Flydubai paid Israeli aviation security official as Trump points to Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
21:22:22 UTC
06:22:22 KST

Israeli authorities increasingly believe the Omani co-pilot accused of trying to crash a flydubai passenger jet acted alone, even as U.S. President Donald Trump continues to suggest Iran may have been behind the attack.
Asked whether he believed Iran was responsible, Trump said, “I do. I personally do.” He has previously suggested a possible Iranian connection based on information he said he was hearing but has not publicly presented evidence. Israeli investigators, meanwhile, have yet to establish an Iranian or other organizational link to the suspect, Hamam al-Hammami.
The comments came hours after Israeli authorities cleared for publication that investigators from the Shin Bet domestic security agency had traveled to the United Arab Emirates and were participating in al-Hammami’s interrogation.
Al-Hammami is accused of attacking the captain of flydubai Flight FZ1073 with an emergency ax and attempting to seize control of the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight on Sept. 30. Passengers intervened after the wounded captain managed to open the cockpit door, and the aircraft eventually landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. The UAE has described the incident as a terrorist attack.
The attack has intensified scrutiny of Israel’s system for securing foreign airlines and screening crews flying into the country. New questions have also emerged over potential conflicts of interest involving senior figures responsible for aviation security at the Transportation Ministry.
After Haaretz reported that Avraham “Avri” Cohen, head of the ministry’s Security, Emergency and Cyber Division, had held a second job in private security for eight years without final authorization, another senior figure in the ministry’s aviation security apparatus has come under scrutiny.
Dvir Rubinstein, one of the founders and the current director of the ministry’s Aviation Security Operations Center, known by its Hebrew acronym MAMLAT, is not a civil servant. He provides services to the Transportation Ministry as an outside contractor while also operating a private company that provides consulting and training services to airlines, including flydubai and Emirates.
That arrangement means Rubinstein has received private payment from flydubai while holding a central role in the Israeli system responsible for dealing with security matters involving foreign airlines, including flydubai.
MAMLAT serves as the Transportation Ministry’s operational center for aviation security and occupies a key position in the mechanism through which Israel approves and oversees security arrangements for foreign airlines operating flights to the country. It works regularly with airlines and government agencies in Israel and abroad.
As part of his role, Rubinstein is responsible for security approvals and permits required by airlines and flights seeking to enter Israel, both in advance and in real time. That makes him one of the principal officials maintaining direct contact with foreign airlines and handling security issues connected to their operations in Israel.
The arrangement has created a situation in which an official responsible through MAMLAT for security matters involving foreign airlines also maintains private business relationships with airlines falling within his professional sphere of responsibility.
The Transportation Ministry said Rubinstein’s outside activities were properly authorized and conducted outside the hours in which he provides services to the ministry. The ministry has not yet responded specifically to questions about his private work for airlines that fall within his professional responsibilities or the implications of those relationships for his MAMLAT role.
A long-running battle over responsibility
The attempted takeover of the flydubai flight has exposed what officials and previous government reviews have described as a broader structural problem in Israel’s security system for foreign aviation rather than an isolated failure.
At the center of the dispute is a position that has become increasingly entrenched among Transportation Ministry professionals: The ministry’s Security, Emergency and Cyber Division does not have the intelligence capabilities, resources or tools needed to assume responsibility for the security of foreign flights entering Israel.
Those concerns predate the current government.
During the tenure of former transportation minister Merav Michaeli and former ministry director-general Michal Frank, ministry professionals formally raised the issue. Frank held at least three dedicated meetings with the National Security Council in which she warned that the Transportation Ministry was not equipped to bear the responsibility.
The National Security Council continued to oppose changing the arrangement, however, and the interagency dispute persisted. Government decisions intended to clarify the division of responsibilities and establish a central coordinating body were not implemented for two years.
As government agencies argued over jurisdiction, aviation and cybersecurity were identified as among the most exposed areas in the security system, according to officials familiar with the discussions.
The organizational problems also extended inside the Transportation Ministry’s security division.
Questions arose over Cohen’s outside employment in private security while he headed the division responsible for protecting national transportation infrastructure. An arrangement allowing him to undertake the outside work had encountered resistance under Michaeli and raised questions about potential conflicts of interest and priorities. It emerged Monday that the approval process had never been finalized.
The concerns over foreign aviation security were raised again after Transportation Minister Miri Regev and ministry Director-General Moshe Ben Zaken took office.
Professional officials told Ben Zaken that the security division could not adequately carry out the mission and warned that the situation represented a genuine security risk. The issue was nevertheless put on hold, according to people familiar with the matter.
One official familiar with the discussions said Ben Zaken had been warned repeatedly but took no action, describing the ministry’s handling of the issue as part of a deep management failure.
Warnings but no dedicated meeting
A review of Regev’s publicly available calendars from 2023 through 2025 also raises questions about the priority given to the issue.
The calendars were analyzed as part of the “Minister Meter” project by Shakuf, an Israeli nonprofit investigative news organization focused on government transparency.
They show extensive attention to aviation matters, including efforts to persuade foreign airlines to resume service to Israel, responses to flight cancellations, aviation agreements and meetings with the Civil Aviation Authority.
But the calendars contain no dedicated meeting specifically addressing the screening of foreign flight crews or the broader security gap surrounding foreign airlines.
That absence stands out because the state comptroller had already warned about weaknesses in the system.
In May 2024, State Comptroller Matanyahu Englman’s office published the public portions of a classified audit examining international civil aviation security. The review covered foreign and private aircraft entering Israeli airspace as well as Israeli aviation abroad and flights departing Israel.
The comptroller recommended that the National Security Council work with the Transportation and Finance ministries, the Civil Aviation Authority, Shin Bet and police to conduct a comprehensive review of the entire civil aviation security system. It also called for a reassessment of government and security Cabinet decisions governing aviation security, some dating to the 1970s, and for clearer responsibility and allocation of resources.
Regev’s calendars show that she continued to meet directly with Civil Aviation Authority officials in 2025. Meetings were recorded Jan. 30, on consecutive days June 11 and 12 with Ben Zaken participating and in a June 27 conference call involving the heads of the Shin Bet and Civil Aviation Authority.
Despite those meetings, no dedicated discussion on the foreign-flight security gap was recorded, even though Cohen submitted several explicit requests for urgent meetings with Regev and Ben Zaken to discuss the deficiencies.
The public calendars provide only a partial picture. The data examined covers 2023 through 2025 and does not include Regev’s schedule in 2026. As is common with ministers’ public calendars, sensitive security consultations, routine briefings and informal conversations may also not appear explicitly or may be listed under broader headings.
Ministry priorities under scrutiny
The calendars also provide a broader picture of how Regev allocated her time during the three-year period.
From 2023 through 2025, she held 160 meetings with municipal leaders from 40 cities and local councils. According to the Shakuf analysis, most were associated with or supportive of Regev’s Likud party.
By contrast, the calendars show no meeting during that period with Tel Aviv-Jaffa Mayor Ron Huldai, a prominent critic of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government.
Those findings do not by themselves establish why particular meetings were or were not held, and the publicly released calendars may not capture every interaction.
The renewed scrutiny comes as investigators across several countries try to determine how al-Hammami was allowed into the cockpit of a Tel Aviv-bound aircraft despite reported warning signs in his background. The Associated Press reported that he had previously been flagged in Oman over extremist views and barred from flying there. No terrorist organization has claimed responsibility for the attack, and publicly available evidence has not established Iranian involvement.
The case has therefore opened two parallel investigations for Israel: one into whether al-Hammami acted entirely on his own or had outside support and another into how the security system designed to protect foreign flights bound for Israel allowed him to reach the cockpit in the first place.

Unknown

Necva Tastan Sevinc
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The European Union warned Monday that escalating violence in Ethiopia and rising tensions with neighboring Eritrea risk triggering a broader conflict across the Horn of Africa.
In a statement issued by its high representative on behalf of the bloc, the EU expressed alarm over the continued escalation and its potential consequences for regional peace and stability.
“This risks triggering a broader regional conflict, with severe consequences for peace and stability across the Horn of Africa,” the statement said.
The bloc called for immediate de-escalation on all fronts, urging those involved to refrain from actions or rhetoric that could heighten tensions.
It also urged parties to the Permanent Cessation of Hostilities Agreement to recommit to its full implementation within the African Union framework.
“Civilians need to be protected at all times, and unhindered humanitarian access must be ensured,” the statement said, stressing that respect for international humanitarian law is imperative.
The EU reiterated that the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states must be respected and called on external actors to refrain from interference.
It urged those actors to use their influence to prevent further escalation and advance political solutions and diplomacy.
Severed ties, accusations
The statement comes amid renewed fighting between Ethiopian federal forces and fighters affiliated with the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), with clashes reported in parts of Tigray, Amhara, and Afar.
The TPLF and federal officials have traded accusations over responsibility for the renewed hostilities.
Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with Ethiopia after Addis Ababa closed its embassy in Asmara and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave. Ethiopia and Egypt also expelled diplomats amid the widening dispute.
Ethiopian military officials have accused Eritrea, Egypt, and Sudan of supporting the Tigrayan-led opposition alliance. The countries have rejected the allegations.
The African Union has urged restraint, warning that renewed fighting risks reversing gains under the November 2022 Pretoria agreement.
That agreement ended a two-year war between Ethiopia’s federal government and the TPLF that killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. Disputes over territory, the return of displaced people, and disarmament remain unresolved.

US warns foreign financial institutions over business with Iran

Breadcrumb
US warns foreign financial institutions not to do business with Iran
The United States on Monday warned foreign financial institutions that if they do business with Iran or its banking sector, Washington could sanction them.
"Foreign financial institutions continuing to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions could be targeted at any time without advance notification and should take immediate action to terminate such activity and relationships," the US Treasury said in an "alert" statement.
The United States launched its war on Iran in late February, killing the country's leadership and demanding it cease any nuclear-related activities.
The war has plunged the Middle East into violence, with Tehran's retaliatory action targeting Washington's Gulf allies and sending global energy and fertiliser prices skyrocketing after it virtually shut a key trading route.
Since late August, Washington has stepped up its campaign to isolate Tehran economically, warning its allies that secondary sanctions would hit them if they continued to conduct transactions with the country's government.
The US Treasury has also announced a slew of new sanctions as part of that push, targeting Iran's financial, cryptocurrency, rail, automotive and manufacturing sectors.
It has also taken action against two banks, one in the United Arab Emirates and another in Turkey, over their alleged aid to the authorities in Tehran.
In Monday's statement, the Treasury said Iran's government operated so-called "shadow banking" channels to circumvent US sanctions, and that foreign financial institutions should aim to identify and avoid any such activities.

Why the difference in Merrett offers?
In regards to the Merrett deal, why was Hawthorns offer considerably less favourable for the Bombers this year than last. Does being a year older make that much of a difference, or is a psychological masterstroke from the Hawks? (Or possibly something else)
- Oscar
It comes down to two things Oscar: Merrett being a year older and him having one year left to run on his Essendon deal compared to two last year.

This year's was 15, 25 and a 2028 second-rounder.

I'm happy to chalk off the Henry Hustwaite part of it, given he's been delisted by Hawthorn, but you might find the value between the two deals to be vastly different if you value Hustwaite as a player.

Zach Merrett's farewell letter to Essendon fans
This has gone up on the Bombers' website, and I'll post it here in full:
To all Essendon members and supporters,
Thank you. Across 13 years and 274 games, your support through the ups and downs has meant the world to me.
I always tried to make you proud. I tried to play with an effort no one could match, and to get up for every game I possibly could. I hope I did that for you.
It feels very strange to be leaving, and it's a time for reflection.
I still remember the night my name was called out at pick 26 in the 2013 draft. My brother rang me from the couch at home and couldn't believe my luck. Celebrating that night with family and friends back home in Cobden, with all four of my grandparents still alive, is something I'll never forget.
Four days later I walked into the Hangar for the first time. Freshly painted white walls, the main oval just mown. I was in awe of Dyson Heppell and Jobe Watson, and my first job on my first day was stretching Jobe's hamstring.
My debut against North Melbourne in 2014 is still one of my favourite memories. Running out in the green sub vest Colin Hooper handed me, in front of 30 or 40 of my closest family and friends and the Bomber Army, and getting the win, was something special. So was being part of Dustin Fletcher's record-breaking game.
Playing 50 games alongside my brother Jackson at Essendon is something we still talk about. We grew up in the backyard in Cobden with plenty of kicks, handballs, tears and tantrums. To end up playing together on the MCG is something our whole family will always be grateful for.
There have been incredible moments and some hard ones. But what I'll take with me most are the relationships: teammates, coaches, staff, volunteers and fans, on and off the field. My family and I are eternally grateful for everything this club has given us.
Essendon will always hold a special place in my heart. It's where I grew up, as a footballer and as a person. Captaining this club was the greatest honour of my career, and I'll never take for granted that I got to lead Essendon.
The club is in great hands with Andy McGrath and the leadership group. I know how much they care about Essendon, and the young players couldn't have better people to learn from.
The future is bright. There is so much talent on this young list, and I can't wait to watch those players grow into great Essendon people and great Essendon players.
In the years to come, I'll be back with a scarf around my neck, cheering on the next generation of Essendon stars.
Thank you,
Zach

Hawthorn's Ben King plan

- Steve
The Hawks cleared the decks a little to get Zach Merrett in, but that may well be a very deliberate play.
Hawthorn is hoping Gold Coast will choose not to match the contract offered to free agent Ben King. If the Suns take that path, they will receive pick seven and the Hawks will give up nothing at all for King.
The alternative is the Suns do choose to match and look to create a trade with the Hawks. The problem there now is that the Hawks don't really have a whole lot to trade anymore. TLDR; The Hawks have managed to get Zach Merrett and force the Ben King deal onto their terms in one fell swoop.

Spanish trade unions plan 24-hour general strike over housing, wages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
21:16:53 UTC
06:16:53 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Spanish trade unions CCOO and UGT announced Monday that they have begun preparations for a 24-hour general strike this fall to demand adequate wages and access to decent housing.
The proposed strike still requires endorsement from both unions’ highest governing bodies, they said in a joint statement, according to parliamentary news outlet Democrata.
The announcement follows the Congress of Deputies’ rejection Friday of royal decree-laws on housing.
The unions said they would coordinate with tenant movements and neighborhood groups, linking their labor demands to ongoing housing protests. A strike date will be agreed with those groups and the Tenants’ Union.
“The demonstrations from last weekend have shown the strength of that demand, and the response must be built among all the organizations that support it,” the statement said.
The unions linked the planned action to their proposals for the sixth Agreement for Employment and Collective Bargaining, which include wage increases of between 4% and 7%, alongside wage review clauses.
Their housing demands include a broad social pact, limits on rental prices, a permanent stock of publicly protected housing, and effective implementation of Spain’s housing rights law nationwide.
The unions also urged employers’ organizations to unblock collective bargaining and ensure wages cover basic needs.
They called on responsible public authorities to effectively enforce regulations protecting the right to housing.

European Solidarity Expels MP Honcharenko Over War-Ending Proposals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
21:15:49 UTC
06:15:49 KST

Ukraine’s opposition European Solidarity party has expelled lawmaker Oleksiy Honcharenko from its parliamentary faction, citing ideological differences over his proposals for ending the war with Russia.
The party announced its decision in a statement on Monday, Oct. 5, explaining that Honcharenko’s views on Ukraine’s future security had diverged from the party’s foundation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Compromises can be part of the path to ending the war,” the statement read. “But Ukraine’s independence, its European future, questions of national identity and the right to determine its own security system are not subject to compromise.”
Honcharenko’s disputed proposals
The expulsion followed days of public debate over Honcharenko’s vision for ending the war, which he first outlined in social media posts on Friday, Oct. 2, arguing that Ukraine was losing the war and should seek agreements with Russia wherever possible.
In a column for Ukrainska Pravda on Sunday, Oct. 4, he proposed that Moscow and Kyiv hold parallel negotiations on specific issues instead of seeking a single comprehensive peace deal.
According to Honchareko, previous peace efforts had stalled because negotiators tried to resolve complex problems, such as territory, security, sanctions, prisoners and guarantees in a single settlement, rather than breaking them into a series of agreements, each with its own timeline and guarantor.
Russia Strikes Kharkiv With Guided Bombs Killing 6, Wounding 59, Including Children
Under his plan, Turkey would guarantee shipping safety, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) would oversee nuclear safety, the Vatican, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar would help return prisoners and deported children, and China would guarantee an end to ground combat.
Honcharenko also proposed gradually lifting restrictions on Russian energy resources in exchange for an end to long-range strikes, the unblocking of the Black Sea and limiting hostilities to the Donbas.
The Donbas, he said, should be addressed only once other agreements are working, with options including freezing the front line without legally recognizing the occupation, a neutral zone or a UN-controlled zone.
He also suggested Ukraine could negotiate a neutral status, provided it keeps cooperating with NATO.
Why the proposals proved divisive
Seizing the rest of the Donbas remains Russia’s main military objective, and Moscow has repeatedly demanded that Kyiv cede the region and withdraw from the parts of the Donetsk region it still controls as a condition for a settlement.
Ukraine, for its part, has rejected those demands as a prerequisite for peace, arguing that its territorial sovereignty cannot be negotiated.
Similarly, it is widely believed that freezing the front line would effectively leave Russian-occupied territory under Moscow’s control; regardless of whether the occupation is formally recognized.
Honcharenko’s suggestion that Ukraine’s neutrality could be discussed also appeared at odds with the country’s constitution, which has enshrined Ukraine’s course toward EU and NATO membership.
His proposal for phased sanctions relief in exchange for a halt to strikes drew criticism as well, with opponents warning that easing pressure on Russia before it ends the war would only reward Moscow’s aggression.
Call for ‘honest conversation’ with society
In its statement, European Solidarity said that responsibility for Ukraine’s negotiating position and diplomatic strategy lies with the authorities that hold a single-party majority and full powers, a reference to President Volodymyr Zelensky and his Servant of the People party.
Citing the public debate sparked by Honcharenko’s proposals, the party said that the government must finally start an honest conversation with Ukrainian citizens regarding a realistic path to a ceasefire and a just peace.
The so-called “resilience plans” and “declarations of strength” no longer answer those questions, the party said, adding that peace cannot come at the cost of giving up what Ukraine has fought for during these five years of war.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has carried out a targeted military operation against the Houthi movement in the Red Sea province of Hudaida, destroying naval weapons depots and thwarting planned attacks on international shipping lanes.
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki confirmed on X that naval units struck Houthi military targets along the coastline, stating that forces "destroyed weapons depots, facilities storing booby-trapped boats and naval mines".
Al-Maliki added that the operation successfully "thwarted a plot for imminent attacks targeting waterways in the southern Red Sea".
The strikes formed part of an escalating multi-front assault.
The Yemeni military announced it launched an offensive to recapture the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, conducting over 1,000 strikes, while the coalition confirmed 100 warplanes flew dawn sorties across the country.
The internationally recognised government declared on Sunday an overarching objective to recover all Houthi-administered territories, which house the majority of Yemen's population.
Bab al Mandab flashpoint
In an urgent statement, Houthi forces claimed sweeping retaliatory strikes against critical infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia.
The group said it launched drones and ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh airport, the Aramco oil refinery in Rabigh, Abha Airport, the Khamis Mushait airbase, Najran, and the Akfa military camp in Asir.
The sharp escalation follows severe territorial shifts last month, when Iran-aligned Houthi fighters seized broad swathes of Red Sea coastline and strategic positions overseeing the Bab al Mandab Strait—a vital chokepoint for international crude and commercial shipping—triggering the deadliest fighting witnessed in Yemen for years.

Mainland Chinese prefer coercion over military force to settle the “reunification question” with Taiwan, and their opinion of the US remains low, although they favour engaging with Washington on trade and security.

Russian Drones Strike Civilian Cargo Ship Carrying Ukrainian Corn, Killing Two
Two people were killed after a civilian cargo ship was struck by two Russian drones in the Black Sea near the Romanian shore, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Reuters reported on October 5.
Romania’s Interior Ministry later confirmed that 11 crew members were rescued after the ship caught fire about 30 nautical miles south of Sfântu Gheorghe.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian attacks on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports and civilian shipping have repeatedly disrupted one of the country’s most important export routes. UNITED24 Media reported that Russia carried out 67 attacks on Ukrainian port infrastructure in July alone, including 35 strikes on civilian vessels in ports and 22 on ships operating through the maritime corridor.
Romanian authorities did not identify the cause of the fire on the cargo ship. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, however, attributed the incident to a Russian drone strike.
“A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Türkiye,” Zelenskyy wrote on X. “Azerbaijani and Indian citizens were on board.”
At the time of Zelenskyy’s statement, Ukraine had confirmed the death of the ship’s captain while another person remained unaccounted for.
“As of now, unfortunately, we know that the ship’s captain was killed. My condolences. The fate of one other person is still being established. Eleven crew members were rescued, one of them injured,” Zelenskyy wrote.
Romania has repeatedly faced Russian drone incursions linked to attacks on neighboring Ukraine. In July, Bucharest expelled a Russian diplomat after three Russian drones entered Romanian airspace over three days, all of which Romanian forces shot down.
Romania’s Interior Ministry stated that a General Aviation Inspectorate helicopter evacuated injured crew members by winch for emergency medical treatment. Coast Guard vessels and the helicopter continued search-and-rescue operations in the area.
Reuters identified the vessel as the Royad Mammadov, flying under the flag of St. Kitts and Nevis. The ship had last docked at Ukraine’s port of Izmail and was heading toward Ravenna, Italy.
Russian authorities had not commented directly on the incident. An earlier Russian Defense Ministry bulletin reported that Russian forces had struck two cargo vessels, according to Reuters.
Ukraine had recently stated that it was ready for a joint ceasefire covering both energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping routes. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha noted that the US, India, Türkiye, and Egypt had submitted proposals, with Kyiv insisting that any maritime truce also protect ports and energy facilities.

‘Muslim NATO’ activates force deployment over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
A three-nation military alliance dubbed the “Muslim NATO” has activated its collective-defense commitments and ordered the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia amid an escalating confrontation with Yemen’s Houthis.
Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan made the decision at an emergency meeting of the Mecca Defense Alliance in Riyadh on Monday after a series of Houthi attacks. In a joint statement they condemned the “attempted targeting” of the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, as well as attacks on Saudi cities and civilian and economic infrastructure.
The group decided to “move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments” and take measures to provide agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their “rapid deployment” in Saudi Arabia. It said the move was intended to boost military readiness and integration and strengthen the three countries’ “collective capacity to confront and counter threats.”
The Emergency Meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee under the Makkah Alliance for Defense reaffirmed the solidarity and unity of our countries in confronting the heinous attacks against the Kingdom and the holy sites. The committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures within the framework of the Alliance in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them.

The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, are a Shiite armed group that has controlled the Yemeni capital of Sanaa and much of northern Yemen for more than a decade. They have accused Riyadh of carrying out extensive airstrikes and hitting civilian targets.

Saudi Arabia first intervened in Yemen in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government after the Houthis had driven it from Sanaa the previous year. Large-scale fighting decreased significantly following a UN-brokered truce in 2022.
Fighting escalated again last month. The Houthis have accused Riyadh of imposing an illegal siege on Yemen, while Saudi Arabia says the group has stepped up missile, drone, and maritime attacks against the kingdom itself and shipping in the Red Sea.
The escalation comes as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed to most shipping and US-Iranian talks on ending the conflict have stalled.
Several Saudi allies have stepped up military support for the kingdom. Britain has agreed to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi warplanes, while France is sending troops, radar, and air-defense systems to help protect the Red Sea oil hub of Yanbu.

Xinhua Headlines: Longer trips, richer experiences: China's National Day holiday reveals shifting tourism trends
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
05:10:57 CST
06:10:57 KST

* Chinese travelers have ventured farther during the National Day holiday, with family trips and experience-oriented travel on the rise.
* Former revolutionary base areas have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about the country's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China.
* More international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country for themselves, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design.
BEIJING, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Five days into China's week-long National Day holiday, millions are still immersed in the sights, sounds and flavors of the season -- traveling, dining, exploring and enjoying the break. Yet this year, the scenes are subtly different.
Travelers have ventured farther as the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday fell just three days before the National Day holiday, while family trips and experience-oriented travel are on the rise, according to travel agencies.
"It points to a fundamental shift in the logic of tourism consumption, as travelers focus more on the quality of time and the richness of their experiences," said Bu Xiting, a researcher with the Communication University of China.
LONGER BREAKS, RICHER CHOICES
Data from Chinese online travel platform Tuniu shows that tours of 10 days or more are particularly popular during this holiday period, accounting for 26 percent of bookings.
Yuan You, an internet company employee, spent three days of her 13-day break in Jiuzhaigou, southwest China's Sichuan Province, before heading to the provincial capital Chengdu for woodworking classes.
"The holiday is rich while maintaining a relaxed pace," she said.
Authorities across the country have rolled out a wide range of activities, consumer vouchers and subsidies to spur holiday spending. Shanghai, for example, has launched about 200 major consumption events, backed by consumer vouchers worth roughly 100 million yuan (around 14.85 million U.S. dollars).
The offerings range from watching films and dining to purchasing digital products and cars, encouraging consumers to explore a broader spectrum of spending experiences.
Cultural institutions, too, are broadening the ways people can experience and consume culture. The Sichuan Museum extended its holiday hours and launched a themed night tour, while Beijing's Zhongshan Park brought museums, cultural institutions and innovative brands together to create a market street featuring culture-inspired products.
As more new energy vehicles hit the roads during the holiday, authorities have taken measures to ensure adequate charging facilities and convenient services.
During last year's eight-day Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, Chinese travelers made 888 million domestic trips and spent a combined 809 billion yuan, according to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism.
This year, data shows that foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 3.4 percent and 5.3 percent year on year, respectively, from Oct. 1 to 3.
RED TOURISM, ROBOTS AND RURAL EXPERIENCES
As China marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, former revolutionary base areas have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about the country's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China.
In Yan'an, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, a street has staged special activities including performances of songs from the revolutionary years and a large-scale bonfire gathering. Visitor numbers on the first day of the holiday rose about 20 percent year on year.
The holiday has also turned some of China's newest robots into part of the consumer experience, putting embodied intelligence to work alongside traditional culture in tourist attractions, shopping districts and ancient towns.
At a cultural district in Chengdu, robots performed dances inspired by local opera's face-changing art and used digital technology to recreate tanghua, a traditional form of sugar painting.
On Chunxi Road, a humanoid robot has gone beyond entertainment to take on the role of a store manager, greeting customers and recommending products rather than simply performing for them.
China's growing network of robot training bases is preparing more machines for roles beyond the factory floor -- and beyond the country's borders. In the first half of 2026, Chinese manufacturers accounted for 97 percent of humanoid robot shipments worldwide, according to a report released at the 2026 World Robot Conference.
Years of efforts to restore the environment and revitalize rural areas are also paying off. On a ridge overlooking the Miyun Reservoir in Beijing, visitors can hike to a viewing platform and enjoy outdoor concerts amid the pine trees.
With roads, infrastructure and public services extending deeper into the countryside, some once-remote villages are emerging as new destinations for holidaymakers.
Caijiagou, a former impoverished hillside village in east China's Shandong Province, has transformed into an art-themed destination, with murals adorning residential walls.
Village official Liang Yunhui said the village has repurposed idle rural homes into cultural spaces such as an art gallery and a musical instrument museum, while hosting events featuring traditional crafts, cultural fairs and folk music. "In total, we have received more than 500,000 visits over the years," he said.
On travel platform Fliggy, the number of users purchasing travel products featuring natural scenery and villages surged by nearly 50 percent from the same holiday period last year.
"More travelers are seeking immersive experiences, from sampling local cuisine and making intangible cultural heritage crafts to watching distinctive performances, allowing them to gain a deeper appreciation of local culture," said a manager with Tuniu.
CHINA HAUL
While many Chinese tourists are venturing farther around the world, more international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country for themselves, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design.
Tennis star Novak Djokovic, in Beijing for the China Open, was seen trying his hand at Chinese calligraphy at the Summer Palace, a former imperial garden. After a match, he used a traditional Chinese seal to put his mark on fans' keepsakes instead of signing autographs.
Huaqiangbei, a sprawling electronics marketplace in south China's tech hub Shenzhen, has become a magnet for foreign shoppers looking to experience China's tech scene firsthand.
Bryan Lamothe-Arice from the United States was browsing smart devices. "I'm particularly interested in the electric bikes and all kinds of flying devices here. I'm going to tell my friends to come here. There are tech products everywhere."
China's border crossings are expected to see about 2.15 million passenger trips a day on average during the National Day holiday, according to the National Immigration Administration.
That growing international interest is also showing up in spending. Overseas visitors spent 263.6 billion yuan in China in the first seven months of 2026, up 27.8 percent year on year, according to the commerce ministry.
(Video reporters: Chen Si, Lin Long, Ji Zijian, Sun Qing and Zhong Chao; Video editors: Zhang Mocheng and Hong Ling) ■

Ethiopia’s Abiy demands access to Red Sea as tensions with neighbours rise
Neighbouring countries say coastal states must govern Red Sea as fighting escalates in northern Ethiopia.
Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has insisted that his landlocked country must have access to the Red Sea, even as neighbouring countries have said responsibility for the sea rests with the states along its shores.
Abiy made the demand as he was sworn in for another five-year term on Monday.
Repeating previous assertions, Abiy said in a speech in Parliament that the country would work to secure a port on the Red Sea, saying that access was critical to Ethiopia’s “civilisation”.
“Based on the principle of give and take, we will work diligently to ensure that Ethiopia has an outlet to the sea,” he said.
Ethiopia lost direct access to the Red Sea in 1993 after Eritrea, formerly a region of Ethiopia, became independent.
Abiy’s call came as Ethiopia’s relations with its neighbours have worsened in recent months, with Addis Ababa accusing Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of supporting opposition forces in Tigray following a resurgence of the fighting against Abiy’s government in the northern region.
For its part, Eritrea has accused Ethiopia of seeking access to the sea through its territory. A separate dispute over Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Nile River has strained relations with Egypt and Sudan, which rely on the river for water.
Four of the five countries bordering the Red Sea – Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia – met on Sunday in Egypt’s New Alamein and called for cooperation on regional issues.
They said governance of the Red Sea was the exclusive responsibility of its coastal states and rejected actions that could affect Egypt and Sudan’s use of Nile waters.
The following day, Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry said discussions over the Red Sea must account for the country’s “legitimate interests and enduring connection” to the body of water.
Somalia’s president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, who attended the Egypt summit, congratulated Abiy on his re-election.
“I look forward to working closely together to strengthen Somalia-Ethiopia relations & advance peace, stability & shared prosperity for our peoples & the Horn of Africa,” he said in a post on X.
Mohamud had previously told Al Jazeera that Somalia did not object to Ethiopia gaining access to the Red Sea through Somali territory but added that the two countries would need to officially negotiate.
Evariste Ndayishimiye, Burundi’s president, also wished Abiy “every success during his renewed mandate”. Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, the chairperson of the African Union Commission, also sent a message of congratulations.

Number of Russians with residence permits rose 61% in Spain after 2021, while falling in Latvia, Estonia, and Czechia
The number of Russian citizens holding valid residence permits in EU countries rose by nearly 105,000, or 14%, from 772,000 at the end of 2021 to 877,000 at the end of 2025. The Volna project reported the figures, citing Eurostat data.
At the end of 2025, Germany had the most Russian citizens with temporary or permanent residency (218,000), followed by Spain (117,000), Estonia (78,000), France (67,000), and Serbia (63,000).
Spain recorded the largest increase: the number of Russians holding residence permits there rose by 44,000, or 61%, over four years. Cyprus ranked second (up 27,000), followed by France (up 14,000).
In some EU countries, however, the number of Russian citizens with temporary or permanent residency fell. The largest declines were in Latvia (down 15,000), Estonia (down 9,000), and Czechia (down 8,000).
Eurostat data indicate that the number of Russians who had settled in the EU rose sharply in 2022 and 2023, then remained largely stable.

Pennsylvania faces largest measles outbreak in decades as case count rises to 1,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
21:09:47 UTC
06:09:47 KST

Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials calculate, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades. The benchmark comes as neighboring New York declared a state of emergency about measles rates there.
Pennsylvania’s health department said Monday 1,004 cases of measles had been confirmed. Five Pennsylvania residents have died after contracting the disease, with 198 hospitalizations.
Lancaster county, with sizeable Amish and Mennonite populations, remains the hardest hit, with 391 cases, according to official figures. Cases numbers have risen over the past three months, with the highest number of infections in the 24-49 age range.
The numbers, however, are not included in a CDC count due to an ongoing dispute between Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, and the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr over how to classify measles-related mortality.
Shapiro has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and Kennedy has publicly questioned whether the state’s recorded fatalities were directly caused by measles. The CDC – which Kennedy oversees – currently lists two measles deaths in the US this year.
Shapiro has expanded access to the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in affected communities.
“I want every Pennsylvanian to know this: measles does not care about your county, your faith, or your social circle,” he said in August. “I urge everyone to take this seriously and to discuss any concerns with their trusted health care provider.”
In New York state, governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency on Monday as well, citing 108 cases in the state as of 3 October.
Ohio, which also shares a border with Pennsylvania, has also reported advancing numbers of cases, with more than 200 this year. Like in Pennsylvania, Ohio has a significant Amish population.
The US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991. As of 1 October, the CDC reported 3,887 confirmed cases this year, along with the highest number of measles-associated deaths in decades.
In addition to Pennsylvania, outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest outbreak with 997 cases reported.
Health officials in Pennsylvania have said the state’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia and attributed the outbreak to low vaccination rates.
According to the Associated Press, the most recent outbreak to surpass 1,000 cases occurred in New York City in the early 1990s. That outbreak infected more than 4,500 people. During the 1989 and 1991 resurgences, 55,000 infections and 123 deaths were recorded, according to Reuters.
The domestic US spread of measles was eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.

ICC unseals Taliban leaders' warrants over persecuting women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
21:07:00 UTC
06:07:00 KST

ICC unseals Taliban leaders' warrants over persecuting women
October 5, 2026
The International Criminal Court (ICC) disclosed on Monday more details about the arrest warrants against two Taliban leaders, while also issuing two more arrest warrants.
The four Taliban leaders are accused of crimes against humanity through the persecution of women, girls and the LGBTQ+ community in Afghanistan since taking power in 2021.
According to the court, warrants were issued in July and September of last year against Hibatullah Akhundzada , the Taliban's Supreme Leader, as well as against Abdul Hakim Haqqani, who heads the country's Supreme Court.
The other two warrants were issued against Education Minister Habibullah Agha and Minister of Higher Education Neda Mohammad Nadim.
The four are charged with persecution on grounds of gender of "girls, women and other persons nonconforming with the Taliban's policy on gender, gender identity or expression; and on political grounds against persons perceived as 'allies of girls and women,'" according to the court.
What does the ICC accuse the 4 Taliban leaders of?
The judges who issued the warrants said that the four implemented policies that saw "severe violations of fundamental rights and freedoms of the civilian population of Afghanistan, in connection with conducts of murder, imprisonment, torture, rape and enforced disappearance."
The Taliban "specifically targeted girls and women by reason of their gender," the judges added, also mentioning persecution against people due to "certain expressions of sexuality and/or gender identity."
The ICC has no jurisdiction to execute the warrants. Still, the move is considered a form of pressure on the Afghan ruling authority.
The Taliban have taken a wide range of measures to restrict women's access to jobs and education beyond sixth grade, as well as barring them from most public spaces.
Women are also obligated to cover their whole bodies apart from their eyes upon leaving home, with a male relative having to accompany them on long trips.
Taliban rejects ICC's warrants
Afghanistan's government spokesperson said the country does not recognize the court's authority.
"We are bound by the rulings of Islamic Sharia and its courts, not by intelligence entities or so-called courts." chief spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said in a statement.
A request for warrants for Akhundzada and Haqqani made last year by former ICC chief prosecutor Karim Khan argued that "Afghan women and girls as well as the LGBTQI+ community are facing an unprecedented, unconscionable and ongoing persecution by the Taliban.”
The UN Human Rights Council has called on the Taliban to drop its "systematic oppression of all women and girls in Afghanistan."
Human rights groups have been calling for the international community to do more against the Taliban's gender-based policies in Afghanistan.

Archer died “suddenly and peacefully at his home between writing sessions” on Oct 5, HarperCollins said.
His editor, Kate Elton, called him a “master storyteller and an editor’s dream”.
The writer had been due to appear at Cheltenham Literary Festival this week to discuss Adam And Eve, what he described as his final novel after 50 years of storytelling.
It was due to be published on Oct 6.
British tabloid The Sun reported that he had been signing books for fans at an event in London on Oct 4.
Archer had revealed in 2014 that he had been diagnosed with prostate cancer.
The author led a life as colourful as the characters in his novels, which sold over 300 million copies, according to his website.
Talented and ambitious, he was a high flyer who could never quite escape the whiff of scandal despite a talent for bouncing back from humiliating setbacks.
Politics and sex were the ingredients which ensured his success as a novelist.
But in real life, the combination led to the downfall of the man who once hoped to become mayor of London.
He was tried for perjury and perverting the course of justice after a friend admitted he had supplied a false alibi during a libel case the peer brought against the Daily Star tabloid in 1987.
Archer had sued the newspaper over a claim he had slept with a prostitute, winning £500,000 in damages.
Ambitious from his earliest years, Archer used his charm and fund-raising abilities to climb almost to the top of the Conservative Party.
MP at 29
He joined the Tories while a student at Britain’s prestigious Oxford University and in 1969, won a resounding by-election victory to become a member of parliament at the age of 29.
His parliamentary career came to an abrupt end in 1974, when he was brought to the brink of bankruptcy by the collapse of a Canadian industrial cleaning company in which he had invested.
However, with typical resilience, he used his experiences as material for his first book Not A Penny More, Not A Penny Less, published in 1975, the first of a series of blockbusters set in the worlds of high finance and politics.
Panned by the critics, they nevertheless earned him a fortune and Archer nursed hopes of a political revival while using his contacts and persuasiveness to raise millions of pounds for the Tories.
In 1985, his labours were recognised by then-prime minister Margaret Thatcher, who named him Conservative deputy chairman, describing him as a model Tory high achiever.
Scandals
But a year after his appointment, he was forced to resign by what he described as a “lack of judgment” after sending £2,000 to a prostitute, Monica Coghlan.
He maintained he only paid the money to help her escape hounding from reporters by going abroad and sued the Daily Star for suggesting otherwise.
In 1992, he was recommended by Thatcher’s successor John Major for a peerage, entitling him to sit in the House of Lords, the upper chamber of parliament.
In 1999, he launched a campaign to become the Tory party’s candidate to become the first elected mayor of London.
But months later, the claim emerged that he had asked a friend, Ted Francis, to provide him with a false alibi against the Daily Star. This forced him to abandon his bid and he was expelled from the party.
In 2001, he went on trial and was found guilty of perjury and perverting the course of justice. He was sentenced to four years in prison, but was granted parole in 2003.
Archer’s long-suffering wife Mary, a scientist, stood behind her husband in his many mishaps.
Famously praised for her “fragrance” by the judge in the 1987 libel trial, she once said: “We’ve explored the further reaches of ‘for better and for worse’ than most couples.”
Archer retired from the House of Lords in 2024. His wife is Chancellor of the University of Buckingham. AFP

Trump says US ready to aid Russia with plague outbreak in Siberia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
21:03:21 UTC
06:03:21 KST

Trump says US ready to aid Russia with plague outbreak in Siberia
Russian authorities quarantine hospital, monitor 200 contacts after suspected pneumonic plague death in Siberia.
President Donald Trump says the United States is ready to help Russia with a suspected pneumonic plague outbreak.
“We are looking at it very strongly. We just heard about it,” Trump said, adding that he had not spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about it but is prepared to offer US support.
“It’s a disease we used to be able to control,” Trump said. “Even with great advancement, the germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don’t work anymore … anyone that has that kind of problem, we will help.”
The World Health Organization (WHO) said based on unofficial information it has received, the “public health risk to the general population appears to be low”.
Earlier on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio downplayed the danger as well. “I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it,” Rubio said.
Russian authorities have quarantined a hospital and are tracing the contacts of an employee at a plague research institute in the remote Siberian region of Irkutsk who died of a suspected pneumonic plague infection. Local media identified the employee as 28-year-old laboratory technician Darya Shipilova.
Official details about the incident have been limited, and Russian media reports say authorities in Irkutsk have placed nearly 200 people under medical observation.
On Sunday, Russia’s official TASS news agency reported that the country’s consumer protection agency, Rospotrebnadzor, said an employee at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown aetiology” or origin. The agency also said it had expanded sample testing from the patient and found no microorganisms associated with her work.
On Saturday, the governor of neighbouring Buryatia region said in a post on his Telegram channel that a woman in Irkutsk had “died, maybe of the plague”.
In a statement to Al Jazeera, a US State Department official said: “We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.”
Pneumonic plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals and their fleas. According to the WHO, the plague is highly infectious and can be fatal if not treated early.
The plague comes in three forms affecting different parts of the body. Pneumonic plague, an infection of the lungs, triggers the patient to cough out infectious airborne droplets.
If identified quickly, antibiotics can treat the disease. Left untreated, it can be fatal in one to six days.

SIR row: Will annul Election Commission orders not in keeping with law, says Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:52:53 UTC
05:52:53 KST

‘Decisions must be unanimous or by majority’, says Supreme Court
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Monday asked the Election Commission, CEC Gyanesh Kumar and ECs S S Sandhu and Vivek Joshi to clarify whether crucial decisions regarding the special intensive revision (SIR) of voter rolls were taken unilaterally by the CEC, and said it would injunct (bar) those decisions by the three-member commission which were neither unanimous nor by majority.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said irrespective of powers vested in the CEC, the law clearly mandates that all decisions must either be by unanimity or by majority among the three members of the EC. “If we come across instances (where CEC has unilaterally taken decisions), we will annul them,” it said.
The statement came after senior advocate Vikas Singh, appearing for a PIL petitioner, strongly argued for an interim direction to the EC to only take decisions by unanimity during pendency of the petition as the amended CEC and Other ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, gave the CEC enormous powers.
The PIL has sought scrutiny of the validity of SIR decisions and ”alterations” in Form 6 for new voters. Singh said since the court could not undo elections, a direction must be issued that in the interregnum, EC must follow the statutory mandate. He pleaded that EC be directed to preserve all records on SIR decisions and Form 6 alteration and produce them before SC for scrutiny.
CEC, ECs need to either rebut or endorse allegations about ‘unilateral decisions’
Let us have some authenticated facts before us through their responses.
They must respond in a clear and transparent manner. If the records show some of the decisions are not taken by majority, we will injunct those. But we cannot put the cart before the horse, the bench said while also issuing notices to the Centre, deputy EC Manish Garg and EC’s director general (IT) Seema Khanna.This has set the stage for the CEC and, more crucially, the two ECs to either endorse or rebut the allegation that important decisions on SIR were taken by Gyanesh Kumar unilaterally and in violation of the law which lays down that the commission’s calls are to be made either unanimously or, failing that, by majority. The allegation, based on a newspaper report, is at the core of the controversy which has reignited opposition to SIR.Senior advocate Vikas Singh, appearing for a PIL petitioner, also questioned the validity of Section 16 of the 2023 Act, which provided that “no court shall entertain or continue any civil or criminal proceedings against any person who is, or was, a CEC or an election commissioner for any act, thing or word, committed, done or spoken by him when, or in the course of acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty or function”.He said this was way beyond the immunity enjoyed even by SC judges and especially when it was not extended even to the PM.Justice Bagchi said, “We will examine the expression ‘or was’. Protection while in office is understandable. Such protection (as provided under Section 16) is perhaps only with regard to the President. It is not given to constitutional court judges under Judges Inquiry Act.”Singh pleaded for suspension of the CEC or divesting him of his authority. When the bench asked who would conduct elections, Singh said the other two ECs would do it. He said in the interim, the SC-mandated selection panel for CEC should be brought back in which the CJI is included along with the PM and the LoP. The 2023 Act replaced the CJI with a Union minister nominated by the PM.
When the bench declined, Singh said the situation was so grave that it could undermine the very basis of our democracy. “Today, the CEC is acting in a manner which is contrary to the statute under which he is appointed. Court should pass some interim orders (restraining the CEC from discharging his functions), otherwise the country will burn,” he said.Patna-based petitioner Rakesh Kumar Singh has sought a direction to EC to “produce before SC the complete original and primary records relating to the matters pleaded herein, including minutes, agendas, approvals, file notings, work allocation and delegation orders, IT-access records, server logs, audit trails and database-change histories concerning the functioning of the commission, ERONet/EClNet, alteration of Form 6 and filing of appeals before the Bengal appellate tribunals”.

Vandenberg Eyes New Launch Support Facilities, Possible On-Site Manufacturing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:48:46 UTC
05:48:46 KST

The Space Force is looking for launch provider’ feedback on its plans to create a new “Mission Development Zone” at Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif.—a space for additional payload processing capacity, test and assembly facilities, and potentially rocket and spacecraft manufacturing infrastructure.
The need for more support services corresponds with a projected surge in launch demand over the next five to 10 years. Vandenberg, which hosts one of the service’s two coastal spaceports, expects its cadence could approach 200 launches per year by the end of the decade—a sharp increase from the 66 space launch missions it supported in 2025.
To meet that higher rate, the range not only needs to designate space for more launch pads and ensure its roads can handle heavier traffic, but it must also make room for the administrative offices, processing facilities, and assembly and test infrastructure that launch suppliers rely on. The Mission Development Zone is Vandenberg’s answer to that challenge.
While officials at Space Launch Delta 30, which oversees the range there, have a vision for what that area could look like, they’re asking industry for input on how to finance, design, construct, and maintain that infrastructure. They also want to hear what types of facilities and layout companies are most interested in.
“Ensuring that United States operators can efficiently process space systems, conduct missions in space, launch, and reenter United States airspace is critical to economic growth, national security, and accomplishing Federal space objectives,” the Delta said in a Sept. 30 notice. “Development and utilization of the MDZ will be in support of maximizing spaceport capability and assured access to space to achieve national security objectives.”
Launch Delta Commander Col. James Horne told Air & Space Forces Magazine during a visit to the base in July that the range is exploring options to lease the land to commercial providers who would then construct their own facilities. He expects they could start breaking ground on MDZ projects as soon as next year.
Along with providing administrative and logistics support, Horne said if there’s industry demand for it, the Mission Development Zone could eventually host rocket factories or commodity plants.
“We are hearing interest,” Horne said. “If you don’t build it here, you have to ship it here either by road or water, primarily. I think as companies look at what their future launch rates may be here, they’re looking at the trade space between, do we build it somewhere and ship it or do we invest capital here to start building that production capacity to enable increased throughput.”
On-site production of both rocket components and key commodities like propellants and purge gases could also make range operations more efficient, potentially reducing chokepoints on base access roads or at Vandenberg’s harbor. Horne noted that a single launch can require as many as 50 commodities trucks moving on and off the base.
“We’ve got to start building the infrastructure to pipe the commodities out to the locations, and then produce them here, potentially,” he said.

McDonald’s hit with US class action alleging AI-powered menu price-fixing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

McDonald’s hit with US class action alleging AI-powered menu price-fixing
WASHINGTON - McDonald’s has been sued in federal court in Chicago in a proposed nationwide class action alleging the fast-food company illegally coordinates menu prices across its franchises and company-owned restaurants through an AI-powered pricing system.
The lawsuit, filed on Oct 2, said McDonald’s violated US antitrust law by conspiring with independent franchisees to fix prices using algorithms trained on nonpublic data.
Reuters reported last week that McDonald’s pricing engine uses machine-learning algorithms to continually analyse data from millions of daily transactions across its nearly 14,000 restaurants.
The lawsuit cited the Reuters article, which said other fast-food companies are also turning to AI to help with pricing and other operations.
“Independent businesses must set their prices independently,” the lawsuit said.
McDonald’s, in a statement on Oct 5, called the allegations speculative and uninformed.
“AI does not set the price of a Big Mac or any other menu item,” the company said. It said franchisees make their own pricing decisions, and that the use of pricing recommendation tools and analytics is widespread across industries.
US plaintiffs have filed a wave of class actions in recent years alleging that companies used algorithms or AI to illegally coordinate prices for hotel rooms, apartment rentals and other purchases.
Lark Turner, a lawyer for the plaintiff, said in a statement, that McDonald’s is “leveraging its troves of data and its franchised system to nickel-and-dime consumers down to the last French fry.”
The plaintiff, an Illinois resident, is seeking to represent a class of potentially millions of McDonald’s customers, the lawsuit said. REUTERS

Saudi Arabia condemns Houthi attacks on kingdom, says group chose military escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:44:23 UTC
05:44:23 KST

Rania R.a. Abushamala
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Saudi Arabia on Monday condemned Houthi attacks targeting civilian facilities and holy sites in the kingdom, saying the group had chosen military escalation despite Riyadh’s efforts to support a political solution in Yemen.
In a statement, the Foreign Ministry denounced the Houthis’ continued targeting of civilians and civilian and economic facilities, as well as what it described as “flagrant and repeated attacks” on the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
It also condemned attacks on the capital Riyadh as well as Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan, Najran, Taif, and Yanbu, along with Saudi vessels in the southern Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Saudi Arabia has said the Houthis targeted Mecca and Medina with missiles and drones, accusations the Yemeni group has denied.
Houthi attacks on other locations in the kingdom, including energy production facilities, have caused civilian injuries and material damage. 
- 'Inherent right' to defend Saudi territory, resources, and sovereignty and to take all necessary measures to protect citizens and residents
The ministry said Saudi Arabia had made sustained efforts since the Houthis’ 2014 takeover against Yemen’s internationally recognized government to support a comprehensive and lasting political solution.
However, it accused the group of rejecting peace and choosing “continued military escalation,” dragging Yemen and its people into further humanitarian and economic suffering “in service of and to implement foreign agendas.”
The kingdom reaffirmed its “inherent right” to defend its territory, resources, and sovereignty, protect citizens and residents, and take all necessary measures to safeguard its security in accordance with international law.
It also renewed its “full political and military support” for Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, government, and people to end the Houthi takeover and restore state institutions.
The ministry urged the international community to fulfill its responsibilities and fully support the Yemeni government in confronting the Houthis and halting the threat they pose to Yemen, the region and the world. 
Reported advances by Yemeni army
The statement followed Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi announcing Monday the launch of an operation dubbed Dawn of Yemen, aimed at restoring state institutions, reclaiming the capital Sanaa, and ending the Houthi takeover.
The Yemeni army subsequently announced that it had taken control of Bab el-Mandeb and the strategic city of Mokha and advanced along the western coast. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
On July 20, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia in response to what they claimed was a Saudi naval and aerial blockade of Houthi-controlled areas in Yemen.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government since 2015 against the Houthis, who are accused of receiving Iranian support and have controlled Sanaa and several provinces since 2014.

‘I’m on a speeding roller coaster’: Freed hostage Liri Albag determined to live life to the fullest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:43:55 UTC
05:43:55 KST

Twenty-one months have passed since Liri Albag was released from Hamas captivity, and her family still chooses its words carefully around her, "walking on eggshells," as her mother Shira puts it.
"It will take a little more time. Everything is still very sensitive," Shira says. "We’re more careful, we give in more and we try to be more understanding. She’s been through enough, and you never know what the trigger will be that causes an outburst or emotional flooding."
Liri: "I feel like I’m on a speeding roller coaster, sometimes up and sometimes down. For the first six months there was euphoria, but over time things began to sink in and the realization of everything I went through hit me."
Shira: "Of course she has difficult days. In the end, she was in captivity. There are lows, there are outbursts. What she’s going through isn’t simple. What she saw on Oct. 7 was trauma that went untreated throughout her entire captivity."
Liri: "They didn’t let us hug, cry or talk to one another. They took even that comfort away from us. At some point we stopped showing emotion or affection. We became apathetic to what was happening."
What helps you cope with the trauma?
Liri: "I’m in therapy, of course, and we also have one another. I know that if I call Emily Damari, Romi Gonen, Agam Berger or Naama Levy, they will always be there for me, and they are the only ones who really understand me. I also have my family and my mother, who is with me day and night."
Have you managed to argue since your release?
Shira: "Not argue, but I’ve gotten angry with her a few times, mainly because she is constantly on the move and never really present. In my opinion, it’s too much running around. She needs to stop for a moment and breathe. A lot of times I told her, ‘Liri, you’re going to collapse eventually,’ because she barely slept and jumped from one thing to another. She came back with a fierce desire to devour life."
Liri: "Before, I would speak to Mom on the phone once a day. Today I talk to her morning, noon and night. The experience of captivity made me look at life differently. I grew up all at once. I’m only 21, but I feel 25."
Good thing you didn’t say you feel like an old woman of 25.
She laughs. "Because at 25 you’re already supposed to make decisions about your future and about making your dreams happen. That’s not something kids my age usually deal with, but I do. I’m already thinking about what I want to be when I grow up."
‘They shot at us, I wasn’t hit’
Liri was born in the community of Matan near Kfar Saba, the third of four children of Shira, 59, and Eli, 60, and sister to Roni, 28, Shai, 25, and Guy, 17. Her parents run a family business importing hardware products for the furniture industry and now live in Moshav Yarhiv, next to Matan.
She enlisted in the IDF in July 2023 and, after completing a course for surveillance soldiers, was sent together with her friends from the course, Naama Levy and Agam Berger, to the Nahal Oz military base. They arrived there on Thursday, Oct. 5, two days before they were abducted.
Much has already been written and said about her abduction. Hamas terrorists who overran the base killed 54 male and female soldiers and abducted Liri along with six other surveillance soldiers: Naama Levy, Agam Berger, Karina Ariev, Daniella Gilboa, Noa Marciano, who was killed in Gaza, and Ori Megidish, who was rescued by the IDF.
On the 277th day of their captivity, footage was released showing them at the moment of their abduction, sitting battered and injured on the floor. During her 477 days in captivity, Liri was moved between 22 hiding places. She spent 103 of those days in underground tunnels. Like the other hostages, she was held in harsh conditions, with almost no food or water.
Liri, were there moments when you genuinely feared for your life?
"Of course. There were quite a few moments like that. The fact that you’re living with armed terrorists, you don’t know when they’re going to explode over something and take it out on you. There was one terrorist I didn’t trust, completely crazy, bipolar, five minutes one way and five minutes the opposite. The only thing that kept us going was knowing they had no interest in us dying, because they would get much more for us if we stayed alive."
Did you know what was happening in Israel while you were there?
"Yes. We asked for a radio and they gave us one, so we were updated. Every now and then I would catch a glimpse of their television on the way to the bathroom, and once I even saw Mom and Dad at Hostages Square."
‘I’m not a celebrity’
Although she spent almost her entire period of military service in captivity, three months after returning home Liri chose to re-enlist and serve in a classified position. In May, she completed her service and posted a photograph on Instagram of herself cutting up her military ID card.
"I felt that I needed to close the circle, to say thank you to the IDF and, above all, to feel like a normal girl again."
Liri met her boyfriend, 26-year-old Tom Skolovin, a fitness trainer who runs a private soccer school at Kibbutz Ein Dor, on Instagram two and a half months after her release. It took six months before she felt comfortable introducing him publicly, in a romantic Instagram video from a day they spent together.
"He says I made the first move, but really he started with me," she says, laughing. "He followed me on Instagram and replied to my story. Then I started a conversation."
What did you write to him?
"I asked him, ‘Who are you and why did you follow me?’ And he wrote, ‘You intrigued me.’ I told him, ‘Well, you intrigued me too. Otherwise I wouldn’t have replied.’ The rest is history. There’s a lot of love between us."
Shira: "Tom is good for her. He boosted her confidence. Here is someone who looks at her not only as Liri Albag the hostage."
How is captivity present in your relationship?
"It’s present in my life, so obviously it’s present in my relationship too. The advantage is that he didn’t know me before. This is the Liri he knows, so he doesn’t compare who I was then with who I am today."
Do you feel that he also walks on eggshells around you, like the rest of the family?
"No, but he’s a sensitive person. We communicate, we talk about everything. He knows what I went through, and he knows how to notice when I’m irritable or when I need more quiet."
Are you thinking about moving in together?
"Obviously it will happen soon."
Shira: "No, wait, not so fast. I’m not letting you go. You’re still a little girl. There’s time," she says, laughing.
Liri: "There’s a distance between Yarhiv and Ein Dor. For now we drive back and forth, but it’s difficult."
You’ve become a sought-after figure at openings and launch events. How do you feel about being a celebrity?
"I’m not a celebrity. I only went to one launch event with my mother. It was cool, but after that I went back to the army and that was it. I may have 80,000 followers, but I don’t work at it. I don’t run a page, I don’t make money from it and I don’t do collaborations. Before captivity, I always joked that one day I’d be famous. I told Agam about it in captivity. I said, ‘See? I knew it,’" she says, laughing. "I don’t want all that celebrity stuff anymore, because at the end of the day I’m a private person."
Is there anything Liri avoids today because of captivity?
Shira: "She can’t watch anything on television except cartoons. Then she asks me or her sisters to sit beside her on the couch, takes my hand and asks us to stroke her and pamper her. Well, she has a pretty good excuse."
Liri: "I tell them, ‘I was in captivity, spoil me,’" she says, laughing.
Shira: "Her relationship with her sisters has become much stronger, and so has her relationship with her brother Guy. They’ve already been through the worst thing imaginable, so everyone is more open about sharing problems and looking after one another. As a mother, it’s wonderful for me to see."
You could see that at the wedding of your eldest daughter Roni a month ago. The video of the two of them dancing together went viral and received more than a million views.
Liri: "First of all, that song, ‘Ma Yihye Machar’ by Pe’er Tasi, accompanied Roni throughout my captivity, especially the line, ‘I will find you among millions of people.’ We were dancing and then suddenly the song came on. She came over to sing it to me, and I couldn’t stop the tears. It was an unbelievable closing of the circle that at her wedding we were dancing together to that song, especially after her husband waited to propose until I came back. I remember that when I returned from Gaza, I hugged him and whispered in his ear, ‘You haven’t proposed yet, I hope.’ He answered, ‘Do you really think I would have done that without you?’"
Shira: "That wedding was our family’s victory party. There were captivity survivors and parents of captivity survivors, people from the Hostages and Missing Families Forum and, of course, the surveillance soldiers who were abducted with Liri."
Are you in touch with other parents?
"We have several parents’ groups, and there isn’t a day when there aren’t conversations there. We meet from time to time too. Not long ago we were at the wedding of Karina Ariev’s sister and everyone came. Now we’re celebrating happy occasions."
Liri: "Knock on wood, let it stay that way. Only happy occasions, amen."
Did Roni’s wedding make you want to get married too?
"I’m not at that age yet, but it’s no secret that I’ve always dreamed of being a mother. After captivity, that desire only became stronger. That’s also the sweetest revenge there can be. At the end of the day, I came into this world to continue it, and I will continue the family line despite them, with at least five children."
