Qalibaf pointed to the Persian Gulf as an example of the consequences of extra-regional involvement, saying that the presence of foreign powers had not brought greater security to the region but had instead contributed to greater insecurity.
He expressed hope that sustained political and economic cooperation between Iran and Armenia would create new opportunities in transit, energy and other sectors.
Mirzoyan described Iran-Armenia relations as strategic, saying continued cooperation between the two governments would further strengthen bilateral ties.
He highlighted the region’s significant potential in transportation, energy and infrastructure and called for broader regional cooperation, including the expansion of Armenia’s transportation links with neighboring countries.

No queues, empty seats and the worst speech ever heard: welcome to the Tory conference | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:34:45 UTC
02:34:45 KST

At the Labour party conference in Liverpool last week, Andy Burnham floated the idea of electoral reform. This week in Birmingham, the Tories have come up with a plan of their own: voting with their feet.
How to put this nicely? Let’s just say that the Conservative party conference is extremely civilised. No queues for the food concessions. No queues to get into any of the halls. In fact, the organisers are delighted that anyone has turned up at all.
This doesn’t feel like a high-octane meeting of a party preparing for government. More like a home counties meeting of the Rotary Club. On current evidence, if there is a general election next year – as Kemi Badenoch is trying to convince us there will be – then the Tories won’t be active participants. More like vaguely disinterested observers. For these four days, Birmingham is a city where you can sit and watch the world pass you by.
Not that those who have turned up seem unhappy. Rather, they are thrilled to find themselves still alive. This time last year, there was a possibility that they faced extinction: under threat from left and right and with a leader in Kemi who looked unlikely to last six months. Since then things have stabilised as Robert Jenrick has been stopped from pulling out their ventilator in the intensive care unit. They are now merely an endangered species. The conference centre is a safari park attraction where we get to see the remnants of the Tory party in a protected habitat.
The morning’s activities take place in what is optimistically called the main hall: a hard-to-find side room with a capacity of about 200. These are way more seats than any of the acts require. First up was shadow transport secretary, Richard Holden, who managed to bore even himself. Still, at least the hall was about a third full. Which, for Rich, is a major result. I’m guessing most of the people there were family and friends.
It was no fuller for the shadow health secretary, Damian Hinds, who stumbled over his notes for five minutes. Weirdly, there were 24 people watching an empty stage online after he had left, while only 17 had been online when he was talking. Or maybe that’s not so weird.
For the afternoon offering we were moved to a slightly bigger hall. This could have been a mistake. It had come billed as a “major speech by the shadow chancellor”. Only we were made to sit through an hour and a half of nothingness – an opportunity to deliberate our own and the Tories’ existential futility – before the main event.
By now at least another third of the audience had left. A wise choice. They clearly had some idea of what was coming. Even 20 minutes of Andrew Griffith can rip your soul in half. If only I had joined them.
Not that the hall was anywhere near full to begin with. First up was the shadow Defra secretary, Victoria Atkins, who had sensibly worked out that no one in their right mind would stay to hear her talk. So instead she positioned herself as a cable TV presenter – there were 53 people watching online – chatting to her guest, Jeremy Clarkson.
This did at least lift the mood in the hall. A genuine celeb was among them for 15 minutes. However, it doesn’t say much for your conference when your most popular speaker is someone who openly says he’s not a Tory party member and has only turned up because he will go anywhere people will have him to talk about farming.
“Wow,” said Jezza. “There’s an awful lot of people here dressed as seats!” Vicky giggled nervously. The rest of the chat came and went perfectly amiably. Jezza did what he does best, giving his best impression of a multimillionaire held back by the incompetence of government. Still, at least he injected some fun. Vicky wanted to know how the farming summer had gone. He replied that the Diddly Squat farm had produced several ounces of hen food because of the extreme heat.
Someone should have told him that Griffith was about to get rid of the Climate Change Committee. If you missed any of this, you will be able to watch extended highlights on the next series of Clarkson’s Farm.
From then on, the conference became one long car crash. A panel with a couple of rightwing hacks droning on about nothing and then another panel in which one businesswoman congratulated herself on not getting stabbed on the train to Brum – apparently all her friends refuse to use trains – and then a businessman sobbing at the thought of billionaires being asked to pay inheritance tax. Some of them are so sick with worry they can no longer sleep.
Finally the main attraction. What would turn out to be a landmark occasion for all party conferences. Because Griffith proceeded to give the worst speech ever heard. Not just in content but in delivery. It was like watching a less sentient version of the PG Tips monkey. Constantly applauding himself and ending his sentences with “Yeah”. What was left of the audience didn’t know where to look.
If Andy really is the future chancellor, then we are truly fucked. Even Mel Stride wasn’t this hopeless. We might as well all pack up now. He was going to build more homes that were uninsulated and might fall down because they were cheaper. He would cut taxes and regulations the Tories had themselves introduced.
“This is our destiny,” he said. And then he dematerialised. It was as though he had been primitive AI and his controller had seen quite enough and decommissioned him. Andy didn’t know he had finished. And neither did anyone else.

Iran protests Norway’s inaction over unauthorized Starlink operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:32:02 UTC
02:32:02 KST

Iran protests Norway’s inaction over unauthorized Starlink operations
TEHRAN— Iran has formally protested to Norway over the continued operation of unauthorized Starlink satellite internet terminals inside Iranian territory, urging Oslo to take immediate steps to halt transmissions that violate Iran's sovereignty and national security.
Iranian Foreign Ministry Director General for International Peace and Security Mohammad Hassan-Nejad Pirkoohi summoned Norwegian Ambassador to Tehran Paul Bjornstad on Sunday and conveyed Tehran’s formal protest over Norway’s failure to take effective action against unauthorized Starlink operations, according to Iran’s Foreign Ministry.
 
During the meeting, Hassan-Nejad outlined the use of Starlink’s satellite communications infrastructure by the United States and Israel to support interventionist activities against Iran.
 
He said Tehran strongly objected to Norway’s continued failure to fulfill its responsibilities as the administration responsible for registering the Starlink satellite network with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU).
 
The Iranian official referred to decisions and conclusions reached by the ITU’s Radio Regulations Board (RRB) over the past several years, saying they require Norway to take appropriate measures to prevent unauthorized Starlink transmissions from operating inside Iranian territory.
ITU has examined the dispute since 2023
The dispute is not new and has been under consideration by the ITU’s Radio Regulations Board since 2023.
According to documents published by the ITU, Iran has repeatedly reported the continued operation of Starlink terminals on its territory without authorization. The Board has also repeatedly urged Norway and the United States to take appropriate measures to have unauthorized Starlink terminals in Iran disabled.
The ITU’s regulatory framework states that transmitting earth stations may operate within a country only when authorized by that country’s administration. The Board has specifically cited Article 18 of the Radio Regulations and Resolution 22 concerning the operation of transmitting earth stations.
At its 98th meeting, the Board concluded that there was evidence of unauthorized Starlink transmissions inside Iran and urged Norway to take all appropriate measures within its capacity to immediately cease such transmissions, including remotely disabling terminals where necessary. The Board also asked Norway and the United States to explain why it had not been possible to disable unauthorized terminals in Iran in the same way that Starlink terminals had reportedly been disabled in several other countries.
The Board subsequently maintained its position. At its 100th meeting, it noted Norway’s unwillingness to enforce earlier decisions requiring the immediate cessation of unauthorized Starlink transmissions, while also noting that Starlink had demonstrated the technical capability to identify and remotely disable terminals operating illegally in a particular area.
At its 101st meeting, the Board said the actions of Norway were not compliant with obligations under relevant ITU resolutions and Article 18 of the Radio Regulations. It nevertheless concluded that it did not have the authority to suspend the frequency assignments of satellite systems because of non-compliance by the notifying administration.
Iran calls for immediate action
Against this background, Hossein-Nejad told the Norwegian ambassador that Tehran had repeatedly followed up on the issue but had yet to see effective action.
He called on Norway to immediately convey and act upon Iran’s request for urgent measures to stop Starlink transmissions operating without authorization inside Iran.
The Iranian official also handed Bjornstad a formal diplomatic note of protest, formally placing Tehran’s objections on record.
The issue has particular significance because Starlink terminals are relatively small and portable, making it difficult for Iranian authorities to identify and locate every unauthorized terminal across the country. The ITU has acknowledged this difficulty, while also noting that the satellite operator possesses the capability to geolocate terminals and remotely disable them.
In its latest published consideration of the matter, the ITU’s RRB said the issue had remained unresolved since its 92nd meeting in March 2023. It again called on Norway and the United States to take appropriate action to have the Starlink operator disable unauthorized transmissions within Iranian territory, while also asking Iran to continue efforts, to the extent possible, to identify and deactivate unauthorized terminals.
The dispute therefore extends beyond a bilateral disagreement between Tehran and Oslo, touching on the international regulation of satellite communications, the obligations of administrations responsible for satellite network filings, and the ability of satellite operators to prevent services from being provided in territories where they have not been authorized.
For Tehran, however, the matter has an additional national-security dimension. Iranian officials have repeatedly accused the United States and Israel of exploiting communications and satellite technologies in support of activities directed against the Islamic Republic. The latest diplomatic protest consequently combines a regulatory demand with a broader objection to the use of foreign technological infrastructure inside Iran's territory without authorization.
Tehran is now calling on Norway to translate the ITU’s repeated recommendations and decisions into concrete measures and to ensure that Starlink transmissions from unauthorized terminals inside Iran are brought to an immediate halt.
Starlink could become a military target
Iran successfully disabled Starlink terminals during events last winter and possesses additional technologies to identify and block their activities, Supreme Council of Cyberspace Secretary Mohammad Amin Aghamiri said. Speaking at an internet businesses conference, he warned that satellite communications infrastructure could become a legitimate military target if used as an instrument of war.
Aghamiri also said Iranian cybersecurity authorities contained the most recent cyberattacks, keeping vital public services operational while minimizing disruptions and public concern during the conflict.

“We also discussed other ideas for protecting critical infrastructure and bolstering air defense. I am grateful for the readiness to help,” Zelesnkyy said on X following the talk.
He also informed Jetten about contacts with the U.S. team and potential trilateral meetings at the technical level between Ukraine, the USA, and Russia. “Realistic proposals that can bring peace closer are important. But Russia must take the negotiations seriously and not try to find more and more pretexts to drag the war out further,” Zelenskyy said.
The President of Ukraine thanked the Prime Minister and the Netherlands for their consistent and resolute support.
In his post, Jetten noted that Russian aggression against Ukraine continues to escalate.
"We saw this again this past weekend, particularly with the air strikes on Kyiv. Russia is deliberately targeting civilian sites and energy infrastructure, seeking to make Ukrainian cities uninhabitable and destroy the economy this winter. We cannot allow this to happen," the Dutch Prime Minister wrote.

Disgraced ex-British prince sues over Epstein raids
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, has taken Thames Valley Police to court over raids on his residences as part of an investigation into his dealings with Jeffrey Epstein.
The former British royal has challenged the legality of search warrants executed in February that saw him briefly placed in custody on suspicion of sharing confidential government information with the convicted American pedophile financier.
The former Duke of York has for years faced separate allegations of sexual misconduct. In 2022, he settled a civil lawsuit with American activist Virginia Giuffre out of court. According to media reports, the former prince had to pay £12 million ($16.3 million) in hush money to the woman, who accused him of raping her in 2001 when she was 17.
Giuffre took her own life in 2025. Her posthumously released memoirs prompted King Charles III to strip his brother of his remaining titles and to evict him from his royal residence last October.
Epstein was found dead in his prison cell while awaiting trial in 2019, in what was ruled a suicide.
On Monday, the press office for Britain’s judiciary announced that Mountbatten-Windsor’s legal claim will be heard in private on Thursday at the High Court.
“The case concerns an application by Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor for a judicial review to quash search warrants issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February 2026,” the judicial spokesperson said, as cited by the media.
The proceedings will be closed to the public at the request of Thames Valley Police, which also confirmed that they are “engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court.”
The former Duke of York previously admitted to associating with Epstein, but insisted that their friendship ended by late 2010 – which was subsequently proven false.
The former prince’s ties to the disgraced financier and convicted sex offender came under renewed scrutiny following the release of the final tranche of the Epstein files by the US Justice Department in February. Some of the emails released indicated that Mountbatten-Windsor used his position as UK trade envoy, which he held from 2001 to 2011, to brief Epstein on investment opportunities in Afghanistan, Singapore, Vietnam, Hong Kong, and China.
Thames Valley Police subsequently raided Mountbatten-Windsor’s home on the Sandringham Estate and his former residence at Royal Lodge in Windsor. He was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, but was eventually released “under investigation” after 12 hours of questioning, and has denied any wrongdoing. He is the most senior member of the royal family to be arrested in modern history.
On Sunday, The Telegraph reported that the police investigation has stalled due to the refusal of the US Justice Department to hand over the unredacted versions of the Epstein files to the UK authorities.
In May, Thames Valley Police said the probe would also look into allegations of sexual misconduct by Mountbatten-Windsor.
The last tranche of the Epstein files included images appearing to show then-Prince Andrew kneeling over a woman lying on the ground, as well as a claim by an anonymous FBI witness that he attended “pedophile ring parties” in the mid-1990s in which minors as young as six were allegedly abused.
Some of the materials released by the Justice Department also appeared to corroborate allegations by Giuffre – one of the most prominent accusers of Epstein.
Commenting on the release of the last batch of the files in February, Russian presidential aide Kirill Dmitriev described the former prince and his “liberal Western friends” as “satanic.”

Dibrugarh's river trade returns after 70 years: First post-Independence cargo from Assam heads to Bangladesh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:29:22 UTC
02:29:22 KST

Dibrugarh on Monday resumed international river trade after nearly seven decades, with Union Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal flagging off a barge carrying 540 metric tonnes of methanol from Bogibeel Terminal to Dhaka, marking the first cargo shipment from upper Assam to a foreign port since Independence.The methanol, produced by state-owned Assam Petro-Chemicals Ltd (APCL) at Namrup, will travel around 768 km along National Waterway-2 on the Brahmaputra before reaching the India-Bangladesh border and continuing through the Indo-Bangladesh Protocol Route. The voyage from Bogibeel to Narayanganj in Bangladesh will cover around 1,300 km.The shipment is being seen as a test of the Brahmaputra's potential as a commercially viable freight corridor connecting the Northeast with overseas markets. Regular methanol shipments to Bangladesh are planned, with the movement enabled by recently established customs and immigration facilities at Bogibeel and Dhubri.The voyage also revives Dibrugarh's river trade nearly 70 years after its historic river ghat shut down. The ghat closed in 1956 as tea shipments shifted to rail, ending regular river bookings from the town.“Our grandparents grew up hearing the steamer whistle at Dibrugarh Ghat.
For 70 years, that whistle fell silent and the ships stopped coming,” Sonowal said. “Today, a ship leaves Dibrugarh for the world once again. The river never failed us. What it lacked for decades was the will to revive it.”The vessel DLB Patkai, pushed by the tug Kushal Konwar, will carry the cargo to Pangaon Port in Dhaka. Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma joined the flag-off ceremony virtually.Sarma described the shipment as a significant moment for the state, saying, “Assam's own product, made in Namrup, is now traveling to an international market on Assam's own river. The Northeast is no longer a frontier. It is India's gateway to the East.”The revival of Dibrugarh's river connectivity has been supported by the Bogibeel passenger and cargo terminal, which opened in February 2024, along with customs and immigration infrastructure and the Jalvahak cargo incentive programme.The route has seen growing activity in recent years. Tata Steel barges reached Pandu through Bangladesh in February 2022, while the river cruise vessel MV Ganga Vilas travelled from Varanasi to Dibrugarh through Bangladesh in 2023.The government is also seeking to expand inland waterways as an alternative freight network. Cargo movement on India's national waterways rose from 18 million metric tonnes in 2013-14 to 218 million metric tonnes in 2025-26, according to the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways.
More than Rs 6,800 crore is being invested in waterways across the Northeast, including the development of National Waterway-2, a ship repair facility at Pandu and last-mile connectivity to Pandu Port.Sonowal said the economic and environmental case for waterways was also significant. “Every ton we move on the river means less fuel burnt and fewer trucks on the highway,” he said.The government is working with Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and Myanmar to develop regional waterway links, with the Dibrugarh-Dhaka shipment potentially opening another freight route for products from the Northeast to international markets.

Trump's Strait May Be Open, But Hormuz Is Not
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:28:52 UTC
02:28:52 KST

Trump's strait may be open, but Hormuz is not
US claims of normal traffic collide with dark transits, million-dollar tanker rates, and $9.99 diesel fuel signs
TEHRAN — The US president insists the Strait of Hormuz is open. Tanker captains, charter markets, insurers, and motorists in the US tell a different story.
That gap — between what the White House announces and what actually moves through the world's most critical energy chokepoint — is now the central front in the information war accompanying the seven-month conflict that began on February 28.
Trump has personally repeated the claim several times in recent weeks. At a White House energy briefing last month, he said the strait was "fully open, totally open" thanks to US naval power. Days later, in a campaign-style speech in Oklahoma, he again declared that "we opened Hormuz" and that oil was "flowing beautifully." Last week, in remarks to reporters before departing for a fundraiser, he repeated that US forces had "kept Hormuz open" and that Iran could no longer "use the strait as blackmail."
The formulation reached its peak when Trump at one point referred to the waterway as the "Trump Strait," suggesting that US escort operations had effectively renamed and reclaimed it.
Maritime reality does not match the rhetoric.
A recent Bloomberg account, based on testimony from a commercial captain transiting the area, described what "open" currently means in practice: a southbound passage attempted in darkness, under radio silence, without normal AIS transparency, and under direct US naval escort — procedures designed for a combat zone, not a commercial lane. Even under those conditions, the report noted, tankers have remained exposed to attack.
That is not a definition of normal traffic. That is the definition of a contested strait.
Charter markets confirm the assessment. Daily hire rates for large tankers operating in the Persian Gulf, which market sources previously placed at around $50,000 per day, are now cited at up to $1.3 million per day for high-risk voyages, once war-risk premiums, security costs, insurance surcharges, and crew bonuses are factored in. No functioning, open strait produces a 26-fold spike in the cost of using it.
Insurers have effectively redrawn the map. Most mainstream cover excludes the northern and central channels without special war-risk approval, forcing traffic into a narrow southern corridor that is congested, slow, and heavily militarized. Delays of days, last-minute voyage cancellations, and owners refusing Gulf orders have become routine.
The security incidents explain why. In recent weeks, at least three commercial vessels have been hit or narrowly missed while approaching or exiting the strait — including a VLCC struck by an unmanned system that forced an emergency diversion, a product tanker damaged by a proximity explosion that injured crew members, and an unarmed bulk carrier and tanker pair that came under fire in an incident the US described as defensive but regional media described as an attack on civilian shipping.
The pattern is consistent: even escorted, even silent, even in darkness, passage is not guaranteed.
The consequences are now visible inside the US itself.
Diesel boards at some US gas stations have displayed $9.99 — not because the price is $9.99, but because legacy signage cannot display double digits. In California, the Midwest, and parts of the Southeast, diesel has in practice exceeded $10 per gallon, while regular gasoline has surged to levels not seen in US history. Trucking companies have warned of cascading food and logistics costs.
Trump has tried to contain the fallout with a familiar toolkit: emergency releases from strategic reserves, public pressure on refiners and retailers to cap margins, temporary waivers on fuel blends, and repeated promises — including a much-publicized pledge of $5,000 payments to voters — to offset the pain. So far, none has restored confidence.
Polling shows fuel prices and inflation are now the top concern for US voters ahead of the midterm elections. Within Trump's own base, the seven-month war — sold initially as a days-long operation, or at most a four-to-six-week campaign — is increasingly described in US media as the most unpopular US military engagement in decades. Republican strategists openly warn that energy prices could cost the party Congress.
It is in this context that Iran has floated a seven-day plan for the full reopening of the strait: a phased, verifiable de-escalation involving a mutual ceasefire on commercial shipping, withdrawal of offensive strike assets from the immediate vicinity of the traffic separation scheme, joint monitoring through regional intermediaries, and a return to normal insurance and AIS operations within one week.
Tehran presents the initiative as proof that closure is a reversible, political decision — not a military fait accompli by the US. Washington has so far dismissed it as a stalling tactic, while continuing to insist the strait needs no reopening because it is already open.
That insistence is the point, analysts in Tehran argue. The conclusion emerging here is twofold:
First, by declaring Hormuz open and traffic normal, Trump seeks to calm US fuel markets psychologically even when he cannot calm them physically. If voters and traders believe the corridor functions, panic buying eases and prices may be contained at the margins.
Second, and more strategically, Washington wants to signal to Tehran that the Hormuz card is already burned — that Iran's principal leverage has been neutralized by US naval power, and that Tehran therefore has no choice but to concede and accept US terms.
In other words, "open" is not a maritime description. It is a political operation.
But a strait where captains sail dark and silent, where charter rates rise from $50,000 to $1.3 million, where civilian ships are still hit under escort, and where US motorists stare at $9.99 signs that cannot tell the truth, is not open by any professional standard.
Trump may have opened his own strait. Hormuz remains closed.

Will Trump roll the dice again? Dostoevsky has the answer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:27:41 UTC
02:27:41 KST

Will Trump roll the dice again? Dostoevsky has the answer
TEHRAN — Many around the world are trying to decode and analyze the character of the current President of the United States — from politicians and analysts to journalists, traders, and market players. After all, the U.S. president wields vast powers, while the mechanisms in the American system for overseeing and constraining those powers are, more often than not, theoretical possibilities on paper rather than practical realities.
One of the biggest questions observers in America and around the world are grappling with today is this: Will Trump once again turn up the flames of war with Iran and launch an attack, or not? First of all, it must be said that the war that began on February 28 has never actually ended. It has had its ebbs and flows — at times more intense, at times quieter — but it has not ended.
Back to the question. Arguably, one of the most logical ways to find an answer would be to look at Trump's own positions. Yet he takes a new stance and makes a new claim every day, and is deeply contradictory on this front. Matters have reached the point where, in a recent campaign speech in Oklahoma, he claimed that Iran was even producing narcotics inside its nuclear facilities. The sheer degree to which Trump treats his audience as fools is at times astonishing.
When conventional, logical approaches fail to solve a puzzle, everyone tries to resort to inventive methods of their own. Here, I want to turn to Dostoevsky for help. The great virtue of writers is that you can count on their help even after their death.
One of Dostoevsky's most famous and captivating works is the novel The Gambler, written in just 26 days, whose dramatic creation was itself driven by the financial pressure of the author's own gambling losses. It makes no difference where a gambler is from or what the instrument of gambling is; throughout history, gamblers have remained utterly loyal to one thing: never walking away from the table. Winners press on to win more; losers press on to recover their losses — both convinced of their luck.
Alexei Ivanovich, the hero of the novel, like every other gambler, is faithful to this unwritten pact. When he wins a handsome sum, he keeps playing to make more; and when he loses for the first time: “With a feeling like a sick qualm, as though I would like to make my way out of the crowd and go home, I staked another fifty gulden — this time on the red.”
The attack on Venezuela was, for Trump — albeit through cheating — the equivalent of a sweet win. But for one addicted to gambling, a sweet win is not only never enough; it further stimulates the instinct. Egged on by the then head of Mossad, the U.S. president fell under the illusion that it was now time to land the whale. Defeating an Iran that has stood against America since 1979 and has outlasted every previous president could immortalize his name in history. Less than a year ago, he had attempted this gamble and lost — and he thought that this time the story would be different.
A war that was supposed to last a few days, or at most four to six weeks, has now turned into a seven-month quagmire for America, with price displays at some gas stations showing $9.99 for diesel — simply because they are physically incapable of displaying a higher figure. Trump's late-February gamble has become the most unpopular American war in decades and has brought his voter base to the brink of collapse.
A rational man in such circumstances would revise his calculations and abandon the folly. But it must not be forgotten that we are dealing with a tired and desperate gambler who has promised each spectator $5,000 to cheer him on louder, who does not shrink from attacking a school and massacring children to secure victory, and who regards sinking an unarmed vessel as entertainment. Losing the gamble is not the main problem; the main problem is his false hope in luck.
Some sources say Trump has stated in closed-door meetings that the reason the war has produced no result is that the attacks were not severe enough.
At the end of Dostoevsky's novel, Alexei, who has lost everything, recalls a memory in which he once had only one gulden left in a game and won 170 with it, and says: “This is a fact — That is what one’s last gulden can sometimes mean! And what if I had lost heart that time, if I had not dared to make up my mind? ... Tomorrow, tomorrow all shall be ended!”

Amcha Yisrael unveils framework for independent October 7 commission of inquiry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:27:37 UTC
02:27:37 KST

- i24NEWS

- Amcha Yisrael unveils framework for independent October 7 commission of inquiry
Amcha Yisrael unveils framework for independent October 7 commission of inquiry
According to the party's plan, the new Knesset would elect the commission's chairperson and deputy by secret ballot from a list of retired judges nominated by lawmakers themselves
The Amcha Yisrael party, led by Ofer Winter, has unveiled a framework for a special commission of inquiry into the events of October 7. The proposal calls for an independent, professional body removed from political control. The party says it rests on three principles: truth, trust and results.
The initiative is led by Netali Shem-Tov, who was evacuated from her home in Metula on October 7, and Sigal Kraunik, whose husband Arik, the Kibbutz Be'eri security coordinator, was killed that day. Attorney Eran Ben-Ari is also leading the effort. The three presented the plan on behalf of the party.
In a statement, the party said: "The fact that no commission of inquiry has been established to date is a disgrace shared by both the coalition and the opposition." It argued that neither camp has an interest in forming such a body, since both share blame for the failure.
Under the proposal, the new Knesset, rather than the government or the courts, would choose the commission's leadership. The process would mirror presidential elections. Knesset members would propose retired judges, and the 120 lawmakers would then vote.
The body would hold full investigative powers and would not face political limits on the direction of its work. It would have to begin within a set timeframe and present preliminary findings to the public within six months. The investigative team would include bereaved families, hostage representatives and others directly affected, who would play an active role.
The mandate would extend beyond the sequence of events on October 7. It would also examine decisions, processes and lessons accumulated over the years, including events and operations surrounding Operation Protective Edge, to the extent they help explain the failure.
The party said a commission that lacks credibility across all segments of the public cannot succeed. "We will spearhead a commission of inquiry that is free from vested interests," the statement read. It added that the effort is owed to the fallen, their families, the wounded, and the country's children, to ensure such a tragedy never happens again.

A military court in Yekaterinburg has sentenced Leonid Melekhin, an activist deported to Russia after a failed U.S. asylum bid, to six years in prison. The court convicted him of “justifying terrorism” over a photo of a Vladimir Putin mannequin hanging from a bridge and an internet comment.
Judge Igor Solomko of the Central District Military Court in Yekaterinburg has sentenced Perm activist Leonid Melekhin to six years in a general-regime penal colony, Mediazona has learned. Melekhin was found guilty on two counts of “public justification of terrorism” (Parts 1 and 2 of Article 205.2 of the Russian Criminal Code). In addition to the prison term, the court banned Melekhin from administering websites and online channels for two years.
The military court had been hearing Melekhin’s criminal case since May 6. The trial was held entirely behind closed doors at the request of prosecutor Maria Otradnova.
Otradnova argued for the secrecy of the proceedings by claiming that the “terrorist danger has increased” in the Sverdlovsk region. She insisted that a closed trial was necessary to “ensure the safety of the participants” in the process and to avoid disclosing the “methods and means of conducting operative-investigative activities.”
An anonymous source close to Melekhin previously told Mediazona that the case against him was initially triggered by a post on the Telegram channel of fellow Perm activist Yuri Bobrov, “Bobr. There and Back Again (An Immigration Diary)”. The post featured two photographs: one showing Melekhin at the U.S.-Mexico border crossing, and another showing a poster and a mannequin hanging from a rope, with a photograph of Vladimir Putin’s face.
“Putin V.V. murderer fascist usurper,” the poster read. “All that is necessary for the triumph of evil is the inaction of good people / a fascist to the gallows.”
However, by the time Melekhin’s case reached the Central District Military Court, it included two separate episodes of justifying terrorism. While the first episode stemmed from the mannequin stunt, the second was reportedly based on an internet comment. It remains unknown exactly what the comment said or where it was posted.
Sergei Fadeev, Melekhin’s current defense lawyer, did not respond to Mediazona’s questions.
In the summer of 2024, the 35-year-old businessman and activist from Perm requested political asylum in the United States but was ultimately denied. Melekhin spent roughly ten months languishing in U.S. immigration detention, spending his final months in the San Luis immigration prison in Arizona, a facility known for its harsh conditions.
Broken by his time in U.S. custody, Melekhin—according to Valery Kuznetsov, his former state-appointed lawyer—“asked to be sent back” to Russia himself, returning via “self-deportation.” Kuznetsov said that Melekhin about a criminal case but went anyway. He was arrested by the FSB immediately upon his arrival in July 2025.

Russia’s oil and gas revenues fall 17% in 2026 despite doubling of Urals crude prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:26:05 UTC
02:26:05 KST

Russia’s year-on-year federal budget revenue from oil and gas fell 17% in the first three quarters of 2026 despite a sharp rise in the price of Russian crude. The decline was driven by lower production and reduced exports amid Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, as well as a stronger ruble, Reuters reported.
From January through September, tax revenue from oil and gas production totaled 5.47 trillion rubles ($64.43 billion), down from 6.61 trillion rubles in the same period of 2025. The oil and gas sector accounts for about 20% of Russia’s tax revenue, and this year’s budget deficit is expected to reach 3% of gross domestic product — nearly twice the level originally planned.
At the same time, the price of Urals crude had risen above $92 a barrel by the end of September, roughly double its level from before the start of the U.S.-Israeli campaign against Iran on Feb. 28. Prior to the American-Israeli operation, Urals crude loaded at the Baltic port of Primorsk was trading at about $45 a barrel. On April 8, the price reached $113.89, its highest level since 2013. Nevertheless, shipments through the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk are significantly down due to risks following a series of Ukrainian attacks and a shortage of available tankers.
Russia is also cutting production. In September, the government lowered its forecast for oil and gas output in 2026 to their lowest levels in 17 years. According to OPEC data, Russia produced 8.718 million barrels of oil a day in August, 5.6% below January’s level of 9.240 million barrels a day. Reuters attributed part of the decline to repeated Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries, which have forced facilities to reduce production and contributed to fuel shortages in some regions.
A stronger ruble is also putting pressure on budget revenue. From January through August, the Russian currency was on average about 9% stronger against the dollar than it had been during the same period a year earlier. Because Russia collects much of its oil tax revenue in rubles, a stronger national currency reduces the domestic value of dollar-denominated export earnings.

A logo sits on display outside the headquarters of UniCredit SpA in Moscow, Russia, on Wednesday, April 17, 2013. (Andrey Rudakov/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Russian President Vladimir Putin allowed the Italian banking group UniCredit to reorganize its Russian subsidiary and sell the new unit, according to an official decree published on Oct. 5.
Moscow has barred companies from countries it has labeled as "unfriendly" — including Italy — from selling or transferring their shares in Russian businesses without approval from the authorities.
UniCredit, one of the few European banks still active in Russia, announced in May that it plans to sell most of its Russian subsidiary — UniCredit Bank Russia — to a private investor from the United Arab Emirates, while retaining control over its payments arm.
Putin's approval paves the way for the reorganization and sale, which UniCredit aims to complete by the first half of 2027.
Banks like UniCredit and Austria's Raiffeisen Bank have faced mounting pressure from European capitals to exit the Russian market since the outbreak of Russia's full-scale war in 2022 and the subsequent sanctions.
At the same time, Western companies face the risk of Moscow seizing or confiscating their assets in Russia as a form of pressure against Western governments.
Only last month, Putin signed a decree on the confiscation of the assets of the Swiss food company Nestle and the French supermarket chain Auchan, and the Kremlin seized control over the Russian subsidiary of Germany's wholesale food retailer Metro AG.

India is one of Russia’s biggest energy buyers. Can it also help broker peace with Ukraine?
India is beginning to take a more active role in efforts to reach a settlement between Russia and Ukraine, Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said. Bloomberg reported that his explicit statement signals New Delhi’s shift toward a more active stance after years of caution over the war, driven partly by its close economic ties with Russia.
Speaking at a Munich Security Conference meeting held away from its usual venue, Jaishankar said India had become “a little bit more involved” in the peace process in recent months. He said New Delhi is now in talks with both Russia and Ukraine:
We are trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue, but going beyond that to cover some immediate concerns which both of them have on grain exports, on energy exports, on non-attack possibilities. So those are ongoing conversations right now.
Jaishankar gave no details about the progress of the talks. He also said India sees Russia, as the Soviet Union’s successor, as a partner that has traditionally helped it in its conflict with Pakistan.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has discussed the war twice in meetings with Vladimir Putin over the past few weeks — first at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, then at the BRICS summit in New Delhi. India’s is the most comprehensive. For the first time, India has offered to play a role,” Sybiha said. He did not specify what India’s proposals involved.
India and China are currently the biggest buyers of Russian energy, and Russian energy’s share of India’s imports has risen sharply since the war began. The U.S. has repeatedly pressured India to stop buying Russian oil in exchange for lifting tariffs. In early 2026, Donald Trump said an agreement had been reached. But India later resumed purchases after war broke out in the Middle East and energy shortages emerged.
Negotiations over a trade deal between India and the U.S. are ongoing. In recent weeks, the talks have been complicated by the U.S. passage of the so-called “sanctions from hell” law. It allows Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying substantial amounts of Russian oil — above all, India.

Ukraine's general fund revenue up 29.7% in 9M, borrowing down 45.7%
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:24:46 EEST
02:24:46 KST

Ukraine's state budget revenue rose 52.0% year-on-year to UAH 4.12 trillion in January-September 2026, including a 29.7% rise to UAH 2.49 trillion in the general fund, the Finance Ministry said on its website on Monday, citing State Treasury data.
General fund cash spending grew much less, by 16.0% to UAH 3.27 trillion, while total budget spending, including the special fund, rose 31.7% to UAH 4.78 trillion, it said.
The growth in general fund revenue is largely due to bigger grants this year, UAH 604.0 billion against UAH 308.8 billion a year earlier, although September grants were smaller, at UAH 34.5 billion against UAH 53.9 billion. The National Bank also transferred UAH 146.1 billion of its profit to the budget in April and May, compared with UAH 84.2 billion in the same months of 2025.
The large gap in total budget revenue and spending from last year is due to the military part of the Ukraine Support Loan, EUR 31.8 billion, which is recorded this year. EUR 17 billion of it remains available for drawdown by the end of 2026.
Value-added tax (VAT) on goods produced in Ukraine brought UAH 255.2 billion in January-September, against UAH 231.6 billion a year earlier, but VAT refunds rose to UAH 170.9 billion from UAH 131.2 billion. In September, refunds fell to UAH 9.9 billion from UAH 15 billion.
Import VAT added UAH 491 billion (UAH 390.3 billion in the first nine months of 2025), personal income tax and the military levy UAH 266.3 billion (UAH 260.9 billion), corporate profit tax UAH 270.0 billion (UAH 219.7 billion), and subsoil use rent UAH 39.1 billion (UAH 31.5 billion). Since July, the military levy has gone to the special fund, where it brought UAH 50.9 billion in three months.
Excise tax brought UAH 231.1 billion (UAH 210.5 billion), import and export duties UAH 48.6 billion (UAH 40.0 billion), and dividends and part of profits UAH 64.5 billion.
Unified social contribution revenue to the Pension Fund and social insurance funds rose to UAH 569.9 billion in January-September from UAH 479.2 billion a year earlier, the ministry said.
Because of smaller grants and the transfer of the military levy to the special fund, general fund revenue fell 6.0% year-on-year to UAH 195.9 billion in September. Including receipts from the military part of the Ukraine Support Loan, it grew 73.7% to UAH 518.4 billion, the ministry said.
In September, VAT on goods produced in Ukraine brought UAH 36.9 billion, against UAH 25.1 billion a year earlier, thanks to smaller refunds. Import VAT added UAH 57.2 billion (UAH 49.9 billion in September 2025), personal income tax and the military levy UAH 36.5 billion (UAH 30.0 billion), corporate profit tax UAH 4.3 billion (UAH 8.1 billion), and rent UAH 3.4 billion (UAH 4.1 billion). Excise tax brought UAH 24.0 billion (UAH 24.2 billion), and import and export duties UAH 5.9 billion (UAH 5.3 billion). Unified social contribution revenue rose to UAH 67.2 billion from UAH 55.7 billion, it said.
Actual state borrowing for the general fund in January-September 2026 was UAH 717.2 billion, or 58.3% of the amount planned for the period, against UAH 1.32 trillion, or 92.9%, a year earlier, the ministry said.
Domestic government bond placements brought UAH 362.1 billion to fund the state budget, against UAH 382.3 billion a year earlier. Of this, foreign-currency bonds raised UAH 55 billion ($450 million and EUR 691 million), against UAH 90.1 billion ($1.44 billion and EUR 638.3 million). Military domestic bonds raised UAH 130.9 billion (UAH 172.0 billion).
External sources provided UAH 355.1 billion, or about $8.0 billion, in nine months, against UAH 938.1 billion, or $22.6 billion, a year earlier. This included EUR 2.44 billion from the EU under the Ukraine Facility, SDR 1.6 billion from the IMF and $2.93 billion under various World Bank programs.
Public debt repayments in January-September 2026 were UAH 438.8 billion (96% of the plan), and debt servicing payments were UAH 275.7 billion (98.5% of the plan), against UAH 450.9 billion and UAH 246.3 billion a year earlier.
The 2026 state budget was initially approved with revenue excluding grants of UAH 2.90 trillion and spending of UAH 4.77 trillion, including UAH 2.61 trillion and UAH 4.38 trillion in the general fund. In June, mainly because of the EUR 45 billion Ukraine Support Loan from the EU, the Verkhovna Rada raised revenue to UAH 5.20 trillion and spending to UAH 6.41 trillion, including UAH 3.38 trillion and UAH 4.50 trillion in the general fund.
Under the Extended Fund Facility program with the IMF, updated in July, general government revenue is forecast at UAH 6.78 trillion this year, against UAH 5.06 trillion last year, and spending at UAH 7.94 trillion, against UAH 6.63 trillion.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky and representatives of the ruling Servant of the People faction have spoken of the need for another increase in defense spending of $27 billion.
General fund cash spending in January-August 2026 reached UAH 2.7 trillion, against UAH 2.23 trillion in January-August 2025, while revenue was almost UAH 2.3 trillion, against UAH 1.71 trillion.

Supreme Court sounds wary of state-based climate change suits against oil producers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:23:46 UTC
02:23:46 KST

Supreme Court sounds wary of state-based climate change suits against oil producers
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Several justices suggested that local and state claims against oil companies may be blocked by the federal Clean Air Act.
- California and nearly three dozen states and municipalities have filed such claims.
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court justices sounded wary Monday of state-by-state lawsuits that could impose huge damage verdicts on energy producers for the effects of global climate change.
Instead, several of them suggested these local and state claims may be blocked by the federal Clean Air Act.
“Interstate air and water pollution are matters for federal law,” said Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh. “We don’t have to reinvent the wheel. This kind of pollution is a federal matter unless Congress says otherwise.”
Justice Elena Kagan appeared to agree. State-by-state lawsuits “really get in way of how Congress decided to regulate greenhouse gases,” she said.
Justice Amy Coney Barrett questioned if states such as Colorado can use their courts to impose regulations on other states. “What if Colorado passed a law purporting to cap emissions in the other 49 states?” she asked.
At issue before the court was the question of whether cities and states may sue oil and gas producers for the damages inflicted by climate change.
California and nearly three dozen states and municipalities have filed such claims, but none have gone to trial. Meanwhile, the Republican-led states and the Trump administration opposed these lawsuits.
The outcome of the Colorado case could affect California’s 2023 lawsuit against the five largest oil companies and other similar litigation.
The eight justices struggled Monday to decide if these lawsuits are a matter for state or federal law.
Justice Samuel A. Alito, a staunch conservative, said he is sitting out the case, presumably because he owns stock in oil companies that would be affected by a ruling. Without him, the court could split 4 to 4 and be unable issue a decision.
That remains a possible outcome, but Monday’s argument kept open the prospect that a conservative majority will rule to block the climate-change suits.
Last year, the Colorado Supreme Court ruled that Boulder County may sue for damages in a local court. In a 5-2 ruling, the state judges said Boulder could sue and seek damages by alleging the oil producers are a “public nuisance.”
In February, the justices agreed to hear an appeal from the oil industry backed by the Trump administration. Its lawyers argued that the Constitution and federal law do not allow for such claims to be resolved in local courts.
Chief Justice John G. Roberts sounded skeptical of opening the door to a wave of climate change lawsuits.
“If you prevail, the next day a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit. How do you think that will work out on the ground?” he asked the lawyer representing Boulder.
For much of the two-hour argument, the justices struggled over whether federal law imposes a limit on such lawsuits, or instead whether states and their judges are free to seek damages for the harm they have suffered.
They did not signal a clear outcome. They could decide to stand aside and allow the suits to proceed in state courts.
“If Boulder’s claims are allowed to go forward, some 90,000 municipalities across the country will have the ability to make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil-fuel producers,” Kannon Shanmugam, a lawyer for the oil and gas companies, told the court.
Attorney Kevin Russell, representing Boulder, agreed Congress could adopt limits on such state lawsuits, but it has not done so. He said the court should not invent new limits to benefit one powerful industry.
So far, judges across the nation have been divided. Some have ruled that federal law preempts or blocks states and counties from suing under state law.
Justice Clarence Thomas has often voted against claims that a federal law or policy “preempted” or blocked states from pursuing their separate rules or policies.
Some legal experts doubted the oil industry would prevail in this case without both Thomas and Alito. But the defection of one conservative could lead to a tie vote.
If the court splits evenly and cannot rule, it would be a major disappointment for the oil industry because it would allow all the climate-change suits to proceed, at least for now.

The Asian Games close in Japan and head to Qatar in 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:23:40 UTC
02:23:40 KST

Breadcrumb
The Asian Games with more athletes than the Olympics close in Japan and head to Qatar in 2030
The Asian Games were a blur, a sports kaleidoscope of 45 countries and regions that went dark on Sunday, officially closed by Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani, the president of the Olympic Council of Asia.
The games featured about 11,000 athletes, more than the Summer Olympics in Paris two years ago, and now they head west to Doha, Qatar, in 2030.
This will be a homecoming. Sheikh Joaan is a Qatari, the younger brother of the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Al Thani.
Amid the whirlwind of 43 sports, many regional specialities were featured, including kurash, kabaddi, and sepaktakraw; the games offered a glimpse of top athletes who will compete again in two years at the Los Angeles Olympics.
China topped the medal table as it has for decades with 169 gold and 341 overall. Japan was second with 83 gold and 269 overall. South Korea (39, 150) was next, followed by India (21, 85), Uzbekistan (21, 70) and Iran (19, 52).
Forty of the 45 countries or regions won at least one medal. The bottom four won only a single bronze medal: Bangladesh, Brunei, Laos and Syria.
Some athletes to watch heading to the Olympics
Japanese 17-year-old Shin Ohashi set a swimming world record in the 200-meter breaststroke (2 minutes, 4.83 seconds), the first to swim under 2:05.
Also in the pool, Chinese 13-year-old female Yu Zidi won the 200 butterfly and the 200 and 400 medley relays. Organisers named her the event's female MVP. Zhang Zhanshou was the other prominent Chinese swimmer, a freestyler who won seven gold medals.
The male MVP was track and field sprinter Puripol Boonson of Thailand, who clocked 9.90 in the 100 and 19.88 in the 200.
India defeated bitter rival Pakistan for gold in men's cricket, and South Korea's men won gold in both baseball and soccer. That granted team members an exemption from mandatory military service at home. Tom Kim also picked up the exemption, taking men's singles golf.
Mixed martial arts also debuted, without the cage and with fighters wearing gloves and shin pads. Proponents talk of a long shot to land in the 2032 Olympics in Brisbane, Australia.
Organisers offer defence of game management
Organisers and the OCA offered an aggressive defence of the games, which were dotted with glitches and major mistakes.
Japanese organisers put on what they termed "sustainable" games, no athletes village, with lodging for athletes on a cruise ship, in hotels, and in temporary containers. The transportation system was also strained by venues stretching from Nagoya, the host city, across central Japan. Swimming was in Tokyo with some soccer in Osaka.
Despite the focus on austerity and "no white elephants", organisers and the OCA added a half-dozen sports to the program. They planned for 15,000 athletes and officials, but they said 17,000 arrived through late registrations.
To cram in more sports, organisers began the basketball competition on Sept. 10, nine days before the official opening. The Olympics often do the same, starting two or three days ahead, but not nine.
"We had some delays of buses and we'd like to apologise for that," Hideaki Omura, the governor of Aichi prefecture and the head of the organising committee, said Sunday. He described the event as having faced "huge challenges."
Some glitches included buses heading to the wrong destination, the North Korean anthem being played at a field hockey match between South Korea and Bangladesh, and an initial scramble to find beds for all 17,000 officials and athletes.
As usual at large events, audible complaints seemed to fade once the event got rolling and the sports took over.
Fallout from the pandemic-delayed Tokyo Games
Nagoya was awarded this event in 2016, before COVID-19 and before the Tokyo Olympics were delayed until 2021. Japan officially spent $13 billion on the Tokyo Games, although a government report said the real number might be twice that much,
Nagoya organisers in 2016 announced a budget of roughly $650 million, but late in 2025 they said the budget had swollen to about $2.5 billion, almost four times as much.
The Japanese advertising giant Dentsu, convicted of bid-rigging connected to the Tokyo Olympics, was kept out of the bidding for Asian Games contracts. Dentsu has wide experience running large sports events and lining up sponsors.
"Yes, the organising committee had challenges," said Husain Al Musallam, the director general of the OCA. "But our duty and responsibility as leaders was to work hard with the organising committee, to help Japan demonstrate to the world that Japan can deliver."

Merz, Macron seek tougher EU measures against unfair trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:23:00 UTC
02:23:00 KST

Merz, Macron seek tougher EU measures against unfair trade
October 5, 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron sent a joint appeal to the European Commission on Monday, calling for tougher EU measures against unfair trade practices by other states.
They said that the existing instruments at the EU's disposal were no longer sufficient.
The appeal did not name any specific country but it seemed most clearly tied to Chinese trade policy, the EU's vast deficit with China, and its dependence on certain key raw materials. The other apparent candidate would be the US, not least under the current unpredictable trade policy stewardship of tariff-loving President Donald Trump.
It also came just a few days before the EU's trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, is set to visit Beijing.
What did Merz and Macron say?
The joint letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for two new measures to be introduced in Brussels.
One would aim at ensuring diversification and preventing companies from becoming too dependent on suppliers from individual companies.
The other would allow another country to be excluded from access to the European single market on an expedited basis if exceptional circumstances made this necessary.
Merz and Macron wrote that this could be used in cases "where third countries deliberately seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field and fair market conditions through political or economic means, leading to serious and systematic distortions of our single market."
The French and German leaders, both struggling to balance economic growth and public spending, said the EU's struggles to maintain global competitiveness and its dependencies on certain suppliers of core materials led to "geoeconomic risks."
"The open and rules-based trading system is being massively compromised by the instrumentalization of trade, systemic market-distorting practices and global macroeconomic imbalances," they wrote. "All this undermines the level competitive playing field for our companies, our position as a sovereign core industrial producer and our capacity for innovations, which leads to increasing dependencies and geoeconomic risks."
Appeal comes ahead of EU China visit, and EU leaders' summit
Monday's letter is what's known in EU diplomatic circles as a "non-paper." These are nonbinding, informal documents shared between EU member states and institutions that are supposed to propose ideas and initiate discussions without officially committing to a position.
It recommends authorizing the Commission to exclude a country from single market access in extreme situations if it sees the need — currently a complicated process that would take some time to arrange and requires approval from member states.
It suggests reversing this process: allowing the Commission to take the step independently, but with member states then having the chance to block it with a qualified majority vote, which the EU currently defines as a vote by a minimum of 55% of member states that also represents a minimum of 65% of the bloc's total population.
The EU's trade deficit with China is vast and growing. The EU put the figure at around €360 billion (roughly $400 billion) in 2025, though China's statisticians reached a more modest tally of $292 billion.
The bloc is also particularly dependent on China for a number of raw materials, not least rare earths, and is increasingly reliant on both the US and China for high-tech imports and services, particularly in computing and the so-called AI sector.
The EU's trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, visits China this week for talks, ahead of an EU leaders' summit next week, on October 15-16. Sefcovic said earlier this year that he hoped to see "tangible results by October" on the question of trade with China, although whether these will materialize is an open question.
Beijing has warned that it could retaliate with changes of its own after learning of the EU's plans, if it perceives a need to.

French authorities must act upon their human rights obligations and stop the disproportionate police response seen in recent days to student protests, Amnesty International said ahead of tomorrow’s planned nationwide demonstrations.
“As children and young people prepare to take to the streets across France, authorities must ensure their safety and security and protect and facilitate the exercise of their right to demonstrate peacefully. Any policing response must be lawful, necessary and proportionate, and authorities must avoid unnecessary and excessive use of force,” said Anne Savinel-Barras, President of Amnesty International France.
Children and young people peacefully demanding their right to education must be protected rather than being beaten, tear-gassed, or arbitrarily detained
Anne Savinel-Barras, President of Amnesty International France
“Footage and testimonies widely reported over the last week raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of tear gas, batons and restraint techniques by police. Tear gas grenades have been discharged recklessly, and rubber bullets have been fired causing serious injuries.
“Authorities must ensure that any response to demonstrations is necessary and proportionate, and that children and young people peacefully demanding their right to education are protected rather than being beaten, tear-gassed, or arbitrarily detained. The priority should be the de-escalation of tensions and authorities must take all available precautionary measures to avoid the need to use force.”
Background
Since 21 September, high school students across France have taken to the streets demanding that their right to education is met through an increase in teacher numbers, smaller classes and decent school buildings, among other issues. Protests have been met with unnecessary and disproportionate force by police, including the unlawful use of tear gas grenades and rubber bullets. The Ministry of Interior announced that there have been more than 5,000 arrests of protesters and stated that 85 per cent of those arrested have been children.
On 27 October, the Senate will discuss a government bill that would make people participating in a gathering that results in property damage, financially liable for up to €10,000, even if there is no proof that they personally caused, contributed to, or incited the damage.
Amnesty France issued a press release on 2 October 2026 on high school protests.
Protests will be taking place on 6 October in cities including Paris (2pm CEST), Lyon (10am CEST, Marseille 10.30am CEST, Toulouse 11am CEST, Bordeaux 11am CEST

Uttarakhand CM Dhami hands over appointment letters to 332 recruits under ESI scheme

2026-10-05
17:19:46 UTC
02:19:46 KST

Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on Monday distributed appointment letters to 332 newly recruited personnel, including 271 appointees in the AYUSH Department and 61 Allopathic Pharmacy Officers under the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Scheme, at an event held at the Mukhya Sevak Sadan at the Chief Minister's Camp Office.Congratulating the newly appointed personnel, Dhami urged them to discharge their responsibilities with a strong sense of service, sensitivity and dedication.The Chief Minister said receiving an appointment letter marks an important milestone in the lives of young people and also marks the beginning of a new responsibility towards public service.He urged the new recruits not to view government service merely as a job, but as an opportunity to bring positive change to the lives of people at the grassroots.He said the role of personnel associated with the AYUSH Department and the ESI Scheme is directly linked to people's health and well-being."People travelling from remote areas to government health centres and hospitals do so with faith in the system. The sensitivity, promptness and efficiency of government personnel further strengthen this trust," Dhami said, urging the recruits to set an example through their work wherever they are posted.
He said every person visiting a hospital or health centre arrives with hope, and the right decision and sincere efforts of healthcare personnel can make a significant difference to the lives of those in need.Dhami said the state government has taken effective steps to make the recruitment system transparent and fair. Along with stringent action against cheating mafias, a strict anti-copying law has also been implemented.He said Uttarakhand's youth are now getting opportunities in government services on the basis of their hard work and merit. More than 35,000 youths have secured government jobs over the past five years, he said, adding that this reflects the government's commitment to a transparent recruitment system.The Chief Minister said Uttarakhand, besides being known as Devbhoomi, has a rich tradition of yoga, Ayurveda and medicinal herbs. The state government is working continuously to develop Uttarakhand as a model 'AYUSH State' and a 'Global Wellness Hub'.He said AYUSH services are being expanded across all districts, Panchakarma services are being modernised, and Ayurveda Centres of Excellence are being established.Through e-Sanjeevani, people are also being provided access to specialist consultations from home, while the 'AYUSH Setu Portal' is another important initiative in this direction.Several homestays across the state have also been linked with wellness services at nearby Ayurvedic hospitals, he said, adding that the government aims to provide visitors to Uttarakhand with a better experience of health and mental well-being through yoga, Ayurveda and Panchakarma.Dhami said healthcare services under the ESI Scheme are also being expanded continuously. Earlier, the scheme was operational in six districts of the state and has now been extended to all 13 districts.A 100-bed ESI hospital has started functioning in Rudrapur, while construction of a 300-bed ESI hospital is underway in Haridwar. Land has also been identified for an ESI hospital in Kashipur. The recruitment process for 47 new medical officers is in its final stage, he added.
The Chief Minister said the state government is committed to providing better and accessible healthcare facilities to every person.He expressed confidence that the energy and capabilities of the newly recruited personnel would play an important role in fulfilling the vision of a developed and empowered Uttarakhand.AYUSH Education Minister Madan Kaushik also congratulated the newly appointed personnel and said the state government is continuously working to strengthen and make AYUSH services more accessible to the people.He said the induction of the new personnel would enhance the department's efficiency and further strengthen AYUSH healthcare services across the state.He also urged them to discharge their duties with dedication, sensitivity and a spirit of service and play an active role in providing better healthcare to the public.

Elon Musk Calls This Documentary a 'Hit Piece.' Here’s Why It’s So Critical of Him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:19:37 UTC
02:19:37 KST

Elon Musk has called the documentarian Alex Gibney many names on X in the last few months: “crackpot,” “douchebag to his core,” “an idiot,” and someone for whom “dogsh*t is worth more respect.” That’s because Gibney made a four-hour documentary about him, “Musk,” which arrives in U.S. theaters October 9.
Gibney has chronicled tech leaders including Elizabeth Holmes and Steve Jobs. But this film has generated perhaps more news and controversy ahead of its release than any of his previous documentaries, in large part because of how strongly Musk and other tech companies have reacted to it.
Musk is waging a war of words over the documentary online, and his lawyer threatened Gibney with a defamation lawsuit. In late September, the Hollywood Reporter wrote that YouTube, Meta, TikTok, and X all declined to run the movie’s trailer on their platforms due to its “political content.” Universal Pictures, which controls the movie’s international distribution rights, also delayed its rollout over political sensitivities before saying that it stood by the film. (A representative for Gibney wrote to TIME on Oct. 5 that international distribution had been "worked out" following an Oct. 2 call with Universal, but did not elaborate further.)
On Sept. 30, Gibney sat down with TIME in Washington, D.C. to discuss why the movie is so critical of Musk, and Gibney’s ongoing fight to distribute it widely. Here are excerpts from the conversation, which has been condensed for clarity.
TIME: Is this movie a hit piece, as Elon Musk says?
Gibney: It's certainly critical, but I think the criticism is earned. This is a rigorous and meticulous investigation of somebody, and it ends up being critical.
I saw the film yesterday and found it incredibly dread-inducing. It literally ends with the destruction of the planet into a fireball.
Yes. That's right.
How are your dread levels these days?
They're really high. Look at all of these tech leaders in Washington, talking about the future of AI. The takeaway seems to be, “We'll just take care of it.”
Having been on that ride with Elon Musk, I don't want him to take care of it. He seems so comfortable with risk that he'd just as soon leave the planet. I posit at the end of the film, it's as if he's betting on whether or not AI will lead us to a moment of extraordinary abundance or basically the end of life on Earth. Who makes that kind of a bet?
Musk just landed a new gig: co-leading Project Meridian, a new Pentagon initiative aimed at shaping the future of warfare.
That's like putting the Joker in charge of the Manhattan Project. This is not a serious person at this moment, but he's being handed enormous power.
You’ve made several docs about Silicon Valley figures, including Steve Jobs and Elizabeth Holmes. In which ways is Musk simply channeling Silicon Valley mythmaking, and in which ways is he distinct?
I think it’s both, but I would draw some distinctions. Steve Jobs, after NeXT [the startup he ran between his Apple stints], surrounded himself with a small group of people who could tell him no, and he would listen to them. And that's what made Apple great. He had a fanatical attention to detail when it came to making products. Elon did just the opposite. He surrounded himself with people who only tell him yes.
I do think, in the “fake it till you make it” sense, that he's straight out of the Silicon Valley mold and similar to Elizabeth Holmes in that way. The obvious difference between him and Elizabeth Holmes is you can drive a Tesla, and the Edison [Theranos’s blood-testing machine] never worked. It’s not worth what its valuation is, but there’s a real car.
Many in Silicon Valley would tell you that failure and mythmaking are part of the pathway to success. Thomas Edison lied about the lightbulb for years, and then he made it work and changed the world. While Musk has plenty of failures, he’s built so many actual things: rockets, cars, satellites.
Yeah, these are real companies with very impressive technology. Seeing those reusable rockets come down—it's really impressive.
But there’s an interesting angle to that SpaceX story, too. Elon has always positioned it that if SpaceX hadn't succeeded on the fourth rocket launch, he would have been broke and everything would have been over.
Lori Garver [former NASA administrator] tells a very different story. The federal government had decided to use him as a test case, and they were going to keep working with him whether that fourth launch went up or not. We're supposed to invest in the lone entrepreneur who gets by without any government help or assistance. Turns out, it's just the opposite. The government has always been his friend—it made SpaceX, it made Tesla profitable at critical moments.
Over your career, you've incurred the wrath of other powerful figures who you’ve made documentaries about: the Church of Scientology, Bibi Netanyahu. What is it like, comparatively, incurring the wrath of Elon Musk?
He threatened to sue over a movie that he hadn't even seen, which made it very much like the Church of Scientology.
That was just part of the playbook. I had just seen him threaten to sue Ro Khanna for citing all sorts of evidence about USAID. So, to some extent, Elon Musk is playing the role I expected him to play.
But I'd be a fool not to be concerned about Elon Musk, both because he's the richest man in the world and also because he has the ear of a president who has turned the Department of Justice into an instrument of revenge.
Have any odd things happened to you, like being tailed or anything like that?
There was somebody, actually, in Camden, Maine. I thought somebody from behind me was following me, and the person in the passenger seat had an iPhone up, photographing me. But what did Hunter Thompson used to say? “Just because I'm paranoid doesn't mean I don't have enemies.” [Thompson was famously paranoid, but the line is actually from Joseph Heller’s Catch-22.]
Many people on X are currently dismissing you as a hack and the movie as a hatchet job. Do you get discouraged over the fact that Musk has a bigger platform than you, and that you won’t be able to change most people’s minds?
I don't get discouraged over the fact that Elon has a microphone, because I think Twitter has become this kind of dumpster fire which houses a collection of cult followers for him, as well as some critics, in order to boost engagement.
But what I do worry about—and I saw it in the initial refusal of Google, Meta, TikTok, and X to run our ads for the trailer—is a kind of unspoken consolidation of power that doesn't want to allow criticism, particularly over the accretion of power and money. That is becoming more and more and more of a worry.
Thankfully, to some extent, there is a cyclical nature to this, because I remember when I did a film called The Trials of Henry Kissinger, no cable network would show it in this country until we put it out in theaters. It played for months at Film Forum, and then started playing around the country. And then there was such public demand for it that finally the network put it on.
Theaters, in this moment, are proving to be a pretty good outlet for critical voices that the streamers and the social media platforms won't allow.
Which of those social media platforms has backed down from blocking the trailer?
YouTube and Meta—both on Instagram and Facebook—are now allowing ads. TikTok is not, and X has said that they would allow them, but we haven't seen any evidence of it.
What does this whole kerfuffle tell us about the status of free speech?
It's being curtailed. I mean, the free-speech absolutist Elon Musk is doing his damnedest to limit speech.
One of the most controversial parts of the film is when Ashley St. Clair, Musk’s ex, says that before the 2024 presidential election, Musk texted her about feeling optimistic about Trump winning because of Musk’s “10,000 lasers in space.” What does that text mean, and what do you hope comes of it being in the movie?
It was there to raise questions. We did not assert that Elon Musk had changed votes in 2024. All we did was show Elon Musk's text to Ashley, where he talks about 10,000 lasers in space. Is that Mini-Me talking? Is he lying to his lover? Or is he boasting about something that he did relating to the fact that he knew before everybody else what the outcome of the election was going to be? That seemed worth putting in.
And it pays off a little bit later in the film, when we begin to wonder what happened to all of the data that DOGE had access to, and did it end up in Elon's hands? And is he going to use it for the 2026 elections? We don't know.
Why should the public care about all of the data that Musk may have had access to through DOGE?
As Geoffrey Hinton, the godfather of AI, says: if you were to train an AI on all the data of every American citizen, you'd have some powerful tools. Either to figure out how or where to devote resources during the election, or develop rhetorical strategies to appeal to people. We know how good Facebook and Instagram are at getting right to what we want, right? So, it's just disquieting on its face.
I think the idea is that, particularly with what Elon Musk is doing with AI: what does AI want more than anything else? Data. And that is a vast amount of data to feed to an AI system.

UK 'threatens to expel Israeli diplomats' over consulate closure

Unknown Publisher
