Breadcrumb
UK 'threatening to expel 27 Israeli diplomats' over E. Jerusalem consulate closure
The UK government has threatened to expel 27 Israeli diplomats from London over Tel Aviv's decision to close the country's consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israeli media reported on Monday.
The warning was reportedly conveyed to Israeli officials in a message seen by Israeli news website Ynet.
The number of Israeli diplomats facing expulsion from London corresponds to the number of British diplomats who will be forced from the British Consulate General if Israel goes ahead with the closure on 8 October.
The closure of the consulate, which opened in 1838, comes as part of Israel's retaliation against Britain over its new sanctions on Israeli settlements. Foreign Minister Ed Miliband announced the new measures in September, which will ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements. Miliband's announcement also underscored that London views Israel's settlements as illegal, in line with international law and guidance from the International Court of Justice issued in July 2024.
As reported by The New Arab last month, the new sanctions do not appear to distinguish between Israel's illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, East Jerusalem, and occupied areas of other sovereign states, including the occupied Golan Heights. Israel has long pushed the view that the occupied West Bank is separate from occupied East Jerusalem, having claimed sovereignty over the entirety of the city.
Local staffers at the consulate have already ceased working at the building, while British diplomats are preparing to leave, according to the report. Sources cited by Israeli media said the UK had not expected such a harsh response from Israel.
Israel's other retaliatory measures include the expulsion of British representatives from the Gaza coordination centre in Kiryat Gat, ending British involvement in the training of Palestinian security forces and blocking 11 British MPs and a lawyer from entering Israel or the occupied Palestinian territories.
The consulate's impending closure comes as ties between London and Tel Aviv continue to be tested by domestic developments in the UK, where criticism of Israel is increasingly appearing in mainstream political discussions.
At the Labour Party annual conference in late September, Miliband told members and activists that they "were right" on Palestine, conceding that the party's previous leadership had made mistakes.
On Sunday, the UK's Green Party voted to become the country's first mainstream political party to consider Zionism a form of racism, a move which drew backlash from Tel Aviv.
Immediately following the announcement, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar added Green leader Zack Polanski to the growing list of British politicians now barred from visiting Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories.

COVID outbreak: passengers from Thailand were not allowed into russia without a temperature check

Russian citizens arriving from Thailand are not allowed to leave the plane until their temperatures have been checked. The reason is an outbreak of COVID, Telegram channel Shot reports, as UNN reports.
Details

Pregnant women give birth fleeing Yemen war as aid funds run dry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:16:05 UTC
02:16:05 KST

Breadcrumb
Pregnant women give birth fleeing Yemen fighting as UN aid funds run dangerously low
A UN agency is warning that it has only a fraction of the financing required to continue its operations amid a significant escalation of fighting in Yemen, where pregnant women are giving birth while fleeing violence and struggling to reach life-saving care.
The UN Population Fund (UNFPA), the UN's sexual and reproductive health agency, told The New Arab that it has been able to mobilise just 6% of the funding required to sustain its immediate operations, securing $1.37 million in total.
The agency requires $22.7 million for the next three months, including $5.7 million in scale-up funding needed to reach 80,000 households and 137,000 women and girls with reproductive health and protection services.
The escalation in fighting, which has seen the Houthis effectively besiege Taiz, the country's third-largest city, alongside government counter-offensives across several provinces including along the west coast, has left women and girls particularly vulnerable and in dire need of aid.
UNFPA estimates that some 3,200 pregnant women need care, with the displacement forcing some women to give birth as they flee the fighting.
Among them was Miriam, who gave birth on the side of a road while attempting to escape the violence.
A UNFPA team later found her sheltering in a cave with her newborn baby, both trembling from the cold. With no skilled medical care available, women travelling alongside Miriam had been forced to help deliver her baby themselves.
"Health facilities and referral systems are already under significant strain, and any further disruption to roads or communications could make it more difficult for people to reach services," UNFPA told The New Arab, referring to concerns for women and children, including pregnant women.
"We continue to stress the need to protect civilians and health facilities, ensure the safety of humanitarian personnel, and allow safe and sustained access for civilians, humanitarian actors and essential supplies."
Attempts to increase aid as Taiz effectively encircled
Yemen's Houthis launched an offensive aimed at taking the Bab al-Mandeb Strait on 3 September, plunging the country back into civil war.
On Monday, the rebel group cut the vital road to Aden at Al-Turbah, the only main supply route to and from Taiz, meaning access is now largely restricted to mountain routes.
UNFPA warned that cutting the main road connecting the city with the rest of government-held Yemen would further restrict access to health care, medicine, food and humanitarian assistance.
"Mountain routes are unsafe and unsuitable for women in labour or those needing urgent obstetric care, increasing the risk of preventable deaths."
Despite this, the agency is working to address the worsening humanitarian crisis and the growing needs of women, including an estimated 600 newly displaced pregnant women and newborns who require emergency obstetric and newborn care.
That care includes "caesarean sections, severe postpartum haemorrhage requiring blood transfusions, and acute neonatal resuscitation", the agency said.
UNFPA has also pre-positioned 55 tonnes of maternal medicines and supplies in warehouses near displacement sites, which should cover 120,000 pregnant women over the next six months, while working to provide further assistance to health facilities in Taiz.
"UNFPA will scale up support to two additional health facilities in Jabal Habashi and Al Mawasit districts of Taiz governorate and one in Tuban district in Lahj governorate by the first week of October," it told The New Arab.
It is also preparing to deploy five mobile teams to provide protection services for women across Taiz, Lahj and Aden, as well as community midwives to respond to the growing wave of displacement across the country.
Those plans, however, remain dependent on the changing security situation.
The impact of the fighting on women has also been highlighted by other aid agencies, with Oxfam's Country Director in Yemen, Derran Puig, telling The New Arab about Fikriya, a displaced mother who fled shelling in Taiz and is now facing the approaching winter without adequate food or shelter.
"Her experiences reflect what we are hearing from displaced families across Taiz," Puig said.
Puig noted that Oxfam had provided cash assistance to 1,400 households, with a further 560 planned, but stressed that needs are continuing to grow as the fighting intensifies.
"We urgently need more support and funding to scale up the response and ensure women and children have access to food, water, shelter and safety."
Women affected nationwide
Though Taiz has been at the centre of fighting in recent weeks, with around 90% of all displaced people originating from the region, according to the UN's migration agency, other areas of Yemen have also seen fighting.
The violence risks expanding further following the government's announcement of a nationwide offensive on Sunday aimed at retaking Houthi-held territory, including the capital Sanaa.
Basma Alloush, Deputy Director of Public Affairs and Communications for the Middle East, North Africa and Ukraine at the International Rescue Committee (IRC), told The New Arab that in Abyan, Lahj and Al-Dhale, where the organisation operates, women are increasingly being forced to choose between their safety and accessing basic services.
"Displaced women tell us they are often too afraid of harassment to collect water or wait in queues for assistance, and for some, that fear is cutting them off from accessing any services just as needs are rising," Alloush said, noting that women also require support to process the fear and trauma they experience.
A community volunteer told IRC staff: "We have lost our homes to war, and now the fear of social stigma and shame are isolating us even further."
For pregnant women, the impact of the war's escalation is particularly severe and is compounded by outbreaks of cholera, diphtheria and croup that are reportedly spreading.
"In many areas, displacement is outpacing humanitarians' ability to respond, and further escalation could deepen that gap for women who already have limited safe options," Alloush said, adding that funding shortages were making the situation worse.
Humanitarian funding cuts worldwide have restricted aid agencies' ability to respond to international crises, with the IRC joining UNFPA in warning that it lacks the necessary funds to tackle Yemen's growing crisis and has already reduced operations due to cuts.
According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, funding from Development Assistance Committee countries fell 23.1% in 2025 compared with 2024 levels and is projected to fall by a further 5.56% in 2026.
"Right now, our capacity to reach everyone in need is limited, and women and girls are among those facing the greatest exposure," Alloush said.

He fled Maduro's Venezuela. Now he leads Ukraine's South American battalion.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:14:53 UTC
02:14:53 KST

He fled Maduro's Venezuela. Now he leads Ukraine's South American battalion.
Colonel Jose David Chaparro takes part in a routine infantry training session in Mykolaiv Oblast, Ukraine, in May 2026. (Nastassia Kantorowicz Torres/ The Kyiv Independent)
At a military training site in Mykolaiv Oblast, Col. Jose David Chaparro, call sign "Katana," does one-arm push-ups with his team. The 59-year-old Venezuelan commands the Bolivar Battalion, a drone unit within the Security Service of Ukraine’s Special Operations Center "A" (Alpha).
"Remember, if you control your breathing, you control it all," he tells the soldiers who struggle to hold a plank position.
He quizzes them on drones. "Apart from pornography, you can also review drone tactics online," he says, and the group laughs.
After training, three recruits are formally inducted into the battalion. Chaparro taps each new member on the shoulder with a katana, the traditional Japanese sword that is also his call sign.
Three years after its founding, the Bolivar Battalion has grown to about 250 soldiers. Most are Colombian, along with a few Chileans, Venezuelans, Italians, Germans, and Portuguese. As Ukraine intensifies recruitment of foreign volunteers, many from Latin America, Chaparro has become more critical of the approach. His unit offers a window into Ukraine's growing reliance on foreign volunteers, and the challenges that come with the recruitment push.
Chaparro was born and raised in San Cristobal, Venezuela. He came to Kyiv in 1989 for a postgraduate law degree and lived through the collapse of the Soviet Union before returning to Venezuela in the late 1990s, where he eventually worked in the government.
From 2001 to 2005, he served as acting consul in Moscow. During that time, he says, the gap between the government's ideology and his own democratic values widened so far that he resigned and returned to Venezuela once again.
In 2013, Chaparro joined students and other protesters who took to the streets and built barricades in San Cristobal, tired of injustices, political repression, food shortages, inflation, and insecurity. By early 2014, the social uprising, known as guarimbas, had spread across Venezuela, and the government of Nicolas Maduro violently cracked down on the protesters. Chaparro's opposition to the regime forced him to flee to Ukraine with his family between 2013 and 2014, he says.
read also
Once in Kyiv, Chaparro joined the barricades once again at Ukraine's EuroMaidan Revolution. Venezuela and Ukraine, he says, "share a mutual enemy: Russia." Moscow backed the governments of Hugo Chavez and Maduro as they repressed dissent in Venezuela.
When Russia's full-scale invasion started in 2022, Chaparro volunteered in the Territorial Defense Forces.
"I knew the enemy very well," he says.
In 2023, he founded the Bolivar Battalion, named after Simon Bolivar, who led Venezuela, Colombia, and Ecuador in their fight for independence from Spanish colonial rule. In 2025, the battalion was integrated into the SBU.
"The first rule I heard from the colonel: stay alive," says a Colombian soldier with the call sign "Billy," who has served under Chaparro for more than a year. He transferred from another battalion, where he says he felt he was being sent on combat missions to die. He knew Chaparro recruited differently and required soldiers to train for a couple of months before signing a contract, unpaid but with living costs covered.
Lt. Col. Kostiantyn Milevskyi, head of the Ground Forces department that coordinates foreigners' military service, says that pre-contract training for soldiers is unusual and probably specific to special operations units, yet he cannot confirm it.
For Chaparro, training ensures his soldiers are committed to the cause and able to fight. Billy says that Chaparro looks after every one of his soldiers. They trust him, Billy says, because they know he will not send them on a mission he would not take on himself. Chaparro is not required to accompany his soldiers to the front line, but he does.
The battalion now operates a range of drones, from first-person-view (FPV) strike drones to fixed-wing reconnaissance drones. It fights in Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. Chaparro says that no soldier has been killed in action since the battalion switched to drone warfare 15 months ago.
Chaparro says Ukrainians have welcomed him with open arms and see him as "just another Ukrainian." But within the military, he says, he has at times faced hostility because he is Latino.
A soldier with the call sign "Aries" recalls a racist remark a senior Ukrainian officer made to Chaparro, telling him to "get out of the house and take your Indians with you." Aries says Chaparro defended his soldiers and nearly got into trouble himself. "Not everyone will stand up for you like that," Aries says.
Military analyst Viktor Kevliuk from the Centre for Defence Strategies estimates that between 10,000 and 16,000 foreign volunteers serve across Ukraine's armed forces. South Americans make up 40%, the largest regional group, he says.
"For Ukrainian society, all of them, they are heroes and will be heroes up to the end of their days."
Kevliuk says foreign volunteers have proven especially valuable amid Ukraine's mobilization problems and an estimated 200,000 absent-without-leave cases as of early 2026, which he attributes partly to combat exhaustion and resistance to conscription among Ukrainians who did not volunteer.
"While foreign fighters help partially alleviate manpower shortages," he says, "they do not offer a systemic solution to Ukraine's broader personnel crisis."
read also
Ukraine's approach to recruiting foreigners has changed considerably since 2022, when it waived visa entry requirements for foreign volunteers. Once in Ukraine, however, many foreign volunteers faced bureaucratic uncertainty over residency, documentation, and their long-term legal status.
In late 2025, the government announced several reforms to change the situation for foreign volunteers. Some, such as pay raises for infantry and noncombat roles, affect every service member, but others were specific to foreign volunteers.
Among the reforms was the formalization of combatant status, so a foreign national can obtain veteran status on the same terms as a Ukrainian. Combined with a residency permit introduced this year, that status opens a path to Ukrainian citizenship.
Since January, Ukraine also permits multiple citizenship for nationals of a government-approved list of countries, meaning some foreigners can see military service as a path to migration without giving up their original citizenship.
"Many, he says, "come looking for a future, or for money, or for opportunities," but have no military experience."
On June 12, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov wrote that reforms aimed at filling 30% to 50% of assault and infantry positions with foreigners would begin rolling out.
Milevskyi says the recruitment process has been deliberately streamlined. The biggest change is financial: Ukraine now covers recruits' travel costs to the country. "No one is giving them money. Ukraine is just paying for tickets, or renting the plane," he says. Once enough recruits sign up to fill a plane, flights are chartered from cities such as Bogota, Colombia, according to him.
Chaparro does not believe the Defense Ministry's recent reforms solve the problem of recruiting qualified soldiers. The challenge, he says, is attracting professional soldiers and retaining them. The South Americans now arriving in Ukraine "are in the most part, frauds," he says.
"They say they can operate a drone, throw a grenade with three hands, yet deliver nothing," he says. Many, he says, "come looking for a future, or for money, or for opportunities," but have no military experience.
Chaparro says the volunteers he fought alongside in 2022 were experienced professionals, and the gap between them and the new arrivals is "like the difference between the moon and the earth."
Milevskyi sees it differently. He says recruits must submit documents "which prove they served in the police, that they were in touch with the army." Asked whether inexperienced recruits were being sent to the front within days, he called it "rumors."
Colombians make up a large share of foreign volunteers, he says, "because of the lifestyle in Colombia and because the salary in the Ukrainian army is double, triple, four times more than they can imagine in Colombia."
Billy says money was not his reason to come and fight for Ukraine. "Money was never the driving factor for me. As a professional soldier I always knew I would come one day," he says. He sees it as his military duty.
Aries, like Billy, was a professional soldier in Colombia. He followed the war and saw TikTok videos saying Ukraine's armed forces needed more troops. Bored with working odd jobs in Spain, he traveled to Ukraine and enlisted. "I like the military life," he says.
A soldier with the call sign "Valera," one of the few women in the battalion, says she came to Ukraine "to fight for what is right and be part of the change." She says money is a secondary motivator.
Chaparro sits at a table, laughing, drinking an espresso, and sharing chicken nuggets with his soldiers. He treats them to food and drinks at a gas station in Mykolaiv Oblast to celebrate the three new members.
"For Ukrainian society, all of them, they are heroes and will be heroes up to the end of their days," Milevskyi says of foreign volunteers.

Israeli lecturer charged over plot to kill hundreds Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:12:57 UTC
02:12:57 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli lecturer charged with plotting to kill hundreds of Palestinians
An Israeli university lecturer has been charged over a years-long plan to kill hundreds of Palestinians in coordinated attacks and forcibly expel Palestinian communities to Jordan, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip.
The mathematics lecturer at Bar-Ilan University planned a wave of attacks targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel, including Bedouins, as well as Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank, according to an indictment filed on Monday.
The plan envisaged 72 Jewish attackers divided into 12 cells carrying out surprise attacks on Palestinian towns and mixed Palestinian-Jewish cities using rifles, pistols, axes and hammers.
It also contained explicit instructions not to show mercy to Palestinian women and children, or stop in response to their pleas during the attacks.
According to prosecutors, the lecturer's ultimate objective was to kill hundreds of Palestinians and terrorise Palestinian communities into fleeing permanently beyond Israel's borders.
The defendant, a man in his 60s from Petah Tikva whose identity is under a court-imposed gag order, called the plan "AYAT", an acronym derived from a Hebrew phrase meaning "the people will carry out the expulsion".
Prosecutors said he developed the plan for nationalist and ideological motives and spent years preparing for its implementation, including conducting reconnaissance, producing detailed operational documents, and attempting to recruit others.
The plan extended beyond attacks by armed civilian cells. According to the indictment, the lecturer sought to recruit collaborators from within the Israeli military who would provide coordinated support, including air force, artillery and armoured bombardment of Palestinian population centres.
In a section titled "How do we carry out AYAT here and now", he set out instructions for participants to carry out mass killings and rapidly seize roads, entrances and exits to Palestinian towns, mixed cities and hospitals.
The document instructed attackers not to show mercy towards women and children or stop when victims pleaded with them, claiming that any hesitation could lead to Jews being killed.
Prosecutors said the killings would be carried out simultaneously and promoted on social media in real time in an attempt to spread fear among Palestinians.
The intended result, according to the indictment, was the flight and permanent expulsion of Palestinian citizens of Israel, including Bedouins, alongside Palestinians living in occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank.
The lecturer allegedly envisioned Palestinians being driven towards Jordan, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip.
Prosecutors have charged him with preparing to commit an act of terrorism under Israel's Counter-Terrorism Law, extortion by threats and obstruction of justice, and have asked the court to keep him in custody until the conclusion of proceedings.

From school blockades to violence: what is driving student protests in France?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:10:56 UTC
02:10:56 KST

Student protests erupted in the Paris region in mid-September and have since spread across the nation, with some demonstrations descending into violent clashes with police.
When students from a school in Créteil, in the southeastern suburbs of Paris, joined their teachers in protest to call for more resources and staff, they could not have predicted that their action would trigger a nationwide movement.
The campaign began on 17 September and quickly gained momentum after videos of the protests spread across social media, prompting students across France to join the call for government action to address overcrowded classrooms, teacher absences, outdated facilities and other grievances.
More than two weeks on from the first protest, student unions have called for pupils to assemble for a day of mass action on Tuesday. Meanwhile, hundreds of schools were totally or partially closed on Monday, after authorities determined that the necessary safety conditions were not in place.
Rioters, clashes, police forces
While many demonstrations have been peaceful, others have been marred by riots and clashes on the margins with law enforcement authorities. According to France's Ministry of Justice, there have been more than 5,060 arrests, with 87% involving minors. Meanwhile, more than 170 pupils, 78 school staff and over 600 police officers have been injured over the course of the protests.
Across France, several schools have been damaged, burned or ransacked. In some cases, rioters have infiltrated the demonstrations.
On Monday, a 15-year-old was reportedly injured by a a police grenade in the northern French town of Lens, leading him to lose his hand. Public prosecutor Etienne Thieffry told the press that it had not yet been definitively established "whether the teenager picked up the grenade" or if it was thrown at him.
In the central French town of Tours, the family of a 16-year old schoolboy lodged a complaint for police violence on Sunday, after he lost sight in his right eye in the preceding days. According to the state prosecutor, the boy’s injuries suggest he could have been hit by a police rubber bullet. In both cases, an investigation is underway.
France's Human Rights League (LDH) has denounced a "global deviation from the rule of law and a disregard for legal frameworks" during police interventions involving school students.
Speaking at a press conference on Monday, Nathalie Tehio, the organisation's president said that international law was not only being "disregarded", but in fact "completely trampled upon."
Yet, Stanislas Gaudon, national secretary for Alliance Police Nationale, a major French police union told Euronews that the police remained focused on ensuring security around the perimeter of schools.
"When there are acts of aggression and the use of force, it's a question of determining the proportionality and the legitimacy of the act."
"If this is done against individuals who have fired at police officers or thrown acid, then the use of force to disperse is necessary. I don't like using the term 'repression' or 'suppression' of student protests. That's not the issue. If there is no disturbance in the public space, then there is no legitimate use of force by law enforcement", Gaudon said.
Politicians drawn into the fray
The ongoing unrest has drawn politicians into the fray, increasing pressure on the government to resolve the situation and respond to students' grievances.
On Friday, Education Minister Édouard Geffray held talks with school unions and staff, alongside parent bodies. That day, French Minister of Justice Gérald Darmanin, stated that violent protests had impacted 735 out of France's 3,700 schools in "one way or another."
On Sunday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced the government's five-point action plan. He said that the government remained committed to preventing class cancellations, improving facilities in partnership with regional authorities, better organising school days, making Parcoursup more transparent (France's platform for university applications), alongside a general pledge to support students.
The hard left has come out in staunch support of the protests, with Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the France Unbowed party, declaring on Thursday, "what we want is for this country’s young people to emerge from this episode with their heads held high."
His critics have accused the politician, along with his party, of stoking and manipulating young people for political gain. Meanwhile, he has stated that his party supports the movement, but isn’t organising it and wants it to be non-violent.
Teacher unions: 'The school system is in crisis'
Speaking to Euronews, Jean-Rémi Girard, a teacher and president of the national union of schools and higher education (SNALC), stressed the dangers of politicising the protests.
"We really have to be very careful not to turn what is happening — regardless of the political side involved — into a political tool, because it is very dangerous."
"We are the ones out there in the field, and we need to be looked after and protected. Because it’s already hard enough to recruit staff given the lack of appeal of our profession; if we aren't protected on top of that, it’s going to be even harder to find teachers in the years to come."
On Friday, a teacher was also sprayed with petrol during a protest near a school in the south of France. A 16-year old pupil has since been placed in police custody.
According to Girard, the grievances raised by students are far from new.
"We are increasingly struggling to replace teacher absences, French classrooms are among the most crowded in Europe, classrooms aren't properly equipped during heat waves. These are things we already know."
"The starting point is that the school system is in crisis, and it has been for a long time," he stated, while underlining that a minority of individuals have perpetrated many of the most intense episodes of violence.
"They come here to cause trouble, and I've seen that."
"We have a group of colleagues who are outside the school to talk to the students, in an attempt to prevent the situation from escalating. Anything can happen and in five minutes the atmosphere can change completely. We are familiar faces for the students, we have an established relationship with them and want to keep and ongoing dialogue."
Many parents support the protests
While some parents have advised their children to stay away from the protests, in some cases forbidding them from going to school, the Federation of Councils of Parents of Students (FCPE), one of France's largest parent associations, has expressed support for students on strike.
"We support calls for our children to study in better conditions", Mustafa Ozcelik, Vice-President of the FCPE told Euronews.
Ozcelik stressed that many parents share their children’s concerns over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and absences, difficulties recruiting teachers for certain subjects, a lack of school doctors and classrooms that become excessively hot in summer.
"School staff, parents and ultimately students themselves want to be able to return to school. Students are smart enough to know whether they should continue protesting or not, it is not up to us to decide. But from the moment they obtain the guarantees they want, everyone will return to school."

United Arab Emirates to launch spacecraft to probe seven asteroids in 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:10:27 UTC
02:10:27 KST

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) is expanding its space footprint with plans to launch a probe to the further reaches of the solar system.
The MBR Explorer, which is set to launch in March 2028, will visit seven different asteroids in the main asteroid belt, which lies between Mars and Jupiter. The spacecraft, which is designed to be fully autonomous, will first perform a flyby of Venus in mid-2028 and a flyby of Earth in spring 2029 to put it on course to the asteroid belt.
One at the main belt, the spacecraft will visit asteroids 10253 Westerwald, 623 Chimaera, 13294 Rockox—then a flyby of Mars—before visiting 88055 Ghaf, 23871 Ousha and 59980 Moza. The final destination, expected to be reached in 2034, is 269 Justitia, an asteroid in the middle main asteroid belt, some 200 million miles from Earth.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Once there, the MBR Explorer will orbit 269 Justitia for seven months before releasing a lander that will attempt to touch down on the space rock to analyze its composition. The asteroid is believed to have formed in the Kuiper Belt, beyond the orbit of Neptune, and could offer clues as to how water and other organic materials were distributed in the early solar system as the planets began to form.
The UAE is among the nations jockeying to carve out room in the space race between the U.S. and China. In 2020, for example, the country launched a probe that entered orbit around Mars in 2021.
The expansion of its space program is also reflective of the country's desire to be less reliant on fossil fuels, which are the UAE’s largest export.
On Sunday royal family member Hamdan bin Mohammed Al Maktoum, defense minister and chairman of the UAE’s Supreme Space Council, said on X that the country’s space sector is currently valued at roughly $12 billion and that the country aims to become one of the world’s top 10 space economies by 2031.

The head of Polish diplomacy highlighted Poland's role in promoting the human rights and democracy agenda. He also stressed the crucial importance of accountability for war crimes and human rights abuses.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Radosław Sikorski pointed out that the erosion of the international legal order and the deepening democratic deficit in many countries of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) require effective mechanisms for holding those responsible for human rights violations and breaches of democratic standards to account. In the context of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine the minister noted that there can be no durable peace between nations and societies if crimes are denied, victims are silenced, and if perpetrators escape accountability.
A just and lasting peace in Europe requires Russia to abandon its neo-imperial policies. To end its aggression against Ukraine. And to stop aggressive and destabilising actions in the region,
stressed the foreign minister.
During the opening session, representatives of the Swiss OSCE Chairpersonship were joined by high-ranking executives of the OSCE Secretariat and autonomous institutions: OSCE Secretary General Feridun H. The Conference will continue from 5 to 15 October. Its participants will take part in sessions on human rights, international humanitarian law, fundamental freedoms, the rule of law, and democratic institutions.
***
The OSCE’s Warsaw Human Dimension Conference is a ten-day event organised by the incumbent OSCE Chairpersonship holder—currently Switzerland—and the Warsaw-based OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR). It has been one of the key events devoted to human rights. Around 1,900 people representing governments and civil society organisations have registered to participate in this year’s event.

Ukraine’s path into the EU may come with a catch for its farmers: limits on subsidies and market access
Brussels may limit Ukraine’s access to agricultural subsidies and the EU food market if it joins the bloc, according to an internal European Commission document cited by the Financial Times.
The proposed restrictions are intended to reassure current EU members, including Poland, France, and Italy, which fear that a massive influx of Ukrainian grain would hurt their farmers. In exchange, Brussels would support efforts to restore Ukraine’s access “to its traditional export markets.”
The EU allocates 55 billion euros a year to agricultural support. The European Commission proposes tying new members’ access to subsidies to reforms and fulfillment of commitments made when joining. It also proposes making it easier to strip members of their voting rights if they violate the bloc’s rules.
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has accelerated EU enlargement, the FT reported, but some member countries now fear that Brussels may lower its rule-of-law and anti-corruption standards for new members. A series of corruption scandals in Ukraine has also deepened doubts about Kyiv’s readiness to join.
In 2022, the EU lifted tariffs and quotas on Ukrainian agricultural products to support Ukraine’s economy. But the influx of cheaper Ukrainian products prompted protests by European farmers, with particularly strong opposition in Poland, Romania, Hungary, Slovakia, and Bulgaria.
In 2024, the EU began reintroducing restrictions on certain goods. On June 6, 2025, it ended the preferential trade arrangement and restored prewar duty-free import quotas to protect its own producers.

Backing student protests a breach of ‘EU values’ – MEP bloc
The right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) group has launched a motion to probe the European Left Alliance (ELA) over an alleged breach of “EU values” and support for student unrest gripping France, Politico has reported, citing an email it has obtained.
Protests have gripped the country for days and have spread to neighboring Belgium. Students are demanding increased funding for public schools and better learning conditions, including more teachers, smaller classes, and repairs to deteriorating buildings. In numerous locations, the protests turned violent, leading to the full closure of some 400 high schools and around 5,000 arrested, mostly teenagers.
The protests have been endorsed by the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed, LFI), which instructed its officials to step in to protect students from riot police yet urged demonstrators to stay nonviolent. The French prime minister’s office, citing intelligence services, accused the party and “its far-left proxies” of organizing the violence altogether. The LFI has strongly denied allegations that it somehow initiated or orchestrated the violent unrest.
The allegations have prompted the motion, which is led by the ECR vice chair Charlie Weimers, to investigate the ELA over the alleged actions of its member, the LFI, Politico reported on Tuesday. The potential probe could ultimately result in an effective ban of the left-wing bloc, namely its deregistration and the loss of EU funding. To put the process in motion, Weimers needs to get a minimum of 180 signatures from at least three political groups within the European Parliament by next Friday. If the initiative garners enough support, the outlet expects a vote during the plenary session on October 19.
The ELA has condemned the looming action by the right-wingers, insisting it was not in breach of the bloc’s values.
“The ECR, whose own members regularly attack these very values, is abusing an EU procedure to try to avert attention from investigations of breaching EU values by the far- and extreme right,” ELA Co-President Catarina Martins said, as quoted by Politico. “Standing with young people asking for better education is not a breach of EU values,” she added.
In France, former interior minister and the leader of the Republicans (LR) party, Bruno Retailleau, called for outlawing the LFI, branding it a “seditious party” that is “fascinated by violence.” The ban demand has been dismissed by LFI leader Jean-Luc Melenchon as “ridiculous” and “absurd,” with the politician mockingly suggesting that the proponents of the allegations against his party apparently been using “telepathy.”

France, Germany seek new EU rapid response tool against trade threats

France, Germany seek new EU rapid response tool against trade threats
French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Monday announced they would develop a new legal tool to enable the EU to respond rapidly to trade wars or measures, such as dumping. While they did not say the proposal was a direct response to the actions of any particular country, it came days before EU Chief Ursula von der Leyen visits China to tackle trade frictions.
French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz have urged the European Union to develop a new legal arsenal to respond faster to any potential trade war with China, according to a letter seen by AFP on Monday.
While it stopped short of explicitly naming the Asian giant, the letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was sent just days before the EU trade commissioner heads to Beijing to tackle trade frictions.
"We need a credible instrument in the hands of the Commission" for decisive action, including the ability to cut off access to the European single market "if needed", Macron and Merz wrote.
The proposed weapon could be deployed in a trade war, for example if a country were to cut off supplies to critical raw materials.
If that happened, "the EU must be able to inflict damage comparable to that being done to us", a German government source said.
The United States and China could retaliate faster and more robustly in any trade war, the source said, warning that the EU's tools were not "as effective".
Read moreG20 trade ministers deadlocked over industrial overcapacity, says US trade chief
Germany and France want to give the Commission the power to respond to a trade aggression within days. Under their proposal, such action would not need approval from the EU's 27 countries, though a weighted majority of states could block it.
Merz and Macron are expected to present their ideas at an EU leaders' summit next week in Brussels.
The new tool could be used against any country but the EU's biggest trade concern is its deficit with China, which Brussels says is inflicting damage on key European sectors.

The Commission is already working on new tools to protect its industries, with one option a European equivalent of "Section 301" – the trade tool Washington has used to probe foreign practices it deems discriminatory, and retaliate with tariffs.
The EU's deficit in goods with China hit around 360 billion euros (around $400 billion) last year, meaning the EU imported far more from the Asian nation than it exported there.
European companies say they are undercut on prices by Chinese rivals in sectors ranging from steel for wind turbines to semiconductors and batteries.
Europe also depends heavily on Chinese supplies of critical raw materials.
Macron and Merz also want a new tool to reduce European dependencies.

Cambrian Patrol expands for largest exercise yet
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:00:24 BST
02:00:24 KST

Exercise Cambrian Patrol has expanded to its largest edition since the event began in 1959, with 140 patrols taking part in a demanding two-day assessment across the Welsh mountains, according to the British Army.
Running from 2 to 13 October, the 2026 exercise has been increased to meet demand from British units and international partners, with additional phases and patrols added to the programme.
The field includes 75 Regular Army patrols, 15 Reserve teams and 13 from University Officer Training Corps units, alongside 35 international patrols and two combined British Army and international teams. More than 350 personnel are supporting the exercise.
Each eight-person patrol begins near Builth Wells after an initial equipment inspection at Beulah, before receiving orders and completing its battle preparation. Teams then cover up to 40 miles across the Welsh mountains over roughly 48 hours before finishing at Sennybridge. Performance is assessed throughout the route, with teams competing for gold, silver and bronze medals or a completion coin.
According to a news update from the British Army, Major Darren Pridmore, Officer Commanding Exercise Cambrian Patrol 2026, said: “This is all designed to test the skills that soldiers need to survive and fight on the modern battlefield. It is a demanding assessment of leadership, resilience, tactical judgement and teamwork under pressure.”
The exercise is delivered by 160th (Welsh) Brigade on behalf of Commander Land Forces, with training direction provided by the Director Land Warfare Centre. Tasks this year include casualty evacuation, intelligence gathering, artillery fire planning, vehicle recognition, simulated chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear incidents, reconnaissance, minefield crossings and attacks on enemy positions.
Organisers have also increased the emphasis on small-unit leadership, placing junior officers and non-commissioned officers in situations where they must make tactical decisions while managing fatigue and maintaining the momentum of their patrol. The 2026 exercise has been adjusted to incorporate lessons associated with contemp rary conflicts, particularly the increased prevalence of persistent surveillance and unmanned aircraft.
Patrols will be tracked by both ground forces and unmanned aerial systems, requiring teams to consider concealment, routes and movement patterns while completing their assigned tasks. Mobility and survivability assessments include crossing the Forward Line of Own Troops, river crossings and navigating minefields during reconnaissance missions.
The exercise also includes a greater emphasis on the collection and integration of battlefield information. Patrols will use safe houses, static sensors and unmanned aerial systems to build an intelligence picture, combining information gathered from several sources before identifying and reporting targets.
Major Pridmore said: “We’ve preserved the spirit of Cambrian Patrol while adapting it to reflect the realities of contemporary conflict.
“From drones and persistent surveillance, to intelligence integration and CBRN readiness, this year’s exercise better reflects the challenges soldiers can expect to face on operations.”
Chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear readiness will also receive greater scrutiny during the exercise, with teams assessed on whether they arrive with the necessary equipment and can continue operating in a simulated contaminated environment.
The changes reflect the Army’s wider effort to adapt training to battlefield conditions in which small units can face persistent observation, widespread use of drones and a greater requirement to combine information from distributed sensors.
Pridmore added: “The battlefield is evolving rapidly and success increasingly depends on close collaboration between operators, innovators and industry.
“Cambrian Patrol provides a unique opportunity to bring those communities together, helping us adapt faster, exploit emerging technologies and maintain operational advantage.”
International participation remains a major part of the event, with 35 overseas patrols taking part alongside British teams this year.
Cambrian Patrol has long been used by foreign armed forces as an opportunity to test their troops against British units in difficult terrain, while exposing participants to different tactical methods and operating procedures.
Major Pridmore said: “The United Kingdom does not fight alone. Future operations will be conducted alongside allies and partners, making interoperability and mutual understanding essential.”
The exercise takes place over terrain around the Brecon area of Wales, where weather, elevation and distance add to the tactical assessments faced by teams. Patrols must continue completing military tasks while carrying their equipment across the route and operating with limited rest.
Once the field phase is complete, teams undergo a detailed debrief and reporting process before their overall performance is assessed and the final medal standard determined.

Knocker device remotely "knocks on wood" to explore long-held superstition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:00:21 UTC
02:00:21 KST

Knocker device remotely "knocks on wood" using smartphone app
Designers Shashwath Santosh and Nithin Eluvathingal have created a small remote device called a "knocker" that attaches to a tree and knocks on wood from afar to explore well-known superstitions.
The conceptual device "knocks on wood for you" when wood is out of reach, according to the design team. It plays on a popular belief that this action rids people of the bad luck gained from saying a future outcome aloud.
"Some believe talking about good luck ruins it unless you knock on wood," said Santosh and Eluvathingal. "But wood isn't always nearby. When wood is out of reach, this internet-connected device knocks on wood for you."
The small, white knocking devices are tied around one or multiple trees via a bright red strap. They each contain a tiny robotic arm and a display screen that flashes a ticker of each knock sent to the device.
Via a corresponding web app created by the pair, a person presses a large red button that reads "knock on wood". The signal transfers to one of the distant knockers, prompting a corresponding robotic arm to give two light taps on its tree.
According to Eluvathingal, the distance is "practically limitless" as the app is Wi-Fi connected and communicates with a central server.
For instance, someone in a cafe in Tokyo could knock on a tree in New York's Central Park, he told Dezeen.
The app also displays how many available devices are online, and confirms the unit number of the individual device that receives the knock.
"Our relationship to thought-frameworks, such as superstitious luck, is a uniquely human experience resulting from centuries of evolution," said the team.
"The knockers borrow from worlds of industrial design, engineering, manufacturing, critical thought, and world-building to celebrate 'the machine' as a medium for this interrogation."
The knockers were designed to be installed as a group, or "fleet", so that the system can receive triggers from multiple people at once.
The project builds on previous work by the pair, then under the studio name Kinky Kashayam, that played on superstitions around black cats as part of a series they call Machines Responding to Superstitions.
"What if we treat superstitions as 'challenges' worthy of commercial design intervention?" said Santosh at the time.
Shashwath Santosh is a designer based in New York who works on "experimental machines" and Google AI, while Nithin Eluvathingal works as a researcher and programmer in Toronto, currently working with McDonald's Canada.
Other conceptual design objects recently created to bring awareness to social issues include a tote bag that converts into a life jacket by a group of New York artists , a stuffed toy designed to resemble a data centre and a device that slows New York Citi Bikes when passing through rent-burdened neighbourhoods.
The photography is courtesy Shashwath Santosh and Nithin Eluvathingal

Scientists may have seen dark matter. If they did, what exactly is it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Scientists may have seen dark matter. If they did, what exactly is it?
A popular idea called a ‘higgsino’ comes close to explaining it, but has some issues
If a recent hint of dark matter is real, it would rewrite physics. Scientists are already trying to read the outline of that new story’s plot. And that’s reignited interest in certain theories, including a long-beloved but increasingly sidelined concept called supersymmetry.
Dark matter is imperceptibly everywhere, an unidentified type of particle pervading the universe but evident based only on its gravitational effects on galaxies and other cosmic entities. On September 1, scientists with the LUX-ZEPLIN, or LZ, collaboration announced they’d seen a signal in their detector that could have been caused by a single particle of dark matter — though it could still be just a blip caused by known physics processes.
In the weeks since the detection, dozens of papers have been posted on arXiv.org purporting to explain what LZ saw. Much interest has focused on a theorized type of particle called a higgsino. If the idea is correct, it would be big. “If we discover it, it would be the first discovery of supersymmetry,” says theoretical physicist Harikrishnan Ramani of the University of Delaware in Newark.
Supersymmetry proposes that for each known particle, there exists a heavier counterpart called a superpartner. It’s an idea that could solve multiple physics puzzles at once, so it has attracted a devoted following of physicists.
One of these hypothetical superpartners, such as the higgsino, could be dark matter. The higgsino is the superpartner of the Higgs boson — a particle discovered in 2012 that explains the origin of mass. “If you asked people in the year 2000, ‘What’s your favorite dark matter candidate?’ probably a lot of people would already have said the higgsino then,” says theoretical physicist Tracy Slatyer of MIT.
In recent years, supersymmetry’s popularity has waned, as particle colliders failed to find evidence for it. But as an explanation for LZ’s dark matter hint, a higgsino seems plausible — at least at first glance. “It comes pretty close to working,” Slatyer says.
Physicists spot a puzzling signal
The LZ detector, located at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, S.D., consists of a large tank of liquid xenon. The detector searches for dark matter speeding through the xenon, crashing into it and sending a xenon atomic nucleus zinging away. That’s expected to be a rare event, since dark matter interacts very weakly with normal matter. In the event LZ found, the nucleus recoiled with particularly high energy. Most types of dark matter would produce low-energy recoils in addition to high-energy ones. But LZ didn’t see any low-energy recoils.
If dark matter were a higgsino, that could explain the absence of low-energy events. The higgsino differs from typical dark matter candidates in that it would have two different masses. A collision would happen only if there’s enough energy to bump the higgsino from the lighter to the heavier mass state. That means lower-energy nuclear recoils wouldn’t happen.
Within a day of LZ’s announcement, several papers on the arXiv put forth the higgsino possibility. “I got pretty excited,” says theoretical physicist Katherine Freese of the University of Texas at Austin, a coauthor of one such paper, which was submitted September 1. “First paper I ever wrote in 24 hours.”
But further investigation made the higgsino explanation seem less plausible. For example, if higgsinos exist, they would interact in the sun and get trapped there due to its gravitational pull. There, according to the concepts of supersymmetry, they would annihilate one another and produce high-energy particles called neutrinos. Those neutrinos should have been observed by a neutrino detector located at the South Pole, called IceCube, Ramani and a colleague reported September 2 at arXiv.org. But no such neutrinos have been seen.
And there’s another potential issue. Slatyer and colleagues noticed a plot in an appendix to LZ’s paper that looks at even higher energies. If LZ saw one higgsino at the energy they reported, they’d expect to see even more at these higher energies, the team reported September 3. But LZ didn’t report anything that looked like dark matter at those energies. The LZ detector wasn’t calibrated for those energies, says LZ spokesperson Rick Gaitskell, a physicist at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “We didn’t make any formal claims about detection or even nondetection in that event region,” Gaitskell wrote in a text message. But, if the data are taken seriously, that makes LZ’s event even more difficult to explain with a higgsino.
There’s wiggle room for higgsinos
Considering all these factors makes the higgsino idea a bit of a stretch. But there’s still a little wiggle room. One possibility is that the higgsino’s mass differs from what theoretical physicists expect it to be, about 1,000 times a proton’s mass. That large mass is chosen to allow higgsinos to explain the amount of dark matter seen in the universe today. So changing it complicates the picture, but could make it align better with what LZ saw.
Additional wiggle room comes from the possible speeds of the dark matter particles in the Milky Way. The particles might reach higher velocities than typically assumed, and that could make the data easier to explain. For a faster higgsino to have shown up in LZ, it would require a larger difference in the two masses of the particle. The resulting bigger energy difference means higgsinos have fewer opportunities to produce neutrinos in the sun, explaining why neutrino experiments haven’t seen those particles.
By playing around with those factors, it’s still possible to make the higgsino explanation work, Freese says. Higgsinos with around 2,000 times a proton’s mass could do the trick, Freese and a coauthor report in an October 2 arXiv paper. “Big picture: We love [the] higgsino, and what we’re doing now is putting in the details that we think are important,” she says.
But, if it’s not the higgsino, “maybe it’s some other particle with the same basic features,” says theoretical physicist Dan Hooper of the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Such particles wouldn’t be subject to the constraints supersymmetry imposes. For example, if the particles collect in the sun, they wouldn’t necessarily create neutrinos, so it doesn’t matter that IceCube doesn’t see them. Hooper and colleagues investigated the possibilities in a paper submitted September 10 to arXiv.org. And in a September 22 arXiv paper, Hooper and colleagues proposed a version of a different class of dark matter particle that could explain two puzzles in one: LZ’s result and mysterious gamma rays, high-energy light, seen coming from the center of the Milky Way.
Other physicists are looking at entirely different ideas, involving hypothesized types of particles such as dark photons. Meanwhile, scientists are eagerly awaiting new results from LZ, to see if additional data hide similar events.
Other dark matter experiments, such as XENONnT at Gran Sasso National Laboratory in Italy, are also taking a look, combing through their existing data to check for high-energy events. LZ’s result “clearly requires a cross-check,” says XENONnT spokesperson Elena Aprile, a physicist at Columbia University.
Even if the result isn’t a slam-dunk for the higgsino — and even though this might not be dark matter at all — scientists are enjoying exploring the possibilities. “I think it’s wrong to throw tantrums over the fact that it’s not the higgsino the way we want it to be,” Ramani says. “Nature might not give us everything we want in one go.”

The party rejects the allegation and blames government neglect for students’ anger. Its leader, Jean-Luc Melenchon, has called for nonviolent action.
The student demonstrations overlap with broader public-sector protests against spending cuts involving teachers, healthcare workers, firefighters, and transportation staff. The movements have added pressure on President Emmanuel Macron, whose approval ratings have fallen to 16-18% in recent polls.

Russia’s Oil Revenue Machine Is Losing Steam—September Income Drops 22%
Russia’s federal budget received about $5.43 billion in oil and gas revenue in September, down 22% from the same month in 2025, according to Finance Ministry data cited by Russian outlet The Bell on October 5.
Revenue improved only modestly from August, rising 7% to roughly $5.09 billion. August itself had already recorded a 16% year-over-year decline, underscoring continued pressure on one of the Kremlin’s most important sources of budget income.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A growing share of that revenue is being offset by government compensation payments to Russian oil refiners, which are designed to cover the gap between domestic fuel prices and prices on the global market. Those payments jumped from about $2.37 billion to $3.67 billion in September.
The increase effectively absorbed the entire rise in mineral extraction tax revenue. Russia collected around $9.68 billion from the tax in September, up from approximately $8.43 billion in August, but the larger refinery compensation bill erased the additional proceeds.
Since the beginning of 2026, Russia has received roughly $65.64 billion in oil and gas revenue, 17.2% less than during the first nine months of 2025. September’s result was broadly in line with Finance Ministry expectations, missing the government’s target for additional oil and gas revenue by only about $120 million.
For October, the Russian Finance Ministry expects roughly $3.47 billion in additional oil and gas revenue.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukrainian long-range strikes had put more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity out of operation.
Recent Ukrainian strikes have hit several Russian oil refineries and related facilities, including KINEF, Ust-Luga, Moscow, Yaroslavl, Perm, Ilsky, Saratov, and Syzran.

Ukraine’s Faster Military Innovation Was “Humiliating” to Watch, Ex-US Army Secretary Says
Former US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll described Ukraine’s rapid wartime adaptation as “humiliating” for the United States, Rolling Stone reported on October 4.
He argued that Ukrainian forces developed more effective weapons despite operating with a far smaller budget.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Driscoll, who resigned as Army secretary in August, focused much of his tenure on modernizing US forces for battlefields increasingly shaped by drones, electronic warfare, and rapidly changing technology, Rolling Stone wrote.
“In some ways, it was humiliating seeing how quickly a nation could change when it needed to,” Driscoll told Rolling Stone. “When you would see what Ukraine’s budget was and how small it was relative to ours and how, despite that, they had better weapons of war, it was a wake-up call.”
Rolling Stone noted that Ukraine’s development of cheap, mass-produced drones demonstrated how quickly the modern battlefield was changing after two decades in which the US military largely focused on counterinsurgency operations in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Driscoll argued that the US military’s procurement system was too slow to keep pace with those changes.
“When you’re an American soldier, you would get to work every day, and you basically step back like 20 or 30 years with tech,” he stated.
In May 2025, Driscoll created the 600-soldier Unmanned Assault Battalion, an experimental “drones first” unit based in Italy that operated its own drone laboratories, tested electronic warfare tactics, and worked with Ukrainian advisers, Rolling Stone reported.
The initiative formed part of a broader effort to adapt lessons from Ukraine to the US military. The Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative combined drones, interceptors, Patriot systems, and satellite intelligence in an AI-enabled network, while Ukrainian drone pilots later trained alongside American and NATO troops during multinational exercises in Germany.

Small island emerges in Lake Zurich amid historic low water level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:56:00 UTC
01:56:00 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
A small island has emerged in Lake Zurich as the water level has fallen to a historic low, Swissinfo reported Monday.
The island is located off the coast of Stafa, a Swiss town on the lake’s eastern shore.
Under normal conditions, only a rock known as the Stafner Stein can be seen at the site.
The lake’s water level currently stands at 405.24 meters (1,329 feet) above sea level, allowing the small land formation to rise above the surface.
Although the island is small, it is large enough for a small boat to moor and for people to stop for a picnic.
The island was last visible 74 years ago, when Lake Zurich recorded its previous major low water level.
It had also emerged in 1909 during a period of exceptionally low water levels.
A mark on the Stafa stone showing the water level recorded at that time has also become visible again after being covered for many years.
The island is expected to remain visible for some time, as the lake is likely to take a while to return to its normal level.
No prolonged period of rain is currently in sight.

Can Yemen's divided coalition turn the tide against the Houthis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:53:56 UTC
01:53:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Can Yemen's divided coalition turn the tide against the Houthis?
When the Houthis launched attacks along Yemen's western coast on 3 September, internationally recognised government-aligned forces were unprepared for what was the largest offensive since the ceasefire signed in 2022.
Their response revealed a series of operational failures that allowed the Houthis to advance across 5,000 square kilometres, seizing the port city of Mocha, several coastal positions, and the islands of Mayyun and Hanish to gain control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Reported accounts of the initial Houthi offensive show that the fragmented government-aligned forces lacked military coordination and timely support from Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The Houthis penetrated opposition communications, tracked troop movements, and cut off frontline units from command. They reportedly relied on Iranian advisers, who provided direct support for their blitzkrieg.
Over the following days, Saudi airstrikes and Yemeni government-aligned counterattacks sought to reclaim lost ground, including areas along the Taiz–Aden route.
Combat is currently concentrated in Taiz province, where the Houthis are attempting to consolidate control over captured territory.
"Their objective is to consolidate gains by securing the mountainous areas overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and blocking the road between Taiz and Lahej and Aden to cut off military support," Yemeni political analyst and journalist Mohammed Al-Qadhi told The New Arab.
"By recapturing these zones lost in 2017, the Houthis shield themselves from government and Saudi counter-offensives, avoiding exposure in the flat coastal areas."
Reports also suggest Houthi troop movements towards Saada province on the Saudi border.
The fault lines in Yemen's anti-Houthi camp
Regional and Western officials told Reuters last week that Saudi Arabia was planning a large-scale offensive against the Houthis, including a possible coastal push to secure Red Sea shipping, or an assault on multiple fronts.
On Sunday, Yemen’s government then announced the ambitious goal of retaking all Houthi territory, with operations beginning at dawn.
So far, according to the Saudi-led coalition, the military has carried out over 1,000 airstrikes using 100 warplanes as part of Operation 'Dawn of Yemen'.
The Houthis effectively encircled the city of Taiz the same day, cutting off the main supply route linking the city to Aden, the capital of the government.
As the war unfolds, the Houthi offensive could expose the limits of Yemen’s anti-Houthi coalition, with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government struggling to overcome fractured command structures and competing political agendas threatening to undermine their campaign.
Yemen's anti-Houthi camp has never been a single bloc, with the Saudi-backed government, represented by the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), an uneasy coalition of rival factions.
Among them is the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a UAE-backed separatist movement that had been represented on the council until January and seeks an independent southern Yemen.
Its offensive to expand control, launched in December 2025, was rapidly reversed by Saudi-backed forces in January, prompting the UAE to withdraw its remaining forces from Yemen.
Tareq Saleh, nephew of the late president Ali Abdullah Saleh, meanwhile, commands the National Resistance Forces (NRF), which favour a unified Yemen but were long backed by Abu Dhabi.
Islah, the Sunni Islamist party with historical ties to the Muslim Brotherhood - an association it denies - has long opposed the southern separatist project and supports a unified Yemen.
The UAE-backed Giants Brigades and National Resistance Forces (NRF) retain distinct command structures, even as Riyadh seeks to bring Yemen's fragmented armed groups under a more unified state command through the Nation's Shield and other security and military structures.
Operationally, the NRF, Giants Brigades, and National Shield Forces (operating under the PLC) maintain separate command structures and logistics rather than a unified field command, while the PLC itself has yet to establish an integrated military leadership.
Coordination is made even harder by lingering anger in the south after the STC's contested dissolution in January, the rise of the southern region of Hadhramawt as an independent political force, and Islah’s mistrust of UAE-backed groups.
"On this basis, a unified front under a single command with a shared offensive objective appears unlikely in the coming months," Ahmed Alshargabi, a research analyst at the Yemen Policy Centre, told The New Arab.
“The more probable outcome is defensive coordination aimed at blocking further Houthi advances toward Lahj, Aden, Bab al-Mandeb and Marib, without any real integration of forces.”
He added that a real alliance depends on an understanding between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, unified funding, southern political guarantees, and an empowered field command.
Rival regional visions for Yemen
The Saudi-UAE rivalry plays a critical role in the anti-Houthi coalition’s internal fragmentation.
As Andreas Krieg, associate professor in Security Studies at King’s College London, explained to The New Arab, Saudi Arabia and the UAE have different interests and cultural approaches to Yemen.
Abu Dhabi does not see a unified Yemen as a necessity, while Riyadh favours a unified sovereign state. The result is a fragmented landscape in which few Yemeni forces have a stake in fighting beyond their own regions.
“It’s unrealistic to think that the southerners will fight in the north against the Houthis, which most southerners see as a problem for northerners,” he told The New Arab.
“Even if there is a reconciliation between the UAE and Saudi Arabia, it’s very unlikely the southerners will volunteer to take the war into northern Yemen. They have no stakes there. So ultimately what we end up with is a shifting stalemate.”
Last week, UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed visited Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh. It was the first visit by a senior Emirati official since a diplomatic rift erupted between the two Gulf states in January.
Alshargabi said the meeting reflects a tactical rapprochement driven by Houthi advances and Riyadh’s reliance on UAE-backed forces, but Abu Dhabi’s potential demands could fuel new instability and leave their rivalry unresolved.
Krieg added that potential UAE support is unlikely to alter the war’s trajectory, given the fragmented command structures and the limited reach of southern forces.
In early 2026, Yemen's government attempted to consolidate southern forces by integrating former STC units into the Interior Ministry, reshuffling commanders, and tolerating hybrid arrangements. Some experts argue that a state monopoly on force is unlikely given Yemen’s tribal loyalties, whereas reducing the number of non-state armed actors is more realistic.
Forging military cooperation among anti-Houthi forces is far easier than achieving political unity, according to Anas Alqaed, director of programmes at the Gulf International Forum, because battlefield coordination requires no formal political agreement.
“The coalition lost ground mainly due to a breakdown in command and control, and fixing that could take anywhere from a few months to two years,” he told The New Arab.
“However, I do not believe the anti-Houthi coalition is ready to reverse the Houthi advance, and we will not see a joint Saudi-Emirati or global coalition form against them until they actively move to close the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.”
After the US declined Saudi Arabia’s request for military support, Riyadh turned to Pakistan and Turkey, signatories of the recent Mecca defence pact. Both have limited their commitments to technical support, while their defence and foreign ministers and military chiefs are due to meet in Riyadh this week.
Riccardo Gasco, foreign policy coordinator at InstanPol Institute, said expectations around the Mecca Pact are inflated, particularly over the prospect of automatic military support.
“Turkey has a clear interest in stopping the Houthis in relation to Bab al-Mandeb Strait as a trade corridor, but strictly automatic military support remains highly improbable,” he told The New Arab.
Among Saudi Arabia's other allies, Britain offered air refuelling, while France announced the deployment of military personnel to the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.
Unconfirmed reports say Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has offered to help Gulf states in a wider campaign against the Houthis. But Krieg argued that "the Israeli intelligence networks in Yemen are very poor", with Riyadh and Abu Dhabi far better placed.
"That is not something the Israelis can deliver," he said, adding that Israeli involvement could further fracture the anti-Houthi camp and fuel Houthi propaganda, while Tel Aviv may use its assistance as a card to play in its push for normalisation.
A new stalemate?
While the fragmentation of the anti-Houthi camp benefits the Houthis and Iran - exerting pressure on a second strategic chokepoint after Hormuz and handing Tehran greater leverage in US negotiations - it also strengthens the Houthis' position against Riyadh.
As the trajectory of the Yemen war remains uncertain, experts lay out several scenarios. One is containment, with the Houthis consolidating gains as far as Bab al-Mandeb and front lines settling around Lahj, Taiz, and Marib.
This would leave Yemen de facto partitioned and Riyadh entering negotiations from a position of weakness.
Alternatively, a limited counter-offensive could see coalition forces retake ground around Dhubab and Mokha, though this would require unified command and Saudi–Emirati coordination.
Other possibilities include regional escalation via attacks on Saudi infrastructure or shipping, or a return to UN-led diplomacy.

Amid suspicions that hostile individuals approached two IDF posts in southern Syria, troops deployed in the area are increasingly concerned that people in nearby villages may be testing soldiers’ vigilance. The two incidents, occurring within a very short period, point to rising tension near the Israeli border.
The first incident occurred overnight between Sunday and Monday, when a 22-year-old Palestinian man living in Damascus was shot by IDF troops after approaching a military post near the Syrian village of al-Hamidiyah. The man, who was captured on the post’s surveillance cameras, was unarmed and carrying only a phone and money.
The second incident occurred Monday afternoon, when two Syrians riding a motorcycle approached the "Police" military post in the Quneitra area. The two were shot by IDF troops and later detained.
No IDF troops were injured in either incident, but the combination of two attempts to approach Israeli military posts inside Syrian territory has raised concern. Among the possibilities being examined is whether those involved were trying to assess how IDF troops would respond to their advance at two locations only a few kilometers apart.
Syrians are prohibited from traveling on roads in the area close to the Israeli border, and certainly from approaching the chain of military posts established by the IDF in the southern sector. The frontier in this part of Syria had remained quiet for many months, but the sequence of incidents over the past day has raised the level of alert.
The IDF is stretched across several fronts and, as in other sectors, is currently operating in Syria in a defensive posture. Some of those defensive activities also include offensive measures, though even those are significantly different in nature from the periods of active ground maneuvering in Gaza and Lebanon.
The shift in operational posture is considered a particularly sensitive period for troops, who are trying to preserve the advantages they have gained and establish a strong defensive line along the Syrian border.
At the same time, the fact that combat forces are now primarily defending rather than attacking has raised concerns about complacency and reduced sharpness, as well as the possibility that their behavior could become more predictable from an enemy’s perspective.
‘A warning sign’
Golan Regional Council head Uri Kellner and Katzrin Local Council head Yehuda Dua issued a joint statement saying: "Two significant and serious incidents in less than 24 hours are already a warning sign that cannot be ignored. We are identifying a recurring phenomenon, and it requires a determined response and a long-term security solution."
"Precisely in days when there is a sense of calm, we must not become confused and we must not return to the thinking that existed before Oct. 7," they said. "Alongside the continued IDF presence and activity in Syrian territory, the State of Israel must continue strengthening security infrastructure in Golan communities, Katzrin and the Druze villages."
The two added: "We are already calling on party leaders and those who will form the next government to commit to continuing to strengthen security in the Golan and to allocate the necessary resources, including remaining in the buffer zone and the Mount Hermon area."
"The security of Katzrin and Golan residents cannot depend on a temporary sense of calm. Our residents are entitled to the same level of security that the State of Israel is obligated to provide to all its citizens."
