US Marine’s Arrest for Murder Tests Okinawa’s New Governor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:52:00 UTC
01:52:00 KST

Okinawa’s new governor had barely begun his effort to improve relations with Tokyo when an alleged killing involving a U.S. Marine confronted him with the prefecture’s most persistent political dilemma: how to support national defense while protecting residents who bear a disproportionate share of its costs.
Okinawa Prefectural Police arrested Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, early on October 4. He is suspected of killing Yagi Anna, a 39-year-old Naha resident, at a hotel and stealing her belongings. Ballard denies the allegations. The Marine Corps has pledged cooperation with Japanese investigators.
The case immediately drew protests from both national and prefectural authorities. Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu summoned U.S. Ambassador George Glass, while Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro summoned U.S. Forces Japan commander Lieutenant General Stephen Jost.
On October 5, before delivering her policy speech to the Diet, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae condemned the incident and demanded full investigative cooperation, tighter discipline, and effective measures to prevent further crimes.
For Governor Koja Genta, who took office on September 30, the timing was especially difficult.
His September 13 election ended 12 years of prefectural leadership opposed to relocating Futenma to Henoko in northern Okinawa. Koja has sought a more cooperative relationship with Tokyo. Effective October 1, he replaced the prefectural division handling opposition to the Henoko project with an office focused on accelerating the return of U.S. military land.
But his cooperation was never unconditional. Koja has acknowledged the need for defense capabilities while demanding advance explanations and local understanding.
In a protest letter read aloud to Lieutenant General Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, and U.S. Consul General Andrew Ou on October 5, Koja said that the recurrence of such a serious crime “leads us to conclude that U.S. military efforts regarding discipline and human rights education are completely ineffective.” He demanded stronger preventive measures and a review of the Japan-U.S. Status of Forces Agreement, or SOFA.
Watson expressed condolences and pledged continued cooperation with the investigation, saying the U.S. military was committed to being “good neighbors” and earning the trust of the Okinawan people.
That exchange reflects a longstanding problem.
Okinawa hosts approximately 70 percent of Japan’s nationwide area of facilities reserved exclusively for U.S. military use. Residents thus experience the alliance through noise, accidents, environmental concerns, and criminal cases, alongside its promised protection against external threats.
In 2025, police cleared 101 cases involving Penal Code offenses by U.S. military personnel, civilian employees, and their families, up from 73 in 2024. These figures count cases, not convictions or individual offenders, and do not establish a comparative crime rate. Nevertheless, there is good reason for scrutinizing measures introduced after earlier incidents, including restrictions on nighttime drinking and joint patrols.
Japan generally has primary jurisdiction over off-duty offenses against Japanese nationals. When American authorities already hold a suspect, however, the SOFA provides for U.S. custody until indictment. Following the 1995 rape of a schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen, Washington agreed to give “sympathetic consideration” to Japanese requests for pre-indictment transfers in murder and rape cases.
Ballard was arrested by Japanese police and remains in Japanese custody. This is therefore not a case of Washington withholding a suspect. The broader question is whether existing arrangements under the SOFA provide sufficient accountability, information sharing, and preventive oversight.
The controversy comes as Japan’s defense buildup in its southwestern islands enters a more operational phase. Tokyo is connecting missile deployments, surveillance, transport, and logistics across Kyushu and the southwestern islands, while U.S. forces develop more dispersed operations.
Plans to store the U.S. Army’s Typhon and HIMARS systems at Kadena and deploy Marine NMESIS anti-ship missiles and MADIS air defense systems to Ishigaki during October’s Keen Sword exercise make cooperation with local authorities particularly consequential. Koja has so far withheld judgment on the storage plan, saying Tokyo has not adequately explained the reasons or its duration.
Koja’s election gave Tokyo reason to expect smoother negotiations. It did not give the Japanese government or the U.S. military a blank check. Anger over this case could make individual decisions on facilities, exercises, and base restructuring politically harder, even without reversing Japan’s overall defense policy.
For Koja, the test is whether cooperation with Tokyo and Washington can produce tangible protection for Okinawans. For the alliance, the stakes are broader: deterrence in Japan’s southwest depends not only on missiles, bases, and military units, but also on the trust of the communities expected to host them.

Medicine shortages will result if drug prices are driven too low | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:50:19 UTC
01:50:19 KST

Without decisive government action, the reported medicine shortages in hospitals will only be the tip of the iceberg (Hospitals in England hit by shortages of common drugs such as paracetamol, 29 September). Medicine supply chains are complex and global, with multiple points of potential failure that are especially sensitive to geopolitical shocks. Brexit has made us even more vulnerable, as we no longer have access to EU medicine reserves, and cross-border logistics are further complicated.
Our research shows that these shortages tend to be concentrated in (off-patent) generic and biosimilar markets. It’s true that low prices for off-patent medicines are important in driving health system savings and promoting affordability. The problem is that when prices are driven an unsustainable low, manufacturers exit, leaving markets with too few suppliers and dangerously exposed to any supply disruption or demand spike. The NHS bears the cost when a shortage does occur, in the form of higher prices, expensive substitutes and a heavy staff burden in managing emergency procurement and, sometimes, rationing. Patients pay the highest price in delayed treatment and worse outcomes.
The government needs to weigh pricing controls against the costly damage that a drug shortage can cause. The answer lies in using regulatory, pricing and approval decisions to encourage competition and nurture supplier resilience. There is a critical balance between affordability and medicine security that needs to be struck.
Amanda Cole
Director, Office of Health Economics

DR Congo boat collision kills at least 30, dozens missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

01:47:50 KST

DR Congo boat collision kills at least 30, dozens missing
Two vessels crashed while navigating the Congo River in Equateur province at night.
A boat collision on a river in the Democratic Republic of Congo has killed at least 30 people, with dozens more reported missing.
Two vessels crashed into one another as they navigated the Congo river, officials said on Monday. The accident took place on Sunday evening near the Ngombe-Lukolela area in Equateur province in the northwest of the country.
The officials said that 30 people had drowned during the incident. Search-and-rescue efforts have been launched to try to find the missing.
Crispin Mputu, interior minister of Equateur province, told the state-owned news agency Agence Congolaise Presse that “a metal vessel named ‘Dieu se cache,’ was coming from Kinshasa,” the country’s capital, when it crashed with a “wooden vessel called ‘HB Super Victoire,’ [that] was coming from Businga”.
“Almost all the passengers on board were trapped underwater, and the boat itself also sank,” he added.
Mputu said the people who drowned have already been buried.
Safety standards
It is unclear what caused the crash. Mputu noted that many accidents have occurred as boats travel at night.
A security officer who witnessed the incident told The Associated Press news agency that the boat travelling from Kinshasa was overloaded with goods.
Boating tragedies are common in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where late-night travel and overcrowded vessels are often blamed.
Poor safety standards and a lack of infrastructure in remote parts of the country also contribute to boating disasters, which have killed hundreds of people in recent years.
In July, a wooden boat transporting students back from state exams sank, killing at least 20 people in the country’s Kasai province.

Ioanna Kuçuradi (1936-2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:47:23 UTC
01:47:23 KST

Ioanna Kuçuradi, a leading Turkish philosopher, has died.
Dr. Kuçuradi was known for her work in the fields of human rights, human health, and ethics. She is the author of Human Beings and Their Values (İnsan ve Değerleri), Ethics, (Etik) Looking at Art Through Philosophy (Sanata Felsefeyle Bakmak), and Human Rights: Concepts and Problems, among other works.
Kuçuradi held several significant professional and public roles. Up until her death at age 89, she was president of the Turkish Philosophy Association and Honorary President of the World Federation of Philosophical Societies. She chaired the High Advisory Council for Human Rights of the Prime Ministry of Turkey and the Turkish National Committee of the UN Decade for Human Rights Education, and served on the National Advisory Council for Human Rights of Turkey, the European Monitoring Centre on Racism and Xenophobia, and the Turkish National Committee of the UN Decade for Human Rights Education.
Until 2005 she was a faculty member in the Department of Philosophy of Hacettepe University, a department she founded in 1968 and chaired for many years. She also founded the university’s Centre for Research and Application of the Philosophy of Human Rights, and created and directed a similar institute at Maltepe University. She was also a holder of a UNESCO Chair of Philosophy from 1998 to 2005. Prior to joining Hacettepe University, she taught at Atatürk University and Istanbul University, where she had earned her BA and PhD in philosophy.
Ioanna Kuçuradi died on October 2nd, 2026.

Badenoch is trying to match Farage step for step – but it’s a dance of death for the Tories | Polly Toynbee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:46:33 UTC
01:46:33 KST

You can walk all the way from Somerset to Sussex without crossing a Tory-run constituency, if you wish. You could also travel through each of the counties of Wiltshire, Hampshire, Dorset and Surrey without setting foot in Tory lands. They are now mainly Liberal Democrat, and there’s not one Tory MP in all of Oxfordshire.
Is Kemi Badenoch bothered? Everything she does seems cleverly designed to keep those places lost to her for ever as she woos Reform voters, unsuccessfully. The more she leans right, the more she repels home counties moderates. Those Reform voters are not coming back, psephologists say. Without reclaiming the old “blue wall”, there is no hope, ever, of a Tory majority, say both Profs Tim Bale and Rob Ford and just about every political authority you care to ask.
Shooting the breeze at the party’s Birmingham conference, you might never guess the Tories still poll four percentage points below the last election, the worst result since the Duke of Wellington was dismissed in 1830 for rejecting electoral reform and defending every rotten borough.
Spot that Wellingtonian legacy in the interview Badenoch gave ConservativeHome. “I march to the beat of my own drum,” she says. Indeed she does, but out of step with the public, not condescending to care what it might be thinking and allowing no shade of disagreement. Removing the Lords whip from Gavin Barwell, Theresa May’s chief of staff, was a deterrent message to anyone taking part in the “festival of ideas” here, a festival of one idea only. Barwell opposed Badenoch’s edict barring any candidate who supports net zero carbon emissions or staying in the European convention on human rights. “I haven’t left the Conservative party. It has left me,” Barwell tweeted plaintively. It has left a great many others, too.
Margaret Thatcher, still holy here, never did that: she had “wets” in her first cabinet and never expelled them from the party. Her ideological obduracy over the poll tax only overcame her later on, and it did for her. But Badenoch is starting out this way. The adulation showered on her by Tories and their press must come from some alternative wonderland where they are not polling in third place at 19%, while their leader, though improved, scores net -15 – compared with Andy Burnham on +7. In polling, more call her “nasty” or “rude” than “strong” or ‘intelligent”.
What demographic is she for? Giving free childcare to parents earning over £100,000 will strike most as a grotesque gesture. Only 4% make £100,000 or more: they don’t think themselves wealthy, but the other 96% of people do. The £700m cost of that policy should go to the dwindling number of deprived two-year-olds getting early years support, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. Already, the children of the best-off are eight times more likely to benefit from funded childcare hours than the most disadvantaged, says the New Economics Foundation. Children arriving at school unready are tomorrow’s Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training). This should have the education secretary, Lucy Powell, rampaging: it’s not about parents, it’s about children’s futures. Badenoch’s pledge to cut some benefits to “subsistence” level deliberately implies the 4 million children below the poverty line are living the life of Riley.
Her responses to Burnham are also out of touch with the times – and even with the Times. While 70% want closer relations with the EU, her party shockingly pledges to rip up any agreement Burnham makes, sabotaging any trade pact on agri-foods or freedom for the young to travel across Europe. Negotiations are at risk of failure if the EU fears Europhobes might ever regain power and reverse it all.
Austerity is still raw in public minds, with overflowing prisons, blocked courts, NHS waiting lists and a million Neets, alongside the housing crisis. What a time for Badenoch to propose £47bn in cuts, with her shadow chancellor now planning even more “in every part of government”.
Instead of beckoning back those moderate-minded home counties, she competes punch for punch with Nigel Farage. Last week, she stripped down the aid budget to £1bn to equal Farage’s policy. Look at their arms race to demolish the civil service: Badenoch started last year by pledging to cut 132,000 civil service jobs, return it to pre-Brexit levels (before all the mundane EU agencies we quit – medicines, chemical safety etc – had to be replicated). Farage was due to cut a mere 68,500 until Danny Kruger upped the ante last month to 250,000 in his “Storm and Sunshine” policy. The latest? The Tories just pledged to kill off the Environment Agency, Natural England and the Climate Change Committee. What do the home counties think of that?
This contest for lowest taxes, smallest state, toughest stance on migrants, harshest welfare cuts and deepest loathing of young people will spiral downwards towards something new and dangerous. Modern British politics has never before had rightwing parties competing as equals. But locked in this dance of death, the politics of bile carries them further from most voters. Tories are dying out: 63 is now the median age of Badenoch’s voters, while Labour’s is 46.
If nothing improves by next conference, the mirage of Badenoch’s rock-solid support will melt away. But what would replace her? Waiting in the wings there is a model of what a Conservative revival might look like – Prosper UK, launched in January.
It tiptoes, praising Badenoch loudly, yet it is running seven events at this conference. That included a small Sunday night rally for electoral reform. It was addressed by former West Midlands mayor Andy Street, now co-chair of Prosper UK with Ruth Davidson It is backed by a formidable array of what was once the One Nation group, now defunct in parliament – or dormant under Badenoch’s rightwards march. No MPs back Prosper UK in public, but the group claims a third of them do secretly, along with 30,000 declared supporters. David Gauke, vice chair, has crept back into the party – he thinks by accident when the membership computer processing his re-application didn’t register he’d been ejected in 2019. In returning, he joined a battalion of remainer luminaries of the centre-right who’d had the whip suspended at the same time, including Kenneth Clarke and Dominic Grieve.
Gauke travels the country speaking to Conservative associations and others. Prosper UK is pro-EU, pro-migration for skilled workers and foreign students, pro-net zero and against the pension triple lock – and Gauke says that “Conservatives should be truth tellers on all these”. But though socially liberal, he’s dry as a bone on fiscal discipline, campaigning for low business taxes, a smaller state and enticing back non-doms – all Hayek, no Keynes. “No one speaks for some 7 million people centre or centre-right,” he says.
Indeed, the country needs a plausibly electable Tory party to put up a fight against Faragism, not a carbon copy of it. If Badenoch is not for turning, to survive it will need to turn her out.
- Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

If the winners of Tysiachovesna-2026 program to support Ukrainian cultural products do not receive funding from the state this year, they will be funded from the budget for the initiative in 2027, Director of the Department of Strategic Communications and Promotion of Ukrainian Culture at the Ministry of Culture Hanna Krasnostup said.
"We haven't been officially told to stop. We're doing everything we can. All 680 winners are counting on the program. Of that number, 150 are scheduled to complete their projects this year. Some winners, whose projects involved co-financing, have already begun work on their projects. And my task now is to ensure everything is done promptly and correctly so that SOE "Center for the Protection of Ukraine"s Information Space' can sign the contracts and make the advance payments," Krasnostup told Interfax-Ukraine, addressing reports of a possible reduction in funding for cultural projects.
She said that as of now, no agreements have yet been signed with the competition winners, but this is expected to happen in the near future.
"We can sign contracts; the draft agreements must include a provision stating that a lack of funds constitutes a force majeure event," the official added.
At the same time, the department head said that if, due to force majeure, someone does not receive funding this year, they will retain their status as a Tysiachovesna-2026 winner, and funding will be provided next year from the funds allocated for this program.
"We'll assess the situation as it develops. If payments aren't made this year, part of the funds will not go toward a new competition but rather toward launching the projects that were selected as winners this year," Krasnostup said.
According to her, in the event of a delay in state funding, the competition winners will not be required to create a cultural product by the previously agreed-upon deadlines. At the same time, in such a case, the Ministry of Finance will be asked to amend the procedure for using the funds and extend these deadlines.
At the same time, she noted that the ministry has not yet withdrawn the funds allocated for Tysiachovesna. According to the monthly allocation schedule, most payments are scheduled to take place in December for projects to be completed in subsequent years.
In this regard, the Ministry of Culture is awaiting further clarification from the government regarding how the situation with continued funding for the current year will unfold.
The department head explained that during negotiations with the winning bidders, the ministry is discussing all possible options.
As previously reported, in late September, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky announced that, to conserve budget funds for defense needs, a number of expenditures would be suspended, including funding for road construction, Resilience Plans, and certain cultural programs.
On September 29, the Cabinet of Ministers adopted a resolution on prioritizing government spending amid the challenging situation with public finances and delays in some planned international funding.
As previously reported, on April 3, the Ministry of Culture launched a call for proposals as part of the initiative to create a Ukrainian cultural product called "Tysiachovesna" (formerly "1,000 Hours of Ukrainian Content"). After August 16, 680 winning projects of Tysiachovesna-2026 were announced across seven categories.
According to Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy and Minister of Culture Tetiana Berezhna, the project is planned to be expanded to include books and online games next year. Berezhna also said that book authors and libraries will be able to join the Tysiachovesna program in 2027. In addition, there are plans to introduce regulations governing the use of artificial intelligence (AI), raise the minimum score required for pitching, and separate first-time applicants from experienced ones.
Furthermore, Berezhna said Tysiachovesna project may introduce clear restrictions in 2027 that would bar artists and performers who collaborated with Russia during the war from participating in the project.
The 2027 state budget allocates UAH 5.4 billion to Tysiachovesna, which is UAH 1.4 billion more than this year.

Three survivors suffered injuries and were evacuated by helicopter belonging to the Romanian General Inspectorate of Aviation. The other eight were reported to be in good condition and were taken aboard rescue vessels.
The Romanian Border Police confirmed that the ship had sunk. Its official statement said a fire had occurred aboard the vessel but did not establish its cause.
Several Romanian media outlets subsequently reported that the vessel may have been hit by a drone. News.ro and Digi24 cited a suspected drone strike in the area southeast of the Pescăruș platform. Radio România Constanța also reported initial information that the ship "might" have been struck by a drone, while stressing that the circumstances had not yet been fully clarified.
The Romanian Naval Authority later said the fire had started following a suspected drone strike. It has not, however, publicly issued a final determination on the cause of the incident.
Reuters also reported on the fire, deaths and rescue of crew members, noting that Romanian authorities had not identified a cause for the blaze. The agency reported that the vessel was owned by Turkish interests and operated under the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian drones had attacked the ship.
"A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian ship in neutral waters carrying corn," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that citizens of Azerbaijan and India were aboard.
The Turkish service of Euronews described the incident as a suspected drone attack involving a vessel linked to Turkey, while noting that Romanian authorities had not definitively determined what caused the fire.
Anadolu Agency reported the incident primarily as a fire aboard a merchant vessel off the Romanian coast. The Royad Mammadov is connected to a Turkish owner but sails under the Saint Kitts and Nevis flag.
Turkish reports said the ship was carrying grain from the Ukrainian port of Izmail to Ravenna, Italy. Turkish media also pointed to increasing risks for civilian shipping in the Black Sea because of the war in Ukraine and said the incident was being closely followed in Turkey because of the Turkish connection and the deaths among the crew.
Romanian media likewise reported that the Royad Mammadov was a Turkish cargo ship transporting grain from Izmail to Ravenna. The vessel was sailing under the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis.
The ship's presence in the area came as commercial vessels carrying Ukrainian goods continue to travel through parts of the western Black Sea exposed to military risks. Romanian authorities clarified that the incident occurred within their exclusive economic zone but outside their territorial waters.
The rescue operation followed an alert received by the Maritime Coordination Center in Constanța at approximately 10:37 a.m., after which rescue vessels were dispatched within minutes. ARSVOM sent the SAR Apollo and SAR Ares, with the SAR Artemis joining later along with a Border Police vessel.
A helicopter operated by the Romanian General Inspectorate of Aviation took part in evacuating the injured crew members, lifting them from the scene before they were transferred for medical treatment.
The incident comes as war-related events involving unmanned aerial vehicles and risks to civilian shipping have increased in the Black Sea. Romania, a NATO member bordering Ukraine, has reported incidents connected to the war in the neighboring country in recent years.
The investigation into the circumstances of the fire aboard the Royad Mammadov is ongoing.

====================================================================================================

BT’s purchase of TalkTalk is cosy – but probably politically sensible | Nils Pratley
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

“All the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest,” thundered Virgin Media O2. It’s not an unreasonable view of BT’s hurried weekend acquisition of TalkTalk. Once upon a time, TalkTalk was seen as a plucky upstart performing the useful role of irritant to BT’s giant Openreach broadband operation. Now the challenger is being consumed by the dominant player via a pre-pack administration that minimises short-term political headaches.
Here’s the problem, though, with the cosy stitch-up thesis. For all the howls of outrage, it’s hard to see what the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, who gave her blessing by issuing a little-used public interest notice, was supposed to do differently. Alternative approaches, notably a chaotic collapse of TalkTalk without a rescue plan for the customers, risked worse outcomes.
OK, perhaps the worst fears of GP surgeries and hospitals being disconnected at a stroke, and thousands of vulnerable customers losing their internet connection, were overdone. But, in Nandy’s shoes, you probably wouldn’t take the risk. TalkTalk, after all, had had months to find a buyer but failed to land a credible deal even when its retail division and its wholesale unit, PXC, were up for grabs separately.
Disappointed would-be buyers blame the reluctance of BT, as the critical supplier to TalkTalk, to extend financial support to a new ownership vehicle. From BT’s point of view, however, one can see why another private equity backer for TalkTalk wouldn’t feel like an improvement on the last one. As it is, BT will be booking £100m as a non-payment of a debt even as it takes control.
The deep problem here is that TalkTalk – Sir Charles Dunstone’s creation more than 20 years ago – hasn’t been doing much real challenging work of late. After going through the refinancing wringer more times than is healthy, it was a financially distressed company. At the last count, borrowings were in the region of £1.5bn, a staggering sum for a loss-making business with only 1.5 million retail customers and 1 million wholesale ones. Telephony, remember, tends to be a low-margin game even when things are going well.
That is not to say the politicians get a free pass. Successive governments have been told many times by the regulator Ofcom that a “supplier of last resort” regime should be in place in the broadband market, just as it is in energy and water. The logic is simple: in extremis, there should be a way for a government-supported operation to step in to prevent sudden disconnections and look for an orderly permanent solution.
The unavoidable fact, though, is that such a regime didn’t exist with TalkTalk. That glaring hole in the regulatory setup needs to be addressed for future cases. But a weekend arrangement with BT, however objectionable in theory, at least has the advantage of not drawing on a penny of public money.
The medium-term regulatory test will be to ensure BT and Openreach can’t abuse the advantage of gobbling TalkTalk. There was a theatrical public exchange of letters between the BT chief executive, Allison Kirkby, and the Ofcom boss, Dame Melanie Dawes. The former pleaded for regulatory mercy, in effect, for removing a political problem; the latter replied that applying the regulatory framework was a statutory duty.
It’s anyone’s guess how that will work out in practice since the wriggle room would seem to be enormous. But the guiding principle hasn’t changed – wholesale operators need to have access to Openreach’s network on reasonable commercial terms. TalkTalk couldn’t make it pay but that, in the end, seems primarily to be a story of its own perilous financing. Wrapping the business into BT is very far from being ideal – but it’s not the worst pragmatic fudge.

====================================================================================================

Mine Blast Tests South Korean Engagement Policy as Pyongyang Rejects Any Contact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:38:00 UTC
01:38:00 KST

On September 21, two mines exploded inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that divides North and South Korea. Three South Korean soldiers were injured in the blast, two of which suffered serious injuries.
Two weeks later, on October 5, the South Korean military concluded that the explosion was caused by a mine North Korea had buried south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) that serves as a de facto border.
“Based on the results of the joint investigation with the United Nations Command (UNC) and scientific evidence, we have made a final determination that our service members, who were carrying out normal DMZ operations south of the MDL, were seriously injured by a plastic antipersonnel mine that North Korea planted south of the MDL under the pretext of so-called border fortification work,” Kwon Dae-won, deputy chief of the South’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said during the military’s press conference on Monday. Both the UNC and the South Korean military assessed that the mines had been buried for at least 12 months.
Along with Kwon’s briefing, the military also said that it had launched an operation to remove the North Korean mines buried around the explosion site by detonating them. It also urged North Korea to offer a sincere apology to the injured service members and to remove the mines it installed in violation of the Armistice Agreement.
However, Pyongyang already rejected these findings and then refused an offer of talks on the border when Seoul released its initial assessment on the cause of the land mine explosion days ago. The dispute now places the engagement policy of South Korean President Lee Jae-myung under direct strain.
To understand the issue, it helps to begin with the geography of the border. The MDL separates the two Koreas, and the DMZ extends for two kilometers on either side of it. The Armistice Agreement forbids hostile acts inside the DMZ and bars any crossing of the MDL without permission from the Military Armistice Commission. The U.S.-led UNC holds the authority to judge violations of the armistice.
Nevertheless, the line has grown difficult to read on the ground. Only around 200 of the 1,292 signs placed along it in 1953 remain intact. Seoul’s Defense Ministry has acknowledged that the baselines of the UNC and the South Korean military differ across roughly 60 percent of the border coordinates.
The September 21 explosions occurred during an operation to clear a path for a joint inspection with the UNC. The inspection was meant to examine terrain changes near the MDL, which military officials suspected were signs of mine-laying by North Korea. The blast site lay about 10 meters south of the line.
On September 28, the South’s JCS assessed a very high possibility that North Korean mines caused the explosions. Forensic analysis detected traces of trinitrotoluene and a brown synthetic material consistent with North Korean plastic antipersonnel mines. Next, investigators found another unexploded North Korean mine near the site. As a result, the South Korean military believes the area held at least four mines.
In addition, South Korean Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul told lawmakers on September 29 that Pyongyang appeared to have planted mines at several locations south of the MDL.
On September 30, Lt. Gen. Kang Hyun-woo of the JCS demanded an apology and responsible measures from North Korea, and he urged Pyongyang to halt its border fortification. Meanwhile, the UNC reported that investigators had identified an active North Korean mine south of the line. The command added that it was addressing the violation through established armistice mechanisms. For now, the military has said that it will announce the final results of its joint investigation at a later date.
North Korea answered with a flat denial from Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of the North’s autocratic leader Kim Jong Un and the main voice on inter-Korean relations. The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), one of the North’s key state-controlled media, carried her statement on September 30.
“The incident is a clear farce reminiscent of the ‘wooden-box mine incident’ which disturbed the world more than ten years ago, in consideration of the time and method of provocation,” Kim said in her statement. “Clearly speaking, our soldiers have never crossed the border.”
On October 2, South Korean Unification Minister Chung Dong-young proposed that the two Koreas should meet to confirm and survey the MDL again. In his view, the fading visibility of the line was a primary factor behind the blast. While Chung said that demanding an apology from North Korea is natural, he opposed resuming loudspeaker broadcasts toward the North as a dangerous step.
Pyongyang replied the same day. Kim Yo Jong rebuffed Chung’s proposal as a “wild dream and unilateral jargon.”
Her statement then turned to the border line itself. “It is the fixed stand of the DPRK government to define the borderline, our sovereign boundary line, through the full exercise of sovereignty, that is, by the use of force, not by means of negotiation,” Kim said. (DPRK is an acronym of North Korea’s official name: Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.)
Behind the rejection stands a fortification campaign that North Korea launched in 2024. In late 2023, Kim Jong Un declared that the two Koreas are hostile states. Since then, North Korean troops have installed barbed-wire fences and landmines along the MDL.
Kim Yo Jong has described the work as a matter of sovereignty with no military purpose. Moreover, her statement published on September 30 said that North Korea had decided to strengthen counterattack capability opposite the 21st Infantry Division of the South Korean army on the eastern front.
South Korean officials counted more than 20 crossings of the MDL by North Korean troops in August alone – more than the 17 cases recorded during all of 2025. A JCS official attributed the crossings to work in unfinished areas. Under the rules of engagement, South Korean forces fire warning shots when North Korean troops cross the line. Pyongyang has threatened swift retaliation should South Korean troops fire directly at North Korean soldiers at work on the border project rather than firing warning shots.
The episode recalls a crisis in 2015 – the same chain of events that Kim Yo Jong mentioned in her own statement. On August 4, 2015, wooden-box mines detonated near the MDL south of Paju and severely injured two South Korean noncommissioned officers. Of the two, one lost both legs and the other lost part of one leg. Six days later, Seoul determined that North Korean troops had deliberately laid the mines.
In response, Seoul resumed loudspeaker broadcasts along the border for the first time in 11 years, and the two sides exchanged artillery fire on August 20. Soon after, senior officials between the two Koreas opened marathon negotiations at Panmunjeom on August 22. Three days later, they reached a six-point agreement. According to the agreement, Pyongyang expressed regret over the explosions and Seoul agreed to halt the broadcasts. The agreement eventually led to further contacts and to reunions of families separated by the 1950-53 Korean War.
Still, the circumstances of 2026 differ from those of 2015. For one, Seoul no longer has loudspeakers along the border because the Lee administration removed them to reduce tensions. For another, Pyongyang has denied responsibility and refused talks. Accordingly, Kang has cautioned against repeating the measures of 2015.
The contrast matters because Lee has pursued de-escalation since taking office. In August 2025, he pledged to restore the 2018 inter-Korean military agreement. His government suspended loudspeaker broadcasts directed at the North in a unilateral concession.
A day before Chung made his proposal for inter-Korean talks, Lee discussed the mine blasts in a speech marking the 78th Armed Forces Day. Lee said he still felt pain over the soldiers wounded in the explosions. Moreover, he pledged that his government would keep pursuing practical measures to lower military tensions with Pyongyang. Lee’s tone contrasted with the warning of retaliation that the North’s state media had published a day earlier.
In this context, many critics in South Korea wondered why Seoul chose to keep to its dovish stance on Pyongyang even after North Korea caused injuries to three South Korean troops., Seoul has stated that it will “take necessary measures” after establishing the facts based on the investigations; however, the military has not yet specified what corresponding measures it would take.
Meanwhile, North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the waters off its east coast from the Wonsan area on October 3. The launch came one day after Kim Yo Jong ruled out any contact with Seoul. The JCS said that the missile flew more than 700 kilometers. However, KCNA claimed on October 4 that the missile, which was reported as an intermediate-range strategic missile, hit a target 1,000 kilometers away.
“We must continue our responsible efforts nonstop to constantly and repeatedly make the enemy recognize the reliability and fatality of our strategic offensive means,” Kim Jong Un said.
A separate announcement by Kim Yo Jong on October 3 addressed the flight distances reported by South Korea and Japan. She said that those figures exposed the limits of the tracking capability of the two militaries. In her account, a wave-like flight path caused the enemy to lose the missile from its first skip points. She described the missile as able to change its orbit at low altitude and said it was equipped with artificial intelligence.
“The enemy always made such a lame excuse that there is a limit to the detection capability because of the curvature of the earth’s surface, but in fact this just serves as a proof of our perfect missile capability and the most scientific ‘evaluation index’ confirming the power and reliability of our weapon system,” Kim said. “In other words, this means that there is no way to avoid this attack.”

Counter-drug policies are data-driven: minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:52 UTC
01:37:52 KST

Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) yesterday said the ministry has always held a zero-tolerance stance toward illegal drug use, but anti-drug policies must be based on scientific evidence and implemented strategically.
Shih made the remark in response to questions about the heated debate over drug policies between two Taipei mayoral candidates over the weekend.
The debate was about Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and his re-election campaign team saying that Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) had discussed decriminalization of drug use and mentioned in an 2014 article that Taiwan should establish community centers that provide drug users with clean needles and controlled substances.
Photo: CNA
Shen said that he was referring to drug-related harm reduction measures, including methadone maintenance treatment and needle and syringe programs, which have been implemented across Taiwan for years.
In Taiwan, methadone maintenance treatment is taken orally.
Shih said anti-drug policy has three main directions, with the first being “stamping out,” which falls under drug enforcement and prevention. The second is anti-drug “publicity,” which is mainly expanding anti-drug awareness campaigns on campuses. The third is “getting clean and treatment,” in which the ministry plays an important role.
Pilot needle and syringe programs have been implemented in Taiwan since 2005, providing sterile needles and injection equipment to people who inject drugs, to prevent HIV and viral hepatitis B or C transmission as a result of sharing or reusing needles and injection equipment, Shih said, adding that it has proven effective for preventing the spread of HIV.
According to ministry statistics, in 2005, injecting drug users accounted for 72 percent of newly reported HIV invfections, a share that fell to 1.7 percent last year. The number of newly diagnosed HIV cases has been declining year by year since 2018, although there was a slight increase last year he added.
Substitution therapy is another harm reduction measure, because “overcoming drug addiction is a long journey, particularly for users of opioids such as heroin,” as it affects the brain and nervous system, Shih said.
Complete recovery requires a phased reduction, he added.
When substitution therapy was launched in 2006, oral methadone was the main substance provided, and oral buprenorphine was introduced in 2011, he said.
Through a comprehensive community-based treatment plan, including substitution therapy, heroin and opioid users have access to medical care that can help them gradually overcome addiction and reintegrate into society, Shih said.
Evidence shows that harm reduction measures can help people with drug addiction break away from criminal syndicates and reduce crime, he added.

For US and China, enmity abides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:51 UTC
01:37:51 KST

US President Donald Trump might tout his “truly great friendship” with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), boasting after their summit last month that the two countries “have never gotten along better,” but beneath the smiles in Washington, the reality remains stark: “strategic stability” is an illusion, while more tit-for-tat military buildup should be expected.
Neither Washington nor Beijing has any intention of easing its security posture in East and Southeast Asia.
This hard truth dims any realistic prospect for a managed rivalry, regardless of upcoming high-level dialogue on trade, artificial intelligence or even the Iran war.
Consider the grim daily routine in the Taiwan Strait. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) continues to dispatch about eight military aircraft and 10 naval vessels a day around Taiwan.
This is “gray zone” pressure designed to force reunification without a direct military attack. Yet, during Xi’s three-day visit, Trump refused to yield to the Chinese leader’s ultimate red line, declining to explicitly voice “opposition” to Taiwanese independence.
While the US president has paused a US$14 billion arms sale to Taipei, after the midterm elections, he might face a Congress even more resolute to arm Taiwan against Beijing’s daily coercion.
The friction is not isolated to Taiwan. On Sept. 24, Chinese navy and coast guard vessels harassed a Philippine resupply mission to Second Thomas Shoal (Renai Shoal, 仁愛暗沙), a sandbank in the South China Sea that is occupied by a Philippine military garrison.
Manila, a treaty ally of the US, disputes the illegal Chinese claims to almost 90 percent of this vast stretch of water.
Washington’s response to Chinese operations in the area has been quietly stepped up: the US Marine Corps practiced fielding an air defense radar system in the Philippines to defend the country’s northern province, a mere 100km from southern Taiwan.
Meanwhile, the US Army is planning to station part of its next-generation Multi-Domain Task Force units in South Korea to ensure US access to the Taiwan Strait and the China seas.
In 2017, Washington deployed a Terminal High Altitude Area Defense air and missile defense system on the Korean Peninsula amid vehement Chinese protests.
As allied naval transits continue to assert that the Taiwan Strait remains an international waterway, the burden of containment is shifting. Allied partners such as Japan, Canada, Australia and New Zealand are increasingly compensating for decreases in publicly announced US passages.
This could not happen without coordination with Washington and is a direct result of the Trump administration’s persistent demands for burden-sharing.
The real danger lies in a deeper, technological race.
A Chinese military expert, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to legal jeopardy in China under the CCP’s new national security laws, said that the battlefields of Ukraine and Iran have proven that the modern era belongs to drones, stealth cruise missiles and advanced ballistic rockets, saying that most large US and Chinese weapons and equipment are worthless, and that the key point is which superpower abandons large-scale arms and systems, devises a new national defense strategy and accelerates the implementation of a new military revolution.
This technological arms contest would paralyze any meaningful bilateral dialogue on AI. While Chinese observers point to upcoming meetings at the APEC summit in Shenzhen and the G20 in Miami as opportunities to stabilize relations, the underlying structural tension tells a different story.
The divergence was laid bare in the post-summit readouts. The White House said that Trump advocated for trilateral arms control negotiations, to include Russia and China.
The Chinese government, by contrast, publicized a consensus on eight outcomes with no mention whatsoever of arms control.
Xi can spin the mantra of “constructive strategic stability,” but his military maneuvers telegraph expansion. The containment-versus-expansion dynamic is here to stay, and Washington must prepare for the long game.
Emanuele Scimia is a journalist and analyst covering foreign affairs and defense issues.
In 40 years of watching politics, I have never seen anything quite like Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) breed of politician. He has a presence that commands attention, and a combination of qualities that appear to be the result of powerful political currents. What is it that makes Shen different? China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

The Presidential Office yesterday condemned what it called a “typical case of transnational repression” after media reports alleging that China has been illegally surveilling the son of President William Lai (賴清德) in the US.
Taiwan strongly condemns such “barbaric” acts that disregard human rights and national sovereignty, and seek to suppress, threaten or even harm people who advocate freedom and democracy or their families, Presidential Office spokeswoman Karen Kuo (郭雅慧) said.
“Such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world,” Kuo said in a brief statement.
Photo: X account of US Attorney Bill Essayli / AFP
She thanked US law enforcement authorities for assisting and protecting Taiwanese, and said Taiwan would continue to work with the US and other democratic allies to jointly combat illegal acts of transnational repression.
The Presidential Office’s comments came after CBS News on Sunday reported that the FBI had arrested Wanying “Heather” Zhang, a California real-estate agent, at Los Angeles International Airport that day on charges of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government. She was about to board a flight to Shanghai.
Zhang, 34, is accused of spying on a “close relative of a Taiwanese government official” in the US, First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli wrote on Sunday in a post on X.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Lai Ting-yu (賴廷與)
Lai Ting-yu, an engineer in his 30s who studied at a US college, works for Dutch electronics company Philips and has a young son, said CBS News, citing Taiwanese media reports.
Zhang allegedly surveilled Lai Ting-yu and “his family — filming their home, vehicles, and reporting information back to handlers” in China, the FBI said on its X account.
Zhang traveled to Seattle last year and, acting at the direction of Chinese officials, sent “photos, videos, and license plate information to those officials,” Essayli said.
She was detained by the FBI at Los Angeles International Airport “attempting to depart for China” on Sunday, he said.
FBI Director Kash Patel cheered the arrest in a post on X, warning foreign adversaries that “America is no longer a safe place to run your espionage operations.”
“Allegedly surveil a foreign leader’s family on US soil for the PRC — and try to catch a flight back to Shanghai? Not happening,” Patel said, referring to the People’s Republic of China.
Zhang, who resides in Irvine, California, “coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection,” Essayli said.
She allegedly flew to Seattle on Sept. 1 last year, rented a black Nissan and drove to Lai Ting-yu’s home, a court document seen by Agence France-Presse said.
Images from a neighbor’s security camera included in the complaint allegedly show Zhang and her associate “appearing to film” the family as they arrived home one evening, CBS News said.
Zhang allegedly texted a Chinese government handler, based on WeChat messages obtained through a search warrant for her iCloud account, the CBS report said.
FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the complaint alleged Zhang had asked her accomplice to use AirDrop to transfer the surreptitiously taken photos over a short distance to avoid leaving a record of the transmission through the Internet.
Zhang was expected to make her initial appearance in federal court yesterday.
Zhang’s husband, Edric Ding, who is also a realtor at the same company, declined to comment, CBS reported.
Zhang’s arrest comes after Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) state visit to Washington, during which Xi told US President Donald Trump to show “prudence” over Taiwan and urged the US to oppose Taiwanese independence.

&quot;The U.S. is closely monitoring the situation&quot; — Rubio issues statement following plague case in Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:37:48 EEST
01:37:48 KST

"The U.S. is closely monitoring the situation" — Rubio issues statement following plague case in Russia
Kyiv • UNN
Marco Rubio said that the U.S. is closely monitoring the death of a laboratory employee in Irkutsk. The facility and several hospitals were placed under quarantine.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States is closely monitoring the case of an employee of a Russian laboratory who died last week after an incident at a research institute studying plague in Siberia, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
"We are watching this situation very closely," Rubio said Monday before departing for Europe. "I don’t think this is a reason for panic, but it does require close attention and monitoring."
As previously reported, Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of the plague-control institute in the city of Irkutsk, fell ill directly at her workplace. She died two days later, during the night of October 2, at a regional hospital in the neighboring city of Shelekhov.
The circumstances in which she fell ill remain unclear. Unconfirmed reports appeared in Russian media that Shipilova may have been infected as a result of an incident in the laboratory. Officials have not publicly confirmed this version.
Local media reported that the institute was subsequently placed under quarantine, while staff were forced to sleep on the floor and on chairs. "Everyone has been isolated since Friday—more than 60 people," a relative of one of the employees named Roman told the news outlet "Siberia.Realities."
According to him, relatives were allowed to deliver food through the checkpoint while tests were being conducted inside the building. Similar quarantine restrictions were introduced at several other hospitals in the city and its outskirts.
Referring to information released by the Russian side about the death, Rubio said it appeared that the laboratory worker had become infected, raising concerns that the disease might have spread inside the facility.
"Of course, the links between the United States and Russia are very limited right now," he said. "But, as with anything else, if something like this gets out, it spreads instantly."
Senior officials in Russia heightened public concern by circulating conflicting information. Alexei Tsydenov, head of Buryatia, which borders Irkutsk, initially wrote that Shipilova had died of plague, but later edited the post, saying that she had "possibly" died from the disease.
Rospotrebnadzor said that Shipilova had died of "pneumonia of unknown etiology." The agency insisted that tests had not detected microorganisms associated with her professional activities and described the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the region as stable.
Authorities in the neighboring city of Baikalsk briefly urged residents to refrain from traveling to Shelekhov and nearby settlements after what was described as unofficial information about possible plague infection emerged. The post was later deleted from social media.
"There are no visible changes in everyday life on the streets, but people are concerned and anxious. Local residents are outraged that they are not being told anything," said Olena Trifonova, a journalist with "People of Baikal," a Russian media outlet operating from abroad and specializing in Siberia.
Despite the absence of a confirmed diagnosis, it appears that precautionary measures have been introduced throughout the region. On Monday, the U.S.-funded radio station Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported that several hospitals in Irkutsk had been placed under quarantine. The outlet confirmed that employees of the institution where Shipilova worked—the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East—had been kept inside the building since October 2.
Patients at Irkutsk City Clinical Hospital No. 1 and the Ivan-Matryonin Children’s Hospital reported that relatives were not allowed to visit them and that people inside were prohibited from going outside.
Local residents reported on social media that certain precautionary measures had been introduced.
Meanwhile, mandatory mask-wearing was introduced at the Irkutsk Aluminium Plant in Shelekhov. The company’s director, Artem Fominykh, called it a preventive measure, saying: "It is better to be safe than sorry." Over the weekend, a number of mass events were canceled in Irkutsk.
Shipilova’s death prompted intervention by high-ranking federal officials responsible for public health. On Friday, Anna Popova — head of Rospotrebnadzor and the country’s chief sanitary physician — arrived in Irkutsk.
She took part in an emergency meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission devoted to the case, which officials classified as a suspected "particularly dangerous infection."
After meeting with Popova to coordinate further action, Irkutsk Region Governor Igor Kobzev urged residents to remain calm. "All individuals who had contact with the sick woman have been placed under medical observation. As of today, no signs of illness have been detected in them, and the results of laboratory tests are negative," he wrote on Telegram.
Kobzev did not mention in his post the information about the laboratory employee’s death. American politicians expressed concern about the incident, which occurred against the backdrop of the Kremlin’s long-standing and unfounded claims that Ukraine had allegedly been secretly conducting biological weapons research with Washington’s support.
Republican Congressman Don Bacon, a senior member of the House Armed Services Committee, wrote on social media: "I remember hearing from Ukraine’s opponents about their so-called biolabs. These were Russian disinformation operations of the highest order. But in reality, it is Russia that has biolabs."
The publication adds that plague remains endemic in some areas of Siberia and Russia’s Far East, where the pathogen is naturally maintained in populations of wild rodents and their fleas.

Handset camera lens manufacturer Largan Precision Co (大立光) reported a 11.47 percent year-on-year decline in revenue for the third quarter yesterday, despite revenue last month hitting its highest level since October last year.
Third-quarter revenue was NT$15.65 billion (US$492.32 million), compared with NT$17.68 billion a year earlier, the company said in a statement.
The figure was below the NT$18.58 billion consensus estimate from a Yahoo Finance poll of 13 analysts.
Photo: David Chang, EPA-EFE
Third-quarter revenue increased 14.53 percent from NT$13.66 billion in the second quarter, as the quarter is usually the peak season for the handset industry. Apple Inc in the quarter launched the iPhone 18 series with variable aperture lenses for which Largan enjoys an exclusive supply share, Yuanta Securities Investment Consulting Co (元大投顧) said.
The iPhone 18 lineup saw strong sales after its launch last month, boosting Largan’s sales to NT$5.78 billion in the month, the highest since October last year, when it posted sales of NT$6.26 billion, the company’s data showed.
Besides Apple, Taichung-based Largan supplies high-end handset camera lenses to Android phone vendors, such as Samsung Electronics Co, Xiaomi Corp (小米) and Huawei Technologies Co (華為).
In the first nine months of the year, Largan’s cumulative revenue was NT$44.86 billion, up 2.12 percent from NT$43.93 billion a year earlier, the company’s data showed.
Largan is to release its third-quarter earnings results at an investors’ conference on Thursday and give sales guidance for the fourth quarter.
During the conference, investors are expected to hear from the company about prospects of new handset sales from major vendors, its progress in pilot production of fiber arrays for copackaged optics, and land purchases for production expansion.
As Largan is pushing into the copackaged optics market, the company has spent several months in research and development on optical communication applications, leveraging its expertise in precision alignment.
The company has sent fiber array samples to customers for validation and plans to establish pilot lines using semi-automated production and invite potential clients for factory visits, with full automation to be introduced upon mass production next year, Yuanta said.
This year, Largan has spent more than NT$8 billion on land and factory buildings across Taichung for production expansion, the company’s regulatory filings showed.

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, an ally of US President Donald Trump, and Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva are to face off in a runoff on Oct. 25 for the top job of Latin America’s powerhouse economy after neither won a majority in Sunday’s vote.
The country’s electoral court in Brasilia said neither the 80-year-old incumbent, seeking his fourth non-consecutive term, nor the 45-year-old son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro would garner the majority vote needed for an outright win.
The court had Bolsonaro with just over 56 million votes to Lula’s 53.7 million, with 99.8 percent of the vote reported.
Photo: AFP
The next presidential term is set to begin on Jan. 5.
The winner will be in charge of Latin America’s biggest economy and a population of 214 million. A win for Bolsonaro would increase US influence in Latin America. If Lula wins, Brazil would keep its distance from Washington and continue to deepen its relationship with China.
Flavio Bolsonaro addressed the press and a small group of supporters, including some wearing green-and-yellow Brazil jerseys and one woman wrapped in the Israeli flag, outside his Brasilia house.
“Brazil wants change, that’s the reading of what happened today,” Bolsonaro said.
“It’s the end of the Workers’ Party era,” he added, in a reference to Lula’s party.
Lula, seeking to be encouraging ahead of an uphill battle to beat Bolsonaro in the runoff, said the result was “unexpected” as he had thought he could win in the first round.
“Tomorrow we start a new campaign,” Lula said. “I am very good in the knockout stage. We will see who has the best plan.”
Lula and Bolsonaro have three weeks to reach moderate voters who did not support them in the first round. Augusto Cury, a writer who finished in third place with 3.4 million votes, said he would not endorse either in the runoff. Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, two candidates who garnered about 5.3 million votes combined on Sunday, have previously said the same.
In the campaign ahead, Lula is expected to try to capitalize on the popularity of his social policies and his rival’s many legal woes.
While the once widely popular Lula saw his approval ratings plummet during his third term, standing up to the US gave him a boost. He also enjoys a strong base of supporters who credit his social policies for improving millions of Brazilians’ lives.
However, he faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into his rival.
Flavio Bolsonaro is likely to lean into his messaging on affordability and link the president to corruption scandals.
He has promised to crack down on Brazilian criminal groups and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy, second only to China. He also has campaigned on releasing his father and bringing him back to politics.
Both candidates face image problems: Roughly half of Brazil’s population disapproves of the Bolsonaro family, and roughly half disapprove of Lula’s Workers’ Party, according to multiple polls.

US defense experts to participate in meetings, war games in Taiwan joint assessment program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:43 UTC
01:37:43 KST

US defense liaisons are to take part in 130 meetings and map-based war games in Taiwan under an expanded joint assessment program, the Ministry of National Defense said in a report.
Sources have previously said that the Pentagon would station personnel at the ministry under a joint program that is to run from this year through 2028.
That program would involve officials from the Office of the Undersecretary of Defense for Policy and researchers from the Institute for Defense Analyses, a US nonprofit research organization that conducts national security studies, the ministry report said.
Photo: Bloomberg
Each organization would assign one representative to work at the ministry’s headquarters in Taiwan.
The Office of the Undersecretary of Defense for Policy advises US defense leaders on national security and defense policy, while the Institute for Defense Analyses conducts federally funded research and analysis on national security and science policy.
The ministry plans to hold 50 in-person meetings and 80 videoconferences this year under the program, which runs from this year through 2028, the report said.
The ministry has allocated funding for the initiative since 2022. Under the arrangement, the Office of the Undersecretary of Defense for Policy commissions the Institute for Defense Analyses to coordinate experts from the US military and research organizations, including the US Indo-Pacific Command, the Defense Intelligence Agency and the National Ground Intelligence Center.
The US liaisons work with the ministry, General Staff Headquarters and the armed services to assess defense and operational issues and provide policy recommendations.
Findings from the program’s first three years have been incorporated into the annual Han Kuang military exercises and training assessments conducted by each service, the ministry said.
Beginning this year, the US is expanding the scope and depth of the assessments and increasing their frequency, the report said.
The ministry said it has budgeted NT$471 million (US$14.82 million) over three years for the program. The NT$152.5 million allocated for next year would cover an expanded research team, the 130 meetings and the costs of stationing the two US liaisons in Taiwan.
The meetings would bring US experts together with Taiwan’s joint staff, service headquarters and frontline units for discussions, on-site inspections and map-based war games, as well as qualitative and quantitative assessments using simulation models, it said.

Photo: CNA
"Eswatini will therefore continue to advocate for Taiwan’s meaningful participation in international organizations and mechanisms where its contribution can benefit humanity," he said.
Kunene, who was previously posted to the UN, said such support was not only "an expression of friendship," but also "a principled position grounded in fairness, inclusion and the practical requirements of effective international cooperation."
In terms of bilateral ties, Kunene highlighted Taiwan- backed rural electrification as an example of how the partnership had improved people’s lives, saying communities across Eswatini’s countryside now "light up like stars" at night.
He also pledged to promote closer cooperation in areas including trade and investment, renewable energy, agriculture, healthcare, digital transformation and artificial intelligence.
Meanwhile, Lai welcomed Kunene to his new post and said the friendship between Taiwan and Eswatini had "stood the test of time" and remained strong despite changes in the international landscape.
Taiwan will also continue working with Eswatini on projects including the Taiwan Industrial Innovation Park while expanding cooperation in agriculture, healthcare, education, trade and technology, Lai said.

Photo: AP

From January to August this year, “8,041 citizens were repatriated by air,” state newspaper the Global New Light of Myanmar said.
While the ship returns have been highly publicized in Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur has not commented on the returns Myanmar says it organized by weekly flights.
The total number of migrants Myanmar has said returned by plane and ship this year is 9,517.
Malaysia said that returnees under its scheme agreed to voluntary repatriation from detention centers, where Myanmar says they had “faced difficulties” after serving sentences for immigration offenses.
However, rights groups report dire conditions in the facilities, and the UN refugee agency says staff were not allowed to verify that decisions to return “were genuinely free and informed.”
More than 100,000 people are estimated to have been killed in Myanmar since a military coup in 2021 unleashed civil war, monitor organization ACLED said.
The Rohingya started fleeing the country en masse to Malaysia before that, escaping a military crackdown starting in 2017 deemed a genocide by rights groups — a charge the armed forces have always denied.
The Rohingya make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to UN data, and have been the focus of recent anti-migrant sentiment.
After the ships carrying the 1,476 migrants docked on Sunday in Thanlyin, just south of Yangon, AFP journalists saw dozens moved to a monastery holding center for ID and health checks.
“Necessary arrangements are continuing to facilitate their swift reunion with relatives and family members, ensuring their safe return to their respective hometowns,” the Global New Light of Myanmar said.

The Web is not ready for millions of rule-bending bots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:39 UTC
01:37:39 KST

Earlier this year an Australian tech worker asked his OpenClaw artificial intelligence (AI) agent whether it could get him higher up on the waiting list for a popular gym class. It did exactly what he wanted, but with an unexpected twist: It found a flaw in the system and canceled the booking of another person on the list.
AI’s next big magic trick is to start doing things for you across the Internet, with new tools like Muse from Meta Platforms Inc and dots from OpenAI working 24/7 to find online bargains, book restaurant tables or check your e-mails for unpaid bills. What is troubling is how these increasingly capable, arguably useful tools have been trained to find creative ways to meet their goals, which could lead to a mess of unintended consequences when unleashed on an Internet full of poorly secured Web sites.
The Australian tech worker’s AI agent had found a loophole and exploited it, without being told to. So what happens when millions of other people’s agents start competing for the cheapest flights or the best movie seats? In the best-case scenario, we would see a smooth and well-functioning network of bots that play by the rules to get the best outcomes for their humans. In the worst: a cybersecurity nightmare.
The Web simply might not be ready. Security firm DataDome said that 65 percent of the more than 20,000 Web sites it tested had systems for detecting or blocking AI agents, and that bot activity hitting login pages rose more than eightfold in the first half of this year.
In some ways, it is hard to imagine these new AI agents causing widespread trouble. They look too cute for a start. Muse has a cartoonish design reminiscent of a Labubu doll, while the vividly covered blobs that represent dots could be characters in a children’s TV show — perhaps part of an effort to ease general mistrust of Meta and OpenAI.
They work well, too. Bloomberg Opinion’s Dave Lee called Muse “the most impressive product Meta has released in years.” He said his agent, which he had christened Harold, had organized his calendar and scoured Facebook Marketplace for good deals.
Meta and OpenAI say they have strong guardrails in place to make sure their agents behave themselves. Muse is kept within an isolated virtual machine — essentially a private computer in Meta’s cloud — while a separate security system controls every request it makes to the Internet, handling payments and making sure a human is consulted before any major task like buying something or sending a message. Dots is monitored in a similar way.
However, even these safeguards do not fix an underlying problem baked into today’s generative AI models through their training, which is a tendency to look for shortcuts, a phenomenon researchers call reward-hacking. (It is also why chatbots are prone to flattery.) The UK’s AI Security Institute noticed a rise in this kind of cheating behavior in coding agents and chatbots late last year.
The inclination to please is what drove OpenAI’s agents to hack Hugging Face a few months ago. OpenAI agents also improperly meddled with the Web sites of dozens of other organizations this year, including the US Securities and Exchange Commission and Australia’s government-run healthcare program. Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company on its own accord.
These last cases happened while the models were being trained or tested, with safeguards deliberately lowered, but the bots’ actions still surprised their developers, and researchers have found that even when they make their tests harder to game, agents keep trying to cheat.
There are signs that AI products would also hunt for loopholes in the wild, particularly in coding. In one instance, a software developer told his AI agent to clear out temporary files from a computer folder without using the “delete” command. The agent then hid that instruction inside a testing tool, and slipped past the filter to clear the files using the command it was told not to.
Now multiply that type of behavior by million of agents, as consumers explore using AI to optimize their lives and work. When Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg launched Muse last month, he said consumers deserved to have access to their own “personal superintelligence” and that the new agents would “make you money.”
Some are not doing that well. When a consumer tech reviewer in Toronto named Matt J. Robb tried using Muse to sell a keyboard on Facebook Marketplace last month, the agent angered the buyer by saying Robb was at home to carry out the transaction, which was not true, according to an account posted on Threads.
The agent had also made a low-ball offer. On top of the risk of cheating, agents can also just make mistakes, and it would likely be end users who pay the price. Robb was left with a negative rating from his angry buyer.
However cuddly these new agents look, the systems behind them are trained to tick a box one way or another. They might do it a little too well.
Parmy Olson is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering technology. A former reporter for the Wall Street Journal and Forbes, she is author of Supremacy: AI, ChatGPT and the Race That Will Change the World. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration
There could be isolated afternoon showers in mountainous areas of southern Taiwan, he said.

Huáhua: Dào shíhou rén hàn chē yídìng dōu hěn duō ba? Nǐmen dǎsuàn zěnme qù?
清清：我們打算一大早開車出門，從新竹開到花蓮，再一路玩到台東。
Qīngqīng: Wǒmen dǎsuàn yí dà zǎo kāichē chūmén, cóng Xīnzhú kāi dào Huālián, zài yílù wán dào Táidōng.
華華：希望不要遇到塞車，祝你們一路順利！
Huáhua: Xīwàng búyào yùdào sāichē, zhù nǐmen yílù shùnlì!
清清：我們已經做好心理準備了。你呢？你有什麼打算？
Qīngqīng: Wǒmen yǐjīng zuò hǎo xīnlǐ zhǔnbèi le. Nǐ ne? Nǐ yǒu shénme dǎsuàn?
華華：我請了兩天假，想趁連假出國走走。
Huáhua: Wǒ qǐng le liǎng tiān jià, xiǎng chèn liánjià chūguó zǒuzou.
清清：祝你出國玩得開心！
Qīngqīng: Zhù nǐ chūguó wán de kāixīn!
翻譯 Translation
Huahua: This Friday marks the start of the National Day holiday weekend. Do you have any plans?
Qingqing: My family and I are planning to visit Hualien first, and then go to Taitung to watch the National Day fireworks.
Huahua: There’ll probably be lots of people and traffic then, right? How are you planning to get there?
Qingqing: We’re planning to leave early in the morning, drive from Hsinchu to Hualien, and then travel all the way down to Taitung.
Huahua: I hope you don’t get stuck in traffic. Have a safe and smooth trip.
Qingqing: We’re already mentally prepared for that. How about you? What are your plans?
Huahua: I took two days off and want to take advantage of the long weekend to travel abroad.
Qingqing: Have a great trip.

1. 國慶 (guóqìng) National Day
2. 連假 (liánjià) long holiday; consecutive days off
3. 出門 (chūmén) go out; leave home
4. 塞車 (sāichē) traffic jam; be stuck in traffic
5. 心理準備 (xīnlǐ zhǔnbèi) be mentally prepared
6. 請假 (qǐngjià) take time off; ask for leave
7. 趁 (chèn) take advantage of (an opportunity / time); while. . .
8. 一路順利 (yílù shùnlì) have a smooth journey; have a safe trip

BILINGUAL STORY 雙語故事

★ Bilingual Story is a fictionalized account. 雙語故事部分內容純屬虛構。
Two red flares rose from the black sea. The men stopped eating beside their stranded tank and stared toward the water. The platoon leader shouted for everyone to get into position. Hsiung Chen-chiu climbed into Tank No. 66 and looked through the sight.
Wooden boats crowded the darkness. Soldiers jumped into the water, holding rifles above their heads, and moved toward the beach. Hsiung was 18 years old. A few hours earlier, the biggest problem he had ever faced was a tank stuck in the sand.
Photo: AI I 照片：人工智慧
Tank No. 66 should have gone back to camp after the exercise. Instead, it was stuck beside the coast. Another tank tried to pull it free. Then one track came off. They worked into the night trying to repair it. Two other tanks stayed nearby.
Hsiung turned the cannon toward the sea and loaded a shell. The cannon kicked. A boat offshore burst into flames. The fire lit the water. More boats. More men. Hundreds of them. He fired again. The fighting continued through the night.
Near dawn, the tide went out. Landing boats were stuck in the mud, but enemy soldiers were already inland. Gunfire hit the tank. Metal rang around Hsiung. Then he heard engines behind them. “Reinforcements!” someone shouted. The engines came closer. And the bullets came faster.
兩枚紅色的信號彈從漆黑的海面升起。守在故障戰車旁的士兵們放下手中的食物，凝視著海面。排長大聲喊叫，命令所有人各就各位進入戰鬥位置。熊震球爬進66號戰車，透過瞄準鏡看了出去。
黑暗的海面上擠滿了木船。無數士兵跳入水中，將步槍高舉過頭，朝著沙灘前進。那一年熊震球才18歲。幾個小時前，他所面臨最大的難題，也不過是一輛陷入沙堆裡的戰車。
66號戰車原本應該在演習結束後返回營區，但它卻卡在海岸邊。另一輛戰車試著把它拉出來，結果履帶反而脫落。他們忙到深夜努力修理，另外兩輛戰車則留在附近警戒。
熊震球將砲管對準大海，裝填了一發砲彈。砲火後座力猛然一震，海上的一艘船隻隨即爆炸起火，火光照亮了水面。更多船隻、更多敵兵，成百上千地湧來。他再次開火，戰鬥持續了一整夜。
接近黎明時分，潮水退去。登陸的船隻擱淺在泥灘上，但敵軍士兵已經進入內陸。槍林彈雨擊中戰車。金屬碰撞聲在熊震球耳邊響個不停。隨後，他聽到身後傳來引擎聲。「援軍到了！」有人大喊。引擎聲越來越近，子彈也呼嘯得更加猛烈。
Epilogue 故事討論
The battle was real. Early on Oct. 25, 1949, Chinese communist forces crossed from Fujian to Kinmen, beginning the Battle of Guningtou. Military studies estimate that the first wave included more than 8,000 soldiers, crossing in about 200 boats, mostly civilian fishing and sailing boats. The previous afternoon, M5A1 Tank No. 66 became stuck near Longkou after a military exercise. Attempts to free it failed, so two other tanks stayed nearby.
When the attack began, all three happened to be near the landing area. No. 66 opened fire, and one early shell reportedly hit a boat carrying ammunition, setting it on fire and lighting the shore. As the tide fell, many boats became stuck near shore, making it harder to bring in more troops. After three days of fighting, the invasion failed, with thousands of Communist soldiers killed or captured. For Kinmen, No. 66’s unlucky breakdown turned out to be a blessing in disguise.
這是一場真實發生過的戰役。1949年10月25日凌晨，中共軍隊從福建渡海進攻金門，展開了「古寧頭戰役」。根據軍方的研究估計，第一波攻勢包含超過8,000名士兵，搭乘約200艘船渡海，其中大多是民間的漁船和帆船。前一天下午，一輛M5A1 66號戰車在演習後不幸陷於壟口附近的沙灘，救援嘗試失敗後，另外兩輛戰車留在現場守候。
當攻擊開始時，這三輛戰車恰好就在登陸地點附近。66號戰車隨即開火，據傳其中一發即早發射的砲彈擊中了載有彈藥的船隻，引發大火並照亮了海岸。隨著潮水退去，許多船隻擱淺於岸邊，導致敵軍難以繼續輸送兵力。經過三天的奮戰，這場入侵行動以失敗告終，數千名共軍士兵陣亡或被俘。對金門而言，66號戰車當年那場不幸的故障，最終反而因禍得福。
