China pressured Munich institute to cancel author event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:37 UTC
01:37:37 KST

The Chinese consulate in Munich last week unsuccessfully pressured a local literary institute to cancel a talk by Taiwanese author Yang Shuang-zi (楊?子), said Chao Yen-ching (趙彥清), director-general of the Munich office of the Taipei Representative Office in Germany.
Tanja Graf, managing director of Literaturhaus Munchen, which organized the event, confirmed the attempted interference, Chao said.
Ahead of Yang’s talk on Thursday last week, officials from China’s consulate in Munich contacted the institute and asked it to cancel the event, offering to fund and arrange an alternative featuring a Chinese author, he said.
Photo: CNA
The institute refused the request, he added.
Yang’s public reading and discussion about her International Booker Prize-winning novel Taiwan Travelogue (臺灣漫遊錄) was overshadowed by controversy involving her interpreter.
Tsao Chang-chen (曹昌振), the Chinese interpreter hired by Literaturhaus Munchen, did not bring a pen or paper on stage for Yang’s talk and said before the event that there would be some political topics he would be “unable to translate,” Chao said.
As Yang’s talk took place during Oktoberfest, the institute hired a local translator who had been recommended by an association of Taiwanese expatriates in Berlin to save money, he said.
Tsao failed to translate the participants’ German remarks for Yang and, when Yang spoke, avoided translating terms such as “Republic of China,” “Taiwan” and “China,” Chao said.
Tsao translated Yang’s reference to China’s “cognitive warfare” as “misinformation,” and when Yang spoke of “the immense threat from China,” Tsao rendered it as a threat from “a very big neighbor,” prompting the organizer to clarify that the neighbor was China, he said.
After receiving complaints from Taiwanese attendees, Chao said he lodged a complaint with Tsao and raised the matter with the event’s moderator, the book’s German translator and Literaturhaus Munchen.
“The organizers were shocked and embarrassed” to learn what had happened, he said.
Several people in the audience tried to ask politically “sensitive” questions during the event, although Yang “answered very well and was not affected by it,” Chao said.
While he said he had no evidence of Chinese involvement in the interpreter controversy, the Chinese consulate had tried to get the event canceled and might also have “exercised influence” over people attending it.
Yang later said the alleged Chinese interference in her event only proved that “literature and politics cannot be separated.”

Envoy prods US on stalled arms sale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:32 UTC
01:37:32 KST

Taiwan’s representative to the US projected confidence that US President Donald Trump would ultimately approve additional weapons sales to Taiwan, which has been waiting for a US$14 billion arms package.
“Obviously the speed could be a little faster, but we hope the United States — the United States understands very well the threat that we are under and, I’m very sure, will be providing us with the necessary equipment,” Alexander Yui (俞大?) said on Bloomberg This Weekend.
Trump’s efforts to woo Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) have sowed uncertainty about the US’ commitment to Taiwan, raising the stakes for the arms sale. Air defenses make up a substantial share of the proposed package, people familiar with the matter have said.
Photo: Screen grab from Bloomberg’s Web site
The US has been “very clear on the fact that there’s no change in US policy towards Taiwan,” Yui said.
The US has not “acquiesced or responded” to Xi’s call to explicitly oppose Taiwanese independence, which would go beyond the longstanding policy that Washington does not support independence, he said.
A senior Trump administration official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Trump would make a determination on the arms package in a fairly short time, without elaborating on the timeline.
Trump, who downplayed the issue when he hosted Xi in Washington last month, has long said he would make the decision “soon.”
Trump has previously described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” in his dealings with Beijing, and has engaged on Taiwan with his Chinese counterpart in a manner that is at odds with longstanding US practice.
With Trump and Xi expected to meet two more times this year at international summits, Yui said the goal is “to make sure that Taiwan is not on the menu.”
Tension over Taiwan also played out as Chinese diplomats ensured at the last minute that the 1951 Treaty of San Francisco would not be displayed during the two leaders’ visit to the National Archives in Washington, a person familiar with the matter said.
China did not sign the treaty, which forced Japan to relinquish its claims to Taiwan without specifying which government would assume sovereignty over the island.
The episode, first reported by National Public Radio, underscored Beijing’s sensitivity over Taiwan, which China has threatened to take by force if necessary.
As US officials look to defuse concerns around support for Taipei, the senior administration official pointed to Trump’s approval of a record US$11 billion in arms sales to Taiwan in December last year.
US House of Representatives Speaker Mike Johnson last week cited Trump’s record on Taiwan, telling Fox Business that Taipei remains a “very important partner, friend and ally.”
The delay in the latest package’s approval was related to “everything that’s involved and going on in the Middle East,” Johnson said.
However, the uncertainty deepened this week after US Ambassador to China David Perdue said Trump had asked Xi whether he wanted to purchase US weapons. Trump disputed the account before musing that selling weapons to Beijing might be a good idea.
A US Department of State spokesperson said US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.
US support for Taiwan has long served as a measure of US credibility in Asia, where allies including Japan and South Korea rely on Washington’s security commitments.
A failure to come to Taiwan’s aid in a crisis could also represent a significant geopolitical gain for Beijing, Bloomberg Economics chief geoeconomics analyst Jennifer Welch said.
Taiwan produces most of the world’s leading-edge semiconductors, making it indispensable to the artificial intelligence boom and the billions of dollars US companies are investing in data centers and advanced computing.
“None of that happens without Taiwan and without the chips that Taiwan makes,” Welch said.
For Taiwan, the more immediate concern is whether Washington would continue providing the military equipment it needs to defend itself against any Chinese attack.
A bipartisan group of US senators urged Trump in May to formally notify Congress of the pending package. Separately, House Democrats called on the administration to reaffirm the longstanding “one China” policy, which recognizes Beijing as China’s sole legal government while acknowledging, without endorsing, its position that Taiwan is part of China.
Washington maintains unofficial relations with Taipei and provides defensive weapons, while intentionally leaving ambiguous whether US forces would intervene militarily in a conflict.
Brookings Institution analyst Ryan Hass, a former National Security Council official, said he expects additional arms sales during Trump’s presidency, potentially through smaller packages after the two leaders conclude reciprocal visits to the APEC summit in China next month and the Group of 20 meeting in Miami in December.
Even so, the delays and conflicting messages are having consequences.
“By introducing so much uncertainty about sort of the steadfastness of the United States,” Trump is “providing tailwind to China’s efforts to induce them to believe that they are isolated and alone in the world to contend with China,” Hass said.

Russian strikes leave Ukraine with almost no spare locomotives, further complicating grain exports
Russian forces have intensified attacks on Ukrainian freight trains in recent weeks, leaving Ukraine with almost no reserve locomotives, Taras Vysotskyi, Ukraine’s minister of agrarian policy and food, told the Financial Times.
Ukrainian authorities are in talks with European allies about supplying locomotives compatible with Ukraine’s track gauge (1,520 mm), he said.
Freight trains carry grain and ore, Ukraine’s main exports, among other cargo.
The loss of locomotives makes it even harder for Ukraine to export grain, the newspaper reported. Attacks on Ukrainian port infrastructure have already severely hampered grain exports.
Vysotskyi estimates that if the ports remain closed, Ukraine will lose at least $8 billion from June 2026 to June 2027.

EDITORIAL: AI and establishment distrust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:30 UTC
01:37:30 KST

Data centers have become one of the fastest-growing infrastructure sectors globally, driven by the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI). However, debates over data centers in the US as well as Asia-Pacific nations have intensified, with public focus shifting from economic growth and technological development to worries about rising costs of living. That has led to construction delays and cancelations.
Opposition to data centers in the US has become a cross-party issue ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. A March Gallup poll found that 71 percent of Americans oppose data centers in their area, with nearly 50 percent saying they strongly opposed them. A Pew Research Center survey in August found that 60 percent of Americans are uncomfortable with new data centers, with 54 percent saying they are concerned about the negative environmental impact, 50 percent about rising utility bills and 49 percent about quality of life.
The US is home to the world’s biggest investors in AI infrastructure and has the most data centers globally. According to Stanford University’s AI Index report, the US has 5,427 data centers, more than 10 times as many as any other country. However, rising opposition has blocked or delayed 45 data center projects in the US in the second quarter of this year, valued at US$68 billion. That followed 75 data center projects valued at about US$130 billion that were blocked or delayed in the first quarter, according Data Center Watch, a research project from 10a Labs that tracks opposition to data center development across the US.
Most of the opposition in the US stems from construction, grid connection and land leasing, which could be resolved over time, Bloomberg reported, citing data compiled by market intelligence platform Currence. Opposition from local communities and politicians is a primary driver of the disruptions, accounting for 52 percent of project cancelations, with regulatory and permission issues accounting for 30 percent, the reports said. Growing public opposition has surpassed financing, grid constraints and critical equipment shortages as the main challenge to data center development.
The growing opposition to data centers, an issue that is uniting Americans across party lines in an otherwise highly partisan era, reflects a more serious concern: public discontent with the political and economic establishments. The Washington Post in July quoted Utah Governor Spencer Cox as saying that data centers embody public anxieties around AI and the economy. Cox — who supports data center development for economic growth and national security, but has called for stricter environmental and consumer safeguards amid public pushback — said data centers have become a tangible target for those anxieties because people feel that “this is something they can fight.”
Analysts from think tanks such as the Brookings Institution have said that while the data-center backlash in the US was triggered by immediate, tangible grievances over potential electricity price hikes, water waste and industrial noise, it was fundamentally fueled by a deeper and broader anxiety about corporate overreach and the unchecked development of AI. Despite the debate over who benefits and bears the costs of data centers, tech giants and US President Donald Trump continue to claim that the expansion is vital for US technological supremacy over China.
Taiwan should watch this issue closely, because grassroots opposition to data centers is spreading to the Asia-Pacific region. Conflicts over data center construction in Japan, Australia and India are sometimes more pronounced than in the US. It remains unclear whether additional restrictions on data centers would weigh on tech giants’ capital expenditure, drive away potential backers and ultimately affect the companies in Taiwan that are in the AI supply chain. Growing policy uncertainties abroad therefore deserve further observation.
The backlash against data centers abroad should not be seen as opposition to AI. Instead, the real question is data center governance, and the answer is that large data centers should bear a larger burden of energy and grid costs because they are big electricity users. Moreover, data center development involves power equipment, cybersecurity, supply chains and national security, but at its core, it is actually about power grid resilience. It is no longer a question of how much electricity can be generated in the AI era, but whether power transmission, substations, energy storage and control systems can withstand new large-scale loads. This is particularly true for Taiwan.
In 40 years of watching politics, I have never seen anything quite like Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) breed of politician. He has a presence that commands attention, and a combination of qualities that appear to be the result of powerful political currents. What is it that makes Shen different? Throughout the past decades of local elections, I have not seen anyone seriously discuss a long-term vision for urban planning, let alone with the kind of clarity and insight that Shen possesses that compels people to keep listening. He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision
Taiwanese writer Chu Yu-hsun (朱宥勳) this month spoke out about the difficulties of judging literary competitions when nearly 40 percent of the novel submissions he reviews appear to be generated by artificial intelligence (AI). He said he would refuse to serve as a judge for any literary award that does not explicitly prohibit the use of AI in creative writing. The use of AI in creative and academic work has become increasingly common. My son, who attends National Chengchi University, says he is exasperated after working to complete assignments on his own, only to receive lower grades than classmates who used
China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising
Freedom of expression is a precious gift from the times, civilization and history, Hong Kong writer Hon Lai-chu (韓麗珠) said on Wednesday last week when she received the Golden Tripod Award, the highest honor in Taiwan’s publishing industry, for her novel Flesh Mountain (祼山). “As a Hong Konger these days, I deeply feel that the freedom to write and publish should not be taken for granted,” she said. She said that for a reason. Nvidia and Hon Hai say their robots improving at building AI components
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

Nvidia Corp and Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密) have improved the efficiency of critical assembly steps for Nvidia’s GB300 NVL72 rack-scale artificial intelligence (AI) platform by using robots, the companies said on Friday.
Nvidia detailed in a technical blog titled “The Machines that Make the Machines” how its operations team and Hon Hai trained robots to assemble critical GB300 NVL72 components, improving manufacturing stability and efficiency.
Success rates for assembly steps exceeded 90 percent, it said.
Photo: CNA
Nvidia also said the two companies focused on assembling the GB300’s tester tray, which is used to verify the functionality and performance of GB300 computing modules before shipment.
Key tasks included bus bar assembly and the insertion of multiple electrical connectors, it said.
For bus bar assembly, Nvidia said a major challenge was getting robots to grasp and transport a metal bar that carries high-voltage electricity to the tray, insert it and secure it with screws at 16 locations.
For multi-connector insertion, robots must lift two large and two small cable-mounted electrical connectors from the tray and insert them into sockets with tight clearances, it said.
According to test data, the automation system hit a success rate of more than 95 percent for bus bar assembly, which requires tightening 16 screws, with a target completion time of 124 seconds.
For multi-connector insertion, involving four cable connectors of different sizes, the success rate ranged from 90 percent to 95 percent, with a target completion time of 72 seconds.
During GB300 tester-tray assembly, Nvidia said flexible automation systems are needed to address uncertainty, because rapid design cycles and relatively low production volumes make fixed automation infeasible.
Robots need to be adaptive and robust enough to handle variations in the assembly process, it said.
Hon Hai, known globally as Foxconn Technology Group (富士康), is one of Nvidia’s major suppliers. The company announced last year that it was working with Nvidia to build a smart manufacturing plant at its production site in Houston, Texas, using Nvidia’s model-driven humanoid robots to produce AI servers.
Hon Hai has said it plans to expand its use of robots developed with Nvidia to other plants in Texas, Wisconsin and California.
The company, which accounts for more than 40 percent of the global AI server market, remains upbeat about the sector. At an investor conference in August, Hon Hai said that its AI rack shipments should more than double from a year earlier this year.

Photo: the CTBC Brothers via CNA

Wang Wei-chen collected three hits and four RBIs, while Huang Wei-sheng also drove in four runs.
The Brothers scored three runs in the first inning, added two in the fifth and pulled away with four in the seventh and three in the eighth.
They are to face the Uni-President 7-Eleven Lions, who qualified by finishing second in the full-season standings, in a playoff series beginning on Friday. The winners are to meet the Wei Chuan Dragons in the Taiwan Series.
The CPBL divides its regular season into two halves, each with a separate champion.
The Dragons earned direct entry to the championship series by winning the first half and finishing with the league’s best full-season winning percentage.

The best-of-seven Taiwan Series is to begin on Saturday next week at Taipei Dome, where the Dragons are to host Games 1 and 2 and, if necessary, Games 5 through 7.
Games 3 and 4, scheduled for Oct. 20 and 21, will also be played at Taipei Dome if the Brothers advance, or in Tainan if the Lions qualify.

Cyber official plans AI testing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:27 UTC
01:37:27 KST

The government would begin black-box cybersecurity testing using agentic artificial intelligence (AI) to imitate hackers next year, the National Institute of Cybersecurity said yesterday.
The institute’s new director, Dennis Kung (龔化中), told a news conference in Taipei that this would be one of the tasks he would prioritize during his term.
Kung, who has private-sector experience in researching and developing networking equipment, smartphones and cybersecurity software, said cybersecurity research should not be limited to product development in laboratories.
Photo: Reuters
The focus should be on closely linking R&D units with frontline defense units, with the experiences gained from defense units guiding the work of the R&D units, Kung said.
The products developed by R&D teams should be used by the defense units as well.
“With the addition of AI-proficient staff, we can produce a cybersecurity defense that truly meets the needs of the government and private sectors in the fast-changing AI age,” he said.
Kung said that he aims to lead the team at the National Institute of Cybersecurity in upgrading four areas of defense.
First, for the government’s annual cybersecurity exercises next year, the institute would run black-box penetration tests, using agentic AI to imitate hackers. Agentic AI would be used in the Cybersecurity Operations and Defense Exercise next year, he said.
Second, the institute would work with international AI firms to use on-premises models to conduct automated source-code scans of software used in key government and critical infrastructure projects, addressing vulnerabilities at the development stage, he said.
Third, the institute would use agentic AI and large language models to analyze millions of pieces of global cybersecurity intelligence in real time each day and turn them into blocking rules for perimeter security devices, he said.
Fourth, the institute would assist the government and the private sector in building a controlled environment for high-intensity AI-powered cybersecurity attacks, Kung said, adding that this would help build a strong, ingrained defensive response.
Kung said that he found that AI can identify vulnerabilities at least 10 times faster than traditional methods. Government agencies should first establish a comprehensive software bill of materials inventory and prioritize repair based on risk levels, he said, adding that they can deploy virtual patches as temporary measures to block threats, rather than attempting to patch every vulnerability indiscriminately.
Kung said the institute would be committed to strengthening Taiwan’s overall cybersecurity capabilities by working with its incident response center and the Administration for Cybersecurity to help domestic companies establish product security incident response teams (PSIRTs).
The initiative is introduced in line with the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act, Kung said.
This year, the institute plans to assist at least 30 companies in establishing PSIRTs to ensure that vulnerabilities can be reported and patched promptly when discovered, he added.
Regarding frequent DDoS attacks targeting media Web sites, Kung said that the institute and the Taiwan Computer Emergency Response Team/Coordination Center are always ready to provide support.

At least 126 Taiwanese targeted in China’s transnational repression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

At least 126 Taiwanese in 140 cases have been subjected to Chinese transnational repression, the Mainland Affairs Council said yesterday, following news reports of the arrest of a woman who was accused of spying for China on President William Lai’s (賴清德) son and his family in the US.
China has repeatedly threatened the safety of those targeted and their families, the council said, adding that such efforts are aimed not only at Taiwan’s president and government officials, but at Taiwanese as a whole to intimidate them and create a chilling effect.
Taiwanese firmly oppose such actions, it said.
Photo: Chung Li-hua, Taipei Times
The surveillance and following of people by local collaborators at China’s direction, such as the targeting of Lai’s son, are federal felony in the US.
However, similar conduct in Taiwan would not be punishable under current law, highlighting gaps in the nation’s legal framework for countering the various forms of transnational repression Taiwanese face, it said.
The government is working to revise the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法) and hopes people will pay greater attention to and support the effort, it said.
Tunghai University Center for Mainland China and Regional Development Research deputy director Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗) said that for the intelligence agencies of any country, prominent political figures and their family members can be valuable sources of intelligence.
For Taiwan and US national security and protective services, safeguarding the president’s immediate family, assessing potential risks and monitoring unusual contacts are already part of their security responsibilities, he said.
The US decision to arrest the suspect involved and bring criminal charges indicates that China’s surveillance of Lai’s family crossed a red line for US law enforcement and national security, Hung said.
The US arrests and criminal charges were a clear warning to the Chinese government through the judicial system, he added.
If surveillance of the president’s family is not stopped, it would be difficult to predict what kind of security threat it could eventually pose, he said.
By taking action now, the US is signaling to Beijing that Chinese Communist Party cannot simply extend the intelligence-gathering and surveillance methods it uses inside China to other countries, he said.

Hsu allowed her son to use a cellphone to document events in the capacity of a staff photographer at important overseas community gatherings, Hung said, adding that the minister disregarded security risks.
The controversy has sparked discontent among overseas Taiwanese communities, Chen said, calling on Hsu to step down immediately and submit to an investigation.
The OCAC said that all travel plans, staffing arrangements and budget expenditures strictly adhere to the Directions for the Overseas Travel Allowance Disbursement (國外出差旅費報支要點) and budget regulations.
All expense declarations and reimbursements are subject to strict supervision by audit institutions, it added.
The OCAC’s dispatch of overseas personnel and official vehicles also complies with operational regulations, and their usage is strictly limited to official duties, with no private use or overclaiming of expenses, it said.

THSRC plans more trains for pre-weekend travelers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:21 UTC
01:37:21 KST

Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp (THSRC) said yesterday that beginning on Thursday, it would operate eight southbound train services from Taipei to Taichung between 5pm and 9pm every Friday consisting solely of non-reserved seat carriages to ease passenger pressure.
The announcement came after the high-speed railway operator faced criticism for not limiting sales of non-reserved seats for the four-day Mid-Autumn Festival and Teachers’ Day weekend last month, resulting in large numbers of non-reserved-seat passengers spilling into reserved-seat cars and leaving many passengers with reserved seats unable to board during the first two days of the holiday.
Statistics from the Ministry of Transportation and Communications showed the number of high-speed rail passengers reached a record-high 347,979 on the first day of the holiday. The system transported approximately 1.788 million people during the four-day long weekend, ministry data showed.
Photo: Wu Cheng-fung, Taipei Times
Railway Bureau Director-General Yang Cheng-chun (楊正君) said last week that pressure on the high-speed system’s capacity is unlikely to ease until all 12 newly procured train sets enter service by 2028.
The THSRC said three of the new train sets are scheduled to begin operations in July next year. Before new trains are added to the service fleet, the high-speed rail operator said that it would implement special service deployment plans designed to maximize its transport capacity during peak or even super peak hours.
The peak hours for the high-speed rail system refer to the period from 5pm to 9pm on Friday, while the super-peak hours occur when the time coincides with the beginning of a long weekend or a major national holiday, it said.
During peak hours, cabins of non-reserved seats are often crowded, particularly in sections north of Taichung, it said.
Starting on Thursday, eight southbound train services would operate at the beginning of every weekend between 5pm and 9pm and provide only non-reserved seats, except business-class cabins. The eight train services would depart from Nangang or Taipei and terminate in Taichung.
Under the special deployment plan, trains would reverse directions directly at the platforms, without returning to the depot, the company said, adding that trains depart again after a 12-minute interval.
This would reduce the train deployment time by one hour and increase capacity during peak hours, quickly transporting southbound passengers and reducing the wait time for northbound passengers, it added.
The company said that the special scheduling would be implemented for the first time on Thursday, the last workday this week before people begin the three-day holiday weekend.
THSRC would run a pair of Taichung-bound train services departing from Nangang or Taipei hourly from 5pm to 9pm that would stop at every station along the way, each with nine to 11 cars of non-reserved seats.
During the Double Ten National Day holiday travel period, 23 additional train services would be provided to help accommodate increased passenger demand, it said.
To encourage passengers to travel during off-peak hours, an extra late-night service would be operated on Thursday, while an additional northbound service would be added on Saturday, it said.

On a monthly basis, revenue rose 25.7 percent from NT$921.77 billion in August, which the company attributed to strong sales of smart consumer electronics products, mainly smartphones. Last month’s figure exceeded NT$1 trillion for the first time in Hon Hai’s history, the company said in a statement.
Third-quarter revenue rose 47.12 percent year-on-year and 20.44 percent quarter-on-quarter to NT$3.27 trillion, also marking a record high for the period, Hon Hai said.
Photo: I-hwa Cheng, AFP
Analysts on average expected revenue to rise to about NT$2.83 trillion in the third quarter, Bloomberg News reported.
Hon Hai said the better-than-expected third-quarter performance was driven mainly by strong growth in its cloud and networking products, electronic components and computing products businesses.
The cloud and networking products business — primarily servers — posted strong year-on-year revenue growth last quarter, as customers accelerated orders for artificial intelligence (AI)-related products, Hon Hai said.
Hon Hai, also known as Foxconn Technology Group (富士康科技集團), is Apple Inc’s primary iPhone assembler and makes servers powered by Nvidia Corp’s AI accelerators.
The company in August said it expected AI server rack shipments to grow by a high double-digit percentage sequentially in the third quarter, with full-year shipments expected to more than double this year. Strong contributions from AI servers are expected to continue at least until next year, it said.
Last quarter, the electronic components business also posted strong year-on-year growth, driven by higher revenue from its major components operations and other businesses, while the computing products business grew strongly on higher average selling prices and front-loaded shipments, Hon Hai said.
In the first nine months of this year, revenue rose 39.53 percent year-on-year to NT$7.67 trillion, surpassing the previous record of NT$5.5 trillion set in the same period last year, it said.
The company said the cloud and networking products and electronic components segments posted the strongest annual growth among its businesses during the period.
In this quarter, growth momentum from AI-related products is expected to continue, while the traditional peak season for information and communications technology products should also support overall performance, Hon Hai said, adding that uncertainties in the global political and economic environment warrant close monitoring.

Taiwan legalized same-sex marriage in 2019 in a first for Asia and is normally a bastion of tolerance in a region where LGBTQ rights are often suppressed or outlawed. Taipei holds its main Pride event later this month, the largest in East Asia.
Taipei police on Saturday afternoon raided the Commander D bar, citing a complaint alleging the bar might be breaching public decency laws. They took 51 people in for questioning and arrested the owner.
Photo: CNA
Chiang, who has previously attended Taipei Pride, said regardless of age, gender, sexual orientation, identity, ethnicity or beliefs, the government must ensure everyone in Taipei has equal rights.

Wanhua Precinct Chief Chen Yung-hua (陳勇華) was also disciplined, Lin said, adding that Chen had requested two reprimands over inadequate supervision and that the request was approved.

“Taipei’s diversity and inclusivity should not only be visible on Pride parade day,” he wrote.
The Commander D raid was one of three operations on Saturday involving gay bars, police precinct spokesperson Chen Yu-cheng said.
Police had in the past conducted “irregular inspections” of the three venues, he said, adding that the precinct inspected 15 entertainment venues on Saturday.

====================================================================================================

Why a journalist is exposing the world’s biggest porn bosses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:19 UTC
01:37:19 KST

There was a time, a few decades ago, when the men who owned the world’s biggest pornography businesses were happy to be famous. They paraded a lifestyle they hoped looked glamorous, appearing in public dressed in silk pajamas or with a woman in swimwear on each arm. Porn moguls like Hustler’s Larry Flynt or Playboy’s Hugh Hefner were household names.
“Say what you want about these old perverts, who once set the tone of our sexual culture, but at least you knew who they were and what they were selling,” Patricia Nilsson writes in her new book, Guilty Pleasure: The Pornification of the Internet, the Economy and Everything Else. “These days, the men calling the shots are nowhere to be seen.”
It’s not that they simply feel shy about posing alongside the women who generate their income, or are wary of giving interviews. The owners of the industry’s biggest companies are so anxious to remain anonymous that we often don’t even know their names. They have understood that it is wiser to live in total obscurity.
Photo: EPA-EFE
UNDER-SCRUTINIZED
So Nilsson’s decision to start investigating pornography for the Financial Times will no doubt have come as a very unwelcome development for these mostly invisible leaders of a sector that has been under-scrutinized for decades. For five years, she subjected the industry to the same deep analysis that a journalist would give to the oil and gas markets. She wondered why, unlike most businesses of a similar scale, pornography companies rarely made the headlines.
“I started wondering: why is there so much porn everywhere? Why is the online world so saturated with images of people paid to have sex?” Nilsson says.
Photo: AFP
She asks at the start of Guilty Pleasure: “We live in a world where as many people have instantaneous access to free porn as to clean water. Why aren’t we more curious about the growing role of pornography in our lives?”
Nilsson, 34, says she belongs to “the first generation that came of age on the Internet, and to whom oceans of free porn was a normal part of life.” This perspective has shaped her calmly pragmatic approach to the subject.
“Of course there are parts of the industry I’m critical of,” she says. “My argument is not that we should be neutral towards porn, but that we need to accept and understand it as a real industry, and ask what its growth and popularity says about the state of our economy and the world of work.”
Photo: AP
Nilsson is in London when we meet — she has British and Swedish citizenship but Polish roots and lives in Frankfurt, where she is approaching the end of maternity leave (she finished writing her book in the exhausting first weeks after giving birth).
TECH NERDS AND BANKERS
Her investigations led to the discovery that the industry’s owners were now tech nerds and bankers, with no particular interest in pornography itself.
“I started realizing: this industry isn’t really about porn any more. I would go to these porn conferences and I couldn’t find anyone who actually worked with porn. I couldn’t find anyone who even knew someone who worked with porn, because all these people were working in [Web] traffic or payment processing,” she says.
I’ve attended a couple of these conferences and have been equally struck by the quantities of men in zipped tech-bro gilets who want to talk about impenetrably dry notions like affiliate marketing, barely acknowledging that they work in the world of explicit adult content.
Nilsson was determined to bring the sector’s leaders out of the shadows in part because she wanted to reveal who was getting rich through porn and how they were doing it. But she also disliked the hypocrisy of these men, some of whom had become billionaires.
“Online sex workers literally have to bare it all; once you put your image out there on the Internet, even if technically you control the IP, it can be very difficult to ever get it down. So it’s terrible if the people profiting from the industry then have the gall to say: ‘I want to protect my anonymity and I don’t really want to be associated with sex work,’” she says. “They don’t want to put their names out there, they don’t want to put their faces out there.”
She was the first person to track down Bernd Bergmair, the mysterious figure who, from 2013 to 2023, owned MindGeek — then the world’s largest pornography company and the conglomerate operating Pornhub. It turned out he was an Austrian former Goldman Sachs investment banker, described as an “uncle type” in expensive clothes, who had been so determined to stay hidden that others in the pornography world described him as a ghost and doubted his existence. Bergmair had written his undergraduate thesis on “financing strategies for corporate acquisitions,” and knew so little about pornography that, early on, he took his competitors out for lunch to pick their brains on how the business functioned.
A banker who had worked in Frankfurt, London, New York and Hong Kong, Bergmair “seemed entirely uninterested in the sex [work] that underpinned the empire he was buying,” Nilsson notes. “He knew it was a highly profitable business and he just cared about ensuring that the structure was safe enough so that he could keep taking his dividends out.”
In 2020, Pornhub removed millions of unverified videos, some of which may have contained nonconsensual pornography, rape, child sexual abuse, violent sexual abuse of women and other abusive content.
‘MASTURBATORY’ MODEL OF THE INTERNET
We’re already familiar with the way pornography companies drove early improvements in the power of the Internet from the 1990s onwards, to enable large quantities of video to be distributed to the maximum number of people at maximum speed. But Nilsson lists half a dozen other ways that pornography has dictated the way we navigate the Internet.
We can also thank pornography businesses for developing reliable, high-quality video streaming, honed by the need for glitch-free camming, where models broadcast live video feeds of themselves to customers and chat to them. And long before influencers started working out what they needed to do to grow and maintain a lucrative social media following, Webcam models were deciding how best to curate online personas to keep audiences’ attention, and elicit generous tips.
Nilsson says her own virtual world is usually full of cheerful sourdough recipes or restaurants that she wants to check out on her next trip to Sicily, but she realizes now that the way “all this lovely, worthwhile content” is transmitted to her phone, and the way she consumes it, is closely based on a model developed by online pornography tech developers. Companies such as MindGeek trade on desire, so they became expert early on at spotting what people browsing the Internet are genuinely interested in.
“Staring at content that is algorithmically engineered to arouse you is a perfect metaphor for our relationship with our devices and the Internet and social media. Pornography is no longer just about sex — its logic of capturing attention through stimulation, keeping us watching rather than doing, is embedded in the online world,” she says.
Social media sites have learned from innovations developed by pornography companies — how to make the stream of content addictive, how to ensure people stay browsing for a little longer.
“We’re often scrolling, and we feel like we’re living these things, but we’re not. We’re stuck in this sort of endless loop of gratification and self-soothing, and we use our phones to calm ourselves down, or just take our mind off things, but we’re not living.”
She calls this the “masturbatory” model of the Internet; a model that feeds us content designed to “make us feel good, to arouse us, to flatter us, to make us linger.”
She traces a clear line from the carefully flirtatious interactions of women stripping online for camming work, trying to get tips from their clients, to the docile and sycophantic tones given by developers to chatbots, “who indulge our fantasies and make us feel better than any person in our real lives can.”
ONLINE OUTRAGE
In parallel, online outrage also has roots in pornography and the competition for hits, she argues.
“If you look at the state of online culture today … we have so much anger and everything feels so extreme. This follows a trend you could see on Pornhub a long, long time ago — where the onslaught of free material meant that content needed to shock more and more to stand out, making pornography become more and more extreme,” she says.
Anyone who followed last year’s race between the British porn stars Bonnie Blue and Lily Phillips to outdo each other by broadcasting themselves having sex with hundreds of men will know what she means.
Nilsson’s primary focus is analyzing the business model, rather than charting the experiences of the women who create the content. She doesn’t soft-soap the extremes of the industry — documenting, for example, the disturbing popularity of “humiliation porn,” which is pornography that involves actors being used sexually by a group of men to the point of gagging or tears. But many of the women she interviews emphasize how the work has given them options. A different perspective is offered only occasionally.
She tells me she felt awkward when she found herself sitting next to a depressed Webcam model at an adult industry event in Prague one evening. Nilsson had been invited to attend by Katya Tiuni, a Ukrainian woman who went into camming in the 1990s to escape the poverty of the post-communist economic collapse. Tiuni later set up a school for women hoping to become online sex workers, teaching them brand development and how to cultivate long-term audience loyalty (more than 10,000 women have attended her Webinars).
But the young woman next to Nilsson was not enjoying the training.
“I was trying to chat about the job and she was just so unhappy, saying: ‘I don’t want to be here, I miss home, I made a mistake.’ It was such a great contrast to Katya’s lean-in feminism, feeling empowered through making money,” Nilsson says.
This woman’s views on the industry do not make it into the book.
Instead, Nilsson is at pains to avoid judgment.
“Historically, much feminist analysis of sex work has come from women who have never done it, or never been in circumstances where it might seem like the best option available. If we are genuinely interested in supporting sex workers, their own accounts of what the work means to them have to be central to the conversation,” she says.
Thinking about what the proliferation of online pornography means for women, like her, who have to “live in a world where the idea that you can buy female attention and affection” has become mainstream, is a “completely different conversation to what it actually means to people who are doing sex work.”
More interesting, she says, is to think about why so many women are opting to go into this world. She wonders what we can learn “about the state of capitalism when so many people are saying: ‘Actually, it’s not going to work for me to get a degree and try to get a job and work my way up because just earning an income, if you don’t have previous assets, is not working any more. I need to hustle to get a down payment on my house.’”
Finally, she is curious about the links between social media and a growing readiness to post explicit content.
“Why,” she asks, “do we have an online culture that has made self-exposure so normalized, and the drive to monetize one’s own image so normalized, that the step to actually selling pornography is not that big for many people?”
Mark Carney built a global profile this year by standing up to US President Donald Trump. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi yesterday called China an “important neighbor” and pledged to build a stable relationship between the rival nations in a policy address.

Photo: Bloomberg
“We will work to ensure communication on shared challenges, promote dialogue to safeguard our national interests, and build a constructive and stable relationship,” she said.
However, she added that Japan would also “firmly assert our country’s positions” and “strongly call for responsible behavior.”
Takaichi also signaled her government would draft a comprehensive plan to deal with population decline, which she called a “quietly advancing national crisis.”
Despite enjoying unusually high approval ratings a year into office, Takaichi is navigating a number of challenges, including rising inflation, market concerns about Japan’s mounting debts and a diplomatic spat with China that has been rumbling since making the comments about Taiwan last year.
The policy speech came after China’s top diplomat last week said ties with Tokyo were “waiting to be normalized again” as he met a former Japanese foreign minister who was leading a trade delegation in Beijing.
China had last year warned its citizens against travel to Japan, and imposed trade restrictions that have reportedly led to big drops in supplies of vital rare earth minerals to Japanese firms.
On population decline, Takaichi promised to formulate a comprehensive strategy by the end of the year. The number of Japanese people living in the country fell below 120 million for the first time in 42 years, according to government data released in July.
She also pledged to ensure she had the trust of the market, repeating her commitment to a proactive and responsible fiscal policy, after her program of expansive government spending rattled markets.
The parliamentary session, scheduled to run through December, is to discuss several bills, including plans to cut a consumption tax on food for two years to curb the impact of inflation on voters’ daily lives.
Takaichi’s speech also included a pledge to support the International Criminal Court after the US targeted the tribunal’s Japanese president, Tomoko Akane, with sanctions in August.

Taiwan’s Rita Chou on Sunday won the Women’s 9-Ball World Championship in Bali, Indonesia, securing the title for the second time.
Chou, 39, defeated defending champion Seo Seoa of South Korea three sets to one (4-1, 1-4, 4-1, 4-1) to claim US$55,000 in prize money.
After splitting the opening two sets on Sunday, Chou won the first three racks of the third. A scratch on the break allowed Seo to pull one back, but Chou capitalized on a failed safety to clear the table and take the set.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Sports
In the fourth set, Chou recovered from a 1-0 deficit, winning four consecutive racks, after errors by her opponent, to seal the championship.
Chou reached the final with straight-set victories against China’s Huang Qingning in the quarter-finals and Japan’s Chihiro Kawahara in the semi-finals.
Seo, 23, had eliminated three Taiwanese players — Chou Chia-chia, Chiang Shui-ching and Wei Tzu-chien — on her way to the final.
Chou’s defeat of the defending champion marked the second time that a Taiwanese player secured two world titles in the women’s 9-ball competition.
Taiwan’s Liu Hsin-mei won the title in 1999 and 2002, becoming the first Taiwanese woman to do so twice.
Chou won her first title in 2023, when she also defeated Seo in the semi-finals and beat Britain’s Allison Fisher in the final.
This year’s tournament, held from Monday to Sunday last week featured 64 players, the organizers said.

Filipino priests bless pets for Saint Francis feast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:14 UTC
01:37:14 KST

It was a day for wagging tails, happy faces and a special annual blessing at a church in the Philippine capital.
Every Oct. 4, Catholics mark the feast day of Saint Francis of Assisi, the patron saint of animals and ecology, remembered for his humility, compassion and deep love for all living things. Many parishes choose the first Sunday of October to hold community animal blessings or Saint Francis service events.
At Malate Church in Manila, parishioners marked the feast by bringing their beloved pets for a special blessing — mostly dogs, but also cats and even a pet snail.
Photo: EPA
“We are blessing the animals and plants and this is so much in relation to the feast of Saint Francis of Assisi ... so the Malate parish has been advocating this one,” said Father Leonito Distor, parish priest of the church.
Parishioners formed a line as they walked up the aisle with their pets, waiting patiently for a priest to sprinkle their companions with holy water.
For pet owners, it was a simple expression of gratitude for the unconditional love, joy and companionship these animal friends bring into their lives every day while honoring Saint Francis’ call to respect and care for all of God’s creation.
“They are part of our family ... not exactly like us in the sense that they can’t speak, but they do have emotions,” said 32-year-old nurse Gaudine Supnet, who owns four Shih Tzu dogs. “I want them to feel, in some way, that we are grateful for their presence in our lives; that’s why we have them blessed.”
The church also organized free pet vaccinations for dogs and cats in the church parking lot.

CGA seizes NT$1.62 billion worth of drugs in largest marijuana bust in a decade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:13 UTC
01:37:13 KST

The Coast Guard Administration (CGA) yesterday at a press conference displayed 815kg of marijuana and other narcotics seized on June 3, marking Taiwan’s largest marijuana bust in a decade.
The drugs had an estimated market value of nearly NT$1.62 billion, according to the CGA.
The CGA said the investigation was led by its Keelung Enforcement Team under the direction of the Keelung District Prosecutors Office, with personnel from various CGA branches and police in New Taipei City and Hsinchu City joining the operation. Investigators closely monitored a suspicious truck with an unusual schedule and deployed teams along the coast of Keelung and in New Taipei City’s Rueifang District (瑞芳), it said.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
At around midnight on June 3, the task force launched a raid at a parking lot in Rueifang as suspects were transferring items from the truck to a passenger car. Authorities seized 1,309 packages containing 766.09kg of dried marijuana flowers, 43.25kg of amphetamine and 5.34kg of mixed drugs, including ketamine, it said.
CGA personnel arrested three suspects at the scene and later tracked down four others, including the alleged ringleader, surnamed Lee (李), it said.
The cases were referred to prosecutors for investigation on charges of violating the Narcotics Hazard Prevention Act (毒品危害防制條例), the CGA said. Prosecutors indicted the suspects on Aug. 24, it added.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰), who attended yesterday’s press conference, said the bust took place on June 3, Taiwan’s Opium Suppression Movement Day, making the seizure particularly significant.
Noting that students across Taiwan were finishing the school year and preparing for summer vacation in June, Cho said the large quantity of drugs could have harmed students’ physical and mental health had the drugs made their way into schools and society.
Cho thanked frontline law enforcement officers for their patience and expertise in carrying out the interagency drug crackdown.
He pledged the government would not only reward their efforts but would also provide stronger support by increasing manpower and upgrading equipment and technology, ensuring that frontline personnel have the resources they need to combat drug trafficking.

Kuai Kuai workers set to vote on ending strike today
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:11 UTC
01:37:11 KST

The Kuai Kuai union’s strike would likely end today after Kuai Kuai Co agreed to union demands, said the Taoyuan City Government’s Department of Labor yesterday.
Department commissioner Lee Hsien-hsiang (李賢祥) made the remark after holding a negotiations yesterday afternoon between the union and the company, during which he said company chairman Chung Yu-lin (鍾育霖) agreed to the union’s demands.
Under the proposed terms, employees who resign following a job transfer would receive four months’ additional pay on top of the statutory severance package, while those who choose not to relocate with the company two years after the plant move would receive eight months’ additional compensation in addition to statutory severance pay.
Photo courtesy of the Taoyuan Confederation of Trade Unions via CNA
Union Chairman Liu Neng-hung (劉能宏) said the union would hold a provisional meeting today to vote on the proposal and would call off the strike if it is approved.
Earlier yesterday, the union, whose members work at the company’s Jhongli factory, voiced their concerns during a protest outside the Ministry of Labor in Taipei, four days after workers began a strike that was later extended indefinitely.
The dispute arose after Kuai Kuai workers learned in July through the news that Kuai Kuai, which has been owned by the San-Ti Group since 2019, sold the Jhongli site to Advanced Semiconductor Engineering for NT$5.67 billion (US$178.37 million).
As part of the deal, Kuai Kuai would lease back parts of the site for up to two years while preparing to relocate.
The deal sparked concern among workers that the company would abandon them and force them into resigning by relocating without paying them severance and other layoff benefits.
In response to the strike on Friday, Kuai Kuai said it would not lay off workers for the two years it remains at the Jhongli site, and would provide statutory severance plus two months’ wages for ensuing layoffs.
Peng Kuei-mei (彭桂梅), a union board member, said the no-layoff pledge “provides employees with no protection at all,” saying that the company could still meet that pledge if workers left on their own, in which case they would not receive severance.
Employees who left after the relocation because the new factory was too far away or had unsuitable working conditions could be denied severance because they were not formally laid off, she said.
To deal with the issue, the union is seeking compensation for any relocation, which could impose a heavier burden on the factory’s many middle-aged and older workers, who might struggle to find new jobs or adapt to a new work location, it said.
Peng questioned the company’s uncertain relocation plans, with Pingtung County and then Hsinchu and Taoyuan being considered but no site being secured.
“How can employees be expected to keep working for two years and believe they will still have jobs afterward?” Peng said.
The union said that a labor broker had twice brought migrant workers to the picket line on Friday last week and asked them whether they wanted to enter the factory to work, in what the union said was an attempt to get them to cross the picket line.
The union questioned whether an employer or broker should be allowed to require migrant workers to make such declarations.
In response to the protest, Chin Shih-ping (金士平), a section chief at the labor ministry’s Department of Employment Relations, reiterated that companies must not subject workers participating in union activities or strikes to “adverse treatment.”
Asked specifically about the broker’s actions, Chin described the circumstances as “complicated” and would require further review before the ministry could take a position.
According to the union, the plant has about 160 Taiwanese employees, including 155 union members, and about 60 migrant workers, mainly from Vietnam and Indonesia, none of whom are union members.

TV host Kevin Tsai faces backlash over Shen event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:09 UTC
01:37:09 KST

Taiwanese television host Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) has faced a backlash in China after he on Sunday attended the opening of Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign headquarters.
Shen has been called a “staunch Taiwanese independence separatist” by the Chinese Communist Party, which has threatened to hold him accountable under its anti-secessionist laws.
A livestream showed Tsai, who previously hosted the popular variety show Kangsi Coming (康熙來了), holding a campaign balloon bearing the slogan “Let Taipei Get Back on Track” and waving a cheering stick alongside supporters, drawing widespread attention online.
Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
Asked about his attendance, Tsai reportedly said he had come to “see what it was like” and hear different perspectives, adding that he might attend events for other candidates and would like to interview them all.
His manager said Tsai’s attendance was preliminary research for possible interviews with both candidates.
Tsai’s appearance at Shen’s event became a trending topic on Chinese social media, with posts labeling Tsai a “separatist.”
Chinese electric vehicle maker Leapmotor, which last month announced Tsai as a brand “partner,” removed promotional content related to the entertainer by Sunday evening and issued a statement reaffirming its commitment to Beijing’s “one China” principle, while fashion magazine Harper’s Bazaar China deleted an interview with Tsai published last month.
Shen yesterday called the backlash unfair, saying that Tsai had simply come to the event to learn about the candidates’ policy platform.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), who is seeking re-election, urged China to respect Taiwan’s free and democratic way of life and not discriminate against people because of their political views.
“I support and respect Tsai’s right to express any views of his own,” Chiang told reporters.
KMT caucus secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said the caucus opposed efforts by Chinese Internet users and businesses to blacklist Tsai, adding that Beijing should respect freedom of speech and democracy.
Taiwan is a democratic and pluralistic society in which everyone has the right to learn about candidates’ policies and ideas, Hsu said.
Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), deputy executive director of Tunghai University’s Center for Mainland China and Regional Development Research, said the incident illustrated how Beijing uses its market power to influence the politics of Taiwanese entertainers.
As China has already branded Shen a “die-hard Taiwanese independence separatist,” publicly attending his campaign event could carry commercial consequences for entertainers in the Chinese market, Hung said.
Political labeling, online pressure and corporate action are used to enforce Beijing’s political red lines, he said.
Businesses know where the political lines are and take steps to protect their interests without direct government intervention, he added.
The incident sends a warning to entertainers, businesses and others who associate with the DPP or politicians whom the Beijing has threatened to sanction, Hung said.
China is seeking to establish boundaries for political engagement by making political associations carry a price, he said.
Once Chinese market pressure spills into Taiwan’s elections, it threatens the autonomy of the nation’s democracy, Hung said.
Beijing does not need to dictate how Taiwanese people vote if it can raise the cost of supporting certain parties and politicians, he added.
By making Taiwanese weigh the risk of losing jobs, endorsements and other commercial opportunities in China before participating in their own elections, Beijing is extending its political red lines into Taiwan’s democratic system, he said.
China can draw red lines in its own market, but it has no right to impose them on Taiwanese, Hung said.

What happens when Chinese AI goes rogue?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:08 UTC
01:37:08 KST

Covering the recent round of artificial intelligence (AI) apocalypse warnings, I have tried to reject this cult-like deference toward all-powerful computer systems and the inevitability rhetoric: If Silicon Valley does not build them first, someone else — likely China — will.
Yet a recent spate of incidents in the US has spurred a fresh, heated debate on the safety of allowing AI systems to act on their own. A growing number of researchers inside the companies involved are also warning of “existential” dangers, with Anthropic PBC even flagging such concerns to investors in its initial public offering prospectus.
For China, the risks of near-term hazards like labor market threats or the more alarming science-fiction scenarios such as hacks on critical infrastructure are making it harder to write off the furor as a distinctly US obsession.
Beijing has dismissed some of these warnings as “fearmongering,” seeing the calls to slow AI development as an attempt to hold China back. However, voices inside the industry have also suggested that frontier risks simply are not being felt as acutely at home because they are further behind the US.
Huawei Technologies Co’s rotating chairman Eric Xu (徐直軍) wondered whether Chinese AI was advanced enough to encounter the “type of risk” US providers were increasingly debating. AI model makers in China “may need to speed up their pace” to reach the level that they could “also feel the risks,” Xu said, while acknowledging the need for balance, according to Reuters. It shows how global debate has devolved in unhelpful ways.
Accelerating the race is the wrong answer on both sides of the Pacific. There are nearly 1,000 large language models in China, according to Bloomberg Intelligence. Competition on this scale already makes even Silicon Valley’s breakneck pace seem muted.
The Chinese industry has also been plowing significantly more resources into agents, or systems that can act more autonomously. Agent misbehavior, especially the Hugging Face Inc incident in July, when one of OpenAI’s agents broke out of its evaluation environment and broke into Hugging Face’s systems, has kicked off this safety reckoning.
As the short-lived OpenClaw frenzy showed, even China’s nontechnical public is willing to experiment with them. It means if agentic AI is inherently more risky, it is likely only a matter of time before we see concerning behavior from Chinese AI tools.
Companies are aware. A DeepSeek paper that includes founder and chief executive officer Liang Wenfeng (梁文鋒) as a coauthor bluntly warns that agent behavior can be “untrustworthy.” Escaping containment is not a distinctly US risk, either. Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 exploited a loophole in a sandbox during cybersecurity testing, US-based Frontier Security said. Some Chinese AI agents have also shown the kind of deceptive and concerning trends that have raised alarm about US tools.
While Beijing has pushed back on some of the “doomerism,” policymakers are paying attention. China last month released AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, a policy document that notably also dropped in English, clearly aimed for Western audiences. It explicitly warns that AI has demonstrated a “self-accelerating trend,” adding that the question of whether this could exceed human control demands attention and vigilance.
Another cornerstone of the latest safety contention is recursive self-improvement, or AI systems that can autonomously advance their own capabilities. It is the development path that spurred an Anthropic researcher to quit and warn that makers of the technology earnestly believe it could “kill us all” within a decade.
As Oxford China Policy Lab research associate Qian Zilan (錢子蘭) has said, China is further along in this regard than many in the West might realize, partly because its researchers describe it in different terms. It all reveals how little visibility each side has into the risks of what the other is building.
In discussing the technology’s risks, Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) has warned — most recently in conversation with US President Donald Trump — that “AI must be kept under human control.”
Xi’s self-interest in maintaining order offers a narrowing window for cooperation on risk mitigation dialogue. It also exposes the limits of the safety protocols that did emerge from the Trump-Xi summit, namely a new “channel” for reporting AI-related incidents.
These hotlines have not always been effective. During the 2023 spy-balloon crisis, the Pentagon tried to reach its Chinese counterparts through a crisis line but Beijing declined the call. Such a setup is also inherently retroactive. Preventative risk sharing also does not have to depend solely on government-to-government talks, especially when regulators might struggle to keep pace with the technical knowledge.
It would be more productive to have outlets where companies and researchers can exchange information more directly.
China has burdensome regulations in place surrounding AI; using it as the boogeyman is no longer a convincing excuse for inaction from lawmakers in Washington.
If Chinese AI systems are just months behind, and the country’s all-out push for agents comes to fruition, it is likely a matter of time before more concerning scenarios emerge from the other side of the Pacific. Policymakers should act before the next incident is more than just a warning shot.
Catherine Thorbecke is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia tech. Previously she was a tech reporter at CNN and ABC News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Nobel medicine prize goes to US, German scientists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:08 UTC
01:37:08 KST

The Nobel Prize in medicine was yesterday awarded to three scientists who created a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.
Karl Deisseroth, 54, Peter Hegemann, 71, and Georg Nagel, 73, have carried out research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.
The Nobel Assembly lauded their work and said the method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries.
Photo: AFP
The assembly said Deisseroth is based at Stanford University in California, while Hegemann is at Humboldt University in Berlin and Nagel at the University of Wurzburg, also in Germany.
Optogenetics opened what the Nobel assembly called a new era in neuroscience, the discovery of a light-controlled switch to turn on and off nerve cells and circuits in the brain to better learn how it works — to start unraveling the pathways that lead to behavior and disease.
It started when Hegemann explored how a single-celled type of green algae can swim toward light. He and Nagel discovered a particular protein that, when illuminated by blue light, opens a channel to create an electrical impulse. Putting that protein into other cells makes them light-sensitive.
Photo: AP
Deisseroth then worked with the gene that controls that protein to create a light-controlled switch for nerve cells in the brains of living mice.
“It’s a very precise set of tools for doing experiments about how the brain works that are pretty hard to do any other way,” the University of Pittsburgh’s Jeremy Berg said.
He was at the National Institutes of Health in the early 2000s when it awarded Deisseroff major funding for “this vision of optogenetics that was pretty much spot-on the way it played out.”
Deisseroth, a self-described night owl, said he was up late in his northern California home working on papers and e-mailing his students. He had just gone to lie down when he got the call from the Nobel Assembly.
“No real sleep was achieved,” he told The Associated Press in a phone call an hour after the announcement.
He said the next task on his to-do list was to pack school lunches for his children, who were still sound asleep.
Thomas Perlmann, the secretary of the medicine committee, said he was able to reach all three winners.
The prize was announced at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about US$1.2 million).
Last year, the prize went to three scientists researching the immune system.

Streamlining the carbon fee system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:08 UTC
01:37:08 KST

In June of this year, the Ministry of Environment completed its first collection cycle under the carbon fee system, the first phase of which targets close to 500 of Taiwan’s largest emitters. The scheme is to be gradually expanded to encompass small and medium-sized manufacturers and commercial service providers that emit less carbon individually but exist in large numbers, with established carbon pricing mechanisms and the option of voluntary reduction plans that qualify companies for reduced rates.
This climate policy, which has significant implications for the green transformation of Taiwan’s industrial structure and its competitiveness in global supply chains, demonstrates the government’s commitment to implementing the Climate Change Response Act (氣候變遷因應法) and achieving its 2050 net zero emissions target. However, implementation faces a number of challenges, including carbon fee rate disputes, stringent approval requirements for voluntary emissions reduction plans, and a lack of carbon accounting capacity among small and medium-sized enterprises. Striking a balance between carbon pricing incentives, international competitiveness, and the burden of corporate transition has become a pressing public policy issue for central government agencies to confront.
Carbon pricing seeks to internalize the external costs of greenhouse gas emissions, directing investment and technological development toward low-carbon innovation. However, if it is designed primarily as a revenue-raising mechanism while neglecting financial support for companies’ efforts to develop and implement emissions reduction technologies, it risks triggering carbon leakage. This occurs when high carbon fee costs prompt the relocation of operations to other countries with weaker environmental regulations, dealing a blow to global emissions reduction efforts and the domestic economy. If the review process for voluntary emissions reduction plans lacks clarity and objective, quantifiable criteria, it risks leaving excessive room for administrative discretion and bias. This could create unfair competition between industries and infringe on businesses’ property rights and freedom of operation.
Strong governance in the transition to a carbon fee system requires a legal framework built on stable rules, transparent procedures and predictability. Drawing on the examples of the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and Singapore’s carbon tax system, earmarking carbon fee revenues for specific purposes and introducing phased tax incentives are essential to maintaining resilience throughout the industrial transition.
Central government authorities should establish a legal requirement that 100 percent of carbon fee revenues be allocated to a specific greenhouse gas reduction fund and be earmarked for subsidies that help businesses upgrade low-carbon equipment, develop green energy technologies and conduct carbon capture, utilization and storage trials. Clear funding mechanisms and due process in the provision of technical support are essential to alleviating businesses’ fears about their viability in the face of double taxation and rising transition costs.
To streamline Taiwan’s carbon pricing framework and help industries make a smooth transition, central government authorities should amend the Regulations Governing Self-determined Reduction Plans (自主減量計畫管理辦法) and establish clear statutory criteria for qualifying for preferential carbon fee rates. The ministry should revise regulations to grant substantial carbon fee deductions directly to companies that adopt renewable electricity and meet statutory benchmarks for improving energy efficiency. It should also establish a streamlined online review system to eliminate regulatory uncertainty in administrative procedures.
Most importantly, the government should establish a public-private partnership to help small and medium enterprises measure their carbon emissions and transition to lower-carbon operations. The Ministry of Economic Affairs and the Ministry of Digital Affairs could jointly assess those enterprises’ digital and green transition needs, develop free, decentralized carbon accounting tools that do not require expensive software, and bring in third-party verification bodies. This would help traditional industries with limited resources establish compliant carbon footprint data and safeguard their ability to compete fairly within supply chains.
The continued rollout of the carbon fee system is key to Taiwan’s transition to net zero emissions and its standing in international green supply chains. The climate crisis demands urgent action, and the path to industrial transition must be grounded in justice, reason and the rule of law. The Ministry of Environment, the Ministry of Economic Affairs and the Executive Yuan should respond directly to the concerns of industry and environmental groups and undertake sweeping reforms to climate regulations and industrial incentive programs across government agencies.
The carbon fee system must be an engine for industrial upgrading in Taiwan. It is critical for national competitiveness and environmental justice that this regulatory framework operates with professionalism, rigor and proper legal procedures — and that every review of fee rates and emissions reduction plans withstands practical scrutiny. Only then can Taiwan turn the climate crisis into an opportunity for transformation and secure a more stable and conducive environment for economic development in the global transition toward a sustainable future.
Roger Lo is a freelancer.

Will the NHI’s new budget help the staff?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:07 UTC
01:37:07 KST

On Sept. 23, negotiations over next year’s National Health Insurance (NHI) global budget reached a conclusion. The NHI Committee set the growth rate for overall expenditure — encompassing hospitals, primary care clinics, dental services and traditional Chinese medicine — at 5.5 percent for next year. This pushes the total budget just above NT$1 trillion (US$31.46 billion) for the first time. It is the second consecutive year that an agreement has been reached to increase the budget, reflecting a consensus among medical professionals and payers on the need for greater investment in healthcare. The question is whether this additional funding can improve working conditions and help retain staff.
The negotiations included almost NT$5.8 billion in additional funding to improve nurses’ pay, which would be included in next year’s budget. How effectively this is allocated remains to be seen. The overall budget increase accounts for the demands of an aging population and rising medical costs. It cannot be treated as a surplus that hospitals and clinics are free to spend as they see fit. The scale of investment and how the money is used are two separate questions, and they are equally important.
Increased government reimbursements under NHI do not directly translate to higher wages for medical staff; healthcare institutions must first decide how to internally distribute the funds. Payment structures certainly affect institutional income, but it is ultimately management that has control over salaries, hiring and staffing schedules. When discussing staff retention, it is critical to ask not just how much the government is investing, but how employers are using the resources they receive.
When healthcare institutions “raise wages,” are these increases to fixed salaries or available bonuses tied to additional conditions? The Ministry of Health and Welfare has said that the average monthly salaries it publicly reports factor in non-regular payments. These averages alone cannot tell us how compensation has changed; if higher earnings are coming from working more night shifts and overtime, it cannot be claimed that working conditions have materially improved.
There are better ways to assess the effectiveness of retention efforts, such as measuring how much of the additional funding is being spent on personnel; how much fixed salaries have increased; and where the patient care workload per shift decreases after new staff are hired. Comparing salaries, actual working hours, vacancies and turnover rates is the only way to understand how much conditions for frontline workers have actually changed. It is worth examining whether or not improved pay for one professional group affects the salaries and workloads of others.
Clarifying how funds are distributed within institutions requires accounting for the different services provided and financial constraints faced by different facilities. Attributing all staffing shortages to the same cause should be avoided. However, responsible resource allocation can still exist under financial hardship; concrete measures for staff retention must be offered alongside explanations of cost pressures.
The NHI Committee’s consensus in negotiations completes just one stage of budget allocation. For frontline medical workers, the most pressing questions remain: Do salaries reflect the work they put in? Can they actually take time off? Can they see a stable future in the profession? It is the employers who control salaries and working arrangements that must provide answers to these questions.
Lu Chun-wei is a dermatologist and assistant professor at Chang Gung Memorial Hospital.
