Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Ukrainian pilots will begin training on French Rafale aircraft in France in the very near future,” Zelensky said. “This is a strong step for Ukrainian combat aviation.”
New aid package as Russia steps up strikes
Paris is also preparing a new package of military supplies for Ukraine, which Kyiv expects to receive soon, Zelensky said. While he did not disclose what the package would include, he confirmed that its contents were on the agenda during the call.
In a post on X, Macron reaffirmed France’s full support for Ukraine.
“With President Zelensky, we took stock of the concrete support we can provide to help Ukraine intercept drones and thwart Russia’s aggression,” he said, noting that France would continue providing support to the country despite intimidation or escalation by Russia.
The call came as Ukraine braces for its fifth winter of war, amid concerns that Russia will continue its campaign of targeting the country’s energy grid and other critical infrastructure.
Beyond the fighter jets, Zelensky said Ukrainian and French teams are continuing work on producing French missiles and aerial bombs in Ukraine.
Russia Strikes Kharkiv With Guided Bombs Killing 6, Wounding 59, Including Children
The groundwork for the cooperation was laid in July, when Paris agreed to support licensed production in Ukraine of AASM Hammer glide bombs, Aster 30 interceptors for SAMP/T air defense systems, and SCALP cruise missiles.
The two countries are also working to advance FREYJA, a Ukraine-led initiative to develop an affordable anti-ballistic missile defense system. Launched in Paris in July, the project brings together Ukraine, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the UK.
Zelensky said he and Macron had discussed ways to speed up the work and agreed to go over the details when they meet in person, though no date has been set publicly.
From 100-jet plan to first 16 aircraft
Zelensky’s latest announcement follows France’s earlier confirmation that it had started preparing Ukrainian pilots for the aircraft.
According to UNN citing French Minister Delegate for European Affairs Benjamin Haddad, the training follows the standard French Air Force path; first, the pilots start on Grob G-120TP light trainers, move on to Dornier Alpha Jet advanced trainers and only then transition to frontline fighters.
Once the course is complete, Ukraine could receive its first four Rafales.
The training is the first practical step in a deal that has been taking shape for nearly a year. In November 2025, Zelensky and Macron signed a letter of intent for Ukraine to acquire up to 100 Rafales.
In July, Kyiv and Paris agreed on a roadmap for the first 16 jets, along with an unspecified amount of weaponry, which is expected to be financed through the EU’s €90 billion ($103 billion) Ukraine Support Loan and other sources.
As part of the same July agreement, France pledged two more SAMP/T air defense systems by the end of 2026 and four to eight upgraded SAMP/T NG systems in the following years.
Deliveries of Aster 30 interceptors, which are in short supply in Ukraine, were also expected to increase from October.

Iran executes two men linked to anti-govt protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:17:47 UTC
01:17:47 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran executes two men linked to anti-govt protests
Iran's judiciary said two men were executed on Monday for involvement in the deaths of four police officers during anti-government protests that peaked in January.
Authorities accused them of murdering the officers in the central city of Isfahan during protests that began in the capital, Tehran, in December over economic grievances before spreading nationwide.
The movement rapidly evolved into large anti-government rallies that peaked on 8 and 9 January, causing unprecedented destruction and thousands of deaths.
"Alireza Sepahi and Alireza Raissi were hanged this morning after the Supreme Court upheld the verdict," the judiciary's Mizan Online website said, without specifying the dates of their arrest or trial.
The court had sentenced the two men, whose ages were not given, to death "for membership in an armed group and undermining national security", Mizan added.
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths in the unrest, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel.
Foreign-based NGOs, citing much higher death tolls, maintain, however, that Iranian security forces fired on protesters.
The number of executions in Iran has risen since the start of the Middle East war, which was triggered in late February by US-Israeli strikes.
In 2025, Iran executed at least 1,639 people, the largest number in any year since 1989, according to the NGOs Iran Human Rights and Together Against the Death Penalty.
Amnesty International says Iran carries out more executions than any country except China.
On Saturday, Iran announced the execution of another man convicted of a raft of charges, including firing a military-grade weapon at police officers during the protests.

The Armed Forces of Ukraine will receive the Varkhan robotic system — technical specifications and battlefield strengths
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian Varkhan unmanned ground complex transports hundreds of kilograms of cargo over dozens of kilometers. The system has all-wheel drive, replaceable batteries and several control systems.
The Ministry of Defence has codified and authorized the Varkhan unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) for supply to the Armed Forces of Ukraine. It is designed to perform a wide range of military logistics missions: delivering weapons, ammunition, equipment, hardware, and more, UNN reports, citing the Ministry of Defence.
Tactical and technical characteristics (TTC) of the Varkhan UGV
The Varkhan UGV was manufactured at a Ukrainian defense enterprise in response to requests from military personnel who need the appropriate equipment to perform logistics tasks. The engineers incorporated all the defenders’ requirements into its design.
The Varkhan unmanned ground platform is highly versatile, reliable, and durable. It is built on an all-wheel-drive chassis with a 4×4 wheel arrangement, dependent suspension, and ground clearance of more than 200 mm. The design ensures good off-road capability and allows the system to move confidently across difficult terrain, in severe off-road conditions, marshland, and sand.
The platform is equipped with quick-release batteries, enabling it to carry out missions continuously.
Strengths of the Varkhan system on the battlefield
The Varkhan unmanned ground vehicle demonstrated high tactical and technical characteristics during testing. Its capabilities are sufficient to transport hundreds of kilograms of cargo over several dozen kilometers. In addition, the Varkhan UGV has several communication/control systems.
The Varkhan system meets the requirements of modern high-intensity warfare:
-  continuous operation; 
-  reliable, durable components and assemblies; 
-  a clear control algorithm; 
-  availability of spare parts and consumables; 
-  high tactical and technical characteristics; 
-  extensive logistics capabilities; 
-  ease of maintenance. 
The Varkhan UGV is part of an ecosystem of integrated solutions. It includes T-Bone ground control stations, antennas, masts, repeaters, and rotary mechanisms.
Combining these products makes it possible to develop integrated solutions for controlling unmanned systems and ensuring stable communications.
It should be recalled
Earlier, the Ministry of Defence codified the Zmiі Mini Strike reconnaissance and strike UGV. It was designed jointly with engineers from one of the most effective combat brigades of the Defense Forces and manufactured taking into account more than four years of wartime experience and analysis of the combat use of ground drones on the battlefield.

ICC unseals arrest warrants for Taliban education ministers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:16:48 UTC
01:16:48 KST

ICC unseals arrest warrants for Taliban education ministers
The International Criminal Court on Monday unsealed warrants for Afghan Education Minister Habibullah Agha, and Higher Education Minister Neda Mohammad Nadeem, accusing two senior Taliban officials of crimes against humanity for denying Afghanistan's women and girls over 12 their rights to an education.
The International Criminal Court on Monday unsealed arrest warrants for two Afghan education ministers accused of committing crimes against humanity through the Taliban government's restrictions on women and girls.
The warrants, for Habibullah Agha, minister of education, and Neda Mohammad Nadeem, minister of higher education, were issued on September 9, 2025 and remained under seal until Monday.
The two officials are accused of gender-based persecution linked to policies that have barred girls over the age of 12 from school and excluded women from higher education following the Taliban's return to power in August 2021.
The ICC warrants were likely to increase international pressure on the Taliban government.
AFP has approached Taliban authorities for comment.
The two warrants against the ministers were issued after the ICC authorised warrants in July 2025 for Afghanistan's Supreme Taliban Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and Supreme Court President Abdul Hakim Haqqani – parts of which have been made public.
Both Agha and Nadeem have played key roles in implementing the supreme leader's vision for Afghanistan.
"There are reasonable grounds to believe" the suspects committed "the crime against humanity of persecution on gender grounds", the court said.
It said the persecution was directed against women and girls, and the deprivation of their fundamental rights was committed "in connection with" other alleged crimes under the Taliban government's policies, including "imprisonment, torture, rape and enforced disappearance".
The court said the alleged crimes were committed in Afghanistan from the Taliban's takeover until at least January 20, 2025.
'Worsening' oppression
The ICC's disclosure of the warrants came the same day the UN Human Rights Council urged the Taliban authorities to repeal their "worsening" and "systematic oppression of all women and girls in Afghanistan".
The council's 47 member countries unanimously criticised that discrimination "and the harms that it has entrenched, which are unbearable, unjustifiable and should shock the conscience of humanity".
The ICC's Pre-Trial Chamber II said it decided to unseal all four warrants – with redactions – after concluding that doing so would not unduly affect ongoing investigations and could "prevent the commission of further crimes by the suspects".
Publication could also "promote cooperation by the international community... in relation to the situation in Afghanistan", it said.
Afghans across the country have told AFP journalists of severe mental health problems tied to the education ban, with teenage girls and women mostly staying at home.
Afghan universities are now men-only zones, where smartphones are banned and students can be chastised if their beards are not long enough.
Some women and girls have tried to continue their education by studying online, but their efforts are hampered by internet and electricity problems across Afghanistan.
Women are increasingly absent from public life and need to abide by a strict dress code when they leave home, covering everything but their eyes.
They are banned from most jobs and a host of public places – including parks – and must have a close male relative escort them on long journeys.
The higher education ban has led to staff shortages in hospitals, multiple healthcare workers told AFP, as women are no longer allowed to qualify as doctors.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

====================================================================================================

Israel is rewriting the Palestinian curriculum in East Jerusalem to erase Palestinian identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:15:52 UTC
01:15:52 KST

Sally Assi, 34, recalled watching her 11-year-old daughter, Aline, a third-grader at Nour al-Huda School in the town of Beit Hanina in occupied East Jerusalem, arrange her drawing supplies before asking her, “Do you know why we draw Jerusalem?”
“Because it’s beautiful… right?” Aline answered.
Assi smiled, but her question to her daughter wasn’t really about drawing. “Jerusalem isn’t just walls and the Dome of the Rock,” Assi told Mondoweiss. “Jerusalem, to our generation and the generations before us, is a living history. It has cities, people, prisoners, stories, dreams.”
What Assi is describing from her kitchen in the town of Betunia, adjacent to Ramallah, is not an isolated worry among Palestinian parents whose children attend schools in East Jerusalem, under the control of the Israeli Ministry of Education. It is the front line of a rapid, Israeli-driven transformation of Palestinian education in the occupied city, where the Israeli curriculum has become mandatory for every first- and seventh-grade class as of this school year, affecting well over a third of Palestinian students in East Jerusalem.
Now, these tens of thousands of Palestinian children, for the first time since Israel illegally annexed and occupied the city in 1967, are using the Israeli curriculum as part of an effort to “Israelize” the schools. In addition, the remaining two-thirds of the Palestinian student body have been subjected to invasive Israeli alterations to the existing Palestinian curriculum, which has included the wholesale deletion of phrases, images, and symbols that denote Palestinian national identity, most significantly references to the Nakba of 1948 and altered phrasings around themes such as Jerusalem, prisoners, and Palestinian heritage.
It’s this quiet encroachment on Palestinian textbooks, as much as the wholesale replacement, that worries Assi most. “We don’t want our children to learn hatred, and we don’t want them to carry pain without meaning,” she said in an indirect reference to Israeli claims that Palestinian textbooks teach children to “hate.”
“But we want them to know the truth,” she added.
For Assi, the issue isn’t one deleted page, one cut poem, or one changed word, but the collective memory of the Palestinian people that is being altered. “Whoever deletes a page from an entire history is asking children to deny a part of themselves,” she said.
A conflict that moved inside the classroom
In East Jerusalem, the fight over education is no longer about the number of schools or classroom seats alone. It has moved into the classroom itself, into the book students open each morning, the terms their eyes land on, the images they study, the history they’re taught, and the narrative that will shape how they understand themselves in their city for years to come.
With the start of the 2026-2027 school year, the Israeli curriculum was imposed on all new first- and seventh-grade classes in municipal schools located in areas under the jurisdiction of the Israeli-run Jerusalem Municipality.
Israel’s own data shows the scale — the share of Palestinian students studying the Israeli curriculum rose to roughly 36% in 2025-2026, and more recent figures put this year’s number at close to 45,000 students, about 38% of all East Jerusalem students.
The Palestinian Authority (PA) Minister of Education and Higher Education, Amjad Barham, detailed to Mondoweiss a set of edits documented in correspondence and circulating records.
“In the first-grade civic and life education textbook, the Palestinian national anthem is marked for deletion,” Barham said. “The documents also describe the removal of a second-grade page containing an image of a prison and an attempt to break free from it, along with the deletion of prisoners’ names”.
In third grade, the poem “Ala Dalauna”, a traditional Palestinian folk song that often appears in nationalist anthems about the homeland, is among the material reportedly cut from the Arabic curriculum. The lesson, “Bride of the Sea,” the commonly used nickname for the coastal Palestinian city of Jaffa, now occupied by Israel, was also altered, its questions rewritten.
The edits surface even where they seem furthest from politics. In mathematics, Barham said, a reference to the “separation and annexation wall” was struck, along with a map of Palestine showing Jerusalem as its capital.
The changes intensify with grade level. From fourth through ninth grade, the documents describe substituted terminology — “mujahid” (freedom fighter) replaced with “defender,” “aseer” (prisoner) replaced with “the wronged” — alongside deleted or revised material on Jerusalem, prisoners, the Palestinian revolution, resistance, settlement, strikes, and select historical events.
“In their place”, Barham said, “content on peace, coexistence, and cooperation has been introduced.” References to the Palestinian village of Umm Khalid were recast in light of its proximity to present-day Netanya, an Israeli city. Language on the Judaization of Jerusalem was rewritten toward a vocabulary centered on peace rather than confrontation,” he noted.
Ma’arouf al-Rifai, spokesperson for the PA-run Jerusalem Governorate — the parts of the West Bank Israel annexed in 1967 and incorporated within the boundaries of Israel’s Jerusalem municipality — warned that Israel’s decision to impose the Israeli curriculum on East Jerusalem’s municipal schools represents “a dangerous and unprecedented escalation,” the most serious since 1967.
In a statement, al-Rifai described the move as a direct assault on the national and cultural identity of generations of Jerusalemites. “The decision is part of a systematic policy targeting Palestinian education in Jerusalem, one aimed at replacing the curriculum with the Israeli narrative in full,” the statement read.
Al-Rifai cited figures showing the scale of that replacement: nearly 45,000 students, around 38% of the roughly 120,000 Palestinian students in East Jerusalem, are now enrolled in the Israeli curriculum. The trajectory, he said, reveals a rapid and dangerous escalation — from 10,347 students in the 2020-2021 school year, to 19,402 in 2024-2025, to 27,041 in 2025-2026.
Six years ago, he noted, the number stood at under 13,000. Fifteen years ago, it was a few hundred.
A trajectory decades in the making
Israeli affairs analyst Esmat Mansour says this shift didn’t begin this year, nor was it imposed by sudden decree. It’s a trajectory that has accumulated for decades, starting with early attempts to impose the Israeli curriculum after the 1967 occupation of East Jerusalem, which was blocked by parent and teacher resistance, keeping the Jordanian curriculum in place for years.
“When the Palestinian Authority was established, the Palestinian curriculum became the city’s reference text,” Mansour told Mondoweiss. “But it never entered classrooms without passing through Israeli review. Books were revised before approval, so the cover stayed Palestinian while the content was reshaped from within. Today, that has escalated into something bolder: direct expansion of the Israeli curriculum itself, not as a marginal alternative but as a primary track competing for the city’s children”.
That pattern of internal revision is exactly what Hebrew University researcher Samira Alian documented in a recent academic study examining 28 social studies textbooks for grades three through ten. She found substantive changes to material on Jerusalem, Palestinian identity, colonialism, Zionism, and the Nakba: altered wording about Jerusalem itself, deleted or amended references to the occupation, changed lesson titles, and removed images tied to the wall and settlements. One textbook, the study found, excluded entire lessons on Palestinian political history, replaced with material carrying none of the same weight.
Imad Hawas, an Arabic teacher at a municipal school in Anata under Israeli jurisdiction, says the change can’t be reduced to a passing word.
“A textbook doesn’t just transmit information,” Hawas said. “It determines how a child learns to name a place, understand events, and connect the past to the present he lives in every day. When the word ‘Palestine’ changes, or a reference to the occupation is deleted, or the image of the wall a child sees with his own eyes on his way to school is altered, the material no longer stays what it was in its original version. It becomes another text, carrying a Palestinian title but different content.”

A former poet laureate and a Pulitzer winner lead TS Eliot prize shortlist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:15:34 UTC
01:15:34 KST

The former poet laureate Andrew Motion and Pulitzer prize winner Jorie Graham are among the 10 poets shortlisted for this year’s £25,000 TS Eliot prize, the UK and Ireland’s most prestigious award for a single volume of poetry.
Motion has been selected for Gravity Archives, while Graham, who was previously shortlisted in 2012, is on the list for Killing Spree.
Motion was the UK’s poet laureate between 1999 and 2009, and has written more than 15 poetry collections, alongside nonfiction books including biographies of Philip Larkin and John Keats. In a Guardian review, Sandeep Parmar wrote that Gravity Archives showcases Motion’s “rooted and resolute eye surveying the mortality of others as well as his own”.
Graham, who has published 16 collections, won the 1996 Pulitzer prize for poetry for The Dream of the Unified Field, a book of selected poems. In 2012, she was shortlisted for the TS Eliot prize for the collection PLACE, which won the Forward prize for best collection.
Along with Motion and Graham, this year’s shortlist features the British poet and writer Keith Jarrett, whose second collection, Hide Me Under the Blood and I Shall Be Satisfied, is also shortlisted for this year’s Forward prize. He is a poetry slam champion, and his work has previously been projected on to the facade of St Paul’s Cathedral.
Other shortlisted poets include Imani Mason Jordan, whose PIVOT is their debut collection; the Canadian poet Sylvia Legris, shortlisted for Sleep Gate; and Shara McCallum, whose collection Behold is her seventh.
“Though very different in voice, style and preoccupation, these 10 collections share a determination to meet the challenges faced in difficult times with closer attention to language,” said chair of judges and poet Leontia Flynn. “Each of these books reminds us why, when nothing else makes much sense, it’s to poetry we turn to reorient ourselves.”
The remaining poets on the list are 2022 Forward prize winner Kim Moore, for The House of Broken Things; Holly Pester, for Cafés; Jana Prikryl, for The Channel; and the Irish poet Billy Ramsell, for Render. Mason Jordan’s PIVOT is the only debut on the shortlist.
Flynn appeared on the judging panel alongside the poets Ishion Hutchinson and Daisy Lafarge. The 10 collections were selected from 174 submissions by 65 British and Irish publishers.
The prize was established in 1993 by the Poetry Book Society to mark its 40th anniversary and honour its founding poet, TS Eliot.
The winner will receive £25,000, with each shortlisted poet receiving £1,500. Last year’s prize was won by the Canadian poet Karen Solie for Wellwater. Other recent winners include Joelle Taylor, Jason Allen-Paisant, Anthony Joseph and Bhanu Kapil.
The shortlisted poets will read from their work at the Southbank Centre’s Royal Festival Hall in London on 17 January, with the winner announced at a ceremony at the Wallace Collection the following day.

====================================================================================================

When growth is not enough: housing and inflation, Sanchez's main challenges before elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:15:22 UTC
01:15:22 KST

Spain's economy is still outpacing the eurozone and employment is at its highest since 2008, but Sánchez's term end is marred by inflation, weak productivity and a housing crisis now dominating the election debate.
The President of the Spanish Government, Pedro Sánchez, will face the snap elections on 29 November hoping that the strong economic figures that have marked much of his time in office will help him overcome a widespread feeling across the country: macro-level growth is not enough.
Spain's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 2.8% in 2025 and is expected to continue expanding at a relatively brisk pace, with growth forecast at 2.4% for 2026, as the European Commission's country report on Spain points out (source in Spanish). Since the pandemic, moreover, Spain has grown faster than the main economies of the euro area.
However, as the protests over the housing crisis that have gripped the country for weeks make clear, that growth has not translated into an improvement in Spaniards' quality of life. The Commission attributes part of this to a sharp increase in the population, driven by migration flows, but also to weak labour productivity.
Hourly productivity has improved since 2019, but productivity per employee and per full-time worker has remained virtually flat. That is one of the main reasons why aggregate growth is not being reflected to the same extent in per capita income in a Spain that Sánchez has governed since June 2018.
Immigration, in fact, has become one of the engines of the Spanish labour market. While employment grew by 2.6% in 2025, the number of jobs filled by people born abroad accounted for 7.9% of all the posts created that year.
The latest consolidated figures nevertheless show that the labour market still has a strongly seasonal pattern. In August, unemployment rose by 44,419 people, to 2,355,918, although this was the lowest figure recorded in that month since 2007. In September, the jobless total increased again, by 23,587 people, which was also a low for that month since 2007.
The main pillar of Spanish growth has been the services sector, and specifically exports of services and tourism. Spain received 58.1 million international tourists between January and July 2026, an unprecedented figure and 4.6% more than a year earlier. Tourist spending rose by 7.8%, reaching a record 82.054 billion euros, according to the Frontur and Egatur data published (source in Spanish) by the National Statistics Institute (INE).
The European Commission stresses that the increase in exported services has helped widen the current account surplus and improve the country's international investment position. But it also warns that a significant share of activity remains concentrated in sectors with relatively low productivity, such as agriculture. More than 82% of the jobs created were in low-productivity activities, limiting the scope for wage growth.
Inflation adds another layer of tension. In September, annual inflation in the country stood at 5%, well above the 3.8% recorded on average in the euro area, and only behind Lithuania (6.1%), Bulgaria (5.6%), Cyprus and Luxembourg (5.2%) and Greece (5.1%).
In September, inflation in Spain stood at 4.9%. The INE mainly attributed the Spanish spike to rising fuel prices and the behaviour of package holidays.
Housing, the big problem
If there is one issue that sums up the imbalance between economic growth and quality of life, it is housing. Here, Spain faces a serious mismatch between supply and demand, both for buying and renting, especially in large cities and tourist areas.
"The severe rate of housing deprivation increased, which indicates poor living conditions", says the Commission's country report. Social housing accounts for barely between 1.5% and 1.7% of the total stock, compared with an average of between 6% and 7% in the European Union.
On top of that, prices have been rising steadily since 2014 and have accelerated in recent years, while high costs are also making labour mobility more difficult.
This is precisely where the economy and politics collided on Monday. After the Government failed to ratify two decrees last week to tackle the housing crisis because it lacked the support of its partners in Congress, Prime Minister Sánchez dissolved parliament and called elections for November.
Thus, the economic balance sheet of Sánchez's term in office so far has two sides: one in which Spain is growing, creating jobs and benefiting from the arrival of foreign workers and the strength of the tourism sector; and another, which GDP growth alone cannot solve, weighed down by low productivity, the loss of purchasing power and the difficulty of accessing housing.

This is precisely where the economy and politics collided on Monday. After the Government failed to ratify two decrees last week to tackle the housing crisis because it lacked the support of its partners in Congress, Prime Minister Sánchez dissolved parliament and called elections for November.
Thus, the economic balance sheet of Sánchez's term in office so far has two sides: one in which Spain is growing, creating jobs and benefiting from the arrival of foreign workers and the strength of the tourism sector; and another, which GDP growth alone cannot solve, weighed down by low productivity, the loss of purchasing power and the difficulty of accessing housing.

Russia burned 628,000 new school textbooks in Kharkiv at the peak of back-to-school season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:14:23 UTC
01:14:23 KST

Russian missiles and drones destroyed 13 million Ukrainian books this summer, The Guardian reported. That is about a third of all books printed in Ukraine this year, the government estimates.
Russia is striking civilian warehouses, including those where publishers store their books. The uncertainty is pushing publishers toward safe international bestsellers, Publishers Weekly reported. "We'll all end up fed up with safe, non-risky books—if there are still publishers around to publish them," said Iryna Baturevych, co-founder of the publishing news outlet Chytomo.
Millions of Ukrainian books on fire
Ranok is one of Ukraine's largest publishing houses and a leader in children's literature and school textbooks. On one day in August, Russia destroyed more than 85% of its stock, The Guardian reported.
Viktor Kruhlov, the publisher's co-founder and chief executive, was on the warehouse floor at its headquarters in Kharkiv. The facility, built on the site of a former bread factory, covered about 10,000 m².
Together with five senior colleagues, he was discussing plans for the upcoming school year, the peak of the distribution season. Moments after the meeting began, a strike hit about 30 meters from where the staff had gathered. Kruhlov heard an explosion and almost at once saw a huge fire. As colleagues tried to put out the flames, a second strike came, and he realized there could be a third and a fourth, so the staff evacuated. Fifty people were on shift that day, and no one was injured, Kruhlov told The Guardian.
Eight million books, including 628,000 new school textbooks, were in the warehouse at the time. None could be saved. Firefighters battled the blaze for a week.
Several editorial staff members who saw the remains of the warehouse for the first time looked shaken as they recognized fragments of books they had helped create.
"When you see what was produced with your brain, with your hands, with your imagination, spoiled by Russia, it's an awful feeling," Kruhlov said.
He predicted shortages at Ranok's stores this fall, when the books in stock run out and there is nothing to replace them.
Literature is part of Ukrainian identity
Kruhlov is convinced that Russia deliberately targeted the book warehouse, but Bohdana Laiuk, Ukraine's deputy culture minister, sees the strikes as part of Russia's broader campaign against warehouses, The Guardian wrote.
"They cannot occupy Kyiv. So they target warehouses around Kyiv to take the possibility of everyday life from us—and books are part of everyday life," she said.
Books also matter to Russia's occupiers, Laiuk said.
"When the Russians occupy, the first thing they do—and we know this from the areas that were occupied and then liberated in 2022 in the Kherson and Kharkiv regions—is to go to the libraries, take the Ukrainian language books out, and destroy them," Laiuk said.
Before 2022, about 70% of the Ukrainian book market consisted of Russian-language titles, most of them imported from Russia.
Russian dominance in Ukrainian publishing developed over centuries, from tsarist bans on publishing in Ukrainian in the 19th century to Soviet Russification. Ukrainian writers were purged, and Ukrainian literature stayed in the shadow of Russian literature, the article notes.
Laiuk calls the dominance of Russian books a form of colonialism. Russia deliberately built its own information space in Ukraine through books, media, and television, she argues, so that everything would be ready for it once its tanks arrived.
Even after independence, a commercially successful Ukrainian-language novel was long seen as unlikely. But at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukrainian bookstores stopped selling Russian imports, and interest in Ukrainian literature grew, from 1920s classics and poetry to contemporary authors and translations.
"So people are asking: what does it actually mean to be Ukrainian? Literary culture gives us the place to understand who we are," Laiuk told The Guardian in 2023.
The future of Ukrainian literature is uncertain
Ranok is now rushing to reprint textbooks and bestsellers: schools need the former, while sales of popular titles will help the publisher make up for lost revenue.
For debut authors and writers of less commercial or experimental books, the situation is particularly difficult. Even before the strike on Ranok's warehouse, some publications had been delayed by attacks on printing infrastructure.
Ksenia Shpak's debut novel, an urban fantasy about a girl displaced from eastern Ukraine to the Carpathians, was due out in February 2025 but was published only that November, the article says. Half of the print run was in Ranok's Kharkiv warehouse when it was attacked.
It was her first published book, and Shpak fears the publisher will now focus on bestsellers and reprint her novel only if money allows. The Ukrainian book market is also feeling demand level off and the cost of living rise, she said.
Despite the loss of 8 million books, Kruhlov remained optimistic. Looking over the ruined warehouse in Kharkiv, he said he planned to rebuild everything—and to do it better.

How light became a remote control for the brain, and won a Nobel Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:14:11 UTC
01:14:11 KST

Optogenetics, the technique that lets scientists control brain cells with light, has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine for their work in light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, a method that lays the foundation "of a new era in neuroscience", the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet announced on Monday.
But what exactly is optogenetics, and how did the laureates develop the technique?
Optogenetics is a method for controlling selected cells using light as a remote control. It allows scientists to switch cells on or off in a living brain and investigate how particular cells and neural circuits influence behaviour.
This new method was given the name optogenetics in 2006, but the story behind the technique began more than a decade earlier, when Peter Hegemann was studying the unicellular alga Chlamydomonas, an organism famous for swimming towards light.
Hegemann wanted to understand what makes algae move towards light. He studied its eyespot, a tiny orange dot on the cell’s surface that detects light. Through a series of experiments, Hegemann and his colleagues identified light-sensitive proteins called channelrhodopsins, which allow algae to detect light and respond to it.
Together with Georg Nagel at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics in Frankfurt, he inserted the algal genes into frog egg cells and human kidney cells and proved that channelrhodopsin was indeed a light-controlled ion channel.
When exposed to blue light, the channel opened in just 0.2 milliseconds, allowing positively charged ions to flood into the cell and generate a tiny electrical impulse.
Years later, Karl Deisseroth, the third laureate, introduced the channelrhodopsin gene into rat nerve cells. By shining blue light on the cells, they could trigger nerve signals, showing that the protein could act as a light-controlled switch. He then used the technique to control nerve cells in the brains of living mice.
For example, scientists could trigger movements in a mouse's whiskers or wake sleeping mice simply by switching on a light.
What does the future hold?
The discovery “provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, in a press release.
Optogenetics is currently used primarily as a research tool. By allowing researchers to turn targeted cell types on or off using pulses of light, it enables scientists to establish direct cause-and-effect relationships between neural activity, brain function, and behaviour.
It allows researchers to map the neurons involved in emotional states such as fear, anxiety or reward. They can also map specific neural circuits governing pain, thirst, attention or aggression.
Optogenetics is also widely used in research into neurological or psychiatric conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, anxiety, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease and epilepsy.
The science has also entered clinical trials to treat retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic disease that causes blindness due to the loss of light-detecting cells in the retina.
By delivering light-sensitive opsin genes into surviving retinal cells, researchers have enabled a blind patient wearing light-emitting goggles to regain partial vision and perceive high-contrast objects.

As Air Force Goes Big on Autonomy, Are Cargo Drones Next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:13:38 UTC
01:13:38 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force’s plans to field 1,000 semi-autonomous fighter and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance drones within just a few years made headlines at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference last month.
But beyond the service’s signature Collaborative Combat Aircraft and Massed Modular Aircraft programs, a half-dozen or so firms are pitching another kind of autonomous aircraft: cargo drones to solve some of the thorniest logistics problems.
Textron Aviation and Merlin Labs unveiled a cockpit-less Cessna equipped with Merlin’s autonomy software and a nose hatch opening to a cavernous cargo bay.
“By pairing a proven aircraft platform with autonomy technology, we’re exploring new approaches to contested logistics operations while also examining how autonomy may enable more efficient cargo aircraft designs that increase usable volume, improve cargo accessibility and support mission sustainment requirements,” Bob Gibbs, Textron’s vice president for defense and special mission sales, said of the company’s Cessna SkyuCourier UX concept.
Reliable Robotics is offering its own modified Cessna 208B Caravan. Its aircraft flew in multiple Agile Flag exercises in 2024, installing actuators, sensors, and other gear in the cockpit and using a human pilot to command high-level direction from a ground station. Reliable announced a $17.4 million deal with the Air Force in 2025 to provide an aircraft for a yearlong test.
In a May blog post, Reliable’s certification flight test lead Chris Baughman wrote that the firm is targeting the start of fiscal 2027 to begin the test, which will focus on the Indo-Pacific region. The company is also seeking FAA certification for its autonomy software to operate in U.S. airspace, targeting 2028 for that certification.
Joby Aviation, which previously acquired autonomy startup Xwing, is also flying a modified Cessna Caravan, racking up 40 hours and 7,000 miles during last summer’s Resolute Force Pacific. Joby did not exhibit at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber, but sought to capitalize on the timing by announcing soon after that it completed 3,199 miles of autonomous flight across the U.S. this summer, including stops at Shaw Air Force Base, S.C., and near Washington D.C. At a press event Sept. 24, Joby’s Head of Defense Policy John Barranco told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the aircraft carried a safety pilot for those flights in case human intervention was needed, but the autonomy software never required a pilot intervention.
Coming at the same time that other vendors are developing autonomous fighters and reconnaissance aircraft with clean-sheet designs, the modified Cessnas might seem like minimalist efforts. But aviation firms see a gap they can fill in the Air Force’s logistics enterprise, a small airlifter that can do jobs that USAF’s workhorse C-130 cannot do as efficiently. The Hercules can haul 40,000 pounds of cargo, and the Air Force has only about 270. A Cessna could be ideal for shorter hops and smaller loads at a fraction of the cost.
“It’s a really robust, reliable existing cargo airframe that’s in the world, and there are many of them, and so we can retrofit a lot of those for the customers,” Barranco said.
USAF officials have spent years talking about Agile Combat Employment—the concept of dispersing small teams of Airmen and aircraft from large bases to operate from remote or austere locations and move quickly to counter adversary long-range missile attacks. But the ACE logistics is complex, especially in the vast and watery Indo-Pacific region.
Having small, unmanned aircraft to island-hop and resupply those forces so they can generate airpower—without taxing manned airlifters—could be a solution.
“Historically it’s about a logistics train where you’re trying to move a really big airframe and move a lot of stuff, and that takes time, and it takes Airmen, and it takes support, and that’s a really important mission,” said Barranco. “Sometimes you need to move a lot less really, really quickly, without standing up a mission, without 24 hours’ notice, without pulling folks together.”
Other concepts are also emerging to chase this possible market. DZYNE Technologies put its autonomous cargo drone, called Grasshopper, on display.
DZYNE and the Air Force Research Laboratory unveiled Grasshopper last May, as a self-guided glider capable of carrying up to 500 pounds after being dropped out the back of a C-130; from there, it could glide tens of miles to resupply troops in “high-risk environments.”
DZYNE has since offered a “Long-Range” powered variant with a turbine engine that can fly “10 times” further than Grasshopper and launched from “standoff” distances.
U.S. Special Operations Command has tested the concept, using the Long-Range Grasshopper in Exercise Trojan Footprint 26 in Romania and North Macedonia, where the drones were launched from a Romanian Air Force C-27J.
But the firms pursuing this niche want more than a narrow special ops use case, focusing on any mission where moving cargo quickly without risking crews could be attractive.
Grid Aero won $6 million in seed funding from the Air Force’s innovation arm, AFWERX, last August. CEO Arthur Dubois compared his company’s drone to a “flying pickup” truck at the time, saying it would be able to carry somewhere between 1,000 and 8,000 pounds from “Guam to Japan,” for example, a trek of some 1,500 miles.
Grid Aero’s Lifter Lite hasn’t made its first flight yet, but the firm was among seven selected in September to compete for the Air Force’s Massed Modular Aircraft program. It’s unclear if Lifter Lite or some other design is what the company envisions as its entry.
Dubois said last year that the idea for Lifter Lite sprang from asking military and commercial air cargo stakeholders about their pain points. For the military, that’s executing logistics in areas where U.S. assets could be attacked.
Lt. Gen. Kenyon K. Bell, deputy chief of staff for logistics, engineering, and force protection, noted as much during the conference: “The era of uncontested logistics is over,” Bell declared. “We will have to continue to fight our way in from a logistics standpoint and be able to sustain and regenerate ourselves while we’re in contact. … That is a concept that we certainly need to think through.”
Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach endorsed the concept of autonomous cargo drones during a media roundtable at the conference, albeit without completely committing to it.
“We believe that there’s some value in that as well,” he said in response to a question. “It certainly could be valuable in the Pacific, with the ranges that we’re talking about. And so we’re looking at several different options and evaluating them, but I would say, no program of record just yet, but certainly taking a look at some demonstrators and the like to see what’s available to us.”
Congress and Pentagon officials are also tuning in. When Undersecretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael culled the department’s list of “critical technology areas” from 14 to just six last November, “contested logistics technology” survived the cut.
The House Armed Services Committee directed the the Air Force to present a briefing on the topic in their version of the 2027 defense policy bill. Lawmakers also expect a proposed timeline for developing an acquisition strategy that could include rapid prototyping. They also want a strategy for the use of “low-cost and attritable Group 4 and 5 unmanned aircraft systems in contested logistics operations.”
Staff Writers Matthew Cox and Stephen Losey contributed reporting.

Britain's national security adviser made an undisclosed visit to Israel last week but failed to reach a deal to prevent the closure of the U.K. Consulate in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem, three sources familiar with the talks said.
Jonathan Powell, whose visit has not been disclosed by Britain's government, held talks with Israeli officials but failed to reach an agreement to keep the consulate open, said the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Israel on Sept. 8 ordered Britain to close the East Jerusalem consulate within 30 days and remove its diplomats from the city, after Britain said it would ban goods made in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
France and Canada joined in the sanctions. Israel has not taken action against them.
The incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel's longtime allies over its unlawful settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law.
The 30-day deadline for Britain to close the consulate runs out on Thursday. Two of the sources said talks were still ongoing, and while an agreement to keep it open was possible, it is unlikely one would be struck by the Thursday deadline.
Asked about Powell's visit and talks with London over the consulate, a spokesperson for Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar told Reuters that it would close on Thursday, as announced.
A U.K. government spokesperson had no immediate comment.
In announcing the sanctions, Britain said that Israel's actions were undermining the possibility of a two-state solution - the idea of a Palestinian state co-existing peacefully alongside Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government openly rejects the idea of Palestinian statehood.
Britain cited Israeli government-backed plans to expand illegal settlements and rising settler violence targeting Palestinians in the West Bank. The British sanctions are to take effect next year.
The British consulate, in the Sheikh Jarrah neighborhood of East Jerusalem, handles the country's relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians.
The British sanctions announcement and Israel's response marked a new low in the relationship between the once steadfast allies. Britain has repeatedly criticized Israel over its violations in the war in Gaza and over Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin

Font size
Bulgaria and 16 other EU member states have called for cohesion and agricultural funding to be maintained in the bloc’s 2028–2034 budget, the Bulgarian government press office said.

Norway plans temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:11:31 UTC
01:11:31 KST

Norway is planning a temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places, amid rising global concern at the spread of the AI-enabled recording devices.
The Oslo government is planning a bill to prevent the use of the camera-enabled spectacles in parks, beaches, museums, shopping centres, schools, daycare centres, healthcare facilities, gyms and public events, although private use would still be allowed.
There is already a growing patchwork of restrictions on the use of the glasses including in UK and US courtrooms and in pubs, cinemas and restaurants where owners have raised privacy fears.
Torgeir Micaelsen, Norway’s minister of digital affairs, said he was “worried that new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without knowing it”.
“We do not want a society where people worry about being recorded without their knowledge, photographed or filmed in places and situations where they are accustomed to not being monitored,” he said.
Norway’s Labour party, which heads a minority government, needs the support of other parties to pass the proposed ban. It said it planned to submit a bill “as soon as possible”, while tasking an expert group with drawing up permanent regulations on the issue.
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta sells “smart” versions of Ray-Ban and Oakley glasses that allow users to film, take photos, make phone calls, play music and execute AI prompts. It has sold at least 9m pairs of the Ray-Ban versions since the start of 2023.
In the UK restaurateurs such as Jeremy King, who created the Wolseley and Delaunay restaurants, and pub chain Wetherspoons have already said they do not want customers using the devices. Cinemas said in August they had begun introducing policies to ban or restrict the use of smart glasses citing both privacy and film piracy concerns.
Last week the governor of California, Gavin Newsom, vetoed legislation that would have penalised citizens for using smart glasses to record people without their permission in changing rooms, doctors’ offices and other spaces people generally consider private. The state already has laws governing unlawful recording.
In France, the child welfare group E-enfance said it had this year received about 20 reports of women being filmed without their knowledge using glasses fitted with a camera, the majority of which involved Meta smart glasses. It said the incidents often followed the same pattern: a young girl or woman approached in a public place, filmed without her knowledge, with the clip then posted on social media in the form of a prank or a street interview.
Meta has stressed that each pair of glasses is fitted with a tamper-proof LED light that blinks white when the user is recording or taking pictures. It advises users: “Not everyone loves being photographed. Stop recording if anyone expresses that they would rather you not.”
A Meta spokesperson said: “We’re excited that our glasses continue to be very popular for listening to music, making calls, or getting live translations, so we’re continuing to expand styles and features around the world. Every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video. It can’t be turned off and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it -- something smartphones and other camera’s don’t have.”

Glasgow city council reaches pay deal with union to avert fire-and-rehire plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:08:14 UTC
01:08:14 KST

Glasgow city council has reached an agreement with the trade union Unison over pay and grading, averting one of the UK’s biggest ever fire-and-rehire exercises.
Talks between the council and the GMB, Unite and Unison unions previously broke down when Unison refused to ballot its members on a new pay and grading system, designed to resolve historical equal pay issues.
The collapse of talks prompted the council to contact 23,000 workers, its entire non-teaching staff, at the end of last month to inform them they were at risk of being dismissed and reappointed, many on less favourable terms. The move led to significant backlash from opposition parties, unions and council employees.
The original proposal that led Unison to walk out of negotiations would have resulted in wage cuts for 11% of staff, but on Monday the council agreed to protect their pay for three years.
Unison said many issues remained unresolved and that negotiations would continue, but that it would ballot its members this month. The council has agreed to continue negotiating on issues including the equality impacts of the new pay structure.
Ricky Bell, the leader of Glasgow city council, said he was “delighted that we have been able to reach agreement with Unison” and “remove the unpalatable prospect of fire-and-rehire”.
“This is a strong and fair deal,” he added. “Both GMB and Unite have already agreed to take it to their members and, with all three unions now engaging with their memberships, we are moving closer to the outcome we have always wanted to achieve: ending pay discrimination in Glasgow city council once and for all.”
Bell emphasised there was no further money to come as part of the package, but said he looked forward to seeing the outcome of the union ballots. He thanked the Scottish government for additional support to help “unlock [the] agreement”.
Chris Sermanni, Unison’s Glasgow city branch secretary, said: “Unison stood firm because Glasgow’s workers deserved better than what was originally put on the table.
“That position has secured significant movement. There’s now a path for Unison members to give their verdict without the immediate threat of dismissal and re-engagement hanging over them.
“The period ahead will be used to keep fighting to give the whole workforce the information they need to make their decision.”
The ballot will last four weeks, with a timeline to be laid out in the coming days.

Sanction Israel to save Palestinian state, officials tell EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:07:40 UTC
01:07:40 KST

Breadcrumb
Sanction Israel immediately to save Palestinian state, officials tell EU
More than 500 former European politicians and diplomats have urged the EU to take immediate action against the Israeli government as it prepares to move forward with the E1 settlement designed to block the establishment of a Palestinian state in the occupied West Bank.
Writing in the French newspaper Libération, the officials called on European governments to agree to an EU-wide trade ban on Israeli settlements and impose sanctions on all banks and companies involved in the settlement project.
Among the names attached to the list are former French prime ministers Dominique de Villepin and Alain Juppe, former Belgian prime minister Yves Leterme, and former EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell.
The E1 area is situated between occupied East Jerusalem and the Maale Adumim settlement bloc. If built, the project would effectively cut the West Bank in two, making a future contiguous Palestinian state impossible.
Israel's attorney-general recently postponed a construction tender for 1,234 housing units until after the 27 October general election, though a second tender for 2,167 units is expected to open two days before the vote.
"The time has undoubtedly come for the EU and its member states to act," the former officials wrote ahead of next week's meeting of European foreign ministers.
"The 27 will meet after another year of violence and ethnic cleansing by the Israeli government against the Palestinian people in Gaza and the West Bank," the op-ed read.
Successive attempts to impose EU-wide sanctions on Israel have been scuppered by close Israeli allies Germany and Italy, which have blocked the qualified majority needed to partially suspend the association agreement.
In the absence of an EU-wide consensus, several European countries are implementing trade bans with Israeli settlements, including France, the Netherlands, Ireland, Spain, Norway and Belgium.
Meanwhile, the UK last month became the first G7 country to announce plans to impose sanctions on Israeli banks, construction companies, and real estate firms involved in the settlements.
"While the fact that some EU member states have taken national action against illegal settlements is to be welcomed, others, notably Germany and Italy, continue to systematically block the adoption of measures at the European level, thus becoming de facto complicit in the weakening of EU values and the two-state solution," the op-ed said.

'Misled the public': BJP rejects Rahul Gandhi’s 'illegal' claims on Form 6 and SIR
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:06:52 UTC
01:06:52 KST

NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party on Monday came down heavily on Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi and accused him of misleading the public over the Supreme Court's observation on Form 6 and the Election Commission's decision on the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra compared Rahul's claims to the Congress leader's earlier statements on the Rafale issue.
"Rahul Gandhi misled the public on two counts. First, he claimed that Form 6 was illegal - specifically mentioning the Bharatiya Janata Party in this context. However, the Court did not declare Form 6 illegal today. It noted that the petition mentioned a modification to Form 6, so the Court said it would look into the matter," Patra said."We had not consented to any such modification. If any modification has indeed taken place, that will become clear only after a notice is issued. Yet, when we read the detailed order and look at the Election Commission's press release dated September 26, 2026, it becomes evident that the Commission had clearly stated there were no changes to Form 6 and that the Supreme Court had validated the declaration form attached to it," he said.
This comes hours after Rahul Gandhi alleged that the CEC had changed Form 6 "illegally and unilaterally", citing the Supreme Court's observation which came earlier in the day."It is now established beyond doubt that Gyanesh Kumar changed Form 6 illegally and unilaterally. This is just one more proof of him abusing his position to help the BJP," Rahul said."He and everyone else involved in this criminal assault on our democracy will be held accountable," he added.The Congress leader also shared a screenshot of the September 26 Election Commission statement which read: "The declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court. For non-SIR period, the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used."In its response, the EC said the order for the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Bihar, issued on June 24, 2025, had received the unanimous approval of the Commission and was subsequently upheld by the Supreme Court in its judgment dated May 27, 2026.EC officials also clarified that Form 6 itself had not been changed, but that a declaration had been attached to the form under the Bihar SIR order, as quoted by PTI.This came after the Supreme Court said it had not approved any modification to Form 6 used by the EC during the SIR exercise in various states."Any modification to Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When records are produced, we would like to see who has modified it," a bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said.
What is Form 6
Form 6 is the application used by eligible voters for inclusion in the electoral roll.The declaration was attached to Form 6 during the Bihar SIR, which began with the EC's June 24, 2025, order. The declaration sought additional details, including information about the applicant's parents.
According to EC officials, the form itself remained unchanged, while the declaration was a separate document attached to it for the SIR exercise. Outside SIR, the forms prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, apply.The declaration was later withdrawn from the EC's online portals.The online version of Form 6 and the declaration also used a single OTP for both, rather than requiring separate OTP verification, which had led to suggestions that the declaration was part of Form 6.

Ukraine’s Farsight Vision Builds Ground Robot Navigation to Work Without GPS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:06:49 UTC
01:06:49 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Farsight Vision Builds Ground Robot Navigation to Work Without GPS
Ukrainian defense technology company Farsight Vision presented a navigation module on October 5 that allows ground robotic systems to orient themselves without GPS by combining laser sensing with 3D terrain data.
Oboronka reported the development on October 5, citing information provided by Farsight Vision. The system generates a real-time point cloud around the vehicle, identifying obstacles, holes, slopes, and other terrain features while refining its planned route.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The solution is based on the concept of a digital twin of the terrain," Farsight Vision stated. The company explained that operators receive a continuously updated model of the surrounding area rather than relying solely on satellite imagery.
Before a mission, the FSV Platform creates a 3D model of the terrain. During movement, the onboard module adds sensor-generated point cloud data to the model, allowing the operator to compare the vehicle's actual surroundings with the planned route.
If GPS becomes unavailable and the ground system loses its position, the combination of the prebuilt 3D model and live sensor data helps restore orientation. The three-dimensional view can also show terrain geometry that may be difficult to assess through a conventional video feed.
Farsight Vision CEO Viktoriia Yaremchuk noted that the company wants to eliminate the need to launch a separate reconnaissance drone simply to guide a ground robotic system. Such support creates additional risk and consumes resources, she added.
"By the end of the year, Farsight Vision aims to enable the drone to autonomously return to the point where communication was lost or to a designated base," Yaremchuk stated. The initial target is several kilometers, with later scaling to 30–40 kilometers at the platform's maximum speed.
Earlier, on September 24, Ukraine codified the domestically produced Varkhan ground robotic complex, a 4×4 platform that can carry up to 300 kilograms over 37 kilometers to positions where sending personnel would be too risky.
Unmanned ground vehicles completed more than 25,000 logistics and evacuation missions in August alone, up from 7,511 in January. Kyiv aims to build at least 50,000 combat and logistics ground robots this year.

Ukraine Adds New Varkhan 4×4 Ground Robot to Its Military Arsenal. Here’s What It Can Do
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:05:58 UTC
01:05:58 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Adds New Varkhan 4×4 Ground Robot to Its Military Arsenal. Here’s What It Can Do
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense has codified and approved the domestically produced Varkhan unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) for use by the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the ministry announced on October 5.
The Varkhan is designed primarily for military logistics missions, including transporting weapons, ammunition, equipment, and other supplies. According to the ministry, the system was developed by a Ukrainian defense company in response to operational requirements provided by the military.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The UGV is built on a four-wheel-drive 4×4 chassis with dependent suspension and ground clearance of more than 200 millimeters. Its design allows the vehicle to operate across difficult terrain, including off-road conditions, marshy ground, and sand.
The platform is also equipped with quick-release batteries, allowing operators to replace power sources and continue missions without extended interruptions.
During testing, the Varkhan demonstrated the ability to transport hundreds of kilograms of cargo over distances of several dozen kilometers, according to the Defense Ministry. The platform is also equipped with several communication and control systems.
The ministry said the UGV was designed for sustained operation in high-intensity combat conditions, with an emphasis on durability, straightforward controls, accessible spare parts and consumables, and ease of maintenance.
According to the statement, the Varkhan also forms part of a broader ecosystem of unmanned-system equipment that includes T-Bone ground control stations, antennas, masts, repeaters, and rotating mechanisms. Together, these components are designed to provide integrated control of unmanned systems and maintain stable communications.
Ukrainian forces in the Sumy region managed to retrieve an unmanned ground vehicle damaged by a mine after receiving help from a local woman who happened to be cycling past the area, Ukraine’s 71st Separate Airmobile Brigade reported.
The brigade said the UGV struck a mine during a combat mission, putting the damaged vehicle at risk of being lost.

Three oil depots, petrol stations and a data centre – Russia continues to inflict damage on Amic Energy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:05:49 EEST
01:05:49 KST

Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Russian attacks have repeatedly caused damage to Amic Energy’s infrastructure in Ukraine. The latest strike targeted an oil depot that had already been seriously damaged at the start of the full-scale invasion.
In the first weeks of the war, Russian troops entered the site. At that time, the oil depot was full of fuel, which Amic Energy reported to the relevant Ukrainian authorities to ensure the supplies were not used by the occupying forces. As a result of the fighting on the depot’s premises, four storage tanks were burnt out and process equipment was damaged. Now this same facility has been hit again — this time by a direct Russian attack.
“The most important thing for us is that none of our employees were harmed. This is by no means Amic Energy’s first loss. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, three of the company’s oil depots, a data centre and several petrol stations have been damaged. And that’s not even counting the petrol stations the company has lost as a result of the occupation of part of Ukraine’s territory. That’s why we understand, not just in theory but from our own experience, just how real these threats are, and what the cost of this war is,” says Gintaras Macijauskas, CEO of Amic Energy in Ukraine.
Despite the damage to its infrastructure, the Amic Energy network continues to operate as normal. The company is stepping up security measures and working on additional solutions to protect its staff, including the installation of mobile shelters near petrol stations.
Amic Energy is also documenting the losses incurred by the company as a result of Russian aggression and is asserting its right to compensation. In 2023, the company filed a claim to this effect with the European Court of Human Rights. According to preliminary estimates, the amount of damages claimed in this case exceeds 300 million hryvnias — approximately 8.5 million euros.

====================================================================================================

Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:05:20 UTC
01:05:20 KST

Flávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, leaving progressive voters reeling.
The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.
“Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now.”
Speaking outside the White House on Monday, Donald Trump told reporters: “Well, it’s a big victory: close but a very, very big victory. Amazing, actually.”
Trump, who is a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, predicted the runoff would be “a very close election”.
The far-right surge was a triumph – albeit an incomplete one – for the Bolsonaro clan and its 71-year-old patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro.
The disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, saw four relatives elected to congress. His 44-year-old wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won a seat in the senate, as did his second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, who is 43. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, 28-year-old Jair Renan Bolsonaro, and the ex-president’s 62-year-old brother, Renato Bolsonaro, both won seats in the lower house of congress.
Across Latin America’s biggest democracy, key congressional and gubernatorial races were also won by staunch Bolsonaristas including Tarcísio de Freitas, who was re-elected as the governor of São Paulo state, and Sérgio Moro, who was elected governor of the southern state of Paraná. Both men were ministers during Bolsonaro’s 2018-22 government.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) will now boast the largest caucus in the senate with 28 of its 81 seats. Combined with the seats of other hard-right parties, that number rises to 43, giving the movement an upper house majority.
Meanwhile, pro-Lula senate candidates, including the former environment minister Marina Silva, the leftwing veteran Benedita da Silva, and the centrist former planning minister Simone Tebet, suffered bitter defeats.
Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, two young Bolsonarista social media warriors, became the best-voted congresspeople in Brazilian history, securing more than 3m votes.
“We are experiencing a revolution … The far right is growing in a very consistent way, election after election,” said Lago, calling the election the worst for progressive and moderate centrist parties since the late 80s.
Lago believed Lula had managed to interrupt the advance of Bolsonaro’s populist movement in 2022, thanks to positive voter memories of his first two terms, from 2002 to 2010. Back then, a global commodities boom allowed Brazil’s first working-class president to fund major social welfare programmes that helped millions escape poverty. “But it was just an interregnum,” Lago said.
Control of the senate should allow pro-Bolsonaro politicians to approve an amnesty for their movement’s charismatic leader, allowing the former president to emerge from the Brasília mansion where he is living under house arrest and reassert his leadership of the far right.
“I think he will be freed and I think he will be very important during Flávio Bolsonaro’s [presidency],” said Lago. “Flávio will be running the country and [Jair] Bolsonaro will be doing what he has always done: leading the revolution.”
The senate majority may also help Bolsonaro’s third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, return from self-imposed exile in the US. The 42-year-old, who has close ties to Donald Trump’s Maga movement, was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison earlier this year for coercion – the result of his lobbying the Trump administration to interfere in his father’s coup trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.
The result is good news for Trump, who has been accused of trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour, and his attempt to expand the conservative “orange wave” sweeping Latin America to its biggest democracy and economy. Recent years have seen a succession of pro-Trump presidents win power in the region, from Costa Rica, Honduras and El Salvador to Chile and Colombia.
One of Trump’s most enthusiastic regional cheerleaders, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, celebrated Bolsonaro’s “historic” victory against “the communist Lula”. “The American continent belongs to citizens who want to live in freedom,” Milei wrote on X.
The prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, wished Bolsonaro “good luck in the final” and celebrated his “great victory”. He wrote on X: “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.”
Speaking after Sunday’s result was confirmed, Lula put a brave face on what analysts called a catastrophic night for the left. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil,” he said, vowing to expose his rival’s “dark past”, which involves well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld and corruption allegations, which Bolsonaro has denied.
But the mood at Lula’s post-election event was reportedly funereal and Bolsonaro goes into the second round as the firm favourite. He is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates – Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema – who, between them, won more than 5.5m votes.
Santos quickly announced he would endorse neither candidate, considering both Lula and Bolsonaro to be “crooks”. Zema has vowed to vote against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) in the runoff, while Caiado has yet to declare his intentions.
Lula’s best hope may be convincing some of the record 33 million Brazilians who did not vote to turn out next time. “He will need to mobilise these apathetic voters who, in a sense, have already abandoned politics, which will be an extremely difficult task,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right.
Rocha has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters and identified “a great deal of voter apathy, especially among those who are not aligned with Bolsonarismo, and who could potentially vote for Lula”.
Although Flávio Bolsonaro has held political office for more than 20 years, “for undecided voters, his main positive characteristic is this idea of ‘renewal’, despite his possible involvement in corruption and with paramilitary groups,” Rocha added.
Lago believed only a dramatic shift from Lula’s campaign – such as changing the candidate, or a severe scandal involving Bolsonaro – could change the election’s outcome. But he was doubtful that would occur.

Brazil's Lula weighs VP Alckmin as next finance minister to woo centrist voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:03:48 UTC
01:03:48 KST

Brazil's Lula weighs VP Alckmin as next finance minister to woo centrist voters
BRASILIA, Oct 5 - Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is considering tapping Vice President Geraldo Alckmin to be his next finance minister if re-elected, two people familiar with the proposal said, in a bid to bolster his fiscal credibility and win over centrist voters after Senator Flavio Bolsonaro beat expectations in the first-round vote.
Under the proposal, Alckmin would remain vice president while also becoming finance minister next year, cementing his authority over economic policy, the sources said, speaking on condition of anonymity because the deliberations are private. The proposal is still under discussion.
The Brazilian presidency did not respond to a request for comment.
Alckmin, a veteran centrist, unsuccessfully challenged Lula for the presidency in 2006 and has served two terms as governor of Sao Paulo. He also ran Lula's Development, Industry and Trade Ministry until earlier this year, making him a key interlocutor with Washington since the US imposed sweeping tariffs on Brazilian goods.
Alckmin is widely considered a moderating force in Lula's government, with strong ties to the business community, although critics say his influence has been overshadowed in Lula's current term by policies widely seen as tilting to the left.
Lula also considered making Alckmin his finance minister in 2022 but ultimately chose Workers' Party member Fernando Haddad as finance minister after winning in both the first and second rounds.
Seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, Lula finished second on Sunday behind Senator Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro and an ally of Trump, in a first-round result that defied most polling forecasts, which had pointed to a narrow lead for the president.
The outcome, along with the electoral success of Bolsonaro's right-wing allies in Congress, sparked a strong market rally on Monday as investors bet a Bolsonaro administration would be more likely to deliver faster fiscal consolidation with broader legislative support.
Since Lula took office, Brazil's gross public debt has risen by more than 10 percentage points of GDP to 82.9%, a key vulnerability for the leftist leader despite inflation running below historical averages, stronger-than-expected economic growth, record-low unemployment and gains in real wages.
In remarks after the first-round results on Sunday, Lula signaled the importance of Alckmin to his runoff strategy, declaring that "no one in this country has the moral authority to lecture me or Alckmin on fiscal policy or fiscal responsibility, given what he did in Sao Paulo state and what we did in Brazil."
Elevating Alckmin could help attract voters concerned about fiscal credibility who are unwilling to back Bolsonaro but have grown disillusioned with what they see as an increasingly populist turn by Lula's government, the sources said. REUTERS
