We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

ANTALYA, Türkiye, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- The 77th International Astronautical Congress kicked off Monday in Antalya, Türkiye's Mediterranean resort city, gathering space leaders, researchers and industry representatives from across the globe.
Held for the first time in Türkiye, the five-day event runs until Friday under the theme "The World Needs More Space."
The event features sessions addressing some of the industry's key priorities, ranging from lunar exploration and satellite systems to artificial intelligence, space security and international cooperation.
During an opening address, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan warned that turning space into an arms race is wrong and dangerous.

Organized annually by the International Astronautical Federation, the congress serves as a major platform for scientific exchange, business contacts and discussions on the development of the global space sector.
According to the semi-official Anadolu Agency, the congress has received 8,330 research abstracts from 108 countries and regions, with more than 4,000 studies selected for presentation in over 180 technical sessions. ■

World Insights: What could shape Brazil's tight presidential runoff
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:13:32 CST
00:13:32 KST

by Xinhua writers Lu Junyu, Chen Haoquan and Wu Hao
RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's presidential election is heading to a runoff on Oct. 25 after a tight first-round vote on Sunday, with Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party and incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party separated by only about 2 percentage points.
The first-round results underscored the continued polarization of Brazilian politics, with the two candidates together securing over 90 percent of valid votes. Over the next three weeks, attention will focus on why the race remains so close, how U.S.-Brazil ties could affect the campaign, and where the two candidates could find additional support.
WHY THE CLOSE RACE?
The first-round vote was highly concentrated around the two leading candidates. Flavio Bolsonaro led the first round with about 47 percent of valid votes, followed by Lula with about 45 percent, while all other candidates received less than 5 percent each.
Brazilian media said the gap of less than 2 percentage points between the two was the narrowest presidential first-round margin since Brazil's return to democracy.
Both candidates also have relatively firm political bases but face considerable public rejection; therefore, the runoff begins with two relatively consolidated political camps, leaving less room to win over committed supporters of the other side, local media reported, citing political analysts.
Under Brazil's electoral rules, voters can decline to support any candidate by casting blank or null ballots, a choice that can also serve as an expression of political discontent.
Low voter enthusiasm has added another layer of uncertainty to the election.
According to official results, with more than 99 percent of ballots counted, turnout in the first round was weighed down by an abstention rate of 21.08 percent, while blank and null ballots together accounted for about 5 percent of votes cast.
A pre-election survey by Brazilian pollster Datafolha found that 47 percent of respondents were less interested in this election than in the previous one. Another poll, by consultancy Quaest, showed that 23 percent were "completely uninterested" in the race, while a further 10 percent said they might abstain or cast a blank or null ballot.
With the two political camps already highly consolidated, supporters of the eliminated candidates and voters aligned with neither side could become more important in the runoff.
For Flavio Bolsonaro, consolidating support from voters who backed other right-wing and center-right candidates will be important. Lula, meanwhile, has sought to appeal to voters outside his traditional base with measures addressing livelihood concerns, including tighter regulation of online betting and help for indebted households.
Turnout will also matter for both sides. With less than 2 percentage points separating the two candidates, mobilizing potential supporters who stayed home could dominate the runoff campaign.
HOW COULD U.S. TIES AFFECT THE RACE?
Beyond the complex domestic political landscape, the United States has continued to affect this year's election. U.S.-Brazil relations have become increasingly strained over the past year, with disputes ranging from tariffs and judicial proceedings to visa restrictions.
The U.S. administration has imposed tariffs on Brazilian goods and criticized the conviction of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was found guilty of attempting a coup after losing his reelection bid, while Lula's government has accused Washington of exerting political pressure on Brazil.
Those tensions have increasingly intersected with the presidential race. U.S. President Donald Trump, who maintained close ties with Jair Bolsonaro, said shortly before the election that he was watching the Brazilian vote "very closely."
Flavio Bolsonaro, son of Jair Bolsonaro, has advocated closer ties with Washington, while Lula's campaign has accused the Trump administration of seeking to interfere in Brazil's presidential election.
But the U.S. factor may prove counterproductive in electoral terms. Pressure from Washington could give Lula more room to emphasize national sovereignty and resistance to foreign pressure.
Daily newspaper Folha de S.Paulo noted that when the United States imposed steep tariffs on Brazilian goods in 2025, Lula's approval ratings rose as his government adopted a stronger sovereignty-focused response. ■

Ireland coach wants UEFA to keep team apart from Israel
Unknown

Breadcrumb
Ireland coach wants UEFA to keep team apart from Israel after contentious games
Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrímsson wants UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future competitions after their contentious Nations League games.
The teams drew 1-1 in Ireland's "home" game in Backa Topola, Serbia, on Sunday, a week after Ireland's 3-0 win in Israel's "home" game in Debrecen, Hungary.
Irish players came under pressure not to play the games because of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza; however, players voted to play, sparking fierce backlash from pro-Palestine supporters.
Ireland's goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu boycotted the match against Israel last Sunday.
Irish players wore black armbands and bowed their heads during the Israeli national anthem before the first match. They repeated the gesture for the second match, when the Israeli players wore black armbands for the 7 October attacks.
Hallgrímsson told Ireland's national broadcaster RTÉ afterwards that he thinks UEFA should keep the sides apart in future.
"There is obviously a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There are not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does," Hallgrímsson said.
"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we have gone through these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."
Contentious pairing
Calls in Ireland to boycott the games against Israel started as soon as the Nations League draw pitted the countries against each other in February. Israel's visit to Dublin would likely have triggered large protests and posed a major security challenge for the local police.
The FAI, which filed a motion the previous November calling on UEFA to ban Israel from club and international competitions, resisted calls for a boycott, arguing the team could face punishing sanctions from UEFA. Ireland is co-hosting the 2028 European Championship with England, Wales and Scotland.
In June, the FAI said it was moving Ireland's home game to Serbia for "operational reasons" and that no fans would be present.
Israel was already playing its home games in Hungary because of the war.
Damaged relations
Relations between Ireland and Israel will not have improved following their meetings on the field. Tempers boiled over at times on Sunday, and a clash occurred before halftime when Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle said an Israeli player spat at him.
"There's been a lot of those incidents that could have escalated," Hallgrímsson said. "We were clever enough to stop it before it went too far. I felt it was kind of the intention to try to intimidate us and make us do something stupid."
An Israeli journalist said at the pre-match press conference the day before that the Irish players had called the Israeli players "monkeys" during the previous match, prompting an immediate rebuke from Irish communications officer Kieran Crowley, who said it was "a lie" and ended the press conference.
Ireland forward Adam Idah, who is Black, was reportedly racially abused by a small number of Israeli fans present during the first match.

Ukraine says its strikes have knocked out more than 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:08:58 UTC
00:08:58 KST

Ukraine's Security and Defense Forces have "put out of action" more than 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity through recent long-range strikes, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said in a statement published by the Defense Ministry on 4 October. These "carefully thought-out" actions were aimed at "bleeding the Russian war machine" and "destroying its military-economic potential," Khmara said.
Ukraine treats Russia's refineries as a priority target because their revenue helps fund the war. Even Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed on 1 October that the strikes had cost Russia 1% of its GDP and had "partially" achieved their goal, Interfax reported.
The ministry did not publish how it calculated the figure.
"The consequences of Ukrainian operations are not always visible immediately. But the effect accumulates and produces a tangible result," the ministry said.
Ukrainian deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory
The ministry named eight recently struck facilities, among others. One of them is the Moscow Oil Refinery, which Ukraine targeted in a massive drone attack on the night of 20 September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The refinery, operated by Gazprom Neft in Moscow's Kapotnya district, supplies about 40% of Moscow's fuel market and 70% of the Moscow region's demand for gasoline and aviation fuel, according to Russian news Telegram channel Astra.
Another was KINEF, which Ukraine has attacked repeatedly. It is Russia's second-largest oil refinery by capacity, and the Ukrainian military struck it on the night of 30 August, setting off a fire at the facility.
The ministry also named the Yaroslavl, Perm, Ilsky, Saratov, and Syzran refineries and the Ust-Luga port complex.
Ukraine triples production and procurement of long-range drones—and this is not the end
This year, Ukraine has tripled the production and procurement of long-range attack drones, the ministry said.
"This is not the limit. We will continue to scale up deep-strike capabilities," the statement said.
International cooperation is part of that push. Berlin will fund the production of additional DeepStrike-class long-range drones in Ukraine, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said after a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group on 15 April. The sides also agreed to jointly develop and produce a medium- and long-range drone system.
Ukraine and Germany also signed an agreement on the joint production of Bars drones, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on 8 July. The Bars' modular design allows it to be used for deep strikes, among other missions.
Oil refinery output has fallen
Russian refineries cut crude oil processing by 14% in the first nine months of the year compared with the same period last year amid Ukrainian drone attacks, according to calculations by two industry sources.
Experts' estimates of the decline differ widely. In August, Serhii Vakulenko of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center put it at 25–28%, while Russian economic commentator Vyacheslav Shiryaev put it at 65–70%, according to Defense-Aerospace.
Fuel production data give a more concrete picture: in July, Russia's gasoline and diesel output was about a quarter to a third lower than in March 2026, the outlet reported.

Russia's military spending masks a longer-term strategy for a prolonged war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:08:52 UTC
00:08:52 KST

What does Russia's rising military budget say about its plans for the war?
Russia's President Vladimir Putin (C) looks on as he visits an observation post during the "Center-2026" strategic command-and-staff exercise at the Chebarkulsky training ground in Chelyabinsk on Oct. 2, 2026. (Alexander Kazakov / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
The Russian government began the month by submitting a three-year budget plan to parliament, proposing yet another increase in funding for its war against Ukraine.
On the surface, the planned increase looks substantial. Russia's overall military budget is set to rise to around 17 trillion rubles (approximately $200 billion) in 2027, up from 12 trillion rubles in 2026 — a 27% increase in nominal spending.
When combined with spending on law enforcement, another heavy budget line, expenditures on the military and security forces account for 43% of the total government spending.
The figures are striking, but experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent cautioned that they can be misleading.
Rather than pointing to a sudden surge in military spending, the latest budget figures suggest that Russia is continuing to gradually build up and sustain its military capacity, signaling a readiness for a prolonged war.
read also
Big numbers
Next year, Russia's military and security forces will get more money than any other sector — only 21% of the 2027 budget is allocated to healthcare, education, and social payments combined. That is generally similar to what is directly funneled to the military, but only half of the number when allocations to security forces are added.
Russia's high military budget would also be maintained in 2028 and 2029, according to the three-year budget plan.
"It's difficult to speculate, but the planned budget hike suggests that (the Kremlin) may intend to recruit more people (into the army) under contract in 2027," said Michael Kofman, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
Guesses on the actual purpose of the increases can only be speculative, argued in turn Pavel Luzin, a researcher with the Center for European Policy Analysis.
On top of the already high military budget, the Russian government can additionally increase funding throughout the year without parliamentary approval, said Sergey Aleksashenko, an exiled Russian economist and former deputy finance minister.
"Basically, the numbers we are seeing, this is what the Kremlin wants us to see," he said. "Around May (this year), the Defense Ministry requested additional funding from Vladimir Putin, and this request was granted."
While Russia does not publish detailed data on military spending, Luzin agreed that the figures for 2026 were likely higher than what was settled in the Russian government's initial budget: "approximately 16-17 trillion rubles, in my assessment," the researcher told the Kyiv Independent.
As for funding on healthcare, education, and social payments, these are set to decrease next year, Russian economist Alexandra Prokopenko found in a recent study.
Nothing dramatically new on the military spending front
The 27% army budget increase may sound significant, but this number is a bit misleading, Aleksashenko said.
"Russian military expenditures are growing step by step, but not as dramatically as (this figure) would suggest, because that number was calculated on the wrong basis," the Russian economist added.
According to him, instead of basing the increase on Russia's initial plans for 2026, these should be compared to what Russia actually spent throughout the year: in that case, the increase would be much lower.
"It's not extraordinary that the government admitted that it will spend at least 17 trillion rubles on the military in 2027," Luzin agreed.
The bulk of the on-paper increase is linked to inflation, specifically cost-push inflation in the military industry, but also salaries and payments to wounded and families of killed Russian soldiers, the researcher added.
"At the same time, the Russian government is also beginning a new round of investments, trying to modernize the sector, because Russia's military industry cannot produce more than it did (at its peak) in 2024," he added.
In fact, Russia's upcoming budget says more about how the government wants to raise money for the war, Prokopenko explained — more than it does about how much money will be spent and on what.
"Officially, Russia's budget deficit is to be cut to 2.2% in 2027, but since the start of the full-scale invasion, the government never managed to stick to the original budget deficit plans," Prokopenko said. "For instance, for 2026, the plan was to keep the deficit to 1,6%, as opposed to 2,6% in 2025, but in the end the projection for this year is 3,2%."
Russia fills its deficit either through taking out money from its National Wealth Fund or by borrowing on the internal market, Prokopenko said.
However, the Russian government is having trouble attracting private businesses and citizens to invest in bonds — as a result, when Russia's Central Bank conducted its most recent bond auction, major state-owned banks bought around 84% of the total sum, Prokopenko said.
To raise money for the war in Ukraine, Russia also raised taxes, for instance by hiking VAT rates to 22% in 2026, by overall increasing income tax the previous year, and by introducing a planned tax on dividends and yields on bonds starting in 2027.
While Russia is clearly looking for money for the war, and the prime role of state-owned banks in financing debt can look awkward, this says little about the actual state of the Russian economy, Aleksashenko said.
"I don't see any problems on the financial or the economic side which would make Putin stop the war," the Russian economist argued.
"He is generally conservative with expenditures, so I don't think we'll be seeing a sudden boost in boots on the ground. As for the cost of this war (to the Russian economy), unfortunately, while it might not be sustainable in the long run, Putin sees the price to pay as acceptable."

A power outage affected thousands of homes and businesses in parts of London on Monday after a fault in an underground electricity network, according to UK Power Networks (UKPN).
Around 32 postcodes, mainly across east London, were affected by the disruption, which began at about 10.32 am (0932GMT).
UKPN, which operates electricity networks across London, southeast England and the east of England, said the outage was caused by a fault in the local underground network.
The disruption affected transport and businesses in the capital. Departure screens at London Liverpool Street station went blank, while some shops and offices were left without electricity. Offices also reported disruptions after Wi-Fi services were cut and computer monitors stopped working.
The Great Northern railway line was also affected, with trains unable to stop at Essex Road station after platform lighting was cut off. Passengers were advised to travel via Old Street or Highbury and Islington and allow extra time for their journeys.
UKPN said it diverted power to restore electricity to 4,989 homes and businesses around 15 minutes after the outage began.
Power was gradually restored, with electricity fully restored across all affected postcodes by the afternoon.
No further details about the cause of the underground network fault were provided.

The Czech Ministry of Defense has canceled a tender to purchase 185 armored vehicles worth 24.7 billion Czech korunas (approximately €1 billion).
This is evidenced by an official notice of the procurement cancellation, published in the Czech public procurement register, according to Ekonomický deník.
The bidding process was halted while awaiting preliminary proposals, which were due by September 30.
The decision was justified by circumstances requiring special attention and economic factors.
Officially, the project involved procuring equipment for the engineering corps, medical services, and military police.
The procurement process became complicated because of the large number of specifications and requirements, which caused potential bidders to lose interest.

Currently, the issue of providing the Czech Army’s medical and engineering units with armored wheeled vehicles remains unresolved.
Previously, the American company Flyer Defense, in partnership with the Czech STV Group, delivered the first batch of F72-HD heavy tactical vehicles to the Czech Republic.
In total, the country is set to receive 46 such vehicles, which the U.S. government is providing free of charge under the Foreign Military Financing (FMF) program in gratitude for its support of Ukraine.

Why the U.S. Bomber Withdrawal From a U.K. Air Base Is Significant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:07:36 UTC
00:07:36 KST

President Donald Trump said Monday afternoon that "threats" had prompted the U.S. to remove all of its B-1 Air Force bombers from the RAF Fairford base in southern England over the weekend. The move came a week after several men were arrested nearby in relation to a suspected terror plot, which the U.K. government believes may be linked to Iran.
When asked if there was a specific threat that led to the bombers being moved, Trump told reporters: “Yeah, I think we can say that. They didn’t fly out by accident. There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy… why should we leave them there? We moved them around a little bit, not very far.”
He added that Washington “actually knows the people that made the threat.” When asked if they are linked to Iran, Trump responded: “They would be linked to Iran.”
A U.S. Defense Department official had earlier told TIME that all the U.S. bombers had been ”re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” but did not offer a specific reason behind the move, instead saying that U.S. bombers “routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements.” The official added that America’s bomber force remains “ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities… anywhere, anytime.” Hours before Trump's remarks, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed the idea that the removal of U.S. bombers was directly connected to the foiled Fairford plot, insisting he has “confidence” in the security of U.S. bases.
A spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the RAF Fairford base remains safe, but refused to offer any specific comment on the military operations of “foreign nations.” The British Ministry of Defense directed TIME to the U.S. Air Force when approached for comment.
The move comes after five men, all U.K. nationals, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses on Sept. 27, following a suspected terror plot nearby RAF Fairford, an airbase used by the U.S. to strike Iran. Officers made the arrests after receiving a tip-off that three "suspicious vehicles" appeared to be heading toward the direction of the base. Amid ongoing investigations, British counterterrorism police arrested a dual British-Iranian national in central London on Oct. 1 on suspicion of terrorist acts in connection with the incident. All arrestees have been released on bail.
David Dunn, a professor of international politics at the University of Birmingham, says the U.S. withdrawal from Fairford is “historic, unprecedented, and an indication of the sense of vulnerability” surrounding U.S. military assets abroad.
“Fairford is normally the place during a crisis where America sends bombers to beef up America's military capability and its formal operating bases, whether that's for operations in Europe, like the Kosovo campaign, or for operations in the Gulf through 2003 onwards, or indeed for operations in Iran,” Dunn tells TIME. “This [removal] is an indication of concerns about the safety of those assets in their forward operating bases.”
Dunn adds “the haste” with which the operation took place over the weekend is also noteworthy, referencing reports that some of the aircraft had only been there for a relatively short period of time, having arrived recently as part of a rotation.
U.K. and U.S. officials suspect Iranian involvement in RAF Fairford plot
Both U.K. and U.S. officials have voiced suspicion of Iranian involvement in the suspected terror plot that has led to several arrests.
Burnham on Sept. 30 said the U.K. believes Iran was likely involved in the incident. “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation,” he said, adding that British forces were “working closely” with U.S. counterparts.
Iran has vehemently denied any involvement. In the immediate aftermath of the initial arrests, the Iranian embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" any attempt to "link Iran to" the arrests made near RAF Fairford. After Burnham’s comments, Iran doubled down on its denial, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accusing the U.K. of “barking up the wrong tree.”
Trump previously said the five men arrested at the scene had been under “investigation” prior to the arrests and were looking to cause “big damage.” Asked whether Iran was involved in the suspect terror plot, he said, “it might be,” but did not offer further details.
Dunn says that although Iran “hasn't got the range to [directly] attack bases in the U.K.,” it does not necessarily remove the potential threat to U.S. assets stationed there. “Iran—by doing things via proxies, organized criminal gangs, or hiring people gangs through payments through the dark web—can still have a military effect and a deterrent effect on the operation of a base like Fairford,” he says.
Counter Terrorism Policing has said it is looking at all angles, citing possible foreign-state involvement as one line of inquiry. It has urged against conclusions being drawn in what is a high-profile and active investigation.
How RAF Fairford has supported U.S. military operations for decades
RAF Fairford is a NATO-designated standby deployment and a U.S. forward operating base for U.S. Global Strike Command, according to U.K. government records. The base, which opened in 1944, has been used extensively by U.S. military aircraft in previous conflicts, including "Operation Iraqi Freedom" in 2003.
The U.S. Air Force describes RAF Fairford as its “preferred” European “bomber forward operating location” and previously said it has used Fairford “nearly continuously” since the base was constructed.
Former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer initially refused to allow U.S. access to U.K. military bases in its offensive strikes against Iran—a move that earned him the wrath of Trump. Starmer changed his position in March, authorizing the U.S. to use bombers based at RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned the base could be a target on account of its use by the U.S. military, insisting it makes the U.K. a “participant in aggression” in the war.
Starmer had previously warned the British public of the general threat posed by Iran. On Feb. 28, in an address to the nation hours after the U.S. and Israel launched its initial strikes against Iran, he said: “Even in the United Kingdom, the Iranian regime poses a direct threat to dissidents and the Jewish community. Over the last year alone, they have backed more than 20 potentially lethal attacks on U.K. soil.”

"But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian ships instead of normal navigation. Pressure is needed to restore global food security. And everyone who is truly interested in this should help."
Romania's Interior Ministry later said 11 crew members had been rescued. The vessel was sinking, while injured survivors were evacuated for emergency medical treatment. Romanian authorities had not provided details about the cause of the fire.
The incident is the latest in a string of Russian attacks that has crippled civilian and commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
Ukraine's maritime corridor, opened in 2023 after Russia withdrew from the U.N.-backed grain deal, has been largely closed again after a spate of Russian attacks, both on port infrastructure and ships themselves, over summer 2026.
The International Maritime Organization has warned that the war poses a "serious and immediate threat" to crews and vessels operating in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.
The latest incident comes two days after a Russian strike on a Liberian-flagged cargo ship in Ukraine's Odesa region killed one person and injured three, according to Ukrainian port authorities cited by Reuters.

Pakistan rolls out fuel subsidies as oil prices squeeze households
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:02:00 UTC
00:02:00 KST

Pakistan has rolled out a nationwide fuel subsidy scheme targeting motorcycle, rickshaw and small-car owners as rising global oil prices put pressure on working- and middle-income households, the Prime Minister’s Office said.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif launched the Prime Minister’s Special Relief Scheme to provide targeted assistance to people who rely on their vehicles for work and daily transportation, particularly those who often fall outside conventional social assistance programs.
Under the scheme, eligible motorcycle, rickshaw and Qingqi users receive 500 Pakistani rupees ($1.78) in fuel relief per week through four tokens a month.
The government has removed an initial 5-liter minimum purchase requirement, meaning users can now receive the full Rs. 500 subsidy regardless of how much petrol they buy.
Owners of cars with engines of up to 800cc, meanwhile, receive a discount of Rs. 100 per liter on 10 liters every 10 days, with three subsidized tokens available each month.
The government also expanded eligibility for motorcycles, rickshaws and Qingqis from vehicles up to 15 years old to those up to 20 years old following public feedback. Vehicles registered on or after Jan. 1, 2006, can now qualify.
Eligible citizens can register free of charge through the government's 9771 SMS service, while a digital system links applicants' national identity, registered SIM cards and vehicle records to help prevent duplicate claims and misuse.
The Prime Minister’s Office said the program was developed rapidly despite Pakistan's limited fiscal space and was intended to shield vulnerable households from the impact of global energy price increases.
Sharif is personally overseeing the scheme, with the government saying further adjustments could be made in response to feedback from recipients.

Britain threatens to expel 27 Israeli diplomats over Jerusalem consulate closure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:01:05 UTC
00:01:05 KST

Britain has warned Israel that it will expel 27 Israeli diplomats from the embassy in London unless Jerusalem reverses its decision to close the British Consulate General in East Jerusalem, according to a message conveyed to Israeli officials and obtained by ynet.
The warning marks a sharp escalation in already strained relations between Israel and Britain, which deteriorated further last month after London announced new measures targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The British government has banned imports of goods from settlements and announced sanctions against individuals and companies it says support, facilitate or profit from settlement activity. Britain considers Israeli settlements illegal under international law, a position Israel disputes.
In response, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar announced a series of measures against Britain, including the closure of its consulate in East Jerusalem, which serves Palestinians and employs 27 British diplomats.
The British Consulate General in Jerusalem operates separately from the British Embassy to Israel. According to the British government, it represents London in its dealings with Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza and handles political, economic, security and consular affairs. Britain recognizes Israel's de facto authority over West Jerusalem but has not recognized sovereignty over Jerusalem as a whole, saying the city's final status must be determined through negotiations.
Israel's decision to close the consulate and revoke the diplomatic credentials of its staff is due to take effect Thursday. Dozens of locally employed staff members have already been dismissed and the British diplomats are preparing to leave.
Sa'ar's other measures included removing British representatives from the international aid coordination center for Gaza in the southern city of Kiryat Gat, ending British involvement in training Palestinian Authority security forces in the West Bank and barring 12 British elected officials and other citizens from entering Israel.
Israel said those barred had been involved in antisemitic or anti-Israel activity or had denied Israel's right to exist.
People familiar with the dispute said British officials were shocked by the Israeli measures and had not expected such a severe response. They were particularly angered by Israel's decision to give the diplomats serving at the East Jerusalem consulate only 30 days to leave the country.
The officials noted that Russia, by comparison, gave Britain four months to close its consulate in St. Petersburg amid a diplomatic dispute involving espionage allegations.
Britain initially refrained from publicly announcing retaliatory measures, believing it could persuade Israel to reverse its decision through quiet, behind-the-scenes diplomacy.
London has now conveyed a more explicit warning, however. British Ambassador to Israel Simon Walters informed Israeli officials that if the closure goes ahead, Britain would respond by expelling 27 diplomats serving at the Israeli Embassy in London — one Israeli diplomat for each British diplomat whose work in East Jerusalem is being terminated, according to people familiar with the message.
Such a move would severely impair the Israeli Embassy's ability to operate. Although the mission employs more than 27 diplomats, the total is not substantially higher.
The embassy has also been without an ambassador for more than a year, since Tzipi Hotovely returned to Israel in September 2025. It is currently headed by chargé d'affaires Chris Cantor.
The British Embassy declined to comment on the report.
Relations deteriorate over Gaza and West Bank
The dispute comes amid a broader deterioration in ties between the two countries over Israel's policies in Gaza and the West Bank.
Britain has increasingly criticized Israeli settlement expansion and settler violence and says its latest measures are intended to preserve the possibility of a two-state solution. In September, Britain joined a group of Western countries warning that Israeli actions in the West Bank were undermining prospects for a Palestinian state.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government has also stepped up its criticism of Israel's conduct in Gaza. In a speech to the UN General Assembly last month, Burnham condemned Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attack and affirmed Britain's support for Israel in the face of threats from Iran, while sharply criticizing the Israeli government's actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who took office in July, has made the Israeli-Palestinian conflict a prominent part of British foreign policy. Miliband, the son of Jewish refugees who fled the Nazis, has repeatedly emphasized both his personal connection to Israel and his opposition to Israeli government policies in Gaza and the West Bank.
At the Labour Party conference in Liverpool last week, Miliband received loud applause during a speech in which he denounced what he described as war crimes in Gaza, attacked Israeli government policy and defended London's decision to prohibit trade in goods from West Bank settlements.
Miliband also acknowledged the domestic pressure facing the government over Gaza, saying millions of people in Britain had been appalled by events there. "We hear you. You were right," he said.
The tensions have unfolded against an increasingly contentious British political debate over Israel and Zionism.
On Saturday, Britain's Green Party conference approved a motion describing Zionism as a "racist ideology" and calling for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel. British media noted that the decision placed the Greens, which have grown substantially in political prominence, in an unusually explicit anti-Zionist position among mainstream European political parties.
The diplomatic standoff now leaves Israel and Britain facing the prospect of one of the most serious disruptions to their bilateral diplomatic representation in years, with Thursday's deadline for the East Jerusalem consulate closure approaching.

American rocket artillery opens fire in joint drill
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:00:04 BST
00:00:04 KST

US Army rocket artillery has opened fire during a joint live-fire exercise with the Singapore Armed Forces, with M270 Multiple Launch Rocket Systems used during Exercise Daring Warrior 2026 at Fort Sill in Oklahoma, according to the US Army.
Soldiers from Bravo Battery, 3rd Battalion, 13th Field Artillery Regiment, 75th Field Artillery Brigade conducted the firing on 21 September alongside Singaporean personnel as part of the bilateral training event.
Imagery released by the US military shows an M270 launching rockets across the Fort Sill training area, with American and Singaporean troops also working together around artillery equipment and command systems during the exercise.
The US Army said the live-fire was designed to synchronise American and Singaporean launch crews, allowing the two forces to practise delivering coordinated precision fires while testing their ability to operate together on the range. Exercise Daring Warrior brings together artillery personnel from the two countries for training involving weapons operation, command and control and the coordination required to employ long-range fires as part of a combined force.
The M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System is a tracked rocket artillery platform operated by the US Army and several allied militaries. Its launcher carries interchangeable rocket and missile pods, allowing it to employ different types of ammunition depending on the mission.
Unlike conventional tube artillery, multiple launch rocket systems are intended to deliver fires over greater distances and can engage targets using guided munitions. The M270 shares ammunition with the wheeled M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, better known as HIMARS, although the tracked M270 carries two launch pods rather than one.
The system has also gained renewed prominence during the war in Ukraine, where M270 and HIMARS launchers supplied by Western countries have been used extensively by Ukrainian forces for long-range precision strikes.
For the American and Singaporean troops at Fort Sill, the emphasis was on operating the systems as part of a combined artillery force rather than simply conducting individual launcher firings.
Photographs from the exercise show personnel from both armies working together during equipment familiarisation and planning activity, as well as operating observation and targeting equipment in the field. Other imagery shows American and Singaporean troops positioned around command posts and tactical vehicles before the live-fire phase, reflecting the wider chain of activity required to identify targets, pass firing information and coordinate launch crews.
The Singapore Armed Forces operates its own M142 HIMARS rocket artillery systems, giving its personnel experience with a weapons family that shares ammunition and elements of fire-control architecture with the M270.
Fort Sill is the US Army’s principal artillery training centre and home to the Field Artillery School, making the Oklahoma installation a regular location for both domestic and multinational artillery exercises. The 75th Field Artillery Brigade is also based at Fort Sill and provides long-range precision fires capabilities to US forces, with subordinate units operating rocket and missile artillery systems.

A ‘phoenix’ planet was born from the ashes of its dead star
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

A ‘phoenix’ planet was born from the ashes of its dead star
The discovery hints that planetary systems can have second beginnings
A dead star’s wreckage may be the birthplace of a new planet.
The existence of second-generation planets was predicted theoretically more than 15 years ago. But this “phoenix” world, if confirmed, would be the first actually spotted, scientists report October 5 in Nature Astronomy.
“A phoenix is reborn from the ashes of its predecessor, and this planet is formed from the ashes of the star,” says astronomer Jamie Williams, of the University of Warwick in Coventry, England.
The finding suggests planetary systems can have a second life even after their stars die.
Before this discovery, this planet formation process has been “more like a hypothesis, more like speculation,” says planetary scientist Zifan Lin of Washington University in St. Louis, who was not involved in the new work. “This is the first time we’ve seen evidence for that process.”
Williams and colleagues found signs of the planet in the atmosphere of a white dwarf called HS 0209+0832. White dwarfs are the small, dense cores left behind after low-mass stars — like our sun — puff up into red giant stars at the end of their lives, ultimately blowing all the outer material away.
These stellar corpses are so dense that most chemical elements sink into their centers, leaving them with pristine atmospheres composed of almost entirely hydrogen and helium. But astronomers have found that between a quarter and half of these stars are “polluted” with elements like silicon and iron, which are found in rock.
These elements probably come from shattered planets that the star devoured as it expanded. “They can be probes into the interiors of planets,” Lin says. Astronomers have also found whole planets that seem to have survived their stars’ demise and still orbit the remaining white dwarf. Ironically, some astronomers think these dead stars could be prime hunting grounds for signs of extraterrestrial life.
HS 0209+0832 was a known weirdo. When the Hubble Space Telescope observed it in 1999, astronomers could tell that the white dwarf contained a mysterious mix of chemicals, but they couldn’t identify them. Since then, there have been more detailed studies of how certain atoms would show up in stellar atmospheres, Williams says.
Reanalyzing those observations showed that the white dwarf contains only trace amounts of silicon and almost no iron, Williams and colleagues found. But it does include a ridiculous amount of niobium. This hard, silvery metal, used in jewelry, rocket systems and superconductors, is rare on Earth and had never been seen in a white dwarf.
“We’ve never observed anything in the universe that’s this niobium-rich before,” Williams says. “We were quite confused at first.”
A clue to how it got there came from the element’s origins. Niobium forms in the slow neutron-capture process, or s-process, which mostly occurs in certain red giant stars as they shed their atmospheres and die. Iron nuclei transform into heavier elements in a series of accretion and decay that can take thousands of years.
Material ejected from a dying star could have coalesced into a new planet full of s-process elements, Williams says. Then the resulting white dwarf could slowly sip on the new planet’s atmosphere, leaving a fresh coat of niobium and other s-process elements on the white dwarf’s face.
To support this idea, the team looked at observations of HS 0209+0832 taken with the TESS space telescope, which hunts exoplanets by observing small changes in the light of their stars as planets orbit. The white dwarf’s brightness changes with a period of about 4.4 days, the team found. That’s too slow to be related to the white dwarf’s own rotation.
But it could be explained by a gas giant planet orbiting very close to the star, about 4 percent the distance from the Earth to the sun or 6 million kilometers. Williams imagines it as a silvery version of Jupiter.
“We’re not really sure, if it’s not a planet, what it is,” he says. “A planet is the most reasonable explanation.”
Our sun will one day meet the same fate as HS 0209+0832’s predecessor. We don’t know enough about second-generation planets yet to say whether our solar system could end up with one after the sun dies, Williams says. “But I think it’s definitely possible.”

Israel was prepared to shoot down FlyDubai plane, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:59:04 UTC
23:59:04 KST

Israel was prepared to shoot down FlyDubai plane after attack on captain, sources say
Israel was prepared to shoot down a FlyDubai plane after the captain was attacked in the cockpit, even with over 150 Israelis on board, two Israeli sources with direct knowledge of the situation told CBS News.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, passengers on board the plane and the flight captain have said.
Israel has a long-practiced procedure for this kind of possible 9/11-style event, according to the sources. After the plane plunged 14,000 feet, the Israeli Air Force tried to contact the cockpit but got no answer. A pre-established committee was quickly roused and a command center established.
Fighter jets were scrambled and Israel's airspace was closed. But Israel called back the jets once it realized that, about 400 miles from Israel, the plane turned toward Saudi Arabia, and the Saudis scrambled their own jets.
The captain of the plane was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. A group of Israeli passengers and FlyDubai staff then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, according to accounts from the plane.
If Flight 1073 had gotten within a certain distance, Israel would have sent jets into Jordanian airspace to investigate, the sources told CBS News.
The Israeli fighter pilots would have gotten as close as possible to inspect the cockpit and try to make visual contact with the pilot to assess the situation, the sources said. They would have then done the same to the cabin to assess the status of the passengers. If there appeared to be panic, they would relay their findings to the Air Force and the pre-established committee.
If it was determined the plane was hijacked, and the potential hijackers maintained radio silence and made no demands, the committee would get the defense minister and the prime minister on a call, the sources said.
The protocol calls for a rogue flight approaching Israel to be shot out of the sky, but only the prime minister could have made that decision. The sources told CBS News that shooting down the passenger jet would be considered better than many hundreds being killed if a rogue plane slammed into Israel's prominent Azrieli buildings, the airport or another "high-value target."
The co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain said during his interrogation in the United Arab Emirates that he had planned the attack even before he was employed by FlyDubai, an Israeli official told CBS News. The co-pilot, identified by sources familiar with the investigation as Omani national Hamam al Hamami, intended to crash the plane at Ben Gurion Airport, the official said, adding that he had flown to Israel in the past.
The attempted hijacking was likely a lone-wolf attack, an early investigation by Israel shows, according to sources familiar with the matter. The investigation is ongoing and all avenues are still being explored, the sources told CBS News.

A NATO official confirmed the plan's existence to the Kyiv Independent.

Subsequently, allied forces would seek to destroy Russian command and control to deliver a quick and decisive victory.
At the same time, the plan said NATO would avoid any provocations on its part while working to counter Russian hybrid attacks.
NATO has not publicly commented on the contents of the plan.
Tensions between Russia and the alliance have surged since the outbreak of the full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022, with Moscow repeatedly issuing threats to NATO members and countries backing Kyiv.
The concerns are further fueled by escalating Russian hybrid attacks and provocations on NATO soil, from drone incursions in Poland and Romania to alleged Moscow-backed sabotage operations in Estonia and Germany.

Protests in France and Spain appear disparate but core issues are the same
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:55:44 UTC
23:55:44 KST

In Spain, tens of thousands of people in 50 cities have taken to the streets amid mounting fury over the country’s housing crisis, their feelings made plain on a banner at the burgeoning protest camp in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol plaza: “You can speculate on watches, jewels, crypto-bros and Ferraris. But not on our fucking homes.”
In France, as high school pupils clash with police in often violent protests over long hours, missing teachers, crumbling classrooms and an opaque university admissions system, the angry slogans include: “More hours in class than for sleep”, “Fund study, not repression” and “I’d like to be worrying about my maths exam, not my future”.
They may stem from different specific grievances, but the two waves of mainly youth-led protest exemplify a growing problem for western European governments: a generation of young people feeling increasingly denied the basic socioeconomic security that, by and large, their parents enjoyed.
The trigger in Spain, where rents have risen by 80% in a decade, was – perhaps ironically – the high-profile eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid after an investment fund increased her rent by 230%. For those spending more than half their income on housing (the monthly rental on a one-bedroom flat can cost an entire median salary), enough was enough.
Rocketing rents, rampant property speculation, the boom in short-term tourist rentals and stagnant wages have combined to make an independent adult life increasingly unachievable for many young workers – and the state is seen not as a neutral mediator, but an active enabler of property speculation.
In France, the protests began in the northern Paris suburbs but quickly spread nationwide, fuelled by young people’s anger at an underfunded education system that, the data shows, entrenches social inequality.
Pupils routinely miss months of teaching owing to unfilled staff absences. Timetables run from 8am to 6pm – among the longest in Europe – in buildings with leaking roofs, cockroaches and collapsing ceilings. In Paris last week, students on high school barricades saw budget cuts as a straightforward assault on their future. In their eyes, a system meant to promote social mobility now prevents it.
Lacking parliamentary majorities and facing varying degrees of budgetary constraint, however, neither government has much room for manoeuvre. Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, on Monday called a snap general election after rightwing parties voted down his emergency housing legislation.
In France, as student protests – and more than 5,000 arrests – forced the closure of up to 500 secondary schools on Monday, the centrist prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has urged local authorities to prioritise filling long-term teacher absences and called urgent meetings to discuss repairing dilapidated school buildings.
Taken together, the two crises highlight some core problems facing mainstream governments. First, young people in particular have come to see incremental measures – targeted tax credits, minor administrative reforms – as sticking plasters on altogether deeper socioeconomic wounds.
Second, facing mounting street pressure and opposition parties eager to exploit it, ruling coalitions – especially those that lack majorities – will struggle. And in France, heavy-handed policing risks alienating young voters from the mainstream even further.
Meanwhile, radicalised opposition parties are actively weaponising the discontent. On the radical left, France’s Jean-Luc Mélenchon – backed by 47% of voters under 35 – has sided openly with the street, while in Spain, leftwing parties Podemos and Sumar have blamed the housing crisis squarely on out-of-control financial capitalism.
At the same time, the populist far right is playing a law-and-order card, with Marine Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) in France seizing on footage of burning barricades to accuse centrist leaders of tolerating “unbridled violence” and Spain’s far-right Vox siding with the main conservative Partido Popular opposition to torpedo Sánchez’s emergency package, framing it as government overreach punishing landlords.
Squeezed from both sides, mainstream governments face a spiralling challenge. When an entire generation concludes that society’s existing frameworks guarantee them neither affordable homes nor functioning schools, political consent starts to evaporate and Europe’s establishment parties risk losing their legitimacy.
As Nando de Anguulo, a 26-year-old protester in Madrid, put it: the protests prove that as things stand, “it is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties – and not the politicians who have to adapt to what the people want. It can’t go on like that.”

NATO Uses Lessons-Learned in Ukraine to Plan Russian Defeat in 3D+ Battlespace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:54:38 UTC
23:54:38 KST

NATO is drafting a strategy designed to defeat a potential Russian attack on its eastern flank quickly and decisively by combining conventional military power with drones and artificial intelligence.
The document, titled “Theory of Victory,” is being developed under NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) Gen. Alexus Grynkewich and is expected to be presented in Poland on Monday, Oct. 12, Bloomberg reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Bloomberg reviewed an unclassified version of the document, which is intended to clarify how NATO would respond if Russian forces entered the territory of an alliance member.
The strategy remains a planning document rather than an indication that NATO believes a Russian conventional attack is imminent.
“The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO’s advantage,” Grynkewich’s spokesperson, Col. Martin O’Donnell, told Bloomberg.
O’Donnell declined to discuss operational details but said the alliance needed to prepare now to deter aggression and prevail if attacked. He also stressed that NATO remained a “purely defensive” alliance.
Drones and AI would support conventional forces
Under the proposed strategy, NATO would initially seek to stop an incursion using land forces and capabilities developed through its Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative.
These would include low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-assisted targeting integrated with conventional weapons and military units.
Russian Authorities Won’t Confirm Pneumonic Plague Outbreak in Central Siberia
After securing freedom of movement, allied forces would attempt to disrupt and destroy the enemy’s command-and-control structure, with the aim of defeating the attacking forces before they could establish a lasting foothold on NATO territory.
The plan emphasizes avoiding unintended provocations while demonstrating enough military readiness to convince an adversary that an attack could not succeed.
It also covers hybrid threats – hostile actions such as sabotage, cyberattacks, interference with infrastructure and covert operations that remain below the threshold of open warfare.
Russia has reportedly ordered its intelligence services to intensify hybrid operations across NATO and EU countries, including possible sabotage against military facilities, critical infrastructure and communications systems.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said there are currently no indications that Russia is preparing a conventional assault on the alliance. However, European governments expect Moscow’s hybrid campaign to continue and potentially intensify.
NATO applies lessons from Ukraine
The strategy reflects lessons from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, where inexpensive drones, electronic warfare and rapidly updated software have transformed even frontline 2D battlefield operations into 3D-plus battlespace operations.
NATO has already been testing drones, unmanned ground vehicles, counter-drone equipment and new communications systems under the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative.
The alliance has also explored an AI-assisted automated defensive zone along its borders with Russia and Belarus. The proposed system would use interconnected sensors, drones and weapons to detect hostile movements while reducing the number of soldiers required to monitor exposed areas.
In July, NATO members agreed to invest more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities over five years. The alliance is also developing a counter-drone marketplace and plans to train five times as many military drone operators by the end of 2027.
Allies face spending and force decisions
The proposal comes as European NATO members sharply increase defense expenditure but debate how to divide funding between tanks, artillery and other conventional weapons and newer technologies demonstrated in Ukraine.
The US reportedly sent allies a questionnaire during the summer asking about their defense spending and support for President Donald Trump’s policies as Washington considered reducing some American military assets assigned to Europe.
The questionnaire also asked whether NATO members could contribute additional forces to Grynkewich’s defense plans.
“Theory of Victory” is therefore intended not only to describe a possible military response but also to show governments what forces and technologies they would need to finance before a crisis begins.
The initiative comes amid growing concern about Russian drone incursions, sabotage and airspace violations along NATO’s eastern flank. Rutte has said the alliance deliberately keeps the precise threshold for activating Article 5 ambiguous, preventing adversaries from calculating how far they can escalate without triggering a collective response.

Leaders of global space agencies gathered in Türkiye's Mediterranean province of Antalya for a special session at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) and discussed international collaboration.
The session brought together senior aerospace officials from Türkiye, the US, Europe, China, India, Canada, and Japan.
Yusuf Kirac, president of the Turkish Space Agency, said orbital activities have expanded in recent years, while securing sustainable and secure access to space has become a logistical challenge that remains insurmountable without collaboration.
“Building the future of space requires collective capabilities, responsible leadership, and effective global cooperation — the IAC’s running theme of ‘The world needs more space’ this year means more space for science and innovation, for opportunities for young people and new ideas, and to ensure the participation of countries from all across the world,” he said.
NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson noted that upcoming Artemis III mission will feature a multinational crew of three Americans, one Canadian, and one Italian space traveler, utilizing orbital docking maneuvers with SpaceX and Blue Origin lunar landers before concluding the mission in 2027.
“We are lucky in the US to have full support of our Congress with funding; for example, they gave an additional $10 billion to our budget last year to help us with our Artemis program, build the Moon base, establish a permanent presence, and then move on to Mars,” he said, noting that the conclusion of Artemis III next year will pave the way for the subsequent Artemis missions.
European Space Agency Director General Josef Aschbacher said space has become a part of daily life with satellite technologies benefiting many areas of society, while the global space economy is expected to triple its current $600 billion valuation to over $1.8 trillion over the next decade.
He added that Europe is seeking ways to boost its robotic and crewed exploration capacity through global partnerships.
The speakers at the special executive session for space agency leaders included China National Space Administration’s Lu Guoping, Indian Space Research Organization’s V. Narayanan, Canadian Space Agency’s Jean-Claude Piedboeuf, and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s Hiroshi Yamakawa.
The event kicked off on Monday and will run until Friday, co-hosted by the Turkish Space Agency and SAHA Istanbul defense cluster, organized by the Turkish Industry and Technology Ministry. Anadolu serves as its global communications partner.

The flydubai co-pilot who stabbed the captain of a flight to Israel last week had planned the attack before joining the airline, according to two Israeli officials familiar with the UAE investigation.
A third source briefed on the probe said the Omani co-pilot had planned to crash Wednesday's flight into Ben-Gurion Airport. He had also flown to Tel Aviv earlier this year and intended to hijack and crash that flight, but ultimately abandoned the plan, the source said.
It was not immediately clear why he changed his mind, though the source said he is believed to have known someone aboard the earlier flight.
The sources spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the investigation. UAE and Israeli authorities, as well as flydubai, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The co-pilot of flydubai Flight FZ1073, which was flying from Dubai to Israel last Wednesday, attacked the captain with an emergency crash axe, the UAE prosecutor general has said, describing the incident as a "terrorist attack."
Two sources have identified the co-pilot as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami. Israeli officials have said he is from Oman but have not publicly named him, while UAE authorities and flydubai have not disclosed his identity
Reuters has not been able to independently reach al-Hammami, who is in UAE custody, for comment. The UAE has not announced formal charges against him, and it is not known whether he has appointed a lawyer. Oman has not commented on the incident.
The two Israeli officials said al-Hammami told interrogators that he applied to flydubai after searching for airlines that operated flights to Tel Aviv.
CBS News reported Sunday that an initial Israeli investigation found that he acted alone.
According to Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, al-Hammami planned to shut down the plane's engines and crash it into skyscrapers in Tel Aviv. The report said he also intended to kill the captain without alerting authorities and reach Tel Aviv before Israeli fighter jets could intercept the aircraft.
Passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot before he could carry out the alleged attack. Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, survived after managing to open the cockpit door. More than 170 passengers and crew were aboard the flight, most of them Israeli.
A reserve flydubai pilot traveling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at an airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia. The co-pilot was detained there and transferred to the UAE on Thursday.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said pilots from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel, including Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to Israel. It remains unclear how al-Hammami was assigned to the Tel Aviv flight, and Netanyahu has since ordered a review of foreign airlines flying to Israel.
An Australian counterterrorism unit is also investigating the co-pilot's ties to Australia. A fourth source said he studied at RMIT University in Melbourne around a decade ago.

Hungary Set to Ease Ukraine EU Veto – But Only After Minority Rights Deal

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:51:17 UTC
23:51:17 KST

Hungary is expected to ease its veto on further progress in Ukraine and Moldova’s EU accession talks this week, potentially clearing the way for negotiations on two additional policy clusters.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar instructed the country’s diplomats not to block letters inviting Kyiv and Chisinau to submit negotiating positions for the next stage of the process, the Financial Times (FT) reported on Monday, Oct. 5, citing two officials.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The two clusters cover the EU internal market, competitiveness, and inclusive growth. Budapest has repeatedly prevented their advancement because decisions at this stage require the unanimous support of all 27 EU members.
The planned move is procedural and does not yet amount to Hungary’s unconditional approval to open the clusters. Budapest’s final political support depends on the Verkhovna Rada adopting legislation expanding education rights for Ukraine’s national minorities.
“The accession process of Ukraine is taking shape, with due process and a realistic approach,” an EU official familiar with negotiations with Budapest told the FT.
Parliament vote remains decisive
Ukraine registered the draft education legislation in parliament on Thursday, Oct. 1 and is expected to hold a vote on Monday, Oct. 12.
The proposed law would give Hungarian-speaking communities and other national minorities whose languages are official in the EU greater opportunities to receive education in their native languages.
Russian Attack Sends Projectile Into Bus at Moldova Border
Schools where more than half of pupils study in a minority language could receive special status. However, the legislation would not extend the same provisions to Russian as it is not an official EU language.
Magyar welcomed the bill, saying it would strengthen legal guarantees for Hungarian-language education and the network of minority schools.
Roughly 100,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Ukraine, mainly in the western Zakarpattia region. Budapest has long argued that Ukraine’s education legislation restricts their linguistic and cultural rights.
Kyiv and Budapest reached an agreement in principle on the community’s language, cultural, educational, and political rights in June, but Hungary subsequently blocked the second and third accession clusters.
If the Rada approves the bill, EU officials could formally advance the clusters before the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 15.
Four clusters could be open
EU accession negotiations are divided into six thematic clusters containing the reforms a candidate country must complete before joining the bloc.
Ukraine and Moldova have so far opened the Fundamentals cluster, which covers the judiciary, democratic institutions, and fundamental rights, as well as the External Relations cluster.
Hungary has blocked clusters two and three multiple times, while other EU members opposed separating Moldova from Ukraine and advancing the two countries at different speeds.
If the internal market and competitiveness clusters are opened, only two clusters would remain: one addressing green policy and connectivity and the another covering resources, agriculture, and cohesion.
The European Commission hopes to open those remaining clusters for Ukraine and Moldova before the end of 2026.
Opening all six clusters would not mean that either country is able to join the EU. Each cluster contains detailed benchmarks and reforms that must be negotiated, implemented, and eventually closed with the unanimous approval of member states.
Magyar has adopted a less confrontational approach toward Ukraine than his predecessor, Viktor Orbán, but has continued to oppose an accelerated accession process. In June, he secured the removal of language calling for faster Ukrainian accession from an EU summit declaration.
The expected compromise would allow Magyar to present the education bill as a diplomatic achievement for Hungary’s minority while enabling Ukraine and Moldova to move forward with their membership bids.

Partner’s Financial Condition Can Change Within Few Months - Dun & Bradstreet
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:51:17 EEST
23:51:17 KST

A one-time check of a counterparty before concluding a contract does not make it possible to fully control commercial risks: a company’s financial condition, its owners, management and payment discipline may change already in the course of cooperation. Therefore, Ukrainian businesses should move from one-time checks to continuous monitoring of key partners.
International business information systems, including Dun & Bradstreet (D&B), make it possible not only to obtain information about a company before starting cooperation, but also to track changes in its profile.
According to Maksym Urakin, Director of Development and Marketing at Interfax-Ukraine and head of the D&B-Interfax-Ukraine business unit, monitoring is particularly important for companies to which a Ukrainian supplier regularly provides deferred payment terms or with which a significant volume of turnover is associated.
“A counterparty may have looked absolutely reliable at the time the contract was signed, but six months later the situation may be different. The company’s debt burden may increase, its owner or management may change, or its payment discipline may deteriorate. If the supplier learns about this only after an overdue payment, managing the risk becomes significantly more difficult,” Urakin noted.
International D&B databases are used to track changes in corporate data and assess business risks. Depending on the information available for a particular jurisdiction, a user can analyze changes in an enterprise’s financial condition, its corporate structure and other characteristics.
This approach is particularly relevant for companies with a large number of customers and suppliers. With hundreds or thousands of counterparties, regularly checking each of them manually is practically impossible.
“Businesses need to identify critically important partners. The greater a counterparty’s debt to the company, or the more strongly the supply chain depends on it, the higher the frequency and depth of monitoring should be,” Urakin believes.
A change in risk indicators does not necessarily require the immediate termination of cooperation. It may serve as a signal to revise the credit limit, shorten the payment deferral period, request additional collateral or conduct a more in-depth check.
A separate area is supplier monitoring. Financial problems at a raw-material producer, carrier or another critically important partner can lead to a halt in supplies even when the Ukrainian company’s own financial position remains stable.
According to Experts Club, Ukrainian enterprises should divide counterparties at least according to their level of financial significance and the potential damage from default or termination of supplies, while the most critical partners should be monitored continuously.
“In a modern risk management system, the question should be not only ‘whom did we check before concluding the contract,’ but also ‘what has changed with our largest counterparties since the check.’ It is monitoring that makes it possible to identify a problem before it turns into a direct financial loss,” Urakin emphasized.
Dun & Bradstreet is an international provider of business data and analytical solutions whose history began in 1841. The company provides tools for business identification, counterparty checks, assessment of credit and commercial risks, compliance, supply chain management and work with corporate data.
The official representative of Dun & Bradstreet in Ukraine is the Interfax-Ukraine news agency. The specialized D&B-Interfax-Ukraine unit helps Ukrainian companies work with international business data, check foreign partners and obtain a D-U-N-S Number.

Ukraine commenced using artificial intelligence-enabled robot guns to bring down Russia's new and fast-moving jet-powered drones, according to its air force on Monday.

Ignat acknowledged that the new system had a small operating radius.
"It can operate at about one kilometer plus (0.6 miles). And it works when conditions are favorable, when the attack approach angle is suitable," he told AFP.
