DHS buys three detention centers in California for $950 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:48:43 UTC
23:48:43 KST

Department of Homeland Security buys two more detention centers in California for $950 million
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- The facilities sold by the GEO Group, a for-profit prison company, are all located in Adelanto, north of San Bernardino.
- The sales reflect Trump administration efforts to avoid oversight from California and other states by placing the facilities under federal ownership, even though they would still be operated by private companies.
- Last year, Congress approved an infusion of $45 billion for immigration detention as part of President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
WASHINGTON — The Department of Homeland Security has purchased two immigrant detention facilities in Adelanto for $950 million, according to the private prison corporation that sold them.
The sale by the GEO Group, a Florida-based government contractor, follows a $1.5-billion sale over the summer of two other California detention facilities by GEO’s competitor, CoreCivic of Tennessee.
The sales bolster the Trump administration’s goal of cementing its capacity to detain immigrants it seeks to deport and reflect efforts to avoid oversight from California and other states by placing the facilities under federal ownership, even though they would still be operated by private companies.
The most recent sale, announced Monday, includes the two buildings that make up the 1,940-bed Adelanto ICE Processing Center and the 704-bed Desert View Annex.
In some instances, contracts have been changed to declare that the centers are simply not subject to local or state laws. In others, ICE has purchased facilities owned and operated by private companies.
Homeland Security has said that California’s laws, which increase oversight of immigration facilities, make federal ownership critical to ensure it retains the detention capacity needed on the West Coast.
A spokesperson, who did not provide their name in an emailed statement, said ICE is “ensuring we have resources to carry out President Trump’s mission.”
Last week, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed more than 20 bills aimed at pushing back against the Trump administration’s immigration agenda. Among them are bills that will authorize the California attorney general to bring civil actions to protect detainees’ constitutional rights, and require the disclosure of public records, such as 911 calls, from the facilities.
Homeland Security has taken steps to avoid those laws, including through the facility purchases. With companies including GEO Group facing what Chief Executive George C. Zoley called “unwarranted litigation” over allegedly unsafe conditions, federal ownership could become part of their defense strategy.
In total, the federal government has now spent nearly $3.2 billion on detention facility purchases, the majority of them in California. CoreCivic sold off two other facilities, in Minnesota and Kansas, in August.
The sales were made possible by an infusion last year of $45 billion for immigration detention from President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act as the administration seeks to expand its immigrant detention capacity.
In its announcement, GEO Group said it will continue managing daily operations at the facilities under the company’s existing contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which is effective through Dec. 19, 2034.
The company said it is engaged in an “active process” with Homeland Security for the potential sale of multiple other facilities. Those sales hinge on GEO Group’s ability to continue managing those facilities under long-term contracts, the company wrote.
“We are pleased with the completion of these important asset sales to the U.S. federal government, and we look forward to continuing to provide high-quality secure support services under our existing long-term contracts with ICE,” Zoley, the company’s CEO, wrote in a news release.
“We are proud of our 40-year public-private partnership with ICE, and we stand ready to continue to assist the federal government in meeting its immigration enforcement priorities,” Zoley added.
Reacting to the news, Rep. Norma Torres (D-Pomona) wrote on X that Congress must continue conducting oversight and hold ICE and GEO Group accountable for conditions in the facilities.
“Taxpayers are being forced to spend $950 million to buy three aging detention facilities and then keep paying GEO Group to run them through 2034,” she wrote. “We’re paying hundreds of millions for the facilities and billions more to operate them, while ICE moves to limit oversight of unsafe conditions. Taxpayers shouldn’t have to foot the bill twice for a broken, for-profit detention system.”
During a shareholder call in August, Zoley said ICE was contemplating buying more than 10 facilities, and that number “could continue to grow.”
“We are pursuing a potential sale of the buildings, but we want to retain the business,” he said on the call. “We consider ourselves primarily a support services operator, and will place particular importance on our ability to continue our support services at any facility sold to ICE.”
GEO Group said it anticipates receiving $705 million in proceeds from the sales, after taxes and transaction fees. The company wrote that net proceeds will reduce the company’s debt and facilitate the repurchase of company shares.
The facilities in Adelanto, about 60 miles northeast of Los Angeles, have been the subject of complaints, lawsuits and visits by members of Congress.
Immigrant rights groups filed a federal class-action lawsuit against DHS this year alleging poor drinking water, food, sanitation and medical care at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center, and a federal judge ordered improvements.
Four people have died at the facility since last year, according to Homeland Security records. The agency often says that detainees receive comprehensive medical care and that, for many, it’s the best they’ve ever had.
A mortality review by ICE investigators for Ismael Ayala-Uribe found that medical staff at the facility made repeated failures and “deviated beyond safe limits of practice.” ICE took down the records, but the investigative publication Project Salt Box downloaded and published them.
Ayala-Uribe, 39, who had fallen ill at the facility, later suffered cardiac arrest at a hospital during a surgery related to a pelvic abscess in September 2025.
More detention space could be coming to California. Last month, Homeland Security signed a $1.2-billion construction contract to expand a federally owned facility in El Centro that ICE previously used but which GEO Group now operates for the U.S. Marshals Service, Project Salt Box first reported.

A Moscow judge has sentenced the former mayor of the Black Sea resort city of Sochi to 15 years in maximum-security prison for corruption, state media reported Monday, citing the Russian Prosecutor General’s Office.
Alexei Kopaygorodsky, 41, served as mayor from September 2019 until May 2024, when he abruptly resigned, citing a transition to a federal post. After the transfer failed to materialize, Kopaygorodsky joined a volunteer army battalion fighting in Ukraine.

His wife Yanina Kopaygorodskaya was sentenced to 10 years in prison for serving as an accomplice, while her assistant Alexander Pasunko was fined 190,000 rubles ($2,200).
Kopaygorodsky and his wife were also ordered to pay fines of half a billion rubles ($5.9 million) each.
In addition, the former mayor was stripped of his state medal, banned from holding public management roles for 14.5 years and will face three additional years after his prison term.
Prosecutors accused Kopaygorodsky of embezzling two municipal land plots and concealing their origin, as well as accepting more than 319 million rubles ($3.7 million) in bribes from business leaders and developers in exchange for favors and protection in 2022-24.
Kopaygorodskaya was also accused of threatening one witness in order to receive false testimony and bribing another witness through Pasunko with half a million rubles ($5,900) while under house arrest.
Both denied the charges.
Earlier in January, a Sochi court seized the family’s assets worth more than 1.6 billion rubles ($18.8 million).
Kopaygorodsky is among at least 10 current and former deputy governors who have faced criminal prosecution since Veniamin Kondratyev became Krasnodar region governor in 2015.

Germany and France agree new trade tool to counter China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:43:27 UTC
23:43:27 KST

Paris and Berlin call for a new EU "systemic reaction" tool that would let Brussels move fast to counter China-driven market distortions, as well as retaliation planning and a revamp of trade defence tools.
France and Germany have proposed new powers for the European Commission to counter market distortions as the EU confronts mounting trade pressure from China.
In a letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday, accompanied by a policy paper on global economic imbalances, Paris and Berlin called for tools to restrict access to the EU market, diversify supplies and prepare for possible retaliation.
Brussels describes its economic relationship with Beijing as unsustainable, with the EU’s trade deficit reaching an estimated €1 billion a day in 2025. It has given China until this month to offer concessions.
The issue is due to come before EU leaders at next week’s European Council summit, where France and Germany will press for urgent action.
"We need a comprehensive framework to complement our toolbox with new legal instruments – in a lean and non-bureaucratic way," reads the letter, signed by President Emmanuel Macron and Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The accompanying paper warns that “a massive industrial shock” is hitting sectors central to Europe’s economic model, including pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, industrial machinery and chemicals.
New powers
The letter calls for a new instrument to be activated "where third countries seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field and fair market conditions by political or economic means, leading to severe and systematic distortions."
The tool would restrict access to the European single market, which Paris and Berlin see as the EU’s main leverage in negotiations with China.
They want decisions taken swiftly through a procedure known as comitology, in which member state representatives scrutinise Commission measures.
Crucially, the instrument would be activated “unless a qualified majority is opposed”, making it easier for the Commission to act.
The tool should also be "country agnostic, capture all market distortions, from a single production to a whole sector, from subsidies to currency manipulation," the policy paper says.
The aim is to allow the Commission to devise tailor-made solutions that reflect the EU's interests and do not place obligations solely on European companies.
According to a source at the Élysée, the goal is to be able to impose tariffs, but also to adopt “any measures that demonstrate the [EU’s] credibility and, above all, its determination to restore a level playing field.”
The response could involve using measures like those included in the EU’s existing Anti-Coercion Instrument, designed to counter economic bullying by foreign countries - which allows the bloc to restrict access to licences and intellectual property rights.
Diversifying supplies
The letter also calls for a diversification instrument, which von der Leyen already announced at the last European Council in June.
According to the paper, it should "reduce European dependencies, resolve existing supply chain concentration and prevent emerging concentration risks – taking into account import concentrations from a given country, company or stakeholder nationality, market share at the global level."
In other words, Berlin and Paris want a comprehensive framework that serves diversification goals in line with the economic security agenda and covers distortions beyond trade.
Preparing for retaliation
The paper acknowledges that retaliatory measures are likely to test the EU's political unity, and that a united front will be crucial in any trade war with China.
"The EU must be prepared and factor in international reactions and potential retaliations to its policies, instruments and measures. Understanding the extent and variety of coercion is essential," it continues.
The proposal calls for an inventory of possible retaliatory measures and an assessment of their impact on each member state, alongside coordination among EU leaders.
Strengthening trade defences
The paper also calls for measures to reduce risks and sever dependencies, urging the Commission to make greater use of trade defence instruments by launching more investigations on its own initiative and reallocating staff and resources to support them.
It also advocates a broader approach to sector-wide trade disputes, when "protection for narrow categories of goods is now insufficient in the face of more systemic distortions and the global dominance of third countries on the whole value chain of specific sectors."
Paris and Berlin also propose targeted changes to anti-dumping, anti-subsidy and safeguard rules to make it harder to circumvent EU trade measures.
This article has been updated to include additional details provided by the Élysée.

Why Al-Turbah and Dhubab are key to Yemen's new offensive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:41:21 UTC
23:41:21 KST

Breadcrumb
Why Al-Turbah and Dhubab are key to Yemen's new offensive
Fighting in Yemen's Taiz province has expanded beyond the traditional front lines around the city, reaching two areas with major strategic importance: Al-Turbah in southern Taiz and Dhubab on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The escalation comes as Rashad al-Alimi, head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced on Monday the launch of "Dawn of Yemen", a wide-ranging military operation that the government says aims to retake Houthi-controlled territory and restore state institutions.
Al-Turbah and Dhubab are particularly important because of the routes they command. Al-Turbah is a key link between Taiz and southern Yemen, while Dhubab overlooks Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world's most important maritime passages.
Here's why the two areas have become central to the latest fighting.
Al-Turbah, Taiz's lifeline to the south
Al-Turbah lies around 75 kilometres south of Taiz city and is the administrative centre of Al-Shamayatayn district and one of the main towns of the wider Al-Hujariah region.
During more than a decade of war, the city has become an important commercial and transport hub.
As traditional roads connecting Taiz with southern Yemen became blocked or difficult to use, the route through Al-Turbah and Al-Shamayatayn emerged as one of the province's main connections with Aden, Lahj and the southern coast.
The city also received large numbers of displaced Yemenis and, until the latest escalation, had largely remained away from direct fighting.
That makes control of the roads around Al-Turbah particularly important. Disrupting them could affect civilian traffic as well as military supply lines between Taiz and southern Yemen.
Local sources cited by media outlets said Houthi fighters entered Al-Turbah on the evening of 4 October following fighting in Al-Safiya, Al-Samsara, Al-Markaz and Al-Bireen, with some reports claiming they had taken parts of the main road towards Taiz.
Government forces, however, said on 5 October that they had regained the initiative on several Taiz fronts.
Sources on the ground told The New Arab that the Houthis had previously established sleeper cells inside Al-Turbah, which emerged after the group advanced into nearby areas.
Clashes subsequently erupted inside the city, with government forces surrounding Houthi fighters in several locations, the sources said.
The significance of the battle, however, extends beyond control of Al-Turbah itself, as whoever controls the surrounding roads gains an important advantage in moving troops and supplies between Taiz, southern Yemen and the western coast.
Fighting around Al-Safiya, Al-Bireen and Al-Turbah therefore threatens one of the main corridors that has kept Taiz connected with the south throughout the war.
Why does Dhubab matter?
Dhubab, in the far southwest of Taiz province, carries even greater strategic significance because of its proximity to the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The strait connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and is a crucial route for international shipping.
Dhubab's position also places it along coastal routes leading towards Mocha and Bab al-Mandeb, making control of the area important for military movements and supply lines along Yemen's western coast.
Government forces said on 5 October that the Dawn of Yemen offensive had expanded into the area.
Armed forces spokesman Colonel Majed al-Nazili said the Giants Brigades and Nation's Shield Forces carried out a flanking operation and seized Bab al-Mandeb and Dhubab military airport.
He also said government forces cut the Dhubab-Mocha road and established fire control over it, leaving hundreds of Houthi fighters surrounded in Dhubab. Some had attempted to escape by sea, he claimed.
According to the government's account, the operation sought to isolate Houthi forces in Dhubab from supply routes towards Mocha while attacking their positions from several directions.
Government forces also said they had secured the strategic Kahboub mountain overlooking the western coast.
The Giants Brigades and Nation's Shield Forces are taking part in the ground offensive, while the coalition has provided air support.
The coalition said around 100 warplanes participated in the operation, targeting what it described as high-value targets.
If government forces consolidate control over Dhubab and surrounding positions, it could alter the military balance around the southern entrance to the Red Sea and restrict Houthi movements along this part of the western coast.
Who is leading Dawn of Yemen?
The government has not published a full command structure for the operation, but several senior political and military figures have emerged.
Abdulrahman Abu Zara'a al-Muharrami, a member of the PLC, is closely associated with the Giants Brigades, which has previously fought the Houthis along Yemen's western coast and other fronts.
Former defence minister and PLC member Mahmoud al-Subaihi has also remained involved in overseeing military fronts.
Major General Hamdi Shukri, commander of the Fourth Military Region, is another key figure. His command covers strategically important territory including Taiz and Aden, while reports in September said forces around Dhubab and other western coastal areas were being reorganised under his leadership.
Al-Nazili, meanwhile, has served as the main military spokesman announcing developments in Dawn of Yemen.
At the top of the command structure is Al-Alimi, who announced on 4 October that government forces were moving from preparations to military operations before formally announcing Dawn of Yemen the following day.
Why are the two fronts connected?
Al-Turbah and Dhubab sit on different sides of the latest battle, but both are important because of the transport corridors they control.
Al-Turbah helps connect Taiz with Aden and southern Yemen, while Dhubab sits on the coastal route towards Mocha and Bab al-Mandeb.
Government forces would therefore seek to secure Dhubab while preventing the Houthis from consolidating control around Al-Turbah and threatening the Taiz-Aden route.
But the offensive remains in its early stages, and battlefield claims from both sides remain difficult to independently verify.

The trial and humiliation of Sami Abu Shehadeh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:40:53 UTC
23:40:53 KST

On Thursday, October 1, Sami Abu Shehadeh appeared before a nine-justice panel of Israel’s Supreme Court in Jerusalem to contest his disqualification from running on the Joint List slate in the October 27 Israeli election. The petition against him had been filed by the Jewish Power Party (Otzma Yehudit), a Kahanist party led by Israel’s hardline National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, who argued the case in person. It won the backing of the Central Elections Committee by a margin of roughly 30 to 4, with support from the attorney general and from parties across the Zionist opposition. The attempt to exclude Arab political representation is increasingly becoming a staple of Israeli politics, as political parties outdo each other in policies designed to symbolically and politically discipline Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Abu Shehadeh is a Palestinian native of Jaffa, a city largely destroyed and emptied of its Palestinian population in the 1948 Nakba, when Zionist militias conducted a widespread ethnic cleansing campaign. He is also the leader of the Balad party, a Palestinian political formation that believes in one democratic state for all peoples between the river and the sea. In the wake of “Operation al-Aqsa Flood” (Tufan al-Aqsa) on October 7, 2023, Abu Shehadeh wrote a short article in the regional Arab newspaper al-Araby al-Jadeed, focusing on the operation’s strategic and political reverberations. The article emphasizes common-sense views that highlight Israel’s racialized discourse, its vengeance economy, the similarities between the surprise of October 7 and the Egyptian crossing of the Suez Canal in 1973, and the political possibilities emergent, in part, due to an event that broke the military and political impasse in Gaza. It speaks of the law of physics that every action produces a reaction, and of history not having started on that fateful Saturday morning.
In the words of its president, Isaac Amit, the Israeli Supreme Court found the article “painful, outrageous, and repugnant,” while acknowledging that the justices differed on its legal implications. The court then asked Abu Shehadeh to withdraw from the race voluntarily, sparing it the need to issue a reasoned ruling. But it was the scene that, perhaps more than anything, encapsulates the humiliation to which Abu Shehadeh was subjected. Here was a Palestinian historian from Jaffa, well aware of the long history of Israeli and Zionist trigger-happy massacres, ethnic cleansing, racist discourse, and sadistic policies, including a carceral regime whose intended purpose is now to force Palestinians to emerge from prison having lost tens of kilograms. Here he was, standing before the law, recanting and justifying an article, and fighting to enter a parliament where he would have had to swear allegiance to a “state” that broke his world.
The dehumanization of Palestinians as political commonsense
The old argument for participation in the Israeli parliament has found new life in the wake of the genocide. Palestinians in Israel speak of the need to stop Israeli rightwing fascism, to secure a new government coalition in which Arab parties could play a role, and to win concessions, specifically around the growing crime syndicates in Palestinian communities inside Israel, as well putting in place a more pliable Israeli government willing to soften its sadism and expand budgets for Palestinian municipalities and local councils (for villages and towns inside Israel). This is a political program that increasingly dismembers Palestinians inside Israel from their history and memory on account of their present conditions. In this sense, the trial was not only that of a Palestinian standing in the presence of an organ that safeguards Israeli Jewish supremacy through the language of legal decorum; it was also that of Sami Abu Shehadeh standing between his history and his present, a self divided against itself and willing to exchange a captive present for its history and memory.
What makes the trial of Sami Abu Shehadeh difficult to dismiss, moreover, is the striking convergence between the electoral strategy of Israel’s right-wing coalition and that pursued by Republicans and centrist Democrats in the United States — the attempt to define the legitimate boundary of political belonging and, by extension, permissible political discourse. The same is also facing Elif Erlap in Berlin in the wake of her strong showing in the September elections. In Israel, however, this strategy has acquired a particular force because the political dehumanization and ostracisation of Palestinian politicians has been allowed to assume the status of something approaching political commonsense, and has not been met by any significant resistance from within Jewish-Israeli society.
The silence and complicity of all major Jewish-Israeli political forces could also serve as a basis for judging Palestinian participation in Israeli elections.
In terms of yielding socio-economic gains, the results of participating are meager for Palestinian communities inside Israel — while coming at a high symbolic and political cost. A part of that cost is how Israel uses it as a propaganda tool, pointing to the participation of Palestinians with Israeli citizenship in parliament as a sign of its “Jewish and democratic” character, even though the legal, symbolic, and political terms suggest that they are included only to be excluded. Participation by Palestinian political parties has historically been contested, and major boycott campaigns have accompanied each round of elections.
The charitable rendition of the argument for joining elections would stress the need for wide participation by highlighting that the right-wing Israeli coalition is itself fearful of a large Arab showing in the election, one that would reduce its seat share and make it almost impossible for the government that led Israel over the past four years to return to power. But what is more interesting for our purposes here is what it means to “stand before the law” for a Palestinian political leader who is willing to denounce himself in the name of a present that he does not meaningfully influence.
The tragedy here is Abu Shehadeh’s complicity in his own fate. He recants the article that he wrote “before the law,” he condemns the Palestinian resistance “before the law,” and he even speaks of being against everything Hamas did, including the supposed systematic mass rape of Israelis – the occurrence of which is widely contested – “before the law.” He looks shaky, and he grants license and legitimacy to a court that, as he was well aware before entering its gate, was geared to exclude him from running in the election. He even agrees to withdraw his candidacy, enabling mainstream media headlines in the West not to speak of a ban on Palestinian politicians in supposedly democratic Israel, but to speak of the withdrawal of a Palestinian politician from running in elections.
Redefining citizenship
What is being redefined here, in part through these legal and political maneuvers, is nothing less than the substance of citizenship itself. It is no longer enough for a Palestinian in Israel to pledge an oath to the state in order to be worthy of standing ineffectively, as an empty symbolic shell, in the Knesset; he must also go through the motions of reflexively condemning every act that any Palestinian commits in resisting the occupation. It is not enough to secure a seat in the Knesset, to speak Hebrew, to stand in solemn quiet while facing an Israeli flag and listening to the Hatikvah (Israel’s national anthem), to abide by its rules and procedures, and to submit oneself to questioning by its judges.
Beyond all that, a Palestinian citizen of Israel must now surrender his memory and live in amnesia. Abu Shehadeh was permitted to speak before the law only when the terms of speaking were already set by a state angrier at an analytical article that names the resistance as resistance than at the moral corruption at the core of the state, which has led it openly to destroy the lives of millions. Abu Shehadeh confessed, as a Palestinian confesses in the presence of an interrogator from Israeli intelligence – and he was excluded anyway.
In part, Abu Shehadeh’s mistake is that he uttered what the settler has always suspected: that the natives of the land, even when they recognize Israel and live side by side with it in everyday life, are ultimately captives, and that upon any sign of a radical change in the power dynamics, they will show their true colors. To write an article that speaks of the political possibilities in the wake of the Tufan and to insist on treating the operation as a symptom of Israeli policy is proof of guilt. It is in the moment of Israel’s shaking to its core that the truth of the native comes out.
What the settler has always suspected appeared to be confirmed by the shock of October 7 and the article Abu Shehadeh wrote, and so the native was summoned “before the law” to be condemned. The court’s task is to stage the discovery and to convert the settler’s suspicion into a procedure that would permit Abu Shehadeh to exclude himself.
Yes, the presence of Arabs as a whole remains a demographic fact that is to be managed and permitted a semblance of political participation, but the Arab at the individual level must be “disciplined” for daring to think that the world might be otherwise.
To be a citizen willing to trade history and memory for the pragmatic needs of the present is still to be held as a suspect. It is to be told that the door is open, only to discover it was never meant for you to pass through. In Kafka’s parable, Josef K. waits at the gate until he dies. The Palestinian citizen is asked to confess at the gate, and then informed that he should commit suicide. Israel was never meant to include Palestinians -it was always meant to exclude them through their inclusion, or to include them through exclusion, until the time comes to “finish the job.”

‘Police can’t remain mute spectators’: Delhi HC dismisses pleas for fresh probe into 2019 Jamia violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:40:51 UTC
23:40:51 KST

Delhi HC rejects SIT probe pleas in Jamia violence case
The Delhi high court on Monday dismissed petitions seeking an independent probe into alleged police brutalities against students during the December 2019 violence at Jamia Millia Islamia. The court observed that police cannot be expected to remain “mute spectator” when a gathering turns violent.A bench of Justices Vivek Chaudhary and Manoj Jain said the police did not enter the university premises at the outset when the assembly was peaceful, but intervened after the situation outside the campus escalated and the crowd moved into the university.“The police intervention, therefore, has to be viewed in the prevailing law and order situation which had developed at that time,” the court said.‘Police cannot be expected to remain inactive’The bench said the right to peaceful protest was not in dispute. Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Constitution protect freedom of speech and expression and the right to assemble peacefully without arms, subject to reasonable restrictions.These rights do not, however, extend to causing any violence or destruction of property, it said.“Once a gathering ceases to remain peaceful and the circumstances disclose violence, commission of cognisable offences or a threat to life or property, the police cannot be expected to remain inactive or as mute spectator merely because the gathering is taking place within a university campus,” the court observed.
The petitions sought an independent judicial inquiry into the violence, an investigation into alleged police excesses and compensation for injured students.“The events of December 2019 undoubtedly generated considerable public concern and gave rise to serious allegations regarding the conduct of various stakeholders,” the court said.The bench noted that protests on December 15, 2019, had escalated into violence around the university, including stone-pelting, burning of buses and other vehicles, damage to public property and attacks on police personnel.The high court also noted shortcomings in the police response, referring to the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) inquiry, which found that the use of tear gas shells inside the university library could have been avoided.It said a university was a place of learning and academic activity, and this “crucial aspect” must be considered while exercising police powers.
“That consideration cannot, however, be taken to mean that the police are prohibited from entering a university campus in all circumstances,” the court said.It added that university authorities should, wherever circumstances permit, be informed and consulted before police intervention. However, an immediate threat to life or property or a rapidly developing law-and-order situation may leave no time for prior communication or permission.The court noted that criminal cases had been registered, an investigation conducted by the Delhi Police Crime Branch's Special Investigation Team (SIT), and charge sheets filed before competent courts. The NHRC had submitted its report in May 2020.“No subsequent incident or material has been brought to our notice to show that the violations of guidelines as alleged in these petitions have continued or have been repeated,” it said.

airBaltic planning up to 700 layoffs across Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:40:00 UTC

airBaltic planning up to 700 layoffs across Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius
Latvian airline airBaltic is planning layoffs that could affect 500–700 jobs across the Baltics, including in Tallinn, as it restructures its business.
airBaltic, which employs nearly 3,000 people across the Baltics, announced Monday it is taking steps to adapt its operations to a new business model, including changes to its workforce.
While the exact number of layoffs is still subject to change, the Latvian flag carrier currently estimates that planned changes could affect approximately 500–700 positions across its bases in Riga, Vilnius and Tallinn.
The airline has already notified the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund (EUIF) of the planned collective layoffs but declined to give estimates by base or employee group, saying more details will be shared with staff this month.
"No final decisions have been made regarding individual employees, and we will engage directly with our colleagues as the next steps are determined," CEO Erno Hildén said, pledging transparency and care throughout the sensitive process.
Long-haul overhaul
The measures aim to improve financial stability, streamline airBaltic's network and boost efficiency. The airline has previously announced plans to reduce its Airbus A220-300 fleet and expand year-round ACMI (aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance) partnerships.
The planned changes will not affect airBaltic's flight schedule, the airline said Monday, with all scheduled flights currently operating as planned.
In mid-September, airBaltic announced it would restructure its financial obligations under U.S. law while continuing to operate normally. The company also secured a new €350 million loan at an interest rate of around 12 percent.
In August, Latvia's Saeima approved a bailout plan for the airline under which the state will provide airBaltic with up to another €30 million in funding and amend the terms of its existing obligations.
airBaltic reported a €44.34 million loss last year, several times smaller than in 2024, while revenue rose 4.2 percent to €779.34.

One of Slovenia’s last glaciers will disappear within days due to warming
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:39:35 EEST
23:39:35 KST

One of Slovenia’s last glaciers will disappear within days due to warming
Kyiv • UNN
The Triglav Glacier, which has been studied since 1946, has shrunk to several patches of ice. The cause is warming and early snowmelt.
The Triglav Glacier in Slovenia, which scientists have been studying since 1946, has shrunk to several patches of ice and may disappear completely within the next few days. Researchers attribute this to climate change and unusually early snowmelt. Reuters reports, writes UNN.
Details
For years, the Triglav Glacier attracted skiers in the summer and has been revered for many generations as a symbol of Slovenia’s alpine heritage.
Scientists have been monitoring the Triglav Glacier since 1946, when it covered about 14 hectares. In recent years, it has effectively ceased to be a glacier in the full sense of the word, meaning that new ice has no longer been forming in it.
"Everything indicates that the very last remnants of ice will literally disappear within the next few days," said Miha Pavšek of the Anton Melik Geographical Institute at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts.
As climate change intensifies, the glacier received less snow than usual last winter, and the snow cover melted unusually early. As a result, the remaining ice was exposed to the summer heat for longer.
"Even a place sheltered from the wind and shaded can no longer save the remnants of these true glaciers," Pavšek said.
Across Europe, which is warming faster than any other continent, glaciers are shrinking.
Pavšek noted that the disappearance of glaciers in neighboring Austria could eventually lead to reduced water flows in the basins of the Drava and Mura rivers, which are important sources of irrigation in Slovenia.

Low water level in Lake Zurich reveals new island

Low water level in Lake Zurich reveals new island
The historically low water level of Lake Zurich is revealing something new: an island is now emerging from the water off Stäfa. Normally, only a rock – the Stäfner Stein – is visible there.
The historic low water level of Lake Zurich – currently standing at 405.24 metres above sea level – has created a new island. This now rises just under 400 metres above the water off the coast of Stäfa. It isn’t large, but it is big enough to moor a small boat there and enjoy a picnic.
+ How much water is left under Switzerland? Nobody can say yet
The small island was last visible 74 years ago, when the previous major low water level was recorded. Before that, it emerged in 1909 during a period of extremely low water levels. A mark on the Stäfa stone indicates the water level at that time and has now been uncovered for the first time in many years.
The island is likely to remain a popular destination for a while yet, as it will be some time before the lake returns to its normal level. There are currently no prolonged periods of rain in sight.

Cabinet wants phones out of schools from January
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The cabinet is calling on all primary and secondary schools to ban mobile phone use starting from January.
In a new proposal from digital economy minister Willemijn Aerdts, children would not be allowed to use their phones on school grounds, rules about children appearing in family vlogs would be tightened and the time children spend scrolling would be limited.
“Online, on social media or in video games, children quickly become exposed and face unacceptable risks,” Aerdts said in the proposal, called ‘Strategy Letter on Children’s Rights’.
Since 2024, there have been national agreements prohibiting the use of phones in the classroom.
The government does not have the authority to order schools to implement the policy and the education ministry will work with schools to come up with an agreement.
Aerdts is also keen to limit how children are used in online content, like family-style YouTube.
The cabinet also intends on commissioning research into sites like Netflix, YouTube, Roblox, Fortnite, ChatGPT, Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok and their impact on children.
Earlier this year, the government has backed an EU-wide minimum age for social media. D66, VVD and CDA agreed in their coalition agreement to push for an enforceable European minimum age of 15.

Murder in Okinawa: The US military’s history of alleged crime in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:37:17 UTC
23:37:17 KST

Murder in Okinawa: The US military’s history of alleged crime in Japan
The murder of 39-year-old Anna Yagi is the latest in a string of crimes involving US personnel on Okinawa.
The murder of a Japanese woman allegedly committed by a US Marine on the southern island of Okinawa has prompted public outrage in Japan, amid a long string of incidents involving American personnel.
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the incident on Monday as a “heinous crime” and said the government had lodged a strong protest with Washington, urging their “full cooperation with the investigation” and “strict discipline among US military personnel”.
About 100 people participated in a rally in Naha, the capital of Okinawa, on Sunday, as news spread that a US marine had, a day earlier, allegedly killed a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in the city and stolen her wallet.
Public broadcaster NHK reported that security camera footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving alone with her belongings. Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description. The suspect has reportedly denied the allegations.
Police identified the suspect as Devin Jacob Ballard and the victim as Anna Yagi.
Kozue Akibayashi, a professor of gender and peace studies at Doshisha University in Kyoto, Japan, said the incident reflects a decades-long issue. “The Japanese government has always chosen the US-Japan alliance over the safety and lives, and voices of the people of Okinawa,” she told Al Jazeera.
Why are US marines stationed in Okinawa?
The United States has about 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan. Okinawa bears a disproportionate burden, hosting about 70 percent of US military facilities in the country, set up under a bilateral security treaty and Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) signed first in 1951 and then revised in 1960.
Japan has the “primary right to exercise jurisdiction” for crimes committed off-base while US personnel are not on duty, while the US has the “primary right” for crimes committed on the base or while on duty.
Okinawa is viewed by Tokyo and Washington as key in deterring potential military aggression from China. “The US and the Japanese governments have always cited ‘geopolitical’ importance of the location of the archipelago to justify not only the presence itself but also the disproportionately high concentration of the US military there,” Akibayashi, at Doshisha University, said.
“However, in reality, it was convenient for the Japanese government to keep the larger number of US troops and military facilities in Okinawa that nobody wants.”
The professor said Okinawa, one of Japan’s 47 prefectures, represents 1 percent of the entire population of Japan and less than 1 percent of the entire Japanese territory.
“Their political voice does not seem to bear significance to the Japanese government,” she added. “Probably more importantly, Okinawa was colonised by Japan in the late 19th century and has always been a subject of discrimination within Japan.”
Okinawa was historically an independent trading nation called the Ryukyu Kingdom before Japan annexed it in 1879. The US held Okinawa, which is 100 kilometres (60 miles) from Taiwan at the closest point, from the end of World War II until 1972.
“Many US military bases located on the main islands of Japan were transferred to the islands of Okinawa … because the mainland Japanese people had started to protest the presence of the US military in their neighbourhood,” Akibayashi said.
The presence of US marines has repeatedly stirred resentment among residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct of personnel.
Have US marines been accused of crimes before?
Yes, there is a long history of crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving accidents allegedly committed by US personnel, triggering protests on Okinawa.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a US marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison.
In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa. The same year, an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.
In 1995, the rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan girl by three US servicemen led to mass protests.
According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since 1972, when the US returned control of Okinawa to Japan. In 2024, the number of arrests hit 80, the highest in 20 years.
Akibayashi said people in Okinawa have been outraged by these crimes, which they see as violations of their basic human rights. “Their lives and even survival have been made insecure and threatened by the US military presence,” she said.
“They have expressed countless times their opposition to and anger at the US military presence, and unequal burden of ‘security’ policies imposed on them throughout the decades. Their protests have been ignored and nullified.”
How did Japan and the US respond to Yagi’s murder?
Japanese authorities have expressed outrage at the murder, while the US pledged full collaboration in the investigations.
Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said, “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.”
Prime Minister Takaichi said Japan had lodged a protest with US authorities and called the crime “exceptionally brutal and vicious”.
The government has urged the US “to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among US military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes”, Takaichi said.
The US embassy and the Marine Corps expressed condolences over the incident and said they were cooperating with the Japanese authorities.
The Marine Corps said in a statement that the suspect, who is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force and based at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was in Japanese custody.
“The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior,” it said.
US Ambassador George Glass posted on social media that he had spoken with Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Okinawa’s governor, offering “our sincere condolences and pledging full cooperation as the investigation continues”.
Akibayashi said that when crimes are committed, “the US government and the military always say they would address the issue or promise tighter discipline”.
“They never worked,” she added.

Nine Dutch restaurants win first Michelin stars
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Nine Dutch restaurants have won Michelin stars for the first time in the 2026 edition of the guide, and two of them went straight in with two stars.
Azurite in Delft, run by chef Mario Ridder, and Suis in Schin op Geul, near Valkenburg, both entered the guide at two-star level, broadcaster NOS reported.

De Librije in Zwolle remains the only three-star restaurant in the Netherlands, a rating it has held since 2004. Nelson Tanate now leads the kitchen following the death of co-owner and chef Jonnie Boer in April 2025.
No Amsterdam restaurant won a new star this year, and Daalder and De Juwelier lost theirs, AT5 reported.
In total, the Netherlands has 119 starred restaurants, the same number as last year.

Europe enters winter with low gas reserves, but Lithuania says supplies are secure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:34:00 UTC
23:34:00 KST

Europe is heading into winter with gas storage facilities at unusually low levels, raising questions about supply security and prices as the continent continues to reduce its dependence on Russian and other imported fossil fuels.
Gas storage facilities across the European Union are about 71% full, below the European Commission’s revised target of 80%. The commission lowered its original 90% target in an effort to avoid panic buying and additional pressure on prices.
Lithuania is less concerned about its own supply. The country stores gas at Latvia’s Inčukalns facility, which is only about 48% full. The underground storage facility is used by all three Baltic states as well as Finland.
Experts say Lithuania has already stored enough gas to meet the needs of households and ensure the security of its gas system.
“The amount of natural gas necessary for household consumers and to ensure the security of the system is currently stored in the facility,” said Matas Taparauskas, a member of Lithuania’s State Energy Regulatory Council.
Based on the amount of gas currently stored, Lithuania has enough reserves to cover its needs during the coldest part of the heating season, he said.
The relatively low level of gas stored in Inčukalns could indicate increased regional pressure if demand were to rise sharply, Taparauskas said.
But Lithuania has an additional safeguard: its liquefied natural gas terminal at Klaipėda.
“The LNG terminal is our main source of gas supply, and we have an interconnection with Poland,” said Agnė Bagočiutė, head of Lithuania’s Energy Agency.
Even during the coldest heating season, Lithuania can meet its gas needs through imports via the LNG terminal, according to energy officials. The country has also signed a gas supply agreement with the United States.
Energy Minister Lukas Savickas said Lithuania should not increase the amount of gas stored underground at any cost.
“We should not increase the amount held in storage at any cost,” Savickas said. “We need to act responsibly so that we can secure the most competitive prices possible. In Lithuania’s case, we see that this has been done.”
Higher prices, tighter supplies
The situation across Europe is more complicated.
The beginning of the year offered few warning signs. Gas prices were even lower than a year earlier. But prices have since risen sharply after the United States launched attacks on Iran, according to the report.
Dan Jørgensen, the European commissioner for energy and housing, said Europe’s dependence on imported energy has already come at a steep cost.
“This year we have already exceeded 100 billion euros in additional payments for energy, without receiving a single additional molecule of gas or oil in return,” Jørgensen said. “That very clearly shows how harmful and unsustainable our dependence on energy resources is.”
Europe is also competing for liquefied natural gas with buyers in Asia, particularly when supplies from the Middle East are disrupted.
Gas prices have become difficult to predict. Futures prices are currently around 73 euros per megawatt-hour, while Bagočiutė said prices could decline somewhat early next year.
Taparauskas said Europe could still fill its storage facilities to 90%, but the key question was how much that would cost.
“Europe would be capable of meeting the requirement to fill storage facilities to 90%, but the main question is at what price,” he said.
The lower EU target was partly intended to prevent countries and companies from rushing to buy gas and driving prices even higher.
The situation varies considerably across Europe. Poland’s storage facilities are nearly full, while Inčukalns is less than half full.
Brussels calls for lower energy use
The European Commission is also urging consumers and businesses to reduce energy consumption and is looking beyond the immediate winter.
“My conclusions are clear: We need to reduce our dependence. We need to replace fossil fuels,” Jørgensen said.
The European Union is expected to publish its assessment of the bloc’s winter preparedness in early October. Member states are also awaiting proposals from the European Commission on measures to reduce energy costs for consumers.

What to know about Spain's November snap election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:33:49 UTC
23:33:49 KST

What to know about Spain's November snap election
Oct 5 - Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has called an early election for November 29 that he hopes will hand him a parliamentary majority but which could just as easily usher in a conservative coalition, as the centre-left bloc trails in most opinion polls.
Here is what you need to know about the election:
POLLS PITCH RIGHT-WING COALITION AS LIKELIEST OUTCOME
• Sanchez's Socialist Party (PSOE) has long trailed in the polls, hovering around 28% and never above 33% throughout his eight years in office.
• Parties further to the left, which will be key for Sanchez to cobble together a coalition, are currently polling at around 8%.
• A coalition between the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox is the only combination projected to win enough votes for an absolute majority in the 350-seat lower house of parliament.
• Voting intention for Vox stands at roughly 18%, propelled by younger and male voters.ISSUES LIKELY TO DOMINATE THE ELECTORAL CAMPAIGN
• Housing will dominate the left's agenda, with Sanchez taking the decision to call the election after protests erupted across the country following the high-profile eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her Madrid home.
• Immigration is likely to be another defining issue, both for Sanchez as one of Europe's loudest advocates of immigration's benefits for society and the economy, recently granting legal status to nearly a million undocumented migrants, and for Vox, which wants far tighter controls. The mass crossing of 72,000 migrants into Ceuta in July has overwhelmed local authorities and triggered major political disputes over Spain's ability to control its borders.
• Corruption: Opposition parties are expected to make corruption a central theme of the election campaign, seeking to tie Sanchez to a series of investigations, trials and convictions involving members of his inner circle and family. Sanchez has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and argued that some of the cases form part of a politically motivated campaign against his government.
CANDIDATES FOR PRIME MINISTER
• Sanchez, the incumbent, will run again for the Socialists, having spearheaded the party since 2017.
• Now seeking a third term after eight years in office, he is already Spain's second-longest-serving premier since the country returned to democracy in 1978.
• Despite a tenure dogged in the past two years by corruption investigations, the Socialist leader is betting that the housing crisis and the prospect of a far-right party coming to power will help mobilise left-leaning voters who might have otherwise abstained.
• Alberto Nuñez Feijoo, former president of the region of Galicia, will run against Sanchez representing the People's Party, which he has led since April 2022.
• A four-time winner of presidential elections in Galicia, Feijoo built a reputation in his years governing the region as a moderate and pragmatic administrator.
• The PP emerged as the largest party in the 2023 general election but failed to secure enough support to form a government, leaving Feijoo as leader of the opposition.
• Since then, Feijoo has sought to position the PP as a government-in-waiting, piling criticism on Sanchez for everything from his policies to the corruption allegations encircling his party.
A CABINET ROLE FOR THE FAR RIGHT?
• Polls project that the PP would rely on far-right Vox to govern, giving a far-right party a role in cabinet for the first time since the death of former dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.
• Its leader is Santiago Abascal, who built his political profile in the Basque Country opposing separatism and co-founded the party in 2014 alongside others defecting from or seeking an alternative to the PP.
• Under Abascal, Vox has evolved from a minor political force into the country's third-largest party. It advocates tougher immigration controls, recentralisation of state powers, lower taxes and the reversal of many progressive social policies.A MOBILISED LEFT? THE 'BROAD FRONT'
• A swathe of parties to the left of PSOE are planning to launch a new common platform called "Broad Front" (Frente Amplio), which will be Sanchez's best hope of maintaining power if it supports the Socialists in coalition as previously. The alliance would replace Sumar, a hard-left platform founded in 2023 by Labour Minister Yolanda Diaz which acted as coalition partner to Sanchez's government in his final term.
• The new front will name a leadership candidate at a launch event on October 17, after Diaz said she would not stand as leader again.
• Podemos, former junior coalition partners to PSOE who take a more critical line than Sumar, has for now refused to join the front, opting to run separately unless open primaries are held.OTHER PARTIES
• Spain's parliament is highly fragmented, giving minor parties that hold just a handful of seats the power to tip the scales on passing policy.
• The country's historically distinct regions feature four separatist parties: EH Bildu in the Basque Country, BNG in Galicia, and two in Catalonia — the left-leaning ERC and the right-leaning Junts.
• While EH Bildu, BNG and ERC have broadly supported Sanchez, Junts has frequently vetoed his government's measures, including the housing decrees that prompted the prime minister to dissolve parliament. REUTERS

On the First Anniversary of the Global Governance Initiative:  From Guiding Vision to Concrete Action
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:33:22 EEST
23:33:22 KST

by Ambassador of China to Ukraine Ma Shengkun
On September 1, 2025, President Xi Jinping chaired the “Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus” Meeting in Tianjin and delivered an important speech titled “Pooling the Strength of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization To Improve Global Governance,” in which he formally proposed the Global Governance Initiative (GGI). Over the past year, the Initiative has evolved from a declaration of principles into practical action, received broad and positive responses from the international community and produced increasingly tangible results.
This year the world has continued to face numerous challenges: the deficits in peace, development, security and governance have become increasingly intertwined. Bloc confrontation and the Cold War mentality have resurfaced. Global challenges have continued to emerge. Unilateralism and protectionism are on the rise. The efficacy of multilateral mechanisms is weakening, and the representation and voice of numerous developing countries in global governance remain seriously inadequate. The international community is calling for more open, fair and efficient international governing mechanisms. It is precisely against this backdrop that the Global Governance Initiative was proposed. The Initiative clearly answers the questions of our times, namely what kind of global governance system to build and how to reform and improve global governance. It also provides a “golden key” to tackling both current and future challenges of global governance.
In essence, the Initiative is underpinned by five core concepts. First, staying committed to sovereign equality. All countries, regardless of size, strength or wealth, are equal in international affairs and should participate in, make decisions in and benefit from global governance as equals. Hegemonism and power politics must be opposed. Second, abiding by international rule of law. It is important to uphold the basic norms governing international relations built on the purposes and principles of the U.N. Charter, oppose the selective application of international law and double standards, and reject attempts to put the domestic laws of a few countries above international rules. Third, practicing multilateralism. It is important to uphold the principle of extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit, safeguard the central role of the U.N. in the international system, and resolve differences through dialogue and consultation. Fourth, advocating the people-centered approach. It is important to strengthen practical cooperation in areas such as poverty reduction, public health and education, and ensure that the benefits of development are shared by all countries more equitably. Fifth, focusing on taking real actions. It is important to focus on concrete issues such as climate change, development financing and AI governance, and address real-world challenges through practical cooperation. These five core concepts are in line with the purposes of the U.N. Charter and align with the U.N. 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
Since its launch, the Initiative has received positive responses from the international community. To date, the Initiative has won the support of nearly 160 countries and international organizations. The Group of Friends of Global Governance has been established in New York, Geneva and Vienna, with its membership expanding from 43 founding members to more than 60 countries. As a dedicated platform for dialogue on global governance, it has substantively engaged in the U.N. agenda. The Group delivered a joint statement at the U.N. General Assembly Briefing on the U.N.80 Initiative and sent a representative to the General Discussion of the 79th World Health Assembly. On May 28, 2026, Foreign Minister Wang Yi attended the meeting of the Group of Friends of Global Governance at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, which brought together representatives from more than 60 countries. The meeting issued a joint communiqué, forging consensus on five key points, including upholding the authority of the United Nations, safeguarding international rule of law, strengthening solidarity and cooperation, and improving global governance. It also put forward nine reform directions covering such areas as promoting U.N. reform for greater efficiency, enhancing the authority of the Security Council, development financing and AI governance.
China has never ceased its efforts to put the Global Governance Initiative into practice. China released the Concept Paper on the Global Governance Initiative and the white paper More Just and Equitable Global Governance: China’s Principles, Proposals and Actions, clarifying the Initiative’s framework and priorities. The International Organization for Mediation (IOMed), jointly initiated by 19 countries including China, commenced operations in Hong Kong in October 2025. It is the world’s first intergovernmental legal organization dedicated to resolving international disputes through mediation. In May 2026, it successfully resolved its first international maritime dispute, involving parties from China and Singapore. In the same month, it held its inaugural Global Mediation Summit in Hong Kong, drawing over 400 representatives from 48 countries and regions. The World Data Organization was established in Beijing in March 2026, and the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization was established in Shanghai on July 16, 2026. These platforms are open to all countries and aim to jointly explore effective governance systems suited to today’s world and capable of addressing various threats and challenges. China has also submitted its 2035 Nationally Determined Contributions to the United Nations, set up the Kunming Biodiversity Fund, and plans to host the Global Governance Forum in the Xiong’an New Area this autumn, where it will work with all parties to develop ideas for reforming and improving global governance.
The first anniversary of the Global Governance Initiative offers an opportunity to look back and, at the same time, marks a new starting point. On September 1, 2026, President Xi Jinping delivered an important speech at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Plus Meeting in Bishkek, systematically elaborating on the vision of an equal and orderly multipolar world. From the four dimensions - sovereign equality and mutual respect; balance, order and the rule of law; multilateralism and dialogue and consultation; mutual benefit, win-win and inclusiveness - he set out a clear direction for advancing the Global Governance Initiative. On September 12, at the 18th BRICS Summit President Xi Jinping delivered a statement titled “Jointly Shouldering the Responsibility of the Times and Striving to Be a Pioneering Force”, reiterating that the Four Global Initiatives provide a systematic solution to the deficits in development, security, civilization and governance. Centered on sovereign equality, international rule of law, multilateralism, the people-centered approach and a focus on real actions, China’s solution is charting a clear path toward improving global governance.
“When the Great Way prevails, the world is for everyone.” Global challenges call for global response, and global governance requires the participation of all countries. More importantly, proposed visions must be followed by concrete actions. As a responsible major country, China has proposed the Global Governance Initiative and made efforts to put it into practice, with the fundamental aim of addressing the current global governance deficit and tackling pressing issues in global governance. Implementing the Global Governance Initiative and building a more just and equitable global governance system will enable more countries to safeguard their own interests and participate in addressing common challenges on an equal footing. China stands ready to strengthen communication and deepen cooperation with more countries, international organizations and regional mechanisms, and work together to build an open, inclusive, clean and beautiful world of lasting peace, universal security and common prosperity.

The Surprising Drama in Taipei’s 2026 Mayor Race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:31:00 UTC
23:31:00 KST

Few would have expected the Taipei mayoral race to become one of the most hotly watched races of the 2026 local elections in Taiwan. With incumbent Mayor Chiang Wan-an of the Kuomintang (KMT) facing off against Puma Shen of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), polling shows Shen doing unusually well for a city that is traditionally seen as a KMT stronghold.
Another reason the campaign is attracting attention: the post is often a stepping stone to the presidency. Past presidents Chen Shui-bian and Ma Ying-jeou both previously served as Taipei mayor.
Taipei is generally understood to be a KMT bastion, given that many of those who came with the KMT to Taiwan in the wake of the Chinese Civil War settled in Taipei. To date, Chen Shui-bian is an outlier as the only DPP mayor of Taipei in history. While Ko Wen-je won the mayorship in 2014 as an independent who had the backing of the pan-Green camp, he was seen as having benefited from his independent political reputation, which did not necessarily link him with the DPP.
Shen running for Taipei mayor, then, was not initially seen as likely to be successful. If anything, Shen was originally seen as having agreed to be something of a political sacrifice for the DPP.
Shen is one of the DPP’s most visible legislators, and it would be a poor look for the DPP to field someone obscure to run in Taiwan’s capital. Taipei, after all, often sets the tone for other political races. Yet Shen was seen as unlikely to win and as having potentially signed up himself for a disastrous race.
In 2022, the DPP’s Taipei mayoral candidate lost by over 10 percentage points. The 2018 race was even more humiliating for the party, with DPP candidate Pasuya Yao finishing a distant third behind both Ko Wen-je and the KMT’s choice.
Shen is an unusual candidate for historically pan-Blue Taipei. Shen, originally an academic specializing in criminology, is best known as the founder of the Doublethink Lab and the Kuma Academy. The Doublethink Lab is Taiwan’s best-known disinformation research organization, while the Kuma Academy is one of the foremost civil defense groups that regularly conducts training in skills that might be useful in the event of a Chinese invasion or other catastrophes. Given this background, Shen is mostly publicly known for being tough on China-related issues.
Shen also played a prominent role in the eruption of the 2024 Bluebird Movement, which was partly sparked by anger over Shen being injured during a scuffle in the legislature.
Running for Taipei’s mayor seat, then, is mostly a test of whether Shen might have a political life beyond serving two terms as a party list legislator. Though Shen is still in his first term, if he did well or at least put a dent in Chiang Wan-an’s vote count, the DPP would likely keep him in rotation for future positions, as one of the party’s more visible younger politicians. Shen is currently 44.
Not many expected Shen to actually be competitive in the race. Survey polls in Taiwan that are not conducted by academic research institutions are largely partisan and are released in order to impact, not reflect, election results. With that caveat in mind, some polls show Shen within a few points of Chiang.
Shen’s campaign has focused on anti-incumbent sentiment by depicting Chiang Wan-an as a handsome but ineffectual figure who does not know about policy and largely relies on aides to provide him with information. Shen’s strong performance during interviews has also benefited him. One interview with a pan-Blue-leaning talk show host went viral due to Shen’s ability to casually answer the host’s questions about a range of policy issues with detailed proposals, without having to rely on notes or other information.
Likewise, analysts have noted that Shen only attacks the Chiang mayoral administration in areas where his own campaign has a detailed counterproposal for how to carry out city governance, thus avoiding a purely negative campaign.
Chiang was also recently hit by two political controversies. The first involved Chiang’s son winning a Taipei city-funded scholarship for a student exchange program with the United States, despite being the mayor’s son and a U.S. citizen. Subsequently, Chiang faced allegations of nepotism, leading Chiang to state that his family would not accept the scholarship.
The second controversy, which is decidedly more bizarre, involved Chiang being found to have discarded a ceremonial stalk of sugarcane he was gifted during a temple ceremony. Chiang threw the stalk by the side of the road after the event ended. Even if an aide was sent to retrieve the discarded stalk, the act was seen as reflecting arrogance and disregard for the common people.
Chiang’s struggle in the polls is surprising. He has sometimes been criticized for being a bit stiff during public speaking events, as well as for gaffes, such as being unable to remember a number of English terms during a speech at Harvard University in a clip that went viral online. Nevertheless, Chiang is usually seen as a leading politician of the KMT. As one of its most prominent younger politicians at age 47, he’s often considered a future presidential contender. Chiang has also differentiated himself from other KMT members by being more progressive on social issues such as gay marriage.
Chiang’s trips abroad during his administration – to Singapore, China, the U.S., France, and South Korea – were largely seen as signaling presidential ambitions, aiming to pad out his diplomatic credentials. Chiang is expected to throw his hat into the ring for the KMT’s 2028 presidential nomination.
With the unexpected rise of Shen in the polls, the DPP will be aiming to do as much damage to Chiang’s future electoral chances as possible.
It is also probable that backlash against Chiang reflects public dissatisfaction with political dynasties. Chiang is the son of former legislator John Chiang – not to be confused with the similarly named former KMT chair, Johnny Chiang, a politician of the same generation as Chiang Wan-an.
Chiang is also the supposed illegitimate grandson of Chiang Ching-kuo and great-grandson of Chiang Kai-shek. Both Chiang Wan-an and his father changed their last names from Chang to Chiang when they decided to seek higher office. Though some questions about the veracity of this claim have been raised – Chiang has refused DNA testing as an invasion of his privacy – the claim that he is descended from Chiang Kai-shek is generally accepted in Taiwanese politics. Notably, Chiang has more commonly referred to Chiang Ching-kuo in public messaging so as to steer clear of controversy about the authoritarian period under Chiang Kai-shek’s rule.
Because of his lineage, backlash against Chiang as the heir of a political dynasty has sometimes erupted into the open, even within the KMT. When passed over for political advancement within the KMT, for example, legislator Hsu Chiao-hsin – another youth politician in the KMT – lashed out at being passed over because her “last name is not Chiang.”
If Shen were, in fact, successful in taking Taipei, it would be a huge political upset. It is probable that talk of Shen as a future presidential contender would materialize immediately. In a similar case, when the KMT’s Han Kuo-yu was successful in winning the Kaohsiung mayorship in 2018 – in what is traditionally considered DPP heartland – this catapulted him to become the KMT’s presidential candidate in 2020
It also led to the political narrative that the DPP’s traditional grip over southern Taiwan was dramatically weakening. Even though Han was removed as mayor in a recall in 2020, the KMT has continued to place high hopes on winning away the DPP’s southern power base.
The DPP has clearly had its eye on making inroads into Taipei for some time. Indeed, the party has often fielded the younger, progressive politicians that emerged in the wake of the Sunflower Movement in downtown Taipei districts that are seen as having rising numbers of upwardly mobile, politically progressive young professionals.
If Shen were to win Taipei in an upset, this would probably be for the same reason that the DPP lost Kaohsiung to the KMT in 2018: city residents growing tired of what they perceived as complacency in governing a presumed electoral safe zone.

Right-wing wave in Brazil's Congress boosts Bolsonaro camp ahead of presidential runoff

Right-wing wave in Brazil's Congress boosts Bolsonaro camp ahead of presidential runoff
SAO PAULO/BRASILIA, Oct 5 - Brazil's right-wing Liberal Party, home to Senator Flavio Bolsonaro's presidential bid, emerged as the biggest winner in congressional elections on Sunday, securing the largest single-party representation in both the Senate and the lower house.
Senator Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, on Sunday won the most votes in the first round of the presidential race, advancing to a runoff against leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on October 25.
During the campaign, the younger Bolsonaro stumped often for allied Senate candidates. His Liberal Party (PL) increased its representation in the Senate from 15 to 28 seats, the strongest result for a party since Brazil's constitution was enacted in the late 1980s, following the country's return to democracy. It also secured 121 seats in the lower house, projections for that chamber showed, up from 98 seats currently.
Combined with other center-to-right parties and blocs, which were projected to win close to 250 seats in the lower house and more than 30 seats in the Senate, the Bolsonaro agenda looks set to enjoy a healthy working majority in the next Congress.
An allied Congress — and particularly Senate — would help the younger Bolsonaro achieve his aim of granting amnesty to his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.
The Senate's pro-Bolsonaro bloc may even be close to the threshold of 54 votes needed to impeach the Supreme Court justices who convicted the far-right former leader.
"I was very happy to see how many Brazilians went to the polls to make their voices heard and didn't stay on the sidelines because they want change," Bolsonaro said after the vote.
Sunday's legislative races, held alongside the first round of the presidential election, renewed all 513 seats in the lower house of Congress and two-thirds of the 81-seat Senate.
Congressional races in Brazil have drawn increasing voter attention in recent elections as lawmakers expand their influence in the capital Brasilia, particularly through greater control over federal spending and leverage over presidential appointments.
Lula's Workers Party, known as PT, also increased its footprint in Congress. The party maintained its Senate presence with nine seats, and a three-party bloc led by the PT was projected to win 88 seats in the lower house, up from 82 currently.
GOVERNANCE CHALLENGES
Even as Lula fights for a come-from-behind victory in the second round of voting, analysts say the next Congress would make his fourth, non-consecutive term an uphill battle.
"Governance would pose a major challenge for President Lula," said Neuriberg Dias, head of legislative watchdog DIAP, adding that a right-wing bloc would work to stifle legislative progress and the functioning of government.
Both political camps have illustrated the difficulties faced by presidents who do not have sufficient congressional backing.
In April, Lula became the first Brazilian president in more than a century to see a Supreme Court nominee voted down amid tensions with center-right Senate President Davi Alcolumbre.
Congress has also overturned dozens of Lula's vetoes since his return to office in January 2023, underscoring lawmakers' growing assertiveness.
Former President Jair Bolsonaro faced similar obstacles, with Congress blocking some of his most prominent policy initiatives, including efforts to loosen gun-control rules and introduce a printed ballot verification system for elections. REUTERS
