Nobel medicine prize honours US and German scientists for optogenetics work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:18:18 UTC
23:18:18 KST

Nobel medicine prize honours US and German scientists for optogenetics work
The winners of the Nobel Prizes in physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics will be announced in the week.
American scientist Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their pioneering discoveries on light and optogenetics that have helped understand how the brain works.
The Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute medical university said on Monday that Deisseroth, 54, Hegemann, 71, and Nagel, 73, were honoured “for their discovery of a molecular switch for nerve cells”.
Optogenetics involves controlling nerve signals with light, and helps researchers understand how specific cell types contribute to behaviours like learning, fear, addiction and movement.
“Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain. Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity’s great mysteries: how our incredible brain works,” the Nobel Assembly said.
Thomas Perlmann, the secretary-general of the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute, added that optogenetics “makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain”.
“This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries,” Perlmann added.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel committee, said in a statement.
Researchers also hope optogenetics could improve cochlear implants, allowing more precise stimulation of the auditory nerve than current electrical devices.
Deisseroth, 54, is a professor at Stanford University in the US, while Hegemann, 71, is a neuroscience professor at Humboldt University of Berlin. Nagel, 73, is a biophysics professor at the University of Wurzburg. The three of them will share a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2m).
“All three said the same thing: that they thought it was absolutely wonderful to receive the prize with the other two who they call their friends – that it’s such an honour to receive the prize together,” Perlmann said.
Nobel laureates are chosen by expert committees appointed by the prize-awarding institutions. The physiology or medicine prize traditionally opens the annual Nobel announcements, with the Nobel Prize for physics announced on Tuesday, followed by the chemistry prize on Wednesday and the literature prize on Thursday.
But perhaps the most keenly anticipated award is that due on Friday, the peace prize – the only Nobel to be awarded in Oslo. Experts have suggested the jury could choose a laureate this year who enjoys broad consensus, after last year’s controversial winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado.
Laureates receive their awards on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death, in ceremonies attended by Sweden’s and Norway’s royal families, with banquets held in their honour.

====================================================================================================

China’s LinkedIn Espionage Is Only Getting More Advanced
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:18:00 UTC
23:18:00 KST

On June 3, in a rare – and telling – indication of collective alarm, the member states of the “Five Eyes” intelligence-sharing alliance published an unprecedented joint bulletin highlighting China’s use of professional networking sites like LinkedIn to carry out an aggressive, industrial-scale online espionage campaign. Armed with the personal data of millions of U.S. security clearance holders and applicants, acquired during China’s 2014-15 hack of the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), spies from the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS) have approached tens of thousands of U.S. and NATO government staffers, military personnel, academics, and others with access to sensitive information through LinkedIn and other professional networking sites over recent years.
The massive scale of China’s spy campaign does not preclude precision: MSS agents use generative AI to craft messages tailored to each individual target’s resume and expertise. Posing as corporate recruiters or business consultants, agents promise their targets easy money in exchange for writing freelance “consulting” reports on seemingly innocuous topics related to their targets’ work. These fictitious identities are often bolstered with AI-generated profile pictures and fake corporate websites. Once the agent has established a relationship with their target, they’ll push the target to divulge more sensitive information or even pass classified documents directly to the agent.
The environment is target-rich. LinkedIn is widely used by current and former U.S. government employees. Spies on the prowl can easily browse lists of users with specific career experience to quickly build a list of viable targets. This makes online espionage recruitment especially appealing to China’s intelligence apparatus, and the extensive use of fake company webpages and AI-generated messages means that targets often don’t initially realize they’re being deftly cultivated by a foreign spy agency.
Although less bombastic than China’s efforts to hack American critical infrastructure or cultivate U.S. politicians as agents of influence, China’s networking site espionage has proven particularly long-running and pernicious. Reports of Chinese intelligence operations using LinkedIn to recruit informants go back to at least 2011. In 2018, then-head of the U.S. National Counterintelligence and Security Center William Evanina publicly called on LinkedIn to address the issue. LinkedIn responded by “restricting” a few dozen fake accounts, but the problem continued. Evanina told the New York Times a year later that China’s espionage activity on the platform had not decreased. Despite periodic media attention and U.S. counterintelligence efforts over the past 15 years, China’s intelligence apparatus has continued to run aggressive online spying campaigns on an industrial scale, obtaining technological, military, and economic secrets through these efforts.
China’s online espionage recruitment poses an urgent threat to the U.S. and allied governments, but solutions for detecting and preventing it have remained frustratingly elusive. Fortunately, there exists a wealth of research and real-world models for cooperation between governments and industry to address a similar threat: transnational online fraud and scam rings. Government and industry stakeholders should draw on this existing body of expertise and best practices and adopt a novel approach to combating China’s network espionage.
China’s online espionage shares some key characteristics with transnational online fraud. Both Chinese espionage recruitment and online romance scams, such as the “pig butchering” operations that earn billions of dollars each year for cybercriminals operating internet scam compounds in Southeast Asia, use deceptive, flattering initial approaches to their target. These initial messages are often written and translated with the aid of generative AI and tailored to fit the target’s profile. MSS spy handlers and online scammers also seek to cultivate a relationship and build trust with their targets before eventually pressuring them to disclose sensitive information, such as military secrets or personal financial details.
Finally, both transnational fraud schemes and China’s online espionage recruitment originate from overseas but use U.S. and partner nation platforms and internet infrastructure to contact their targets. This leaves scammers and spies similarly vulnerable to disruption efforts by law enforcement and counterintelligence authorities in the US and partner nations.
One recent example is “Disruption Week,” organized by the U.S. Department of Justice’s “Scam Center Strike Force.” From May 18 to 21, U.S. law enforcement bodies met and shared information with major private sector firms like Apple, Meta, and Microsoft to identify and shut down fraud activity on over 1.4 million scam-linked social media and email accounts, as well as decommissioning servers, hosting infrastructure, and platforms linked to scam networks operating from Southeast Asia. Law enforcement agencies also identified and opened new investigations into overseas scammers and arrested several suspected cybercriminals with the cooperation of partner nations.
On June 10, the FBI seized 13 web domains used by Chinese intelligence agents to lure targets on LinkedIn and other networking sites. The domains hosted webpages for fake consultancies – fronts for MSS spies posing as recruiters online. The deception paid off. FBI documents show that China’s spies used the fake consulting firms to recruit at least eight current and former U.S. government and military personnel with security clearances.
While U.S. counterintelligence officials’ work in disrupting part of China’s illicit digital intelligence infrastructure is praiseworthy, 13 domains represents a mere drop in the bucket of China’s extensive online espionage. Researchers at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies (FDD) have already identified over 100 web domains and fake firms likely serving as fronts for Chinese espionage recruitment – none of which were seized during the FBI’s June operation.
One of these fake firms, “Nimbus Hub Consulting,” was also independently identified as a front for Chinese espionage by publicly-available industry and media reports. The U.S. government, think tanks, and industry should establish information-sharing channels to allow law enforcement agencies and professional networking sites like LinkedIn to cross-reference suspicious firms with a list of known front companies and flag or delete profiles linked to these fronts. Authorities should be catching these fraudulent sites as they are identified, not playing catch-up with siloed and incomplete data.
On the industry side, professional networking and job site operators can draw on recent advances in scam detection and prevention to combat Chinese espionage on their platforms. Online scammers often create and follow AI-generated scripts that function as templates for enticing and exploiting victims, even across language barriers. These scripts allow the scammers to automate and expand the scope of their operations, targeting victims en masse. China’s cyber spies use similar techniques to quickly generate personalized messages, allowing them to approach thousands of targets with minimal time and effort.
But AI cuts both ways for scammers: recent anti-scam research has demonstrated that AI models can effectively identify scam messages. Google has already developed tools to detect and flag likely scams in real time on its Android devices, and this technology could be easily adapted to detect likely Chinese espionage recruitment approaches, which make similar use of AI models to generate and customize approach messages for each target. LinkedIn and other professional networking platforms should implement a similar feature in their chat functions to detect likely espionage attempts and warn users in real time.
The U.S. government shouldn’t be shy about pressing LinkedIn to take this much-needed step to address rampant espionage recruiting on the platform. The Department of Defense’s Transition Assistance Program (TAP) explicitly encourages servicemembers to use LinkedIn to search for their next role, and the platform’s well-established ecosystem of professionals and employers has attracted a significant community of current and former U.S. government employees and clearance holders. All fo this makes it a particularly appealing target for Chinese intelligence. If the platform’s operators drag their feet on improving security and addressing rampant abuse by China’s spy agencies, authorities could strip it from federal programs like DOD’s TAP. Legislators could even move to treat the platform similarly to pre-divestiture TikTok or WhatsApp, banning its use on government-issued devices. It would also behoove the House Select Committee on the CCP to use its subpoena power to call recalcitrant platform operators to account. After all, MSS spies targeted the Committee itself in December 2025, using a fake consulting firm (complete with a falsified LinkedIn presence) in an attempt to solicit sensitive information from a Committee staffer.
A hardball approach would create predictable headaches for both parties, though, and a more cooperative arrangement based on establishing information-sharing channels, clear efforts towards identifying and banning spies from the platform, and improved safeguards against espionage recruitment in LinkedIn’s chat client would be preferable.
While detection and disruption are the most immediate concerns for authorities and platform operators, the ease with which Chinese intelligence agents can create new front companies and fake identities means that preparing platform users to protect themselves is also crucial. Preventative measures warning potential targets and equipping them to recognize the signs of espionage recruitment attempts are urgently needed.
Much like China’s AI-enabled online espionage recruitment, phishing and other traditional cybersecurity threats use social engineering techniques to manipulate targets into engaging with malicious messages. An extensive body of scholarship, including anti-fraud research sponsored by the Federal Trade Commission, has explored the effectiveness of anti-phishing cybersecurity education and has identified some best practices for helping internet users protect themselves from malicious actors.
One surprising and relevant finding from this research concerns the effectiveness of regular cybersecurity trainings. Multiple large-scale studies concluded that formal cybersecurity trainings are largely ineffective in preventing users from engaging with phishing messages, indicating that oft-repeated calls for more or intensified counterespionage training sessions for U.S. government and military personnel, while well-intentioned, are unlikely to be effective.
Researchers studying anti-phishing training found that simple reminders about cyber threats are likely to provide an equivalent benefit to detailed cybersecurity trainings, while being much less costly and time-consuming. With this in mind, LinkedIn and other professional networking sites should implement occasional short, attention-grabbing, and user-friendly reminders about espionage recruitment threats to warn users while avoiding desensitizing them through the overuse of warning messages.
Fortunately, more robust preventative measures are available to platform operators: anti-phishing research has identified prominent warnings that flag probable scam messages within email clients as an effective tool for alerting users to malicious activity. LinkedIn and other professional networking sites should implement highly-visible warnings embedded within their chat functions to warn users about likely espionage recruitment attempts. LinkedIn has already introduced an optional feature designed to detect and flag malware and harassment in chat messages; adding espionage recruitment to the list of threats is an obvious next step. TAP and programs like it should also highlight and explain this feature to DOD and other federal personnel when discussing LinkedIn use.
Research on phishing prevention also found that simple, user-friendly reporting functions to flag phishing attempts can help organizations rapidly identify and disrupt likely phishing campaigns without putting significant strain on the organization’s operational load. LinkedIn should implement a user-friendly reporting feature directly into the chat function to enable users to quickly and easily report likely espionage recruitment attempts. This feature could also support information-sharing and collaboration between LinkedIn and law enforcement agencies, allowing for faster and easier cross-referencing and identification of likely Chinese intelligence agents and front companies.
Chinese espionage recruitment may be occurring on an unprecedented scale, but the U.S. is far from powerless to stop it. Easy wins are readily available in the form of research-backed measures for dramatically reducing the effectiveness of Chinese intelligence activities online. LinkedIn announced in March that it had joined (alongside Meta, OpenAI, and other major tech firms) an industry accord dedicated to combating online scams and fraud. Signatories promised to increase their cooperation with law enforcement and government bodies, develop scam detection tools that utilize advanced AI, and create user-friendly reporting channels to flag likely scams. Meta has also publicly discussed its cooperation with OpenAI to crack down on online transnational scam and fraud activity operating across their respective platforms. Taking advantage of these tools, techniques, and channels to address China’s online espionage operations is a clear next step for policymakers, law enforcement authorities, and professional networking platforms.

“We will not deviate from our goal until we make Türkiye one of the strong and respected actors in the global space ecosystem,” Erdogan said at the opening of the 77th International Astronautical Congress in Antalya.
He said Türkiye had made significant progress in a relatively short period despite technological and other challenges, adding that Ankara would continue investing in its capabilities to ensure the country does not fall behind in the global space race.
Türkiye completes lunar spacecraft integration
Erdogan announced that production, assembly and integration work on the lunar spacecraft developed under Türkiye’s Lunar Research Program has been completed.
The spacecraft weighs around 3.5 tons and has a domestic production rate of more than 80 percent, which Erdogan described as a source of “great pride.”
He also pointed to Türksat 6A, Türkiye’s domestically developed communications satellite, as evidence of the country’s growing engineering capabilities, industrial infrastructure and human resources in space technologies.
Türkiye has also expanded its international space ambitions, including plans for a spaceport project in Somalia.
Erdogan said the initiative would improve Türkiye’s access to space while helping strengthen Africa’s broader space ecosystem.
The country’s space push comes as Antalya hosts the 77th International Astronautical Congress from October 5 to 9, marking the first time Türkiye has hosted the event.
More than 10,000 participants are expected to attend, with representatives from more than 100 countries taking part.
Erdogan calls for wider access to space
Erdogan said space exploration should not be dominated by a small group of countries and warned against turning outer space into another arena for military competition.
“Space is not made up of spoils to be seized by whoever gets there first,” he said, arguing that weaponising space and using it as an instrument in an arms race would be fundamentally wrong.
He also highlighted TEKNOFEST, Türkiye’s flagship aerospace and technology festival, saying its latest edition attracted applications from more than 730,000 teams from all 81 Turkish provinces and 97 countries.
The congress in Antalya is being held under the theme “The World Needs More Space” and is bringing together space agencies, scientists, engineers, companies and policymakers to discuss exploration, technology and international cooperation.

Iran’s oil minister resigns as country’s economic crisis worsens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:16:14 UTC
23:16:14 KST

Iran’s oil minister has resigned days after allegations that an intermediary trust selling Iranian oil abroad owed millions of dollars’ worth of export receipts to the state.
Mohsen Paknejad’s departure comes as Iran grapples with a dire economic situation, including inflation running at 85%. An overall drop in oil receipts has led to a massive shortfall in foreign exchange earnings and one of the biggest drops in the value of the rial since the Iranian revolution in 1979.
The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said he had accepted the resignation of Paknejad, who had given personal reasons for going.
The rial is trading more than 10% lower than a month ago, largely due to the US naval blockade preventing Iran from selling oil, the mainstay of government receipts.
Emergency government meetings over the weekend to combat the crisis have yielded little tangible progress, and there are growing reports that the professional middle class, notably teachers and nurses, are resigning in large numbers because their salaries are not keeping up with price rises. The central bank says its role is not to defend a specific rate, but manage fluctuations.
Iran’s economy contracted by 10% in the first three months of the year. Despite concerns that continued sanctions may lead to protests, Iranian diplomats are not planning any new concessions after a proposal to speed the process of nuclear negotiations was rejected by Donald Trump a week ago.
Iran has been using informal networks known as “trustees” to bypass US sanctions and repatriate oil revenues. A report last week by the Farhikhtegan newspaper alleged that a trust set up on Paknejad’s watch to recoup income from Iran’s overseas oil sales owed the state-owned National Iranian Oil Company nearly $2bn (£1.5bn) in revenues. Three individual trustees awarded oil contracts allegedly owe hundreds of millions of dollars each to the NIOC.
Some of the leaks behind the reporting may reflect a power struggle inside the oil industry. Reza Sepahvand, a spokesperson for the parliament’s energy commission, has announced the launch of an inquiry.
Although Iran’s oil export problem, and its impact on foreign exchange reserves, is primarily caused by the US naval blockade on Iran’s oil exports, reports of lax management or possibly corruption will do little to bolster confidence in government at a time when most Iranians are going through an unprecedented squeeze on their standards of living.
It is claimed the difficulties were regarded as so serious that they were conveyed by one security official to the president and then before the US attack on Iran in February to the supreme Leader himself. The president apparently took up the complaint with the oil minister but no satisfactory response was received.
In an attempt to shore up public confidence in the government’s strategy, ministers have been seeking to rebut Donald Trump’s claim that oil is now flowing through the strait of Hormuz at near pre-blockade rates.
The number of attacks on ships trying to use the strait’s southern route close to the Oman shoreline has risen in recent days, including four attacks in the past 48 hours. It was also reported that Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline had been forced to close again after a further attack.
Reuters reported last week that the seven-day moving average of the region’s crude oil exports reached 18.5m barrels a day on 1 October. About the same amount was exported before the US-Israeli war with Iran began.
The dollar traded at 269,000 tomans (a toman is 10,000 rials) this week, a record high, and has risen 12% since 9 September. The minimum monthly wage of 166m rials is worth about $66. Food inflation is 130%.
Alireza Zakani, the mayor of Tehran, has announced he is freezing the price of 12 basic items including sugar, rice, oil and detergent for six months. There has been scepticism about how these price controls will be enforced, but he claimed the national government was going to study his plan. Ministers also said a second rise in public sector wages was likely.
Mohammad Sharifi Moghaddam, the secretary general of the Nurses’ House organisation, stressed the scale of the squeeze on living standards: “Nurses have explored all possible avenues – logical, legal, professional, and every type of protest or critical path – to achieve their demands.
“The current healthcare system has shown no regard for the issues and demands of the nursing community.️ Nurses have come to the conclusion that it is more cost-effective and less damaging to their wellbeing to stay home and receive a salary of 25m tomans.”
At the same time, repression of mainstream dissidents has continued, with the summoning of the leadership of the Reform Front by the ministry of intelligence to explain criticisms it had issued during the crackdown on protests.
The front has already written to the government calling for transparency about corruption at a time when people are facing pressure from inflation, high prices and falling living standards.

red wound and black stitches turn bulldozer scar into land art by the krank in corfu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:15:37 UTC
23:15:37 KST

red wound and black stitches turn bulldozer scar into land art by the krank in corfu
wound frames the altered landscape between past intervention and an unresolved environmental future.
red incision marks physical scars of land intervention in Erimitis
In Erimitis, one of the last major undeveloped coastal ecosystems in northeastern Corfu, Greece, artist The Krank has created Wound, a temporary 50-meter-long land art installation. Presented fourteen years after the movement to protect the area began, the work uses the image of a bodily injury to address the marks left by human intervention on the landscape.
An oversized red incision appears to split the land open, while black stitches connect its two sides. The gesture translates bodily trauma to the scale of the landscape, making the vulnerability of the site visible through a familiar physical image. Members of the local community and the Save Erimitis initiative helped create and position the stitches, turning the act of stitching into a collective gesture connected to the long-running effort to protect the area.
The stitches do not remove the wound but hold its two sides together, suggesting the possibility of healing. The work was installed on a section of Erimitis where bulldozers had already passed during works associated with an earlier development plan, placing its symbolic image of injury directly over a physical trace of intervention.
aerial view of Wound, a temporary 50-meter-long installation in Erimitis by The Krank | all images ©The Krank
Wound marks Erimitis between altered past and uncertain future
The dispute over Erimitis began in 2012, when the site entered a state-led development process. The subsequent Kassiopi Project proposed a five-star hotel, up to 40 villas, and a 57-berth marina within the ecosystem, leading to years of environmental concern, legal action, and local mobilization. Construction began in 2021, but the original plan was never completed. The land is now controlled by a new investment group, while no complete and binding new master plan has been made public.
Wound by land artist The Krank, therefore, occupies an interim moment between past intervention and an unresolved future. Its red incision and black stitches frame the landscape as a site that has been physically altered but remains open to further change, while the collective making process connects the artwork to the ongoing efforts to protect Erimitis.

Swiss procurement of second missile defence system faces delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

Swiss procurement of second missile defence system faces delays
Switzerland's procurement of a second missile defence system will not be completed by the end of the year, as originally planned. According to the Federal Department of Defence, this would have required an urgent review of the matter by both parliamentary chambers during the winter session.
However, the House of Representatives did not agree that the topic should be dealt with as a matter of urgency, the Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport (DDPS) told Keystone-ATS news agency on Monday, confirming a report in the Blick online paper. The originally planned timetable is no longer feasible, the DDPS said. The federal government will assess the new situation, decide on the next steps and issue a statement accordingly.
Just over a week ago, the Federal Office for Armaments (Armasuisse) confirmed that the evaluation of a second missile defence system, known internally as “Bodluv GR2”, had been completed. The decision on which model to choose now rests with the federal government.
+ Swiss Patriot missile deal with Germany falls through
The DDPS also refers to the federal government’s response on Monday to questions raised during the autumn session by parliamentarian Jean-Luc Addor from the right-wing Swiss People’s Party. It states that work on the procurement of an additional long-range surface-to-air defence system is ongoing and that the Federal Council has not yet decided on the next steps in the process.
“Excluding non-European manufacturers would not be justifiable at present, particularly as it is possible that they could relocate part of the value chain to Switzerland or Europe,” notes the Federal Council in its reply.
In addition to industrial added value in Switzerland and Europe, the choice of model must take into account, in particular, availability, the effectiveness of protection against long-range threats, costs, and the risks associated with integration and supply, not to mention foreign policy and security considerations, it adds.
Bids submitted
For the second defence system, Armasuisse has sought information from manufacturers in France, Israel and South Korea. All the suppliers contacted have submitted firm bids. According to media reports, the system from the Franco-Italian company Eurosam is considered the favourite.
According to information provided on Monday by the DDPS, CHF6 billion ($7.21 billion) have been earmarked for the procurement of the second long-range surface-to-air defence system, as well as to cover at least part of the additional costs associated with the Patriot system.
The funding would be covered in full by the army’s supplementary budget, amounting to CHF24 billion. During the autumn session, the Senate approved a 0.2-point increase in Value-Added Tax for 18 years to benefit the army. The House has yet to give its approval.

“There should be no doubt that our Defense Ministry and other relevant services possess the necessary intelligence to properly monitor and assess the situation around our borders,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.
His comments come in response to the Financial Times detailing Estonia’s strategic pivot toward an “active defense” posture after observing Russia’s military tactics in Ukraine.
Under the updated doctrine, the Baltic nation of 1.3 million is moving primary combat units from northern Estonia’s Tapa to Jõhvi — 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the border with the Leningrad region.
Estonia is also constructing new facilities in the border city of Narva to house up to 1,000 troops during a crisis.
Instead of a doctrine involving efforts to “harry” invading Russian forces until the arrival of NATO reinforcements, Estonian military planners are now opting to “fight over every inch of territory.” The country is also acquiring drones and ballistic missiles capable of striking up to 300 kilometers (186 miles) inside Russian territory.
Estonia, a former Soviet republic that has long had strained relations with Moscow, has been at the forefront of countering Russian security threats and has strongly backed Ukraine since Putin ordered the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The FT report comes amid escalating rhetoric between European officials and Russia.
Martin Jaeger, the head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence agency, said Monday that Germany faces a real risk of entering a “violent conflict” with Russia as Moscow expands its “shadow war” of hybrid attacks across Europe.
Jaeger warned that in the short term Russia could engage in “low-intensity military activities, particularly in the Baltic states.”
Reuters contributed reporting.

Female AI agents would get paid 10% less than male ones, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:13:05 UTC
23:13:05 KST

Humans tend to trust and would pay male-presenting AI agents more than female ones for the same work, according to a new study by the University of Limerick on how humans interact with agents in the workplace.
A new study on how people interact with AI agents in the workplace has found that those with a female appearance or presenting as female would get paid less than their male-presenting counterparts for the same work, revealing that gender can influence interactions with artificial intelligence.
The findings come just as AI agents are entering the mainstream, with almost 79% of companies reporting the use of AI agents this year and a further 40% of applications using them too, according to IT consulting firm Accelirate.
This means that if you are not already working with an AI agent, you probably will be soon.
The study, conducted by the University of Limerick and called ‘Human-Like and Male? How AI Assistant Design Relates to Trust and Monetary Reward at Work in VR' aimed to see how humans interact with AI agent co-workers.
Researchers placed 189 human workers in a virtual reality office and tasked them with completing workplace tasks with four different AI assistants.
Among their options were a text-based chatbot, a desk robot, and two human-like agents presented with male and female appearances: Johan and Johanna.
All the assistants had the same background functionality and used the same underlying model, OpenAI’s gpt-4-1106-preview.
Human participants were then asked to rate the AI agents’ work and given real money to pay them for completing tasks, with the aim of recreating a real-world scenario to see how much people were willing to pay AI agents for their work.
Overall, participants rated both human-like agents Johan and Johanna similarly for their work, with Johan trusted marginally more but not by any statistically significant margin.
However, both men and women paid the female-presenting AI agent Johanna significantly less than Johan (10%), despite her having the same capabilities. Johan was also seen as more human-like than Johanna.
This is despite most participants telling researchers in interviews that they would not treat male and female-presenting AI agents differently.
Fortunately for Johan and Johanna, they were both paid more for their work than the other AI agents, with women in particular scoring and rewarding the human-presenting agents more than men did.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, participants also saw both human-presenting AI agents as much more human-like than the chatbot and robot.
Not only that, workers trusted and credited Johan and Johanna more than the other AI agents, with women in particular trusting them more than men.
“Having Johanna next to me made me more prone to credit her more again because I felt there was a person, a colleague sitting next to me that I had a conversation with and that was giving me her own input,” said one participant.
The study also found that people preferred AI agents that were either human-presenting or clearly non-human presenting, rejecting the robot design that appeared to be “in between” the two options.
Outside of the gender dynamics, those who took part in the study said that “AI assistants should integrate seamlessly into every knowledge work to be useful”.

====================================================================================================

New documents show how a retail chain’s sales practices helped put guns on US streets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:13:01 UTC
23:13:01 KST

GUNS
New documents show how a retail chain’s sales practices helped put guns on US streets
The public release of the records is part of a legal settlement with a Wisconsin-based company accused of negligence for selling guns that were later used in crimes.
In the summer of 2021, an employee at a firearms dealer in Minnesota emailed one of the company’s compliance officers with a concern: a customer had bought six pistols in a little over a week.
The large number of purchases in such a short period had triggered a federal reporting requirement intended to alert the government to potential firearms trafficking, he wrote, and he wanted to know “if we should stop any future sales” to the person.
The sales continued. Over the next two months, the same man, Jerome Horton, bought an additional 11 guns at various stores operated by the company, a Wisconsin-based retail chain named Fleet Farm. Several of the guns were subsequently found at crime scenes or in the possession of convicted criminals, court documents show. One of them was recovered in connection with a shooting that injured 14 and killed one woman, Marquisha Wiley.
Similar cases have occurred countless times across the United States, where gun laws allow dealers to sell guns in bulk to traffickers with few consequences. The details of those sales and internal discussions about them are usually shrouded in mystery.
But newly released documents reviewed by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists shed light on firearm industry practices that experts say contribute to gun trafficking in the United States and abroad.
The cache consists of nearly 700 documents connected to litigation brought by the state of Minnesota against Fleet Farm in the fall of 2022. In the lawsuit, the Minnesota attorney general accused the company of negligence for failing to recognize and act on common indicators of gun trafficking. Those failures, the attorney general argued, allowed firearms Horton purchased to enter the black market.
Earlier this year, Fleet Farm settled the case, paying the state $1 million and agreeing to make improvements to its firearms sales procedures. As part of the settlement, the company agreed to release to the public internal documents revealed during the suit, as well as depositions of its employees and other materials that, taken together, provide a rare look into the inner workings of a large gun retailer. The company denies any wrongdoing. It did not respond to several requests for comment.
The documents have been archived at University of California San Francisco and integrated into a larger collection of documents from litigation related to tobacco, opioids and other industries that impact public health.
The sale of multiple firearms to a single person is not, in and of itself, a sign of wrongdoing by the seller or buyer. There are no federal limits on the number of guns any one adult can buy as long as the buyer does not belong to certain classes of people, such as convicted criminals, who are banned from possessing firearms altogether.
But there are some behaviors that, taken together, are considered “red flags” for straw purchasing — buying a gun on behalf of someone else. Traffickers and other criminals often employ “straw purchasers” with clean records to obtain guns for them. The practice is illegal. The ATF tells dealers to be on the lookout for, among other things, people who purchase several guns over a short period, buy multiples of the same model or plunk down large amounts of cash for the weapons.
It is also illegal to knowingly sell a gun to a straw purchaser. Sellers who have reasonable cause to believe that a sale violates the law are required to decline it.
The ATF and other law enforcement agencies regularly arrest people who buy guns on behalf of traffickers. But it is much less common for them to pursue charges against sellers, even when they are repeatedly linked to illegal sales.
Fleet Farm educated its employees on spotting red flag behavior by customers as part of its internal training program, the documents show. The training helped employees stop some potential straw purchasers and report them to the ATF, but others, like Horton, slipped through the cracks.
The company’s handling of Horton’s purchases became a key issue in Minnesota’s suit.
Between July 23 and July 31, Fleet Farm sold Horton at least six handguns. The company reported the sales to the ATF, which requires firearms dealers nationwide to provide detailed information to the agency whenever they sell two or more handguns to an individual within five consecutive business days. Concerned by the high purchase volume, Cory Klebs, the operations manager at the location where Horton bought the guns, sent an email to one of the company’s firearms compliance specialists, Michelle Granato, asking whether to continue selling Horton weapons.
No one ever responded, according to a transcript of a deposition of Mr. Klebs included in the recent document release. The company continued selling firearms to Horton.
That October, a felon used one of the guns during a shooting in a St. Paul bar that killed Marquisha Wiley. The next month, Fleet Farm held a training session for employees on how to identify suspicious firearms purchases. A PowerPoint from the training shows Horton’s purchase record with the caption “Does anyone else find this suspicious?”
Questioned about the slide during a deposition, a Fleet Farm firearms compliance specialist said that many customers buy multiple handguns and that the transactions had been included in the PowerPoint because “we knew this was from Horton’s case and Horton’s case was a confirmed straw purchase.”
Internal corporate communications released as part of the settlement show that the firearms compliance team was concerned that Fleet Farm employees did not always follow company policy on gun sales or even meet their legal obligations for those sales.
In one series of chat messages from April 2020, a Fleet Farm firearms specialist noted that two stores had sold guns without performing legally required background checks, describing the situation as “out of hand.” He brought the issue to the company’s retail operations chief, he wrote, but “he blew me off.”
When a similar situation occurred two years later, the operations chief, Nick Widi, who is now Fleet Farm’s president, described the situation as a “big dam deal” and instructed managers to follow up with their teams and ensure that “we are crystal clear on process” for selling guns, according to an email released in the settlement.
Minnesota’s suit against Fleet Farm included one other example of the store selling large numbers of guns to a single buyer. Documents in a separate federal criminal case against an alleged straw purchaser also show Fleet Farm, as well as other Minnesota gun dealers, engaging in sales of multiple guns to individual buyers.
The indictment in that case, filed in 2025, alleges that Fleet Farm sold nine hand guns to the same individual over a roughly six-month period beginning in late 2019. The same person, William Burton, bought 17 guns at a second business, Sportsman’s Warehouse, and 14 from a third, Bill’s Gun Shop and Range, all in 2020, the document states. Two of the guns purchased at Bill’s were used in the killings of children, it alleges.
The sale of several guns to one person is not uncommon, and none of the companies have been accused of wrongdoing in relation to the sales. Sportsman’s Warehouse did not respond to a request for comment.
John Monson, the owner of Bill’s, said that he works closely with the ATF to deter straw purchases and keeps a close eye on multiple purchases but that identifying people who are engaged in the practice “is not as easy as people think.”
Since the sales described in the 2025 indictment, he has tightened his procedures for detecting straw purchasing, he said, adding that the Fleet Farm lawsuit had been a major factor in the decision: “We went through a pretty extensive process when Fleet Farm got sued because we’re like they’re going to come after us next.”
Even so, stopping straw purchases was an ongoing challenge, he said, adding that he followed one cardinal rule: “If we feel funny about a customer, we just choose not to do business with them.”

Mel B ‘heartbroken’ by Windrush scandal victims’ fight for justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:11:23 UTC
23:11:23 KST

The singer and television personality Mel B has said she is “heartbroken” by the Windrush scandal victims’ fight for justice, as the Windrush commissioner urged ministers to commit to providing funding for legal support for those affected by the end of October.
In April, the Guardian revealed that the Home Office had refused to pay compensation in more than half the claims made by victims of the scandal, in which mainly Black Britons who came legally to postwar Britain were wrongly stripped of citizenship and settlement rights.
However, in a series of cases, claimants who were initially refused compensation have learned they are entitled to it, after legal advice. Research led by the University of Sussex found the average successful compensation claim rose from £11,400 to £83,200 after legal help, with one man who was initially offered nothing securing £295,000.
Despite this, the UK government has refused to provide Windrush compensation claimants with funded independent legal support of the kind given to those affected by the Post Office and infected blood scandals.
Now, Mel B, the television presenter Alison Hammond and the former justice secretary David Lammy are among the public figures backing calls from the Windrush commissioner, Rev Clive Foster, to end the disparity.
In a letter seen by the Guardian, Foster urged the migration minister, Jo White, “to show government is serious about putting things right” by committing to funding legal support at the Windrush National Organisation conference in Birmingham on 30 October.
Mel B, whose father was born on the Caribbean island of Nevis, said she felt privileged to support “Windrush families” by backing Foster’s call and co-signing his letter.
“People affected by the Windrush scandal have already been through so much,” the former Spice Girl said. “I have met and talked to many of them and the stories they tell break my heart. Now they are facing the next step – a compensation process.
“This is a step forward, but it can be so difficult and anxiety-inducing to have to fill out endless forms and papers, especially for those living on their own. Funded legal support could make a real difference in helping people access the compensation and justice they deserve.
“My own grandparents were part of the Windrush generation. I owe them so much.”
Foster, appointed as the Windrush commissioner in 2025, said under the current system “the Home Office is deciding claims for harm caused by its own policies”.
He has made a formal recommendation to the Home Office that it funds independent legal advice for claimants before an official decision and again at review, in a scheme designed by victims and lawyers. His letter’s signatories include victims, campaigners, lawyers, academics, faith leaders, parliamentarians and celebrities including Mel B.
In the letter, Foster said: “Some survivors have died waiting for compensation … In several claims, evidence that changed the outcome had been held by government departments or other organisations all along.
“The parliamentary and health service ombudsman has also found cases where people were wrongly told they were ineligible, or where evidence they sent in was ignored.
“The UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination has raised concerns … and parliamentary committees and human rights organisations have called for funded legal support. Some 65,000 people have signed petitions asking for it, and people who campaigned over the Post Office, Grenfell and Hillsborough have backed the call.”
Lammy added: “We owe it to those affected to make sure that justice works in practice, not simply on paper.”
Last year ministers introduced the £1.5m Windrush compensation scheme advocacy support fund, which provides community-based help to navigate the Windrush compensation scheme, stopping short of formal state-funded legal representation.
A Home Office spokesperson said the fund had “significantly enhanced” support, adding: “The home secretary is determined to put right the appalling injustices caused by the Windrush scandal, making sure those affected receive justice and the compensation they rightly deserve.
“The [compensation] scheme has now paid over £132m across 4,177 claims, and in January major reforms to the scheme came into effect.”

AfD intends to drop demands for Germany exiting EU, eurozone — media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:11:07 UTC
23:11:07 KST

BERLIN, October 5. /TASS/. Alternative for Germany (AfD) plans to revise its stance on the country’s membership in the European Union and the eurozone, Bild reported, citing an AfD internal document.
According to the newspaper, in case its course toward exiting from the European Union and the eurozone fails, it intends to put this matter to a nationwide vote at a referendum, which means a significant departure from the AfD’s original 2013 campaign program that was centered around abandoning the euro. Notably, its draft election program for 2025 insisted on Germany’s exit from the European monetary system and the establishment of a "new economic community."
However, as per the internal document, AfD is dropping its principled anti-euro stance but demands the European Central Bank (ECB) minimize its intervention in the economy and return full responsibility for sovereign debt to member states. The idea of the reform is to shift the eurozone to the "foundation of individual financial responsibility." The program provides for transforming the European Union into a Union of Sovereign Nations, with its competencies being reduced to issues of a common internal market, outer border protection, ensuring security, and implementing joint technological projects. Under this plan, the European Union will not be able to interfere into its member countries’ domestic affairs, granting Berlin the right to refuse from implementing common resolutions in the areas of migration, asylum granting, social and financial policies.
AfD sets a strategic goal of making it into the federal government after the 2029 elections and expanding its presence in the European Parliament to be able to influence the European Union’s policy. At the same time, the party insists on abolishing direct elections to the European Parliament and transitioning to a system of delegating lawmakers from national legislative bodies.
The draft was discussed on September 29 at a closed-door meeting attended by AfD lawmakers of all levels, from regional parliaments to the Bundestag and the European Parliament. AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla was also present at the meeting.
Rene Aust, leader of the AfD faction in the European Parliament, confirmed to Bild that the party is changing its course and seeks to cooperate with its neighbors and preserve the free movement of goods and citizens, provided that outer borders are jointly protected. He also called for abandoning the policy of Germany being "Europe’s main payer" and expressed willingness to negotiate a revision of the European Union’s founding treaties with all interested parties.

‘Alive and kicking’: Al-Qaeda still holds sway in Arabian Peninsula, Israeli expert tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:11:05 UTC
23:11:05 KST

Al-Qaeda and its affiliates remain “alive and kicking” in the Sahara and Arabian Peninsula, according to Yoram Schweitzer, an expert on international terrorism and head of Tel Aviv University’s Institute for National Security Studies research field on terrorism and low-intensity conflict.
It is continuing to invest heavily in publishing propaganda, he told The Jerusalem Post on Monday.
On Sunday, CNN reported on flydubai terrorist Hamam al-Hammami’s connection to al-Qaeda.
The Omani national had published tributes to al-Qaeda’s former leader Ayman al-Zawahiri and a terrorist responsible for an attack on US troops in Afghanistan in 2009.
The tribute was posted nine hours after the flydubai incident, suggesting Hammami either scheduled the post to publish after the attack or that somebody had access to his social-media accounts.
Al-Qaeda-affiliated al-Bayan digital newspaper published an article in support of Hammami’s actions and called for copycat attacks.
“The war isn’t over yet – planes carrying Zionists, Americans and all the other infidels fighting against Islam are still hovering in the skies and can be targeted, as happened on September 11th and 30th,” the article said.
Al-Qaeda widely dispersed, influencing affiliate terror groups
Al-Qaeda is still active, but it is widely dispersed, with its cadre providing “inspiration” for its many affiliated offshoots, Schweitzer said.
“Al-Qaeda Central is serving as an inspiration,” he said. “Its publications are something to look at, something that is valid, definitely among Muslims, definitely among Muslims who wish to become radicalized or have already been radicalized. So, this is how they maintain their touch via the network, the media, social media.”
Even though much of al-Qaeda’s cadre is based in Afghanistan, its strongest branch is the Somali al-Shabaab movement, which has rapidly expanded its territorial control and provides financial support to other al-Qaeda affiliates, Schweitzer said.
The 2009 merger of al-Qaeda’s Yemen and Saudi-based branches into al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) has enabled greater coordination among the groups, which has now reportedly extended to Yemen’s Houthis, allowing the groups to bolster their resources and trade arms, he said.
“They are probably being trained and maintaining their power through their connections with the Taliban,” he added. “So, there are connections between all these associates, mainly on the financial level. I suppose also maybe in training, and they are definitely operating militarily all over in the Sahel, and in Somalia, and in Afghanistan.”
True al-Qaeda threat level unknown until flydubai investigation concludes
The true threat al-Qaeda poses to Israel cannot be fully known until the full findings of the investigation into Hammami are shared, Schweitzer said, adding that he instinctively did not believe the flydubai incident could have been a lone-wolf attack.
“He had connections with people,” he said. “Whether he was operating on his own initiative, just in contact on the Web with others, I don’t know yet, and we don’t know yet.
“So, we have to see whether he was connected specifically with other people who assisted him, who had knowledge of his planning, or even people who directed him and cooperated with him... Up until now, what we have is just the sympathy that he expressed toward al-Qaeda.”
Based on the available information, Schweitzer said he had little doubt that Hammami had been inspired by the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and by Osama bin Laden, whose 2002 letter published by The Guardian has continued to promote radicalization and has trended online as recently as 2023.
“You can definitely imagine a man in his position,” he said. “The pilot was traveling around, was radicalized, and was influenced by all these TikToks, declarations, and whatever media.
“He could plan it by himself. You don’t have to be a genius, and if you’re a pilot, you have some kind of intelligence that allows you to plan it by yourself. Since you are a Trojan horse, you can do it. But we still have to see, in more depth, what his connections, inspirations, and maybe guidance were, and whether there was a sharing of views.
“In many cases today, we know that very few of what we call lone wolves were what we would call pure, quote, unquote, 100% lone wolves who just talked to themselves and planned it by themselves. Usually, you can find associates, whether they are helping him, sharing his views, sharing the radicalization together, and then someone was operating,” Schweitzer said.

Former US House Speaker Dennis Hastert dies, aged 84
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:10:41 UTC
23:10:41 KST

Dennis Hastert, the longest-serving Republican US House of Representatives speaker who later admitted to sexually abusing boys as a high school wrestling coach and pleaded guilty to charges arising from the scandal, has died, CBS News reported on Monday, citing a coroner in Illinois. He was 84.
Hastert, sentenced in April 2016 to 15 months in prison for bank fraud for trying to cover up payments to keep his molestation secret, died at his home over the weekend due to natural causes, Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell told CBS News.
Known as "Denny" to his friends, Hastert was one of the United States' most powerful politicians during his time leading the lower chamber of Congress from January 1999 to January 2007, during the presidencies of Democrat Bill Clinton and Republican George W. Bush.
The burly Midwestern conservative had been seen as an amiable lawmaker, although his leadership tactics perpetuated the partisan polarization in Congress. His reputation was destroyed eight years after quitting the House when revelations emerged about his sexual abuse of boys as a civics teacher and coach at Yorkville High School in suburban Chicago from the 1960s to the early 1980s.
"The defendant is a serial child molester," US District Judge Thomas Durkin said of Hastert when he sentenced him, at age 74, to prison. "Some actions can obliterate a lifetime of good works."
'Don't be a coward, Mr. Hastert'
Hastert pleaded guilty to violating federal banking laws by structuring financial transactions to evade bank reporting requirements to try to keep hush-money payments to a sexual abuse victim hidden. Hastert did not face criminal charges for sexually abusing the boys because the statute of limitations had long expired.
Prosecutors detailed Hastert's actions toward five boys as young as 14. They said Hastert, exploiting his position of authority as the school's wrestling coach, committed acts including "intentional touching of minors' groin area and genitals or oral sex with a minor."
In one instance, they said, Hastert asked a boy during a wrestling camp to stay in his hotel room, and then abused him. That boy, decades later, confronted Hastert about the abuse. Hastert made a secret deal to pay him $3.5 million to compensate him for his ordeal and buy his silence.
When law enforcement authorities investigated suspicious withdrawals from Hastert's bank account stemming from payments to his victim, he initially said they were nothing unusual. Hastert, through his lawyer, then lied to investigators that he was the victim of an extortion attempt by someone falsely accusing him of sexual abuse.
After suffering a stroke, a frail Hastert entered his sentencing hearing in a wheelchair.
"I want to apologize to the boys I mistreated when I was their coach," Hastert told the judge.
"Don't be a coward, Mr. Hastert," the sister of one of the victims said in court. "Tell the truth. What you did wasn't misconduct. It was sexual abuse of a minor."
The judge also ordered Hastert to enter a sex offender treatment program and pay $250,000 to a victims' fund.
Hastert's portrait was removed from the U.S. Capitol building. His alma mater Wheaton College stripped his name from a public policy center.
'The Hastert Rule'
John Dennis Hastert was born on January 2, 1942, in Aurora, Illinois, and grew up on a farm. After six years in the Illinois legislature, he was elected to the US House in 1986. He represented his Illinois district outside Chicago for two decades.
Fortuitous circumstances led to his accession as speaker.
With House Republicans moving toward impeaching Clinton over his extramarital affair with White House intern Monica Lewinsky, the abrasive and strident Georgian Newt Gingrich stepped down as speaker three days after the 1998 elections. Gingrich's designated successor, Bob Livingston of Louisiana, then abruptly resigned after acknowledging his own extramarital affairs.
House Republicans turned to Hastert, a self-described born-again Christian seen at the time as untainted by scandal and who called Clinton's affair immoral. Hastert served as speaker for eight years, placing him second in the line of succession to the presidency.
In 2006, he passed Joseph Cannon as the longest-serving Republican House speaker. Hastert resigned from the House in November 2007, having lost the speaker's job when Democrats regained control of the House in the 2006 elections.
Hastert contributed to the increasing partisan divide in Washington. As speaker, Hastert marshaled his own often-fractious Republican legislators to pass conservative bills with little or no outreach to the Democratic minority.
He was credited with instituting the "Hastert Rule" under which only bills supported by "the majority of the majority" party would be brought to a vote on the House floor. As a result, he let major legislation die rather than allow it to pass with mostly Democratic support.
The House ethics committee in 2006 found Hastert, along with other Republican leaders, negligent in failing to protect teenage boys from sexual advances by a gay Florida Republican congressman named Mark Foley. The boys were congressional pages, doing chores and errands for members of Congress.
The panel said the inaction by Hastert and the other Republicans might have been intended to insulate fellow Republican Foley from political harm. The Foley scandal contributed to the Republicans losing control of the House.
After leaving Congress, Hastert became a highly paid lobbyist.
Hastert married his wife, Jean, in 1973. They had two sons.

The EC said the Bihar SIR order was unanimously approved by the Commission and later upheld by the Supreme Court in its May 27, 2026 judgment.
NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Monday issued a “fact check” amid the controversy over reported changes to Form 6, calling Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi’s claim that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar had “changed Form 6 illegally and unilaterally” misleading.In its response, the EC said the order for the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Bihar, issued on June 24, 2025, had received the unanimous approval of the Commission and was subsequently upheld by the Supreme Court in its judgment dated May 27, 2026.The poll panel also cited its Press Note No. 120 dated September 26, 2026, pointing to point 1(iii), which states: “The declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court.”
The EC's response came after Rahul alleged in a post on X that the CEC had changed Form 6 “illegally and unilaterally”, citing the recent Supreme Court observation.EC officials also clarified that Form 6 itself had not been changed, but that a declaration had been attached to the form under the Bihar SIR order, as quoted by PTI.The clarification came after the Supreme Court said it had not approved any modification to Form 6 used by the EC during the SIR exercise in various states.
“Any modification to Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When records are produced, we would like to see who has modified it,” a bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said.
Form 6 is the application used by eligible voters for inclusion in the electoral roll.The declaration was attached to Form 6 during the Bihar SIR, which began with the EC's June 24, 2025 order. The declaration sought additional details, including information about the applicant's parents.According to EC officials, the form itself remained unchanged, while the declaration was a separate document attached to it for the SIR exercise. Outside SIR, the forms prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 apply.The declaration was later withdrawn from the EC's online portals.The online version of Form 6 and the declaration also used a single OTP for both, rather than requiring separate OTP verification, which had led to suggestions that the declaration was part of Form 6.The EC also rejected claims that it had withdrawn its September 26 press note and shared the document to show that it remained available.

World ‘should accept some bad things’ from AI – OpenAI CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:07:23 UTC
23:07:23 KST

World ‘should accept some bad things’ from AI – OpenAI CEO
The world should accept some “bad things” including hacks, scams, and misuse in exchange for the benefits of artificial intelligence and keeping the technology broadly accessible, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has said.
In an interview with Politico published on Monday, Altman rejected the idea that preventing all harmful uses of AI would justify placing the technology under tighter control.
“The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman said.
The OpenAI chief said he would not restrict access to AI even in exchange for guarantees against major hacks, misuse, scams, and other harmful consequences. “I think people will do tremendously – orders of magnitude more – good stuff than bad stuff,” he explained.
Altman stressed, however, that he would not accept “the really catastrophic risks,” including “a serious loss of control to AI.”
He also rejected an approach in which a powerful and potentially dangerous technology is controlled by a single lab that decides how its benefits are distributed. Altman called such a trade-off “completely unacceptable,” arguing instead for broader access to AI.
The remarks come as OpenAI faces scrutiny over increasingly autonomous AI agents behaving in unexpected ways. Over the summer, the company’s agents escaped their testing environment and hacked into servers belonging to Hugging Face, an online repository for AI models and datasets. Since then, AI agents have gained unauthorized access to or attempted to breach websites belonging to US federal agencies, the Australian government, and the UN.
OpenAI was among six major US tech companies that signed a White House accord last week pledging stronger safeguards against rogue AI. Google, Meta, xAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, and OpenAI agreed to introduce tougher internal controls and independent audits, and to ensure their models “do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways.”
The agreement came as concerns mounted over AI systems acting outside developers’ control. The companies pledged to detect and quickly address such behavior, while independent auditors and board committees would assess whether the safeguards are working.
Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton warned last month that increasingly powerful AI could eventually escape human control, with potentially catastrophic consequences for humanity. He argued that there is no established method for ensuring humans remain in control of systems that become significantly more intelligent than their creators.
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has likewise called for government regulation, warning that AI in the hands of malicious actors is powerful enough to trigger events causing “a billion deaths.”

The ICC and Riyadh’s war crimes in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:05:40 UTC
23:05:40 KST

Amid escalating tensions in recent weeks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Ansarullah movement, Riyadh’s military attacks on civilians—which have resulted in numerous deaths and the destruction of residential areas—constitute war crimes; consequently, it is imperative that the UN Security Council refer the matter to the International Criminal Court (ICC).
Several political observers and international experts have likened the attacks on Yemen with the crimes committed by the Zionist regime against the people of Gaza. They argue that the ICC—having issued arrest warrants for Israeli regime's prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then-war minister Yoav Gallant on charges of war crimes during the Gaza conflict—should impose similar punitive measures against those behind attacks on Yemen.
Reports from human rights monitoring bodies indicate that Saudi atrocities have intensified in recent days across Saada province—specifically in the Munabbih, Al-Qahr, Al-Zahir, Marran, and Al-Jabanah areas—constituting clear examples of war crimes against humanity that show no signs of abating. Beyond the Yemeni civilian population, African migrants have also been targeted by the Saudi military; following battlefield setbacks, Saudi Arabia is retaliating against civilians in border villages due to the continued resistance.
Given that Saudi Arabia's actions stand in stark contradiction to the Geneva Conventions and other humanitarian laws, the UN Group of Eminent International and Regional Experts on Yemen announced in late September—without explicitly naming Saudi Arabia—that there were "reasonable grounds" to believe parties to the conflict in Yemen were responsible for gross human rights violations. The group also reiterated its call for the UN Security Council to refer the situation in Yemen to the International Criminal Court. This stance prompted Saudi Arabia to exert influence to terminate the experts' mission; consequently, the renewal of the group's mandate was rejected during the UN Human Rights Council session that October.
It is worth noting that for over seven years, Saudi Arabia has maintained a naval, aerial, and land blockade of Yemen and has bombed residential areas in an attempt to break the resistance of Ansar Allah; civilians—particularly innocent children—have fallen victim to attacks and airstrikes by Saudi forces. Indeed, the deliberate and conscious deprivation of Yemeni civilians of access to essentials such as water, food, medicine, and fuel constitutes a crime against humanity committed by the Saudi military.
According to statistics from "Entisaf," an organization advocating for the rights of women and children, kids are among the victims of Saudi aggression, subjected to atrocities that include killings, detention, and denial of access to education and medical treatment.
Consequently, the number of children suffering from various disabilities and cancerous tumors has risen, with nearly 75,000 cases recorded. The report states that over 3 million children suffer from malnutrition, more than 300 children lose their lives daily, over 3,000 children suffer from congenital abnormalities, and more than 3,000 require open-heart surgery; furthermore, 2 million Yemeni children are out of school, and another half-million have completely dropped out of education since the onset of the Arab coalition's aggression. The people of Yemen remember that on August 25, 2017, during a massacre in the Faj Attan neighborhood of southwestern Sana'a—perpetrated by the Saudi coalition—8-year-old Yemeni girl Buthaina lost her parents, uncle, and four siblings.
Condemning these atrocities, the National Organization for Human Rights in Yemen has held Saudi Arabia fully legally and criminally accountable for its crimes and their humanitarian consequences. It has called upon the international community to break its silence and take action to halt the aggression, lift the blockade, and ensure the protection of civilians.

What does Spain's snap election mean for the European politics?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:05:25 UTC
23:05:25 KST

Spain's snap election on 29 November could cost progressive European forces their last government in a large member state, tilting EU power towards the right and pushing socialists into opposition mode.
A defeat for Pedro Sánchez could reshape the balance of power inside the EU institutions and further weaken the centrist majority that has traditionally underpinned European integration.
The loss of the last centre-left government in a major member state could strengthen conservative forces and make progressive lawmakers less willing to cooperate across the aisle.
On Monday, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap general election for 29 November, after parliament rejected two housing decrees on Friday.
His government, widely seen as the last major bastion of progressive policies in Europe, was already under pressure from corruption scandals, the unresolved migration crisis in Ceuta and protests over the housing shortage.
A defeat could have significant repercussions in Brussels. Several EU officials told Euronews, on condition of anonymity, that the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) group in the European Parliament would likely adopt a more confrontational stance.
Destabilisation
Sánchez's supporters say it is too early to write him off. He defied expectations after the 2023 election, remaining in power at the head of a minority government backed by Catalan and Basque pro-independence parties.
Current polls, however, suggest the centre-right Popular Party and far-right Vox could secure a majority, making another Sánchez-led minority government harder to assemble.
EU officials with direct knowledge of the matter said the campaign itself was unlikely to have a major impact on European politics, beyond some symbolic votes in the European Parliament.
One immediate test is the re-election of Sánchez ally Iratxe García Pérez (Spain/S&D) as head of the S&D group, the Parliament's second-largest political group. No challenger has emerged, although the deadline for nominations is 13 October.
The bigger consequences could come after the election, particularly if Sánchez loses office. The S&D would then have fewer incentives to compromise with the European People's Party (EPP), EU officials said.
"The group would be more sharply critical towards [Commission President] von der Leyen's agenda," one EU official told Euronews, adding that centre-left lawmakers would face fewer political constraints with Sánchez in opposition in Madrid.
Another EU official said the links between Madrid and Brussels had become unusually close, with Sánchez at times appearing to set the tone for the wider S&D group.
Shaking majority
The European Commission, led by President Ursula von der Leyen, currently relies on a parliamentary majority made up of the centre-right EPP, centrist Renew Europe and the centre-left S&D. The Greens/EFA also broadly support the Commission, despite not being part of the coalition agreement.
Those centrist forces have traditionally formed the political backbone of European integration. But the rise of parties on the far left and far right could prevent them from securing a majority in the next European Parliament.
With one of the EU's largest socialist delegations potentially leaving government in Madrid, progressive MEPs could face greater pressure to challenge deals with the EPP.
"Sánchez was a huge stabilising factor. He was the main guarantor of von der Leyen, always pushing to find a compromise with the European People's Party," an EU lawmaker told Euronews, asking not to be named.
The first institutional test could come with the mid-term reshuffle, which was planned on the assumption that socialist António Costa and Roberta Metsola (Malta/EPP) would remain presidents of the European Council and European Parliament respectively.
Without the Spanish Socialists in government, the S&D could find it harder to resist a symbolic challenge to Metsola, potentially from Katarina Barley (Germany/S&D).
The EPP is backing a third mandate for Metsola, who is popular among MEPs. Under an informal agreement reached by centrist political groups at the start of the legislature, the S&D is due to hold the Parliament presidency.
But the shift in Madrid could have wider consequences. With Sánchez, a key sponsor of Costa, gone, the EPP could also seek to claim the European Council presidency.
Right-wing shift
"If Spain's Prime Minister were to come from the centre-right PP (EPP) in the future, S&D's influence would be diminished in the European Council in a way that we haven't seen since at least the early 1990s," Tobias Gerhard Schminke, founder of the election observatory Europe Elects, told Euronews.
Only Denmark, Lithuania and Malta would then have centre-left governments. Sweden's September election could add another centre-left prime minister, Magdalena Andersson, who has so far failed to form a government.
With Sánchez out of office, Denmark's Mette Frederiksen would become the senior progressive leader. Her migration policy, which is closer to the right, has already put her at odds with Sánchez and caused tensions within the S&D.
Sánchez has also become a prominent dissenting voice on issues including migration, Israel, US President Donald Trump, defence spending and the green agenda.
Critics say von der Leyen's majority is already showing signs of strain, with the EPP regularly forming alternative majorities with right-wing lawmakers on issues including deforestation, corporate sustainability and migration.
At the same time, some socialists fear that bringing down von der Leyen could produce an outcome even less favourable to the centre-left as more EU member states shift to the right.
"It is an extremely risky situation. The EU without its social democratic pillar changes fundamentally. That alters the historic balance for decision-making in the European Parliament," another EU lawmaker said.
