Heritage is identity: Iranian archaeologist exposes scale of war destruction to historic sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:33:29 UTC
22:33:29 KST

Heritage is identity: Iranian archaeologist exposes scale of war destruction to historic sites
TEHRAN – An Iranian archaeologist, Sonia Shidrang, highlighted in a global webinar hosted by the International Committee on Archaeological Heritage Management (ICAHM), a scientific committee under ICOMOS, that the 40-day war with the United States and the Israeli regime left 149 historical sites across 20 provinces damaged, and that Iran's cultural heritage now demands a response grounded in international law, rigorous documentation, and a concrete protection plan.
The ICAHM Webinars 2026 took place on Sep. 30, chaired by Matt Whincop, ICAHM Secretary General, and focused on the theme "From Vulnerability to Resilience: Protecting Cultural Heritage from Natural and Anthropogenic Disasters."
The program featured two speakers addressing heritage protection from complementary angles. Professor Hatice Pamir from the Department of Archaeology of Mustafa Kemal University, Turkey, presented "Earthquakes and the Archaeological Heritage of Antioch on the Banks of the Orontes River: Lessons Learnt from Fieldwork," focusing on seismic threats to archaeological sites.
Shidrang followed with "Iranian Cultural Heritage Under Fire: Documentation, Risk, and a Plan for Protection," examining conflict-related risks and strategies for safeguarding heritage. Together, the talks spanned both natural and human-induced disasters, reflecting the webinar's central concern with building resilience for cultural heritage.
Shidrang, a faculty member at Shahid Beheshti University, opened with a reminder that heritage is not merely about ancient monuments. "It is about identity. It is about memory. It is about the shared story of humanity," she said, adding that war's direct and indirect effects on tangible and intangible cultural heritage are irreversible and irreparable.
According to the Iranian Ministry of Cultural Heritage, the joint US-Israeli military campaign that began on February 28, 2026, severely damaged districts, houses, prominent buildings, museums, and cultural sites. The Ministry has called the destruction "a clear violation of international law" and "a threat against the historical memory of humanity."
Among the damaged sites are five UNESCO World Heritage properties: the Golestan Palace in Tehran, the Naqsh-e Jahan Square complex and Imam Mosque in Isfahan, and the Trans-Iranian Railway, which was struck at five stations on the final night of the conflict.
Shidrang anchored her presentation in the 1954 Hague Convention for the Protection of Cultural Property in the Event of Armed Conflict, noting that Iran is a State Party to the Convention and its Protocols. She cited Article 3, which requires states to prepare in peacetime to safeguard cultural property, and said the Ministry moved valuable artifacts to secure storage and installed protective coverings before and during the war. She also pointed to Article 4(1), which obligates parties to refrain from any act of hostility directed against cultural property; Article 6, which provides for the Blue Shield emblem to mark protected sites; Article 7, which requires respect for cultural property to be integrated into military regulations; and the 1999 Second Protocol, which establishes individual criminal responsibility for violations. Iran, she noted, installed Blue Shield markers on museums and historic buildings. "The distinctive emblem has legal force under Article 6 only if parties are aware of it and choose to respect it," she said.
The scale of the destruction, according to the Ministry's latest estimates by early summer, included five UNESCO World Heritage sites, seven historical fabrics, and 54 museums damaged to varying degrees. 74 sites were damaged by blast waves, 42 by strikes on their buffer zones, and 33 by direct strikes on their premises. Tehran Province ranks first with 83 damaged sites, nearly half of the total; of these, 36 are inscribed on the National Heritage List, and six were completely destroyed, including the Rafi Nia Synagogue and the Pasteur Institute. Isfahan Province ranks second with 27 sites, followed by Kurdistan with 13, Khuzestan with 12, Kermanshah with five, Lorestan with four, Qom with three, and other provinces with 15. The financial estimate of damage, initially calculated at approximately €27.08 billion, has now risen to €36.10 billion, with more than €7.22 billion of that representing damage to the Golestan and Sa'dabad Palace complexes alone.
The Golestan Palace, a UNESCO World Heritage site, was severely damaged on March 1, 2026, when an Israeli missile struck a nearby building in the Grand Bazaar. The Shams-ol-Emareh structure was hit, and the head of the Marble Throne statue was severed. The Tehran Grand Bazaar was also severely damaged. The Sa'dabad Palace complex was hit by five bunker-buster bombs on March 16, 2026, collapsing roofs and walls across three palaces, shattering 6,000 square meters of glass, and causing structural failure at the Omidvar Brothers Museum.
Despite the destruction, Iran was not passive. On the first day of the war, the National Museum of Iran transferred all movable objects from its exhibition halls to secure storage and then protected large, immovable objects in place. Fire-resistant thermal insulation was wrapped around artifacts, sandbag walls were erected, and metal framing reinforced them against shrapnel and heat.
Shidrang said that, according to the Iranian Ministry of Cultural Heritage, emergency protection is now complete, with buildings prioritized by age and structural strength. As of this summer, emergency restoration had been completed at 10 sites, including the Golestan Palace, Sa'dabad Palace, the Glassware Museum, and the Museum of Contemporary Art, along with two buildings in West Azerbaijan and several sites in Isfahan, Zanjan, and Qom. Restoration is underway at 21 sites, including the Museum of Decorative Arts and Chehel Sotoun Palace in Isfahan and the Khosrowabad and Moshir Mansions in Kurdistan. Documentation for structural reinforcement of the Blue Dome of Maragheh has been completed, documentation of Baba Taher's Tomb in Hamadan is in progress, and debris-clearing of the Falak al-Aflak buffer zone in Lorestan has been completed by military institutions.
The Secretary-General of the Iranian National Commission for UNESCO has reported the compilation of several thousand pages of documentation concerning damage sustained by the nation's educational and cultural infrastructure and cultural heritage during the recent wars. He further stated that, through UNESCO's follow-up, a number of countries—including Japan and South Korea—have signaled their readiness to contribute to the reconstruction of Iran's cultural heritage, with some €2.5 million in assistance having been pledged.
Shidrang also pointed to reports showing that, from the first days, the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, in cooperation with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, initiated extensive consultations and correspondence with international bodies, issuing six statements and nine letters to organizations including UNESCO, the International Council of Museums (ICOM), ICOMOS, and the World Tourism Organization. UNESCO, ICOMOS, and ICOM were informed of the details of the damage and condemned the attacks. ICOMOS condemned the destruction "whether intentional or incidental" and recalled that cultural heritage must not be considered a target, while ICOM called on all parties to comply with their obligations under the 1954 Hague Convention and its Protocols. Iran has cited international legal instruments including the 1954 Hague Convention, the 1972 World Heritage Convention, the 2003 Intangible Heritage Convention, UN Security Council Resolution 2347, and legal mechanisms related to the Hague Tribunal. However, despite these efforts, no adequate response was given to Iran's requests for international assistance for reconstruction.
Based on the 1954 Hague Convention and the current situation, Dr. Shidrang proposed a five-point protection plan. The first point calls for accelerating Blue Shield implementation and enforcement, accompanied by formal notification to all parties through UNESCO and the 1954 Hague Convention Secretariat, because the distinctive emblem has legal force under Article 6 only if parties are aware of it and choose to respect it. The second calls for safe haven and evacuation protocols, extending protective covering, sandbagging, and structural reinforcement to immovable heritage where possible and invoking the International Register of Cultural Property under Special Protection under Article 8 for the most significant sites. The third calls for a no-strike list and military coordination, formalizing UNESCO-provided coordinates into a no-strike list communicated through military channels, with Article 7 specialist personnel embedded in command structures to advise on cultural property protection and with the "military necessity" exception interpreted narrowly and documented transparently. The fourth calls for emergency funding and technical support, with UNESCO, ICOMOS, ICCROM, and the Blue Shield establishing a joint emergency fund for immediate stabilization, documentation, and conservation—not as a matter of politics, she said, but to fulfill the obligation to protect the cultural heritage of all humanity. The fifth calls for legal accountability and monitoring, documenting the damage for future legal proceedings before the International Criminal Court, the International Court of Justice, or other mechanisms, and establishing a standing monitoring mechanism—perhaps a joint UNESCO-ICOMOS-ICOM task force—to receive, verify, and publish reports on cultural heritage damage in the conflict zone.
The session, chaired by ICAHM Secretary General Matt Whincop, concluded with an exchange regarding the future of Iranian heritage management within the international arena. As the international community continues to grapple with the protection of the world’s shared past, the collaborative efforts exemplified by the webinar highlighted the vital necessity of fostering institutional partnerships.

Quote: "Ukraine has repeatedly proposed concrete steps to de-escalate the situation and ensure security in the Black Sea. There have also been relevant proposals from third countries. But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian vessels instead of normal maritime navigation. Pressure is needed to restore global food security. And everyone who is genuinely interested in this must help."
Background:
- Earlier, Romanian authorities reported that two people had been killed in the attack.
- Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, previously said that the international community should help resume the global trade route in the Black Sea.
- Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said Ankara is stepping up its diplomatic efforts to resume grain exports through the Black Sea and has received a positive signal from Ukraine on the matter.

Russia Repeatedly Tests Romanian Air Defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:27:06 UTC
22:27:06 KST

A suspected drone fell near Romania’s border with Ukraine and started a fire on Friday, Oct. 2, without national air defense radars reporting an incursion, adding to concerns over NATO’s ability to detect and stop aircraft crossing its eastern frontier.
Romanian authorities were investigating the object’s origin. Their initial statement described it as possibly an aerial drone and did not confirm that it was Russian.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The alert came during Russian drone attacks on civilian sites and infrastructure across the Danube in Ukraine. At about 5 a.m., authorities received reports that an object had fallen near Plauru in northern Tulcea County. Firefighters and military teams secured the area. No casualties or material damage were reported.
Local Mayor Tudor Cernega told Euronews Romania that the object fell in a harvested field roughly 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Danube and 1.5 kilometers (0.9 miles) from homes. He said residents had received no air-raid alert that night.
Romania faced another alert early Monday, Oct. 5, when radar detected an aerial target near Vylkove on the Ukrainian side of the border. Two Spanish F-18 fighters scrambled from Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base, and authorities warned residents in northern Tulcea County at 2:34 a.m. No incursion into Romanian airspace was detected, and the alert ended at 3:23 a.m.
Repeated breaches, different responses
Recent incidents have included aircraft briefly entering NATO territory, drones disappearing from radar and debris recovered after explosions. Those events have not all produced shootdowns, but official accounts also record fighter deployments and other responses.
India Moves to Broker Black Sea Deal Between Russia and Ukraine
On the evening of Sept. 27, a drone entered Romania near Ceatalchioi and disappeared from radar approximately 10 minutes later near Somova, according to a Defense Ministry account carried by Agerpres. Two Romanian F-16s took off to monitor the situation. The statement did not report a shootdown.
On Sept. 29, the ministry confirmed finding a crater and drone fragments near Gropeni in Brăila County. Investigators established that an explosive payload had detonated on impact, causing a limited fire on agricultural land.
Poland reported a separate violation on Sept. 23, when a Russian military Mi-8 helicopter crossed from Kaliningrad near Braniewo. According to Polish operational command, reported by Notes from Poland, it penetrated no farther than 300 meters (about 980 feet) and remained in Polish airspace for 42 seconds. Poland scrambled fighters and placed ground forces on standby.
Earlier in September, Estonia reported drones entering its airspace after flying along its eastern border. Allied aircraft responded from Ämari Air Base. The foreign ministry’s statement linked the threat to Russia’s war but did not identify the drones’ operator.
NATO forces have also destroyed intruding drones. As Kyiv Post reported in July, Romanian forces shot down three drones over three consecutive days. Authorities identified the first as a Russian Shahed-type drone, and Bucharest subsequently expelled a Russian diplomat.
Pressure to strengthen drone defenses
On the Ukrainian side of the border overnight Oct. 1–2, the Air Force reported 108 incoming Russian drones, including 47 jet-powered Shaheds. It said air defenses shot down or suppressed 88, approximately 81% of the total. That figure combines different methods of neutralization and is not a count of aircraft physically shot down.
Across NATO’s eastern flank, repeated alerts have increased pressure to strengthen defenses against drones rather than rely on fighter deployments alone.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania reportedly requested €500 million ($570 million) in urgent EU assistance for drone defenses. Kyiv Post’s Sept. 23 report, citing Finland’s Iltalehti newspaper, said the three countries’ defense ministers had sent their request to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The reported request had not been publicly announced.
Sabotage allegations and NATO’s response
The airspace incidents come alongside allegations of Russian operations against European businesses supporting Ukraine.
On Sept. 29, Estonia accused Russian intelligence services of ordering an August arson attack on Milrem Robotics, a defense company in Tallinn. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the perpetrators had been apprehended and that Estonia had summoned Russia’s ambassador. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov rejected the accusation as baseless.
In a separate maritime incident, Russian border guards held the cargo ship Västerbotten for several hours on Oct. 1 while it was heading to Estonia’s Sillamäe port. The Cypriot-flagged vessel was in Russian territorial waters and subsequently continued to its destination.
Estonia’s Transport Administration said Russia had not explained the detention. An official also noted that states can inspect ships in their territorial waters, so the detention alone did not establish an unlawful action.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said the alliance’s responses to Russian hostile activity will not always be public or match Moscow’s actions directly.
Speaking alongside Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius in Brussels on Sept. 29, Rutte said: “You will not always see them public. They will not always be symmetric. It will not always be tit-for-tat.”
Romania’s latest statements illustrate the continuing detection problem: a suspected drone fell near Plauru without a recorded incursion, while a separate radar alert three days later prompted fighter launches without a confirmed border crossing.

The indictment against Vladimir Bortko, the director of "Bandit Petersburg," who called for a nuclear strike on Ukraine, has been sent to court, UNN reports, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General and the Security Service of Ukraine.
Details
The Security Service of Ukraine has completed its pretrial investigation into Russian director, screenwriter, and former State Duma deputy Vladimir Bortko, who promotes Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine.
The SBU investigators have now submitted the indictment to the court. The offender faces up to 8 years in prison with confiscation of property.
The investigation established that the suspect publicly calls for the continuation of the war, denies Ukrainian statehood, and advocates the use of tactical nuclear weapons against our country.
The SBU recalled that Bortko is known for the Russian television series "Bandit Petersburg" and "Streets of Broken Lanterns." He combined his work in cinema with political support for the Kremlin regime.
During the investigation, Security Service officers documented numerous episodes of his provocative statements between 2017 and 2026.
Thus, on the air of the "Komsomolskaya Pravda" radio station, he once again called for a nuclear strike on Ukraine. In addition, he advocated seizing Kyiv and then the entire territory of our country.
On the basis of the evidence collected, Bortko has been charged under two articles of the Criminal Code of Ukraine:
▪️ Article 436 (propaganda of war);
▪️ Part 3 of Article 436-2 (the production and dissemination of materials in which Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine is justified, recognized as lawful, or denied, committed repeatedly and using the mass media).
Since the suspect is located in Russia, comprehensive measures are underway to bring him to justice.
The investigation was conducted under the procedural guidance of the Office of the Prosecutor General.

Cocaine Boatmen Are Being Blown Up By US Airstrikes, But The Drugs Keep Flowing From Colombia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:25:00 UTC
22:25:00 KST

That has left the work of identifying these men to local communities and journalists, such as a consortium led by the Latin American investigative outlet CLIP that was able to collect the names, or at least some information, about 19 men killed between September 2 and May 5.
When reached for comment, the U.S. Southern Command declined to discuss how they identify targets, but said that “every narco-terrorist neutralized” as part of the campaign “was an affiliated member of a Designated Terrorist Organization, actively transporting illicit material along known trafficking routes in international waters.” 
In their update on Operation Southern Spear one year in, U.S. officials were less bullish than their president, but said the campaign had driven a 60 percent reduction in illicit maritime activity in the Eastern Caribbean region that includes La Guajira. They also touted a 65 percent reduction in the Western Caribbean and a nearly 50 percent reduction in key areas of the Eastern Pacific.
The Trump administration does not disclose how it measures success, but a July report issued by the Washington Office on Latin America, a rights advocacy group, noted that available evidence suggested the military campaign was having little to no impact on the supply of cocaine reaching the U.S. 
Catalina Niño, a project coordinator at the local branch of the German pro-democracy non-profit Friedrich Ebert Stiftung, noted that “there is nothing to indicate that the strategy is achieving its supposed objective.”
“There is no evidence that the strategy works, not even in terms of physical proof, because destroying the boats leaves no evidence behind. There are no individuals to prosecute, and there is no verifiable evidence that there were drugs on those boats in the first place,” she said. “It is impossible to obtain evidence in this regard.”
When reached for comment, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said that “all of these decisive strikes have been against designated narcoterrorists bringing deadly poison to our shores, and the President will continue to use every element of American power to stop drugs from flooding into our country and to bring those responsible to justice.”
Colombia’s presidency did not respond to requests to comment. The country’s deputy ombudsman, Paula Aponte, said in a statement that her office has sought further information from other state agencies on the Colombian nationals believed to have died in the attacks, but with little success. 
Searching for a Body 
Down one dusty dirt road in Riohacha sits a single-story brick home where a grief-stricken Wayúu family has been waiting for a boatman to return since May. The family, who lives without running water, has traveled across the peninsula to look for his corpse. They also constantly scan social media, where graphic videos of casualties from decimated boats circulate.
“He hasn’t appeared. They have asked about him even in the Dominican Republic,” said a distraught woman who answered the door to the family’s home and identified herself as a neighbor.
The woman explained that without a body, the man’s mother refuses to accept his death. 
But many believe the moment his life ended was captured in the video accompanying a Southern Command press release announcing a May 4 missile strike on a vessel “operated by Designated Terrorist Organizations” in the Caribbean Sea.
“Two male narco-terrorists were killed during this action,” the press release declared. 
After that announcement, word quickly spread in La Guajira that the men might be from the Wayúu community that has inhabited this desert for hundreds of years.

Sánchez bets it all on housing ahead of Spain’s snap election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:24:11 UTC
22:24:11 KST

Tarps and tents fill the Puerta del Sol square following an extraordinary parliamentary session to vote on a government housing decree in Madrid on Oct. 2, 2026. | Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez hopes his country’s dire housing crisis has become so bad that it overshadows the other challenges Spain faces.
Nationwide protests over skyrocketing rents and real estate speculation have rocked Spain in recent weeks, prompting the Socialist leader to call snap elections for Nov. 29 on Monday.
Sánchez, who is under pressure over the ongoing migrant crisis in Ceuta, as well as corruption cases involving members of his family and close political allies, is aiming to capitalize on popular discontent over housing to pull off a long-shot reelection — while portraying Spain’s conservative opposition as an obstacle to solving the problem.
Advertisement
But critics have questioned the wisdom of the prime minister casting himself as a champion of housing rights when his time in power has coincided with a deepening of the current crisis.
Valeria Racu, spokesperson for the Spanish Tenants’ Union, which has spearheaded the housing protests, said Sánchez had “no track record to boast about” and called his Socialist Party “a party of landlords.”
“We’re done with these politicians,” she added. “We’re not falling for their nonsense anymore.”
Pablo Simón, a political scientist at Madrid’s Carlos III University, thinks the prime minister’s electoral bet made sense.
“The current outlook for Sánchez is dire,” he said. “Even if you ignore the migrant crisis in Ceuta — which isn’t going to be solved anytime soon — and the ongoing corruption cases, he’s still leading a minority government that can’t pass any legislation, with negative inflation steadily undermining his claim that Spain is doing great in economic terms.”
By making the election about housing, Simón added, the prime minister is seeking to shift the conversation away from corruption in his inner circle and the national defense issues surrounding Spain’s North African exclaves, and toward the social issues championed by the left.
Advertisement
A nationwide crisis
Spain’s housing crisis is rooted in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, when banks sharply restricted mortgage lending to ordinary families.
“The cash didn’t disappear from the market, it just ended up in the hands of investors,” said Spanish National Research Council housing expert Javier Gil. “What we see in Spain is a new cycle led by speculative, non-residential demand.”
That cycle resulted in a “tenant generation” unable to access home ownership not simply because of a lack of housing, he added, but because high-income investors have bought homes as assets.
The price hikes have been particularly punishing for young Spaniards. According to the latest figures from Spain’s National Statistics Institute, 69% of Spaniards aged 18 to 34 live with their parents — a rate surpassed only by young people in Croatia.
The same tourism boom that resulted in generated €200.7 billion in 2024, equivalent to 12.6% of GDP, has drawn real estate investors to major cities and tourist destinations. Although Sánchez’s government has taken steps to rein in the short-term rental market, the number of nights spent in tourist apartments has doubled since he took office in 2018.
Advertisement
Population growth has added pressure in major urban centers. Spain has gained more than 3 million residents since 2015, including 793,000 in Madrid, 556,000 in Barcelona and 279,000 in Valencia — all cities where housing costs have risen sharply.
Sánchez has not been blind to the crisis, calling housing the country’s “great constitutional challenge.” In 2023, he pledged to use “all state resources” to provide 184,000 public and affordable rental homes.
But when the government last provided a detailed accounting of the effort, in August 2024, it said only 14,000 homes had been “made available to citizens” through a social scheme. Some 60,000 other properties were reported to be in various stages of development.
The recent rollout of the government’s new housing portal, CASA47, was similarly underwhelming. It initially listed just 638 homes, none of which were in markets like Madrid or Barcelona, where the crisis is particularly acute.
“Sánchez’s Socialist Party has spent years claiming to want to tackle the housing market, but in practical terms it’s followed the same approach as right-wing parties,” Gil said. “They’ve avoided questioning the status quo or proposing structural limits or transformations.”
Even last week’s housing decrees — which included plans to curb speculative practices, extend eviction protections for vulnerable tenants until 2030 and automatically renew existing rental contracts, and which were ultimately rejected by lawmakers — contained only minimal measures unlikely to substantially address the crisis, Gil added.
Advertisement
“There’s a clear disconnect with the public mood,” he said. “Right now there is a widespread feeling in society that people have had enough and want greater market intervention.”
Questionable pivot
Despite his mixed record on the issue, Sánchez is determined to campaign as a housing champion.
Before parliament is dissolved, he plans to have the Council of Ministers reapprove the housing bills rejected by lawmakers last Friday. The measures could then be voted on by the legislature’s standing committee, which remains active after dissolution.
The move, which is clearly aimed at keeping the issue alive ahead of the election, has been denounced as a cynical ploy by Spain’s conservative opposition.
Center-right People’s Party lawmaker Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo last week said the government’s only substantial housing measure had been “giving a whore an apartment in the Plaza de España,” referring to allegations that former Transport Minister José Luis Ábalos used kickbacks to finance a flat for his mistress.
Ábalos, who was sentenced to a 24-year prison sentence after being convicted of influence peddling and other crimes in June, denies the accusation.
Advertisement
The far-right Vox party has likewise ridiculed Sánchez’s housing pivot, arguing that the government’s migration policies made the housing shortage worse and saying Sánchez should instead focus on the needs of Ceuta’s residents.
The attacks illustrate how difficult it will be for Sánchez to keep the election debate focused on housing rather than corruption and migration.
“It’s obvious he doesn’t have a great track record on housing, but he’s trying to do his best with the electoral cards he’s been dealt,” Simón said. He predicted the Socialist leader would campaign less on specific measures than on broad social issues and the threat posed by the rising far-right.
“He did this in the last election, in which he sidestepped a review of his government’s performance and centered the conversation on the implications of a PP-Vox government,” he said. “Housing is the pretext to call the election and center the conversation on social issues.”
It’s unclear whether that strategy will appeal to the thousands of Spaniards who have taken to the streets over the past week.
Racu said the Tenants’ Union wants politicians to commit to enacting indefinite rental contracts, legally mandated rent reductions, an end to evictions and speculative purchases, and a major expansion of public housing by reclaiming homes held by banks and investment funds.
Advertisement
She declined to say what protesters should do if none of the parties running in the election commit to meeting their demands.
“Voting is important, it’s a right that was won through bloodshed, suffering, and violence in the face of the Francoist dictatorship,” she said. “But democracy and people’s power reside in much more than a vote every four years.”
“In eight days of people power, we have done more for housing than eight years of progressive government,” Racu added. “Whoever governs, this is not going to stop. Politics is returning to where it always should have been: the streets and the people.”

Prosecution of Tren de Aragua Accused Mastermind Deemed Complex Case
Unknown

2026-10-05
13:24:00 UTC
22:24:00 KST

Reported by
A suspected cybercriminal who allegedly bankrolled the notorious Tren de Aragua gang through a multimillion-dollar ATM fraud scheme was arrested and will remain behind bars to face a complex prosecution in Nebraska, just days after the Venezuelan was blacklisted by the Treasury Department.
In a news conference Saturday in Omaha that began with, “well we got him,” FBI Special Agent in Charge Eugene Kowel said Anibal Alexander Canelón Aguirre, an alleged computer whiz and hacker tied to the transnational gang, was captured on the high seas.
During his news conference, Kowel said the FBI in Omaha received assistance from the U.S. Coast Guard and the FBI's Critical Incident Response Group. Canelón Aguirre, he said, was subsequently transported by sea and air to the District of Nebraska.
The FBI’s web page for its most-wanted fugitives now shows a red bar across his photo reading “Captured.”
However, Kowel’s account contrasts with statements made just weeks earlier by FBI Director Kash Patel. During a Senate hearing, Patel announced the fugitive’s capture in Venezuela without explicitly naming him or providing further details.
“Our overseas apprehension of (Canelón) Aguirre demonstrates our relentless focus on bringing to justice those who target Americans,” Kowel said on his LinkedIn page. “We'll continue working with our partners to dismantle and disrupt the activities of Tren de Aragua in our communities.”
Through a court-appointed defense attorney in Omaha, Canelón Aguirre pleaded not guilty on Friday to the four-count indictment. He was denied bail while awaiting trial in what a federal judge deemed a complex prosecution—meaning the Venezuelan won’t have a speedy trial.
Magistrate Judge Michael Nelson said he ruled that Canelón Aguirre was a flight risk “based on the totality of the record before the court, given the defendant's lack of ties to this country or this community, his ties to a foreign community, the nature of the offense itself, and the fact that the defendant does not have legal status in the United States and therefore cannot lawfully work here … there's no conditions or release that will reasonably assure his appearance for future court proceedings.”
Canelón Aguirre is alleged in his December 2025 indictment to have been the mastermind of a scam to help fund Tren de Aragua, a notoriously violent Venezuelan organized crime group. It said he allegedly led a multi-million dollar ATM fraud scheme.
In a news release Friday, the Justice Department said its investigation “focused on a widespread ATM Jackpotting conspiracy that has been tied to the designated foreign terrorist organization TdA. To date, 120 defendants have been charged in the District of Nebraska for their role in this conspiracy.”
Canelón Aguirre, 50, faces charges of bank fraud, bank fraud using a computer, conspiracy to commit laundering and conspiracy to provide material support to a designated terror organization. He faces up to 30 years in prison.
The judge ordered prosecutors and the court-appointed counsel to file motions by October 23 and set an October 30 date for Canelón Aguirre’s next court appearance.
Canelón Aguirre’s arrival in the Nebraska courtroom followed by two days his elevation by the Treasury Department to the list of specially designated nationals, making him a pariah in the global financial system. The listing cited his ties to Tren de Aragua.
Days after his court appearance, however, the exact circumstances of how Canelón Aguirre was brought to the United States remained unclear, complicated by conflicting official statements.
While Kowel stated the fugitive was captured on the high seas, FBI Director Kash Patel announced during a Senate hearing just weeks earlier that he had been captured in Venezuela, without naming him or providing further details.
Article 69 of Venezuela’s constitution prohibits the extradition of its citizens. When asked by OCCRP, the FBI, State Department and Venezuelan government all declined to discuss details of the case.
One possibility is that Canelón Aguirre was expelled from Venezuela when apprehended in international waters. That was the method used last March when alleged South American drug kingpin Sebastian Marset was arrested by Bolivian forces and rather than being extradited, a diplomatic procedure, was expelled to Peru, from where he was quickly brought to the United States to stand trial in Virginia.
The FBI provided few operational details, offering no information on how the operation was carried out and whether Venezuelan authorities assisted in the capture of Canelón Aguirre.
OCCRP was among the first to warn of the nascent criminal organization spreading into the U.S. in its November 2023 series Narcofiles: The New Criminal Order.

Airstrikes and artillery hit north Ethiopia after Tigray capital's fall, aid sources say
Oct 5 - Airstrikes and artillery fire hit northern Ethiopia's Tigray region overnight into Monday morning, aid sources said, almost two weeks into clashes between federal government and rebel forces that have raised fears of wider fighting.
Air attacks killed at least 17 people northwest of Tigray's capital Mekelle - which federal Ethiopian National Defence Force soldiers took over the weekend - according to a bulletin circulated among humanitarian groups.
The bulletin added that government forces exchanged artillery fire with fighters loyal to the Tigray People's Liberation Front - the region's dominant political force which is part of a rebel alliance aiming to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.
Spokespeople for Abiy's office, the federal forces and the TPLF did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the reports, which Reuters could not confirm independently.
Analysts say the fighting threatens to escalate into a wider conflict, with Ethiopia accusing Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting the armed opposition. All three countries have denied this.
Last week, Ethiopia and Eritrea, which fought a border war from 1998-2000, severed diplomatic ties over the allegations.
WORST ESCALATION SINCE 2020-2022 CIVIL WAR
The fighting since September 23 is the worst escalation of violence since a 2020-2022 civil war in Tigray that resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths.
In that war, federal forces captured Mekelle within a month before the TPLF reclaimed it seven months later.
On Monday morning, Ethiopia's military and Tigrayan forces exchanged heavy artillery fire close to the Tekeze River near the town of Mai Tsebri, according to the humanitarian bulletin.
Overnight, airstrikes killed at least nine people in Adwa, which is about 100 km (60 miles) northwest of Mekelle, and eight in Sheraro in northwestern Tigray, the bulletin said.
It did not say who launched the airstrikes.
Another aid worker confirmed the strikes in Adwa, but did not have information about casualties.
In Mekelle, which Tigrayan forces left without a fight, daily life was returning to normal, with shops reopening and phone and internet access returning a week-long disruption, residents said.
US WARNS ETHIOPIA AND ERITREA AGAINST CONFLICT
Analysts are closely watching the Ethiopian military as it advances northward toward the Eritrean border.
Eritrean forces fought in support of Ethiopia's federal government in Tigray during the 2020-2022 war following a 2018 normalisation of ties between the longtime foes that won Abiy the Nobel Peace Prize.
Relations soured afterward, in part over landlocked Ethiopia's public insistence that sea access is vital for its security and economy.

Merz and Macron want the EU to hit back harder — and faster — against trade threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:21:10 UTC
22:21:10 KST

BERLIN — The European Commission needs the power to act much faster against trade threats, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron urged in a joint letter on Monday.
The leaders of the EU’s two most powerful and populous countries want Brussels to be able to act more quickly and decisively in a trade confrontation — while making it harder for EU capitals to block action.
The proposal seeks to strengthen the hand of Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič, who flies to Beijing on Thursday for the final round of talks in a four-month process where Brussels is seeking to rebalance the EU’s trading relationship with China.
Advertisement
Merz and Macron said the Commission should be empowered to restrict, or even completely cut off, imports from countries seen as creating “severe and systematic distortions” in the single market. In their letter and a joint position paper, they call for urgent action, saying the EU’s existing trade defense toolbox “does not suffice anymore.”
“Without delaying the full use of the existing set of instruments, we need a comprehensive framework to complement our toolbox with new legal instruments — in a lean and non-bureaucratic way,” they wrote.
One senior German official, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly, described the tool as a “second-strike weapon” that could be deployed in the event of an escalating trade war.
“We can see that certain players have important, powerful instruments at their disposal,” the official said, pointing to the sweeping so-called Section 301 tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s dominance of critical-mineral supply chains. The EU, they explained, needed its own countermeasures.
“When trade rules are not respected, we need to be credible regarding the fact that access to the internal market cannot be guaranteed,” said an official from Macron’s office, noting that “dialogue does not preclude our determination to protect our most vulnerable sectors.”
The French official said the procedure for activating the new measures should be based on the one that already exists for anti-dumping cases. This allows the Commission to take action without first seeking a green light from EU capitals.
Advertisement
“We can’t keep waiting — for months or sometimes even years,” the French official said.
A new bazooka
While the joint letter doesn’t mention China by name, it clearly relates to the bloc’s €1-billion-a-day trade deficit with the world’s leading exporter and growing concerns about the impact of Chinese overcapacity on European industry.
The existing Anti-Coercion Instrument, also known as the EU’s trade “bazooka,” in theory gives the Commission enormous powers to restrict imports in response to actions that are considered economic coercion.
In practice, however, activating the ACI requires months of investigation and the support of a qualified majority of EU governments. Divisions among capitals have previously complicated efforts to agree on trade measures targeting China.
The new instrument proposed by Berlin and Paris — which could either update or replace the ACI — would make it much harder for EU member countries to block swift action. Commission measures would stand unless a “reverse” qualified majority of countries voted to block them.
Bernd Lange, who heads the European Parliament’s trade committee, welcomed the Franco-German letter as a step forward. The German Social Democrat negotiated on behalf of the Parliament during the development of the ACI, pushing unsuccessfully to give the Commission more leeway to activate the instrument.
Advertisement
“It was so complicated,” Lange said. “If there is now a shift in the mindset of the Council, it’s really good.”
Watershed moment
Sander Tordoir, chief economist at the Centre for European Reform, called the letter and position paper a “watershed” moment.
“What the two leading European capitals are signaling is that they want to flip the switch and have a more structured, comprehensive set of policies to slow down the impact of the second China shock on European industry,” said Tordoir, who has advocated that Europe adopt U.S.-style 301 tariffs in the past.
Germany’s shift toward a more aggressive trade posture is particularly significant given Berlin’s previous reluctance to back stronger EU trade defenses.
“One of the major actors watering down the ACI back in the day was in fact Germany,” Tordoir said. “Germany has transitioned from hesitator-in-chief on stronger European trade tools to actively backing a number of concrete proposals.”
The document is part of broader Franco-German negotiations on the EU’s top economic files. The talks were launched by Macron and Merz after a joint ministerial meeting in Cologne in July, when the two leaders said they were converging on a more aggressive stance toward China.
Advertisement
The Franco-German letter also calls on the Commission to take new steps to diversify European supply chains and lessen dependency on Chinese imports. The Berlaymont has already announced that it is developing a diversification instrument aimed at encouraging manufacturers to wean themselves off cheap Chinese imports. It plans to publish the proposal by the end of the year.
Hans von der Burchard reported from Berlin, Giorgio Leali from Paris and Carlo Martuscelli, Jordyn Dahl and Camille Gijs from Brussels. This article has been updated.

Scottish and Japanese engineers will send whisky and ingredients into orbit for five years. The experiment will study the maturation of alcohol in space.

Details

Nobel medicine prize goes to scientists who put the brain under a light switch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:19:44 UTC
22:19:44 KST

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries that laid the foundation for optogenetics, a technique that allows researchers to control nerve-cell activity with light.
The Nobel Assembly honoured the trio for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, a field that has fundamentally changed the study of the brain.
By combining genetics with light, scientists can activate or silence specific groups of nerve cells, allowing them to investigate how individual neural circuits contribute to processes such as learning, fear, addiction and movement.
From algae to the living brain
The breakthrough began in the early 2000s, when Hegemann and Nagel were studying how single-celled algae detect and move towards light.
They identified a light-sensitive protein called channelrhodopsin. When exposed to blue light, the protein opens a channel that allows charged particles to enter the cell, generating an electrical signal.
Deisseroth later introduced the gene responsible for channelrhodopsin into nerve cells. In 2005, he demonstrated that blue light could trigger nerve signals in those cells, and by 2007 the technique had been used to control neurons in the brains of living mice.
The discoveries gave neuroscientists a powerful way to investigate the brain with unprecedented precision.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee.
A tool with medical potential
The technique has helped researchers identify neural circuits associated with memories, emotions and behaviours that are relevant to neurological and psychiatric disorders.
Its use in humans remains highly limited, but optogenetic approaches have begun moving towards clinical applications, including research aimed at treating certain forms of blindness. Scientists are also studying its potential for conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and epilepsy.
Deisseroth, 54, is a professor at Stanford University. Hegemann, 71, is a neuroscience professor at Humboldt University of Berlin, while Nagel, 73, is a biophysics professor at the University of Würzburg.
The three laureates will share a prize of 12 million Swedish kronor, with the awards to be formally presented in December.
When Nobel Assembly Secretary General Thomas Perlmann called the scientists to tell them they had won, all three expressed their delight at sharing the prize, saying they considered it “absolutely wonderful” to receive the honour together.
The award recognises a scientific breakthrough that has moved neuroscience closer to understanding how individual cells and circuits shape the complex workings of the brain.

Three Scientists Win 2026 Nobel Prize In Medicine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:19:00 UTC
22:19:00 KST

The 2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine has been awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their discoveries involving light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, the Nobel academy announced on Monday.
Optogenetics combines optics and genetics to enable non-invasive stimulation of neurons. The Nobel Assembly said the technique has significantly changed scientists' understanding of the brain by allowing researchers to identify neural circuits involved in specific memories, feelings and behaviors relevant to neurological and psychiatric disorders.
"The impact of optogenetics extends far beyond understanding the healthy brain, it has also helped revealed how brain circuits are disrupted, with implications for conditions such as blindness, depression, addiction and dementia," Abdel El Manira, a Nobel committee member and professor of neuroscience, said after the announcement.
In clinical medicine, researchers are using optogenetics in efforts to restore sight in people with visual impairment. The field is also expected to potentially contribute to treatments for neurological and sensory disorders including Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.
Peter Hegemann is a leading specialist in photobiology and is regarded as one of the founders of optogenetics. He is a neuroscience professor at Humboldt University of Berlin in Germany.
Georg Nagel is a biophysicist and professor of neurophysiology at the University of Würzburg in Germany. Karl Deisseroth is a professor of bioengineering and psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University in the United States.
The researchers' work came together after Hegemann studied how a single-celled species of green algae moves toward light. Hegemann and Nagel identified a protein that opens a channel when exposed to blue light, producing an electrical impulse. Introducing the protein into other cells makes them responsive to light.
Deisseroth later worked with the gene responsible for the protein to develop a light-controlled switch for nerve cells in the brains of living mice.
The medicine award is the first Nobel Prize to be announced this week. Laureates in physics, chemistry, literature and peace will be announced in the days leading up to Friday.
Last year's medicine prize was jointly awarded to Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell of the United States and Shimun Sakaguchi of Japan for their discoveries concerning peripheral immune tolerance.
The prizes will be presented at ceremonies in Stockholm, Sweden, on December 10.
Each Nobel Prize comes with a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor, equivalent to slightly more than €1 million or .2 million.

Estonia is preparing for possible Russian provocations by moving troops closer to its border with Russia and buying weapons capable of striking deep inside Russian territory, the Financial Times reported.
Under its new “active defense” strategy, Estonia has expanded and modernized a base in Jõhvi, 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the border with Russia. The headquarters of the First Brigade has relocated there from Tapa, Estonia’s main military base, about 150 kilometers (93 miles) from the border.
Estonia is also building a new base in Narva designed to house 1,000 troops. The plan calls for 200 troops to be stationed there permanently, while the base could accommodate another 800 in the event of a crisis on the border.
Estonian military officials believe Russia is unlikely to try to seize the border town of Narva but do not rule out provocations meant to test how NATO’s collective defense clause functions.
As part of the “active defense” strategy, Estonia signed contracts in 2025 to buy nine American-made HIMARS systems with missiles that have a range of up to 300 kilometers (186 miles), as well as nine South Korean Chunmoo multiple rocket launchers with a similar range, the Financial Times reported.
Military and intelligence officials believe Russia is not ready for a full-scale war with NATO, at least not within the next couple of years, the FT reported, but they intend to do everything possible “to make aggression against us unthinkable.” “Our aim is clear: to keep the enemy and the destruction of war away from Estonian territory,” the Defense Ministry said.
European countries, especially those bordering Russia, have said repeatedly in recent months that they fear Russian provocations designed to pressure NATO into abandoning its support for Ukraine. Latvia’s intelligence services made a similar statement in the summer of 2026.

Peeter Kaldre: A dangerous moment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

Peeter Kaldre: A dangerous moment
As the United States scales back its military role in Europe, the continent faces a dangerous test: strengthening its own defenses while Russia intensifies its threats and war against Ukraine.
It is appalling that 500 million people (Europe) have to ask 300 million people (the United States) for protection against 140 million people (Russia). That is what NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said recently when the subject of reducing the U.S. military presence in Europe came up. Rutte is certainly not the first to put it this way, but it illustrates the situation European security now finds itself in.
How to shoot yourself in the foot
The U.S. plan to reduce its military contribution to NATO and delegate more responsibility to European countries is nothing new; nearly every U.S. administration has talked about it. Why should the United States have to defend wealthy Europe when Europeans themselves barely lift a finger for their own defense? The difference is that the Donald Trump administration has now begun to act and the first cuts are already taking place.
All this is happening at a time when Russia is waging a full-scale war in Europe against Ukraine and is increasingly threatening European countries that support Ukraine.
The September 15 issue of Foreign Affairs featured an article by three security experts — Franklin C. Miller, Eric Edelman and Walter B. Slocombe — pointing to the risks posed by such a U.S. plan. The authors refer to a new security strategy completed last year that calls for shifting the focus from Europe to Asia and the Middle East.
The article lists military capabilities that the Americans want to cut in Europe but that Europe will not be able to replace anytime soon. Its conclusion is that such a policy threatens America itself — in other words, the United States would be hurting itself.
The U.S. military presence in Europe prevents potential adversaries from growing stronger and becoming a threat to the United States. One example cited is that, for the first time in many years, the United States did not take part in a NATO exercise in the North Atlantic that practiced countering Russian submarines. Those same nuclear-armed submarines are designed to approach the U.S. coast...
The story of the Dead Hand
Now the United States is pulling back, but Europe is simply not ready to replace the Americans. One way forward is through so-called coalitions of the willing, one example being the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), led by the United Kingdom and comprising the Baltic and Nordic countries.
The JEF does not have to wait for NATO's Article 5 to be formally invoked; it can act immediately. Jamie Murray, commander of the British contingent stationed in Estonia, put it well: We are ready to go into battle immediately. There are currently 900 British troops in Estonia, with another 300 to be added next year.
We should also bear in mind that the United Kingdom has nuclear weapons, as does France. Although their combined arsenal cannot be compared with Russia's, the Kremlin still has to take it into account. In theory, NATO's collective defense provides for the possibility of using nuclear weapons, including in Estonia's defense. Finland's recent decision to allow nuclear weapons into or through the country in the event of a threat was a powerful statement.
Incidentally, Finland and Sweden seem to have been transformed since joining NATO. Sweden recently announced that if Russia attacks, Sweden will strike targets deep inside Russia.
As for nuclear weapons, Russia has recently begun threatening their use again. Some time ago, Vladimir Putin warned Europe at the Valdai forum that if European countries were planning to take action against Kaliningrad, Russia could resort to nuclear weapons.
There has also been renewed talk of the so-called Dead Hand, an underground system in the Urals that can launch nuclear weapons even if the country's political leadership has been eliminated. It is one of those "nice" Kremlin stories whose veracity cannot be taken for granted.
Nuclear weapons are, after all, Russia's last resort. It cannot defeat even Ukraine with conventional weapons, let alone prevail in a potential conflict with all of Europe. Before it comes to that, however, there are the so-called hybrid tools to try: sabotage, assassinations, election interference and so on. And, of course, brutal strikes against Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, along with disingenuous appeals to foreign countries to move their embassies out of Kyiv.
The aim is to frighten Europe into abandoning its support for Ukraine or at least scaling it back. Putin understands very well that if European support for Ukraine continues, it will be almost impossible for him to subjugate the country.
A very dangerous period lies ahead. Russia may be tempted to make some move against Europe before next month's U.S. congressional midterm elections. Those elections could significantly change Washington's hitherto lenient approach toward Russia.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Is it hard to make friends with the Dutch or is it you?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:17:45 UTC
22:17:45 KST

Is it hard to make friends with the Dutch or is it you?
Molly Quell
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Our regular columnist wants to know whether the Dutch are really so hard to make friends with – or is the problem you?
“It’s just so hard to make friends with the Dutch,” the woman seated next to me bemoans. I’m at a dinner party made up mostly, but not entirely, of internationals.
In fact, a Dutch woman seated across from us agreed. She’d recently moved to The Hague after living in Groningen for the past few years and was apparently also struggling to meet people.
It’s an oft-heard complaint in international circles.
Pretty much every organisation catering to internationals in the Netherlands has some advice for how to achieve this virtually impossible feat.
“Many locals have their own social groups that they have maintained since childhood,” the Leiden International Center patiently explains.
The city of Amsterdam sets the bar low. “A neighbour doesn’t have to become a friend (although they might!) – even just being on nodding terms with the people living around you can help you feel at home,” it advises.
There are dozens of threads on Reddit from the recently relocated who are struggling to find connections amongst the Dutch.
True to form, one Dutch poster replies: “We don’t know you, you might just be unlikable for all we know.”
While this may be harsh – sorry, direct – it’s also probably the truth.
You might not be unlikeable in an existential sense. You’re probably a nice person who has friends and loved ones that just happen to live elsewhere. But to the average Tina, Henk and Luca, you just don’t bring much to the table.
First, let’s start with the idea that Dutch people establish their social roster before evacuating the womb.
It is true, in my experience, that Dutch people maintain the friendships they made in childhood and university. This is also true of literally everyone. I concede that the country is small, which makes it easier to keep up with those friendships.
But really, most of us make our friends prior to our early 20s. You just choose to leave yours behind for clogs and tulips. Now your lineup is empty and you’re clawing for a position on a team with few openings.
Which leads me to my second point: there is a reason most of us make friends early in life. It is significantly easy to make friends prior to reaching adulthood. The foundations of primary school friendships are “The other child was randomly selected to sit next to me” and “Who wants to play the same game at recess.” You go to school all day, you see these people all the time and you haven’t yet been downtrodden by the stresses of life.
Now you need to find more of a connection than “I like playing in the sandbox with you” and you need to find the time to make that connection, somewhere between working, exercising, raising your children, spending time with your partner and remembering to order a shower curtain. (If my husband is reading this, I am sorry – I forgot again.)
Even the aforementioned Dutchie at my dinner party was struggling. It’s not simply because you’re a foreigner, it’s just hard to make friends post-graduation.
It is, however, also because you are a foreigner. Dutch people do speak English but that doesn’t mean they want to speak their second language all the time. The language barrier also makes it harder for you to mesh into a group. If you make a Dutch friend and they invite you to their birthday party, you’re now forcing everyone in the circle to switch to English.
Plus, you don’t share the same cultural references, the same jokes, the same base understanding of the world. None of this is insurmountable but it all makes it more difficult to form a bond.
If you came here looking for advice on how to make friendships with the Dutch, you’re in the wrong place. This isn’t an advice column. Making friends as an adult is challenging and you’re playing that game on hard mode by trying to do it across cultural and language differences.
In the meantime, you can try just nodding at people. Maybe eventually one of has them just moved from Groningen and is also desperately trying to convince others that they are likable.

‘Not in my name’: Kosovo rallies to remove stain on legacy of freedom struggle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:17:39 UTC
22:17:39 KST

Last week, when thousands of Kosovars and Albanians converged in Pristina for a massive rally, there was a sense of deju vu among the people of Europe’s youngest country.
Carrying placards and posters, the protesters rent the air with full-throated cries of “Jo ne emrin tim” — not in my name – the same Albanian phrase splashed across posters in Kosovo’s capital.
The October 1 protests were the largest of the daily rallies being held in the capital’s central square since September 16, when former president and one of the most prominent figures of Kosovo’s independence movement Hashim Thaci was found guilty of war crimes by a special court in The Hague.
Kosovars have rejected the conviction of Thaci, 58, who was the political chief of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), an ethnic Albanian group that battled Serb forces for Kosovo’s independence in a bitter conflict that claimed more than 13,000 lives.
An estimated one million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes during the fighting.
Since the ruling, Kosovars and Albanians have gathered in the capital every single night to defend his legacy.
On Thursday, their numbers swelled tenfold as the rally coincided with a historic commemoration that directly illuminates the current unrest.
October 1 holds a special place in the history of the country, which gained independence from Serbia on February 17, 2008.
It is widely accepted that the student uprising on October 1, 1997, was a major catalyst in the country's path to independence after years of bloody struggle against the Serbian regime.
Many view the September ruling against Thaci and three other members of the now-disbanded KLA as tarnishing the legacy of the people’s resistance.
Gazmend Syla, a member of the KLA Veteran’s Association, describes the protests as “the only response of a nation facing the threat of annihilation".
A 78-day campaign of NATO air strikes against Serbian forces eventually forced Belgrade to withdraw from Kosovo.
Serbia still does not recognise Kosovo, though more than 100 countries do. Türkiye was one of the first countries to recognise Kosovo after its declared independence.
Echoes from the past
Back in 1997, Kosovo was officially still part of a crumbling Yugoslavia.
Tens of thousands of students had gathered in the city on October 1 to protest the outlawing of their native language by the regime of convicted war criminal Slobodan Milosevic, as he strove to hold onto the remnants of Yugoslavia after the Balkan wars.
It was followed by a formal ban from national schools and universities, forcing Kosovar Albanian students into underground learning centres.
They had assembled for a peaceful protest, with student leader Bujar Dugolli even releasing white doves at the beginning of his speech to symbolise their intentions.
Serbian police greeted them in riot gear and did not wait long before unleashing unrestricted violence with batons, tear gas and water cannons. Hundreds of students were injured or arrested.
Nearly three decades have passed, but Albanian protesters in Pristina’s square still share their resolve, even as they feel similar humiliation and indignation.
When the special court in The Hague decided that Thaci and three co-defendants were guilty of a series of war crimes, it hit a raw nerve for Albanians in Kosovo and the broader region.
In Albania’s capital Tirana, the City Council declared the four men honorary citizens in an act of solidarity.
Failed dialogue and armed resistance
Before the Kosovo War officially began, youth-led protesters had believed they could convince a heavy-handed government in Belgrade to change course through non-violent resistance.
That belief was shattered when police response signalled mercilessness and the impossibility of dialogue.
Trust in the Democratic League of Kosovo – the main political body which was organising a pacifist resistance at the time – collapsed virtually overnight.
And very next month, the Kosovo Liberation Army, a secretive resistance movement that Thaci would have commanding authority over, made its first public appearance in late November 1997.
What has angered Kosovars most is how the case against Thaci was built – based mostly on anonymous witnesses.
“Witnesses say they were packed into crowded basements or shut into rooms without toilets,” says Agron Leka, a former member of Kosovo’s Youth Assembly.
“How do you think other Albanians were living at the time? My mother was always in hiding. A sniper shot her cousin while she was next to him,” Leka tells TRT World, indicating that Albanians faced worse situations during the war.
Ignoring the truth
The public reaction underscores a fundamental friction. The court operates on a sterile legal paradigm that struggles to accommodate a complex historical truth: that an irregular guerrilla force can commit operational violations while simultaneously serving as the primary shield for an existential survival campaign.
Inside one of Pristina’s war museums, exhibition assistant Besnik Tafa explains that the public is emotionally removed from Thaci’s past.
“They are more so reacting to the sentence. It feels like a great injustice compared to some of the Serbian commanders,” he tells TRT World.
He points to Sreten Lukic, the former head of the Serbian Police in Kosovo, who was sentenced to 20 years for crimes against humanity, including the deportation and persecution of Kosovar Albanians, and Yugoslav army chief Dragoljub Ojdanic, who received 15 years for the same crimes.
For much of the population, it’s difficult to comprehend how Thaci can receive a harsher punishment than those implicated in a campaign of ethnic cleansing.
Anila Shala, who has been protesting regularly in Pristina, was born after the war but, like countless others, carries the bloodstains in her lineage.
“How is this supposed to make me think of my uncle?” she asks. He had joined the armed resistance after Shala’s grandfather was murdered during state-sanctioned violence.
She also fears that legally dismantling the credibility of KLA commanders will, by extension, undermine all the veterans who wrote the state's founding chapter.
“You can’t say the verdict is directed at a few individuals. If you say the father is a criminal, and the mother is a criminal, then their entire family is probably criminal,” she tells TRT World.
The shock and anger were so visceral across the country that it sent Kosovo’s highly fragmented parliament into historic unified action.
Lawmakers unanimously declared the court’s decision “unacceptable” and passed a formal declaration rejecting “any attempt to question Kosovo’s liberation war or to equate the people who fought for freedom and survival with the regime that oppressed them".
While the ruling initially galvanised cooperation, it has now created further division. Kosovo’s parliament must elect a new president by October 6.
Now, KLA-aligned parties are threatening to boycott and collapse the whole process if the government does not announce strict measures to contest the ruling internationally.
Prime Minister Albin Kurti is trying to empathise with the people without outright offending the Western members of the court, whom Kosovo depends on for hundreds of millions of dollars in aid annually.
The real danger, in Kosovars’ eyes, is that Thaci’s sentencing invites revisionism into their narrative.
Rina Kastrati, another exhibition assistant, believes the international community will paint the ruling with a broad brush.
“Kosovars can hold duality. We know our history. Other countries will mostly know the headlines (about Thaci’s conviction),” she tells TRT World.
In the international arena, the guilty verdict risks flattening the power asymmetry in Kosovo’s existential battle, falsely implying that guerrilla fighters had comparable capacity to commit comparable crimes as Belgrade’s state machinery.
For Kastrati, whose father’s life was saved by resistance fighters, the legal equation is intolerable.
“The KLA is part of the reason why I’m alive,” she adds.

What do we know about the suspected Iranian plot to attack UK's Fairford airbase? - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:16:43 UTC
22:16:43 KST

The United States has removed its fleet of bombers from a British airbase a week after five men were arrested nearby on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts as part of a suspected Iranian plot, the details of which remain largely unexplained.
Below is what we know so far:
What happened?
Police were called to RAF Fairford, 90 miles (145 km) west of London, early on Sunday, September 27, and arrested five suspects who were released on bail a day later.
A local farmer had called police, saying she saw three large white vans parked near the base and a group of "hooded and masked men" running into a field nearby. The Times reported that another person who contacted the police was one of the five arrested.
Armed officers responded to the calls and made the arrests in the Whelford area, about a mile from the base, before evacuating nearby properties and searching three vehicles.
The five were initially arrested on suspicion of offenses under the Explosives Act and later on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.
What happened next?
US President Donald Trump said those involved in the plot had planned "big damage," while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also pointed to the "hands of a foreign actor."
In July, Iran's Revolutionary Guards had said the base was a legitimate target.
British counter-terrorism police later confirmed they were considering whether a foreign state had been involved, before Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced on Wednesday there might have been an Iranian link.
A 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national was then arrested in London on Thursday, in what police called a "hugely complex" investigation.
A week after the initial arrests, a Pentagon official said all US bombers deployed to RAF Fairford had returned to their home stations in the US, without giving a reason.
A NATO military source said on Monday: "It is still believed that Iran poses an acute threat to US assets in the UK."
What has Iran said?
Iran has dismissed accusations that it was involved and on Thursday summoned the British ambassador in Tehran over the issue.
What about those arrested?
Counter-terror police have said the investigation is complex. They have said no explosive devices had been found as part of the investigation, but that a quantity of petrol had been recovered during searches of the vehicles.
The five men detained were all British nationals aged between 23 and 25 who lived in London, police said, before they announced they had released them all on bail.
The dual UK-Iranian national arrested on Thursday was also later released on bail.
They remain under investigation and are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others.
Trump said he would not have released the suspects on bail.
Why would Fairford be a target?
Fairford, which opened in 1944 and was used by Allied troops for the D-Day invasion of Normandy, has this year been used by US forces targeting Iran after Britain approved a US request for the base to be used for defensive strikes.
It is one of the US Air Force's only European airfields suitable for heavy bombers and is the preferred base for such operations. It played a key role in both the first Gulf War in 1991 and the invasion of Iraq in 2003.
Britain said in July its armed forces were ready to protect Fairford after Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned it not to allow US bombers to fly from the base. The Guards said any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target.
The bombers deployed there were big enough to carry the large precision-guided "bunker-busting" weapons which are designed to penetrate fortified weapons stores.

Ayhan Şimşek
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Germany is planning to build a new naval base in the northwestern city of Emden amid a worsening international security environment, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said Monday.
"This is significant for us, because it will be a major naval base," Pistorius said during a ceremony in Emden, where top officials signed a letter of intent for the base.
"From here we can quickly reach the North Atlantic and the North Sea," he said.
“The strategic location is also crucial - particularly with regard to our NATO allies, our shared training and operational areas, as well as joint training activities,” he added.
The new base will be Germany's fifth major naval base and is expected to ease the load on Wilhelmshaven, now the navy's most important site on the North Sea.
Defense Ministry sources said Wilhelmshaven will remain central, and the Emden base will complement it.
Pistorius said Germany has decided to expand its navy in response to rising international threats and a worsening security environment and to meet its commitments to NATO deterrence.
"We currently have the smallest navy in the history of the Bundeswehr, and at the same time the largest and most extensive set of tasks. So the navy must grow, and it will," he said.
"Given the current international security situation, especially with a view to the Baltic Sea, but above all the North Sea and the North Atlantic, this is of decisive importance, because with it we increase the deterrence of Germany and NATO," he said.
The planned naval base is expected to be a multibillion-euro investment, according to media reports. It is supposed to reach full operational readiness in 2030, and the site could eventually be home to up to 2,000 military and civilian personnel.

Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is secure a day after the US air force suddenly withdrew a dozen B-1 bombers from the Gloucestershire base over security concerns about a possible threat from Iran.

Aircraft trackers reported that an entire squadron of 12 B-1 bombers based at Fairford had redeployed from the British base to the US on Sunday, a rapid movement that the Pentagon confirmed on Sunday evening.
US officials told the New York Times commanders had received new information about an Iran-backed plot against the base, which has been on high alert for more than a week. Some of the bombers left so quickly that refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled to support their flights to the US.
A report on ITV News said the US feared a multiple drone attack, similar to Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb, in which cheap small drones launched from trucks destroyed 10 Russian bombers in a coordinated attack in June last year.
But UK sources cast doubt on whether Iran had the capability to launch such a complex operation 2,700 miles away. The Ukrainian operation took about 18 months to plan.
Donald Trump said on Monday that the US had withdrawn the bombers from the base because of “some threats”, without saying what they were.
“There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy – we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit, not very far,” Trump said.
UK sources indicated they were not aware of a new terrorism threat to the base and that they would be surprised if Iran could orchestrate a fresh attack, a week after five men from London were arrested late at night having driven to a village near the base in white vans with an unclear purpose.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Monday that the redeployment of the bombers was not tied to the arrests and tried to downplay any discrepancies with the UK. He said the US was confident in the security of all its bases and “with the Brits, we’ve worked very closely for a long time, including on this investigation, and they couldn’t be more cooperative”.
Downing Street’s comments were the first made by the UK in the light of the US withdrawal. Neither the Ministry of Defence nor Gloucestershire police commented when asked if there was any additional threat to residents near the base. Other UK officials indicated they had not been briefed on US thinking.
RAF Fairford has already been on high alert for several weeks amid heightened US concern that Tehran could try to instigate an attack on the base, which was used for US air force bombing runs against Iran earlier this year. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that the base was a legitimate military target.
The hasty redeployment arguably represents a victory for Iran, forcing US bombers to retreat without any kind of attack taking place, though some experts said Washington was engaging in a wider redeployment that could lead to a scaling up of operations against Iran after the US midterm elections in November.
It is unclear what level of threat Tehran could pose to a base in the heart of the UK, though Iran destroyed a US Awacs radar plane on the tarmac during fighting in March. Missiles fired from Iran may be able to reach the UK but would be likely to be shot down first, and a drone attack would be a high-risk operation close to the base.
Experts cautioned there remained a lack of information. “Airfields are hard to defend, but the US could be making a point or just being very cautious,” said Matthew Savill, an expert with the Royal United Services Institute.
Developments in the UK have not so far matched the apparent level of US concern. The five men from London were arrested in Whelford, next to the base, on suspicion of carrying explosives, but they were not charged.
No explosive devices were found in the search of the vans or the men, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. All five were released on bail a day later.
Trump said afterwards that he was surprised they had been allowed out on bail. “We know everything about them, we would not have released them,” he said.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been more muted. He said last week that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, but developments in the British investigation, led by counter-terrorism police, have been limited.
A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparing acts of terrorism, but he was also released on bail on Saturday. Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the events in Gloucestershire were continuing, counter-terrorism police said.
