To state school alumni starting university, I say this: be proud of your background | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:22:39 UTC
21:22:39 KST

“So, where did you go to school?” On the face of it, it doesn’t seem like a loaded question. I was mostly bemused when I first started university 20 years ago and found myself being asked it repeatedly by other students. Why were they so interested? Surely no one would have heard of the north Wales comprehensive I had attended? When they countered my baffled reaction with “Charterhouse” or “Marlborough”, how was I supposed to respond? When one student said, of another, “He went to Winchester, you know”, I stared blankly at him, not understanding why he was telling me about someone else’s day trip to a city in Hampshire (“Oh, did he have a nice time?”). It was strange, new territory.
Asking someone where they went to school is often not an innocent question. It is a way of “placing” you on a social scale. As thousands of freshers settle in to their first terms at university, a significant proportion will be battling with this dawning awareness that Britain runs on a network of private schools whose alumni often seem to know, or know of, one another. State-school students might have been dimly aware of it before, but nothing puts it into sharper focus than freshers’ week. It’s clear that little has changed since my own student days. I was saddened to read recent reports of classism at St Andrews, which led to a student’s announcement that she would not return this academic year: “Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” she said. The pervasiveness of private school culture, as I suppose you could call it, remains nationwide and deeply embedded.
It’s a shock, as a young person, to go from being the majority – state-educated – to suddenly feeling like the minority, and in some stark cases being made to feel “less than” as a result. It’s why I admire Sophie Pender’s 93% Club so much. Pender set up the initiative while she was at Bristol University, where she was mocked for her working-class background, to bring renewed focus to the fact that the vast majority of people educated in the UK – 93% in fact – attended state school, and to offer them a professional career mentoring and networking alternative to the “old boys” that is a de facto benefit of private school attendance.
Pender’s new campaign, Made in State School, aims to shift attitudes by issuing red plaques to celebrate some of the nation’s finest state school alumni – from David Attenborough and Jacqueline Wilson to Jessica Ennis-Hill and Marcus Rashford. She even presented a plaque to Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference last week. She is right when she says that state schools have a PR problem. They are often framed, in rightwing media especially, as dystopian, rough, a hardship that has to be overcome, as opposed to what they actually are: symbols of British excellence, innovation and creativity.
So often the media conversation takes the default assumption that private schools are inherently better than state schools, and that it is always in a child’s best interests to attend one. When you hold opinions like mine – that in rejecting the local state school, you are choosing a form of segregation – they can sometimes feel uncomfortable to express. My industries, media and publishing, are dominated by people who went to private school (half of newspaper columnists are privately educated). Education is a sensitive topic, and this can sometimes have a silencing effect.
So allow me to lay my cards on the table. Sending your child to private school encourages them to believe that they are better than other children. We have seen where this leads, in the behaviour of some of our leading politicians. The cultures of abuse that have been able to thrive at boarding schools that prioritised reputation and prestige over safety have left many victims in their wake.
We should be lauding the benefits of state schools. Being more socially mixed, they teach children openness and confidence. Being able to interact with people from a huge range of backgrounds is a vital life skill. State school kids are often hilarious – there is a unique sense of humour that comes from inclusion; from having seen it all. In the case of mixed-gender schools, they give you a far more developmentally appropriate understanding of the opposite sex. Perhaps due to a combination of socially repressed poshness or a lack of exposure to girls, the ex-public schoolboys at my university often seemed genuinely terrified of the working-class young women they were now expected to study alongside.
I wouldn’t go as far to say that it’s impossible to be cool and to have gone to private school, but let’s be honest, it’s harder. University was the first place I went where privilege was a status symbol, and it was discombobulating to be treated with derision by someone who wouldn’t have lasted two minutes in the roasting competition that was your morning registration. Well, you might say, “cool” shouldn’t matter – but as the Made in State School plaques demonstrate, cool people often go on to do radical, groundbreaking, culture-defining things.
I won’t rehash some of the toxic attitudes I experienced that first term, mostly from public schoolboys, but the scales fell from my eyes. Someone with less confidence and weaker politics might have put on a voice and tried to fit in. Which is why I want to say to any university fresher who feels that way now to hold their head high. These people’s parents chose to purchase educational advantage for their offspring – which was their prerogative – but that doesn’t make them better than you. You’ve still ended up in the same place, without the astronomical costs of private school tuition fees and largely off your own back! Being made in state school is something to be proud of. Become comfortable owning it, and using it to lift others up. We’re the 93%, after all.
- Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist

Turkey weighs military support for Saudi Arabia under Mecca pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:21:13 UTC
21:21:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Turkey weighs military support for Saudi Arabia under Mecca defence pact
Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan are set to hold high-level defence talks in Riyadh on Monday as Ankara signals its readiness to support the kingdom against continued Houthi attacks under the countries' newly signed joint defence pact.
Foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs from the three countries will attend a meeting of the Political and Defence Strategic Committee established under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed on 7 August.
The talks come as Turkey steps up its engagement with Saudi Arabia amid growing questions over what military support Ankara could provide Riyadh, including expanding defence industry, intelligence cooperation and expertise in drone warfare.
Turkey's foreign ministry said Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Defence Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of the General Staff Selcuk Bayraktaroglu would attend the meeting.
Fidan is expected to outline Turkey's position on consolidating the alliance and its next steps, as well as assess threats to peace and stability in the region and discuss developments impacting the three countries' shared security.
According to the ministry, Fidan will stress the importance of the alliance in providing a combined and effective response to threats and preventing regional crises.
He is also expected to reaffirm Turkey's "strong support" and solidarity with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks and stress that attacks targeting holy sites, including Mecca, are unacceptable.
Ankara is also expected to emphasise the importance of securing international trade routes and resolving regional conflicts through peaceful means.
Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Friday that Iran had proposed political engagement with the Houthis, an initiative expected to be discussed at the emergency Riyadh meeting.
Dar said Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan would determine their next steps during the talks.
The alliance is also expected to establish its secretariat in Riyadh, with Pakistan nominating retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood as its first secretary-general.
Mecca defence pact takes shape
The Political and Defence Strategic Committee, comprising the three countries' foreign and defence ministers and chiefs of staff, is responsible for directing activities under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
It held its first meeting in Istanbul on 31 August, when officials discussed the technical work required to institutionalise the alliance.
The countries' foreign ministers also met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, where they discussed regional developments and issued a statement condemning attacks on Mecca, which the Houthis denied carrying out, as well as attacks on Saudi civilian and economic infrastructure.
The military chiefs of Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan subsequently met in Riyadh on 25 September.
Saudi Arabia's defence ministry said the commanders reviewed threats facing the kingdom and discussed strengthening military cooperation, intelligence sharing and coordination between their armed forces.
They also agreed to begin translating commitments under the Mecca pact into "effective military cooperation".
Fidan later said regional developments and military threats facing Saudi Arabia from both the north and south had been discussed.
He said Turkey's chief of staff had briefed President Recep Tayyip Erdogan following the technical military talks in Riyadh, adding that the Turkish armed forces possessed the capabilities and expertise required to respond to threats.
Erdogan has stressed that the pact should not be viewed as an alliance directed against Iran, Israel or any other country.
In an interview with Newsweek, he said the agreement was based on Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises the right to self-defence. Under the agreement, an armed attack against one of the three countries is considered an attack against all parties.
Erdogan said the response would depend on the requirements of the country under attack and could range from intelligence, logistical and ammunition support to broader military assistance.
What could Turkey provide?
Attention has increasingly turned to what Turkish support for Saudi Arabia could look like in practice.
Fidan said on 20 September that Ankara would consider Riyadh's military requirements as it confronted continuing attacks, while stressing that Saudi Arabia should not be drawn into the conflict between the United States and Iran.
Turkey's growing defence industry could become a central component of that support.
Ankara has developed significant capabilities in drones, missiles, smart munitions and artillery, while its armed forces have accumulated experience in conflicts involving armed groups and irregular forces.
Turkey provided extensive military support to Azerbaijan during the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war and intervened in support of Libya's internationally recognised government in 2019, where Turkish drones helped shift the military balance.
It has also conducted repeated military operations in northern Syria and Iraq and exported drones to countries including Ukraine and Ethiopia.
Those capabilities have prompted speculation that Ankara could provide Saudi Arabia with military advice, intelligence support and advanced weapons without becoming directly involved in fighting.
Ufuk Necat Tasci, a professor of international relations at Canakkale Onsekiz Mart University, told The New Arab that Fidan's comments signalled that Ankara was positioning itself firmly alongside Riyadh.
"Politically, this statement indicates that Turkey will enter the equation in favour of Saudi Arabia. Time will reveal whether this intervention will be direct or indirect," he said. "Nevertheless, Turkey does not want to remain neutral towards the attacks on Saudi Arabia during this period, because this alliance, as is clear, has raised concerns in both Israel and Iran."
Drones and air defence
Merve Suna Ozel Ozcan, an international relations academic at Kirikkale University, cautioned against interpreting Turkey's position as signalling direct military intervention.
"Fidan's statement should be interpreted from the perspective of solidarity, not war or aggression," she told TNA.
She noted that defence industry cooperation was among the clearest areas in which Ankara could assist Riyadh, particularly through drone technology.
Turkey and Saudi Arabia already have an agreement involving the Bayraktar Akinci combat drone, with Turkish defence company Baykar and Saudi military industries pursuing local production and technology transfer.
Ozcan said the nature of Houthi warfare meant Saudi Arabia required more than additional advanced air defence systems such as the Patriot and THAAD.
Riyadh also needed additional defensive layers, she said, particularly cheaper systems capable of countering large-scale drone attacks.
Such cooperation could offer the clearest indication yet of how the Mecca agreement will move from a political commitment to a functioning defence alliance, as Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan seek to define how collective defence will work in practice.

The proposed interaction was informal, Chaudhary said, adding that there was no need to “blow it out of proportion”. (File photo)
NEW DELHI: 'One nation, one election' JPC chief and BJP MP PP Chaudhary on Monday gave a clarification amid the, now cancelled, proposed meeting of the parliamentary panel with Supreme Court judges, saying that it was SC that called the meeting and then cancelled it.Chaudhary claimed that Supreme Court had set the meeting for October 6 at 4.30 PM via an email sent to the committee’s Director on September 22.
“Many members were not aware that the Supreme Court itself had scheduled the meeting. Through an email dated the 22nd, the Supreme Court informed our Director that it had fixed the meeting for the 6th at 4:30 PM. When the Supreme Court later cancelled the meeting, we also cancelled it and issued a notice to all the members. Since the meeting had initially been scheduled by the Supreme Court, we had informed all members accordingly,” he added, as quoted by ANI.
Chaudhary further said the proposed interaction was informal and there was no reason to attach undue significance to it. He also pointed to previous instances of discussions between parliamentary committees and the judiciary. "The committee and the Supreme Court also said that if it is not appropriate, this issue should not be escalated.
If both sides can hold a discussion, that is fine; if not, that is fine as well. There is no need to lay so much stress on this matter or blow it out of proportion," he said, speaking to ANI after the JPC meeting, held earlier in the day.He cited previous committee proceedings to argue that such interactions were not unprecedented."Earlier, regarding committee matters like the Education Bill and several others, as Mr Wilson stated, he had advised the committee to discuss matters with them. There are several past precedents of holding discussions with the Supreme Court. So there was nothing wrong with it either. And if the Supreme Court did not consider it appropriate, there is no issue at all," Chaudhary said.Further talking about the release of its report, he added, "Look, the process is currently ongoing; we are hearing the stakeholders. Once all members convey that there is no further need to hear anyone, and after gathering the opinions of all the members, we will submit the report,."The clarification came after former Union minister and Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal criticised the proposed interaction, calling it "unconstitutional". Sibal had said the separation of powers under the Constitution meant that courts, rather than Parliament, determine the constitutionality of legislation."I have never heard in the history of India till date that a parliamentary group holds a meeting in the Supreme Court regarding a law (One Nation One Election), to tell the Supreme Court judges what this law actually is. I am talking about 'One Nation One Election'... I have never heard of such a thing in my legal career. This is unconstitutional," Sibal said at a press conference.The JPC is examining the Constitution (One Hundred and Twenty-Ninth Amendment) Bill, 2024 and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024, which seek to provide the statutory framework for synchronising elections to the Lok Sabha, state assemblies and Union Territory assemblies.
Chaudhary also referred to a letter by DMK MP P Wilson, saying there were precedents for such interactions. "You will receive the details regarding that. It has happened in the past. It is stated in Mr Wilson's letter; he placed that letter before the committee," he said.The JPC met at the Parliament Library Building in New Delhi on Monday as it continued its deliberations on the two Bills. Chaudhary said the committee was still in the process of hearing stakeholders and would submit its report once members were satisfied that all necessary views had been heard.

Ukraine warns of fake government and media sites tied to Russian intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:19:32 UTC
21:19:32 KST

Ukraine's security agency claims that Russia is impersonating official government sites to spread disinformation and collect personal data.
Russian intelligence services are creating fake websites, social media pages, and messenger channels to imitate Ukrainian government agencies, security bodies, media outlets and senior officials, Kyiv has said.
According to the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), these fake resources copy official names, logos, photographs and branding in an attempt to appear legitimate.
The agency said it had recorded a key increase in such manipulative activities and had already identified and blocked more than 50 resources that copied the SBU’s own branding and appearance.
Fake accounts have also been created in the names of senior Ukrainian officials. Previous examples include Telegram accounts impersonating President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, First Lady Olena Zelenska, former presidential office chief Andriy Yermak and former SBU chief Vasyl Maliuk.
Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation has also warned about fake accounts using the names and photographs of security officials to publish supposed insider or exclusive information.
In some cases, operators repurpose older Telegram channels, including cryptocurrency pages, by changing their names and branding to make them appear official.
The goal: information and influence
The SBU says the fake resources are mainly used to spread disinformation and collect personal data.
By copying government agencies, officials or media organisations, Russia can present false or misleading information as though it came from a legitimate Ukrainian source.
The SBU says these campaigns aim to destabilise the political and social situation inside Ukraine and weaken the country's position internationally.
The same resources can also be used to collect information from users. Fake pages and channels may encourage people to follow an account, click on links, send messages or provide personal details.
According to the SBU, Russian intelligence services also target users who interact with fake pages and messenger channels and may compromise their accounts to obtain personal data. The agency says this information can later be used in recruitment operations or to gather confidential information.
Russian intelligence services are particularly interested in information about the combat and operational activities of Ukraine's defence and security forces, according to the SBU.
The fake resources can therefore serve several purposes at the same time. First, they can spread disinformation, attract users by posing as trusted sources and direct them towards links or accounts that can be used to collect information.
This tactic often relies on small differences that can be difficult to spot, like different usernames for fake accounts. Meanwhile, a fake website may closely copy the design of a government or media page but use a different web address.
Ukrainian authorities are therefore advising users to check account names, web addresses and verification badges carefully, avoid suspicious links and rely on official sources.

Farsight Vision Presents Navigation Module for UGVs That Operates Without GPS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:19:06 UTC
21:19:06 KST

The Ukrainian-Estonian defense company Farsight Vision has unveiled a new navigation module for unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) that helps them navigate the terrain in the absence of a GPS signal.
Company representatives discussed the development with Militarnyi.
The solution combines a laser sensor with 3D data from the FSV Platform. While in motion, the system generates a point cloud around the UGV, identifies obstacles, pits, slopes, and other terrain features, and helps refine the vehicle’s position.
The system is based on the concept of a digital twin of the terrain. A 3D model of the area is created in advance on the FSV Platform, against which data from the UGV’s sensors is subsequently cross-referenced.
While in motion, the laser module scans the space around the vehicle and updates the model with current data. Thanks to this, the operator sees not only a static satellite map but also the actual condition of the route in real time.
“Our goal is to eliminate the need to launch a reconnaissance drone just to escort the UGV, as this creates unnecessary risk and wastes resources,” Victoria Yaremchuk, CEO of Farsight Vision, noted.
The module’s key function is UGV localization. If the GPS signal is lost, the system can compare the sensor’s current data with a pre-built 3D model and help the operator restore the UGV’s spatial orientation.
The operator can control the UGV via a ground station, and after connecting to the FSV App, receives an additional 3D view of the route and the surrounding terrain.
By the end of the year, Farsight Vision plans to enable the UGV to autonomously return to the point where communication was lost or to a designated base several kilometers away, and subsequently scale this capability up to 30–40 km.
In May 2025, Farsight Vision presented technology for building 2D and 3D terrain models that can be used for route planning and operations in areas where satellite navigation is unavailable.
The new module continues Farsight Vision’s overall concept of creating an autonomous navigation ecosystem.
Militarnyi previously reported on the integration of the company’s software into the Mara and Besomar “photodrones” and a system for predicting signal loss zones for UAVs.

A Return to the Roots and a Graphic Revolution — Gears of War: E-Day Game Release
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:15:51 EEST

A Return to the Roots and a Graphic Revolution — Gears of War: E-Day Game Release
Kyiv • UNN
The Gears of War prequel will take players to the first Locust attack and will be released on PC and Xbox Series S|X. The price in Ukraine starts at UAH 2,299.
October 2026 will be one of the busiest months of the year for the gaming industry. Already on Tuesday, October 6, gamers will have the opportunity to play a large-scale prequel to the cult Gears of War franchise. The shooter Gears of War: E-Day will take players 14 years before the original game, with young Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago at the center of the story, writes UNN.
Details
Gears of War: E-Day takes players back to the series’ origins and tells the story of the day humanity first encountered the Locust invasion. The events take place 14 years before the original Gears of War, with young Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago at the center of the story. Players will have to survive the first hours of Emergence Day, when an ordinary city turns into a battlefield within minutes.
The first game in the series was released way back in 2007. According to the plot, which unfolds on the planet Sera, humanity was at war with itself over an energy resource—Imulsion (a glowing underground liquid). The Coalition of Ordered Governments won this war. Just a few days after the long-awaited peace treaty was signed, hordes of monsters—the Locust—suddenly attacked from underground. On the very first day, a quarter of the planet’s population was killed.
In desperation, the Coalition activated the Hammer of Dawn satellite weapon. The weapon burned down major cities and destroyed billions of people and Locust, but it did not solve the problem: the monsters hid deep underground.
Fourteen years after Emergence Day, former Sergeant Marcus Fenix, who was serving a prison sentence for desertion, is freed by his friend Dominic "Dom" Santiago.
Marcus is assigned to Delta Squad. Their goal is to infiltrate the Locust underground tunnels and activate the Lightmass bomb to destroy the enemy’s lair.
The new installment will use Unreal Engine 5, allowing the developers to significantly enhance the detail of the environments, lighting, and characters themselves. The familiar cover-based firefights remain at the core of the series, but E-Day makes them more dynamic thanks to additional verticality and movement options.
It should be noted that the game will be released only on PC and Xbox Series S | X, meaning it will not be playable on PlayStation. The developers of Gears of War: E-Day consider Xbox exclusivity an advantage, as it allowed them to focus on a single hardware platform and achieve high graphical quality at 60 FPS with hardware-accelerated ray tracing.
For The Coalition team, Microsoft’s decision to return to an exclusives policy became a source of pride. Creative director Matt Searcy and art director Arjan Henbeck believe that the opportunity to present such a project confirms the studio’s technical expertise.
According to the creators, working with a limited range of hardware made it possible to avoid spending resources adapting the game for numerous platforms and to get the most out of Unreal Engine 5. The technologies used include MegaLights, which makes it possible to illuminate scenes simultaneously with hundreds of dynamic light sources, and Lumen global illumination.
"This way, we can ensure high quality," the developers noted.
According to them, the impressive graphics, smooth animation enabled by the motion-matching system, and photorealistic cutscenes rendered in real time became possible because quality was prioritized over the goal of releasing the game on every competing platform.

MOSCOW, October 5. /TASS/. Russia regrets that a joint statement could not be adopted following today’s meeting of the Moscow format of consultations on Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, the Russian president’s special representative for the country, told journalists.
"When drafting the final joint statement, we encountered one problem – that problem was that our Afghan and Pakistani colleagues didn't see eye to eye. We regret this," he said.
"Our Afghan colleagues felt that this year, in the text [of the draft joint statement], Afghanistan was mentioned too often in a terrorist context. To be honest, this surprised us, because the same wording and expressions were used in last year's text, [after] the seventh meeting. "The Moscow format can work and continue to exist without this joint statement. But it would be more in line with tradition, more proper. The Moscow format remains as a platform, but it is not a platform for resolving bilateral disagreements; it is a platform for coordinating regional cooperation."
The Moscow format was established in 2017 on the basis of a mechanism of consultations involving special representatives of Russia, Afghanistan, India, Iran, China, and Pakistan. Its first meeting was held on April 14, 2017, with the participation of deputy ministers and special representatives from 11 countries, including Afghanistan. The main goal of the format is to promote national reconciliation in Afghanistan and to ensure the fastest establishment of peace in the country. Special representatives and senior officials from Afghanistan, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, China, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan took part in the current meeting. Parents in Finland turn to AI for free school pictures
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:14:04 EEST
21:14:04 KST

It's that time of year again: the school semester is underway, and many kids have already had their annual photo day.
But this year, there's a twist. Some parents in Finland are feeding preview images of their kids' portraits into AI tools to wipe away the copyright text.
As some families debate the issue on social media, the Finnish school photographers' association said it has learned of isolated cases where photos have been used without permission.
That means the photographer does not get paid for their work.
According to the association's vice chair, Outi Simström, there is a common misunderstanding about the sector's earnings model.
"A photographer is not paid by the school or daycare for coming in and photographing the children. The entrepreneur's income comes from families voluntarily buying the pictures they want," Simström said.
50-year copyright
Photographs have at least 50 years of protection under related rights, said Emilia Hodge, a specialist in intellectual property law.
As a general rule, photographs may not be copied or published without the photographer's permission. If a photograph qualifies as a copyright-protected work, the protection lasts considerably longer.
Simström also warns parents about the risks of using AI.
"When we're talking about a picture of a person, and especially a minor, it's material and personal data of a kind that I would always recommend thinking carefully about which external digital service you upload these images to. Afterwards, they can't easily be removed."
Using photographs without permission is hardly a new phenomenon, according to Mikko Säteri of Finnfoto, the umbrella organisation for Finland's photography associations.
For around a decade, parents have captured pictures by removing watermarks with various tools and software. AI, however, has added a new dimension to the practice.
"AI can enlarge an image file enough to make a printable copy from it," he explained.
Säteri said photography businesses are now having to develop new ways to protect their images and track down those used without permission.
School photography is a Finnish tradition going back 160 years. But Säteri said he is now concerned about whether these businesses can survive in the age of AI.
School snaps feature prominently in Säteri's own home, as they do in many others.
"I think it's wonderful to see photographs of my daughters from different periods lined up on the fridge."

The United States has withdrawn all B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Britain due to reported "new threats," though the British government insisted Monday the site is safe.
Police were called to the base in southwest England on Sept. 27 after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in "suspicious" activity.
The scare prompted a counterterrorism probe and forced evacuations at 85 homes near the airbase, which was used by the United States to launch strikes on Iran.
Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but "a quantity of petrol was recovered," according to counterterrorism police.
A statement from a Pentagon official Sunday said "we can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States."
The statement noted that "operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time."
An unidentified U.S. official told CNN that the bombers were moved after "an unspecified new threat," with the source calling the latest threat a "real world incident."
It was unusual to move the bombers back to their home stations instead of deploying them to another base in the region, the official reportedly said.
Two U.S. officials told the New York Times that the bombers were moved after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against the base.
One American official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but the situation became urgent in the past 24 hours, the Times reported.
Asked whether the base was safe, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham's official spokesman said: "Yes."
"We have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world," he told reporters.
Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel theft, as energy prices in the U.K. hit record highs this week.
Burnham has said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident, a charge rejected by Tehran.
Six London-based Britons arrested in the September incident, including a U.K.-Iranian dual national, all men in their mid-20s, were released on bail, drawing rebuke from Washington.
"I wouldn't have done that," U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters, as his Secretary of State Marco Rubio alleged a "foreign actor" was involved.
Iran's embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.
Adding to the mystery, British media reported that officers were alerted to the incident by one of the initial suspects, but police have not commented on the reports.
Security at the base had reportedly been heightened recently.
Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran," and U.S. bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing at the base.
Fairford is the only airbase on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.
The incident came after a farmer living in the village of Whelford, near the airbase, called the police after seeing three vans blocking a road and a group of masked men fleeing the scene.
Aerial footage of the vans showed they appeared to contain barrels, and at least one was marked with a fake logo and phone number, giving the false impression that it was owned by a legitimate diesel delivery firm.

Accept ‘bad things’ in return for benefits of AI, says Sam Altman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:13:36 UTC
21:13:36 KST

Sam Altman says he believes the world should accept “bad things” happening with AI in exchange for the benefits of the technology.
The chief executive of OpenAI cited hacks, scams and “other bad things that will happen” in an interview that sparked an instant backlash from critics of the big AI companies. His comments came after one of his company’s safety experts resigned, saying at the weekend that its “culture is broken”.
In an interview released on Monday, Altman was asked about how OpenAI’s approach to safety differed from that of Anthropic, which has called for the industry to slow down after one of its researchers quit, warning that AI experts believed “it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.
“I think there’s a lot of daylight,” Altman said. “One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use AI widely].
“I do think the lighter touch regulatory stance we advocate for comes with an accepting of the fact that some bad things are going to happen as society figures out the resilience.
“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying we will make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams or all the other bad things that will happen because I think that people will do tremendously – orders of magnitude – more good stuff than bad stuff.”
The interview for Politico’s Decoded podcast drew a strong response from Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida. He said he had “no dice” with the idea “a handful of tech oligarchs get to make that decision [on safety] for the rest of us”.
His state last week asked a judge to bar OpenAI from developing new AI models without third-party approved guardrails.
Gary Marcus, a prominent AI sceptic and professor emeritus at New York University, said Altman was “saying the quiet part out loud: suck it up, so you can make us rich and powerful”.
Altman also reignited a feud with Elon Musk, telling Vanity Fair: “I don’t like bullies, and I think Elon’s a bully.”
He had been asked if the AI industry could “grow up” and work together.
“I think once in a while you got to punch a bully back in the nose,” Altman said. “And I also think Elon, like many bullies, only respects people who do. So if you want me to be able to work with him, maybe you should be happy I hit back once in a while, but I will work with Elon, of course.”
Altman co-founded OpenAI with Musk in 2015 but earlier this year Musk alleged in court that Altman, OpenAI, and the company’s president, Greg Brockman, unjustly enriched themselves and broke a founding contract. Musk’s claim was dismissed by a judge and jury.
OpenAI was hit by multiple safety crises over the summer, including when a swarm of its AI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website. Other agents accessed Australian government data. In the interview with Vanity Fair, Altman warned of “a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems” from rival open-source models. He suggested OpenAI could help its customers defend against the risk.
The company has scrapped the release of a cutting-edge model but Altman’s comments reflect a more bullish mood ahead of a stock market flotation.
The wave of public and political concern last month about the potentially catastrophic consequences of fast-progressing AI agents that act beyond human intent had led to hopes of US-wide or even international safety agreements.
However, Donald Trump and AI bosses including Altman and Dario Amodei of Anthropic signed a far more laissez-faire pact at the White House last week. The US president said he wanted the companies to “self-police” to limit the risks from AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons.
Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and Google DeepMind and as chief scientist at the UK’s AI Safety Institute, said warnings about AI risks understated the dangers.
“There’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems,” he said, adding that actions taken over the next two to 10 years would be decisive.
OpenAI’s David Robinson announced his departure at the weekend, saying “the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough” as they sprint from one product launch to the next.
His view was endorsed by Miles Brundage, an AI policy researcher who worked at OpenAI for six years. He said he regretted helping “spread the idea of iterative deployment”, which may have made sense when AI was less powerful “but makes no sense at all after many deaths have been tied to AI and as we’re careening towards extinction-level risks”.

Vagus Nerve Stimulation Could Help New Skills Stick
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:13:07 UTC
21:13:07 KST

Vagus Nerve Stimulation Could Help New Skills Stick
Scientists found that stimulating a major body-to-brain nerve after practice may open a hidden window that helps new skills stick.
- Date:
- October 5, 2026
- Source:
- Tohoku University
- Summary:
- Stimulating the vagus nerve after practice helped mice develop stronger long-term motor learning, revealing a potentially important window when the brain is still locking in a new skill. The effect was linked to rhythmic changes in brain blood vessels, hinting that body-to-brain signals may help prepare the brain for lasting change.
- Share:
Why do some new skills seem to click almost instantly while others remain frustratingly difficult even after repeated practice? The difference may involve more than talent or effort. It may also depend on whether the brain is in the right condition to turn practice into lasting learning.
Learning does not happen independently of the rest of the body. Internal organs constantly send information to the brain through the vagus nerve, one of the nervous system's major communication pathways. Researchers at Tohoku University who study super network brain physiology have now shown in mice that stimulating this nerve after training can strengthen long term motor learning. Their findings point to a previously overlooked role for communication from the body to the brain in helping new skills persist.
The findings were published in iScience on August 25, 2026.
The Vagus Nerve and Learning
The vagus nerve serves as a major information highway between the brain and the body. It carries signals from internal organs to the brain while also transmitting instructions from the brain back to those organs. Scientists can influence this pathway using vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), which is already clinically approved for treating several disorders.
Earlier research has mainly explored VNS as a form of neuromodulation that changes activity in neurotransmitter systems. The new study suggests there may be another important mechanism involved: rhythmic changes in blood vessels inside the brain.
To investigate this possibility, the researchers created a small cuff electrode designed to stay attached to the left cervical vagus nerve in mice. They then tested VNS during horizontal optokinetic response (HOKR) learning, a cerebellum dependent eye movement task that teaches mice to improve their ability to follow moving visual stripes. The response is similar to the automatic eye movements a person makes while standing on a platform and watching a train move past.
The Biggest Effect Appeared After Practice
The researchers applied VNS after each training session rather than during the learning task itself. The stimulation did not immediately improve performance while the mice were training. Instead, the benefits became apparent later.
On following days, mice that received VNS showed stronger long-term learning. This pattern suggests that the stimulation may influence processes that happen after training, when the brain is consolidating what it has learned into more durable memory.
"The key point is that VNS was delivered only after training," says Professor Ko Matsui. "Our findings suggest that VNS may open a hidden window of opportunity for enhanced learning by making the brain environment more receptive to long-lasting change."
Rhythmic Changes in Brain Blood Volume
The team next looked for changes inside the brain that might accompany the improved learning. They measured blood volume activity near the cerebellar flocculus, an area involved in HOKR learning.
Using fiber photometry, the researchers found that a single round of VNS produced a two phase vascular response. Local blood volume briefly decreased before rising after a delay. When VNS was repeated, it created rhythmic oscillations in blood volume.
Those vascular rhythms also appeared to be related to learning. Mice with larger blood volume oscillations generally showed better learning by Day 5, suggesting that changes in the brain's vascular environment could be connected to the longer lasting effects of the stimulation.
"Our brains may be more strongly influenced by the body than we imagine," says lead author Junyu Chen. "By tuning the brain's metabolic environment, including rhythmic vascular movements, we may eventually unlock capacities that would otherwise remain latent."
Exploring the Brain-Body Connection
Future research will focus on refining stimulation protocols and determining more precisely how communication between the brain and body supports long term plasticity.
By studying this two way communication pathway in greater detail, scientists hope to better understand how learning becomes lasting and how that process might eventually be enhanced.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Tohoku University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Junyu U. Chen, Yoko Ikoma, Ko Matsui. Vagal nerve stimulation induces vascular oscillations and enhances long-term learning. iScience, 2026; 29 (9): 117413 DOI: 10.1016/j.isci.2026.117413

Armenia has long been one of the easiest places for Russians to relocate. New residency rules are about to make staying there more complicated.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:12:14 UTC
21:12:14 KST

Armenia has long been one of the easiest places for Russians to relocate. New residency rules are about to make staying there more complicated.
In a recent survey, Meduza readers named Armenia one of the most comfortable countries for Russians to emigrate to. But starting November 1, new rules for obtaining a residence permit will take effect in the republic. The authorities are introducing quotas on residence permits, moving document submission online, and for the first time setting clear financial requirements for foreign entrepreneurs. This matters for Russians: opening a sole proprietorship in Armenia and obtaining a residence permit through it is one of the most popular ways to legally remain in the country. We explain how this path works, what’s changing, and how the changes will affect Russians who have moved to the country.
Andrey Frolov, an editor at the emigrant entrepreneur community Kovcheg Business, helped us sort out the details. He himself moved to Armenia in 2022, opened a sole proprietorship there, and obtained a five-year residence permit.
Basic rules for staying legally in Armenia
Russians don’t need a residence permit to live in the country for years
Russian citizens can enter Armenia without a visa and stay up to 180 days per visit. The official “180 days a year” rule holds up on paper, but in practice it isn’t applied, says Andrey Frolov: “The limit applies per entry. That’s why many people spend years doing visa runs, leaving for Georgia, for example, and returning. Formally, such trips aren’t provided for by law, but in practice they work.”
Those who don’t want to make endless trips to the border have another option: obtaining official registration, which lets Russians stay in Armenia indefinitely. This right is enshrined in a separate 1997 interstate treaty, and current disputes over Armenia’s membership in the Eurasian Economic Union don’t affect it. The privilege doesn’t extend to citizens of other countries.
In March 2025, the Armenian parliament passed a law launching the process of joining the European Union. Leaders of Eurasian Economic Union countries are demanding that Yerevan hold a referendum so voters can finally choose a course: the EU or the Eurasian Economic Union. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan acknowledges that holding membership in both blocs at once is impossible. These developments haven’t changed Armenia’s legal status in the EU or the Eurasian Economic Union, but they have fueled political and economic tensions.
You can register at the “passport office” with or without the property owner present. If the owner isn’t there, police will check whether the applicant actually lives at the stated address. A Meduza source advises staying home during business hours for the first week and a half to two weeks after submitting documents to catch a visit or call from the local precinct officer. No lease agreement is required for this procedure.
An important detail: the registration stamp must go exclusively in the foreign-travel passport. A mark in an internal Russian “passport” (ID) will make it invalid in Russia, and it’s impossible to replace the document abroad. A damaged document will also cause problems when applying for a new foreign-travel passport at a consulate.
Legally linking registration to the internal passport without damaging it will be possible only after obtaining a temporary residence permit or a residence permit (more on that below).
Keep in mind that if your 180-day limit for staying in Armenia expires while your documents are being processed, you face a fine of 50,000 drams. The law doesn’t provide for automatic deportation or an entry ban, though it technically leaves authorities the right to apply extreme measures.
Hi, I’m Vladislav Gorin.
I’m the host of Meduza’s daily Russian-language daily news podcast. This summer, the Russian authorities opened a criminal case against me — not for committing a crime, but for telling the truth about Russia and its war against Ukraine.
Because the Kremlin has branded me a criminal, I can’t go home. I also can’t safely travel to countries like Turkey — even though it’s a NATO member — because I could be arrested and extradited to Russia. I can’t even renew my passport at the consulate anymore.
None of this is going to stop me. I know there are hundreds of thousands of people in Russia who don’t want this war and who still believe in freedom and democracy, and they deserve access to independent journalism. Please support Meduza so I can keep reaching them.
Who needs an Armenian residence permit, and when
First and foremost, resident status is necessary for anyone planning to apply for a Schengen visa or other foreign visas. Not all embassies and consulates in Armenia accept tourist visa applications from Russians who have only registration: many require a temporary residence permit or a residence permit.
The document also comes in handy for flights outside the CIS when returning to Armenia. There are known cases of Russians with only registration running into trouble boarding flights to Armenia at foreign airports, because the simplified stay procedure for Russian citizens rests on a bilateral treaty not reflected in other countries’ national laws. Staff at foreign airlines, relying on general databases, may conclude that a passenger has exceeded the permitted annual limit (formally 180 days) and refuse to let them board.
A residence permit also provides access to resident banking rates: several local lenders offer favorable terms exclusively to holders of that status.
It also solves verification problems with international services. Ordinary registration isn’t enough to pass verification on platforms like Payoneer or set up YouTube payments, but a residence permit avoids those difficulties.
Another reason to get the document is long-term planning: a residence permit can protect against legislative changes. Russia or Armenia could revise the terms of the bilateral agreements governing registration rules at any moment, and no expert can predict when, or whether, that will happen. Full residency status neutralizes that risk.
Armenian migration law allows for a residence permit on several grounds: employment, study, business, family ties, and Armenian ancestry. One of the most accessible routes — applicants need only a minimal package of documents at the application stage — and one of the most popular is obtaining a residence permit through entrepreneurial activity. That status not only grants the right to reside but also legalizes your income, reducing the likelihood of problems with banks and tax authorities during audits.
So what should those who also want to legalize their income do
Open a sole proprietorship. This can be done in a single day (but be prepared for difficulties with banks)
The first step is to get a social security number (SSN). Without it, you can’t open a business or a bank account, or even make a free appointment with a doctor. Yerevan almost always has lines for an SSN, but in cities an hour and a half to two hours from the capital, it can be obtained the same day you apply, according to Frolov. Keep in mind that an SSN application can’t be used to register your place of residence: that’s handled strictly at the “passport office” tied to your address.
Once you have your SSN, you can move on to registering as a sole proprietor. In Yerevan, that can be done in a single day at the Unified Public Services Center. You’ll need a notarized translation of your foreign-travel passport (you can find a notary via this link) and your SSN, and you should be ready to explain verbally what you plan to do. The registration certificate is issued on the spot. Which activity code you’re assigned hardly matters: accountants determine the nature of your business from the wording on your invoices, based on the actual description of services. Frolov himself, for example, works as an editor, though his documents list him as a publisher of printed materials.
The next stage, opening a bank account, is where things get more complicated. Verification of an entrepreneur’s documents is handled separately from verification of an individual and takes about a week. Banks usually ask for contracts with clients and an accountant, and sometimes for proof of registration at your address.
The main thing Frolov warns about is that local banks’ requirements are often unpredictable. Bank staff may demand a diploma or a contract with a local company, contrary to official regulations. In such cases, he advises not arguing but simply switching to a different branch.
Two more important nuances are worth knowing in advance:
- Problems with dollar transfers. If an Armenian bank’s correspondent bank is Bank of Georgia, transactions in U.S. dollars will almost certainly be rejected.
- Difficulties with online payment processing. Setting it up can take weeks, or even months. Even so, there are success stories, such as the PayLink service from Ameria Bank.
A separate difficulty can arise with Russian clients, though not on the Armenian bank’s side. For Armenia’s local tax authority, the State Revenue Committee, the origin of the money doesn’t matter as long as the income is legal and the client isn’t under U.S. or EU sanctions. Russian companies, however, are often required to pay VAT in Russia out of their own pocket when working with a foreign sole proprietor, which is why many decline such cooperation.
‘Zero percent taxes’ is a myth. But you can pay little.
Immediately after registration, a sole proprietor is placed on the general taxation system, with VAT and profit tax. To switch to the simplified regime, you must file an application within 20 days of registration, then confirm the status by February 20 every year — a task an accountant usually handles. Miss the deadline, and you’ll pay the maximum rates for the entire year, which is why the Meduza source advises finding an accountant before opening the business.
Hiring a specialist isn’t legally required, but all reporting and the taxpayer’s personal account are kept exclusively in Armenian. Accounting services for a sole proprietor issuing several invoices a month cost 25,000–30,000 drams a month.
The main tax regimes for sole proprietors:
- Turnover tax (simplified scheme). It applies as long as annual income doesn’t exceed 115 million drams. Rates depend on the type of activity (for example, 10% in retail and 1.5% in newspaper sales), but it mostly comes down to 10%.
- IT sector. A preferential regime of the same turnover tax applies, with a 1% rate for a closed list of high-tech activities. The previous “IT certificates” haven’t been issued since 2025, as the rules have changed.
- Microentrepreneurship. A 0% rate applies to turnover up to 24 million drams a year.
Most of the rumors swirl around “microbusiness” status. In practice, Frolov said, there’s no complete freedom from taxes in Armenia — a myth common among Russians moving to the country. Only the turnover tax is zeroed out. The stamp duty and the medical insurance contribution, both paid once a year, remain. This regime also doesn’t suit everyone: Armenia’s tax code lists prohibited types of activity. You can’t open a food service business under “microbusiness” status in Yerevan, for instance, though you can in other cities. Tutors, artists, and jewelers most often choose this status.
There’s a separate trap tied to the wording on documents. Since 2025, providers of legal, accounting, and consulting services no longer have the right to work under the simplified regime. The expert advises not writing the word “consulting” on invoices at all if you’re actually providing other services, such as development or design. Otherwise, the tax authority will immediately switch you to the general system with VAT.
Consider the risks. The main ones aren’t in Armenia, but in Russia.
As long as a person remains a Russian tax resident — which requires spending at least 183 days in the country over 12 months — they must pay Russian personal income tax on all their income, including income that passes through an Armenian sole proprietorship. Russia’s Federal Tax Service monitors Russians’ foreign accounts more closely than Armenia’s tax authority monitors the foreign accounts of Russian residents, Frolov said.
One more important detail: although a double taxation treaty is in effect between the two countries, in practice it often doesn’t operate strictly by the book. If you’ve registered income in Russia as a sole proprietor or as a self-employed person, you won’t be able to credit tax you’ve already paid there against your Armenian taxes — you’ll have to pay another 20% in income tax to Armenia’s budget. The situation is different for regular personal income tax.
For example, if 13% has already been withheld from Russian income, the Armenian tax authority allows paying only the difference: 7%. Formally, the treaty works differently: you’re supposed to pay the full 20% in Armenia and then seek a refund from Russia’s Federal Tax Service. However, local agency takes a more accommodating approach and allows a credit for tax already paid in Russia.
Armenia requests data from Russia’s tax authority only on its own citizens. Emigrant communities aren’t aware of any such requests regarding Russians yet, though that could change at any moment.
A separate issue is notifying Russian authorities about obtaining a residence permit. Ignoring that requirement carries administrative and criminal liability. There’s no need to report Armenian registration at a place of residence, which follows from an official response from the Interior Ministry obtained by members of one emigrant community. Formally, there’s also no need to report a temporary residence permit, but an analysis of court practice conducted by Kovcheg shows that security forces may consider any such document subject to disclosure.
The obligation to report a residence permit arises only after entering Russia: you have 60 days to do so. The length of the visit doesn’t matter — even if you leave after just a few days, the deadline keeps running.
What’s changing in Armenia’s migration laws in 2026
Residence permits used to be issued ‘by eye.’ Starting November 1, there will be clear rules and quotas.
Before the reform, the process was simple: open a sole proprietorship, pay turnover tax for two to three months, and submit documents. There were no clear income requirements. Decisions, according to Andrey Frolov, were made “frankly by eye”: some people got a five-year residence permit, others got one for a year, and some were rejected.
Starting November 1, the rules will become stricter and more formal:
- for a residence permit based on a sole proprietorship, you’ll need to show turnover of at least one million drams in the 60 days before applying, or keep that amount in the business account;
- for an LLC, you’ll need to contribute two million drams to the charter capital — if the company doesn’t pay taxes for 180 days, the residence permit is revoked;
- it will no longer be possible to get a five-year residence permit right away: applicants will first be issued a one-year permit, then can apply for a five-year one after three years of continuous residence.
The government will also set annual quotas for each type of legalization. Once a limit is reached, the electronic system will automatically start rejecting new applicants. As of the end of September, the size of the quotas still hadn’t been announced, not even for 2026.
What else is changing? Documents will now have to be submitted online. Applications for the special 10-year residence permit, including for people of Armenian descent, will no longer be accepted (documents already issued will remain valid). A new investment-based residence permit will appear, though the minimum amount required for it hasn’t been named yet. Some specialized sources link the reform to Armenia’s negotiations with the European Union on visa liberalization.
You can still try to catch this departing train: applications from those who manage to submit documents before November 1 will be reviewed under the old rules. But open appointment slots ran out back in June, and the only hope now is people who booked a slot in a panic and are canceling it. Checking the system regularly gives you a chance of catching a freed-up slot, though the odds are slim.
For the smallest businesses, the reform could turn out to be good news
The main paradox of the changes involves “microbusiness” status, which had been a trap for those counting on a residence permit. Entrepreneurs under this status don’t pay turnover tax, so they can’t show a history of tax payments when submitting documents — a gap that, according to the Meduza source, usually led to rejection.
The new rules require not tax payments but a certain level of turnover or a certain amount in the business account, conditions that owners of “microbusiness” status can meet fairly easily. Frolov expects more entrepreneurs to pursue this path to legalization after November 1. The first results from reviews of such cases should appear as early as December and January.
There’s also a risk: under the new law, an entrepreneur can be stripped of their status for not paying taxes for six months. How that rule will apply to businesses with a zero rate is still unclear.
In other cases, the conditions for obtaining a residence permit will get worse: instead of a five-year permit right away, applicants will get a one-year permit and a three-year wait.
Moving family members will become harder, and the path to citizenship will take more than three years
The new migration rules change the terms for those planning to move with family. Here’s what that will look like:
- Family reunification isn’t possible under a one-year residence permit, an old legal norm that will remain in place even after the reform. Family members can be legalized under the five-year status, but obtaining that status will become harder. A spouse and children will be issued documents for only one year, which will have to be renewed annually. Previously, family members’ residence permits obtained through reunification were automatically tied to the validity period of the main applicant’s cards.
- Certain difficulties also arise with the residence permit based on an employment contract (a temporary residence permit, or work permit). That status functions much like a residence permit and can also be used to obtain documents for family. Russians, however, don’t need a work permit under Eurasian Economic Union rules, which creates a gap in the new regulations. It’s still unclear how migration authorities will handle such situations — only practice will show.
The reform is also affecting Russians’ long-term plans. Right now, people can apply for citizenship through residency after three years of living with legal status. Armenia’s Interior Ministry has proposed tightening those rules, but parliament hasn’t yet taken up the bill. Meanwhile, according to Kovcheg and other specialized communities, citizenship is rarely approved for people without Armenian roots, and applicants are often rejected without explanation.
Difficulties also await those counting on a passport for the whole family. In practice, the three years of legalization set out in the law will stretch into a much longer period for relatives, since the process factors in the time needed to process each intermediate status and the wait for a five-year residence permit. The actual time spent in the country before filing will end up exceeding three years.
Despite all the difficulties, Frolov is confident that the entire legalization process in Armenia can be completed independently, without “facilitators.” The only thing you’ll need in any case is money for government fees, accounting and financial services, as well as notarized translations. For handling the paperwork yourself, you can use publicly available spreadsheets maintained by the “Armenia: Residence Permits, Banks, Taxes” community, which collect current regulations, document lists, and breakdowns of nonstandard situations.

EU monitors 'very closely' suspected outbreak of pneumonic plague in Russia

Brussels and Washington are "closely" monitoring the evolution of a suspected plague outbreak in Siberia following the death of a lab worker.
The European Commission is monitoring the suspected outbreak of pneumonic plague in Siberia, Russia, "very closely" and stands ready to coordinate a response among member states if necessary.
The situation came to light following the death on 2 October of a lab worker of the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute who is said to have broken a test tube containing the plague pathogen. Her death was attributed to a "pneumonia of unknown aetiology".
The incident prompted precautionary measures in the region. Roughly 200 people who had been in touch with the lab worker have been placed under strict medical observation.
Russian authorities have so far refrained from confirming the existence of a plague outbreak, but the reports have heightened alarm worldwide.
"We are aware of the reports concerning the laboratory incident in Russia, seemingly involving a pathogen causing plague," a Commission spokesperson said on Monday.
"Public health is always a priority for us, so we are in touch with our experts from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control," the spokesperson added.
"We monitor very closely what is going on."
Pneumonic plague is a fast-moving lung infection caused by Yersinia pestis that spreads through infectious respiratory droplets during close contact. It has a high mortality rate but can be effectively treated with modern antibiotics.
"We are much better prepared for any pandemics" after COVID, the spokesperson said, noting that countries have antibiotic stocks at hand.
The Commission is using the World Health Organisation (WHO) to get updates from the Russian authorities, whose contacts with their European counterparts are severely restricted since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
For now, the executive does not intend to convene a dedicated meeting nor adopt emergency measures.
The response of Brussels mimics that of Washington.
The US State Department has said it is "closely" monitoring the situation and urged Moscow to provide "accurate" information "quickly and openly". The Commission also stressed the need for "timely and transparent reporting".
The plague has been absent in Europe for more than 50 years.

US gives Estonia 13 reconnaissance drones to boost border security
The United States has provided Estonia with 13 Skydio X10D drones to help the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) monitor hard-to-reach areas along the country's borders.
U.S. Ambassador to Estonia Roman Pipko and PPA Deputy Director General Veiko Kommusaar signed the transfer agreement for the 13 small unmanned aircraft systems (sUAS) at Tallinn's Miinisadam Naval Base on Monday.
Following the signing, PPA personnel conducted a demonstration flight for the officials.
Skydio X10D drones are small enough to be carried by hand, can be launched quickly and are equipped with both daytime and thermal cameras, allowing officials to monitor hard-to-reach areas around the clock, the U.S. Embassy said in a press release.
"These transfers represent both the U.S. commitment to Estonian security and the expertise that our Estonian partners bring to their work every day," Pipko said.
"I believe continued cooperation in this area will strengthen both of our borders and make our two countries safer," the ambassador continued, adding that U.S. border officials could learn from their Estonian counterparts.
The transfer of the drones was funded by the U.S. State Department's Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs (INL), with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) implementing the program.

Russia is seeking new routes for grain exports after a sharp collapse via the Black Sea — intelligence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:09:29 EEST
21:09:29 KST

Russia is seeking new routes for grain exports after a sharp collapse via the Black Sea — intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
Russian wheat shipments through the Black Sea have fallen sharply. Russia is redirecting cargoes to the Baltic, Murmansk, and China, but the routes are limited.
Russia is attempting to redirect its grain exports to the Baltic Sea, northern ports and China after a sharp reduction in shipments via the Black Sea. At the same time, the new routes have limited capacity, high transportation costs and other logistical obstacles. This was reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service, UNN writes.
In the second ten-day period of September, Russia shipped only 347,000 tonnes of wheat, compared with 1.3 million tonnes during the same period in 2025. Novorossiysk handled 72,500 tonnes, compared with 696,000 tonnes a year earlier
It is noted that Moscow is attempting to divert some cargoes to the Baltic, northern ports and the Far East. The Ultramar terminal in Ust-Luga has begun accepting grain. In September, applications for its delivery by rail amounted to approximately 260,000 tonnes. Even at maximum capacity, this route can handle about 500,000 tonnes per month. Russia's southern ports, by contrast, have annual capacity of more than 60 million tonnes. Last year, they handled nearly 90% of Russia's seaborne grain exports.
Russia is also attempting to ship grain through Murmansk. Russian Railways approved the first shipment — 40,000 tonnes from Stavropol Krai. The port is suitable for large vessels and operates year-round, but its distance from the main grain-producing regions makes the route excessively expensive. Additional costs are estimated at $18–25 per tonne ($720,000–$1 million for a 40,000-tonne shipment).
In the east, Russia is increasing shipments through China. The volume of the "New Overland Grain Corridor" rose from 2.3 million tonnes in 2024 to 5.8 million tonnes in 2025. For 2026, approximately 9 million tonnes are expected
However, according to the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, there are also strict restrictions here: railway infrastructure, terminal capacity, tariffs, phytosanitary requirements, including the absence of a phytosanitary protocol for Russian winter wheat, and Chinese quotas.
Russia cannot quickly create a replacement for the Black Sea system. This requires railways, elevators, transshipment facilities, insurance, vessels and permanent buyers. There is clearly insufficient capacity for this in the Baltic and Murmansk. The Chinese route also has its own limitations. Russia can distribute some of its grain across other routes. But it is unable to assemble a new system of the same scale from them, the intelligence service states.

WFP releases August report on Iran

Unknown Publisher

21:07:50 KST

WFP releases August report on Iran
TEHRAN – The World Food Program (WFP) has released a report, expounding on activities in Iran over the month of August.
In August, WFP food assistance reached 35,711 beneficiaries, including Afghan and Iraqi refugees, through a hybrid combination of in-kind food and cash-based transfers (CBT).
Refugees are assisted with a staple food basket, which includes fortified wheat flour (a ration of 9 kg per person, reduced from 12 Kg since the month of November 2025 due to funding shortfalls).
Under CBT modality, WFP continued to provide cash assistance to support the essential living costs of vulnerable refugees. The transfer is IRR 8 million (USD 5.2) for households headed by men and IRR 9 million (USD 5.8) for households headed by women.
By August, WFP Iran helped ease the financial burden associated with the gluten-free dietary needs of 60 refugee celiac patients from WFP’s beneficiaries by providing them with an extra cash amount of IRR 9.7 million (USD 6.3) per person as a replacement for their usual food entitlement.
WFP supported 409 refugees with disabilities across eleven settlements, each receiving an additional monthly cash support of IRR 3 million (USD 1.9), on top of their regular aid. Initially launched in two provinces, the initiative was gradually expanded to cover 11 settlements in Saveh, Semnan, Bani Najar, Sarvestan, Bezileh, Abazar, Rafsanjan, Bardsir, Jahrom, Meybod, and Torbat-e-jam.
The school feeding program and education incentives are suspended due to summer holidays, and will resumed with the start of the new academic year.
In August, WFP supported 27 income-generating projects in 18 settlements to improve economic resilience and self-sufficiency for 299 refugees, 38 percent of whom were women, and the remainder were youth. These activities included welding, tailoring, baking, farming, and other trades, providing opportunities for women and youth to develop practical skills, strengthen social connections, and actively engage with their communities.
As part of the response to the recent escalation, WFP started to provide cash transfers affected Iranian households, with the first round completed reaching 340 households, of which 327 were male-headed households.
Assistance was provided according to household size: IRR 210 million (USD 139.1) for households of one to three members; IRR 350 million (USD 231.9); for households of four to five members; IRR 420 million (USD 278.3) for households of six or more members.
In 2025, WFP sustained food assistance to some 33,300 vulnerable refugees living in 20 settlements across 13 provinces, including 404 refugees with disabilities (40 percent women) who received monthly cash top-ups. About 183 women and 190 men received WFP livelihood support.
WFP doubled cash transfer values since January 2025, safeguarding access to food amid price volatility and protecting the most vulnerable households.
Assistance remained uninterrupted, with targeted adjustments: wheat flour entitlements reduced from 12 kg to 9 kg (Nov-Dec) and school snacks paused (Oct-Dec) to stretch limited resources.
To promote girls’ education and reduce barriers to attendance, approximately 2,629 girl students received cash incentives as part of WFP’s commitment to empowering young women. Some 9,261 boys and girls and their teachers benefitted from WFP school snacks.
For more than four decades, the Islamic Republic of Iran has hosted Afghans fleeing conflict and hardship. In 2025, WFP remained essential to protecting the food security of vulnerable refugees residing in 20 settlements, where households rely on shelter, education and primary health care by the Government and other humanitarian actors, complemented by WFP’s monthly food assistance (through cash and in-kind modalities).
The program’s focus is on maintaining a dignified minimum basic needs while prioritizing those with the highest vulnerability, including households headed by women and persons with disabilities.
Operations are implemented in close collaboration and coordination with the Center for Alien and Foreign Immigrant Affairs (CAFIA), WFP’s primary governmental counterpart, and with International Non-Governmental Organizations (INGO) and UN agencies, mainly the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), to ensure coherent refugee support and referral pathways.
Despite a complex year, marked by economic volatility and temporary operational risks, WFP sustained core assistance to settlement refugees. To safeguard purchasing power, WFP increased cash-based transfer values by 100 percent in January 2025 following the recommendation of a settlement-specific Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB) assessment; this was complemented by a one-time cash top-up to cushion households during market instability and reduced income after the Iran-Israel 12-day conflict.
Targeted adjustments preserved program continuity: wheat flour entitlements were reduced from 12 kg to 9 kg per person for November-December, and the school snacks program was suspended for October to December.
These measures limit service disruptions while protecting life-saving transfers for the most vulnerable. Livelihood activities were scaled down given funding shortfalls and corporate efficiency measures, with WFP continuing to explore cost-effective, resilience-building options that can be re-activated as resources allow.
By December 2025, Iran continued to be one of the world’s largest refugee-hosting countries, sheltering approximately 2.5 million Afghans, including 773,000 individuals with official refugee status. Among them, around 35,000 critically vulnerable refugees reside in 20 settlements across 13 provinces.
MT/MG
