Acoustic tomography to assess hidden decay in Şişli’s century-old trees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:07:49 UTC
21:07:49 KST

Local experts view a color scan of an old trunk in Şişli, as sound waves map deep inner decay with strict care. (AA Photo)
An estimated 200 large and old trees in Istanbul’s Şişli district will undergo acoustic tomography to detect internal decay that may not be visible from the outside and assess their risk of falling, with authorities aiming to preserve them in place wherever possible.
The survey will cover trees in parks and gardens as well as those lining busy streets and located in areas with heavy pedestrian and vehicle traffic. Century-old trees at the Darülaceze complex, where residents spend much of their time, will also be examined.
In the first stage, experts will record each tree’s height, trunk structure, crown diameter, lean and branching pattern. Its approximate age will be established through previous records and, where necessary, by examining annual growth rings obtained with an increment borer. Some plane trees in the district are estimated to be more than 100 years old, with some reaching 130-150 years.
Acoustic tomography will then be used to examine the trees internally without cutting into or otherwise significantly damaging them. Sensors placed around the trunk transmit sound waves, whose travel speeds vary depending on whether they pass through healthy tissue, decayed areas or cavities. The measurements are used to create a three-dimensional picture of the trunk and identify where decay begins and how far it extends.
If decay is detected, measurements will be repeated at different heights to determine its full extent. However, the presence of decay alone will not automatically lead to a tree being removed. Experts will combine the tomography results with the tree’s physical characteristics and local wind data, including the strongest recorded winds, to calculate its potential risk of falling.
According to Istanbul University-Cerrahpaşa faculty member Serhun Sağlam, the project was prompted in part by the recent collapse of a large plane tree in the Teşvikiye neighborhood. Although the tree had appeared healthy, significant decay extending from its roots into the trunk was found after it fell.
“An old tree with decay does not necessarily mean we will cut it immediately,” Sağlam said, adding that pruning to reduce crown weight, cleaning visible cavities and installing mechanical supports could be used to lower the risk.
Removal would be considered only when a tree has reached an irreversible condition and can no longer be safely maintained. In such cases, it would be replaced with a new tree.

Türkiye condemns Israel’s renewed work in southern Syria

Türkiye on Oct. 5 condemned Israel’s resumption of excavation work along the so-called “Sufa 53” line in Syria’s southern Quneitra province.
In a written statement dated Oct. 5, the Turkish Foreign Ministry condemned what it described as Israel’s “attempts to create new faits accomplis in Syria.”
The ministry called on the international community to take “effective and decisive steps without delay” to end Israel’s expansionist policies, which it said were escalating regional tensions, and to ensure Israel’s withdrawal from occupied Syrian territory.
Ankara said it would continue to support Syria’s sovereignty, political unity and territorial integrity and take necessary steps in coordination with countries in the region.
Israeli forces resumed excavation work on Oct. 4 west of Al-Asha village in Quneitra as part of a project known as the “Sufa Line” or “Sufa 53,” according to the Syrian media.
Military vehicles and bulldozers were seen digging near the separation line with the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights and extending a route through rural areas from northern to southern Quneitra, reports said.
Israel began work on Sufa 53 in mid-2022 near Hadr in northern Quneitra before extending the project south through nearby areas.
Israel says the fortifications are intended to prevent possible attacks by Iran-backed armed groups.
Construction continued after the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in December 2024 and intensified as Israeli forces expanded their presence in and around the separation area in southern Syria.
Local residents have reported extensive damage to grazing land, trees and wild vegetation that provided an important source of income for families in the area.
Syria’s Foreign Ministry also condemned the renewed work on Oct. 4, describing it as a “flagrant breach” of the 1974 disengagement agreement, which established a buffer zone and separation of forces between the two states.

Bhutan’s ‘Mindfulness City’ Hides a Dark Reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:07:00 UTC
21:07:00 KST

On September 22, Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay of Bhutan stood at the podium at the United Nations General Assembly and made a direct sales pitch to foreign investors. “I stand before you today not as a prime minister, but as a salesman,” he told world leaders, openly seeking foreign investments to advance the concept of the Gelephu Mindfulness City (GMC).
For Chet Nath Timsina, Tobgay’s speech was deeply personal. Timsina was 20 when he and his family were evicted from southern Bhutan in the early 1990s after being coerced into signing a “voluntary migration form.” He resettled in New York in 2009 and has called the state home ever since.
Living just 250 miles from the United Nations headquarters, Timsina watched only half of Tobgay’s address. “I saw him just talk about GMC, which I feel is another way to disturb the living places of the Nepali-speaking population in Bhutan,” he said. The GMC is being developed across a vast tract of southern Bhutan, a region home to large Nepali-speaking communities, including thousands of families expelled in the early 1990s.
The Haunting Land Beneath the City
Tobgay told the U.N. that Bhutan wanted economic transformation without losing “what makes Bhutan, Bhutan.” But whose culture defines that identity?
In February 1989, under the “one nation, one people” policy, Bhutan removed Nepali from schools in the south. Human Rights Watch reported that ethnic Nepalis viewed such “Bhutanization” measures as attacks on their cultural identity, contributing to mass demonstrations.
Bhutan’s government then began to force the Nepali-speaking community out of the country entirely. In 1997, the United Nations’ refugee agency reported that about 92,000 Bhutanese refugees were living in seven camps in Nepal, plus another 15,000 living outside the camps. By 2015, more than 100,000 Bhutanese refugees were resettled in eight Western countries, the vast majority in the United States.
That history matters because the GMC is being presented not merely as an investment zone but also as a model for Bhutan’s future. The project’s promotional language combines ecological preservation, Buddhist values, technology, finance, and international investment, promising economic growth alongside environmental stewardship and human well-being.
Yet even today, Nepali remains absent from Bhutan’s southern schools. A project marketed as “mindful” development must also address the cultural rights and historical experience of the people whose homeland it is transforming.
The issue is not whether Bhutan wants to develop the south, nor whether foreign investors are interested in a new economic hub on the Bhutan-India border. Bhutan has every sovereign right to pursue economic development. The problem is that the language of a blank slate can obscure the history of the land on which the new city is being built.
The hard-sell to foreign investors also masks the reality of life in Bhutan today. The government continues to detain political prisoners, with international human rights organizations, alongside U.N. experts, documenting dozens of them being held for decades following unfair trials, arbitrary detention, and torture. The Global Campaign for the Release of Political Prisoners in Bhutan, a community-led advocacy organization, alongside other international watchdogs, has consistently raised deep concerns regarding the inhumane treatment of these prisoners.
Other international NGOs have also raised alarms as citizens and journalists continue to face criminal charges, fines, and jail terms under strict defamation and national security provisions for exercising freedom of expression online and offline. In recent months, The Diplomat exclusively reported how Bhutan has unjustly accepted dozens of former refugees deported from U.S. soil, only to leave them in limbo near the India-Nepal border, effectively rendering them stateless.
It was against this backdrop that Tobgay, during his recent speech, called for “judicial independence” for the GMC.
Why Bhutan Needs the GMC
For decades, Bhutan’s economy has depended heavily on hydropower and tourism. That model generated significant revenue and helped preserve the country’s distinctive environmental and cultural policies, but it did not produce enough private-sector employment for a growing, educated population. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) reported that youth unemployment stood at 17.8 percent in the third quarter of 2025 and identified outward emigration as a continuing structural concern. It has also warned that Bhutan needs to expand beyond hydropower and low-productivity sectors to create private-sector jobs and retain young workers.
The strain is especially visible in the growing number of young Bhutanese leaving the country in search of better opportunities. King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck even visited Australia, home to the largest Bhutanese community abroad, in October 2024. In Sydney, Canberra, and Perth, he addressed large crowds of expatriates, urging young professionals to acquire skills, save, and eventually return to help build the country’s future.
The GMC, in part, is designed to address that same challenge by creating new economic opportunities and attracting investment that could give young Bhutanese more reasons to stay or return.
The tiny Himalayan kingdom between India and China has deep economic and strategic ties to India, particularly in hydropower and trade. GMC allows Thimphu to widen its economic relationships while preserving those longstanding partnerships. At an Indian government foreign policy panel in June, participants highlighted the GMC’s ambitions to attract international investment while emphasizing the growing role of Indian private investment. In that sense, the GMC is part of Bhutan’s effort to expand the kingdom’s strategic autonomy in a volatile region.
The Forgotten Landowners
However, Bhutan is attempting to attract foreign investment to a contested, grief-soaked land – where dozens of Nepali-speaking citizens were tortured and killed in uprisings and countless others died in exile without reclaiming their homes. The GMC project thus risks turning unresolved history into someone else’s investment opportunity.
Currently based in Colorado, Hari Prashad Adhikari, a former National Assembly member from the GMC-affected area, was among thousands whose properties were seized by the regime before their eviction. In his book, “Ethnic Cleansing in Bhutan: A Stigma to 21st Century,” he recounted how his family lost their homes, farmland, and orchards. He valued his family’s lost property, business assets, and foregone income at 29.4 million Bhutanese ngultrum in 1990 prices, equivalent to roughly 204 million ngultrum (about $2.1 million at current exchange rates), using the IMF’s projected 2026 inflation rate.
While property claims from the past remain legally and politically complex, their existence poses a tangible risk for international investors. Capital cannot flow smoothly into a state developing lands once subject to mass displacement without transparent mechanisms to address the claims of those who were forced to leave.   
Now living in Adelaide, Australia, 76-year-old Bhanu Adhikari said he spent two years in prison after being accused of violence against the government following protests in the early 1990s. For a little over two decades, he called the very land now designated for GMC his home. While he was away, he says, corrupt officials forged documents to seize his family’s seven acres of fertile land and other properties for a fabricated price of just 51,000 ngultrum, roughly $500. His mother-in-law, Beni Maya Rai, who died in Adelaide in 2025 at the age of 91, had long wished to return to her ancestral land, carrying memories of the home she had lost. 
For Adhikari, the GMC’s promise of a peaceful future cannot erase that history.
“If foreign investors are involved in the GMC project, we will try to seek legal counsel to hold them accountable and pursue compensation for the land the Bhutanese government looted from us,” he said.
From the Beldangi refugee camp in Jhapa, Nepal, where still close to 7,000 refugees continue to live awaiting a durable solution, Tilak Rai as the chairperson of the Bhutanese Refugee Representative Repatriation Committee (BRRRC), views the mega-project as a direct continuation of past injustices.
Calling the GMC an attempt to purify the regime’s atrocities against the Nepali-speaking population, Rai noted that even those currently living in the affected area are denied proper compensation and silenced by fear of retribution.
“The BRRRC appeals to the international community to prevent Bhutan from turning seized ancestral land into a high-tech façade designed to erase our history,” he said.
Rai’s concerns from across the border are now being echoed by people who still live on the affected land in Bhutan. The landscape there is already undergoing a rapid, state-directed overhaul. Recent months have brought intensive land leveling, corporate partnership pacts and construction progress across the special administrative zone, anchored by heavy development at the Gelephu International Airport site in Samtenling, Sarpang.
The airport will affect 552 landowners across roughly 1,400 acres, with authorities offering replacement land, tokenization, or monetary compensation. But affected residents have raised concerns over land fragmentation, the loss of land across generations, and whether they can remain in Sarpang. In an earlier expansion of the airport, 11 landowners appealed their replacement-land allocations, expressing dissatisfaction with the substitute plots.
Meanwhile, authorities have invited proposals for a 256-unit housing project intended primarily for relocated families. The concerns are therefore not confined to those who were driven from southern Bhutan decades ago; people who remain on the land today are also confronting questions of compensation, relocation and what development will mean for their homes and livelihoods. As the airport moves toward its 2029 target, those questions remain central to the project’s transformation.  
What Investors Need to Know 
The GMC’s economic promise depends on international credibility, yet the IMF has already identified significant fiscal and financial risks associated with the project. Its independent tax regime could affect Bhutan’s national tax base, while the legal relationship between the GMC and the rest of the country still requires clarification in areas including labor, goods, and capital mobility.
Addressing the refugee question would not require Bhutan to halt economic development in the south. Economic modernization and historical reckoning can proceed together. Bhutan could establish an accessible historical record of the southern districts affected by the displacement of the 1990s, create a transparent process for documenting property claims and determining which claims have a legal basis, and incorporate the history of the region into the GMC’s own cultural and educational institutions rather than presenting the area as an untouched landscape awaiting transformation. 
The country’s leaders have invited investors to become co-founders of a new city. That invitation comes with a responsibility on both sides. Investors should ask not only what industries the GMC will create, what tax incentives it will offer, or what returns it might generate. They should also ask what kind of historical and institutional framework they are entering.
Timsina and others in the diaspora see a cruel repetition unfolding in real time: “Watching Mr. Tobgay talk about building a future on the land I was evicted from felt like opening an old wound that never truly healed for me and my family.” 
Although neither of us originally came from the GMC-affected area, our families originally lived not that far from that region. We were children when our families were forced out of Bhutan, and we grew up in exile carrying memories of a home we barely knew. We are not arguing against development or investment in the south. But a city promoted to the world as “mindful” cannot claim a new beginning while leaving the people displaced from this land and the circumstances of their displacement outside the story.
A decade from now, the GMC may be fully operational, drawing thousands of visitors and investors, and most people may know little about the circumstances that preceded its construction.
Many of those forced from southern Bhutan have since rebuilt their lives elsewhere and become citizens of other countries, but they still cannot return, even as visitors. Our children will grow up with memories of Bhutan that come largely from the stories we tell them, and as they grow older, they will have the opportunity to look into that history for themselves.
Whatever the GMC becomes, the story of how this land was taken from those who once called it home will, at the very least, remain part of what we pass on to them. For investors in the project, that history may come with a cost, too.

Kosovo Moves To Curb Hague Tribunal Powers On Eve Of Deadline To Elect New President
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:06:51 UTC
21:06:51 KST

PRISTINA -- Police fired tear gas at protesters outside Kosovo's parliament on the evening of October 5 as a dispute over proposed restrictions on a Hague-based war crimes court became entangled with a last-minute political standoff over electing the country's next president.
Some protesters threw fireworks and glass bottles toward the parliament and the police as demonstrators demanded lawmakers complete passage of legislation that would sharply restrict the jurisdiction of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.
Six officers were injured and 11 civilians sought medical attention during the protests. Three protesters were taken to a police station for further judicial processing.
Parliament approved the bill in a first reading earlier on October 5, with all 91 participating lawmakers voting in favor. But a second reading and final vote remained uncertain after the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) tied its support for electing a president to passage of the legislation, while Prime Minister Albin Kurti's ruling Vetevendosje party insisted the president should be elected first.
Kurti and PDK leader Bedri Hamza met on October 5 in an attempt to break the impasse, but no agreement was announced. At around 7 p.m., Vetevendosje lawmakers were seen leaving parliament.
The standoff comes just hours before an October 6 constitutional deadline to elect a president. Failure to do so would trigger parliament's dissolution and fresh parliamentary elections.
Several hundred supporters of the Kosovo Liberation Army -- including veterans of the former guerrilla force -- had gathered outside parliament earlier in the day and said they would not leave until the legislation was fully approved.
The PDK proposed the changes following last month's war crimes convictions of four former KLA leaders, including former President Hashim Thaci.
Kurti backed the initiative despite describing the proposed changes as rushed and saying there had been little time to analyze them. He said the appeals process remained the route to challenging the convictions and called for a coordinated national strategy.
The second opposition party, the Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK), which has 18 seats in the 120-seat parliament, said it could not support the initiative. Lawmaker Jehona Lushaku-Sadriu warned that parliamentary approval would not guarantee implementation and that the changes might have no legal effect.
Ramush Haradinaj of the opposition Alliance for the Future of Kosovo (AAK) called for a second reading later the same day. The bill must undergo detailed committee scrutiny before a second reading, although parliamentary rules allow procedural deadlines to be waived under certain conditions.
The proposals would cap prison sentences at 15 years, allow appeals to Kosovo's Supreme Court, require sentences to be served in Kosovo, and make those convicted eligible for presidential pardons.
The bill would also limit the court's jurisdiction to offenses mentioned in a 2011 Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe report, which addressed allegations including postwar organ trafficking. It would also narrow the period covered by the court from January 1998–December 2000 to July 1, 1999–December 2000, excluding the wartime period.
Legal experts warn, however, that parliamentary approval alone would not establish whether the changes could take effect.
The PDK submitted the bill on September 21, five days after the court sentenced former President Hashim Thaci and former parliamentary speaker Jakup Krasniqi to 25 years in prison each, former parliamentary speaker Kadri Veseli to 18 years, and Rexhep Selimi to 13 years.
All four were convicted of war crimes and acquitted of crimes against humanity. Their defense teams have announced plans to appeal.
PDK leader Bedri Hamza says the initiative aims to strengthen oversight and accountability rather than dismantle the court. Kosovo's government cleared the bill to proceed on October 2.
The dispute over the legislation has complicated an already difficult effort to secure the votes needed to elect a president.
Hamza has said the PDK, which holds 22 seats, is prepared to provide the necessary votes for the presidential process once parliament completes approval of the court legislation. Vetevendosje, by contrast, wants the presidential vote to take place first.
Kurti had met separately with Hamza and LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku over the weekend in an effort to find a way forward before holding another meeting with Hamza on October 5.
A presidential candidate needs 80 votes in the first two rounds or 61 in a third. At least 80 lawmakers must participate for the election to proceed.
Kurti's Vetevendosje holds 53 seats, while his government was elected with 62 votes. PDK participation could provide the numbers needed to hold the presidential vote.
A first-reading vote would not complete the legislative process; committee scrutiny and a second reading would still follow. Parliament can waive procedural deadlines under certain conditions.
Ehat Miftaraj, director of the Kosovo Law Institute, told RFE/RL in reporting published on September 30 that lawmakers may propose amendments but must respect Kosovo's international commitments.
These include a commitment to consult the European Union on legislative changes affecting the court's mandate or related proceedings and to allow its work to continue until relevant investigations and proceedings are completed.
Visiting Pristina on October 1, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said decisions on legislative changes were for Kosovo to make but judicial independence must be guaranteed. She said the court's mandate must be fully respected and stressed the verdict concerned individual responsibility, not Kosovo's resistance.
The US State Department had not responded by publication to RFE/RL's request for comment.
Miftaraj said amendments concerning the court could face review by the Specialist Chamber of the Constitutional Court in The Hague.
The Specialist Chambers told RFE/RL for the September 30 report that they had not been consulted. They declined to comment on political initiatives, saying they remained focused on ensuring fair, impartial, and secure trials.

Europe’s Proposed Defense Union Would Put Ukraine at Its Core
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:03:34 UTC
21:03:34 KST

A group of Members of the European Parliament (MEO) is pushing for the creation of a European Defense Union that would work closely with NATO while giving European countries greater capacity to defend themselves independently, with Ukraine envisioned as a key partner.
MEP Reinier van Lanschot, one of the initiative’s proponents, outlined the proposal in a comment to Ukrinform news agency.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The proposal comes as Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine and uncertainty over US security policy have fueled calls for greater European defense capabilities, van Lanschot said.
“We have come to the conclusion that in the face of Russia’s fierce war of aggression and the unreliability of the United States, Europe must be able to defend itself independently,” he said.
He added that they still believed NATO was of immense value and wanted to strengthen the Alliance, but that Europe must also be capable of autonomous defense.
The proposed defense union would operate within NATO while retaining the ability to act independently if NATO’s collective-defense mechanism under Article 5 were not invoked, according to van Lanschot.
He described the concept as “separable but not separate” from NATO, meaning the European structure would remain integrated with the alliance while maintaining its own capabilities.
Ukraine envisioned as key defense partner
Van Lanschot said Ukraine should play a central role in the proposed European security architecture, alongside other non-EU partners such as Norway and the UK.
Guterres’s Successor Will Need Russia’s Blessing
“A European Defense Union can function effectively only if our most important partners – such as Norway, the United Kingdom, and Ukraine – are involved. Ukraine currently has the strongest army in Europe and is the most technologically advanced,” he said.
According to van Lanschot, European countries’ perception of Ukraine has changed significantly since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
He said the EU’s approach had shifted over the past five years, from initially focusing on helping Ukraine withstand the war to recognizing that “we now need Ukraine’s help” to become more technologically advanced and stronger itself.
“Ukraine as a partner has a lot to offer,” the MEP added.
The proposal would also allow Ukrainian military personnel to voluntarily participate in a future European Rapid Reaction Force, according to van Lanschot.
Proposed European security structure
The proposed union would include six main components: a European Security Council, a European Military Staff, a European Military Intelligence Center, a European Strategic Support Unit, a European Rapid Reaction Force, and a European deterrence mechanism based on Article 42.7 of the Treaty on European Union, which provides for mutual assistance among EU member states.
The European Security Council would serve as the union’s main political decision-making body. Its decisions would be made by qualified majority rather than unanimity, according to the proposal, in an effort to avoid the deadlocks that have repeatedly affected EU foreign and security policy.
The proposed structure would also be designed to complement rather than replace NATO.
The initiative comes as the EU debates how to strengthen its own defense capabilities and reduce its dependence on the US.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said during her State of the Union address last month that Europe needs its own mechanism for urgent consultations when an EU member faces a security threat, modeled on Article 4 of the NATO treaty.
She also proposed establishing a European Security Council that would include Ukraine.

€4 million apartment sale highlights Tallinn's changing housing market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:03:00 UTC
21:03:00 KST

€4 million apartment sale highlights Tallinn's changing housing market
Tallinn's housing market is seeing growing demand for higher-quality homes and luxury properties, even as developers face rising inventories and questions about the city's future housing needs.
The most expensive apartment in Estonia was sold this summer in Kalamaja's first high-rise. An entire floor changed hands for nearly €4 million. The property has 340 square meters of living space and a terrace almost as large, offering views of the sea and Tallinn's Old Town when the weather is clear.
Real estate analyst Tõnu Toompark said there has recently been more activity in the luxury property market, but deals like this remain rare.
"An apartment transaction worth more than €1 million is still something very exceptional, but it happens every month. Broadly speaking, 70 percent of apartments under development, or even slightly more, are two- and three-room apartments," Toompark said.
Most buyers are not looking for an entire floor. A living room and a couple of bedrooms would be enough. But even the price tag on a three-room apartment can take the breath away of someone earning the average salary.
New developments in Tallinn are asking more than €5,000 per square meter. A more affordable 85-square-meter, three-room apartment in the Uus-Volta quarter is available for €460,000. Want to live one floor higher? An apartment of the same size will set you back nearly half a million euros.
A parking space costs an additional €25,000 and a storage unit another €8,000. Hopefully, your pockets are not completely empty by then because the home still needs to be furnished.
Uku Tint, development director at Endover, said the company has the highest sales turnover among Tallinn developers this year, although its inventory of apartments still awaiting buyers has also grown.
"Our customer segment consists of people changing homes — in other words, they already have a home and are moving to a newer one in a better area, meaning people's expectations have risen," Tint said.
Someone earning the average salary who does not already own a home to sell should instead look for a family apartment in Mustamäe or Lasnamäe, Tint said. Or perhaps outside Tallinn altogether, in developments springing up on fields where apartments are more affordable.
According to Reigo Randmets, CEO and owner of real estate developer Reterra, the rule of thumb is that on the fields of Rae Municipality you can get one more room than at Hipodroomi in Tallinn.
Around 1,000 apartments, a kindergarten and a commercial quarter are planned for Hipodroomi. Randmets said people buying apartments today are more likely to be purchasing a home for themselves rather than a property to rent out. The area surrounding the building is also playing an increasingly important role in their choice.
"People belong above ground, while we direct cars underground or away from the buildings. People don't want to live in a parking lot and send their children there to play," Randmets said.
Tint added that customers have become very knowledgeable.
"They're looking for quality. Awareness has also increased about things like indoor climate. What should the humidity level in a room be? Is it too low or too high? What about ventilation — is the air fresh enough? But in addition to quality, it's the same story when you go outside: you want to be able to walk without getting hit by a car, you want a green environment and you want a gym nearby," Tint said.
The city also wants families with children to move into new developments and requires apartments of different sizes. To reduce construction costs, developers are allowed to build fewer expensive parking spaces. Ultimately, however, the developer still determines the price of a home.
Kristi Grišakov, head of the planning and architecture service at the Tallinn Urban Planning Department, said large apartments are often marketed in practice as luxury products and are therefore more expensive.
Real estate analyst Tõnu Toompark said the picture is not as bleak as it may seem when browsing real estate listings. Wages have recently risen faster than apartment prices.
"If I look at how many average monthly salaries I have to pay today for a comparable two-room apartment in Mustamäe or Haabersti and how many I had to pay 10 years ago, it's almost exactly the same. There is clearly a perception in the market that prices are too high, but the reality — the numbers — doesn't support that," Toompark said.
As new developments rise across the city, bank buildings in central Tallinn are looking for a new purpose. SEB is moving its headquarters closer to the harbor, LHV's new office is being built next to its old one and Swedbank has moved from Liivalaia tänav to Arter. Developers are interested in whether buildings where home loans were once issued could one day become homes themselves.
"SEB is not yet under active consideration. It's such an unusual building that adapting it for residential use will certainly be interesting, not to mention the question of how the surrounding area would function as a residential environment. The Swedbank building is certainly one of the more difficult cases because of noise. Is it even possible to create residential units there or would that require a very extensive reconstruction of the building itself? At the same time, educational institutions and public transportation are all available there. But because the area has been used as a workplace, bringing a residential feel and greenery there will certainly be a challenge," Grišakov said.
But there is no avoiding an uncomfortable question: Will there be enough people to live in all these homes in the future?
"What we're seeing now is that the population trend itself is also undergoing a major shift. If Tallinn's population, for example, no longer grows very significantly and neither does Estonia's population and we can also see from demographic trends that younger generations are no longer having children at the same rate, then it makes even more sense to ask: Who are we building homes for, and how many should we build?" Grišakov said.

How everyday technology is helping wounded IDF veterans reclaim independence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:01:44 UTC
21:01:44 KST

Three years after October 7, a different kind of reality unfolds away from the headlines. For thousands of wounded soldiers and civilians, recovery is a long and demanding process that requires persistence, support and hard work every day.
While there are no quick fixes, the right intervention can have an immediate and meaningful impact. Through initiatives led by the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee (JDC) and its partners, innovative approaches are opening new possibilities for rehabilitation and helping people focus more fully on recovery.
When Adi Timor pushes himself too hard during a workout, the consequences are immediate. If his prosthetic leg does not sit properly for even half a mile, he can spend the next two days unable to walk. That uncertainty is part of his life now. But so is running.
Before he was wounded in the war, Adi was a reserve officer and fitness trainer preparing for his first marathon. Today, as he works his way toward achieving his rehabilitation goal of running again, some of the technology helping him is surprisingly ordinary: smart lighting, automated shutters, a voice assistant, a robot vacuum and a high chair he can lean on while cooking or washing dishes.
These adaptations make his home manageable enough that he can push himself harder in training, knowing he will be able to still function independently afterward. “The solutions in my apartment give me a safety net,” he said. “They allow me to train at a level that pushes the boundary and really see what I’m capable of.”
The principle of improving daily independence and restoring a sense of control is at the heart of Tech for Heroes, a program developed by JDC, Beit Issie Shapiro and Restart Global. 
JDC has worked for more than a century in Israel to address social challenges and expand opportunities for the country’s most vulnerable people.
Since the launch of Tech for Heroes ten months into the war, 428 wounded people, including soldiers and victims of terror attacks, have received 1,280 technology solutions tailored to help them navigate daily life more independently at home, in self-care, at work or school and in the world around them. 
The devices range from smart-home systems and noise-filtering headphones to kitchen appliances and air purifiers, helping people who were injured physically or emotionally function more independently by addressing specific challenges in their daily lives.
‘Five minutes with my daughter is a whole world’
Amir’s path home looked very different. After October 7, he joined ZAKA teams helping recover the bodies of people murdered at the Nova festival site, in kibbutzim and at military bases in southern Israel. The work continued for months, including assisting archaeologists and accompanying remains for burial. Then came an instruction for which, he said, no one could really prepare him: We’re done - Go home.
For the first six months, he could not hold his young daughter. The barrier was not physical. It was smell. Babies have a distinctive scent, he explained, but his mind had begun transforming ordinary smells into those connected to what he had encountered while recovering bodies. “At its worst, it was the smell of burned flesh,” Amir said. “That is a smell you never forget. It is the worst smell there is.”
When Tech for Heroes became involved, a specially trained occupational therapist from the program spent time learning from Amir and his wife about the challenges they were facing. At the time, Amir was avoiding family interactions, unable to take part in cooking or meals and spending most of his days alone on the balcony coping with his PTSD symptoms.  
Among the solutions the Tech for Heroes team identified was an air purifier and an electric indoor grill. Cooking smells had become triggers for Amir, and the combination between the two appliances helps clear odors quickly enough that he no longer has to retreat while his family prepares or eats food. “It removes the effect of the smells from the apartment, which means I don’t have to wait several hours after they eat,” he said. “I can even sit with them at the table, be with my kids, even if I’m not eating and have no appetite, or I can sit in front of the television while my wife cooks.”
“Being able to hold my daughter for five minutes is a whole world.”
Amir’s experience is one of thousands emerging from the war’s unprecedented rehabilitation needs. According to the Defense Ministry Rehabilitation Department, more than 25,000 newly wounded men and women entered the rehabilitation system between Oct. 7, 2023, and July 2, 2026, with 65% coping with psychological distress or PTSD. Many are young reservists whose injuries continue to affect daily life for them and their families long after they return home.
A shattered face, and a reason to leave the room
Oren, whose name has been changed to protect his privacy, was injured when a rocket-propelled grenade struck the military vehicle he was in during the war. His face was severely damaged by the blast and shrapnel, and a fellow crew member was killed next to him. “When I came back from the hospital, I suddenly realized that things were not working for me, not physically and not emotionally,” he said.
He struggled to sleep and often retreated to his room when his children came home. Brushing his teeth became difficult because parts of his mouth had lost sensation. Household chores consumed energy he did not have, and eating was difficult because chewing could be painful.
A specialized electric toothbrush helped improve Oren’s oral hygiene, while kitchen appliances such as a blender and an electric grill made preparing and eating food easier. He also received a robot vacuum cleaner that helped him participate in household routines. 
Some of the biggest effects came indirectly. Because the robotic cleaner runs on a schedule, the floor has to be cleared first. Aligning his schedule with the robotic cleaner helped him get out of bed and become active like nothing else managed to do. Easier meal preparation also made it more likely that he would sit at the table with his family. 
“And once you are sitting together, conversations begin: ‘How are you? How was your day? How was school? How was kindergarten?’” He said. “That has a much broader impact on the family, because otherwise I might simply stay in my room.”
The technology is only the starting point
According to findings from the Tech for Heroes impact study, participants reported that their sense of independence increased from 80% to 91% after six months of using the technology solutions. By the second survey wave, 97% reported improved quality of life, and 77% said the technology enabled them to do things they had been unable to do since being wounded. 
While the findings highlight the value of expert guidance in selecting technological solutions tailored to individual needs, rehabilitation professionals note that the work does not end with providing a device.
Anat Shpilberg, a psychologist who heads an intensive rehabilitation program for people coping with PTSD at the Rehovot branch of the National Institute for Neuropsychological Rehabilitation, said technology can also affect therapy. After referring several participants to Tech for Heroes, she said “The technology brought emotional and psychological issues to the surface that might otherwise have taken much longer to emerge, if at all."
Noise-filtering headphones may make public transportation possible again for someone whose sensitivity to noise has made a bus or train unbearable. Devices designed to regulate breathing and engage several senses, can help some patients ground themselves as anxiety surfaces. “What helps one person will not necessarily help another, so that personalization is essential,” Shpilberg said. “Patients need to feel that someone sees them, understands them and validates the daily challenges they are experiencing.”
That personalization is built into Tech for Heroes. Participants complete a questionnaire and meet with an occupational therapist who specializes in adapting technology. During the process, they identify challenges in daily life and determine which technologies can best address them, adjusting solutions as needs change. 
“Behind every statistic is a wounded servicemember working to reclaim independence and rebuild meaningful daily life. We’ve learned how simple, accessible technology can make a difference, even when the challenges are complex.” said Efrat Shaprut, director of JDC's Division for Independent Living for People with Disabilities, Resilience and Mental Health.
“This unique model brings together professional expertise, personalized solutions, and compassionate human support. Recovering from injuries that affect both physical and mental health requires an approach that is sensitive, flexible, and centered on the individual. There are no shortcuts in recovery, yet technology can profoundly support the process." 
‘I know I can function in my own home’
For Adi, independence does not mean pretending his leg injury no longer matters. It means knowing that on a bad day, when his body has reached its limit, his home will not become one more obstacle. “What mattered most to me was being independent and not dependent on other people,” he said. “I know that even if I’m tired from physical therapy or training, I can still manage my own home.”
He is now testing how far he can go again: running, surfing, studying and rebuilding the life he envisioned before he was wounded.
For Amir, progress can mean sitting at the table while his family eats. For Oren, it can mean getting out of bed and creating a daily routine. The technology itself may be no more remarkable than a smart light switch, a kitchen appliance, an air filter or a high chair. What it is helping restore is much larger: The ability to take control over their own lives.

Flydubai incident fuels row over Israeli security failures
Unknown

2026-10-05

Breadcrumb
Flydubai incident fuels political row over Israeli security failures
A major security and political row has erupted in Israel over the flydubai incident, as questions mount over how an Omani co-pilot accused of plotting to crash the passenger jet was repeatedly allowed to fly into the country despite reported warnings over weaknesses in the screening of foreign air crews.
The controversy has widened beyond Israel's security agencies and transport ministry, with opposition politicians accusing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government of presiding over another serious security failure and then seeking to turn the narrowly avoided disaster into political capital.
Hamam al-Hammami, the Omani co-pilot accused of attacking the Indian captain of flydubai flight FZ1073 on 30 September, allegedly told investigators that he had planned to crash the aircraft into Israel's Ben Gurion Airport, according to Israeli reports.
Other accounts, however, have offered different versions of his alleged plans. Israeli news site Ynet reported that Hammami intended to target a US military base in Jordan if he was unable to reach Ben Gurion Airport.
The investigation remains ongoing and the precise motive and intended target have not been independently established.
A picture emerging from reports over the weekend portrayed Hammami as a possible lone actor who had allegedly spent months planning an attack, with no evidence so far publicly establishing that he acted on behalf of an armed organisation or foreign government.
Some Israeli reports claimed Hammami had considered carrying out an attack on previous flights and used earlier journeys to Tel Aviv to gather information. One report alleged that he had considered crashing an aircraft during a flight to Israel in July but abandoned the plan because of his friendship with a crew member.
Warnings over security gaps
The incident has instead intensified scrutiny of apparent gaps in Israel's own aviation security arrangements.
Haaretz reported that Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency had repeatedly warned the transport ministry in recent years about weaknesses in the monitoring of foreign flight crews and passengers.
Sources involved in securing flights to Israel told the newspaper that Shin Bet had previously recommended transferring responsibility for screening foreign airlines and their passengers to Israel's civil aviation authorities.
Israel's National Security Council reportedly made a similar recommendation last year, but the transport ministry opposed the move and retained control over screening and oversight.
A 2024 Israeli state comptroller report examining the years 2022 and 2023 had also identified serious shortcomings in aviation security, including arrangements covering aircraft operated by foreign airlines.
Although the transport ministry formally bears responsibility, according to Israeli media reports, both Shin Bet and Mossad were aware of difficulties facing the ministry's security division but did not intervene.
Yedioth Ahronoth reported that the incident had exposed a fundamental question for which Israeli authorities still appeared to have no clear answer on who was actually responsible for protecting passengers on foreign flights bound for Israel.
Haaretz also reported that none of the transport ministry, Shin Bet or Mossad had taken responsibility for failing to examine information previously supplied about the Omani co-pilot, despite all three having legal access to databases containing information supplied by airlines.
Netanyahu's office said on Sunday, four days after the incident, that the prime minister had instructed National Security Council chief Shmuel Ben Ezra to appoint an official to conduct a comprehensive review of security arrangements for foreign civilian aviation travelling to Israel.
The announcement came despite the National Security Council having already examined the issue last year.
Netanyahu exploiting incident ahead of elections
The security controversy has also developed into a bitter political dispute after Netanyahu sought to highlight the actions of Israeli passengers who intervened after the Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door.
Netanyahu met passengers involved in the incident and released footage of the encounter, while presenting the episode as an example of "Israeli heroism" and suggesting that warnings he had issued shortly before the incident demonstrated his awareness of looming security threats.
His opponents accused him of attempting to claim political credit for the prevention of a disaster that they said exposed failures under his own government.
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, said Netanyahu's government had "learned nothing from October 7", arguing that Transport Minister Miri Regev should resign or be dismissed.
Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, described the incident as evidence of what he called the government's broader failures and accused Netanyahu and his ministers of sacrificing public safety for political interests.
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett was similarly scathing.
"Instead of investigating and drawing lessons to prevent the next disaster, Netanyahu and Miri Regev are celebrating the failure that happened on their watch," Bennett remarked.
He drew a direct comparison with the failures surrounding the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks, accusing Netanyahu and his ministers of complacency and neglecting security.
Avigdor Lieberman, leader of Yisrael Beiteinu, placed responsibility on Shin Bet and called for its chief, David Zini, to resign.
"The culture Netanyahu has created, according to which no one is responsible for failures while successes always have one father named Bibi, must stop," Lieberman said.
Israeli commentators draw October 7 parallels
The criticism has extended into the Israeli press, where several prominent commentators have compared the failures exposed by the flydubai incident with those preceding the 7 October attacks.
Writing in Haaretz, military analyst Amos Harel said Netanyahu had quickly embraced the "heroes" of the incident and attempted to associate himself with the successful prevention of the alleged attack.
Netanyahu and sympathetic Israeli media outlets have pointed to remarks he made at Tel Nof airbase the previous day, when he warned of attempts by Israel's enemies to disrupt the country's elections.
Harel, however, wrote that subsequent checks with security agencies showed there had been no specific intelligence warning concerning such a plot.
Instead, he said, officials had been assessing a combination of broader risks, including the election period, Jewish holidays, the anniversary of the 7 October attacks and increased general warnings about possible attacks on Israelis abroad.
Harel argued that the incident required a comprehensive investigation, accountability for the security failures and immediate action to close existing gaps.
Yedioth Ahronoth columnist Nahum Barnea also compared the episode with 7 October, pointing to what he described as the same pattern of institutional negligence before a crisis, civilians acting decisively when disaster struck, and political leaders subsequently avoiding responsibility.
"The similarity between the two disasters, the one that happened and the one that was prevented, sends chills down the spine," Barnea wrote.

Uncrewed vessel completes remote subsea ROV trials
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:00:44 BST
21:00:44 KST

ACUA Ocean and Forssea Robotics have completed a three-week trial in Plymouth integrating a remotely operated underwater vehicle with an uncrewed surface vessel, demonstrating more than 40 remotely controlled deployments from shore, according to the companies.
The trials paired Forssea Robotics’ 170kg ARGOS remotely operated vehicle, or ROV, with ACUA Ocean’s USV Pioneer, using a Sonardyne Mini-Ranger 2 ultra-short baseline positioning system to track the underwater vehicle.
All launches, dives and recoveries were commanded remotely from shore, with the combined system controlled from ACUA Ocean’s Remote Operations Centre at Turnchapel Wharf in Plymouth. Forssea personnel simultaneously supervised operations from the company’s headquarters in Sète, France.
The programme was carried out under a contract with the European Space Agency and was intended to test whether inspection, survey and light-intervention tasks normally supported by crewed vessels could instead be conducted using an uncrewed surface platform.
More than 40 ROV deployments were completed during the programme, including eight launch-and-recovery cycles during a single day. The companies said ARGOS reached and inspected the seabed in water deeper than 20 metres while operating with up to 35 metres of tether.
Trials also included inspection work on the wreck of the Poulmic, a seabed feature and a concrete target block in Cawsand Bay, with the ROV locating and filming the targets.
ACUA and Forssea said operations were conducted in one-metre waves with winds averaging 18 knots and gusting between 20 and 30 knots. The companies also reported an operation south of Plymouth Breakwater in waves reaching around two metres, which they said had no effect on the ROV.
The positioning arrangement used a Sonardyne Mini-Ranger 2 USBL system mounted aboard Pioneer to track a WSM6+ transponder carried by ARGOS. Both manual station keeping and dynamic positioning were used to keep the surface vessel and ROV in position during the trials.
A live ROV dive was also streamed to Eckernförde in Germany for the Cyber Innovation Hub of the Bundeswehr, demonstrating how the underwater system could be monitored remotely from another country while being operated from the UK.
According to a joint news update from ACUA Ocean and Forssea Robotics, ACUA Ocean CEO Neil Tinmouth said: “These trials prove we can open a weather window that conventional crewed vessels cannot work in, giving operators a wider weather window for inspection campaigns. Just as importantly, running inspection campaigns from an uncrewed surface vessel takes significant cost out of the work – fewer support vessels, fewer people offshore and far less weather-related downtime.”
The companies are targeting offshore energy operators, subsea inspection and maintenance providers, critical infrastructure operators and survey organisations with the combined system.
ACUA Ocean describes Pioneer as an uncrewed surface vessel designed to provide endurance and seakeeping for remote maritime operations, while Forssea’s ARGOS is a compact ROV intended for inspection, survey and light-intervention work. Forssea supplied the underwater vehicle with a dedicated integration kit for use aboard the USV, allowing the two systems to operate as a single remotely supervised package. The ROV can also carry different payloads depending on the inspection or survey task being undertaken.
Gautier Dreyfus, CEO of Forssea Robotics, said: “All of us at Forssea are hugely proud of this milestone and impressed by Pioneer’s sea-state capabilities. Seeing how smoothly the ROV integration and the multiple launch-and-recovery sequences went over the past few weeks was hugely satisfying. My congratulations to the ACUA engineering teams – we are excited to see what comes next.”
The work forms part of a wider industry effort to reduce the requirement for large crewed support vessels during routine subsea inspection and monitoring. Uncrewed surface vessels can carry sensors or deploy underwater systems while operators remain ashore, reducing the number of personnel required at sea.
ACUA and Forssea said the configuration is intended for work around offshore wind farms, pipelines and other subsea infrastructure, where repeat inspection and monitoring missions can require vessels to remain on station for extended periods.
During the Plymouth programme, the partners focused on proving repeated launch and recovery of the ROV, maintaining communications and positioning between the two platforms, and controlling the combined system remotely during operations in coastal waters.

Two decades of U.S. data challenge an evolutionary explanation for the gender-equality paradox
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:00:33 UTC
21:00:33 KST

Two studies that tracked Americans for two decades or more found that as the United States grew wealthier and more gender-equal, psychological differences between men and women did not grow, and in a few cases they shrank. The findings, published in Social Psychology and Psychological Reports, provide evidence against a popular evolutionary explanation for why such differences appear larger in richer, more egalitarian countries.
The research addresses a phenomenon known as the gender-equality paradox. This concept refers to the observation that differences between men and women in personality, academic strengths, and mental health often appear larger in countries with higher levels of gender equality and economic prosperity.
A study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that higher living conditions were associated with larger sex differences in personality and depression across different countries, though differences in math, sexual behavior, and partner preferences were smaller. Similar patterns have been observed in education, with another 2024 study showing that differences in girls’ and boys’ relative academic strengths, with girls relatively stronger in reading and boys in math and science, are consistently larger in wealthier, more gender-equal nations.
To explain this paradox, many evolutionary psychologists point to the resource hypothesis, sometimes called the free expression hypothesis. This framework proposes that humans possess innate, sex-specific tendencies rooted in early human evolution, when, according to this view, men and women faced different pressures that shaped different psychological traits.
On this account, when a society meets its citizens’ basic material needs and relaxes strict social rules, individuals are finally free to express their true, biologically driven gender differences. Under this theory, a highly developed country removes the struggle for basic survival, allowing men and women to naturally drift toward distinct, gendered interests and emotional patterns.
“The study was motivated by a long-standing debate about the so-called gender-equality paradox,” Gabriele Prati, an associate professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Bologna and the author of both studies, told PsyPost.
“The problem is that most of the evidence supporting this explanation comes from comparisons between different countries at a single point in time,” he explained. “Countries differ in many other respects—history, culture, institutions, religion, economic structure, and social norms—so a correlation between gender equality and sex differences does not necessarily tell us what happens when equality or economic resources actually increase.”
A more direct test is to follow what happens within a single society as it changes. Prati did this in two longitudinal studies, which follow the same people over many years, tracking Americans across a period of rising wealth and gender equality.
The first study, published in Social Psychology, analyzed data from the Midlife in the United States project, which included a nationally representative sample of 7,108 adults. At the start of the study, participants averaged 46 years old, and 52 percent were women. Prati examined three waves of data collected between the mid-1990s and 2014. During this nearly twenty-year span, the United States experienced documented increases in its gross domestic product, a standard measure of economic prosperity, as well as an overall increase in gender equality.
Participants completed surveys assessing their personality traits, including extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, openness, and neuroticism. The surveys also measured altruism, trust, negative emotions, and clinical depression. At the start, women scored higher than men on most of these measures, including negative emotions, agreeableness, and neuroticism, while men scored slightly higher on openness. The research aimed to determine whether the psychological gaps between men and women widened as the societal conditions improved, exactly as the resource hypothesis would predict.
The findings did not support the evolutionary resource hypothesis. The gap between men and women in altruism, trust, negative emotions, and all major personality traits remained unchanged over the nearly twenty-year span. For depression, the gender gap actually shrank. Women were still more likely than men to meet the criteria for depression in 2014, but the gap narrowed because women’s odds of depression fell by about 38 percent while men’s did not change.
Prati also tested the hypothesis at the individual level by looking at changes in household income adjusted for household size. Rising income was not followed by growing differences between men and women. The two associations that did emerge ran opposite to the theory’s predictions: higher income was followed by slightly lower conscientiousness among women and, at the edge of statistical significance, a higher likelihood of depression among men.
“The main takeaway is that greater prosperity and gender equality did not make men and women progressively more psychologically different in the way predicted by the resource hypothesis,” Prati said.
“An important broader lesson is that a pattern observed when comparing countries is not necessarily evidence of the mechanism producing that pattern,” he noted. “Following people and societies over time provides a more direct test, and in this study that test did not support the resource hypothesis in its current form.”
To test the hypothesis in a different developmental stage, Prati conducted a second study, published in Psychological Reports, focusing on adolescents and young adults. This research used data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health, which tracked a nationally representative sample of 6,504 Americans from 1994 to 2018. Over five survey waves, participants grew from middle and high school students into adults in their late thirties. This dataset allowed Prati to examine different outcomes in younger people: math and science grades, scores on a picture vocabulary test, self-reported willingness to take risks, self-esteem, and depressive symptoms.
Once again, the results did not support the predictions of the evolutionary framework. Gender differences in math and science grades did not change between the mid-1990s and the end of high school, differences in vocabulary scores did not change between 1994–95 and 2001–02, and differences in willingness to take risks did not change between 1996 and 2018.
Just as in the adult study, the gender differences in depressive symptoms decreased over time. The gap in depressive symptoms, on a scale from 0 to 3, shrank from 0.14 points in 1994–95 to 0.10 points in 2008–09, and the self-esteem gap, in which boys typically score higher, shrank from 0.16 to 0.05 points on a five-point scale by 2001–02. Prati describes these changes as very small to small, but they ran opposite to the theory’s prediction.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. Both studies rely on data from a single country, and tracking these changes in countries with different cultural histories or economic structures might yield different patterns.
In addition, because the same people were aging while society changed, the studies cannot fully separate the effects of societal change from ordinary development. The self-esteem gap, for example, tends to narrow as teenagers become adults.
Another detail to keep in mind is the way certain traits were measured. Some, such as risk-taking and trust, were assessed using a single survey question, which might not capture their full complexity. The datasets also lacked some of the measures most central to the theory, such as interest in working with things versus people, so future studies could test whether those show different patterns.
It is also possible that two decades is not long enough to observe deep cultural shifts in how gender differences are expressed. However, Prati notes that the hypothesis does not specify how long these effects should take to emerge, and that there is no clear reason to expect individual income gains to take decades to have an effect.
“We should be cautious about concluding that giving people more economic resources and greater gender equality naturally reveals or amplifies innate psychological differences between women and men,” Prati added. “Differences between women and men are likely shaped by a much more complex combination of social, cultural, environmental, and possibly biological influences.”
The study, “No Evidence for the Evolutionary Resource Hypothesis as an Explanation of the Gender-Equality Paradox: A Three-Wave Longitudinal Analysis of Sex Differences in the United States,” was authored by Gabriele Prati. The study, “The Gender-Equality Paradox: A Longitudinal Test of the Free Expression or Resource Hypothesis Among Adolescents,” was also authored by Gabriele Prati.

Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for corn gado gado | Quick and easy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:00:24 UTC
21:00:24 KST

I am still making large, nourishing and vibrant salads, with gado gado being one of my favourites. It is a well-loved Indonesian salad, and something I devoured almost daily when we travelled around the islands many moons ago. It is also an excellent way of eating an abundance of veg, and can be made to suit your taste. If I was going all out, I’d add tofu or tempeh, some prawn crackers and beansprouts, but feel free to make the bowl as you wish, with whatever you have to hand – have a play.
Charred corn gado gado
For those who have a peanut allergy, this dressing works well with good-quality almond butter, too.
Prep 10 min
Cook 30 min
Serves 4
2 tbsp vegetable or groundnut oil
1 tbsp red Thai curry paste
80g pure peanut butter, crunchy or smooth
2 tbsp soy sauce
1 tbsp light soft brown sugar
200ml coconut milk
Sea salt and white pepper
Juice of 1 lime, plus 1 lime, quartered, to serve
300g baby potatoes
4 large eggs
150g green beans, trimmed
2 ears of corn
100g baby spinach, washed
½ bunch coriander, leaves picked and chopped
Start by making the dressing. Pour the oil into a small saucepan, add the curry paste and fry, stirring, for a few minutes. Stir in the peanut butter, soy sauce, sugar and 175ml of the coconut milk, then season with salt and white pepper, and bring to a gentle boil.
Add the lime juice and simmer for five minutes, until thick, rich and creamy. Add the remaining 25ml coconut milk, simmer for a further minute, then take off the heat and leave to cool.
Meanwhile, get the rest of the salad ready. Put the potatoes in a pan of salted cold water, bring to a boil and cook for about 15 minutes, until tender. Boil the eggs for seven minutes for just-set yolks, give the beans six minutes and the corn five minutes.
Drain everything, leave to cool, then stand the corn ears upright and carefully cut off the kernels. Assemble the bowls with all the different components in sections: a quarter of the potatoes, the green beans, the shaved corn, a handful of spinach leaves and a boiled egg cut into quarters. Drizzle over the cooled sauce, and serve topped with a scattering of coriander and with a wedge of lime for squeezing over.

Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:00:24 UTC
21:00:24 KST

On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.
Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.
Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.
Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.
After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.
Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.
“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.
“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”
On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.
“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”
Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.
When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”
The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.
In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.
“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”
With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.
She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.
“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

Extreme heat putting births in jeopardy, U.N. climate chief warns
Nadi, Fiji — Extreme heat is increasingly linked to problems such as premature births or underweight babies, the U.N. climate chief warned on Monday as Fiji hosted talks ahead of a major summit.
This week's meetings in the city of Nadi and on the atoll nation of Tuvalu are aimed at drawing the world's attention to life on the front line of climate change in the Pacific.
They are a precursor to the larger U.N.-sponsored global climate summit, known as COP31, to be held in Turkey next month.
Highlighting the need for urgent action, United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell cited a new survey showing more than two-thirds of health professionals across five continents had seen complications caused by intense heat in the past five years.
"Climate-driven extreme heat during pregnancy is increasingly linked to premature birth, stillbirth, low birth weight, and maternal complications," he said.
The Plan International charity said in a separate report on Monday that climate disasters were also increasing the risk of child marriage and teen pregnancies, in part through their impact on the health and education services on which girls depend.
The South Pacific is among the most vulnerable regions in the world to global warming — from rising sea waters jeopardizing homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching.
Fiji's climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, called for commitments from developing nations to a "just transition" with support for "countries in the world that suffer the most."
A U.N. report released in August found developing countries needed $310 billion to $365 billion to adapt, yet had only $26 billion in adaptation finance available in 2023.
"We rely on and we appeal to countries to commit to climate finance," Tabuya said.
Australia — the head of this year's climate negotiations and a major coal exporter— faces accusations of hypocrisy: Its sales of the fossil fuel have boomed on the back of demand caused by the Middle East conflict.
Tabuya told journalists there had been "frank discussion" on Monday with her Australian counterpart Chris Bowen and Pacific officials.
"Yes, we have sentiments expressed from certain countries," she said, when asked if she backed calls from other Pacific leaders for Australia to halt expansion of coal and gas projects.
"But for the Pacific, it's important at this pre-COP that we find common ground. There will be things that we disagree on, but we can agree to disagree," Tabuya said.
Refocusing on limiting global warming
Also high on the agenda is a push by Pacific leaders for the world to stick to a target of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) — a threshhold that was breached in 2025 — and give more attention to the impact on oceans.
"Keeping 1.5 alive means hope — hope for Tuvalu, hope for Kiribati, hope for small island atolls around the world," Bowen told journalists.
"We can actually come to this conversation and say, 'as a fossil-fuel exporting nation, we can bring something different to the table,'" he said.
Sea levels are also rising at a record pace, driven by warming oceans and glacier melt, according to the August U.N. report. 
.
Up to 1.2 billion people could be displaced by 2050, with Pacific island countries experiencing sea level rise at twice the global average, it said. 
Regional leaders have pitched the pre-COP as a chance to bring the world to the Pacific, and they are keen to show the impact climate change is having on the region.
In Naidiri Village, a marine protected area an hour's drive south of Nadi, locals described efforts to combat coral bleaching and improve ocean health.
"Countries that don't cause climate change are being affected," Joseva Kunagado, 21, told AFP.
Manoa Duwai, who set up Naidiri Village's marine protected area more than a decade ago after realizing what the damage wrought by overfishing is, said they were experiencing climate change "every day."
"The sea level is rising, and a heat wave earlier this year," he said. "A message to the developed countries: Do remember, don't forget."
Delegates will also take a one-day trip on Tuesday to low-lying Tuvalu, which is already laying plans to relocate its population if it's consumed by the ocean.
Tuvalu is one of the world's least visited countries and the highest point in its capital, Funafuti, is just 6.6 feet above sea level.

The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese foreign agent at the Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese President’s family.

FBI Director Kash Patel appeared to laud the arrest on social media. “Foreign adversaries take note: America is no longer a safe place to run your espionage operations,” Patel wrote. “Allegedly surveil a foreign leader’s family on U.S. soil for [China]—and try to catch a flight back to Shanghai? Not happening.”

China, meanwhile, has long branded Taiwan’s leader William Lai Ching-te as a separatist and a “destroyer of peace.”
During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s recent state visit to the U.S., President Trump said of the topic: “We didn’t spend a lot of time talking about Taiwan.”

The latest report from the U.S. Congressional-Executive Commission on China continues to warn about Beijing’s transnational repression activities, including intimidation and the targeting of Hong Kongers, Uyghurs, Tibetans, Taiwanese figures, and other Chinese dissidents.
Sen. Rick Scott (R, Fla.) posted on X: “This is only further PROOF of what we already know—they’re actively infiltrating our country and threatening our national security.”

Authorities filed a criminal complaint against Zhang in federal court, CBS News and Fox News reported, with an affidavit from an FBI special agent.

Essayli, speaking to Fox News Sunday, said that Zhang was a naturalized U.S. citizen.
“She was conducting surveillance on behalf of the Chinese government," Essayli told Fox News. “And she was spying on a relative of the President of Taiwan here in the U.S.”
Essayli, in his X post, added that Zhang “used tradecraft to avoid detection” and that “she never notified the Attorney General she was acting for a foreign government.”
Under federal law, those who act as agents for other nations without prior notification to the U.S. Attorney General may face up to 10 years in prison, fines, or both.

The complaint alleged that a home security camera near the victim’s house recorded Zhang and the individual “appearing to film” the victim and his family.
The complaint does not name the victim, but CBS News reported, citing unidentified law enforcement sources, that the target was Ting-yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Lai.
Zhang then allegedly messaged one of her Chinese government contacts, according to the complaint, where she sent: “Saw him. Young male. It’s that young one.” She then sent two license plate numbers, which the FBI agent found were both registered to the victim. The FBI agent wrote in the complaint that they were able to access details of Zhang’s messages following a search warrant on her iCloud account.
“If [China] were to wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to [China],” the FBI special agent wrote.

UN upholds housing as a human right on World Habitat Day
