UN upholds housing as a human right on World Habitat Day
Representatives from governments, civil society and academia meeting in Muscat, Oman on Monday called for urgent action to address a global housing crisis affecting nearly 3.4 billion people.
They gathered to commemorate World Habitat Day which this year focuses on the theme of Adequate Housing for All.
“Adequate housing is not a luxury. It is a foundation for a dignified life and for sustainable cities,” said Anacláudia Rossbach, Executive Director of UN-Habitat, the agency that promotes sustainable urbanization.
She stressed that “housing needs to be treated as a public priority alongside land and basic services”, underlining the need for greater investment in communities and cooperation across government, the private sector and civil society.
Millions living in slums
In his message for the day, UN Secretary-General António Guterres called adequate housing for all “the foundation of dignity, security, and opportunity.”
He noted, however, that more than three billion people worldwide are denied this universal human right.
“Over one billion live in informal settlements and slums, and many more experience homelessness or have been displaced by conflict, disasters, and climate change,” he added.
Trapped in poverty
The President of the United Nations Habitat Assembly, Nga Kor Ming, reminded participants that behind the numbers are real people.
Mr. Ming – Malaysia’s Minister of Housing and Local Government – highlighted the plight of families living in homes without legal protection, or even basic sanitation and clean water, whose children suffer preventable diseases.
“A house without clean water, safety or legal security is not a home. It is a poverty trap,” he said in a video message. “Therefore, to deliver adequate housing for all, we must move away from quick fixes to systemic transformation.”
More than four walls
Ms. Rossbach explained that under the UN human rights framework, housing is considered adequate when it meets seven criteria that include availability of services, habitability, affordability, location and accessibility.
“Adequate housing means much more than a physical structure with four walls and a roof,” she said.
“A family may have a roof and still spend so much on rent that there is little left for food, education, or healthcare. A home may be affordable, but located far from jobs, schools, or transport.”
Everyone at home
The UN Secretary-General upheld that “investing in adequate housing and transforming informal settlements reduces poverty, tackles inequality, builds climate resilience, and fosters peaceful and inclusive societies.”
He called for coordinated action by national and local governments, building stronger partnerships, and better use of data in decision-making.
“The international financial architecture must also be reformed to mobilize the adequate, predictable, and affordable financing developing countries need to invest in housing at scale,” he added.
The Secretary-General ended his message with an appeal to the international community.
“On this World Habitat Day, let us treat housing as a public good and build a world where everyone has a place to call home,” he said.
A month of action
World Habitat Day is observed annually on the first Monday in October.
It marks the start of UN-Habitat’s Urban October – a month-long campaign to advocate for housing and sustainable urban development that concludes on World Cities Day, 31 October.

ICC unseals four arrest warrants over Taliban persecution of women and girls

ICC unseals four arrest warrants over Taliban persecution of women and girls
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has made public four arrest warrants against senior Taliban figures, accusing them of persecuting women and girls in Afghanistan, which amounts to a crime against humanity.
In a decision on Monday, judges unsealed warrants for Taliban Supreme Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and Chief Justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani, whose existence was announced in July 2025, and for two further suspects, Habibullah Agha and Neda Mohammad Nadim.
The four warrants were issued between July and September 2025.
The court said there are reasonable grounds to believe all four are criminally responsible for ordering, inducing or soliciting persecution, a crime against humanity under article 7(1)(h) of the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty.
Punished on gender grounds
It says the persecution was carried out on gender grounds against girls, women and other people who did not conform to the de facto Taliban government’s policy on gender, gender identity or expression. It was also carried out on political grounds against people seen as “allies of girls and women”.
According to the court, the crimes were committed in Afghanistan from 15 August 2021, when the Taliban seized power, until at least 20 January 2025.
Violation of fundamental rights
Judges found that the Taliban had put in place a policy that led to serious violations of the civilian population’s fundamental rights and freedoms, linked to murder, imprisonment, torture, rape and enforced disappearance.
While some Taliban rules applied to everyone, the court said girls and women were specifically targeted because of their gender.
Through decrees and edicts, they were severely deprived of their rights to education, privacy and family life and of the freedoms of movement, expression, thought, conscience and religion.
Other Afghans were targeted because certain expressions of sexuality or gender identity were considered at odds with Taliban policy.
The judges also found that people seen as opposing these policies – even passively, or by failing to act – were targeted as political opponents. They included those described as “allies of girls and women”.
Systemic harm
In the warrants, the judges said that the Rome Statute’s definition of gender goes beyond a purely biological idea of sex, in line with current developments in international law.
They said it must recognise the socially constructed roles, behaviours, expectations and hierarchies traditionally linked to people because of their sex – commonly known as gender norms – when assessing gender-based persecution.
The court added that such persecution covers not only direct violence, but also systemic and institutionalised harm, including the imposition of discriminatory social norms.
The ICC Prosecutor applied for the first two warrants on 23 January 2025, and judges issued them on 8 July that year, initially under seal to protect victims and witnesses and safeguard the proceedings, though the court disclosed they existed.
At the time, the ICC Prosecutor said further applications against other senior Taliban members would follow.

Extreme heat making pregnancy a ‘new fault line’ in climate crisis
Pregnancy and childbirth have become a “new fault line in the global climate crisis” as extreme heat worsens, the head of the UN climate action body (UNFCCC) warned on Monday, calling for maternal and newborn health to be built into countries’ climate plans.
Speaking in Fiji at an event organized by global charitable foundation Wellcome, ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, UNFCCC chief Simon Stiell said a deep test of climate action was “far, far simpler” than degrees, targets and finance: “whether we protect life at its most fragile”.
“Rising temperatures mean rising danger in pregnancy,” he told first day of the pre-COP ministerial meeting, noting that extreme heat during pregnancy is increasingly linked to premature birth, stillbirth, low birth weight and maternal complications.
Health workers sound alarm
Mr. Stiell cited new data, released on Monday, from a survey commissioned by Wellcome of maternal health professionals in five countries across five continents.
Some 73 per cent reported that heat-linked cases or complications had increased over the past five years, while 81 percent were concerned or very concerned that extreme heat would increasingly out maternal, foetal and newborn health at risk without more action.
Nearly all respondents had cared for a pregnant woman or baby whose health they considered had been affected by extreme heat.
“Behind those numbers are human stories: an expectant mother’s journey to clinic delayed by dangerous heat; a midwife working through unsafe temperatures; a newborn needing specialist care,” Mr. Stiell said.
‘No cool place to go’
While no one is immune, he stressed that the risks and impacts are not shared equally. People working outdoors, living in unregulated housing, travelling far to a clinic or relying on facilities without water, power or cooling “cannot be protected by advice alone”.
“‘Staying cool’ is simply not an option when there is no cool place to go,” he said.
“A safe birth is already too often shaped by geography, income and access to care. Without action, extreme heat will widen that injustice.”
For small islands and other nations that “did practically nothing to create this climate crisis”, Mr. Stiell said, the findings underscore the need for support at scale.
He called for the tripling of adaptation finance agreed at COP30 in Belém to be delivered and for nations to work with the whole financial system to make $1.3 trillion a year for developing countries a reality.
Three priorities
Mr. Stiell set out three priorities:
- Making pregnancy and newborn care part of adaptation, heat and health planning;
- Turning evidence into protection through guidance, training, heat alerts and safer facilities;
- Improving data to show where risks are growing and which interventions work;
“What is not named in a plan is too often not funded, not measured and not protected,” he said. “Harm that is not counted is too easily ignored.”
He commended the COP31 Presidency of Türkiye and Australia’s President of Negotiations for making health a key priority, building on Brazil’s work last year.
“A changing climate must never be accepted as a reason pregnancy and birth become less safe,” he said.
“A newborn’s healthy start must never depend on a family’s ability to escape the heat.”

Security, sacrifice or opportunity: Visions differ over effective climate action
Should the world move away sharply from fossil fuels, or manage a slower, more careful retreat?
That question underpinned many of the speeches from global leaders at this year's High-level Week General Debate in New York, as climate change emerged as one of the defining fault lines dividing Member States.
UN News reviewed some of the key speeches to assess where those divisions are.
Leaders offered sometimes very different visions of what action should look like – from Pacific nations demanding a rapid move away from fossil fuels to energy producers stressing security, affordability and a more gradual transition.
Who, what, when
Across the statements, the main points of division were about how fast energy systems should change, what role fossil fuels should continue to play, and who should shoulder the cost of both the transition and the damage already being inflicted.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres – who made climate a central theme to this year’s High-level Week – opened the General Debate by calling for immediate action.
“A future beyond fossil fuels is in sight. The question is how?” he said, urging governments to adopt national plans to transition away from fossil fuels, with clear timelines and protection for workers and communities.
Pacific islands under threat
Some of the strongest calls for speed came from low-lying Pacific Island States, whose territories face threats to their very existence due to rising sea levels and intensifying floods.
The President of the Marshall Islands said the growing likelihood of overshooting the limit set by global leaders in Paris 10 years ago to keep an increase in temperatures to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, demanded a much faster response.
“A much accelerated transition away from fossil fuels is the only logical response. Continued investment in fossil fuels is not only immoral but irrational,” she said.
Tuvalu similarly called for a “fast, fair, just, and orderly transition away from fossil fuels”, alongside action to reduce both methane and carbon dioxide emissions.
Don’t jeopardise the economy
But other countries laid out more gradual or mixed pathways.
Saudi Arabia argued that climate action and energy security are compatible. It stressed “the importance of not excluding any source of energy” and of pursuing “realistic and comprehensive transition pathways” that deliver energy security, climate protection and economic development together.
Nigeria stressed that the climate transition should not come at the detriment of development.
“We reject the false choice between development and climate action,” the Vice President said.
Nigeria’s Energy Transition Plan aims for net-zero emissions by 2060 while combining renewable energy and clean cooking with gas as a transitional fuel.
Venezuela also backed decarbonisation, but warned that an imposed transition could threaten food security, employment, production and affordable energy.
Brazil similarly prioritised energy security.
“We have achieved self-sufficiency in oil and will continue to explore the potential of new reserves, such as those in the Equatorial Margin. But we will not abandon the environmental agenda,” its President said, before pledging to advance the country’s decarbonisation roadmap.
Climate transition: An opportunity
On the other hand, several States sold climate action as an economic opportunity rather than sacrifice.
The UK linked clean energy, of the type provided by wind and solar, to jobs, growth and reindustrialisation.
In a similar vein, Lesotho launched a Just Energy Transition Fund, which is intended to strengthen renewable energy capacity, achieve energy independence for the country, and help build an economy based in part on renewable-energy exports – with potential jobs for young people and women.
Portugal also presented renewables as a way to reduce dangerous energy dependencies. It said more than 70 per cent of its energy production comes from renewable sources and that its carbon-neutrality target has been brought forward to 2045.
Climate change dissenters
The United States stood further apart from much of the climate framing.
President Donald Trump promoted expanded fossil fuel production and mocked previous warnings about global warming.
He cited “people who said we'll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming, a name since reborn to climate change because the planet was cooling, not warming, and nobody was dead.”
He stated that his administration successfully halted an international “global carbon tax” on shipping from Member States of the International Maritime Organization (IMO), asserting that “there is no global government.”
Who pays – and on what terms?
For many developing and climate-vulnerable countries, financing emerged as another major fault line.
Nepal described climate disasters as a development emergency: damaged roads, schools, homes and clean-energy infrastructure can wipe out years of progress, while forcing poorer countries to borrow to rebuild.
It called for grant-based support rather than more debt and criticised the difficulty of accessing existing mechanisms.
“Climate finance must not become a bureaucratic maze through which vulnerable countries spend years proving that they need help,” Nepal’s Prime Minister said.
Seychelles went further, bringing in international law. It argued that mitigation, adaptation, technology transfer and loss-and-damage finance “are not acts of charity—they are legal obligations,” and called for affordable long-term finance and debt relief.
When climate change threatens the map
For small island States, climate change also became a question of sovereignty.
“The sea does not negotiate. It does not read communiqués. And it does not recognise a veto,” the Bahamas Prime Minister told the Assembly.
The Bahamas endorsed the Declaration on Sea-Level Rise, saying it affirmed that its statehood and boundaries would endure despite rising seas. Tuvalu likewise highlighted provisions affirming continuity of statehood and sovereignty and safeguarding established maritime zones and rights.
The Marshall Islands also said its existing boundaries and baselines should endure as seas rise, while calling for accessible finance for adaptation and loss and damage.
From promises to implementation
Several leaders also pointed to practical measures already underway.
Pointing to commitments to protect 30 per cent of land and seas, France’s President held up recent progress on environmental protection as proof that multilateral action can work.
Others proposed concrete ideas for furthering cooperation. Nepal, for example, proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, led by Nepal, India and China, to share satellite data and expertise, monitor dangerous glacial lakes, strengthen early-warning systems and coordinate cross-border disaster assistance.
At the same time, several leaders voiced frustration with the gap between commitments and delivery.
Türkiye said it wanted the major upcoming UN-backed international climate conference, COP31, which it will host in November, to become an “Implementation COP.”
Denmark made a similar argument. “The challenge before us is no longer a lack of solutions. We have the solutions. We know what is required. Now we need to deliver,” the Danish Ambassador said, also calling for COP31 to focus on implementation and “real-world results”.

Don't miss: Watch Saturn shine and Halley’s Comet debris streak across the sky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:59:17 UTC
20:59:17 KST

Don't miss: Watch Saturn shine and Halley’s Comet debris streak across the sky
- Date:
- October 5, 2026
- Source:
- NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
- Summary:
- October skywatchers can see Saturn at opposition, catch meteors from Halley’s Comet during the Orionid peak, and watch the Moon sweep past the famous Pleiades star cluster. Moonlight may obscure some Orionids, but the best viewing should come before dawn after the Moon sets.
- Share:
October offers several memorable sights for skywatchers, including Saturn at opposition, the Orionid meteor shower, and a close pairing of the Moon and the Pleiades, also known as the Seven Sisters.
Skywatching Highlights
- Oct. 4: Saturn reaches opposition, making the ringed planet visible for much of the night
- Oct. 6: A thin crescent Moon appears close to bright Jupiter before sunrise
- Oct. 21-22: The Orionid meteor shower peaks; moonlight may interfere, so look before dawn after moonset
- Oct. 27-28: The Moon passes near the Pleiades star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters
Saturn leads October's celestial lineup, followed later in the month by meteors linked to Halley's Comet and a close encounter between the Moon and one of the best known star clusters in the night sky. Together, these events make October a busy month for anyone looking up after sunset or before dawn.
[See Video Link After Article.]
Saturn Reaches Opposition
On October 4th, Saturn reaches opposition, offering one of the best viewing opportunities of the year for the ringed planet.
Opposition occurs when Earth moves between the Sun and Saturn. From our perspective, Saturn then appears on the opposite side of the sky from the Sun. As a result, the planet rises around sunset and remains visible for much of the night.
Saturn is also drawing scientific attention because of unusual activity in its atmosphere. Astronomers have long studied a hexagon shaped jet stream stretching nearly 20,000 miles across the planet's north pole.
More recently, observations from NASA's Hubble Space Telescope revealed a ten sided atmospheric wave surrounding Saturn's south pole. The feature, located in the southern hemisphere, appears to be growing stronger. That gives researchers a rare chance to observe a massive atmospheric structure as it develops.
Orionid Meteor Shower Peaks in October
The Orionid meteor shower reaches its peak during the night of October 21st and into the morning of October 22nd.
These meteors come from small pieces of material left behind by Halley's Comet. Although the Orionids appear to originate from the direction of the constellation Orion, individual meteors can flash across any area of the sky.
Viewing conditions will not be ideal for the entire night this year. A bright waxing gibbous Moon is expected to overpower some of the fainter meteors.
The best opportunity to see the shower may arrive during the few hours before dawn, after the Moon has set. For better viewing, find a dark location away from bright lights, allow your eyes time to adjust, and scan as much of the sky as possible.
The Moon Meets the Seven Sisters
Another striking sight arrives on the night of October 27th into the 28th, when the Moon passes close to the Pleiades star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters.
The Pleiades have inspired stories in many ancient cultures. Part of their widespread importance may come from the fact that the cluster can be seen from nearly every part of the world.
To find the pairing, look toward the east during the evening as the Moon and the Pleiades rise higher in the sky. To the unaided eye, the cluster looks like a slightly hazy group of 6 to 7 stars.
No special equipment is required to see the Pleiades, but binoculars or a telescope can reveal the cluster in much greater detail.

Data Centers in the Asia-Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:59:00 UTC
20:59:00 KST

As artificial intelligence receives continued investment and media hype on promises that it will remake the global economy, investment is pouring into digital infrastructure, particularly data centers. The Asia-Pacific region is experiencing its own data center boom with resource consumption emerging as the defining flashpoint between digital infrastructure ambitions and the communities hosting them. Water is the most acute concern: hyperscale facilities draw millions of liters daily in regions already facing groundwater depletion, drought, or agricultural competition for supply, from South Asia’s water-stressed corridors to Central Asia’s shrinking basins. But energy demand runs a close second, as straining grids raise the threat of higher electricity prices and increased pollution from fossil fuels despite decarbonization targets adopted by countries and companies around the region. Other issues such as land acquisition and construction disruption — noise, dust, traffic, and questions over fair compensation — add a further layer of friction, particularly where regulatory oversight and environmental impact assessment requirements have not kept up with construction.
Underlying Asia’s data center buildout is a deeper grievance: that the benefits of digital infrastructure (tax revenue, jobs, grid investment) are diffuse and national, while the costs are concentrated and local. As protest activity spreads from established flashpoints like South Korea to newer markets including Japan, Malaysia, Indonesia, and India, politicians are taking notice and regulation aimed at controlling data center resource consumption is spreading across the region.
Australia has moved to become the first country to bring data center location, energy, and water requirements under a single national regulatory framework. On July 15, 2026, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that the National Framework will require large-scale operators to become “net-generators” of power, meaning that they must fund their own generation capacity and grid connection costs rather than passing them to consumers. In addition, operators must meet mandatory energy efficiency and water conservation standards. A new Office of AI will coordinate design of the framework, which is intended to replace the current fragmented state-by-state approval system and streamline compliance. The proposal follows growing community concern over data centers straining local grids and drinking water supplies, and reflects lessons drawn from overseas markets where rapid buildouts have provoked local backlash. Legislation is expected early next year, pending agreement with state and territory governments at the National Cabinet.

Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:58:00 UTC
20:58:00 KST

Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What to know
October 5, 2026
What you need to know about plague
- There are three forms of plague, all caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
- The three forms of plague are bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.
- Bubonic plague is the most common form, it does not spread from person to person. If untreated, the bacteria can move through the body and bloodstream, causing septicemic plague, which causes internal bleeding and organ failure.
- If the the bacteria reach the lungs, they cause pneumonic plague. Pneumonic plague is highly contagious as it can pass from person to person through the air, via coughing, for example.
- If untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.
Speculation over the death in a Russian plague laboratory
Following the death of a Russian laboratory worker, there is speculation about an outbreak of pneumonic plague, a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs. Russia denies there is a broader risk to the community.
Russian officials have said the laboratory worker's death was not caused by a plague pathogen. The 28-year-old died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Russia's Interfax news agency, citing Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's disease-control agency. According to that agency, samples taken from the woman showed no microorganisms "related to her professional activities." This contradicts earlier information.
Local media had previously reported that the woman, who worked at an institute dedicated to fighting plague, had dropped a test tube.
She reportedly died on Friday, October 2, 2026, at the district hospital in Shelekhov, a town near Irkutsk in Siberia.
According to official Russian figures, two hospitals and a children's clinic were placed under quarantine. Local reports said staff at the institute were being quarantined at their workplace. The US news site Axios has reported that around 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under observation. There were no further reported infections.
Even so, distrust of how Russia handles information persists. On one of DW's Russian-language social media channels, a user wrote: "It wouldn't surprise me if this turns into a disaster now, both in terms of the spread and the quarantine measures."
Pneumonic plague: a fast-moving lung infection
All that is known for certain, at time of writing and first publication (October 5, 2026), is that pneumonic plague is highly contagious.
Pneumonic plague is a form of plague that infects the lungs. Like every form of the disease, it is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals, such as rodents and in the fleas that feed on them.
The World Health Organization describes the pneumonic form as the most virulent type of plague.
Its incubation period can be as short as 24 hours, and it is the only form that passes easily from person to person through respiratory particles released when a sick patient coughs. This is why, according to the WHO, it can trigger severe epidemics.
Symptoms appear quickly: high fever, headache and weakness, followed by a rapidly worsening pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and a cough that often brings up blood.
A person can catch pneumonic plague by breathing in the bacteria directly, or by developing it when bubonic and/or septicemic plague go untreated and spread to the lungs.
What is the difference between bubonic and pneumonic plague?
Pneumonic plague is not a separate disease. It is one of three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.
All are caused by the same bacterium.
What sets them apart is where the infection settles in the body, and that shapes how the disease spreads and how deadly it is.
Bubonic plague is the most common form and the one most people think of when they hear the word "plague." It usually follows a flea bite. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells into a painful lump known as a bubo. According to the WHO, it rarely spreads between people.
If bubonic plague goes untreated, the bacteria can move further through the body. If they spread into the bloodstream, the disease can become septicemic plague, which causes bleeding under the skin, tissue death in the fingers and toes, and organ failure. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the illness becomes pneumonic plague, the form that can pass from person to person through the air. Both septicemic and pneumonic plague can also develop directly, without a bubo appearing first.
Left untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.
Pneumonic plague treatment: antibiotics within the first 24 hours
Pneumonic plague is curable, but only if treatment starts quickly. The WHO warns that without treatment it can kill within 18 to 24 hours of the first symptoms.
Common antibiotics can cure the infection, and recovery rates are high when patients are treated within about a day of falling ill.
Speed is what decides the outcome. Doctors are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation and to start antibiotics as soon as plague is suspected, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The drugs themselves are not rare or specialized. They are standard, widely used antibiotics, and patients usually need a course of up to two weeks. To stop the infection spreading, patients are kept in isolation, and wearing masks helps protect those around them, the WHO says.
Preventive antibiotics and isolation for close contacts
People close to a patient are treated as well, even if they have no symptoms. Both the WHO and the CDC recommend a seven-day course of preventive antibiotics for close contacts of anyone with pneumonic plague.
The WHO does not recommend a plague vaccine for the public. It reserves vaccination for high-risk groups, such as laboratory staff who work with the bacterium and health workers.

WMA members must call for release of detained Palestinian medics
Members of the World Medical Association have a duty to uphold their commitment to the protection of healthcare workers everywhere.
More than 1,700 healthcare workers have been killed during the genocide in Gaza. Israel has detained hundreds more without charges. Doctors, nurses and paramedics who stayed to treat the wounded have themselves become casualties of this war.
When medical staff are killed, imprisoned or disappeared, it is not only they who pay the price. Patients lose the people they rely on to keep them alive.
This is something delegates who gather in Rotterdam this week for the General Assembly of the World Medical Association (WMA) must remember. The fate of their Palestinian colleagues should be put on the table, not as a debating point, but as a test of whether the world’s governing body of medical ethics still means what it says.
The WMA already recognised the seriousness of these issues last year by adopting a resolution on the protection of healthcare in conflict. That was an important step and a welcome reaffirmation of the principles of medical neutrality. The challenge now is to ensure this is followed by the commitment of every medical association to explicitly support it and to use its influence to pressure governments to act.
If the WMA Assembly needs a single face for this file, it could be the one of Dr Hussam Abu Safia, the paediatrician who was the head of Kamal Adwan Hospital, the last functioning hospital in northern Gaza until Israeli forces stormed it in December 2024.
He’s been held now for more than 22 months without charge under Israel’s Incarceration of Unlawful Combatants Law, which permits indefinite detentions. He reportedly continues to endure prolonged solitary confinement, beatings, severe weight loss and untreated pre-existing conditions. An international petition for his release has drawn the signatures of more than 970 medical professionals from 41 countries.
Alongside him stands Dr Mazen al-Rantisi, the 71-year-old family physician from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, known as the “doctor of the poor”. He was arrested in June in a predawn raid on his home.
In addition, our longtime Doctors Without Borders (MSF) colleague, Dr Mohammed Hassan Ali Obeid, a respected 43-year-old Palestinian orthopaedic surgeon and father of three children, has been detained under the Unlawful Combatants Law in Israel for more than 600 days without charge.
Although detained health workers have been released, more than 80 remain in Israeli custody alongside at least a dozen arrested from the West Bank.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has recorded 1,000 attacks on healthcare, which have resulted in more than 1,000 deaths and 1,700 injuries in Gaza since October 7, 2023. Roughly 90 percent of Gaza’s health infrastructure has been destroyed or damaged. In August 2025, United Nations experts stated that the systematic destruction of the health system amounts to “medicide”.
In the West Bank, where no wartime emergency provides cover, the WHO also documented more than 1,000 attacks on healthcare since October 7, 2023, with 42 deaths and at least 218 injuries.
Ambulances are stopped at checkpoints and their crews taken. Medics trying to reach people injured in settler attacks have themselves been obstructed. Dialysis and oncologic patients stay home because the checkpoints make the journey to treatment impossible. Healthcare workers have been shot, detained and killed during Israeli military raids.
All of this represents Israel’s deliberate and systematic endeavour to dismantle Palestinians’ capacity to provide care. This is consistent with its clear and blatant disregard for Palestinian life.
The WMA Assembly should speak plainly about what is happening. It should call publicly for the release of detained Palestinian doctors, including Abu Safia, al-Rantisi and Obeid. It should press for independent access to those still being held. And it should back independent investigations into attacks on healthcare in Gaza and the West Bank with the findings made public regardless of where they lead.
This is an opportunity to collectively pressure fellow medical associations, political authorities and any relevant bodies to take action.
What lies before the Rotterdam assembly is a duty. One that reaffirms loudly, structurally, universally the founding proposition of the WMA: that membership carries an ethical responsibility, which does not flex with geography or alliances.
Healthcare workers are not targets. Either a white coat is worth protecting everywhere, or it is protected nowhere. The test is not simply whether we affirm these principles, but whether we uphold them when it matters most.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Family, peace and financial stability are most important to Bulgarians today
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:56:44 UTC
20:56:44 KST

News
What are the values of modern Bulgarians?
Family, peace and financial stability are most important to Bulgarians today
Monday 5 October 2026 13:57
Monday, 5 October 2026, 13:57
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The question of what Bulgarians value most is not merely a philosophical one. Over the years, sociological agencies and research institutes, as well as international and humanitarian organisations, have explored it in an effort to gain a clearer picture of the society in which we live and the direction in which it is heading. How long is the road between the goals we set as a society and our desire for a better world for ourselves and our children?
In the spirit of human values and critical thinking, we examined some of the largest sociological surveys conducted in Bulgaria and Europe, considered their commissioners and objectives, and attempted to bring together data from the past nearly ten years to answer the question: what are Bulgarians like today and what do they care about?
The latest major nationally representative survey on the subject was conducted in September 2026 by Progress Consult, commissioned by a major German hypermarket chain operating on the Bulgarian market. The study has been conducted periodically since 2017, tracking changes in the value system of Bulgarians and the factors that determine their quality of life.
PHOTO Progress Consult
The index is calculated on the basis of 82 specific factors grouped into seven areas: health, finances, family and relationships, personal goals, career, education and leisure. It compares the importance of each factor to people with the extent to which it is actually present in their lives.
The main finding this year is that health and financial well-being are the most important concerns for Bulgarians. Personal health ranks first in importance among respondents, followed by the health of their loved ones. Financial security has recorded the largest increase, rising from eighth place in 2022 to third place in 2026.
For the first time, personal freedom and autonomy have entered the top ten most important values, rising from 18th to 10th place in terms of importance to Bulgarians.
According to the author of the study, sociologist Dr Rosen Kutelov, data from the past four years show that Bulgarians have moved “from a state of acute anxiety to an adapted state of insecurity”. In his words, people are responding by narrowing their social circles, focusing on those closest to them and creating a protected personal world, with a practical approach and higher expectations for their own well-being. The survey provides supporting evidence: in 2022, 33.8% considered the broader social environment extremely important, while in 2026 the figure fell to 29.6%.
According to Kutelov, the greatest discrepancy in the lives of Bulgarians is between their desire for financial security and the extent to which they actually achieve it.
PHOTO BGNES
Peace, family and security are the most important values according to the results of the second-largest national survey, conducted among 1,003 adults on the subject “The Values That Connect Us”. It was carried out in early 2023 by Trend polling agency at the request of communications agency Interpartners Group.
In the survey, 46% of respondents identify peace as the leading value. In earlier similar studies, family had ranked first, but against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine, peace moved to the top in 2023. Family ranks second in importance at 37%, followed by security at 36%. 
For the youngest respondents, the most important values are peace, freedom and human rights. The study reveals an interesting comparison between security and freedom, with the results clearly showing the preference in Bulgarian society: if forced to choose, 52% of respondents place security above freedom. People aged 18 to 39, predominantly men, however, are more likely to favour freedom. The findings are, of course, a reflection of the ongoing war in Ukraine and the emerging new conflicts in the Middle East.
Considerably further down the list in the 2023 analysis of 14 values are freedom of expression (14%), democracy (13%), tolerance (11%) and equality (9%). Gender equality comes last, at 4%, although in practice Bulgarians express strong support for it. As many as 83% categorically reject the statement that women should be subordinate to men, 77% believe household chores should be shared, and 70% do not accept that men should earn higher salaries than women. 
Children stand out as a key value for couples in Bulgaria, while marriage as an institution is losing significance in contemporary Bulgaria, with 55% saying that getting married is not necessary.
PHOTO Pixabay
As regards a sense of belonging to a larger group of people, the largest share of participants, 53%, say that for them this is Bulgaria, while 22% identify with their local community and only 6% with the European Union. The authors believe this indicates a continuing distance from the EU following Bulgaria’s accession to the bloc in 2007.
As for education, historically an important value for Bulgarians, Trend’s findings show that 90% of respondents believe education and healthcare should be completely free, while 81% think the state is obliged to provide a job for anyone who wants to work. The sociologists reject the easy explanation that this is simply a legacy of the past, noting that the figures among the youngest respondents are almost identical to those for society as a whole. 
In this context, 62% believe that success in Bulgaria depends on whom you know. The same view is held by 56% of the youngest respondents and 61% of those with higher education. The majority do not believe that a person in Bulgaria can succeed through hard work or become wealthy through honest means.
The Holy Synod of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church
PHOTO patriarshia.bg
As regards values related to faith and religion, Bulgaria displays institutional trust without deep religiosity. This conclusion can be drawn from data by Gallup International Balkan from a survey conducted for the Bulgarian National Television between 28 March and 5 April 2024 among 805 people, through face-to-face tablet-assisted interviews, using a representative sample of the adult population. Sociologists note that trust in the Church has remained stable in recent years, ranging between 40% and 50%. Some 49.7% of respondents say they trust the Church, while 34.1% take the opposite view.
A separate survey by the same agency in August 2024 shows that trust in the Church stood at 43.1%, compared with 35.8% expressing distrust, and adds an important detail: three quarters of people identify as Orthodox Christians, but just under two thirds say they believe in God. Trust among the youngest respondents is low.
The international picture is similar: according to a 2022 global survey by the World Association of Gallup International, 53% of Bulgarians describe themselves as religious, placing Bulgaria among the moderately religious societies worldwide.
PHOTO BTA
The moral compass of young people: human rights, security and anxiety
A detailed portrait of young Bulgarians can be found in the findings of the Friedrich Ebert Foundation’s 2024 study “Optimism about the Individual, Pessimism about Society”, conducted in partnership with the Ivan Hadzhiyski Institute of Sociology. The study covers young people aged 14 to 29 in 12 countries in Southeast Europe.
When asked which values related to democracy are most important to them personally, Bulgarians under the age of 29 rank human rights first (24%), followed by security (20%) and economic well-being (14%). Equality (7%) and democracy (5%) remain at the bottom of the list. The idea of emigration is not unfamiliar to 74% of those surveyed.
 A secondary analysis of the same data also reveals a gender difference: young women seek protection through solidarity and rights, while young men place greater emphasis on strength, order and economic pragmatism.
The researchers note an overall high level of anxiety among Bulgaria’s active population. According to Associate Professor Boris Popivanov, one of the authors of the study, young people’s fears are primarily existential, concerning life, health and the future. They are most often worried about the healthcare system (47%), war (44%) and climate change (42%). 
Another trend highlighted by the findings is increased civic and political engagement among young Bulgarians: 21% say they are interested in the country’s political life, compared with just 7% in the same study in 2018.
PHOTO European Parliament
Where do we stand against the backdrop of Europe?
According to a large-scale Eurobarometer survey conducted in February-March 2025 on the values that the European Parliament should defend, Bulgarians put peace first (45%), followed by democracy (32%) and the protection of human rights (22%). 
A Eurobarometer survey conducted at the end of 2021 found that 25% of Bulgarians wanted European institutions to protect respect for national identities, cultures and traditions, compared with an EU average of 14%. Gender equality was considered important by only 11% of Bulgarians, compared with 24% across the EU.
As many as 48% of Bulgarians believe that their voice is not taken into account in the European institutions.
PHOTO magnific.com
In conclusion, we can say that at the top of the moral pyramid of contemporary Bulgarians stand their families and loved ones. The succession of political crises and financial instability, inflation and armed conflicts in recent years has turned the desire for peace, security and financial stability into a leading aspiration for Bulgarians. Security is placed above freedom, particularly among older people, while trust in institutions remains low. Most troublingly, democratic principles and equality among people continue to lose ground in the personal value systems of Bulgarians today. This can only raise further questions about the nation’s bright European future.

China Focus: Global businesses eye opportunities as China import expo nears
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:56:23 CST
20:56:23 KST

SHANGHAI, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- With one month to go before the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE), companies from around the world are preparing to gather in Shanghai in east China, bringing products ranging from advanced manufacturing equipment and medical technologies to African coffee and Syrian soap.
The annual expo, the world's first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports, has become a major platform for foreign companies seeking access to the vast consumer and industrial markets of the world's second-largest economy.
Since its launch in 2018, the CIIE has drawn participants from more than 180 countries, regions and international organizations. Overseas exhibitors have made about 27,000 appearances at its business exhibitions, with over 3,400 new products, technologies and services making their debuts.
This year's event, scheduled from Nov. 5 to 10, comes as China begins its 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) with a renewed push for high-standard opening up and stronger domestic demand.
For some companies, this year's CIIE will be their first.
Austria's WFL Millturn Technologies, a machine tool manufacturer that entered the Chinese market more than 20 years ago, shipped its exhibits from the industrial city of Linz in August.
WFL Managing Director Stefan Hackl said the company decided to join the CIIE given China's role at the heart of the global manufacturing chain, and hopes to use the expo to expand further in the Chinese and Asia-Pacific markets.
"I don't see any good reason why we will not be successful in China in the upcoming decades," Hackl said.
Singapore-based Perennial Holdings Private Limited is another newcomer.
The company has established China's first wholly foreign-owned tertiary general hospital in Tianjin in northern China. Since opening, the hospital has received patients from more than 40 countries and regions, while the company is pursuing further healthcare investments in more Chinese cities.
"When you invest in China, you are investing in the most competitive market in the world," said Pua Seck Guan, executive chairman and CEO of Perennial Holdings.
Pua added that China's opening up of its healthcare sector could create more opportunities for foreign investors.
The newcomers arrive as China continues to widen market access for foreign businesses. In 2025, the country registered 70,392 newly established foreign-invested firms, a record high and up 19.1 percent year on year. In the first half of 2026, the number rose 5.3 percent from a year earlier, with foreign direct investment in actual use reaching 402.14 billion yuan (roughly 59.71 billion U.S. dollars).
China is also seeking to expand imports as it works to boost domestic consumption and pursue more balanced trade. In August, imports increased by 21.7 percent, with growth exceeding that of exports for a sixth successive month.
The opportunities offered by the CIIE extend beyond large multinational companies. Nearly 13,000 overseas micro, small and medium-sized enterprises have participated in the first eight editions.
Syrian businessman Muhannad Shakally is preparing for his 9th CIIE. When he brought traditional Syrian soap to the inaugural expo in 2018, he was testing the Chinese market.
Today, monthly orders exceed five tonnes, equivalent to around 20,000 bars. "They sell almost as soon as they arrive. I don't even keep inventory," he said.
This year, he plans to introduce aromatherapy products and Syrian herbal teas, hoping to bring more products from his country to Chinese consumers.
For years, the CIIE has provided free booths to exhibitors from the world's least developed countries. This year, organizers will upgrade a dedicated section for Asian and African products, with measures to help African businesses tap opportunities created by China's zero-tariff policy.
Since May 1, China has applied zero-tariff treatment to imports from all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations, while expanding market access through measures including upgraded "green channels" for products such as dried chilies, coffee beans, cashews and wild aquatic items.
An official delegation from Cote d'Ivoire will make its first appearance at the CIIE's business exhibition, showcasing cocoa, coffee, cashews and kola nuts.
"We are very happy to participate for the first time. This will be a good opportunity to showcase Cote d'Ivoire to the world," said Rami Koné, an official with the country's export agency.
Einar Tangen, a senior fellow at the Center for International Governance Innovation, said small and medium-sized enterprises from the Global South, particularly those in Africa, were once on the margins of global trade. China, he said, has provided them with opportunities to share in the benefits of its opening up and development. ■

Feature: Healing little hearts: Kabul's new hospital brings life-saving surgery to Afghan children
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:56:08 CST
20:56:08 KST

KABUL, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- In a country grappling with profound healthcare shortages, a newly opened cardiac hospital on the outskirts of Kabul has begun offering specialized treatment for children living with congenital heart defects, restoring their ability to breathe freely, reclaiming their childhood smiles, and enabling them to envision a healthier tomorrow.
Supported by the Afghan Red Crescent Society, the 50-bed facility provides free diagnosis, treatment, and cardiac surgery to young patients from every corner of Afghanistan.
For countless children whose conditions have stolen their vitality and placed crushing emotional and financial burdens on their families, the hospital stands as a rare beacon of hope.
Mohammad Hassan, father of five children all afflicted with heart defects, journeyed nearly 390 km from the northern province of Jawzjan to Kabul, driven by a single, desperate hope to save his three-year-old daughter.
Having already lost one child to the same condition, Hassan now faces the ordeal with a mixture of anxiety and fragile optimism, seeking care that his family could never have afforded independently.
"I am happy that she is being treated here. Our financial situation is very difficult, and we could not afford the cost of treatment," Hassan told Xinhua.
A private hospital had demanded 300,000 afghanis (about 4,550 U.S. dollars) for his daughter's treatment -- an impossible sum for a daily-wage laborer struggling to sustain his household. With tears welling in his eyes, Hassan recalls the infant he could not save.
"My two-month-old daughter had a hole in her heart. She could not receive treatment and passed away," he said.
Naz Mohammad, father of a five-year-old girl, discovered his daughter's heart defect only after returning from work abroad.
He sought diagnosis at private hospitals, yet the prohibitive costs and his family's dire financial circumstances left essential care beyond reach. "Private hospitals have asked us to pay between 120,000 and 200,000 afghanis for her treatment. I cannot afford it," he said.
He now confronts a protracted wait of six months to two years, as throngs of families priced out of private care converge on the public facility.
Yet Naz Mohammad clings steadfastly to hope that his daughter's turn will arrive, that she will receive the treatment she urgently needs, and that she will grow up healthier with a brighter future ahead.
Dr. Abdul Wali Atmanzai, head of the cardiac hospital, explained that the facility commenced operations approximately two months ago, delivering diagnosis and treatment for children with heart defects, including those born with holes in their hearts.
For many low-income families, such specialized care had long been inaccessible. To date, 154 children have undergone surgery at the hospital, with four to eight procedures performed daily.
All services are provided entirely free of charge. "All services, from hospitalization and medical examinations to surgery and medicines, are provided free of charge," Dr. Atmanzai told Xinhua inside his office.
Atmanzai observed a rising tide of demand, with 20 to 30 new patients registering each day. While comprehensive national statistics remain unavailable, he estimates that more than 100,000 children across Afghanistan may be living with heart defects.
Without timely diagnosis, adequate facilities, and access to specialized surgery, many children forfeit their chance at life-saving intervention. "At the national level, 20 to 25 percent of such children may lose their lives," he said.
For Atmanzai and his colleagues, every successful operation transcends the surgical theater. It represents the restoration of a child's smile, the easing of a family's anguish, and the rekindling of hope for the years ahead. ■

Ukraine Is Running Out of Spare Locomotives as Russian Strikes Threaten Exports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:56:06 UTC
20:56:06 KST

Ukraine is seeking replacement locomotives from European partners after Russian strikes nearly exhausted its reserves, threatening the rail deliveries that keep the country’s Black Sea exports moving.
Ukraine is negotiating with countries whose railways use the same track gauge, the FT reported, citing Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi. The talks are aimed at securing additional rolling stock to replace equipment lost in Russian attacks.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The pressure is already being felt at one of Ukraine’s major maritime gateways.
Mykyta Hrubov, chief executive of port operator TIS, told the newspaper that three locomotives had been lost in the area around the company’s terminal at the port of Pivdennyi. He described the shortage as a bottleneck in port logistics.
Russia has intensified attacks in recent weeks on trains carrying grain and iron ore, two key Ukrainian export commodities. The losses threaten the inland transport network on which maritime trade depends.
Restoring port operations therefore leaves another challenge unresolved: getting enough cargo to the berths. A shortage of locomotives can constrain shipments even when conditions allow vessels to load and sail.
Ukraine had already appealed publicly for help replenishing its locomotive fleet before the latest report. On Sept. 15, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Russian attacks had damaged or destroyed more than 500 locomotives since the full-scale invasion began, with more than half of those losses occurring in 2026.
Russian Attack Sends Projectile Into Bus at Moldova Border
He urged partners to help find locomotives compatible with Ukraine’s 1,520-millimeter track gauge and provide financing to accelerate purchases of new equipment.
The request highlights a practical constraint on replacement efforts: Ukraine needs locomotives that can operate on its railway network.
Sybiha said the railway also carries essential supplies and evacuates civilians from frontline areas, making replacement locomotives necessary to sustain both economic activity and humanitarian operations.

Zheng Qinwen advances China Open last 16
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:55:55 CST
20:55:55 KST

Zheng Qinwen of China hits a return during the women's singles round of 32 match against Marie Bouzkova of the Czech Republic at 2026 China Open tennis tournament in Beijing, China, Oct. 5, 2026. (Xinhua/Sun Fei)
BEIJING, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- China's Zheng Qinwen battled past 18th seed Marie Bouzkova of the Czech Republic 7-6 (3), 4-6, 7-5 to reach the women's singles round of 16 at the China Open on Monday.
Zheng earned the first break of the match, but Bouzkova responded by converting a break point in the sixth game. The set went to a tiebreak, where Zheng pulled away to win 7-3.
Bouzkova made the stronger start to the second set, taking a 3-0 lead before holding off Zheng's attempts to recover and forcing a decider.
The players traded service holds for much of the final set before Zheng converted her second match point to seal the victory.
"Bouzkova is a very steady player, so I need to be patient, and I need to balance between forced and unforced errors," reflected Zheng right after the match.
Zheng will meet Alina Charaeva of Armenia in the next round. ■

Trio win Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels, optogenetics
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:55:47 CST
20:55:47 KST

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine is announced in Stockholm, Sweden, Oct. 5, 2026. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel were awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, the Nobel Assembly at Sweden's Karolinska Institute announced. (Xinhua/Lyu You)
STOCKHOLM, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Three scientists have been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the prize on Monday for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, the Nobel Assembly at Sweden's Karolinska Institute announced.
According to the institute, optogenetics is a method that shows how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviors in the living brain.
"Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel discovered a remarkable protein, channelrhodopsin, in a single-celled alga. Karl Deisseroth transformed the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells. The laureates have laid the foundation of a new era in neuroscience," the institute said in a press release.
Karl Deisseroth, born in the United States, is a professor at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University. Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, both born in Germany, are professors at Humboldt University of Berlin and the University of Würzburg, respectively.
The laureates will share a prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (about 1.19 million U.S. dollars). ■

At least 10 dead, several missing after boat collision in western DR Congo
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:55:44 CST
20:55:44 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- At least 10 people were killed and several others remained missing after two boats collided on the Congo River in western Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the DRC's official news agency reported Monday, citing provincial authorities.
The accident occurred overnight from Saturday to Sunday in Equateur Province, according to the reports. "The provisional toll stands at around 10 dead, several missing and 57 survivors," Chrispin Mputu, provincial interior minister, was quoted as saying.
The accident was caused by a collision between two vessels, one traveling from the capital, Kinshasa, and the other from Businga in neighboring Sud-Ubangi Province, the official said.
Search and rescue operations are continuing, local media reported. ■

S. Korea accuses DPRK of planting landmines south of MDL, demands apology
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:55:44 CST
20:55:44 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- The South Korean military on Monday accused the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) of planting landmines south of the military demarcation line (MDL), demanding an apology from Pyongyang.
Kwon Dae-won, vice chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), told a press briefing on the final investigation results that South Korean soldiers, who performed routine demilitarized zone (DMZ) operations south of the MDL, sustained severe injuries due to plastic anti-personnel landmines planted by the DPRK south of the MDL.
Kwon explained that the conclusion was based on the joint on-site investigation between the South Korean military and the United Nations Command from Sept. 26 to 29.
Kwon strongly urged the DPRK to immediately remove all landmines installed and offer a sincere apology to the South Korean service members who were injured in the explosion.
The incident occurred on Sept. 21 near the MDL, where three South Korean soldiers from the army's 25th division were injured while conducting a mission inside the southern side of the DMZ dividing the two Koreas.
Kim Yo Jong, department director of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea, said on Oct. 2 that South Korea intended "to plunge the situation in the Korean Peninsula again into a critical state" over a recent mine explosion along the border.
In a press statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), the senior DPRK official called the mine explosion a "farce" created by Seoul, adding that Seoul's conclusion was "groundless." ■

Pakistani PM stresses teachers' role in national progress on World Teachers' Day
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:55:44 CST
20:55:44 KST

ISLAMABAD, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said Monday that educational institutions and teachers lay the foundations for national progress and prosperity, emphasizing their contribution to shaping the future of the country.
In a message to mark World Teachers' Day, Sharif said teachers are instrumental in nurturing young people, developing their abilities, expanding their knowledge and instilling values that help shape societies.
Pakistan's development is closely linked to the quality of its education system and the dedication of its teachers, the prime minister said.
He stressed the need for an inclusive and future-oriented education system capable of responding to artificial intelligence, climate change, technological advancement and the changing demands of the job market.
Highlighting the country's efforts, Sharif said the government is committed to providing teachers with professional training, modern educational resources and a conducive teaching and learning environment.
The government is also pursuing curriculum reforms and expanding technical and vocational training to equip young people with skills aligned with industrial and employment needs, he said.
A new generation imbued with the values of integrity, compassion, tolerance, discipline, creativity, mutual respect and patriotism would be capable of shouldering the responsibilities of the future, he added. ■

NEW DELHI, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Three people, including an 11-year-old boy, were killed after a boat carrying them capsized in a wetland in India's northeastern state of Assam on Sunday, police said Monday.
The boat capsized at the Merbil wetland in the Ghilamara area of Lakhimpur district, about 418 km northeast of Dispur, the seat of Assam's state government.
Police have attributed the boat capsizing to rising water levels in the wetland.
Boat capsizing incidents are common in India as many people, especially in rural areas, use traditionally made boats as a mode of transport. ■

Philosophers Among Recent ARC Future Fellowship Winners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:55:02 UTC
20:55:02 KST

The Australian Research Council last month announced the winners of its latest round of Future Fellowships.
.
The fellowship awards are roughly AU $1 million, and are intended to support 4-year projects.
The philosophy faculty named in this recent round of fellowships include:
Guillermo Badia (The University of Queensland)
A project to develop new many-valued logics to help machines reason about data that is scored with numbers, probabilities, security access levels, etc. This is a significant issue since a great deal of information we handle in daily life comes in this form. This project expects to improve how we ask questions of complex databases by producing novel techniques and explore how much time and memory computers need to answer them. This has potential for applications in AI, secure data access and disease tracking, among others. The expected outcomes are novel logical tools for understanding and optimizing queries. Benefits include the development of distinguished expertise in Australia to lead in logic for advanced data technologies.
Stephanie Collins (Monash University)
This project aims to build a new ethical framework for business corporations, in light of recent Australian corporate scandals. It expects to generate a rigorous, philosophically grounded framework that reimagines what business corporations are and what they are for, using an innovative methodology that engages business ethics advisors and policymakers in ethical dialogue. Expected outcomes include new ethical principles to guide corporate governance and regulation, focused on the energy, care, and banking sectors. By reconceiving how business corporations can be contributors to wellbeing, the Fellowship’s benefits will include a positive transformation in how we understand and conceptualise ethics in business.
Nicholas Evans (Monash University)
This project aims to develop a comprehensive, unified ethical framework for decision making in Australian health security covering preparation for and responses to naturally occurring disease pandemics, biological weapons, and laboratory containment failures. The project expects to generate new knowledge in bioethics, using innovative and interdisciplinary methods to identify ethical responses during public health crises, and understand Australians’ beliefs about government preparation and responses to those crises. Expected outcomes of this project include novel bioethical frameworks in public health, improved trust in Australian pandemic response, and ethics guidance for Australian public health and national security policymakers.
Peter Evans (The University of Queensland)
Quantum theory works, but it fails to provide a clear picture of how and why it works. This project aims to address this problem by building a philosophical framework that places observers inside the scientific picture. Drawing on tools in philosophy and quantum physics, this framework expects to rethink objectivity for the quantum age, and demonstrate practical utility through case studies in optical clock networks and quantum devices. Expected benefits include a transformative new understanding of quantum reality, strengthened dialogue between science and humanities, and reinforced Australian research capacity and leadership in the rapidly growing quantum sector.
Luara Ferracioli (The University of Sydney)
This project aims to assess the ethics of demographic renewal, the process by which new citizens join a political community over time. Low fertility rates around the world raise the question of whether it is legitimate and ethical for liberal democracies to adopt pro-natalist polices, thereby encouraging citizens to have more children than they would otherwise. This project expects to generate new knowledge in political philosophy and public policy by developing a new theory of family formation policies. 
Sandra Leonie Field (Monash University)
This project aims to investigate fundamental questions of human agency: when are my desires just passively ‘from the outside’ and when do they count as active and ‘really mine’? Developing underappreciated theoretical resources from the great 17th century philosopher Spinoza, the project will generate new knowledge about Spinoza’s philosophical system and new knowledge in political philosophy concerning individual and collective agency. Expected outcomes include a novel Spinozist theoretical paradigm for political philosophy, and enhanced research capacity through the development of an Early Career Researcher network.
The full list of Fellowship winners is here.

Officers involved in strikes on Ukraine were among eight killed in Tu-95MS crash in Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:55:00 EEST
20:55:00 KST

Officers involved in strikes on Ukraine were among eight killed in Tu-95MS crash in Russia
Eight military personnel were killed when a Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed in Russia's Amur Oblast on 29 September. At least three of them were officers involved in combat missions or their preparation, according to the Book of Executioners, a Ukrainian project documenting Russian war criminals and people who betrayed Ukraine.
Source: Russian media outlets Mediazona and The Insider
Details: Russian media outlets reported that the names of those killed had been posted in the Selskiye Novosti (Rural News) social media group for Seryshevo, a settlement near the Ukrainka strategic air base. OSINT analyst duke garland was the first to flag the post.
A photo featuring the portraits of the eight men killed was also released by Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky district in Amur Oblast. He said the local authorities would ask the long-range aviation command to put the crew forward for state awards.
Mediazona verified the list and confirmed that all eight served in Russia's strategic aviation.
According to the media outlets, those killed are:
- Andrei Lobanov, 40
- Vladislav Moskovskikh, 31
- Artur Yenokian, 30
- Mikhail Kotyshev, 23
- Sergei, 47, whose surname is reported as Monsevich by Mediazona and Moisevich by The Insider
- Vladimir Kelip, 55
- Fedor Pavlyukov, 43
- Andrei Gerasimov, 36.
The OSINT analyst believes the portraits in the announcement follow the standard order in which Tu-95MS crew members are listed. On that basis, Lobanov was the crew commander, Moskovskikh the co-pilot, Yenokian the navigator, Kotyshev the navigator-operator (responsible for operating the bomber's mission systems), Monsevich the flight engineer, and Kelip the radio operator. Pavlyukov and Gerasimov were likely passengers or inspectors.
Mediazona says the quality of the photograph makes it difficult to establish the military ranks of all those killed with certainty.
The Insider checked the names against the Ukrainian Book of Executioners database and found Lobanov, Pavlyukov and Gerasimov in its records. Details about them had been added before the plane crashed.
As of November 2025, Major Andrei Lobanov was listed in the database as the deputy commander of a Tu-95MS squadron of the 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment, based at the Ukrainka airfield. According to the project, he directly commanded the unit and personally participated in combat missions.
Lieutenant Colonel Fedor Pavlyukov is listed as the regiment's deputy commander for flight training. He commanded a Tu-95MS squadron from August 2021 to April 2024. According to the project, he was responsible for preparing flight personnel for combat missions and directly led the unit.
Furthermore, in March 2022, Ukrainian intelligence included Pavlyukov on a list of Russian long-range aviation pilots who, according to its data, were being prepared to participate in the war against Ukraine.
Andrei Gerasimov is listed in the Book of Executioners as a major and commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in the 121st Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment. According to the database, he commanded the unit and personally took part in combat missions. However, Mediazona's casualty list gives his rank as lieutenant colonel.
Ukrainian serviceman and blogger Anatolii Shtefan also reported that at least three of those killed were involved in organising and executing missile strikes on Ukraine. Shtefan did not specify whom exactly he was referring to.
According to Port Amur, cited by The Insider, there were nine military personnel on board. The bodies of two of the crew members were not found immediately. The Russian Ministry of Defence initially reported six dead and one taken to hospital.
Background:
- On 29 September, the Tu-95MS crashed near the village of Krasnoyarovo in the Mazanovsky district in Amur Oblast.
- The Russian Defence Ministry claimed that the bomber was conducting a training flight without ammunition when it crashed in an unpopulated area. Regional authorities said the crew steered the aircraft away from residential buildings, and no one on the ground was injured.
- The Russian Defence Ministry sent an Aerospace Forces commission to the site to establish what caused the crash. Kommersant reported that investigators had tentatively attributed it to a technical malfunction. The Insider notes, however, that no conclusions about the cause of the crash have been publicly confirmed.
- According to Mediazona, most of those killed had served at the Engels strategic bomber airbase in Saratov Oblast before moving to the Ukrainka airbase. According to the outlet, Russia began pulling its strategic bombers out of Engels after Ukraine launched its first drone attacks on the airfield.
- After the Security Service of Ukraine carried out Operation Spider's Web, the Ukrainka airbase in Russia's Far East became one of the main bases for its strategic aviation. According to The Insider, a Tu-95MS combat mission from the base, involving stopovers at Engels or Olenya airfield, missile launches and the return flight, can cover more than 12,000 km and last around 23 hours. The outlet notes that flights of this length accelerate wear on the aircraft and their engines, shortening their service life.

Data of over 10M customers exposed in cyberattacks on Japanese firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:54:43 UTC
20:54:43 KST

Faisal Mahmud
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Two Japanese companies have reported major data breaches following unauthorized access to their computer systems, potentially exposing information belonging to millions of customers, local media reported Monday.
Monogatari Corp., operator of the Yakiniku King barbecue restaurant chain, said information belonging to more than 10 million customers was leaked after unauthorized access to its reservation and rewards app, according to Kyodo News.
The compromised information included customers’ names, email addresses, phone numbers and membership numbers.
The breach was detected Friday, the company said, adding that it had found no evidence so far that the leaked information had been misused.
Separately, Daiwa Securities Group said data belonging to around 110,000 customers of its brokerage unit may have been compromised following unauthorized access to a contractor-operated server, Kyodo reported.
The intrusion occurred between Friday evening and Saturday morning on a server operated by Scala Communications Inc., which provides Daiwa Securities with an online customer inquiry management service.
Potentially exposed information includes names, email addresses and account numbers.
Including inquiries that contained no personal information, around 220,000 pieces of data may have been affected.
Daiwa said the compromised information could not be used to conduct transactions, including online trades.
The brokerage has also found no evidence so far that the potentially compromised information has been published or circulated online.

Association of Ukrainian Cities urges PM to unblock municipal funds
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:54:42 EEST
20:54:42 KST

The Board of the Association of Ukrainian Cities appealed to Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky, demanding the immediate resumption of payments to local communities.
Despite municipalities having funds in their accounts and complying with the requirements of Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 590, key financial settlements have been blocked in Ukraine since September 9. As a result, communities are unable to purchase fuel for ambulances and special equipment used to clear rubble after enemy shelling. In addition, funding for the repair and equipping of medical, educational and social facilities, preparations for the heating season and the arrangement of Points of Invincibility has been completely halted. The restoration of damaged infrastructure and energy facilities, as well as implementation of resilience plans, are under threat.
"Blocking settlements by communities with energy resource suppliers, fuel suppliers, repair crews, waste removal companies and others is leading to consequences that the aggressor has failed to achieve through shelling since the beginning of the full-scale invasion," the Association of Ukrainian Cities said in its appeal.
Village, settlement and city mayors are drawing the Ukrainian prime minister's attention to the fact that without the immediate unblocking of community payments, the conditions for the operation of state and international institutions, educational, medical and social facilities in all Ukrainian communities will be destroyed.
The Board of the Association of Ukrainian Cities called on the prime minister to halt the accrual of penalties against communities for failure to repay loans and make timely payments due to the absence of an official decision to block settlements, and also to initiate bringing to account government officials whose actions or inaction have halted the operation of all municipal services in the country.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
