Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (AFP File Photo)
Israel held official ceremonies on Oct. 5 to mark the third anniversary of Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023 attack, which triggered the Gaza war, as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sought to fend off mounting criticism over the assault ahead of a critical election.
“There will be no Hamas rule in Gaza. Anyone who was involved in the attack against us and held our hostages is living on borrowed time,” Netanyahu said during the state ceremony.
The Oct. 7 attack killed 1,221 people in Israel and saw 251 others taken hostage, according to Israeli figures. Israel’s ensuing war on Gaza has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, while large parts of the territory have been reduced to rubble and severe humanitarian deprivation continues.
Netanyahu has faced intense criticism at home over the security failures surrounding the 2023 attack, with his popularity falling to critical levels ahead of elections scheduled for Oct. 27.
Critics have accused the prime minister of prolonging the war for political reasons, even at the cost of delaying the return of Israeli hostages.
His persistent opposition to the establishment of a state commission of inquiry into the failures surrounding the attack has also come under fire, particularly as demands for an investigation into the government and military’s handling of the crisis have intensified.
The latest controversy was fueled by a series of reports in the Israeli press alleging that the leader of the United Arab Emirates had personally warned Netanyahu about a possible Hamas attack in October 2023.
The reports triggered a political firestorm in Israel and were followed by further accounts that Egypt had similarly warned Israel of an impending Hamas assault, but that Netanyahu ignored the warnings.
Speaking at the Oct. 5 ceremony, Israeli military Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir acknowledged the army’s failure to protect civilians during the attack, pledged thorough investigations into the failures and called for renewed vigilance.

Thousands of protesters blockaded a bishop inside a church in a Polish village on Sunday – and some even physically attacked him – amid anger over the dismissal of a popular long-serving local Catholic priest.
As a result, police were called in and, after efforts by negotiators to calm the crowd failed, officers escorted the bishop away from the premises after midnight.

The incident took place in the village of Grojec, near the city of Oświęcim in southern Poland. The municipality has an official population of around 3,200, but local media – including the Gazeta Krakowska newspaper and Fakty Oświęcim website – report that around 3,000 people gathered on Sunday evening to protest.
They were angered by the decision to remove local priest Józef Zborek, who has served in the parish for almost 30 years, from his position.
The diocese of Bielsko-Żywiec says the priest was found in church proceedings to have been guilty of “serious and proven irregularities in the performance of his duties”. However, the actual nature of his offences has not been publicly revealed, with the church noting that, under canon law, only Zborek himself can do so.
The case against him was initially reported in 2024. The priest repeatedly appealed against the decision, taking the case to the Vatican. However, the decision to remove him was upheld, with Zborek removed from his position on Saturday.
On Sunday, Roman Pindel, the bishop of Bielsko-Żywiec, visited Grojec to meet with the parish council and discuss the situation. Afterwards, he proceeded to the local church to attend the Eucharist.
However, before his arrival, thousands of people had gathered around the church, holding signs saying “Don’t take away our parish priest”. Some burst inside and disrupted the ceremony.
Asked about the reasons for Zborek’s popularity, one woman told Gazeta Krakowska that he had accepted children who had been turned away by other priests for first communion and had “no problem baptising illegitimate children”.
News website Onet reports that one local theory is that the priest was removed from his position because he had not charged parishioners for sacraments. Churches in Poland generally expect people to make payments in return for sacraments such as baptism, confirmation and marriage.

The bishop reiterated that only Zborek himself was authorised to disclose the reasons for his dismissal.
But, with a large, angry crowd still gathered outside and blocking all exits, the bishop was evacuated under the protection of officers at around 1 a.m.

The City Duma will select the city's next mayor from a shortlist presented by Governor Veniamin Kondratyev.

A local court began hearing a lawsuit against Naumov’s administration over the construction project.
Media reports say that residents objected to a general infrastructure plan adopted by the city under Naumov’s leadership, with some 27,000 residents commenting on the plan, sparking mass protests.
Complaints against Naumov’s administration have also piled up due to the administration’s failure to manage winter weather emergencies and stalled transit projects.

French public broadcaster drops plan to use Israeli firm for political program: Report

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
France Televisions scrapped plans to use an Israeli company to develop an interactive tool for a political program after internal concerns were raised over the handling of viewers’ personal data, French investigative outlet Mediapart reported Monday.
The public broadcaster had reportedly planned to work with Terrific, an Israeli company specializing in e-commerce, on an interactive platform called Agora for the relaunch of France 2’s political program, L’heure de verite (The Hour of Truth), scheduled for Oct. 8.
The platform was intended to allow viewers to send questions to presidential candidates and participate in polls in real time, according to the report.
Mediapart reported that the project could have involved the collection of data on the political preferences of users of France Televisions’ Franceinfo website.
The outlet also reported that Terrific CEO Israel Grintz co-founded a company in 2018 that markets political campaign targeting tools.
France Televisions ultimately abandoned the project and assigned the work to its own technical teams, according to Mediapart.
The broadcaster told Mediapart that Terrific had proposed a public-interaction system for television programs, including political programs, but that tests conducted by its editorial and technical teams had not been conclusive.
Mediapart also reported concerns over another Terrific-developed advertising tool, Shoppable, used on the France.tv platform.
The tool was removed from the platform on Sept. 3 after users reported that their antivirus software had detected risks related to phishing and personal data.
France Televisions’ technical teams had found the tool was collecting data that could contribute to creating user profiles, including a unique identifier, URLs of pages visited and certain content metadata.

Bulgarian Foreign Ministry proposes higher long-stay visa fees for foreigners

News
Bulgarian Foreign Ministry proposes higher long-stay visa fees for foreigners
Monday 5 October 2026 13:23
Monday, 5 October 2026, 13:23
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Bulgaria's Ministry of Foreign Affairs is proposing a 20% increase in the fee for accepting and processing applications for a Type D long-stay visa. The proposal has been published on the government’s Public Procurement Portal, BTA reports.
A Type D visa is issued to foreigners wishing to establish long-term or permanent residence in Bulgaria.
The proposal would raise the fee from €100 to €120. The ministry’s arguments state that a study has been conducted of the fees charged by other EU countries for the issuance of national long-stay visas. The current Bulgarian fee is below the average level, which, according to the ministry, creates fiscal, administrative and migration-related risks.
The fee also has a regulatory effect, with its lower level compared with those in other Schengen countries making Bulgaria an attractive “entry point” for migration pressure and attempts to abuse rights. The ministry also points to increased administrative pressure on Bulgarian consular services and migration authorities.

2026-10-05
11:10:05 UTC

Ukraine ranks fifth in Europe for defense startup founders, with 82 Ukrainian entrepreneurs building companies in the sector.
The figure comes from The State of Defence Tech 2026, a new report by Dealroom and Resilience Media.
Despite having one of Europe’s largest developer communities, and despite defense startups attracting 37% of all venture capital invested in Ukraine, the country receives a disproportionately small share of European investment.
In 2026, Dealroom recorded just $19.8 million in funding for Ukrainian companies, placing Ukraine 10th in Europe.
Since 2020, Ukrainian companies have raised a total of $46.5 million. However, according to ecosystem estimates, the actual figure could reach $100 million when deals not captured in the statistics are included.
Meanwhile, the European defense technology market is experiencing record growth of 309%, raising $7.4 billion as of September 2026.
Defense startups now account for 11.1% of the overall European venture capital market, while their share in EU countries has reached 15%.
Germany led Europe in investment volume with $3.5 billion, followed by Finland with $1.2 billion and the UK with $932 million.
Ukrainian defense tech companies are also attracting increasing amounts of U.S. capital. In particular, investor Axon invested $10 million in Buntar Aerospace and funded Farsight Vision.
Notable investors in the domestic market include Ukrainian fund Resist.UA and the Ukrainian Startup Fund.
Unmanned systems remain the main driver of the market, attracting $4.7 billion across 40 funding rounds.
Counter-drone solutions raised $1.2 billion, while maritime robotics attracted $796 million – more than in all previous years combined.

Tensions rise as Yemen army launches broad strikes against Houthis
Unknown

2026-10-05
11:09:57 UTC
20:09:57 KST

A Yemeni man inspects melted foam inside a factory after a strike that Houthi authorities-run media attributed to Saudi Arabia, in the Shamlan neighbourhood of Yemen's capital Sanaa on Oct. 4, 2026. (Photo by Mohammed HUWAIS / AFP) /
The Saudi-led military coalition announced on Oct. 5 its participation in the new Yemen government offensive targeting the Iran-backed Houthis, with 100 warplanes used in dawn strikes to provide air cover for ground forces.
“100 fighter jets participated at dawn today in Operation ‘Dawn of Yemen,’” coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki wrote on X, using the name for the new offensive announced on Oct. 4.
“Round-the-clock air support for the Yemeni armed forces on the ground.”
He said the coalition has secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets as part of the ongoing campaign.
The coalition’s announcement came after the Yemeni military said it launched a broad set of strikes against Houthi targets on Oct. 5, after the country’s internationally recognized government declared a
new campaign to retake all territory.
The Iran-backed Houthis have made fresh gains in recent weeks, capturing swaths of the country’s Red Sea coastline and territory around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key chokepoint for international shipping.
At war against the government, the Houthis launched a lightning offensive in September that has killed hundreds of combatants on both sides and, according to U.N. figures, forced more than 145,000
people to flee their homes.
Hours after the government announcement, Yemen’s military spokesman said its forces launched over 1,000 “strikes against artillery and rocket launcher positions, defensive fortifications, approach and reinforcement routes, supply lines and logistics assets, combat reinforcements” belonging to the Houthis.
The government strikes, however, have yet to blunt ongoing Houthi advances on the ground. 
On Oct. 4, the group effectively encircled the key city of Taiz after cutting the main supply route linking the city to the interim government capital of Aden.
“It is a significant development, but I think it is still too early to say that we are witnessing a decisive turning point,” Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group, told AFP.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.
The fighting in Yemen has also drawn in Saudi Arabia, leader of an anti-Houthi military coalition since 2015, with the group regularly claiming attacks on the kingdom’s territory in recent weeks and declaring a blockade of its ships in the Red Sea.

PROFILE - Who are the winners of 2026 Nobel Medicine Prize?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:07:29 UTC
20:07:29 KST

Rabia Ali
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Three scientists whose work has transformed the study of the brain have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries that allow researchers to control nerve cells using light.
Karl Deisseroth of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel of the University of Wurzburg, were awarded the prize “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics,” the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet said Monday.
Their discoveries helped establish optogenetics, a technique that uses light-sensitive proteins to control the activity of nerve cells and study how neural circuits influence functions such as memory, feelings and behaviour.
Here is a profile of the three scientists and the work that led to the Nobel Prize.
 
Karl Deisseroth
American scientist Karl Deisseroth is a neuroscientist, bioengineer and practicing psychiatrist at Stanford University.
He received an undergraduate degree in biochemical sciences from Harvard University in 1992 before earning a PhD in neuroscience and an MD from Stanford in 1998 and 2000, respectively.
He also completed a medical internship, postdoctoral training and an adult psychiatry residency at Stanford.
Deisseroth's research focuses on understanding and manipulating neural circuits. His work helped turn channelrhodopsin, a light-sensitive protein discovered by Hegemann and Nagel, into a tool for controlling neurons.
In 2005, Deisseroth showed that neurons containing the protein could be activated with blue light. Two years later, he demonstrated the technique in the brains of living mice.
 
Peter Hegemann
German biophysicist Peter Hegemann was born in Munster in 1954.
He studied chemistry at the University of Munster and Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich before receiving his PhD in biochemistry from the Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry in 1984.
He later led a research group at the institute, became a professor at the University of Regensburg and joined Humboldt University of Berlin in 2004.
Hegemann became interested in how the single-celled green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii detects light and moves toward it.
His research helped identify channelrhodopsins, light-sensitive proteins that form channels in cell membranes. Together with Nagel, he showed that these proteins could make cells respond to light.
 
Georg Nagel
German biophysicist Georg Nagel was born in Weingarten in 1953. He studied biology and biophysics at the University of Konstanz before completing his doctorate at Goethe University Frankfurt in 1988.
He subsequently carried out postdoctoral research at Yale University and Rockefeller University in the US. He returned to Germany as a research group leader at the Max Planck Institute of Biophysics in Frankfurt.
Nagel joined the University of Wurzburg in 2004.
He held a professorship in molecular plant physiology until 2021 and is now a senior professor at its Institute of Physiology, where his research includes membrane transport, artificial light receptors and their optogenetic applications.
Nagel and Hegemann's work on channelrhodopsin showed that light could trigger electrical changes in cells, providing a crucial foundation for optogenetics.

INTERVIEW - Civilian 'space race 2.0' with China closer than US would like right now: NASA deputy chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:04:41 UTC
20:04:41 KST

INTERVIEW - Civilian 'space race 2.0' with China closer than US would like right now: NASA deputy chief
Matt Anderson tells Anadolu that US leads 'in all 3 sectors of space,' hints at 'exciting news' soon
Beril Canakci
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
ANTALYA, Türkiye
The civilian race to the Moon between the US and China is tighter than Washington would like, NASA's deputy administrator said Monday, signaling that the space agency will soon make a major announcement.
"We won the first space race in the 60s and early 70s, and right now the space race 2.0 ... the civilian space race ... is closer than we would like right now," Matt Anderson told Anadolu on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) in Türkiye's Mediterranean province of Antalya.
"But we're going to be confident, and we have some exciting news to announce very soon," he said, without elaborating.
China has set a goal of putting astronauts on the lunar surface by 2030 and said the development of its Long March 10 heavy-lift rocket, Mengzhou crew spacecraft, and Lanyue lunar lander is on track.
NASA flew four astronauts around the Moon on its Artemis II mission in April. The agency later turned Artemis III into an Earth-orbit test flight planned for 2027 and now aims to return astronauts to the lunar surface with Artemis IV in 2028, for the first time since Apollo 17 in 1972.
Anderson, a retired US Air Force colonel, was sworn in as NASA's 16th deputy administrator in May.
'Peaceful exploration' vs national security
Asked whether the new race is about prestige or science, Anderson said NASA's focus is "the scientific exploration and discovery," adding that the Artemis era is "very different" from the Apollo program of the 1960s.
"We're going to the lunar surface to stay, building a permanent presence in moon base to learn more about the surface, and ultimately what we call the third space race is pushing on to Mars and beyond," he said.
On concerns over an arms race in orbit, Anderson said: "I do think the United States is leading in all three sectors of space right now."
He drew a line between NASA's mission and the military's. "We do separate NASA's peaceful exploration of space and then the national security side of space, which is the US Space Force and US Space Command," he said, adding that NASA likes to partner with other government agencies.
Last month, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the country has "on-orbit space control weapons," the first time a US official publicly confirmed the existence of weapons in space. Russia and China responded by accusing Washington of launching an arms race in space.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans placing nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not explicitly prohibit conventional arms.
Space station's 'responsible' end
Anderson said NASA is "very proud of our almost 26 years of continuous presence in low Earth orbit" aboard the International Space Station (ISS).
"When the time comes for the ISS's days to end, we have already contracted a company to have a very responsible manner of de-orbiting the ISS down to Earth," he said.
The ISS has been continuously crewed since November 2000. In 2024, NASA picked SpaceX to build a dedicated US Deorbit Vehicle under a contract worth up to $843 million, designed to guide the station to a controlled reentry over a remote ocean area once operations end, currently planned for 2030.
Data centers in orbit, AI autonomy
On plans to place data centers in space, Anderson said the "barrier to entry to get to space right now is still very high," citing launch costs.
"But if the opportunity presents itself for either private industry or governments, and there's a way to make money and help things on Earth, I would welcome that," he said.
In January, SpaceX asked the US Federal Communications Commission for permission to deploy up to 1 million satellites that would operate as solar-powered data centers for artificial intelligence.
Asked whether granting AI autonomy in space is a cause for concern, Anderson said: "No, I don't think we should be worried about it."
"(US) President (Donald) Trump just recently convened the best experts in super intelligence across the globe to talk about this very thing. I'm just confident that in the right hands, with the United States leadership, it'll be working out really well," he said.
Trump hosted leading tech executives at the White House on Sept. 29, where companies signed a voluntary, non-binding pact called the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, as his administration pushes to use the term "super intelligence" in place of "artificial intelligence."
Expanding international partnerships and Türkiye's role
Anderson said he is "really excited for the future of Türkiye in the space community," noting that the country has just joined the Artemis Accords.
"With that, Türkiye can now help us, with all the other members of the Accords, go up and build our Moon base. That can help the engineers of Türkiye, the scientists, and maybe even astronauts," he added.
Türkiye signed the accords on Sept. 1 at NASA headquarters in Washington, becoming the 71st signatory, with Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir signing on behalf of the country.
Launched in 2020 by the US and seven founding countries, the non-binding accords set out common principles for safe, transparent, and peaceful civil exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
"Space is a national priority, and clearly, with signing the Artemis Accords, under (Turkish) President (Recep Tayyip) Erdogan's leadership, it is a national priority for Türkiye. So, we look forward to that partnership and see where it goes from here," he said.
Türkiye plans to launch its first domestically built lunar spacecraft in early 2027, according to Kacir. Turkish astronaut Alper Gezeravci flew to the ISS in January 2024 as the country's first person in space.
Describing his agenda in Antalya, Anderson said the congress is about "building trust, teamwork, and ultimately some training" with fellow Artemis Accords countries.
"This is a great way for the United States, and for NASA in particular, to work with the other space agencies, work with the other governments, to see where we can build all our objectives," he said.
IAC 2026, running on Oct. 5-9, is organized by the International Astronautical Federation and hosted by the Turkish Space Agency, with SAHA Istanbul as co-host. It is the first time Türkiye is hosting the congress.

Schneider Electric shares plunge on record $22.6bn PTC deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:04:38 UTC
20:04:38 KST

French energy technology group Schneider Electric has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Boston-based PTC for $22.6bn (€20.1bn) to expand its industrial AI business. The French company's shares plummeted on Monday following the announcement.
Schneider Electric, one of Europe's most valuable companies, saw its shares plunge after confirming an agreement to buy US-based industrial design software company PTC.
The deal is expected to be the largest acquisition in Schneider Electric's history, as the company seeks to expand its industrial AI capabilities using product and engineering data.
The French energy technology group will pay $205 per share for 100% of PTC's shares in cash, valuing its equity at $22.6bn (€20.1bn) and the business, including debt, at $23.7bn (€21.1bn).
The deal "creates a leading, scaled, open and interoperable industrial software and AI franchise", Schneider said in a statement, adding that PTC's board had agreed to the deal. The offer represents a 42.3% premium to PTC's last closing share price.
Schneider said the deal would combine industrial software and AI to help customers design, manufacture, operate and maintain products more efficiently, using industrial data to guide decisions and improve performance.
Olivier Blum, chief executive of Schneider Electric, said: "The acquisition of PTC represents an important step forward in our ambition to lead the new era of Energy and Industrial Intelligence. Together, we are creating the industry’s most complete Software & AI powerhouse and highest-quality portfolio bridging the physical and digital worlds."
The move comes amid concerns that advances in artificial intelligence could undermine software companies' business models by offering cheaper alternatives to their services.
PTC’s valuation this year had fallen as low as 13.1 times the next 12 months' earnings, according to MarketWatch, citing FactSet.
The publication cited analysts at Jefferies who warned that fears of AI disruption had depressed software valuations, allowing Schneider to buy PTC at a decade-low valuation, but could continue to weigh on Schneider's shares after the deal.
PTC's chief executive Neil Barua said: "We gain substantial scale and resources to accelerate innovation, advance our Intelligent Product Lifecycle vision, and expand our business into more geographies and end markets to serve more customers."
The Boston-based company has more than 7,000 employees and serves more than 30,000 customers. It generated roughly half of its revenue in the Americas in its 2025 financial year.
Schneider expects to issue up to €17bn in debt and up to €6bn in new shares to pay for the deal.
The company said it expects annual cost savings of €250m by the third year after completion, alongside approximately €800m in additional revenue from combining the businesses.
Schneider also expects to pause share buybacks in 2027 and 2028, before accelerating purchases to complete its existing €2.5bn–€3.5bn programme by the end of 2030.
The deal is expected to close by the third quarter of 2027, subject to customary conditions, including approval from PTC shareholders holding at least a majority of its outstanding shares and the required regulatory approvals.
Schneider's shares were down more than 9% in morning trading in Paris following the announcement.

Peru prison inmates sew 'pope dolls' ahead of pontiff's visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:03:46 UTC
20:03:46 KST

Peru prison inmates sew 'pope dolls' ahead of pontiff's visit
LIMA, Oct 5 - Behind the steel bars of Lima's Chorrillos Women's Prison, the rhythmic clatter of sewing machines and the snip of scissors mark a rush to meet a deadline.
Inmates of the high-security prison are hand-stitching velvet dolls and stringing together beaded necklaces, all bearing the face of Pope Leo, ahead of his November 6-17 trip to South America. The initiative, part of Peru's "productive prisons" program, aims to fund the women's reintegration into society.
"Right now, we are in 'pope mode'," said Nanny, an inmate who asked to remain anonymous as she carefully stuffed a doll with cotton. "We found out last year the pope held a Peruvian ID card, so we launched the idea of making a doll for everyone — children and adults alike."
The pope, born in the US as Robert Prevost, is a naturalized Peruvian who served as a missionary and bishop in the country for decades before Pope Francis brought him to Rome in 2023. He was elected pope in May 2025.
For the women, the work provides a mental escape and a way to support their families from afar. "We lose personal contact with our children, who suffer the most," Nanny said. "We may not be there in body, but we are there in soul and heart."
Among piles of fabric scraps, 78 inmates craft items ranging from $9 stuffed toys to intricate bracelets that are sold outside the prison.
For Judith Vargas, a Colombian national incarcerated for six years, the workshop is a rare chance to learn. "It distracts me and teaches me things I didn't know, like making earrings and necklaces," she said.
Prison warden Doris Nakandakari said while the program teaches vocational skills, the inmates are hoping for a spiritual reward. "Their greatest wish is for the pope to visit them ... to give them a blessing and the courage to keep moving forward," she said.
Peru is the final stop on Leo's regional tour, which includes Uruguay and Argentina. REUTERS

Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Launch Site, UAV Storage Facility and Command Post
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck several Russian military facilities in temporarily occupied territories on October 4 and overnight into October 5, including a drone launch site, a command post, and a UAV storage facility, Ukraine’s General Staff reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In the Donetsk area, Ukrainian forces hit a site used by Russian troops to store, prepare, and launch attack drones. According to the statement, systematic strikes on such facilities are intended to reduce Russia’s ability to deploy attack UAVs and use them against Ukrainian civilian infrastructure.
Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian communications hub in the Donetsk area.
In the temporarily occupied Berdiansk area of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian troops targeted a Russian command post and a drone storage facility. A Russian military repair unit was also hit near Liubymivka in the Zaporizhzhia region.
In addition, Ukrainian forces carried out strikes against concentrations of Russian personnel near Komysh-Zoria in the Zaporizhzhia region, Uspenka in the Luhansk region, and Donetsk.
The latest operations follow a Ukrainian long-range drone strike against Russia’s Khanskaya military airfield in the Republic of Adygea overnight on October 4. According to Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), the attack struck a Russian Su-35 multirole fighter and a Su-34 fighter-bomber.
The SBU said the operation was carried out using long-range drones operated by its Alpha Special Operations Center. The Khanskaya airfield is located approximately 500 kilometers from Ukrainian-controlled territory.

Russia Cuts Coal Prices, Yet China and Türkiye Imports Keep Falling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:03:31 UTC
20:03:31 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Cuts Coal Prices, Yet China and Türkiye Imports Keep Falling
Russian coal exports to China fell 10.8% year over year in January-August 2026 as higher logistics costs, import duties, and stronger competition eroded Moscow’s position in one of its key markets.
The Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine (SZRU) reported the figures on its official website on October 4. Russian suppliers delivered 53.15 million tons of coal to China during the eight-month period, losing ground to Mongolia and Indonesia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the agency, Mongolian coal imports surged 48.9% to 78.39 million tons, while Indonesia supplied 121 million tons. China imported 310 million tons of coal overall during the period.
Mongolia benefits from a shared land border with China and zero import duties, while Russian coal faces tariffs of 3% to 6%. Australia and Indonesia also receive zero-duty treatment under free-trade arrangements.
Russian producers are already offering discounts of around 10%, but further reductions could make exports unprofitable. Transport costs are adding further pressure, with the cost of shipping coal from Russia’s Vostochny port to China rising 45.5% from the start of 2026 through September 11.
Thermal coal exports could face the strongest pressure as Russian suppliers compete with Chinese mines while absorbing higher rail and freight costs. Russian railway tariffs increased again in October, while stronger demand for open freight wagons has raised transportation expenses.
The agency added that the pressure is also spreading beyond China. Russian coking coal exports to Türkiye fell 30% during the first seven months of 2026, with no shipments recorded in July, while coal deliveries to Russia’s southern ports dropped 33% that month compared with June.
The slump in southern deliveries coincides with mounting maritime risks in the Black Sea, where Ukrainian drone attacks on commercial vessels bound for Novorossiysk have driven up shipping costs.
Shipowners have pulled dozens of coal-transporting vessels from the region or halted operations altogether, and bulk carrier availability dropped by 21% in a single month. In early August, carriers serving the route raised freight rates by up to fourfold, while war-risk insurance premiums climbed to double or triple base freight rates.

Russian Armor Appears Less Often as Ukrainian Drones Keep Striking in Kharkiv
Ukrainian forces reported destroying a Russian tank, an artillery piece, and multiple transport vehicles in the northern Kharkiv region, according to a statement published online by Ukraine’s 16th Army Corps on October 5.
The strikes were carried out by drone operators from the Hart border brigade in the South Slobozhanskyi direction, where the unit reported that Russian armored vehicles have been appearing less frequently.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The strikes come as Ukraine reports exceptionally high Russian losses across the front. According to Ukraine’s General Staff, Russia lost an estimated 46,230 troops killed or wounded in September, while Ukrainian forces also regained territory in the Donetsk region and continued to slow Russian advances.
“The sky here is under the watchful control of UAV operators from the Hart border brigade,” the 16th Army Corps stated.

“The result of another such attempt was a struck tank, a gun, and several vehicles that the enemy used to support its units,” the statement noted.

“For Russian equipment, appearing in Hart’s sights is far from a promising prospect,” the 16th Army Corps stated.
Days earlier, Ukrainian FPV operators from the 423rd Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment destroyed a Russian T-54 tank that had reportedly been moved nearly 9,000 kilometers from storage facilities in Russia’s Far East. The Soviet-era vehicle had been fitted with additional protective structures but was still struck deep behind Russian lines.

French students set fire to Paris school entrance on eve of nationwide day of action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:02:26 UTC
20:02:26 KST

More than 400 schools were disrupted by late morning, as the government promised a bill to dock family benefits over damage.
A 15-year-old student had his hand blown off during a protest in northern France on Monday, authorities said, as demonstrations disrupted hundreds of schools on the eve of a nationwide day of action.
A police union source said the student, in the town of Lens, appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, hoping to throw it back, when the device exploded in his hand.
Students have been protesting over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities. Tuesday's day of action has been called by the Union syndicale lycéenne (USL), a high-school students' union.
Among the schools hit was the Vauquelin secondary school in Paris's 13th arrondissement, where "around ten hooded and masked young people came up to the entrance", according to headteacher Carole Zerbib. They "brought bins and inflammable items" to the doorway and then set them alight, she told French news channel BFMTV.
As a result, the school will remain closed for the day. "These are criminal acts that fall under the law and must be punished in the harshest possible way," said Jean-Didier Berger, France's junior interior minister.
Demonstrations and tensions were also reported outside the Voltaire, Sophie-Germain and Turgot high schools in Paris, as well as in the cities of Lyon and Lille. "Around forty higher-education sites" are also expected to be disrupted, Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste told the radio station Sud Radio.
By late morning, 413 schools had been or were still "subject to actions or disruptions since the start of the day", according to France's education ministry. That represents a 27% fall compared with the same time on Friday, although 40% of the schools had not previously been affected.
"Vandals pay" bill
In response to the violence seen in recent days, government spokesperson Maud Bregeon told news channel CNews that a bill known as "casseurs-payeurs", or "vandals pay", would be examined in the Senate on 27 October.
"It will allow us to dock family benefits… for damage caused by adults or minors" and "to introduce a form of collective responsibility", she said.
Mathilde Panot, who leads the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) group in the National Assembly, told public broadcaster franceinfo that "there is no political response" to the high-school students' demands, only "a policing response".
Tuesday's day of action, dubbed "Act III", is backed by a broad alliance of education unions. The centre-left Socialist Party (PS) has also called on people to stand "alongside" high-school students.

Former Prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched legal action against Thames Valley Police to challenge the lawfulness of search warrants that led to his arrest earlier this year, according to a judicial spokesperson.
A private High Court hearing is due to take place Thursday before Justice Hilliard to determine whether documents relating to Mountbatten-Windsor’s application for judicial review can be made public, according to British media reports.
Thames Valley Police is opposing the release of the documents.
The legal challenge stems from warrants issued by an Old Bailey judge that enabled police to search Mountbatten-Windsor’s residence on the Sandringham estate and his former home, Royal Lodge in Windsor, in February.
Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on Feb. 19 on suspicion of misconduct related to the sharing of confidential material with Epstein, who amassed a fortune as a financier before being convicted over sex crimes and dying in jail in 2019.
Mountbatten-Windsor was interviewed under caution and subsequently released while the investigation continued.
A High Court judge later granted Mountbatten-Windsor permission to challenge the legality of the police force’s actions in relation to the searches.
According to the Daily Telegraph, it is the first time a member of the royal family has challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of King Charles I in 1649.
Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied wrongdoing in connection with his association with Epstein and rejected claims of personal gain linked to his trade role.
According to files released in January, Andrew sent Epstein details of his upcoming official trips as trade envoy to Singapore, Vietnam, the Chinese city of Shenzhen, and Hong Kong in October 2010, and the following month apparently shared official reports from the trips.
Thames Valley Police confirmed that its investigation remains ongoing.
“Whilst our investigation into misconduct in public office continues, we are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the central criminal court. As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further,” a spokesperson for the force that carried out the arrest told the BBC.

Should you be ‘poop maxxing,’ or ‘fiber maxxing’? Experts explain what’s healthy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:01:52 UTC
20:01:52 KST

The eyes may be the “window to the soul,” but the gut is the window to our health. Our stools contain a wealth of information—about our nutrient balance, our metabolism and even warning signs of disease.
Gut fanatics on social media have jumped in on the promise of poo. Known as “poop maxxing,” or more politely, “fiber maxxing,” there is a swell of enthusiasm for high-fiber foods, regular bowel movements and the quest for a healthy gut.
Put bluntly, unless you have specific symptoms (more on these in a moment), there is no reason to obsess over your excrement. But there is some truth to these trends, microbiome experts say.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“I think that poop maxxing and fiber maxxing are some of the more legitimate health trends that I’ve heard about,” says Bill Sullivan, a microbiologist at Indiana University.
The reason why has to do with the power of fiber, he says. A person’s recommended daily fiber intake depends on age and sex, but the U.S. Department of Agriculture has historically recommended ranges from 22 to 34 grams for adults.
“There is sound evidence that if you increase the amount of fiber up to the recommended levels—you don’t need to go beyond that—you are going to gain a lot of physical and mental health benefits, no question,” Sullivan says.
Here’s everything you need to know to help maximize your gut health.
What does poop have to do with my health?
The gut is “the biggest endocrine organ you have in your body,” says Justin O’Sullivan, a professor of genomics at the University of Auckland in New Zealand. The gut also contains at least 100 million neurons—earning it the nickname “second brain” for its likely role in influencing our mood. “Sometimes we just don’t realize how core to us it is in many ways,” O’Sullivan says.
Our gut is “loaded” with trillions of bacteria, fungi and viruses that together support and influence our physical—and mental—well-being, Sullivan says. Bacteria produce vitamins and short-chain fatty acids that serve as “a potent anti-inflammatory,” as well as the hormone serotonin, which helps regulate appetite, he adds.
Bacteria are also responsible for the mucus barrier along your gastrointestinal tract that prevents toxins from leeching into the bloodstream, Sullivan says.
Research even suggests gut health may shape aging, Sullivan says. Long-lived healthy adults tend to have microbiomes that are richer in bacterial diversity than those of their chronological peers, with the former having gut bacteria that look more like those of younger, healthier adults. The reason why is a mystery—scientists are still working to untangle whether a healthy gut drives longevity or is a by-product of it.
One way to find out how the gut shapes health is to conduct clinical trials involving fecal transplants. In one study involving teens with obesity, for instance, O’Sullivan and his colleagues found that participants who ingested fecal transplant capsules loaded with healthy gut bacteria had better metabolic health years later than those who didn’t. O’Sullivan is also researching how the microbiome may support gut function in people with autism and aid in the treatment of anorexia nervosa.
How can I tell if my gut is healthy?
It’s not totally clear how your microbiome influences your overall health, Sullivan says. A combination of genetics and environment shape this relationship. But, he adds, “if you’re eating a healthy diet of real foods that are rich in fiber, if you’re getting sufficient exercise [and] a good night’s sleep and engaging in stress reduction to the best of your ability, you’re doing the very things that are going to cultivate a healthy microbiome.”
The Bristol stool chart—a tool doctors use to get assess your poop’s consistency—can also offer a guide to indicate “whether you’re on track with things,” Sullivan says, but there’s no reason to fixate on your feces during each trip to the bathroom.
In general, poop that comes out consistently “really hard and cracked” or like “little, tiny balls,” is unknot ideal, O’Sullivan says, because it may indicate constipation. The same is true on the opposite end of the spectrum—you don’t want stools that are like liquid. Somewhere in the middle, with a consistency he describes as “like peanut butter,” is best.
It’s also worth noting that some variation in your stools’ color and texture is normal, but if you see blood in the toilet, “that is definitely worthy of seeking medical attention,” Sullivan says. Red blood may be a sign of hemorrhoids, diverticulosis (small pouches in the colon), and more, while black or tarry feces can be a sign of internal bleeding in the colon, small intestine or stomach—and is linked to cancer, ulcers and inflammation.
What foods should I eat to get more fiber?
Whether or not you are fiber maxxing consciously, if you’re interested in boosting your gut heath, your best bet is to “eat the rainbow,” Sullivan says. “Eat a wide variety of different foods, as many as your taste buds will allow.”
“The diversity feeds your microbiome,” O’Sullivan adds. Building gut diversity takes time, but “having fiber, having plant material, having nuts, seeds, protein—all of those things feed your biome.”
Both soluble and insoluble fiber are important for gut health. Soluble fiber helps form that essential, slimy gut barrier and “mops up” cholesterol from the body, Sullivan says. Insoluble fiber keeps you regular, helps prevent hemorrhoids and feeds anti-inflammatory bacteria species in the gut.
But both experts have a warning: be careful not to overload your body with too much fiber, because that can cause cramping and diarrhea. “I would recommend a slow and steady change,” Sullivan says.

Photos: Yemen’s hospitals struggle to operate amid persistent power outages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:01:07 UTC
20:01:07 KST

In Pictures
Photos: Yemen’s hospitals struggle to operate amid persistent power outages
Families in Aden endure sleepless nights and spoiled food as blackouts become a defining feature of daily life.
Aden, Yemen – In this coastal city long accustomed to sweltering, humid summers, the absence of electricity can reshape an entire day.
When the power cuts out, fans and air conditioners fall silent. Sleep becomes difficult. Students race to finish their homework before darkness arrives. Children spill onto the streets while young men drift towards the sea in search of moving air and cooler waters.
Inside hospitals, where treatment cannot be postponed until the lights come back on, electricity carries a different weight altogether.
Yemen’s power crisis predates the current war. Even before the conflict, only about 55 percent of the population had access to electricity from all sources, which is among the lowest rates in the Middle East and North Africa.
Since 2015, damage to infrastructure, fuel shortages and ageing generation and distribution systems have left supplies even more fragile.
In Aden, power stations continue to face repeated shutdowns, leaving residents without electricity for long periods. Insurance premium increases on tankers carrying fuel to Aden have also reportedly made the crisis worse.
An assessment by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published this year said Aden was receiving just two to six hours of electricity a day as structural weaknesses and fuel shortages caused frequent outages.
As the sun sets over the city, a second part of the day begins. Homes and businesses slip into darkness, punctuated only by small lights powered by batteries and solar systems. Residents often do not know how long the latest blackout will last, or how long the power will stay on once it comes back.
During the summer, when temperatures in Aden climb towards 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit), the consequences are hard to escape. Residents in the city interviewed in the middle of the year said their homes had become almost unbearable during the prolonged power cuts that plague the city. The heat does not always disappear when the sun goes down.
“Sometimes the power comes back while we are asleep, so we wake up to use it. Our lives have become tied to when electricity comes and goes,” one resident said. For her family, an outage is measured not just in hours but in problems. Children are unable to sleep, food spoils in warm refrigerators and housework must wait.
When the heat inside becomes too much, Youssef heads for the coast. The sea, he said, is no longer just a place of recreation but a refuge from the unbearable heat of the city.
“When the electricity is off for hours, it is very difficult to stay inside,” he said. “There is no fan and no air conditioning, and the humidity makes the heat worse, so we come to the sea.”
Towards the end of the day, young men and families gather along the waterfront. Some swim. Others simply sit beside the water and wait for the city to cool. But the sea cannot solve Aden’s electricity crisis. Hours later, Youssef returns home and sometimes finds the house exactly as he left it.
“Sometimes we get back and the power is still out, and we start waiting all over again,” he said.
For children like Mohammed, Saeed and Abdullah, blackouts have changed where childhood takes place. When their homes become too hot, they move into the street, running between houses or sitting with other children until late.
“It gets hot inside the house, so we come down and play in the street,” one of the boys said. “We play football or sit with our friends. Outside is better when the electricity is off.”
For them, a blackout is not an extraordinary event. It is part of the life they have grown up with.
The effects follow them into the classroom. In Aden, the United Nations Development Programme documented more than 7,000 students and teachers struggling in dark, stifling classrooms during power cuts. The installation of solar systems at eight schools and an education office has helped. One teacher reported that some students had fainted due to the heat.
At home, preparing for exams can depend on a rechargeable lamp or a small solar system if they have one.
In hospitals, there is no option but to simply wait out the darkness. Operating theatres, intensive care units, laboratories, medical refrigerators and dialysis machines all depend on continuous power.
The World Health Organization (WHO) says recurring power cuts disrupt lifesaving health services across Yemen, forcing facilities to rely on combinations of grid electricity, generators and solar systems.
In 2025, the WHO supplied about 4.33 million litres (1.14 million gallons) of fuel to 177 health facilities across the country to keep generators and essential equipment running.
Zeina Ahmed, a kidney patient, watches tubes carry her blood to a dialysis machine.
“For people at home, a power cut means heat and darkness. For us here, the first thing we think about is whether we will be able to have our dialysis or not,” she said.
“I come to the hospital knowing that I need this session. If it is delayed, I keep thinking about when I will get it and whether the machines will continue to work.”
After years of unreliable grid supply, solar panels, batteries and generators have become familiar parts of Yemen’s landscape.
They sit on rooftops, providing power to the homes, businesses and schools that can afford them.
More than half of Yemen’s homes now rely on solar power in some form, according to the WHO, while hospitals and other health facilities are increasingly adopting solar systems to keep essential services running.
Families who can afford to buy larger panels and batteries can power more appliances. Others might have just enough electricity for a light, a fan or a phone charger – a fragile shield against the dark and the heat.

Bloomberg: NATO developing "Theory of Victory" over Russia using drones and AI
NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich is developing a strategy for achieving a swift victory in the event of a Russian attack on the Alliance's eastern flank, with a particular focus on integrating new defence technologies such as drones and artificial intelligence.
Source: Bloomberg, which obtained an unclassified version of the document titled Theory of Victory, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Grynkewich is due to present the document in Poland on 12 October. Officials and diplomats familiar with the matter said it is intended to explain how the Alliance would respond to a potential invasion of NATO territory.
The document is also intended to show allies how NATO will integrate conventional weapons with new capabilities that have emerged since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, as well as to encourage greater defence investment and better preparedness, the sources said.
The strategy emphasises NATO's defensive nature and the need to avoid unintended provocations, while making clear the need for a collective response to hybrid threats.
The strategy stresses that by demonstrating its readiness, NATO aims to convince an adversary that victory is impossible.
However, if NATO is attacked, the Alliance would seek to halt the invasion using a combination of ground forces and other assets under the NATO Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative – a concept based on the use of low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-powered targeting.
Grynkewich's spokesperson, Colonel Martin O'Donnell, declined to discuss the details of the plan but stressed that the Alliance is "purely defensive".
"The Supreme Allied Commander Europe's theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO's advantage. Given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked," he said.
Background:
- Martin Jäger, head of Germany's Federal Intelligence Service, has said he sees a risk of violent conflict with Russia and that the confrontation has taken on a new and dangerous quality.
- Media reports have also indicated that Estonia is relocating a key brigade from the town of Tapa to Jõhvi, 50 kilometres from the Russian border, as part of the launch of an "active defence" strategy in preparation for possible Russian aggression.
- Meanwhile, Lithuania and Poland are jointly developing an international civilian evacuation plan that could be implemented if some residents of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia need to be evacuated across the border.

T-7A Red Hawk links up with simulators in first LVC flight
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:00:55 BST
20:00:55 KST

US Air Force instructor pilots have flown a T-7A Red Hawk trainer while digitally linked to ground-based simulator cockpits, the first live-virtual-constructive (LVC) flight between the aircraft and its Ground-Based Training System inside Air Education and Training Command, according to the US Air Force.
The flight took place on 16 September at Joint Base San Antonio-Randolph, Texas, and involved instructor pilots from the 99th Flying Training Squadron alongside civilian simulator instructors from the 12th Training Squadron. Red Hawk aircraft APT-4 was flown by Lt. Col. Michael Trott, the 99th FTS commander, and Lt. Col. Phillip Bourquin, the squadron’s operations officer. On the ground, two simulator cockpits were flown by Robb Erickson, a retired Air Force colonel, and Ryan Sparkman, a retired lieutenant colonel, both civilian simulator instructors with the 12th TRS.
According to AETC, the simulators were connected to the airborne jet through secure, high-bandwidth tactical data links while it manoeuvred in local military training airspace, giving instructors on the ground the same operating picture as the crew in the air. The architecture allows the jet and simulator cockpits to track one another’s flight parameters, sensor sweeps and weapons employment at the same time. In practice, that means a student in a simulator can fly as a virtual wingman or adversary against a real aircraft, while instructors inject constructive threats such as surface-to-air missile rings, electronic warfare jamming and simulated enemy aircraft into both sets of cockpit displays.
Erickson, who leads the 12th TRS T-7A civilian simulator instructors, said in the release: “Accomplishing this capability for the first time inside AETC represents a paradigm shift in how we train and build combat-ready aircrews.” He added: “When APT-4 took flight, we weren’t just flying another training sortie. We established a live, bi-directional data link fusing an airborne aircraft directly into our simulators and synthetic battlespace.”
The Air Force says LVC training lets aircrews rehearse fifth and sixth generation tactical scenarios without the cost, maintenance demands and airspace limits of putting large numbers of real adversary aircraft in the air. “The power of LVC lies in its density, complexity and interconnectivity,” Erickson said. “By tethering our simulators directly to the live aircraft out in the airspace, student pilots can experience the realistic, sensor-saturated operational environment they will face in front-line fighters and other combat aircraft.”
Sparkman was quoted in the release as saying: “The synthetic injection we proved today challenges aircrews with threat presentations and sensor-management puzzles that were impossible to replicate on our legacy flying platforms.”
That legacy platform is the Northrop T-38 Talon, which has trained US Air Force fighter and bomber pilots since the early 1960s. Boeing, partnered with Saab, won the Advanced Pilot Training competition in 2018 with what became the T-7A, under a contract covering up to 351 aircraft and 46 ground-based training systems. The programme has since experienced delays linked to issues including the escape system and flight control software, pushing back its entry into service. The 99th Flying Training Squadron, which traces its lineage to the Tuskegee Airmen, inspired the Red Hawk name and the aircraft’s red tail markings.
AETC says the flight sets a technical baseline for modernising the undergraduate pilot training syllabus as the 12th Flying Training Wing prepares to receive the production fleet. “This initial flight confirms that our core digital architecture is sound,” Erickson said. “Proving that the T-7A and our simulators can communicate and fight together in the same virtual sky keeps us squarely on track to deliver cutting-edge training for tomorrow’s warfighter.”

Christa Pike’s lawyers had warned execution would be ‘difficult and perhaps cruel’ due to her veins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:00:55 UTC
20:00:55 KST

A former lawyer for Christa Pike says he was not surprised that Tennessee botched its attempt to execute her because attorneys had warned that problems accessing her veins could make the procedure dangerous and potentially cruel.
James Crowson, who represented Pike during part of her post-conviction appeals, said he had followed the case from afar before the failed execution at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville on 30 September.
“Well, I can’t say I’m surprised,” said Crowson, who represented Pike while working for the Tennessee Post-Conviction Defender. “I knew that there were a number of defense filings saying that she had compromised veins, and that was going to be a difficult and perhaps cruel procedure for her because it was going to put her at risk for exactly what happened.”
Pike, 50, on Sunday remained hospitalized and on a machine helping her breathe after Tennessee administered two doses of pentobarbital that failed to kill her, as far as an attorney now representing her knew, the lawyer said on the CNN program State of the Union.
“She’s still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill – we don’t really know the prognosis yet and may not know for several days,” Stephen Ferrell, an assistant federal defender, said to CNN host Jake Tapper.
Ferrell told Tapper that he had not been able to personally see Pike, but “this is the extent of what we know”.
Pike’s attorneys allege improperly placed intravenous lines allowed the drug with which she was injected to enter tissue rather than her bloodstream, leaving both arms severely injured.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has maintained that it followed every step of the state’s lawful execution protocol. And the department said the protocol did not permit additional procedures after the steps carried out on Wednesday.
Crowson said the accounts that officials followed the written protocol and that the execution was badly mishandled are not necessarily contradictory.
“The state comes up with a protocol and, typically, states that are inclined to impose the death penalty don’t really include medicine or science in the discussions when they’re coming up with these protocols,” he said.
Crowson said the reported injuries appeared consistent with the concerns raised before the execution, citing the theory that the drug entered surrounding tissue instead of circulating properly through Pike’s bloodstream.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at the Knoxville Job Corps. Pike was 18 at the time. Her then boyfriend and co-defendant, Tadaryl Shipp, was 17 and was ineligible for the death penalty. He received a sentence of life imprisonment.
That gap in punishment based on a small age difference remains significant to Crowson. He said it illustrates what he views as the capricious nature of capital punishment.
“She’s a few months older than the young man that was engaged in the same conduct, and she’s been fighting for her life now for 32 years,” Crowson said. “He’s still in prison, but hasn’t been subjected to the death penalty.”
He said the age of 18 that was decisive for Pike “just seems like an arbitrary number”.
Crowson represented Pike during a stage of her post-conviction case about 16 years earlier and said he visited her “dozens of times” on death row. He said he last spoke with her in 2009.
He described Pike at the time as “very superficially charming” and attentive to people around her. But he said the person he knew bore little resemblance to the teenager whose crime sent her to death row.
“I never saw the Christa that committed those crimes that put her in prison,” Crowson said. “That person exists, obviously.”
The core of the post-conviction appeal, he said, was ineffective assistance of counsel. His team argued that Pike’s original attorneys failed to adequately present evidence about her mental illness, brain damage and history of severe childhood abuse during the sentencing phase.
Pike ultimately exhausted her appeals without ever getting relief, despite her attorneys’ offering evidence of being diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike had said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”
Crowson more recently said “there was a lot that was left out” at the time of Pike’s conviction.
“Would it have made a difference? I don’t know. There are a lot of people who feel very strongly, and her crime was grisly and horrifying.”
What happens next depends on whether Pike ultimately survives the botched execution – and, if she does, the extent of any lasting injuries.
Crowson said he expects intense pressure on Bill Lee, Tennessee’s governor, to commute Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment if she recovers. If she suffered serious neurological damage, he said, questions about her competency would become central to any attempt by Tennessee to execute her again.
The fallout of the botched execution widened on Saturday when Lee announced that Frank Strada, the Tennessee Department of Correction commissioner, would resign later in October. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted executions in the state for the remainder of the year.
Strada’s resignation was a predictable consequence of a botched execution now under national scrutiny, according to Crowson, who said: “Whenever you have a disaster like this, there’s going to be some fallout.”
Furthermore, Pike’s was at least the fifth execution Strada had botched since 2022 in Tennessee as well as Arizona, where he previously worked, according to death penalty lawyers.
Crowson said he hopes that Pike’s case results in the government taking a closer look at the death penalty as a functional legal punishment. He said there is a clear pattern between people who are sentenced to death and their history of trauma and mental illness not being accounted for during trial and sentencing.
“I think we as a nation have a strange relationship with mental illness,” he said. “It’s just so often discounted and mocked. It’s unfortunate.”

Crime videos push liberal voters toward stricter laws but not the political right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:00:33 UTC
20:00:33 KST

When exposed to videos of retail crime, voters in a highly liberal city adopted tougher, more conservative stances on local criminal justice policies. The participants did not, however, alter their broader political identities or overall ideological leanings. These findings were published in the The Journal of Social Psychology.
In psychology, a concept called terror management theory explores how people manage their deep-seated awareness of their own mortality. The theory suggests that reminders of death or existential threats create intense anxiety. To cope with this discomfort, individuals often seek comfort in structured, predictable, and historically conservative worldviews.
Decades of research on this topic have yielded mixed results regarding how people vote under stress. Some experiments show that threats push people toward the political right. Other studies suggest that threats cause polarization, driving both liberals and conservatives further toward their respective extremes.
Recent political shifts in the United States provided a real-world testing ground for these ideas. In California, voters recently considered revising a state law known as Proposition 47. Originally designed to reduce prison populations by classifying minor thefts as misdemeanors, the law has faced intense debate in recent years. Critics have argued that the $950 threshold for a felony charge encouraged organized retail theft, as offenders faced minimal legal consequences.
University of San Francisco psychologist Violet Cheung-Blunden and her colleagues wanted to see if fear-inducing media could sway voters in a deeply liberal area. They designed two experiments to test whether videos about local crime could alter decisions on Proposition 47. The researchers also wanted to know if this exposure would change the participants’ general political identities.
In the first experiment, the research team recruited 206 adults from the San Francisco area during the week leading up to the election. The researchers asked the participants about their preexisting political beliefs, including their views on authority, immigration, and economics. The participants were then randomly assigned to watch one of two short videos.
Half of the group watched a video showing local tourist attractions, like the construction of the Golden Gate Bridge, to serve as a baseline comparison. The other half watched a compilation of news clips and online videos depicting organized looting and retail theft in the city. After watching the videos, the participants completed a mock exercise to revise Proposition 47.
The participants were asked to propose the ideal dollar amount for classifying retail theft as a felony. They also had to provide the minimum and maximum amounts they would be willing to accept on a ballot. Finally, the participants rated their current overall political orientation on a scale ranging from ultra-liberal to ultra-conservative.
The participants who watched the crime video proposed a markedly lower minimum and ideal dollar threshold for felony charges compared to the group that watched the tourist video. In practical terms, exposure to the crime footage prompted these voters to adopt a stricter, more punitive stance on retail theft. They became more conservative on the specific issue of criminal justice.
This shift toward a conservative policy position did not translate to a broader ideological change. The participants’ self-reported political orientation remained anchored to their initial beliefs, and they did not shift toward the political right overall. A single exposure to threatening media was not enough to uproot their overarching political identities.
The researchers also looked for evidence of political polarization. They checked whether the crime video caused initially liberal participants to become more liberal and initially conservative participants to become more conservative. The data did not support this idea, as the participants largely maintained their general ideological footing.
To ensure the reliability of these initial patterns, Cheung-Blunden and her team conducted a second experiment with 98 college students in San Francisco. This study followed a nearly identical procedure to the first one, but it took place in a controlled laboratory setting. The researchers also had all participants watch a five-minute breathing and relaxation video before viewing their assigned footage.
This relaxation step was intended to reduce baseline mood variations among the students. By calming the participants first, the researchers hoped to make any emotional reactions to the subsequent tourist or crime videos easier to measure. The results of the second experiment ended up mirroring the first.
The students exposed to the crime video proposed substantially lower dollar thresholds for felony theft across all three categories. Just like the community adults, the student participants embraced a tougher stance on crime after viewing the threatening footage. Once again, this shift toward a stricter crime policy did not alter the students’ broader political identities.
The crime video failed to move the student participants’ overall political orientation toward the right. The researchers also found no indication that the threatening footage caused the students’ general political views to become more polarized. The students’ overarching political ideologies remained stable, even as their position on a specific local policy shifted.
While the experiments show how media exposure can alter specific policy preferences, the results come with a few boundaries. The studies took place in a highly liberal city, meaning the participants likely sat further to the political left than the average American voter. The second experiment also included a high proportion of female participants, who generally reported more liberal leanings than male participants in the study.
These demographic skews mean the findings might not neatly apply to voters in more conservative or politically divided regions. Additionally, the researchers point out that their experiments measured political shifts using a mock policy threshold and a general ideology scale. Future research could incorporate a wider range of political choices, such as preferences for specific political figures in an actual election.
It is also difficult to know if the crime videos specifically triggered a deep fear of mortality, as terror management theory suggests. The footage might have simply provoked general anxiety about safety and social order. Future studies will need to directly measure the specific types of emotional discomfort that drive voters to change their minds on public policy.
The study, “Threat-Induced Conservatism in a Liberal Electorate: Issue-Based Shifts without Ideological Transformation,” was authored by Violet Cheung-Blunden, Serena Rajkumar, Yuka Hirata, Caelyn A. McDonough, and Chonhei Liao.

Switzerland set for referendum on Malaysia trade deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Switzerland set for referendum on Malaysia trade deal
GENEVA – Switzerland looks on course on Oct 5 to hold a referendum on a trade deal with Malaysia, with opponents believing the agreement endangers tropical rainforests and lacks proper safeguards against forced labour.
Campaigners handed in 85,000 signatures at the Parliament buildings in the Swiss capital Bern on Oct 5, public broadcaster RTS said.
To trigger a referendum under Switzerland’s direct democracy system, 50,000 valid signatures must be collected within 100 days of publication of a new law. The Swiss Parliament completed its approval of the trade deal in June.
The authorities will now have to verify the signatures.
If approved, the referendum would likely go ahead in the first half of 2027.
The free trade agreement is between Malaysia and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) that brings together Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland, all countries outside the European Union.
The EFTA-Malaysia Economic Partnership Agreement was signed at EFTA’s ministerial meeting in Tromso, Norway, in June 2025. Negotiations began in 2012.
The agreement comes into effect once the domestic ratification processes in the contracting states have been completed, Switzerland said when the deal was signed.
“For Malaysian palm oil, Switzerland has agreed to a market-compatible and quota-based reduction in tariffs so as not to adversely affect domestic production of vegetable oils,” the authorities said at the time.
“The agreement also includes a comprehensive section on environmental protection and labour rights. Among other things, it contains specific provisions to ensure that palm oil traded under the agreement is produced sustainably.”
In Switzerland, palm oil is primarily used in processed foods, cosmetics and cleaning products.
The Alliance Against Tropical Deforestation umbrella organisation led the collection of signatures against the deal.
The agreement “plans to lower tariffs on 12.5 million kg of palm oil, without effective measures against rainforest deforestation and forced labour”, the alliance says.
“In doing so, Switzerland is helping to accelerate the destruction of a rainforest in Malaysia that is already critically threatened, while jeopardising the rights of plantation workers and indigenous communities.
“Furthermore, this agreement risks restricting the right of farming families to freely save and exchange their seeds,” it claims.
According to EFTA figures, Switzerland exported €890 million (S$1.28 billion) of goods to Malaysia in 2025, led by pharmaceutical products at €255 million, and machinery and mechanical appliances at €191 million.
Imports from Malaysia to Switzerland were worth €622 million, led by electrical machinery at €244 million, and machinery and mechanical appliances at €109 million. AFP

Estonia industrial output jumps 4.5% in August on energy surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Estonia industrial output jumps 4.5% in August on energy surge
Estonia's industrial production rose 4.5 percent year on year in August, with output up in all three sectors and energy production surging nearly 57 percent, Statistics Estonia reported.
Manufacturing however grew just 1.2 percent, dragged down by wood and food production, while electrical equipment was the strongest contributor, up 12.2 percent.
The rise of 4.5 percent seen in August 2026 took place at constant prices compared with August last year. Output increased in all three industrial sectors: by 25.3 percent in mining, by 56.9 percent in energy production and by 1.2 percent in manufacturing.
Commenting on the results, Riin Kadarik, lead analyst at Statistics Estonia, said that,as in July, manufacturing output continued to grow in August, despite the decline in production volumes in the two largest manufacturing activities.
"Output fell by 0.6 percent in the manufacture of wood and by 3.8 percent in the manufacture of food products, which was mainly due to the decreased production of dairy products. The biggest contributor to the growth in manufacturing production was the manufacture of electrical equipment where output was up by 12.2 percent year on year, supported by increased production in the manufacture of electric motors, generators and transformers," Kadarik said.
In July this year, production volumes increased in two thirds of the manufacturing activities. In August, however, output grew in less than half of the manufacturing activities. There were five economic activities with a significant increase in output — in addition to the manufacture of electrical equipment, production volumes increased notably in the manufacture of machinery and equipment not elsewhere classified (n.e.c), which rose by 19.7 percent; coke and refined petroleum products (20.4 percent), fabricated metal products (6.9 percent) and motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers (up 19.1 percent).
Looking at the major industries, in addition to the manufacture of wood and food products, output also fell by 2.1 percent in the manufacture of computers, electronic and optical products.
In August 2026, 66.2 percent of the total production of manufacturing was sold to the external market, a little higher than in July. Compared with August 2025, the sales of manufacturing production increased by 6.4 percent at current prices according to working-day adjusted data. Domestic sales increased by 3.7 percent and export sales by 8 percent.
The output of the energy sector was up by 56.9 percent in August at constant prices. Based on the volume of production, electricity production increased by 43.3 percent and heat production by 46.5 percent year on year.
"Electricity production was boosted by the significant increase in wind and solar energy production. Also, electricity exports were much higher. The substantial year-on-year increase was also due to the fact that electricity production in August last year was lower than usual," Kadarik added.
The increase in mining output was driven by the greater extraction of oil shale and stone, sand and clay.

Pro-Trump and Pro-Russia Dodik Hails Election Victory in Bosnia and Herzegovina
Unknown
