Over the summer the Florida Department of Health proposed dropping hepatitis B, chickenpox, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine requirements for kids in pre-K through grade 12. While the law technically still requires children to receive vaccinations against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, and tetanus to attend school in Florida, religious exemptions are already higher there than the national average. And the newly proposed vaccine rule makes exemptions even easier to obtain, parents will now be able to opt their kids out of vaccination based on “sincerely held moral or ethical belief(s).” Parents would also be able to keep a child’s vaccination records, or lack thereof, from being tracked by the state’s immunization registry.
In a study published last Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA, researchers used computer modeling to assess what would happen if Florida were to drop its MMR vaccine mandate. According to their projections, a dropped mandate in Florida could trigger the largest measles epidemic seen in the United States in nearly half a century.
Even without a completely dropped mandate, a decrease in childhood vaccination due to more individual exemptions will leave Florida more vulnerable to outbreaks. The researchers found that vaccinating a child against measles is three times more effective in reducing disease transmission than vaccinating one adult. That’s because measles is really contagious under scenarios of close contact. And kids together in school spend a lot of time in close contact with one another.

The operation of Palanca-Mayaki-Udobne border checkpoint between Moldova and Ukraine has been suspended following the impact of a shell near the Moldovan checkpoint as a result of Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure, leaving a border guard with minor injuries, the Border Police of the Republic of Moldova reported on Monday.
"The Border Police reports that on October 5, 2026, an incident occurred in the area of the Palanca-Mayaki-Udobne checkpoint as a result of Russia's attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Around 09:38, a shell fell near the Palanca checkpoint, which, after hitting the ground, bounced and struck a shuttle bus parked near the barrier," the report states.
According to preliminary information, the shell damaged the bus and the dispatcher's booth. One border guard sustained minor injuries, and no other casualties were reported. Citizens are advised to refrain from traveling to this area.
In addition, the Border Police, together with the Customs Service, is continuously monitoring the situation to resolve it and maintains contact with the relevant authorities of Ukraine.

Italian Cooperation Promotes the Pineapple and Avocado Supply Chains in Cuba
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:10:55 CEST
19:10:55 KST

Participants in the Italian Cooperation project “CubaFruta,” which promoted the pineapple and avocado production chains in the four rural municipalities of Matanzas, gathered in Havana. The project “is a concrete example of cooperation between Italy and Cuba, based not only on financial resources but also on institutional relationships, the exchange of knowledge, trust, and joint efforts,” said the Italian ambassador, Simona De Martino, as she opened the workshop presenting the results, which was attended by producers, decision-makers, municipal governments, universities, and scientific institutions involved in the initiative. Several participants highlighted that one of the main outcomes was the exchange of knowledge and expertise among the municipalities of Los Arabos, Colón, Calimete, and Jagüey Grande. In particular, they emphasized how crucial the role of women was to the results achieved by CubaFruta. In this regard, the director of AICS in Havana, Silvia Fuligni, highlighted how the initiative promoted gender equality through training programs, greater participation of women in decision-making roles, and the development of new economic opportunities, such as the “Fruit Houses” established in the four participating municipalities. The following organizations collaborated on the CubaFruta project: AICS Havana, the Institute for Research in Tropical Fruit Growing, the Cuban Ministry of Agriculture, the Agricultural Entrepreneurship Group, the Institute for Food Industry Research, with funding from Italian Cooperation (Ministry of Foreign Affairs) and support from the Ministry of Commerce.

Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Su-35 and Su-34 Fighters in 500-Km Drone Raid
Unknown

10:09:44 UTC

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Su-35 and Su-34 Fighters in 500-Km Drone Raid
Ukrainian long-range drones struck a Russian Su-35 multirole fighter and a Su-34 fighter-bomber at the Khanskaya military airfield in Russia’s Republic of Adygea overnight on October 4, according to Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The SBU said on October 4 that the operation was carried out by drones operated by its Alpha Special Operations Center. The airfield is located roughly 500 kilometers from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
According to the agency, the strike hit a Su-35—one of Russia’s most advanced operational fighter aircraft—as well as a Su-34, a key platform used by Russian tactical aviation. The SBU estimated their export values at approximately $100 million and $50 million, respectively.
Both aircraft can carry guided aerial bombs, which Russian forces regularly use against Ukrainian positions along the front line and against cities farther from the battlefield. The SBU also reported that its drones struck an ammunition depot located on the airfield.
Khanskaya, located near Maykop, is used by Russian military aviation and has previously hosted Su-34 and Su-35 aircraft. The facility also serves Russia’s military pilot training system and has been targeted by Ukrainian long-range strikes before.
Earlier on October 4, open-source footage and satellite fire-detection data indicated a fire at the airfield following the overnight drone attack. NASA’s FIRMS system detected thermal anomalies in the area of the facility.

Officials Claim Stable Health Situation in Irkutsk After Anti-Plague Institute Worker’s Death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:09:42 UTC
19:09:42 KST

Russian health authorities maintain that the health situation in Siberia’s Irkutsk region remains stable amid concerns surrounding the death of a lab worker at a local anti-plague facility, state media reported Sunday.
The female employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East was hospitalized last Tuesday with symptoms of severe pneumonia and died on Thursday.
The lab worker was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” according to a statement from consumer safety watchdog Rospotrebnadzor cited by Interfax.
Media reports have described the suspected infection as pneumonic plague, which affects the lungs and can spread between humans through respiratory droplets.
Alexei Tsydenov, head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, initially claimed the employee had died of the plague, before modifying his statement with the word “maybe.”
Rospotrebnadzor said that laboratory analysis of material from the patient did not reveal any microorganisms associated with her work handling dangerous pathogens.
Earlier reports claimed the lab worker may have broken a test tube containing live bacteria.
According to Interfax, the institute’s special commission and Rospotrebnadzor concluded that no emergency or security breach had occurred. The watchdog noted that no other infectious disease complaints had been registered among institute employees over the preceding 10 days.
Rospotrebnadzor said all close contacts were placed under medical observation with daily laboratory testing, which detected two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus, but no other infections.
Irkutsk region Governor Igor Kobzev said in a video published Monday that family members and close relatives under quarantine could be discharged next week.
Local media reported that, contrary to earlier reports, area hospitals continued to operate on standard schedules aside from localized precautions.
The Kremlin on Monday referred all questions about the issue to Rospotrebnadzor.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Washington was closely monitoring the situation.
"We're watching and monitoring it closely," Rubio told reporters before leaving for a trip to Europe. "I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause just to keep an eye on it."
Rubio, citing what Russia has released about the death, said it seemed there was a worker in the lab who was infected and there was concern the disease may have spread internally.
"There's very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia, obviously,” he said. "But like anything else, something like that gets out, it just quickly spreads."
A European Commission spokesperson said Monday that Europe was also “very closely” monitoring the situation.
“We are aware of the reports concerning the laboratory incident in Russia, seemingly involving a pathogen-causing plague,” the spokesperson said.
Plague is endemic to Siberia, the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak, as the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, is present among the small wild mammals in its vast wilderness and their fleas. It is rare for Russians to fall ill with plague, however, though cases in other parts of the world — notably Africa — occur every year.
Reuters contributed reporting.

Construction Begins in France on FDI Frigate for Sweden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:09:41 UTC
19:09:41 KST

French shipbuilder Naval Group began construction of the first Luleå-class frigate for the Swedish Navy on October 2.
According to the company’s official website, construction began just one month after the contract was signed. Construction officially began with a steel-cutting ceremony at Naval Group’s shipyard in Lorient, France.
“Today, it is a great honor for us to begin production of the FDI Luleå in Lorient. All Naval Group sites and teams are fully committed to the successful delivery of the program, in close cooperation with FMV in both France and Sweden,” said Vincent Martino-Lagarde, Naval Group’s Head of Surface Ships.
Naval Group signed the contract for the construction of four frigates on August 31, 2026. The contract is valued at approximately €4.3 billion.
Sweden plans to receive the frigates between 2030 and 2034: the first, HMS Luleå, in 2030; HMS Norrköping in 2032; HMS Trelleborg in 2033; and HMS Halmstad in 2034.
The Swedish version of the frigates will carry several locally produced systems. These include Saab lightweight torpedoes, the RBS 15 anti-ship missile system, the Giraffe 1X radar, the Trackfire remotely operated weapon station, and BAE Systems Bofors 57 mm and 40 mm naval guns. At the same time, Sweden has already begun training personnel to operate the new ships.
FDI (Frégate de Défense et d’Intervention) is a French class of first-rank, multi-purpose frigates developed by Naval Group as a more compact alternative to the FREMM frigates.

Ukraine’s Answer to Russian Jet Drones Could Arrive This Month—Small Anti-Aircraft Missiles
Ukraine expects to begin deploying several types of small anti-aircraft missiles against Russian jet-powered drones in the second half of October.
The announcement was made by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on October 4.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy, the new interceptors have not yet been deployed operationally, but Ukraine expects to see the first results later this month.
“There are several types of them. We will obviously see the results this month. Toward the end, in the second half of this month, we expect to see the results. You asked about their use and how widespread it is. So far, there has been no such use. It is yet to happen,” Zelenskyy said in response to a journalist’s question.
The president added that production of the missiles could be rapidly scaled up if they demonstrate strong results in intercepting Russian drones.
The planned deployment is part of Ukraine’s broader effort to develop new systems capable of countering Russia’s increasingly frequent use of high-speed, jet-powered attack drones. Ukraine is also developing five high-speed interceptor drone models for this purpose, Zelenskyy told the Financial Times, as reported by RBC-Ukraine on October 2.
One of the five designs has advanced sufficiently for production to potentially reach around 400 units by the end of October, while the remaining four are still undergoing testing.
Alongside new air defense capabilities, Ukraine is working to expand its domestically produced long-range strike weapons. The country expects its FP-9 ballistic missile, which its manufacturer says has sufficient range to reach Moscow, to be ready this fall.
Zelenskyy told Reuters on October 3 that he had personally contacted Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point and urged the company to accelerate development of the FP-9 following the first combat use of Ukraine’s shorter-range FP-7 ballistic missile.

Russia’s First New Division of 2026 Reveals How Much Its Army Has Changed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:09:32 UTC
19:09:32 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s First New Division of 2026 Reveals How Much Its Army Has Changed
Russia has created its first newly reported division of 2026 and already committed it to fighting around Kostiantynivka—but the formation’s structure also shows how deeply years of losses have reshaped the Russian army.
The new 84th Motor Rifle Division was formed within Russia’s 3rd Combined Arms Army, formerly the 1st Army Corps of the so-called “Luhansk People’s Republic,” according to Defense Express, citing data from the Unit Observer project on October 3.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Its core was built around the existing 4th Motor Rifle Brigade, which had already been reinforced with two additional motor rifle regiments before becoming the foundation for the new division.
Russian forces have now deployed the formation in the Kostiantynivka sector, one of the most heavily contested areas of the Donetsk region.
Defense Express noted that this is the first reported case in 2026 of Russia creating a new formation at division level.
The pace is slower than in previous years. Three new divisions were reported in 2025, all created largely by expanding existing brigades. In June of that year, reports emerged that the 200th Motor Rifle Brigade could form the basis of the new 71st Division. Later, Russia also moved ahead with two new naval infantry divisions that had been planned several years earlier.
The contrast with 2024 is sharper still. Russia reportedly created seven new divisions that year. Before the full-scale invasion, the Russian army had roughly 12 divisions. By early February 2025, that number had risen to 23.
But the number of divisions does not tell the whole story. Defense Express points to a significant change in how Russia is structuring them.
Before February 2022, the core of a standard Russian motor rifle division typically consisted of two motor rifle regiments and a full tank regiment.
Reference figures for the prewar structure showed a division with as many as 12,000 personnel, roughly 187 tanks, 240 infantry fighting vehicles, 72 to 90 152mm artillery systems, 36 120mm mortars and 26 Grad multiple-launch rocket systems.
New formations created during 2024 and 2025 increasingly followed a different model: three motor rifle regiments supported by only a tank battalion rather than an entire tank regiment.
That is a major reduction in organic heavy armor. The 84th Division appears to continue that trend. Its predecessor, the 4th Motor Rifle Brigade, had already been supplemented with two motor rifle regiments before being expanded into the new formation.
Defense Express argues that the shift reflects two pressures Russia has faced throughout the war: enormous losses of armored vehicles and continuing personnel attrition.
Previously, reports emerged that Russian forces suffered 46,230 personnel losses in Ukraine in September, marking their highest monthly total recorded in 2026.
The September figure surpassed the previous monthly highs recorded during the summer, when Russian personnel losses reached 42,860 in July and 42,020 in August.

Ukraine May Have Turned 700 Km/H Bars Strike Drone Into Jet-Powered Interceptor

Ukraine May Have Turned 700 Km/H Bars Strike Drone Into Jet-Powered Interceptor
Ukraine may have adapted its Bars long-range jet-powered strike drone into an air-defense interceptor, with the system reportedly showing the highest effectiveness among Ukrainian interceptor drones currently used against Russian aerial targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy highlighted the Bars system during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on October 4.
“Second—interceptor drones. Bars have shown positive results. They currently have the highest percentage. Others are also catching up. God willing, there will be this kind of competition in the good sense of the word,” Zelenskyy said.
It remains unclear whether Zelenskyy was referring to a modified version of the existing Bars strike drone or a separate jet-powered interceptor carrying the same name.
Ukraine and Germany already have an agreement covering joint production of Bars drones, while Ukrainian jet-powered platforms originally designed for deep-strike missions have also been adapted for interception tasks.
Zelenskyy said the Bars interceptor currently has an interception effectiveness of around 30%. He also said Ukraine is expected to receive 2,000 Bars systems produced in cooperation with Germany, with funding already provided by the German side.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukrainian forces currently destroy around 50% to 55% of Russian jet-powered drones, sometimes reaching 60%, while conventional Shahed-type drones are intercepted at a rate of around 85% to 92%, depending on the composition of each attack.
Production of jet-powered interceptors remains constrained by engine availability and financing. Zelenskyy previously said Ukraine imports large numbers of engines while also producing some domestically, though local output remains insufficient.
The Bars platform has been under development since 2023 and has undergone more than 40 engineering upgrades.
Depending on configuration, different versions can reportedly reach ranges of up to 1,000 kilometers, carry payloads of up to 60 kilograms, and exceed speeds of 700 kilometers per hour.
Bars was developed as a modular platform with DeepStrike, MiddleStrike, and FrontStrike configurations, allowing fuel capacity and payload to be adjusted for different missions.
The platform also incorporates artificial intelligence technologies, including machine vision in its targeting systems. Neither the Ukrainian government nor the manufacturer has publicly confirmed that the Bars interceptor identified by Zelenskyy is directly derived from the long-range strike version.
Earlier, Ukraine deployed more than 12 automated .50-caliber gun turrets in Kyiv to counter Russian jet-powered drones, with another eight systems set to be installed across the Kyiv region.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 2,020 Troops, 47 Artillery Systems in One Day

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian forces also lost two tanks and four armored combat vehicles during the latest reporting period, bringing cumulative losses to 12,393 tanks and 25,487 armored vehicles.

Russia’s estimated cruise missile losses remained at 5,126, while naval losses stayed unchanged at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Ukrainian and Russian forces clashed 177 times across the front over the latest reporting period.

Russia’s Tu-95MS Goes Down With Three Officers Linked to Missile Strikes on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:09:08 UTC
19:09:08 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Tu-95MS Goes Down With Three Officers Linked to Missile Strikes on Ukraine
Three Russian strategic aviation officers linked to missile strikes against Ukraine were among those killed when a Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed in Russia’s Amur region in late September.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on October 4, the officers were identified as Lieutenant Colonel Fedor Pavlyukov and Majors Andrey Gerasimov and Andrey Lobanov. A photograph of the deceased crew was published by Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky District in the Amur region.
The Tu-95MS crashed near the village of Krasnoyarovo on September 29 during what the Russian Defense Ministry described as a training flight. Russian authorities said six crew members were killed and one person survived with injuries.
Pavlyukov served as deputy commander for flight training with Russia’s 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment and previously commanded one of its Tu-95MS squadrons, according to data cited by Militarnyi from the Ukrainian database Book of Executioners. Ukrainian researchers linked him to the preparation and execution of missile strikes against Ukraine.
Gerasimov was a Tu-95MS squadron commander with the 121st Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment, which is associated with Engels-2 airbase in Russia’s Saratov region. According to the same database, he participated in combat sorties and may have been involved in organizing cruise missile launches during strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Lobanov served as deputy commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in Russian military unit 75715. Militarnyi, citing previous reporting by 24 Kanal, said Lobanov commanded a Tu-95MS during a May 29, 2023 combat sortie in which its crew launched six air-launched missiles at Ukrainian critical infrastructure.
The crash occurred as Russia continued moving Tu-95MS bombers between Engels-2 and Ukrainka airbase in the Amur region following Ukrainian strikes against strategic aviation facilities.
According to Militarnyi, Engels-2 is used to prepare aircraft and load Kh-101 air-launched cruise missiles, while the more distant Ukrainka base allows Russia to disperse its strategic aviation fleet. Such deployments can require flights exceeding 12,000 kilometers and lasting close to 24 hours.
The Soviet-designed Tu-95MS remains one of Russia’s primary strategic missile carriers and has been repeatedly used to launch Kh-101 cruise missiles against Ukraine.
Earlier, on October 1, a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter crashed in the Voronezh region, killing all three crew members. The helicopter was reportedly shot down by a Russian Su-35 fighter after being misidentified as a Ukrainian drone during a large-scale drone attack.

US Army tests counter-drone tech at Mexican border as cartel drone use rises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:09:07 UTC
19:09:07 KST

US Army tests counter-drone tech at Mexican border as cartel drone use rises
YUMA, Arizona, Oct 5 - The US Army is testing counter-drone technology in the US-Mexico border area, seeking to sharpen its defenses against the growing threat of drone use by cartels and emulate the rapid battlefield innovation happening in Ukraine's war with Russia.
At Falcon Peak, a US Northern Command exercise held in September in Arizona, soldiers watched as defense firms demonstrated radars, interceptor drones, autonomous gun systems and other technologies designed to detect, track and destroy small unmanned aircraft.
Army officials said drones crossing the southern border are typically systems sold commercially and used by criminals for surveillance linked to their smuggling and human trafficking operations. Brigadier General Brian Filler, deputy commander for operations at Joint Task Force Southern Border, told reporters the military detected 378 drone incursions in the previous 30 days and that the trend was increasing.
"We are seeing largely commercial off-the-shelf available drones," Filler said, adding that most carry surveillance cameras and are often observed alongside cross-border movements.
The US military said earlier this month it had downed 11 cartel drones using lasers since deploying the technology along the southern border in August.
LEARNING FROM UKRAINE
Military planners are racing to keep pace with lessons from Ukraine, where drones have transformed the battlefield and driven rapid innovation in both offensive and defensive systems.
Military officials caution that cartel-operated drones are not comparable to the sophisticated battlefield ones seen in Ukraine or the Middle East. But they say the border offers a valuable operational environment to test equipment, train soldiers and evaluate how systems perform outside controlled laboratory conditions.
The exercise highlighted the Pentagon's growing embrace of venture-backed defense technology firms. Since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, investors have poured billions of dollars into companies such as Anduril, Shield AI, Saronic and a wave of smaller drone and counter-drone startups seeking military contracts.
Anduril's Ghost drone was featured in the demonstrations, as well as the radar-and-camera detection system produced by Teledyne FLIR, the "Bullfrog" counter-drone automated machine gun produced by Allen Control Systems and an interceptor drone sold by Powerus, which went public on Thursday, merging with a company backed by sons of US President Donald Trump.
Officials said part of their goal is replicating the rapid iteration cycle seen in Ukraine.
"We tend to look at Ukraine and we say, 'I am so impressed with how quickly they can adapt on a daily or weekly basis,'" Brigadier General Matt Ross told reporters.
"What we should really do is replicate that process." REUTERS

Trump's deportation push forces dozens of LGBT migrants onto hostile terrain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:08:57 UTC
19:08:57 KST

Trump's deportation push forces dozens of LGBT migrants onto hostile terrain
DAKAR, Oct 5 - Two years ago, a mob assaulted Abdou Latifou and threatened to kill him after he was seen kissing the man he loved.
He fled his home in the West African nation of Togo and sought refuge in the United States, according to his asylum application.
Latifou rejoiced last November when a US immigration judge ruled it was not safe for him to be sent home.
“I told myself, ‘From this day on, I’m entering a world where I’m free to live as myself,’” he said.
In June, though, Latifou was forced onto a US deportation plane — not back to Togo but to Sierra Leone, a nation where gay men can be sentenced to life in prison under colonial-era laws.
President Donald Trump's administration has deported tens of thousands of people to third countries, enabled by deals with impoverished foreign governments.
Latifou's case is one of 40 documented by Reuters where migrants granted US legal protection after being persecuted for their LGBT status were deported to third countries in Africa that either criminalize same-sex relations or have been described by the State Department as hostile to LGBT people.
Reuters has tracked the fate of all 40 – including people from across Africa, as well as Iraq, Jamaica and Russia – by interviewing a dozen deportees and immigration lawyers and reviewing hundreds of pages of legal documents.
Sixteen remain in the countries they were deported to and some are still detained. Sixteen others, like Latifou, were repatriated to their home countries against their will. Nine are in hiding in third locations. One Ghanaian man is no longer in contact with his lawyers or relatives, they said.
Sending people “to a third country where they face the very persecution we recognized makes a mockery of our protection systems,” said Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former senior US immigration official.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement "does not enforce the law on the basis of sexual orientation, that would be illegal,” Chandler Rebel, a spokesman for the Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, said in a statement. "Third country removals are an essential public safety tool.”
A NEW TACTIC
Third-country deportations were rare before Trump’s second term.
But since he returned to office and began a wide-ranging immigration crackdown, more than 40,000 people in total have been deported to countries not their own by ICE and Border Patrol, according to preliminary government data shared with Reuters, far higher than previous estimates from advocates. About 900 were sent to African countries.
In a February order, in a case challenging the policy, US District Judge Brian Murphy highlighted the risks facing gay people. The government’s claim that those targeted had not explicitly asked not to be deported to repressive third countries was an “absurdity,” he wrote.
“No person could reasonably be expected to make detailed, prophylactic claims about every country on Earth to which she might have a valid claim against removal.”
On Tuesday, the Supreme Court put a hold on Murphy's ruling, allowing the administration to continue third-country deportations. The court will hear arguments in December.
HOSTILE GROUND
The 40 cases documented by Reuters involve deportations to three countries that explicitly criminalize same-sex sexual acts: Sierra Leone, Cameroon and Eswatini.
In three other countries that do not have such laws on the books -- Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea and the Democratic Republic of Congo -- the State Department has previously documented abuses against LGBT people, including “corrective rape” and conversion therapy.
Government spokespeople for the six countries did not respond to requests for comment.
Bridget Crawford, director of law and policy at Immigration Equality, an LGBT advocacy group, said the US has repeatedly granted asylum to LGBT people from these countries. Her group has helped 12 Cameroonians and one person from Congo win asylum in recent years.
But more than half of the 40, including Latifou, were not eligible for asylum because they did not apply for it in countries they passed through before illegally entering the US. This was disqualifying under Biden-era restrictions that a federal court vacated in May.
The judge in Latifou's case granted a lesser protection, barring the government from deporting him to Togo but allowing his removal elsewhere.
After being flown to Sierra Leone, Latifou said he was held for two weeks in a hotel under police surveillance.
Guards then put him on a flight back to Togo. He arrived with a few items of clothing and $100 to his name.
He traveled to his village to see his mother, but a relative soon warned him that he was not safe and helped him cross the border to Benin. He continued on to Ivory Coast, where he lives with a friend and works as a security guard.
Same-sex relations are not illegal in his new home, but Ivorian activists have reported rising homophobic violence, and Latifou avoids the Togolese community, “so I don’t get recognized.”
“When an individual is no longer in ICE custody then ICE will no longer be responsible for them," Rebel, the DHS spokesman, said.
'UPSIDE DOWN'
Many of the deportees who spoke to Reuters said they wound up wherever someone would take them in.
A bisexual Ghanaian woman was deported to Cameroon in January and remained there for seven months.
Unable to speak French, the primary local language, and fearing for her safety if she returned to Ghana, she went to live with a relative in northern Nigeria, where penalties for same-sex sexual acts can include lashes or death by stoning.
Most days she does not leave the house, she said.
A gay man from Ghana -- deported to Sierra Leone, then forcibly repatriated -- has spent four months hiding out in the forests of neighboring Togo. He survives on small sums of money sent by his mother, he said.
Most nights he sleeps on a blanket on the ground, seeking cover in an abandoned, half-finished house when it rains.
A 44-year-old Mauritanian man who lived in the US for more than a decade was detained by ICE in January and flown to Eswatini, a small southern African kingdom he had never heard of.
He spent a month and a half in a mosquito-infested prison with no hot water, he said in an interview.
He finally agreed to be flown back to Mauritania, then slipped over the border into Senegal, where the government recently doubled the maximum penalty for same-sex sexual acts.
Now staying with relatives in a remote town, he is trying to find out if any countries in Europe or Asia might accept him.
“My life just got turned upside down,” he said. REUTERS

Unidentified object found in sea off Helsinki turns out to be from old shipwreck
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:08:53 EEST
19:08:53 KST

A metal object was found floating in the sea in the Kustaanmiekka area off Helsinki on Saturday evening.
The Finnish Navy's initial assessment is that the object is likely a mechanical component from a very old shipwreck.
Police released a photograph of the object on Sunday, describing it as a relatively heavy, funnel-shaped metal object measuring around 40 centimetres.
Later on Sunday, the police said they do not suspect a crime and will no longer investigate the matter, as the object is considered harmless.
Object resembles ship's searchlight
Maritime archaeologists from the Finnish Heritage Agency also believe the object could have come from an old shipwreck.
However, the experts emphasised that their assessment was based on the photograph released by police, in which only part of the object is visible.
According to Sami Brczyski, an employee of the Museum Department, the object resembles a ship's searchlight. Such searchlights were primarily installed on ships during the first half of the 20th century.
Riikka Alvik, a specialist researcher and maritime archaeologist at the Finnish Heritage Agency, said it was right to report the discovery to the authorities.
She noted that the object also resembles parts of Soviet torpedoes.
"The parts of the Soviet torpedoes looked quite similar. Therefore, reporting the discovery was absolutely correct. Furthermore, a collision with a large metal object floating in the water is always dangerous for ships," says Alvik.
Object found in busy shipping channel
The object was found in a shipping channel used by passenger vessels travelling to and from Helsinki. It was discovered by a fisherman who happened to be in the area, according to the Gulf of Finland Coast Guard District.
Police received a report from the Border Guard at around 19:20 on Saturday about an unidentified metal object floating in the water south of the Kustaanmiekka strait.
The police requested assistance from the Finnish Navy to identify the object. It was towed to the Santahamina naval base later that evening.
Both the police and the Gulf of Finland Coast Guard District cordoned off the area, bringing ship traffic to a halt for several hours.
Fintraffic told the Finnish News Agency STT that the restricted area was located south of Särkkä and Suomenlinna and west of Vallisaari.
The area is used by vessels travelling to and from the Katajanokka terminal and Olympia Terminal in Helsinki's South Harbour.
Passengers on the Viking XPRS ferry told Finnish tabloid Ilta-Sanomat on Saturday evening that they had been unable to leave Helsinki for Tallinn because of the operation.
The ferry was scheduled to depart at 20:00. According to Yle's information, it eventually left Helsinki at around 02:00 on Sunday.

Trump heads to Nebraska as Republicans defend Senate seat
GRAND ISLAND, Nebraska, Oct 5 - US President Donald Trump arrived in Nebraska on Monday to rally Republicans and promote his economic record, taking his message of new investment and manufacturing to a state where farmers and truckers face sharply higher diesel prices and voters worry about inflation.
His stop in the city of Grand Island is part of Trump's 32-day sprint to the November 3 midterm elections, a campaign in which he is spending considerable time in Republican strongholds. Trump has urged Republicans to “pretend” he is on the ballot, arguing that voters should view the midterms as a referendum on his administration and economic record.
"With your support, just 29 days from now, Nebraska is going to defeat the radical-left Dumb-o-crats once again," Trump said in the opening moments of his remarks.
His party is trying to persuade voters that investment, manufacturing and economic growth under Trump outweigh the pain of higher prices stemming from the unpopular US-Israeli war on Iran.
But Republicans enter the final weeks of the campaign facing a difficult national political environment. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday found Trump's approval rating at 32%, matching the lowest reading of his political career, while registered voters preferred Democrats over Republicans 44% to 37% when asked which party they would support in the midterms. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%, with 28% undecided.
The poll also found Trump's support weakening among Hispanic voters, a group that helped propel him to victory in 2024. Just 24% of Hispanic Americans approved of his performance, while 52% of Hispanic registered voters said they planned to vote Democratic in the November 3 election, compared with 26% who planned to vote Republican.
Reuters polling and analysis have also found Republicans' opponents competitive in a number of states Trump won by double digits in 2024, including Nebraska. Trump carried Nebraska by more than 20 percentage points in 2024, but public polling consistently shows a competitive contest between Republican Senator Pete Ricketts and independent Dan Osborn.
ORGANIZERS ADD HUNDREDS OF CHAIRS
Supporters packed the Heartland Events Center in Grand Island, many wearing Trump's signature red shirts and others sporting University of Nebraska attire in the same shade. Organizers brought out hundreds of additional chairs to accommodate supporters in the rear of the arena, as the crowd filled available seating ahead of Trump's remarks.
Trump has grown agitated at recent reporting of empty chairs and early departures at his signature rallies.
For many, the draw was the unusual sight of Trump in the Republican-heavy state of Nebraska. He has only visited the state about six times since 2016 and not once since 2022, public records show.
"I am not sure I will ever see him in person again and didn't want to miss this. He doesn't come here often," said Nancy Rhodes, a 54-year-old stay-at-home-mother who drove an hour to see the president.
Rhodes said Trump's decision to start a war with Iran has made things more expensive - and may hurt Trump's party's chances of retaining power - but said disarming Iran's nuclear program was worth the cost.
Trump started his campaign swing last week with stops in Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama and Ohio, reflecting his goal of energizing voters in Republican-friendly states while making himself the central messenger for a party facing concerns about his political standing.
He told reporters on Monday that he plans to travel nearly every day until the November 3 midterms, including stops in Iowa and Michigan.
The president spent part of the weekend pushing to end the twice-yearly clock change, saying farmers support permanent daylight saving time because it would give them more sunlight later in the day. He even publicly shared Republican Senator Tom Cotton's cellphone number as the two sparred over the issue. REUTERS

Australia launches ambitious cardiovascular disease data platform

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:07:53 CST
19:07:53 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Australia has launched a national data platform to accelerate the discovery of new risk markers for heart attack and stroke.
The Australian Cardiovascular Disease Data Commons is a cloud-based research platform linking major Australian health cohorts and analytical platforms, with more national and international datasets to follow, according to a statement released Monday by Australia's Baker Heart and Diabetes Institute.
The institute described it as "one of the most ambitious plans to harness cardiovascular disease data globally and accelerate research and clinical translation."
Professor Peter Meikle from the institute said the project brings together large cohorts with genomic, metabolomic and proteomic data, as well as stored blood samples, to validate existing risk markers and discover new ones.
Meikle said the platform would help researchers assess how well polygenic risk scores work for Australians and develop the first combined lipidomic and genetic risk tool for coronary artery disease, a leading cause of death worldwide.
Up to 27 percent of heart attack patients have none of the well-known risk factors, including high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes or smoking, when they present to a general practitioner, the institute noted. ■

MADRID, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez announced Monday that Spain will hold an early general election on Nov. 29.
Sanchez announced the decision in a video statement from the Moncloa Palace at 9 a.m. local time (0700 GMT), saying he would convene an extraordinary cabinet meeting later that morning to dissolve parliament and call the election.
The decision followed parliament's rejection on Friday of two government decrees aimed at easing the housing crisis and strengthening protections for tenants. The People's Party, Vox and the conservative Catalan party Junts per Catalunya voted against both measures.
The rejection highlighted the fragile parliamentary position of the coalition government led by Sanchez's Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE), which has relied on support from smaller and regional parties to pass legislation.
The PSOE has led Spain's government since 2018. Its parliamentary group holds 121 seats in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies, while its coalition partner, the left-wing alliance Sumar, holds 26. The coalition has therefore needed support from other parties, including the Basque Nationalist Party and the Catalan Republican Left.
Sanchez said he was seeking renewed public support and a broader progressive majority to advance his government's agenda. He also acknowledged that his government had made mistakes and had not achieved all its objectives.
The announcement came amid widespread protests over Spain's housing crisis, with demonstrators gathering in Madrid and other cities over the weekend to demand government action. ■

Scientists discover a human brain gene that can jump through DNA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:06:28 UTC
19:06:28 KST

Scientists discover a human brain gene that can jump through DNA
- Date:
- October 5, 2026
- Source:
- Cornell University
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a human gene with a remarkable double life: it appears to play an important role in brain cells while still retaining the ability to jump around the genome. Called BC200, the gene evolved millions of years ago from a mobile piece of DNA known as a transposon, but unlike most genes that arose this way, it never lost its mobility. Researchers even found BC200 embedded inside a human poxvirus, suggesting it may have jumped from infected skin cells into the virus.
- Share:
For the first time, scientists have identified a human gene that appears to serve an important biological role while still retaining the ability to move around the genome.
Researchers at Cornell University made the discovery after finding a human genetic element inside a poxvirus. Their analysis showed that the element, known as BC200, is not only associated with brain function but also behaves like a jumping gene, meaning it can move and insert itself into genomes.
A study published Sept. 24 in Science reports that BC200 combines traits that scientists had not previously seen together in a human gene.
A Brain Gene With a Mobile Past
BC200 is expressed mainly in neurons, but its evolutionary history traces back millions of years to a transposon, also known as a 'jumping gene', a non-coding genetic element capable of relocating itself and inserting into new places in a genome.
Transposons can sometimes be harmful because they are able to insert stretches of DNA into genes and interfere with normal function, potentially contributing to disease. Over evolutionary timescales, however, they can also be useful. Their activity can help regulate existing genes or contribute genetic material that eventually becomes part of new and beneficial genes.
About half of the human genome is made up of transposon-derived DNA. Most of these elements are no longer active, and only a very small fraction can still move and copy themselves within genomes.
"Genes that come from transposable elements and that are repurposed for cellular functions are typically no longer transposable," said Cedric Feschotte, a senior author of the study. "BC200 was itself created from a mobile element but has retained its mobility and yet it is also clearly serving a cellular function. Somehow evolution hasn't been able to untangle these two things."
A Rare Genetic Jump Into a Virus
Scientists have documented a handful of cases in other species in which transposable elements moved into viruses. One early example came in the late 1980s, when researchers working with cultured moth cells observed a transposon moving from those cells into a baculovirus, a type of virus that infects insects.
BC200, however, is found only in humans and closely related primates. Scientists first identified it in the late 1980s as a highly abundant non-coding RNA in human neurons.
Its exact physiological role remains uncertain, but evidence suggests that BC200 may help regulate how neuronal messenger RNAs are translated into proteins.
BC200 also appears at low levels in germ cells - sperm and eggs - which means it may have the potential to create new insertions in the genome that could be inherited by future generations.
Possible Links to Skin Cells and Disease
The researchers also think BC200 may have made its jump into the molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV) while the virus was infecting skin cells, since those are the only cells known to be infected by MCV.
The gene has also attracted attention because it is expressed abnormally in some tumors and appears at elevated levels in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease. That raises the possibility that BC200's ability to move could also play a role in disease.
Feschotte said the team now wants to investigate whether the molluscum contagiosum virus uses BC200 to manipulate human host cells for its own benefit.
The researchers are also interested in learning more about BC200's connection to diseases such as breast cancer and other tumors, where the gene is abnormally expressed. One key question is whether BC200 is actively jumping in cancer cells and, if so, whether those movements are creating mutations.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Cornell University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Pu Gao, Ellen J. Pritham, Cedric Feschotte, Cheng Sun. Escape of the BC200 gene to a human poxvirus reveals its persistent transposition in primates. Science, 2026; 393 (6818): 1342 DOI: 10.1126/science.aeh3441

The Republican consensus on Israel is starting to fracture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:05:47 UTC
19:05:47 KST

The Republican consensus on Israel is starting to fracture
Christian Zionism made Israel central to conservative politics. America First and younger Republicans are testing that consensus.
The Republican Party’s powerful alliance with Israel — repeatedly reaffirmed during President Donald Trump’s second term — is rooted in conservative Christianity’s rise as a political force more than half a century ago.
The Reverend Billy Graham’s relationship with President Richard Nixon helped bring evangelical politics into the White House. Graham later regretted his political entanglement, particularly after Watergate, but the opening remained. In the late 1970s, Jerry Falwell’s Moral Majority mobilised conservative evangelicals into a potent Republican constituency that Ronald Reagan incorporated into his conservative coalition. Israel became increasingly central to that identity, with many evangelicals viewing support for the Jewish state through a biblical rather than purely strategic lens. Leaders such as televangelist John Hagee and Christians United for Israel later built an institutional network that translated religious conviction into political pressure. What began as evangelical access to Republican presidents became a durable political infrastructure.
For Christian Zionists, this alliance is about more than religious affinity. Many view Israel as central to biblical prophecy, including end-times interpretations and the anticipated return of Jesus Christ. These beliefs elevated support for Israel from a foreign-policy preference to a religious commitment. As evangelical voters became a core Republican constituency, politicians had strong electoral incentives to embrace that commitment, bringing theology, party loyalty and strategic interests into closer alignment.
The political heirs
Today’s Republican leaders inherited that system.
Mike Johnson of Louisiana, the speaker of the US House of Representatives, embodies its contemporary influence. He has invoked biblical passages to portray the relationship between the US and Israel as more than a conventional strategic partnership. His speakership gives him considerable influence over legislation, congressional spending and debates over US military assistance to Israel.
Senator Ted Cruz of Texas has repeatedly framed his support for Israel in explicitly Christian terms. Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas represents a more nationalist, hawkish version of the alliance. His effort to replace “West Bank” with “Judea and Samaria” in federal terminology illustrates how biblical language can enter government policy.
Former Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee, now Trump’s ambassador to Israel, represents the same intersection of evangelical Christianity and Republican politics. His defence of Israeli settlements and rejection of conventional territorial terminology reflect a worldview in which biblical claims carry substantial political weight.
These figures did not create the alliance; they are its current custodians. Their influence extends beyond rhetoric. Congressional votes on military assistance, diplomatic protection and sanctions translate political commitments into policy. Christian Zionist organisations sustain that influence through church networks, lobbying, grassroots mobilisation and direct engagement with elected officials, keeping their priorities prominent even when other Republicans question overseas commitments.
Trump and the America First complication
President Donald Trump strengthened the evangelical alliance with Israel while introducing a competing force into Republican foreign policy: America First.
His administration’s recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and relocation of the US embassy fulfilled a longstanding Christian Zionist priority. Yet Trump’s coalition also includes voters sceptical of foreign entanglements, overseas military interventions and extensive foreign assistance. This creates a tension within the Republican consensus.
For Christian Zionists, support for Israel can constitute a biblical obligation. For some America First Republicans, the question is whether that commitment advances a clearly defined American interest. The positions overlap but are not identical.
The tension sharpens when support for Israel risks a wider war, additional deployments or prolonged US involvement in the Middle East. The Iran war has exposed precisely this contradiction, forcing Republicans to confront the point at which support for Israel collides with America First opposition to prolonged military involvement abroad. Religious conservatives may regard biblical commitments as decisive while more isolationist Republicans question the financial costs, potential American casualties and responsibilities Washington assumes on behalf of other countries.
Trump has sought to accommodate both constituencies, but their competing priorities have become increasingly difficult to reconcile.
The generational crack
A more consequential challenge may be emerging among younger Republicans.
A Pew Research Center March survey found that Republicans overall viewed Israel more favourably than unfavourably, by 58 percent to 41 percent. Among Republicans aged 18 to 49, however, 57 percent held unfavourable views. Older Republicans remained substantially more favourable. A separate Pew survey in May found that 42 percent of Republican-leaning Americans aged 18 to 29 viewed Israelis favourably, compared with 83 percent of those aged 65 and older. Although the surveys measured different populations and questions, both revealed a pronounced generational divide.
These findings do not mean younger Republicans have abandoned Israel or oppose the US-Israel relationship. They do suggest that the constituency underpinning the alliance is becoming less uniform.
The reasons extend beyond ideology. Younger Americans encounter the conflict through social media, reporting on Gaza and images of civilian suffering. Some question whether religiously grounded foreign-policy commitments serve American interests. Others support Israel while opposing particular Israeli government policies. Unfavourable views of Israel should not automatically be equated with hostility towards Israelis or rejection of the bilateral relationship.
Nevertheless, a generation increasingly divided over Israel may prove less receptive to appeals treating support for the country as an unquestionable test of conservative identity.
A changing Republican inheritance
Israel has developed into more than a foreign-policy priority. For millions of conservatives, support for Israel has been part of the Republican Party’s religious and moral identity.
That legacy remains powerful, but its foundations are shifting. Younger Republicans came of age during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, Trump’s nationalism, scepticism towards foreign intervention and Israel’s war on Gaza. Their questions increasingly concern not only theology but also national interests: What does US support for Israel accomplish, what does it cost and when should religious conviction yield to strategic considerations?
Such questions may reshape the coalition without immediately dismantling it. Evangelical organisations retain substantial resources, access to political leaders and the capacity to mobilise voters. Their congressional allies hold positions of considerable influence, and changing public opinion does not automatically translate into new party platforms or congressional votes.
Yet the growing divide between older evangelical voters and younger Republicans presents a longer-term challenge. Christian Zionism succeeded so thoroughly that its premises became Republican orthodoxy. But an alliance sustained by religious conviction, institutional influence and partisan loyalty becomes harder to preserve when a new generation questions those underlying assumptions.
For decades, support for Israel could be presented simultaneously as foreign policy and faith. Increasingly, younger Republicans may demand a different justification, one grounded in demonstrable US interests rather than religious obligation alone. Whether Republican support for Israel can survive that shift may become a defining test of the party’s evolving identity.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Reuters was unable to independently contact al-Hammami, who is being held in the UAE, for comment. However, according to the publication, the UAE has not brought any formal charges against him, and it is unknown whether he has appointed a lawyer. Oman has not commented on the incident so far.

Nobel Prize for Medicine awarded to three scientists for their work in optogenetics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:05:01 UTC
19:05:01 KST

STOCKHOLM, October 5. /TASS/. The 2026 Nobel Prize for Medicine has been awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute announced on Monday.
The three scientists were selected as the winners for their work ‘concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics’, the Assembly explained in a press release.
"The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2026 is awarded for optogenetics - a method that makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviors in the living brain. Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel discovered a remarkable protein, channelrhodopsin, in a single-celled alga. Karl Deisseroth transformed the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells. The Laureates have laid the foundation of a new era in neuroscience," the press release reads.
According to Per Svenningsson, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, "optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of."
Optogenetics, a groundbreaking method for controlling nerve signals with light, has rapidly gained global impact and fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain, the Assembly continued. "Using optogenetics, researchers have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders. In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment. Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity’s great mysteries: how our incredible brain works," it concluded.

Saudi-led coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said 100 fighter jets were providing support to Yemeni government forces battling the Houthis.
He said the coalition had secured “air protection” over the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets during the ongoing campaign.
The claims and the scale of the campaign could not immediately be independently verified.
Houthis seize key town as fighting escalates
The Houthis captured the town of Turbah on Sunday, shortly before Yemen’s internationally recognized government announced a major military operation against the rebels.
The renewed fighting has revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year ceasefire.
Turbah lies on a major road linking Taiz with the southern port city of Aden, which serves as the interim seat of Yemen’s government. For years, the town served as an important position for government forces defending Taiz against the Houthis.
The rebels had already seized several villages and areas on the outskirts of Taiz, advances that could help them encircle Yemen’s third-largest city.
The latest Houthi gains follow a rapid offensive along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast that began in early September.
The rebels captured the strategic city of Mokha and several Red Sea islands, gains that allowed them to control the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints, through which roughly 12% of global trade passes.
In an announcement Sunday, the Saudi-backed Yemeni government said it was mobilizing troops throughout territory under its control.
Rashad al-Alimi, head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, said in a televised speech that the operation was aimed at “recovering the remaining territories” held by the Houthis and called on the international community to support his government.
Hours later, al-Malki pledged “full operational support” for Yemeni government forces until the Houthis were “eliminated.”
He also said Saudi Arabia reserved the right to take all necessary measures against Houthi missile and drone attacks on the kingdom during the nearly three-month escalation.
Saudi-backed forces launch counteroffensive
On Monday, factions aligned with the Saudi-backed coalition said they had begun offensives against Houthi positions east of coastal areas seized by the rebels.
The forces attacked Houthi positions in Dhubab, on the coast of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to Col. Majed al-Nazili, a spokesman for the Saudi-backed forces.
The Giants Brigades, another government-aligned force, said it had launched a “decisive military operation against the Houthi militias” in the Bab el-Mandeb area.
Al-Alimi said in a post on X that the operation, dubbed “Yemen Dawn,” was intended to restore state institutions, “liberate” the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa and end what he called the Houthi “coup.”
The latest escalation began in mid-July, when the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa airport to prevent an unauthorized Iranian flight from landing.
The rebels responded with missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces and announced a blockade of Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, later attacking several Saudi-linked vessels.
In September, the Houthis intensified their campaign, advancing rapidly down the Red Sea coast in their largest territorial push in years.
The capture of Turbah “will likely severely constrain Yemeni government-aligned forces’ ability to reinforce and resupply front-line positions” across Taiz province and in the city itself, the Washington-based Institute for the Study of War said.
“Disrupting resupply has military value, of course, but controlling all the roads in and out of areas to the north of Turbah also prevents government forces from retreating out of the city,” the think tank wrote in an analysis Sunday.
Civil war flares again after four-year ceasefire
Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, when the Houthis swept south from their northern stronghold, captured Sanaa and forced the internationally recognized government into exile in Saudi Arabia.
The conflict has created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises and killed more than 150,000 people.
The latest round of violence has killed more than 800 people and wounded more than 3,600, according to the United Nations.
More than 145,000 people have been displaced within Yemen, according to the U.N. migration agency, while more than 3,000 others have fled across the Red Sea to Djibouti.
Last week, the health ministry run by Yemen’s internationally recognized government warned that the renewed fighting was severely affecting medical services across Taiz province.
The ministry said health facilities in coastal, western and southern parts of the province had either closed or were operating only partially.

Construction of the plant near Balbieriškis was expected to begin this autumn, with production scheduled to start late next year or in the autumn of 2027. The facility is planned on a 30.6-hectare site in the village of Ąžuolai.

Raccoons taking over the Curonian Spit; hunting to be permitted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:03:31 UTC
19:03:31 KST

Raccoons on the Curonian Spit are being counted and monitored, and authorities are preparing a plan to combat this invasive species; hunting is likely to begin as early as spring.
Saulius Rumbutis, a staff member at the Tadas Ivanauskas Zoology Museum, noted that while there appears to be a significant number of raccoons on the Curonian Spit, it is difficult to determine exactly how many are present. He estimated the population to be between 50 and 100 individuals.
Raccoons are nocturnal animals that typically hide during the day. Rumbutis explained that they often choose large tree hollows or simply fallen trees—such as pines—for shelter; they climb up to sleep during the day and venture out at night in search of food.
The highest concentration of raccoons has been observed near Juodkrantė. As omnivores, these animals tend to stay near inhabited areas where food is more plentiful. Rumbutis noted that raccoons feed on mollusks and will also eat the eggs or chicks found in bird nests. If they happen to find something like a slice of pizza discarded in a trash bin, they will certainly eat that as well.

Trump’s recent statements on the economy are even more bonkers than usual | Steven Greenhouse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:53 UTC
19:00:53 KST

Donald Trump recently made a bold claim about his abilities, writing on Truth Social: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”
But in the days before and after that post, Trump made one mind-boggling statement after another, including one that raised the possibility of cutting off all trade with dozens of the US’s trading partners. The president’s statements had many experts questioning not just his intelligence, but also whether he – and the outlandish policies he was proposing – were a clear and present danger to both the US economy and the world economy. Public respect for Trump’s economic sense has fallen so low that just 7% of Americans think he should take the lead in regulating AI, according to a recent WSJ poll.
Responding to Trump’s reckless statements, one prominent advocacy group, Republicans Against Trump, derided him as “Dumbest. President. Ever.”
Economists and corporate executives were especially alarmed by two Trump statements. First, he wrote on Truth Social: “I’ll stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit” if the Federal Reserve doesn’t cut interest rates.
The second disconcerting statement was: “If we stopped Trading with every country that we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year.”
Not only is Trump’s arithmetic childishly silly here, but any college student who took Econ 101 knows that if a trade-dependent nation like the US suddenly ended all trade with dozens of countries, that would lead to economic disaster. What’s more, it was worrisome that Trump views himself as almighty emperor with the power to singlehandedly halt hundreds of billions of dollars in trade.
If Trump ordered the US to terminate all trade with every place with which it has a trade deficit – that includes China, Mexico, Taiwan and the European Union – many US manufacturers would quickly find themselves in desperate straits, unable to obtain critically needed computer chips, rare earths, auto parts, aluminum and much more. As a result, many factories would be forced to close. Not only that, many farmers would be crippled because they couldn’t import the fertilizer they need, while many homebuilders would have to stop work because they couldn’t import needed lumber.
Those were by no means Trump’s only recent mind-boggling statements.
Two days before the Federal Reserve raised its short-term interest rates to 3.75% to 4% to combat inflation, Trump was on a tear, badgering and bullying the Fed, telling it not only not to raise interest rates, but to cut rates sharply. “We should be at 1% or half a percent,” Trump said. Again, anyone who took Econ 101 knows that cutting rates so sharply and so low will push prices skyward at a time when the Fed and consumers already think inflation is too high. And let’s not forget that Trump was the guy who promised to reduce prices on day one as president.
With that statement, the self-described “stable genius” president showed his utter failure to understand one of the most basic teachings of Econ 101 – when interest rates are extremely low, like 1%, that heats up the economy and that revved-up economic activity fuels inflation. The University of Michigan economist Justin Wolfers called Trump’s demand for a 1% interest rate “the dumbest thing ever said by a president”.
Then there was this whopper. Trump said that if the Fed bowed to his demands and slashed interest rates, “we could have a GDP [growth] of 14, 15, 16 and 20.”
Those numbers are absurd, fantastical. Considering that the US economy grew at a moderate 2.2% rate in this year’s second quarter and rarely grows faster than 5%, talk of 20% growth is delusional. Since the second world war, the US economy has grown at a rate at 20% or higher just once. That happened in the third quarter of 2020 due to extraordinary circumstances – in that quarter, myriad businesses rushed to reopen after the worst pandemic in a century caused many to suddenly shut down during the previous quarter. (GDP plunged at a 28% rate that quarter.)
Then there was this colossally wrong-headed statement about trade: “The word ‘Deficit’ is nothing more than a fancy word for LOSS.” Trump coupled that assertion with his misbegotten statement that the US would magically be $1.5tn richer if it terminated all trade with every nation with which it has a deficit.
This shows an infantile understanding of trade – and a stunning blindness to its mutual benefits.
To explain how inane Trump is being here, let’s hypothesize for a second that in the US-France trade relationship, the only goods traded are wine and bourbon. Under Trump’s ludicrous logic, if the US buys $2bn of wine from France, and the French import $1bn worth of Kentucky bourbon, the resulting $1bn trade deficit means the US is simply giving away $1bn to France.
Trump bafflingly sees that as an outright $1bn loss. Blinded by ignorance, ideology or an idée fixe, Trump fails to see that that’s not a harmful $1bn “loss” – rather, Americans are getting $1bn worth of fine wine to enjoy. No doubt wine lovers across the US see that as a gain and certainly not as a $1bn loss.
Bottom line, Trump’s delusional statements on the economy show that he is becoming more detached from reality and from rational understanding of how the world works. One can’t help but wonder why his economic advisers don’t stop him from making such ridiculous and at times dangerous statements. If Trump turns his absurd economic notions into reality, as he has done in his ugly, unnecessary trade war with Canada, that will be more bad news for Americans.
Voters should realize that Trump, with his failure to grasp basic economics, is a danger to the economy. He has brought us higher prices, slower GDP growth, and constant economic chaos and uncertainty. His tariffs and disastrous war against Iran have hit the great majority of Americans in their wallets and pocketbooks.
Tragically, Trump’s Republican supporters in Congress either cheer him on or remain dismayingly silent while Trump does serious damage to the economy and to the finances of millions of struggling families. Americans shouldn’t forget this when they vote in November’s midterm elections.
- Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

MVRDV designs modular concrete street furniture to be occupied in "unexpected ways"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:46 UTC
19:00:46 KST

MVRDV designs modular concrete street furniture to be occupied in "unexpected ways"
Colourful concrete modules are combined to form impromptu hangout spots in the Barcode collection, designed by architecture studio MVRDV for Barcelona street furniture manufacturer Escofet.
The range consists of three basic building blocks – steps, slopes and a joint table and bench – that can be joined together to create an atlas of different topographies.
MVRDV founding partner Jacob van Rijs, who led the project, says he hopes the collection will encourage citizens to take ownership over their cities and appropriate urban infrastructure in a way that suits their needs.
"Too often, the design of urban spaces can feel formulaic – benches and other elements are selected from a catalogue and placed in the most predictable places," he says.
"This collection is built around a different approach: human occupation becomes the centrepiece of any design, with a creative collaboration between the individual elements, the arrangement made by an urban designer, and the unexpected ways that the public will occupy them," Van Rijs continued.
Barcode consists of three basic building blocks that can be adapted with add-ons like planters. They come in Escofet's eight different concrete colours, including red, green and yellow alongside more muted grey, white, beige and black.
The Tribune module consists of a set of broad steps for climbing and sitting, while the smooth slope of Dune invites lounging. Desk is a more traditional set-up of a table framed by two benches for al fresco eating or working.
All three modules have the same height and width, so they can be lined up to form a continuous surface. MVRDV envisions them being used in one long line – hence the name Barcode – or combined into more compact two-by-two "islands".
Considering all the different variations, MVRDV says the collection includes 72 different choices of elements that can be combined into nearly "infinite variations".
Previous adventures in street furniture from the studio, which was founded by Van Rijs alongside Winy Maas and Nathalie de Vries in 1991, include a giant woven floot mat that provided seating in Bangkok during the city's design week and bright-blue play areas for a 200-metre-long park beneath a Mumbai flyover.
All renders and photography courtesy of MVRDV.

European defence tech funding hits record levels
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:00:38 BST
19:00:38 KST

European defence technology startups have raised a record $7.4 billion in venture capital so far in 2026, nearly three times the $2.6 billion raised across the whole of 2025, according to Dealroom and Resilience Media.
The figures are contained in The State of Defence Tech 2026, which projects European defence-tech investment could reach $10.5 billion by the end of the year if current activity continues.
The report also records a marked increase in US involvement in European defence technology companies. American investors now account for 47 per cent of European defence-tech funding, compared with 17 per cent in 2020.
Much of the increase in investment has been concentrated in large funding rounds. Dealroom and Resilience Media said so-called mega-rounds, including Helsing’s $1.8 billion Series E, account for more than 85 per cent of European defence-tech funding recorded so far this year.
Across NATO members and allied countries, seven funding rounds of at least $1 billion have involved Anduril, Helsing, Saronic, Shield AI, Quantum Systems, ICEYE and Castelion. Defence startups across NATO countries have raised $27.1 billion in venture capital during 2026, around 1.9 times the amount raised during the whole of 2025.
Defence technology now accounts for 11.1 per cent of European venture capital investment, according to the report, rising to 15 per cent when considering the 27 European Union member states.
The pool of investors participating in the sector is also expanding. Dealroom identified 455 investors involved in at least one European defence deal during 2026 to date, compared with 408 during 2025 and 114 in 2020.
Specialist defence investment funds participated in 25 per cent of European defence funding rounds this year, up from 18 per cent in 2025 and 12 per cent in 2024. The report said private equity, project finance, debt and grants contributed a further $2.4 billion to defence companies across NATO and allied countries during 2025.
Germany is currently the largest European market for defence-tech venture funding, driven in part by investment in Helsing, Quantum Systems and Stark. German startups have raised $3.5 billion during 2026 and $5.9 billion since 2020, while Munich is identified in the report as Europe’s leading defence-technology hub.
According to a news update accompanying the report, Leslie Hitchcock, co-founder and publisher of Resilience Media, said: “National security, defence and technological innovation are now inseparable. Across NATO alliance countries, there is an urgent need to strengthen the infrastructure underpinning our collective security and resilience. For Europe, technological sovereignty must mean building together in the face of common threats.”
She added: “This is both a strategic imperative and a major economic opportunity: to build companies that protect peace and democracy while transforming defence, cybersecurity, energy and other critical infrastructure.”
US investors have become increasingly prominent within that European market. The report identifies Axon, Accel, Founders Fund, Y Combinator, General Catalyst and Lightspeed among the most active American investors in European defence technology during 2025 and 2026.
Among European investors, the NATO Innovation Fund recorded 12 defence-tech funding round participations since 2025, while Lakestar recorded ten, making them the two most active investors identified in the report over that period.
Klaus Hommels, Founder and Chairman of Lakestar, said: “Europe’s military leaders have been clear with us: if we want to build and retain critical defence capabilities in Europe, we also need sovereign European financing. The demand for these technologies is there and now the capital must follow. This record investment shows that Europe is beginning to recognise defence technology as a strategic necessity, not a passing investment trend.”
Despite the increase in funding, the report identifies areas where European companies remain behind global competitors. It describes Europe as relatively strong in quantum technology, photonics, space and drones, while identifying gaps in areas including AI chips and processors, launch vehicles, humanoid systems and communications satellites.
European quantum startups alone have raised $2.1 billion so far in 2026, with investment projected to reach $2.9 billion by the end of the year.
The value of European venture-backed defence startups has reached a combined $44 billion, according to the report, with companies founded since 2020 accounting for 77 per cent of that total.
Exit activity is also expected to increase. Across NATO and allied countries, defence-tech exits are projected to rise to 31 during 2026, compared with an annual average of around eight between 2021 and 2024. Exit value reached $18.6 billion during 2025, although the report said activity remained heavily concentrated in the United States.
The study also examined the movement of personnel between government, the military and the defence technology investment sector. Sixteen per cent of commercial leaders at European defence-tech companies were found to have military or defence ministry experience, while the proportion rises to 34 per cent among investors working at specialist defence funds.
Harry Mead, co-founder and CEO of Augur, said: “It’s reassuring to see European investment responding to the current threat environment. But this isn’t turning into deployed capability fast enough. The enemy are at the gates: Europe can’t afford to wait for new systems and legislation.”
“Our adversaries know this and are adept at exploiting the lag between identifying the problem, funding a solution and deploying it. We already have the infrastructure. What we urgently need is to make our sensors and systems more intelligent, so that operators can always stay a step ahead of our adversaries.”
The report is being presented at the Resilience Conference in London on 5 October, bringing together defence technology companies, investors and military and government representatives from the UK, NATO, Ukraine and other European countries.
