Celebrity admiration is linked to submission to authority, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:32 UTC
19:00:32 KST

People who strongly admire celebrities tend to be more deferential to authority and more attached to traditional norms, according to new research published in Psychological Reports. The findings suggest that strong emotional attachments to famous figures relate to a preference for established social order and conventional norms, even after accounting for a person’s general political orientation.
People often form one-sided emotional connections with famous actors, musicians, and social media influencers. While these parasocial relationships are common and can sometimes provide a sense of community, intense celebrity admiration involves spending excessive time and effort focusing on a favorite public figure. This level of absorption is sometimes linked to negative outcomes. For instance, a 2021 study covered by PsyPost indicated that higher obsession with celebrities was associated with lower performance on tests of vocabulary and fluid intelligence.
The idea that celebrity admiration might be tied to authoritarianism is not new. Researchers proposed in 2001 that people inclined to defer to authority might gravitate toward celebrities, who are often treated as authorities on a range of topics, but their study of British participants found no association between the two.
Since then, the understanding of authoritarianism has shifted. The authors of a 2010 paper argued that right-wing authoritarianism is better understood as three related but distinct sets of attitudes: authoritarianism (which involves aggression and strict control), conservatism (which focuses on submission to authority and preserving the status quo), and traditionalism (which centers on adhering to old-fashioned lifestyles and morality).
Nearly 25 years after that first study, and amid shifts in celebrity culture and politics, the researchers sought to test which specific dimensions of authoritarianism are actually associated with celebrity admiration, especially once general political ideology and demographic factors are taken into account. The team was led by Ho Huynh, a senior lecturer in the School of Medicine and Psychology at the Australian National University.
“We know that celebrities have undue influence over people and that celebrities typically endorse liberal-leaning causes (e.g., climate change, immigration, abortion),” Huynh told PsyPost. “We were surprised to learn through our previous work that people who admire celebrities tend to self-identify as more politically conservative.”
“In the current work, we wanted to see if celebrity admiration would extend to right-wing authoritarianism,” Huynh continued. “This work might help to explain the contradiction of why politically conservative people in the United States might be more attracted to celebrities despite the stereotype that celebrities tend to hold liberal views.”
To investigate this, the researchers recruited 331 adults living in the United States through the online crowdsourcing platform Prolific. The sample was deliberately balanced during recruitment to contain an equal mix of self-identified liberals, moderates, and conservatives, meaning it is not nationally representative. About 54 percent of the participants were women, and all were 18 or older, with an average age of about 40.
Participants completed the brief seven-item version of the Celebrity Attitude Scale, a questionnaire that asks people to indicate their agreement with statements about their favorite famous person. This scale measures two levels of admiration. The first is a lighter, entertainment-social level, which includes enjoying keeping up with news about the celebrity or discussing them with friends. The second is a more intense, pathological level, characterized by feelings that the celebrity is a soulmate or that the fan shares a special, indescribable bond with them.
The participants also completed a survey assessing the three dimensions of right-wing authoritarianism. For example, participants rated their agreement with statements like “Obedience and respect for authority are the most important virtues children should learn.” Finally, they provided demographic information, including their education level, socioeconomic status, and their overall political orientation on an 11-point scale ranging from completely liberal to completely conservative.
The initial results showed that both forms of celebrity admiration were linked to higher scores on all three dimensions of authoritarianism. The links were strongest for conservatism (correlations of 0.32 for the lighter form and 0.45 for the intense form, on a scale where 0 means no relationship), moderate for traditionalism (0.19 and 0.32), and weak for authoritarian aggression (0.15 and 0.13). Only the intense form was linked to political conservatism, and modestly so (a correlation of 0.19).
To see if these links held up under closer statistical scrutiny, the researchers ran a series of models that controlled for the participants’ age, gender, education, socioeconomic status, and general political orientation. This step helped rule out the possibility that the connection simply reflected factors like political conservatism, which was linked to authoritarian attitudes and to intense admiration.
After accounting for these factors, celebrity admiration consistently predicted right-wing conservatism and right-wing traditionalism. Demographics and political orientation explained about 24 percent of the variation in conservatism scores; celebrity admiration added 9 percent (lighter form) or 13 percent (intense form) on top of that. For traditionalism, it added only about 2 to 4 percent.
“The association between celebrity admiration and authoritarian submission seems to be robust and reliable, indicating that people who worship their favorite celebrity tend to prefer more dominant authorities,” Huynh explained. Asked what the average person should take away, he said: “People who report admiring their favorite celebrity are more likely to submit to authority and prefer traditional norms. These trends might help explain why people who admire celebrities may self-identify as more politically conservative.”
However, the relationship between celebrity admiration and the third dimension, authoritarianism (the demand for strict punishment of rule-breakers), did not remain robust. Once demographics and political orientation were factored in, intense admiration no longer predicted authoritarian aggression. The lighter form remained a statistically detectable predictor, but it accounted for only about 1 percent of the variation, and the authors do not consider this strong evidence of a link. The authors suggest this may be because people who heavily admire celebrities tend to see the world as fair, with people getting what they deserve, and so may feel less need to support harsh punishment for rule-breakers.
Huynh sees this boundary as an encouraging sign. “Celebrity admiration was not related to authoritarian aggression, which involves strictness and social control,” he noted. “This finding showed the limits of celebrity admiration, which is positive and worthy of optimism.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study measured these traits at a single point in time, so the direction of the relationship is unknown. Intense absorption in celebrity culture might lead someone to adopt more authority-respecting and traditional views, or people who already hold such views might be more drawn to celebrity culture. When the researchers flipped their statistical model, higher authority-submission scores also predicted more celebrity admiration, a pattern consistent with either direction.
The list of control variables was also limited, missing related traits like narcissism and a preference for social hierarchies. Additionally, the survey asked participants to focus on their favorite celebrity but did not distinguish between typical entertainers and political figures. Because modern politics has become heavily focused on personalities, admiring a politician might function differently than admiring a musician or actor.
“This research was not about political celebrities, but celebrities generally,” Huynh said. “Some people may want to view these findings through the Trump presidencies, but only 5 out of 331 people in the study listed Donald Trump as their favorite celebrity. As such, these findings represent the associations between celebrity admiration and endorsement of different aspects of right-wing authoritarianism more broadly.”
Finally, the study only included participants from the United States. Cultural values, political structures, and the nature of fame vary widely around the world, so these connections might operate differently in other countries.
Huynh suggested another direction for future work. “An interesting next step would be to examine the associations between celebrity admiration and left-wing authoritarianism (e.g., hostility toward people in power, support for censoring opposing views, and rejection of traditional values and norms),” he said.
The study, “Idols and Ideologies: Examining Associations Between Celebrity Admiration and Right-Wing Authoritarianism,” was authored by Ho Phi Huynh, Joshua L. Williams, Marla F. Jorgensen, Amy Dicke-Bohmann, and Lynn McCutcheon.

Gambling Is Sending More People to the ER
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:07 UTC
19:00:07 KST

Legalizing gambling can come with big health problems.
That’s the conclusion of a recent study out of Ontario, published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, which found that after the Canadian province legalized betting on individual sports events in 2022, emergency department visits for gambling disorders doubled. Most of the people who landed in the emergency department were men, and almost one third of the visits led to hospitalizations.
“This rise in severe presentations might be a bit of a warning signal of a wider increase in harms across the general population,” says Ryan Forrest, a public-health doctoral student at the University of Toronto and one of the authors of the study. “We think about things like financial distress, family and relationship problems, worsening mental health—and those things are not captured in the emergency department data.”
The authors of the Ontario study projected how many people would normally end up in an emergency department every year, and then compared that to what they saw after online betting on single sporting events became legal in Ontario. Emergency department visits were 154% higher than they would have been had the law not been changed, Forrest says. The visits were concentrated among men aged 10-44.
Many of the patients showed up at the emergency room with major depression and suicidality, and some had other mental-health or substance-abuse diagnoses, Forrest said. Doctors at the emergency department noted in patients’ records that gambling had contributed to those other issues.
A separate study by some of the same researchers also found that calls to ConnexOntario, Ontario’s free 24-hour mental health and addictions helpline, were 200% higher than they would have been had the law not been changed. That study found that the people reaching out for help were almost exclusively boys and men aged 15 to 44.
“There’s two data sources telling us there is a real health signal happening here,” Forrest says.
The mental-health consequences of expanding betting
The study is a warning to the U.S., which has seen sports gambling proliferate since 2018 after the Supreme Court struck down a law barring most state-authorized sports gambling, allowing states to decide for themselves whether to allow sports betting. Since then, dozens of states, including New Jersey, Tennessee, and New York, have legalized sports betting. Many states also allow online casino games. Gambling has spread in Canada, too, after the country legalized betting on single sports events in 2021.
Therapists in the U.S. say they are already seeing the mental-health consequences of the legalization of sport betting across the U.S., along with the results of more exposure to prediction markets. Birches Health, the largest provider specializing in the treatment of gambling disorder in the U.S., has seen the number of 18-to-34 year old clients grow more than twofold since 2024, according to Cynthia Grant, vice president of clinical for Birches Health.
“There’s more people gambling,” she says, “and when you have more people gambling, it simply means that there’s more people who are going to develop a problem.”
Grant says that clients are mentioning prediction markets 200% more often than they did last year, according to the company’s analysis of its initial clinical assessments. Prediction markets allow people as young as 18 to place wagers; sports betting is restricted to people over 21.
“It’s just not a regulated environment out there,” she says. “People’s lives are being ruined; their relationships are being destroyed, their retirement accounts are gone.”
One of the reasons younger people are seeking treatment may be that they are starting to gamble earlier, she says. It’s not just prediction markets: some kids are given lottery scratch tickets for gifts, she says, or they’ll participate in family fantasy sports wages. “Those are the memories that people talk about” in therapy, she says. Kids are also exposed to gambling with online games that encourage them to chase a reward, or through hobbies like collecting Pokemon cards, in which they are betting that they’ll get a valuable card in an anonymous pack.
The standard treatment for gambling disorder is cognitive behavioral therapy, Grant says, because people with a gambling addiction often have distorted thinking and believe that they can beat the system. But often, she says, people don’t even know that gambling disorder is a mental-health condition and that insurance can cover care. Studies show that suicidal ideation and suicide risk is 5 to 10 times higher in people with gambling disorders than in the general population.
An under-regulated betting landscape
Both Grant and Forrest say that the unregulated nature of gambling in both Canada and the U.S. leads to more people ending up with mental-health problems—but that there is little investment in tracking those problems. There has been no money set aside by the Canadian government to track whether it leads to more public-health problems, Forrest says.
“You compare that to something like when cannabis was legalized, there were huge amounts of grants given out to monitor these kinds of policy changes,” Forrest says.
Most apps don’t have automatic spending limits that prevent people from losing too much money gambling, and most take a hands-off approach to users who act in a way that suggests they have an addiction. In a recent ProPublica story, a reporter posed as a problem gambler and found that rather than flagging his behavior, the app tried to incentivize him to keep going.
“The way that online systems work right now do not protect people at all who are prone to behavioral addictions,” Grant says, “and that, to me, is very dangerous for my clients.”
“Bartenders have rules about how much they can serve someone,” Grant says. “Police can issue a DUI—there are efforts to stop people who are potentially causing harm. But that does not happen in the gambling space.”

The Case Against Wearing Headphones in Public
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:06 UTC
19:00:06 KST

I keep losing my wireless headphones. When I do have them with me, they’re often out of battery. So one day earlier this summer, I decided to ditch them.
It felt like a huge step, as I’d long used in-ear tech as a shield from the auditory chaos of London. But what happened felt transformative. I was surprised at how present I was without them.
During my first headphones-free commute, I smiled at strangers. I noticed the stops on the train line, something I never do when I rely on an app to tell me when to get off the train through my earphones. That one journey made me wonder if I had accidentally outsourced the joys of my city life to my phone.
In 2026, we have become remarkably good at filling every quiet moment: Spotify on the train, podcasts while walking, Google Maps telling us where to go, our phones providing something to look at whenever there’s a lull.
The scale of this is striking. Ofcom’s latest research found that 93% of U.K. adults listen to some form of audio every week, and more than a quarter listen to podcasts weekly. Hundreds of millions of people worldwide listen to podcasts.
There’s also a fascinating social angle. Research published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology found that people often avoid talking to strangers because they underestimate how enjoyable those interactions will be. And research into constant smartphone connectivity published in Current Directions in Psychological Science suggests that our devices can cause us to miss the emotional benefits of casual interactions by effectively replacing them.
It turns out that there might be a psychological reason why being without headphones has felt so unthinkable. Psychotherapist Jack Worthy tells me that our earliest impulses as newborns are approach and avoidance. “We approach what feels interesting, exciting, or otherwise potentially rewarding. We avoid whatever feels dangerous, disgusting, or boring.” Our emotional life proceeds from these drives, and these drives evolved to promote our survival and success.
Our headphones give us the power to dial in to highly appealing experiences and tune out everything we’d rather avoid in the environment. If our homes serve as refuge from the outside world, our headphones create a tidy micro-environment inside our heads.
I decided to continue my experiment, spending a month commuting without earphones at all.
After a week without them, I started observing fascinating new details about streets that I had walked countless times. One seismic discovery was that the nearest train station to my flat is a two-minute walk away. Google Maps had shown me the longer route, hauling me around the local houses for more than double as long, which in London may as well be wasted hours.
Without headphones, I found myself overhearing bizarre conversations. Like the girl next to me on the train, who had found a Rhode lip gloss in her boyfriend’s car when she is a Rare Beauty girl. She assured her friend that it could not have been her lip gloss because she would never buy anything from Hailey Bieber—after all, she is a long-time Selena Gomez fan. “I can’t believe how Hailey Bieber stole Justin Bieber from Selena Gomez, and now someone else is stealing my man!” she wailed with her head held between her knees and her friend rubbing her back.
Another time, I witnessed a man nearly lose his mind after a stranger accidentally smeared dirt onto his white shoes. The man exploded, yelling at this innocent stranger. It was a captivating fight, and I was absolutely glued. How could this man be fuming about a simple mistake? Imagine if I’d missed the spontaneous subterranean soap opera because I was listening to a podcast.
My absolute favorite eavesdropping moment was when two women in leather outfits and cowboy boots boarded the train and sat opposite me. The woman next to the window said her stressed boyfriend Keith had just bought the couple a flat, so she didn’t feel she could pressure him for an engagement ring. I was glued to their ridiculous conversation and, when they got off, sad that I couldn’t listen in anymore, as her requests were getting more and more ludicrous with every outburst.
“I don’t see him proposing to that nutter!” said the old man next to me, and we shared that rarest of joyous things: a communal laugh.
“Good luck to Keith! Lots going on, poor fella.”
I couldn’t believe I had been missing out on so much drama. Looking back, I realized how rarely I let myself be bored, instead always reaching for distraction.
Psychoanalysis uses the term “reverie” to define a particular kind of constructive, necessary daydreaming, points out Worthy. “In therapy, reveries refer to the daydreams, memories, and associations occurring to the analyst during a session.” A sensitive, attuned analyst interprets those reveries to understand what’s happening between themself and the patient.
If you’ve ever experienced a sudden moment of inspiration in the shower or on a run, if the solution to a sticky problem revealed itself to you spontaneously, you know something of what it means to use reverie. You let your mind unfold in unintentional directions, and your unconscious mind showed you what your conscious mind was missing.
If we’re always moving through the world with headphones in, listening to music or podcasts or books, we’re compromising our mind’s space for revery, says Worthy. There’s less room for the constructive daydreaming our mental processes use for creativity, problem-solving, and synthesizing.
By the end of the month, I had no desire for headphones. When the train got too loud, I would put them on just to cancel the screeching sounds of the metal wheels. But when it got calmer, off they came, and I was ready for the next drama. Now I’m excited for spontaneous comedy to pepper my commute and give me unexpected pick-ups throughout my day.
My friends complain about how people rarely approach each other in London. During my no-headphones experiment, there have been some headlines for me, too: I got asked out on the streets as well as on the tube. Not that it led to anything romantic, but it wouldn’t have happened if I had my headphones on.

Press review: White House names AI czar as Greece, Germany seek Ukraine aid audit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 5. /TASS/. The latest threats from Vladimir Zelensky could provoke a tougher response from Russia, while the White House appoints an AI czar. Meanwhile, Greece and Germany call for an audit of assistance to Ukraine. These stories topped Monday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Zelensky’s decisions could doom Ukraine to tougher response from Russia
The intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine were a direct result of recent statements from Vladimir Zelensky and his actions, Russian authorities explained. In particular, the Kiev regime has announced plans to attack Russian refineries again and plans to acquire the FP-9 missile, which is capable of reaching Moscow. In response, the Russian Armed Forces will increase strikes targeting "military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure in Kiev and other Ukrainian regions," the Russian Defense Ministry warned. The Russian Foreign Ministry said the goal would be to deprive Zelensky of the ability to escalate the conflict or harm the Russian economy. Meanwhile, the United States has taken a wait-and-see approach before the congressional elections.
Since the EU itself is unable to meet all Kiev's demands for increased financial assistance, the issue of seizing frozen Russian assets is being raised once again, Fernand Kartheiser, a member of the European Parliament from Luxembourg, told Izvestia. "All this indicates that the EU's policy regarding Ukraine is untenable even in the medium term, for Ukraine is a money pit. Voters in EU countries will never agree to further cuts in spending on social needs and other important budget items in order to continue to channel funds into this `black hole’ - Ukraine," the MEP said.
Disagreement about the forms, sequence and pace of support for Ukraine persists in Europe. A number of EU countries, for example, have refused to expedite the allocation of funds from a €90 billion loan for Kiev. This increases the likelihood of individual countries acting through bilateral agreements with Kiev, said Ivan Loshkarev, associate professor at the Department of Political Theory at MGIMO University. Apart from Germany, Nordic countries, primarily Sweden and France, may take a more proactive position. The latest escalation by Kiev is also meant to demonstrate that Russia is also suffering losses from the conflict, Loshkarev emphasized. This will probably allow Ukraine to demonstrate some fragmented progress in its attempts to delay peace. Zelensky rather views the idea of launching talks as an undesirable scenario that will again raise questions about the prospects of his tenure as president, the political scientist noted, and his term of office expired back in May 2024.
Zelensky’s calls to escalate the conflict further pose a direct security threat to which Moscow could respond with tough and exhausting military-technical measures, experts interviewed by Izvestia argued. According to them, today, Russia has a major arsenal of high-precision weapons enabling it to immediately increase the intensity and pace of combined attacks on key enemy targets.
Russia’s retaliatory measures are long-term and systemic, military expert Vasily Dandykin emphasized, with the list of targets also expanding. The West and Kiev should not expect to protract the conflict for another 18 to 24 months, for their defense capacities are designed for a much shorter period, so experts expect radical changes on the front line within the next few months already.
Kommersant: White House installs new authority to mitigate AI risks
US President Donald Trump has decided to appoint National Intelligence chief Jay Clayton as AI czar. A Clayton-led working group will have to present a report on the risks and potential of advanced AI technology within the next 120 days and recommendations to the government regarding potential regulation in this sphere. Russian President Vladimir Putin last week called imposing limits on the use of AI technology in security an existential issue facing humanity. However, neither the US nor Russia is currently ready to place major limits on their AI potential in defense.
Artificial Intelligence was among the key topics discussed at a recent summit between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington. The two leaders agreed to launch a regular interdepartmental dialogue on AI, including a separate communication channel for emergency discussions of major incidents related to the uncontrollable behavior of AI systems. However, no restrictions on the development of AI technology were discussed as there is fierce competition between the US and China in this sphere, and neither of them intends to hold its potential in check for the time being.
However, neither the US nor Russia is seemingly ready for outside-imposed restrictions. The Washington Post reported recently, citing sources, that the two countries’ delegations succeeded in having the requirement that AI-based systems must operate predictably and reliably removed from a document currently being drafted as they joined efforts at a UN debate. The clause made the consideration of ethical factors in using lethal autonomous systems and the stipulation requiring human verification of military targets selected by AI algorithms prior to a strike mandatory.
Jennifer Kavanagh, a senior fellow and director of military analysis at Defense Priorities, a US-based think tank, who took part in the latest meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club, called the approaches of both Washington and Moscow quite logical in an interview with Kommersant. The US decision to refrain from imposing restrictions on AI stems from the fact that it views AI as a sphere of advantage over China, she explained. It is reluctant to restrict itself in order to prevent China from catching up with it, she noted. Meanwhile, Russia is facing different threats, mostly amid the continued Ukraine conflict and rearmament in Europe. In both cases, the benefits of using AI can help offset the disadvantages faced by Russia, the expert added. Against this backdrop, Kavanagh said, it is logical that both the US and Russia are seeking to avoid committing themselves to restricting what they view as their areas of advantage.
As Kommersant reported earlier, the only actual restriction lately agreed by P5 or the five permanent members of the UN Security Council, namely, Russia, the US, China, France and Britain, is that the decision to use nuclear weapons amid the widespread adoption of AI technology, including in the military and military-nuclear sphere, will always be made by humans. Even though the P5 members have not issued joint statements on this matter, they have expressed individual views on the subject.
Izvestia: Greece, Germany demand audit for assistance to Ukraine
The opposition in Germany and Greece is calling for an audit of how the financial and military aid delivered to Kiev has been used, Izvestia has learned. According to them, the money ends up in the pockets of Ukrainian officials, while the weapons are resold to other countries. Berlin has been a main donor, and Greece has Patriot interceptor missiles needed by the Ukrainian army.
Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kiev on an unannounced visit with a pledge of another €1.3 billion in support. Experts believe that due to corruption scandals in Kiev, control over the use of European funding will be tightened further.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party could establish committees at the next Bundestag to investigate the use of financial and military aid transferred to Ukraine, Steffen Kotre, a member of the German parliament from AfD, told Izvestia. "It is well known that money from Germany and other countries ends up in the pockets of corrupt Ukrainian politicians. It is also known that weapons intended for Ukraine have surfaced in Serbia and other countries. As soon as the AfD enters the new Bundestag with 25% support or more, investigative committees will surely be established that will deal with these issues," Kotre announced.
In Greece, the Greek Solution parliamentary faction made a similar demand to audit weapons supplies to Kiev, its leader Kyriakos Velopoulos told Izvestia. "Any military supply to Ukraine is tantamount to high treason. <...> We will give every bullet sent to Zelensky a check, holding everyone who has harmed the Greek economy, Greece’s national interests or Greek defense capabilities responsible," he warned.
According to Yegor Sergeyev, a senior researcher at the Institute of International Studies of the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO), a German audit will be more dangerous for Kiev. Berlin is not only one of its main donors, but it can also influence broader EU decisions. Control over the use of financial aid could be somewhat tightened, he said. However, the financial flow from Europe will not stop completely as the EU needs Ukraine mostly as a political instrument, he argued.
European countries are increasingly discussing audits of the use of resources supplied to Kiev even as this idea has not materialized anywhere yet. This would require political changes that may happen very soon, with a parliamentary election expected in Greece next year as France will elect a new president, while the German parliament could possibly be dissolved ahead of time.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: India, Pakistan balancing on the brink of war
There is a dangerous tension in relations between India and Pakistan. Two people were killed near the Bedian strategic border sector. India blamed the incident on Pakistani saboteurs or Islamist terrorists, while Pakistan claimed that locals who had lost their way there were to blame. The incident took place in an area disputed by the two countries over the use of the Indus River. However, there is no information on whether the October 2 shooting was somehow related to that dispute.
Islamabad and New Delhi again accused each other of an armed provocation as envoys were summoned to the two countries’ foreign ministries. Pakistan claimed that Indian border guards had opened fire on three unarmed Pakistani civilians, killing two of them and injuring one. India rejected these accusations as biased and groundless. The Indian Foreign Ministry told the Pakistani charge d’affaires that the Pakistani side had continued to send terrorists and drug traffickers across the border.
On the face of it, India has an advantage over its long-time opponent: it has a larger Army, and Pakistan is embroiled in a conflict with Afghanistan. The actual situation is more complicated. India, which has traditionally pursued the policy of non-alignment, has no close military allies. True, it is a member of QUAD, a US-led alliance with Japan and Australia, but the United States has shown no desire to get involved in the dispute between India and Pakistan.
Meanwhile, Pakistan, for one, has a close military partner, if not a true ally - China, formally a neutral party. However, Beijing has actually provided military assistance to Pakistan, Alexander Lukin, academic director of the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia at the Russian Academy of Science, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. "As usual, China says disputes should be resolved in line with UN decisions. And it actually supports Pakistan which has signed a strategic partnership with China. The two countries maintain broad contacts, including military ones. China has established an `economic corridor’ toward the Indian Ocean on Pakistani soil. This corridor runs through a Pakistani-controlled area of Kashmir. However, India considers the whole of Kashmir to be its part. Consequently, the territorial conflict is in effect trilateral, given China controls an area in Kashmir under the 1963 agreement with Pakistan regarding border demarcation. Since India regards all of Kashmir as its own land, it does not recognize this agreement between Pakistan and China. In short, while China is formally neutral, in reality, it sides with Pakistan," Lukin concluded.
Vedomosti: Russian coal prices at Baltic ports reach three-year high
In September, export prices of Russian coal at Baltic ports rose to a more than three-year high, according to data from PBS Index, seen by Vedomosti. On September 25, Free-on-Board (FOB) prices of thermal coal with a calorific value of 6,000 kcal/kg at Baltic ports climbed to $89/metric ton. The last time a higher price was recorded was in April 2023. The prices increased by 13% last month, or were up 31% from January.
The rise in export prices is driven by the increased cost of coal on the global market, high demand in Turkey, and rising dry-bulk freight rates resulting from the reorientation of shipments from terminals in the country's south to Baltic ports, a PBS Index representative explained to Vedomosti.
Active purchases by China and the risk of reduced exports from Indonesia are also driving up the export price of Russian coal, said Yegor Vershinin, an analyst at the Finam financial group. Another factor behind the rise is the escalating political crisis in the Middle East, which has affected global energy prices, Boris Krasnozhenov, Head of Investment and Sector Analysis at Alfa-Bank, added.
Rising gas prices globally will help sustain demand for coal at least until the end of this year, therefore Russian fuel export prices will continue to increase, Alexander Kotov, a partner in consulting at NEFT Research, argued. According to him, thermal coal prices at Baltic ports will rise to $100/metric ton, given favorable market conditions.

Omega Has New Bond Watches Even if There Isn’t a New James Bond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

It's been five years since James Bond was on the silver screen in No Time to Die. For fans of the secret agent, the wait has been arduous, made even harder by the fact that Amazon, which now owns the franchise, still hasn't chosen a successor to Daniel Craig, let alone started filming Bond's resurrection.
But if it's seemed like a long haul for fans, just think how it has felt for Omega, which counts on a steady stream of Bond action to regularly inject lots of lovely cash into the company via watch releases linked directly to the films. Omega's last official Bond film tie-in watch was the titanium No Time to Die Seamaster prematurely launched back in 2019, ahead of the film’s then Covid-delayed release in 2021.
Considering that Swatch Group’s net profit collapsed by almost 90 percent to $32 million in 2025 (though, thankfully, things look rosier so far this year), we shouldn't be surprised that Omega isn't bothering to wait for Jeff Bezos to put his white cat down and proceed with world domination. As there's no new Bond or Bond film to work with, Omega has decided to launch 007-themed watches anyway—not just one, but an entire collection totaling six Seamaster Divers.
You can hardly blame the brand. When Omega first strapped a Seamaster to Pierce Brosnan's wrist in 1995's GoldenEye, it reportedly saw a 20-fold sales increase. In 2012, Omega's then-president Stephen Urquhart even told Variety that Omega’s sales “look like a stock market chart” that peaks during promotion of Bond films, then sinks afterward. “The films have had a very marked influence on sales,” Urquhart conceded.
The new “James Bond and Spectre” collection is themed around good and evil, with three watches bearing the “007” symbol of James Bond, and three the octopus-like motif of Spectre, the fictional global terrorist organization in the series.
The six Seamaster Diver 300M watches share the same movement. However, the two non-limited stainless-steel editions are the core pieces, available individually at $8,600 each—one with a blue aluminum dial dedicated to James Bond, and the other black for dastardly Spectre fans. Both come on a brushed mesh bracelet.
The James Bond edition has a grade 5 titanium bezel, while the Spectre edition boasts a black ceramic bezel ring to match the dial's blackened grained finish.
The remaining four Seamasters are split across two limited-edition numbered sets—one dedicated to Bond, the other to Spectre—capped at 77 boxes each. At a cool $89,800 per pair (Omega won't sell them individually), you get one stainless-steel model on a brushed mesh bracelet, and a second in platinum-gold on leather.
Each set comes in a presentation box with an additional NATO strap, strap-changing tool, cuff links, a cord bracelet, a loupe, a leather travel pouch and card holder, and papers. In the James Bond set, the strap keepers are engraved with 007; in the Spectre set, the strap keepers carry the Spectre emblem.
This collection is not the first time Omega has sought to leverage its Bond connection without a film peg. Back in May of this year, Omega unveiled the Seamaster Diver 300M Chronograph “007 First Light,” a new 44-mm chrono tied to 007 First Light, a James Bond game developed by the same studio responsible for the Hitman franchise. Originally designed as an in-game gadget, Omega turned it into a production model.
Back in 2012, there was the Seamaster James Bond 007 50th Anniversary watch with a red number 50 on the bezel. In 2019, there was an On Her Majesty's Secret Service edition Seamaster to mark 50 years of the 1969 film, limited to 7,007 pieces. Then, in 2022, Omega released a Seamaster to coincide with 60 years of Bond movies.

====================================================================================================

A life in episodes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
34 minute listen
When I was about 15, alone in the flat one afternoon, I sneaked into my mother’s writing desk and found a small pocket calendar from 1946 pushed to the back of a drawer. I had grown up with my mother and her parents, not knowing who my biological father was, or how I had come about; the question was simply never asked. I turned, with a kind of dread, to the entries from nine months before I was born. In mid-March there was an ordinary note – ‘Party at the Academic Association’; she was training as a laboratory technician in Lund and liked the students’ company – and on the following day, in her hand, five words: ‘God, what have I done!’ I still remember the shock of standing there with the diary, half-guilty for trespassing on her private papers, and saying aloud, over and over: ‘That’s me – that’s me. What have you done? I’m a mistake.’
For half a century, the scene stayed as it was: fixed, private, finished. Then, about a decade ago, I posted it – to several hundred old acquaintances and strangers – on Facebook. I was in doubt; I felt faint embarrassment at making it public, but this was itself part of what I wanted to examine. Why was it shameful? What did the shame tell me about myself? And would saying it out loud, to strangers, do anything to drain the memory of its sting? The answers came from my readers, and one of them showed me something I could not have seen on my own.
Betty, a friend from the years we were postdocs together at Stanford, had heard me tell the story in person long ago, and she said the written version was missing something: my voice, the intonation and the look on my face. What look, I asked – had I played it for sympathy, had I ironised it? ‘Absolutely flat,’ she wrote. ‘No affect. A Max von Sydow deadpan. But yes, you ironised.’ I had not known that about myself: that I’d delivered the central wound of my origins with no expression at all and turned it into a dry joke.
That discovery, prompted by a reader’s response, was one of the first signs that writing one’s life in public could change how memory and narrative take shape. Writing an autobiography or memoir was traditionally a solitary undertaking. Authors worked through papers, memories and past events largely on their own, occasionally consulting family, friends or colleagues. Only after years of private work would the manuscript reach the public. Readers encountered the finished account, with little sense of the revisions, doubts and shifts in understanding that had shaped it.
Social media has fundamentally disrupted these conditions. By publishing sequential episodes of my life every few days, however, I have turned my autobiographical drafts into a continuing dialogue with my readers. Their real-time responses have made me reconsider how I understand my professional achievements, my personal relationships and myself. The question that drives it is not what happens when you put a memoir on Facebook, but a quieter one: what happens to self-image when it is formed in public?
As a professional historian of science, I have always been fascinated by biographies, autobiographies and memoirs – viewing them not merely as raw material for writing history, or even microhistories, but as distinct accounts of the past in their own right. Yet now, writing my life story piece by piece in public, I’ve begun to question whether a life can ever be framed, genuinely, as a coherent narrative – and whether that uncertainty might be a good thing.
I chose to focus on the personal context, developing an approach I termed existential scientific biography
I first tried my hand at full-scale life-writing in 1986, shortly after I finished my first book, on the history of Swedish ecology. Almost accidentally, I met with Niels Kaj Jerne, the Danish immunologist who had been awarded the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine just two years earlier. ‘I have saved some papers,’ he casually remarked as we sat talking over a glass of wine in the kitchen of his large villa in southern France. We went up to the spacious attic room, where he parted the shutters and gestured towards the ancient Roman aqueduct, the Pont du Gard. Yet, I had no interest in antiquity; my attention was entirely arrested by the hundreds of grocery bags from the local supermarché lined up across the stone floor. They were stuffed to the brim with intimate letters, private diaries, raw laboratory protocols, rough article drafts, and decades of correspondence with colleagues around the world. He had kept virtually every scrap of paper that had passed through his hands from his youth onwards.
I can still vividly recall the thrill of exploring this unique archive. That afternoon set in motion a seven-year cooperation. At the outset, we discussed the possibility of weaving biography and autobiography together; we toyed with the idea of a book in a parallel format, with my biographical text on the left-hand pages and his personal recollections on the right – auto/biography as interlocution.
The vision of a side-by-side account soon faded, however, because Jerne – who was then in his mid-70s – lacked the stamina to draft his own memoir. Instead, through hundreds of hours of conversation, I managed to elicit a wealth of memory fragments that continuously enriched, and occasionally disrupted, my developing account of him.
Jerne’s unusual candour about his personal and intimate life led me, early on, to view his private and scientific realms as an integrated whole. Most of my colleagues in the history of science viewed biography as an ancilla historiae – a handmaid to history – and thus focused on the social and cultural context of researchers and their work. In contrast, I chose to focus on the personal context, developing an approach I termed existential scientific biography. As a lifelong admirer of Søren Kierkegaard, Jerne enthusiastically embraced this framework.
Jerne died in 1994. By the time my book about him, Science as Autobiography, appeared in 2003, I had been appointed professor of the history of medicine at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark. There, I hoped to focus on medical biography and autobiography. But I quickly became absorbed in transforming the university’s medical history museum into Medical Museion. My life-writing went on standby for several years.
It was only upon retiring 10 years ago that I found myself free to resume my fascination with life-writing, now with the roles reversed: after decades spent writing the lives of others, I would become my own subject. The decision was sparked one afternoon while I was clearing out my office at the museum. I suddenly realised how much material I had accumulated without having given it a second thought while I lived my life ‘forwards’, as Kierkegaard once put it.
My almost 50-year-long academic paper trail was a cornucopia of manuscripts, bundles of correspondence, lecture notes, meeting minutes and calendars. These were not in shopping bags on a stone floor, but in magazine files and stacks on office shelves. Yet the emotional impulse was the same as in Jerne’s attic room in Languedoc 30 years earlier, and I was seized by an irresistible urge to reconstruct my own life. It was high time to begin understanding life ‘backwards’. I was about to turn 70 and I realised – much like Socrates – that the unexamined life is not worth living. What had I achieved? How had I used my talents, and what mistakes had I made? Could I go to my grave without answering such questions?
Who, besides myself, could be interested in the answers? Unlike Jerne, I was not a well-known figure – but that was, paradoxically, a virtue. For me, the examined life mattered as a souci de soi, an act of self-care. I thought of the writing exercise as a present-day, healthy ageing counterpart to the late-medieval and early modern ars moriendi – the art of dying well.
I spent three years reading and taking notes, year by year, page by page
And for others, I thought, my autobiography might be of interest as an experiment and an example: I wanted my readers to focus on questions of genre without being distracted by the historical (in)significance of the subject.
I packed the professional papers into removal boxes and set up an archive room in the basement at home, adding my private papers – school essays, diaries, personal letters and photographs – and also downloaded tens of thousands of work-related files and emails from the university server. I then spent three years reading and taking notes, year by year, page by page. Much was factual and emotionally neutral. Some old articles stirred a sense of pride; others were downright embarrassing. Angry letters from former intimate partners were particularly painful to revisit.
The emotional rollercoaster had its counterpart in the labour of memory. I would lie on the bed with the curtains drawn and earplugs in, to stifle sensory impressions, transporting myself in imagination to the many places I had lived, visited and worked, and the people I had met, trying to capture my immediate feelings of pleasure, joy, longing, unease, sorrow or fear as I recalled them. These deliberately summoned memories were then supplemented by the thousands of fragments that surfaced as I worked my way through the archive.
Archival documents and memories are the obvious source materials for anyone writing their autobiography – and gathering them had so far been exactly the solitary labour the genre is known for: the lone author behind drawn curtains, exhuming papers and interrogating memory. But few authors go further and seek out the people they have encountered throughout their lives. As an experienced oral historian – both for the history of ecology and, later, for the Jerne biography – I had already spent hundreds of hours interviewing others about their lives. So it was a natural step to turn the same method on myself, and supplement the archival records and my own memories by contacting people from my past – childhood and adolescent friends, schoolmates, teachers, former colleagues, and even former girlfriends – in order to flesh out and contrast my self-image with their perspectives. Some declined; others had little more than banalities to offer (‘you were tall and thin’), but many were surprisingly candid. Over the years, I have spoken with several hundred acquaintances and colleagues, and have renewed a couple of lost connections – though not romantic ones. These conversations were the first breach in the traditional solitude of the genre.
It was almost inevitable that my autobiography would be existential. I wanted to understand how my years as an academic researcher and teacher were interwoven with my life as a whole: upbringing and education, personality and aesthetic preferences, political and moral commitments, social and personal relationships. Inspired by the French philosopher Pierre Hadot, I conceived of my intellectual work as ‘a form of life’; I therefore regarded my archives, memories and conversations with friends, colleagues and acquaintances as ‘spiritual exercises’ that could help me towards greater self-awareness. In the words of Michel Foucault: as a ‘technology of the self’.
In addition to the existential approach, there was yet another aspect of life-writing that I brought with me from my experiences with Jerne, namely the cooperative construction of a life story. And what makes that construction possible, at scale and with readers, is the medium.
What is new in my project is the move onto social media. For me, this was no great leap: a decade before I began the memoir, I had begun blogging, and later Tweeting, extensively about the museum’s transformation. So, when I embarked on my autobiography, writing it on social media felt entirely natural.
I chose Facebook – it lends itself to longer texts, and it was where many of my old friends and colleagues were already. I posted several times a week: striking memories, interesting documents I had read, engaging conversations with old schoolmates, and, not least, spontaneous reflections on genre. I wrote in Swedish, my mother tongue, in my adopted Danish, and in English, as the mood took me. The posts formed a florilegium: a gathering of flowers in the original sense of the word. Gradually, I accumulated friends and followers, who began responding to the life I was putting before them. A dialogue was quietly getting under way.
After a few years of unstructured writing, I began to proceed systematically, still on Facebook, of course, but now in a feuilleton format – a serial form published in instalments. One might suppose that my inspiration was the serialised novel of the 19th century, but my actual model was not Dickens, Dostoevsky or Dumas; it was the dramaturgy of the television series: the division into seasons, the thematically coherent episodes, the tension between what is resolved and what is left open – and the cliffhanger.
I have provisionally divided the feuilleton into 16 seasons, from childhood to a final season about my autobiographical work and my second set of children. I do not write and publish them strictly chronologically, but in the order that satisfies my curiosity and nostalgic cravings. (Though once I have started a season, I see it through chronologically in its entirety before moving on to the next.)
I have no master plan telling me in advance which parts of my life will matter
An episode is a thematically coherent Facebook post of 300-500 words that takes a specific situation or experience as its point of departure. Working from a raw file of letters, diary entries and present-day reflections, I winnow the material and try to render what happened clearly enough for some meaning to emerge. Each episode must be able to stand alone, intelligible and engaging even for those who only occasionally follow my Facebook feed.
How many episodes a season holds emerges only in the writing, as readers’ comments spur new insights and new episodes. And above all, I have no master plan telling me in advance which parts of my life will matter.
An average episode takes roughly a day to formulate. I begin with a private draft written from my own authorial perspective, then copy-and-paste it to the Facebook text box and continue working, now with the reader’s gaze in mind. It is often only when writing the Facebook version that my inner reader discovers weaknesses that my inner author had overlooked – much as a writer catches in the proofs what they missed in the manuscript. Sometimes, the point of an episode only becomes clear just before I press ‘send’ at lunchtime and wait for the responses that come in throughout the afternoon and evening.
Working at this pace, I can publish three or four episodes a week; across the whole project, I have posted almost 2,000 times, serving up autobiography as soap opera.
The crucial difference between writing one’s autobiography in traditional book form and writing it as a feuilleton on social media is the possibility of entering into a dialogue with readers from the earliest stages. The profile currently has more than 1,000 followers from Sweden, Denmark, the UK and the US, and each post usually draws at least a handful of comments; occasionally as many as 200. Most responses come from a core group of around 100 regular participants; they come from every walk of life, and some of the sharpest remarks come from readers with no scholarly training at all. In recent years, however, this engagement has diminished, partly reflecting a general trend on social media, but perhaps also a waning interest in the project itself (another similarity with TV series).
The comments vary widely. Some followers recount similar experiences; others correct factual details or suggest literature for contextualising the episode; still others offer alternative interpretations. The best exchanges have the intensity and quality of a good seminar with a small group of students or colleagues. Like in-person seminars, I respond to every comment, often revising language that might give rise to misunderstanding.
No single exchange has been revolutionary; what matters is the accumulation – hundreds of small corrections and re-readings, settling slowly into a different sense of who I have been. I do not know what the next episode will look like, how the season will end, or what shape the whole will take.
The deepest corrections altered the account of the person I was. In the season about my years as a PhD student, I describe an event relating to a former partner, Lone. We had lived together in Copenhagen in the mid-1970s, but the relationship was troubled, as I remember it, because of her mood swings, which I attributed to her diabetes. I left her for someone else and then stopped thinking about her almost entirely. Years afterward, she suddenly wrote to me, saying she had been evicted from her flat and asked for help. I did not answer. On my 40th birthday, she sent me an envelope lined with red silk paper, empty inside. I did not answer that either. It was only when I began the memoir decades later that I searched for her in the Danish public registry and discovered she had died in her early 40s, alone as far as I could tell. I then remembered I had once promised her I would be there when she died and plant daisies on her grave, and felt guilty about not having fulfilled my pledge.
What the post did not give me, the readers did in their comments. An old neighbour, Eva, who had known Lone, supplied a fuller portrait than I had been able to manage on my own; I had been writing, I admitted to her in the comments, ‘under the influence of my memory of the bad aspects of the relationship’. Another reader, Barbro, caught me in a single line: people would describe her own personality much as I had described Lone’s, she wrote – and she had never had diabetes. I had inadvertently conflated Lone’s difficult personality with her chronic illness in a way that exonerated my decision to leave her. A third reader, Kristina, asked what I thought the empty envelope had meant. I tried to deflect: I had been blank then and was blank now. She refused the deflection – she had not asked what I thought back then, she had asked what I think now. When I still had no answer, she offered one: a beautiful container with nothing inside, a friendship promised for a lifetime that turned out to be air. The process was forcing the container open, allowing a small, late act of atonement when another reader, Carolina, suggested I plant the daisies anywhere beautiful, since I had no grave to find. But I have still not planted them.
I had to defend – or reconsider – my gaze in real time, under the scrutiny of people I respect
Readers are no gentler with my professional life than with my private one. Now and then, they puncture the version of myself I have just offered. In one post, I recounted an episode from the final year of my PhD studies, when I attended the Swedish annual meeting for historians of science. The morning’s keynote, by the most powerful professor in the field just back from a sabbatical at Berkeley, had struck me as a long and self-satisfied catalogue of the distinguished colleagues he had met and the dinners he had attended. My irritation grew with the square of the elapsed minutes. When the floor opened, I put up my hand and asked, with deliberate weight on the adjective and no softening preamble, whether he had got any intellectual benefit from his trip as well. There was a silence, then scattered tittering. The chairman immediately declared coffee break, and I felt like a king for a few minutes amid the other doctoral students’ admiration (‘How did you dare?’), until the keynote speaker’s own student looked at me with a dry smile and said: ‘There you’ve evidently destroyed your career in Swedish history of science.’ He was right; I took my future ambitions to Denmark.
I posted this as a cautionary anecdote, but some of my readers declined to let it stay one. One refused the heroic frame: I was not brave, Mats said, but rather ‘naive and insensitive’; I could have asked the same legitimate question in a way that sought an answer rather than an audience. I conceded: ‘Yes, it was provocative and foolhardy.’ An American colleague, Richard, turned the story over and read its underside – call it instead ‘How I began my career in Denmark’ – and I had to agree that leaving the Swedish history-of-science milieu was my intellectual salvation. My Danish colleague Jes moved the lens onto vanity itself: gracious answers existed that would have honoured the question without diminishing the questioner, but they require the one quality rarest in academic life, ‘the absence of a dominating vanity’ – and then he caught his own pretension in the act of saying so.
Between them, the three readers dislodged the small monument I had built to my own courage and showed me the vanity inside it. The thread also made me admit that this was not a single youthful lapse but a pattern: I had done the same to a leading European scholar a few years later.
Sometimes, the dialogue puts the act of telling itself on trial. I once posted a memory from a conference in the 1980s, dominated in my recollection by a young female doctoral student wearing a Mickey Mouse T-shirt that prominently accentuated her breasts – an image that, at the time, had prompted hushed, stereotypical jokes among the male attendees about ‘Mickey’s ears’. I described it as a moment in which she deliberately played on her gender.
The reaction from my Facebook readers was swift and polarised. A younger colleague attacked the post as sordid, accusing me of reproducing today the same objectifying male gaze I claimed merely to be reporting from the past. Another woman read the student’s choice as a breaching experiment – a conscious subversion of the grey academic dress code. A third defended my right to report the past as I remembered it, noting the ‘Lutheran asceticism’ often demanded of female academics, and offered her own counter-anecdote about a male presenter whose thin linen trousers had distracted an entire audience.
The dialogue did not correct my memory, but it forced me into an uncomfortable ethical confrontation with my own role as narrator. Was I documenting the past, or was I still looking through that same 1980s lens? The ethical practice lies in exactly this friction: the feuilleton format made it impossible to hide behind polished, retrospective wisdom. I had to defend – or reconsider – my gaze in real time, under the scrutiny of people I respect.
Lessons like these keep me drawn to the feuilleton format. My readers have helped to make these years of autobiographical writing the most absorbing, enjoyable and meaningful of my long academic life. To paraphrase Socrates again: the examined life, in dialogue with others, is truly worth living.
I recently scored very highly on the ‘openness’ scale in a Big Five personality test, which puts a psychological gloss on the entire project. The feuilleton format showed my preference for living with open questions and unresolved interpretations, rather than striving towards a finished account of my life.
My openness also had an intellectual precedent in my training as a historian of science. There, I had learned to distinguish between ‘ready-made science’ and ‘science in the making’, as Bruno Latour had put it. The lesson was not to build historical writing on published articles and textbooks alone, but to regard research as a provisional process through which facts are slowly assembled and stabilised.
I think of my autobiographical writing on social media as something similar. It is, in the most literal sense, an autobiography in the making.
Even so, when I began this project, I took it for granted that it would arrive somewhere – that the long labour of extracting from archives, summoning memories, and talking to others would eventually compose itself into a coherent narrative of my life.
This is a common conception of autobiography as a genre. The French autobiography scholar Philippe Lejeune holds that it is a retrospective prose narrative; within identity research, life stories are regarded as a fundamental form of self-understanding – the view being that we all live in and through stories about ourselves, and that a good life means shaping a unified life story. Narrativity is seen as a moral ideal: the good, examined life is, by definition, a narrated life.
Each episode must be readable on its own; the reader need not know everything that has preceded it
But there are dissenting voices. The British philosopher Galen Strawson distinguishes between those who experience themselves diachronically, as a single self unfolding through time, and those who understand themselves episodically. Such people experience their lives as a sequence of fragments rather than as a coherent whole, and yet can be fully reflective and morally serious. Strawson’s chief witness is Michel de Montaigne – perhaps the greatest autobiographer in world literature – who moves freely between fragments, paradoxes and unfinished reflections in an open-ended exploration that never resolves into a story.
I learned how stubborn the narrative assumption can be when I tried to enlist my readers on Strawson’s side. Scarcely a year into the project, I posted a link to his seminal article ‘Against Narrativity’ (2004), expecting nods of agreement. Instead, I got a quarrel that ran late into the night. One of my sharpest readers, Christian, objected that we are not one story but many small, situational ones. I held my ground: I knew my own past as a heap of fragments, not as a plotted tale. Only afterwards did I see what the argument had really been about. Christian was reading continuity and coherence into my life even as he denied doing any such thing.
Looking back at my own feuilleton, I realise I am closer to Strawson’s episodic self-understanding than to the retrospective narrative of classical autobiography. I did not begin with the vision of telling a story about myself: I began with the basement archive, the memory fragments and the conversations with friends. I bring out letters, diary entries, remembered images and the voices of others, trying to do justice to a situation, a mood, a conflict, a crossroads. Each episode must be readable on its own; the reader need not know everything that has preceded it, nor guess what is to come. If there is a Bildungsreise, it is full of detours, interruptions, dead-ends and retreats. If there is a moral, it is local and provisional – not a step in an overarching arc of personal development.
The form itself works against tidying. Because I publish short, self-contained episodes in rapid succession, it is difficult to reshape what I have written into a narrative without readers noticing; any attempt to harmonise the whole after the fact runs up against episodes already published. The open feuilleton thus becomes a safeguard against the kind of retrospective and self-flattering narrativity that Strawson warns against.
I once caught myself doing the very thing the open feuilleton is supposed to protect against – and the form saved me from myself. Something I had carried as private shame for most of my academic life was a compulsion to raise my hand at conferences and seminars. After one such meeting in 1979, I had written in my diary that, as usual, I could not restrain myself, giving in to a ‘pathological drive’ to dominate the room with my questions: ‘I am conditioned to the moment of questioning a speaker. I cannot keep my mouth shut. My heart pounds; I feel an irresistible compulsion … What is this inner need to show myself off in company?’ The pattern was unmistakable: wherever I sat – a hundred people in the room, time for only two questions – I had to ask one of them; I could count on my fingers the few occasions I managed simply to listen. And immediately afterwards, always, the shame: not at the behaviour, which was harmless enough, but at being unable to govern the impulse. I posted this and asked whether others knew the feeling. They did, and the thread ran long and serious into the afternoon, 90 comments in all.
What I had not noticed was that, in copying out the diary entry for the post, I had reduced five words to an ellipsis. That evening I went back to the original to see what the ellipsis had swallowed. The five elided words were: ‘compare Harry Belafonte on Arholma’. I knew at once what they meant. The summer I was 11, the only child in a roomful of adults at a guesthouse on the island of Arholma, a summer resort north of Stockholm, I had been coaxed into singing and had chosen Belafonte’s ‘Banana Boat Song’. A few shaky verses in, my great-uncle said, loudly, to the room: ‘Can’t someone shut that child up?’ The line had landed like a whiplash and lodged there.
The genuinely unsettling discovery was not the buried memory itself, but what I had done with it. I had, in fact, already written an episode connecting that humiliation, explicitly, to the seminar compulsion – and when I sat down to write about the compulsion the second time, I had forgotten the connection completely and even pruned the clue out of my own quotation. I posted the recovery the next day as what it plainly was: a specimen of forgetting, almost in a Freudian sense – that one can write about a painful thing in a detached, factual way and still keep mislaying it, precisely because it is too uncomfortable to hold. The form had caught me, in public and across two days, in the act of reading my own life badly – and only the second reading, prompted by the readers and by going back to the source, set it right.
My own misreading is only part of what the feuilleton reveals. The comment threads are full of readers trying to connect the dots on my behalf – tracing long arcs and identifying turning points. This impulse to discern patterns arises after the episodes are published, in the encounter between the stream of fragments and readers inclined to see them as links in a unified life narrative. In that sense, the feuilleton functions as a laboratory for watching how narrativity emerges in reception rather than in the act of writing itself. I repeatedly discover that my critics read more continuity, more purpose and more personal development into the material than I did myself when writing it – Christian, in our quarrel, was only the earliest and bluntest case.
I do not see this as a pessimistic conclusion, but as a liberating one. Strawson’s critique helps me calibrate my ambitions: to aim for fidelity to the fragments rather than the false comfort of a whole. If one thinks – as many narrativists do – that the essential task is to shape a unified self-narrative, the temptation is always there to smooth over ruptures, play down contradictions, and tidy away whatever doesn’t fit. The drive for narrative risks crowding out the unpredictable, the messy and the recalcitrant that make up much of our lived experience.
What I resist is not coherence but the imperative to impose it
The process matters far more to me than the result; even so, I have not ruled out publishing the final text as a book. But that intention sits uneasily with everything I have just argued: to edit the stream of episodes into a single volume risks imposing a coherence that was never there. Perhaps a narrative will emerge in the editing; perhaps it will not.
Autobiography, as I now practise it, is a series of soundings of how I relate to episodes from my life in light of today’s feelings, knowledge and relationships. What I resist is not coherence but the imperative to impose it.
This is also why I no longer regard autobiography as a final report on a life, in which questions such as ‘What have I achieved?’ or ‘What mistakes did I make?’ find definitive answers. The questions I now ask myself are different: how do I bear the consequences of what I have done? Which ties from the past do I wish to affirm, which must I accept, and which can, and should, I try to dissolve? The feuilleton has become a way of living with my past: testing my reactions against those of others, reconsidering my judgments, and trying out different descriptions of the same event.
When I return to Kierkegaard and Socrates, I do so with scepticism towards the self-image I held when I began packing my papers into removal boxes. To live forwards and understand it backwards need not mean capturing my life in a single narrative stream. It may be that I never finish understanding but continue to try – episode by episode.
Socrates’ reminder that the unexamined life is not worth living is too easily heard as a demand that the examined life be a well-told one. I would put it differently today: the too neatly narrated life risks becoming a poorly read one.

Democrats in Key Senate Races Embrace 'Capitalist' Label
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

In the past, Democrats rarely felt the need to explain their position on capitalism. They could campaign on fixing a rigged economy, reducing corporate power, or raising taxes on the rich without feeling compelled to affirm their belief in the economic system itself.
This election cycle is different. 
“I am a capitalist,” James Talarico, a Texas Democrat, told TIME last month, after complaining that Republicans were trying to paint him as a socialist in his bid for Senate against Ken Paxton.
“I’m not a socialist,” Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, his fellow Senate candidate in Michigan told TIME in May, who then praised the efficiency of capitalism to “allocate resources.”
The two Democrats are among the most prominent examples of candidates in tight races making their support of capitalism crystal clear amid the growing visibility of the Democratic Socialists of America and a string of victories by candidates on the party’s left. Republicans in races across the country—and at the White House—have pointed to those trends as they increasingly embrace “socialist” and “communist” as catch-all attacks against all Democrats.
The defensive pose from Democrats is a broader trend than just a few Senate races: Sixty Democrats, including 10 sitting members of Congress, signed a pledge this summer from the newly formed Promise to America declaring, “We are capitalist, not socialist.” The collective was organized by centrist Democratic Reps. Tom Suozzi of New York and Adam Gray of California, the only two Democrats in 2024 to flip congressional districts won by President Donald Trump. “We believe in a growing, fair, and competitive economy that rewards hard work, innovation, entrepreneurship, and ownership,” their pledge reads.
But not every Democrat facing the socialist label has gone so far as to embrace capitalism. In Maine, Troy Jackson, a former state Senator with ties to Bernie Sanders, replaced Graham Platner as the party’s Senate nominee in July with the support of the DSA. When asked by TIME whether Jackson views himself as a capitalist, Jackson’s campaign declined to answer but pointed to his past comments on socialism.
“I see myself as a Mainer and a working-class person,” he told NBC News in July when asked if he’s a socialist. “You know, we have socialism in the state with public schools, with plowing the roads, tiring the roads … I don’t see myself as anything but a guy that wants to make good change for people I care about.”
Asked on Morning Joe on July 28 about whether he supported the DSA’s policies, Jackson said he didn’t. What he did support, he said, was “a government that works for everyday people, small business owners, workers” and others who depend on the government to work for them.
Jackson's approach illustrates the broader ambiguity Republicans are exploiting. A Democrat can campaign against concentrated wealth, corporate influence and economic inequality without necessarily rejecting capitalism, just as a Democrat can support universal health care or stronger labor protections without identifying as a socialist.
Vance wields ‘socialist’ charge in Florida
Vice President J.D. Vance sharpened the Republican attack in Florida last week, accusing Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon of embracing socialism and not belonging in the country because of those views. The remarks came as Vance campaigned alongside Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, who is fighting to keep the seat she was appointed to when Marco Rubio became Secretary of State, and offered a blunt version of the argument Republicans have been making against Democrats around the country.
“Ladies and gentlemen, when Angie Nixon calls herself a socialist, I think the right response is to say: ‘Then get the hell out of here. You don’t belong in America if those are your views,’” Vance said.
Nixon presents a more complicated case than many of the Democrats facing the socialist label. The Florida state representative has been an unabashed progressive throughout her decade in state politics and joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June. But the DSA did not endorse her Senate campaign, and Nixon has said she does not agree with all of the group's positions. She has also resisted the idea that her affiliation with the organization determines her political identity.
“I’m a capitalist who believes that we need some strong regulations,” Nixon said on NBC's Meet the Press in August. She has separately described herself as a social democrat who believes in strong safety nets. Republicans have nonetheless made the DSA connection central to their case against her, and Moody has described the race as a choice between “freedom or socialism.”
For Nixon, as for El-Sayed and Talarico, the question is therefore becoming part of the larger campaign conversation about what kind of economic politics Democrats are offering. But Nixon’s case also shows why the labels can be difficult to apply cleanly: she has joined an organization that calls itself socialist and shares some of its policy goals, but describes herself as a capitalist and rejects some of its positions.
Talarico rejects ‘crony capitalism’
Talarico has perhaps taken the most expansive approach to the question. In an interview with TIME in September, the Democratic Senate nominee rejected the socialist label and offered his own definition of capitalism, one rooted in competition, private enterprise, and a stronger middle class.
“I think Democrats should reclaim the principles of capitalism, 'cause that's not what we have right now,” Talarico said. “We don't have capitalism. We have crony capitalism, where the people who succeed in this economy are those who can afford to pay for politicians, those who can pay for access and control.
Republicans have accused Talarico of backing a “Democrat Socialist agenda” and even saying that his policies would amount to “destroying capitalism.” The attacks are unfolding in a race that Democrats view as one of their most significant opportunities to compete in Texas in a generation.
“Dr. King once said that we have socialism for the rich, and rugged individualism for the rest of us,” Talarico told TIME. “If we're going to get back to real capitalism, it means that all of us are going to get compensated for our labor, for our work, for the wealth that we create.”
In Michigan, where recent polls show El-Sayed leading Republican Rep. Mike Rogers for an open Senate seat, the National Republican Senatorial Committee has called El-Sayed a “radical socialist.”
Much like Jackson in Maine and Nixon in Florida, El-Sayed supports Medicare For All and believes corporate power needs to be curbed. But El-Sayed says those positions do not require a broader ideological commitment to socialism.
“I actually think that at the small and local scale, capitalism is a great way to allocate resources, as long as everybody has access to it,” El-Sayed told TIME.
—With reporting by Philip Elliott
