The U.S. deported a former political prisoner to Nicaragua. He's now in prison again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Jeffrey Jarquín, a former Nicaraguan political prisoner who said he was tortured for opposing President Daniel Ortega, was jailed at Managua’s Modelo prison immediately after the U.S. deported him.
- His case underscores growing concern that the Trump administration is deporting Nicaraguans to a country where they face persecution, despite international protections against forced returns.
- U.S. deportations to Nicaragua more than doubled in the first seven months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, according to Human Rights Watch.
A former political prisoner who said he was tortured for leading protests against Nicaragua’s authoritarian government was arrested and jailed immediately after he was deported there from the United States last week, according to relatives and human rights advocates.
Jeffrey Jarquín, 35, was taken directly from the deportation flight to Nicaragua’s notorious Modelo prison, where he had been held previously for participating in pro-democracy marches that were violently repressed by President Daniel Ortega.
Jarquín was among thousands of Nicaraguans who took to the streets in 2018 to demand Ortega’s resignation and free elections. He helped occupy two public universities, and later took refugee inside a small Catholic church as it came under fire from pro-government militia forces — an incident that became emblematic of the country’s embattled protest movement.
More than 25,000 people have been expelled to ‘third countries’ under Trump, including to dangerous and conflict-ridden nations such as the Central Africa Republic.
Jarquín was imprisoned for nine months, and later told journalists and human rights investigators that guards burned his genitals with cigarette butts. He was released in 2019, spent a short period in Costa Rica and later sought political asylum in the United States.
The Trump administration has levied sanctions on Ortega and his family members and has repeatedly criticized his government, with Juan Pablo Segura, deputy assistant secretary of State for Western Hemisphere affairs, describing it recently as a “brutal dictatorship that is stealing, lying and murdering.”
Yet journalists, human rights advocates and political dissidents who were persecuted for promoting democracy in Nicaragua are increasingly being targeted for deportation as the Trump administration narrows access to asylum and expands the pool of migrants eligible for removal.
U.S. immigration agents have recently begun arresting members of a high-profile group of Nicaraguan political prisoners who were freed in a 2023 State Department deal, flown to the U.S. and granted temporary humanitarian parole and the chance to apply for asylum.
The U.S. has sent some Nicaraguan migrants as far away as Africa under a Trump administration program that deports asylum seekers and others to “third countries” where they have no ties.
Journalists, human rights advocates and dissidents who were persecuted in Nicaragua and sought safety in the U.S. are increasingly being targeted for deportation.
But other Nicaraguans are being sent home, despite warnings from human rights advocates that such deportations may violate the international ban on “refoulement” — returning someone to a country where they face persecution or torture.
“The United States sent him to the very prisons where he had already been tortured,” said Muriel Sáenz, an activist who represented Jarquín during an immigration bond hearing.
Jarquín, she said, is a victim of political persecution who has been sent “back into the hands of his tormentors.”
Jarquín was arrested in Miami in February after being accused of assault. A judge dismissed the case, but while Jarquín was detained, immigration agents initiated deportation proceedings against him. An immigration judge denied him asylum, according to his advocates.
They said Jarquín agreed to be deported but asked to be sent to a third country. Instead he was put on a plane to Managua last week.
U.S. deportations to Nicaragua have risen sharply under Trump. An analysis of government data by Human Rights Watch found that the U.S. deported more than 6,300 Nicaraguans between January and July of this year, compared with 3,323 during the same period in 2025.
In Miami’s Nicaraguan community, Jarquín was known as a vocal opponent of the Sandinista regime, often carrying a megaphone to protests. He posted photos on social media of himself alongside U.S. Republican leaders who have also criticized Ortega, including U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
At 81, Ortega is the longest-serving leader in the Americas. He rules the country with his co-president and wife, Rosario Murillo.
The pair, former revolutionaries who decades ago helped overthrow a brutal right-wing dictatorship, have tightened their grip on power in recent years, closing media outlets and nongovernmental organizations and jailing or expelling virtually all of their political opponents. Nicaragua’s government did not respond to inquiries about the Jarquín case.
His friends and family members say they don’t know when they will see him again.
“His life is in danger back in Nicaragua,” said Ronmell López, a friend. “We demand that the dictatorship ... respect his life and safety.”
“For Nicaraguan deportees, the risk of persecution is real,” said Juan Pappier, deputy director of the Americas division at Human Rights Watch. “The United States government knows Nicaragua is one of the most authoritarian governments in the hemisphere and should take robust steps to ensure nobody is sent back to torture or abuse.”
Linthicum reported from Mexico City. López reported from Jacksonville, Fla.

Trump calls it a war, then a 'military conflict.' Why the Iran fighting keeps changing names
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

When is war not ‘war’? In Iran, according to the U.S.
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Over seven months of conflict with Iran, Trump administration officials try to avoid calling the hostilities a ‘war.’
- Like previous administrations, both Democratic and Republican, the White House aims to avoid having Congress invoke the War Powers Resolution.
- Only Congress can declare war, so presidents have avoided the word to avoid securing congressional approval for military actions.
WASHINGTON — Late September in the Oval Office, President Trump declared, “Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. We’re gonna win that war very soon.”
It wasn’t the first time he’s described the hostilities as “war.”
On Feb. 28, the day U.S. and Israeli began bombarding Iran, he warned that “the lives of courageous American heroes may be lost, and we may have casualties. That often happens in war, but we’re doing this not for now. We’re doing this for the future, and it is a noble mission.”
But throughout seven months of back-and-forth strikes with Iran, Trump administration officials, and sometimes Trump himself, have performed verbal acrobatics to avoid the “W” word.
Senior administration officials loosely tossed around “war” during the first stages of conflict, but with polls showing the war in unpopular and congressional support waning, “war” and even “Operation Epic Fury” have become taboo among members of the Trump administration.
Trump has called attacks on Iran a “military operation,” “military decimation,” “excursion” and “skirmish.”
At a White House press briefing last month, Vice President JD Vance attempted to clear the air when a reporter asked about a potential end to what she called a “war in Iran.”
“I wouldn’t call it a war right now,” Vance said. “Major combat operations lasted for about six weeks.”
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth tread carefully in front of the Senate Appropriations Committee in July, repeatedly referring to a “conflict” in Iran that needed additional funding to continue.
On May 5, during the first of two delicate ceasefires with Iran, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced an end to the objectives laid out in Operation Epic Fury and the beginning of “Project Freedom” — an effort to escort merchant ships through the Strait of Hormuz.
In April, Trump announced the blockade of Iranian ports. When asked about whether the blockade constituted an act of war, Rubio replied, “That’s not an act of war, that’s a defensive measure. It’s a counter to what they have decided to do.”
Senior Trump officials have maintained that the conflict can no longer be viewed as war because the intensity of strikes between the two countries has been reduced.
The “end” of Operation Epic Fury, the name Trump used when he announced hostilities on Feb. 28, was declared on May 5 — 60 days after the fighting began.
The timing was no coincidence. Under the War Powers Resolution of 1973, a president must cease all hostilities abroad after 60 days if there is no congressional declaration of war.
Legal and political considerations
Under the Constitution, only Congress declares war, but past presidents have routinely circumvented this rule by exercising their authority to direct the military and initiate strikes on targeted nations.
Nearly every modern president, from Dwight D. Eisenhower to Trump, has used this justification to undertake military action without the declaratory approval of Congress.
Congress can also choose to approve an Authorization for Use of Military Force, which grants the president legal authority to conduct military operations overseas.
Unless Congress sets a time limit on the authorization, authority to use the legal justification to launch military strikes can theoretically span multiple administrations.
Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), a former constitutional law professor at American University, said that presidents of both parties have avoided the term “war” when attempting to evade congressional approval of hostile action abroad.
“Trump has followed some of his predecessors in playing word games with the war power,” Raskin said. “What makes his case so extreme is that he proudly described it as a war and depicted it in glorified military terms.”
In March, seven days into the fighting, Trump said, “The war itself is going unbelievably. It’s as good as it can be.”
Congress has not officially declared war since World War II. The Vietnam War, the invasion of Afghanistan and both wars in Iraq were all approved by Congress under the umbrella of an Authorization for the Use of Military Force.
This year Congress has not approved such an authorization for the action with Iran. Fourteen Senate votes for a War Powers Resolution to curb Trump’s war efforts have failed in the chamber so far.
According to a CNN/SSRS poll last month, only 26% of Americans approve of the Trump administration’s handling of the Iran war.
Raskin said that he believes Trump’s terminology has shifted with the public mood, adding that he hasn’t heard any of his Republican colleagues “play along with the semantic games.”
“When things have turned south in the fortunes of this war, he has tried to pretend it’s something else,” Raskin said. “I think that has just further enraged the population.”
Past handling of congressional war power
The administration’s declaration that Operation Epic Fury had concluded echoed May 2003, when then-President George W. Bush stood in front of a banner reading “Mission Accomplished” aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, approximately six weeks after Operation Iraqi Freedom began.
“Major combat operations in Iraq have ended,” Bush said. “And now our coalition is engaged in securing and reconstructing that country.”
Despite the victory lap, combat operations in Iraq and across the Middle East continued through the aughts. The Iraq war wouldn’t officially end until 2011, with President Obama’s signature.
Obama himself relied heavily on the 2001 Authorization for the Use of Military Force — passed by Congress under Bush — in his military campaign against Islamic State during his presidency.
According to Council on Foreign Relations data, Obama launched 542 drone strikes and killed 3,797 people in Yemen, Pakistan and Somalia without renewed approval from Congress.
A case more analogous to Trump’s comes in former President Truman’s unilateral decision to deploy U.S. troops to Korea in 1950. The Truman administration forwent congressional approval altogether and used United Nations Security Council resolutions to justify the intervention against Communist forces in the north, according to a White House news release from the time.
There were many critics of this exercise of executive war powers, most notably, Ohio Republican Sen. Robert A. Taft, who argued that Truman had usurped congressional war powers.
However, that Congress still provided monetary support, granting Truman military funds and extensions to the draft to raise additional troops for the Korean War effort. According to historical Gallup polls, 78% of Americans in 1950 approved of U.S. intervention in Korea.
Trump sticking with ‘war’
While Vance and other administration officials continue to avoid “war,” it does slip out now and then. Trump has been, perhaps, the most discordant messenger of the administration when discussing Iran.
After referring to the “war” on social media and public interviews more than a dozen times, Trump backed Vance’s comments about the Iran war no longer being active as he spoke to reporters in the Oval Office in September. He refuses to call the conflict a “war,” Trump said, because “you are supposed to get approval.”
“I call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us,” Trump said.

Parliament resumes work with packed legislative agenda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:59:02 UTC
18:59:02 KST

(AA Photo)
Lawmakers will open the new legislative year on Oct. 6 with a number of previously submitted bills on the agenda, including a proposal to regulate the Turkish Red Crescent and legislation covering digital accommodation platforms.
The nine-article bill on the Turkish Red Crescent’s duties and powers, as well as its rights and exemptions, is expected to be the first item on the Turkish parliament’s agenda.
Under the proposal, no other legal entity could be established with the aim of exercising the exclusive rights and fulfilling the obligations granted to the Turkish Red Crescent under international agreements.
Services and products produced directly by the Turkish Red Crescent or companies and affiliates in which it holds more than a 50 percent stake would be classified as strategic purchases during disasters, emergencies and extraordinary periods.
Such purchases could be made directly from the Turkish Red Crescent or its majority-owned economic enterprises, affiliates and companies without being subject to the Public Procurement Law.
The bill would also allow the Red Crescent to receive social assistance data held by the Family and Social Services Ministry under a protocol, subject to the Personal Data Protection Law. The data could be accessed only to the extent required for the organization’s duties and by authorized personnel.
The parliament’s Planning and Budget Commission is also scheduled to meet on Oct. 6, with Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan expected to brief lawmakers on the bank’s activities and monetary policy implementation.
The meeting comes as authorities investigate a financial turmoil involving investment funds that has affected more than 455,000 people.
A separate bill submitted to parliament on Aug. 11 covering tourism and accommodation services offered through digital platforms such as Airbnb, TravelGo and Booking is also expected to be discussed by the relevant commission.
The proposal would require digital accommodation platforms to obtain authorization from the Culture and Tourism Ministry. If approved, the measure would create a framework for Booking to resume operations in Türkiye after being inaccessible in the country for about nine years, subject to ministry oversight.
The bill would bar foreign digital accommodation platforms from conducting activities outside the scope of their authorization and from selling or marketing other products.
Meanwhile, the assembly is also expected to hold weekly group meetings, with the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) is scheduled to meet on Oct. 6.

Three politicians facing criminal charges have been elected to Latvia’s 15th Saeima, and once their mandates are approved, parliament will have to decide whether to consent to the continuation of criminal proceedings against them, LETA has found.
The Saeima Rules of Procedure state that parliament’s consent is also required for the continuation of criminal proceedings in cases where criminal prosecution began before the mandate of a Saeima member was approved.
The Rules of Procedure also stipulate that an MP who has committed a criminal offence is considered expelled from the Saeima from the day a conviction enters into force.
Ainārs Šlesers (LPV), a current Riga City Council member who has been elected to the Saeima, is charged in the so-called second digital television criminal case. Several other people have also been charged in the case, including former Prime Minister Andris Šķēle.
The Supreme Court previously overturned an acquittal handed down by Riga Regional Court in the criminal case and sent the case back to Riga Regional Court for a new hearing.
Rūdolfs Brēmanis (SV/AJ), another current Riga City Council member elected to the Saeima, is accused of defrauding and embezzling 102,721 euros
 belonging to the Latvian state during his diplomatic career. The case is still before a court of first instance.
Former Rēzekne mayor Aleksandrs Bartaševičs (Together for Latvia/LPV), who has also been elected to parliament, is facing charges in two separate criminal cases.
The prosecutor’s office recently referred a case to Latgale District Court in which Bartaševičs is accused of exceeding his official authority during the implementation of a recreation centre project in Rēzekne.
Meanwhile, Vidzeme District Court in Gulbene is hearing another criminal case in which Bartaševičs is accused of disclosing restricted-access information and of deliberately failing for 16 years to declare information about property acquired abroad and other substantial income in his public official declarations.

Estonia moves troops closer to Russian border amid shift in strategic thinking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:57:01 UTC
18:57:01 KST

Estonia's 1st Brigade, the main combat-ready element of the country's land forces, will be moving to a newly expanded base less than 50 kilometers from the Russian border, placed to better meet a possible Russian attack.
The move, revealed in comments by the unit's commander, Tarmo Kundla, published in the Financial Times on Oct. 5, comes amid increased awareness of Russian military designs on the Baltic country.
The 1st Brigade will relocate from its previous base in Tapa to the town of Johvi, just west of the city of Narva on the Russian border.
Narva is often seen as a potential flashpoint of hybrid or kinetic attacks not only due to its location, but because the majority of its population is Russian-speaking, a common tool of Russian propaganda to justify aggression.
According to Kundla, the brigade's move is connected to a shift in strategic thinking for the Estonian military, which relies on the airpower of NATO forces based in the region — as well as on the deterrent of the alliance's Article 5 — to protect against an attack from its much larger neighbor.
“We have to start from the border and win from the first battles,” Kundla said, explaining that the move will help the army to fight with a posture of "active defense," allowing immediate return strikes on targets deeper in Russian territory in the event of an invasion.
Although Moscow has failed to achieve any of its strategic aims in almost five years of full-scale war against Ukraine, Russia's war has led many countries on NATO's eastern flank to amp up defense spending and reassess military doctrine, as the nature of warfare itself has undergone a paradigm shift.
In recent years, the Trump administration's open questioning both of the United States' status as Europe's security guarantor, and of Article 5 itself, has unnerved NATO members on the eastern flank.
In 2026, Estonia announced a record 42% increase in defense spending, reaching 2.4 billion euro ($2.69 billion), or around 5.4% of the small country's GDP.
With the extra spending also came procurement of new weapons systems, including U.S.- and South Korean-built rocket systems that could strike St. Petersburg.
“We are in the process of changing everything,” said a military policy official at Estonia’s defense ministry quoted by the Financial Times.
“The reality is that the [Estonian defense planning] has been the same for the last 10 years. But Russia is already planning to double its forces across our border.”

After years of displacement, Syrian Christians return home as children go back to schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:56:09 UTC
18:56:09 KST

After years of displacement, Syrian Christians return home as children go back to schools
Christian schools resume role after some were seized by former regime, others used as shelters for displaced families
Ahmet Karaahmet, Hisam Sabanlioglu and Lina Altawell
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
IDLIB, Syria / ISTANBUL
‘The school was renovated over nearly two years and is now ready to resume education,’ Father Lucas Bashrafa tells Anadolu
Christian schools in Syria are resuming their educational role after years of disruption, as families displaced by the war return to their hometowns following the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime.
Some of the schools had been seized by the former regime, while others were transformed into shelters for people displaced from their homes by bombardment and security crackdowns.
Children from Christian families returning to their communities have also begun re-enrolling in schools where they studied before years of displacement interrupted their education.
Christian clergy members say the reopening of the schools can help restore their role in promoting peaceful coexistence, education and development, while expressing hope for a Syria where freedoms and rights are protected.
‘Rights returned to their owners’
Father Lucas Bashrafa, priest of the church in Qunaya village in the Idlib countryside, said the village school belongs to the Franciscan friars and has resumed its role after years of closure.
“Rights have returned to their owners. The school was renovated over nearly two years and is now ready to resume education,” Bashrafa told Anadolu.
“The school was seized by Syria’s now-dissolved Baath Party in 1971, placing the building under the control of the former regime,” he said.
During the years of war, the building was turned into a shelter for displaced people forced to flee their communities because of bombardment by the former regime’s forces in Idlib and its countryside, he said, adding that it remained in use as a shelter for 10 years.
“I hope the school will once again become a center for peaceful coexistence, education and development,” Bashrafa said.
“The fundamental mission of the Franciscan friars in the region is to promote love and peace among people and villages,” he said.
“The school had previously been an important educational center for residents of surrounding villages,” he added.
“Some of the teachers who are teaching at the school today were once students here,” Bashrafa said.
He expressed hope that Syria would return to days “when education, development, freedom and rights are protected and restored to their owners.”
“We thank God for this blessing and for this new step in our lives,” he added.
Qunaya was among several Christian villages that experienced widespread displacement during the war waged by the Assad regime from 2011 to 2024.
Around 20,000 people lived in the predominantly Christian villages of Ghassaniyeh, Yacoubiyah, Jdeideh and Qunaya in western Idlib before the war began.
Between 2013 and 2015, amid some of the harshest years of the conflict, intensive bombardment by former regime forces and accompanying clashes forced most residents to flee, reducing the remaining Christian population to around 500.
Students return to classrooms
Hanna Jalf, a student from Qunaya, told Anadolu that she and her family fled to the central city of Hama after the war began before returning to their village following the fall of the former regime.
She said she resumed her education after returning home.
“I studied ninth grade here and passed. I got a good result and moved on to 10th grade,” she said.
Jalf said conditions in Qunaya are good now and encouraged other families who have not yet returned to come back to their homes.
Syria’s new government is also working to rehabilitate Christian schools across the country to restore their educational role.
Last month, Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh announced the reopening of the Holy Land School in the Jisr al-Shughur area of Idlib countryside after it had been closed for nearly 60 years.
“This scene is part of the Syria we dreamed of … a Syria for all its people,” Saleh said at the time.
The reopening was part of a series of school openings in Idlib province amid efforts to rehabilitate educational infrastructure in the country.
On Dec. 8, 2024, Syrian opposition forces entered Damascus and announced the overthrow of Assad’s regime, ending his rule from 2000 to 2024. Assad had inherited power from his father, Hafez Assad, who ruled from 1970 to 2000.

Geran-4 Gets Russian Engine and New Navigation System — DIU

09:54:56 UTC
18:54:56 KST

Russia’s Geran-4 jet-powered drone has received a locally produced engine and a new optical navigation system.
The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine reported this on the War&Sanctions portal.
Russian forces began using an upgraded version of this UAV in the fall of this year.
A new MOKH module based on the high-precision PNI5GA magneto-inductive sensor manufactured by U.S. company PNI Sensor has been integrated into the Geran-4 design.
The sensor operates together with the SADRA inertial module, reducing gyroscope drift and improving the accuracy of autonomous navigation.
In addition to satellite and inertial navigation, the enemy has added the Susanin electro-optical correlation system.
It compares images from an optical sensor with a reference image stored in the computer’s memory to adjust the route from the launch point to the target.
Instead of the Chinese Telefly TF-TJ2000A turbojet engine, Russians installed a locally produced equivalent manufactured in Alabuga.
According to Oboronka, engines assembled in Russia undergo additional testing and modifications due to poor manufacturing quality in China. Among the debris, investigators found a turbocharger impeller with Russian markings and drilled holes for weight balancing. Such modifications reduce the centrifugal force acting on the component at high rotational speeds and lower vibrations that can lead to engine failure.
To effectively strike bridge structures and power transmission line towers, the enemy has equipped the drone with a new KRSN shaped-charge cutting warhead.
The remaining electronic modules and components of the UAV remain identical to those used in previous versions of the Geran drones.
The Geran-4 jet-powered attack UAV features a flying-wing aerodynamic configuration and is designed to strike targets at medium and long ranges. The fuselage is approximately 3 meters long, the wingspan exceeds 2.5 meters, and the launch weight is estimated at 200–250 kg, with a warhead weighing up to 50 kg.
The drone is equipped with a turbojet engine that enables it to reach a flight speed of 400–500 km/h and provides an effective range of 400–600 km. Its onboard control system combines satellite navigation, an inertial module, a magnetometric unit, and an electro-optical correction system for autonomous guidance to the target.

Is Iran losing control of the Strait of Hormuz?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:54:19 UTC
18:54:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Is Iran losing control of the Strait of Hormuz?
As Iran and the US take tentative steps towards a deal to re-open the Strait of Hormuz, there may be signs that Tehran's biggest source of leverage is being eroded.
Iran has long viewed its ability to paralyse the strategic chokepoint as its own version of a nuclear bomb, a Trump card which, if used, could trigger a global energy crisis of historic proportions.
Immediately after the US and Israel launched the war on 28 February, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) did just that, moving decisively to block the strait and trapping a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas inside the region.
But its ability to apply the thumbscrews to the global economy has been threatened in recent weeks as the US military facilitates covert oil shipments through the strait and Arab producers reconfigure export routes.
More oil is now leaving the region than at any point during the seven-month war, weakening Tehran's hand as it tries to negotiate permanent control over the strait.
Arab oil exports are rebounding
Middle Eastern crude exports excluding Iran returned to pre-war levels in September despite Iran and its allies escalating attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure.
Estimates by data tracking platform Kpler indicate that Arab countries shipped at least 16.5 million barrels of oil out of the region per day during the month.
Much of the rise was powered by Saudi Arabia, which responded to the attack on its Red Sea pipeline last month by surging exports through the strait.
Shipping data tracked by Bloomberg shows that the kingdom's Hormuz shipments rose to more than three million barrels per day in the first three weeks of September, more than triple the amount in August.
Exports through Hormuz have slowly ticked up since June, when the Pentagon launched a coordinated effort to get energy supplies onto the global market. Backed by US air cover, Gulf states have snuck millions of barrels of oil through the narrow stretch of water by using shadow fleets to evade Iranian fire.
The US attempt to prise open the waterway has dovetailed with moves by Arab states to find new ways of getting their oil out of the region. Saudi Arabia has re-routed its crude to the Red Sea via its East-West Pipeline while the UAE has relied on its terminal at Fujairah on the other side of the strait. Iraq has trucked millions of barrels of oil across the Syrian desert to the Mediterranean.
"Iran appears to have lost significant leverage over the Strait of Hormuz," said Ria Reddy, Iran team deputy lead at the American Enterprise Institute's Critical Threats Project.
"If commercial vessels can continue to transit the strait at high rates despite Iranian threats, Iran has less ability to use the strait to compel the US and other states to accept its demands," she told The New Arab.
The rise in Arab oil exports isn't the only way in which Tehran's control has slipped. The US blockade has turned the tables on Iran, trapping its oil in the region and depriving it of billions of dollars of vital revenues.
Dozens of its ships have been struck by US forces, in what the Trump administration has described as a "tanker for tanker" policy aimed at deterring IRGC attacks on maritime traffic.
Energy crunch continues
With no end in sight to the war, the millions of barrels of oil now making their way out of the region have had little impact on global prices, which continue to be influenced by heightened geopolitical risk and spiralling freight rates.
The unlocking of Hormuz has coincided with a 57% surge in the price of Brent, which peaked at $110 in mid-September following the Houthi takeover of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the crucial Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Neither has it helped to curb shortages of fuels such as gasoline and diesel, whose prices have surged to record highs due to ongoing bottlenecks at refineries worldwide.
The US-led effort also appears not to have had the same success with raising gas shipments from Qatar, which remain far below pre-war levels. Last month, gas prices in Europe and Asia climbed to their highest levels since 2022 amid supply fears ahead of the winter.
All of this means that Iran continues to have a large say over the trajectory of the global economy, despite millions of barrels of crude now transiting the strait every day.
"Resumed oil exports in the Strait of Hormuz is not synonymous with stabilisation," Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East security at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab.
"Iran still retains the capability to resume retaliatory drone and missile strikes on Gulf critical infrastructure and oil production sites," she said.
Danny Citrinowicz, a senior researcher at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), said that although the US has weakened Iran's control of the strait, it has so far failed to achieve its overarching goal of stabilising the global energy market.
"Iran retains the ability to target tankers, threaten commercial shipping, and make passage through the strait increasingly difficult and expensive," he said.
"As a result, Washington's operational achievements have yet to produce the economic outcome it ultimately needs. Oil prices remain elevated, in part because of higher insurance premiums, tanker shortages, and the continuing risk to commercial shipping."
Tanker war
Iran's sporadic attacks on ships have prevented a normalisation of maritime traffic in the strait, keeping freight rates at record highs, extending the freeze in the insurance market, and maintaining pressure on oil prices.
September saw a notable uptick in attacks on tankers, with 21 vessels confirmed hit by Iranian projectiles, up from 12 the month before, according to data collected by conflict monitor ACLED.
"September has seen the largest number of successful Iranian attacks on commercial ships since March, when the war was at its peak," Valentin d'Hauthuille, ACLED's Middle East regional team lead, told The New Arab.
Washington has for the moment gained the upper hand in the strait, but Iran's continued ability to threaten ships raises questions about the long-term viability of its escort operation, he said.
That said, the US's destruction of its coastal radars and surveillance systems is making it increasingly hard for it to use them. There are signs that the damage is forcing it to resort to cruder means of disrupting maritime traffic.
"Iran appears to have adopted less effective methods of tracking and attacking vessels, including the use of fast attack craft to visually identify targets and shore-based rocket launchers to deploy mines," the Critical Threats Project's Reddy said.
"These adaptations suggest that Iran faces greater difficulty identifying, targeting and consistently disrupting shipping at scale."
Widening the battlefield
Iran's say over the future of the strait extends beyond what happens in its immediate neighbourhood to other parts of the region, where its allies have been able to further tighten global energy markets.
Oil and gas prices spiked last month after Houthi forces and Iraqi paramilitaries mounted a one-two punch on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea exports, in the same day taking over the Bab al-Mandeb strait and disabling Aramco's East-West oil pipeline.
Since the ceasefire in Yemen collapsed in July, the group has struck several refineries on the kingdom's Red Sea coast and closed the chokepoint to Saudi-linked ships.
However, horizontal escalation has had limited success for the Axis of Resistance, with Arab producers proving resilient to these multi-pronged attacks and swiftly finding new export routes when one is closed down.
Oil traders may have been spooked by September's attack on the Saudi pipeline, but, in the end, it made little impact on the kingdom's ability to export. Aramco was able to quickly divert flows to Hormuz and brought the pipeline back online in only two weeks.
It also involves a degree of risk which Iran has thus far not been willing to fully take on. Iran has refrained from targeting the UAE since signing the ill-fated peace deal in June, allowing shipments to Fujairah to continue. Neither has it tried to disrupt Iraq's overland shipping route through Syria, a move which would only anger Baghdad and risk pushing it further into America's orbit.
War of attrition
Despite the intense US bombing campaign, the IRGC is believed to still possess thousands of drones and a sizeable missile inventory. There are also signs that China is shipping components to Iran's military to help it maintain production lines and replenish its stockpiles.
This means that, unless there is an end to the war or the US can accomplish the unlikely feat of fully destroying its offensive capabilities, Iran will likely be able to disrupt shipping for many months to come.
The sustainability of the US's operation is less certain. It may be succeeding in getting more oil through the strait at the moment, but it remains an open question about how long it can keep this up.
Months of deployment are putting US forces under increasing strain, with commanders recently warning that continuing the war is unsustainable. Missile interceptor stockpiles are dangerously low, naval forces are fatigued, and the concentration of assets in the region is harming the military's readiness elsewhere around the world.
Moreover, the cost of the operation is currently running at around $2 billion every month, according to the Congressional Budget Office. The Pentagon has put the total cost of the war at more than $45 billion up to the middle of September - and that's without factoring in the costs of replenishing missile inventories and repairing the damage at US bases.
Despite this, the Pentagon appears to be preparing to resume the full-scale war following November's midterm election, last week dispatching another carrier strike group and up to 10,000 additional troops to the region.
The Trump administration is hoping that economic pressure will push Tehran into accepting its conditions for an agreement and recently renewed its attempts to collapse Iran's economy.
The new wave of sanctions dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, together with the naval blockade, has piled more pressure on Iran's economy, sending inflation surging to 73% year-on-year in September and the Iranian rial plunging to a record low of 2.7 million to the dollar.
Meanwhile, the economy shrank more than 10% year-on-year between 21 March and 20 June, while the vital oil and gas sector contracted more than 26%.
RUSI's Ozcelik said that, while large portions of the Iranian public appear to be backing the government's twin calls for resilience and resistance, that may change in the coming months as the economic crisis continues to intensify.
"Tehran may find it harder to convince large segments of the public that they are winning the war and that resistance against the US is worth the heavy toll on the cost of living, hyperinflation, and shrinking economic opportunities," she said.
Matthew Hoare is a journalist at The New Arab
Follow him on X: @matt_h_9

Oil exports from the Middle East, excluding Iran, exceeded their pre-war average last week, Kpler data showed, as pipelines helped bypass the Strait of Hormuz despite continued attacks on shipping.
Despite attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, crude oil exports from the Middle East Gulf region, excluding Iran, returned to pre-war levels in September, according to maritime tracking firm Kpler. The recovery followed changes to the region’s export routes.
"At least 16.5 mbd (million barrels a day) left the region between 1 and 28 September, matching the pre-war average excluding Iran. That is 10.5 mbd above March's monthly average," said the firm.
However, 40% of those exports now bypass the Strait of Hormuz, compared with 17% before the war, with pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates providing key alternative routes. Most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore.
The figures cover crude oil and condensate.
The export figures include shipments via the Red Sea, which exporters increasingly use to bypass Iran’s attempted blockade of Hormuz. Around a fifth of the world’s oil supplies passed through the strait before the conflict.
Oil prices remain well above their pre-war levels. International benchmark Brent crude futures for December delivery traded at $102.25 a barrel on Monday morning, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate traded at $90.50 a barrel.
Brent futures were around $72 before the war. The disruption to shipping through the strait has sent shock waves through the global economy, prompting countries to scramble for alternatives and sending fuel prices soaring.
Iran continues to claim control over the waterway, and ships travelling without its authorisation risk attack. Nevertheless, more vessels are getting through, while alternative routes are operating at full capacity.
Despite the recovery in exports, experts warned that conditions remained far from normal. A US blockade of Iranian ports continues to restrict a large share of Iran’s own oil exports.
Saudi Arabia has benefited from the reopening of its East–West pipeline, which connects its main oil fields in the east to the Red Sea terminal at Yanbu, bypassing Hormuz.
The pipeline shut down on 11 September after strikes launched from Iraq and resumed operations on 22 September, Kpler analyst Amena Bakr said last week.
The UAE also has a route around Hormuz through its pipeline linking Abu Dhabi’s oil fields to Fujairah, a terminal on the Gulf of Oman outside the strait.
The recovery in exports comes as the seven core members of OPEC+, which comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, including Russia, agreed on Sunday to leave their production targets unchanged for November, in line with expectations.
The seven countries produced about 25 million barrels of crude oil a day in August, up 630,000 barrels a day from July, according to OPEC’s September report.

Eurozone business activity grows at fastest pace in 41 months in September
Unknown

2026-10-05

Mucahithan Avcioglu
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Eurozone private sector activity expanded at its fastest pace in nearly three-and-a-half years in September, with the composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) rising to a 41-month high, S&P Global said on Monday.
The final composite PMI output index climbed to 53.1 from 52.0 in August, while the services business activity index increased to a 10-month high of 53.0 from 51.6.
Readings above 50 indicate expansion, while those below that threshold signal contraction.
Output growth accelerated across both manufacturing and services, rounding off a robust third quarter as demand improved and employment increased.
All five countries covered by the composite survey recorded growth for the first time since November. Spain led the expansion, followed by Ireland, while Germany’s upturn accelerated. Italy and France registered more modest growth.
New orders increased at their fastest pace in 41 months, supported by the strongest rise in orders from foreign clients in more than 4 1/2 years.
Outstanding work increased for the first time since June 2022, prompting companies to hire additional staff, although employment growth remained marginal.
“The collective signal from the PMI surveys is one of GDP growing at a 0.4% quarterly rate, with momentum accelerating as we head into the fourth quarter,” said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
He said IT-related services showed particularly strong growth, supported by artificial intelligence investments, while consumer-oriented services remained resilient despite higher energy prices.
Inflationary pressures also intensified, with input costs and selling prices rising at their fastest rates since May. Services firms increased their charges at the sharpest pace since February 2024.
“A renewed upturn in price pressures signalled by the survey meanwhile hints at eurozone inflation running closer to 4% than the ECB’s (European Central Bank's) 2% target,” Williamson said.
Combined with accelerating growth, the figures would fuel speculation about more aggressive monetary policy tightening, he added.

Kuwait strips 415 of citizenship, including billionaire

Breadcrumb
Kuwait strips hundreds more of citizenship under six new decrees, including billionaire businessman
Kuwait has issued six decrees revoking the citizenship of 415 people, including prominent billionaire businessman Mahmoud Haider, as well as those who obtained nationality through them as dependants.
According to the decrees published in Kuwait's official gazette, citizenship certificates were withdrawn from six people and their dependants under Article 21 bis (A) of the 1959 Kuwaiti Nationality Law and its subsequent amendments.
A second decree revoked the citizenship of 286 people and their dependants, while a third stripped 14 people of their nationality.
A fourth decree revoked the citizenship of 25 people and their dependants, while a fifth affected another 41 people. A sixth decree stripped a further 43 people and their dependants of Kuwaiti nationality.
Kuwait began its nationality review campaign in 2024, saying it aimed to tackle fraudulent citizenship claims, including cases involving dual nationality or citizenship acquired through marriage. Kuwaiti law also allows nationality to be revoked on grounds of national interest and state security, provisions that rights organisations say have been applied broadly and with little public explanation.
The campaign has expanded significantly this year, with citizenship revoked from politicians, footballers, musicians and other public figures, including 1982 World Cup goalkeeper Ahmed al-Tarabulsi, singer Abdulmohsen Al Muhanna and composer Yousef Al Muhanna.
Rights groups estimate that at least 50,000 people have lost their Kuwaiti citizenship since 2024, warning that the campaign has raised growing concerns about due process, transparency and the risk of statelessness.

Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:52:07 UTC
18:52:07 KST

The Nobel prize in physiology or medicine 2026 has been awarded to three scientists for their work investigating the mysteries of the brain.
Karl Deisseroth of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of the Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg have been awarded the prize “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”.
The Nobel assembly at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden, announced the winners on Monday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000).
The 2026 award is the 117th time the prize has been given. Of the 235 laureates – including the latest winners – only 14 have been women and none have been awarded to black scientists.
In a nutshell the trio’s research led to the development of a light-sensitive switch that can be used to control nerve cells in the living brain, switching them on or off.
Jonathan Levin, the president of Stanford University, said the subsequent discoveries by Deisseroth, along with those of his fellow laureates, have deepened understanding of neural circuits and how they shape feelings, behaviour, and more.
“Their implications are profound, not only for understanding the human brain, but for opening possibilities into new treatments for neurological and psychiatric disorders,” he said.
The work had its origins in research by Hegemann, who wanted to explore how a green alga called Chlamydomonas swam towards light. “He discovered that its eye spot contains a light-sensitive protein that converts light almost instantly into an electrical signal, allowing the alga to move,” said Abdel El Manira, a professor of neuroscience at the Karolinska Institute and member of the Nobel assembly.
Nagel and Hegemann identified the proteins, called channelrhodopsins, and working with frog egg cells they revealed that when the proteins were exposed to blue light, they allowed charged particles – or ions – to flow into the cell, producing an electrical impulse.
Further work by the pair revealed that when the genetic instructions for one of the proteins were inserted into human or mouse kidney cells, those cells became light sensitive.
Deisseroth took the discovery even further, using rats to demonstrate that by introducing the gene for a channelrhodopsin into nerve cells, it was possible to produce electrical signals in them using light.
He and his colleagues later applied the approach to nerve cells in the motor cortex of the brains of mice, allowing them to use light – delivered by tiny optic fibres passed through their skull – to trigger movement in the rodent’s whiskers.
Subsequent work in mice showed the approach could also be used to investigate which networks of nerve cells were involved in the formation of particular memories, including fear.
While rooted in basic science, the team’s work has already had real-world implications, opening up a field of medicine known as optogenetic therapy.
In one trial it was used to partially restore the sight of a man who went blind as a result of retinitis pigmentosa, a condition that results in damage to light-sensitive cells in the retina.
In that case, the genetic instructions for making a channelrhodopsin were delivered by means of a harmless virus into retinal ganglion cells in the man’s eyes.
He was then kitted out with light-stimulating goggles that captured pictures of the world around him and converted them into single-wavelength images that were projected on to his retina using pulses of light.
Prof Botond Roska, the director of the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel who co-led the study, welcomed the announcement of the Nobel laureates.
“This is truly wonderful news. I hope this helps to boost all efforts on optogenetic vision restoration to bring back vision to blind patients,” he said.
Anna Wedell, a professor at Karolinska Institute and a member of the Nobel committee for physiology or medicine, said the laureates’ work had provided new possibilities to map which cells were responsible for which functions, and which cells communicated with each other, opening up a new understanding of the function of the brain.
“We’ve had anatomical maps and correlations, but now we have a tool that can provide cause-and-effect relationships so we can get a functional map of the brain, exactly pinpoint which cells do what, which cells are responsible for creating behaviours or even emotions and memories in the brain,” she said.
Wedell said that by studying animals to understand how a normal, healthy brain worked, it was then possible to explore what happened when thing went wrong – for example in the case of diseases such as dementia, epilepsy and addiction.
“By understanding which cells are active in these diseases in the mouse, we can also understand where to look in the human,” she said.

Japanese leader calls woman's murder, allegedly by U.S. Marine in Okinawa, "heinous crime" as outrage spreads

Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving incidents by U.S. personnel have long sparked protests on the island, which bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of U.S. military facilities in Japan. 
The new case involves Lance Cpl.     Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old U.S. Marine stationed at Futenma Air Station in Okinawa, who was arrested on suspicion of killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.

The officer asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station, where he was arrested, NHK reported.
His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo news agency reported.

Emotions run high
Around 100 people participated in a rally in Naha on Sunday, holding up placards stating their "strong protest" against the murder, Japanese media reported.
Okinawa native Sorane Sakihama, 24, who organized a similar rally in Tokyo on Sunday, said she cried upon learning about the woman's death.
"We couldn't protect her. That made me so angry and sad," the university student told AFP, adding that she was planning to organize another protest in front of the U.S. Embassy for Tuesday evening.
"I want to ask them — what are these soldiers stationed here for? They might say they are here to protect lives or boost security. But how can they say that when a life was taken by their own?"
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters on Monday that "the government will work with the United States to thoroughly make sure there will be no recurrence, and reduce burdens on local residents."
News of the Marine's arrest immediately prompted Japan's foreign affairs and defense ministers to summon senior U.S. officials to convey their "extreme disappointment" and "lodge strong protests," Kihara said.
The incident came just a few weeks after Okinawa elected Genta Koja as its new governor, ending the eight-year rule of his predecessor, who had long pushed for a major U.S. military base to be moved off the island.
Koja, 42, accepts a central government plan to keep the U.S. Marine Corps' Futenma air base on Okinawa's main island, but to move it to a less populated location.
Calling the murder-robbery "extremely malicious in nature," Koja told reporters on Sunday it had "hugely shocked residents here who are forced to live side-by-side with the bases, and instilled new fear in them."
"I am infuriated," Koja said.
He said the incident showed U.S. efforts to "educate soldiers and improve their behavior have not been functioning at all."
Koja said he will travel to Tokyo "soon" to lodge a protest with top government officials, including Takaichi.
On Monday, U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass said on social media that he is telling U.S. military commanders this week they need "to hold our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity." He also said that he and Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, discussed the "next steps in strengthening that bond of trust with our Japanese partners and base-hosting communities."
Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today it hosts 70% of America's military facilities and most of the 50,000 U.S. troops based in Japan.
There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military on the island. The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to prefectural police.
A Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison last year.
In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
Under a bilateral status of forces agreement, the case is being handled by the Japanese authorities because the suspect was not on duty and was arrested off base.
Japanese prosecutors started examining the suspect's case on Monday to determine whether to press formal charges in the coming weeks.
If convicted, he could face life in prison or the death penalty.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to pass order on plea seeking suspension of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations that he took decisions on the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls without the consensus of the two other election commissioners.A bench led by CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana also issued notice to the Centre, Election Commission of India and its three commissioners on a plea that alleged that the powers vested in the poll panel as a multi-member constitutional body were being exercised without following the collective decision-making mechanism mandated by law.The bench also rejected the poll body's claim that the top court had upheld the declaration attached to Form 6, making it clear that it had not approved any modification to the form.
What the top court said
Justice Suryakant said that any modification of Form 6 - the application citizens use to register as new electors - had not been approved by the top court. “Any modified Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When record is produced, we would like to see who has modified. But, your prayers appear jumbled up,” the CJI said.
The top court said that the transaction of business within the poll panel “has to be unanimous” and if it finds that certain decisions were taken by CEC without the required unanimity, it could reconsider or recall those decisions. “They are expected to take unanimous decisions. If there is no unanimity, it has to be by majority. If records show some decision was not unanimous, etc., we will injunct those decisions and say they are ultra vires. Can we ex parte come to a decision that all decisions were unilateral? We expect them to respond in a clear, transparent manner.”
“Let's first have authenticated information on that. We can always annul any decision,” the bench added.
“We presume that decisions are taken by Election Commission as per law,” the court said.
What is the controversy
A report by the Indian Express claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR, alleging that some were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.
The report said the poll panel's software added a requirement for ancestral details and a link to the previous SIR in Form 6, the voter registration form, without the legal amendment required under election rules.
The poll panel however rejected the charges and said changes in the form were upheld by the Supreme Court . "The declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court. For non-SIR period, the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used," it had said.The poll panel had also said that differences of opinion are normal in institutional deliberations and maintained that all its orders are legally valid and follow the prescribed procedures.

How to select, clean, and store fresh button mushrooms safely
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:48:34 EEST
18:48:34 KST

How to select, clean, and store fresh button mushrooms safely
Kyiv • UNN
Fresh button mushrooms should be firm, dry, and free of spots and unpleasant odors. Store them in a paper bag in the refrigerator for 3–5 days.
Champignons are often used for soups, salads, pizza, sauces, and other dishes; however, before cooking, the mushrooms need to be properly prepared. UNN explains in more detail what to look for when buying champignons and how to prepare them for cooking.
How to choose fresh champignons
First of all, you should inspect the mushrooms. Fresh champignons should be firm, dense, and uniform in color, with white or cream-colored caps. Also pay attention to the mushroom’s surface — if it has become shiny or slimy, or is covered with a sticky coating, it is better to avoid such mushrooms. You should also not buy champignons if they have dark, yellow, or black spots. Another important detail is the stem: its cut should be fresh, not dark and dried out. The smell is also important, as fresh champignons have a characteristic mushroom aroma. However, if they smell musty, rotten, chemical-like, or damp like a basement, it is better not to eat them.
How to clean champignons before cooking
Before cooking, champignons should be inspected and any remaining soil or other dirt should be removed. If the mushrooms are small, young, and almost clean, it is not necessary to peel them. Instead, it is enough to wipe the cap and stem with a clean napkin or brush, and cut off the bottom part of the stem, where particles of soil may remain.
Large champignons can, if necessary, also be cleaned of the thin skin on the cap and any dirt on the stem. If the mushrooms are heavily soiled, they can be cut into several pieces to make it easier to inspect the surface and remove the soil.
For quick cleaning, you can also use flour: place the champignons in a deep bowl or saucepan, sprinkle them with several spoonfuls of flour, cover the container, and carefully shake it. After that, the mushrooms should be wiped with a clean napkin, and some of the dirt should come off together with the flour.
If only a small amount of soil remains on the mushroom’s surface, you can simply wipe the champignons with a clean napkin instead of washing them.
Do champignons need to be washed?
Champignons should not be left in water for a long time, as they quickly absorb moisture, which can make the mushrooms watery and affect their texture and, consequently, their taste during cooking. If the mushrooms need to be washed, they can be quickly rinsed under cold running water. After that, the champignons should immediately be placed on a paper towel and dried.
How to store champignons
Fresh mushrooms are recommended to be kept in the refrigerator. A paper bag is suitable for storage, as it helps prevent excess moisture. Fresh champignons should not be left for too long after purchase. They should be used within 3–5 days.
Before cooking, the mushrooms should be inspected once again. If their smell, color, surface, or firmness has changed during storage, such champignons should not be eaten.

🔴 Nobel Prize in Medicine jointly awarded to ​Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann ​and Georg Nagel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:47:22 UTC
18:47:22 KST

Nobel Prize in Medicine jointly awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel
The Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded Monday to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).
The Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded Monday to three scientists working on the mechanisms the brain uses to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells.
Karl Deisseroth, 54, Peter Hegemann, 71, and Georg Nagel, 73, have carried out research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. They are based at universities in Germany and the United States.
The Nobel committee lauded their work, writing on X that the method “is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries”.
The Nobel Assembly said Deisseroth is based at Stanford University in California, while Hegemann is at Humboldt University in Berlin and Nagel at the University of Wurzburg in Germany.
The prize was announced at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, kicking off Nobel week.
Last year, the prize went to three scientists researching the immune system.
Monday's medicine prize is followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday and literature on Thursday.
After Friday’s peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Oct. 12.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organisation.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

MPs actively use AI to submit spam amendments to 2026 budget draft – committee chair
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:44:29 EEST
18:44:29 KST

Technological development, especially artificial intelligence (AI), is one of the reasons for the surge in amendments to the state budget draft, posing a challenge compounded by the traditional submission of expenditure-increasing amendments without specified funding sources, Budget Committee Chair of the Verkhovna Rada Roksolana Pidlasa stated in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine.
"While previously MPs' assistants spent days and nights writing these spam amendments, like increasing or decreasing every single line in Appendix 3 of the state budget by UAH 1, now an AI like Claude or Gemini can write 2,000 amendments in 3 minutes," Pidlasa said.
She recalled that the trend toward an increasing number of amendments to the government's draft state budget has been growing in recent years, with a 19-year record broken previously at 3,339 amendments.
"I think there could be even more this year. Technological development is strongly facilitating the submission of amendments," the committee chair said.
According to her, AI-generated amendments are indistinguishable from those written by humans, whereas these amendments must still be processed by actual people rather than artificial intelligence.
Pidlasa stated that the use of AI has not led deputies to search for realistic sources of additional revenues to balance proposals for increased expenditures.
"This year is the same as always: deputies have many ideas on how to spend money, but not very many on where to get that money, and even fewer of those ideas are realistic. Many amendments regarding additional expenditures are submitted without any coverage sources. Or it is written that 'coverage will come from increased VAT revenues next year.' But how that increase in VAT revenues will happen remains unknown to anyone," the Budget Committee Chair said.

Ethiopian troops retake regional capital from rebels (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:43:30 UTC
18:43:30 KST

Ethiopian troops retake regional capital from rebels (VIDEO)
Ethiopian government forces and allied fighters have retaken the capital of the northern Tigray region, which rebels seized less than two weeks ago.
Fighters from the pro-government Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) announced in a post on Facebook on Sunday that they had “completely taken control” of Mekelle.
Footage shared by the TPF and dated October 3 shows armed men in military uniforms and vans moving through the streets, with horns sounding as people cheer. The forces entered the city center on Saturday afternoon, followed by federal troops, Reuters reported, citing a source close to the militia.
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which governs the region, acknowledged its retreat in a statement posted on Facebook. It said the regional administration “has decided to temporarily leave Mekelle and operate from another location, while our forces continue carrying out their military operations.”
Residents reported looting of government offices during the withdrawal, while internet and cellphone disruptions have hampered verification of developments, AP reported.
Federal troops also recovered Mekelle’s airport, which TPLF fighters seized on September 23, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to the city and two other Tigrayan destinations.
The East African country has struggled to secure lasting stability since an African Union-mediated peace agreement signed in November 2022 ended the two-year Tigray war, which killed hundreds of thousands. The conflict grew out of a power struggle between the federal government and the TPLF, whose decades of dominance in national politics ended when Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office in 2018. Disputes over disarmament, territory, and the return of displaced people remain unresolved.
The latest escalation followed the formation of an opposition alliance between the TPLF and six other armed groups, including former battlefield enemies, seeking to oust Abiy. On September 24, the Ethiopian National Defense Force said it had killed 272 TPLF fighters and wounded another 260 in a counteroffensive. Tigray’s regional authorities said their troops entered a “defensive battle” after federal forces attacked them with aircraft, drones, and artillery.
The fighting has also deepened a regional diplomatic crisis, with Ethiopia accusing Egypt, Eritrea, and Sudan of supporting the rebels. All three deny the allegations. Ethiopia announced the closure of its embassy in Eritrea and expelled ten Eritrean diplomats on Thursday, citing Asmara’s “direct and indirect acts of hostility.” Eritrea responded by severing ties, claiming Addis Ababa was plotting to take its ports and backing Eritrean opposition groups to pursue regime change. Addis Ababa also ordered an Egyptian diplomat to leave within 48 hours. Cairo retaliated by giving an Ethiopian Embassy counselor the same deadline.

UK reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align with EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:43:22 UTC
18:43:22 KST

The UK is reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align itself with the EU and strengthen its case to be included in new legislation designed to protect the European manufacturing sectors including autos and chemicals.
It is understood the EU has raised the question of tariffs with the UK as part of the discussions on the “Made in Europe” legislation, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act.
The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely. Brussels believes the UK would have to introduce tariffs to create a level playing field to qualify for inclusion in the scheme and match the tariffs of up to 45% it has levied on Chinese cars since October 2024.
Imposing tariffs on Chinese cars would probably prompt a hostile response from Beijing and test Andy Burnham’s desire for a reset in the post-Brexit relationship with the EU.
It would also involve a lengthy World Trade Organization process. It took the EU 13 months between the launch of the investigation into state subsidies in production and transport lines and finally imposing tariffs in October 2024.
The UK has been lobbying hard to be included in the legislation, which will require manufacturers to procure components from the continent to protect against the growing presence of China in supply chains, particularly the auto and chemicals sector.
A government source pointed to comments from the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, last week, saying tariffs on Chinese EVs were “always kept … under close review”.
If tariffs were to be imposed, the move would be a break with the previous government policy. Keir Starmer’s government positioned itself as a strong ally to China, viewing it as an important source of economic growth rather than a risk to British manufacturing.
The UK has consistently argued it does not need trade barriers in the way Brussels does because it does not have the huge trade deficit – now running at more than £1bn (€1.18bn) a day – that the EU is struggling to contain.
China’s increasing trade with the EU – not only in finished products such as cars but also in components – is causing deep concern about cannibalisation of native industries in European capitals. The EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, is visiting Beijing this Wednesday for talks over a reset in trade relations.
Experts said last week the UK car industry faced a “difficult trade-off”, with Chinese investment a potential “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.
However, Nissan’s chair in Europe, Massimiliano Messina, recently said Europe “cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market” through imports via Great Britain.
Nissan is in talks with the Chinese company Chery to manufacture cars in its Sunderland plant, but this would still align with the EU’s Made in Europe policy.
The EU views Chinese manufacturers based in Europe, employing EU staff, as less of a threat to its indigenous industries. Chinese brands made by BYD in Hungary, for example, will not be subject to import duties.
Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said any consideration of tariffs needed to be based on “robust evidence” and maintain a rules-based open and competitive market, adding: “Trade restrictions can have unintended consequences. 
“The immediate priority is a pragmatic agreement recognising the UK as a trusted ‘Made in Europe’ partner as the exclusion of UK-built vehicles would severely damage both our highly integrated industries, jeopardising the €80bn trading relationship.”
Brands such as BYD, Leapmotor and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to the latest industry figures.
BYD has almost doubled its share of the UK market in September 2026 compared with September 2025, with 5.75% of the market, according to figures from the SMMT released on Monday.
In the year to date, BYD’s share has gone up from 2.2% to 3.93%, with 68,000 BYD cars sold up to the end of September, closing in on BMW, which shifted 91,000.
Jaecoo’s share has rocketed, increasing by 223%, with 58,000 new cars sold in the year so far, while Leapmotor sales have soared by a phenomenal 765% – up from about 1,500 cars sold in 2025 to more than 13,000 in the year so far.
A UK government spokesperson said: “We have not put tariffs on Chinese EVs. We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector’s and UK’s national interests.”

Commander-in-Chief Drapatyi moves away from predecessor Syrskyi's micromanagement – UP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:43:00 EEST

Commander-in-Chief Drapatyi moves away from predecessor Syrskyi's micromanagement – UP
Mykhailo Drapatyi, Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, has chosen to move away from the micromanagement practised by his predecessor Oleksandr Syrskyi, opting instead to decentralise command.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda article (English translation to be available soon)
Quote: "The first word brigade and corps commanders use to describe the first few months of Drapatyi's tenure is 'freedom'. Unlike his predecessor, who would tell some brigade commanders how and where to fight – even specifying the coordinates where a position should be set up – Drapatyi has chosen a different approach. He has opted to decentralise command, moving away from the 'micromanagement' that has already become widely known to the public."
Details: Ukrainska Pravda understands that the commander-in-chief no longer commands troops directly but does so through the troop groupings of the relevant operational commands, in line with the military chain of command. This means that soldiers receive their orders from their immediate commanders.
After taking office, Drapatyi also somewhat reorganised the system of troop groupings. In particular, he disbanded the Skhid (East) Grouping of Forces, commanded by Viktor Nikoliuk – presumably because he was dissatisfied with Nikoliuk's performance – and merged Dmytro Voloshyn's Kursk Grouping of Forces into Mykhailo Shandar's Pivnich (North) Grouping of Forces.
There are now six troop groupings operating across the entire front: Pivnich (North), Pivden (South), Zakhid (West), the Joint Forces Grouping, and two recently established by Drapatyi – Centre, commanded by Andrii Biletskyi, and Azov, commanded by Denys Prokopenko.
Ukrainska Pravda sources say the move away from hands-on management of brigades and corps has brought another change: Drapatyi no longer spends several hours every day hearing reports from all commanders, as Syrskyi did.
"Syrskyi would hear reports from everyone every day and could give specific instructions on how to respond to developments, including where troops should advance… Drapatyi doesn't do that; that's the job of the troop grouping commanders. Drapatyi focuses on strategic and systemic issues. And when commanders do speak to the commander-in-chief, he isn't interested in a standard report on 'what happened', but in statistics, analysing problems and finding solutions – in other words, what conditions need to be created for a particular commander to accomplish their mission. And that's the right approach," a senior military officer told Ukrainska Pravda.

Head of German intelligence warns of the threat of an "armed conflict" with Russia

BND chief Martin Jäger said there is a real threat of an armed conflict between Germany and Russia. The intelligence service sees no signs of a large-scale attack on NATO.
The President of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND), Martin Jaeger, considers the threat of a military confrontation between Germany and Russia to be real. Die Welt reports this, UNN writes.
Details
"The confrontation in which we are engaged with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous quality: Germany is at risk of being drawn into an armed conflict with Russia," Jaeger said on Monday during an open hearing of the Bundestag’s Parliamentary Oversight Committee.
According to Jaeger, Russian intelligence services are operating "highly professionally and ruthlessly." "The threat of attacks on targets in Germany remains real and current. We must counter it."
As an example of this escalation, he cited an attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, for which Berlin blamed Russia.
"No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany. We did not seek this confrontation. Russia is imposing it on us, seeing us as its main adversary. Because we do not accept Russia’s revisionist, expansionist policy and its aggressive war against Ukraine," Jaeger said.
According to the official, the Russian leadership seeks "to ensure for the future that political decisions directed against Moscow are not made in Berlin or other European capitals." This results in "increasingly aggressive actions by Russian intelligence services" against Germany and other states.
"Russia is waging a shadow war against us. This undeclared war cannot be described using traditional military or legal categories. We are not in a state of defense, yet we are still under attack—that is precisely what a shadow war is," the official said.
"Russia seeks to undermine Europe’s political support for Ukraine. We must be prepared for attempts at intimidation and further interference. Nuclear threats will likely be heard again," the head of the BND added.
However, according to Jaeger, at present the intelligence agency sees no signs of a large-scale Russian attack on NATO territory. Nevertheless, "Russian military action on a limited scale" is possible, particularly in the Baltic states, the head of Germany’s intelligence service уточнив.
