Estonia to Move Troops to Russian Border Under “Active Defense” Strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:12:54 UTC
18:12:54 KST

Estonia is moving some of its troops closer to the Russian border as part of a new “active defense” strategy.
The Financial Times reports that the main units of Estonia’s 1st Infantry Brigade, the country’s main combat force, will be permanently stationed in Jõhvi instead of Tapa.
Jõhvi is located about 50 km from the Russian border, while Tapa is approximately 130 km away.
To accommodate the troops in Jõhvi, Estonia is building new military facilities. The country is also constructing a military base in Narva that will be able to accommodate up to 1,000 troops.
Around 200 troops are expected to be stationed there in peacetime, with up to 800 more deployed in the event of war.
The changes are part of a broader review by Estonia’s Ministry of Defense of its military strategy, as the country shifts to an “active defense” concept introduced in May 2026.
The concept calls for defending the country directly from the border and attempting to stop an enemy at the earliest stage of an attack. As part of this approach, Estonia is acquiring modern weapons and long-range artillery, including HIMARS multiple launch rocket systems.
Militarnyi previously reported that, after four months of training, Estonian troops carried out their first live-fire exercises using the country’s own HIMARS rocket systems.
The wartime structure of the Estonian Defense Forces includes more than 43,000 positions. About 4,200 are assigned to active-duty personnel, while the rest are reservists and members of the Estonian Defense League (Kaitseliit).
As of 2026, the Estonian Division forms the core of the land component of the Estonian Defense Forces. It is the country’s largest land formation, reports directly to the Commander of the Defense Forces, and is integrated into NATO’s command structure.
The division includes the 1st and 2nd Infantry Brigades, a headquarters and signals battalion, an ISTAR reconnaissance battalion, and artillery, engineering, and logistics battalions.
The division’s main maneuver unit remains the 1st Infantry Brigade. It comprises the Scouts Battalion, the Kalev and Viru infantry battalions, an air defense battalion, a combat support battalion, headquarters and signals companies, and an anti-tank company.
The brigade also trains conscripts, who are later transferred to the reserve.
The 2nd Infantry Brigade is primarily responsible for the southeastern part of the country. In peacetime, it consists of a headquarters in Tartu, the Kuperjanov Battalion in Võru, a combat support battalion, and a support and communications company. In wartime, the brigade is expanded with reserve units.
In addition to the division, the Estonian Defense Forces include the Cyber Command, Support Command, Military Police, Special Operations Forces, and other units.

The JCS said the mines were discovered about 10 meters (33 feet) south of the Military Demarcation Line, suggesting they had been “planted” there rather than swept into the area, Yonhap News reported.

You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you want to play in this era and what role Spain should play. Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez arrives to attend the EU Summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels, on June 18, 2026. (AFP File Photo)
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Oct. 5 called a snap election for Nov. 29, after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.
The defeat on Oct. 2 was just the latest political setback for the Socialist premier, one of the few European prime ministers from the left still in power.
“To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people,” Sanchez, in office since 2018, said in a televised address, adding his aim was “to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament.”
Tens of thousands of protesters marched in Madrid and other cities in Spain on Oct. 3 to demand affordable housing.
The government’s proposed measures, which included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants, were voted down by opposition parties in Spain’s parliament.
The defeat infuriated those protesting the country’s increasingly expensive housing market and underscored the difficulties his minority coalition government faces in passing legislation.
Spain has been operating under its 2023 budget, the last national spending plan passed by Sanchez’s government, for several years.
The demonstrations extended a crisis that has gone on for more than a week, triggered by the eviction last month of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid flat where she had lived for decades.
Hundreds of protesters have been occupying a tent city set up more than a week ago in the heart of Madrid to press for reforms.
Recent opinion polls have generally placed the main opposition conservative Popular Party (PP) ahead of the Socialists.
Housing has for years been a top concern for Spaniards as supply falls short of demand, with rents and house prices rising as elsewhere in the European Union.
Average rents in Spain have almost doubled over the past decade, while asking prices for homes have risen by about 90 percent, according to real estate website Idealista.
Abascal’s eviction catalyzed long-running anger about runaway housing costs.
The pensioner was forced to leave the Madrid flat where she had lived for more than seven decades after it was acquired by an investment company that sought to increase her rent by 275 percent, say housing campaigners.
The backlash led the new owners to reach a deal allowing her to return to the flat at a low rent.
The housing bills Sanchez’s leftist coalition had presented to parliament were rejected after the Catalan separatist party Junts, on whose support the government relies, voted against them, arguing they were hastily drawn up and would make the housing crisis worse.
Sanchez defended his government’s record in his address, pointing out that under his leadership Spain’s economy has grown faster than those of its main European peers.
But after eight years in power, Sanchez is also under pressure from corruption scandals involving people close to him, including his wife and top figures in his Socialist Party.
While polls put the PP ahead, they suggest the party would fall short of an absolute majority in parliament and would need the support of far-right Vox to govern.

'New pace, new height': PM Modi-Parmelin talks put India-Switzerland ties on fast track
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:06:29 UTC
18:06:29 KST

File photo: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Swiss President Guy Parmelin at Hyderabad House for bilateral talks, in New Delhi on Monday
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Swiss Confederation president Guy Parmelin held wide-ranging talks in New Delhi on Monday, with the two sides discussing ways to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, mobility, infrastructure, defence, nuclear energy and critical technologies.The talks came as India and Switzerland seek to build on the India-EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA), which entered into force last October and is set to complete a year of implementation this week.Addressing a joint press statement after the talks, PM Modi said the relationship between India and Switzerland had gained fresh momentum and highlighted the two countries' cooperation in innovation, infrastructure and advanced technology.“India-Switzerland friendship is centuries-old... Innovation, infrastructure and advanced technology are strong pillars of our foundation today. With the Summit today, we are going to give a new pace and height to our partnership,” PM Modi said.
India eyes $100 billion investment under TEPA
PM Modi said TEPA was an ambitious blueprint for investment, innovation, jobs and shared prosperity and set out a target of attracting $100 billion in investment into India and creating 1 million direct jobs over the next 15 years.
“I am very happy to welcome the president of Switzerland to India. First of all, I would like to appreciate his commitment to India-Switzerland relations. With his personal support, last October we implemented a historic Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement between India and the European Free Trade Association, or EFTA, countries,” PM Modi said.
“This is India's first FTA with any economic bloc in Europe,” he added.The Prime Minister said India and Switzerland had also taken decisions to increase market access for Indian exports to Switzerland and facilitate investment between the two countries.He said the measures would support exports of Indian agricultural products, pharmaceuticals, textiles and engineering goods, while encouraging Swiss investment in sectors including biotechnology, life sciences, banking, insurance, food processing and sustainability.
Defence, nuclear energy and infrastructure on agenda
The talks also expanded beyond trade and investment, with PM Modi saying the two countries had identified new opportunities for military exchanges and defence production cooperation.“We also agreed to further deepen nuclear energy cooperation,” he said.PM Modi pointed to projects such as the Varanasi ropeway, Noida's Jewar airport and railway and tunnelling projects in mountainous regions as examples of India-Switzerland infrastructure cooperation.The two sides also signed an agreement covering transport, mobility and infrastructure, with PM Modi inviting Swiss infrastructure companies to increase investment in India and participate in capacity-building, design and manufacturing.People-to-people ties were another focus of the discussions. PM Modi said the Migration and Mobility Partnership Agreement and Young Professionals Agreement signed during the visit would create new opportunities in Switzerland for Indian students, researchers, professionals and young people.
Parmelin calls visit a ‘stepping stone’
Parmelin, who is on a three-day State visit to India, described the trip as an opportunity to further strengthen the long-standing relationship between the two countries.He said India and Switzerland shared democratic values as well as trust and mutual respect, and described his visit as a “stepping stone” towards deepening their partnership.The Swiss president's visit is also significant for TEPA, which was signed in March 2024 after nearly 16 years of negotiations and came into force in October 2025. The EFTA countries — Switzerland, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway — have committed to investing $100 billion in India over 15 years under the agreement.Parmelin is scheduled to attend the second India-EFTA Prosperity Summit on October 7, marking the first anniversary of TEPA's implementation.
Swiss business delegation accompanies Parmelin
Parmelin arrived in New Delhi earlier on Monday and was accorded a ceremonial reception at Rashtrapati Bhavan before visiting Rajghat to pay tribute to Mahatma Gandhi. He was accompanied by a delegation of senior officials and business representatives.External affairs minister S Jaishankar also met Parmelin and said he appreciated the Swiss president's commitment to deepening the India-Switzerland partnership and building on the promise of TEPA.
According to the ministry of external aaffairs, Switzerland is India's largest trade and investment partner among the four EFTA countries.More than 330 Swiss companies currently operate in India across sectors including engineering, services, precision instruments, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, while Indian companies in Switzerland have a presence in areas including IT, pharmaceuticals and machinery.Parmelin will also meet President Droupadi Murmu, who is scheduled to host a banquet in his honour. The visit is his first State visit to India and his second trip to the country this year, after his participation in the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi in February.

Details
Brent crude futures fell 72 cents, or 0.71%, to $101.59 per barrel at 06:34 GMT (09:34 Kyiv time), while the price of U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude stood at $90.05 per barrel, down $1.05, or 1.2%.
The price of Brent crude lost most of its gains last week, while WTI fell 1.6% after G7 countries agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel fuel and oil from emergency reserves and pledged to refrain from restricting energy exports under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump.
Trump ruled out a U.S. ban on diesel exports following the G7 decision03.10.26, 14:37 • 8731 view

ICE gasoil futures rose more than 2% to $1,390.25 per barrel on Monday.
Experts' opinion

Qatar partners with Euroclear to widen foreign access to government debt market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:05:03 UTC
18:05:03 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Qatar’s central bank and Euroclear, a Brussels-based provider of securities settlement and custody services, announced Monday a collaboration to establish an international settlement link aimed at widening foreign investor access to the country’s domestic government debt market.
The initiative will allow international investors to access Qatari government bonds and sukuk, or Islamic bonds, through Euroclear’s infrastructure, while giving issuers access to a broader and more diversified pool of capital.
The collaboration is expected to boost liquidity, improve market efficiency and deepen international capital flows into Qatar. It aligns with the country’s Third Financial Sector Strategy and Third National Development Strategy for 2024-2030.
The link will cover eligible Qatari riyal-denominated conventional government bonds and sukuk.
Euroclear Bank will act as the issuer central securities depository, while Edaa, Qatar’s central securities depository, will serve as the investor depository for local investors. Qatar Central Bank will act as issuer and paying agent.
Euroclear Chief Executive Valerie Urbain said the collaboration would “simplify market access, enhance liquidity and strengthen Qatar’s appeal to global investors.”

German defense company ARX Robotics and Ukrainian company Roboneers have entered into a strategic partnership to jointly develop and integrate unmanned ground systems.
The agreement was signed in Kyiv on October 4 in the presence of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
That same day, Zelensky and Merz attended the Ukrainian-German Business Forum, where the two sides reached several agreements covering the defense industry, unmanned systems, air defense, and energy.
The new agreement between ARX Robotics and Roboneers provides for deeper technical integration of the two companies’ systems, as well as joint research and development activities.
“Together with Roboneers, we are providing Ukrainian forces with a powerful yet intelligent fleet of unmanned ground systems at scale,” Witfeld said.
Under the partnership, the combat experience gained from operating robotic platforms in Ukraine will also be used to develop future ground systems for the armed forces of Western countries.
ARX Robotics supplies Ukraine’s Defense Forces with GEREON-family unmanned ground systems. In May, the company signed a contract to supply Ukraine with several hundred more of these systems, which is expected to increase the Defense Forces’ fleet fivefold. According to the company, its systems constitute the largest fleet of Western-made unmanned ground systems deployed in Ukraine.
The current agreement expands cooperation between ARX Robotics and Roboneers, which already includes the joint production of the Ukrainian Lynx Pro unmanned ground system. In June 2026, the companies announced the establishment of a joint venture, ARX Industries, as part of the Build with Ukraine initiative.
In July, soldiers from the 123rd Brigade deployed an unmanned ground system from a maritime unmanned platform onto the occupied Kinburn Spit. The operation is believed to have involved a Roboneers-produced Lynx unmanned ground system equipped with a PKT machine gun.
In September 2026, the company also codified the combat version, the ShaLynx PRO Mk.19 (M), which combines the Lynx PRO platform with the remotely controlled Shablya weapon station and a 40 mm automatic grenade launcher.
Earlier, Roboneers also integrated the Shablya MK-19 combat module onto the Volya-E unmanned ground system, transforming the logistics platform into a remotely controlled fire-support system.
The companies’ cooperation comes amid a rapid increase in the number of unmanned ground systems in the Ukrainian Defense Forces. In April, the Ministry of Defense announced plans to contract 25,000 unmanned ground systems during the first half of 2026. In July, the ministry reported that it had contracted more than 22,000 Ukrainian-made unmanned ground systems for 2026.

Ministry of Defence Sanctuary Awards
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

Ministry of Defence Sanctuary Awards
The annual Sanctuary Awards recognise outstanding conservation and sustainability efforts across the Ministry of Defence (MOD) estate.
The Sanctuary Awards have been recognising outstanding conservation and sustainability efforts across the MOD estate since 1991.
The awards celebrate and encourage group and individual efforts that benefit sustainable development, environmental and heritage conservation, utilities and resource-saving measures, sustainable construction and procurement or community awareness on land or property that the MOD owns or uses in the UK and overseas.
35th Sanctuary Awards 2026: Shortlisted entries
Winners will be announced on 17 November 2026. You can sign up for the free Sanctuary Awards 2026 live feed online.
Many congratulations to the 14 projects that have been shortlisted for the 35th Sanctuary Awards 2026:
- 507 Specialist Team Royal Engineers – A1 Steam trust, Darlington Railhead Construction Project (A1 Steam Locomotive Trust, Darlington)
- AA Wick Marsh Ranges (AA (Wick Marsh) Ranges, Fingringhoe, Colchester)
- Aldershot’s Training Area – sustaining military capability (Aldershot Military Fieldcraft Training Areas)
- Barton Stacey Flyfishing Club (Barton Stacey Training Area)
- Beckingham Cadet Training Centre – sustainable construction (Army HQ, Andover)
- Devonport Open Days (HMNB Devonport)
- Group Captain Maurice Dixon (RAF Leeming and RAF High Wycombe)
- Sq Ldr Don Earl (RAF High Wycombe)
- Exercise Druid Sacrifice (RAF Valley)
- Find it in Plymouth – supply chain resilience at Devonport (HMNB Devonport)
- FuelActive – cleaner fuel for Team Leidos’ fleet (Defence Fulfilment Centre, DM Beith, MOD Bicester, JHC FS Aldergrove, MOD Kineton, MOD Longtown, DM Gosport, HMNB Portsmouth)
- Lydd Ranges Sea Defence Project (Lydd Ranges)
- Project Life (National Armaments Director Group Bicester)
- SPINNERET – microgrids for operational energy (MOD Bovington Camp)
Nominations were sought in the following categories:
- Climate Change Resilience Award – projects or activities focused on taking action to enhance climate resilience through adaption.
- Energy Award – for energy of fuel projects that decrease energy demand, increase energy efficiency and/or increase energy resilience through sustainability.
- Environmental Enhancement Award – projects focused on wildlife, biodiversity, environmental research, or tackling pollution or contamination issues.
- Heritage Award – projects focused on archaeology, historic buildings, historic parks or gardens, landscape preservation, museum collections, or heritage education or public engagement.
- Individual Achievement Award – any individual who has made a significant personal contribution to MOD’s sustainability or conservation ambitions.
- Social Impact Award – grass-roots sustainability projects focusing on community engagement, green spaces, wellbeing or facilitating public access.
- Sustainability Improvement Award – for projects that demonstrate sustainability improvements through implementation of circular economy principles (including reducing resource consumption or waste and recycling), sustainable procurement, sustainable construction or refurbishment projects, and improvements in equipment or systems through eco design.
The Operational Capability Award will be chosen from the shortlisted nominations and awarded to the project which best delivers enhanced operational capability through sustainability and climate considerations.
And the Silver Otter Trophy will be chosen from the category winners and awarded to the best Establishment, Conservation Group or community led project or individual conservation effort on the MOD estate.
For queries please email: DIO-Sanctuary@mod.gov.uk

Swiss government backs VAT increase to fund 13th pension

Swiss government backs VAT increase to fund 13th pension
The Swiss government has supported an increase in Value-Added Tax (VAT) to pay for the 13th payment of the Swiss old-age and survivors' (AHV/AVS) pension.
On Monday, the government advocated a rise of 0.4 percentage points, from 8.1% to 8.5%, ahead of the referendum on November 29. A double majority will be required for the vote.
To fund the 13th AHV/AVS pension, which will be paid from December 1, CHF4.2 billion ($5.06 billion) will be required in 2026. This figure is expected to rise to around CHF4.5 billion in 2030 and CHF5.4 billion in 2040.
Parliament has opted for funding solely through VAT, rejecting a parallel 0.2-point increase in employees’ contributions. The 0.4-point rise in VAT will generate CHF1.5 billion per year.
+ Swiss Senate backs mixed financing for 13th pension
The reduced rate will remain at 2.6%. The VAT increase for the accommodation sector will be 0.2 percentage points, rising from 3.8% to 4%.
This change will not be sufficient in the long term. In its AHV2030 reform proposal, the government has included a scenario for additional funding for the 13th pension. Both the left and the right have voiced criticism.

British cavalry tests horses for battlefield patrols
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:01:42 BST
18:01:42 KST

The British Army has been experimenting with the use of horses for reconnaissance, patrol and security tasks in terrain where military vehicles may struggle to operate, according to imagery released by the Ministry of Defence.
Soldiers and Military Working Horses from the Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment took part in a mounted combat capability experiment on the Barossa training area at Sandhurst, exploring how mounted troops could support battlefield activity beyond the Regiment’s familiar ceremonial duties.
The training was conducted across difficult terrain and focused on environments where conventional vehicles could face restrictions, giving soldiers an opportunity to examine how horses might provide an alternative means of moving personnel during reconnaissance and security operations.
Images from the exercise show Household Cavalry soldiers conducting mounted patrols in pairs while using the SA80 sighting system to locate and track simulated enemy positions. The experiment focused on reconnaissance, patrol and security roles, with troops required to operate from horseback while maintaining observation of the surrounding terrain and identifying potential enemy activity.
The use of horses gives mounted personnel a different mobility profile from troops operating in vehicles, particularly across ground where access routes may be narrow, broken or otherwise unsuitable for conventional platforms. The Sandhurst activity was specifically intended to examine their use in such environments rather than establish a new Army-wide mounted combat role.
According to the MOD caption accompanying the imagery, the activity drew on lessons from international partners while exploring how mounted troops could contribute to patrol and security missions.
Military horses have historically been used for reconnaissance, transport and mounted patrols, although mechanisation removed them from most frontline roles during the 20th century. The Sandhurst experiment examined whether some of those characteristics could still have relevance in specific modern operating environments where access, terrain and mobility create problems for vehicles.
The mounted patrol serial took place on 23 September at the Barossa training area, with soldiers and horses working together to test reconnaissance and security techniques in terrain selected to challenge conventional movement.

The euro slid to its weakest level against the US dollar since May 2025 on Monday, as France's debt troubles and Spain's political turmoil, capped by a snap election call, fuelled fears of a fresh eurozone crisis and of contagion across the bloc's bond markets.
The euro fell to a 17-month low against the US dollar at the start of the week, as fiscal and political risks in Paris and Madrid revived memories of the eurozone debt crisis.
The euro touched $1.1161 during Asian trading, after four consecutive weekly losses, and stood at around $1.12 at the European open, recovering slightly.
Analysts at Dutch bank ING warned in a note on Friday that the market could "easily add another 2% in risk premium to the euro" if the bond sell-off extended.
The spread between French and German 10-year bond yields stands at roughly 146 basis points, after the largest weekly increase in 17 years last week, according to data provider LSEG.
France's 10-year yield rose to 4.917% in early trading on Monday, close to last week's 24-year high, after closing Friday at around 4.856%.
French Finance Minister Roland Lescure insisted last week that France remained a solid borrower, unveiling a 2027 budget that aims to cut the deficit from 5.4% of GDP to 5%, ahead of next spring's presidential election.
Spain added to the political uncertainty on Monday, when Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap general election for 29 November, after the parliament rejected two of his minority government's housing decrees on Friday.
Spain's 10-year yield was mostly steady between 4.07% and 4.09% on Monday morning, leaving its premium over German debt at around 65 basis points, less than half of France's current gap.
Against this backdrop, European stocks were mixed at the open.
The Euro Stoxx 50 fell 0.4%, and the broader Stoxx 600 rose 0.6%.
France's CAC 40 fell more than 1%, while Spain's IBEX 35, which slipped into the red after Sánchez's announcement, was 0.4% higher.
Meanwhile, Germany's DAX, Italy's FTSE MIB, the UK's FTSE 100 and the Netherlands' AEX traded between 0.1% and 0.3% higher.
Contagion fears test the ECB
Last week's sell-off also hit Italian, Belgian and Greek bonds, while German debt drew safe-haven demand. Italy's premium over Bunds neared 110 basis points on Thursday.
Analysts at Belgian bank KBC wrote in a note on Monday that there had been "clear contagion towards the likes of Belgium or Italy" since then.
The turmoil leaves the European Central Bank in a bind.
It has raised rates twice since June to tame inflation, which hit 3.8% in September, but traders have pared bets on more hikes.
Its Transmission Protection Instrument, a bond-buying backstop created in 2022, has never been used.
Speaking at a think tank event on Thursday, Joachim Nagel, head of Germany's Bundesbank and a likely candidate for the ECB's next presidency, said the central bank's focus was price stability, not "certain spread levels".
Asked about France, ECB President Christine Lagarde told French daily La Croix last week that "when your debt is close to 120% of GDP and not on course to be brought under control, it's a serious matter".
However, Lagarde asserted that "it's not 2008 or 2011".
Wall Street rallies after weak jobs data
US stocks climbed on Friday after the American economy added just 29,000 jobs in September, far fewer than expected, prompting traders to pare bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike in October.
The S&P 500 rose 0.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average 0.5% and the Nasdaq Composite 1.2%.
US futures were mostly flat on Monday, except for the Nasdaq-100, which was about 0.5% lower.
The minutes from the Fed's September meeting are due on Wednesday.

The Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea.

Ex-Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon to appear at New York City hearing on AI
NEW YORK – Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who warned that artificial intelligence could become too powerful for humans to control, will testify on Oct 5 at a New York City Council hearing, alongside representatives of some of the world’s biggest AI companies.
Coxon will appear at the request of Council Speaker Julie Menin, who has urged AI whistleblowers to testify as city lawmakers weigh a package of bills aimed at establishing safeguards around the technology, according to people familiar with the matter.
Coxon quit Anthropic in September and issued a stark warning about the race to develop increasingly powerful AI, accusing his former employer and OpenAI of “gambling with our lives”. He confirmed he plans to testify on Oct 5.
The hearing will put some of the industry’s most vocal critics in the same room as representatives of Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet’s Google and Meta.
Former Google DeepMind researcher Alex Turner and Daniel Kokotajlo, executive director of the AI Futures Project and a former OpenAI researcher, are also expected to testify, according to one of the people. Turner confirmed he plans to attend the hearing. Kokotajlo could not be reached for comment.
Menin’s office said Anthropic will be represented by Logan Graham, head of its Frontier Red Team, which tests advanced AI models for their capabilities and risks.
OpenAI will send Morgan Dwyer, head of policy development and operations; Meta will send Shane Cahill, an AI policy director; and Google will be represented by AI policy executive Alice Friend.
A spokesperson for Google declined to comment. Representatives for the other companies did not respond to requests for comment.
The hearing is part of an effort by New York officials to play a larger role in regulating an industry that has expanded rapidly in the city, even as much of AI regulation remains the province of federal and state governments.
One proposal before the council, sponsored by Menin, would give whistleblowers a portion of fines or penalties recovered from AI companies following reported violations.
Other legislation under consideration would allow people harmed by AI systems to sue developers under certain circumstances and require third-party validation of some systems before they can be deployed in the city.
OpenAI, Anthropic and Google agreed to appear after Menin’s office warned that they could be subpoenaed, while Meta had committed to attending earlier, Bloomberg News previously reported. The council subpoenaed SpaceX’s artificial intelligence unit after it failed to respond to requests to appear.
Officials from Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration will also testify, including Samuel Levine, commissioner of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, and Sarah Milstein, deputy commissioner at the Office of Technology and Innovation. BLOOMBERG

Bulgarian National Television Ends the Ukrainian-Language News Program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:01:00 UTC
18:01:00 KST

The Bulgarian National Television (BNT) has ended its Ukrainian-language news broadcast, presenter and editor Maria Plachkova, a Bessarabian Bulgarian, said in a Facebook post.
The program was launched in 2023 for Ukrainian citizens who came to Bulgaria and began building new lives there after the outbreak of the war.
“The Ukrainian-language news on Bulgarian National Television is ceasing broadcast,” Plachkova wrote, describing it as a great honor to have worked as the program’s presenter and editor since it began.
She said the broadcasts covered developments in Ukraine as well as Ukrainians living in Bulgaria, focusing on their lives, stories and experiences between the two countries.
Plachkova began her journalism career in Ukraine by producing a Bulgarian-language program for the Bulgarian community there. She later described the Ukrainian-language program in Bulgaria as a continuation of that connection.
“And in Bulgaria, from the very beginning, we spoke about Ukraine - about what was happening there, about Ukrainians in Bulgaria, and about our shared history and culture,” Plachkova wrote.
She also expressed gratitude for Bulgaria’s support for Ukraine since the beginning of the full-scale war and said Bulgarians in Ukraine had a role connecting the two countries, cultures and peoples.
“Bulgaria has supported Ukraine since the very first days of the full-scale war, and I am sincerely grateful for that—especially today, when this support matters so much. We, the Bulgarians of Ukraine, have the distinct honor and responsibility of serving as a bridge between two states, two cultures, and two peoples,” Plachkova said.
For her, she added, the program went beyond reporting news because each broadcast involved people and their personal experiences and hopes. She described the broadcasts as a form of support and assistance that gave Ukrainians an opportunity to be heard, while thanking everyone who had contributed to the program.
In an earlier social media post, Plachkova had indicated that the Ukrainian-language broadcast could be discontinued.
She said she had worked at BNT for four and a half years and had spent the last three as editor and presenter of the Ukrainian-language news. She said she first learned about the program’s low viewership and the conclusion that there was insufficient interest when the issue was presented to the Council for Electronic Media (CEM).
“I have been working at BNT for four and a half years, and for the last three, I have served as the editor and presenter of the Ukrainian-language news. I learned about the low viewership figures and the conclusion regarding a lack of interest only during the presentation before the Council for Electronic Media (CEM). Prior to that, I had not been made aware of any such analysis or any decision concerning the format's future,” Plachkova stated.
She said she had repeatedly raised the issue with BNT management and submitted letters with questions and proposals for developing the program but received no response.
Plachkova also said the broadcasts were mainly posted on BNT’s website rather than YouTube, while business trips and opportunities to produce reports on location had been suspended.
“The news broadcasts were published primarily on the BNT website without being uploaded to YouTube, and business trips and opportunities for on-site filming were suspended. Therefore, I believe that the assessment should take into account not only viewership figures but also the way the content was produced and distributed,” she said in a statement on September 25.
She argued that the Ukrainian-language news was part of BNT’s public service role and was important for people living, working or staying in Bulgaria.
“To me, the Ukrainian-language news is part of BNT’s public service mandate and is significant for people living, working, or staying in Bulgaria. Consequently, I believe that before a final conclusion is reached regarding the necessity of this information product, it is important to consider all circumstances surrounding its creation, distribution, and viewership,” Plachkova stated on September 25.
The latest broadcast currently listed in the Ukrainian-language section of BNT’s website was published on July 17, 2026.

It’s time to abolish ICE | Amy Fischer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:00:52 UTC
18:00:52 KST

ICE must be abolished.
That’s the conclusion we at Amnesty International have reached after documenting the chilling pattern of human rights violations across the US during immigration enforcement operations.
ICE’s record of violating human rights has been documented for more than two decades, but our latest findings show that the abuses go well beyond a series of incidents. Instead, under the Trump administration, there is a clear pattern that has reached a new and dangerous scale.
In large-scale immigration enforcement operations in Chicago, Minneapolis-St Paul, New Orleans and Washington DC, we documented federal agents repeatedly racially profiling and arbitrarily detaining people based on their perceived race. Agents also targeted workplaces and neighborhoods that they associated with Black and brown immigrant communities. I spoke with dozens of people – including Indigenous people, Black and brown US citizens, and people with legal immigration status who were also racially profiled, stopped and arbitrarily detained.
In all of the cities, people told me about federal officers using intimidation and unlawful force, including lethal force, against people they were attempting to detain, as well as community members observing or defending their neighbors. Agents broke down doors with guns drawn, smashed vehicle windows without justification and threw people to the ground. They used teargas and pepper spray against protesters and observers in public places, often impacting children and the surrounding neighborhoods. They also used facial recognition technology, drones and helicopters to unlawfully surveil people and intimidate them at the same time. As a Washington DC resident, I remember the helicopters shaking the windows of my home.
We documented abuses inside detention facilities as well. I heard harrowing stories from people who were held for prolonged periods in overcrowded and unsanitary facilities not designed for long-term detention, with minimal food, no access to healthcare, and severely restricted access to lawyers. We have concluded that these conditions constitute cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment and, in some circumstances, may amount to torture. We also documented unlawful incommunicado detention and possible acts of enforced disappearance, including cases in which families and lawyers could not locate people in ICE custody. I listened to panicked family members desperately seeking their loved ones who had been snatched by masked men in their communities, without a trace and no way to locate them.
The significance of our findings is not simply the brutality of individual incidents. It is their consistency. These violations were committed across four cities, involving different communities, operations and agents, yet they were strikingly similar. They are characteristic of the Trump administration’s cruel mass detention and deportation machine, including an immigration enforcement system in which safeguards have been weakened, oversight dismantled and accountability having become nothing more than a buzzword.
When a pattern of human rights violations is so undeniably occurring and completely embedded within an institution, for decades, and with pervasive impunity, the only solution is to start over. That’s why we are calling for ICE to be abolished.
The Trump administration’s deliberately cruel and racist practices have left entire communities across the US living in fear. Families are being torn apart. My friends are being deported. People are afraid to leave home to go to work, take their children to school or seek medical care.
The United States has an obligation to respect and protect the human rights of all of us. Immigration enforcement does not exempt any government from that responsibility. Yet the Trump administration has turned the country’s immigration enforcement system into a monster which repeatedly violates people’s rights.
ICE is not an inevitable feature of the US government. It was created in the aftermath of 9/11 to turn immigration into a national security issue, and has been problematic since.
However, the scale and horror that we have witnessed since January 2025, fueled by billions of new dollars and persistent impunity, has reached new levels. It has become clear that no amount of defunding, training or disciplinary measures will be enough. The extent and scale of the abuses and failures we documented lead to only one possible road to justice: ICE must be abolished.
But we can’t stop there. A future without ICE is not the end of the work. It’s a threshold step toward building an immigration system that complies with international human rights law and standards, centers family unity and compassion, and does not rely on cruelty and fear.
In fact, across the four cities we investigated, communities have refused to accept cruelty and fear as inevitable. People have built rapid-response networks and hotlines. They walk neighbors to school and work. They provide food, financial assistance, legal support and medical care. They document abuses. They support families who have been torn apart. They protect one another. Their solidarity shows us what communities can do when people refuse to abandon one another.
We don’t have to look farther than these communities to know that we can create a future where all of us are cared for, ICE agents don’t have free rein to terrorize our communities, where government power is subject to accountability, and where every person can enjoy their human rights.
It is past time to build an immigration system grounded in human rights and human dignity. It starts by abolishing ICE.
- Amy Fischer is director of refugee and migrant rights at Amnesty International USA

Shortages of crucial HIV medicines due to aid cuts are a ‘warning’, say experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:00:52 UTC
18:00:52 KST

Aid cuts have affected HIV drug and test supplies across the world, with some providers reporting they are out of stock of key medicines, according to a survey of 40 countries.
Organisations providing HIV care revealed that more than half (55%) had run out of stock within the past year, with a critical scarcity of HIV tests and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) – a prescription medicine that people take to reduce the risk of getting HIV.
The survey by the International Planned Parenthood Federation (IPPF), a network of organisations in more than 170 countries dedicated to sexual and reproductive health, rights and justice, showed that at the time of questioning, 40% of its members reported they had run out of all stock of a product and 60% had at least one product at low stock levels.
Mallah Tabot, a senior adviser at IPPF Africa’s regional office, said: “These shortages are a warning of what happens when funding becomes uncertain and the supply systems communities depend on grow fragile.
“We cannot let decades of progress against HIV be undone simply because products aren’t available. This is not a distant risk – it is already happening.
“HIV infections are rising in a number of countries around the world and lives are being lost,” she added.
Findings from the 40 member associations that responded to the survey revealed that HIV rapid diagnostic tests were the most critically affected product across all respondents.
Testing is provided by almost every responding member association, yet 17 reported low stock and a further five reported no availability, meaning that more than half cannot offer sustained HIV testing at the point of care.
Oral and injectable PrEP were also scarce, with 12 member associations reporting low stock or none at all. Without reliable access to these basic commodities, there will be gaps and interruptions in care for people seeking healthcare from IPPF member associations.
In general, respondents from the Arab world, Asia and Oceania, Europe, the Americas and the Caribbean said supplies, including condoms and antiretroviral therapy, were unreliable.
Lori Miller, an HIV adviser for IPPF, said: “Our partners already have what it takes to deliver integrated HIV prevention, testing and treatment – the clinic networks, digital infrastructure, health workforce and community trust to reach people with care – but unreliable supplies are letting them down.”
An estimated 40.9 million people were living with HIV worldwide last year, when there were 570,000 Aids-related deaths recorded, alongside 1.2 million new HIV infections.
In 2025, HIV responses around the world were disrupted by cuts that threatened to stall years of progress. That year, there was a fall in aid spending of about 23% compared with 2024, leading the UN to warn in June of the risk of a resurgence of the HIV epidemic.

‘Defend our men!’: fears for women’s rights in Latin America over plans to counter gender violence laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:00:52 UTC
18:00:52 KST

The Chilean senator Vanessa Kaiser is on a mission. In her view, men are under attack and need to be protected from the wrongs that feminism has brought about, including a barrage of false accusations of gender-based and sexual violence. “I want to be the first minister in the history of the west to defend men,” she says.
“I want to defend you against the idea that, simply for being born male, you are guilty,” she said in July, speaking about a proposed bill that would create sanctions for falsely reporting domestic violence and sexual assaults. “Because now, on top of all the burdens we already had, thanks to those horrible ideologies called feminism and the gender perspective, we have to defend our men.”
Kaiser’s comments capture a belief gaining ground across Latin America: that laws introduced to protect women from violence have gone too far, leaving men vulnerable to malicious accusations. Now, politicians across the region are beginning to turn that argument into legislation.
In Bolivia, Chile, Argentina and Peru, lawmakers have proposed bills that would toughen punishments and, in some cases, create new procedures for people found to have made false reports, with a particular focus on cases involving domestic, sexual or gender-based violence.
Individually, the measures are presented as safeguards against fabricated allegations. Taken together, women’s rights groups say they reflect a growing – and disturbing – narrative that women routinely misuse laws intended to protect them, one they say risks making victims too afraid to report abuse in the first place.
That the bills have been presented almost in “parallel” suggests that conservative groups campaigning against women’s rights are pursuing a broader and coordinated regional strategy, according to Paula Ávila-Guillén, director of the US-based Women’s Equality Centre. “The likelihood of it being a coincidence is very low.”
And the proposals are advancing despite scant evidence that such cases of false accusations are widespread – and that false reporting already exists as a criminal offence in each of the countries concerned.
In Bolivia, MPs have proposed an amendment to Law 348, the country’s legislation on violence against women, which would introduce prison sentences of up to six years for falsely reporting gender-based violence.
Another bill, approved in general terms by senators in July, would toughen penalties for false criminal accusations more broadly, while creating aggravated penalties for allegations involving gender-based violence and sexual offences.
In Argentina, a bill pending before the senate would also significantly increase penalties for false accusations. A version approved by a senate committee in April would raise the current maximum sentence from one to three years, and to as much as six years for allegations involving gender-based violence, sexual offences or violence against children. A newer version removes the explicit reference to gender-based violence, replacing it with “serious intentional crimes” – an undefined category that lawyers warn could still encompass many of the same cases.
Chile has gone further, proposing a special procedure for alleged false complaints arising from family court proceedings, which include cases of domestic violence – and sexual offences. The procedure could be triggered after an acquittal, dismissal or other decision rejecting an allegation, with a finding against the complainant potentially leading to compensation, public retraction and criminal proceedings.
In Peru, lawmakers have proposed harsher penalties specifically for false allegations involving violence against women or the family, with sentences of up to six years in prison.
In Bolivia, supporters of a similar bill say the measures are necessary to protect people wrongly accused of serious crimes and reinforce the presumption of innocence. Defending the proposal in a the legislative assembly, the senator José Manuel Ormachea, from the right-wing Alianza Libre party, said: “We need regulations that counterbalance Law 348 [outlawing violence against women].”
In Chile, Kaiser presented the bill as a response to what she describes as widespread abuse of the justice system. “Today, false accusations are a tumour in our society, spreading like cancer, claiming more and more victims,” she said on the senate television programme Profundidad de Campos.
But researchers say there is little evidence that false accusations are a serious problem.
Official national statistics on false accusations do not exist in Chile. In Bolivia, false-accusation claims accounted for 0.13% of all the cases filed in 2024, according to the public prosecutor’s office. In Argentina, a report from the public prosecutor’s office found that false-report investigations represented about one in every 1,000 criminal cases examined between 2023 and 2025 – just 0.09%. In jurisdictions able to break the cases down further, only 8% of all false-report cases related to gender-based or intrafamilial violence.
The far greater problem, critics say, is that violence often goes unreported. In Chile, data shows that most gender-based or sexual violence is never reported at all. In a 2024 government survey, just 12.1% of women who had experienced sexual violence said they had reported their most recent experience.
Meanwhile, only 15% of women who were victims of femicide in Argentina in 2025 had previously reported violence, according to the country’s national femicide register. Another survey found that among women who had experienced violence from their partner, 77% had not filed a complaint.
“For years women have been afraid to report because nobody believed them,” says Ávila-Guillén. “This risks sending us backwards, even to before the #MeToo movement, where women are not only discouraged from reporting sexual violence and harassment, but now also risk being sent to prison if the accusation is not successful.”
In Bolivia, Martín Vidaurre, a policy coordinator for Ipas, an international non-profit organisation specialising in reproductive health, says women already face significant barriers when reporting violence, from an overstretched justice system to economic obstacles and institutional prejudice. Yet a powerful counter-narrative has taken hold: that women routinely abuse the system through false reports.
“There’s a narrative that when you report a case, a man can immediately go to jail. There’s a narrative that women use this law against men when they are bad to them, when they want to divorce them,” he says. “They’re saying that this law, 348, against the violence against women, is actually a law against men.”
Vidaurre says that in practice women may report abuse but later abandon proceedings because they cannot afford legal costs, while overstretched prosecutors, police and judges struggle with heavy caseloads.
Similar conditions exist in Peru. Susana Chávez, a prominent women’s rights advocate and director of Promsex, which defends reproductive rights, says victims often report only repeated or extreme violence, and can then face scepticism from police, lengthy court proceedings and a large backlog of cases when they do so. Some abandon their cases because an abusive partner makes continuing to support their children conditional on dropping proceedings. “It’s very difficult, already, to confront the issue or speak out against it,” she says.
It is against such a backdrop that campaigners see the growing focus on false allegations as part of a much larger political battle.
Chávez described the proposals as part of “a very organised, very large packet” pushed by an anti-women’s rights faction that has also sought to dismantle sexuality education, remove references to gender and eliminate inclusive language. “It’s a very coordinated, orchestrated agenda,” she says.
Over the past decade, women’s movements have become an increasingly powerful force across Latin America. Ni Una Menos (Not One [woman] Less), which began in Argentina in 2015 as a protest against femicide, spread rapidly across the region, while the “green wave” for abortion rights helped propel important reforms in Argentina, Mexico and Colombia.
At the same time, conservative movements have increasingly mobilised against what they describe as “gender ideology” – a label used to challenge policies ranging from abortion and sexuality education to LGBTQ+ rights and protections against violence against women.
“We have a very strong presence of the ultra-conservative sector in the [Peruvian] congress,” says Chávez. “These policies put at risk the entire spectrum of sexual justice and reproductive justice. It is a very complex amalgam that sets women back by at least 50 years.”
In Argentina, Natalia Gherardi, lawyer and director of the feminist organisation Latin American Team for Justice and Gender, sees the proposed bills as part of the same ideological fight. Since taking office, the government of the far-right president, Javier Milei, has abolished the ministry of women, gender and diversity and later shut down its successor office for protection against gender-based violence, while cutting or scrapping a series of programmes aimed at supporting women and LGBTQ+ people. It has also sought to remove femicide from the penal code as a specific category.
“The government in Argentina has built a cultural battle around the idea that feminism has gone too far, and that women should be put back in their place, and that all gender-based violence allegations are an invention of feminism,” she says.
The series of false accusation bills has now attracted the attention of the regional body responsible for monitoring countries’ compliance with the Belém do Pará convention, the inter-American treaty on violence against women.
In August, the committee of experts of Mesecvi, the convention’s monitoring mechanism, issued a strong warning over the initiatives in Argentina and Bolivia. It said the proposed legislation could create an additional legislative barrier to justice, increase fears of retaliation and deepen the re-victimisation of women.
“It is very serious,” says Mónica Maureira, vice-president of Mesecvi. “There is a concerted strategy at the regional level; that is, there are multiple countries in the region that are imposing laws with similar characteristics.”
The committee has also been monitoring similar proposals in Guatemala, Uruguay and Paraguay, Maureira adds.
For Gherardi, the danger lies in the effect such laws could have on women considering whether to report abuse at all. “It will prevent women from looking for protection,” she says.
“If you can’t turn to the judiciary for protection then who will you turn to?”

Plant Life exhibition imagines a future where "plants return as the dominant source"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:00:25 UTC
18:00:25 KST

Plant Life exhibition imagines a future where "plants return as the dominant source"
From a fire jacket grown from fungi to building blocks made from algae and oyster shells, the latest exhibition at Melbourne's National Gallery of Victoria (NGV) explores humanity's relationship with the plant world through design.
Called Plant Life: The Nature of Design, the exhibition features more than 60 works that span furniture, architecture, decorative arts, craft, photography and film.
It spotlights how plant-based materials can be a vital alternative to non-renewable materials and focuses on global Indigenous communities' engagement with the natural environment.
"For most of human culture, up until the discovery and refinement of petrochemical-based products, everything was effectively either plant-, animal-, or mineral-based," senior curator of contemporary design and architecture at NGV Ewan McEoin told Dezeen.
"So this idea of cyclical life was fundamental for thousands of years, across all cultures. What we're trying to do is look at a future where plants return as the dominant source."
A new locally made biomaterial was selected to fabricate the display plinths and surfaces throughout the exhibition.
Called Plantbord, the hemp board was developed by Australian designer Joost Bakker and sustainable building material supplier Forest One. It was bound with the bio-resin Plantics, which, according to McEoin, is the world's first 100 per cent bio-based thermosetting resin.
Here, Dezeen selects eight of the most interesting design and material innovations from the exhibition:
Urgent Is The Rhythm bio-masonry blocks by Kate Scardifield
Sydney-based artist and material researcher Kate Scardifield developed a new building material by combining algae and oyster-shell waste.
In this work, more than a tonne of algae biomass, collected from aquaculture industries in New South Wales and Queensland, was mixed with oyster-shell waste to form biomasonry blocks.
Melbourne-based architecture studio Edition Office designed a series of speculative architectural drawings to imagine buildings made from the material.
It envisions algae being processed into blocks, tiles and facade panels to form the building while being cultivated on site at a vast agricultural scale and storing carbon as the building blocks are constructed.
Ecotono Shiringa bio-leather jacket by the Awajún people of the Peruvian Amazon and Mozhdeh Matin
Lima-based textile studio Mozhdeh Matin has worked with the Awajún people of the Peruvian Amazon to develop a plant-based leather jacket.
The indigenous community, which is the guardian of the local shiringa forests, collects milky sap from the trees through shallow cuts on the bark. This is then applied to cotton, which is dried or smoked into a leather-like waterproof material.
These traditional techniques tap shiringa trees without cutting them down, a technique that Matin hopes to preserve.
Activist Emma Håkansson's film Shiringa: Fashion Regenerating Amazonia accompanied the jacket at the exhibition, documenting the indigenous community and their relationship with the forests.
Ply Loop Chair by Joris Laarman
Dutch designer Joris Laarman has created the Ply Loop Chair, using a plant-based thermoset resin derived from agricultural waste streams to bind plywood.
The new material, called Plantics, replaces the conventional toxic urea-formaldehyde adhesives that are commonly used in furniture. According to Laarman, it is non-toxic, recyclable and biodegradable.
The continuous looping form of the chair was enabled by digital design and fabrication.
Sensbiom 2.1 by Crafting Plastics
Crafting Plastics, an interdisciplinary studio focusing on circular design, has developed a web-like plant-based plastic alternative that turns pink when exposed to ultraviolet (UV) radiation.
Sensbiom 2.1 is a modular architectural installation made from the material, which can be used as partitions or light-filtering surfaces.
The biopolymer lattices change colour in response to UV radiation, allowing the otherwise invisible environmental conditions to be perceived by viewers.
Resting Place daybed by Fernando Laposse
Designer Fernando Laposse has created a daybed using patches of fabrics dyed with avocado-seed pigment and marigold flowers to cover the surface of the piece.
The patchwork was informed by the Japanese Boro technique, where damaged textile is repaired through patching. It was stitched with images of guns and chainsaws to reference repairing a broken system.
Laposse aimed to raise awareness of the surging global avocado demand, which has led to a social and ecological crisis in Mexico, where the majority of the world's avocados are grown.
Banet dining chair naked by Bart Schilder
Dutch designer Bart Schilder created this dining chair with hemp fibre and fungi.
The inner core of the chair was made primarily of hemp fibre and fused with mycelium, a root-like network of fungi that acts as a natural adhesive.
The growth of the fungi was stopped through drying and heat treatment to ensure no living fungi remain in the chair core.
According to the designer, producing this dining chair generates approximately five kilograms of carbon dioxide — roughly one seventh of an equivalent plastic chair.
Lanh My A black silk by Lo Silk
Vietnamese fashion house Lo Silk has created a traditional Ao Dai – one of Vietnam's most recognisable female ceremonial dresses – using Lanh My A, a rare black silk textile.
The black dye was achieved through a plant-based process, unique to the town of Tan Chau in Vietnam's Mekong Delta region.
The silk is soaked in the resin of mac nua, the fruit of the Diospyros Mollis tree, whose resin darkens through oxidation. The resulting textile was then sun-dried, washed and beaten repeatedly in Mekong River water to further deepen the blackness.
Mycelium Wildfire Jacket, by Judith Glover, Tien Huynh, Mohamad Arekha Bentangan and Alexi Freeman for RMIT University
Industrial designer Judith Glover, material scientist Tien Huynh, microbiologist Mohamad Arekha Bentangan and bio-designer Alexi Freeman have collaborated to develop this fire jacket using fungi-grown materials for a new commission from RMIT University.
The prototype was fabricated from mycelium leather, a biomaterial cultivated from fungal networks grown from agricultural waste in controlled environmental conditions.
According to the team, the material is able to self-extinguish when exposed to flame, through further manipulation that extends its durability, fire resistance and thermal insulation.
The photography is by Sean Fennessy unless stated otherwise.
Plant Life: The Nature of Design will be on display at The Ian Potter Centre: NGV Australia from 28 August 2026 to 7 February 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

Staples Print and Marketing Services Review: Fast Holiday Gifts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

I print all the time, and not just because I test printers, but because I like paper. It doesn't matter if they're documents, photos, posters, or banners; I like artifacts—everything is better in physical form. And it's not just dinosaurs like me; while eschewing digital media, Gen Z is embracing printed matter, too (see, the kids are alright).
I've lost track of how many photo books I've printed over the years—mostly one-offs of little projects, fun things for friends, and maybe five copies at most. I'm not a photographer anymore, but old habits die hard, especially when you see the way people react to paper books. The response to a book, versus showing someone your latest Instagram post, is not even comparable.
With the holiday season kicking off, it seems apropos to point out that photo books make great gifts, as do mugs, prints, and my personal favorite for kids: photo puzzles. I've tested dozens of printing services over the years, and one of my favorites for holiday gifts is Staples.
You can order Staples prints online through the company's website, which features a variety of tools to help you design your photo gift, be it a mug, print, or puzzle. The print quality is great, and the online tools are well done and easy to use. But while ordering online is convenient, it's not why I like Staples for printing. It's because I can go to my local store and talk to actual human beings about my printing needs.
Printing can be tricky, and preparing your digital files exactly how the printer wants them isn't always easy. Best practice is to provide a high-res, flattened PDF file in CMYK color, but if you don't know what that means or how to get your file into the right format, fear not. The best way to print, even if you do know how to format it accurately, is to bring the file to your local Staples and talk to the print and marketing specialists there. They can catch potential issues before you print, and in most cases they can print a proof (sometimes at a reduced size, but still a proof) so you can see what you're getting beforehand. This is one advantage over online-only services.
Another big advantage is that you can get your gifts the same day if you pick up in-store. If you're in a rush this holiday season, remember that tip. You can even order online and pick up in-store to save yourself a trip, just be sure the place your order before noon.
Want to really step up your game? Here's my pro tip. Head to your local Staples to place your order, but have them print it at a Staples production center. Tell the store to have the production center send proofs for you to approve in person. This eliminates the same-day advantage, as it will likely take several days—sometimes as much as two weeks—but the printing quality will be better.
What's the quality like? I printed a couple of 11-ounce mugs—other options include a 15-ounce mug and a 17-ounce travel mug—and the results were on par with other services I've tested. I happen to like the shape of the Staples mugs a little more than what I got from others, but that's more personal preference than anything. For the design, you can choose a premade template and upload a photo of your choice, or you can start from scratch and design your own mug. As with all Staples printing services, you can choose same-day pickup if you want five or fewer. For larger orders, you'll need to get them delivered.
The photo options, like mounted prints, are nice. The print quality here lags behind dedicated photo services like our top picks, Mpix and Printique, but for the price it's quite good (both Mpix and Printique are more expensive). They offer canvas prints, metal prints, foam-backed prints, and posters up to 36 by 48 inches.
Staples is also a great place for business printing. I'm in the process of transitioning back to running a business, and the first thing I did wasn't setting up an Instagram account or doing anything with social media. The first thing I did was print business cards. Staples online business card maker is fantastic. And if I had a physical presence for my business, I'd have printed banners and posters and signs and everything else. Because we live in the real world, and if you want your business to succeed offline, you're going to need to print.

No plane, no gain: US aviation sanctions ground ordinary Iranians while missing the regime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

An 86-year-old father stranded in California shows the real human toll of US air sanctions on Iran
Borzou Daragahi for The Straits Times
- The US sanctions on Iran's aviation sector have severely restricted travel and commerce, causing cancellations and complicating access to medicines and essential goods.
- These sanctions mainly hurt ordinary Iranians, increasing economic hardship with soaring inflation, job scarcity, and disrupted education and migration plans.
- Experts doubt sanctions will force regime change, warning they may strengthen Iran's leadership while lacking a clear, cohesive US strategy.
AI generated
ISTANBUL – Hossein-Reza’s plans to leave Iran for a trip to see friends and family in the Netherlands in October were waylaid by the US’ imposition of sanctions on the country’s aviation sector in August as part of Operation Economic Outcast – Washington’s attempt to isolate Iran economically.
Would he be able to secure a ticket to Amsterdam, he wondered? Would he be forced to travel by road to neighbouring Turkey or Armenia?
While some respond to such uncertainty with anxiety or even dread, Hossein-Reza, a 40-something documentarist, was relaxed.
After a year in Iran that included chaos and gunfire in the streets, warfare in the skies, internet blockages and economic devastation, as well as questions about the country’s very future, he is taking the travel hiccup in his stride.
“I never even try to book a ticket until a day or two before I have to leave,” he said in an interview, on the condition that his full name not be published.
The Iranians who spoke to the press did so under heavy risk, withholding their full names for fear of official reprisals for communicating with foreign journalists.
The US has placed some of the toughest financial restrictions on Iran ever imposed on an adversary – and the sanctions continue to intensify as the conflict drags on.
The pressure campaign has gone far beyond travel bans on targeted individuals or sanctions on the weapons trade or dual-use goods to include, since September, punishments of third-country companies that do business with 27 airlines and companies in Iran’s civilian airline sector and restrictions on the country’s auto and rail industries.
The result has complicated the supply of some crucial medicines into the country as well as any travel and commerce.
Flights to a number of neighbouring countries – including Iraq, Azerbaijan and Oman – have been cancelled.
However, air travel to Russia and China has not been affected, and sporadic flights to the major air hubs of Istanbul and Dubai continue.
A video posted on social media platform X on Sept 24 showed a flight crew aboard an Iranian Varesh Airlines flight from Tehran to the Tajikistan capital of Dushanbe returning home after its route through Azerbaijani airspace was denied.
The severe sanctions on aviation add to what many describe as growing despair and malaise among many ordinary Iranians.
“Iranians will be resilient as long as there is hope,” said one Western diplomat who recently left Tehran, speaking on condition of anonymity as he was not authorised to speak to the media. “But if there’s no light at the end of the tunnel, there is less reason to stay steadfast.”
Hamidreza Ahmadi, a Tehran tech entrepreneur, described growing frustration among ordinary Iranians as they struggle to understand the uncertainties the conflict has thrust upon their lives.
He described frustration over contradictory statements and goals by US President Donald Trump – from regime change, to a peace deal, to halting a nuclear programme supposedly destroyed in 2025, to reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which was already open before the war began.
“Geopolitically, everyone’s very, very confused,” he said. “Like, what do you mean America’s almost out of munitions? How could that be? They see Iran is getting weaker. They feel that. But they also see a bunch of Iranian missiles and a bunch of drones landing.”
Iranians describe difficulties in securing jobs, with youth unemployment rates estimated to be as high as 50%, a freezing of investment and business expansions, as well as price increases, including for subsidised fuel and petroleum products that are the lifeblood of the Iranian economy.
Prices for some drugs have tripled, according to local reports, while food prices have soared.
Iran’s year-on-year inflation reached 84% in August.
“Sanctions are something that, wherever you are on the political spectrum, affect you on a daily basis, and nobody can see a way out of it,” Ahmadi said in an interview.
In theory, sanctions are supposed to punish the regime rather than ordinary people.
But compliance experts say companies effectively refrain from doing even non-restricted commerce with entities linked to a country as heavily sanctioned as Iran.
Brett Erickson, founder of Obsidian Risk Advisors, a US consultancy focused on international crime and due diligence, told The Straits Times: “Most companies are going to de-risk and just not assume the legal hurdles that need to be jumped through.
“And that’s something we see with Gaza and Yemen and so many countries where technically, it is allowed. But in reality, we see huge shortfalls as a result of companies not wanting to assume the risk.”
Pharmaceuticals and foods are specifically excluded from sanctions, but companies often refrain just to avoid the hassles and hurdles of any trade with Iran.
Trump administration officials and their supporters know that the sanctions hurt ordinary Iranians. But this is precisely the goal – raise public frustrations to a level where the people turn on the regime. Beyond sanctions, the US has very few options, experts said.
“The problem with sanctions is we’ve plucked all the low-hanging fruit,” Alan Eyre, a former US State Department official who was part of the team that negotiated the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran, said in an interview.
“We’ve plucked all the high-hanging fruit. We’ve cut the tree down. So it’s not as if there are a lot of super-duper effective sanctions that we haven’t used.”
The latest round of sanctions significantly differs from previous rounds because they focus on an entire sector of the economy, regardless of whether an individual or company is involved in any activity deemed harmful by the US.
Erickson said: “It essentially just cuts off the entire industry, regardless of whether it has a nexus to someone who is sanctioned by the US.
“It is a very significant measure. And again, it does need to be understood that the overwhelming hardship will be shouldered by the civilian population. Obviously, things can be transshipped into Russia and China and other countries that refuse to play ball, and that will be significant for the Iranian government.”
Observers are closely watching how aggressively Washington attempts to enforce sanctions on third countries such as Turkey or the United Arab Emirates, as well as China, which has vowed to ignore them.
But the sanctions may be the most severe that Iranians have faced, and potentially the hardest to circumvent.
Ali Ahmadi (no relation to Hamidreza Ahmadi), a fellow at the Switzerland-based Geneva Centre for Security Policy who regularly travels between Iran and the West, said: “They figure out how to operate within the parameters of the sanctions.”
Ali Ahmadi was recently in Tehran and booked a flight on an obscure airline, which was cancelled at the last minute, but he managed to rebook on a different airline. “When I called the website I was buying the tickets from, they said, pick one of the more reputable, bigger names because they already know how to get through the sanctions,” he recalled.
Others have found the new restrictions more challenging.
Maziar, a 42-year-old in Tehran, is struggling to bring his frail 86-year-old father home from a trip to visit relatives in California.
“I’ve been trying to figure out the least exhausting path for my dad to get back to Iran,” he said, asking that his family name not be disclosed.
“We were hoping to use the Dubai route. But that’s no longer an option. We’re going to wait it out a bit longer and hope for a better option, and if the situation doesn’t change, we’ll have to use the land border crossing via Turkey.”
Even Iranians sympathetic to the US are angered by the latest US sanctions.
One impact of the latest round of restrictions has been the cancellation of the English-language proficiency tests required for overseas employment or education because the companies running the paid exams fear the wrath of the US Treasury Department.
Iranians who spent years on plans to study or move abroad have suddenly found their dreams thwarted. “On paper, sanctions are supposed to make the government weaker, but how is cancelling tests making the government weaker?” said one Tehran resident, who asked that her name not be published.
Even as prices of food and medicine in Iran increase, there have been no reported shortages of luxury goods – another sign that the sanctions are mostly squeezing the poor.
Observers have criticised the US strategy as rudderless, aimed more at satisfying Washington hawks’ demands for action rather than part of a cohesive strategy.
Ahmadi from the Geneva Centre said: “Within the context of US policy as a whole, pressure for pressure’s sake has become ossified. Like you’ve got to do something.
“What’s the next measure? Do that. Istanbul Airport is probably kind of vulnerable to US sanctions. Okay, we’ll threaten to sanction them. There’s no strategy here.”
Iran experts, including former US officials, have publicly voiced doubt that ratcheting up economic pressure will convince the Iranian government to give in to US demands – in fact, it could have the opposite effect.
Eyre, the former State Department official, said: “The people running Iran think that if they just show any weakness in the face of all this pressure, it’s going to lead to them being swept out of power. That’s why sanctions are unlikely to work.”

France becomes Europe’s ‘weakest link’ under Macron’s leadership — news agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:59:26 UTC
17:59:26 KST

NEW YORK, October 5. /TASS/. Nearly 10 years of President Emmanuel Macron’s rule have turned France into Europe’s "weakest link," Bloomberg reported.
Macron came to power in 2017 as a business-oriented politician who sought to bring about an "economic and political revolution" in France. However, the president’s political movement will "be effectively over" after he leaves office in 2027, and the promised "revolution" never led to a change in France’s economic policy, in which government spending plays a significant role compared to other Western countries, the article noted.
"After a decade of political missteps and global cataclysms that made government spending his (Macron’s - TASS) go-to solution, popular anger is rising, growth is sinking, debt is soaring and investors are dumping French assets in a global bond market rout that has made it the euro area’s weakest economic link," William Horobin, the article’s author, pointed out.
According to him, the final battle to preserve the legacy of "Macronomics" will be the passage of next year’s French budget in parliament. Even if the minority government puts together a credible budget proposal, Macron’s potential successors, opposition leaders Marine Le Pen Le Pen and Jean-Luc, who are leading in the polls, could roll back all of his reforms. "The messy end" to a decade in power contrasts with the proclaimed vision of making France "the powerhouse of a retooled Europe with the heft to stand for itself as [US President] Donald Trump undermines NATO from within," the author stressed. The conflict in Ukraine and the difficulty of balancing relations between the US and China only increase the likelihood that populist political forces will come to power in France, which "threatens to overtake what’s left of the post-World War II order," he argued.
According to Horobin, key moments of Macron’s presidency include the attempt to reform fossil fuel taxation in 2018, which led to mass protests by the Yellow Vest movement, a radical increase in government spending following the pandemic and energy crisis, costing the treasury approximately 262 billion euros, and the decision to call for early parliamentary elections in 2024. France’s public finances and Macron’s political capital have not recovered since then, the author emphasized.
