Polymarket goes to court to overturn Dutch gambling ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:56:40 UTC
17:56:40 KST

Polymarket goes to court to overturn Dutch gambling ban
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
US prediction platform Polymarket has gone to court in The Hague to overturn a Dutch ban on its services, arguing that it sells financial products, rather than bets.
The company confirmed the case to the Financieele Dagblad. The judges will reportedly be asked to decide whether betting on real-world events counts as gambling, which the Dutch gambling regulator Ksa says that it is.
Polymarket argues that it is more like trading in derivatives, which should be supervised by financial markets regulator AFM.
Polymarket users buy contracts that pay out in USDC, a type of cryptocurrency whose value is equal to the US dollar, if a particular event does or does not happen. The company says this is comparable to futures contracts traded on financial markets.
Fines and bans
The Ksa ordered Polymarket to stop serving Dutch users in an order dated January 20 and made public on February 17. It said the platform was offering games of chance without a licence and threatened a penalty of €420,000 a week, up to a maximum of €840,000.
Polymarket stopped Dutch users from placing bets later in February, but the regulator ruled it had acted too late and in May demanded €420,000, and rejected the company’s objection in June.
The platform drew widespread attention in the Netherlands after users staked millions of dollars on the outcome of the October 2025 general election.
Only sport
According to the Ksa, Dutch law only allows betting on sport, so a licence would not be an option for Polymarket either.
“Prediction markets are on the rise, in the Netherlands too,” Ksa director Ella Seijsener said in a statement in February. “These types of companies offer bets which are not allowed on our market under any circumstances, not even by licence holders.”
Last week, MPs voted down a motion from the far-right Forum for Democracy (FvD) asking the government to look into regulating prediction markets as a separate category within gambling law.
Gambling lawyer Micha Schimmel told the FD he gives Polymarket’s case little chance. He pointed to a 2015 ruling which found that a service can be a financial product and still count as gambling. Polymarket is also banned in France and Germany.

VKG pushes back cellulose plant timeline as search for investors continues

VKG pushes back cellulose plant timeline as search for investors continues
The company has yet to find a way to build its bioproducts plant in Europe at a low enough cost to compete on the global market.
When VKG unveiled plans to build a cellulose plant in summer 2021, the company hoped to open the facility in Ida-Viru County five years later. Instead of opening the plant, however, the company is still searching for potential investors this year.
This year, VKG also relinquished a 10-year long-term contract with the State Forest Management Center (RMK) for the purchase of raw materials.
According to VKG CEO Ahti Asmann, the company is looking for ways to make the project more profitable.
"The situation with the bioproducts plant is complicated. We have indeed been in talks with investors and we have come to understand that using a conventional European approach and European prices may make it difficult to compete globally," Asmann said.
After the designated spatial plan was established in spring last year, the company's CEO hoped investors could be found within a year. Under current plans, the company aims to reach an investment decision by the first quarter of 2028. If it has not found an investor by then, the company will assess whether it makes sense to proceed with the planned plant in Lüganuse Municipality.
"We are currently looking for a way to structure the project so that it is competitive and so that the investment can be made at a more reasonable cost," Asmann said.
If the company finds an investor by 2028, the plant is currently expected to begin operations in 2030, four years later than originally planned.
The estimated cost of the plant has risen by 50 percent from the original estimate, from €800 million to €1.2 billion. VKG has invested €2 million in the project to date.
VKG plans to use low-value wood at the plant to produce cellulose, dissolving pulp and biochemicals, with end products used in the textile and biochemical industries, as well as in the paint, food and pharmaceutical industries.
As a byproduct, the bioproducts plant would generate 800 gigawatt-hours of electricity per year. That would amount to around 10 percent of Estonia's current annual electricity consumption.

UK Green Party votes to equate Zionism with racism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:55:56 UTC
17:55:56 KST

On the 4th of October, the UK Green Party voted to classify Zionism as a form of racism, sparking condemnation from British Jews and anger from the Israeli government—which stated it now views the party as an organization that supports terrorism, reports Reuters.
The party, which garnered 6% of the vote in the 2024 parliamentary elections, stated that it regards Zionism as an ethno-nationalist political project and reiterated its call for the UK Labour government to end arms sales to Israel. Zionism is a religious-nationalist political movement advocating for the gathering of all Jews in their historical homeland, the re-establishment and strengthening of a Jewish state, Jewish immigration to Israel, and the displacement of Arabs from the region.
In its statement, the Green Party also noted that the proposal underscores the party's support for the right to self-determination and calls for the creation of a single democratic state within the territory of historic Palestine.
The definition of Zionism—which inspired the founding of the modern State of Israel and addresses the rights of other peoples within Israel and adjacent territories—is a subject of controversy. Jewish groups sometimes describe this as the right to self-determination.
Despite objections from several high-ranking representatives, the Green Party's proposal received majority support within the party:
 1,022 members voted in favor, while 813 voted against. Party leader Zack Polanski did not participate in the vote.
Several British Jewish groups have already condemned the vote. The Progressive Judaism movement stated that the Green Party has made antisemitism part of its policy and has become a racist party. The movement added that the fact that some Jews supported the proposal does not mean it will not be used against others.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar has decided to ban Polanski from entering Israel. The ministry stated that, according to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's definition, the party's proposal constitutes antisemitic rhetoric because it denies Jews the right to self-determination.
On the 3rd of October, Green Party Deputy Leader Mohtin Ali—a supporter of the proposal—told Sky News that the main driving force behind it was the high number of Palestinian casualties in Israel's war against the terrorist group Hamas. He pointed out that the proposal clearly defines Zionism, describing it as an ethno-nationalist movement, ethnic cleansing, and genocide.
The British government regards the actions of Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank as ethnic cleansing,
 though it has noted that the question of whether Israel is committing genocide is a matter for the courts to decide. Israel—which denies both ethnic cleansing and the commission of genocide—called on other British political parties on the 4th of October to condemn the Green Party's vote, stating that the Green Party had adopted not only the color green from Hamas but also an ideology calling for the destruction of the State of Israel through armed struggle.
Polanski and other Green Party representatives said they would continue to speak out against the heinous crimes of Benjamin Netanyahu's government, emphasizing that there is no contradiction in supporting the rights of both Palestinians and Jews.

Spain’s PM Pedro Sanchez calls snap election amid housing crisis

Yemeni government forces claim control of Bab el-Mandeb Strait from Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:54:55 UTC
17:54:55 KST

Sahin Demir
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Yemeni government forces have taken control of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb area from the Houthis as part of the ongoing military operation, “Dawn of Yemen,” the army said Monday.
Military spokesman Lt. Col. Majid Abdullah al-Nuzayli said the pro-government Southern Giants Brigades and Nation’s Shield forces had “successfully taken control of Bab el-Mandeb.”
In a series of statements on US social media platform X, al-Nuzayli said government forces also took control of Dhubab airport and cut the road between Dhubab and Mokha.
He said hundreds of Houthi fighters had been surrounded in the Dhubab area and called on them to surrender, adding that some Houthi fighters later fled by boat via the sea.
Bab el-Mandeb is a strategically important waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea and is a key route for international shipping.

Spain PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:54:25 BST
17:54:25 KST

Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests
- Published
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called an early election for 29 November after recent defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis.
Speculation about a snap election had been building over the weekend after parliament rejected two decree laws put forward by the minority government to protect tenants in the rental market.
The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after she was unable to afford a sharp rent rise has sparked nationwide protests and increased pressure for housing reform.
In a televised address on Monday, Sánchez said that to push reforms through he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites".
Housing has not been the only issue causing problems for Sánchez's leadership in recent months, with his party having been caught up in numerous corruption scandals and facing pressure on other cost-of-living issues and immigration.
"We have made mistakes and have not achieved everything we had set out to do," Sánchez said, acknowledging there were still "a lot of problems to solve, particularly in the areas of inequality, of public services and access to housing".
Sánchez's left-wing coalition government is made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, and does not have a majority in parliament.
Spain was not due to hold a general election until the summer of 2027 at the latest.
Sánchez has been prime minister since June 2018. His Socialist party finished second in the last election, in 2023.
Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, it fell short of a majority.
Sánchez remained in power after striking agreements with left-wing parties and securing support from Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.
Speaking after Monday's announcement, the leader of the People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said: "At last, Spaniards will be able to decide".
The opposition leader said it would not be "just another election", but a chance for voters to choose between "decline or change, lies or change, incompetence or change, division or change, corruption or change".
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people took to the streets in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona, calling for greater protections for tenants.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis when she was forcibly evicted from her Madrid home on 23 September.
A legal glitch allowed her landlord to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650. It was later lowered to €1,650 - still €300 more than her monthly pension.
She was removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years, and was later admitted to hospital.
Her lawyer has since said she will be able to return to her home, but the incident has prompted widespread anger over housing.
The left-wing coalition government responded with two decree laws in an effort to defuse the protests.
The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".
The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas.
The political right argued the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Juan Bravo of the People's Party said last week "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".
Sánchez's leadership has been marred by numerous corruption scandals in recent months.
In April, his wife Begoña Gómez was charged with corruption after a two-year criminal investigation.
She is accused of using her relationship to advance her private career - allegations she denies, and which have been dismissed by Sánchez as a right-wing attempt to undermine his coalition.
In May, police raided the Socialist party's headquarters in Madrid as part of an investigation into allegations an operative was paid to carry out a misinformation campaign. The party has denied the allegations.
And in June, Sánchez's former transport minister, José Luis Ábalos, was jailed for 24 years after he was found guilty of being involved in a network that received kickbacks from the sale of face masks during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The Spanish prime minister also came under scrutiny for his handling of the Ceuta migration crisis over the summer, when tens of thousands of people entered the territory from Morocco without authorisation.

US rushes bombers out of UK base over new terrorist threat – NYT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:53:55 UTC
17:53:55 KST

‘Iran-linked terror plot’ behind US bomber evacuation – NYT
The US has rushed to withdraw bombers from an airbase in the UK after receiving new threat information about an alleged terrorist plot against the facility, the New York Times reports, citing sources.
The announcement cited by the NYT comes a week after five men were arrested in what was trumpeted as a high-level security operation near RAF Fairford, which hosts US bombers used in the war against Iran. However, after a hysterical media reaction in the UK, the five, all British citizens in their early 20s, were released on bail the following day.
Days later, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham claimed that London had “strong indications” that Iran could have been behind the incident, which only came to life after a local farmer called the police, having seen a group of men run from their white vans on a country road when caught in the headlights of her car.
All 12 US Air Force B-1 bombers were withdrawn over the weekend, allegedly after commanders received new warnings concerning a possible Iranian-backed plot against the base, two anonymous US officials told the NYT on Sunday.
Some aircraft had reportedly only arrived the week before as part of a routine rotation. According to the NYT’s sources, the withdrawal was deemed so urgent that several bombers took off without aerial refueling support. At least three bombers reached their home base in South Dakota by Sunday, the officials said.
According to one source, the information was connected to threat warnings that surfaced three weeks earlier, but new details received over the preceding 24 hours alarmed commanders and increased the urgency of withdrawing the bombers. The details were not disclosed.
The Pentagon’s European Command confirmed that the aircraft left England but declined to comment on any new warnings.
“We can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford are redeploying to their home stations in the United States,” the command said in a statement. “US Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements.”
Iran has denied having any involvement. The embassy in London accused Britain of promoting “Iranophobia.” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi rejected Burnham’s allegation, saying he is “barking up the wrong tree.”

Ukraine faces US$8bn loss due to closure of ports
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:53:00 EEST
17:53:00 KST

Ukraine faces US$8bn loss due to closure of ports
Ukraine risks losing at least US$8 billion in export revenue from June 2026 to June 2027 if its Black Sea ports remain closed.
Source: The Financial Times, citing an estimate by Ukraine's Minister of Agrarian Policy Taras Vysotskyi
Details: According to Vysotskyi, such a shortfall would equal approximately 20% of Ukraine's total export revenue for the past year. This represents a forecast based on a prolonged port shutdown, rather than already recorded losses.
Ukraine had planned to export 64 million tonnes of agricultural products this year. However, without the resumption of maritime shipping, Vysotskyi estimates that at best only half of this volume will be successfully exported.
As the FT reports, Russian attacks on vessels and port infrastructure have effectively halted operations along the primary maritime export route. Road transport is significantly more expensive and cannot compensate for its loss.
Even a resumption of shipping would not mean a return to previous volumes. Shota Khajishvili, owner of the Risoil terminal in Chornomorsk, told the publication that following the attacks, the company could operate at only 30% capacity – loading two vessels simultaneously instead of five.
Background: The European Commission proposes to significantly restrict Ukraine's access to the EU agricultural market and agricultural subsidies even after accession.

Israel's mental health crisis in the wake of Oct. 7 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:52:00 UTC
17:52:00 KST

Israel's mental health crisis in the wake of Oct. 7 attacks
October 5, 2026
Warning: This article contains references to death by suicide that some readers may find disturbing.
As October 7's third anniversary approaches, Ronen Shalev's body tells him something's coming.
"You start shivering," he tells DW. "It's not just one day and you move on. We have many graves to visit, many families to meet. It's a difficult time and you feel it in your body."
Both of his children attended the Nova Party in Israel's south, where almost 400 people were killed in a terrorist attack carried out by Palestinian militant group Hamas and its affiliates in Gaza. In total, roughly 1,200 people were killed in the attack and around 250 were taken hostage.
The attack triggered the war in Gaza, during which Israel has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and displaced much of the territory's population.
Shalev's son, Roee, was shot and hospitalized, but he survived. Roee's partner, Mapal Adam, was killed in front of his eyes. Shalev's daughter, Lior, also made it out.
Shortly after that day, Shalev's wife Gavriela went missing, before her body was found in a burned car with a goodbye letter. "She couldn't handle the sorrow from that day," Shalev says.
At the same time, his son Roee's post-traumatic symptoms started emerging, mostly in the form of extreme mood swings. "He went to treatment to please me, but he didn't really believe in it. He thought he was OK, that he was strong," Shalev remembers.
Two years after Gavriela's death, Roee couldn't take it anymore, either.
"I'm alive, but I'm dead within," Roee wrote in his goodbye message, which he posted on his Instagram account. "I'm sorry."
A country in post-traumatic state
Since October 2023, Israel has been grappling with a mental health crisis of unprecedented scale.
According to a report by Israel's State Comptroller from February 2025, some 39% of the Israeli public reported suffering from post-traumatic symptoms, depression, anxiety or a combination of the three, on a medium or severe level.
This amounts to some 3 million people, 600,000 of whom could suffer severely. However, the report also found that the number of people receiving mental health treatment had only risen by 1% since October 7, 2023, a difference of around 60,000 people.
Among the affected groups are survivors of the attack, as well as people evacuated from their homes in Israel's south and north due to the war.
Noga Dagan-Buzaglo is a researcher with the Adva Center, a think tank focusing on inequality in Israeli society. She wrote an extensive paper about Israel's mental health system and its challenges post-October 7.
She tells DW that while the country's mental health budget did increase due to the war, it was too little, too late, as the health system faced an ongoing crisis that was not handled properly.
"The biggest challenge is convincing people to work in Israel's public mental health system, both due to lower wages in comparison to the private sector and due to an overload of work," she says.
Sedatives often the go-to solution
The current situation affects mental health professionals, too. Research by the University of Haifa found that 84% of the therapists who treated people affected by the October 7 attack showed traumatic symptoms themselves, and some 45% of them said they feel mentally exhausted.
Israel's Health Ministry has repeatedly said it has increased funding and job openings for the country's public mental health system, but staffing shortages remain, especially in peripheral regions in the far north and south.
Because of these issues, the report said waiting times for treatment through Israel's public healthcare system were longer than six months. In some cases, Dagan-Buzaglo says, patients had to wait more than a year before receiving help.
Mental health NGOs and volunteers try to fill the gaps, often struggling themselves under the workload. This also leads to an increased use of prescription medications. Some people turn to substances like alcohol and drugs.
The Israeli Ministry of Health said earlier this year that it had registered a rise of between 13% and 17% in the prescription of sedatives, sleep aids and antidepressants.
Those who suffer from the situation the most are the ones who cannot afford to pay a private therapist. Dagan-Buzaglo labels the Israeli public health system's response to the situation as "simply bad."
Soldiers at risk
Combat soldiers have received a special focus when it comes to Israel's mental health crisis.
Statistics published by the Israeli parliament and the IDF suggest a sharp rise of suicide cases among reservists: from a maximum of one annual case in the six years preceding the war to 11 cases in 2024, as well as nine cases investigated as suspected suicides in 2025. This does not include ex-soldiers who committed suicide due to trauma after the end of their service.
Dagan-Buzaglo, a researcher at the Adva Center, says that while professionals receive better pay and conditions working for the army, the lack of personnel is still apparent. "In the army, too, the length and quality of treatment are by far not at an adequate level."
To start solving the problem for both civilians and soldiers, she believes the system needs more support. "We have to acknowledge the fact that trauma is not over after a year. This means investing money."
Breaking the taboo
Ronen Shalev holds regular lectures and talks about the importance of mental health, often to groups of soldiers. He believes this is the best way to continue his son's legacy of fighting to live on.
Shalev, who himself was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), says he made a choice to live his life to its fullest.
His message: The taboo regarding suicidality — which still exists across Israeli society — needs to be broken. "This is especially true regarding those who say they are strong. They're the scary ones as they're less likely to receive treatment."
For Shalev, speaking publicly about his family's experience has become part of his own recovery — and a way to encourage others to seek help before they reach a crisis point.
"Life, with all its pain, is still worth deciding in favor of," he said.
If you are suffering from serious emotional strain or suicidal thoughts, do not hesitate to seek professional help. You can find information on where to find such help, no matter where you live in the world, at this website: https://befrienders.org/
Edited by: Andreas Illmer

Israel bars UK Green leader after party votes to define Zionism as racism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:51:14 UTC
17:51:14 KST

UK Jewish groups say the motion stokes hatred after a string of attacks on their community, while the government and other parties have condemned a policy that even at least three out of five Green MPs opposed.
Israel has barred the leader of Britain's Green Party Zack Polanski from entering the country after the party's members voted to define Zionism as racism.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar took the decision on Sunday evening, hours after the vote at the left-wing party's annual conference, Israel's foreign ministry said. It called the resolution "a clear antisemitic text" and described the ban on Polanski as a "first step".
"The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle," the ministry said.
Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, called the party's decision "a disgrace".
"Zionism is the national liberation movement of the Jewish people, and it forms the basis for the Jewish people's right to a state and a national home in the Land of Israel," Herzog said on X.
The motion passed by 1,022 votes to 813. It states that Zionism will be "treated as any other form of racism" and commits the party to supporting a "single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine".
Jewish groups warn over safety
The vote comes at a time of heightened fear among British Jews. The Board of Deputies of British Jews said the motion stoked "anti-Jewish hatred after a year in which British Jews have been murdered attending their synagogue, stabbed in the streets, and seen their community buildings firebombed".
Two worshippers were killed in an attack on a Manchester synagogue on Yom Kippur last year. In March, ambulances run by a Jewish volunteer service were set alight in Golders Green, north London, the first in a string of arson attacks on synagogues and other Jewish sites in the capital. Two Jewish men were stabbed in the same neighbourhood in April.
Last week, two Iranian nationals were charged over an alleged plot to carry out an attack in Manchester around this year's Yom Kippur.
The Community Security Trust, which monitors antisemitism, recorded 1,926 incidents in the first half of 2026, its second-highest half-year total, including a record 135 assaults.
Ahead of the Green Party vote, the heads of the Board of Deputies, the Community Security Trust and the Jewish Leadership Council wrote to the party.
"This motion would make the Green Party the first electorally significant UK political party in living memory to adopt what appears to be an overtly antisemitic political platform," they said.
UK parties condemn vote
Bridget Phillipson, chair of the ruling Labour Party and minister for women and equalities, condemned the decision.
"It is shameful to vote against a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine and to condemn the vast majority of British Jews and Jews around the world as racist for supporting Israel's right to exist," she said in a party statement.
The opposition Conservatives described the Greens as "toxic to its core".
"British Jews should not have to disclaim a belief in Jewish self-determination and the existence of Israel in order to be accepted by a British political party," said Chris Philp, the party's shadow home secretary.
Divisions in the party
"This has been a serious and deeply felt debate within our membership," a Green spokesperson said.
In a joint statement, Polanski and the party's MPs said there was "no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people".
The motion exposed divisions in the party. At least three of its five MPs opposed it, and Polanski, who is running to become an MP in former prime minister Keir Starmer's London constituency, skipped the vote.
He said earlier this week that the "displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people" was "clearly racism".
United Nations investigators have accused Israel of committing "genocide" in the war in Gaza, a finding that Israel has rejected.
The Greens, who hold five of the 650 seats in Britain's parliament, have surged in popularity under Polanski, attracting voters dissatisfied with the centre-left Labour government's stance on the Israel-Hamas war. Polls show his popularity has taken a hit in recent months following several missteps.

Hackers get personal information on 8.8 million people in Denmark government data leak
- Hackers illegally accessed Denmark's national registry, stealing personal data of around 8.8 million people, including names, addresses and social security numbers.
- The breach affected data beyond Denmark's six million population, including deceased and emigrated individuals, raising serious concerns.
- The authorities are investigating the incident, which involved hacking a company with legal registry access; the hackers remain unidentified and access has not yet been revoked.
AI generated
COPENHAGEN – Hackers broke into Denmark’s national registry and gained access to personal information on millions of people, the digital affairs ministry said on Oct 5.
“The administration of the national registry (Central Person Register) has found that unauthorised individuals obtained illegal access in particular to the names, addresses and CPR numbers of around 8.8 million registered people”, including those who have died or emigrated, the ministry said in a press statement, referring to Denmark’s social security numbers.
“This is an extremely serious incident,” Christina Egelund, digital affairs minister said in the statement.
“Together with all the relevant authorities, we are in the process of mapping out the full extent of the incident,” she added.
Denmark has a population of around six million, but the national registry has information on 11 million, including data of those who have died and people who have emigrated from the country.
An investigation has been launched into the incident, with the hackers not yet identified, the statement said.
They broke into the national registry by hacking into a Danish company that legally had access to it, the government said, adding that the access has not been revoked. AFP

Budget 2027: Accounting Chamber identified risks related to UAH 1.5 trillion in loans and defense spending
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:50:22 EEST
17:50:22 KST

Budget 2027: Accounting Chamber identified risks related to UAH 1.5 trillion in loans and defense spending
Kyiv • UNN
The 2027 Budget includes more than UAH 1.5 trillion in external loans without identified creditors. The Accounting Chamber considers the forecast overly optimistic.
The draft State Budget of Ukraine for 2027 includes more than UAH 1.5 trillion in external loans, but potential lenders have not yet been identified. The Accounting Chamber of Ukraine reported this, pointing out the risks and analyzing defense expenditures, UNN reports.
Details
"The draft State Budget of Ukraine for 2027 provides for attracting more than UAH 1.5 trillion in external loans, while the potential lenders for these loans remain unidentified. Another UAH 131.3 billion in revenue depends on the planned tax changes coming into force. According to the Accounting Chamber's assessment, this creates risks of insufficient funds being received to finance state needs," the post says.
The total amount of financial resources in the state budget for 2027 is reportedly planned at UAH 8.03 trillion, "which is 12.9% more than the amount approved for 2026." "More than half of these resources — UAH 4.32 trillion, or 53.7% — is planned to be received in the form of grants and loans from international partners," the post says.
At the same time, auditors noted that the timely and complete receipt of these funds will determine the possibilities for financing the planned state expenditures. Of these funds, UAH 1 trillion 822.9 billion constitutes external borrowing, the Accounting Chamber stated.
"The forecast regarding the feasibility of attracting foreign funds in precisely these amounts is assessed by the Accounting Chamber as overly optimistic. After all, potential lenders for UAH 1.5 trillion — 88.8% of external borrowing to the general fund — have not yet been identified. Therefore, the failure to receive the necessary amount of financial support from international partners will be the key risk to the financing of the state budget in 2027," said Accounting Chamber Chairwoman Olha Pishchanska.
Expenditures: the main priority is security and defense
State budget expenditures for 2027 are planned at UAH 7.3 trillion.
Budget expenditures on security and defense are planned at UAH 4.855 trillion, or 66.8% of all expenditures. Of this amount, UAH 1.5 trillion is allocated for payroll, including servicemen's monetary allowances. Another UAH 264.9 billion constitutes a reserve for the security and defense sector. State guarantees of up to UAH 30 billion are also provided.
"At the same time, if hostilities intensify or the prices of fuel, weapons, and imported components rise, the need for funds may increase. Even taking the allocated reserve into account, there may be a need for additional funds, primarily for the procurement and repair of weapons and military equipment. Therefore, the Accounting Chamber emphasizes the need for a more detailed assessment of the planned expenditures in this area," the Accounting Chamber's statement says.
The budget also provides UAH 570.9 billion for social protection and social security. In particular, UAH 292.8 billion is allocated for pensions, UAH 42.3 billion for housing subsidies and benefits, and UAH 38.1 billion for support for families with children.
The Accounting Chamber separately drew attention to the significant difference in approaches to remuneration in state bodies.
In particular, it is proposed that a reference amount of UAH 2,331 be applied to employees of certain state bodies whose remuneration is regulated by special laws, as well as to employees of tax and customs authorities. By contrast, the subsistence minimum for able-bodied persons, amounting to UAH 3,691, is proposed for determining the basic amount of judges' official salaries. This approach increases the planned amount of payroll expenditures in the judicial system.
The state budget deficit and debt burden
The state budget deficit for 2027 is planned at UAH 1.67 trillion, or 15% of GDP. The total amount of state borrowing will be UAH 2.37 trillion.
At the end of 2027, state and state-guaranteed debt is projected at UAH 12.7 trillion. Its ratio to GDP will increase from 105% to 113.9%.
Debt repayment and servicing are allocated 15.1% of all state budget expenditures — UAH 1.2 trillion. As of July 2026, nearly 80% of the debt was denominated in foreign currency. The depreciation of the hryvnia beyond the projected level creates a risk of an increase in the debt and the costs of its repayment and servicing.
Recommendations of the Accounting Chamber
Based on the results of its examination of the 2027 State Budget, the Accounting Chamber recommends that, during the finalization of the draft State Budget of Ukraine for 2027:
-  clarify and provide additional justification for the sources of budget financing, in particular external borrowing; 
-  take into account the existing reserves for increasing certain state budget revenues; 
-  assess the adequacy of the expenditures envisaged for the security and defense sector; 
-  eliminate legal inconsistencies. 
The conclusions and proposals of the Accounting Chamber, as noted, have been submitted to the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine for consideration during the review of the draft Law of Ukraine "On the State Budget of Ukraine for 2027."
We remind you
The 2027 Budget draft envisages a deficit of 15% of GDP and debt exceeding 110% of GDP. UAH 4.885 trillion is planned to be allocated to security and defense.

Dozens Detained at Moscow Communist Party Rally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:48:55 UTC
17:48:55 KST

Moscow police detained around 60 people on Sunday during a Communist Party rally commemorating the 1993 constitutional crisis, after the event spiraled into a protest against alleged fraud during last month’s parliamentary elections.
An estimated 2,000 people gathered for an annual memorial honoring those killed during an Oct. 4, 1993, standoff when President Boris Yeltsin ordered tanks to shell the Supreme Soviet parliament building to dissolve opposition to his administration.
Eyewitnesses told the Telegram news channel Ostorozhno Novosti that police officers charged into the crowd after chants of slogans like “Down with the Tsar!” “Freedom for political prisoners!” and “For fair elections!” broke out against the ruling United Russia party.
United Russia won a record number of seats in the State Duma during the country’s first wartime parliamentary elections last month. The Communist Party — the largest Kremlin-approved systemic opposition faction — won fewer seats than in previous elections.
The Communist Party said 65 “mostly young people” were detained at the tail end of the rally on Sunday afternoon.
“Efforts are underway to release the detainees and provide them with the necessary help,” the party said in a statement on its Telegram channel.
Senior Communist Party lawmaker Dmitry Novikov said that officers began releasing some detainees later on Sunday evening.
The independent outlet Sotavision reported that authorities held several participants overnight pending court hearings.
News outlets underscored that authorities had approved the rally.
The exiled outlet Agentstvo reported that these were the largest detentions at a Communist Party rally since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
On Monday morning, Communist Party leadership issued a statement challenging the voting process and electoral pressure on its candidates.

Shell injures border guard at Moldova-Ukraine border, hits bus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:47:01 UTC
17:47:01 KST

A projectile that fell on the grounds of the Palanca-Mayaky-Udobne border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova ricoched from the ground, struck a passenger bus and a control booth, and lightly injured a Moldovan border guard on Oct. 5, Moldova's Border Police said.
The incident occured at 9:38 a.m. local time, as Russia carried out attacks against Ukrainian infrastructure, the border police said, according to Moldovan media NewsMaker and Zairul de Garda.
Moldova's General Police Inspectorate said it closed the border crossing for the duration of its investigations and urged drivers to avoid the area, NewsMaker reported.
Overnight, Russia launched 205 attack drones of various types, including 49 jet-powered drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down 172 drones, including Shahed-type, Gerbera, and other drones, as well as two Banderol loitering munitions, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at three others.
"The security environment around Moldova has become more difficult," Moldovan PM Vasile Tofan said during a press conference in Brussels on Oct. 5. "Russian drones and missiles pose a serious risk to our population and infrastructure."
Kaja Kallas, the EU's High representative for Foreign Affairs, also condemned Russian violations of Moldovas airspace with missiles and drones.
"This is completely unacceptable. The Kremlin is putting lives at risk across the continent. Moscow's aim behind these actions is to create fear and paralyze our decision making," Kallas said.
Palanca borders Ukraine's Odesa Oblast, which Russia regularly attacks with drones and missiles. Russia's attacks on Ukraine frequently lead to violations of Moldova's airspace and explosions on the country's territory.
On Oct. 3, five Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated Moldova's airspace and exploded on the country's territory during Russia's latest overnight attack against Ukraine, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said.
"(Russia's) war is dangerously reaching Moldova," Sandu wrote in a post on X on Oct. 3, condemning the attack. "Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped."
Drones invaded Moldova's airspace three separate times on Sept. 30, as Russia launched a day-long attack against Ukraine overnight and into the following afternoon.
On Sept. 24, suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova overnight, amid a sustained mass drone and missile attack on Ukraine.
On Aug. 16, NATO fighter jets shot down a suspected Russian drone that violated Romanian airspace near the Moldovan border, Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta confirmed.
A day later, on Aug. 17, a Russian S-8000 Banderol cruise missile entered Moldovan airspace during a Russian attack on Odesa, before crashing in a cornfield approximately 3 kilometers (1.8 miles) outside of the village of Talmaz, in the Stefan Voda district of Moldova.

Truck driver damages century-old Hengchuen City Wall gate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:46:22 UTC
17:46:22 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Police arrested a truck driver after he damaged the West Gate of the Hengchuen City Wall, Hengchuen Police Station Traffic Police Squad Leader Chung Ping-feng (鍾秉峰) said on Monday.
Chung said the driver, surnamed Chen (陳), scraped the historic structure while driving through the West Gate Sunday morning, causing minor damage, per CNA. The incident is considered a violation of the Cultural Heritage Preservation Act.
The Ministry of Culture installed barriers in January to prevent vehicles from passing through the West Gate and damaging the historic structure, per PTS. However, the ministry removed the barriers following pushback from local communities.
The ministry opted to use road signs as a temporary replacement for the barriers. The local township office has called on GPS navigation services to stop directing traffic through the gate.
Residents expressed dissatisfaction with the government’s handling of the issue, arguing that without cameras and other complementary measures, road signs alone would do little to protect the historic site, per Liberty Times.
In 1871, Ryukyu fishers drifted ashore in the Hengchuen area after experiencing a shipwreck and were later killed by Indigenous tribes, per National Cultural Heritage Data Base. The incident and the killing of a Japanese national in southern Taiwan in 1872 led the Empire of Japan (1868-945) to invade the Hengchuen area, as the ruling Qing dynasty did not view the eastern part of Taiwan as its territory.
The Japanese invasion would later be known as the Mutan Village Incident, when Japan invaded and destroyed Mutan Village, which was chiefly made up of Paiwan people. Afterwards, Japan attempted to establish a long-term base of operations in the area. The Qing dynasty dispatched official Shen Baozhen to the village to negotiate with Japan.
Shen advised the Qing government to establish a formal governing body in the area and construct city walls, which were completed in 1879. The Hengchuen City Walls are the most complete surviving city walls in Taiwan from the Qing Dynasty (1644-1912).

Taipei Zoo celebrates International Zookeeper Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:46:13 UTC
17:46:13 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Zoo marked International Zookeeper Day on Sunday by showcasing how positive reinforcement helps animals cooperate with routine medical exams.
In the past, veterinary procedures often required anesthesia or physical restraint. Advances in animal behavior science have allowed keepers to train animals to participate voluntarily in procedures, reducing stress and the need for restraint or anesthesia, per a zoo press release.
Animals can be trained to stand on scales, open their mouths for dental examinations, extend their paws for blood draws or injections, enter transport carriers, and lie down for X-rays or ultrasound scans.
At Taipei Zoo, the panda care team has trained giant pandas to cooperate with blood pressure checks, blood draws, injections, and tooth brushing. The pandas can also be trained to position themselves for X-rays and ultrasound examinations. Keepers have also used behavioral training to assist with treatment for the elderly giant panda Yuan Yuan, including spinal laser therapy.
The approach is also used with pregnant animals. Keepers train orangutans to position themselves near examination windows so veterinarians can conduct ultrasound examinations. Malayan tapirs can similarly be trained to lie down and tolerate ultrasound equipment for pregnancy monitoring, per the press release.
Taipei Zoo said such cooperation requires long-term, consistent training and close interaction between keepers and animals. Regular behavioral training allows keepers to monitor subtle changes in animals' health and shifts veterinary care toward prevention rather than emergency treatment. The zoo said daily training is largely invisible to visitors, but it is an important part of modern animal care and welfare.

The Kuai Kuai workers' union held two labor dispute mediation sessions with the Taoyuan City Government, but both ended without an agreement. On Sept. 18, 94% of union members voted to authorize a strike, which began at 5 a.m. on Friday.
The company has said it will not lay off workers for two years after the relocation. However, the union said employees who later quit because of longer commutes or unsuitable working conditions could lose their right to severance pay, per CTEE.
The Taoyuan Confederation of Trade Unions said many employees have remained at the factory because it is close to home and allows them to care for their families. It said relocation would increase commuting costs and could also disrupt childcare and other family responsibilities.
The group also criticized the company for failing to announce a final relocation site. It said possible locations shifted from Pingtung to Hsinchu and then back to Taoyuan, leaving workers uncertain about where they may have to work, per SETN.
The labor ministry said it respects the union's legal right to strike and warned the company against unfair treatment of participating workers. It also urged both sides to continue negotiations and said it would work with local governments to help resolve the dispute.
Kuai Kuai is a well-known Taiwanese snack maker best known for its namesake corn puffs and other packaged snacks. According to the economics ministry, the company currently reports annual revenue of more than NT$1 billion (US$32 million).

Last month, Defense Minister Martin Herem said during a public lecture that Tallinn could not afford to keep mobilized troops in the field for long.
“I have jokingly said that if we get to the orange zone there and carry out mobilization, but Russia does not attack, then it would be economically more correct to attack ourselves,” he said. “Then at least we will know when it will start, and we will not waste food and air in vain”
Russian President Vladimir Putin responded to the remark with an idiom: “The circus has left, but the clowns remain.” He added that Moscow has no plans to attack Estonia or any other NATO member.
Commenting on the FT report, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova echoed the president, saying it belongs in the funny pages.
Russian diplomats previously cited Herem’s remarks as examples of what they described as aggressive rhetoric by senior officials in NATO countries. The Russian Foreign Ministry has formally warned the bloc against attacking Russian territory or imposing a blockade on the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, saying the country’s response could involve “all weapons” in its arsenal.
While NATO poses as a purely defensive organization, it has a history of military interventions on foreign soil and does not rule out preemptive attacks. Last week, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said European members of the bloc should have been capable of attacking Iran themselves to eliminate what was described as a nuclear threat from Tehran. He argued that Europe’s military buildup should eventually allow it to conduct such operations without relying on the US.
Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania have all sharply increased military spending in recent years and are reportedly seeking additional procurement funds from the EU budget. Farhadi criticizes Hollywood’s perspective at Rio Film Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:44:43 UTC
17:44:43 KST

Farhadi criticizes Hollywood’s perspective at Rio Film Festival
TEHRAN – Renowned Iranian filmmaker Asghar Farhadi discussed the perceived dominance of American cinema and cautioned against viewing Hollywood as a reliable source for authentic portrayals of foreign cultures.
Farhadi, who is in Brazil for the presentation of his latest film “Parallel Tales” at the Rio Film Festival, made the remarks during a panel, ISNA reported.
The two-time Oscar winner was asked about “Argo” winning Best Picture just a year after “A Separation” won Best International Film at the Oscars. “I watched the film at the time it came out and felt it was a ‘Hollywood thing’,” Farhadi said.
In “Argo,” loosely based on a true story, director Ben Affleck plays a Latino exfiltration specialist who masquerades as a Hollywood producer to rescue six Americans held captive in Tehran during the US hostage crisis in Iran.
“The problem with these kinds of films in Hollywood [and] some people in the United States [is that] they look at the world from up to down,” he added. “Someday you should ask them: Why do you feel you’re up and we’re down? I don’t understand why they have this ego that they’re up.” The Iranian director then said Americans often claim to “have democracy,” but they don’t. “You don’t have democracy. It’s a lie.”
Farhadi then recalled spending time in the US a few years ago when working on a project and, during research, travelling to San Francisco to speak with incarcerated men. “I met some people in prison who are Black, [some who come] from other countries, and the real America was there. But people in the world don’t see that part of the United States.”
“I have this problem when they feel they are up and they think, ‘[others] should be like us,’” he continued. “Even if it’s in a good way and they want to be kind to you, they wish ‘one day you’ll become like us,’ and no, I don’t want to.”
Still on “Argo,” the director said movies like that “are not deep.” “They make these movies for money; it’s a business. And in these films, it’s always a white guy from the United States saving others. My question is: Why? Why does an American go to Cuba or Iran to save people? People understand they can save themselves. Who asked you to come and save us?”
Asked about how he broaches politics in his films, the renowned filmmaker said that, whenever “you talk about society, you are talking about politics.” “Even when you talk about family life, their relationships, their difficulties and problems, indirectly you are talking about politics. In my films, I always try not to talk about politics directly because, to me, that is a bit far from cinema. The cinema that I believe is the kind of cinema that gives space to audiences to discover things about themselves.”
The director then brought up Abbas Kiarostami’s “Fellow Citizen” as Iran’s “most political film.” The 1983 documentary heavily trails drivers across the streets of the Iranian capital. “He made a documentary about car drivers in Tehran, but when you see people, the way they talk to the police, the layers are very political.”
“Media and cinema don’t give you a complete image of people’s ordinary life,” he added. “But the thing about empathy is that, all around the world, people are similar to each other. Cinema is based on hate and love. And [when it comes to] hate and love, everywhere is the same. A love between a mother and child in Brazil and in Tehran is the same. The way they express it is different, but the core is the same.”
Farhadi said that when he watches a Brazilian film, he soon forgets he is watching a story from another place in the world, and feels it is a “film about us” as people. “If one day people can travel to other countries, and if they shake hands, that’s the best way to know people, not through media. I don’t believe media can give us the whole image.”
On this, the filmmaker emphasized how his last two films, “A Hero” and “Parallel Tales,” are about how we see others and how we are seen in return. They are also heavily influenced by “how social media has shaped our lives.”
“When we see something in the media, we should be careful,” he continued, adding that most information replicated by mainstream media about Iran, for example, comes from “very simple knowledge” of real life in the country. When a singular discourse is perpetuated, the director implied, it means people are “ready to accept” when someone says “they are the enemy.” “This is something the media is doing, because the most powerful media belongs to powerful people. This is the problem.”
Farhadi spoke very briefly about his next film, reiterating it will be shot in Persian. Enquired as to whether the film might deal with the current war in Iran and the conflict in Palestine, the director said: “Not directly,” suggesting the current political climate might have an underlying effect on the story despite not being the subject of his project.
“The Salesman” helmer also recalled how “Parallel Tales” was supposed to be shot in the US: “I stayed there for three years, writing, searching, casting. I did casting in the US with American actors, very big names. But every day that I came back to my home, I told myself: I cannot connect with this. Something is wrong. It was a big problem. One night I decided to change.”
SS/SAB

Three years on: Israel is asphyxiating Gaza and dismantling the means of survival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:41:58 UTC
17:41:58 KST

- Israel is continuing its genocide in Gaza, Palestine, where the space in which people can live is shrinking and the conditions for survival are being systematically destroyed.
- Governments must act now to ensure that Israel stops the destruction and killing, and prevents ethnic cleansing, in Palestine.
Amman / Jerusalem – Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warns that Israel is progressively asphyxiating Gaza, Palestine, and continuing its genocide: the space in which people can live is vanishing, while the conditions people need to survive are being systematically destroyed through continued violence, the deliberate blockade of essential supplies, and the destruction of healthcare and vital infrastructure.
In the past year, the physical trapping of people in Gaza has been made increasingly definitive by the establishment of Israel’s Yellow Line. Originally presented as a temporary, first-phase military withdrawal position and a key part of maintaining the so-called ceasefire – it is now reinforced by military positions, berms and ongoing demolitions and has continued to move west, squeezing people into a smaller and smaller area. Israeli forces now occupy approximately 65 per cent of Gaza, using the line to draw a clear border around this area.
As the Yellow Line moves, the threat to people living nearby becomes increasingly immediate, compounded by the uncertainty of approaching a line that is not clearly or consistently demarcated. People risk being shot by Israeli forces when they approach it, and MSF teams continue to treat people with gunshot wounds sustained nearby. Its encroachment is also disrupting the delivery of essential assistance: MSF water trucking has had to stop when shooting occurs near communities living close to the Yellow Line.
“The Yellow Line cannot be treated simply as a line on a map,” says Amande Bazerolle, MSF head of emergency response in Gaza. “It has become a mechanism of encirclement and ethnic cleansing, while cutting communities off from the infrastructure, healthcare, water and other essentials they need to survive.”
The Yellow Line cannot be treated simply as a line on a map.
Amande Bazerolle, MSF head of emergency response in Gaza
Violence is not confined to the areas around the Yellow Line. In June and July alone, despite a so-called ceasefire, MSF teams treated more than 1,200* cases of violent trauma across Gaza, including blast injuries, burns, gunshot wounds and injuries resulting from physical assault.
Over the past three years, our teams have treated more than 200,000 trauma cases*, including injuries resulting from intentional physical violence, while Israel’s military offensive has killed more than 74,000 people, including more than 20,000 children.
As Israel confines Palestinians into increasingly limited areas, families are being pushed into overcrowded and unlivable conditions, without sufficient access to clean water, sanitation services, shelter, or healthcare. These conditions are contributing to the spread of disease.
MSF teams have treated more than 11,000 cases of skin diseases, such as scabies, this year alone, while seeing more than 1,500 cases of chickenpox in June and July. MSF distributed around 2.1 million litres of drinking water per day in August, yet the scale of need remains far beyond what can be met under these restrictions. 
“Most people have less than six litres of domestic-use water per day and limited access to basic hygiene items such as soap and detergent,” says Dr Murad Asaliyya, medical activities manager in Gaza. “We are treating gastroenteritis, acute respiratory infections, a lot of skin conditions, hepatitis, bacterial skin infections, scabies and lice.”
“At the same time, we are facing severe shortages in terms of medical supplies,” says Dr Asaliyya. “Even the cream we need to treat scabies has been restricted by the Israeli authorities.”
At the same time, we are facing severe shortages in terms of medical supplies. Even the cream we need to treat scabies has been restricted by the Israeli authorities.
Dr Murad Asaliyya, medical activities manager in Gaza
Over the past three years, access to healthcare has deteriorated dramatically, with hospitals increasingly running out of basic supplies and patients unable to access essential medicines and treatment. Restrictions on essential supplies, such as engine oil and spare parts, are also crippling the infrastructure needed to keep hospitals, ambulances and water systems running, with generators already breaking down and water-trucking operations reduced.
The destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system and damage to more than 80 per cent of all structures in the Strip, alongside the lifelong physical and mental health impacts of repeated violence and displacement, will extend far beyond the present and prevent any meaningful recovery for years to come.
Nor is this crisis limited to Gaza. Since 2023, violent settler attacks, military operations and raids on homes, displacement camps and agricultural land, illegal settlement expansion, displacement, home demolitions and movement restrictions have rapidly escalated across the West Bank and East Jerusalem, particularly this year. Patients at MSF clinics tell teams about homes being demolished by Israeli forces, attacks by settlers, and livestock being stolen. The policies of violence, harassment and forced displacement affecting Palestinians extend beyond Gaza, causing further fragmentation of Palestine.
“It will take generations to recover from the harm that has already been done over the past three years, and in the preceding decades, while the excruciating consequences of Israel's ongoing genocide are still being felt every day,” says Bazerolle. 
“Destruction, displacement and deprivation have become normalised — practices Israel is carrying out with impunity,” says Bazerolle. “Governments must act now to ensure Israel stops the destruction and killing, prevents ethnic cleansing, and stops denying Palestinians the means of survival.”

Iran says it disabled Starlink terminals during January protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

17:40:57 KST

Sahin Demir
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Iran claimed Monday that it had successfully disabled Starlink terminals during nationwide protests in January and has other tools to counter the satellite internet service.
According to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, head of Iran’s National Cyberspace Center, said Tehran had successfully disabled Starlink terminals during the protests.
“For the first time, Iran managed to successfully disable Starlink terminals during the coup in January,” Aghamiri said, using the Iranian authorities’ description of the protests.
He claimed that Western media had also reported at the time that Iran had successfully carried out an operation to disable Starlink terminals.
“That important technical operation, which was completely successful, is one of our tools, and we also have other tools at our disposal to counter Starlink,” he added.
Aghamiri’s comments came in response to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who displayed a Starlink terminal during his address to the UN General Assembly in New York on Sept. 24.
Netanyahu said the device allowed Iranians to access information, accusing Tehran of spending large sums of money on internet censorship.
Iran witnessed widespread anti-government protests in January, with demonstrations intensifying on Jan. 8 and 9 amid clashes between protesters and security forces.
Iranian authorities imposed a nationwide internet blackout on Jan. 8 as the protests intensified.
Starlink remained one of the few ways for Iranians to access the internet during the blackout, although reports at the time indicated that the satellite service was also experiencing significant interference and disruptions.
Aghamiri said the disruptions were caused by an Iranian operation targeting Starlink terminals.
Starlink, operated by US space technology company SpaceX, provides internet connectivity through a network of satellites.

Bar-Ilan lecturer indicted over plot to kill hundreds of Arabs in coordinated attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:39:42 UTC
17:39:42 KST

A Bar-Ilan University mathematics professor accused of planning coordinated terrorist attacks intended to kill hundreds of Arabs has asked to be released to house arrest, telling a court that he does not pose a danger and has “exams to grade” at home.
The professor, around 60 and from Petah Tikva, has been in custody since Sept. 17. The investigation began after the Shin Bet domestic security agency received initial information about his alleged plan, after which the case was transferred to the Central District police’s major-crimes unit.
Prosecutors have asked that he remain in custody until the conclusion of legal proceedings. He is charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism under Israel’s Counter-Terrorism Law, extortion by threats and obstruction of justice.
At a hearing Monday at the Lod District Court, the defendant’s attorneys also asked that the gag order preventing publication of his name remain in place. They argued that the indictment “could harm the State of Israel internationally” and said members of his family in Australia could also suffer if he were identified.
The judge extended the gag order until noon on Oct. 7.
The indictment alleges that the professor spent years developing a detailed plan he called “Ayit,” a Hebrew acronym for a phrase meaning “The People Will Carry Out Transfer.”
Under the plan, prosecutors say, he intended to recruit 71 additional Jewish attackers and divide a total of 72 participants, including himself, into 12 six-person terrorist cells. At least half were supposed to hold firearms licenses.
The cells were allegedly to arm themselves with pistols, rifles, axes and hammers and launch simultaneous surprise attacks in mixed Jewish-Arab cities and Arab and Bedouin communities, with the goal of killing hundreds of people and driving Arabs and Palestinians permanently toward Jordan, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip.
Alleged plan included help from within the IDF
The indictment describes an even broader element of the alleged plan: assistance from people the defendant hoped to recruit from within the IDF.
Prosecutors say he envisioned sympathetic military personnel providing coordinated support to the attacking cells, including Air Force strikes on Arab population centers and assistance from artillery and armored forces.
In written instructions described in the indictment, the professor allegedly called for mass killings and the rapid seizure of friction points, roads, entrances and exits to Arab communities, mixed cities and hospitals.
One passage allegedly instructed participants not to show mercy, including toward women and children, and not to stop in response to pleas.
According to prosecutors, the professor believed simultaneous mass attacks, amplified in real time on social media, would prompt Arab citizens of Israel, including Bedouins, as well as Palestinians in east Jerusalem and the West Bank, to flee.
The alleged preparations stretched from February 2023 until his arrest last month and included reconnaissance trips, detailed handwritten documents and repeated attempts to recruit others.
Prosecutors say his thinking began after the May 2021 intercommunal violence and intensified following the Oct. 7 attack and subsequent war.
‘I don’t see who I am dangerous to’
During the court hearing, the professor argued that he should be allowed to return home.
“In my opinion, I am not currently dangerous to anyone. I can be released to house arrest,” he told the court.
“My life has been completely turned upside down. I have so many things to do and financial matters to take care of,” he said.
He also expressed fear for his safety in custody.
“I don’t see who I am dangerous to. If they want to publish this, do it without my name,” he said. “All the prison guards are Muslim and I am afraid. Israel is a small country. Some of them tell me they know what I am accused of. I am alone there.”
“I am a professor at Bar-Ilan and I worked until my arrest. I have exams to grade at home,” he added.
The professor also said he had developed the plan “because of Oct. 7, not for myself,” although the indictment alleges that his preparations began months before the Hamas attack.
“I didn’t do anything for myself. I buried my life for three years,” he said. “I don’t think I should be punished.”
Disguises, reconnaissance and failed recruitment attempts
According to the indictment, the defendant spent roughly a year and a half attempting unsuccessfully to recruit supporters and partners.
He allegedly conducted reconnaissance around the Bedouin community of Tuba-Zangariyye in northern Israel to study access routes and determine how it could be attacked. Prosecutors say he intended the community to be one of the plan’s central targets.
Investigators also allege that he went to considerable lengths to conceal his identity during his recruitment efforts.
He is accused of wearing a face mask, hat and sunglasses, identifying himself under the false names “Menachem” or “Menachem Livneh,” and using the phones of passersby to contact people connected to his recruitment efforts.
He allegedly wrote his documents by hand instead of using a computer and prepared instructions explaining how participants should avoid detection.
Alleged attempt to recruit Feiglin
The indictment also says the professor sought to involve Zehut leader Moshe Feiglin in his plans.
According to prosecutors, he intended first to recruit Feiglin and then, with his help, identify additional participants.
The professor allegedly planned to invite preselected activists to a Zehut election gathering without initially telling them why. At the event, prosecutors say, the participants would be informed that they had been recruited for a terrorist attack scheduled for the following day and would be given detailed operational instructions.
He attended two public events held by Feiglin and attempted to arrange a meeting and deliver a summary of his plan, but Feiglin did not respond to any of his approaches, according to the indictment.
About a month ago, prosecutors allege, the professor wrote Feiglin a threatening letter criticizing him for refusing to cooperate and warning that he would publish the letter if Feiglin did not assist him, in what the defendant allegedly believed would cause political damage ahead of the election.
Two days later, he allegedly went to Feiglin’s home and handed the letter to a neighbor, asking her to deliver it.
He later attended a Zehut event at Jerusalem’s Mahane Yehuda market and, through another woman, delivered several copies of the letter to the party’s director-general along with another letter containing a similar threat.
Zehut said after the indictment was published that Feiglin and the party leadership contacted police immediately after receiving the threatening and extortion letters and filed a formal complaint.
Feiglin thanked police for handling the case and called for the legal process against the professor to be pursued fully.
Bar-Ilan suspends professor immediately
Bar-Ilan University said the professor would be suspended immediately pending the conclusion of the legal proceedings.
“Bar-Ilan University condemns in the strongest possible terms and is deeply appalled by the acts attributed to the lecturer in the indictment. The University’s leadership calls upon the police and the prosecution to pursue the matter to the fullest extent of the law, should the allegations be substantiated.
“The University has, and will continue to have, zero tolerance for conduct of this nature, conduct that is fundamentally incompatible with the values we share as Jews, as Israelis, and as human beings, and that stands in clear opposition to the values of Bar-Ilan University.
“The lecturer will be suspended from his duties with immediate effect, pending the conclusion of the legal proceedings.”
Prosecutors argue that the alleged conduct, which they say extended over several years, reflects an extremist ideology that led the defendant to formulate a detailed, multi-stage plan for mass killing.
In their request to keep him detained until the end of proceedings, prosecutors said the alleged nationalist and ideological motivation, the extensive preparations and the heightened security tensions during the period demonstrate what they described as an immediate danger to individuals, the public and the state.

One day behind bars: Students and incarcerated women break prison stigma in Thailand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:39:26 UTC
17:39:26 KST

One day behind bars: Students and incarcerated women break prison stigma in Thailand
“Your mind follows the thread, one by one, row by row. You know? It’s like meditation. I don’t like machines.”
Weo, a prisoner at the Central Women’s Correctional Institution in Bangkok, prefers to sew by hand. She tried the sewing machine, but noticed that her mind was calmer when threading with her fingers directly. By not using a machine, she can produce a unique pattern that is hard to find in conventional shops.
She is explaining this to a group of design students who, sketchbooks in hand, are walking through the rows, observing the women who sew.
As time passes, some lose their initial apprehension and sit across from them, picking up fabric samples. Others ask about the products they are making. Some borrow their needles and, with the women’s guidance, try a bit of sewing themselves. A few sit on the floor in the basket-weaving corner with the women who have, by now, mastered the skill.
Today, the students have left the classroom behind to spend their morning at Thailand’s first women’s prison, where approximately 150 women learn weaving, knitting and machine sewing to make marketable products.
The students’ task is to design a product that these women can manufacture during their sentences.
Through the wall
The initiative, launched in November 2025 by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and the Thailand Institute of Justice (TIJ) pairs design students with incarcerated women to create modern, sustainable products that can be sold outside prison.
Earlier this year, 22 students visited the prison and interacted with the women who are now manufacturing new products. Their designs had to appeal to modern consumers, be practical and tell a story linked to rehabilitation that would raise awareness of the critical role vocational training plays in reducing recidivism.
“The stigma surrounding those who have made mistakes has long been a wall in our society. To help them cross that barrier, we must restore their human dignity,” said TIJ’s Chontit Chuenurah.
“By weaving their stories into these products, we use the creativity of the youth to build a bridge between the prison and the outside world, replacing fear with understanding.”
Under the theme Through the Wall, the initiative seeks to dismantle physical and social barriers, helping incarcerated women return successfully to society, she added.
“The project aims to create prison-made goods that appeal to modern consumers while equipping correctional officers with essential marketing skills,” said Aki Okanan, former prison reform expert at UNODC.
The project also raises international awareness of the role of rehabilitation and vocational training in reducing re-offending she added.
Time well spent
A panel of judges evaluated nine projects from 19 students in a competition earlier this year.
The winner was Time-Made, featuring intricately smocked watch straps.
For the students behind the design, time has a two-fold meaning: the sentence that prisoners can reduce by working in prison, and the time that people outside value, a privilege sometimes taken for granted.
“We wanted our product to remind people that we can use time carefully and meaningfully. That we can watch our time,” says Game, 21, co-winner of the competition.
First steps
All designs received support for product development and marketing, and the winning product, together with a selection of others, will be produced in collaboration with partner correctional facilities.
Natty, also 21, has been studying lifestyle products for three years. She had expected the prison to look gloomy and scary and was surprised to find the workroom bright and airy. Still, she noticed that most prisoners used dark colours.
“I want to take the skills they have and show them brighter fabrics and see what happens,” she said.
Sitting by Weo’s side, Ana*, from Latin America, tells the story of how she was caught attempting to smuggle cocaine into Bangkok. After four years in prison, she can produce perfect stuffed animals and is fluent in Thai, although she has never seen Thailand outside prison.
“I heard it’s beautiful here, but it doesn’t matter. After this, when I manage to get back to Brazil, I will start an import business and sell stuffed animals from Thailand. I know how to do it. I have the connections, and I speak the language.”
As the students pass through the gates and security controls to leave, their enthusiasm wanes. Although the prisoners cannot leave, this collaboration connects them to the outside world, the first step in reintegration.

Israel marks October 7 anniversary as national memorial day
October 5, 2026
Israel is observing a national memorial day on Monday for those killed in the October 7, 2023 Hamas terror attacks and the soldiers who died in the Gaza war, Israeli media reported.
Two state ceremonies are being held at Mount Herzl in Jerusalem, where President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other senior officials are expected to attend, The Jerusalem Post reported.
More memorial events, rallies and ceremonies are planned across the country with schools, municipalities and communities also holding events throughout the day.
Flags at state institutions, police stations, prisons and military bases were lowered to half-mast, reports said. The memorial fell on October 5 this year due to the Hebrew calendar, which is lunisolar.
October 7 terror attacks set of chain of events
The Hamas terror attack on October 7 killed some 1,200 people in Israel, with the Palestinian militant also taking another 251 hostages into Gaza. It was the single deadliest day for Jewish people since the Holocaust.
The October 7, 2023, attacks had massive consequences not only for Israeli society but also for Palestinians in Gaza, where Hamas had maintained power since the territory last held elections in 2006.
Following the Hamas attacks, the Israeli military began a war targeting Hamas in Gaza. The European Union, as well as the United States, Germany, and other countries, classify Hamas as a terrorist organization.
Israel's war on Hamas left more than 73,650 Palestinians dead in Gaza , most of them civilians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.

Tory plan to cut energy efficiency rule for builders will cost new home owners £1,000 a year, says thinktank
The Tory proposal to get rid of the Future Homes Standard (see 8.51am and 3.33pm) has been described as the equivalent of a £1,000-a-year “new homes tax” for homeowners.
E3G, a climate change thinktank, has made the argument on the basis that, without the rule, which requires new homes to have low-carbon heating, owners will pay at least £25,000 more in running costs over 25 years.
The UK’s shadow chancellor will announce today that the Conservative party would axe the Future Homes Standard if elected. This policy cuts energy bills and emissions in new build homes by requiring builders to fit new homes with heat pumps and solar panels instead of gas boilers. Heat pumps and solar panels offer dramatically lower running costs than homes fitted just with gas boilers, to the tune of around £1,000 a year in a 3-bed house.
The small additional upfront cost is quickly recovered by homeowners and protects them from price shocks on the volatile fossil fuel market. If the government builds all its promised 1.5 million new build homes to the Future Homes Standard, this will save bill payers around £35bn on their energy bills over 25 years, and stops 41m tonnes of dangerous carbon dioxide from being released into the atmosphere.
Cutting this policy would be a disaster for first time buyers and businesses working in one of the fastest growing sectors in the UK economy.
