&quot;Hornets&apos; Nest&quot; a year later: expert examinations, investigation, and the struggle of the families of deceased Odrex patients
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:11:49 EEST
17:11:49 KST

"Hornets' Nest" a year later: expert examinations, investigation, and the struggle of the families of deceased Odrex patients
Kyiv • UNN
Almost a year has passed since the release of the documentary film “Hornets' Nest.” The families of deceased patients spoke about the current status of investigations and court proceedings concerning the circumstances of treatment at Odrex.
Almost a year has passed since the publication of the documentary film "The Hornet’s Nest", in which relatives of deceased Odrex patients shared their truth about treatment at the Odesa clinic. According to them, it resulted in complications, enormous bills, and the deaths of their loved ones. Even before the film was released, its subjects contacted law enforcement authorities. The UNN investigated what stage the investigation and court proceedings have reached.
Seven years without an expert examination — the case concerning the death of Svitlana Huk’s husband
Svitlana Huk’s story began back in 2019. Her husband turned to Odrex with a thymus tumor. According to the widow, doctors convinced the family that surgery was necessary and that the treatment had positive prospects.
After the surgery, the man’s condition sharply deteriorated, and several days later he died in intensive care.
Svitlana said that the family paid about $42,500 for the treatment. After her husband’s death, the clinic filed a lawsuit demanding that the widow pay an additional approximately UAH 900,000. This concerns civil case No. 522/19678/19, filed by Dim Medytsyny LLC, operating under the Odrex brand, against Svitlana Huk to recover a debt under a medical services agreement.
For her part, Huk filed a lawsuit against Dim Medytsyny LLC. Her civil case No. 522/10741/22 concerns the protection of consumer rights in the provision of medical services, partial invalidity of the transaction, and compensation for material and moral damages.
In addition to the civil disputes with the clinic, criminal proceedings No. 12022162510001375, registered under Part 2 of Article 190 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, are also ongoing. As part of these proceedings, the investigation must establish the circumstances surrounding Svitlana Huk’s husband’s treatment and provide them with a criminal-law assessment. However, after seven years, the case has still not reached the key stage — a full forensic medical examination.
And this is despite the fact that the examination is supposed to answer whether the treatment strategy was chosen correctly, whether the surgery was justified, whether the doctors complied with medical standards, and whether there is a causal link between their actions and Svitlana’s husband’s death.
However, Huk has been unable to obtain such a conclusion for years. The case materials were sent to expert institutions repeatedly, but the examination was never carried out.
Kyiv twice explained its refusal to conduct the examination by citing the absence of a pathological autopsy and the impossibility of reliably establishing the cause of death. Among the reasons for its refusal, Lviv cited the absence of an approved list of paid services, as well as the fact that the entries in the inpatient medical record had been made in Russian, which, according to the bureau’s position, prevented their objective examination.
At that point, the plan was to translate the documentation into Ukrainian and send the materials to the experts again. However, as Svitlana Huk told UNN , it has still not been possible to obtain the necessary expert conclusion.
Even as part of the criminal proceedings, Kyiv refused to conduct the examination for the third time,
Olha Melai — questions about the documents and a blocked investigation
Olha Melai’s husband underwent chemotherapy at Odrex. Because he needed regular drug infusions, he was offered the installation of a special port — a procedure that clinic staff described as minimally invasive and uncomplicated. However, after the intervention, Ihor Melai ended up in intensive care in critical condition and later died. In total, the treatment and medications cost the family more than UAH 2.5 million.
After her husband’s death, Olha had questions about the medical documentation: according to her, the discharge summary contained practically no information either about the port insertion itself or about the consequences of the intervention. The widow contacted law enforcement authorities and handed investigators copies of documents confirming payment for the treatment, while the investigator said that the medical record was to be submitted for a forensic medical examination.
Melai contacted law enforcement. Based on her statement, criminal proceedings No. 42025163030000200 are being investigated under Part 3 of Article 190 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. She provided the investigators with copies of documents confirming payment for treatment, and the investigator said that he intended to submit the medical record for a forensic medical examination.
Not limiting herself to the criminal proceedings, Melai contacted the Ministry of Health and asked it to verify the medical records concerning her husband’s treatment at Odrex for discrepancies and possible falsification. The Ministry instructed the Health Department of the Odesa Regional Military Administration to conduct a clinical and expert assessment; however, the inspection could not be carried out. The Department explained that the Odrex clinic had not provided the patient’s medical documentation, citing its seizure by law enforcement as part of the criminal proceedings.
After that, Melai herself contacted the police, asking them to grant the Department access to the seized materials. At the same time, she submitted requests to the National Health Service of Ukraine and the eHealth system to verify the data concerning her husband’s treatment and his electronic medical records.
Thus, almost a year after the criminal proceedings were opened, the question of what exactly happened during Ihor Melai’s treatment and whether any violations occurred still remains without a final answer.
Khrystyna Totkailo’s father was promised that his voice would be preserved
In August 2024, Khrystyna Totkailo learned that her father had cancer. The family lives in Kyiv, so they initially contacted Feofaniya Hospital. According to Khrystyna, after a consultation, the doctors concluded that aggressive chemotherapy before radical surgery was too risky in his case.
According to Khrystyna, surgeon Ihor Bielotserkovskyi was also present at that consultation. He was the one who suggested that the family contact the Odesa-based Odrex clinic, where his wife, oncologist Maryna Bielotserkovska, worked. Khrystyna recalls that the family was told that this was where her father could receive treatment in a way that would preserve his larynx and voice.
At Odrex, the man was prescribed a five-day course of chemotherapy, with another course planned. He was also fitted with a feeding gastrostomy. Khrystyna said that she repeatedly asked staff to monitor its condition and change the dressings, but, according to her, there was no proper care for several days. Before he was discharged, it was discovered that a through-and-through opening had formed in the area of the gastrostomy.
After returning to Kyiv, her father’s condition deteriorated sharply: his kidneys began to fail, and wounds appeared in his mouth. Khrystyna claims that she did not receive clear answers to her questions about the prescribed treatment and her father’s condition.
The family paid more than UAH 250,000 for the treatment. It was not possible to save her father—he died. After his death, Khrystyna contacted law enforcement.
After his death, Khrystyna contacted law enforcement. Based on her statement, criminal proceedings No. 42025163030000197 are being investigated.
Recently, I was informed that the investigator in the case had been changed and that the documents had been sent for examination. For now, this is all the information I have about the progress of the proceedings. It is difficult for me to obtain more detailed information because I am in Kyiv, while the investigation is being conducted in Odesa,
Several years have already passed, yet the families still have not received definitive answers. The investigations have been accompanied by delays, changes of investigators, and difficulties in carrying out examinations. At the same time, the relatives of deceased Odrex patients continue to fight for the right to know the truth about what happened to their loved ones.

Bulgaria Starts Free Flu Vaccination for Children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:10:00 UTC
17:10:00 KST

Free seasonal flu vaccinations for children have begun in Bulgaria, with 75,000 doses of a nasal vaccine secured for the current winter season, according to the health authorities.
The nasal vaccine is expected to be the main option initially available through general practitioners. It can be given to children aged 2 and older and does not require an injection.
Under the national program, free vaccination is available to all children up to and including age 7, as well as children with chronic conditions through age 17.
Another 50,000 doses of injectable flu vaccine for children have been allocated, with the first deliveries expected to reach Bulgaria at the end of October. Delays in vaccine deliveries are affecting both doses supplied under national programs and vaccines intended for sale in pharmacies.
Annual flu vaccination is recommended because vaccine formulations are updated to correspond with the flu strains expected during the season. Vaccination is considered particularly important for young children and people with chronic conditions because they face a higher risk of severe illness and complications from influenza.
Bulgaria has already recorded its first seasonal flu case of the new season. The patient has been hospitalized in Sofia for treatment.
The appearance of the first cases marks the beginning of the active respiratory infection season and highlights the importance of prevention.
Doctors also advise maintaining good personal hygiene, ventilating rooms regularly and limiting contact with others when symptoms of flu or another viral infection develop.

At the same time, however, the safety of the nuclear power plant depends directly on the operational readiness of the equipment located on the Zaporozhye Thermal Power Plant’s grounds. Specifically, we are talking about electrical equipment on the grounds that redirects electricity from the Ferrosplavnaya high-voltage lines to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant. Two weeks ago, due to constant Ukrainian shelling, a transformer that powered this equipment was damaged. And for two weeks now, emergency diesel generators have been maintaining the operational capability of these critically important systems," he said.

It explained that 134,422 buildings were completely destroyed, while 13,848 sustained severe damage and around 328,627 housing units were damaged.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, and destroyed around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure.

Bolsonaro's surprise lead over Lula sends Brazil elections to runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:05:00 UTC
17:05:00 KST

Brazil's right-wing Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro secured a surprise lead over President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s election, sending it to a runoff in three weeks.
In a result that defied opinion poll projections showing Lula in the lead, Flavio Bolsonaro scored 47% of the vote to the incumbent's 45%.
If Bolsonaro triumphs in the Oct. 25 election, the Latin American powerhouse will join a steady rightward march in the region in recent elections, a trend championed by U.S. President Donald Trump.
The election results included a series of landslide wins for the right in parliament in a massive setback to Lula, who at almost 81 is seeking a fourth term in office to cement his legacy.
"I admit I was convinced I would win in the first round. The game is about to start. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people," the 80-year-old said.
The veteran leftist has branded the election a battle between democracy and "barbarism," warning voters that Brazil's sovereignty was at stake in the face of U.S. pressure.
Flavio Bolsonaro was a little-known senator a few months ago when his father anointed him his political heir, unable to run himself as he serves a 27-year sentence for an attempted coup after losing a 2022 election bid.
However, his father's powerful name won over the country's conservative base and he slid past Lula despite a campaign marked by scandals and mudslinging.
"I am truly happy with the result," Flavio Bolsonaro said after results came through, hailing the "very real possibility" of a run-off victory.
Voters in the deeply polarized nation were jaded by familiar choices and few voted with conviction.
Oscarina de Oliveira, a 62-year-old caregiver, said she had planned to vote for Lula, as she always has. But "when I got there, I switched to Bolsonaro. Just to see what happens, to see if anything changes."
Carolina Botelho, a political scientist at the Rio de Janeiro State University, said that the leading candidate in the first round has won every election in Brazil since the end of the country's military dictatorship in 1985.
With 56 million votes, Flavio Bolsonaro's first round performance outdid that of Jair Bolsonaro in 2018, when he was elected and 2022.
It emerged during the campaign that Flavio Bolsonaro was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic "Dark Horse" about his father.
For many voters, this did little to move the needle.
"Things are truly terrible. As far as I'm concerned, the left just doesn't work anymore," said tech worker Joao Batista, 36, in the Rocinha favela, saying he was fed up with the "horrible" expense of basic goods.
Flavio Bolsonaro highlighted Sunday that as president he will have the possibility of appointing four justices to the powerful Supreme Court – which convicted his father and has been at the center of key political and criminal scandals.
The elections proved a triumphant comeback for the Bolsonaro family after Jair Bolsonaro lost a re-election bid in 2022, leading to violent riots in the capital and his conviction last year for attempting a coup.
Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro and another one of Jair Bolsonaro's sons, Carlos Bolsonaro, both secured seats in the senate.
Jair Bolsonaro's youngest son Jair Renan, 28, was elected as a federal lawmaker.
Flavio has cast himself as more "moderate" than his firebrand father, but his critics were concerned.
"Flavio is a danger to Brazil, he represents a step backward. We can see everything his father did...He really destroyed Brazil," said Anderson de Almeida, a 45-year-old doorman.
Trump had said he was watching the election "very closely," but did not endorse Flavio Bolsonaro.
The US president has wielded tariffs and sanctions to pressure Brasilia over complaints ranging from the trial against his ally Jair Bolsonaro to alleged unfair trade practices.
Lula repeatedly warned him not to "meddle" in the elections.
Revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, Lula made a dramatic comeback to office in the 2022 elections after being jailed on a corruption conviction for 18 months.
The charges, thrown out on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him.
In his third term he oversaw a drop in inflation and unemployment, but voters complain about a high cost of living and as in many Latin American nations, citizens are fed up with high levels of crime and violence.

Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces seized key positions on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait on Monday, military and government sources said, as they fought to reverse last month's advances by the Iran-backed Houthis and drive them from the vital waterway.
The government forces have taken large parts of Dhubab district, which overlooks Bab al-Mandeb, and are asserting full control over the area with heavy air support from a Saudi-led coalition, three military sources and one government source told Reuters.
Houthi-aligned media had earlier denied that government forces had made advances in the area.
Fighting has raged along several frontlines in Yemen for weeks after a dormant civil war erupted in a spillover from the US-Iran conflict, with the Houthis seeking to control the vital Bab al-Mandeb Strait and firing missiles and drones at Saudi cities and infrastructure.
With Gulf energy exports already restricted by Iran's closure of the Hormuz Strait, the fighting in Yemen has threatened another major oil export route, pushing up global prices and raising new risks in a region already aflame.
Saudi Arabia backs offensive to retake territory
The internationally recognized Yemeni government announced on Sunday the launch of its offensive to recapture territory, with President Rashad al-Alimi swearing to fight "until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia."
Saudi Arabia, which arms and trains Yemeni government forces, is backing the military campaign with air power and has sought logistical help from allies to push back the Houthis, restore free traffic in the Red Sea, and end the group's attacks on its territory.
While the war has raged on several frontlines in Yemen, the heaviest fighting has been in the southwest, both in the coastal area near the strait and in the hills around the city of Taiz, where the Houthis are trying to surround government forces.
A Houthi-run news agency on Monday cited a military source as saying that the group had driven government forces from the al-Mawasit district of Taiz province, reaching the home of Alimi, head of Yemen's interim presidential council.
The mountainous district sits close to the main road running from Taiz to Aden, the last route that government forces have had into the city, which has been on the frontlines since early in the civil war.
Yemen's conflict began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in the following year with an air campaign aimed at restoring the government and ousting the Iran-backed group.
The fighting quickly ground to a bloody stalemate, with most frontlines stalled, leading to a major humanitarian crisis in what was already the poorest Arab state, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022 that held until this summer.

Spanish PM Pedro Sanchez calls snap November election as far-right looms and polling lags
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:04:03 UTC
17:04:03 KST

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called an early election for November 29 on Monday, in a bid to strengthen his mandate after a fragmented parliament rejected the government's key housing decrees last week amid widespread protests.
"We need to renew people's support," Sanchez said in a televised address. "We need to mobilize and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain."
The premier also acknowledged having made mistakes and falling short of campaign promises.
"I also know that part of that social majority is dissatisfied today," he said.
Sanchez has stood out globally for taking a strong stance on progressive issues from Palestinian statehood to defending multilateral institutions and cracking down on "tech oligarchs," even as a series of setbacks and scandals weakened his position at home.
Sanchez skilled at cobbling together coalitions
Facing the electorate now is a risky move as Sanchez's Socialist Party is trailing in opinion polls. However, he has been boosted by proposals to tackle a mounting housing crisis that were well received but were struck down by right-wing MPs on Friday, leading to planned new public protests about housing.
An election defeat would spell the end of one of Europe's last few left-leaning governments at a time when the far-right is making unprecedented gains across the region as a growing swathe of European voters desert the center ground.
Opinion polls suggest a coalition led by the conservative People's Party (PP) with the support of Vox is the most likely outcome in Spain, ushering a far-right party into central government for the first time since the return of democracy after the death of dictator Francisco Franco.
Still, Sanchez, a wily political operator, has proven time and again his ability to surprise those who had long written him off.
Despite never winning enough votes to form a majority government, he has cobbled together a series of fragile and seemingly impossible coalitions including voices from the far-left to the separatist right to remain in power for three successive terms lasting eight years.
But growing fragmentation among his partners has meant the government has passed little in the way of legislation in its third term and failed to pass a budget since 2023, even as Spain's economy has continued to be one of the best performing in the developed world.
Sanchez moves as rival ousted
Sanchez took office after leading a move to oust center-right Mariano Rajoy in the wake of major corruption scandals within Rajoy's People's Party. However, senior members of Sanchez's own Socialist Party have in the past year faced allegations of graft, dragging down the party's already weak approval rating, which has hovered at around 26-31% throughout his tenure.
Against the odds, he won a second four-year term in office in 2023 despite heavy losses in earlier regional and local elections by negotiating support from a loose alliance of parties in parliament.
That was achieved after promising a highly controversial amnesty for pro-independence Catalan leaders in exchange for their support, a move still bitterly remembered by many voters as a betrayal of Spanish unity.
Sanchez won early plaudits for moves including the exhumation of Franco from a mausoleum the dictator built for himself outside Madrid, and the reform of a labor law that has seen unemployment fall to its lowest level in almost two decades.
He cemented his humanitarian and pro-immigration credentials early by saying in June 2018 that Spain would accept the Aquarius migrant rescue ship and its 629 passengers, after Italy and Malta both refused to let the ship dock in their harbors.
As other European countries have toughened their policies towards foreign arrivals, Sanchez has consistently argued that immigration is essential for sustaining Spanish growth by plugging gaps in key sectors such as construction, agriculture and hospitality and for providing revenue to prop up Spain's strained welfare system.
More recently, his refusal to agree to US-led demands to increase defense spending to 5% of GDP while pivoting toward China has rattled US President Trump and some European leaders concerned about the threat of the bloc being flooded with Chinese goods.
Sanchez's housing measures provided a rare chance for the Socialist leader to pitch himself as the leader of a mobilized left and distract from the more politically damaging issues of the migrant crisis in Ceuta and corruption scandals, said Lorenzo Bernaldo de Quiros, economist and president of consultancy Freemarket Corporate Intelligence.
"This is a window of opportunity," de Quiros said. "If he does not call elections fast, (those topics) will return to center stage."

====================================================================================================

New documentary 'To Kill a Nazi' details Holocaust survivor's key role in Entebbe rescue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:03:54 UTC
17:03:54 KST

As I interviewed Boaz Dvir, the director of the new documentary, To Kill a Nazi, which had its Israeli premiere last week at the Haifa International Film Festival, it was impossible not to talk about the big story of the previous day - the hijacking of the flydubai flight that was foiled by Israeli passengers.
That was because this incident made To Kill a Nazi incredibly topical, since it tells the story of the extraordinary life of Michel Cojot, a French Holocaust survivor who became obsessed with assassinating the Nazi official Klaus Barbie, who was responsible for deporting his father to Auschwitz.
Later, Cojot was a passenger on the Air France flight that was hijacked to Entebbe. Much of the film details Cojot’s role in giving crucial information to Israeli authorities that enabled them to conduct the Operation Thunderbolt raid, one of the most successful and spectacular military rescues in history.
The documentary, narrated by Jason Alexander, will be shown on October 6 at the Menachem Begin Heritage Center in Jerusalem and is being screened around the world, including at the Jewish Film Festival in Australia, the Chelsea Film Festival in New York, and the Silicon Valley Film Festival later this month.
Cojot spoke in interviews about how, when he became a victim in the 1976 hijacking, he felt as if he had been given a second chance to prove himself because not long before that, he had located Barbie in Bolivia but had chosen, gun in hand, not to murder him.
A whole army behind the Entebbe hijackers
My first question was what Dvir thought Cojot would have done had he been on the flydubai plane. “He would have joined those guys in storming the cockpit. Absolutely. In fact, when they landed in Entebbe, he got a few Israelis together and contemplated doing exactly that: overtaking the four terrorists.
“What changed his mind was seeing the Ugandan soldiers and noticing that the head hijacker, Wilfried Bose, was huddling with them. He realized that even if we take over the plane, there are these soldiers; there’s a whole army behind them.”
The story of Cojot’s experience in the Entebbe hijacking and his role in making Operation Thunderbolt possible could have easily been the subject of an entire documentary.
“It was drawn out and intense… The world was fixated on Entebbe for that whole week,” recalled Dvir, who grew up in Israel and was fascinated by the hijacking as a nine-year-old.
“My father woke us up that Sunday morning and said the words: The IDF did it,” said Dvir, a journalism professor at Pennsylvania State University, in addition to his work as a documentary filmmaker.
Much later, he planned to make a documentary about a different Michel – Michel Bacos, the Air France captain of the plane hijacked to Entebbe. Bacos became a hero because he said he had turned down the chance to be released early on, but chose to remain with the hostages.
But as Dvir researched Bacos’s story, he realized that a release of the flight crew was never on the table; the hijackers needed them there because the plane was a new kind of Airbus that almost no one knew how to fly.
While interviewing survivors of the hijacking, one name came up again and again: Michel Cojot. “They said: ‘There was a French hero there, and his name was Michel. Not Michel Bacos: Michel Cojot.’ That’s how I discovered this complex, fascinating Jewish character.”
While it has always been rumored that an Israeli firm designed the Entebbe airport terminal and gave the Mossad and the IDF the blueprints, Cojot, who was among the second group of hostages released before the raid, provided more crucial information, Dvir said.
“What really made the [Israeli] military hesitate was the reports from the other released hostages, one by one, telling them the terminal was rigged, that it was booby-trapped. You can’t storm a building that’s booby-trapped. The whole building explodes. Everything goes up in flames, and everybody dies. That was really holding them back. Then Michel assured them it was not.”
Cojot had checked the boxes that supposedly held the explosives and knew that they were empty.
“He went as far as taking photographs. Can you imagine? You’re a hostage, and you’re taking photos of the terrorists?… He’s making diagrams, taking notes, sneaking them to his son [Olivier, who was held hostage with him at first and was released with the first group]…
Cojot's father killed in Auschwitz, survived by hiding
“When I interviewed Israelis who were part of the rescue mission, they knew about Michel Cojot. I wasn’t breaking the news. They nicknamed him ‘Colonel Cojot.’ They thought he was a French military guy.”
Cojot’s plan to get information to the Israeli authorities worked, but he clearly risked his 12-year-old son’s life to carry it out. He even tasked Olivier with destroying Israeli passports in secret, so the hijackers wouldn’t know which hostages were Israeli.
This choice to turn his son into his assistant during the hijacking becomes even more complex and interesting when you look at Cojot’s own childhood. Cojot was born in France in 1938 to Jewish parents; when he was still a child, his parents acquired false identity documents. His name was changed several times so that he could escape deportation to the death camps.
But one day his father was caught and sent to Auschwitz, where he was killed. Cojot and his mother hid during the rest of the war, and she married a man after that who adopted Cojot.
Cojot went on to receive an MBA from Columbia University and had a successful career with the consulting firm, McKinsey & Company in France. He also married and had three children. But he was haunted by the loss of his father and blamed himself for not being able to save him, although he was just a child at the time. He could not enjoy living a normal life, and trained his own children on how to survive if there were ever another Holocaust.
GRADUALLY, HE became obsessed with a desire to take revenge on Barbie, who was responsible for the deportation of his father. After the war, Barbie was living openly in Bolivia, where he trained government-backed militias. Cojot even persuaded McKinsey to open an office in Venezuela that he headed, so he could more easily track Barbie.
The film shows how the Holocaust survivor managed to insinuate himself into Barbie’s inner circle, but also that, when Cojot was finally alone on a street with Barbie, he chose not to kill him.
“He was not a killer. He never fully explains it, not in his interviews or his book. It isn’t clear. Maybe it was subconscious, a feeling rather than a thought… ‘Don’t do it, don’t stoop to his level; you’re trying to get rid of evil, and now you’ll attach yourself to it if you kill him.’”
Not long after that, Cojot boarded the Air France flight and felt that this gave him a second chance to bring down evil. Besides sharing critical information with Israeli authorities, he also tried to bring this intelligence to the French government, but an official who answered the phone on Friday told him to call back on Monday; he spent a great deal of time trying to discreetly influence Bose, one of the hijackers. When the raid began, Bose could have killed the hostages, but he did not.
“Bose was such a hardcore guy. Why didn’t he throw the grenade or shoot the hostages? He knows he’s about to die. This is his life mission. He’s been a terrorist for a while, one of the leaders of the international terrorist movement connected with [infamous terrorist known as Carlos the] Jackal.
“There’s no doubt in my mind that Michel got to him. Michel played a tricky psychological game. I like to look at actions, and Michel convinced him to take several actions that harmed their cause.”
Chief among these actions was persuading the hijackers to release two groups of passengers.
“Releasing hostages doesn’t help the hijackers. First, they bring information to people planning a rescue. Second, it diminishes the hijackers’ power, which rests on how many hostages they hold. Fewer hostages from fewer countries means less power,” said Dvir.
“There was no reason to release them. They were protected by Idi Amin and Ugandan soldiers. The airport cafeteria was feeding everybody. But Bose let Michel manipulate him.”
Cojot wrote about how he shared his story of coming close to killing Barbie with Bose, and tried to convince him that if he were to kill Jewish hostages, he would be acting just like a Nazi.
Looking back on Cojot’s complicated life and legacy, Dvir said, “So many survivors don’t want to know or talk, or want to create their own bubble. I don’t blame them; life is difficult. Michel couldn’t do that. He always had to know the truth.
“Then he’d figure out how to deal with it. Painful, damaging, helpful; it didn’t matter. He had to know. That is the aspect of his life I personally relate to. I have the same obsession. What is the truth? Not what I want it to be. What is it, really?”
Speaking again about the flydubai incident, Dvir added, “I keep coming back to landing in Israel to show this film on the day of this attempted hijacking: Is there something going on? Some sort of divine intervention? Is Michel’s spirit here?”
See the film’s website tokillanazi.com for a full list of screenings.

ANU adds three new artworks to 'October 7' exhibit as Israel marks third anniversary of massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:03:20 UTC
17:03:20 KST

ANU – Museum of the Jewish People in Tel Aviv will mark the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre with an evening exploring the role of art in expressing grief, preserving memory, and finding hope, on the evening of October 5.
The event, called “We Shall Yet See Better Days: Art and Hope Rising From the Fracture,” will introduce three new works to the museum’s October Seventh exhibition, which opened shortly after the attacks.
Curated by Michal Houminer and Carmit Blumensohn, the exhibition brings together works by 25 artists, documentary photography, and Israeli songs associated with the period.
The new works, created by graduates of the University of Haifa’s School of Design, examine how the events have shaped Israeli society and its visual language.
Tamara Kloss’s Compassion Fatigue explores the proliferation of memorial stickers in public spaces, asking how repeated exposure affects our response to individual stories of loss.
Yael Lerner’s I Saw a Dove uses the familiar symbol of peace to examine the fragility of hope in Israel, while Yehuda Feldmer’s Shalom traces the word’s visual and cultural meanings from the Bible to the present. All three artists will discuss their work during the evening.
Art as a path to healing
Artist and designer Gabi Zaltzman will give a lecture titled “You Can’t Cancel Spring: Optimistic Creativity in Difficult Times,” drawing on his work and personal experiences to explore how art, humor, and creativity can sustain people through uncertainty.
“Art is a powerful force that allows us to reflect, ease suffering, perhaps heal, and begin to create hope,” said museum CEO Oded Revivi.
The museum will also offer guided tours on October 5 and 7.
ANU is located on the Tel Aviv University campus.

Saudi Arabia turns to Pakistan, Turkey as US refuses to intervene against Houthi threat - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:03:20 UTC
17:03:20 KST

For decades, the relationship between Saudi Arabia and the US has centered on an often-mentioned but rarely tested supposition: If the kingdom were attacked, America would come to its rescue.
But recent events have shown that much-vaunted security umbrella to be a leaky one.
Last month, Iran-aligned Yemeni rebels blitzed through Yemen's coast and threatened to shut down Saudi Arabia's Red Sea lifeline. But the Trump administration, reluctant to open a new front in its war with Iran, rebuffed Riyadh's calls to come to its rescue.
That has left the kingdom searching for friends beyond Washington, for allies ready to put rockets where the rhetoric is and assist in a fight Saudi Arabia considers existential.
Over the last few months, as Persian Gulf nations contended with the fallout from the Israel-US war on Iran, Saudi Arabia has supercharged its military-focused diplomacy. In July, it announced a 15-nation maritime alliance to safeguard shipping through the Red Sea, the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the Gulf of Aden.
NATO-style Mecca Joint Defense Agreement established in fallout of Iran war
Soon after came the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a NATO-inspired security pact where any attack on Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan would be regarded as an attack against all three.
And this week, Saudi Arabia's race to rally allies spurred a detente of sorts with its frenemy the United Arab Emirates, with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman - the country's de facto ruler - and defense minister's brother receiving the Emirates' vice president for the first high-level meeting since the two sides fell out over Yemen late last year.
There have even been reports of possible cooperation between Saudi Arabia and Israel against the Houthis, a notable development - if true - for two countries with no formal diplomatic relations.
The Saudi overtures come at a sensitive time for the kingdom. The standoff between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz has largely cut off Saudi Arabia's main export channel, and attacks on its energy infrastructure are lowering its oil output.
As a result, the kingdom saw a 25% contraction in "oil activities," according to official economic data, triggering an almost 5% decrease in the country's gross domestic product between April and June, compared with the first quarter of the year.
Houthis escalate war against Saudi Arabia, Yemen
That reduction forced painful cuts to Vision 2030, the prince's signature policy aimed at remaking Saudi Arabia. So-called giga-projects, such as the Line and Trojena, have revised their ambitions downward amid the financial realities of a Saudi Arabia under fire.
And all that was before the Houthis got involved.
The Houthis had been fighting the Saudis since 2015 in Yemen's civil war that killed hundreds of thousands of people before settling into a stalemate and an uneasy ceasefire in 2022.
But in July, Saudi Arabia attacked the airport in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, to prevent the landing of an Iranian plane carrying high-ranking Houthi officials. That set off a flurry of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure, and the Houthis' announcement of a blockade against Saudi shipping on the Red Sea - now the main corridor for Saudi energy exports.
Then in September, the Houthis overran Yemen's coastal cities, snapping up materiel left behind by Saudi-backed government fighters and seizing control of territory near the Bab al Mandab strait.
A few days later, the Saudis accused an Iranian-backed militia in Iraq of coordinating with the Houthis to hit the East-West Pipeline, the vital infrastructure that had allowed Saudi Arabia to reorient its oil from Hormuz to the Red Sea.
All that pushed the Saudi crown prince to turn to the US for help - and he had reason to think it would come: Late last year, the US signed a strategic defense agreement with the kingdom, designated it a major non-NATO ally, and agreed to sell it advanced F-35 fighter jets.
Mohammed also has something of a personal relationship with US President Donald Trump, who made Saudi Arabia the first stop of his first overseas tour in 2025 after being reelected and boasted that he had garnered almost $1 trillion in Saudi investments into the US economy.
Trump initially seemed receptive to the prince's entreaties but reportedly pulled back just as US warplanes were set to take off for sorties on Houthi targets. Later, he told Fox News that Washington was "in constant communication with the Houthis and that they've agreed not to fight the United States."
The Houthis have also assured European nations, which have been wary of provoking the rebels' ire, that they won't attack their shipping either. Last month, France and the UK said they would offer defensive assistance to Saudi Arabia, while Greece is operating US-made Patriot missile batteries in the kingdom.
With the US hesitating, the expectation is that Saudi Arabia's partners in the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement will form the international cavalry to help, but that has yet to manifest itself on the ground.
This week, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif said his country was "bound" by the pact to defend Saudi Arabia.
"That means whatever means are available at our disposal, they'll be available to Saudi Arabia also," he said.
Pakistan already has 8,000 troops in Saudi Arabia, along with 16 Chinese-made JF-17 Thunder fighter jets, combat drone squadrons and a surface-to-air missile battery. But it's unclear whether they have participated in attacking the Houthis.
Turkish officials, meanwhile, say they have "no issues meeting" Saudi Arabia's "military needs," especially on technical matters.
The Houthis say any party attacking them will face retaliation.
"By God, if Turkey and Pakistan become involved, we will strike them with an iron fist," said Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior member of the Houthis, in an interview on Iraqi television.
Observers say Saudi Arabia is gearing up for a ground offensive aimed at preventing the Houthis from consolidating their gains on the Red Sea coast and reversing the tide. The plan is for Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighters to lead the charge.
"It will be mostly an air campaign for the Saudis, with Yemenis and maybe Pakistanis on the ground, though I doubt the latter will get involved beyond being on the border," said Bernard Haykel, a professor of Near Eastern Studies at Princeton University.
There is little chance the US would contribute to such a fight with boots on the ground. But it could provide intelligence and logistical support, just as it did during Mohammed's 2015 foray into Yemen. The US Navy could also launch strikes, as it did when the Houthis blockaded the Red Sea in 2025, before Trump declared a ceasefire.
In any case, although Saudi leaders may not expect Washington to get involved, their fear is that the US will forge another agreement with the Houthis to the exclusion of Riyadh's concerns, Haykel said.
"The Saudis want a signal that the US is in the background as support if something happens," he said.
"They'd love to have it in the center of everything. But if they can't, they want to make it seem like America is fully on board without necessarily being in the battle."

An Ireland football staff member has alleged that an Israeli player spat at him during a tense Nations League match Sunday, as political tensions surrounding the fixture spilled onto the pitch.
Damien Doyle, Ireland’s head of athletic performance, made the allegation as players and staff headed toward the tunnel at halftime during the 1-1 draw at the TSC Arena in Backa Topola, Serbia, according to The Irish Times.
Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson said the incident would be considered by a disciplinary committee.
“I felt like they were trying to intimidate us from kick-off,” he said, according to The Irish Times, adding that he gave his players credit for remaining calm.
Israel coach Ran Ben-Shimon said he had already gone to the dressing room and did not see what happened, while the Israel Football Association declined to comment.
The incident added to a highly charged match between the teams, which was played behind closed doors after the Football Association of Ireland moved the fixture to a neutral venue in Serbia, citing operational challenges.
Ireland players wore black armbands and bowed their heads during Israel’s national anthem. They also again refused the traditional pre-match handshake.
On the field, Troy Parrott gave Ireland the lead from a penalty in the 39th minute before Israel captain Dor Peretz equalized shortly after halftime.
Israel hit the post twice in the second half, but neither side found a winner. The draw left Ireland third in Nations League Group B3 on five points, while Israel remained bottom with two, according to the Football Association of Ireland.
The match followed Ireland’s 3-0 victory over Israel in Hungary on Sept. 27.
The two games drew strong political attention in Ireland because of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, with calls for the Football Association of Ireland to boycott the fixtures. The association proceeded with the games after warning that withdrawal could lead to UEFA sanctions.
Hallgrimsson said after Sunday’s match that he was “absolutely delighted” the two-game series was over, describing the past two weeks as difficult for his team.
He has also called for UEFA to ensure that Ireland and Israel are not drawn together again, according to The Guardian.

More Than 5,000 Arrested as French School Protests Escalate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:01:00 UTC
17:01:00 KST

Between 400 and 500 schools across France will be fully or partially closed on Monday because of ongoing student protests, Education Minister Edouard Geffray said, with 24 schools already having been burned or ransacked since the movement began.
Geffray said Sunday that lessons would be “totally or partly suspended” at around 400 to 500 high schools because security conditions “have not been fulfilled.” He said the number of affected schools would be similar to Friday's figure but promised a “partial, progressive return to lessons.”
More than one-third of the 468 schools in the wider Ile-de-France region around Paris will be closed Monday because of the demonstrations, regional president Valerie Pecresse told Franceinfo.
The protests began at a Paris school on September 17 before expanding nationwide last week, with some demonstrations turning violent as teenagers clashed with security forces. Police have at times used tear gas and batons to disperse students.
Students at French high schools, known as lycées, have complained about high teacher absenteeism, excessively long school days and deteriorating facilities, along with other grievances.
At an open-air meeting in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, students spoke Sunday about their complaints.
One student from a deprived district said, “The violence is unleashed.” She referred to a student who had lost his teeth after being hit by a police rubber bullet and another who had suffered an eye injury.
A 16-year-old student named Campion held a placard reading, “They say they are listening to us but prefer to gas us.”
“I don't understand why the government deploys so much force against a case that is valid: our education, our future,” he told AFP.
Geffray accused far-left infiltrators of having “hijacked” the movement and engaging in extreme violence. He said the situation created a risk for both staff and students and reported that 78 education workers had been injured.
“They were deliberately targeted because they were employees of the national education system,” Geffray said.
Organizers have called for demonstrations to continue Tuesday, citing the government's lack of “concrete measures.”
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu sought to respond to the students' concerns Sunday by establishing a timetable that calls on local authorities to prioritize filling vacancies created by long-term absences and unfilled positions.
Lecornu also scheduled a meeting with regional presidents for Tuesday to discuss renovating the country's frequently deteriorating school buildings.
More than 5,000 people have been arrested since the protests began, 85% of them minors.
A 16-year-old was detained Sunday over an attack on a teacher in the southern town of La Ciotat. The 59-year-old teacher was hit and doused with gasoline near a high school demonstration Friday.
In Belfort in eastern France, footage emerged last week showing several youths kicking and beating a police officer who was on the ground, prompting strong reactions from officials.
The prosecutor said two youths, Bulgarian nationals aged 15 and 17, had been arrested and placed under investigation for suspected aggravated violence.
The lawyer for one of the youths, whom the officer had attempted to arrest before the assault, said his client had filed his own complaint alleging attempted murder.
Amnesty France criticized what it called “disproportionate police violence” during the demonstrations last week and said students must be able to express their grievances.
“Authorities must allow young people to exercise these rights without fear of being hit by tear gas grenades or batons, or being arbitrarily taken into police custody,” said Anne Savinel-Barras, president of Amnesty France.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez rejected the characterization of the police response, saying security forces “are not cracking down on young people” but are instead “protecting” students who want to “peacefully voice their demands.”

U.S. Withdraws All B-1B Strategic Bombers from RAF Fairford
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:00:51 UTC
17:00:51 KST

The United States has withdrawn all B-1B strategic bombers deployed at the British RAF Fairford airfield.
The Pentagon and U.S. European Command (EUCOM) confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine the redeployment of the aircraft to their permanent bases in the United States.
On October 4, 12 B-1B Lancer bombers previously stationed in the United Kingdom left the air base throughout the day.
“We can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” the U.S. defense agency said in a statement to TWZ.
The Pentagon emphasized that the redeployment does not affect U.S. strategic bombers’ ability to conduct combat missions. B-1Bs, B-2s, and B-52s can carry out long-range combat missions directly from the continental United States.
The redeployment took place amid a counterterrorism investigation surrounding the airfield.
On September 27, British law enforcement received reports of three suspicious vehicles traveling toward RAF Fairford. Police detained five men aged between 23 and 25 near Welford. Police later released all five detainees on bail with restrictions, but they remain subjects of the investigation.
Britain’s Counter Terrorism Policing said they are investigating several possible lines of inquiry, including the possibility that the detainees may have been acting on behalf of a foreign state.
On September 30, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were indications of Iranian involvement in an alleged plot to carry out a terrorist attack near RAF Fairford.
On October 1, police detained another man in London as part of the investigation. The British-Iranian national was suspected of preparing a terrorist attack. On October 3, he was released on bail, while the investigation remains ongoing.
However, as of now, British law enforcement has not publicly presented evidence conclusively establishing Iran’s involvement in the incident.
RAF Fairford plays an important role in U.S. strategic bomber operations in the Middle East. At the beginning of hostilities with Iran, the British government officially allowed the United States to use RAF Fairford for designated operations against Iranian missile forces.
The UK government said that U.S. operations from British bases were aimed at destroying Iranian missiles that posed a threat to allies and shipping. The first U.S. bomber deployed as part of this mission arrived at RAF Fairford in March 2026.
On July 22, the U.S. Air Force used B-1B Lancer to strike Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps facilities in Iran. The aircraft performed combat missions using the British RAF Fairford airfield.
On March 2, U.S. B-1Bs were used to strike ballistic missile production and storage facilities in Iran.
The scale of the U.S. deployment at RAF Fairford was so significant that organizers canceled the Royal International Air Tattoo 2026 air show in May.

Nobel Prize 2026 kicks off: Who will win the medicine award?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:00:45 UTC
17:00:45 KST

Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine for their research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics — a method that "provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of."
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2026 is awarded for optogenetics — a method that makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviours in the living brain, the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet announced on Monday.
German scientists Georg Nagel, Peter Hegemann and US scientist Karl Deisseroth won the Prize, laying foundation "of a new era in neuroscience", the institute said in a statement.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine in a press release.
“This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries,” the committee wrote on social platform X.
Last year's prize was shared by two US-based scientists, Mary E Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell, and their Japanese peer Shimon Sakaguchi for their discoveries in peripheral immune tolerance.
The three were awarded for "their groundbreaking discoveries concerning peripheral immune tolerance that prevents the immune system from harming the body," the institute said in a statement. Experts called the findings critical to understanding autoimmune diseases such as Type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and lupus.
The honour has been awarded 117 times to 235 laureates between 1901 and 2026.
Monday's medicine prize is followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday and literature on Thursday.
After Friday’s peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on 12 October.
The prize this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about €1.09 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates, or an organisation.
The award ceremony will be held on 10 December, the anniversary of the death of Alfred Nobel, a wealthy Swedish industrialist and the inventor of dynamite who founded the prizes. He died in 1896.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's Rita Chou (周婕妤) won her second Women's 9-Ball World Championship after defeating defending champion Seo Seoa of South Korea 3-1 in Sunday's final in Bali, Indonesia, per UDN.
The 39-year-old Chou, nicknamed the "Big-Eyed Girl," earned NT$1.75 million (US$55,000) in prize money. The victory also made her the second Taiwanese woman to win the annual pool tournament twice, matching Liu Hsin-mei's (柳信美) record from 1999 and 2002. She previously won the world title in 2023.
Chou advanced to the final after defeating China's Huang Qingning in the quarterfinals and Japan's Chihiro Kawahara 3-0 in the semifinals. She then overcame Seo, who was seeking her second consecutive title.
The tournament, held from Sept. 28 to Sunday, featured the world's top 64 female competitors. Taiwan sent seven players, including Wei Tzu-chien (魏子茜). Wei reached the semifinals, where she lost 3-1 to Seo and finished with a bronze medal.
Seo defeated two other Taiwanese players, Chou Chia-chia (周家嘉) and Chiang Shui-ching (江水淨), on her way to the final.
President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) congratulated Chou after her victory, praising her performance and encouraging Taiwan's billiards players to continue competing internationally.
The Ministry of Sports said in a press release that Taiwan's billiards players have achieved increasingly strong results at international competitions and that it will continue providing resources and logistical support to help athletes compete on the world stage.

Taiwan Coast Guard's second long-distance patrol ship begins construction

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Kaohsiung-based Taiwan International Shipbuilding Co. held the keel-laying ceremony for the second of six Coast Guard ocean patrol vessels in Kaohsiung on Friday.
A keel is the ship's structural foundation that runs along the bottom center from the bow to the stern, according to a press release. Laying the keel marks the official start of a ship's construction.
Siraya, the first of the six cutters, was launched on Nov. 1, 2025. It is named after one of the country's Indigenous groups, and other ships in the class will follow the same pattern.
The builder said the new patrol ships use reinforced steel for the hull and frame. The front uses an axe bow design that anchors the vessel for added stability in rough seas.
The builder said the displacement volume is about 5,000 metric tonnes. It added that the ship has a hybrid propulsion system for 30-day missions from cold, high-latitude regions to the tropical Indian Ocean.
The builder said the ships will secure maritime safety, enforce fishery laws, and support salvage operations. It noted that the ships will be delivered by 2031.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan High Speed Rail Corporation will add two southbound trains per hour on Friday evenings, with most cars offering non-reserved seating, to ease crowding during peak travel hours.
The additional service will operate every Friday between 5 p.m. and 9 p.m., THSRC said last Monday. Eight extra southbound trains will depart from Nangang or Taipei during the four hours and terminate at Taichung, per CNA.
All cars on the additional trains will offer unreserved seating except business class. THSRC said the busiest section for unreserved passengers is north of Taichung, where heavy crowds can also affect travelers with reserved seats.
The changes follow severe crowding during the Mid-Autumn Festival and Teachers' Day holiday period. A record 347,970 passengers used the high-speed rail on Sept. 24, while nearly 1.79 million traveled between Sept. 24 and 29, according to Economic Daily News.
Some passengers with reserved seats nearly missed their trains because of the crowds. Business-class passengers also complained that people with unreserved tickets had entered their cars.
To increase capacity, the operator will reverse trains directly at station platforms before sending them back into service. The arrangement will allow trains to begin their return journeys within about 12 minutes and reduce waiting times for northbound passengers, per TVBS News.
Before the regular Friday service begins, the new arrangement will first be used on Thursday during the National Day holiday travel period. Two extra southbound trains per hour will run to Taichung that day, while selected services will provide nine to 11 cars with unreserved seating.
A late-night train will also be added on Thursday, followed by an extra northbound service on Friday. The measures are intended to increase capacity before new trains enter service next July, per CTEE.

Estonia is moving troops closer to the border with the Russian Federation and preparing for a possible conflict — FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:59:41 EEST
16:59:41 KST

Estonia is moving troops closer to the border with the Russian Federation and preparing for a possible conflict — FT
Kyiv • UNN
Estonia is transferring a brigade to Jõhvi, 50 km from the border with the Russian Federation, and implementing an active defense strategy. The country is purchasing HIMARS and Chunmoo.
Estonia is redeploying a key brigade from the city of Tapa to Jõhvi, 50 kilometers from the Russian border, as part of launching an “active defense” strategy in preparation for possible aggression by russia. Estonian officials told the Financial Times, reports UNN.
Details
According to officials, Estonia is continuously moving troops closer to the border with Russia and purchasing weapons capable of striking deep into Russian territory, as this frontline NATO country prepares for possible aggression by moscow beyond Ukraine.
However, Estonia’s armed forces and intelligence chiefs do not believe that russia is seeking a full-scale war with NATO, at least over the next two years, but they are convinced that the russian federation is preparing for a possible future conflict with this Baltic state. This has prompted the country, which has no air force of its own, to adopt an “active defense” strategy.
“We have to start at the border and win the first battles,” said Colonel Tarmo Kundla, commander of Estonia’s First Brigade, the country’s main combat force.
Under the new strategy, his unit will be permanently redeployed from Tapa to Jõhvi, 50 km from the Russian border, where large new facilities for housing soldiers are currently being built.
“Deterrence is not working. The critical period for resolving this issue for all of us in the Baltic countries is the next one to four years,” said a representative of Estonian military intelligence.
“For deterrence to be credible, we must make aggression against us unthinkable. Our goal is clear: to keep the enemy and the devastation of war away from Estonian territory,” Estonia’s Ministry of Defence emphasized.
In May, the Estonian government introduced the term “active defense” into its national security concept. Since then, the country’s armed forces have begun a quiet but radical reorganization. From Tapa, Estonia’s main military base, elite units are being permanently redeployed to positions closer to the Russian border. In addition to the new base in Jõhvi, a base designed to accommodate 1,000 servicemembers is also being built in the border city of Narva.
Over the past year, the country has signed contracts to purchase nine American Himars multiple-launch rocket systems, M57 ballistic missiles with a range of up to 300 km, as well as nine South Korean Chunmoo MLRS units with a similar range. It should be noted that the distance from Estonian border bases to Russia’s St. Petersburg is 260 km.
During the decade following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2014, Estonian military strategists developed a defense doctrine shaped by the country’s history and geography. Under this approach, in the event of aggression, the country’s conscripts would rapidly mobilize and conduct a tactical, almost guerrilla-style defense to impede Russian forces and inflict losses on them until NATO reinforcements arrived.
However, observing russia’s actions in Ukraine, Estonia’s military leaders concluded that such a plan would not work. They now believe that the kremlin does not care about losses, fighting to retain captured territory even after everything on it has been destroyed.
Estonia now plans to fight for every inch of territory and deliver powerful strikes against russia hundreds of kilometers behind the front line from the first day of any invasion.
At the same time, Tallinn’s greatest concern is the possible end of the war in Ukraine, after which russia could redeploy tens of thousands of battle-hardened troops to NATO’s borders. Estonian intelligence believes that this is precisely why the Baltic countries need to use the coming years to strengthen their defenses and deter russia.

Shipowners seek protection from drones after wave of attacks in the Black Sea and the Middle East - FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:53:08 EEST
16:53:08 KST

Shipowners seek protection from drones after wave of attacks in the Black Sea and the Middle East - FT
Kyiv • UNN
Following attacks in the Black Sea and the Persian Gulf, shipowners have sharply increased demand for counter-drone systems. Protecting a tanker costs around $500,000.
Commercial shipping companies are rushing to strengthen their fleets' protection against drones following a wave of attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and the Middle East. Financial Times reports, writes UNN.
Details
Counter-drone specialists, including Marss, Drone Defence and D-fend, said they had seen a sharp increase in the number of inquiries from shipowners, with particularly strong interest among companies involved in transporting oil and gas cargoes and operating in the marine energy infrastructure sector.
Commercial vessels, the publication writes, are increasingly becoming targets of attacks in the Persian Gulf and the Black Sea, as parties to conflicts seek to disrupt critical supply chains for goods, while shipowners willing to operate in dangerous waters are setting record freight rates for their vessels.
D-fend Solutions Chief Marketing Officer Jeffrey Starr told the Financial Times that the company, founded by Israeli cybersecurity experts and specializing in taking control of hostile drones before safely landing them, was seeing "huge demand" from the shipping sector.
"We are seeing shipowners, shippers and naval forces facing an asymmetric threat that is driving a significant increase in inquiries about our technologies," he said. "This threat from unmanned aircraft is no longer confined to areas of intense combat."
According to Chief Executive Richard Gill, rival company Drone Defence has recorded an increase in inquiries from oil tankers and gas carriers, as if shipowners can protect their vessels, "they will be able to choose riskier routes."
John Stawpert, maritime director at the International Chamber of Shipping, said the threat posed to the industry by drones had increased in recent years, "from both surface and airborne platforms, and this is particularly relevant in areas of active conflict, such as the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea and the Black Sea."
According to the International Maritime Organization, more than 20 sailors have been killed in the Persian Gulf by drone and missile strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran in late February, while around 30 people have been killed in the Black Sea this year.
The cost of chartering a supertanker to pass through the Strait of Hormuz reached a historic high of $1.2 million per day last week for voyages to China, compared with an average of about $79,000 per day in September last year.
Marine energy infrastructure, including pipelines, cables and wind farms, has also become a target, the publication notes. European security services report surveillance using drones and, in some cases, covert attacks, while NATO countries are increasingly voicing concern over Russian interference in European waters, the publication writes.
According to several counter-drone specialists, until recently demand for anti-drone technology at sea came mainly from superyacht owners seeking protection from paparazzi.
"Superyachts were one of the areas where it all began ... and a significant number of top yachts are protected by the Nidar system," said Marss Development Director Rob Bullock.
The company is now seeing a "step change" in the development of vessels serving the offshore oil and gas industry, as "the technology and software for integrating it have reached a price point at which the costs of lost days due to such threats justify the investment."
Nidar systems operate by using onboard surveillance technologies, such as radar and cameras, to detect approaching threats. More advanced systems may include kinetic means of response, depending on the laws of the region in which the vessel operates.
Drones can also be disabled by jamming GPS signals or disrupting their control frequencies.
Hill said that a radar system with cameras and a signal-jamming system would cost approximately $500,000 for an oil tanker. Ships that cannot afford such technologies resort to more primitive means of protection against drones, such as nets and suspended water tanks, to confuse the drones or cause them to explode before they reach critical parts of the ship, the publication writes.
The key task for counter-drone companies is to develop systems capable of accurately targeting drones in conditions of heavy seas and withstanding exposure to corrosive salt water.
Starr said that D-Fend, whose technology was used to protect U.S. ports during this year's FIFA World Cup, had created a "reinforced, protected version" of its system for maritime applications, which had become "an excellent growth driver."
But keeping pace with the constantly changing threat is an ongoing struggle.
"It's an endless cycle," Bullock said. "Just when you think you've deployed the best thing you've ever deployed, it changes. Everything is moving so fast."

Lithuanian media organisations on Monday condemned what they described as pressure on journalists and executives at news portal 15min following an investigation by the outlet and international partners into the founders of financial group Bankera.
The organisations said the campaign showed characteristics of a strategic lawsuit against public participation, or SLAPP, which they said can be used to intimidate and financially exhaust media outlets and discourage reporting on matters of public interest.
According to 15min, data about its employees and their family members has been collected without justification, journalists have been followed at events, and articles distorting the truth have been published through a newly created website and social media accounts. Outdoor advertising has also been purchased to promote the articles, the portal said.
15min has received dozens of complaints and claims and has been reported to the Office of the Inspector of Journalist Ethics, the Commission for Ethics in Public Information, the Bank of Lithuania, the Radio and Television Commission of Lithuania, the State Territorial Planning and Construction Inspectorate, the Media Support Fund, the Culture Ministry and the Special Investigation Service.
Statements on the situation were issued by the Internet Media Association, the Association of Professional Journalists, the Lithuanian Journalists’ Union and the National Press Association.
The organisations said the case had characteristics of a SLAPP campaign, in which a flood of complaints, claims and lawsuits is intended not to seek justice but to silence criticism, intimidate journalists and financially weaken media organisations.
“News organizations and journalists become the target instead of the publication itself being challenged,” Lina Bušinskaitė, chairwoman of the Internet Media Association, said in a statement.
“We urge state institutions to take this case seriously because pressure on the media undermines one of the fundamental principles of democracy,” she said.
The controversy follows an investigation published last year by 15min and the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), an international investigative journalism network.
Further reading
The investigation reported that tens of millions of euros raised from investors through a cryptocurrency token offering were transferred via Pervesk, a Lithuanian company supervised by the Bank of Lithuania, to Pacific Private Bank in Vanuatu.
According to the investigation, the funds raised through the token offering seven years ago ended up at Pacific Private Bank, which was acquired by Bankera founders Vytautas Karalevičius, Mantas Mockevičius and Justas Dobiliauskas.
The investigation reported that funds were subsequently transferred to accounts belonging to the founders and companies linked to them. Those companies were used to acquire real estate, according to the report.
In mid-September, 15min reported that the Bankera founders had been formally suspected, following an investigation lasting more than a year, of misappropriating assets worth at least 45 million euros.
15min is owned by Lithuanian media group 15min Group, which also operates news agency BNS, radio stations M1, M1 Plus, Lietus, M1 Dance and Laluna, as well as Žmonės, Ji and Legendos magazines and the Žmonės Cinema home entertainment platform.

JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russian authorities said a 27-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute was hospitalized on Sept. 29 with symptoms of severe pneumonia. She died during the night of Oct. 1-2.
Russian media reported that she had contracted pneumonic plague, although authorities have not publicly confirmed that diagnosis.
One version reported by Russian media said the woman had recently returned from a work trip to Buryatia, where a plague outbreak had been detected near the border with Mongolia.
Another theory suggested she may have accidentally broken a test tube containing the plague bacterium at a laboratory.
Russia’s consumer protection watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, rejected the laboratory accident theory, saying no emergency involving pathogenic microorganisms had been recorded.
Hospital quarantined, 189 people hospitalized
The Shelekhov hospital where the woman died was placed under quarantine. Authorities identified 189 people who had been in contact with her and hospitalized them for observation.
Guterres’s Successor Will Need Russia’s Blessing
Irkutsk Region Governor Igor Kobzev said on Oct. 2 that none of the hospitalized people showed signs of the disease and that laboratory tests had returned negative.
The following morning, authorities in the nearby city of Baikalsk urged residents to temporarily avoid traveling to Shelekhov and neighboring settlements because of the reported plague death.
The warning was later deleted.
What is plague?
Plague is a serious infectious disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It has several forms, including bubonic, pneumonic and septicemic plague.
People most commonly contract plague through bites from infected fleas carried by rodents.
Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and can spread between people through respiratory droplets. Unlike bubonic plague, it can therefore spread directly from person to person.
The disease can be treated with antibiotics if detected early. Without treatment, however, pneumonic plague can be rapidly fatal.
Russia’s last recorded case was in 2016
Russia’s last officially recorded human case of plague was reported in 2016 in the nearby Altai region.
A 10-year-old boy contracted the disease after skinning a marmot and developing an infection through damaged skin. He survived after receiving timely medical treatment.
The reported case in Irkutsk has not been publicly confirmed as plague by Russian health authorities, leaving the circumstances surrounding the woman’s death unclear.

All-inclusive to adventure: The top experiences that will shape ultra-luxury travel in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:50:49 UTC
16:50:49 KST

Planning next year’s ultra-luxury escape? All-inclusives, celebrations and privacy are among the experiences driving high-end traveller habits.
Is it too early to start thinking about New Year’s resolutions? Well, if more travel in 2027 has been on your mind, perhaps a luxury trip should make that list, too.
Offering inspiration for high-end tourism, Virtuoso’s 2027 Luxe Report draws on insights from more than 3,100 travel advisors across more than 50 countries to reveal what will shape luxury travel in the coming year.
According to those surveyed by the global network of agencies, 59% of advisors predict spending on trips will increase modestly and 13% forecast a significant increase, while a further 23% expect spending to remain at 2026 levels.
This suggests that luxury travellers are “not simply maintaining current levels but accelerating their prioritisation of meaningful experiences and investing more in access, quality and time”, Virtuoso said, adding that “value and safety” have become increasingly important in deciding where they go and how they travel.
In 2027, Europe is set to dominate the luxury travel map, with seven of the top 10 most popular global destinations. Following Japan in first place, Italy, France, Greece and Spain make up the top five, while Croatia, South Africa, Portugal, the UK and the US are in the top 10.
Celebrating milestones, excitement to explore a new destination, and spending time with loved ones are the top three reasons why affluent travellers will be jetting away next year.
Other leading travel trends include multigenerational family travel, immediate family travel, and expedition cruising.
Top ‘ultraluxe travel’ experiences
Virtuoso’s survey found that advisors saw a 47% increase in “ultraluxe travel”, which covers exclusive use, private or exceptionally high-end experiences.
So, what will shape the experiences of the high-end traveller next year?
Luxury all-inclusive experiences
All-inclusive experiences top the ultraluxe travel list for 2027. In a separate report, Virtuoso said that “these days, the best all-inclusive properties are rewriting the script”. The company added that “tasting menus take the place of buffets, private villas reign over cookie-cutter rooms, and service is genuine and personal, never transactional.”
Celebration travel
From destination weddings and anniversaries to family gatherings, graduations and milestone birthdays, celebration travel ranks second among the ultraluxe travel experiences. According to Virtuoso’s research, Greece, Bali, Maldives, Italy and French Polynesia rank among the top five honeymoon destinations for 2027.
Privacy
With social media’s ability to quickly turn obscure destinations into must-see, overcrowded spots overnight, for the luxury traveller, privacy means avoiding the queues and camera clicks, while being able to move through the world with minimal friction.
Hyper-personalised experiences
Luxury travellers are no longer satisfied with splurging on a trip abroad just for the sake of it. They are instead pursuing encounters that are personal. According to the report, personal enrichment and education ranked eighth on the top 10 motivations for why the affluent will travel next year.
From the tarmac to bed and board, luxury travellers’ tastes are shifting from generic, off-the-shelf experiences to ones shaped by their exact preferences, which provides a sense of exclusivity. This can include private tours or one-of-a-kind dining experiences catered around their preferences.
Active and adventure trips
Rounding up the ultraluxe travel experiences list are active and adventure trips, with “seeking adventure” ranking 10th among affluent travellers’ top motivations for travel in 2027. Virtuoso’s research found Antarctica, South Africa, Iceland, Costa Rica and Kenya as the top five most popular adventure travel destinations for next year.

Ethiopia's govt. forces push back TPLF to retake Tigray capital
