07:46:00 UTC
16:46:00 KST

Ethiopia's government-allied fighters entered Mekelle, the capital of Tigray region, Sunday after the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front announced its withdrawal amid renewed fighting.
The TPLF last month seized the Mekelle airport and the city, one of Ethiopia’s largest. In a statement Saturday, it said its forces had pulled out. They had done so in the previous two-year war, which ended with a peace agreement in 2022, apparently to spare the city from destruction.
Ethiopian Airlines had suspended flights to Mekelle and the Tigrayan cities of Axum and Shire after the rebels seized the airport. The African Union urged restraint, warning that renewed tensions threatened the 2022 agreement.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has tried and failed to subdue Tigray’s rebellious leaders in recent months, with TPLF Chairman Debretsion Gebremichael openly challenging him.
Debretsion said Thursday that the fighting was a "continuation of the previous war” and that his fighters would keep attacking and defending Tigray from its enemies.
After federal troops take control of Mekelle, Abiy is very likely to leave regional security in the hands of the Tigray Peace Force, which comprises former members of the TPLF armed wing, Tigray Defense Forces, according to Jalale Getachew Birru, an analyst of Ethiopia for ACLED, an independent global monitor that collects, analyzes and maps data on conflict.
The Tigray Peace Force is fighting alongside federal troops against the TPLF.
Severe disruptions to internet and cellphone networks have made gathering and verifying information from Tigray difficult, although some connectivity was reported Sunday.
Residents of Mekelle told The Associated Press Saturday that federal forces had retaken the airport, although details were scarce.
Civilians looted government offices and hauled away equipment from police headquarters in Mekelle as TPLF-allied fighters withdrew, a local business owner, who witnessed the departures and looting, said Sunday.
The looting targeted the TPLF administration office, the regional police headquarters and some shops, Filmon Equar Hailu said.
Speaking by phone from Mekelle, Filmon said he saw some TPLF-allied fighters with light weapons leaving the city, some on foot. Departures began in small groups about three days ago and continued through Saturday afternoon, he said.
Small groups of fighters from the Tigray Peace Force entered Mekelle, Filmon said, adding he heard celebratory gunfire overnight into Sunday morning.
The TPLF is one of seven opposition groups that declared an alliance late last month whose objective is to remove Abiy. He rose to the premiership in 2018 and was reelected earlier this year. In addition to once being Tigray’s ruling party, the TPLF was the dominant group in a coalition that ruled Ethiopia between 1991 and 2018.
The fighting has brought renewed hardship to civilians still recovering from the previous war. Residents have described fears of renewed isolation following the suspension of flights. They also reported that roads connecting Tigray and Afar had been closed to civilian traffic.
The conflict is also testing regional alliances, with Ethiopia charging that the TPLF is likely getting support from Eritrea and Egypt. Relations between Ethiopia and Egypt have been cold in recent years because of a large power dam on the Nile River that is opposed by Cairo over concerns it could diminish the amount of water received in Egypt.
Abiy also angered Eritrea over his stated wish for Ethiopia to gain sovereign access to the Eritrean Red Sea port of Assab.
Ethiopia on Thursday closed its embassy in Eritrea and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave Addis Ababa, the federal capital, citing their alleged "involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia’s national security.” Eritrea retaliated by saying it was cutting diplomatic ties with its neighbor.
Egypt denies supporting the TPLF, and Eritrea says Abiy is trying to externalize an internal conflict.
Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki traveled to Egypt on a working visit at the invitation of his counterpart there, Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel said Saturday.
Afwerki and President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi would "discuss further enhancement of bilateral ties during the visit,” Yemane said on X.

Bulgarian cabinet to criminalise customs violations, tighten control on gambling
We Continue the Change proposes total ban on gambling advertising

Under amendments to the Gambling Act adopted in 2024, the period after which a person can request to be removed from the register was reduced from two years to 30 days. valentino asks guests to bring books to its runway show for donation to public libraries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:45:22 UTC
16:45:22 KST

valentino’s ‘antibiblioteca’ looks to unread books to rethink the value of clothes
presented at bibliothèque sainte-geneviève in paris, the collection explores accumulation, memory and possibility, while guests contribute books from their shelves to be donated to public libraries.
VALENTINO TURNS THE RUNWAY INTO A LIBRARY OF POSSIBILITIES
Alessandro Michele stages Valentino’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection at Paris’s Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève as an encounter between clothing and everything that remains unknown. Titled Antibiblioteca, the show takes its starting point from the idea of the antilibrary, a collection of unread books whose value lies precisely in what they might still contain. In Michele’s formulation, fashion can operate in much the same way. Garments do not need to be worn, owned or consumed to have meaning. They can exist as possibilities.
Guests were asked to bring a book from their own shelves, chosen with the thought that someone else might want to read it, with the books later donated to local libraries. The invitation to the show was designed as a catalogue of imaginary books, with titles for books that do not actually exist. They can only be imagined, setting up the idea behind the show: that there is value in what we have yet to discover, just as there is value in clothes that may never be worn. Antibiblioteca looks at the collection as a cluster of ideas and possibilities, whether or not they ever become part of someone’s wardrobe.
the show MOVES THROUGH BIBLIOTHÈQUE SAINTE-GENEVIÈVE in paris
The concept draws on Nassim Nicholas Taleb’s account of Umberto Eco’s library in The Black Swan. Taleb describes the unread books in Eco’s collection as more valuable than the books he has already read because they represent the limits of his knowledge and the possibility of discovering something beyond it. Alessandro Michele extends this argument from books to clothes. Every fashion collection contains objects with different futures. Some garments will appear briefly on a runway, some will survive primarily through photographs and moving images whole others will enter wardrobes and remain almost untouched. Their existence does not begin or end with their practical use.
Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève’s long wooden reading tables, green lamps, iron railings and densely occupied bookshelves create an environment organized around concentration, memory and accumulated knowledge. Against this architecture, the models introduce another kind of archive. The clothes are temporary, moving through a space built to preserve what came before. Books remain on shelves while the Italian fashion house‘s collection passes between them, producing a quiet contrast between permanence and ephemerality. The effect is also a reminder that fashion itself is an archive. Its forms return, mutate and acquire new meanings. Historical references can become contemporary propositions, while an image from a runway can continue to circulate long after the garment has disappeared from view.
WHY ALESSANDRO MICHELE GIVES FASHION ROOM TO REMAIN UNREALIZED
Michele’s idea also questions how we measure the value of fashion. If a garment is judged only by how often it is worn or how useful it is, we miss much of what fashion can do. A runway look can become an image, a memory or an idea. It can suggest a new shape or a different way of seeing the body. It can stay with us long after the show, even if it is never worn. This connects to Giorgio Agamben’s idea of potentiality, which Michele uses to describe the possibilities that remain open before something becomes real.
A fashion show brings together clothes that may never enter everyday life, while showing us what that life could look like. There is something hopeful in this idea. An unread book is not useless because it has not been opened, just as an unworn garment is not without value because it stays in a wardrobe or exists only as an image. Both hold the possibility of something that has not happened yet.
project info:
name: Antibiblioteca
fashion house: Valentino | @maisonvalentino
creative director: Alessandro Michele | @alessandro_michele
collection: Spring/Summer 2027
location: Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève, Paris, France

Presidential election in Bulgaria to be decided in a runoff: Alpha Research
Monday 5 October 2026 10:29
Monday, 5 October 2026, 10:29
PHOTO alpharesearch.bg
Font size
The presidential ticket of incumbent head of state Iliana Iotova and Kiril Valchev has the support of 44.5% of those who have definitely decided to vote on 25 October, according to a poll by Alpha Research. The candidates Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev is in second place with 26.1%, while Kostadin Kostadinov and Petar Volgin are third with 10.5%.
Speaking to bTV, sociologist Boryana Dimitrova stressed that the figures reflect the preferences of those who were firmly decided to vote at the start of the campaign, and that changes remain possible before election day.
“We are talking, first, about a certain runoff and, second, with a very high degree of probability, a runoff between the two leading presidential tickets,” Dimitrova said. She qualified her statement, however, by noting that shifts in the standings cannot be ruled out before the end of the campaign.
According to her, 30% of those firmly decided to vote could still change their choice. She also pointed out that nearly 40% of those who say they will not vote are motivated by disappointment with politicians, while around 24% believe there is no politician who represents them.
The poll also shows strong public demand for a live televised debate between the main candidates, with 62.6% saying such a debate should be held before the first round. According to Dimitrova, society needs clearly stated positions and greater clarity about the candidates’ visions.
The Alpha Research survey was conducted from 24 September to 1 October using the agency’s own funds and among 1,000 Bulgarian adults, BGNES reports.

Breadcrumb
US withdraws all bomber aircraft from UK's Fairford airbase
The United States confirmed Sunday that it has withdrawn all B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford, a British airbase at the centre of a counter-terrorism probe after a mysterious security incident last month.
Police were called to the base in southwest England on 27 September after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in "suspicious" activity.
The scare forced evacuations at 85 homes near the airbase, which was used by the United States to launch strikes on Iran.
Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but instead "a quantity of petrol was recovered," according to counter-terrorism police.
A statement from a Pentagon official said Sunday "we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States."
The statement noted that "operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time."
Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel thievery, as energy prices in the UK hit record highs this week.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident, a charge rejected by Tehran.
Six London-based Britons arrested in the incident, including a UK-Iranian dual national, all men in their mid-20s, were released on bail, drawing rebuke from Washington.
"I wouldn't have done that," US President Donald Trump told reporters, as his Secretary of State Marco Rubio alleged a "foreign actor" was involved.
Iran's embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.
Heightened security
Adding to the mystery, British media reported that officers were alerted to the incident by one of the initial suspects but police have not commented on the reports.
Security at the base had reportedly been heightened recently.
Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran," and US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing from the base.
Fairford is the only airbase on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.
The incident came after a farmer living in the village of Whelford, near the airbase, called the police after seeing three vans blocking a road and a group of masked men fleeing the scene.
Aerial footage of the vans showed they appeared to contain barrels, and at least one was marked with a fake logo and phone number, giving the false impression that it was owned by a legitimate diesel delivery firm.

The Main Intelligence Agency (GUR) of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine has published details on the War & Sanctions portal regarding a new version of Russian jet-powered Geran-4 UAVs, which the Russia began deploying in the fall of 2026.
"The updated Geran-4 notably contains a new MOK unit, based on a high-precision magneto-inductive sensor (magnetometer) PNI5GA manufactured by PNI Sensor (USA). The MOK operates alongside the SADRA inertial navigation module and reduces the drift of its gyroscopes, increasing the accuracy of the UAV's autonomous navigation," the DIU press service reported on its Telegram channel.

"To effectively strike (cut through with a shaped jet) bridge structures and power transmission line supports, the enemy has begun using a new KRSN warhead (cumulative-cutting special payload). The Chinese Telefly turbojet engine has been replaced by a localized Russian-produced equivalent manufactured in Alabuga," the DIU stated.
According to intelligence data, the rest of the electronic units and components remain unchanged and identical to previous Geran models.

Russia Hides Potential Pneumonic Plague Outbreak After Fatal Lab Breach
A health scare in Siberia is raising questions over what Russian authorities are trying to hide, as public warnings vanish, officials avoid naming the infection, and emergency measures quietly expand.
A suspected case of pneumonic plague has triggered emergency measures in Russia’s Irkutsk region after a 28-year-old employee of an anti-plague research institute died and nearly 200 people were placed under medical observation, while Russian officials have avoided publicly identifying the disease.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Sun on October 3, Daria Shipilova, 28, who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, reportedly died from plague, prompting the isolation of 189 people and an emergency response involving Russia’s top infectious disease official.
Shipilova was hospitalized in the town of Shelekhov with severe pneumonia-like symptoms before her death. The Shelekhov district hospital was subsequently placed under quarantine as health authorities began tracing people who may have come into contact with her.
Russian outlet Lyudi Baikala reported that Shipilova worked as a laboratory technician and may have been exposed on September 25 after breaking a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen. The circumstances of the reported incident have not been officially confirmed.
Despite the scale of the response, authorities in the Irkutsk region have stopped short of publicly confirming pneumonic plague. Governor Igor Kobzev referred only to a suspected case of a “particularly dangerous infection,” saying identified contacts had been placed under medical observation and had so far tested negative.
Russia’s chief sanitary official and head of Rospotrebnadzor, Anna Popova, rushed more than 2,600 miles from Moscow to Irkutsk to oversee the emergency response, according to The Sun, yet Russian authorities have still refused to publicly name the infection behind the alarm.
The Sun reported that 189 people were isolated—114 in one hospital, 63 in another, and 12 at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute. Antibiotics reportedly disappeared from some pharmacy shelves amid panic buying, while authorities canceled public events.
The head of neighboring Buryatia, Alexey Tsydenov, initially said Shipilova had died from plague, only to later soften his statement to say she “may have died from plague.”
The information surrounding the suspected outbreak has also begun disappearing. Authorities in Baikalsk deleted a warning urging residents to avoid travel to Shelekhov, while Kremlin-linked REN TV removed five posts mentioning plague.
Russian epidemiologist Mikhail Favorov, now based in the US, told The Sun that Popova’s personal intervention suggested the situation was “terrible” and “critical,” while accusing authorities of concealing the full circumstances surrounding the case.
Despite the quarantine, emergency response and nearly 200 people being placed under observation, Russian officials continue to publicly describe the case only as a suspected “particularly dangerous infection.” As of October 4, however, authorities said those under observation showed no symptoms and had tested negative.
The suspected plague case comes amid broader concerns over infectious diseases in Russia. In September, researchers identified the drug-resistant tuberculosis strain EurA1.1 in several Russian regions, while the country recorded around 48,000 tuberculosis cases in 2025, including tens of thousands involving drug-resistant forms of the disease.

Waste management, farmers feel the squeeze as diesel prices soar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:41:00 UTC
16:41:00 KST

Waste management, farmers feel the squeeze as diesel prices soar
Estonia's rising diesel prices are putting pressure on waste collection businesses and farmers alike, leaving both grappling with sharply higher operating costs.
Amid the ongoing crisis in the Middle East, diesel prices in Estonia have climbed to around €2 a liter this fall. For waste management provider Eesti Keskkonnateenused, the increase means it may have to negotiate higher waste collection fees with local governments before the end of the year.
Southern regional manager Mart Laidmets said waste collection contracts are generally signed with local governments for several years at a time, with an option to extend them, but such sharp fuel price hikes are difficult to anticipate.
"We have no choice but to negotiate with local governments about whether and by how much they are willing to raise prices," Laidmets told ERR, adding that the company was already close to the limit of how much it could offset rising costs through greater efficiency.
Eesti Keskkonnateenused's southern region operates a fleet of about 30 vehicles, using roughly 60,000 liters of diesel a month to serve Tartu, Estonia's second-largest city, as well as further-flung regions including Setomaa Municipality.
Higher fuel costs are also being passed on by the company's transport partners, Laidmets noted, including those hauling waste and other loads between Tartu, Tallinn and Võru.
'Where can I save that money?'
Farmers are feeling the impact as well. Jõgeva County grain farmer Tõnis Soopalu said filling up his tractor's 450-liter tank has soared, more than doubling from €270 to €550. That's enough fuel, he noted, for a single workday.
During the busiest periods, when combines and grain dryers are running, his farm can go through more than 1,000 liters of diesel a day.
"When it comes to cutting costs, the big question is, where can I save that money?" Soopalu asked. Cutting back on inputs can reduce yields, while skipping necessary work or stopping the dryer could damage the grain.
While the farmer said there was no reason for panic yet, he acknowledged the volatility was making it harder to plan costs. Rising natural gas prices are another concern as well, because gas is used to produce nitrogen fertilizer.
"If oil prices stay this high, we've seen before that it's not sustainable for very long," Soopalu said. "Right now, it's a question of how much will be produced, whether it will be produced at all and what availability will look like. There's plenty to worry about."
--
Editor: Aili Vahtla

Bpost increases cost of sending parcels and letters from 1 January 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:39:15 UTC
16:39:15 KST

From 1 January, Belgian postal services provider Bpost is increasing rates for sending letters and parcels. On average, a stamp will cost around 8 per cent more. Sending a small parcel from a post office will cost 40 cents more.
Bpost increases cost of sending parcels and letters from 1 January 2027
According to Bpost, the price rises are necessary because “Belgians’ postal habits continue to change rapidly.”
The postal operator bases its claim on the most recent study by the Belgian Institute for Postal Services and Telecommunications (BIPT). In 2025, only 22 per cent of respondents said they still sent letters, compared with 41 per cent five years earlier.
“As volumes fall, the cost per letter rises for us. This is because the costs of staff and sorting centres remain the same,” says spokesperson Mathieu Goedefroy. “That is why the price increase is unavoidable.”
Here’s how the prices are changing
Standard postage stamp: 1.63 euros becomes 1.77 euros
Priority postage stamp: 2.52 euros becomes 2.73 euros
Registered post: 9.85 euros becomes 10.76 euros
Sending a parcel at the post office: 8.60 becomes 9 euros
Post within Europe: 3.07 euros becomes 3.36 euros
International post: 3.29 euros becomes 3.58 euros
Another important point to note: older stamps will remain valid next year as well.
Parcels to cost 4.5 per cent more on average
Sending parcels is therefore also set to become more expensive. To send a parcel from a post office using the ‘bpack 24h’ service – for parcels within Belgium that are usually delivered the next working day – you currently pay 8.60 euros. Bpost is raising this to 9 euros.
Prices for other domestic parcels are rising by an average of around 4.5 per cent, depending on the weight and type of parcel. According to Bpost, anyone wishing to send a parcel as cheaply as possible is advised to send it outside peak periods, create a shipping label online and have the parcel delivered to a collection point.
Surcharge during peak month
As in previous years, a €1 surcharge will be applied during the busy period between Black Friday and Christmas, as the number of parcels rises sharply at this time.
These price rises may not be the end of the story. According to Bpost, depending on inflation, prices could be increased by up to a further 3 per cent in the course of 2027.

Head of Jewish Greens says she may leave party over ‘Zionism is racism’ vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:38:32 UTC
16:38:32 KST

The head of the Jewish Greens has said she may leave the party after it voted to adopt a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.
Vivien Lichtenstein said that while opinion among Jewish members of the party was split on the motion passed at its annual conference in Brighton on Sunday, she said she believed it was unhelpful and it was “possible” she might quit.
It comes as anger grows among some in the party about the decision of Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, to miss the vote and to encourage supporters to do the same so they could instead campaign for him in Holborn and St Pancras before the parliamentary byelection for the seat next week.
Polanski sought to have the conference postponed so the party could focus on his efforts to win Keir Starmer’s former seat. When the Greens’ executive committee refused this, the party contacted members, encouraging them to get refunds on their conference tickets to campaign.
Sunday’s binding policy motion was passed by 1,022 votes to 813, and some Greens say more effort by Polanski could have stopped it.
One long-standing member said: “There’s so much anger at his disinterest in such a critical issue. You can’t run a party on vibes alone.”
The motion was opposed by four of the Greens’ five MPs, and is expected to face a legal challenge under equality laws. Polanski did not take a side but justified the motion’s broad argument by pointing to the death toll in Gaza.
Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Lichtenstein condemned the motion: “I don’t think it’s helpful, and it doesn’t make any difference whatsoever to Palestinians.”
Asked if she would remain in the party, she said: “I haven’t decided yet. Certainly it’s quite possible that I will leave the party, and I’m giving it a little time, and to talk with colleagues.”
The motion says Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism”. It calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”.
Some Jewish Greens have expressed concern that this will mean they could face disciplinary action for belonging to Jewish organisations that officially support Zionism, even synagogues. Supporters of the motion, which was led by a group called Greens for Palestine, have said this would not happen.
Asked about this issue, Lichtenstein said she was less worried about being personally targeted than about the potential impact on organisations. She said: “I’m not concerned about people accusing me of supporting Israel’s right to exist, and therefore, I’m a racist, which of course is not the case. I’m just concerned that this is a very bad motion …
“What concerns me is that the party might accuse UK organisations, Jewish organisations, and also Israeli-Jewish and joint Arab-Jewish organisations, of being Zionist and therefore racist. I support an awful lot of those sorts of organisations that are working against the occupation, and even go out on the ground to assist Palestinians.”
The idea of calling for a single Palestinian state was not an issue for all Jewish Greens, Lichtenstein said, but party policy had been that it should be “up to Israelis and Palestinians to choose their future, one state or two”.
The chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, described the motion as “poisonous antisemitism” and a “threat to British Jews and to Britain”.
He said he was “appalled” by the motion, claiming the Green party had resurrected a “discredited and dangerous slander” first promoted by the Soviet Union.
“All decent people will see this for what it is: poisonous antisemitism, a threat to British Jews and to Britain,” he said.
Israel barred Polanski from entering the country in retaliation for the motion, which the Israeli foreign ministry said “constitute[d] a clear antisemitic text”.
It is understood some Green members are consulting lawyers over whether the policy could be challenged for breaching equalities legislation.
Adam Wagner KC, the barrister who led a case that concluded Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour party broke equalities laws over antisemitism, said such a case would have a good chance of success. “I think there is a strong risk that the motion as passed contravenes the Equality Act 2010, which applies to political parties, as it will discriminate against and harass people who hold Zionist beliefs and Jewish people more generally,” he said.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday announced early elections for Nov. 29 after parliament rejected two government housing decrees amid mounting protests over the country’s housing crisis.
Speaking at his official residence in Madrid, Sanchez said he would convene his Cabinet later Monday to begin the process of calling the election.

Sanchez said housing, inequality and public services remained challenges, and called for renewed public support to continue his coalition’s reforms.

The legal fight stems from the issuing of warrants by an Old Bailey judge that allowed police to raid Mountbatten-Windsor’s residence on the Sandringham estate, and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, in February. Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Jeffrey Epstein files.
A high court judge subsequently granted him permission to challenge the legality of the force’s actions over the searches.
According to the Daily Telegraph, which first reported Mountbatten-Windsor’s legal challenge, it represented the first time a member of the royal family had challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649.
Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on his 66th birthday in relation to allegations that when he was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender.
Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with the late financier.
Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on 19 February and interviewed under caution before being released under investigation.
Misconduct in public office can cover a wide range of conduct, including sharing confidential financial information, financial misconduct, wilful neglect of duty and sexual misconduct. It also covers corruption and improper interference, conflict of interest, perverting the course of justice, dishonesty or fraudulent conduct, and misconduct leading to personal gain.
Thames Valley police said: “While our investigation into misconduct in public office continues, we are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the central criminal court. As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further.”
Mountbatten-Windsor has been approached for comment.

The Russian Foreign Ministry has repeatedly emphasized that Russia’s sovereignty over these territories, which is established under international law, is beyond doubt.
On October 1, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the plenary session of the 23rd meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club that Moscow seeks good and neighborly relations with Tokyo. According to the president, both countries have areas of mutual interest. However, Russia’s approach to ties with Japan has not changed, whereas Tokyo’s attitude toward Moscow has, Putin said, emphasizing that Japan had imposed sanctions on Russia.

Elections in Bulgaria: Low Turnout Forecast as Yotova Leads Presidential Race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:35:02 UTC
16:35:02 KST

The Iliana Yotova-Kiril Valchev presidential ticket leads with 44.5% among Bulgarians firmly decided to vote, while the Andrey Gyurov-Georgi Kandev pair has 26.1%, according to Alpha Research's first survey since the official start of the presidential campaign.
The study was conducted with Alpha Research's own funds among 1,000 adult Bulgarians selected through a two-stage quota sample. Researchers used direct standardized interviews on tablets at respondents' homes, with fieldwork running from September 24 through October 1, 2026.
Sociologist Boryana Dimitrova said the current figures make a runoff between Yotova and Gyurov certain, although changes among the leading candidates remain possible before the campaign ends.
Kostadin Kostadinov and Petar Volgin are third with 10.5%. Alpha Research said both the second-placed ticket and the representatives of Vazrazhdane are currently drawing support beyond their traditional party bases.
The agency estimates voter turnout at around 37%, corresponding to between 2.4 million and 2.6 million people. In another presentation of the survey, turnout was estimated at 37-38% of the electorate registered by the Central Election Commission.
Interest in the presidential election at the beginning of the campaign is lower than it was for the snap parliamentary election on April 19, Dimitrova said. She does not expect substantial mobilization during the remaining weeks, although the campaign could still affect voter attitudes.
Disappointment with politicians is the leading reason cited by people who say they will not vote. Around 40% give that explanation, while about 24% say there is no candidate who represents them.
The group of potential non-voters includes people who regularly abstain as well as voters who participated in April but have become disillusioned again. Alpha Research said those who do not see a suitable candidate include supporters of GERB and the DPS, along with some right-wing voters.
Overall, about one-quarter of respondents say no politician represents them. Among those who will not vote, 41.9% cite disillusionment with all politicians, 25.6% point to the absence of a candidate who represents them and 20.2% say they have no interest in politics. Another 9.5% say they will abstain because they believe the election result is already predetermined.
Many voters have yet to settle on their choice and are expected to decide during the campaign or even on election day. Of those firmly committed to voting, 70% have already made a definite choice, while 30% remain open to changing their preference.
The Yotova-Valchev ticket starts the campaign with the strongest institutional and personal support, Dimitrova said while presenting the findings on bTV. “At the start of the campaign, the Yotova-Valchev ticket enters with distinctly higher institutional and personal support,” she said.
Dimitrova described the 26.1% result for Gyurov-Kandev as “a strong position,” saying it showed a significant electoral base and room to expand support beyond the traditional right-wing and liberal-right electorate.
She said a runoff after the October 25 presidential election was highly likely and gave the top two tickets the strongest probability of reaching the second round.
“We are talking, firstly, about a certain runoff, and secondly, a runoff that, with a very high degree of probability, will be between the top two presidential candidate pairs,” Dimitrova said, while noting that the rankings at the top could still change before the campaign ends.
According to her, 30% of those firmly decided to vote could still change their choice. “Nothing is settled at the start of the campaign,” Dimitrova emphasized.
Kostadinov and Volgin remain third with 10.5%, a result close to the level achieved by Revival in the April parliamentary election. Their ticket is also among the few leading presidential pairs to have been nominated directly by a political party.
Dimitrova said the Kostadinov-Volgin candidacy was also intended to consolidate Revival's position. While the top two tickets were nominated by initiative committees and backed by political parties, their campaign is focused on mobilizing the party's own electorate.
The remaining candidates currently receive between roughly 1% and 3%, although movement within that range remains possible because some voters make their final decision during the campaign or shortly before election day.
Alpha Research considers it virtually impossible at this stage for a candidate ranked fourth or lower to move into the top two, while changes in the order of the leading candidates cannot be excluded before the campaign concludes.
The agency's findings therefore point to a runoff, with a contest between the two leading presidential tickets considered the most likely scenario, while the remaining three weeks of campaigning could affect voter mobilization and behavior.
One major campaign question concerns the votes of GERB and the DPS, both of which have decided not to participate in the presidential election. Nearly half of the electorate of each party says it will not vote.
Among GERB supporters who intend to participate, between 20% and 25% favor Gyurov-Kandev, around half as many support Yotova-Valchev, and fewer choose other candidates such as Kostadinov-Volgin. DPS supporters tend to favor Yotova-Valchev.
“There is a possibility of a surprise between the two rounds. If the leadership of either party, for one reason or another, calls on its supporters to vote for a specific candidate, that could happen,” Dimitrova said.
A televised debate is also strongly expected, with 62.6% of respondents saying one should be held between the leading candidates even before the first round. Dimitrova said voters need clearly stated positions and a better understanding of the candidates' visions.
Political scientist Teodor Slavev said on bTV that criminal incidents and political conflicts during the campaign could further discourage voters.
“This is not the first time we have witnessed activity involving the criminal underworld, the Prosecutor's Office, and the Ministry of Interior during an election campaign,” Slavev said while discussing the murder of Iliyan Filipov.
He said the killing in Plovdiv had divided public opinion between those who believed the state was collapsing and those who saw the rapid arrest of the alleged contract killer as evidence of a functioning state. Slavev said both interpretations were exaggerated and argued that criminal cases in Bulgaria had often attracted substantial attention during investigations before later fading from public view in court.
Tsvetanka Andreeva said political conflicts were also extending beyond the presidential campaign and could become a central factor in the political contest. She said the ruling party had an opportunity to take fewer risks because its candidate was the incumbent president, while Progressive Bulgaria was beginning to intervene within the opposition.
Andreeva referred to Friday's clashes in parliament between the authorities, represented by Rumen Radev, who took the parliamentary rostrum, and the opposition, which she described as fragmented but highly critical and harsh.
She said the confrontation had a history involving Radev and the Movement for Rights and Freedoms (DPS) and traced it to the dispute between Ahmed Dogan and Delyan Peevski. According to Andreeva, the party structures had sided with Peevski at that time, while Radev had sided with Dogan.
In her view, Radev was intervening in the DPS in an effort to secure the party as a future partner, which she said required him to attack its current leadership.
Andreeva said Peevski had publicly challenged Radev to substantiate invoices with documentation or resign, describing this as evidence of high stakes in the confrontation.
She also said DPS lawmakers had alleged that corruption involving highway guardrails had occurred under the administrations of Galab Donev and Rumen Radev, including a 160% price markup that Donev himself had acknowledged.
Andreeva linked the Plovdiv murder to what she described as connections between oligarchy, organized crime and political projects. “We are talking about a businessman who is a sponsor of a ruling party,” she said.
Slavev said the combination of these developments was discouraging voters and could result in lower turnout. He argued that both leading presidential tickets had an interest in this because their campaigns were fragmented and largely taking place within the echo chambers of their respective supporters.
He said the contest was narrowing toward the core electorates of Progressive Bulgaria and PP-DB, while a significant share of voters had still not said how they planned to vote.
Slavev also referred to allegations concerning pardons for drug addicts and the detention in Greece of “Kartofa,” who had accused Kandev.
“We need to monitor all these developments very closely during the election period,” Slavev said.

Pro-Russian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik declared his party the winner in Bosnia and Herzegovina's elections held on Oct. 4.
Dodik was not on the ballot, but Zeljka Cvijanovic from his Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) party is poised to retain her seat in the country's tripartite presidency, according to preliminary results.
The Balkan country held elections for the presidency, shared among the Croat, Serb, and Bosniak ethnic groups, as well as for regional and cantonal governments, under a complex political system established after the 1992-1995 Bosnian War.
"If it had not been for (U.S. President) Donald Trump's magnificent victory, we would probably be political corpses today," Dodik told his supporters, while also thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin, who voiced support for the SNSD before the elections.
Dodik, known for his separatist and pro-Moscow views, served as the president of Republika Srpska — Bosnia's Serb-dominated entity — between 2022 and 2025.
In 2025, he was stripped of office and barred from running for six years for defying the country's international envoy.
With over 95% of the votes counted, Denis Becirovic of the Social Democratic Party (SDP BiH) is set to retain his Bosniak seat in the presidency, and Bosnian Croat nationalist candidate Darijana Filipovic has claimed victory in the race for the Croat seat.
Dodik's SNSD is also expected to retain power in the Republika Srpska local parliament and presidency.
The vote was marked by a relatively low turnout, with 42% of voters casting ballots, down almost 10% from the 2022 elections.

Spanish PM Sanchez calls snap Nov. 29 polls amid housing crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:33:00 UTC
16:33:00 KST

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday called a snap election for Nov. 29, seeking to bolster his mandate after parliament rejected key housing decrees following widespread protests.
"We need to renew people's support," Sanchez said in a televised address. "We need to mobilize and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain."
The premier also acknowledged having made mistakes and falling short of campaign promises.
"I also know that part of that social majority is dissatisfied today," he said.
Sanchez has stood out globally for taking a strong stance on progressive issues from Palestinian statehood to defending multilateral institutions and cracking down on "tech oligarchs," even as a series of setbacks and scandals weakened his position at home.
Facing the electorate now is a risky move as Sanchez's Socialist Party is trailing in opinion polls. However, he has been boosted by proposals to tackle a mounting housing crisis that were well received but were struck down by right-wing MPs Friday, leading to planned new public protests about housing.
An election defeat would spell the end of one of Europe's last few left-leaning governments at a time when the far-right is making unprecedented gains across the region as a growing swathe of European voters desert the center ground.
Opinion polls suggest a coalition led by the conservative People's Party (PP) with the support of Vox is the most likely outcome in Spain, ushering a far-right party into central government for the first time since the return of democracy after the death of dictator Francisco Franco.
Still, Sanchez, a wily political operator, has proven time and again his ability to surprise those who had long written him off.
Despite never winning enough votes to form a majority government, he has cobbled together a series of fragile and seemingly impossible coalitions including voices from the far-left to the separatist right to remain in power for three successive terms lasting eight years.
But growing fragmentation among his partners has meant the government has passed little in the way of legislation in its third term and failed to pass a budget since 2023, even as Spain's economy has continued to be one of the best performing in the developed world.
Sanchez took office after leading a move to oust center-right Mariano Rajoy in the wake of major corruption scandals within Rajoy's People's Party.
However, senior members of Sanchez's own Socialist Party have in the past year faced allegations of graft, dragging down the party's already weak approval rating which has hovered at around 26-31% throughout his tenure.
Against the odds, he won a second four-year term in office in 2023 despite heavy losses in earlier regional and local elections by negotiating support from a loose alliance of parties in parliament.
That was achieved after promising a highly controversial amnesty for pro-independence Catalan leaders in exchange for their support, a move still bitterly remembered by many voters as a betrayal of Spanish unity.
Sanchez won early plaudits for moves including the exhumation of Franco from a mausoleum the dictator built for himself outside Madrid, and the reform of a labor law that has seen unemployment fall to its lowest level in almost two decades.
He cemented his humanitarian and pro-immigration credentials early by saying in June 2018 that Spain would accept the Aquarius migrant rescue ship and its 629 passengers, after Italy and Malta both refused to let the ship dock in their harbors.
As other European countries have toughened their policies towards foreign arrivals, Sanchez has consistently argued that immigration is essential for sustaining Spanish growth by plugging gaps in key sectors such as construction, agriculture and hospitality and for providing revenue to prop up Spain's strained welfare system.
More recently, his refusal to agree to U.S.-led demands to increase defense spending to 5% of GDP while pivoting toward China has rattled U.S. President Trump and some European leaders concerned about the threat of the bloc being flooded with Chinese goods.
Sanchez's housing measures provided a rare chance for the Socialist leader to pitch himself as the leader of a mobilized left and distract from the more politically damaging issues of the migrant crisis in Ceuta and corruption scandals, said Lorenzo Bernaldo de Quiros, economist and president of consultancy Freemarket Corporate Intelligence.
"This is a window of opportunity," de Quiros said. "If he does not call elections fast, (those topics) will return to center stage."

China's Wang Zisai wins fourth straight Trampoline World Cup title

RICCIONE, Italy, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- China's Wang Zisai won the men's individual trampoline title on Sunday, completing a sweep of four consecutive World Cup events and securing the overall World Cup title.
Just a week earlier at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Wang and two-time world champion teammate Yan Langyu dominated the men's individual event. The day after returning to China, they immediately left for Italy for the latest World Cup stop.
"Honestly speaking, it was hard to compete back-to-back, but I had to chase my goal, especially when it's so close," Wang said.
The 2026 Trampoline World Cup comprises six stops. Wang had previously won three consecutive events in the Netherlands, Switzerland and Portugal, beating two-time Olympic champion Ivan Litvinovich of Belarus in the Netherlands and Portugal.
One of Wang's main goals in Riccione was to practice alternating between routines with different difficulty values while also seeking to secure the overall World Cup title.
Rather than attempting his maximum difficulty in every round, Wang varied the difficulty of his routines. He used a difficulty score of 21.900 only in the second preliminary round and the final, opting for 19.500 in the first preliminary round and semifinal.
Wang delivered a steady performance in the final to win with 66.020 points. Yan took silver with 64.870, while 20-year-old Portuguese Gabriel Albuquerque finished third with 64.140.
"I'm very happy to have won four consecutive titles, but I'm also well aware that the World Championships are still ahead of me," Wang said.
The 39th Trampoline and Tumbling World Championships will be held in Nanjing, China, from November 4 to 8.
In the women's synchronized trampoline event, Zhang Xinxin, who won the world synchronized title last year, teamed with 18-year-old Zhang Yu for their first major competition as a pair.
The duo won the title with 49.690 points. Zhang Yu and Zhang Xinxin also finished third and fourth, respectively, in the women's individual event. ■

Here is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany hitting the headlines on Monday, October 5, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Air traffic in Stuttgart suspended due to hoax bomb threat
Germany's Stuttgart Airport saw the temporary suspension of all departures and arrivals due to a bomb threat that turned out to be a hoax.
Police looked into a claim a man had made to an employee that he had been carrying a bomb in his luggage, which resulted in the terminal being evacuated and all air traffic being stopped.
Germany's Federal Police said no threat was detected, and the airport's operations resumed shortly after the threat was found to be not true.
The 24-year-old man who claimed to be carrying a bomb is under investigation for allegedly disturbing the peace by making threats of criminal offenses.
German Book Prize best novel award goes to Shida Bazyar for 'The Gaps'
The 2026 German Book Prize has been awarded to Shida Bazyar for her novel "Die Lücken" (which could perhaps be translated as "The Gaps"), with the jury describing her book as "a novel against ambivalence."
The book is set in fictional community, Heimesbach in Hunsrück, "in which 90 years of German history have nested themselves in the walls and the biographies," as the prizegivers put it.
"The novel leads us through the years and the heads of those who shaped the village: from Jewish families who lost everything, via Nazi profiteers, who later reinvented themselves as innocent hangers-on, through the Sharifi and Karimpour families, who fled from Iran decades later," the book prize writes. "Shida Bazyar succeeds in providing a virtuoso storytelling mosaic about the burden of history, the lie of the new start, and the desire to finally find a home."
The jury praised Bazyar's storytelling format in particular, saying it was an ideal vehicle to convey disparate and yet interconnected ideas.
"The author chooses compelling literary strategies: The view of an omniscient narrator, and the caleidoscopic structure of the text make it possible to jump between times and to create both closeness and distance at the same time," they wrote in their explanation for the award.
The 38-year-old Bazyar was born in Germany to Iranian parents who fled in the 1980s.
"It's not so easy for me to truly experience joy, I have to say," Bazyar said in her acceptance speech. "Because it is quite a strange feeling when you write a novel about people who were persecuted, terrorized and murdered. To then be truly happy about its success, that doesn't seem quite right to me." Therefore, Bazyar said, she'd like to dedicate the accolades to the people the book is about.
Bazyar also made this year's shortlist for the International Booker Prize for her debut novel from 2016, "The Nights are Quiet in Tehran," which became a hit when translated into English in 2025.
READ — Merz, Macron call for tougher EU tools against unfair trade
Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have written to the EU's Ursula von der Leyen, saying the bloc needs tougher — and faster — means to respond to unfair trade practices by third countries.
Their appeal names no names but it seems most likely to have China in its crosshairs, or just maybe the US under Donald Trump's erratic trade policies.
This comes days before the EU trade commissioner heads to Beijing for talks, and just over a week before this month's EU leaders' summit, where the issue might well come up again.
Merz tells pupils: Do better in school than I did
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has returned to his former high school on a visit marking the school's 100th anniversary, telling pupils they should aim for better grades than he managed.
Merz graduated from the Friedrich-Spee-Gymnasium in Rüthen, western Germany, 51 years ago.
"Do a slightly better Abitur than I did," the chancellor told pupils, referring to Germany's school-leaving qualification that allows students to attend university.
Merz has kept his exact final grade a closely guarded secret. Last year, he joked that his school certificate was locked in a safe at home.
He did, however, suggest that his overall grade was somewhere around 3.8 — a relatively poor result in Germany's grading system.
Merz has previously said he lacked discipline and motivation at school and at one point had to repeat a year.
"I didn't have difficulties with school; the school had difficulties with me," he joked on Monday.
He said things improved after he changed schools and moved to Rüthen, where mathematics and physics eventually became two of his favorite subjects.
Hundreds of pupils greeted Merz on his return, with some calling out "Hello, Chancellor" as he arrived.
The visit came less than a week after Merz presented the German School Award in Berlin, where he said he wanted to focus more personally on education policy and visit schools more frequently.
Germany plans new naval base in Emden
Germany plans to build a new naval base in the northern city of Emden as it expands its armed forces.
The federal government and the state of Lower Saxony signed a declaration of intent for the project on Monday, the Defense Ministry said.
Germany currently has only one North Sea naval base, in Wilhelmshaven. The ministry said it would not have enough capacity to accommodate the navy's planned expansion.
"New ships and boats need berths. Our soldiers need accommodation and training facilities," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said.
Pistorius said the new base could create up to 2,000 military posts and that Emden's access to the Atlantic made it an ideal location.
Lower Saxony Premier Olaf Lies said the aim was for the base to be operational by the early 2030s.
Chinese high-tech could be security risk — domestic intelligence agency
High-tech goods from China, such as electric vehicles or even robot vacuum cleaners, could represent a security risk, the BfV domestic intelligence agency has warned.
BfV head Sinan Selen told a hearing of parliament's intelligence oversight committee in Berlin that the issue was of "great concern" to him.
"I already see substantial shortcomings that create potential for abuse," he said.
Data collected via the products could be passed on to "state agencies", he said, leading to risks including "potential shutdown of entire products."
"In terms of resilience and availability (this) could confront us with problems," he said.
The warning comes as sales of high-tech products to Germany are growing and Chinese manufacturers compete ever more strongly with their German counterparts.
Deutsche Telekom targets billions in AI savings
Deutsche Telekom plans to use artificial intelligence and automation to cut annual costs by around €2.5 billion ($2.9 billion) by 2030.
The target covers the German telecommunications giant's operations outside the United States.
Deutsche Telekom is already using AI for repetitive tasks in network operations, customer service, software development and administration.
Its "Frag Magenta" chatbot handled around 2.6 million customer service calls in the first half of 2026, the company said.
At T-Mobile US, in which Deutsche Telekom holds a majority stake, AI agents now handle 40% of customer contacts.
Outside the US, Deutsche Telekom expects savings from AI and automation to reach €1.1 billion by 2027 and €2.5 billion by 2030.
"AI is fundamentally changing Deutsche Telekom," CEO Tim Höttges said. He said the technology was improving networks and customer service while opening up new business models."
IN DEPTH: Germany trainer Klopp's first internationals
The German football team has had its first four international matches under its new coach, Jürgen Klopp — a mixture of success, failure and in-betweens.
DW analyzes Klopp's methods and relationship with the team as shown over the past couple of months in this article: Klopp's first Germany internationals: What did we learn?
Social Democrat groups oppose coalition's working week reform
Grassroots groups within the Social Democrats (SPD) — the junior partner in Germany's conservative-led coalition government — have spoken out against plans to "flexibilize" the working week in a position paper.
In question is a paragraph in the coalition agreement that speaks of "the possibility of a weekly rather than a daily maximum working time."
The conservative Christian Democrat (CDU)-Christian Social Union (CSU) bloc has pushed to have a maximum number of hours that can be worked per week rather than the current daily standard limit of eight hours.
Although the four SPD groups fundamentally accept the idea, they are calling for strict controls, among other things wanting collective labor agreements under which both parties work out details as "a necessary prerequisite."
They also say exceptions should made in certain sectors where illegal employment is prevalent.
Employers' associations in June objected to the idea of collective labor agreements as a coercive measure when it was put forward by the Labor Ministry, leading to its retraction, with the CDU saying that it went against the coalition agreement.
The position paper submitted by the SPD groups could thus lead to a new split in the coalition, stating as it does: "It is not in keeping with a modern reform of working hours regulation or a better compatibility of work and family when bosses can decide alone when employees can knock off work."
German court sets limits on deportation detention
Germany's Federal Court of Justice (BGH) has ruled that a person facing deportation cannot be detained as a flight risk simply because their past behavior suggests they might try to avoid being deported.
The case concerned a stateless Palestinian man who sought asylum at a police station in Germany in April 2023. Austrian authorities had already issued a decision requiring him to return.
A court in the German city of Duisburg ordered the man detained while his transfer was being arranged.
The courts argued that his previous actions indicated a risk that he would try to evade deportation. He had lived in Austria since 2020, where two asylum applications had been rejected, and had also applied for asylum in Belgium and Germany.
But the man had never explicitly said that he intended to avoid deportation.
The BGH ruled that his behavior alone was not enough to establish this particular ground for detention.
A person's words do not necessarily have to state the intention literally, the judges said. But it must be "clear and unambiguous" from what the person says and the circumstances that they intend to evade deportation.
The court found that the man's detention from May 7 to June 6, 2023 had therefore violated his rights.
German immigration law provides several other grounds on which people can be detained pending deportation.
IN DEPTH: Two German scientists in Nobel-winning trio
Peter Hegemann from Germany's Humbolt University and Georg Nagel from the University of Würzburg have won this year's Nobel Prize in medicine alongside their US colleague, Karl Deisseroth.
You can read more about their achievements in this article: German and US scientists win Nobel Prize in medicine
Germany at risk of 'violent conflict' with Russia — intelligence chief
Germany is facing a growing risk of a violent confrontation with Russia as Moscow continues a campaign of hybrid warfare with other countries in Europe, the head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence service warned on Monday.
Speaking before the Bundestag at the annual public hearing of intelligence chiefs, Martin Jäger said: "The confrontation we are facing with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous dimension."
"Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia — the attempted attack in Leipzig is just one example," he said.
"No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany," he added.
Jäger was referring to a drone attack at Leipzig airport in August that the German government has blamed on Russia.
Russia has repeatedly denied any intention of attacking NATO
countries, with President Vladimir Putin, however, saying on Thursday: "But if we are subjected to aggression, we will have no choice but to respond."
Draft bill aims to help domestic abuse victims move house
The Justice Ministry has put forward a draft bill making it easier for domestic abuse victims to leave joint tenancy contracts and obliging perpetrators to pay for any ensuing costs.
"The path to a self-determined and safe life after domestic abuse is often still a long one," Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig told newspapers from the Funke media group.
"We want to make it a bit easier," she added.
She said the draft bill aimed to give domestic abuse victims clear legal rights against their abusers, including being able to demand that the latter pay any costs arising from the premature termination of the joint lease.
More protection for others in the household
The bill also envisages increased protection for children and relatives of victims.
Under current German law, family courts can impose bans on domestic abusers taking up contact with or approaching their victims but not other members of the same household.
Hubig said the draft law foresaw such protections being extended to other people dependent on the abuser without any separate application being made.
According to police statistics, nearly 266,000 people in Germany were affected by domestic abuse in 2024, 70% of them women and girls.
The Justice Ministry has said the real figure is likely to be much higher, estimating that 95% of cases go unreported.
E-vehicle subsidy program has 'exceeded our expectations' — environment minister
Since May, the German government has paid out subsidies to 100,000 households wanting to procure an electric vehicle, Environment Minister Carsten Schneider told the mass-circulation Bild newspaper on Monday.
Schneider, from junior coalition partner the Social Democrats (SPD), said the program, worth €3 billion ($3.36 billion), had "far exceeded our expectations."
He said that every additional electric vehicle protected households from high fuel prices and made the county less dependent on expensive oil imports and international conflicts.
According to the Bild article, half of households applying for the subsidy had a maximum annual income of €45,000 and three-quarters of them €60,000.
Schneider said he found it particularly important that this graduation of payments according to income functioned properly.
Preliminary assessments have shown that less than 15% of households that applied for the subsidy were looking to buy vehicles from China, contradicting expert views that Chinese automakers would profit the most.
Left Party takes Economy Minister Reiche to top court
The Left Party is taking a row about a remark made by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche to the Constitutional Court after Reiche failed to give a declaration to cease and desist on time.
Reiche had posted a remark on the official Instagram site of her ministry saying: "Antisemitism and expropriation endanger Germany and the economy."
The comment refers first to the unproven accusation that the Left Party is antisemitic in its ideology and then to the Left Party's plan to socialize apartments from corporate landlords in a bid to reduce skyrocketing rents in the capital.
Reiche doubled down on her criticism of the socialist party in comments she made during a visit to Ukraine over the weekend, telling the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild she feared a national loss of growth if a leftist coalition took power in Berlin.
"What the Left Party represents here in Berlin and the people that it represents is dangerous not only for Berlin but for our country," she said.
The Berlin branch of the Left Party has accused the Christian Democrats (CDU), to which Reiche and Chancellor Friedrich Merz belong, of carrying out a "large-scale campaign" against its top candidate, Elif Eralp, who won recent state elections in Berlin.
It has taken legal action over similar statements on CDU interior ministry websites in various states, criticizing the use of official government channels to denigrate another party.
The ministries in Saxony and Schleswig Holstein withdrew the statements, but those in Baden-Württemberg, Brandenburg and Hesse have so far not done so.

Scientists use AI to identify enzymes that could degrade plastic pollutants
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:31:40 CST
16:31:40 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Scientists in Australia are using artificial intelligence biotechnology to identify enzymes that could potentially break down plastic and other harmful pollutants.
Researchers are combining machine learning technology and biochemistry to filter millions of enzymes stored in biological databases around the world and identify candidates that could degrade harmful pollutants, according to a recent statement from Australia's Murdoch University.
Murdoch University PhD candidate Joseph Boctor said in his review published in Nature Reviews: Earth & Environment that the key to finding the right biological fit to combat each pollutant was likely hidden within existing data.
Machine-learning tools could mine millions of unexplored biological data to find suitable enzyme candidates, Boctor said, adding the machine-learning pipelines use knowledge from previously characterized enzymes to predict how enzyme structures could interact with target pollutants and break them down.
Boctor said the approach could help to more rapidly address pollutants already present in the environment while scientists develop bioplastic alternatives.
He said persistent pollutants such as PFAS and microplastics could cause health problems, with agricultural soils now containing around 23 times more microplastics than oceans.
The team at Murdoch University's Bioplastics Innovation Hub, a collaboration with the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization, Australia's national science agency, is now focusing on testing, validating and scaling the identified enzymes for bioremediation efforts. ■

NEW YORK, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Coast Guard suspended its search at sunset Sunday for the six people aboard a medical jet that crashed off Nantucket Island, in the U.S. state of Massachusetts, the agency said in a statement.

"Given the information shared by authorities and the conclusion of the search-and-rescue phase, we must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement on Sunday. ■

Migration was one of the main topics on the agenda of last week’s Justice and Home Affairs Council in Luxembourg.
This Council followed the Munich Migration Meeting on 26 September, where several ministers called for faster returns, stronger external border controls and a bigger operational role for Frontex.

He also wants the EU to do more migration diplomacy with key countries of origin and transit, including Bangladesh, Pakistan, Gulf countries, Egypt, Libya, and Morocco, with the aim of addressing migration routes before people reach EU borders.
Leaders agreed to move ahead with the new EU return regulation and make return procedures faster and more effective, including through closer cooperation with countries such as Morocco.
