Unearthing the Ground: Architecture and the Politics of Waste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

In 1948, Robert Moses established the Fresh Kills Landfill on the western shore of Staten Island. The site, chosen for its remote marshland and cheap land value, was meant to be temporary, but by 1955 it was the largest landfill in the world, receiving up to 29,000 tons of refuse per day at its 1991 peak. By 2001, after more than fifty years of continuous operation, Fresh Kills covered 2,200 acres, roughly three times the area of Central Park, and was, unspectacularly, visible from space. When it started, Moses didn't expect to design a dump but, without calling it that, a new landform with four artificial hills rising up to sixty meters above sea level built entirely from the accumulated residue of eight million daily lives.
That landform is now, slowly, becoming a park. James Corner Field Operations won the international design competition launched by the city in 2001, producing a master plan called Lifescape that will take thirty years to complete. The landfill's four mounds are being capped, planted, and gradually opened to the public. Methane from decomposing waste is captured and fed into an energy system as the wetlands are being restored around the engineered hills. Evidence of New York's consumption transformed into a feat of ecological engineering and an act of institutional memory management (a way of making a city's most embarrassing landscape slowly look like something it was always meant to be).
The world generates roughly two billion tonnes of municipal solid waste per year, a figure projected to reach three and a half billion by 2050. A significant portion of that volume ends up compressed, layered, and graded into the earth at the urban periphery. The landfill is, in this sense, one of the most common acts of territorial production in the modern world; a new landform, engineered and deliberate, built from the accumulated residue of daily life. Architecture has spent considerable energy thinking about what cities build up; maybe it's time to think more about what they build under.
The Ground
A landfill is one of the few construction projects in which the material and the structure are the same thing. The engineering behind a modern sanitary landfill works from the bottom up: a liner system of compacted clay and high-density polyethylene prevents leachate (the liquid produced by decomposing waste) from contaminating groundwater; a network of pipes collects landfill gas, primarily methane, for energy recovery or controlled burning; drainage systems manage stormwater across slopes designed to shed rather than absorb.
What this engineering conceals is the basic territorial act that landfilling represents. A landfill is not just a place where waste goes; it is a political decision about urban planning, about what ground is worth using for waste. This geopolitical decision has consistently been made in the direction of land that is cheap, peripheral, and inhabited by people who lack the political power to refuse or contest it. Looking again to Fresh Kills, that required a 525-acre landfill gas collection system and a series of geocomposite layers, geomembranes, drainage nets, and protective fill; Robert Moses chose marshland in Staten Island because it was expendable. But in other places, mostly in the Global South (where most landfills are located), communities have not been consulted, and most of the security layers described have not been applied. According to the World Bank, over ninety percent of municipal solid waste in low-income countries is disposed of in open dumpsites or burned in the open air.
The sociologist Robert Bullard, in Dumping in Dixie, documented how hazardous waste facilities, landfills, and industrial sites were disproportionately located in African American communities across the southern United States. Not by accident but through a consistent pattern of regulatory and planning decisions that treated certain neighborhoods as more available for environmental burden than others. Bullard's work established the field of environmental justice, and his central argument (that the geography of waste disposal follows the geography of inequality) has since been replicated in studies across dozens of countries, lending theoretical structure to political movements that had long described the same pattern.
Developing countries account for roughly eighty to ninety percent of the world's mismanaged waste, despite generating far less of it per capita than wealthy nations. The United States, representing four percent of the global population, generates twelve percent of global municipal waste. The infrastructure to manage that waste domestically exists and is regulated and maintained; what is lacking is the political will to confront the full cost of consumption at home, rather than externalizing it toward territories with less capacity to push back. The landfill is, in this sense, one of the most legible maps of global inequality; find the dumpsite, and you find the community whose civil and public power was suppressed.
The Trade
Since the 1980s, wealthy nations have explored a mechanism of international commerce that exported growing quantities of waste to lower-income countries. Around five million tonnes of plastic waste are exported each year globally, with seventy-one percent originating from just ten high-income countries, seven of them European. A 2023 analysis published in Grist found that official UN data undercounts this flow by 1.8 million metric tonnes annually because of "hidden" plastics embedded in textiles, contaminated paper bales, and miscategorized materials. The EU alone ships more than three million kilograms of plastic waste to the Global South every day. This transfer of environmental cost from those who produce it to those who lack the political standing to refuse it is called "waste colonialism".
The same logic runs through carbon markets, where wealthy nations and corporations purchase offset credits generated in developing countries, externalizing the cost of compliance toward territories with less capacity to negotiate. The voluntary offset market has grown from two billion dollars in 2020 toward a projected two hundred and fifty billion by 2050, with the primary sources of carbon credit generation concentrated in developing countries whose forests, soils, and land are purchased by corporations in the Global North as a mechanism for avoiding domestic emissions reductions. Researchers have documented land grabs, displacement of Indigenous communities, and restrictions on land access as consistent byproducts of offset projects in Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, and across sub-Saharan Africa; projects that generate, on average, only 0.08 jobs per hundred hectares of land involved.
The Basel Convention, adopted in 1989, was the international community's response to a series of egregious cases: the 1988 Koko incident in Nigeria, where Italian companies illegally dumped 3,800 tons of hazardous waste, burying drums of toxic chemicals in a farmer's backyard in exchange for a small monthly payment; and the Khian Sea affair, in which a ship carrying incinerator ash from Philadelphia was refused by multiple countries before dumping its cargo off the coast of Haiti. The convention sought to regulate and, eventually restrict, the trade in hazardous waste from wealthy to less-wealthy nations. Its goals have remained largely unfulfilled. The United States, notably, hasn't even ratified the convention, and sent more than 800 million pounds of plastic waste to Mexico, Malaysia, India, Vietnam, and others in the year following the introduction of stricter rules in 2021.
The displacement of the trade accelerated sharply after 2018, when China implemented its National Sword policy and stopped importing plastic waste from foreign countries. For over two decades, China had been the world's largest importer of waste plastics, processing materials that wealthy nations classified as recyclable but that often could not be sorted or sold domestically at a profit. When China closed its ports to these shipments, the trade rerouted to Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand, and the Philippines, absorbing much of the redirected flow. According to data analyzed by the nonprofit Basel Action Network, Malaysia received 1.4 billion kg of plastic waste annually (between 2021 and 2023); Vietnam received a billion kg and Turkey nearly a billion. Ghana receives approximately 150,000 tonnes of electronics annually, on top of a domestic e-waste stream estimated at 215,000 tonnes per year in total.
Agbogbloshie, a neighborhood on the Korle Lagoon in Accra, has been described as the world's largest e-waste dump, a "digital dumping ground" processing millions of tons of discarded electronics from Europe and North America. That characterization has since been substantially contested, as repeated studies have found that the scrapyard at Agbogbloshie processes between 10,000 and 13,000 metric tons of e-waste annually (a significant quantity but far below the figures circulated in global media campaigns that served Western environmental narratives). More importantly, the framing of Agbogbloshie as a passive recipient of Northern waste obscures the economic logic and political economy of the site. Alice Mah and Grace Akese have argued that informal recycling provided livelihoods for thousands of migrant workers (an estimated 8,000 workers), organized through its own governance structures, labor hierarchies, and market relationships.
When the Greater Accra Regional Minister demolished the scrapyard in 2021, announcing that he was "taking possession of Agbogbloshie" as part of a sanitation and "beautification" campaign ("Let's Make Accra Work"), researchers noted the parallels with nineteenth-century colonial logics of urban hygiene. The urban geographer Neil Smith called it "urban revanchism", a forceful reclamation of urban space from marginalized groups in the name of order, hygiene, and development.
The Future
A landfill is, among other things, a stratigraphic record of consumption, layering what a city produced, used, and discarded across decades. Archaeologists have long recognized this. William Rathje's Garbage Project, launched at the University of Arizona in 1973, spent decades excavating landfills to study what Americans actually discarded, as opposed to what they reported discarding. Rathje found that newspaper, not food, was the dominant material in American landfills, and that supposedly environmentally conscious decades had left more durable waste than less conscious ones. The landfill, he argued, was a more accurate record of daily life than any survey or census. What the global geography of waste disposal reveals is that the cost of consumption is rarely borne by those who consume.
Architecture's role in this geography has been, on its best days, to make the consequence visible. Munich's Olympiapark artificial hills designed with the debris of war; Lisbon's Parque das Nações oil refinery decommissioned in the 1980s whose lands were revitalized for the Expo'98; or the CopenHill waste-to-energy plant in Copenhagen that proposes that waste infrastructure need not be expelled to the periphery. Despite their differences, these are all examples of architecture as a decision about memory, not just material.
According to the World Bank's What a Waste 3.0 report, published in 2026, global waste generation is expected to grow from 2.56 billion metric tonnes in 2022 to 3.86 billion metric tonnes by 2050 (a fifty percent increase under a business-as-usual scenario) with the fastest growth in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, the regions least equipped to manage it. Thirty percent of waste generated worldwide is already not managed properly. Rich countries, representing sixteen percent of the global population, produce thirty-four percent of the world's waste. What that trajectory means for architecture is that more waste means more landfills, more incineration plants, more transfer stations, more contaminated ground, more communities asked to host what other communities produce. Whether architecture's response will be to design those facilities better, to make them more visible, or to ask more fundamentally who built the system that requires them in the first place, is a question that each project will answer differently, and none of them will answer completely.

"Bond market turmoil and euro weakness have raised fears that France’s problems could spread to the eurozone, similar to the debt crisis more than a decade ago, and force the European Central Bank to help shore up French debt. Some analysts, however, said it was still too early to judge whether the risk of contagion was increasing," the publication writes.
Meanwhile, Ninghui Liu, head of investment strategy and research for the Asia-Pacific region at State Street Investment Management, said that "France’s fiscal position is becoming increasingly unstable, while the market has only been reacting since last week."
"For now, I think this is more a story about a country than a euro crisis," he added.

Suspected Plague Death Sparks Quarantine Across Russia's Irkutsk Region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:22:19 UTC
16:22:19 KST

Nearly 200 people have been placed under medical observation in Russia’s Irkutsk region following the death of an anti-plague institute employee from a suspected or possible case of plague, according to Russian officials and local media reports.
Local media reported that 189 people were being monitored after an employee at an anti-plague research institute in Irkutsk became ill. Alexei Tsydenov, head of neighboring Buryatia, said on social media that the woman had died from an unspecified form of plague.
Russia’s public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said the employee had instead been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology” and that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk region, as well as in the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov, remained stable.
The agency said expanded testing had found no microorganisms connected to the employee’s professional activities.
Local reports on Friday said a 27-year-old employee of an anti-plague institute had developed suspected pneumonic plague after returning from a work trip to Buryatia, where an outbreak had reportedly occurred near the Mongolian border. The report cited the Russian Telegram channel Mash.
The case was later identified as involving Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute in Shelekhov.
The United States is monitoring reports of the suspected case and the quarantine measures in Russia, according to Axios, which cited a Trump administration official. “We are aware of reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia. We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners,” a State Department spokesperson told RFE/RL on October 4.
The State Department called on Russian authorities to “share accurate information quickly and openly,” while saying plague can be treated with commonly available antibiotics, especially when treatment begins early.
A US Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson also said the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention was working with the State Department and that protecting US citizens remained the department’s “highest priority.”
White House officials are also following developments and Russia’s quarantine measures. Senior administration officials said the government was aware of the reports and was considering possible responses.
There are currently no direct commercial flights between the United States and Russia, and Washington has not announced additional travel restrictions over the suspected case.
The reports have raised concerns among some US lawmakers and former officials, including over Russia’s history of biological-weapons research.
Representative Don Bacon, a Republican from Nebraska and senior member of the House Armed Services Committee, connected the reports to longstanding Russian allegations that US-supported laboratories in Ukraine were involved in biological-weapons research.
“I remember hearing from anti-Ukraine voices about their so-called bio labs. It was Russian disinformation ops at their best. But in reality it is Russia with the bio labs,” Bacon wrote on social media.
Russia has repeatedly accused Washington and Kyiv of operating biological-weapons facilities in Ukraine, claims rejected by both governments and unsupported by independent investigations.
The Soviet Union maintained a large offensive biological-weapons program during the Cold War despite being a party to the 1972 Biological Weapons Convention. Defectors and later investigations documented military research involving pathogens including plague and efforts to create antibiotic-resistant strains.
That history has become part of the political discussion surrounding the Irkutsk case. However, there is no public evidence that the laboratory involved was developing plague as a weapon or that Shipilova’s death was linked to an offensive biological-weapons program.
Former Republican Representative Adam Kinzinger of Illinois separately urged a broad suspension of air travel involving Russia. “The whole world needs to ban ALL flights to and from Russia,” Kinzinger wrote on social media.
He later called for flights from Russia to be stopped and for Russians to be prevented from entering other countries until the situation had been clarified.
The case has centered on Shipilova, whose death was reported on October 2.
Independent Siberian outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal) reported that Shipilova accidentally broke a test tube containing bacteria that cause pneumonic plague on September 25 while working at the institute. The outlet said she subsequently became seriously ill and died on October 2.
Russian authorities have not confirmed that account. Rospotrebnadzor said Shipilova had been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology” and that further tests were conducted because of her professional activities, but no microorganisms associated with her work were detected.
The agency also said the institute had recorded no accidents involving pathogenic microorganisms.
Precautionary measures have nevertheless been introduced. Around 200 people who may have been in contact with Shipilova have been placed under medical observation or isolation, while hospitals in the region have imposed restrictions.
Several hospitals in Irkutsk were reportedly closed for a three-week quarantine, according to Lyudi Baikala. The facilities named in the report included City Hospitals No. 1, 3 and 10 and the Ivanovo-Matreninsk Children’s Clinical Hospital.
A healthcare-sector source told the outlet that Irkutsk doctors were “openly talking about plague,” although the disease was not mentioned in official documents. The Kyiv Independent said it could not verify the claims at the time of publication.
The measures have also fueled speculation because Russian officials initially avoided publicly referring to plague, while local and independent reports described a possible laboratory accident involving Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes the disease.
The director of the Irkutsk Aluminum Plant in Shelekhov, Artem Fominykh, ordered employees to wear masks on October 2 “due to the current situtation in our region” and urged workers to seek immediate medical attention if they developed symptoms.
Fominykh said on October 4 that the mask requirement was a routine measure in response to seasonal respiratory illness.
Authorities in Baykalsk asked residents on October 3 to temporarily avoid travel to Shelekhov and nearby settlements because of the reported plague case, but the warning was deleted less than two hours later.
“Due to unofficial information about a confirmed case of plague in a person in the city of Shelekhov, we ask you to limit visits to Shelekhov and nearby settlements until the circumstances surrounding this threat are clarified,” the Baykalsk city administration said in a post at 8:28 a.m. local time.
Lyudi Baikala reported that the post was removed at 10:21 a.m.
Pro-Kremlin broadcaster REN TV also deleted Telegram posts reporting the number of people hospitalized, with all five posts concerning the reported spread of plague later removed.
Tsydenov, the governor of Buryatia, which borders Irkutsk region, appeared to confirm Shipilova’s death from plague in a social media post on October 2. While rejecting reports that she had visited Buryatia, he wrote that the woman had died of plague.
He subsequently edited the post to add the word “possibly.”
Irkutsk Region Governor Igor Kobzev has also made limited public comments about the case. On October 2, he referred to a “particularly dangerous infection” while reporting on a meeting of the regional commission on sanitation and epidemic prevention.
Kobzev spoke publicly about Shipilova’s death for the first time on October 4, without naming her and instead referring to her as “an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute.”
“Preventive measures are being carried out in the region under the strict supervision of Rospotrebnadzor (Russia's national public health and consumer protection agency),” Kobzev said.
Kobzev did not directly mention plague, saying instead that the employee had contracted “pneumonia of unknown origin,” according to Rospotrebnadzor.
“No microorganisms linked to the employee's professional duties were detected in samples taken from the patient,” Kobzev said.
He added that no infectious diseases had been reported among institute employees over the previous 10 days and that everyone who had contact with the patient had been identified, examined and placed under medical observation with daily laboratory testing.
Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium that normally circulates among wild rodents and fleas. Its pneumonic form affects the lungs and can pass between people through respiratory droplets during close contact.
The disease can develop rapidly, while modern antibiotics can be highly effective when treatment starts promptly.
The possibility of pneumonic plague would help explain efforts to identify and monitor people who had close contact with Shipilova, but quarantine and monitoring do not establish that she had plague or that an outbreak has occurred.
There is currently no publicly confirmed evidence of wider transmission among residents of Irkutsk.
The Irkutsk case has also drawn comparisons with another incident in Russia. In April, Russian authorities sought to play down another outbreak involving cattle that had spread through parts of Siberia since February, saying it was under control and caused by pasteurellosis, a relatively minor bacterial infection.
Veterinarians and independent journalists challenged that account, citing mass slaughter, village lockdowns and secrecy they said were more typical of a foot-and-mouth disease outbreak.

Spain’s PM Pedro Sánchez calls snap election after housing law fails to pass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:22:01 UTC
16:22:01 KST

Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has once again staked his political future on a snap general election called after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency legislation to tackle the housing crisis.
Sánchez, who has been in office since 2018, used a televised address to communicate his decision, which had been widely expected. The next general election had been due before the end of next summer.
Announcing on Monday morning that an early general election would be held on 29 November, the prime minister defended his government’s social, environmental and humanitarian record – and admitted it had made mistakes – but said it was time to let the Spanish people have their say.
“It’s up to you now,” he said. “A glance at the horizon shows us that the world is in a very complex era of transformation and transition. It’s a time of great tension, of climate emergency, and of social and technological changes – including highly disruptive advances in artificial intelligence. It is, therefore, a time of great dangers, but also – if we know how to seize the moment – of great opportunities. You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you wish to play in this era, and what role you want Spain to play as well.”
Sánchez’s gamble is being seen as a pragmatic move from a seasoned political risk-taker. His minority coalition government with the small, leftwing Sumar alliance has faced a turbulent time in parliament since the prime minister secured his return to office by striking a controversial deal with Catalan pro-independence parties in the aftermath of the inconclusive snap general election he called three years ago.
Unable to pass a budget since 2023, with his party and inner circle beset by corruption allegations and his government facing enduring pressure over its handling of the mass crossing into Spain’s north African enclave of Ceuta over the summer, he appears to have decided another snap vote is his best chance of survival.
Sánchez repeated his familiar assertion in Monday’s address that the choice was between his progressive government and a Spanish right that would curtail freedoms and turn back the clock on hard-won advances.
“You, the men and women of Spain, must decide whether you want to join the far-right wave that rolls back progress wherever it governs, or to ensure that Spain remains a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility,” he said.
“You must decide whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forwards, and whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society.”
The government’s efforts to tackle the housing crisis were set out in two decrees that contained a range of measures – from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room – but were voted down in congress last Friday by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence party Junts.
The PP, which is leading the polls but which may need to rely on Vox’s support to form a national government, said it believed construction, and not regulation, was the best way to tackle the crisis.
The votes were met with an angry response from the crowds who had gathered outside congress, eliciting boos and cries of “Shame” and “Your profits, our misery”.
The PP welcomed news of the snap election. “At last, the Spanish people will decide,” said the party’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo. “This isn’t an election like previous ones. This is about Spain beating Sánchez.”
Vox, which already governs with the PP in four Spanish regions, hailed the decision. The party’s leader, Santiago Abascal, said Vox would fight to ensure that Spaniards “are not discriminated against in their own homeland” when it came to housing and benefits. He also said his party would focus on “remigration” in order to reverse what he called “the migrant invasion”.
Long-brewing fury over the high cost of renting and the precarious nature of many tenancies exploded late last month following the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was removed from the home in Madrid where she had lived for 70 years. Abascal said she could not possibly afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Her plight prompted tens of thousands of people to take to the streets to protest, and saw a huge tent camp reminiscent of the 2011 indignados movement spring up in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square.
Over the weekend, large demonstrations were held across the country as protesters stepped up their demands for urgent action on the housing crisis. Authorities said 70,000 people had taken part in a protest in Madrid on Saturday, while organisers put the figure at 500,000.
Sánchez will be hoping that the focus on housing, and the right’s rejection of his government’s plans to address the crisis, will mobilise voters.
The housing issue has served to deflect attention from the government’s much-criticised handling of the continuing crisis in Ceuta, which was sparked when about 70,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours.
Members of Sánchez’s administration, his party and his inner circle have also been battling a series of corruption allegations over the past two years.
In July this year, the prime minister’s brother, David Sánchez, was banned from holding public office for nine years after being found guilty of administrative misconduct relating to his hiring by a socialist-led council in the south-western region of Extremadura.
Meanwhile, Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gomez, is due to face trial after a judge charged her with embezzlement, influence peddling, corruption in business dealings and misappropriation of funds at the end of a two-year investigation.
David Sánchez and Begoña Gómez have both denied any wrongdoing, and the prime minister has previously accused his political and media enemies of launching a “harassment and bullying operation” against his family.

Spanish PM Sanchez calls snap election as pressure mounts over housing crisis
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday called an early election for November 29. Facing the electorate now could be risky, as Sanchez's Socialist Party is trailing in opinion polls.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said Monday he would call an early election on November 29, after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his government.
"To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people," Sanchez, in office since 2018, said in a televised address, adding his aim was "to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament".
In recent weeks, Spanish residents have demanded solutions from the government over housing affordability, holding protests in cities across the country after public outrage grew over the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid last month.
Read moreSpanish lawmakers vote down affordable housing bills in blow to Sanchez’s government
Right-wing opposition parties joined forces to scuttle two emergency decrees in Parliament that included measures to reduce evictions and real estate speculation.
The setback sparked wide speculation that Sanchez could consider moving up a national election from next year.
Sanchez has been Spain’s prime minister since 2018, making him one of Europe’s longest-standing leaders.
Sanchez has stood out globally for taking a strong stance on progressive issues from Palestinian statehood to defending multilateral institutions and cracking down on "tech oligarchs", even as a series of setbacks and scandals weakened his position at home.
Facing the electorate now is a risky move as Sanchez's Socialist Party is trailing in opinion polls.
An election defeat would spell the end of one of Europe's last few left-leaning governments at a time when the far-right is making unprecedented gains across the region as a growing swathe of European voters desert the centre ground.
Opinion polls suggest a coalition led by the conservative People's Party (PP) with the support of Vox is the most likely outcome in Spain, ushering a far-right party into central government for the first time since the return of democracy after the death of dictator Francisco Franco.
Still, Sanchez, a wily political operator, has proven time and again his ability to surprise those who had long written him off.
Despite never winning enough votes to form a majority government, he has cobbled together a series of fragile and seemingly impossible coalitions including voices from the far-left to the separatist right to remain in power for three successive terms lasting eight years.
But growing fragmentation among his partners has meant the government has passed little in the way of legislation in its third term and failed to pass a budget since 2023, even as Spain's economy has continued to be one of the best performing in the developed world.

"Define core work and cut unnecessary tasks" — Burnout risk remains high for workers in Finland
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:18:06 EEST
16:18:06 KST

Workers in Finland have reported a modest improvement in their ability to cope with the demands of their jobs, according to the latest 'How is Finland doing?' study by the Finnish Institute of Occupational Health.
Some 43 percent of working people in Finland now rate their ability to deal with their jobs as excellent, up from 39 percent a year earlier.
But at the same time, the risk of burnout remains high. One in four workers either has an elevated risk of burnout or is likely already experiencing it.
Researchers said administrative demands and conflicting roles contribute to exhaustion. They say workplaces should focus on reducing these pressures.
"We often talk about the amount of work, but it is not necessarily the number one risk factor. What seems to have a greater impact is that rigid operating methods, inadequate tools, the slow flow of information or conflicting expectations create unnecessary friction at work," said researcher Jie Li.
"I would encourage people to define core work and to eliminate tasks that do not support your goals."
Other risk factors include job insecurity, excessive workloads, monotonous tasks, as well as physical strain.
Yle News reporter Hannah Anderson looks into Finland's stressed out workers.

Anti-migrant protesters scuffle with police in Gosport after Channel rescue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:16:56 UTC
16:16:56 KST

Two people have died and two more have been injured trying to cross the Channel in a small boat, French authorities have said, while 12 anti-migrant protesters on England’s south coast were arrested after what police described as “violent disorder” as they opposed the rescue of nearly 150 more people on a second vessel.
Even though the number of small boat crossings has fallen in recent months, the incidents come amid growing unrest in some quarters partly fuelled by far-right agitators.
Authorities in the Pas-de-Calais area said one man in his 30s and another in his 40s died during the overnight crossing from the French coastal town of Berck towards England’s south coast. Two women were taken to hospital after suffering burns over large parts of their bodies.
A spokesperson for the Pas-de-Calais prefecture said: “An investigation has been opened by the Boulogne-sur-Mer public prosecutor’s office to determine the circumstances surrounding the deaths. François-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, thanks all the services involved, particularly the firefighters, for their intervention and commitment during this operation.”
Anticipating the arrival of another boat, demonstrators gathered in Gosport in Hampshire on Sunday night. It was the second time protesters had targeted the town amid rumours of rescued people disembarking there.
Referring to the 12 arrests, Hampshire and Isle of Wight police said there had been assaults on a police officer and on an emergency worker, as well as affray and racially aggravated public order offences.
A crowd of about 350 people had gathered and a handful of officers were treated at the scene for minor injuries.
Simon Dodds, an assistant chief constable, said: “Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest. Our position on this has been clear that we will investigate thoroughly and take robust action against anyone responsible.
“Last night saw a number of incidents that were clearly not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe.
“Our officers did not deserve to be assaulted as they worked incredibly diligently on Sunday to ensure the safety of everyone in the area. Neither do they, or anyone from our partner agencies, deserve to be singled out online or subjected to abuse via social media. We will work with our colleagues across policing to address any online threats.”
There were similar scenes last month when protesters gathered in the area expecting migrants to arrive on a dinghy but they were ultimately taken to Dover by sea.
On Sunday evening, several rescued people were seen arriving at a marina in Gosport after being transported onboard two RNLI boats. Their dinghy was shadowed by French rescue vessels while in the Channel until it was met by RNLI boats in English waters, according to ship tracking data.
The Home Office said 149 people were believed to be onboard. It said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to protect our border. We have established contingency plans to make sure we can securely disembark, check and process all small boat arrivals. Migrants will be transported to short-term holding facilities in Kent, where they will be processed as normal and undergo stringent health, security and biometric checks.”
Departures from so far west on the northern French coast have been rare in recent years, but it is the third such crossing in a month. In September, British rescue boats collected passengers off a dinghy that had spent about 30 hours at sea after setting off from Normandy.
The 51 people, who refused help from the French coastguard, arrived in Dover after being transferred to Border Security Command boats. It had been expected they would be taken to Gosport, with hundreds of protesters gathering after coaches and ambulances were seen in the area. Six people were arrested by officers that evening.
The provisional total for Channel crossings this year is 19,451. This is down 43% on this time last year and 23% below the figure at the same time in 2024.

Israeli forces blow up abandoned building in military raid into southwestern Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:16:02 UTC
16:16:02 KST

Sahin Demir
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Israeli forces blew up an abandoned building during an incursion into the western Damascus countryside in southwestern Syria on Monday, Syrian media reported.
Syria Alikhbariah TV said Israeli forces entered agricultural land between the town of Beit Jinn and Mazraat Beit Jinn before demolishing the abandoned building.
The broadcaster did not provide further details about the raid or report any casualties.
The Beit Jinn area has witnessed repeated Israeli military activity in recent weeks.
On Sept. 18, Israeli forces shelled the outskirts of Beit Jinn, days after another Israeli force raided agricultural land around the town with about 10 military vehicles, two tanks and a bulldozer.
Parts of southern Syria have witnessed repeated Israeli incursions and attacks, including raids, searches, arrests and the establishment of military checkpoints.
Israel has occupied most of the Syrian Golan Heights since 1967. Following the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024, Israel declared the 1974 disengagement agreement void and seized the demilitarized buffer zone and other positions, including the Syrian side of Mount Hermon (Jabal al-Sheikh).
Damascus has demanded that Israeli forces withdraw to their positions before Dec. 8, 2024, while reaffirming its commitment to the 1974 agreement.

They spent weeks identifying the dead after October 7. Some ended up in a psych ward
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:15:28 UTC
16:15:28 KST

One after another, the trucks entered the base. The large company logos on them revealed their previous purpose: fresh meat, sausages, ice cream. Finally the food had arrived, someone said.
Others were less optimistic. Then the doors opened, and with them, the smell. Bodies. Piles of dead bodies, one on top of the other, and intertwined. This was the scene at the Sde Teiman army base in the south a few days after October 7.
In those days, Sde Teiman was a mirror image of the Shura army base in central Israel. The bodies of soldiers and civilians were brought to Shura, while the bodies of people thought to be terrorists were brought to Sde Teiman. All told, about 1,600 bodies were found in Israel, and many more were found in the Gaza Strip near the border fence.
According to Naor Paz, a reservist, one time the body of a member of a community's security squad was found. He had apparently taken the Kalashnikov off a dead terrorist and himself fell in battle.
At first, the dead Israeli was mistaken for a dead Hamas man. In another case, the body of an Israeli woman was found among bodies of Gazans removed from a vehicle that, on October 7, was hit by a combat helicopter while on its way back to the Strip.
On paper, the identification mission wasn't complex: Unload the trucks, place their contents into refrigeration containers, and take a DNA sample from each body. The samples were sent to labs, where they were cross-referenced with state databases and personal items provided by the families of the missing. When a match was found, the body was removed from the refrigeration container and transferred to Shura.
But this dry description fails to capture the reality. When bodies were intertwined, it was often impossible to tell whose arm or leg it was. For DNA purposes, "we took teeth or a piece of a nail with a hammer and chisel," Paz says. "If not much was left of him, we would take a piece of bone."
And there were other challenges. "Some bodies were collected only after a few days, sometimes weeks, and were decomposing," Paz says.
According to some soldiers, the chaos was also worsened by the performance of Zaka, the organization that recovers dead bodies. "The army evacuates every limb in a separate bag," Paz says. "Zaka sees a hand, then a body, thinks they're connected, and puts them in the same bag, as if they were putting together a puzzle."
For example, one soldier recounts a case of intertwined hands. "Fingers really between fingers," he says. "At first, they thought they belonged to the same person, but it turned out to be two different people."
At the camp, it was hardly possible to avoid the dead. As Paz puts it, "We slept not far from the bodies; we even ate next to them. At first, I couldn't eat anything. After a few days, I ate some carbs, but no meat – to this day, I still can't."
The smell was unbearable. "They gave us eucalyptus oil for the mask, but it didn't help; everything penetrated," Paz says. "When I got home, my wife asked me to throw away my clothes because of the smell. Even after I showered four times, she still smelled the stench. It stuck to my skin. To this day, I shower three times a day because I think I still have clotted blood on my hands."
Not only the smell was seared into him. "We put a body bag into one of the containers, and suddenly a head fell out, right next to me," Paz says. "I had to pick it up with my hands and put it back in."
He managed to cope with the sights, smells and everything else. Or so he thought. After all, he had prepared for this moment for years in a special department at Home Front Command.
Then came September 2025 and a phone call from his commander. It was a conference call; he saw his friends on the screen, all but one. "Israel killed himself," the commander said. There were 12 soldiers in the department; now there were 11.
Israel Amar was a 34-year-old ultra-Orthodox man from Beit Shemesh near Jerusalem, married and a father of three. He volunteered for reserve duty again and again. One day, while on leave at home, he left with his rifle for a public park, where he took his own life.
A month before Amar killed himself, he had been sent for a psychiatric evaluation. The diagnosis: "no evidence of suicidality."
In the days after Amar's funeral, Paz's condition worsened. That was the trigger for everything, he realizes now. He didn't go to work and was always drinking alcohol. Then came a fit of rage. "I broke half the house," he says. Memories flooded his mind; the wall of suppression broke.
Breaking point
Alon Elharar suffered a similar experience. "We found two spines, and next to them we saw Hebrew letters," he says. "After another look, we realized it was the emblem of a school shirt."
A few days later, the identification came through – an Israeli adult and child who had been burned alive, among many bodies of Palestinians. Two officers in the Southern Command confirmed the details to Haaretz.
"I was a young father, and that was everything to me," says Elharar, who is married with two children. "To see such annihilation and death in the most personal context possible; it hit me hard. It was a breaking point."
Elharar, who is from Jerusalem, wasn't even supposed to be there. In his role in the reserves, he's responsible for training soldiers in body identification. His job is only to instruct them.
But in the first days of the war, when he heard about a shortage of soldiers at Sde Teiman, he volunteered. "I thought it was an incredibly important mission – to find people who didn't deserve to be there," he says.
After a little over a week, the soldiers had completed checks on all the bodies that had been brought to Sde Teiman. But two months later, the soldiers were called back to the base. "In the first round, there was chaos, a mess," Paz says. "DNA was lost along the way, there were clerical errors, so they wanted us to do everything again."
There was also a lack of information on several people classified as missing. "For some, nothing was known about them; we didn't even know if they had been murdered or abducted, so we looked for answers among the bodies."
Paz says the soldiers built profiles of the missing, listing identifying marks like tattoos or dreadlocks. "We had to tear the shirts off the bodies and take everything out of the pockets, because some [Gazans] had stolen things from Israelis. We found necklaces, wallets, maps of kibbutzim, soldiers' IDs," he says. And there were also weapons: grenades, magazines and explosives.
"The bodies were frozen, so we had to thaw them," he says. "Some were decomposing; there were maggots everywhere, and limbs were missing. In some, facial features were visible; in others, not."
According to Paz, in the second round, remains of two Israeli civilians and two foreign nationals were found: an agricultural worker from Thailand and an asylum seeker from Eritrea. There would be several more rounds; in some, more advanced equipment was used to scan the bodies. A special unit at Southern Command was responsible for extracting remains from burned vehicles.
"They used special vacuums," one officer says. "The ash was taken for DNA tests. Several mysteries were solved that way. Israelis, that's all that was left of them: a little ash."
It's unclear how many of the bodies brought to Sde Teiman turned out to be Israelis. Some say 14, others 16, some even 30. One reason is that some rabbinical personnel only count the bodies of Jews.
Then there were the bodies of five Gazan workers who were in Israel on October 7 and were murdered by Hamas. The IDF Spokesperson's Unit was unable to answer questions on this matter.
Continuing to search
Elharar remembers the day he realized that something in him had changed. It happened after a year of continuous reserve duty. "I realized I wasn't okay," he recalls. "I became short-tempered at home with my wife, with the children. I felt that something in my basic human experience had been undermined."
He thinks about death. "I can be sitting on a bus, and it hits me, severs me from my surroundings. Thoughts about what would happen if one of my children died – what would his funeral be like? And how would I hold him? These are thoughts I didn't have before. Death is very present in life. In every joyful moment, I think about the inevitable end."
Today, Elharar is being examined by the Defense Ministry's Rehabilitation Department, but for the time being, he's back in reserve duty. "To tell the truth, I think it's a bit of an escape," he says.
For Paz, the diagnosis is clear: a 40 percent disability rating for post-traumatic stress disorder – for only five years. This is the Rehabilitation Department's new policy, to reduce recognition of permanent PTSD.
"I received the results and felt anger, frustration," he says. "I gave my all so that families would have a grave to visit, and this is what I get in return."
As he puts it, "I've been to so many psychiatrists, and all of them wrote that my condition is severe, that I can't be rehabilitated. My psychologist told me that it's a miracle I'm still alive. My disability isn't temporary, it lives with me every day. I can't go to the supermarket, I barely eat. I can't be in crowded places, I isolate myself, I lash out at the children, I don't recognize myself anymore."
Paz's wife gave birth while he was on reserve duty. "She called me to come, and I got there half an hour before the birth," he says. "When I saw the baby, I couldn't feel anything. Nothing. There was no joy, zero emotion, I was disconnected. It took me four months until I agreed to hold him; I waited for him to grow. At first, he felt like another body part."
It's a feeling of emptiness, Paz says. "I haven't cried in two years; there's no emotion. I'm numb, nothing makes me happy. I can start washing dishes, and my mind goes elsewhere. The water can run for hours. My wife went down to part-time work because she knew I couldn't function with the children."
Even today, Paz is obsessed with people's identifying marks. "I look at people passing by and focus on their hair color, their tattoos. I don't see people, only marks."
And his nights are haunted. "I sleep about three hours a night," he says. "I go to sleep at 2 and wake up at 5." In that short span, he has nightmares – from his days in Gaza as well as at Sde Teiman. After the mission at the base, he volunteered to accompany an armored force in an attempt to locate hostages in the Nuseirat refugee camp. But something went wrong.
"We were inside a building, and there was a tremendous noise," he says. "Somebody from the observation post shouted, 'Terrorist, terrorist.' Then an anti-tank missile was fired at our area, hitting right nearby." The tanks "started firing at the terrorist. A few days later, I came home and decided I wasn't going back."
The nightmares sometimes make him violent in his sleep. "I once lashed out at my wife," Paz says. "For two and a half months, I slept on the couch because I was afraid of hurting her."
He recently checked himself into a mental health facility for three months. "I do everything they tell me, but I don't feel any improvement," he says. "I've lost a part of my soul; I wish something would help."
The skeletons around him
Some veterans take even more drastic steps. For six months, Shlomo Arnon has been living in a locked ward at a psychiatric hospital. "I have no expected release date," the 29-year-old says in a video call.
He was at both Shura and Sde Teiman; he served hundreds of days in reserve duty. He was diagnosed with PTSD and recognized with a 70 percent permanent disability. In the eyes of many professionals, he's one of the war's most severely mentally wounded.
"I saw countless faces of dead people," he says. "One was swollen like a balloon, one was black, another red, one had no face left at all. They all come back to me in flashbacks, in nightmares. At night I scream, I scream my soul out."
It isn't much better when he's awake. "I suffer from fits of rage, breaking everything around me. I'm on tranquilizers and painkillers. I have a hard time taking a shower because I still feel like I'm washing a body," he says. "Because I had so many attacks and so many tremors, I would bang my head against the wall out of frustration, and that damaged my memory."
Arnon, who is from Jerusalem, is married and a father of three. Before the war, he worked in archaeological excavations. Now, in his dreams, he digs in the earth and discovers dead people.
"I lost everything," he says. "My youngest daughter doesn't know me; the middle one calls me Shlomo, not Dad. I'm disconnected from my family, from my friends. At first, they came to visit, but after that, I became one of the crazies."
In the ward, he sees skeletons, but living ones, people who look like bags of bones. "When they show pictures of themselves from two or three years ago, you see gorillas, human beings," he says. "This war has broken so many people, crushed them."
At least 13 other soldiers who served in body identification at Sde Teiman have been hospitalized in locked wards at psychiatric hospitals, sources at the Rehabilitation Department say.
"There were cases where people were completely burned, nothing left of them. I would pick up the last remnant with two fingers," Arnon says.
"There were cases where I would open the bag and see that the whole body was gone, only a few bones remained. There were maggots everywhere. Blood dripping. I found myself walking with a human hand, moving it from place to place."
One time, he tried to pull a body out of a truck. "But I didn't have the strength anymore; it was heavy, so I fell inside," he says. "I was entirely covered in bodies, in blood. It was a moment I said aloud to God, 'Take me, free me from this life.'"
But he stuck to the mission, striving to maintain his humanity. "It was important to me to respect everybody," he says. "Some people wanted to desecrate the bodies of the terrorists. There was a lot of anger; it created a lot of tension among the guys.
"But I didn't allow it, despite everything they did. ... I covered them, I tried as much as possible to act with respect. For me, we're all human beings – Jews, Muslims and Christians."
Arnon's condition is severe, but he's not despairing. "I'm not looking for peace; I'm looking for healing. I believe that it will be good; I hope that with all my heart," he says.
"Maybe I'm completely messed up, but it was for a sacred purpose, for the bereaved families, for the fallen, the victims. I gave my soul for them, and with a full heart. I'd do it again."

EXPLAINER - What is Israel’s ‘Sufa 53’ military project in southern Syria?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:15:03 UTC
16:15:03 KST

Abdulsalam Fayez and Tarek Chouiref
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Israeli forces restarted excavation work Sunday west of Al-Asha village in Syria's southern Quneitra as part of a project known as the “Sufa Line,” or “Sufa 53,” according to Syria Alikhbaria TV.
Military vehicles and bulldozers were seen digging near the separation line with the occupied Syrian Golan Heights, extending a route that runs through rural communities from northern to southern Quneitra.
For residents, the project has meant the loss of agricultural land, damage to grazing areas and vegetation, and changes to the natural flow of rainwater in a province where many families depend on farming and livestock.
 
What is Sufa 53?
Israel began work on Sufa 53 in mid-2022 near Hadr in northern Quneitra before extending it south through areas near Jubata al-Khashab, Al-Hamidiyah, Qahtaniyah, Bir Ajam and Bariqa toward Al-Asha.
The project includes a military road roughly eight meters wide, deep trenches, earth berms reaching about five meters in height, observation posts and military positions.
Israel claims that the fortifications are designed to prevent possible attacks by Iran-backed armed groups.
Construction continued after the fall of the Bashar al-Assad government in December 2024 and intensified as Israeli forces expanded their presence in and around the area of separation in southern Syria.
Syrian accounts say Israeli troops have moved between 300 and 1,000 meters into the area in some locations as work on the project expanded.
 
Farmland lost, livelihoods hit
The impact has been particularly severe on agricultural communities.
Local authorities previously estimated that around 12,000 dunams (1,200 hectares) of land in northern and central Quneitra had been affected by Israeli construction.
In Jubata al-Khashab alone, local officials said around 7,000 dunams (700 hectares) of land had been lost, while another 6,000 dunams (600 hectares) belonging to Al-Hamidiyah and Al-Hurriyah were taken over for the project.
Residents have also reported extensive damage to grazing land, trees and wild vegetation that had provided an important source of income for local families.
Quneitra media director Mohammad al-Saeed previously told Anadolu that the project had caused widespread damage across the province, while access to affected areas remained limited.
Mohammad Mazen Maryoud, mayor of Jubata al-Khashab, said the trenches had disrupted rainwater flows and contributed to soil erosion, directly affecting farming and livestock.
Residents also say the construction has come alongside repeated Israeli raids, detentions, checkpoints and restrictions on access to agricultural land.
Syria’s Foreign Ministry on Sunday condemned the renewed work on Sufa 53, describing it as a “flagrant breach” of the 1974 disengagement agreement and a violation of international resolutions.
The ministry warned that continued Israeli incursions and military activity threatened regional security and stability and undermined international law.
Damascus reaffirmed its right to exercise sovereignty over all Syrian territory and urged the international community to uphold Syria’s territorial integrity and act against continued Israeli violations.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez announces snap election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:14:41 KST

Spain’s Pedro Sanchez announces snap election amid housing crisis
Sanchez calls early vote after Parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has announced a snap general election after Parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.
Sanchez said on Monday the vote would take place on November 29. “We need to renew people’s support,” he said in a televised address.
“We need to mobilise and win a much larger progressive majority in Parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain.”
In recent weeks, Spaniards have demanded solutions from the government over housing affordability, holding protests across the country after public outrage grew over the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid last month.
The government said more than 70,000 people took part in a housing protest in the capital on Saturday.
For years, housing has been a top concern for Spaniards as current levels fall short of demand. According to real estate website Idealista, average rents have almost doubled over the past decade, while asking prices for homes have risen by about 90 percent.
In his announcement, Sanchez acknowledged having made mistakes and falling short of previous campaign promises.
“I also know that part of that social majority is dissatisfied today,” Sanchez said.
Opposition ahead in polls
But facing the electorate is a risky move for Sanchez. Opinion polls suggest that a coalition led by the conservative People’s Party (PP), with support from the far-right Vox party, is the most likely outcome in the election.
If they win, it will be the first time since the death of dictator Francisco Franco that a far-right party has entered central government.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo urged voters to bring his party to power in the election.
“The question I put to voters is whether they want four more years of what we’ve been living through, or whether they want to give change a chance,” he said in a televised address.
If Sanchez loses the election, it will also mark the end of one of Europe’s last left-leaning governments as the far right continues to gain ground across the continent.
Sanchez has stood out worldwide for his strong stance on progressive ideas, from defending the rights of Palestinian people to defending multilateral institutions and cracking down on tech oligarchs.
The prime minister, who has never won enough votes to form a majority government, has brought together a series of fragile and seemingly impossible coalitions, ranging from the far left to the separatist right, to remain in power for three successive terms, lasting eight years.

Ahead of COP31 in Türkiye, Fiji hosts Pacific leaders with focus on oceans, blue economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:14:29 UTC

Riyaz ul Khaliq
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Pacific leaders on Monday gathered in Fiji for preparatory talks ahead of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), which will be held in Türkiye next month, with the host nation urging greater focus on oceans and the blue economy.
“The ocean and blue economy must be central to our climate negotiations, and we must integrate the ocean-climate nexus into those negotiations,” said Lynda Tabuya, Fiji’s minister for environment and climate change.
Tabuya was addressing the gathering in Fiji’s city of Nadi, which is hosting the Pacific Pre-COP31 meeting this week, FBC News reported.
The Pacific communities “depend heavily on the ocean for food, livelihoods and economic activity, making greater investment in ocean protection and sustainable development essential,” she said, calling for limiting global warming to the 1.5-degree target and stressing the need for climate finance to reach vulnerable communities faster and more fairly.
Tabuya said Fiji will push for stronger action on clean shipping, renewable energy, sustainable fisheries and ocean conservation.
“Our ocean is central to the climate solution and climate action cannot succeed without that being front and center.”
The UN’s COP31 conference will be held in the Mediterranean city of Antalya from Nov. 9-20.

Spain’s Sánchez calls snap elections for Nov. 29
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:13:21 UTC
16:13:21 KST

Pedro Sánchez attends an extraordinary parliamentary session to vote on a government housing decree, in Madrid on Oct. 2, 2026. | Javier Soriano/AFP via Getty Images
Already weakened by the corruption cases battering his Socialist Party, Sánchez took a further knock this summer when he faced fierce blowback over his handling of the ongoing migrant crisis in the North African exclave of Ceuta.
But the bitter topic of unaffordable housing — something that tops the list of voters’ concerns in Spain and which has sparked nationwide protests — has finally prompted Sánchez to call an early election in an apparent bid to seize a campaign battleground he believes could work to his advantage.
Although Sánchez has established a reputation as a master of the political bounce-back, he faces a steep climb to turn this latest crisis to his advantage.
Polls overwhelmingly suggest that the country will vote in an administration led by the center-right People’s Party, currently supported by 34% of the electorate, compared with 26% backing the Socialist Party. The PP would likely partner with the far-right Vox party, which is projected to score 18%, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.
In calling for an election, Sánchez warned of the surge of the far right.
“You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you wish to play in this era, and what role you want Spain to play,” he said in his address to the nation.
“You must decide whether to join the far-right wave that drives regression wherever it governs, or whether you want Spain to remain a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility,” he added.
Advertisement
Mixed track record
Sánchez used the televised address announcing the snap elections to highlight what his minority coalition government had achieved since coming to office in 2023.
The prime minister emphasized the strides Spain has made on the economic front, becoming “the fastest-growing economy in the entire European Union, leading in job creation,” and underscored the continued investments in green energy that have made the country a renewables powerhouse.
He also highlighted his own role on the international stage, where he has gained prominence as one of the Western leaders to most forcefully condemn both Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the conflicts in Gaza and Iran, and clashed with tech giants such as Elon Musk.
Sánchez said Spaniards could be proud of a government that “denounces genocidal figures while others remain silent and fights the tyrants, oligarchs, and speculators who seek to destroy our children’s future to line their own pockets.”
While insisting that his government had “transformed Spain into a global benchmark for peace, feminism, and prosperity, allowing us to achieve the best economic, social, and environmental results of any democratic government in our country’s history,” Sánchez also acknowledged that many Spaniards felt “dissatisfaction.”
Average citizens are not feeling the impact of Spain’s strong growth and record employment figures. Inflation outpaces salary gains, leaving most households with little additional purchasing power as prices and housing costs surge.
Advertisement
Moreover, episodes like last year’s Iberian blackout tarnished the prestige of the country’s green energy network, and the international response to the ongoing Ceuta migrant crisis has raised doubts about Spain’s heft on the global stage.
Sánchez admitted his government had made mistakes and “not managed to achieve everything we set out to do.”
“Many injustices remain to be corrected, many social goals to be attained, and many problems to be solved — particularly regarding inequality in public services and access to housing,” he said. “But the fact is that to do more, we need to renew and expand public support in order to undertake the deep reforms required for citizens to reduce these levels of inequality.”
Polls favor conservatives
Although Sánchez has established a reputation as a master of the political bounce-back, he faces a steep climb to turn this latest crisis to his advantage.
The PP, which has called for snap elections almost from the moment Sánchez renewed his hold on power at the end of 2023, reacted to the news with the short tweet: “AT LAST.”
The snap election caught Spain’s fractured far-left parties scrambling to regroup. That’s a problem for Sánchez’s Socialists, who need the groups to their left to unite behind a viable electoral alliance in order to form a fresh coalition government.
Advertisement
With Deputy Prime Minister Yolanda Díaz declining to run for reelection, the Sumar group — junior partners in Sánchez’s coalition government – is still searching for a leader, which is expected to be unveiled on Oct. 17, when the party rebrands as the “Broad Front.”
Health Minister Mónica García is the frontrunner to be lead candidate, with Culture Minister Ernest Urtasun running as the main figure in Catalonia.
It remains unclear whether that project will be able to incorporate Spain’s other major far-left party, Podemos, or figures such as longtime housing activist and former Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau, who has signaled a willingness to return to frontline politics.

2 Iranian police officers killed in armed attack in southeastern Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:12:24 UTC
16:12:24 KST

Sahin Demir
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026

Mideast oil exports exceeded pre-Iran war levels: Kpler data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:11:51 UTC
16:11:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Mideast oil exports exceeded pre-Iran war levels, according to Kpler data
Middle East oil exports, excluding Iran, surpassed their pre-war levels last week, despite attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, according to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler.
For the first time since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran at the end of February, the weekly average of shipments rose for several days above the pre-conflict average of 18 million barrels per day.
Crude oil exports reached pre-war levels in September, with at least 16.5 million barrels leaving the region excluding Iran, Kpler said on Wednesday.
"Forty percent now bypass Hormuz, and most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore," Kpler said, adding that most of the oil flowed through Saudi and United Arab Emirates pipelines.
These figures include flows via the Red Sea, a route increasingly used to bypass the blockade Iran is attempting to impose on Hormuz—where around a fifth of the world's petroleum supplies crossed before the conflict.
Iran still claims control over the strait, and ships without its authorisation risk coming under attack, but more and more are making it out, and alternative routes meant to bypass the waterway are operating at full capacity.
Despite the rebound, experts stressed that the situation was far from normal, and Iran remains deprived of a large share of its own exports by a US counterblockade of its ports.
Saudi Arabia is benefiting from the reactivation of its East-West pipeline, which links the kingdom's main oil fields in the east to its Yanbu terminal on the Red Sea, allowing it to bypass Hormuz.
Shut down on September 11 after being hit by strikes launched from Iraq, the pipeline resumed operations on September 22, Amena Bakr, an analyst at Kpler said last week.
The United Arab Emirates is also able to bypass Hormuz thanks to its pipeline linking Abu Dhabi's fields to Fujairah, a terminal just outside the strait on the Gulf of Oman.
Around 0310 GMT on Monday, Brent North Sea crude for December delivery fell 0.79 percent to $101.44 a barrel.
Its US counterpart, West Texas Intermediate for November delivery, dropped 1.20 percent to $90.02.

Annual inflation eases below 30 pct in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:09:41 UTC
16:09:41 KST

Türkiye’s annual consumer inflation stood at 29.73 percent in September, below market expectations of 30.3 percent, according to official figures released on Oct. 5.
Consumer prices rose 1.84 percent month-on-month, the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) said on Oct. 5.
Annual inflation fell below 30 percent for the first time in 57 months [since November 2021], said Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek on a social media post, commenting on the latest data.
“Disinflation is spreading across the board, excluding transportation. In September, food inflation decreased by 8.4 points compared to the same period last year, reaching an annual rate of 27.6 percent,” he noted.
“To limit the impact of recently rising oil prices on inflation, we are gradually phasing out the sliding-scale tax mechanism [eşel mobil] in gasoline following diesel,” he added.
Şimşek noted that the Central Bank calculates that inflation would have been 7 points lower this year had there been no war.
“We are continuing our policies aimed at increasing the supply of housing and food. In 2027, the reduction in inertia in service inflation, particularly in rent and education, and the weakening of commodity price increase effects will contribute to the decline in inflation,” said Şimşek.
According to TÜİK data, food and non-alcoholic beverage prices, one of the largest components of the consumer price index, fell 0.2 percent from the previous month.
Transportation prices increased 2.79 percent, while housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuel costs rose 2.71 percent.
Transportation contributed 0.49 percentage points to monthly inflation and housing added 0.33 percentage points. Food prices reduced the monthly reading by 0.05 percentage points.
On an annual basis, food and non-alcoholic beverage prices rose 27.62 percent, transportation costs increased 35.1 percent, and housing prices climbed 39.99 percent.
These groups contributed 6.73, 5.96 and 4.84 percentage points, respectively, to annual inflation.
The core C index, which excludes energy, food and non-alcoholic beverages, alcoholic beverages, tobacco and gold, increased 28.7 percent annually and 2.14 percent monthly.
The B index, which excludes unprocessed food, energy, alcoholic beverages, tobacco and gold, rose 29 percent annually and 2.01 percent month-on-month.
Of the 174 expenditure subclasses tracked by TÜİK, prices increased in 133, declined in 35 and remained unchanged in six.
With September inflation data now released, investors will shift their focus to the Central Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee meeting on Oct. 22, when policymakers are due to announce their next interest rate decision. The bank’s final rate-setting meeting of 2026 is scheduled for Dec. 10.
As widely expected, the Central Bank on July 23 kept its policy rate unchanged at 37 percent, extending its monetary policy pause for a fourth consecutive meeting.
Meanwhile, Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan is scheduled to deliver a presentation to lawmakers at the Turkish parliament’s Planning and Budget Commission on Oct. 6.
Karahan is expected to provide a comprehensive presentation covering global developments, the Turkish economy, inflation and monetary policy.

Russia Upgrades Geran-4 Drones With Better Navigation and New Warhead, Ukraine Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:09:37 UTC
16:09:37 KST

Russia has upgraded its Geran-4 attack drones with technology designed to make them harder to disrupt and more accurate, Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) agency said.
The new version, which Russia has started using this autumn, can navigate more precisely without relying entirely on satellite signals and carries a new warhead designed to damage bridges and power infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
One of the upgrades is a small magnetic sensor made by US company PNI Sensor. It helps the drone understand changes in its position and correct errors in its onboard navigation system, improving its ability to stay on course.
Russia has also added an optical navigation system called “Susanin.” In simple terms, the system uses a camera to compare what the drone sees below with images stored in its computer.
This allows the drone to recognize where it is and follow its planned route even without relying on GPS or other satellite navigation.
A similar system is being used on the newer Geran-5 drone, according to Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
The upgraded Geran-4 also carries a new warhead designed specifically to attack infrastructure. It can use a powerful shaped charge to cut through bridge structures and supports carrying high-voltage power lines.
Russia has also replaced the Chinese-made engine previously used on the drone with a Russian-made version produced at the Alabuga industrial facility in Russia’s Tatarstan.
Guterres’s Successor Will Need Russia’s Blessing
Most of the drone’s other electronic components remain unchanged, HUR said in a report published on its War&Sanctions portal.
What is the Geran-4?
The Geran-4 is a relatively large, jet-powered attack drone designed for long-range strikes. It is about 3.6 meters (11.8 feet) long, has a 3.05-meter (10-foot) wingspan and can carry a warhead weighing up to 50 kilograms (110 pounds).
It has a maximum takeoff weight of about 450 kilograms (992 pounds). Its cruising speed is around 320 km/h (200 mph), while its maximum speed is 350 km/h (217 mph).
The drone has a reported range of about 770 kilometers (479 miles) and can fly at altitudes of up to 4 kilometers (2.5 miles).
Geran-4 vs. Geran-5
The Geran-5 is a larger and more powerful member of the same family.
It is about 6.5 meters (21.3 feet) long and weighs up to 850 kilograms (1,874 pounds) – almost twice as much as the Geran-4. It can carry a warhead weighing up to 90 kilograms (198 pounds).
The Geran-5 has a cruising speed of 450–600 km/h (280–373 mph) and a range of about 950 kilometers (590 miles). It can fly at altitudes of up to 6 kilometers (3.7 miles).
In simple terms, the Geran-4 is smaller and lighter, while the Geran-5 is a much larger platform capable of carrying a heavier warhead and flying faster and farther.

Norway to propose temporary ban on AI glasses in some public places
COPENHAGEN – Norway’s government said on Oct 5 it plans to propose a temporary ban on the use of AI glasses in selected places, saying it is concerned people could be photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without their knowledge.
The proposal mirrors a broader global backlash against smart glasses equipped with cameras over privacy concerns.
The ban could apply to places where the public regularly gather, such as parks, beaches, museums, shopping centres and public events, the government said in a statement.
“I am worried that new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without knowing it,” Digitalisation and Public Governance Minister Torgeir Micaelsen said.
It could also apply to schools, playgrounds and youth clubs and to privacy-sensitive places such as doctors’ offices, swimming pools and gyms with changing rooms.
The government said it was not eyeing a total ban and that private use, and use where others are not at risk of being filmed without consent, would still be allowed.
It said it would examine which technology the ban would cover, including whether it would apply to glasses with camera and audio recording, glasses with camera and AI functions or also other body-worn technology with camera, audio recording and/or artificial intelligence.
The minority government said it would present a Bill to Parliament as soon as possible, and would also set up an expert group to advise on permanent national regulation of body-worn technology. REUTERS
