Middle East oil exports top pre-war levels despite attacks, new shipping data shows
Middle East oil exports exceeded pre-war levels in September, new shipping data showed on Monday, as Gulf producers ramped up cargoes despite attacks on vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz.
Merchant ships transiting the key chokepoint face a “heightened and increasingly unpredictable kinetic threat” given the recent sharp increase in traffic, Reuters reported, citing Marisks, a shipping intelligence service.
Over the seven days to 30 September, crude oil exports averaged 18.3m barrels per day, according to provisional data from Kpler. In the 12 months before the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, crude exports from the region averaged about 18m bpd.
Cargoes exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days in September, including transits via Hormuz, the Red Sea and exports from terminals.
Before September, oil shipments from the region matched or exceeded pre-war levels on a handful of days in June and July, Kpler data showed, after Washington and Tehran reached a memorandum of understanding to end the war but it has since lapsed.
The export surge has been driven by Saudi Arabia exporting from both the Red Sea and the Gulf, three weeks after an ttack on its East-West pipeline on 10 September, Kpler said.
Also, Iraq’s state-owned Oil Tanker Company and some refiners have chartered tankers to load Basrah crude inside the strait, after Baghdad secured Iranian permission for Iraqi oil tankers to pass through Hormuz.
Energy intelligence firm Vortexa said that the 14-day moving average for Middle East crude and condensate exports hit 18.6 million bpd, exceeding the 10-year seasonal average and returning to pre-conflict levels. (Condensate exports are a mixture of low-density liquid hydrocarbons that remain liquid at standard atmospheric pressure.)
Senior market analyst Xavier Tang at Vortexa said.
Most of this month-over-month increase seen in September comes from Saudi Arabia, which is ramping up exports to regain market share from other Middle Eastern countries.
This increase in Middle East supplies will also help alleviate tightness in the oil market, especially for Asian refiners.
Liquefied natural gas cargoes exiting the strait of Hormuz also rose in September to their highest levels since February.
Almost 3bn barrels of oil supply have been lost since the start of the conflict, according to Amin Nasser, chief executive of Saudi Aramco.
Speaking at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London, he said 1bn barrels of oil had been released from global stocks, Reuters reported.
Refilling all inventories would equate to an extra 2m barrels per day (bpd) of demand over the next 18 months. Global daily oil demand is just over 100 million bpd.
Saudi Arabia’s maximum sustainable production capacity of 12 million bpd could be made available within days, Nasser said, as its strategic reserves and flexibility in its system have remained intact.
But adding to the supply pressure, much of the remaining 6bn barrels or so in storage is “not practically available,” Nasser said – up to 90% is in pipelines or is needed to ensure the minimum volume for storage tanks to operate.
Saudi Arabia has ways to bypass the strait of Hormuz and Nasser told the conference that Aramco is assessing additional routes, as well as making use of more overseas storage to help cover short-term disruptions.
Its East-West pipeline allows Saudi Arabia to move oil to its Red Sea terminals. Nasser said that without that pipeline, Brent crude futures would have hit $200 per barrel.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, reversed earlier moderate losses and is trading 42 cents, or 0.4%, higher at $102.63 a barrel.

INTERVIEW – Japan bets on space autonomy as global competition accelerates: Country’s space chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:54:58 UTC
15:54:58 KST

- Tokyo aims to increase H3 launch frequency to make rocket a ‘trusted vehicle’ and internationally competitive
- Japan’s MMX mission, due to launch Oct. 20, seeks first-ever sample return from Mars’ moon Phobos   
Japan is doubling down on its ability to reach and operate in space on its own terms, the head of the country's space agency said, as competition in orbit intensifies and a Japanese probe prepares to depart for the moons of Mars.
"We'd like to focus on the autonomy regarding space. That means, for example, autonomous access to space and autonomous activity in space," Hiroshi Yamakawa, president of the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), told Anadolu in Antalya, host of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026).
"Those two are very important for Japan. That's why we are developing rocket technology and also satellite technology," he said.
Yamakawa, who has led JAXA since April 2018, said these capabilities serve Japan's national space policy goals in three areas: space security, the space economy and space exploration.
"We would like to further strengthen those technological capabilities to realize national space policies and contribute to our daily life, economy and national security," he added.
Japan's space program dates back to 1955, when a University of Tokyo team led by engineer Hideo Itokawa test-fired a 23-centimeter experimental rocket known as the "Pencil" in Kokubunji near Tokyo.
 
‘Already an operational rocket'
To secure sovereign launch capabilities amid an increasingly competitive commercial launch sector dominated by global industry players like SpaceX, Japan is ramping up operations of its flagship H3 launch vehicle.
First launched successfully in early 2024 as a joint project between JAXA and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries to replace the H-IIA, the liquid-fueled rocket is designed as Japan's primary heavy-lift workhorse.
Addressing how Japan plans to maintain competitiveness, Yamakawa pointed to the upcoming milestone flight of the vehicle.
“Autonomous access to space is vital for Japanese space activities, and the H3 rocket is at the heart of that endeavor,” he said. “We will launch H3 rocket number 10 this month. And that means our H3 rocket is already an operational rocket.”
He added that JAXA aims to step up the frequency of missions.
“We would like to further increase the launch cadence -- I mean the number of launches in the near future -- so that we can make the H3 rocket a trusted vehicle and also an internationally competitive rocket.”
The 10th H3 launch is scheduled for Oct. 20 from the Tanegashima Space Center in southwestern Japan and will carry the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft.
 
‘Transformable robot’ heads for Mars
Yamakawa described MMX as a milestone for Japanese planetary exploration.
"It will be the world's first sample return mission for Martian moon Phobos. And it's so exciting to ... move on to the next step," he said.
MMX is designed to study both of Mars' small moons, Phobos and Deimos, land on Phobos, collect at least 10 grams of surface material and bring it back to Earth, with the return planned for 2031. NASA, the European Space Agency, France's CNES and Germany's DLR are partners in the mission, and the spacecraft carries a small rover, Idefix, built by the French and German agencies.
Scientists hope the samples will help settle whether the two moons are captured asteroids or debris thrown into orbit by a giant impact on Mars.
Yamakawa said the mission could shed light on the origin and evolution of the Martian moons, of Mars itself and of the solar system as a whole.
He also stressed the engineering challenge.
"From an engineering point of view, it is really a kind of transformable robot, because it will change its shape and function," he said.
He explained that the spacecraft will shed parts of itself at each stage: separating a module after arriving at Mars, releasing hardware used for the landing once it has touched down on Phobos, and finally dropping a capsule carrying the samples into Earth's atmosphere on its return.
The mission follows JAXA's Hayabusa and Hayabusa2 probes, which brought back samples from the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu.
 
Space debris 'the biggest issue'
Yamakawa's remarks come weeks after US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said in September that the US Space Force has "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," the first official US acknowledgment of weapons in orbit.
China's Foreign Ministry responded by urging Washington to stop expanding its military buildup in outer space and preparing for war there, while Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said space "must be free of any weapon."
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not explicitly prohibit conventional weapons.
Asked about rising geopolitical tensions in space and the possibility of conflict beyond Earth, Yamakawa framed space security in terms of keeping orbit usable.
"Space security in Japan means a sustainable use of outer space. For example, the biggest issue is the space debris," he said.
"Space debris collision with active satellites will be a big issue for everybody."
He said JAXA tracks debris using ground stations, telescopes and radars, with a constant focus on preventing collisions with operational satellites.
"That's the biggest issue, and also that's the most important thing to engage," he added.
 
‘Promising area' for Japan-Türkiye cooperation
Welcoming the host nation of IAC 2026, Yamakawa commended Türkiye's recent strides in space exploration, citing the country's first human spaceflight mission to the International Space Station (ISS) in early 2024 and the deployment of its domestically built Turksat 6A telecommunications satellite.
“I think Türkiye has made big progress recently in the space arena,” he said.
He underscored that the two nations already share a history of orbital and satellite cooperation, pointing to the Japanese Experiment Module (Kibo) on the ISS, through which Turkish microsatellites have previously been deployed, alongside ongoing satellite data sharing for disaster management and Earth observation.
“I think space is a promising area for further collaboration,” he said, adding that further developing cooperation with Türkiye is one of Japan’s objectives at the congress.

Americans withdraw bombers from British Air Force base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:54:31 UTC
15:54:31 KST

Following arrests made a week ago near the Royal Air Force (RAF) base at Fairford and the launch of an investigation into a suspected terrorist plot, the US has withdrawn its bombers from the base, the BBC reports.
US officials confirmed on the 4th of October that the bombers—reportedly around a dozen B-1s—had been withdrawn from Fairford and returned to their home bases. The US did not disclose the reason for the withdrawal, but the decision follows an incident on the 27th of September, when police received reports of three suspicious vehicles near the RAF base. Five men were initially detained on suspicion of plotting a terrorist attack but were subsequently released on bail. A sixth man was later arrested and also released on bail.
Sources within the British government have not disputed that the US decision was linked to the incident near the RAF base. The BBC understands that this was a military rather than a political decision, and that US military officials discussed the matter with their British counterparts. The British Ministry of Defence has not commented on the withdrawal of the bombers. 
Flight tracking data indicates that the B-1 bombers departed the RAF base at Fairford on the 4th of October.
A few days after the events at the RAF base, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated there were serious indications of Iranian involvement in the incident but provided no further details. Tehran has denied involvement.
British police arrested five men—aged 23 to 25—in the early hours of the 27th of September after suspicious vehicles were spotted near the base. All are British citizens residing in London. They were initially detained on suspicion of transporting explosives, and charges of preparing a terrorist act were subsequently brought against them. The men were later released on bail; police stated that this decision was part of the investigation and based on experience and strategy. On the 1st of October, a sixth man was arrested in London on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. The police counter-terrorism unit confirmed that he, too, was released on bail on the 3rd of October.
RAF Fairford has also been used by the US Air Force for several decades. In recent months, after the British authorized the use of the base for preparations for strikes against Iran, B-1 and B-52 bombers have used it as a staging point en route to the Middle East. 
In July, Tehran stated that any base linked to strikes against Iran would become a legitimate target for its forces.
Following the initial arrests—and prior to the arrest of the sixth man—US State Secretary Marco Rubio told Fox News that other countries were involved in the incident. He did not provide further details. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed surprise that the five detainees were released on bail.
Many of the deployed B-1 bombers are equipped with guided bunker-busting bombs, which feature reinforced casings designed to successfully strike hardened or underground targets. They are also capable of carrying air-to-ground missiles. Depending on the target's location, each mission from the US could now take 12 to 15 hours, involving mid-air refueling. The Pentagon has emphasized that its bombers remain capable of successfully carrying out missions anywhere and at any time, even if they must take off from the continental United States.

Second U.S. Navy carrier ready to fly MQ-25 drone tanker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:53:15 UTC
15:53:15 KST

- USS Ronald Reagan (CVN 76) became the second U.S. Navy carrier able to fly the MQ-25A Stingray after its control center was installed in August.
- All 11 ship modifications were completed at once in 17 months, while the MQ-25A's initial operational capability may slip to 2029.
USS Ronald Reagan (CVN 76) has become the second U.S. Navy aircraft carrier equipped to fly the MQ-25A Stingray, the service’s carrier-based drone tanker, after crews finished installing an Unmanned Air Warfare Center aboard the ship in August.
The center is the shipboard control room for the MQ-25A. It houses the MD-5C ground control station that operators use to command the drone. The Unmanned Carrier Aviation Program Office, known as PMA-268, manages the effort.
USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) received the first operational installation in March. On USS Ronald Reagan (CVN 76), the U.S. Navy took a faster route. Instead of spreading the work over several years in phases, the team completed all 11 ship modifications at once within a single 17-month period.
That window matches the carrier’s recent overhaul. USS Ronald Reagan (CVN 76) spent 17 months in a scheduled dry-dock maintenance period at Puget Sound Naval Shipyard in Bremerton, Washington, starting in March 2025, and left for sea trials on Sept. 3.
“With each new install and milestone, we are closing the gap for our warfighters to give them the capability, capacity, and lethality they need to win the fight,” said Capt. Daniel Fucito, PMA-268 program manager.
The control station combines several parts: the U.S. Navy’s command, control, communications, computers and intelligence network, Lockheed Martin’s MDCX software and hardware for planning and running missions, and other government-built equipment. The U.S. Navy has built shore, at-sea and expeditionary versions of the MD-5 so the MQ-25A can be flown from almost anywhere.
Next, the ship’s crew and the program team will run pier-side and at-sea tests to confirm the system is ready to support the drone.
The MQ-25A, built by Boeing, is meant to take over aerial refueling duties now handled by F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, freeing those fighters for combat missions and extending the range of the carrier air wing. It is the U.S. Navy’s first operational unmanned aircraft designed to fly from a carrier deck.
The program has faced long delays. A test aircraft first flew in 2019, but the first production-representative MQ-25A did not fly until April 25 this year, at Boeing’s facility at MidAmerica Airport in Illinois. In May, the Pentagon approved the program for low-rate initial production. The U.S. Navy plans to buy 76 aircraft in total.
The drone is expected to move to Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland, later this year to prepare for carrier qualification testing. Earlier plans called for the first MQ-25A to deploy aboard USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) in 2026, but production problems and carrier availability pushed that back. The U.S. Navy defines initial operational capability as three MQ-25As with trained crews ready to deploy on a capable carrier, and a Pentagon report in April estimated that milestone could slip to 2029.

Eyewear chain Hans Anders will stop selling Meta camera glasses following demands from privacy advocates concerned about the so-called “pervert glasses”.
The devices, the most popular version is sold by Meta, look like normal glasses but allow users to film and take photos covertly.
Victim advocacy group Offlimits says it is helping hundreds of women who have been filmed without their consent, many of whom have seen those images distributed online or through social media groups.
“Hiding a camera in an everyday object facilitates transgressive online behaviour,” the organisation’s director Robbert Hoving said in a statement. They are calling on Meta to stop selling the eyewear, and said they would take the tech giant to court if sales were not halted.
Dutch privacy watchdog AP warned last week that sharing images made with camera glasses violates GDPR rules unless permission is given by everyone in the image.
Last month, the consumer watchdog Consumentenbond issued a warning about the glasses, noting that it was possible to manipulate or cover the indicator light to make it even harder to tell images were being captured.
MPs have called for a full ban on the glasses but the cabinet is opposed to a board measure and wants to see other restrictions put into place.
Last week, Instagram removed a video by Roel Maalderink in which the satirical journalist films himself asking the employees of parent company Meta how they feel about the controversial camera glasses.

Oman grounded him, UAE hired him, Israel missed him: How Flydubai attack nearly became catastrophe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:51:49 UTC
15:51:49 KST

Oman identified signs that pilot Hamam al-Hamami was undergoing Islamist radicalization and grounded him. He was reassigned to a desk job at Oman Air but was not dismissed. Flydubai later hired him, after checks that focused on his criminal record but did not uncover his earlier radicalization concerns, and eventually allowed him to fly a sensitive route to Israel.
Israeli authorities, meanwhile, were supposed to identify the security significance of a pilot from a country with which Israel has no diplomatic relations operating a passenger flight into Ben Gurion Airport. That did not happen.
Only the resistance of the Indian captain and the actions of Israeli passengers prevented what investigators now believe could have become a mass-casualty attack. In the aftermath, Israeli oversight bodies have traded blame over who was responsible for detecting the threat.
According to a Wall Street Journal report cited in the investigation, Oman Air had identified al-Hamami’s radicalization, sent him to a deradicalization program and removed him from flying duties. But it did not revoke his international pilot’s license or warn neighboring Gulf states or international aviation authorities that could have prevented him from being hired elsewhere.
When al-Hamami reached Flydubai in 2025, the airline conducted a criminal-background check but did not contact Oman and did not examine whether he had a record of ideological radicalization.
The investigation into al-Hamami in the United Arab Emirates is continuing, including efforts to determine whether he acted alone or under the direction of a state or terrorist organization. At this stage, investigators increasingly believe he attempted to crash Flydubai Flight FZ1023 on his own initiative.
Al-Hamami grew up in Dubai, and investigators are examining a trip he made to Syria as a teenager during the country’s civil war, including whether he became radicalized while staying in the country where his mother was born.
He later obtained a visa for Australia and, according to reports, studied engineering at RMIT University in Melbourne for three years. The university says he did not complete his studies, while a local newspaper reported that his visa had been canceled. Reports also say he later studied for an aeronautical engineering degree through Buckinghamshire New University in England remotely.
Israeli and Emirati investigators are now trying to determine whether early signs of radicalization appeared during his time in Australia. A dedicated Australian team is also examining his contacts and conduct while he lived there, while authorities in Abu Dhabi are investigating Flydubai employees involved in his recruitment.
Suspected plan to crash at Ben Gurion Airport began months earlier
Israeli officials said Sunday that al-Hamami’s interrogation indicated he intended to crash the aircraft at Ben Gurion Airport.
According to the emerging account, he waited until the plane was over Jordan before trying to seize control, intending to continue toward Israel as though the aircraft were making a normal approach before crashing it into the airport and causing mass casualties.
If he could not reach Ben Gurion, investigators believe, al-Hamami planned to crash the aircraft into a U.S. military base in Jordan.
The investigation also indicates that the Omani pilot had considered carrying out the attack as early as July, but postponed it because of a personal connection with one of the crew members aboard the flight, whom he allegedly decided to spare.
Investigators also believe al-Hamami landed in Israel in June and had prepared himself to become a “martyr.”
A major factor in thwarting the alleged plan, alongside the actions of Israeli passengers and the replacement pilots who ultimately stabilized the aircraft, was the struggle put up by Indian captain Smith Machachar.
Investigators say al-Hamami planned to strike Machachar repeatedly with an emergency axe until he lost consciousness, then take control of the aircraft and crash it.
After al-Hamami was subdued and the plane stabilized, the replacement pilots requested permission to land in Jordan. Jordanian authorities initially refused after learning there was a suspected hijacking aboard the aircraft.
Channel 13 reported that al-Hamami told investigators: “I searched and checked which airline flew to Tel Aviv, and that’s why I chose Flydubai. I tried to get into all the airlines. I planned the operation before I was even hired by the company.”
According to an investigation by the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, al-Hamami disconnected the autopilot, seized the controls, shut down the engines in flight and pushed the control column forward with full force.
The aircraft lost 16,000 feet of altitude in less than a minute.
Netanyahu orders review based on recommendation made more than two years ago
Five days after the attempted crash, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly acknowledged for the first time that the incident exposed significant failures and security gaps.
According to his office, Netanyahu instructed National Security Council chief Shmuel Ben Ezra to “appoint an examiner to conduct a thorough review of all aspects of the security of foreign civil aviation to Israel.”
It remains unclear how quickly the review will proceed or whether the security gaps it identifies will be closed promptly.
The review ordered by Netanyahu will be internal, however, and the person heading it will not have investigative or enforcement powers. Ben Ezra’s National Security Council has already been responsible for addressing the issue.
In May 2024, State Comptroller Matanyahu Englman published a report on the security of international civil aviation to and from Israel, identifying serious deficiencies and gaps, including in security arrangements for foreign airlines.
One of its main recommendations was that the National Security Council coordinate work among the Transportation Ministry, Finance Ministry, Israel Airports Authority, Shin Bet domestic security agency and police to formulate a comprehensive new aviation-security policy.
Who is responsible for screening foreign pilots?
On paper, responsibility for foreign flights lies with Israel’s Transportation Ministry.
Its Security, Emergency and Cyber Division, through the Aviation Security Operations Center, is tasked with assessing the security risk posed by foreign flights and issuing security instructions to airlines.
The ministry argues, however, that it is not an intelligence agency and lacks the tools to perform intelligence background checks on crew members and passengers. Its procedures therefore depend partly on security arrangements in the countries of origin and on commitments provided by the airlines themselves.
In the case of the Flydubai flight, it emerged that the Transportation Ministry had never received the crew list.
The Emirati airline had committed to vetting its own crew members and had even told Israel that it had introduced restrictions into its scheduling system designed to prevent pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from being assigned to Israel-bound flights.
Despite that commitment, al-Hamami, an Omani citizen, was assigned to the flight.
It also emerged that under Israel’s 2023 National Passenger Analysis Center law, the Transportation Ministry’s security division is permitted access to a database containing information on crew members aboard foreign flights. Since the database was created, however, the ministry had not requested such access.
The security division is also facing a significant manpower shortage.
Between 2022 and 2025, eight employees left the division, while its official staffing allocation fell from 21 positions to 19. Six of those positions are part-time jobs intended for students and senior citizens, and at least two senior posts are listed as vacant but unfunded.
In practice, according to published figures, the division operates Israel’s transportation security and emergency apparatus with only about 10 permanent full-time employees.
The proposal to establish a single agency with overall responsibility for aviation security is also far from new.
A proposal to create a national aviation-security authority was submitted to the prime minister as early as 2011. According to the Transportation Ministry, two committees headed by the National Security Council subsequently recommended establishing such a body.
Those recommendations were never implemented.
Following the attempted Flydubai attack, responsibility for addressing the issue has now returned to the National Security Council, this time under Netanyahu’s directive to conduct a “thorough review” of the entire security system.
Danny Shenar, who headed the Transportation Ministry’s security division for 25 years, warned that the risk is not limited to Dubai.
Major airports such as Athens have sophisticated security systems, he said, but smaller airports on islands and in peripheral destinations often have far weaker safeguards, even though flights depart from them directly for Israel.
“That is where the danger lies,” he warned.
Radical posts and a deleted social-media trail
Al-Hamami, an Omani citizen, was born in the United Arab Emirates to an Omani father and Syrian mother and spent part of his life in the UAE.
According to a LinkedIn profile bearing his name that was deleted after the attempted crash, he worked at Oman Air for seven years, until February 2025.
In 2024, while still serving as a first officer at Oman Air, extremist material was reportedly found in his possession. He nevertheless remained employed by the airline in a desk position.
CBS reported a somewhat different account, saying he had worked for Oman’s national airline only “for a short time” and that he was suspended from flying after accessing extremist websites.
According to the same LinkedIn profile, he joined Morocco’s Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and left six months later, in January 2026. The airline, however, said al-Hamami completed three months of training but was never ultimately employed by the company.
A diplomat from a Gulf state told AP that the pilot underwent standard security checks before he was hired, but that those checks appeared to focus on whether he had a criminal record rather than examining his broader background or possible signs of radicalization.
CNN reported that only two posts appeared on the LinkedIn account associated with al-Hamami, both published on Wednesday, nine hours after the attempted attack.
It was unclear who uploaded them, CNN said, though the network raised the possibility that the posts had been scheduled in advance.
The first contained a series of videos filmed from the cockpit of Boeing 737 MAX aircraft, the same model as the Flydubai jet al-Hamami allegedly tried to crash.
One clip, according to CNN, was filmed at Dubai International Airport and showed the person behind the camera zooming in on an El Al aircraft.
The cockpit screen visible in the footage showed the flight number of an Oman Air flight from Dubai to Muscat on Oct. 11, 2023, several days after the Hamas massacre in southern Israel.
The post included additional videos showing El Al aircraft, as well as one Arkia plane, and ended with footage of al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri, Osama bin Laden’s successor, who was killed in a U.S. strike.
A second post on the deleted LinkedIn account featured an AI-generated image depicting Islam’s three holy cities, Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem, connected by a continuous glowing path. A song heard in the background included statements rejecting “humiliation,” while the speaker said he did not fear death and was defending his honor.
CNN also reported that an account on X bearing the pilot’s name, which has since been deleted, contained extremist religious views.
The network said the account had contained around 3,000 posts. Some described his mother’s difficulty finding him a prospective wife willing, at his insistence, to wear a niqab, the Muslim face covering that leaves only a narrow opening for the eyes.
“They all refused. Then my mother told them, ‘My son is a pilot,’ and suddenly they all agreed,” read one post from February 2022.
Another post, from January 2022, expressed opposition to men and women working together: “How many respectable and religious young women were ruined in mixed workplaces of men and women and manipulated?”
In another post, he wrote: “I don’t know how you have the patience to talk to one girl for four years. Most girls I talk to last two or three days, and I give them 100 tests, including the whore test. Thank God, none survived more than a week with me.”

Brussels government reaches agreement on 2027 budget

Unknown Publisher

06:50:58 UTC
15:50:58 KST

Yesterday evening the Brussels regional government reached agreement on the Brussels Region’s 2027 budget. “There will be cuts to public spending, and there will be no across-the-board tax increases for the people of Brussels,” Brussels PM Boris Dilliès (Francophone liberal MR) said after the breakthrough.
Brussels government reaches agreement on 2027 budget
The agreement follows a difficult two days of budget talks. Details of the agreement have emerged.
In a press release, PM Dilliès and Brussels Finance Minister Dirk De Smedt (Flemish liberal Anders) announced that in 2027 the deficit will be reduced by 719 million euros.
Where will the savings be made?
Within the government itself and by reducing the workforce
Vacancies will no longer be filled automatically.
Staff will be deployed in a more targeted manner through internal mobility.
The reform of government departments will continue, including the merging of services.
Changes to road tax
The government is committed to ensuring that the cost is not passed on to the people of Brussels. It states that it has made a firm commitment to economic growth through:
A doubling of the BeHome allowance, the financial relief measure in Brussels designed to compensate resident homeowners for increases in the property tax.
A reduction in supplementary personal income tax by 1 percentage point.
A reform of the annual road tax: from the second half of 2027, there will be an exemption for those driving a small city car or a zero-emission vehicle (ZEV).
One of the most difficult discussions centred on the transport operator MIVB. “We have finally decided not to implement the planned fare increase,” De Smedt told VRT NEWS.
“Revenue was lower than anticipated. We have compensated for this by cutting operating expenditure.”
Funding shelters and housing
Francophone socialist government ministers Ahmed Laaouej and Karine Lalieux say last weekend’s budget talks resulted in a “responsible budget” with targeted investments in healthcare, social action and housing.
In their press release issued last night they announced a number of measures:
More than 1 million euros will be allocated to ‘prevention’, including cancer screening and a heatwave plan.
The Region is allocating 1.8 million euros for the provision of shelter for homeless families through Samusocial, the humanitarian emergency service that provides immediate assistance, shelter, and medical and psychosocial support to people experiencing homelessness and social distress, and is earmarking 6.3 million euros for the prevention of addiction.
Funding for measures against early school leaving is being increased by 5 million euros, supplemented by 1 million per year from the French Community Commission (COCOF).
Brussels’ municipalities and local social services centres will receive around 15 million euros extra in 2027.
For housing, the agreement allocates 104 million euros for the construction of over 1,000 social housing units.
Rent subsidies will be maintained, and 131 million euros will be allocated for the recapitalisation of the Brussels Regional Housing Company (BGHM).
Laurent Hublet (Francophone centrist Les Engagés), Employment and the Economy Minister, noted that there will be no changes to the price of service vouchers or to child benefit as is happening in Flanders.

U.S. Air Force gives B-52 a new satellite comms system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:47:22 UTC
15:47:22 KST

- The U.S. Air Force fielded the IRIS satellite communications prototype on B-52 bombers, with multiple kits installed on aircraft as of April 1.
- Built by Shreveport-based Outerlink Global Solutions, IRIS uses Iridium satellites and was funded through a $26 million contract awarded in 2023.
The U.S. Air Force has fielded a new satellite communications system on B-52 Stratofortress bombers, giving crews a way to send voice, data, images and video to commanders far beyond the range of line-of-sight radios.
Air Force Global Strike Command said the system, called IRIS, is now in operational use on the bomber, though it remains a prototype. As of April 1, multiple IRIS kits had been installed on aircraft and delivered to the 49th Test and Evaluation Squadron at Barksdale Air Force Base, Louisiana, for training and operational employment. The command did not say how many B-52s carry the system.
IRIS was developed by Outerlink Global Solutions, a small company in Shreveport, Louisiana, near Barksdale. It combines a satellite communications terminal with equipment on the aircraft and on the ground. The system works with Iridium’s Certus service, which runs on the Iridium NEXT constellation of low-Earth-orbit satellites and offers global coverage. Outerlink has said the Certus terminal provides data speeds of up to 704 kilobits per second. IRIS is set to replace the Global Iridium Bomber Set, which the B-52 has used since 2017.
“Fielding IRIS gives our crews a modern tool to stay connected, share information, and execute the mission in dynamic and contested environments,” said Maj. Gen. Ty Neuman, commander of 8th Air Force and the Joint-Global Strike Operations Center.
In June 2022, the 49th Test and Evaluation Squadron flew the first demonstration of IRIS on a B-52 at Barksdale. A team from the 608th Air Operations Center tracked the flight and checked voice and data transfers from the aircraft, including images and video.
Global Strike Command then used an AFWERX Small Business Innovation Research Phase II contract to integrate Outerlink’s commercial system onto the bomber. In August 2023, the effort moved to a four-year, $26 million Strategic Funding Increase contract, the first such award designated to the command. The program helps small businesses move technology from prototype toward real use.
Testing picked up this year. In March, ground and flight tests showed IRIS could hold a reliable connection while the B-52 was airborne. The 49th Test and Evaluation Squadron and the 608th Air Operations Center confirmed end-to-end performance through approved military network routes, and the B-52 program office signed off on airworthiness before further flight testing later that month.
“We had a clear operational need, the right partner capabilities, and engaged stakeholders working together to deliver capability operators needed and are using today,” said Maj. Gen. Peter Bonetti, director of Global Strike Command’s strategic plans, programs and requirements.
The Air Force Reserve’s 307th Bomb Wing at Barksdale also contributed to the effort, along with the B-52 program office.
The B-52 has flown for more than 70 years and remains central to U.S. long-range strike and nuclear deterrence. The U.S. Air Force plans to keep the bomber flying into the 2050s, with upgrades including new engines and a new radar under the B-52J modernization.
Global Strike Command said IRIS will go through more testing and evaluation as it matures, and that it is still deciding on a long-term beyond-line-of-sight communications solution for the bomber fleet.

US will receive a shipment of Belarusian fertilizer after sanctions against Minsk are eased - FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:47:19 EEST
15:47:19 KST

US will receive a shipment of Belarusian fertilizer after sanctions against Minsk are eased - FT
Kyiv • UNN
In October, 30,000 tonnes of Belarusian potash will be delivered to New Orleans. The shipment is being made amid Washington's easing of sanctions.
The first shipment of Belarusian potash fertilizers to the United States in four years is expected to arrive at the Port of New Orleans in October, amid Washington's gradual easing of sanctions against Belarus's potash industry. This is reported by Financial Times, according to UNN.
Details
"According to the pricing agency Argus, on September 15, Belaruskali loaded 30,000 tonnes of granular muriate of potash (MOP) onto a vessel owned by a company from the Marshall Islands at the Russian port of Bronka (St. Petersburg). According to vessel-tracking data from the commodity platform Kpler, unloading is scheduled to take place at the Port of New Orleans (Louisiana) on October 14," the publication writes.
According to the publication, this will be the first shipment sent to the United States after sanctions against Belarus's potash industry were eased as part of a broader agreement concerning the release of political prisoners. The United States imposed sanctions in 2021 after Belarusian ruler alexander lukashenko brutally suppressed pro-democracy protests the previous year.
At the same time, according to available data, between 2017 and 2021, belarus exported an average of 635,000 tonnes of potash fertilizers to the United States every year. These fertilizers are widely used to enrich soil with potassium and increase the yields of agricultural crops.
"The availability of fertilizers on the global market has declined substantially because of the conflict in the Middle East, which effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz. Although more and more oil tankers are using this route, lured by record freight rates, the profitability of transporting other goods is insufficient to compensate for the potential risk of an attack by Iran," the publication writes.
As noted, in September, President Donald Trump said that the United States was working on a "large-scale deal" to purchase fertilizers from belarus. Almost 80% of potash fertilizer imports into the United States come from Canada. He claimed that such imports would cost "significantly less" than purchases from Canada, which is engaged in a trade conflict with Washington.
At the same time, analysts believe that belarus is nevertheless unlikely to substantially increase supplies to the United States in the near term or compete with Canadian prices.
"The main reason for Trump's large-scale deal on potash fertilizers is to reassure his electorate ahead of the midterm elections, as well as to reassure the Belarusian side," believes Balazs Jarabik, a partner at the analytical firm R Politik.
"The shipment of Belarusian potash fertilizers accounts for only a small share of the 5.6 million tonnes of this product imported by the United States last year. Nevertheless, it indicates a cautious warming of relations between the United States and belarus—a country that has found itself internationally isolated because of its brutal suppression of dissent and its assistance to russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022," the publication writes.
Recall
U.S. President Donald Trump stated that Washington was working on a large-scale deal to purchase potash fertilizers from belarus. The specific parameters of the future deal have not yet been announced.

Japan on Monday called on the US to “thoroughly enforce discipline” among its soldiers deployed in the country, amid protests over a murder-robbery case allegedly involving a US Marine.
“Japan and the United States will work together to thoroughly prevent a recurrence,” the Japanese government's top spokesman, Minoru Kihara, told reporters in Tokyo.
The statement came after a US Marine Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday over alleged robbery and murder of a local woman in southernmost Okinawa, which hosts bulk of some 50,000 US soldiers deployed in Japan under a defense treaty.
He was arrested a day after the alleged murder of Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the prefectural capital Naha on Saturday.
Ballard was sent to prosecutors on Monday, but he has denied the charges, according to Kyodo News.
The incident caused outrage in Okinawa and outside with Japanese foreign and defense ministries summoning US ambassador as well as commander of US Forces in Japan.
According to Jiji Press, some 100 people held protests outside the Okinawa prefectural government building on Sunday.
“How much longer do we have to bear all of this?" the protesters asked.
Tokyo has protested to the US at “various levels,” said Kihara, who is minister in charge of mitigating the impact of US forces in Okinawa, which has seen many crimes involving American forces, angering natives.
Tokyo will "continue to urge the US side to thoroughly enforce discipline” among its soldiers in Japan, said Kihara.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said it was "extremely regrettable" that such a crime had occurred and lodged "strong protest" over the incident.
Japan has called for "full cooperation" of the US with the investigation and "strict discipline among US military personnel" to prevent a recurrence, Takaichi told a parliament session on Monday.
Joining the Sunday protests against the incident, a woman in her 40s said: “I feel it's a contradiction that a serviceman stationed at a US military base in Okinawa to protect Japan has killed a civilian.”
George Edward Glass, US ambassador to Japan, said he was speaking with US military commanders “about how we continue to hold our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity.”
Glass said he discussed with Okinawa-based Marine Air Ground Task Force commander Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson "our next steps in strengthening that bond of trust with our Japanese partners and base-hosting communities," according to a statement on US social media platform X.

Sinkevičius, Nausėda and Kasčiūnas seen as Lithuania’s most influential politicians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:44:00 UTC
15:44:00 KST

Lithuania’s political and professional leaders have ranked Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, President Gitanas Nausėda and conservative leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas as the country’s most influential politicians, according to an annual survey published Monday by news portal Delfi.
Former President Dalia Grybauskaitė and former President Valdas Adamkus followed in the survey, along with former conservative Prime Minister Ingrida Šimonytė and Vytautas Landsbergis, former parliament speaker and the first head of state after Lithuania restored its independence.
The top 10 also included Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys, Liberal Movement leader Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen and Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas, a Social Democrat.
The survey of experts, politicians and civil servants – what Delfi calls “elite” – was conducted by the Reitingai magazin. A total of 1,143 people were surveyed from July 9 to Sept. 1.
Sinkevičius received 598 votes from the respondents, followed by Nausėda with 565. Kasčiūnas and Grybauskaitė each received 435 votes.
A separate nationwide public opinion survey produced a different order. Nausėda was named the most influential politician by 38.3% of respondents, followed by Adamkus at 27.9% and Grybauskaitė at 27.2%.
The same three politicians occupied the top three positions in last year’s public ranking.
They were followed by Šimonytė, Čmilytė-Nielsen, Remigijus Žemaitaitis, leader of the Nemunas Dawn party, Sinkevičius, Kasčiūnas, Landsbergis and Kaunas Mayor Visvaldas Matijošaitis.
The public opinion survey was conducted by Spinter Tyrimai from July 18-25 among 1,017 respondents ages 18 to 75 across Lithuania.
When the “elite” and public opinion surveys were combined using Delfi’s methodology, Nausėda ranked first with 43.7%, followed by Sinkevičius with 33.6% and Grybauskaitė with 32.6%.
Delfi has conducted its annual ranking of Lithuania’s most influential people for 12 years. The rankings cover several categories, including politicians, business and economics, public officials, civil society, media, sports and entertainment.

Total student debt falls for the first time, to €28 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:43:15 UTC
15:43:15 KST

Total student debt falls for the first time, to €28 billion
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The total amount of student loans owed in the Netherlands has fallen for the first time, according to national statistics office CBS.
Students and former students owed €28 billion at the start of 2026 – €800 million less than a year earlier. The fall is due to fewer students taking out loans since the basic grant was reinstated for higher education students in the 2023-2024 academic year.
The grant was scrapped in 2015 and replaced with a loan system, leaving a generation of students to borrow to cover their living costs.
Some 1.5 million people had student debts in January, a figure that has now fallen for three years running. The number of current students with a loan has dropped to around 400,000, down 210,000 since 2023.
The number of former students with debt is still rising, but more slowly. It went up by just over 6,000 this year, compared with 28,000 a year earlier, and now stands at more than 1.1 million.
People owing large debts are also more common. Some 145,000 people owe €50,000 or more, twice as many as six years ago, and almost 5,000 owe at least €100,000. At the other end of the scale, almost half of all borrowers owe less than €10,000.
The average debt has risen by €5,900 since the loan system was introduced, to €18,300. Current students owe €15,600 on average, €1,000 less than last year, while former students owe an average of €19,200.

Fears wombats 'buried alive' after 'devastating' council blunder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:40:22 UTC
15:40:22 KST

in brief
- A council says an investigation is underway after rabbit-control works filled in wombat burrows.
- Volunteers say burrows housing wombats were blocked with soil and rocks.
A local council is under fire after a rabbit-control program inadvertently sealed off wombat burrows, leaving volunteers searching for missing animals.
Nillumbik Shire Council in Melbourne's outer north-east says it is "devastated" and has launched an investigation into the incident, which occurred during rabbit-control works carried out across at least 30 local reserves from June to August.
But for the volunteers who had spent months treating local wombats for the potentially deadly skin condition, mange, the council's response has done little to ease concerns about the fate of animals they can no longer find.
"When they went back to look for them, to give them their next dose of treatment, they found not only could they not find their wombats, but they found the holes had been filled in, and rocks placed in to stop them getting in or out," Suzanne Teese told SBS News.
Teese is a committee member of Wildlife Rescuers, a community group that worked alongside Mange Management to try to free the trapped creatures.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Around a dozen volunteers quickly responded to a call for help.
"They found a couple of wombats who they were able to release, but they know there are many more that were lost," she said.
The contractor was carrying out what the council has described as a "non-chemical, non-poison approach" to rabbit control, which includes "warren-closure techniques".
"They either didn't know, or they weren't taking care, but they have filled in the wombat burrows," Teese said.
In a recent statement, Nillumbik Shire Council said it was "saddened and devastated" by the news and had ordered the contractor to complete an investigation and deliver a full report.
But for Georgie Purcell, a state upper house MP for the Animal Justice Party whose electorate covers some of the impacted areas, the council's response is not enough.
"Wombats were literally buried alive under their watch. It is one of the most horrifying examples of animal cruelty that has come across my desk in some time," Purcell said.
"Strongly worded statements won't deliver justice for these animals and neither will asking the people that were responsible for the literal entombment of wombats to investigate themselves."
The extent of the impact remains uncertain. Volunteers say some wombats were found dead and two were rescued after the burrows were filled in, but have not specified how many animals may have died. Others remain missing.
Purcell said any investigation should be completed independently, or by the state's conservation regulator.
"This is a galling and concerning response from a local government area which is home to such a large population of native burrowing animals," she said.
SBS News has contacted Nillumbik Shire Council for comment.
It's been "a kind of personal tragedy" for those working closest with the wombats, Teese said.
"You do develop an ongoing relationship with these animals because you're treating them in the field, over such a long period of time," she said.
Marie Wynan has lived with wombats for nearly forty years, following generations of wombats through her work.
As a director at the Wombat Protection Society of Australia, she said she's seen too many cases of wombat burrows being filled.
With mothers and their joeys often separating throughout the day, Wynan said it can be difficult to confirm if a burrow is active before it is filled.
"They're being buried a lot. They cannot dig themselves out," she said.
Wynan said the highly intelligent species is a crucial part of local ecosystems and biodiversity.
"There are not two wombats that are the same. Every single one has got different personalities and different temperaments," she said
"Some get on with some individuals, and then they have clashes with another.
"They're just like us, just like a community."

"For Ukraine, the scale and structure of the agricultural sector· <…> and the very high levels of productivity warrant the examination of targeted arrangements that would significantly limit financial support and market access for products such as wheat and grain," the newspaper quoted from the document containing the European Commission's proposals.

Other proposals aim to simplify the procedure for stripping countries that violate EU financial laws of their voting rights. The document also outlined punitive measures for EU candidate countries to "ensure continued fulfillment of commitments undertaken during accession negotiations and provide targeted remedies where serious shortcomings risk undermining the proper functioning of the union," the newspaper emphasized.
Ukraine has held EU candidate status since the summer of 2022. On July 14, 2026, Irish Minister of State for European Affairs and Defense Thomas Byrne announced that the EU had launched accession talks with Ukraine on the second of six negotiation clusters. The negotiation process is divided into 33 sections, or chapters, which are unevenly grouped into six clusters. The talks do not guarantee EU membership nor set a timeline.

According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,393 tanks, 25,487 armored combat vehicles, 157,985 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,733 artillery systems, 2,182 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,688 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,859 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.

Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

====================================================================================================

Researchers develop high-efficiency NEV wireless charging system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:36:05 CST
15:36:05 KST

GUANGZHOU, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Researchers from Chinese and British institutions have developed a wireless charging system for new energy vehicles (NEVs) with conversion efficiency exceeding 98 percent.
The system could support the large-scale use of autonomous vehicles and has potential in sectors such as rail transit, industrial robots and low-altitude aircraft.
A fully automated charging solution that requires no manual intervention is seen as key to the commercial rollout of autonomous vehicles. Inductive power transfer is widely regarded as an ideal route to such charging.
But mainstream ferrite-core solutions face challenges in efficiency, power density and thermal stability. Improving power density and thermal stability while maintaining high efficiency has been a core bottleneck for wireless charging technology.
Researchers from the Dongguan Institute of Materials Science and Technology in south China's Guangdong Province, under the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), worked with the City University of Hong Kong, the University of Cambridge and the Institute of Physics under the CAS to develop a 20 kW-class wireless charging system for NEVs based on nanocrystalline alloys, achieving conversion efficiency of 98.51 percent.
Their study, recently published in Nature Communications, describes a magnetic core structure resembling an overpass that can meet the long-term high-temperature requirements of wireless charging.
The magnetic core strip produced by the team measures 440 mm long, 330 mm wide and 4 mm thick. Its thickness is only half that of traditional ferrite solutions, yet it can carry higher power density.
The system's performance is expected to be further optimized and charging efficiency improved. The Dongguan Institute of Materials Science and Technology is also pushing forward its industrial application.
According to the institute, the new system can be applied not only to autonomous vehicles but also extended to rail transit, industrial automated guided vehicles and low-altitude aircraft.
In September, China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and eight other government departments announced the five-year plan for the intelligent connected NEV industry from 2026 to 2030. The plan proposes that by 2030, vehicles with autonomous driving functions will achieve large-scale application in China, with highly automated driving in scenarios such as highways, urban expressways and some urban roads. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Longer trips, richer experiences: China's National Day holiday reveals shifting tourism trends
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:36:03 CST
15:36:03 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Five days into China's week-long National Day holiday, millions are still immersed in the sights, sounds and flavors of the season -- traveling, dining, exploring and enjoying the break. Yet this year, the scenes are subtly different.
Travelers have ventured farther as the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday fell just three days before the National Day holiday, while family trips and experience-oriented travel are on the rise, according to travel agencies.
"It points to a fundamental shift in the logic of tourism consumption, as travelers focus more on the quality of time and the richness of their experiences," said Bu Xiting, a researcher with the Communication University of China.
LONGER BREAKS, RICHER CHOICES
Data from Chinese online travel platform Tuniu shows that tours of 10 days or more are particularly popular during this holiday period, accounting for 26 percent of bookings.
Yuan You, an internet company employee, spent three days of her 13-day break in Jiuzhaigou, southwest China's Sichuan Province, before heading to the provincial capital Chengdu for woodworking classes.
"The holiday is rich while maintaining a relaxed pace," she said.
Authorities across the country have rolled out a wide range of activities, consumer vouchers and subsidies to spur holiday spending. Shanghai, for example, has launched about 200 major consumption events, backed by consumer vouchers worth roughly 100 million yuan (around 14.85 million U.S. dollars).
The offerings range from watching films and dining to purchasing digital products and cars, encouraging consumers to explore a broader spectrum of spending experiences.
Cultural institutions, too, are broadening the ways people can experience and consume culture. The Sichuan Museum extended its holiday hours and launched a themed night tour, while Beijing's Zhongshan Park brought museums, cultural institutions and innovative brands together to create a market street featuring culture-inspired products.
As more new energy vehicles hit the roads during the holiday, authorities have taken measures to ensure adequate charging facilities and convenient services.
During last year's eight-day Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, Chinese travelers made 888 million domestic trips and spent a combined 809 billion yuan, according to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism.
This year, data shows that foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 3.4 percent and 5.3 percent year on year, respectively, from Oct. 1 to 3.
RED TOURISM, ROBOTS AND RURAL EXPERIENCES
As China marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, former revolutionary base areas have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about the country's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China.
In Yan'an, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, a street has staged special activities including performances of songs from the revolutionary years and a large-scale bonfire gathering. Visitor numbers on the first day of the holiday rose about 20 percent year on year.
The holiday has also turned some of China's newest robots into part of the consumer experience, putting embodied intelligence to work alongside traditional culture in tourist attractions, shopping districts and ancient towns.
At a cultural district in Chengdu, robots performed dances inspired by local opera's face-changing art and used digital technology to recreate tanghua, a traditional form of sugar painting.
On Chunxi Road, a humanoid robot has gone beyond entertainment to take on the role of a store manager, greeting customers and recommending products rather than simply performing for them.
China's growing network of robot training bases is preparing more machines for roles beyond the factory floor -- and beyond the country's borders. In the first half of 2026, Chinese manufacturers accounted for 97 percent of humanoid robot shipments worldwide, according to a report released at the 2026 World Robot Conference.
Years of efforts to restore the environment and revitalize rural areas are also paying off. On a ridge overlooking the Miyun Reservoir in Beijing, visitors can hike to a viewing platform and enjoy outdoor concerts amid the pine trees.
With roads, infrastructure and public services extending deeper into the countryside, some once-remote villages are emerging as new destinations for holidaymakers.
Caijiagou, a former impoverished hillside village in east China's Shandong Province, has transformed into an art-themed destination, with murals adorning residential walls.
Village official Liang Yunhui said the village has repurposed idle rural homes into cultural spaces such as an art gallery and a musical instrument museum, while hosting events featuring traditional crafts, cultural fairs and folk music. "In total, we have received more than 500,000 visits over the years," he said.
On travel platform Fliggy, the number of users purchasing travel products featuring natural scenery and villages surged by nearly 50 percent from the same holiday period last year.
"More travelers are seeking immersive experiences, from sampling local cuisine and making intangible cultural heritage crafts to watching distinctive performances, allowing them to gain a deeper appreciation of local culture," said a manager with Tuniu.
CHINA HAUL
While many Chinese tourists are venturing farther around the world, more international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country for themselves, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design.
Tennis star Novak Djokovic, in Beijing for the China Open, was seen trying his hand at Chinese calligraphy at the Summer Palace, a former imperial garden. After a match, he used a traditional Chinese seal to put his mark on fans' keepsakes instead of signing autographs.
Huaqiangbei, a sprawling electronics marketplace in south China's tech hub Shenzhen, has become a magnet for foreign shoppers looking to experience China's tech scene firsthand.
Bryan Lamothe-Arice from the United States was browsing smart devices. "I'm particularly interested in the electric bikes and all kinds of flying devices here. I'm going to tell my friends to come here. There are tech products everywhere."
China's border crossings are expected to see about 2.15 million passenger trips a day on average during the National Day holiday, according to the National Immigration Administration.
That growing international interest is also showing up in spending. Overseas visitors spent 263.6 billion yuan in China in the first seven months of 2026, up 27.8 percent year on year, according to the commerce ministry. ■

====================================================================================================

UK nuclear umbrella comments prompt Estonia defense debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:35:00 UTC
15:35:00 KST

UK nuclear umbrella comments prompt Estonia defense debate
A remark by the head of the Royal Navy about the UK's nuclear umbrella for Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) partners has prompted debate in Estonia over whether it can deliver on regional defense.
Experts say no separate guarantee is being offered, and that conventional capability — not nuclear reassurance — is what matters most for Estonia and the region.
The JEF is a UK-led defense cooperation framework covering the Nordic and Baltic countries, one of its main aims being to strengthen deterrence in the Baltic Sea region. The jointly developed crisis-response measures complement NATO, and the Joint Expeditionary Force is intended to be the first responder in the event of a threat. The UK is the sole nuclear power in the 10-member state JEF.
Royal Marines General Gwyn Jenkins, who is First Sea Lord and Chief of the Naval Staff, told "Aktuaalne kaamera": "The Baltic Sea is vital to the UK's security – I draw no distinction between our own territorial waters in the Atlantic or in the North Sea, and in the Baltic; we are all part of the same operational space."
Jenkins recently told Finnish paper Iltalehti that the JEF also offers partner countries its so-called nuclear umbrella. According to security expert Meelis Oidsalu, this does not in fact mean that any separate guarantee is being offered, while the British are not changing their existing nuclear policy.
"There is no actual need for any of that, as their longstanding doctrine provides for the protection of NATO allies, and that public doctrine does not say that this has to be an Article 5 operation. So perhaps we were simply being reminded of something important," Oidsalu said.
Oidsalu added that during periods of attritional warfare or a limited war of conquest, the threshold for using nuclear weapons is very high, hence why the UK should actually focus more on developing conventional capabilities.
"They recently held a defense review, and it found that an enormously large sum of money ultimately goes on funding a questionable nuclear capability, while funding for the army and, to some extent, naval capabilities has been somewhat poor. They have already taken some steps in drone warfare, but not as much as they could," Oidsalu continued.
According to Oidsalu, this also raises the question of how capable the British will be in the future of fulfilling the role as regional military leader.
Reserve Maj. Gen. Neeme Väli likewise said the UK has been constantly plagued by a lack of resources on military matters, and that this had impacted on deployments to Estonia.
"For example, the UK's plans concerning the deployment of a brigade to Estonia changed only a few months ago. Initially, there was talk of an armored brigade, but now entirely different capabilities are being discussed. I personally think this statement is also connected to the fact that there simply are not as many resources as originally planned," Väli told "Aktuaalne kaamera."
Former defense minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform) was less skeptical, saying: "I would by no means underestimate British capabilities. It is in our interests that they not only say these things but also act on them. And I believe they will."
There are currently 900 British troops in Estonia. The new contingent arriving in Estonia next year will be about 300 personnel larger than the current one. The UK's land deployment to Estonia has been its largest worldwide for several years now.
Estonia is also in talks with France, also a nuclear power but not part of JEF, to join its enhanced nuclear deterrence initiative, Prime Minister Kristen Michal said last month.

15:34:31 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye’s automotive market is on track to end 2026 with a decline after three years of strong sales performance.
According to data from the Automotive Distributors and Mobility Association (ODMD), passenger car and light commercial vehicle sales fell 24.3 percent year-on-year in September to 83,469 units. Passenger car sales dropped 27.8 percent to 63,736 units. In the first nine months of the year, the overall market declined 13.4 percent from a year earlier to 803,465 units.
Hakan Tiftik, head of the ODMD, said recent developments in financial markets, alongside global economic challenges, have led some consumers to postpone purchasing decisions.
“Recent developments in financial markets have also caused consumers to delay their buying decisions. Promotional campaigns may support purchasing decisions in the short term, but consumers need easier access to financing,” he said.
Tiftik said the slowdown had accelerated during the summer months and could not be explained solely by base effects following exceptionally high sales levels over the past two to three years.
“Of course, it is important to take into account the very high sales levels recorded over the last two to three years. However, it is not sufficient to explain the current slowdown solely through base effects,” he said.
Looking ahead, Tiftik said financing conditions, consumer confidence, vehicle prices, developments in the used-car market and promotional campaigns would be key factors shaping demand in the final quarter of the year.
“Under current conditions, we expect the total automotive market to reach between 1.1 million and 1.2 million units by the end of the year,” he said.
Recalling that limited access to credit remains one of the biggest challenges facing the market, Tiftik said the situation has made vehicle ownership increasingly difficult, particularly for middle-income consumers.
Tiftik also noted that recent developments in financial markets had led some consumers to postpone purchases. While he did not explicitly mention the issue, his comments came amid the recent crisis involving investment funds in Türkiye.

Estonia relocates troops closer to Russian border – FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:34:00 EEST

Estonia relocates troops closer to Russian border – FT
Estonia is redeploying a key brigade from the city of Tapa to Jõhvi, located 50 km from the Russian border, as it prepares for potential Russian aggression.
Source: European Pravda, citing Financial Times
Details: According to Estonian officials, the country is continuously moving troops closer to the border with Russia and procuring weapons capable of striking deep into Russian territory as it prepares for possible aggression by Moscow beyond Ukraine's borders.
The FT writes that Estonian military and intelligence chiefs do not believe Russia is seeking a full-scale war with NATO, at least not within the next two years. Meanwhile, they are convinced that Moscow is preparing for a possible future conflict with Estonia.
This has prompted Estonia, which has no air force of its own, to shift to an "active defence" strategy.
"We have to start from the border and win from the first battles," declared Colonel Tarmo Kundla, commander of the First Estonian Brigade, the country's primary fighting force.
His unit is being permanently redeployed from Tapa to Jõhvi, where large new facilities are currently being constructed to house soldiers.
"Deterrence is not working. The critical period to address that, for all of us in the Baltic states, is in the next one to four years," noted an Estonian military intelligence representative.
Meanwhile, the Estonian Ministry of Defence emphasised that they must make aggression against the country "unthinkable".
"Our aim is clear: to keep the enemy and the destruction of war away from Estonian territory," the Ministry of Defence stressed.
In May, the Estonian government introduced the term "active defence" into its national security concept. Since then, the country's armed forces have initiated a quiet but radical reorganisation. Elite units are being continuously redeployed from Tapa, Estonia's primary military base, to positions closer to the Russian border. Additionally, a new base for 1,000 military personnel is under construction in the border city of Narva.
Over the past year, the country signed contracts to acquire nine American HIMARS multiple-launch rocket systems, M57 ballistic missiles with a strike range of up to 300 km and nine South Korean Chunmoo MLRS with a similar range. It should be noted that the distance from Estonia's border bases to Russia's St Petersburg is 260 km.
In the decade following the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2014, Estonian military strategists developed a defence doctrine shaped by the country's history and geography. Under this approach, in the event of an attack, conscripts would rapidly mobilise and engage in a tactical, quasi-guerrilla defence to delay Russian troops and inflict casualties until NATO reinforcements arrived.
However, after observing Russia's actions in Ukraine, Estonian military leaders concluded that such a plan would not work. They now believe that the Kremlin pays no heed to casualties when fighting to hold captured territory, even after everything on it has been destroyed.
Estonia now plans to fight for every inch of territory and inflict powerful strikes against Russia hundreds of kilometres behind the frontline from the very first day of any invasion.
"Militarily this is very demanding. We cannot shape the enemy [by retreating or tactically luring them into situations]. We have to build our lines today. It is forward defence," stated Kundla.
Estonian military intelligence is particularly apprehensive about potential limited actions targeting a border objective – specifically, the small, predominantly Russian-speaking city of Narva. This could serve as a provocative test of NATO's resolve, aimed at fracturing the alliance.
Background:
- As reported, Estonia's defence spending in 2027 and beyond will exceed 5% of GDP, with total national defence expenditure reaching €2.2 billion.
- Neighbouring Lithuania, together with Poland, is developing an international civilian evacuation plan to be utilised should it become necessary to evacuate portions of the populations of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia across the border.

SC raps Centre, Delhi police over recent rape incidents
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday stressed the need for stronger measures to prevent crimes against women in Delhi, saying authorities must create an environment where women feel safe while walking on the streets or travelling by public transport.A bench led by Justice JB Pardiwala was hearing a suo motu case initiated by the court over recent rape cases and other crimes against women in Delhi-NCR."There appears to be a feeling that women are not safe in city particularly in some vulnerable pockets," the court observed, flagging concerns over the safety of women in certain parts of the national capital.The bench told the Centre and Delhi Police that the focus should be on preventing crimes rather than dealing with them after they have occurred."We must ensure every woman in NCT Delhi feels safe, whether walking at 10 PM or travelling by metro or road," the court said.The Supreme Court also said deficiencies in the system should not create conditions that allow crimes to take place."Deficiencies, if any, should not facilitate commission of crime," the court said."What is important is to prevent crime, not what you do after crime is committed," it observed.
The court also stressed the need to create a strong deterrent for those who may be inclined to commit such offences.“Unless you don’t create such fright in the minds if the criminals ki ab kuch kiya toh mar jayengey (if we commit such a crime we will die) you will not be able to prevent such crimes”, Justice JB Pardiwala said.
“You need to create a fright, a fear in the mind of a man who is prone to commit such officers”, the judge said.The Supreme Court told Delhi Police that it should take a firm approach against those accused of committing serious crimes against women, while also referring to concerns that could be raised under Article 21, which guarantees the right to life and personal liberty.The court said authorities should not be deterred from taking strict action against those accused of rape and other serious offences because of criticism from human rights groups.
