TAELON7’s Limbo Engawa Installation Moves From Accra to Art Omi in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Art Omi and Limbo Museum have presented Limbo Engawa, a two-part site-specific installation by TAELON7, led by architect Juergen Benson-Strohmayer. First presented at Limbo Museum in Accra, Ghana, on March 12, 2026, the project was reconfigured for Art Omi's Sculpture & Architecture Park in Ghent, New York, where it opened on September 19, 2026. Developed as a joint commission between the two institutions, the project uses a modular architectural system to explore how spaces for gathering and exchange can respond to different landscapes, climates, and cultural contexts.
The installation takes its name from the Japanese architectural term engawa, which describes a transitional zone between interior and exterior, as well as between private and communal space. Across its two presentations, the concept is interpreted through lightweight, movable structures that establish relationships between architecture and its surroundings. While the architectural language remains consistent, the installation changes according to the conditions of each site, making its movement between Accra and the Hudson Valley an integral part of the project.
In Accra, Limbo Engawa was installed within the unfinished concrete structure of Limbo Museum and across its surrounding grounds. The intervention responded to the relationship between the incomplete building and the cultivated landscape around it, introducing spaces for sitting, resting, and gathering among the existing structures. Modular components, including oversized daybeds inspired by woven beds commonly found within unfinished buildings, were combined with steel profiles and salvaged billboard strips to create lightweight structures that could be assembled on site.
Related Article
Modular Installation Reimagines Unfinished Structures at Limbo Museum in Accra, Ghana
At Art Omi, the installation has been adapted to a markedly different setting within New York's Hudson Valley. The 120-acre Sculpture & Architecture Park is characterized by fields, wetlands, and wooded areas, contrasting with the urban and unfinished context of the Accra installation. Here, Limbo Engawa takes the form of a freestanding landscape pavilion, with shaded areas providing places for visitors to pause and gather while framing views across the surrounding landscape.
The change in setting also shifts the role of the architectural threshold. In Accra, the installation mediated between an unfinished building and the land surrounding it, while at Art Omi it establishes a transition between a freestanding structure and the open landscape. Its modular construction and reusable components remain consistent, while the configuration responds to the different scale, climate, vegetation, and patterns of movement at the New York site.
The two presentations are conceived as related configurations rather than identical versions of a single site-specific structure. By allowing the installation to be dismantled, transported, and adapted, the project tests how an architectural system can retain a shared spatial and material language while responding to different conditions. Commissioned jointly by Limbo Museum and Art Omi, Limbo Engawa connects the two institutions through a temporary architectural intervention that changes with its context. Support for the project is provided in part by the Austrian Cultural Forum in Accra.
Juergen Benson-Strohmayer is a chartered architect in Austria and Ghana and the founder of TAELON7. His work spans architecture, research, and making, and has developed through projects across Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire, Sudan, Ethiopia, and Austria. Founded in Accra in 2024, Limbo Museum is an experimental cultural institution housed within an unfinished concrete structure, while Art Omi is a nonprofit arts center in New York's Hudson Valley encompassing a sculpture and architecture park, gallery, residency programs, and arts education initiatives.
In other recent installation news, Amman Design Week returns from October 2 to 17, bringing more than 220 designers and participants together across exhibitions, installations, and public-space projects in Jordan. In Aarhus, James Turrell's As Seen Below – The Dome forms the centerpiece of ARoS Aarhus Art Museum's new underground expansion, The Next Level, designed by Schmidt Hammer Lassen and located beneath Musikhusparken. In Copenhagen, Kengo Kuma and Associates' Earth | Tree transforms a former industrial hall at Copenhagen Contemporary through timber, brick, and light, marking the studio's first exhibition in Scandinavia.

Bulgaria Reports 2.8% Budget Gap as Spending Rises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Bulgaria's budget deficit reached a projected €3.6 billion, or 2.8% of forecast GDP, by the end of September 2026, according to preliminary budget execution estimates released by the Ministry of Finance.
Revenue, grants and donations under the Consolidated Fiscal Programme (CFP) are expected to amount to €33.9 billion by the end of September, equivalent to 68.4% of the annual targets set in the 2026 State Budget Act. This represents an increase of €3.4 billion, or 11%, compared with the same period in 2025, the ministry's press office said.
Tax receipts accounted for most of the growth, increasing by €2.4 billion, or 9.8% in nominal terms, year-on-year. Revenue from grants and donations rose by €1.5 billion, while non-tax income declined by €0.6 billion compared with September 2025, mainly because state-owned enterprises paid lower dividends in 2026.
Despite the increase in revenue, CFP spending, including Bulgaria's contribution to the European Union budget, reached €37.5 billion by September 2026, representing 66.1% of the annual projections. For comparison, expenditure totaled €33.7 billion during the corresponding period last year.
The increase in spending was mainly driven by social and health insurance payments, including pensions, as well as personnel expenses, capital investments and other expenditure.
Higher pension payments following indexation under the so-called Swiss rule on July 1, 2025, and July 1, 2026, contributed to the rise. Other factors included the increase in the minimum wage in January 2026 and adjustments to salaries reflecting accumulated inflation in 2025, also effective from January 2026.
Capital expenditure also recorded substantial growth, reflecting investments and projects implemented under the Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP), the Municipal Investment Programme and other capital spending.
As of September 30, 2026, Bulgaria had paid €0.9 billion from the central budget toward its contribution to the EU budget. The payment was made under the legislation governing the EU's own resources that was in force at the time.
The Ministry of Finance will publish detailed statistical data and an information bulletin on state budget execution and key CFP indicators on its website at the end of October 2026. The reports will be based on monthly cash execution data submitted by first-level budget spending units as of September 2026.

(DHA Photo)
Türkiye needs to create new tourism narratives, diversify its destinations and develop more experience-based tourism products to strengthen its position in the global tourism market, says Kaan Kaşif Kavaloğlu, head of the Mediterranean Touristic Hoteliers and Operators Association (AKTOB).
Kavaloğlu said Türkiye has been examining successful destination management models in countries such as France and Spain. He noted that Antalya and Istanbul account for around 80 percent of the country’s tourism activity and argued that spreading tourism more broadly across the country would support further growth.
He said Spain promotes 17 destinations separately and stressed the importance of coordination between central and local authorities in tourism planning. He also pointed to Türkiye’s potential in city, resort, ski and winter tourism.
According to Kavaloğlu, Türkiye should expand beyond its existing tourism hubs and create new destinations, noting that the country’s tourism potential extends beyond the traditional sea, sand and sun model. He said visitors could be offered a wide range of experiences, including history, art, cultural heritage, gastronomy, shopping, rural tourism, hot-air balloon rides, paragliding, skiing and thermal tourism.
Antalya hosts approximately 17 million foreign tourists annually, creating a significant tourism ecosystem and supporting employment in the region, he said.
Commenting on calls to target fewer but higher-spending tourists, Kavaloğlu argued that Antalya should preserve its current tourism volume while attracting more qualified visitors, saying the ecosystem built around 16.5 million to 17 million tourists should not be disrupted.

Spanish PM Pedro Sanchez gambles on Nov 29 snap election to end Parliament deadlock

MADRID – Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called an early election for Nov 29 in a bid to strengthen his mandate, after a fragmented Parliament rejected the government’s key housing decrees last week amid widespread protests.
The snap vote is a high-stakes gamble for Sanchez, whose Socialist Party trails in nearly every opinion poll.
An electoral defeat would spell the end of one of Europe’s last few left-leaning governments at a time when the far right is making unprecedented gains across the region as a growing swathe of European voters desert the centre ground.
However, Sanchez, a wily political operator, has proven time and again his ability to surprise those who had long written him off.
“We need to renew people’s support,” he said in a televised address on Oct 5. “We need to mobilise and win a much larger progressive majority in Parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain.”
He also acknowledged having made mistakes and falling short of campaign promises.
“I also know that part of that social majority is dissatisfied today,” he said, but vowed to fight for Spain to remain “a bastion of openness, social justice and environmental responsibility”.
Spain’s blue-chip index was flat after the announcement, while Spanish government bonds were broadly steady.
The main opposition People’s Party (PP) wrote “AT LAST” in a post on X, with its leader, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, set to hold a news conference later on Oct 5.
The conservatives have been calling on Sanchez to dissolve Parliament and call early elections for most of the current legislature.
Progressive and wily leader
Sanchez has stood out globally for taking a strong stance on progressive issues from Palestinian statehood to defending multilateral institutions and cracking down on “tech oligarchs”, even as a series of setbacks and scandals weakened his position at home.
Recently, he has been boosted by proposals to tackle a mounting housing crisis that were well received but were struck down by right-wing MPs on Oct 2, leading to massive protests by housing activists across the country.
Opinion polls suggest a coalition led by the PP with Vox’s support is the most likely outcome in Spain, ushering a far-right party into central government for the first time since the return of democracy after the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.
Still, despite never winning enough votes to form a majority government, Sanchez has cobbled together a series of fragile and seemingly impossible coalitions, including voices from the far left to the separatist right, to remain in power for three successive terms lasting eight years.
But growing fragmentation among his partners has meant the government has achieved little in the way of legislation in its third term and failed to pass a budget since 2023, even as Spain’s economy has continued to be one of the best performing in the developed world.
Vox leader Santiago Abascal warned the election result would be unpredictable despite favourable polling for the right. “Surveys said the same thing in 2023 and Sanchez managed to form a majority with all his accomplices,” he told TV channel Antena 3.
Rival ousted
Sanchez took office after leading a move to oust centre-right Mariano Rajoy in the wake of major corruption scandals within Rajoy’s PP. However, senior members of Sanchez’s own Socialist Party have in the past year faced allegations of graft, dragging down its already weak approval rating which has hovered at around 26% to 31% throughout his tenure.
Against the odds, he won a second four-year term in office in 2023 despite heavy losses in earlier regional and local elections by negotiating support from a loose alliance of parties in Parliament. That was achieved after promising a highly controversial amnesty for pro-independence Catalan leaders in exchange for their support, a move still bitterly remembered by many voters as a betrayal of Spanish unity.
Sanchez won early plaudits for moves including the exhumation of Franco from a mausoleum the dictator built for himself outside Madrid, and the reform of a labour law that has seen unemployment fall to below 10% – its lowest level in almost two decades.
He cemented his humanitarian and pro-immigration credentials early by saying in June 2018 that Spain would accept the Aquarius migrant rescue ship and its 629 passengers, after Italy and Malta both refused to let the ship dock in their harbours.
As other European countries have toughened their policies towards foreign arrivals, Sanchez has consistently argued that immigration is essential for sustaining Spanish growth by plugging gaps in key sectors such as construction, agriculture and hospitality and for providing revenue to prop up the strained welfare system.
More recently, his refusal to agree to US-led demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP while pivoting towards China has rattled US President Trump and some European leaders concerned about the threat of the bloc being flooded with Chinese goods.
Sanchez’s housing measures provided a rare chance for the Socialist leader to pitch himself as the leader of a mobilised left and distract from the more politically damaging issues of the migrant crisis in Ceuta and corruption scandals, said Lorenzo Bernaldo de Quiros, economist and president of consultancy Freemarket Corporate Intelligence.
“This is a window of opportunity,” he said. “If he does not call elections fast, (those topics) will return to centre stage.” REUTERS

Five consecutive days of intense rain and thunderstorms have left flooded land, destroyed roads and serious damage in rural areas across much of Crete, an island counted among the Mediterranean's most important tourist destinations.
Measurements by the National Observatory of Athens illustrate the volume of rain that fell, mainly on the island's mountainous regions. According to the network of automatic weather stations operated by the Observatory/meteo.gr, 91 millimetres of rain had been recorded by 15:10 on Sunday alone at Xyloskalo, in the Chania region of western Crete, at the entrance to the Samaria Gorge, one of the island's best-known natural attractions.
One millimetre of rain corresponds to one litre of water per square metre. This means that 91 millimetres is equivalent to 91 litres of water for every square metre of surface. The National Observatory reported that high rainfall totals were being recorded, mainly in Crete's mountains, for a fifth consecutive day.
Even larger amounts of water were measured on the Lasithi Plateau, a fertile upland basin at an altitude of around 840 metres in eastern Crete. According to the head of the Crete Development Organisation, Thodoris Ninos, about 440 millimetres of rain fell in the area in just two days, or roughly 440 litres per square metre.
He added that average rainfall in the area over four days of the severe weather reached around 470 millimetres, in a region where total annual rainfall normally ranges between 700 and 900 millimetres.
The huge inflow of water was also evident at the Aposelemis dam, about 30 kilometres east of the city of Heraklion, which is a key source of drinking water for the Heraklion urban area and parts of eastern Crete. The reservoir's reserves rose from around 9.26 million cubic metres on 30 September to more than 12.7 million cubic metres on 4 October.
The difference exceeds 3.4 million cubic metres of water in just four days. The Crete Development Organisation estimates that the level may continue to rise, as water from the Lasithi Plateau is still flowing into the reservoir.
Between 1 October and midday on Sunday, the Fire Service received 485 calls across Crete. Crews carried out 96 pump-outs of floodwater and 101 transfers of people to safe locations. An 80-year-old livestock farmer who had gone missing in Karines, in the regional unit of Rethymno, was found dead, and the authorities are investigating the exact circumstances of his death.
The impact was not confined to eastern Crete. Damage was reported in all four of the island's regional units: Chania in the west, Rethymno in the central-west, Heraklion in the centre and Lasithi in the east. Floods and landslides hit mountain villages, farming and livestock areas, as well as stretches of the coast with heavy tourist activity.
Satellite mapping by Copernicus
Greece has activated the European Union's Copernicus Emergency Management Service – Mapping, under activation code EMSR933, to produce maps of the affected areas through the analysis of satellite imagery.
The data will be used by the authorities to map the flooded areas, assess the damage and plan recovery operations. The request was submitted by Greece's civil protection authority and approved by the European Union.
Lasithi: Plateau turned into a lake
The most serious agricultural damage is being reported on the Lasithi Plateau, one of Crete's key farming areas. Large tracts of land were covered by water and mud, rural roads were damaged and potato and vegetable crops were inundated.
Cretalive, citing local figures, reports that around 3,000 tonnes of potatoes and vegetables may have been destroyed and that roughly 85% of the area's crops lie within the affected plain. The final losses have yet to be calculated.
On Lasithi's southern coast, Ierapetra and tourist resorts to the east of the town, such as Ferma, Koutsounari, Agia Fotia and Makry Gialos, were hit by torrents and landslides. Roads were blocked or badly damaged, vehicles were swept away and dozens of people had to be moved from hotels and other accommodation to safe locations.
Rethymno: Rivers overflow and destruction in Mylopotamos
In Rethymno, mountainous Mylopotamos was among the areas that took the heaviest hit. In Zoniana, a river burst its banks and the streets turned into torrents, while mud and debris caused damage to homes, the road network and infrastructure.
Between 30 and 40 residents were evacuated from their homes, according to local reports, while damage to the water supply network left villages without water. On the slopes of Mount Psiloritis there were also significant losses of livestock, with farmers reporting dozens of dead or missing animals.
In the municipality of Amari, damage to the road network and continuing difficulties in getting around led to in-person schooling being suspended on Monday.
Heraklion: Damage from the mountains to the tourist coast
In the regional unit of Heraklion, problems were recorded both inland and along the coast. In the municipality of Malevizi, Cretalive reports extensive damage to the rural road network, boreholes and irrigation systems, particularly in mountain settlements.
The impact was also felt on some of the best-known tourist beaches of northern Crete. Nea Kriti reported large quantities of mud, reeds, wood and other debris washed up on the beaches of Ammoudara and Karteros, while in Hersonissos erosion led to the loss of a significant part of the sandy shore.
Chania: Damage in Platanias and people trapped in Samaria
In western Crete, serious damage was recorded in the municipality of Platanias. In Apopigadi and Palaia Roumata, sections of rural roads became impassable, while the mayor of Platanias told the Athens-Macedonian News Agency of damage to roads, water networks, chestnut orchards and livestock facilities. The municipality plans to request that a state of emergency be declared in the area.
A special operation is also under way in the Samaria Gorge. By Sunday evening, eight employees of the National Park remained stranded in a safe spot after the hiking trail turned into a raging torrent. They were in good health, had food, medicines and means of communication, and had been instructed not to attempt to move until the water level dropped.
Government delegation in the affected areas
On Monday an expanded government delegation is travelling to Crete to assess the damage and coordinate recovery efforts. A meeting is scheduled at the Region of Crete headquarters, followed by site inspections in Mylopotamos, Ierapetra and the Lasithi Plateau.
The delegation includes the ministers for Infrastructure and Transport and for Climate Crisis and Civil Protection, along with government officials responsible for agricultural production and natural disaster recovery.
The recording of damage is still under way, particularly in the farming sector and on the road network. In many areas the full picture is expected to emerge only once the waters recede and access has been restored.

EU, China to hold Beijing talks to avert trade war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:23:13 UTC
15:23:13 KST

Pedestrians walk past the Berlaymont building, the EU Commission headquarters, in Brussels on October 2, 2026. (AFP Photo)
EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic will head to Beijing on Oct. 8 for two days of make-or-break meetings with Chinese officials to try to stave off a trade war.
The European Union has toughened its stance towards Beijing to defend businesses against what it believes is unfair competition in critical sectors including cars.
Increasingly European leaders and observers warn of a "China Shock 2.0", used to describe Chinese firms' shift into more high-tech manufacturing, which is threatening many traditional EU industries.
The first shock in the early 2000s saw a glut of cheap, more low-tech exports from China hurt manufacturers not just in Europe but around the world.
EU and Chinese officials have been locked in talks since June to address Brussels' concerns about the current trade imbalance.
The EU is simultaneously preparing to boost its trade defence toolbox — but Beijing has threatened to retaliate against any moves targeting China.
Sefcovic raised the stakes for this week's meetings in summer when he warned the EU expected "tangible results by October" from the process.
But experts cautioned against expecting too much from this week's meetings.
"There may be a few crumbs, but I would not expect any kind of major breakthrough," Penny Naas, director of the Brussels office of German Marshall Fund of the United States (GMF) think tank, said.
There could be "agreements on some specific issues, rather than any broad settlement of the trade relationship", said Zhu Tian, professor of economics at the China Europe International Business School (CEIBS) in Shanghai.
It is clear Brussels is aware the talks won't solve all of its woes, with the commission working in parallel on new tools to protect European industries, which are expected to be presented to leaders in December.
What the EU wants is to cut its trade deficit with China.
It hit around 360 billion euros in 2025, meaning the EU imported far more from the Asian nation than it exported there. China has a lower figure of around $292 billion but expects the deficit to rise further this year.
The EU's trade enforcement chief, Denis Redonnet, said sectors facing "sustained and abnormal" import increases included machinery, textiles, basic metals and chemicals.
There were "potentially worrying trends for almost a quarter of all imports into the EU at the moment", driven mainly by Chinese goods, Redonnet told the European Parliament last week.
Sefcovic said the EU wanted to deliver on three main objectives including tackling export surges from China to the bloc's market, especially in critical sectors, and increasing exports from Europe to China.
Brussels also wanted "a system of export licensing for rare earths and other products" after major producer China introduced restrictions on them last year.
Europe hopes to manage Chinese exports through voluntary limits, for example on hybrid cars shipped to the bloc, but an EU official said Brussels wants to include other products. Beijing has said it firmly opposes import quotas.
China has limited room for manoeuvre because of weak domestic demand, which means the government relies on exports to sustain growth levels.
Since the bloc does not expect significant changes by China, the EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said it was also steaming ahead with preparing new tools.
Several EU nations including France have pushed for a "European equivalent of Section 301" — the trade tool U.S. President Donald Trump used to probe foreign practices Washington deems discriminatory, and retaliate with tariffs.
Responding to reports last week about such a tool, Beijing warned it would "respond resolutely" to "discriminatory restrictive measures."
The EU knows they are not empty threats: China previously retaliated against the bloc's trade defence moves with duties on European cognac, and conducted anti-dumping probes into pork and dairy products.
Brussels is also developing a tool that would support businesses, through funding, to diversify their suppliers in critical sectors.
It is still unclear, however, how far the EU as a whole would be willing to go against China — for fear of provoking Beijing.
Germany, which is especially exposed since its biggest trading partner is China, has been especially cautious — though Berlin's stance has hardened as it worries Chinese overcapacities are hurting its export-led economy.
Europe has "the ability to do something more aggressive to stem this China 2.0 shock", GMF's Naas said. "The question is, will they?"

Bosnia Election Highlights Split Between Pro-Russian Dodik Camp and Ukraine Supporters
Unknown

2026-10-05

15:22:00 KST

Bosnia and Herzegovina’s elections have highlighted a sharp geopolitical divide: pro-Russian politician Milorad Dodik’s Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) retained its dominance in Republika Srpska, while three of the four leading parties in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina have taken positions supportive of Ukraine.
A Bosniak left-leaning moderate, a pro-Russian Serb nationalist, and a Croatian nationalist were leading the race for Bosnia’s three-member presidency, according to results from more than 90% of polling stations released by the Central Election Commission, as cited by Reuters.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Denis Bećirović, a Bosniak from the Social Democratic Party (SDP-BiH) and a member of the current presidency, led in the Bosniak-Croat Federation with 26.66% of the vote, ahead of the candidate from the centrist and traditionalist Bosniak Muslim Party of Democratic Action (SDA).
Darijana Filipović of the nationalist but pro-European Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ-BiH) was also leading in the federation with 14% of the vote.
In the Serb-majority Republika Srpska, Željka Cvijanović of the pro-Russian SNSD led with 55.34%, according to the election commission.
The results were broadly in line with expectations and projections released ahead of the vote, although turnout was low at 42.2% across Bosnia’s two entities, the Bosniak-Croat Federation and Republika Srpska.
Germany Pledges €1.3B Defense Package During Merz Kyiv Visit
The election also included voting for the national parliament and regional legislatures in the two entities.
Notably, voting continued at some polling stations after the 7 p.m. deadline because of delays involving Bosnia’s newly introduced electronic voting system, Central Election Commission head Jovan Kalaba told reporters in Sarajevo.
The election commission redesigned ballots and introduced biometric voter identification and electronic scanners, saying the measures were intended to curb electoral fraud.
Bosnia caught between Russia and the EU
The election comes as Bosnia and Herzegovina remains caught between competing foreign influences, with the EU seeking to advance the integration of the Western Balkans while Russia works to preserve its influence, particularly in the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska.
Dodik, leader of the SNSD and a prominent pro-Russian Bosnian Serb politician, traveled to Moscow last week and met with Russian President Vladimir Putin shortly before the election.
Dodik, who has repeatedly advocated greater autonomy and independence for Republika Srpska, remained a central figure in the campaign despite being barred from holding public office and therefore not appearing on the ballot. His SNSD was expected to retain its position in the entity.
He also made a series of statements during the campaign that fueled concerns about renewed instability. At the SNSD’s final pre-election rally, attended by Russia’s ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Igor Kalabukhov, Dodik told supporters that Bosnia was “dead” and “an impossible country; there is no point to it.”
After the vote, Dodik claimed that his party had won both the race for the Serb seat on Bosnia’s tripartite presidency and the presidency of Republika Srpska.
“We have won the member of the (Bosnian) Presidency, and the president of the Republika Srpska. An unexpectedly high result,” he said in Banja Luka, the entity’s largest city.
The election took place against a backdrop of widespread voter frustration over an economic slowdown, the slow pace of EU accession, and a prolonged political crisis. Ethnically based parties have repeatedly blocked decisions by Bosnia’s weak central government, deepening political deadlock.
Bosnia received EU candidate status in December 2022 and approval to open accession negotiations in 2024. Formal talks, however, have yet to begin because the country has not completed key reforms, including measures to strengthen judicial oversight and combat corruption.
The country’s complex political system was established under the 1995 US-brokered Dayton Peace Agreement, which ended the 1992-95 Bosnian War and divided Bosnia into two autonomous entities: the Bosniak- and Croat-majority Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska.
The two entities are linked by a weak central government and a three-member presidency, while an international High Representative oversees implementation of the Dayton agreement.
Bosnia also remains deeply divided along ethnic lines, with nationalist parties representing its three main communities: Muslim Bosniaks, who make up about half the population; Orthodox Serbs, who account for roughly a third; and Catholic Croats, who comprise around 15%, according to European Pravda.

Yemen launches major military operation against Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:18:00 UTC
15:18:00 KST

Yemen launches major military operation against Houthis
October 5, 2026
Yemen's military and a Saudi-led coalition launched an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi fighters on Monday, a day after Yemeni Presidential Council chief Rashad al-Alimi announced the lofty goal of retaking all territory held by the Iran-backed rebel group.
The Yemeni military said Monday operations were commencing in the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, while the Saudi-led coalition said it had hit Houthi "military targets" in the town of Hodeida on the Red Sea coast.
A coalition spokesman on X said that naval forces had "destroyed weapons depots, facilities storing booby-trapped boats and naval mines" and had "thwarted a planned attack" targeting waterways in the southern Red Sea.
Yemeni officials said forces allied with the internationally recognized government retook the crucial town of Dhubab just north of strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Sunday's announcement came after Houthi fighters captured a key road linking the key southwestern city of Taiz with the government-held city of Aden, effectively isolating Taiz. The rebels have besieged Taiz for more than a decade.
More than 70 people were reportedly killed in fighting around Taiz over the past day, according to AFP news agency.
Houthi's claim new strikes on Riyadh
Meanwhile, a Houthi military spokesman said Monday that ballistic missiles and drones targeted King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and an oil refinery in the Red Sea city of Rabigh.
The spokesman said the Aramco refinery in Rabigh was also hit along with military sites and smaller airports in the south.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities on the reported strikes.
Mecca alliance to deploy forces
In response to the latest escalation, Turkey, and Pakistan agreed on Monday to deploy troops as part of the collective defense agreement under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement the two countries signed in August with Saudi Arabia.
The move came after an emergency meeting in Riyadh.
In a joint statement, the trio "reaffirmed their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom's security and territorial integrity."
The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
The three countries condemned the Houthis' targeting of Saudi Arabia's two holiest cities, Mecca and Medina, as well as agreeing to provide the "agreed military forces and capabilities," which will be deployed in Saudi Arabia.
How did the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Houthis escalate?
The latest developments come amid an escalation between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is supported by Saudi Arabia, reviving Yemen's civil war after a four-year ceasefire.
A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia collapsed in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace.
As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Last month, the Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a vital global shipping route — from government hands, even as Al-Alimi called for support from the international community.
At the same time, Houthi's have been launching long-range attacks at targets in Saudi Arabia.
The Iran-backed Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen's more populous western areas since the start of Yemen's civil war in 2014.

Why ordinary investors struggle to buy into the robotics boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:15:45 UTC
15:15:45 KST

Most of the companies building the robots of the future are still private, leaving ordinary investors with limited options such as Tesla, diversified industrial groups or new vehicles like RoboStrategy, a Nasdaq-listed fund whose shares trade at more than twice the value of its assets.
Anyone hoping to bet on robots taking over factories, warehouses and homes runs into the awkward fact that shares of the start-ups at the centre of the frenzy cannot be bought on a stock exchange.
What is available is a carmaker betting its future on robots, industrial groups for which robots are one business among many and a new breed of listed funds charging handsomely for access.
Euronews breaks down the options ordinary investors currently have to gain exposure to robotics, and the risks each one carries.
Buying Tesla for the robots
Tesla is currently one prominent route. As Elon Musk said last year, about 80% of the company's value will come from Optimus, its humanoid robot, while its robotaxis add another robotics angle.
Yet, buying Tesla today still mostly means buying a carmaker. Its automotive business generated $20.5 billion (€18.1bn) of its $28.2 billion (€24.9bn) revenue in the second quarter of this year, almost 75%, while Optimus has yet to record any sales.
"By the end of next year, I think we'll be selling humanoid robots to the public," Musk declared at the World Economic Forum in Davos back in January.
Tesla has since begun building the robot at its Fremont plant in California, but Musk has warned that "Optimus production will be extremely slow at first, as everything is new. This is not like making a car."
"Many Tesla investors own the shares to access Elon Musk's entrepreneurial skills. The vehicle sales keep the lights on and help to fund the more adventurous ideas, including robotics," Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at UK investment platform AJ Bell, explained to Euronews.
However, that ambition does not come cheap.
"European car manufacturers typically trade on less than 10 times forward earnings. In contrast, Tesla trades on 165 times forward earnings. That suggests a lot of the 'blue sky' element is factored into the shares, and investors are having to pay up for it," Coatsworth said.
Most robots are not humanoids
Humanoids also draw attention out of proportion to their share of the market.
About 7,000 were sold worldwide last year for industrial and professional use, against 603,000 industrial robots installed worldwide, according to the International Federation of Robotics (IFR).
The industrial leaders rarely offer a clean bet either.
Robots made up 44% of sales at Japan's Fanuc in the year to March and only between 7% and 10% of revenue at Swiss-Swedish group ABB in the last two years.
On top of that, rather than list its robotics arm separately as originally planned, ABB agreed to sell it to Japan's SoftBank for $5.4 billion (€4.7bn).
Germany's KUKA left the stock market in 2022 after Chinese appliance maker Midea took full control. Siemens, meanwhile, makes the software and controllers that run automated factories, not the robots.
A listed fund of private robot makers
None of the options mentioned offers a direct stake in the start-ups themselves, and that is the gap RoboStrategy is trying to fill.
The fund, which began trading on the Nasdaq in May under the ticker BOT, holds stakes in private robotics companies and has publicly traded shares, so anyone with a brokerage account can own a slice of its investments.
Well-known robotics start-ups such as Figure AI, Dyna Robotics and Apptronik each made up close to a fifth of its net assets in June.
The fund is run by Andrew Kang, co-founder of crypto investment firm Mechanism Capital, who wrote on X in May that when he first looked at robotics two years earlier, "most venture capitalists I consulted with recommended not to invest in the space."
Sentiment has turned fast since then.
Robotics start-ups had raised $18.8 billion (€16.6bn) this year by mid-June, more than in record-breaking 2025, according to data platform Crunchbase, which tracks information about private and public companies, including start-up funding rounds.
Vehicles like RoboStrategy exist because companies now stay private far longer.
The median US tech company that listed in 2025 was 12 years old, against only four back in 1999, according to University of Florida professor Jay Ritter, who is known as "Mr. IPO" given his more than 40 years of pioneering research into initial public offerings.
In the US, stakes in private companies are largely reserved for wealthy "accredited" investors. Paul Atkins, chair of the US Securities and Exchange Commission, said in March that this kind of exposure "should not be reserved for those who satisfy a certain wealth threshold or are deemed to be sufficiently sophisticated."
However, access does come at a price, even for these new funds.
RoboStrategy's shares opened at $27.34 on Friday, about 2.4 times the fund's net asset value of $11.35 per share at the end of August. The fund's shares hit a peak of $59 back in May.
"It's a scarcity premium which can happen with a hot investment area [...] investors might feel it is worth paying a premium to invest in RoboStrategy if it means getting early exposure to companies that could be tomorrow's market champions," Coatsworth explained to Euronews.
That premium can shrink fast.
For instance, buyers in early July paid almost four times the value of the underlying assets and have since lost about a quarter of their money, even though net asset value per share rose by 27% over roughly the same period.
Investors also pay a 2.5% annual management fee, with total yearly expenses of almost 4%, and the fund's private stakes are valued on estimates rather than market prices.
"An investment in RoboStrategy is speculative and involves a high degree of risk, including the possible loss of your entire investment," the fund warns on its website.
There is a precedent for investors suffering heavy losses as a fund’s premium shrinks.
Destiny Tech100, a fund holding stakes in private firms such as SpaceX and OpenAI, traded at a premium of around 2,000% to its asset value within two weeks of listing on the New York Stock Exchange in 2024. Its shares closed at $99.79 on 8 April that year, but by 12 April they had fallen to $29 — a drop of about 71% in four days.
"It's important for investors to know what they are getting for their money and to realise when they are paying more than the underlying value of assets," Coatsworth cautioned.
Robotics ETFs
Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) generally trade closer to their net asset value, though they mostly hold listed companies. For example, Roundhill's humanoid robotics ETF counted Tesla, Chinese robot maker UBTech and Hyundai among its biggest holdings at the end of June.
"There are several robotics ETFs on the market that trade at net asset value, meaning that investors don't have to settle for the first thing they find," Coatsworth said.
Even when a robot maker does list, it can be out of reach.
For example, China's Unitree soared 460% on its debut in August on Shanghai's tech-focused STAR Market, where foreign investors generally need a special licence to buy newly listed shares.
Until more of the sector's leaders go public, investors wanting a pure bet on robots will pay for it one way or another, through a carmaker, a conglomerate or a premium.

glazed passage frames lake views through this compact japanese house
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:15:07 UTC
15:15:07 KST

glazed passage frames lake views through this compact japanese house
minimalist house by FORM / kouichi kimura architects uses gaps, levels, and light to shape its interior.
Two-volume minimalist house opens a continuous Lake view
Minimalist House by FORM / Kouichi Kimura Architects is a residence for a single owner on a hill above a lakeside town in Shiga, Japan. Instead of treating single-person living as a reason to reduce the house to a compact footprint, the design uses the individual as its base unit, reducing the composition to essential spaces while allowing views, light, wind, and sound to shape the interior.
Measuring roughly 70 sqm, the house is composed of a two-story main building and a single-story annex connected by a glazed passageway. The gap between the two volumes creates a continuous sightline from the road through the house toward the lake, while also forming an intermediate space between the interior and landscape.
The interior uses framed views and split levels to define space
Openings are positioned as frames for specific views, limiting the amount of landscape visible at once and bringing attention to individual scenes beyond the windows. In the main building, the kitchen and dining areas occupy the first floor, while the living room and bedroom are located above. FORM / Kouichi Kimura Architects designs both levels to follow open layouts, connected vertically by a double-height space. Variations in floor and ceiling heights subtly define the different areas without fully separating them.
The upper living space is also designed for listening to music, with the double-height volume allowing sound to resonate through the room. High-side windows bring in natural light, casting changing shadows across the walls and floors throughout the day. The annex contains the washroom and shower room, separating these wet areas from the main living spaces. Moving between the two volumes through the glazed corridor creates a transition through the surrounding light, breeze, and landscape.
By organizing the house around a single occupant, the design uses a minimal spatial composition to create a sense of depth beyond its physical dimensions. The separation of volumes, framed views, and connection to the surrounding environment shape a residence where architecture and landscape remain closely connected.
project info:
name: Minimalist House
architects: FORM / Kouichi Kimura Architects | @form.kouichi_kimura.architec
location: Shiga, Japan
floor area: 71,56 sqm
site area: 271,10 sqm

Expert: Russia attacking civilian infrastructure as it has made no front line gains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:15:00 UTC
15:15:00 KST

Expert: Russia attacking civilian infrastructure as it has made no front line gains
Russia's escalating attacks on Ukraine and threats against the West are signs of its failure to achieve a breakthrough on the battlefield, former ambassador to NATO Jüri Luik tells ERR in an interview.
What do you make of Russia's so-called new approach, with its emphasis on long-range strikes and unrestricted attacks on civilian infrastructure?
First, of course, it shows that Russia has been unable to break through the front line and the Ukrainians are now actually managing to retake territory. So the Russians really have only one option left and that is long-range bombardment. They have also begun bombing civilian targets, which is a war crime.
They are clearly testing whether they can reach a point where the Ukrainians simply surrender because their cities are no longer habitable: bridges are destroyed, reservoirs are destroyed, power plants are destroyed. But it is hard to imagine that actually happening. The bombing will certainly continue, but it will not break the Ukrainians' resolve.
In addition to terrorizing Ukrainian cities, Russia is also trying to exert greater pressure on the West. As part of these attacks on cities, embassies have been warned to leave because it is going to become very dangerous. Then there is all the rhetoric about having arms factories that produce weapons for Ukraine in their sights and using nuclear weapons if necessary. The hybrid attacks being carried out in the West have also become more dangerous. What should we make of all this?
As for the Russians' demand that embassies leave Kyiv, they have actually done this several times already and it is clear that no embassy is going to leave Kyiv because of it. It is a form of propaganda pressure.
If anything, the opposite is true. Chancellor Merz was in Ukraine just yesterday and demonstrated very clearly what he actually thinks of the Russians' threats, particularly given that he also brought an economic delegation and businesspeople with him. It was all a signal to the Russians that we do not take their warnings seriously.
To what extent could this intimidation nevertheless have an effect, for example, on societies in Western or Southern Europe? We have a somewhat different attitude here because we have been hearing threats like these all along, but there have been quite a few alarming articles in the international media in recent months. Could that eventually have an impact? Russia does not even have to do very much itself if we are already frightening ourselves.
There are a great many analyses in the international media that are often completely baseless and interpret one Russian move or another as a threat indicating that some kind of attack on NATO countries is being planned. There is actually no such information. It is simply a case of fear making things seem worse than they are.
Of course, we all have to remain vigilant. And there is no doubt that these articles can influence public opinion. But it seems to me that solidarity among European countries in support of Ukraine remains quite strong at present.
Putin's threats are also very specific — the issue of Kaliningrad, for example. I do not think the general public across Europe necessarily knows exactly what Kaliningrad is or what issues are associated with it. So for now, I do not think this will have a significant impact.
This week, Putin spoke at length about his views at the Valdai Forum. He portrayed the current situation as one in which Russia is under attack and has to defend itself and so on, which turns the logic completely on its head. But there was also an interesting moment when he said Russia had gained 1,300 kilometers of territory during September. Analysts at the Institute for the Study of War, for example, went so far as to compare the claim to hallucinations because it differs so greatly from what they are actually seeing on the front line. What could that tell us? Is Putin simply trying to portray the situation more favorably or could he himself already be receiving distorted information?
He is certainly trying to portray the situation more favorably. When analyzing the Valdai speech, we also have to bear in mind that much of it was intended for his domestic audience, even though it is said to be aimed at an international audience. In reality, of course, it was disseminated primarily in Russia.
If you look at the speech analytically, there was not very much that was new: Russia is not to blame, Russia was forced to start the war because Russia was threatened and so on. He has essentially been saying this all along; the only question is the exact wording.
Perhaps the accusation about a possible blockade of Kaliningrad and the statement that Russia could use nuclear weapons in response added a new dimension, although Putin has threatened the use of nuclear weapons before as well.
How has the West and NATO responded so far to Russia's increasingly brazen approach?
I think NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte's response was very good. First, he said that NATO is a defensive alliance and, of course, no one intends to attack Kaliningrad militarily. That is completely absurd.
The Russians know that very well, too, because they have simply withdrawn all their forces from Kaliningrad. If they genuinely believed someone intended to attack Kaliningrad, they obviously would not do that.
In fact, we now have this paradoxical situation in which Kaliningrad's location among NATO countries — within NATO's perimeter, so to speak — actually protects Kaliningrad. Not a single Ukrainian drone has struck Kaliningrad. So, paradoxically, the situation is precisely the opposite.
The second point, and a very important one, is what Rutte said about NATO defending every inch of its territory. Whenever the Russians make some kind of threat, it never hurts to reiterate that NATO has Article 5 and that we will defend our territory. And that is what Rutte did.
More generally, though, NATO is a rather blunt instrument. It is designed for war and, naturally, when it comes to everything below the threshold of warfare, NATO as an organization has difficulty determining how to respond. Not every action is something to which you can respond by immediately going to war.
So when it comes to provocations that remain below the Article 5 threshold, NATO cannot do very much directly. NATO member states, however, can. And NATO provides the security framework that allows countries to act more boldly. It also enables them to provide assistance to Ukraine because we have to recognize that if countries were entirely on their own, they would be much more cautious about giving their weapons to Ukraine.
There is still a degree of risk involved, but because collective security exists, each individual country is more willing to give its weapons to Ukraine. So NATO plays a very important role here, but it is not a direct striking force.
When we talk about these increasingly dangerous hybrid attacks — here in Estonia, there was also discussion this week about the Milrem case — how could countries respond to Russia in the face of such attacks?
There are several options and I think some of them are probably not public and fall within the realm of other kinds of activities. But there is, of course, political and diplomatic pressure, as Estonia applied by summoning the Russian chargé d'affaires.
Most importantly, however, there should be more and more support for Ukraine. In Estonia's case, military aid may no longer be particularly noteworthy in itself, but everything we do to urge the European Union to impose sanctions more actively and forcefully and everything we do to restrict the entry of combatants into the European Union — these are all countermeasures in response to these provocations.
And I think the most powerful response actually came from [German Chancellor Friedrich] Merz. Clearly also in response to the Leipzig provocation where there was an attempt to attack civilian aircraft with armed drones, Merz went there and put an enormous military aid package on the table. I think that message in itself was quite significant.
Is there any hope of hearing something about peace talks in the near future or is that essentially a dead issue for the time being?
I think it is essentially a dead issue, although that does not mean there will be no meetings or news about it.
On the one hand, Putin harshly criticized the Europeans, but when it came to the United States, he was much more nuanced and stressed that Russia is interested in negotiations. He also raised one specific issue — the question of Ukrainian neutrality.
That, of course, demonstrates what we have always known: For Putin, the issue is not only Ukraine as a territory, but also what Europe's postwar security system will look like. And we can see that he is already trying to shape it through his statements. This is part of his negotiating tactics, which we naturally have to watch very closely. None of this is in our interests.
--

London police urge students to reschedule October 7 pro-Palestinian march
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:13:09 UTC
15:13:09 KST

London’s Metropolitan Police on Friday publicly urged organizers of a large pro-Palestinian demonstration planned for Wednesday, October 7, to move the march to another date, citing serious concerns over its impact on Jewish students and staff on the third anniversary of the Hamas massacre in Israel.
The march is expected to set out at noon from King’s College London and end at University College London (UCL), with organizers calling on participants to protest Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip. Against the backdrop of the sensitive date, the Metropolitan Police issued an unusual public appeal to the organizers on Friday asking them to reschedule the demonstration.
Senior police officer James Harman, who is responsible for operations at the Metropolitan Police, said during a briefing at Scotland Yard that “serious concerns” had been raised about the demonstration’s impact on students and faculty members, particularly Jews, both because of the date chosen and because of the planned route between major academic institutions in the British capital.
Harman said police had tried to contact the organizers but had struggled to identify anyone willing to take formal responsibility for the event.
He publicly called on them to change their plans, saying organizers and participants should consider the distress such a demonstration could cause on a day when many members of the Jewish community will mark three years since the October 7 attack.
Pro-Palestine groups in universities across London
The march is being organized under the name University of London Coalition, an umbrella organization of pro-Palestinian student groups at universities across London. In publicity ahead of the demonstration, organizers called for a “Palestine free from the river to the sea” and described the war in Gaza as part of what they called “78 years of genocide.”
One of the event advertisements also featured the red triangle symbol, which in recent years has been associated with Hamas videos.
London police said that if the organizers refuse to move the march, officers will consider measures intended to reduce disruption and harm. Police have already contacted four universities attended by students associated with the coalition and asked their administrations to take steps to ensure that Jewish students and staff can study and work without feeling threatened, excluded, or targeted.
In its letters, the police emphasized that it recognizes the importance of freedom of expression, peaceful protest, and academic debate. At the same time, it cited figures from the Community Security Trust showing that the number of antisemitic incidents at British universities remains significantly higher than levels recorded before October 2023.
Zero-tolerance approach towards hate crimes
Scotland Yard stressed that police do not have the authority to cancel a demonstration solely because of its date or political message. They may, however, impose strict conditions on the route, timing, and conduct of a march when there is a risk of serious public disorder, significant disruption, or intimidation of the public.
Hundreds of police officers are expected to be deployed across London during the coming week because of a series of demonstrations and events. Police said they would adopt a zero-tolerance approach toward hate crimes, incitement to violence, or expressions of support for terrorist organizations.
The October 7 march is expected to be one of the most sensitive tests for British police since the start of the war. Three days later, on October 10, another large march by pro-Palestinian organizations is expected to take place in central London, with police estimating that up to approximately 10,000 people could attend.
According to Metropolitan Police figures, the groups that make up the Palestine Coalition have held dozens of large demonstrations in London since October 2023. Police said 35 of those demonstrations cost approximately £26.6 million in direct expenses. Including the cost of diverting officers from other duties, the total estimated cost rises to about £90 million.

Transportation Ministry official overseeing foreign airlines also consulted for flydubai - report

From North to South: Israel bows its head in remembrance of October 7 massacre

Three years after the October 7 massacre, Israel will mark Monday, October 5, as the national memorial day for the attack and the war.
Two state ceremonies will be held at Mount Herzl, while dozens of ceremonies, rallies, testimony sessions, and memorial events will take place nationwide.
Memorial Day was established by law to take place on Tishrei 24, two days after the Simchat Torah holiday. This year, it falls on October 5, two days before the Gregorian anniversary of the attack.
Throughout the day, flags will be lowered to half-mast at state institutions, police stations, prisons, and IDF bases, while radio and television broadcasts will be adjusted to reflect the nature of the day.
It will remain a regular workday, not a public holiday, and no nationwide siren is expected to sound.
Two state ceremonies to be held at Mount Herzl
At 11:00 a.m., the national memorial ceremony for those killed by Hamas on October 7, as well as soldiers who have been killed since the outbreak of the war, will be held at Mount Herzl.
Alongside the bereaved families and senior government officials, President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Defense Minister Israel Katz, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, Israel Police Commissioner Daniel Levy, Shin Bet chief David Zini, and Mossad chief Roman Gofman will attend.
Herzog, Netanyahu, and Katz are expected to speak.
The ceremony is expected to conclude at 12:15 p.m.
The HaLeom and International Convention Center (ICC) parking lots will open at 8:00 a.m., with free shuttles from both locations to Mount Herzl. Transportation via light rail from the Jerusalem Navon train station to Mount Herzl will also be free.
At 2:00 p.m., the national memorial ceremony for victims of terror will be held at the Victims of Hostile Acts Memorial at Mount Herzl, also in the presence of senior state officials and bereaved families. Attendees may enter between noon and 1:45 p.m.
Entry to both ceremonies must have been arranged in advance, and attendees will be asked to present identification. Weapons will not be allowed.
Education system, nation marks the day
Alongside the ceremonies at Mount Herzl, memorial events will begin across the country in the morning.
Schools across the country will also mark the day with memorial ceremonies and special activities. The Education Ministry has distributed teaching materials, documentation, and memorial content tailored to different age groups.
At 9:30 a.m., the Technion-Israel Institute of Technology will hold a memorial ceremony, and at 10:00 a.m., Nahariya will hold its municipal rally at City Hall Square.
At 11:00 a.m., a testimony session will be held in Nesher with Golan Avitbol of Kibbutz Be'eri, who will speak about the survival, loss, and recovery the kibbutz community experienced.
At the same time, a remembrance ceremony will take place at the military cemetery in Modi'in, while an educational experience marking the memorial day will be held at the National Campus for the Archaeology of Israel in Jerusalem.
At noon, Tel Aviv University will hold a rally at the memorial site opposite the Cymbalista Synagogue and Jewish Heritage Center, which will be open to the public.
An hour later, at 1:00 p.m., the Holon Institute of Technology will inaugurate a memorial monument for alumni and students who were killed during their service or during terror attacks.
From the Galilee to the Shfela: Memorial events in cities
Municipal ceremonies and community events will take place across the country during the afternoon and evening.
In Ashkelon, the municipal ceremony, "We Are All One Human Tapestry," will be held at 4:30 p.m. in the presence of bereaved families and with the participation of youth movements and several organizations.

Jeremy Strong plays Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg in 'The Social Reckoning', Stephen King's 'Carrie' is adapted for the small screen, and Tate Britain revives the rebellious creativity of the 90s. Here's what to look out for this week.
The dark side of social media takes centre stage in this week's biggest movie release: The Social Reckoning.
A dramatisation of the 2021 whistleblower scandal, it tells the story of former Facebook (now Meta) employee Frances Haugen, who leaked documents revealing the company's prioritisation of profits over public health.
At a time when technological anxieties continue to dominate our lives, it's unlikely to be a comforting watch — but at least there's solace to be found in a trip back to the 90s at London's Tate Britain. The museum has put together a nostalgically joyful showcase of the decade's art and fashion in Britain, exploring how they shaped and were shaped by the rebellious culture of the time.
Similarly, 90s pop rock queen Sheryl Crow is releasing a new album that utilises her old school sound in a rallying cry against the divisions of today.
Keep scrolling to find out more about this week's highlights.
Exhibitions
The 90s: Art and Fashion
When: 8 October 2026 - 14 February 2027
Where: Tate Britain (London, UK)
Beanie Babies, girlbands, pastel-coloured shell suits — the 1990s were an era of many things. But more than anything, they have come to represent a version of life we will never get back.
The last decade before the internet, social media and smartphones took over, the 90s had an unbridled sense of optimism. This is reflected in the art and fashion of that time, with the Young British Artists (YBAs) movement giving rise to rebellious new visions from the likes of Damien Hirst and Tracey Emin, while designers like Vivienne Westwood and Alexander McQueen transformed the runway into theatrical spaces for subversion. This, in turn, shaped the energy and image of the era, which the Tate Britain explores through a diverse collection of iconic photographs, paintings, clothing and more — expertly curated by former editor-in-chief of British Vogue, Edward Enninful OBE. Find out more here.
Christoph Schlingensief: It’s not my problem anymore, deal with your own shit
When: 9 October 2026 - 17 January 2027
Where: Gropius Bau (Berlin, Germany)
From satirical gore-films to political performance art, the works of German artist Christoph Schlingensief remain some of the world's most boundary-pushing. By blending his skills in theatre direction, filmmaking and performance art, he consistently created installations that challenged the political and social issues of the time — many of which feel just as relevant today. Sixteen years after his death, the Gropius Bau museum reflects on his works from the late 1990s to the late 2000s, including Schlingensief's remarkable large-scale installation 'Kaprow City', which was originally created in 2006 for a rotating, labyrinthine room.
Bonus highlight: From 9 October, the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris is showcasing more than 250 works from the late French painter Gustave Fayet’s personal art collection. Find out more here.
Movies
The Social Reckoning
Where: Cinemas
When: 9 October
It's been sixteen years since The Social Network came out — a film about Mark Zuckerberg's creation of Facebook and subsequent bitter legal battles. Since then, social media's rot has continued to spread, resulting in lawsuits, safety concerns and growing distrust against the tech billionaires who now harness so much of the world's power and influence. As depressing as all of this is, it also makes for rich sequel material, which Aaron Sorkin (who wrote the previous movie) has now delivered. Starring Mikey Madison (Anora), Jeremy Strong (Succession) and Jeremy Allen White (The Bear), the movie documents the 2021 whistleblower scandal, which saw a Facebook employee leak damning information about the company to the Wall Street Journal.
Bonus highlight: Andrew Garfield stars in The Uprising, a new action-packed drama about the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. It's out in UK cinemas from 9 October, with a staggered rollout across the rest of Europe to follow.
TV series
Carrie
Where: Prime Video
When: 7 October
American filmmaker Mike Flanagan has become a trusted source for two things: supernatural TV series and Stephen King movies. Now he's combined the two with a fresh adaptation of King's 'Carrie' — the story of a young, isolated and bullied girl (Summer H. Howell) living with telekinetic powers. Unlike the previous 1976 and 2013 movies, Flanagan's series reportedly expands on King's original story, re-contextualising it to the present day and developing character backstories along with Carrie's supernatural abilities. Perfect spooky season watching.

Music

For freed Israeli hostages, every moment is now precious
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:10:04 UTC
15:10:04 KST

For freed Israeli hostages, every moment is now precious
TEL AVIV, Oct 5 - Taken with their children or alone. Held for weeks, months or years. Confined in captors' homes or Hamas tunnels as war raged above them. Israeli former hostages seized on October 7 say they now cherish even the smallest moments of freedom.
Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack was Israel's single deadliest day. The militants rampaged through villages, a music festival and army bases, killing 1,200 people and dragging 251 hostages back to Gaza.
They included civilians, soldiers, men, women, children and elderly people, Israelis and foreign nationals. Most were freed in return for Palestinian prisoners during ceasefires between Israel and Hamas, but dozens did not survive.
"Freedom has completely changed the way I see life," said Emily Damari, 30, who was abducted wounded from her home in Kibbutz Kfar Aza and released in January 2025.
Her ordeal taught her not to take anything for granted, she said. "One day in captivity feels like one week. You want to give up at every moment, but I did not," said Damari, who has recently married and launched a clothing line in Israel.
"Today, I open the fridge and I say thank you. I drink cold water and I say thank you. I am thankful for everything, big things and little things. Gratitude has become central to who I am," said Damari. "Being free, at home, surrounded by my family and my people is something I will never take for granted again."
"I CHOOSE LIFE"
Eli Sharabi, 54, was seized from nearby Kibbutz Be'eri. His British-born wife Lianne and their two daughters Noiya, 16, and Yahel, 13, were slain by the attackers. His brother Yossi was taken hostage and killed in Gaza.
In February 2025, Sharabi was released, appearing emaciated and skeletally thin, from 491 days of captivity which he says included being held in a tunnel, hungry, shackled and beaten.
"I learned in captivity how precious every moment and every choice can be, and I carry that understanding with me now. I choose to look ahead, to keep going and to use the life I have in a meaningful way," said Sharabi.
Since his release he has helped establish the Shalva Sharabi Family Centre in the southern city of Ashkelon with the disability charity Shalva, to treat families coping with trauma and disabilities, in commemoration of his own family lost.
"I choose life. I choose to keep living fully, while carrying Lianne, Noiya, Yahel and Yossi with me in everything I do."
His wife and daughters believed deeply in caring for others, he said. "Their kindness and care for others will continue. Families will walk through these doors and receive help, care and hope in a place that carries their name. That gives me strength and makes me very proud," said Sharabi.
SLOWLY BUILDING A FUTURE
Hagar Brodutch was seized from Kfar Aza with her three children and her neighbours' daughter who fled to their house after her parents were killed. They were freed in a brief truce in November 2023.
Life after captivity, she said, can be far more complicated than sometimes portrayed.
"The daily struggle is immense, especially for children. I believe it will take many more years before captivity becomes just a shadow that walks alongside us, rather than something that defines who we are," said Brodutch.
Recently, Brodutch, 43, has begun taking classes in pastry baking, for which she has long had a passion.
"This is about much more than learning how to bake. It is about finding a new path, creating something with my own hands, and slowly building a future," she said.
"During my time in Hamas captivity, I began to understand that if I were released, returning to my previous life and working in management might no longer be possible," said Brodutch.
"I chose pastry as a form of therapy, but also as a way to create something new for myself, with the hope that one day it could become my profession," she said.
Kfar Aza was one of the hardest-hit communities in Hamas' attack. Aviva Siegel, 65, was kidnapped with her husband Keith. She was released in November 2023, but Keith was held until February 2025.
Aviva joined the hostage release campaign movement in Israel while her husband was still being held. Their reunion and her children and grandchildren, and even strangers she meets, give her strength every day, she says.
"I feel that I’m not alone and that there's so much love in this world and we need to keep it with both our hands," she said. "I feel very, very lucky to be alive." REUTERS

Japanese media artist's first major overseas show debuts in Taichung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:09:36 UTC
15:09:36 KST

TAICHUNG (Taiwan News) — Renowned Japanese media artist Manabe Daito has launched his first major overseas solo exhibition, “Relational Time – Life Beyond Simulation,” at the Taichung Arts Museum.
Hong Kong-based media art veteran Kwong Joel curated the exhibition, which features three site-specific installations commissioned for the museum’s galleries.
The show integrates real-time computation, AI agents, physiological signals, light, and sound into dynamic sensory environments.
Manabe has achieved international acclaim for designing tech-driven stage performances, including the Rio Olympics closing ceremony, and collaborating with global icons such as Sakamoto Ryuichi, Perfume, and Bjork.
The exhibition marks a pivotal personal transition for Manabe, who began coding at age 10. After four decades of programming, the rapid rise of generative AI over the past year triggered a profound identity crisis, leading him to stop writing code entirely for a month.
“The arrival of AI has, in a sense, liberated humanity from the labor of coding,” Manabe said, acknowledging initial fears that his technical skills would become obsolete.
Instead of replacing his creativity, AI expanded it. The new exhibition incorporates over 21 million lines of code generated with AI assistance—a scale impossible through human effort alone.
Although he initially considered touring past works, a visit to the Taichung museum inspired him to design entirely new installations tailored to the building's architecture. Manabe said that AI allowed him to realize concepts long constrained by technical limits, reigniting his passion for artistic exploration.
Kwong emphasized that the core theme of relational time centers on how technology intersects with local culture and perception. Although Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Japan are geographically close, audience interactions with media and AI differ across cultures, he said.
Kwong added that visitors do not need prior technical knowledge to experience the exhibition. Rather than static displays, the installations constantly evolve based on real-time audience participation, environmental data, and AI agent responses, he said.
Each visitor leaves a subtle digital trace, subtly altering the environment for subsequent viewers.
Throughout his career, Manabe has treated the human body as a laboratory, from early muscle-control works to recent brain-decoding projects. For him, exploring technology and body modification is not about abandoning humanity, but examining fundamental sensory questions, such as why music compels people to dance.
The exhibition is on view in Galleries A, B, and C at the Taichung Arts Museum through Jan. 3, 2027.
Manabe Daito launches his first major overseas solo exhibition at the Taichung Arts Museum. (Taiwan News, Lyla Liu video)

Taiwan plans COP31 activities despite lack of official invitation

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Environment Minister Peng Chi-ming (彭啓明) confirmed Monday that despite not being invited to the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, Taiwan will hold climate meetings at home and join related events during the summit.
COP31 will be held in Turkey from Nov. 9-20. Taiwan cannot participate as an official party to the talks because it is not a UN member.
Despite its exclusion, the country's climate policies have gained international recognition, Peng said, per CNA. He cited overseas recognition of the country's carbon fee system and cooperation with other countries on emissions trading.
During COP31, Taiwan plans to hold international climate cooperation meetings and participate in related events, Peng said. Environment ministry officials and research groups will also follow the negotiations and gather information on developments at the conference, per CTS News.
Taiwan has sent officials, researchers, businesses, and civil society groups to participate in COP-related activities in previous years despite not being an official party. Ahead of COP30, the environment ministry formed a team to track negotiations and promote the country's climate policies internationally.
The ministry plans to use this year's conference to explain its key climate policies and its progress in cutting carbon emissions. Peng said the outreach would help the international community better understand its climate efforts.
According to the environment ministry, Taiwan introduced its carbon fee system in 2025 as part of efforts to reduce industrial emissions. The system applies to power, gas, and manufacturing facilities that emit more than 25,000 metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per year.
The government aims to cut net greenhouse gas emissions by about 28% from 2005 levels by 2030. It has also set a target of reducing emissions by about 38% by 2035.
