As Iran war smolders, shunned Eritrea looks to come in from the cold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:09:24 UTC
15:09:24 KST

As Iran war smolders, shunned Eritrea looks to come in from the cold
ASMARA, Oct 5 - When Halima Mohammed was six, her parents dropped her off in the desert at Revolution School, where the children of Eritrean guerrilla fighters were raised while their parents fought for independence.
Wounded fighters taught grammar when they weren't carrying rifles. Mothers and fathers appeared only rarely before melting back into the mountains and deserts of a war that would rage for three decades before Eritrea seceded from Ethiopia in 1993.
Halima, 56, is now education minister of Eritrea, where that revolutionary struggle still hangs heavily over one of the most secluded and regimented societies on Earth.
She presides over a schooling system that binds the future of the country's children into the service of the state. All teenagers must undergo army training towards the end of high school before being assigned mandatory and often indefinitely long roles in the military or in national service, mainly low-paid civilian jobs like teaching and policing.
"All school graduates are getting at least a job to work, and they are getting their salary. And at the same time, they are serving the country," Halima told Reuters, which was granted rare access to the nation. "If you are going to have more freedom, first you have to have a country, you have to have national security, because we paid a lot for Eritrea."
Eritrea has long been isolated by the West, which views the East African country as among the most repressive in the world, while the government in Asmara has itself pursued a policy of political and economic seclusion. No elections have been held since the nation became a sovereign state in the 1990s. Independent media outlets were shut down in 2001. Hundreds of thousands of Eritreans have defied strict travel restrictions, which bar most working-age citizens from leaving the country, to abscond overseas.
This small country of fewer than 4 million people has nonetheless acquired new geopolitical significance this year, during the Iran war, owing to its 1,000 km coastline along the Red Sea shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia. The route has proved a critical alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which was the primary export route for Gulf energy shipments before it was effectively closed by the conflict. Attacks on Red Sea trading vessels by Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, which faces Eritrea across the route's southern chokepoint, have made Eritrean waters potentially the most secure transit corridor.
"Eritrea sits astride some of the world's hottest geographical real estate," said Murithi Mutiga, Africa program director at the International Crisis Group, a Brussels-based think-tank. "The war in the Gulf has highlighted the importance of the Red Sea as an alternative outlet for that region. It's no wonder outside powers are courting Asmara."
There have been signs of warming ties with the world: Last month, Washington removed its sanctions on Eritrea, which were imposed over the role of the country's military in the Tigray conflict in Ethiopia in 2020-22. The State Department said the Trump administration made the decision "to advance US regional interests."
Reuters interviewed several senior government figures during a recent trip to Eritrea, as well as dozens of Eritreans at home and abroad, to piece together a picture of a society largely walled off from the modern world.
The officials pressed a consistent message: Eritrea is ready to engage and trade, they said. It is prepared to open up to investors keen to tap its gold, copper and potash. It is looking at reforming its school system to give young people more say over their destiny.
Yet beneath these aspirations lies a state shaped by its leaders' iron conviction that national survival depends on stringent internal security and military vigilance against Ethiopia, its larger neighbor.
In recent years, the countries have been at loggerheads over landlocked Ethiopia's demands that Eritrea grant it commercial and naval access to the Red Sea, particularly the port of Assab near their border. Ethiopia, which had access to the coastline for decades before Eritrea broke away, has cast maritime access as a matter of urgent national security. Meanwhile, Asmara has said it fears Addis Ababa will try to take Assab by force.
Getachew Reda, the Ethiopian premier's adviser on regional affairs, said Addis Ababa has never threatened to use force or violate Eritrea's sovereignty. He said that Eritrea poses a security threat because of its readiness to fund insurgencies within Ethiopia, an allegation denied by Asmara.
Getachew said access to the Red Sea is a matter of economic necessity for Ethiopia, a country of 130 million people, and that his government is willing to come to a peaceful arrangement with Eritrea such as a long-term lease deal on the use of ports.
Last week, the countries cut diplomatic ties, with Ethiopia expelling Eritrean diplomats and Asmara retaliating.
Eritrea has not always been isolated from the West; it enjoyed friendly relations with the US and several European nations in the years following its independence before diplomatic ties collapsed in 2001 when Asmara cracked down on political opponents and journalists.
THE CAPITAL ABOVE THE CLOUDS
Asmara, Eritrea's highland capital, seems a city suspended in time.
Elderly men, many of them veterans with wheelchairs or crutches, linger over macchiatos at dusk beneath fading Italian signs at Bar Vittoria and Bar America, legacies of the Italian colonial rule that preceded Ethiopian control.
Tightly controlled internet access is sparse and slow. Few people bother staring at phones. Young people drink unlabeled bottles of beer from the state-owned factory. Almost no cars can be seen on the streets amid severe government fuel rationing, save a few battered taxis that have survived in an economy ground down by decades of Western sanctions.
Even as ministers spoke of reform and engagement, many ordinary Eritreans remained reluctant to discuss politics.
Conversations often end the same way. A glance over the shoulder. A lowered voice. A polite smile. "It's better not to," several people said when questions turned to national service or political freedoms. Others only agreed to speak if they weren't identified.
Walking through a residential district of Asmara, the sound of applause drifted out from an old cinema. An information session for Sawa was underway.
Little epitomizes the tensions tearing at the fabric of the nation more than Sawa, a remote military camp in the desert near the border with Sudan. This is where teenagers must go to complete their final year of secondary school and undergo military training.
In the cinema, rows of teenagers due to leave home for Sawa faced a stage where a young woman clicked through a PowerPoint presentation filled with photos of students in camouflage uniforms, marching in formation and studying in classrooms.
The presenter, 24-year-old Luna Ermias, wore jeans, sunglasses pushed onto her head and braces that flashed when she smiled. She spoke passionately.
"I was there in 2019," she told Reuters afterwards. "It teaches you to rely on yourself. You manage your money, your time. You meet people from every part of Eritrea."
ESCAPING ACROSS A BURNING DESERT
Many don't share her enthusiasm.
Muse said he was 17 when he decided he would rather run than report to Sawa. He felt sure if he stayed, his life would never be his own.
He packed almost nothing. He slipped away from home under the cover of darkness, hoping to cross the border with Ethiopia before the authorities caught him.
He didn't make it.
Muse said he spent the next six months in prison. When he was released, he added, he wasn't sent home. He was instead deployed in the military to Assab, the Red Sea port.
He escaped again. This time he succeeded.
He crossed the blistering Danakil desert into Ethiopia before reaching another East African country, where Reuters interviewed him. The journey cost him thousands of dollars paid to smugglers, money borrowed from relatives already living abroad.
Reuters reviewed Muse's asylum documents and spoke to three family members who corroborated his story. The news agency couldn't independently verify all elements of the account given by the teenager, who asked for his full name and location to be withheld.
His story isn't unique. According to the United Nations, more than 679,000 Eritreans are living as refugees or asylum seekers abroad, a significant chunk of the nation's small population. Human Rights Watch and many other rights groups say the prospect of prolonged compulsory service has driven generations of young people to flee, often risking perilous journeys across the Sahara and Mediterranean.
The Eritrean government did not comment on the details of Muse's account, though said asylum seekers normally fabricate claims to be granted asylum.
The government disputed the UN figures, saying a significant portion of those classed as refugees are actually from neighboring countries who posed as Eritreans to secure fast-tracked asylum and social benefits. It said Eritrean youths were not primarily driven away by national service but rather drawn abroad by external factors including economic incentives, family reunifications and generous asylum policies in the West.
Germany, Switzerland, Sweden, Britain and the US are among the most popular Western destinations for Eritrean refugees and asylum seekers, according to the UN.
DREAMING OF MERCEDES-BENZ
Not everyone who wants to leave manages to do so.
In Asmara, Reuters met a mechanical engineer who was among Sawa students to achieve top grades and was therefore allowed to attend university. He spoke avidly about German engineering. He'd dreamed of working for Mercedes-Benz one day. Instead, he was assigned to a government job as an auto mechanic.
"You don't study what you want," he said. "Even if you finish university, you often don't work in your field."
At around 2,300 Nakfa ($153) a month, he said, his salary barely covers basic necessities. Saving enough to pay smugglers or finance a life abroad felt impossible.
Officials in Asmara maintained that Western governments and rights groups have long misrepresented Eritrea's national service program by overlooking the security pressures the country faces from Ethiopia, with which it shares one of Africa's most turbulent relationships.
Eritrea emerged from the 30-year independence war, which killed tens of thousands on both sides, only to fight another devastating border conflict with its neighbor seven years later. Persistent regional violence has further cemented a sense of permanent mobilization inside the young state.
Halima, the girl left in the desert a lifetime ago, now sits behind a polished wooden desk in the Ministry of Education in Asmara, housed in the striking red Casa del Fascio, built during colonial rule as the Eritrean headquarters of Italy's National Fascist Party.
With four children of her own, she doesn't dismiss the frustrations of young Eritreans. Her ultimate goal, she says, is to replace compulsory national service with vocational colleges and technical schools. But all plans are subordinate to national security.
"First we have to think about Eritrea. We have to protect it," she said. "As a mother, first I have to think about Eritrea." REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Setting a table two millennia later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:06:27 UTC
15:06:27 KST

(AA Photo)
Setting an ancient banquet table is no longer just a dream. An underwater excavation launched last year off the coast of Adrasan, west of Antalya on the Mediterranean coast of Türkiye, revealed just how magnificent a banquet table might have been two thousand years ago. Exactly 2,100 years ago, a ship laden with ceramic tableware traveling from east to west off the coast of Adrasan likely sank after being caught in a storm. It appears the ship set sail from the port of Rhosus — now known as Arsuz — and its entire cargo consisted of Rhosus pottery, which had gained renown throughout the Roman world. Rhosus pottery was made in Antioch, today’s Antakya, and is known in the literature as “Eastern Mediterranean Sigillata,” which was regarded as the most valuable pottery of the eastern Mediterranean.
Was the cargo destined to Rome?
The ceramics were likely bound for Rome. What is interesting is that while trading ships of that period typically carried mixed cargo, this ship was loaded exclusively with tableware — and packed to the brim. One cannot help but wonder whether this was a special commission. Who knows — perhaps it was for a grand celebration in honor of a Roman emperor, or perhaps a lavish wedding. We know from the Roman writer, orator, and statesman Cicero himself that such commissions were placed in those days. In a letter written to his friend Atticus in 50 BC, Cicero recounts that he had commissioned the famous “Rhosica Vasa” — the pottery vessels from Rhosus — for him. Thanks to this correspondence, we understand that pottery made in Antioch and shipped from Arsuz was highly sought after in Rome.
To date, 6,511 pieces have been recovered from the shipwreck intact and unbroken, while the remainder are in good enough condition to be easily restored to their initial glory. The key factor in their preservation was a brilliant innovation in packing technique: a layer of clay was applied between the plates and bowls to prevent them from breaking. This kept them from clattering against one another as the ship rocked in the waves. As a result, almost the entire cargo has survived intact to the present day with minimal loss. Another notable feature of the find is not merely its sheer size, but its variety: the plates and bowls are not all of the same type. We are talking about a tableware set comprising 122 different shapes and sizes, each designed and made for different purposes.
What was served?
So, what exactly was eaten at such a magnificent banquet? The vessels recovered from the wreck include deep bowls, wide trays, and large serving platters — a variety that reflects how important display and ostentation were at wealthy Roman tables. Throughout the meal, fresh and dried fruits like bunches of grapes and figs were kept on hand for snacking. While commoners relied on wheat or barley porridge, the wealthy enjoyed flat, wheel-shaped loaves of bread paired with cheeses, some wrapped in fig leaves for preservation. These banquets also featured wild game and poultry like duck and goose. Usually roasted over an open fire, game birds formed the centerpiece of the finest feasts and were likely presented on these large, tray-like platters.
Food trade in ancient Rome
Undoubtedly, alongside the pottery traded across the Mediterranean basin, foodstuffs were also shipped to far-off destinations. Liquid commodities such as olive oil and wine — as well as dry goods — were transported in earthenware amphorae. Smoked, dried, and salted fish were particularly popular. However, the most prized item was the fermented fish sauce known as garum — the gourmet delicacy of its day. Products and sauces crafted in one corner of the Mediterranean routinely found their way to tables on the opposite side of the sea.
Just as the red plates of Antakya-Arsuz were famous, so too were those produced in Sagalassos, perched high in the Taurus Mountains. Ceramics made in Sagalassos were shipped to the port of Alexandria in Egypt, which in turn sent back a wealth of local goods — the most prized being salted fish. In those days, Sagalassos was a center of luxury and entertainment where the finest delicacies were sold at the Macellum, a type of Roman gourmet market. Archaeological analysis revealed that fish bones uncovered at the market belonged to species unique to the Nile Delta in Egypt, providing tangible proof of an extensive trade network stretching from Alexandria all the way to the peaks of the Taurus Mountains.
Secret flavor: Garum
Some of the flavors of ancient Rome, however, no longer exist today. Foremost among these is the fish sauce known as garum. It is said that wealthy Romans of the time could not refrain from adding a few drops of garum to every meal. It was an indispensable flavoring, much like soy sauce in Chinese cuisine. Of course, there were also varieties of varying quality. The city of Cádiz, Spain, was a leading center for garum production. The sauce made there from the innards of Atlantic tuna found buyers throughout the Roman world. Today, the remains of these ancient garum workshops have been restored, and Cádiz hosts a museum dedicated to the famous sauce.
While garum was once indispensable, it later disappeared almost completely. It survived on a very small scale on a few Greek islands, on Gökçeada in the Aegean Sea, and on the Princes’ Islands off Istanbul. Today, however, there are sporadic efforts to revive it. In Spain, Michelin-starred chef Pere Planaguma produces a garum he calls “Escata.” To make it, he partnered with a sardine canning factory in Catalonia. He collects the factory’s waste — bones, heads, tails and fish innards — and ferments them using traditional methods. As the fish matter decomposes and settles to the bottom, it leaves a clear, amber-brown liquid on top. According to those who have sampled it, the result is excellent. Personally, I find it far too fishy and think it is best left in the depths of history.

The 2026 Nobel winners will be announced between Oct 5 and 12, starting with the Nobel Prize in Medicine on Oct 5. (AFP photo)
Donald Trump’s intense campaigning last year for the Nobel Peace Prize has left the awarding committee treading carefully for this year’s pick, experts said ahead of next week’s prize announcement.
The U.S. president’s outspoken calls to be given the accolade put the five-member committee under unprecedented pressure last year.
The situation grew even more delicate when the laureate, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, later gave Trump her Nobel gold medal, judging he deserved it after the capture of President Nicolas Maduro.
The Nobel jury knows it is being closely watched by the U.S. president again this year.
“There’s always a lot of lobbying, and ultimately perhaps also attempts to exert pressure on the committee,” the secretary of the Nobel committee, Kristian Berg Harpviken, told AFP in an interview.
“So in one sense we’re very used to that.”
According to several experts, the Trump saga could lead the committee to choose a laureate who enjoys broad consensus when the name is revealed on Oct. 9.
“After last year’s prize, maybe they’re seeking a less controversial situation this year,” the acting director of the Peace Research Institute of Oslo, Haakon Gjerlow, told AFP.
His favorite pick would be a joint prize to Save the Children and Mykola Kuleba, a Ukrainian children’s rights activist campaigning for the return of Ukrainian children illegally taken to Russia from occupied territories.
The other closely-watched Nobel is that for literature, to be announced on Oct. 8.
After honoring Hungarian author Laszlo Krasznahorkai last year, the Swedish Academy that selects the literature laureate could this time go for a woman writer, possibly from Latin America, according to some literary critics surveyed by AFP.
“In recent years, there has been a lot of talk about the ‘Latin American literary miracle’, this new generation that came after the male authors devoted to magical realism, like Gabriel Garcia Marquez,” said Lina Kalmteg, literary critic at Swedish public radio SR.
“In this new wave, it’s women who are taking the lead, with writing often tinged with feminism, but also often quite dark and violent, punctuated by surreal touches,” she noted.

October 7 families join election race with hope of healing Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:03:58 UTC
15:03:58 KST

October 7 families join election race with hope of healing Israel
TEL AVIV, Oct 5 - One was inspired by her son's last stand trying to fight off attackers rampaging through a kibbutz. Another by her son's final words as militants tossed grenades into a bomb shelter packed with fleeing revellers from a music festival. A third by the brothers he campaigned to bring home from captivity in Gaza.
Three years since Hamas' October 7 attack, at least nine Israelis from families directly caught up in the deadliest day in the country's history are running for parliament in an election this month. They represent parties running the gamut of political views, but all say they aim to heal Israel's wounds.
The militants who burst into southern Israel in 2023 killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages to Gaza. Michal Hirsch Negri's son, Roee, died fighting Hamas attackers in Kibbutz Be'eri, where 1 in 10 residents were killed.
Soon after the surprise attack began, Roee, newly married and on a career path in high-tech, scrambled comrades in his reserve counter-terrorism military unit, who later recounted their last moments with him.
"He told them: 'We are not looking at the bodies. We are here to save people. We are here to save our country.' And this is a sentence that is engraved in my heart," said his mother.
Hirsch Negri, 60, is running in Together, led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and part of an alliance of left, right and centre parties aiming to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's nationalist-religious coalition.
"Everyone knows what's bad. Everyone knows what is broken. Talking about how bad it is or how bad the government is won't get us anywhere. My Roee, he always looked at the situation, analysed it and said, okay, now what can we do to fix it?"
'ON A MISSION'
One of her running mates is Noam Tibon, 64, a former general whose son was trapped with his young family in their home on Nahal Oz, another kibbutz attacked by Hamas. Tibon and his wife set out from Tel Aviv to rescue their son, battling en route with Hamas militants and evacuating wounded to hospital.
"October 7 was the biggest failure in our history and I saw it with my own eyes," he said. Netanyahu has rejected blame for the security breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation.
Sharon Sharabi, 51, running in the right-wing Israel Our Home party, says he witnessed Israel's leadership failings when he campaigned for a deal to free Gaza hostages, including his brothers Yossi and Eli, both seized by Hamas from Be'eri.
Yossi did not survive captivity. Eli, whose wife and two teenage daughters were slain in the kibbutz, was released in early 2025 after almost 500 days.
"I understood that even after the hostages come back, that I can't stand aside and let mediocre people keep running the country," Sharabi said. "I understood that I have to leave my life behind, to go on a mission to remedy, to return the state of Israel to its true values."
Not all see removing the coalition as the path forward. Talik Gvili, whose police officer son Ran was the last Israeli hostage whose remains were recovered from Gaza, was personally chosen by Netanyahu as a candidate on his party's slate.
"I am continuing the mission Rani was on. He went to defend Israel," she said in a party campaign video. "I want a strong leader, someone I can count on," she said of Netanyahu. "He promised to bring Rani home and he did. He promised to make a change in the Middle East and he did."
'CONTINUE AFTER ME'
But most of the candidates from October 7 families support parties aligned against Netanyahu, driven by what they see as failings on that day and since.
Shira Shapiro, 51, is running as a candidate for Yashar, a new opposition centrist party led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot whose own soldier son was killed in Gaza.
Shapiro said she and other parents of October 7 victims "are trying to take this pain and give it meaning, to grow from it. This is also what we need to do on a national level."
Her eldest son Aner, a 22-year-old off-duty soldier and musician, had attended the Nova music festival attacked on October 7 and took cover with 26 others in a roadside bomb shelter.
As the Hamas men lobbed grenades into the packed shelter, Aner tossed them out. His last moments were caught in dashcam footage, an audio recording made by one of the victims before she was killed and a photo taken by a survivor.
Aner told the others that if he is hurt, they must continue.
"I hear his voice say 'continue after me', he meant continue throwing the grenades but I hear his voice saying 'continue after me'," said Shapiro. "And I have to continue after him. And that's why I'm here." REUTERS

Ukraine scrambles for money to fight war as Russian strikes batter economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:03:45 UTC
15:03:45 KST

Ukraine scrambles for money to fight war as Russian strikes batter economy
KYIV, Oct 5 - Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, is struggling to survive. Russian airstrikes have brought the city's huge steel plant and mines to a standstill, dragging the local economy to its knees.
Mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said the sprawling industrial city — which stretches along the banks of the Inhulets River — was doing everything possible to ensure its hospitals remain open, the lights remain on in kindergartens and schools, and buses keep running.
"In Kryvyi Rih, the situation is actually worse than anywhere else, apart from the front line itself," Vilkul, 52, a former mining executive, said in a video address.
The financial squeeze on the city of about 600,000 people underlines the challenges facing Ukraine as the government navigates its biggest budget crisis since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Last month, the city's largest employer — ArcelorMittal's hulking mining and steelmaking complex — suspended its operations following a series of Russian ballistic missile strikes that darkened its furnaces.
The prospects for next year, Vilkul said, are bleak.
"It's about survival. Right now, we need to survive," he said.
It's a scene played out across Ukraine's once-mighty steel industry, which accounted for a tenth of economic output before the war. Giant mills in Zaporizhzhia in the southeast and other industrial cities stand silent and exports have stopped.
An escalation in Russia's drone and missile strikes this summer destroyed factories and warehouses across Ukraine, damaged ports and railways, and forced shops and businesses to close, slowing the growth of the economy and tax revenue.
Meanwhile, the technology-driven war is becoming ever more expensive for Ukraine to fight.
Billions of euros in foreign loans have been delayed by failure to pass bills including unpopular tax reforms and anti-corruption legislation demanded by Ukraine's Western allies, leaving a gaping hole in state coffers.
Ukraine needs $56 billion to fund that gap this year —equivalent to about a quarter of its economic output. Of that, $27 billion is military spending.
To bridge the shortfall, Ukrainian officials met European partners in Brussels last week to discuss bringing forward disbursements due next year under a €90-billion ($101-billion) EU loan. The European Commission and Ukraine said they had identified funds to close the gap this year.
But three sources familiar with the talks said accelerating these payments risked increasing budget pressure next year - at a time when looming election campaigns in European allies including France and Poland could erode support for Kyiv.
Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi acknowledges the situation is "challenging". The government has been forced to freeze non-essential spending — including reconstruction of damaged buildings and infrastructure — to prioritise military spending, public sector wages and pensions.
"All resources should be channelled into critically important areas," Koretskyi told reporters.
WAR COSTS SOAR, DOMESTIC REVENUES FALL
Two years ago, a single day of fighting cost Ukraine $140 million, but that figure has jumped to $190 million, according to Roksolana Pidlasa, the head of parliament's budget committee. And that does not include direct military support to Kyiv from its Western allies.
Rising costs are driven partly by the need for expensive medium- and long-range weapons capable of striking Russia's oil refineries and military factories to reduce Moscow's ability to continue its war.
Plus, the wage bill for an expanded army is higher than ever before, and the state must support a growing number of military families of disabled or deceased soldiers.
"Expenditure will continue to rise," Pidlasa told a conference in Kyiv. "This is one more pragmatic reason why the US and Europe need to act faster to force (Russia) to end this war."
In the first nine months of this year, Ukraine spent more than $44 billion on defence alone, data showed. That does not include in-kind military support from allies.
In the same period, the government was able to raise only about $42 billion in tax revenue as the economy slowed.
Pidlasa said that in the first nine months of this year Ukraine's budget lost over 49.5 billion hryvnias ($1.1 billion) in tax revenue because of Russian attacks that not only damaged property and goods, but disrupted logistics and shut shops and businesses for hours at a time.
By the end of the year, the cumulative losses could rise to 70 billion hryvnias, the government estimates.
"We have not a temporary but a structural problem with the revenues at the very time when spending really requires resources," said Oleksandra Myronenko, an economist at the Centre for Economic Strategies, a Kyiv-based think tank.
Some Ukrainian businesses have started to scale back operations. Others have put capital expenditure on hold as the country braces for a difficult winter. Business sentiment and economic expectations are darkening.
Vasyl Khmelnytskyi, founder of an industrial park in the city of Bila Tserkva near Kyiv, said he had scrapped plans to build three new factories.
"The risks are simply too great right now — both for the business and for the people," he said in a Facebook post.
Ukraine's agricultural sector — its largest source of export revenues — has been particularly hard hit. Russian attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea ports led to a 36.6% fall in grain exports year-on-year in September.
About $40 billion in export revenue is at risk this year as a result of the blockade, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said.
Even with tens of billions of euros in foreign support, Ukraine's economy is expected to grow only between 0.5% and 1.5% this year, economists say — down from 1.8% in 2025.
FOREIGN AID IS DELAYED
During more than four years of intense fighting, Ukraine has been able to maintain macroeconomic and financial stability thanks to fiscal support from its Western partners, receiving nearly $200 billion since Russia's invasion.
But $29.5 billion in foreign aid is now at risk this year because of delays in passing reforms, Koretskyi said. The government has postponed about $900 million of capital spending until December, in the hope the legislation will be passed.
The aim is to pass all the required legislation in parliament by October 15, Koretskyi said.
"Only then we will get all the money," Koretskyi said. "This is absolutely vital. It needs to be done as soon as possible."
Legislators are now discussing the budget for next year. The government has proposed record defence budget spending of $110 billion. This figure does not include direct military aid.
Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko has estimated that the unfunded budget gap for the next year is already more than $32 billion.
Part of the solution, Marchenko said, is to use frozen Russian assets in Europe to fund Ukraine's budget. EU countries immobilised some €210 billion of Russian central bank assets after Moscow invaded Ukraine.
"Ukraine continues to mobilise domestic resources, but the scale of Russia's war puts clear limits on our capacity," Marchenko said on X. REUTERS

World’s largest annual gathering dedicated to space opens in Türkiye’s Antalya

2026-10-05

Beril Canakci
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
The world’s space community gathered in Türkiye’s Mediterranean city of Antalya on Monday for the 77th International Astronautical Congress, bringing together space agency chiefs, astronauts, scientists, engineers, industry executives and policymakers to discuss the future of space.
The five-day congress, running through Oct. 9 at the NEST Congress and Exhibition Center in Belek, is being held in Türkiye for the first time.
The theme for this year is "The World Needs More Space."
More than 10,000 participants from over 100 countries are expected to attend the event, which is organized annually by the International Astronautical Federation (IAF).
Often described as the world’s largest annual space gathering, the congress combines scientific and technical sessions with exhibitions, business meetings and high-level discussions. This year’s program will cover subjects ranging from lunar exploration, satellites and artificial intelligence to space security, sustainability and international cooperation.
The event has attracted a record 8,330 research abstracts from 108 countries, with more than 4,000 presentations scheduled across over 180 technical sessions.
Türkiye is hosting the congress under the coordination of the Industry and Technology Ministry, with the Turkish Space Agency as host and SAHA, a Turkish defense and aerospace industry cluster, as co-host. Anadolu is the event’s global communications partner.
The event comes after Türkiye signed the Artemis Accords at NASA Headquarters in Washington, DC on Aug. 31, becoming the 71st signatory to the international framework outlining principles for peaceful, transparent and sustainable exploration of the Moon, Mars and beyond.
On Sunday, Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir hosted the traditional Ministers and Members of Parliament Meeting in Antalya, bringing together ministers, parliamentarians, space agency heads and senior representatives from 38 countries. The meeting adopted the Antalya Declaration, a Turkish-initiated text calling for peaceful, sustainable and responsible approaches to space, which was endorsed by 32 participants from 21 countries.

My search for the perfect Italian aperitivo in Verona
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:00:50 UTC
15:00:50 KST

I arrived in Verona, I admit, without a particularly clear idea of what aperitivo meant. In Italy, the ritual – broadly, a drink and something small to eat before a meal – speaks a different dialect in every city.
Milan has turned it into a polished after-work institution. In Venice, it is more itinerant: an ombra (a small glass of wine) along with a cicchetto (a bite-size snack) and then on to the next bacaro (one of the city’s traditional wine bars). Verona follows another logic.
Veronese wine writer Angelo Peretti has described the osteria (the traditional tavern at the heart of the city’s drinking culture) as a Verona institution: somewhere its social life takes shape over a gòto (the local word for a glass of wine), usually with something small to eat at the counter, often while standing.
I thought I understood. Then, at about 9.30am one morning, while drinking coffee opposite the Teatro Filarmonico, I noticed that aperitivo had already begun without me. A woman ordered a bianchetto, a small glass of white wine. A couple, already defeated by the heat, asked for two spritzes. Two friends shared a bottle of sparkling wine.
Nobody had announced that it was “aperitivo time”. More strikingly, nobody seemed to find any of this unusual.
That was when my search really began. I decided not to look for one type of bar, or even one type of drink. What mattered was whether I would actually stop there for an aperitivo – alone, with friends or simply while waiting for dinner.
Caffè Monte Baldo
At Monte Baldo, which opened in 1909, the counter was still being set up, with a man I took to be the owner assembling the day’s tartine (small open sandwiches with various toppings). A very young waitress offered to help me choose a wine. There were more than 30 wines by the glass, mostly priced between €5.50 and €11. I chose an alta langa, a traditional-method sparkling wine from Piedmont, partly because the bottle was still unopened. They opened it without hesitation.
With lunch ahead, I ordered two tartine: baccalà mantecato (Veneto’s creamy stockfish spread whipped with olive oil) and boiled egg with anchovy. Both were excellent: fresh bread, generous toppings, clearly just made. The tartine cost €4.60; the wine €7.
As I was leaving, a man walked in carrying a motorcycle helmet. Before he had time to order came the question: “Your usual?” However many tourists pass through Verona, somebody still has a usual.
8.5/10
Antica Bottega del Vino
This is one of Verona’s great wine institutions. I arrived before 7pm, as the tartine counter was being filled. The mood was formal: staff in crisp uniforms and a queue of slightly bewildered tourists. With one person serving, it moved slowly as he explained the wines, €3 tartine and where to eat them – at the bar, at small indoor tables, or outside.
I chose an €8 glass of franciacorta, Lombardy’s traditional-method sparkling wine, with two tartine: pancetta coppata (cured pork neck wrapped in pancetta) and gorgonzola cream. Both were generously topped, though the bread, while perfectly decent, wasn’t anything to write home about. Total: €14.
As I drank, nearby tables were laid for dinner and reserved signs appeared. I asked whether I should move. “Absolutely not.” Those few aperitivo tables, I was told, stay for drinkers unless the place is exceptionally busy.
6.5/10
Tor-Tor
A sommelier I trust at one of Verona’s grander restaurants sent me to Tor-Tor, perhaps revealing more interest in wine than in the finer points of aperitivo. Still, it seemed worth a punt. Tucked down a side street behind the Arena, every outdoor table was taken; inside, a regular occupied the counter, deep in wine talk with the owners.
The blackboard and a small wooden menu board revealed a serious selection of natural wines, with plenty from Veneto. I went for a €7 orange wine – white grapes fermented in their skins – which came with popcorn, then added two €2 polpette (small savoury balls, one meat, one aubergine) plus €1.50 olives dressed with oil and chilli.
The polpette did the job nicely; the wine was excellent and expertly recommended. The crowd was overwhelmingly local, and the regular at the counter was still talking wine when I left.
8/10
Osteria Ai Preti
Just across the Adige river in Veronetta, on the edge of Verona’s main tourist circuit, Ai Preti feels like a neighbourhood local. It is large, with dark wood throughout, and has the sort of retro look that comes from never having tried to look retro.
Two counters divide the food between cold tartine and hot snacks. I chose one with baccalà mantecato, another with caramelised onions, and a horse meat polpetta. Tartine cost €2, the polpetta slightly less; with a €4 glass of wine, the whole aperitivo came in under €10.
By 7.45pm, both displays were almost bare, although my polpetta seemed freshly cooked. The crowd looked entirely local, paying far more attention to one another than to the labels. Magazines lay around for anyone drinking alone. Here, aperitivo felt like the working day quietly unwinding.
7/10
Velvet
I was early for dinner. The restaurant next door was still closed and I had half an hour to kill. Filling the gap before dinner is, after all, the primary function of the aperitivo.
Velvet occupies part of a 15th-century palazzo. There is a handsome counter with stools, though I chose a small table. Three nearby tables were already occupied by a more dressed-up crowd than I had encountered in Veronetta, drinking and talking without much hurry.
There was plenty of wine on the list, but I went for a €12 negroni. It arrived with fried plantain crisps, cashews and little savoury pastries with tomato – at no extra cost. A separate food menu offers more substantial bites, including edamame falafel and chicken wings.
By the time I’d finished my drink, the restaurant next door was open. Half an hour neatly accounted for.
8/10
Osteria da Morandin
Morandin was the only place I visited twice. My first visit was almost accidental – a glass of wine became dinner – so I returned a week later, just before 9pm, to make sure I hadn’t simply got lucky. On paper, its long afternoon closure, from 2.30 to 7pm, had been my only doubt.
It was another punishingly hot evening in Veronetta. Every outside table was taken and the fans inside did little more than move the heat around. I was wearing absurd red-and-blue striped trousers. A man I took to be one of the owners, there as a customer, noticed our near-matching trousers and came over for a high five. “They say we look like we’re in pyjamas. They don’t understand fashion.”
Wines run from €2.50 to €6 and, even at that relatively late hour, the cicchetti display was the fullest I had seen: battered vegetables, frittata, prawn skewers, €1.30 meatballs with tastasal (seasoned pork mince) and €1.80 tartine. I chose a durello, the crisp local sparkling wine from the Lessini hills, a meatball and a tuna-and-egg tartina.
The waiters were run off their feet; regulars greeted one another and foreign voices were scarce. Fifteen minutes later, I asked about dinner. “Full.” Ten minutes on, a table appeared. Aperitivo had not replaced dinner; it had made staying for it irresistible.
10/10

Pasture lives: the rebel cheesemakers preserving an Alpine tradition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:00:49 UTC
15:00:49 KST

My journey into the world of storico ribelle began with a shared passion for photography and the mountains. A close friend of mine lives in the Orobie Alps. He loves the mountains and the natural environment that surrounds him, and we share the same passion for photography. When I finally went to visit him, I discovered a way of experiencing the mountains that was very different from the one I knew growing up in the Apennines, where I come from.
What struck me was not only the landscape, but the relationship people still have with it. Here, I discovered a world where the mountain is not simply a place to visit or explore, but a place to live and work. A world where cheese is still a tradition rather than an industrial product, and where the rhythms of the seasons, the animals and the daily work of the alpeggiatori – the mountain herders – are still deeply connected.
There was a poetry in this way of life that immediately inspired me. Waking before sunrise, milking, making cheese, moving with the animals and working until darkness: there was almost no separation between life and work.
I felt compelled to photograph this world. I wanted to tell the story of people who continue to choose a demanding way of life in a time when agriculture is increasingly industrialised and traditional knowledge is disappearing.
In the Orobie Alps, cheese is inseparable from the landscape that gives it life. Steep pastures, stone shelters and seasonal migration have shaped a rural culture for centuries. Animals move with the seasons, milk follows them, and cheese becomes a way of preserving a way of life.
Storico ribelle was born from this tradition – and from a decision to defend it. For generations, bitto cheese was made in small Alpine dairies and exchanged locally for essentials such as grain and salt. During summer, herders moved their animals progressively higher, following the pastures. Along the routes, calecc – simple stone shelters – were used for milking and transforming fresh milk into cheese. The wheels were taken to mountain cellars, or casère, where they could mature for years.
In 1996, the introduction of the bitto DOP (protected designation of origin) brought new regulations. Some producers considered the requirements incompatible with the traditional Alpine system they wanted to preserve. They chose to continue making cheese according to their own methods, outside the DOP. Eventually, a new name emerged: storico ribelle, or historic rebel.
The name reflects resistance, but the deeper story is one of continuity: preserving a relationship between livestock, pasture, milk, cheese and mountain life. That relationship can still be found across Val Gerola, Valtellina and Val Brembana.
At Alpe Pedena, Oreste Pedrelli, 56, has spent the last 10 years herding. He has been making cheese since he was eight, learning the craft from his grandparents. At Alpe Ancogno Soliva, Carlo Duca works with his brother Luigi. Their cheese is renowned for its extraordinary ageing potential, with some wheels maturing for up to 10 years.
At about 2,000 metres, Trona Vaga is the highest storico ribelle Alpine pasture. Manuele, born in 1988, runs the pasture with his partner, Erica, who came to cheesemaking from a completely different background. She studied languages and taught herself the craft as an adult.
Their stories reveal that tradition can be inherited, but it can also be chosen. This is particularly important among a younger generation. Michele Sassella, 15, continues the practice with his mother and sister in memory of his father, Alfio, who dedicated his life to protecting mountain breeds, natural farming rhythms and Alpine biodiversity.
Davide Peregalli, 16, has spent his summers at Alpe Vesenda since he was eight. Gioele Pedercini, 17, has already completed three summer seasons as an Alpine herder while studying agriculture. Valentina, 20, brings another perspective: with a degree in agricultural studies, she is the young cheesemaker at Alpe Orta Soliva.
They represent a generation that is not simply inheriting tradition, but deciding whether it has a future.
That future is fragile. Climate change is already affecting the tradition: scarce rain, increasingly violent storms, and pastures turning yellow even at high altitude. At the same time, increasingly demanding regulations make small-scale cheesemaking more expensive and labour-intensive. Yet the work continues.
Quality here comes with an extraordinary human cost. It means waking before sunrise, working throughout the day and going to bed after sunset. Every hour follows the animals. Milking, often by hand, is followed by transforming fresh milk into cheese. There is little distinction between work and life.
Storico ribelle represents more than a product. It is the result of pasture, animals, knowledge and time – and of people willing to resist the disappearance of a world.
The rebellion began with a choice not to follow a prescribed system. Today, its future depends on another choice: whether a new generation will continue to climb the mountain, care for the animals, make the cheese – and keep alive a way of life that exists almost nowhere else.

Apple iPhone 18 Pro review: big changes for small differences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:00:49 UTC
15:00:49 KST

Apple’s smaller Pro iPhone gets the best kind of spec bump for 2026: longer battery life, faster chips and a fancy new variable aperture for the main camera.
The iPhone 18 Pro is one of a pair of slab phones launched alongside Apple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, and is the cheapest of the new phones, with a regular iPhone 18 yet to be announced.
It isn’t exactly low cost, priced from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099), with a £100 or equivalent rise over previous models courtesy of RAMageddon.
Having fully revamped the design of the body for the iPhone 17 Pro, the new model is a modest refinement. It is 7g heavier and the back glass now matches the colour of the aluminium body, which is available in a handful of new shades.
Apple has shrunk the amount of the screen taken up by the Face ID camera, allowing the dynamic island to show three continuing tasks, up from two on previous devices. It also now shows the 3/4/5G indicator next to the signal level when playing music, which is a most appreciated feature for public transport commuters sorely missed on previous models.
Otherwise, the 6.3in screen is one of the very best on a phone: super bright, crisp and smooth, while being big enough without making the phone enormous. An anti-glare coating makes it much easier to see outside, too.
Specifications
- Screen: 6.3in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)
- Processor: Apple A20 Pro
- RAM: 12GB
- Storage: 256GB, 512GB or 1TB
- Operating system: iOS 27
- Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing
- Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS
- Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)
- Dimensions: 150 x 71.9 x 8.75mm
- Weight: 211g
Faster chip and longer battery life
The 18 Pro has Apple’s new A20 Pro chip, which is about 27% faster than the A19 Pro in last year’s model, with about 45% faster graphics performance. Since the A19 Pro was no slouch, that’s quite the leap and puts it miles ahead of the competition, ready to handle anything.
The phone has a redesigned cooling system for longer peak performance, too, which is especially useful for running games on top settings.
The battery lasts a solid six hours longer than the iPhone 17 Pro, managing to stretch to about two days between charges with more than six hours of active screen use across apps, browsing, messaging and photos. Even with the heaviest of use while out and about, the 18 Pro managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. Most people will only need to charge it every other day.
iOS 27 with new Siri
The 18 Pro ships running iOS 27, which was released for the rest of the iPhone line on 14 September. It refines the relatively controversial Liquid Glass redesign from last year and speeds up the system, including app launches. But the big new addition is Apple’s revamped Siri, backed by Google’s AI technologies.
Siri AI, as the new system is called, is significantly more capable of understanding and answering questions than previous iterations. It is a chatbot like most other AI assistants, but it is less chatty and sycophantic than others, being more likely to just get the job done. As well as a choice of voices, there are sliders to control how fast it talks and how expressive its responses are. It has its own app where you can review previous interactions, but it is accessible anywhere on the phone via the side button, is built into Spotlight search and can see what’s on your screen, including when using the camera.
It can also offer suggestions, such as adding an event to your calendar from the messages or mail apps, and attempts to display relevant information from your emails in the phone app when you call a business. But Siri can only do so if you use Apple’s apps, so if you use WhatsApp for texting and Gmail for your email, none of it works.
Sustainability
The battery will last more than 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £119. Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £349. The specialists iFixit awarded the phone a seven out of 10 for repairability.
It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
Camera
The 18 Pro has a similar camera system to last year’s 17 Pro with one big addition, a variable aperture for the main camera.
That means it has a very good 18MP centre stage selfie camera on the front and three 48MP cameras on the rear: main, 0.5x ultrawide and 4x telephoto.
The ultrawide is one of the best on a phone, handy for landscapes and group shots. The 4x telephoto is very good too, full of detail and manages lower light settings well. It shoots excellent photos with a crop zoom to reach 8x before digital zoom is required, which is a little behind rivals with 5x/10x telephoto zooms.
The variable aperture on the main camera can be left on automatic or controlled manually. It allows the camera to open wider than previous models for better low light performance, speeding up night mode shots and reducing unwanted motion blur.
But it also enables a number of creative uses, such as making starbursts by narrowing the aperture when shooting lights, which is very fun, or controlling the depth of field in your photo. However, because the iPhone’s camera is tiny compared with an APS-C or full-frame camera, the difference in depth of field – where the foreground and background of the image are either in focus or blown out for a nice bokeh effect – is pretty minor. When shooting something up close, manually closing the aperture to f/4.0 can bring things in the foreground or background into focus, but otherwise the difference for most shots is small.
The 18 Pro’s camera has a number of other useful upgrades. My favourite is AI-powered focus tracking that keeps a subject in focus as it moves about or into and out of the frame, which has been one of the best features of a Pixel camera for years and is extremely handy for fast-moving children or pets.
Apple has also added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles feature to customise how the camera shoots photos beyond what was introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, including film simulation. Finally, the new Apple Reference Image feature can sign an image for authenticity, on a per pixel level directly on the sensor, to help later prove a shot is not AI-generated, similar to a digital negative.
The camera shoots some of the very best video on a phone, too. New for this year is the ability to convert a regular video to a cinematic one after the fact, a bit like the excellent automatic portrait mode for photos.
Price
The iPhone 18 Pro costs from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099).
For comparison, the iPhone 17 costs £899, the iPhone Air costs £1,099, the iPhone 18 Pro Max costs £1,299, the Google Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra costs £1,359.
Verdict
The iPhone 18 Pro is an iterative upgrade on an already great device from last year. Inside, it has some quite big changes, but their impact is fairly minor on the whole experience.
The new A20 Pro chip is super fast, but you can’t really notice the difference day to day, as previous iPhone chips have already been very quick. The extended battery life is great, but most people will still have to charge it every other day. The smaller camera cutout in the dynamic island now shows three continuing activities instead of two. Even the variable aperture in the main camera makes only a small difference to image quality unless you’re really trying to get creative.
The screen is fantastic and big enough. The aluminium body feels great to hold. The cameras are some of the best on a phone and even Siri is better now.
All of these things add up. The 18 Pro is without doubt the best iPhone ever made and at this size is one of the very best smaller phones available. It’s just not a transformative change unless you’re upgrading from a much older model and it now costs even more thanks to RAMageddon.
 Pros: relatively compact, great screen, better dynamic island, longer battery life, great cameras, variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.
Cons: small upgrade on last year, expensive, heavier than previous model, AI tools still lag behind top competitors.

Holiday cottage company insisted on a death certificate to amend our break
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
06:00:49 UTC
15:00:49 KST

We booked a break with Sykes Holiday Cottages for 11 of us to celebrate my mum’s 80th birthday last February. The cost was £2,400, paid for by my 87-year-old dad, but it was my husband who made the booking.
In January, my husband was diagnosed with aggressive lymphoma, and he died 10 days before the trip. My parents and some other members of the party still planned to take the holiday, and my dad informed Sykes of the death, since my husband was their point of contact.
Sykes declared that the booking could not be honoured in my late husband’s name and that they would need a copy of his death certificate to move it into my name. We did not have one since an inquest into the death had been ordered.
Sykes said a copy of my marriage certificate would suffice. I submitted this, only to be told that “an official document recognised by the state that confirms the passing of the deceased” was required.
We provided a screenshot of the inquest listing from the coroner’s court website but were advised that this was not sufficient evidence.
My GP wrote a letter confirming the death, but Sykes did not reply, and by then we were all too distressed to continue.
Later, Sykes sent numerous emails to my late husband’s email address asking whether he had enjoyed the stay. We never received a refund, and I have not felt emotionally strong enough to do anything further before now.
TB, Huddersfield, West Yorkshire
I could hardly believe what I was reading as I trawled through Sykes’s correspondence. Its response, on being informed of your husband’s untimely death, was to send him an email asking for information.
When Sykes received the requested marriage certificate, the company simultaneously stated in an email that this provided sufficient proof for the booking to be transferred to your name, and that the booking could not be transferred without an official confirmation of death.
The GP letter confirming the death merely elicited an email saying Sykes would be in touch. By then, the trip was two days away. Sykes still did not amend the booking name, nor did it acknowledge the link to the coroner’s inquest listing.
The next you heard from them was the first of several emails addressed to your late husband hoping that he had enjoyed the holiday. When you asked them to stop using his email address, Sykes apologised for the “inconvenience”.
Four days later, when you had to complain about another such email to him, you were told unapologetically that feedback forms are sent automatically. By then, Sykes had been informed multiple times over a fortnight that your husband had died.
Sykes, I discover, does not have an official bereavement policy which, given the size of the business, is poor enough. But empathy does not require an official mandate and you received none.
Its onerous name change requirements are more suitable for a visa application than checking into a Cumbrian cottage. It refunded the £2,400 pronto when I got in touch and added £150 in “goodwill”. I think that’s a paltry sum for the distress it caused, but you have accepted it so you can put the ordeal behind you.
A spokesperson said: “We have contacted the family directly to apologise and resolve the matter, and are reviewing our processes to ensure situations like this are always handled with the care and sensitivity they deserve.”
Hats off to first-class customer service
Our spirits need some good news, so here are some tales of how customer service ought to be.
“We bought a secondhand Scandibørn bed from a third-party seller and found four screws were missing,” writes CC. “They were so specialist that no shop even knew what they were called. We contacted Scandibørn with low expectations of help, but they immediately offered to send us the missing screws for free. Exemplary customer service, which has earned a customer for life.”
MS, meanwhile, raises his revamped hat to Tilley. “Thirty years ago I bought a Tilley hat, which became a constant companion on walks and holidays. It was beginning to show its age and, since the label promised a lifetime guarantee, I contacted Tilley. I was asked to submit photographs and was promptly invited to choose from three designs. The replacement was dispatched within days, with a handling charge of £20. Sadly, this one will outlast me.”

Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject to our terms and conditions.

Fund repayments in focus as parliament resumes work

Parliament will resume legislative work on Oct. 6, with payment problems affecting about 450,000 fund investors expected to feature in debates alongside bills on the Turkish Red Crescent and foreign accommodation platforms.
Lawmakers are expected to raise the fund payment issue through parliamentary motions. Officials from the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) are also considering safeguards to prevent similar problems.
Options include caps on the combined holdings in individual stocks of funds managed by the same company, minimum thresholds linked to stress tests and early warning mechanisms.
Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan will brief the Planning and Budget Commission on Oct. 6 on global developments, Türkiye’s economy, inflation and monetary policy. He is also expected to discuss the possible monetary policy implications of disruption in the fund market.
The General Assembly will first debate a bill setting out the Turkish Red Crescent’s duties, powers, rights and exemptions.
The proposal would make the organization solely responsible for receiving and using cash and in-kind aid sent to Türkiye by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, the International Committee of the Red Cross and national societies.
Meanwhile, the Public Works, Reconstruction, Transportation and Tourism Commission will consider legislation regulating foreign online accommodation platforms, including Airbnb and Booking.com.
The bill would require these platforms to obtain permits from the Culture and Tourism Ministry. Existing operators would have three months to apply after the legislation takes effect.
Platforms would also pay a contribution of 0.075 percent to the Türkiye Tourism Promotion and Development Agency, calculated on their digital services tax base.
The legislation could pave the way for Booking.com to resume domestic reservations made from within Türkiye, which have been restricted since 2017.
Political parties will also resume their parliamentary group meetings on Tuesdays and Wednesdays, with leaders expected to address the fund payment problems.

Donald Trump has criticised the UK authorities decision to release six men on bail after they were arrested following an incident near airbase RAF Fairford.
The United States confirmed Sunday that it has withdrawn all B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford, a British airbase at the centre of a counter-terrorism probe after a mysterious security incident last month.
Police were called to the base in southwest England on 27 September after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in "suspicious" activity. The scare forced evacuations at 85 homes near the airbase, which was used by the United States to launch strikes on Iran.
Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but instead "a quantity of petrol was recovered," according to counter-terrorism police.
A statement from a Pentagon official said Sunday "we can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States." The statement noted that "operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time."
Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel thievery, as energy prices in the UK hit record highs this week. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident, a charge rejected by Tehran.
Six London-based Britons arrested in the incident, including a UK-Iranian dual national, were released on bail, drawing rebuke from Washington.
"I wouldn't have done that," US President Donald Trump told reporters, as his Secretary of State Marco Rubio alleged a "foreign actor" was involved. Iran's embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.
Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran," and US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing from the base. Fairford is the only airbase on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.

Governor SBP unveils market-based, sustainable Pasban Remittance Reward Scheme with Rs16 billion in annual prizes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:58:37 UTC
14:58:37 KST

Governor State Bank of Pakistan, Mr. Jameel Ahmad, inaugurated the Pasban Remittance Reward Scheme. The market-based rewards initiative has been launched under the auspices of the Pakistan Banks Association (PBA) by the banking industry. It offers Rs16 billion in annual cash prizes to recognize and reward remittance customers using banking channels for home remittances sent to Pakistan. The scheme is funded entirely by the banking industry and does not entail any burden on the national exchequer. Developed under the patronage of the SBP, the scheme aims to further encourage overseas Pakistanis to use formal banking channels for sending remittances to their families and loved ones in Pakistan.
Speaking at the launch ceremony, Governor SBP Mr. Jameel Ahmad said that the SBP and the Government have been working closely with the PBA over the past few months to develop a self-sustaining and market-oriented remittance scheme that can continue to facilitate, encourage, and attract workers’ remittances from overseas Pakistanis through formal channels. He said that workers’ remittances are the backbone of millions of families across Pakistan. They help meet household expenditures, support education and healthcare, and provide resources for investment and economic opportunity.
The governor also highlighted the substantial strengthening of the country’s external account position. He noted that the external current account deficit, which had reached unsustainable levels in FY22 – causing a rapid depletion of foreign exchange (FX) reserves, has now been brought to manageable levels, supporting a sustained buildup in FX buffers. SBP’s FX reserves, which fell below US$3.0 billion in February 2023, now stand at US$21.4 billion. He emphasized that, unlike in the past, the continued strengthening of FX buffers has been driven primarily by FX purchases from the market rather than an accumulation of external debt. The Governor appreciated the contributions of overseas Pakistanis and highlighted the exceptional performance of workers’ remittances, which reached a record US$41.6 billion in FY26, compared with US$21.7 billion in FY19, nearly doubling over the period.
Governor, Mr. Ahmad, emphasized that these figures represent more than an improvement in key indicators; they reflect hard-earned stability and resilience that can help break the boom-bust cycles and place the Pakistan’s economy on a more sustainable growth path. He noted that the Government and the SBP have undertaken a range of policy and reform measures to support this turnaround. To promote exports, the Government provided tax incentives in the current year’s budget, while SBP, in coordination with stakeholders, designed targeted long-term financing and performance-based rebate schemes. The scope of the Roshan Digital Account (RDA) scheme has also been expanded to allow foreign investors and Pakistani residents, with declared foreign assets, besides overseas Pakistanis to invest through RDA channels. SBP has undertaken outreach initiatives, including a recent awareness session in the UK. In addition, IT companies and freelancers have been facilitated in opening foreign currency accounts and retaining export proceeds in those accounts.
The Governor also noted that the Government had introduced Home Remittance Incentive Schemes over the years to encourage the use of formal channels. These schemes helped develop the market, brought more financial institutions into the ecosystem, expanded Pakistan’s domestic and global reach, and strengthened the infrastructure needed to process growing volumes of remittances. As the market developed and the cost of these schemes increased, the Government and SBP undertook a planned and gradual transition towards a more sustainable, market-oriented model, in close coordination with the banking industry. Mr. Ahmad appreciated the banking industry’s continued support in strengthening formal remittance channels, noting that the launch of Pasban represents a further step in this transition. He said the initiative would help maintain the attractiveness of formal channels while recognizing the important contribution of overseas Pakistanis to Pakistan’s economy. The Governor also appreciated the Pakistan Banks Association and the banking industry for their partnership in developing and launching the scheme.
Briefing participants on the initiative, Muneer Kamal, CEO & Secretary General, PBA, said that the Pasban Scheme is the latest in a series of coordinated steps by SBP, the Government and the industry to support the external sector. He explained that this scheme builds on the remitter incentive banks have funded since July 2026, bringing the industry's annual commitment to close to Rs. 100 billion. He further added that this year, banks voluntarily cut the Export Refinance Facility markup by 3.0 points to 4.50% on new loans and rollovers, within the PKR 1,052 billion ERF limit, supporting the Government's export-led growth agenda alongside the Export-Import Bank's financing for exports of SME sector.
Mr. Kamal also briefed participants on the key features of the scheme. He apprised the forum that:
Mr. Zafar Masud, Chairman, PBA, said: "Pakistan's banks have consistently stepped up, taking over the Rs. 80 billion remitter incentive, cutting export refinance rates for our exporters, taking private, agricultural and SME lending to record levels, and supporting circular debt resolution. Overseas Pakistanis are an equally important part of this story, and the Pasban Scheme recognises their contribution, in partnership with SBP and the Government."
The draw results will be announced publicly on the following dedicated webpage of the Scheme, and on the websites and official social media handles of banks and PBA: https://1link.net.pk/pasbanrewards

The inaugural round of Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission (BJC) was held in Islamabad on 16-17 September 2026. The meeting marked the formal launch of the Commission, as envisaged in the 2013 China-Pakistan Agreement on Boundary Management System. 
The Pakistan delegation was led by Mr. Bilal Mahmood Chaudhary, Director General (China), Ministry of Foreign Affairs, while the Chinese delegation was led by Mr. Li Ya, Deputy Director General of the Department of Boundary and Ocean Affairs of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Senior representatives from various Ministries and Departments participated from both sides, including the Ministries of Foreign Affairs, Defense, Interior, Commerce, Communication and relevant Customs, Survey and other boundary management authorities.
Both sides described the establishment of the Commission as a vital milestone in further strengthening the Pakistan-China All-Weather Strategic Cooperative Partnership. The discussions at the inaugural meeting covered wide-ranging matters related to border management and cooperation, including cross-border coordination, movement of goods and people, joint border survey and people-to-people linkages.
The meeting concluded with the signing of minutes of the meeting to reaffirm the mutual consensus and set out the framework for future cooperation under the Commission. Both sides agreed to hold the next meeting of the Commission in China at mutually convenient dates.

Under Pakistan’s Chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State (CHS) for 2026–27, the first meeting of the Council of National Coordinators (CNC) of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) would be convened in Islamabad from 28–30 September 2026. The meeting would be chaired by the National Coordinator of the SCO for Pakistan and attended by National Coordinators from SCO Member States, along with representatives of the SCO Secretariat.
The National Coordinators would discuss a wide range of issues relating to SCO cooperation and coordination, including the programme of activities under Pakistan’s Chairmanship, preparations for upcoming SCO meetings and events, and other matters on the agenda of the Organization.
As the Chair of the SCO CHS for 2026–27, Pakistan would seek to advance the Organization’s objectives under the theme “Turning Vision into Action: Connectivity, Innovation and Shared Prosperity.” In this regard, Pakistan’s Chairmanship would focus on promoting greater connectivity, fostering innovation, enhancing economic cooperation, and strengthening people-to-people contacts, with a view to translating the shared vision of Member States into practical and mutually beneficial initiatives. Pakistan would work closely with all Member States and the SCO Secretariat to advance these priorities and further strengthen cooperation within the SCO.
The meeting marks an important initial engagement under Pakistan’s Chairmanship and would contribute to preparations for various high-level engagements and activities to be undertaken during the Chairmanship, including the meeting of the SCO Council of Heads of State to be hosted by Pakistan in August 2027.

Welcome to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

During the week, Ambassador Shafqat Ali Khan, Pakistan’s first Ambassador to the Republic of Armenia, presented his credentials to the President of Armenia. The appointment marks an important step towards strengthening mutually beneficial relations between Pakistan and Armenia and expanding cooperation in areas of common interest.

The Charge d’ Affaires was asked to convey to the Government of India that Pakistan strongly rejects this irresponsible action and urged India to strictly adhere to international law and bilateral agreements, particularly those aimed at preventing incidents at sea.
The Charge d’ Affaires of Pakistan’s High Commission in New Delhi will lodge a similar demarche with India’s Ministry of External Affairs this afternoon.

The action now rests on the other side. Pakistan has entered into mediation directly.
