So, that is operational, and the two countries are working at their respective competent levels. Further comment on this would not be possible at this stage.
On the next steps for the Makkah Agreement, as was announced in Istanbul, the meeting took place, and further meetings will be held in Pakistan, Saudi Arabia as well as Türkiye, in a sequential manner to further solidify the mechanisms.
(Khawaja Nayyar Iqbal, Media Today): Sir, the disastrous situation in the Middle East is now shifting to Makkah. So, does Pakistan understand that this is part of any great game? Does it mean an exacerbation of a regional war between Muslim countries?
Spokesperson: I think, depending on the geography, there have been countries that have been having their issues, and, as you know, regarding the Houthis’ issue, it is a militant organization, and there is also a government in Yemen.
Our effort in Yemen has been that peace and security should prevail, there should be reconciliation, and the situation should not impact the whole region.
In the context of a regional war between Muslim countries, I don’t think that kind of situation exists.
(Shaukat Piracha, AAJ News): Since you look after South Asian affairs as well, another ugly scene was witnessed at the Asian Cricket Championship when the Pakistani Interior Minister, who happened to be the head of the Asian Cricket Council, was there, but the winner, the Indian team, did not come up. This was also witnessed last year with the men’s team. How has sportsman spirit been deteriorating over the period of time? There is a craze for cricket in the subcontinent. Why are these things happening, sir?
(Muhammad Saleh Zafir, The News): Pakistan has refused to send its Pakistani hockey team to India.
Spokesperson: Spokesperson: So, it is regrettable that the BCCI reportedly declined to allow the Indian women’s team to go on stage and receive the trophy from Mohsin Naqvi Sahib, who is the President of the ACC. As rightly pointed out, this is not the first time it has happened. Last year, they did exactly the same thing, with the Indian men’s cricket team refusing to go and receive the trophy.
So, things have been kind of weaponized and securitized in every aspect of the relationship. Unfortunately, everything has happened because of the Indian stance, basically.
From Pakistan’s perspective, sports should not be weaponized, and they should be allowed to take place. But coming to your question, sir, precisely because of this reason, we do not see a point in sending a cricket or hockey team to India.
So, that is the point: we would not be sending our team to India, but we would be very happy to play against India in a third country, as we are currently playing cricket. So, that is the policy.
(Mateen Haider, WE News): This question is on the Palestinian situation. Israel is planning to launch a ground offensive in Gaza once again, and that plan has been made public. So, this is going to be a blatant violation of the Gaza peace accord and the Board of Peace. On the other hand, there are reports that the United States is planning to send an additional 2.8 billion dollars’ worth of ammunition and weapons to the Israeli government. So, how do you see this contradiction within the U.S.? On the one hand, it is promoting peace in Gaza. On the other hand, it is providing weapons to Israel, and Israel is openly killing Palestinians. This ground offensive is likely and will jeopardize peace in the region. Your comments, please.
(Anwer Abbas, 24 News): Sir, I want to know whether, in respect of Israel’s expected attack on Palestine, we can threaten Israel under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement.
Spokesperson: Spokesperson: I think our policy is very clear on Palestine. Like Jammu and Kashmir, Palestine has been a very important foreign policy issue for Pakistan, and we have been a strong supporter of a two-state solution, basically, with the State of Palestine being established in accordance with UN Security Council resolutions, along the 4 June 1967 borders, with Jerusalem as its capital.
The establishment of that state is important. So, our entire diplomacy, basically, you can say, in this region, revolves around protecting the legal rights of the Palestinian people. We have been talking about stopping the aggression by Israel, providing them with the humanitarian support they so much need, rebuilding the infrastructure there, and bringing it up as a normal, functioning state that is able to stand on its own.
So, what Israel is doing has been frequently condemned. I would say that it is a serious issue, and Pakistan strongly condemns any action that Israel takes against the innocent Palestinian people, including this kind of aggression. It is not only Palestine that is facing this; our brotherly countries, like Lebanon and Syria, are also affected.
What we see is that Akhand Bharat in our neighbourhood and similar greater Israel expansionist policies in Israel are being pursued full scale by Israel. So, the world has to take note of this situation, and we strongly condemn any action by Israel against Palestinians. So, that’s it.
(Syeda Qurat ul Ain, Independent Urdu): Geo has reported that a major internal inquiry report has been obtained by Geo News, stating that 12 billion rupees was illegally collected from citizens in one year through unlawful channels for document attestation. It also says that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs was approached for comment. Can you please share your comment on this set of documents?
(Mateen Haider, WE News): It is widely reported that online attestation at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is facing technical hitches. The technical system developed by the National Information Technology Board (NITB) is extremely faulty. People are facing great problems with online attestation, particularly apostille attestation, which is required by a number of countries. In the past, we have seen the Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister hold an extensive meeting on this particular issue and direct the Foreign Office to facilitate citizens in the timely attestation of their documents. Citizens regularly pay the prescribed fees, but despite that, there is a mafia operating outside the Foreign Ministry, as pointed out by the media. So, what measures are being taken to streamline this attestation system, make it transparent and easily accessible to the people, and ensure timely attestation?
(Aijaz Ahmed, GNN News): I want to add to this that, in my personal experience, one of my colleagues visited here and requested my assistance with the apostille attestation of his documents. I referred him to the official channel for processing his documents. He paid 15,000 rupees to an agent outside the ministry and got his documents apostilled in half an hour.
(Syeda Qurat ul Ain, Independent Urdu): It’s a follow-up question. Can you please confirm whether the outgoing Foreign Secretary saw the report and, according to Geo News, ignored it and appointed officers on different postings / assignments, and, according to the report, it was suggested that these upcoming postings should be put on hold.
Spokesperson: I think it is the responsibility of the media to exercise caution while reporting and mentioning names. Sometimes, baseless allegations can tend to spread, and they become like news, and the news becomes authentic because it is shared by Geo. So, the Foreign Office takes pride in upholding the highest standards of professionalism and integrity.
With regard to the questions raised by the three of you, I would say that the Foreign Office has no information or record pertaining to the so-called inquiry that you are referring to. We do not subscribe to or pay heed to this kind of activism. While the ministry believes in transparency and accountability, we strongly reject such unverified and baseless claims.
That was part one of the question. Coming over to the second part, which Mr. Mateen asked, regarding the situation, I’ll just give you a broad outline. Every day, 17,000 to 18,000 documents are attested at the ministry and the four camp offices in the capitals. So, 18,000 documents—you can imagine how many people come every day—and this is the situation.
The ministry has taken various steps for the facilitation of applicants and the documentation process, which include the QR code system and the courier system, because there were people living in far-flung areas who would otherwise have to come to Islamabad, wait in line, and submit their documents. This online procedure was adopted with different QR services. Companies were hired, powers of attorney were executed digitally, and, for the first time, basically, in the last one year, it has happened that a person sitting in another country can have his power of attorney digitally verified here in the ministry. There is also an integrated database with HEC and IBCC. Now, you do not have to physically go and get it attested, bring it back, and have it counter-attested. It is done online, and it is done in minutes.
Because the requirement is so huge, there was a need to have evening shifts. So, in Pakistan, probably, it is the only ministry where we have a morning shift and then also an evening shift.
So, that is the factual situation. Before the introduction of apostille attestation back in 2024, applicants had to go through a lengthy three-step process. They would have the document attested in one place, then come to the Foreign Ministry, and then go to the embassy, and so on. Each time they travelled to another country, the document would have to be attested again.
Now, with this apostille system, which was introduced in 2024, 120 countries are accepting documents attested by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs here in Islamabad. So, that has eased the burden not only in financial terms but also physically. Imagine 10 million Pakistanis living abroad, and each time they have to go and get a paper attested again and again and again. Now, with the apostille system, attestation done once is applicable to 120 countries. So, it has massively reduced the burden on the people.
And, of course, the media would not easily report this kind of thing. This is the factual situation. But I totally understand that if there are a large number of people, not everybody gets the job done on the first go, so there have to be improvements. I think the ministry is keen to improve its system.
The Foreign Secretary has especially placed the best possible officers, with clean records, in the Consular Department. Some of them are literally outstanding in their work and have very clean records.
We have generated 3.4 billion rupees in the last two years. Before, it used to be a smaller amount. Now, this is almost 3,000 rupees per document. But the documentation is done online, and the payment is made online, so it is not like somebody is receiving the money in cash. It goes into the accounts, and there are POS systems in the Consular Department as well, so it is done through those.
(Journalist): The Journalist pointed out that the fee for Apostille attestation of documents was increased to Rs. 3000/- so how do you claim that overall the initiative has economized the cost of attestation.
Spokesperson: Probably, you didn’t hear my earlier response that it used to cost every Pakistani hundreds of dollars because attestation had to be done not once but at multiple tiers. After having the document attested in Islamabad, you had to get a counter-attestation from the embassy, then go to a foreign country and get the attestation of the Embassy of Pakistan there, and then get it counter-attested by the local authority. So, there were multiple attestations, and we had a lot of expenditure there. This has actually reduced the overall burden.

On the 46th Meeting of the Council of the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:58:18 UTC
14:58:18 KST

On 14th September 2026, the 46th meeting of the Council of the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO RATS Council) was held in Islamabad under the chairmanship of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan.
The meeting was attended by delegations from the competent authorities of the Republic of Belarus, the Republic of India, the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Republic of Kazakhstan, the People’s Republic of China, the Kyrgyz Republic, the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, the Russian Federation, the Republic of Tajikistan, the Republic of Uzbekistan, as well as representatives of the Executive Committee of SCO RATS.
During the meeting, current issues on the international agenda in the field of ensuring regional security were discussed.
The SCO RATS Council condemned the new military attacks against the Islamic Republic of Iran and reaffirmed the SCO’s previously expressed position on this issue.
Expressing condolences to the Government and people of Iran over the tragic deaths of Iran’s Supreme Leader, Seyyed Ali Khamenei, as well as to the families of those killed, the Council reaffirmed its position on preserving Iran’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity and supported efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions, establishing peace and ensuring stability in the region.
The Council reviewed the implementation of previously adopted decisions of the SCO RATS Council concerning the coordination of cooperation among the competent authorities of the SCO Member States in combating terrorism, separatism and extremism, and approved work plans of the Executive Committee of SCO RATS and expert groups on the most pressing issues of the countering the “three forces of evil”.
Decisions were adopted on the establishment and improvement of information infrastructure to strengthen interaction among the Parties. 
An agreement was reached to conduct in 2027 a joint information operation in the field of countering terrorism, a practical seminar for the use of the Internet for terrorist, separatist and extremist purposes, as well as joint counter-terrorism exercise of the competent authorities of the SCO Member States to identify and prevent the use of the Internet for terrorist, separatist and extremist purposes.
The Thirteenth International Scientific and Practical Conference on cooperation between the SCO Member States and the SCO observer state in the field of countering terrorism, separatism and extremism is scheduled to be held in the Republic of Kazakhstan.
Issues concerning the organizational and staffing support of the activities of the Executive Committee of SCO RATS were considered.
For their personal contribution to the development of SCO RATS activities and the strengthening of cooperation among the competent authorities of the SCO Member States and officials of the Executive Committee of SCO RATS were awarded.
The chairmanship of the SCO RATS Council passed from the Islamic Republic of Pakistan to the Russian Federation. An agreement was reached to hold the next meeting of the SCO RATS Council at the premises of the Executive Committee of SCO RATS in Tashkent.
The meeting was held in a businesslike and friendly atmosphere.

Antalya declaration backs peaceful use of space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:55:37 UTC
14:55:37 KST

Representatives from 21 countries have adopted the Antalya Declaration supporting the peaceful and sustainable use of space, Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır said on Oct. 4.
The text was endorsed by 32 ministers, lawmakers and space agency heads at a meeting ahead of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC).
Kacır said it was the first joint declaration adopted at the congress’s ministerial and parliamentary meeting.
Türkiye initiated the declaration and prepared it in consultation with the International Astronautical Federation (IAF) and international partners, he said, urging other countries and international organizations to sign.
The meeting brought together representatives from 38 countries to discuss space law, exploration missions, greater participation by developing countries and a sustainable space economy.
“Progress in space is meaningful only when it produces tangible benefits for people on Earth,” Kacır said, highlighting the role of space technologies in daily life, economic activity and disaster management.
He also stressed the growing contribution of private companies and startups, saying innovation required public support, long-term financing and predictable regulations.
More than 300 companies working in space technologies operate in Türkiye’s technology parks, Kacır said. Work has also begun to establish a dedicated space technology park in Ankara.
Türkiye plans to launch its first lunar spacecraft in early 2027, he added. The craft will have more than 80 percent domestic content and use a hybrid propulsion system developed in Türkiye.
The congress runs from Oct. 5 to 9 in Antalya. Organized by the IAF, it is hosted by the Turkish Space Agency and co-hosted by SAHA Istanbul.

Yemeni army says 1,747 Houthis ‘neutralized’ in over 1,100 military operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:54:41 UTC
14:54:41 KST

Sahin Demir
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
The Yemeni army said on Monday that its forces had “neutralized” 1,747 Houthi members in 1,122 military operations across several fronts in the country.
Military spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said in a statement on US social media platform X that the operations targeted artillery and rocket-launcher positions, defensive fortifications, approach and advance routes, supply lines and means, reinforcements and military buildups, as well as command structures and command-and-control centers belonging to the Houthis.
He said the operations were conducted in Saada, Al-Jawf and Taiz provinces, as well as along Yemen’s western coast.
According to al-Nuzaili, the operations involved warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles, rocket launchers, and snipers.
He said the operations also destroyed or disabled 364 military vehicles and transport and supply assets.
Al-Nuzaili added that government forces would continue their operations to retake state territory and institutions and extend national sovereignty.
Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi on Sunday announced the launch of comprehensive military operations against the Houthis, saying the armed forces, security forces and other military formations had been ordered to retake the territory held by the group.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
Fighting has intensified since July, with a major escalation in September that saw the Houthis take control of the strategic city of Mokha, and advance to Mayyun Island overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The group has also targeted Saudi Arabia, including energy sites.

Merz’s bloc hits new low as AfD widens poll lead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:52:59 UTC
14:52:59 KST

Support for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU bloc has fallen to 18 percent, while the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has reached 30 percent, a nationwide INSA poll showed.
The survey for Bild, published on Oct. 3, marked the conservatives’ lowest reading and the AfD’s highest in the pollster’s records. The AfD gained one percentage point from the previous week, while the CDU/CSU lost one, widening the gap to 12 points.
The Social Democrats (SPD), Merz’s coalition partner, and the opposition Greens each stood at 14 percent. The Left party received 10 percent.
The poll also found that 79 percent of respondents were dissatisfied with Merz’s performance, with the same proportion dissatisfied with the government overall.
INSA surveyed 1,202 people and put the maximum margin of error at 2.9 percentage points.
The findings follow regional election defeats for Merz’s Christian Democrats in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6 and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sept. 20, where the AfD finished first.
Merz described the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result as a “disaster” but pledged to press ahead with reforms.
The chancellor, who took office in May 2025 promising to revive Germany’s economy, has struggled to advance economic and welfare reforms with his SPD coalition partners.

Europe turns to reserves as diesel supplies tighten
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:51:58 UTC
14:51:58 KST

Fuel prices are on display as a cyclist passes a petrol station in Lazdijai, Lithuania on Oct. 3, 2026. (Photo by Petras Malukas / AFP)
Europe’s reliance on imported diesel has left it exposed to sharp price increases as refinery disruptions in the Middle East and Russia restrict supplies, prompting governments to tap emergency reserves.
The Group of Seven agreed on Oct. 2 to release 100 million barrels of crude oil and fuel over four months through the International Energy Agency (IEA), with substantial diesel supplies to be released in the first 20 days.
The move follows a rise in the EU’s average diesel pump price to a record 2.24 euros per liter, about 41 percent above its prewar level, according to European Commission figures published on Oct. 1.
Before the Iran war, the Middle East and Russia supplied nearly a third of global diesel exports, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Gulf shipments in August fell to a quarter of their prewar level, while Russian exports dropped to about a fifth of May volumes, the newspaper said.
U.S. refiners have helped cover the shortfall but are also operating close to capacity.
European refineries have limited scope to increase production quickly, leaving the region dependent on imports.
The EU held 36 million metric tons of emergency diesel stocks at the end of June, equivalent to roughly two months of consumption, the Journal reported, citing Eurostat.
Alan Gelder, a senior vice president at energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie, told Euronews that a large release of diesel reserves could reduce pump prices by 0.10 to 0.15 euros per liter.
“Any further release only buys time, as global diesel supply is still below global diesel demand,” he said.
Releasing stocks would also reduce Europe’s protection against further supply disruptions. Rebuilding them would depend on increased production and exports from the Middle East, Kpler analyst George Shaw told Euronews.
IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol warned at an event in Istanbul on Oct. 2 that higher diesel prices would soon push up inflation worldwide.
In Türkiye, diesel on Istanbul’s European side cost 97.10 Turkish Liras per liter on Oct. 1, down from 100.31 liras on Sept. 17. It remained about 61 percent above its prewar price of 60.30 liras.

Myanmar says nearly 1,500 citizens repatriated from Malaysia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:50:24 UTC
14:50:24 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Myanmar on Monday confirmed that nearly 1,500 of its nationals who completed sentences for unlawful residency and other immigration offenses were repatriated from Malaysia.
Three Burmese vessels, including a hospital ship, docked in Yangon on Sunday morning, “completing a smooth and successful repatriation to the motherland,” the Information Ministry said.
Officials from the military, locally known as Tatmadaw, and the relevant ministries coordinated to repatriate 1,476 citizens.
Burmese Navy vessels UMS Mottama, sea-going hospital ship UMS Thanlwin, and UMS Sinphyushin had departed Yangon on Sept. 24 for repatriation, arriving at Lumut Port in Malaysia on Sept. 28.
The next day, Malaysia began repatriating 1,476 nationals, part of a larger group of some 5,000 nationals.
The first group comprised 1,370 men, 79 women, 20 boys, and seven girls, aged between eight and 60.
“Necessary arrangements are continuing to facilitate their swift reunion with relatives and family members, ensuring their safe return to their respective hometowns,” the ministry said.
Burmese authorities have also repatriated 1,905 citizens from Cambodia since January.
Malaysia's repatriation decision has raised concerns with the UN and other groups.
UNHCR spokesperson Matthew Saltmarsh told journalists in Geneva last week that the agency was “concerned by the reported imminent return of some 1,500 individuals ... with ongoing armed conflict and widespread violence and human rights violations across Myanmar.”
"Under international law, no one should be sent to a country where they may face persecution, torture, serious harm, or other threats to life, liberty, and security," he said.
Saltmarsh added that the UNHCR remains committed to engaging with the Malaysian government through technical support, policy dialogue and capacity building to develop accessible and effective protection measures.

Delhi: Detentions reported during protest over alleged sexual harassment of women journalists by police officials
Several protesters were detained as they held a demonstration outside the Parliament Street police station in New Delhi on Monday over the alleged sexual harassment of women journalists by police personnel during the October 3 protests against India's chief election commissioner, reports said.
The protesters were reportedly staging an overnight demonstration demanding an examination of the CCTV footage of the alleged incident and an action on the complaints.
"We went back and again asked for the CCTV footage, but they did not provide it. They did not register an FIR (First Information Report) or give us any update on the case. Instead, we were detained," news agency PTI quoted a protester as saying.
Three women journalists have alleged that they were sexually harassed by police personnel while covering Saturday's protest in New Delhi demanding resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
One of the journalists alleged that an assistant commissioner of police (ACP) groped her.
The Delhi Police said in a statement police that the complaints were referred to the Crime Branch for a "fair and impartial enquiry."
The Indian Express reported that one of the alleged victims was among the 17 protesters who were taken on a bus to Delhi Cantonment police station on Monday morning,
The Cockroach Janata Party movement's legal affairs head Ratna Singh said that the journalist who alleged sexual harassment by an ACP was among the detained.
Singh claimed that she was told that the detainees were assaulted by the police.
"Two of those detained were allegedly brutally beaten," she wrote on X.
There is yet to be a statement from the Delhi police on Monday's detentions and alleged assaults.
Rahul Gandhi slams Delhi Police
Opposition Leader Rahul Gandhi railed against the Delhi Police over the alleged mistreatment of female protesters and journalists.
"What's happening in Delhi right now follows a single pattern: silence any woman who dares to ask questions," he wrote on X, as he shared an interaction with two women journalists who alleged harassment at a Delhi police station last month.
The Congress leader alleged that those "entrusted with the responsibility" to protect women were now the ones "posing a threat to them".
"Hundreds of people were detained at Jantar Mantar. Female protesters alleged that male police officers misbehaved with them. Cameras were snatched from female journalists, and they were dragged around. Not even an FIR was filed on a journalist's complaint," Gandhi said.
Supreme Court issues notice to Election Commission of India, no suspension for Gyanesh Kumar
The Supreme Court on Monday issued notice to the Election Commission of India (ECI), seeking the poll body's response to petitions against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls.
The pleas sought action against Kumar following an investigative news report which claimed that the poll panel, headed by him, took decisions on voter list changes despite objections from two of three election commissioners.
India’s top court said on Monday that after considering ECI’s response, if it finds that decisions were taken by the top poll official without the required unanimity, it would reconsider or recall those decisions, news agency ANI reported.
"If records show some decision was not unanimous etc., we will injunct those decisions," legal news portal LiveLaw quoted the court as saying.
The Supreme Court declined to pass any interim order to suspend Kumar, an action sought by one of the petitions.
India's Modi holds talks with Swiss President Guy Parmelin
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday held bilateral talks with visiting Swiss President Guy Parmelin at the Hyderabad House in New Delhi.
India and Switzerland exchanged a number of Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) after their leaders reviewed progress in a range of areas of bilateral cooperation, including trade, investment, technology and culture.
The two nations countries took "several important decisions to increase market access for India's exports in Switzerland, and to make investment between the two countries smoother", Modi said at a joint press conference with Parmelin after the talks.
"This will increase the export of India's agriculture, pharma, textile, and engineering goods to Switzerland. At the same time, we will attract new Swiss investment in India's important sectors such as biotech, life sciences, banking, insurance, food processing, and sustainability," the Indian leader added.
India and Switzerland also signed a mobility agreement on Monday which Modi said would lead to more opportunities for Indian students and professionals in Switzerland.
Parmelin described his visit to India as a "stepping stone towards further growth".
"It is the right moment to celebrate how far we have come together but, even more importantly, to shape our joint future," he told the media.
Parmelin last visited India in February 2026 to participate in the AI Impact Summit but his latest trip marks his first state visit to the country.
The Swiss President is accompanied by a high-level delegation of senior officials and business leaders.
Parmelin kicked off his visit earlier on Monday by placing a wreath at Mahatma Gandhi's memorial, Raj Ghat.
India's Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar also met with the Swiss leader.
Jaishankar wrote on X that he was "confident" that Modi and Parmelin's meeting would "further the engagement" between the two nations across " a wide range of domains."
In a statement earlier this week, India's Foreign Ministry emphasized the significance of Parmelin's visit and his participation in the 2nd India–European Free Trade Association (EFTA) Prosperity Summit, which will be held on October 7 to mark the inaugural anniversary of the landmark India-EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA) coming into force.
"Among EFTA countries, Switzerland is the largest trade and investment partner of India," the foreign ministry in New Delhi said.
India-US trade talks have reached a 'plateau' — says Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman
India and the United States have reached a "plateau" in their trade deal negotiations where further concessions from either side could be difficult, Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said at the Munich Leaders Meeting being held in New Delhi on Monday.
Sitharaman described the agreement as a "hard and very rigorously negotiated" one.
The minister said that negotiations were still ongoing.
"Although we like to believe that both sides have reached a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult, But Maybe if there are rooms to operate from, both sides would do it," she said.
India and the US first announced negotiations for a bilateral trade agreement in February 2025 but the deal remains in a limbo.
Multiple rounds of talks have been held between representatives from New Delhi and Washington but there has been no significant breakthrough as differences persist over issues including tariffs and market access.
Last week, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said last week that an agreement was not "imminent".
“We truly have identified the universe of items that are sticking points. We're working diligently toward them," he said.
On Monday, Sitharaman said the trade balance between the two nations was in India's "favor".
"They would want to reduce that imbalance," she said, referring to the US.
The Munich Leaders Meeting in the Indian capital is being hosted by the Munich Security Conference and organized with the support of India's foreign ministry.
Supreme Court to hear petitions against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over SIR decisions
The Supreme Court on Monday is scheduled to hear a batch of pleas seeking the suspension of Election Commission of India chief Gyanesh Kumar over decisions related to the country's controversial voter roll revisions, allegedly taken unilaterally, India media reported.
Critics say a nationwide voter-verification exercise — called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — which began last year, has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters by striking their names from electoral rolls
Kumar has been under intense public scrutiny after the Indian Express daily reported that two of his fellow election commissioners raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months regarding voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral roll data, but those concerns were not taken into consideration.
Kumar heads the three-member commission, which has overseen the voter roll revisions.
The Election Commission of India rejects allegations of wrongdoing and says the process removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also prevents the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Opposition parties and critics allege that the changes to voter lists benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), a charge the party denies.
Kumar is yet to make a comment on the allegations against him.
On Monday, a three-judge bench, headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, is expected to hear petitions over the decisions taken by Kumar allegedly without the approval of the two election commissioners.
One of the petitions is seeking a declaration that the chief election commissioner cannot take decisions for the ECI without the concurrence of the other two Election Commissioners, legal news website LiveLaw reported.
The other seeks a revocation of the 14 reported decisions allegedly taken unilaterally, along with the constitution of an independent judicial inquiry commission or a special investigation team headed by a retired judge of the Supreme Court to probe the allegations against Kumar.
The hearing comes after thousands of protesters and opposition supporters rallied in Delhi and Mumbai over the weekend to demand Kumar's resignation.

Hundreds of French schools closed amid protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:48:00 UTC
14:48:00 KST

Hundreds of French schools shut, teen loses hand in protests
October 5, 2026
Several hundred schools in France closed totally or partially on Monday amid security fears following a wave of nationwide student protests, the education minister has said.
The protests by pupils complaining of poor conditions began at one Paris school on September 17 but last week mutated into sometimes violent demonstrations across the nation.
A 15-year-old boy in the northern town of Lens sustained a severe injury to his hand amid one of the protests on Monday. French news agency AFP cited a police union source as saying he appeared to have picked up a sting ball grenade, another term for a type of tear gas grenade also often called a blast ball, and it exploded in his hand.
The demonstrations have started to dominate France's political debate just a few months before presidential elections that will choose a successor to Emmanuel Macron, who is approaching term limit.
Why are the schools staying closed?
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Sunday that lessons would be totally or partly suspended in some 400 to 500 high schools on Monday, as the security conditions "have not been fulfilled."
According to Geffray, the schools were being closed mainly as a precaution, with more large protests planned for Tuesday.
Geffray said the number of schools remaining closed on Monday would be similar to that on Friday but that there was planned to be a "partial, progressive return to lessons."
He said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" and 78 education staff members injured since the protests began.
"There are activists — particularly from the far left — who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Geffray said.
"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he added.
Valerie Pecresse, the president of the Ile-de-France region surrounding the capital, said that more than a third of the 468 schools in the region would be shut on Monday.
What are the school protesters saying?
The protesting teenagers at French upper high schools, called Lycees, have complained of high rates of absenteeism by teachers, school days that are too long and dilapidated facilities.
They have also protested at the lack of adequate cooling on hot summer days, with some towns seeing temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) last summer in a country without widespread air conditioning.
Organizers have called for the protests to continue on Tuesday, saying the government was still failing to propose "concrete measures" to remedy the situation.
On Sunday, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu urged local authorities to make it a priority to fill gaps left by long-term absences and unfilled posts.
He also called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss renovating school buildings that are often in poor condition.
Violent incidents at the school protests
The protests have been marked by several violent incidents, with security forces sometimes using tear gas and batons to disperse the young protesters.
More than 5,000 people, 85% of them minors, have been arrested since the start of the movement.
On Sunday, a 16-year-old was detained after a 59-year-old teacher was hit and doused with gasoline on the sidelines of a protest in the southern town of La Ciotat.
Last week, a group of young people was filmed beating and kicking a policeman on the ground in the eastern town of Belfort.
The French branch of rights group Amnesty International last week described the action taken by police as "disproportionate."
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has, however, defended security forces, saying they were "not cracking down on young people" but rather "protecting" school and university students wishing to "peacefully voice their demands."
Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

Flydubai co-pilot’s chilling 9/11-style plan: Kill captain, fly normally – then crash at Ben Gurion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:45:00 KST

Flydubai co-pilot’s chilling 9/11-style plan: Kill captain, fly normally – then crash at Ben Gurion
- The Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami planned to kill the captain, continue the flight normally, and deliberately crash into Ben Gurion Airport or other targets in Israel or Jordan.
- Al-Hammami chose flydubai because it flies to Tel Aviv and gathered information on Ben Gurion Airport during a previous visit; he abandoned an earlier attack plan due to a crew friend.
- The captain fought back during the cockpit attack, the plane landed safely, and investigations are ongoing into al-Hammami's motives, security clearances, and possible extremist links.
AI generated
New Delhi – The Omani co-pilot accused of attacking the captain of a Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight allegedly chose the airline because it operated flights to Israel, and he allegedly planned to crash the aircraft into Ben Gurion Airport, according to Israeli media reports citing details from his interrogation.
Hammam al-Hammami, who is in custody in the United Arab Emirates, allegedly intended to kill Indian captain Smit Machchhar, continue operating Flight FZ1073 normally, and obtain landing clearance before deliberately crashing the aircraft into a building or another plane at the airport.
The plan, according to the reports, was designed to delay detection until the aircraft was close enough to its target that the authorities would have little time to intervene.
Israeli media reported that al-Hammami planned to seize control while the flight was over Jordan as it approached Israeli airspace. If he could not reach Ben Gurion Airport, he allegedly considered targeting a skyscraper in Tel Aviv or a US military installation in Jordan.
Co-pilot allegedly chose flydubai for its Tel Aviv flights
Fresh details reported by Israeli outlets suggest the alleged plot may have predated al-Hammami’s employment with flydubai.
A report cited by The Jerusalem Post said al-Hammami had researched airlines flying to Tel Aviv before applying to flydubai.
“I looked into which airline flies to Tel Aviv. That’s why I chose flydubai. I planned it even before I was accepted,” he reportedly told investigators.
The Jerusalem Post separately reported, citing an Israeli source familiar with the interrogation, that al-Hammami said he had researched airlines operating Tel Aviv routes and chose flydubai as a result.
Reports also said he had flown to Ben Gurion Airport several times after joining the Dubai-based carrier and used a June visit to gather information for the alleged attack.
He reportedly intended to carry out the plan in July but abandoned it at the last moment because one of the crew members on that flight was a friend.
Captain fought back after cockpit attack
The alleged plot unravelled on Sept 30 after al-Hammami attacked Machchhar inside the cockpit with an emergency crash axe.
Machchhar later said the co-pilot had asked to pray shortly before the assault.
“The blows kept coming. I realised that it’s not the aircraft; it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me,” Machchhar said while recounting the attack.
Despite being seriously injured, he managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing crew members and others aboard the flight to intervene and restrain the co-pilot.
Two off-duty flydubai pilots travelling as passengers later took control of the aircraft and landed it safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Reuters reported that the aircraft lost more than 16,000 feet of altitude in about 30 seconds during the incident.
Machchhar is recovering after the attack and has spoken to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about the incident.
Security scrutiny widens after attack
The case has also triggered questions over how al-Hammami was cleared to fly to Israel.
Officials familiar with the case have said he had earlier been removed from flying duties in Oman over concerns about extremist material or views. The Associated Press and other international outlets have reported that the authorities are now examining how those concerns were handled before he later joined flydubai.
The Israeli authorities have, meanwhile, ordered a review of security arrangements for foreign civil aviation after the incident.
Investigators in the UAE and other countries continue to examine whether al-Hammami acted alone and whether he had links to any extremist organisation. Reuters reported that no evidence of Iranian involvement had emerged, while the wider motive and possible external links remained under investigation. THE STATESMAN/ASIA NEWS NETWORK

14:44:29 KST

Pro-Russia Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik – who is serving a six-year ban from holding public office for defying rulings of Bosnia’s international envoy and Constitutional Court, claimed victory on Sunday, saying his party would hold a “vast majority”.
The former president of Bosnia's Serb statelet, Milorad Dodik, said his party had retained power in the entity and its seat on the shared presidency, as preliminary results showed a drop in turnout for Bosnia's general elections.
Dodik led the declarations for a dizzying number of posts to be decided in the general elections in a complex system that has held the partitioned Balkan country together since the 1995 peace deal.
The key race was for the tripartite presidency, split between Bosnian Muslims or Bosniaks, and the Serb and Croat ethnic groups. Dodik's Serb nationalists ran on a platform of greater autonomy and secessionist rhetoric.
"If it had not been for (US President) Donald Trump's magnificent victory, we would probably be political corpses today," he told supporters in Banja Luka, in a speech that also thanked his close ally, Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"But now, thanks to the new environment, we are political winners," he added.
The 67-year-old was not on the ballot after being convicted of overstepping his powers and banned from the presidency for six years.
But he remains a central figure in the Bosnian-Serb Republika Srpska entity.
With 95% of the ballots counted, according to electoral officials, his candidate, Zeljka Cvijanovic, was firmly on track to retain her spot in the presidency.
Meanwhile, Bosniak presidential incumbent Denis Becirovic also claimed victory after results showed him leading a tighter race for his seat.
"A freedom-loving, anti-fascist and civic Bosnia and Herzegovina is alive," Becirovic, from the Social Democrats party, told supporters in Sarajevo.
Bosnian Croat nationalist candidate Darijana Filipovic also claimed victory in her bid for the Croat presidential seat.
Dodik's party was also projected to retain power in the Serb entity's parliament and local presidency by a large margin.
The US-brokered ‘Dayton agreement’ ended the 1992-95 conflict but entrenched divisions that often paralyse decision-making.
It divided Bosnia into two semi-autonomous entities –s the Serb-run RS and a Muslim-Croat federation – linked by a weak central government.
Turnout dropped nearly 10% from the last election in 2022, to around 42% on Sunday, according to official figures.
In the Muslim-Croat federation, Becirovic advocates a path toward the European Union and NATO.
But if Dodik's party returns to the presidency, it would almost certainly mean the political deadlock that has blocked the necessary reforms for years would remain.
After two decades in power, Dodik and his party have repeatedly clashed with the country's central authorities and vocally oppose EU membership.
Croat nationalist parties are also pushing for electoral reform. They want a greater say in choosing the Croat member of the presidency in the entity they share with the more numerous Bosniaks.

Maldives begins survey to identify sites for solar photovoltaic systems

2026-10-05

14:42:56 KST

MALE, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- The Maldivian government has begun a nationwide survey to identify suitable locations for solar photovoltaic systems as part of efforts to generate 33 percent of the country's electricity from renewable energy by the end of 2028, state media PSM News reported on Sunday.
Survey teams are visiting islands across the country to identify suitable land and building rooftops for solar installations and collect the technical information needed for future projects.
The government said the program is intended to accelerate the expansion of renewable energy generation and reduce the Maldives' dependence on imported fuel.
In August, the government launched a project to establish solar hybrid systems on 25 islands. Once completed, the project is expected to save more than 3 million liters of diesel annually and cut carbon dioxide emissions by 8,400 metric tonnes.
Work also began in December on a 100-megawatt floating solar project being carried out by an external company. The Ministry of Economic Development, Transport and Trade said the project is expected to be completed in 2027.
The government estimates that reaching its 33-percent renewable energy target by the end of 2028 could save about 42 million U.S. dollars annually in fuel expenditure. ■

Feature: Justice for "comfort women" -- Philippine exhibition calls for acknowledging wartime atrocities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:42:40 CST
14:42:40 KST

People visit the exhibition "Courage in Chaos: Narratives of Women and War" in Manila, the Philippines, Oct. 5, 2026. (Xinhua/Rouelle Umali)
MANILA, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Pointing to her distant grandma's portrait at an exhibition in the Philippines' capital, Manila, Jonna Zapanta said with a heavy heart that her relative was abducted by Japanese troops in 1942 and became a "comfort woman" victim, and that sorrow dwells in her eyes.
"My family once did not want to spread this intergenerational trauma to me, and rarely spoke of this relative," said Zapanta, creative director of the exhibit "Courage in Chaos: Narratives of Women and War," on view from Oct. 1 to 14.
However, while sorting through "comfort women" archives, she stumbled across a survivor with the same family name as her grandmother. After pressing her grandmother for details, she found out the survivor was her grandmother's cousin who suffered a whole life by Japanese wartime atrocities -- a fate shared by many "comfort women."
"Eighty-one years have passed since the end of World War II, yet the Japanese government has still not issued a formal apology to 'comfort women,'" said Zapanta.
Organized by Lila Pilipina, an organization fighting for justice for Philippine wartime sexual slavery victims, the exhibition showcased exhibits including dozens of portraits of WWII "comfort women" victims, paintings and handcrafted works made by the survivors, and anti-war slogans and books.
Between 1942 and 1945, approximately 1,000 Filipino women and girls were forced into sexual slavery as "comfort women." For many survivors, the suffering lingered long after the war ended.
At the gallery wall, hand-drawn works by late "comfort woman" Remedios Felias depicting Japanese troops committing sexual violence against Filipino women, who scream with contorted faces, gained wide attention.
"Many young people today did not live through the Japanese occupation of the Philippines. We hope these paintings and photographs help people understand the sufferings of comfort women," said Sharon Cabusao-Silva, coordinator of Lila Pilipina.
Cabusao-Silva said only a handful of survivors remain, among whom most are elderly and frail. Lila Pilipina tracks their health and supports them with material assistance.
Another set of comics at the exhibition recounts a more recent episode: In 2017, a memorial statue honoring "comfort women" was erected in Manila, only to be removed months later following intense diplomatic pressure from Tokyo.
"It is so shameful and a disrespect for history to remove the 'comfort women' statue in the Philippines," said Teresita Ang-See, a Filipino civic leader. She added that Filipinos must never forget the crimes committed by Japanese troops against them, and wars should not occur again in the country.
Tourists also write on sticky notes and affix them on the gallery wall, with messages such as: "Justice for all our Lolas (grandmother in Tagalog)," "Tribute to the victims of war," "For the continuing fight for the Lolas."
"I can hardly imagine what suffering these Lolas went through. I am deeply inspired by their courage as they persisted in living and fighting," said Irish Keng, a student at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines. She added that it is her first time learning that countries in Asia, including China and the Republic of Korea, endured similar historical trauma.
Cabusao-Silva said "comfort women" in the Philippines and other countries victimized by the Japanese military in WWII deserve justice and recognition.
Commenting on Japan's military moves in recent years and the Japanese government's remarks on historical issues, she said the Japanese government should not launch a war again. "It's high time the Japanese government recognizes its responsibility." ■
People visit the exhibition "Courage in Chaos: Narratives of Women and War" in Manila, the Philippines, Oct. 5, 2026. (Xinhua/Rouelle Umali)

Estonia mulls longer truck driver hours in emergencies to secure supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:41:00 UTC
14:41:00 KST

Estonia mulls longer truck driver hours in emergencies to secure supplies
The Climate Ministry says it wants truck drivers to be allowed to work longer in emergencies to help prevent disruptions to supplies of essential goods.
Estonia is continuing to prepare for a variety of crises which could affect the country, and the transport sector is included in these preparations.
The ministry is preparing a legislative amendment which would allow professional drivers to work longer hours and take less rest than current law allows in emergency situations. This may be necessary, for example, to ensure supplies of essential goods such as medicines or motor fuel during a crisis.
Priit Tuuna, chief specialist at the Ministry of Climate's roads and railways department, told ERR that Estonia has not faced a situation in recent years in which an exemption from working and rest time requirements has been needed. However, that does not mean the country should not be prepared for such situations, he added.
"The coronavirus period was difficult, but it did not directly create a need for operational intervention on our part. However, if we look at neighboring countries and European Union countries in general, unforeseen situations can arise in which rapid action is needed. Natural disasters have happened, for example, and some countries have suffered major storm damage. In such cases, the need for transport has also risen," Tuuna said.
In such situations, the working and rest time requirements could be relaxed by ministerial regulation. For instance, the daily driving time could be extended, the daily rest period shortened, or the deadline for a driver's next rest period could be postponed.
Though longer working hours also increase driver fatigue and the risk of traffic accidents, the ministry says this temporary risk is still smaller than the harm society would suffer if the supply chain for essential goods were to be disrupted. As is the case right now, employers would still remain primarily responsible for ensuring that employees get sufficient rest during a crisis.
"Even now, under normal circumstances, it is the company's own responsibility to ensure that the way its staff's work is organized does not conflict with the rules laid down by law. If an emergency situation arises, it will also be very clearly specified that, for example, one additional hour of driving is permitted. Both the employer and the driver must then comply with that," Tuuna said.
Kersten Kattai, head of the national road transport association (Eesti Maanteetranspordiliit), said he did not believe there was a significant risk that professional drivers would become excessively fatigued during a crisis, particularly when everyone would likely be on heightened alert.
"We still assume that emergencies are emergencies and that both professional drivers and the people assigning them work will retain their common sense and good judgment," Kattai said.
Under the Estonian Constitution there are two definitions covering a state of emergency and a state of war, plus two lesser tiers; of these latter two, the "Emergency situation" (eriolukord) was declared during the Covid crisis.

The FBI arrested a woman at Los Angeles international airport (LAX) as she was leaving the country and accused her of spying on the Taiwan president’s family for China.
Wanying Zhang, also know as Heather, surveilled the Taiwanese president’s son and his family for the Chinese government while in the United States, according to the FBI.
Zhang, 34, was arrested on charges for working for China without registering as a foreign agent as legally required, first assistant US state attorney Bill Essayli of California’s central federal district announced on social media. Zhang took photos and videos of her targets and sent license plate information to Chinese officials, he said.
Citing real-estate licensing and listing records, the Los Angeles news outlet KTLA reported that Zhang was a licensed real-estate salesperson based in the southern California city of Irvine.
She was arrested as she was departing for a flight to China. Her nationality was not clear, and it was also not immediately clear if she had an attorney representing her.
She was due to appear on Monday in federal court in Los Angeles.
Taiwan’s presidential office confirmed relatives of the Taiwanese president, Lai Ching-te were the targets. The office did not specify if it was the president’s son, saying that “this is a classic case of transnational repression”.
“Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts – which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families – as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
The Chinese embassy in the US did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday. And the foreign ministry in Beijing was closed for holidays.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949. But China claims the island as part of its own territory.
Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and China do not belong to each other. He also has said the “People’s Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan”.
China considers Lai a separatist and has called him a “destroyer of peace”.
While in office, Lai has stepped up spending on defense for Taiwan – notably pledging to increase defense spending from 3% to 5% of the GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defense system.

More young boys starting ADHD medication
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:38:18 EEST
14:38:18 KST

An increasing share of young boys in Finland are being prescribed medication for ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder).
Last year, 3.1 percent of boys aged six to eight began ADHD treatment, according to social insurance agency Kela. That was up slightly from 2.9 percent starting medication the previous year.
In total 4,160 boys in the age group were taking ADHD medication last year, equivalent to 5.3 percent of all six- to eight-year-old boys.
The proportion starting treatment varied considerably across the country. North Savo recorded the highest rate, with just over five percent of boys in the age group beginning medication.
Helsinki had the lowest, at around 1.5 percent.

German prosecutors investigate possible sanctions violations by tenants of Russian House in Berlin
The Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office is investigating possible sanctions violations by tenants of the Russian House Russian Houses are cultural centres established in other countries to promote Russia's language and culture and Russian education. They also serve as platforms for Russian state propaganda and soft power cultural centre, which was closed by German authorities in response to Russia's attempted attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport.
Source: the prosecutor's office in a comment to German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The German government decided to close the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin in September. However, a bookshop called MnogoKnig selling Russian literature, a canteen and a visa agency continue to operate within the building.
It remains unclear who exactly is running these establishments and who is profiting from their activities.
The Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office confirmed that it is investigating possible violations of EU sanctions.
"Investigations are ongoing against unknown persons or tenants of the Russian House for violations of the Foreign Trade and Payments Act," the Berlin Public Prosecutor General's Office told Süddeutsche Zeitung in response to an inquiry.
As the Russian House in Berlin is part of the structure of Rossotrudnichestvo (the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States' Affairs, Compatriots Living Abroad, and International Humanitarian Cooperation), which has been on the EU sanctions list since 2022 because of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, providing it with funds is prohibited.
"For example, payments are considered a violation if they benefit a person who is on the sanctions list," Germany's Finance Ministry said in response to an inquiry. Therefore, any payment from which Rossotrudnichestvo benefits constitutes a sanctions violation.
By imposing sanctions on the Russian agency, Berlin also terminated a 2011 German-Russian agreement that had formed the basis for cultural cooperation between the two countries. However, the cultural centre in the German capital remains Russian property, as another agreement from 2013 provides for a 99-year lease term.
Background:
- On 1 September, Germany directly accused Russia of carrying out a hybrid attack at Leipzig Airport in early August and announced retaliatory measures, including the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin.
- Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said that, following Germany's decision to terminate the agreement governing the operation of the Russian House in Berlin, Russia would respond by closing all three branches of the Goethe-Institut in the country – in Moscow, St Petersburg and Novosibirsk.

Middle East oil exports recover to pre-Iran war levels despite Hormuz attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:35:00 UTC
14:35:00 KST

Middle East oil exports recover to pre-Iran war levels
October 5, 2026
Middle East crude oil exports, excluding Iran, rose back above pre-war levels in late September despite continued attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, according shipping data from trade intelligence firm Kpler.
Exports exceeded the pre-war average of about 18 million barrels per day (bpd) on four days in the final week of September, reaching 19.5 million to 22.5 million bpd, according to the data and analytics platform.
When the Strait of Hormuz closed following the start of the Iran war, the seven-day average non-Iranian crude leaving the region fell by 72% in 10 days, Kpler said.
How was Hormuz bypassed?
The recovery has relied on alternative routes and ship-to-ship transfers.
In September, about 40% of crude left the Gulf without crossing Hormuz, compared with only 17% before the Iran war.
According to Kpler, more than 70% of the crude changed tankers offshore in the Gulf of Oman in August. In comparison, almost no Gulf crude changed tankers in the Gulf of Oman before the war.
Additionally, Saudi Arabia also increased exports through the Red Sea, while the UAE used its pipeline to Fujairah.
The primary exporters of crude oil in the region were:
- Saudi Arabia
- the United Arab Emirates
- Iraq
Iran, however, remains the major exception, with its exports still well below the pre-war average, primarily due to US policies.
Attacks on ships around Hormuz continue
Meanwhile, attacks on vessels have continued around Hormuz. At least seven incidents have been reported in recent weeks.
On October 1, a tanker, Kazimah III, was reportedly struck by an unknown projectile, according to maritime intelligence firm Marisks. All crew members were evacuated safely.

On World Architecture Day 2026: A Call to Build Better, Build Differently, and Share Resources
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

The International Union of Architects designates the first Monday of October as World Architecture Day each year, aligning it with the United Nations' World Habitat Day. This year, both occasions are drawing attention to the global housing crisis as a fundamental element of human dignity, inclusion, and well-being. The UIA's motto reads: "Housing is a Human Right. Build It." The organization calls on architects to contribute to advancing equitable access to housing through design, research, and advocacy. From a holistic perspective, the crisis consists not only of a shortage of residential buildings, but of multiple, interconnected barriers to accessing an adequate place to live. The challenge calls on the dual nature of the architect's work: the capacity for abstract design thinking, and the practical knowledge to transform material reality. For architecture to make the right to housing a reality, both capacities must be put into practice: building new governance structures, different models of shared ownership, designs for alternative forms of cohabitation, and new, environmentally sustainable construction systems.
According to the United Nations, more than 3 billion people lack access to adequate housing, more than 1.1 billion people live in informal settlements, and hundreds of millions experience homelessness that goes unrecorded. Although the right to adequate housing is recognized in international human rights instruments, the most urgent responsibility lies with populations whose vulnerability is intensified by conflict, disaster, and climate change. Within this framework of habitat, the UN calls for approaches that respond to the needs of lower-income households, displaced populations, and people with no access to formal housing at all. This call to action begins with a basic premise: the housing crisis is a multidimensional problem that goes beyond the need to build more. It also demands building better, sharing more, and making full use of what already exists, so that housing becomes not only accessible, but a guaranteed right for a population that will keep changing over time.
The International Union of Architects (UIA) is a global non-governmental federation uniting professional organizations of architects from more than 120 countries and territories. From a disciplinary standpoint, it recognizes the severe shortage of housing as one of the most pressing challenges facing cities and communities worldwide. For housing access to be respected as a fundamental right, first it must never be treated as a luxury asset. For the UIA, engaging with this problem means going beyond design practice to contribute to housing policy, affordability, and equitable access, while implementing practical, sustainable, and context-responsive approaches to material solutions. This year, on World Architecture Day, the organization explicitly invites architects worldwide to promote creative strategies to meet the demand for housing through lectures, exhibitions, webinars, and other forms of public outreach. Sharing knowledge is also central to this goal, through architectural education that prepares future generations to address real-world challenges.
Build Systems to Distribute
A systemic problem calls for systematic solutions. In market societies, housing is predominantly understood as a private asset, increasingly scarce, and a guarantee of economic security. This view is not compatible with the notion of a right, a legal principle that guarantees access regardless of each citizen's purchasing power. In terms of land management policy, community organizations, local governments, and private practices have organized around the world to offer alternatives to the most common systems of provision within their own territories. The initiatives presented below include new legislation for the allocation and construction of housing units, models for the deconcentration of ownership and the liberation of housing from speculation, financial support structures, and measures to facilitate more and better housing.
Housing Affordability Crisis: Architectural and Policy Responses from Spain, France, Australia, and the United States
Housing Affordability Drives New Limits on Short-Term Rentals Across European Cities
"If You Build Ugly Social Housing, You Will Create Social Problems": An Interview with the OBEL Award 2026 Recipients
Building, Taxing, and Financing: New York City's Recent Measures to Tackle the Housing Crisis
The United States Enacts Sweeping Housing Reform Legislation to Expand Affordable Housing
Build Structures to Enable New Ways of Living
A problem of volume calls for collective solutions. Disciplinary perspectives on contemporary habitation point to the difficulties arising from the ways we occupy and share spaces, which have become problematic from a social and environmental perspective. When discussing the need to build more, questions arise about whom to build for, for how long, and at what cost. The acceptance of differences in ways of life and family structures is an opportunity to renew the domestic environment. Observing life cycles and patterns of movement influences the details of design itself, as well as the spatial distribution of functions traditionally associated with housing. Climate pressure forces us to consider new ways of occupying territory, from the individual unit to the larger complex. The reflections and examples presented below call for observing contemporary habitation from a broader perspective to respond to variability through design.
Has Architecture Ever Been Entirely Human? Beatriz Colomina and Mark Wigley on the Microbial Nature of Architecture
"Promoting Another Way of Living Together": In Conversation with Cristina Gamboa of Lacol
Building Autonomy: Latin American Communities Bringing Life's Systems Into Architecture
Co-Living: Rethinking Home for Temporary Belonging and Mobile Lifestyles
Khudi Bari: Architecture for Climate Displacement
Rebuild to Make Use of What Already Exists
This societal-scale shift in sources of employment, modes of transportation, perceptions of the environment, and life expectations contributes to the obsolescence of structures that were once necessary. On the other hand, conflict, in its social and environmental dimensions, brings new strategic imperatives for reconstruction and reinvention. Armed and discrimination-based conflict among human beings has resulted in waves of displacement, separating communities from their emotional attachments and places of belonging. The environmental pressure caused by human settlements in various territories lies at the origin of what we call natural disasters. The ideas below address renewal and inventiveness through two forms of rebuilding: transforming what we no longer use and restoring what has been destroyed.
"For Decades We Have Valued the New More than the Old": In Dialogue with OBEL Award 2025 Winners HouseEurope!
Renovation and Everyday Life: How Latin American Architecture Reinvents Existing Spaces
"The Homes of Tomorrow Are Already Built": European Citizens' Initiative for the Right to Housing Opens Signature Collection
Responding to Displacement: Architectural Strategies Across Latin America
Beyond Emergency Shelters: Modular and Vernacular Architecture in Post-Earthquake Reconstruction
Build a More Sustainable Industry
Finally, in reflecting on the concepts and circumstances surrounding construction, it is worth acknowledging that architecture is also an industry. As such, it is historical, extensive, and, from a methodological standpoint, fairly static. It is not only a means of materializing housing, but also a means of employment and a significant source of consumption. In the midst of a crisis, new methods of execution come into play. The stories presented here highlight initiatives, both historical and ongoing, that offer alternatives to the conventional practices of the construction industry. Material and political dimensions intersect, prompting reflection on less hierarchical ways of organizing labor and more creative uses of building materials.
Building as Political Practice: USINA and the Legacy of Collective Construction in Brazil
Radically Collective: The Legacy of Cuba's Microbrigadas Housing Program
How Labor Shortages Are Reshaping Architecture
From Selecting to Making: When Architects Become Material Producers
City Governments Transform Industrial Buildings into Circular Construction Hubs in New York, London, and Brussels

US Supreme Court hears bid to shut the door on climate suits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:25:00 UTC
14:25:00 KST

US Supreme Court hears bid to shut the door on climate suits
- The US Supreme Court will hear Suncor v Boulder, a key climate lawsuit where Boulder accuses oil companies of causing climate change and hiding fossil fuel dangers.
- The case could impact about 40 similar lawsuits and raise issues on federal law pre-emption, possibly ending or limiting many climate claims.
- Justice Samuel Alito recused himself over conflicts, making a 4-4 court split possible that would let Colorado’s case continue to trial without a Supreme Court ruling.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US Supreme Court was hearing arguments on Oct 5 in a case that could determine the fate of dozens of climate lawsuits seeking damages from oil companies for their role in global warming and for concealing the dangers of fossil fuels.
Known as Suncor v Boulder, the dispute began in 2018 when the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, sued ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy, claiming they “knowingly caused and contributed to the alteration of the climate” while “concealing and/or misrepresenting the dangers” of their products.
Suncor operates a refinery in Colorado, while ExxonMobil has deep ties to the Rocky Mountain State. The plaintiffs say they have suffered hundreds of millions of dollars in losses from wildfires, flooding and other weather extremes stemming from climate change linked to the burning of fossil fuels.
It is one of around 40 similar suits brought by cities, states, tribes and other local jurisdictions, modelled on successful litigation against tobacco and opioid producers.
Kannon Shanmugam, representing the oil giants, told the justices during opening arguments that the case “involves an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct”.
“Our constitutional system does not permit state law to be used in that manner,” Shanmugam said.
The companies contend such suits aim to impose an enormous “carbon tax” that could bankrupt the energy industry – that they are an illegitimate attempt to regulate greenhouse gas emissions, and are essentially asking the court to make them all go away.
After failing to move the case to federal court, the companies lost bids to have it dismissed in state court and at Colorado’s Supreme Court.
US President Donald Trump’s administration filed a brief urging the US Supreme Court to take up the case, and the justices agreed.
The court will consider whether federal law – specifically the Clean Air Act – pre-empts Boulder’s claims, whether the Constitution itself bars such suits and whether it can review the case before a trial has taken place.
If the justices focus on the last question, “that essentially just kicks the can down the road” since the wider questions would likely be raised later, Katrina Kuh, a professor of environmental law at Pace University, told AFP.
A ruling on the federal law questions, however, would matter for many pending suits.
“It could extinguish them entirely,” said Kuh. Or the justices could narrow them – allowing Colorado, for example, to apply its state law only to emissions within the state.
Alito recusal
The questions also bear on so-called “climate superfunds” – laws in New York and Vermont that would make polluters pay for climate resilience projects.
New York’s was struck down by a federal judge in September, and an adverse Supreme Court ruling could shut the door to it being revived on appeal.
Conservative legal scholar Jonathan Adler, a William & Mary law professor who filed a brief supporting Boulder, told AFP he disagreed with the oil companies’ legal theories and believed such cases are “viable” – without offering a view on the underlying merits.
He added that Justices Amy Coney Barrett, Neil Gorsuch and Clarence Thomas bear the most watching because “all three of them have shown some scepticism towards broad pre-emption arguments”, though he said they are also likely to be sceptical of suits of this nature.
Ahead of the hearing, ultra-conservative Justice Samuel Alito recused himself after critics called on him to step aside over his oil and gas stock holdings.
Conservatives still hold a 5-3 majority without Alito, but a 4-4 split is now possible – which would leave the Colorado ruling in place and let the case proceed to trial. AFP

Australia's illegal tobacco boom is taking a heavy toll. But new data offers a glimmer of hope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
