In brief
- The peak body for the convenience industry is calling on the government to cut the tobacco excise.
- It comes as new data from Queensland shows a jump in legal cigarette sales after new enforcement laws took effect.
Convenience store owners across Australia are being threatened, attacked and extorted as the illegal tobacco trade strips billions from legal cigarette sales, the industry's peak body says.
Owners have lost $3 billion in legal cigarette sales in the past five years, according to the Australian Association of Convenience Stores chief executive Theo Foukkare.
"Some of our members are being stood over, threatened and asked to pay protection money. They have been ram-raided, they have been held up at gunpoint," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP).
"The safety of the 80,000 frontline staff that our members employ around the country has gone backwards."
Foukkare is among dozens of industry experts and economists calling on the federal government to slash the tobacco excise, as Labor insists the tax is a good thing and urges states to crack down on illegal trade.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Legal cigarette sales jump in Queensland
Assistant Customs Minister Julian Hill has pointed to data out of Queensland to bolster the arguments.
The state's legal tobacco sales rose 55 per cent in the first month after new enforcement laws took effect in November and remained at least 40 per cent above previous levels for the next six months, data supplied by major retailers to the Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette Commissioner shows.
Nationally, the market remained almost flat across the same time period.
"We cannot overstate the emphasis on shutting down retail premises that are blatantly selling illegal products in high streets," Hill told AAP.
Foukkare said a roaring underground trade meant sales of legal cigarettes in Queensland were still well below what they were five years ago.
In other states, the picture was even bleaker.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said his state had successfully begun closing shops selling tobacco without a licence, yet crime was moving to the streets.
"We're actually seeing them now trying to change their business model. So this is why we do need to be one step ahead," he told reporters on Monday.
Foukkare said Queensland's success was likely because it had shut down illegal stores in blitz suburbs and beyond, meaning people needed to drive large distances for illegal products.
However, people were now using WhatsApp and meet-ups to sell cigarettes.
Modelling from Tulipwood Economics, commissioned by the association, showed that freezing the excise and legalising but regulating smoking cessation tools like nicotine pouches would generate $6.2 billion in GST over four years.
"It's time for you [the government] to change your position on tobacco control policy because you have absolutely failed everybody in Australia on this," Foukkare said.
"Stop being so pig-headed and stuck in ideology."
Government resists calls to slash excise
The Coalition has vowed to slash the tobacco excise by 80 per cent if elected, dropping the average price of cigarettes from between $50 and $40 to roughly $16-$26.
Opposition leader Angus Taylor said the cut would take the oxygen out of the thriving black market, which he called "economic terrorism".
"Our strong plan will attack the gangs where it hurts by taking away their massive price advantage, taking away their customers, and taking away their profits," he said.
One Nation wants to slash the tax by 75 per cent and freeze indexation for five years.
NSW Premier Chris Minns has long advocated for an excise cut.
Hill waved away the criticism, accusing the Coalition of being in "some crazy bidding war" with One Nation.
Queensland-based calls to Quitline, a national hotline for smokers trying to quit, more than doubled in the days following large enforcement operations, which he said indicated the crackdown was causing some smokers to quit.
"This is a really positive by-product of strong enforcement at the retail level," Hill said.
Public health groups have warned that cutting the excise and making tobacco cheaper could reverse decades of decline in smoking rates and have serious ramifications for the health of Australians.

Tooth with jade inlay reveals ancient Maya skill as dentists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:20:13 UTC
14:20:13 KST

A study of a pre-Hispanic molar with a jadeite inlay concludes it was treated while its owner was still alive. The find is the first documented case of such an inlay in a Mayan back molar.
A single molar can provide new clues about the knowledge and skills of the ancient Maya in dentistry. A study published (source in Spanish) in the journal 'Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports' analyses a lower first permanent molar with a jadeite inlay on its surface and concludes that the tooth was modified while the patient was still alive.
The tooth belongs to a pre-Hispanic osteological collection at the Popol Vuh Museum of Universidad Francisco Marroquín in Guatemala. The researchers found a well-defined cavity at the point where the four main cusps of the molar meet, in which the jade piece was firmly fixed with a cementing material.
"The cavity is perfect," explains Elma Vega-Lizama, a dental anthropologist at the Autonomous University of Yucatán in Mexico and co-author of the study, in comments reported (source in Spanish) by 'National Geographic'. "It is really a good procedure: well executed, clean."
The location of the inlay is particularly significant. Dental modifications documented among the ancient Maya were concentrated mainly in the anterior teeth, such as incisors and canines, and generally had an aesthetic purpose or were linked to social identity. In this case, however, it is a posterior molar, so the researchers rule out the idea that its function was purely ornamental.
To determine whether the intervention had been carried out before or after death, the researchers used cone-beam computed tomography. The images revealed extensive dystrophic calcification of the pulp chamber, a biological response indicating that the tooth was alive when the inlay was placed. In addition, the pulp chamber was well preserved and showed features consistent with a young adult individual.
The authors point out in the article that this find is "the first documented case of an occlusal inlay in a posterior tooth among the ancient Maya", that is, the first documented case of an inlay in the occlusal surface of a posterior tooth among the ancient Maya. The discovery broadens current interpretations of this civilisation's dental knowledge.
The mystery of its purpose
The exact purpose of the intervention, however, remains unclear. The researchers, from Universidad Francisco Marroquín, the Autonomous University of Yucatán and the Popol Vuh Museum, believe it may have had a therapeutic or palliative purpose, although they also leave open the possibility that it formed part of an unusual symbolic practice. The article stresses that it cannot be proved with certainty whether the inlay was used to fill a carious lesion.
The case is particularly striking because, despite the high prevalence of caries and abscesses among Mesoamerican populations, there is little evidence of interventions intended to relieve these conditions. The researchers also recall that the ancient Maya had considerable experience with dental drilling techniques. According to the study, "less than 4% of the drilling reached the pulp chamber".
The tooth analysed is therefore an exceptional case in Maya dental archaeology. For the authors, it shows that dental modifications in this civilisation were more varied than previously thought and underlines the need to continue investigating the more unusual dental interventions of ancient Mesoamerica.

‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:19:45 UTC
14:19:45 KST

The population of New Zealand’s endemic wētāpunga – believed to be the world’s heaviest insect – is officially “recovering” thanks to a groundbreaking breeding programme that has overseen the release of 11,000 insects into the wild.
“The future of wētāpunga is looking bright,” said Dr Chris Green, an honorary researcher at the department of conservation, who documented the success of the project for the New Zealand Journal of Zoology. Green co-authored a report released on 2 October that outlines the success of the breeding programme.
“Eleven thousand individuals for release is extraordinary and outstanding.”
A female wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse. Its body can grow up to 10cm long (nearly 4in) and its leg span can be as wide as 20cm.
It is the largest of 70 wētā species and was once found across parts of the North Island before predation from introduced species and habitat loss contributed to their decline. By the 1990s, they were considered “endangered” and are now presumed extinct in the wild on New Zealand’s mainland. The insects reside primarily on a smattering of predator-free islands in Auckland’s Hauraki Gulf and off the coast of Northland.
But their fortune is starting to change. Over the past 15 years, tens of thousands of wētāpunga have been bred at Butterfly Creek, a wildlife facility, and Auckland zoo, enabling the release of wētāpunga across new predator-free islands and some mainland reserves north of Auckland.
Butterfly Creek and Auckland zoo established husbandry techniques that, over time, have been scaled up to rear large numbers of wētāpunga in communal creches. The young wētāpunga – or nymphs – are fed a three-part diet of fresh foliage, fish flake protein and leaf litter. The protein is “critical” to the survival of the youngest nymphs, Green said.
Once big enough to protect themselves, the insects are transferred to their new habitat. The efforts have led to 45 separate translocations to wild habitats, which is “a very high number in any recovery of a species”, Green said.
Monitoring on two islands has shown wētāpunga have established self-sustaining populations, with fourth and fifth generations born there, in what Green said was a marker of success. As a result, the species’ conservation status has improved from “nationally endangered” to “nationally recovering”.
“It’s so exciting, because we are unable to report that for so many of our other threatened species,” Green said.
New Zealand is particularly vulnerable to species decline because of its high rates of endemism and problems with introduced pests.
Green said the country was at the forefront of invertebrate recovery work and he was not aware of any other examples of breeding programmes working to this scale, or with such success.
By documenting the project’s work, he hopes other institutions will feel encouraged to develop their own programmes.
“That’s the extraordinary aspect of it – that we’ve been successful,” he said. “If other institutions can get into that sort of position, then there can be huge benefit for threatened species in New Zealand.”

Taipei prosecutors uncover EV charging station investment scam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:17:42 UTC
14:17:42 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taipei District Prosecutors Office on Monday indicted Farxun Energy Co. CEO Hsieh Po-chun (謝博鈞) and 25 others over an alleged illegal investment scheme involving the company's Fafago green energy charging stations, with prosecutors seeking a 16-year prison sentence for Hsieh, per UDN.
Prosecutors said the company raised about NT$219.05 million (US$6.8 million) from investors between January 2024 and April 2026 by advertising investments in electric vehicle charging stations on Facebook, at franchise exhibitions, and in investment seminars in Taipei, Taichung, and Kaohsiung.
The company allegedly charged NT$300,000 per charging-station investment and guaranteed a minimum monthly return of NT$3,520, equivalent to an annualized return of 14.08%. After three years, investors could reportedly have the company buy back the investment for NT$210,000 or continue under “buy two, get one free” and “buy three, get two free” arrangements, per CNA.
Prosecutors said investors had no role in selecting sites, installing equipment, or operating the stations, while returns were not linked to the actual revenue of individual charging stations. The company had installed fewer than 200 charging stations in 2024 but continued soliciting investments, prosecutors said.
Investigators allege the company used new investment funds to pay returns and bonuses to earlier investors rather than building charging stations corresponding to the investments, creating a structure prosecutors described as resembling a Ponzi scheme.
The investigation also found that funds moved through related companies and personal accounts, with some withdrawn in cash to obscure their source. Prosecutors said more than NT$43.87 million was transferred to a company established under Hsieh's son's name, per Money-Link.
The company stopped paying investors in April, prompting complaints and an investigation. In June, the Ministry of Justice's Investigation Bureau and police searched 21 locations and questioned 14 people as part of the investigation, per a Ministry of Justice press release.
Prosecutors charged the defendants under the Banking Act, aggravated fraud, and money-laundering laws. Hsieh faces additional aggravated fraud and money-laundering allegations, while prosecutors are seeking 16 years in prison for him.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The FBI arrested a 34-year-old California woman at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday for allegedly surveilling President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) son and his family on behalf of Chinese officials.
Zhang “Heather” Wanying, an Irvine realtor, was arrested while preparing to board a flight to Shanghai and charged with acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government, per CBS News. Law enforcement sources told CBS that the alleged surveillance target was Lai’s son, Lai Ting-yu (賴廷與).
According to the FBI criminal complaint, Zhang and an accomplice traveled to Seattle in September 2025 and took photographs outside the suburban home of the family of a high-ranking Taiwanese official. The complaint says Zhang and a man identified as “Individual 1” flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue, and went to the residence.
Images from a neighbor’s security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two “appearing to film” Lai, his wife, and their child as they arrived home that evening, CBS News reported. Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler, “Saw him. Young male. It’s that young one,” and “I am videorecording,” followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.
The FBI said it obtained the messages from Zhang’s iCloud account under a search warrant. FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt wrote in the Saturday complaint that information about the whereabouts of relatives of senior Taiwanese officials, including photographs of their homes and vehicles, could have intelligence value if China sought leverage over Taiwan’s president in a potential future conflict.
The complaint alleges Zhang maintained contact with at least two people suspected of working for the Chinese government. She was introduced to one of them through a classmate at Beijing’s University of International Relations, which the FBI said has close ties to China’s Ministry of State Security, UDN reported.
Zhang allegedly met the official in a private room in Changsha during a trip to China in June 2025 and accepted a surveillance assignment. She later messaged the official, “I can handle this,” and on Aug. 26 said she would be busy with work in Los Angeles that week and might travel to Seattle the following week.
Zhang is a licensed California real estate agent with JC Pacific Capital Inc., while her husband, Edric Ding, also works at the company, according to UDN. Lai Ting-yu is an engineer in his 30s who studied in the US and now works for the Dutch electronics company Philips.
Lai earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in 2012, followed by a master's degree in bioengineering innovation and design from Johns Hopkins University and a doctorate in bioengineering from the University of Washington.
Taiwan’s Presidential Office described the alleged surveillance as a case of transnational repression and thanked US authorities for protecting Taiwanese citizens, per Reuters. Presidential Office Spokesperson Karen Kuo (郭雅慧) condemned the alleged conduct as “barbaric,” saying it disregarded human rights and the sovereignty of nations.
First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli said Zhang used “tradecraft” to avoid detection and never informed US authorities that she was acting on behalf of a foreign government, Reuters reported. Zhang is scheduled to appear Monday in federal court in Los Angeles.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Eric Schmidt, the former CEO and chair of Google, said Saturday that a conflict in the Taiwan Strait is likely to become a “drone war.”
“There is a publicly discussed plan to protect the Taiwan Strait,” Schmidt said in an interview with The Economist in Kyiv. “I don’t know, but I’m assuming that will ultimately be a drone war and not a ship war.”
“If you think about it, you don’t really want to put a ship that close to China; you want to put a drone ship with drones in it, because you do not want people to be killed,” he said.
Schmidt added China has a large number of land-to-sea missiles and the US would need interceptors to counter them.

At a conference in Los Angeles last year, he suggested that Taiwan could learn from Ukraine’s experience by using explosive sea drones similar to those Ukraine has used against Russian forces in the Black Sea to help prevent a Chinese landing.
His comments echo “Hellscape,” a defense strategy proposed in 2024 by Admiral Samuel Paparo, the commander of US Indo-Pacific Command, that involved deploying large numbers of unmanned systems in the Taiwan Strait to disrupt a potential Chinese attack.
Schmidt has visited Taiwan several times. Last year, the Special Competitive Studies Project, a nonprofit he founded to promote US competitiveness in emerging technologies, held its third annual global summit in Taipei.

Guterres’s Successor Will Need Russia’s Blessing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:15:00 UTC
14:15:00 KST

António Guterres is approaching the end of his decade as UN secretary-general with little public trust in Ukraine, a bitter dispute with Israel, and a Security Council that remains vulnerable to obstruction by the governments it is supposed to hold accountable.
His tenure produced tangible achievements, including an agreement that reopened Ukrainian ports to grain exports during Russia’s invasion. But his cultivation of Moscow and disputes over his advocacy on Gaza have sharpened questions about how he uses the authority he does possess.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The next secretary-general will inherit those disputes and the same institutional constraints as well as please Moscow to avoid a Russian veto.
A credibility problem in Ukraine
The difficulty of maintaining relations with Moscow without obscuring its responsibility for aggression predates Guterres.
In June 2016, his predecessor, Ban Ki-moon, provoked an angry response from Ukraine’s UN ambassador after emphasizing Russia’s role in ending the conflicts in Ukraine and Syria and safeguarding human rights. Ban supported Ukraine’s territorial integrity but continued to court Moscow’s cooperation.
Guterres inherited that approach. During a May 2021 visit to Russia, he thanked Putin for Russia’s support for the UN and sought deeper cooperation, including on human rights. Russia had already occupied Crimea for seven years.
Guterres maintained the UN’s support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity, and reports issued under his name documented abuses in occupied Crimea. His public diplomacy nevertheless continued to present Moscow as a partner whose cooperation should be cultivated.
Demining Syria: How Not to Let Word Games Bury the Work
His October 2024 visit to the BRICS summit in Kazan especially intensified Ukrainian anger. Kyiv contrasted his acceptance of Putin’s invitation with his absence from the Swiss peace summit that June. Putin was already subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant.
The UN’s account of their meeting said Guterres reiterated that the invasion violated the UN Charter and international law. That objection did not undo the diplomatic recognition conveyed by his attendance.
Distrust toward the UN also extends beyond summit appearances. In Kyiv Post’s 2022 reporting on the treatment of Ukrainian staff, a former employee of the UN-related International Organization for Migration alleged that international colleagues left before the invasion while local staff lacked adequate evacuation arrangements.
In a separate Kyiv Post interview, Ukraine’s then UN ambassador, Sergiy Kyslytsya, criticized inconsistencies within the Secretariat, saying some officials offered their own interpretations of the aggression rather than following the General Assembly’s position. These were allegations about management and institutional discipline, areas where the Secretariat bears responsibility regardless of Russia’s veto.
A November 2025 survey commissioned by the New Europe Center illustrates Guterres’s standing in Ukraine: roughly one in four respondents trusted him, while more than half distrusted him. The telephone survey of 1,000 respondents recorded trust at 25.1% and distrust at 56.7%.
Gaza showed he could use the office forcefully
Guterres’s response to the Israel-Hamas war demonstrated his willingness to use the office’s formal powers to press for action.
On Dec. 6, 2023, he invoked Article 99 of the UN Charter for the first time in his tenure, formally drawing the Security Council’s attention to the danger posed by the war in Gaza. He pressed for a humanitarian ceasefire and warned that civilian protection and aid delivery were collapsing. He had not formally invoked the provision over Ukraine.
His language also triggered a confrontation with Israel. At an October 2023 Security Council meeting, Guterres said Hamas’s attacks “did not happen in a vacuum,” citing the Palestinians’ experience of alleged occupation despite their historically documented rejection of proposals for a two-state solution.
Questions about his judgment also arose during the controversy surrounding Francesca Albanese, the independent UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories. Albanese has drawn criticism for describing allegations of “mass rape” during Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023 attacks as fabrications and defense of Hamas as “a political force.”
Although independent rapporteurs do not report to Guterres, his spokesman defended her against US sanctions in July 2025, calling sanctions on special rapporteurs a dangerous precedent.
Still, despite deep investment in the Gaza war, Guterres’s intervention also exposed the limits of his authority: Two days after he invoked Article 99, the US vetoed a resolution calling for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire.
His diplomacy did produce results
The strongest counterweight to a wholly negative assessment is the Black Sea Grain Initiative, brokered by the UN and Turkey in July 2022.
Before Russia withdrew a year later, the agreement enabled exports of more than 32 million metric tons (35 million US tons) of grain and other foodstuffs to 45 countries. It restored an outlet for Ukrainian agriculture and helped stabilize international food markets.
The arrangement depended on Russian cooperation. When Moscow withdrew in July 2023, Guterres could not compel it to maintain the agreement.
There were administrative reforms, too.
In 2019, the UN created new management and operational-support departments and delegated more authority to managers. Those changes did not resolve the Security Council’s central problem: permanent members can block substantive decisions even when their own conduct is at issue.
Russia’s seat is a responsibility of member states
Russia’s continued occupation of the Soviet Union’s Security Council seat remains disputed by Ukraine.
The UN’s membership record states that Boris Yeltsin notified the organization in December 1991 that Russia would continue Soviet membership, including its permanent seat.
In his 2022 interview with Kyiv Post, Kyslytsya argued that Moscow had bypassed the necessary admission procedures. He also acknowledged that even Ukraine’s closest allies were not ready to accept that argument.
The challenge has not resulted in Russia’s removal.
Resolving it is a matter for governments acting through UN institutions, rather than an administrative decision the secretary-general can impose.
The same distinction applies to Security Council reform. Under Article 108, Charter amendments require adoption by two-thirds of the General Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of UN members, including all five permanent Council members.
The UN’s 2024 Pact for the Future renewed commitments to Council reform. It did not remove Russia’s veto or the requirement for permanent members to ratify Charter changes. As Kyiv Post argued in 2022, calls for reform have repeatedly collided with Moscow’s ability to obstruct action against itself.
What happened to more assertive secretary-generals?
In the same 2022 interview, Kyslytsya described the officeholder as “a secretary more than he is a general.” He contrasted that limited role with Dag Hammarskjöld’s willingness to confront Moscow.
Hammarskjöld died in a September 1961 plane crash while seeking to negotiate an end to fighting in the Congo. The circumstances remain unresolved. Kyslytsya explicitly declined to claim he had been murdered, as his broader argument concerned the resistance an assertive secretary-general encounters from powerful states.
He also credited Kofi Annan, one of the more popular UN chiefs, with effectively carrying out his mandate, while emphasizing that the permanent members constrained even successful officeholders.
What the public wants from the next chief
A new UN Foundation survey suggests respondents want more than competent administration.
Among 5,000 people surveyed across 20 countries, 84% considered the UN necessary. But 52% of all respondents chose the assessment that it remained necessary while struggling to deliver.
Preventing and ending armed conflicts was the leading priority, selected by 58%. Respondents were more likely to want a diplomat, crisis manager, or moral voice than a leader primarily focused on internal reform.
Among those skeptical of international institutions, weak enforcement and domination by powerful countries were leading concerns. Both involve the authority governments are willing to give the organization.
The survey used nonprobability samples of 250 people per country and did not include Ukraine. Its findings describe those surveyed, rather than a representative verdict from the world’s population.
The candidates inherit the same constraints
The seven candidates in the race bring different experiences and approaches to Moscow.
Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), presents his management of nuclear crises as preparation for the job. But his handling of Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia has drawn criticism.
In April, Greenpeace Ukraine challenged his suggestion that joint Ukrainian-Russian use of the plant was technically possible, arguing it risked legitimizing the occupier’s role.
The IAEA did document Russian military personnel and equipment at the site. However, the dispute concerns whether Grossi’s pursuit of practical arrangements sufficiently challenges Moscow’s control, rather than whether he acknowledged the military presence at all.
Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan, who leads UN Trade and Development, combines economic expertise with experience as a national vice president.
Her negotiations to remove obstacles to Russian food and fertilizer exports formed part of the UN’s grain diplomacy, giving her experience with the bargaining that characterized Guterres’s approach.
Guyana’s UN ambassador, Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, has taken a clearer public position on withdrawal. In a January 2025 Security Council statement, she demanded that Russia immediately remove its forces from Ukraine’s internationally recognized territory.
The other contenders are former General Assembly President María Fernanda Espinosa, former Senegalese President Macky Sall, former Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki, and Uganda’s Olara Otunnu, a former UN special representative for children and armed conflict. Former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet withdrew in September.
A-Baki is particularly concerned given her Moscow agenda sympathies. During her UN candidate hearing, she suggested Russia could stop the war and Ukraine could decide against joining NATO. She also said borders should be respected. That places her approach at a different point from Rodrigues Birkett’s explicit demand for Russian withdrawal.
Regardless, any successful candidate will need at least nine Security Council votes and no permanent-member veto, meaning that whoever gets elected will have to be Kremlin-blessed.

Samoa PM apologises after Nazi salute video emerges
Pacific island nation’s leader says 2007 video showing him saying ‘Heil Hitler’ does not reflect his beliefs.
Samoa’s Prime Minister La’auli Leuatea Schmidt has apologised after previously unseen video showed him leading a Nazi salute and saying “Heil Hitler” at a family gathering.
Schmidt issued the apology on Monday after the Samoa Observer, a local newspaper, published the seven-second clip the previous day.
The footage was recorded at a Schmidt family reunion on the island of Savai‘i in July 2007, when he was an MP and deputy speaker of parliament.
In the video, Schmidt is holding a microphone as he leads a “hip hip” exchange with the group before telling those present to raise their right hands and say “Heil Hitler”.
About a dozen people visible in the footage appear to follow him.
Radio New Zealand said it had independently verified the footage through its correspondent in Samoa.
Schmidt said on Monday that the words and gesture were inappropriate regardless of what was intended at the gathering and apologised for the offence they could cause.
“I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism,” he said, adding that the episode did not represent his beliefs or the values of Samoa’s government and people.
The apology followed criticism from academics contacted by the Samoa Observer.
Richard Evans, a historian of Nazi Germany, told the Samoa Observer by email that the footage was “shocking and disturbing”.
The paper also quoted University of Canterbury academic Anne-Marie Brady as saying Schmidt should explain and apologise.
Schmidt, who became prime minister in 2025, has made strong public expressions of support for Israel.
He wore a Jewish prayer shawl at his swearing-in, where a shofar, a horn used in Jewish religious ceremonies, was sounded.
He has also pledged to open a Samoan embassy in Jerusalem before the end of 2026, a step taken by only a handful of countries because of the city’s disputed status and Palestinian claims to East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state.
In his Monday statement, Schmidt said he considered the controversy addressed and would focus on the country’s economic and social challenges.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday refused to pass an interim order seeking the suspension of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and issued notice to the Election Commission of India, CEC and the other two election commissioners on a plea challenging decisions taken by the poll body on Special Intensive Revision.A bench led by CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana heard pleas filed by Patna resident Rakesh Kumar Singh and advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi. Coral reefs are bleaching in extreme heat. Could underwater umbrellas save them?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:02:27 UTC
14:02:27 KST

Underwater shades could help corals survive extreme heat, but researchers stress that they’re not a catch-all solution.
Can an umbrella work underwater? The answer appears to be yes, just not for the reason many might imagine.
Around the world, marine heatwaves have put coral at risk of excessive heat stress. When ocean temperatures get too hot, stressed corals can expel the microscopic algae that live in their tissues, causing them to turn white and lose their main source of food – a phenomenon known as bleaching that is occurring with alarming frequency.
A group of scientists in Florida believes that underwater umbrellas could mitigate the damage.
“Heat-related coral bleaching is probably the biggest threat to reefs worldwide,” says Karen Neely of Nova Southeastern University, lead author of a research article published this week in Frontiers in Marine Science. “Solutions like shading can offer temporary protection on small scales.”
How underwater umbrellas protected Florida corals
The study came together after a record-breaking marine heatwave struck the Florida Keys in 2023.
At most sites, every kind of coral bleached, and branching corals – species that grow in tree- or antler-like formations, such as the aptly named staghorn and elkhorn corals – were almost wiped out. At one inshore site, more than half of the corals researchers monitored lost some or all their living tissue.
“This study stemmed directly from that event: we wanted to provide proof of concept for tools to save targeted corals in similar future events,” says Neely.
The following summer, the researchers selected 40 colonies belonging to two species of brain coral in the lower Florida Keys.
Half were left exposed and half were fitted with floating shades made from PVC frames and nylon mesh – like underwater parasols suspended about 30 centimetres above the coral.
The shades, the researchers stress, were not used to cool the water. Instead, they reduced the intense sunlight and ultravioletradiation that can make bleaching worse.
Divers began monitoring the corals in July 2024 and installed the umbrellas in August, when summer heat intensified. They continued until November, when temperatures cooled, tracking changes in their colour and the algae living inside their tissue.
Despite 2024 seeing the second-highest level of heat stress recorded at the site since 1985, some of the shaded corals began to regain their colour after the umbrellas were installed. The exposed corals became paler during the hottest part of the experiment.
But the umbrellas are still a temporary fix, the researchers stress.
Covering entire reefs would be impractical, so they see it primarily as a way to protect vulnerable corals during extreme heat. Ultimately, though, long-term protection depends on limiting the warming of the seas.
“Scaling is the big limitation of this study,” Neely explains. “Shading is not a cure-all.”
Marine heatwaves are bleaching reefs worldwide
Globally, ocean temperatures continue to break records. On 22 August, the average global sea surface temperature outside the polar regions reached 21.1°C, the highest daily temperature recorded.
Meanwhile, extreme heat is hitting coral reefs more often. In August, the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network reported that bleaching events now occur roughly every five to six years, compared with about once a decade in the past.
Although corals can recover from bleaching when sea temperatures cool, frequent marine heatwaves can leave too little time for damaged reefs to repair themselves.
The most recent global bleaching event began in 2023. Between 2023 and 2024, hard coral cover fell by 8.9 per cent globally – the largest one-year decline on record.
By March 2025, 84 per cent of the world’s reefs had experienced temperatures hot enough to cause bleaching, while parts of Australia’s Great Barrier Reef recorded their largest annual losses of living coral in almost 40 years of monitoring.
Although coral reefs cover less than 0.2 per cent of the ocean floor, they are vital to life, both underwater and on land.
They provide food and shelter for at least a quarter of all marine species, including many fish caught for food, and are a natural shield for coastlines.
While underwater umbrellas may be able to prevent marine heatwaves, the Florida study suggests they could give these important creatures at least some protection as temperatures rise.

Alexandra Albazini who loves Bulgarian and dreams of a master's degree in Sofia

Daniela Goleminova
Interview
Alexandra Albazini who loves Bulgarian and dreams of a master's degree in Sofia
Monday 5 October 2026 07:05
Monday, 5 October 2026, 07:05
PHOTO Daniela Goleminova
Font size
For 17 years, Italian national Alexandra Albazini has worked as a translator at the European Commission in Brussels. She says that from an early age she became fascinated by learning foreign languages, seeing them as a way to discover new worlds, cultures and peoples. This passion has made her a true linguaphile.
Today, Alexandra has an excellent command of seven languages: Italian, English, French, Spanish, German, Slovenian and Russian, and for the past four years she has also been learning Bulgarian. She already speaks it well, albeit with a slight accent.
PHOTO Daniela Goleminova
“I still make a lot of mistakes. I study Bulgarian online with a teacher who lives in Bulgaria, in Sofia. I know Russian and Slovenian, and I love the Slavic world. I am interested in its culture and way of life, in what Bulgarians think, who they are and how they live. I am interested in books and I want to learn the language so that I can read Bulgarian books. I read contemporary literature, including Georgi Gospodinov. At the moment, I am reading Georgi Markov’s two-volume Dispatches from the Past (ed. also known as In Absentia Reports About Bulgaria),” Ms Albazini says.
She says she has visited Bulgaria three times to attend in-person Bulgarian language courses. In the future, she plans to enrol in a master’s programme at Sofia University “St Kliment Ohridski” to deepen her linguistic knowledge of contemporary Bulgarian.
Sofia University Saint Kliment Ohridski
PHOTO BNR
“I didn’t manage to do it this semester, perhaps I will next semester. It is very difficult because they require all the documents to be translated and apostilled,” she explains.
How do Alexandra Albazini’s family and friends feel about her passion for mastering Bulgarian, which is not among the world’s most widely spoken languages?
“My friends and acquaintances say it’s madness,” the polyglot says with a smile. And will learning foreign languages continue to be valued in the future?
“I don’t know how young people will think tomorrow. For me, it is very interesting and important to understand what other people and different nations think and say, and what they write. And as Fyodor Dostoevsky said: ‘Beauty will save the world!’” Alexandra Albazini concludes.
PHOTO Private archive
She says she enjoys working as a translator at the European Commission because it gives her the opportunity to hear all the languages. She does not approve of the fact that English has increasingly become the predominant language spoken in the European institutions in recent years. There are, of course, many difficulties and challenges:
“You never know what the speaker is going to say. Sometimes people speak very quickly, which makes it difficult for the interpreter, because you have to think, translate and speak at the same time. Technical terminology is a real challenge at live meetings, which is why an interpreter has to prepare every day,” the Italian translator explains.
PHOTO Private archive
Alexandra Albazini admits with a smile that she sometimes makes mistakes when interpreting, but stresses that they are not significant and often go unnoticed because work in the interpreting booth is a team effort. If she makes an inadvertent mistake, her colleagues quickly help her correct it.
How are digitalisation and artificial intelligence changing the work of translators? Could AI eventually replace human interpreters?
“I don’t use artificial intelligence because I don’t like it. I am still trying to work without it. If a translation is produced using artificial intelligence, the translator then has to check it. I don’t believe artificial intelligence will completely replace humans, because natural intelligence is very complex. It is not just about words, but about reading, listening, everything that is there,” Alexandra Albazini explains.

The best road trips to spot Europe’s most impressive wildlife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

Planning a wildlife escape? These European road trips combine spectacular scenery with some of the continent’s best opportunities for spotting animals in the wild.
Europe has many charms, and its wide variety of wildlife is certainly among them.
Across the continent, travellers can spot everything from flamingos and starlings to deer, seals and golden eagles. Many of them can be spotted from the road, meaning they’re accessible to a majority of tourists.
Now, car rental company Avis has ranked Europe’s best wildlife driving routes, taking into consideration the reliability of sightings, proximity to airports, how practical and compact each road trip is, and its popularity online, specifically in terms of Google search volume and appearances on Instagram.
Southern England’s New Forest topped the list, followed by Denmark’s part of the Wadden Sea, while Spain appears twice in the top 10.
These are the best driving routes for spotting wildlife across Europe.
Five European scenic drives where you can spot wildlife
New Forest wildlife drive, England
At the top of the ranking is the New Forest in the south of England. This beautiful spot scores 93 out of 100 on the Avis wildlife routes index, for various reasons.
A 32km drive starting in Lyndhurst and travelling through Bolderwood and Rhinefield Ornamental Drive and finishing up in Brockenhurst takes just 45 minutes to one hour – one of the speediest wildlife drives on the list.
This area is particularly famous for its native, free-roaming native New Forest ponies, but visitors can also expect to see the likes of fallow and roe deer and buzzards soaring overhead.
Autumn is an ideal time to visit, with October playing host to the deer rut, the annual mating season for the creatures.
Wadden Sea (Route 11), Denmark
In second place is Denmark’s Wadden Sea – or Route 11 – route, which comes in with a score of 80 out of 100.
Driving from Ribe via the Gammel Hviding marshes to Skærbæk covers around 65km and takes approximately one to 1 hour and 25 minutes to drive.
Expect to see migratory birds, seals and harbour porpoises around the wider Wadden Sea landscape.
This route is also the most accessible in the ranking, as Esbjerg Airport is just 30km away.
In the autumn, visitors can experience Denmark’s famous Black Sun phenomenon, where starling murmurations flock overhead in shifting patterns before heading to roost.
Ebro Delta birding drive, Spain
Third on the list is the Ebro Delta birding drive in Spain’s Catalonia, scoring 74 out of 100.
The route runs for just 25km, which can take approximately 45 to 60 minutes to drive, although there’s so much to see here that wildlife lovers may want to allow a full day for stops.
The route takes in Poblenou del Delta, Pont de Través, Encanyissada, Migjorn and Alfacada and encompasses lagoons, wetlands and rice fields which are variously home to bird species including flamingos, glossy ibis, purple herons, spoonbills, marsh harriers and waders.
While the late spring and summer are particularly good for spotting breeding birds, September and October bring spectacular displays of migrating species.
Camargue wildlife drive, France
The Camargue wildlife drive in France, with a score of 73 out of 100, is in fourth place.
The route is approximately 90km long and takes 2.5 hours, although it can take longer if drivers take more stops. It runs from Arles to Étang de Vaccarès and Pont de Gau and on to Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer.
Pink flamingos are the star attraction here, but visitors can also spot herons, the famous white Camargue horses and black bulls.
September is the best time to see the flamingos, but all the other creatures can be easily seen all year round.
Scotland’s North Coast 500
The iconic North Coast 500 in Scotland ranks in fifth, scoring 71 out of 100 – and it’s by far the longest route in the top five.
In fact, the full circuit covers some 830km and requires about 14 to 16 hours of driving, which most people usually choose to spread across several days.
The route takes drivers from Inverness through Black Isle, Wester Ross, Durness, Dunnet Head and John O’Groats and to Inverness. Those who take it can see habitats which are home to red deer, pine martens, harbour seals and golden eagles.
May to September might provide the most favourable conditions for a road trip, but autumn is a great time to visit for those who want to see the red deer rut.
Europe’s top 10 best driving routes for spotting wildlife
- 1. New Forest wildlife drive, England
- 2. Wadden Sea (Route 11), Denmark
- 3. Ebro Delta birding drive, Spain
- 4. Camargue wildlife drive, France
- 5. Scotland’s North Coast 500
- 6. A149 North Norfolk Coast, England
- 7. Monfragüe National Park roads, Spain
- 8. Hortobágy Route 33, Hungary
- 9. Lake Kerkini wildlife drive, Greece
- 10. Andøya scenic route, Norway

Intelligence Everywhere: Inside Europe’s Next Technology Era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:00:53 UTC
14:00:53 KST

Partner Content presented by Qualcomm
Intelligence is moving closer to where data is created. From smartphones and computers to glasses, cars and industrial devices, AI is becoming embedded across the technologies that shape everyday life.
As AI expands beyond traditional computing environments, it is increasingly being delivered across devices and the cloud. "Our vision is intelligence everywhere," says Wassim Chourbaji, SVP and President Europe, Middle East and Africa, Qualcomm.
“It’s where the data is created at the edge, but also in the data centre,” explains Wassim Chourbaji. “We call it hybrid AI, and it’s really an orchestration between intelligence at the edge and intelligence in the data centre.”
Rooted in Europe
For Qualcomm, this transformation builds on more than 35 years in Europe, with R&D centresacross France, Germany, Sweden, Ireland, Spain and Italy. “Our platforms combine connectivity, high-performance, low-power compute and AI,” says Chourbaji. These technologies are relevant to a wide range of industries, and Qualcomm partners with European industries including automotive, energy, robotics and industrial applications. “We like innovation. We like to drive partnerships, and you will see us very excited about the future and what we’re building in Europe.”
Qualcomm’s approach also builds on academic collaboration and open innovation. Amira Alloum, Director of Engineering and R&D Europe, Qualcomm, highlights collaboration with institutions including the Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology, Politecnico di Milano and the University of Manchester.
These collaborations reflect a broader conviction at the heart of Qualcomm's approach where industry, academia and developers can build on each other's work. That philosophy also extends to open-source communities.
A prime example is Arduino, the open-source electronics platform now under Qualcomm’s umbrella. Fabio Violante, VP & GM of Arduino, points to the platform’s 36.7 million development environment downloads last year as proof of the power of open communities.
“Distributed innovation means having anybody contributing to some form of knowledge,” says Violante. “This is a massive democratisation, lowering the barrier to entry to technology. People who have a problem can now just assemble their solution with a few clicks.”
Beyond Connectivity: The Role of 6G
As intelligence spreads across devices and data centres, the networks that connect them must evolve as well. "6G is not just a new generation of connectivity," says Wassim Chourbaji. "It's connectivity, but also distributed computing and sensing."
In Cork, Qualcomm’s teams are already working with new spectrum and conducting trials for 6G. “Everything is about bridging the gap between theory and reality,” explains Jarbas Pinheiro,Senior Engineer, QT Technologies Ireland Limited. “We invest a lot in research, simulations, prototypes and field trials.”
One of 6G's most promising capabilities is “transforming the network itself into a platform that perceives the physical world in real time,” Alloum explains. By leveraging integrated sensing, the network can create live virtual replicas of physical environments, mapping vehicles, drones, pedestrians, and infrastructure in real time without relying on physical cameras or additional sensors.
Defining Europe’s AI Future
As AI becomes further embedded in daily life, localised implementation and data sovereignty are becoming increasingly important considerations. “I truly believe AI is local by nature,” Chourbaji says. “It understands our dialects, our thinking. So it has to be with the local culture.”
This places Europe in a strong position to benefit from the transformation. “Europe is extremely well positioned in this transformation,” he says, pointing to the region’s industrial base, research capabilities and the need for robust AI and telecom infrastructure.
The opportunity for Europe is not simply to adopt AI technologies, but to help shape their development and deployment. By combining infrastructure, industrial expertise, talent and open innovation, the region has many of the ingredients needed to play a leading role in the next phase of AI.

Internet Watch Foundation reports huge rise in AI child sexual abuse material
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:00:49 UTC
14:00:49 KST

AI-generated child sexual abuse material is proliferating online, with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025.
Analysts at the Internet Watch Foundation have found more photorealistic child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2026 than for the whole of the prior year. The UK-based IWF, which monitors abuse material globally, said it had assessed 6,310 AI images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse, 40% higher than last year’s total of more than 4,500.
Instances of AI-made child sexual abuse material have been rising for several years, with a huge surge in videos in particular, although the latest IWF figures refer to still images only. The majority of the images seen by analysts were of girls, and of children aged seven to 13.
The IWF said the figures underlined the need for new statutory regulation on AI.
Andy Burnham’s government has not signalled that a new bill focused on the technology is imminent. Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, has said “nothing is off the table” in terms of fresh regulation, but that the test for any legislative proposal will be: “Will it make the British people safer?”
Hannah Swirsky, the head of policy at the IWF, said she backed calls from parliamentarians for “binding legislation on AI” to compel companies to build safer models. “It is incumbent on tech companies to build tools which cannot be abused this way,” she said. This problem has been created by technology, and if companies won’t build tools which are safe by design.”
AI-generated child sexual abuse material is illegal in the UK and the government has also made it illegal to adapt an AI model to create abuse material or to distribute such models to others. Developing a model designed to produce hyper-realistic child sexual abuse material carries a criminal sentence of up to five years.
A government spokesperson said: “UK law is clear that child sexual abuse material is illegal, regardless of whether it is AI-generated or not. We are going further by banning AI models that are used to create this type of abuse material and produce sickening, hyper-realistic imagery that often contains the likeness of real children.”
AI has also enabled online predators to create explicit images of children. The Report Remove service, which blocks intimate images from appearing online, has received 420 reports from children concerning images of themselves that they believed had been faked or manipulated to appear explicit. The number has already exceeded its 2025 total of 397.
The use of AI tools to create abuse tools has led to the National Crime Agency and IWF encouraging parents and guardians to keep pictures of their children off social media. The guidance suggests making social media accounts private or sharing pictures of children through a “close friends” group only.

BBC morale dented by gradual ‘bloodletting’ after weeks of job cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

14:00:49 KST

Morale at the BBC has been severely dented by a gradual “bloodletting” that has seen plans to shed as many as 2,000 staff slowly announced over several weeks, members of the corporation’s staff have warned.
More internal meetings have been called for this week to discuss further details of the cuts, which aim to save £500m. Some staff already fear that further waves of cuts will follow soon after in the new year.
It is expected that BBC Scotland and BBC Three will both be made online-only channels as part of a bid to save money, the Guardian understands.
The BBC is having to make the cuts as a result of its serious financial challenges, which have seen its cash revenues fall at an alarming rate over the last year. Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, has said he was not fully aware of the pressures when he took the job.
The drawn-out process of announcing the cuts comes as a result of the BBC’s decision to tell the teams affected as soon as possible, department by department.
However, many acknowledge the result has been a “drip, drip” of announcements that has added to the low morale at New Broadcasting House. “We have our problems, but we seem to be creating new ones,” said one insider.
Referring to yet another internal announcement on further job losses, another BBC figure said: “The bloodletting continues.”
Closing the linear channels for BBC Three and BBC Scotland will be one of the most difficult moments in the latest savings programme. Insiders said the viewing numbers could not justify keeping them on the air.
Brittin has made a series of comments suggesting the corporation has too many linear channels, when viewing habits have switched to catchup viewing on the BBC’s iPlayer platform.
Sweeping redundancy plans have been announced across the BBC, from the news division to local radio and its relatively new media tech division, where 110 compulsory redundancies will be made, with 280 roles closing in the division in total.
Redundancy pay terms are also being reviewed. The BBC has already announced a reduction in local news correspondents, as well as making existing correspondents carry out general reporting duties. Local radio will also be made more regional.
While children’s television has been protected, with the BBC touting its children’s programming as a high-quality antidote to online slop, even staff in that division have been asked to come forward should they wish to take voluntary redundancy.
Gallows humour has already gripped some BBC staff. Managers had to chastise staff after one online call about cuts last week, after it was flooded with disapproving emojis.
Meanwhile, some presenters have begun to refer to the cuts on air. BBC Look North’s Peter Levy joked last week that the “BBC cuts are starting” after a weather presenter could be heard but not seen by viewers during an update.
Some staff are now asking when the cuts will end, given some have been told cost savings have been divided into “waves” and more could be coming next year. One staffer feared a “doom spiral” of weaker output and an increase in the number of people unwilling to pay the licence fee.
“The challenge is real but the reality playing out over weeks and weeks … is likely to make that challenge worse and not better anytime soon,” they said.
Any future plans will be shaped by weekly talks taking place between the BBC and the government over its future funding model, which could see the licence fee widened to include anyone who watches a streaming service.
Currently, only those who watch live television on any platform, or watch the iPlayer, have to pay the fee.

====================================================================================================

Social care for disabled adults is in as much crisis as support for elderly people – so why is the government silent about it? | John Harris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:00:48 UTC
14:00:48 KST

Seemingly brilliant conference speeches are often followed by a hangover, and so it has arguably proved with Andy Burnham’s. It was, it has to be said, something of a triumph, but there is now a familiar sense of nagging angst over how his big idea of a national care service is actually going to work. But equally, it doesn’t seem unreasonable to be more generous and patient. The policy issues are vast. The new PM’s commitment to serious change is clear. And having been urgently needed for years, the basics of what he wants – personal, home-based care delivered free at the proverbial point of need – will be on their way if Labour wins the next election.
Here, though, is a question that is much less finely balanced. Neither Burnham’s speech nor the much shorter address given by Yvette Cooper, the new health and social care secretary, contained a single mention of what roughly half of England’s social care budgets are spent on: provision for working-age disabled adults. Why not? I get the politics: fixating on older people’s care and the pensions triple lock makes everything clear and relatable. But England’s fragmented, unreliable system for younger disabled adults is in need of the same radical level of reform, and it’s the source of just as much fear and worry for the people who either depend on it, or eventually will do.
I am one of them. In fact, I suffer from two sub-types of what we might call Care Dread. My mum is 83, my dad is 90, and they currently pay for visits from domiciliary care workers whose frequency is only going to go up. My son James – who is autistic and has learning disabilities – has just turned 20. He currently goes to a brilliant further education college, but my partner and I will soon face what special needs parents call “the cliff edge”: a switch from education to adult social care, which will bring on a bucket-load of questions. Could he be helped into employment? If he stays at home, what support and everyday stimulation is our local council going to pay for? If he goes into supported living, how do we guard against what I have heard about from other mums and dads: long days spent plonked in front of the TV, the odd trip out, and the possibility of housemates with completely different needs?
The list of fears goes on; it haunts all parents in our position. A new focus of worry, moreover, has just been added: proposals to axe the health element of universal credit (which has already been almost halved this year to £217 a month) for young people with disabilities and health issues, and replacing it with new work schemes. To quote from the Guardian’s report, that plan comes with assurances about the measures not applying to “those with the most severe and debilitating disabilities”, which rather implies the grimly familiar official belief that you can easily grade disabilities from “mild” to “profound”, when lots of conditions show that you can’t (autism is one good example). But the proposals also underline why social care for disabled people has to be a big part of whatever detailed plan Burnham, Cooper and their comrades come up with.
We know that the crossbench peer Louise Casey’s independent commission on adult social care has been convened to consider both older people’s care and support for working-age disabled adults. But evidently, the government is much keener on talking about the former than the latter. Indeed, when I contacted the Department of Health and Social Care, I was sent a comically bland and noncommittal response: “The prime minister has made clear that he wants to see rapid progress on adult social care reforms … Baroness Casey’s commission will outline what a national care service should look like, and as part of the review, the commission will explore and consider the options for supporting working-age disabled adults as well as older people in need of care.”
Jim Kane is the CEO of Community Integrated Care, a not-for profit that seeks to provide supported living and residential care for about 3,000 autistic and learning-disabled adults. “People who have disabilities absolutely have to be front and centre of everything that’s discussed,” he told me last week. “But I also want to be supportive of what the PM’s trying to do, because I don’t believe in my heart that he’s going to ignore disabled people.”
There is so much to put right. Even in cases of disabled people who rely on benefits to live – the personal independence payment and universal credit, mostly – many councils’ care systems subject them to a means test. That means they snatch money as a contribution to the cost of care, whether that’s received at home and in what officialspeak calls “the community”, or through supported living. The learning-disability charity Mencap alerted me to the experience of Fred – who has Down’s syndrome and autism and is deaf– and his mum, Annabel, who live in Somerset. “What many people do not realise,” says Annabel, “is that the local authority charges Fred £147.54 a week from his benefits to pay for his care. This leaves him with just £201.56 a week to live on, which amounts to £10,481 a year.”
Two other issues were explained to me by Alison Bloomer, the editor of the expert online magazine Learning Disability Today. First, hundreds of thousands of disabled people are on waiting lists for the initial care assessments that councils endlessly evade and delay. At the moment, for people up to the age of 25, the special educational needs and disability (Send) tribunal – where decisions can be appealed – and education, health and care plans, which set out the support a young person is entitled to, offer some means of challenging councils’ decisions and conduct, though the government still seems set on degrading both mechanisms. And this is her second point: that dependence on the social care sector, by contrast, means the weakest kind of accountability. If you have a grievance, your only real hope is either the local government and social care ombudsman or your MP.
In his speech, Burnham made moving reference to “the care we give to each other” via the state. But how do we define that? If my son starts to live within the care system, will he still get to indulge his passions: the Strokes, guitars, hillwalking? As Kane put it: “The social care system deals in safety. Have people got a roof over their heads? Have they got food? That’s about it, and it doesn’t even do those that well sometimes: we’ve all seen the scandals. How does it help individuals build relationships? Can they even choose the people that they live with? You know, ‘Who are my friends? Can I have education? Can I pursue my hobbies?’”
The chances of a system being able to consistently meet such fundamental needs are made slimmer by the appallingly low pay rates of care staff (the government is moving on this, although progress towards an adult social care fair pay agreement is still ongoing). Kane would like his employees to be thought of as the equivalent of Band 3 workers in the NHS. But there is now a 28.6% gap between the two groups, and he cannot close it because of the dire financial position of just about all councils.
These are the deep issues that any credible national care service will have to solve. Furious disabled people’s organisations are calling for a National Independent Living Service to be at the core of the reforms, but that will only happen if these issues are talked about – not just on conference podiums, but in the kind of Treasury circles where the best of intentions can too easily wither away. “If we want people to live genuinely fulfilled lives, there’s a price tag that’s different to the one we’ve got now,” Kane told me. Such is yet another quandary faced by this embattled but confident new government, and a vivid reason why so many of us have to keep on pushing.
- John Harris is a Guardian columnist
