Nik Sharma’s recipes for spiced French onion soup and Indian-style Turkish eggs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:00:48 UTC
14:00:48 KST

While purists might scoff and find the combination of spices in my French onion soup a little blasphemous, do give it a shot. Nigella seeds are the best flavour-enhancer for onions, while using ghee instead of butter adds a warm, nutty, caramel flavour. Then, my Indian-inspired twist on çılbır, the classic Turkish breakfast of poached eggs with yoghurt. It features my go-to poached egg method, which I learned from Nigella Lawson.
Poached eggs with green chutney and yoghurt (pictured top)
Stirring the barely simmering water right before adding the egg creates a vortex, forcing the egg white to wrap around the yolk, cradling it and keeping it intact and compact.
Prep 10 min
Cook 35 min
Serves 2
For the green chutney
2 tbsp pumpkin seeds
1 tsp cumin seeds
200g coriander, tender leaves and stems, plus a few sprigs to garnish
1 green chilli, such as bird’s eye, serrano or jalapeño
60ml ice-cold water
2-3 tbsp lime or lemon juice
1 tbsp grated fresh ginger
1 garlic clove, peeled and chopped
1 tsp sugar, or honey or maple syrup, plus more as needed
Fine sea salt
For the yoghurt
480g plain full-fat Greek yoghurt
1-2 garlic cloves, peeled and grated
Fine sea salt
For the poached eggs
4 large eggs
4 tsp lemon juice
Toasted sourdough, preferably buttered or drizzled with olive oil, to serve
To make the chutney, toast the pumpkin seeds in a small, dry saucepan over medium heat, stirring often. After a minute, add the cumin seeds and continue toasting for a minute and a half to two minutes, until they turn fragrant and light brown (if they burn, discard them and start again). Put the pumpkin, cumin seeds, coriander, chilli, ice-cold water, lime juice, ginger, garlic and sugar in a blender, and blitz smooth; if need be, add a few more tablespoons of ice-cold water, one at a time, to loosen – the chutney should not be very runny. Taste and season with salt and more sugar as needed. The chutney can now be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to three days.
Fill a medium saucepan with enough water to submerge a whole egg, bring it to a boil on a medium-high heat, then turn down the heat to a simmer. Put 2½cm water in a second medium saucepan and bring it to a low simmer.
To make the yoghurt, in a medium metal bowl, mix the yoghurt and garlic, then season with salt. Set the bowl over the second saucepan, and whisk for two or three minutes, until smooth and creamy. Spoon the yoghurt into two serving bowls.
For the poached eggs, crack one egg into a fine-mesh strainer set over a small bowl, and let the loose, liquid portion of the egg white drain for about 10 seconds. Gently transfer the remaining egg to a small bowl and add a teaspoon of lemon juice. Stir the simmering water in the first saucepan with a spoon – the water should barely be bubbling – then carefully slide in the egg. Repeat with the second egg. Leave the two eggs to poach undisturbed for three or four minutes, until the whites turn opaque, then, using a slotted spoon, lift out the eggs, allow any excess water to drain off, then place them on top of the yoghurt in the serving bowls. Repeat with the remaining two eggs.
Top the eggs with generous spoonfuls of chutney, garnish with sprigs of coriander., and serve with toasted sourdough.
Nigella-scented French onion soup
Prep 15 min
Cook 2 hr
Makes 4
55g ghee, or unsalted butter
1.6kg yellow onions (about 4 large ones), peeled and halved through the root, then thinly sliced
2 garlic cloves, peeled and grated
2 tsp nigella seeds
Fine sea salt
4 sprigs fresh thyme
2 tsp black peppercorns
1 bay leaf
945ml low-sodium vegetable stock
2 tbsp white or yellow miso
2 tbsp plain flour
2 tbsp dry sherry, or apple cider vinegar
For the croutons
8 slices sourdough baguette (about 13mm-thick) 
115g grated gruyere
2 tsp nigella seeds
2 tsp thyme leaves
In a Dutch oven or large, heavy-based saucepan, melt the ghee over a medium heat. Add the onions, garlic, nigella seeds and a tiny pinch of salt, toss to coat the onions, then cover and leave to cook, stirring occasionally to prevent scorching, for about 30 minutes, until the onions turn soft and translucent.
Take off the lid, turn the heat to low and cook for about another hour (they might take longer), until the onions turn golden brown; if at any point the onions start to stick and burn, add a few tablespoons of water.
Meanwhile, wrap the thyme, peppercorns and bay leaf in cheesecloth and tie with kitchen twine. Put the bag in a medium saucepan, add the stock and 240ml water, then whisk in the miso. Bring to a boil, then turn down to a simmer, cover and leave to steep at a low simmer for 30 minutes. Remove and discard the spice bag.
Stir the flour into the onions and cook on a medium-high heat, stirring, for about two minutes, to cook away the raw flour flavour. Turn the heat to low, add the sherry, then stir in 240ml of the hot stock to ensure there are no flour lumps. Scrape the bottom of the pot to release any stuck-on browned bits, then gradually stir in the remaining stock. Bring to a boil, then turn down the heat to low and simmer for six to eight minutes, until slightly thickened. Taste and season, if need be.
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/400F/gas 6. To make the croutons, put the baguette slices on a baking sheet and bake for 12-15 minutes, until golden brown, flipping once halfway. These can be made up to a day ahead and stored in an airtight container at room temperature.
Heat the grill to high and put an oven rack 15cm from the grill. Put four 600ml ovenproof crocks on a baking sheet and divide the soup evenly between them, filling them to at least 6mm from the top. Top each bowl with two slices of the toast, sprinkle with the gruyere and nigella seeds, then grill for about a minute, until the cheese bubbles and melts. Garnish with the thyme leaves and serve hot.
- These recipes are edited extracts from Fundamentals of Flavor: 100 Recipes for the Science of Better Cooking by Nik Sharma, published by Chronicle Books at £35. To order a copy for £31.50, go to guardianbookshop.com

====================================================================================================

‘I didn’t know what to do’: collapse of providers of high-end digs leaves students in shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

“It was dead in the middle of summer, it was a shock,” says Nathalie Sriwiboonrattan. The fourth-year game design student at Abertay University was at home with her family thousands of miles away in Thailand when she discovered the owner of her Scottish studio flat had abruptly gone bust.
“I was like, my hands are tied. I’m not in the country. I don’t know what to do,” she says. Sriwiboonrattan was forced to act quickly to secure new housing for the academic year, which has just begun, paying £850 to have her possessions moved.
Her sudden upheaval was emblematic of the wider crisis in student housing. While UK universities face a financial crisis, providers of accommodation are grappling with falling international student numbers, a cost of living squeeze and higher borrowing and build costs, exacerbated by the Iran war, affecting upgrades at older properties.
A string of tower blocks known as purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA), targeted at more affluent students, have run into financial difficulty.
It had been touted as the ultimate student living: smart city centre blocks with gyms, cinemas and rooftop terraces have sprung up across the UK. A world away from the traditional image of dirty and dingy shared digs, the flats have offered a spacious alternative for their relatively affluent residents – often international students. Now, some sit half empty, and several schemes have gone bust.
Sriwiboonrattan was among nearly 70 students in Dundee who were left scrambling to find accommodation in late July after the collapse of the owner of Marketgait Apartments, a 116-room city centre block that had a concierge and a shared games lounge with a pool table.
Despite the boom in housing developed by financial institutions in recent years, many students heading off to university this term faced a different dilemma. Rents at the tower blocks have grown much faster than maintenance loans for British students, leaving PBSAs financially out of reach.
Meanwhile, the cost of living crisis has put financial pressure on students seeking university-owned or managed accommodation, while rising rents have hit those wanting to live in shared private rentals. Underlining the scale of the shortage of affordable housing, the students’ union in Bristol included an emergency support number for the housing charity Shelter in an email to new students.
At PBSAs, the national average rent, excluding London, is £191 a week including bills, according to the website StuRents.
At the top end, en suite rooms in Manchester command a weekly rent of £170 to £320, whereas in London, en suite rooms are £250 to £650 a week, and studio apartments in Bloomsbury cost between £550 and £800 plus.
“I wasn’t able to get into PBSA because it is very expensive in Birmingham,” says Soham Chougale, 23, a student at University College Birmingham. “I am an international student, so my working hours are capped at 20 hours [a week in term time], which means I can’t afford to live in PBSA,” says Chougale, the education officer at UCB Guild of Students.
He lived in university-owned dorms for the first two years of his aviation management degree and now shares a two-bedroom privately rented flat with a friend. On campus, he paid £660 rent including bills a month during the first year, which rose by 10% in his second year; now he pays £700 rent a month, excluding bills.
While living on campus “gave me the best feeling of community” and “I still have those friends that I met on the first day”, the wifi was patchy, some facilities were broken and there was a mouse infestation, he recounts.
“PBSA can be quite pricey,” says Matthew Pointon, a real estate analyst at Capital Economics, but adds: “Normally professionally managed buildings are better in terms of quality.”
In London, which attracts the richest students, there is still demand for upmarket accommodation, but outside the capital, there is an oversupply in some cities, such as Coventry, Leeds and Nottingham.
This week, university staff began strikes in Dundee, Edinburgh and Nottingham over budget cuts, with the industrial action threatening to wipe out a term of teaching for many students.
In Nottingham, demand has fallen from a pandemic peak of 46,295 beds in 2022-23 to 42,290 beds in 2025-26, while 7,700 more PBSA beds came on to the market, the student housing charity Unipol calculated.
The number of students arriving from China has stagnated, and those from the new growth countries India, Pakistan and Nigeria are much more cost-conscious than the pre-Covid students from China, says Martin Blakey, an adviser on student living and the former chief executive of Unipol.
Deniz Yalçın, the chair of the Newington-Meadows branch of the Living Rent union in Edinburgh, says: “In Edinburgh, we’re seeing an explosion of PBSA despite the fact that this type of development is not needed and actually fuels the housing affordability crisis here.
“Many of them lie empty during most of the year, using the Fringe [festival] to bolster profits. Some have even been bought by the council to become temporary housing.”
Richard Ward, the head of research at StuRents, says the key issue is the big gap between maintenance loans and rents, after double-digit rental growth at PBSA blocks and shared houses in recent years.
Maintenance loans have declined in real terms because of below-inflation increases and frozen parental income thresholds. “And what have we seen? More students commuting,” Ward says. “Outside of London, you’re talking about £300 rent a week to make a new PBSA scheme viable. Well, your average British student is paying about £160 a week.”
Occupancy rates at the tower blocks range between 71.3% in Glasgow, 69.9% in Coventry, 89.7% in Bristol and 95.3% in Exeter, as of August, according to StuRents.
Student housing providers are increasingly focusing on the cities with the best universities. Unite Group, the UK’s largest developer and manager of student accommodation, has stepped up sales of unwanted sites.
The loss-making group aims to slim down its portfolio to 55,000-60,000 beds in 20 cities compared with 72,000 beds in 29 cities at present, “to increase alignment to the UK’s strongest universities, where student demand is robust and growing”. Unite reduced rents and tenancy lengths in Nottingham, Leicester and Sheffield, the “most challenging” cities, earlier this year, and rooms start from £99 a week in Coventry.
About 95% of new student beds are being built in cities with Russell Group universities, up from 81% last year, according to the property agency Knight Frank, by investors such as Blackstone, KKR and Greystar. The Russell Group is an association of 24 established UK universities including Cambridge, Oxford, Durham, Edinburgh, Manchester and King’s College London.
Smaller PBSA operators are struggling, with average occupancy levels of 85% across the sector, Unipol estimates. The housing association Sanctuary has been trying to sell student assets of more than 5,600 beds, across 21 properties in eight locations across the UK, for nearly two years, and in July said the buyer had “sought to revisit pricing assumptions” citing changes in economic and market conditions.
Investors poured £164m into the PBSA sector between April and June, one of the lowest quarterly levels on record, although total investment of £2.3bn in the first half was ahead of 2025, according to Knight Frank research. Only 13 deals were completed during the second quarter.
In response to the sector’s headwinds, several PBSA owners plan to rent some floors to young professionals, while one block in Leeds that is only 50% full could partly be used for short-term hotel stays.
In Dundee, Sriwiboonrattan has found alternative accommodation – a studio in the nearby Parklands block – which has a sky lounge with city views, gym and rooftop terrace – where she is paying weekly rent of £240, with financial support from her family. At Marketgait, she says the “walls were thin” with noise coming in from neighbours and lifts unreliable, so she prefers her new surroundings now the initial shock has dissipated.
Others still face a bleak picture, with the freshers’ week parties fading into the memory and the academic year now in full swing. Lewis Wilson, the vice-president for higher education at the National Union of Students, says: “The whole system is broken around student finance and student loans. Some students are going homeless, some students are relying on food banks.” A quarter of student unions now provide a food bank or food pantry.
Wilson, who graduated from the University of Sussex two years ago with a law degree, argues that PBSAs need to be better regulated, and become more affordable. “For the students on lower incomes like I was, I would never have been able to afford a PBSA,” he says.
The government says: “We expect higher education providers to consider the supply, and affordability of student accommodation in relation to their anticipated student intakes and across all years of study at least five years ahead.
“Recognising the inherent uncertainties in student demand and housing delivery timelines, providers should engage with the local planning authority on need.”

Spacon fills Edition Denmark in Seoul with vintage Danish furniture and found objects

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

Spacon fills Edition Denmark in Seoul with vintage Danish furniture and found objects
Copenhagen studio Spacon brought touches of its home country to Seoul with a showroom and cafe for the Edition Denmark brand that evokes the "layered feeling of a home".
The 50-square-metre space was designed for a South Korean brand that sells Danish products. In a nod to the hospitality culture found in both countries, the central Seoul store also has an eatery next door.
"For us, the project was about an exchange between two cultures and the things we already share," Spacon founding partner Malene Hvidt told Dezeen.
"Both cultures have strong traditions around gathering, and we wanted the cafe and shop to connect these everyday rituals in a natural way."
The studio designed the one-storey spaces in Seochon, Seoul, to be closely connected, and visitors can buy some of the tableware and products from the cafe.
In both the Edition Denmark cafe and the showroom space, Spacon used a lot of wood, which plays a big part in Danish design and interiors.
"Wood became the foundation of the interior because we wanted the space to feel warm, familiar and lived in," Hvidt said.
"Solid cherry wood is combined with terracotta tiles, woven cord stools and bespoke textile lamps, bringing in softness and references to Danish craft and architecture."
To further underline the connection to Danish culture, Spacon added classic Danish furniture pieces, including the Folkestolen chair by designer Børge Mogensen.
"We wanted the space to have the personal and layered feeling of a home, combining our custom furniture with new and vintage Danish pieces, art and smaller found objects," Hvidt said.
"We also created wooden and aluminium trays engraved with Danish flowers, as small gestures at the intimate scale."
In the cafe, Spacon wanted to create a calming feel and used moss-green stained wood and terracotta to add colour and warmth, while next door it went for a starker material palette.
"The shop has a slightly different character, with a mirrored ceiling opening up the small space and reflecting the objects on display," Hvidt said.
The store is the first project in a long-term collaboration between Spacon and Edition Denmark, which was founded by Dane Johan S Fuglsbjerg and creative director Ji Eun Lee.
Other recent projects by Spacon include a pavilion for the Rosenborg Castle in Copenhagen and an exhibition at the Danish Architecture Center.
The photography is by Seongju Mun and Mihyun Son.

Foreign workers become increasingly vital to Lithuania’s agricultural sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Foreign workers are increasingly filling labour shortages in Lithuania’s agricultural sector, with farmers warning that demand for workers from abroad will continue to grow as it becomes harder to recruit locals.
Farmers say reducing bureaucratic barriers for foreign workers is necessary because many farms would struggle to operate without them.
Youbaa Acharaz came to Lithuania from Morocco to study. Back home, he lived near the beach and worked as a surfing instructor. Now he works as an assistant at the Berčiūnai agricultural company in Panevėžys district.
“The work here is hard. There is always something to do,” Acharaz told LRT TV. “But I really love animals and I like nature. At first, it really smelled bad here, but now it smells like flowers to me. I got used to it.”
The farm employs workers from several countries, including Morocco, Ukraine, Turkey, Bangladesh and India. According to the company’s veterinarian, most had no previous experience working with livestock.
“One said, ‘My grandfather kept camels.’ I don’t know if that can be considered experience with animals, but yes, at first they were even afraid of cows,” veterinarian Artūras Abromaitis said.
The smells were among the biggest challenges for new workers, he said. Some even wore gas masks while working during the winter.
“The gas masks had frozen to them, but they kept working,” Abromaitis said.
The company began recruiting foreign workers after it could no longer find enough Lithuanians willing to take the jobs.
“Here in Lithuania, nobody wants to go to a farm where it smells bad. That’s the culture,” Abromaitis said. “If you talked to people abroad, they would say it is an honourable job, honest work.”
Data from Lithuania’s Employment Service show a sharp increase in the number of foreign citizens working in agriculture. About 2,000 foreigners worked in the sector last year, compared with more than 5,000 this year.
Foreign workers are generally taking jobs for which employers have the greatest difficulty finding local workers.
Giedrė Sinkevičė, deputy director of the Employment Service, said the problem was particularly acute in rural areas, where the population is declining as young people move to larger cities.
“People are naturally disappearing from rural municipalities,” Sinkevičė said. “Young people leave for the big cities, and the competition for workers in rural areas is the most intense.”
She also pointed to “social barriers” that can make it harder for some people to enter formal employment: “When people have addictions or commitments that make them reluctant to be formally employed.”
The head of the board of the Lithuanian Vegetable Growers Association, Paulius Adriejavas, said Lithuanians had once helped farms in other countries by working abroad. Now, he said, foreign workers are helping prevent Lithuanian farms from collapsing.
He expects demand for foreign workers to increase and called for solutions that would make it easier for them to come to Lithuania, including increasing quotas.
“We simply need to solve this. If we do not find solutions quickly, every year we will suffer direct losses because there is not enough labour,” Andriejavas said.
As Lithuanian farms become increasingly modernised, they are also looking for more skilled workers. More than 500 foreign citizens currently perform highly qualified jobs in the agricultural sector.

Aleph Alpha unveils German-language AI model for public infrastructure

German AI company Aleph Alpha has released a new language model called Kolibri for use in public administration and industry, designed to run on infrastructure that customers control themselves, the Heidelberg-based firm said at the weekend.
With the move, Aleph Alpha is seeking to strengthen its position in the competition for AI solutions suited to government and industrial use from Europe. The market is considered strategically important, as many organizations prioritize data protection, transparency and control over the infrastructure they use.
“Expertise to develop competitive AI models”
Kolibri shows that there is “the talent and expertise in Germany to develop competitive AI models,” chief executive Ilhan Scheer said on Saturday.
AI sovereignty means preserving the freedom to make decisions through the ability to develop and advance this technology independently, and giving customers control over how they use it, he said.
Co-founder Samuel Weinbach said, “We have tailored Kolibri specifically to the requirements of German-language applications … so that it can reason in German.”
This was an important step for customers in making AI usable in everyday workflows, he said.
Aleph Alpha, headquartered in the south-western city of Heidelberg, employs around 200 people at four locations in Germany.
AI solutions for public administration and industry
Aleph Alpha has for years positioned itself as a European provider of “sovereign” AI solutions for government and industry.
At the end of April, Aleph Alpha and Canadian AI company Cohere announced a “trans-Atlantic merger,” though in practice the deal amounts to an acquisition of Aleph Alpha by Cohere.

Cambodian PM says educators play pivotal role in equipping youth to navigate dynamic global landscape

13:52:17 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet said on Monday that teachers played a crucial role in equipping youth with the skills necessary to navigate a constantly changing world.
In a statement posted on his official social media platforms to mark World Teachers' Day, Hun Manet said Cambodia celebrated the event under the national theme: "Teachers are the pillars of modern pedagogy for building 21st-century human resources."
"Teachers' Day highlights the pivotal role of educators in building youth competencies to thrive in a rapidly shifting global landscape," he said.
Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Education, Youth and Sport Hang Chuon Naron added that the celebration offers an opportunity to express gratitude to educators and highlight their indispensable role in Cambodia's socio-economic development.
"In this new era, where Artificial Intelligence (AI) has penetrated all aspects of society, it is essential to utilize modern pedagogy to develop our human resources," he said during the World Teachers' Day 2026 Celebration in Phnom Penh.
He stressed that teachers are vital in nurturing students' critical thinking, teamwork, creativity, problem-solving abilities, and capacity for lifelong learning.
Flavio Bonetti, UNESCO Representative to Cambodia, echoed these sentiments, stating that as emerging technologies like AI continue to profoundly reshape the world, it is vital to ensure teachers remain at the center of learning.
He highlighted that with UNESCO's support, the Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport has developed Cambodia's first National Information and Communications Technology (ICT) and AI Competency Framework for Teachers.
He added that this framework will serve as a blueprint for building digital skills, enabling educators to use digital tools and AI both effectively and ethically.
Alongside this initiative, and following ministerial approval, a National EdTech Innovation Hub is currently being established at the Phnom Penh Teacher Education College with UNESCO's backing, Bonetti said.
The Hub aims to promote research and innovation in ICT and AI within education, while developing new Continuous Professional Development (CPD) courses to help teachers build these competencies.
"We must continue to build on the progress made and ensure that investments in education remain a priority so that all learners in Cambodia can benefit equally from these gains," Bonetti said. ■

This industry adds €65 billion to the European economy, but is its bad reputation fair?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:47:58 UTC
13:47:58 KST

The cruise industry is attracting younger travellers, but how is it addressing concerns over emissions and overtourism?
In recent years, we’ve seen demonstrations at ports across Europe against the cruise industry over environmental and overtourism concerns.
But has the cruise industry unjustly become the poster child for the travel industry’s problems, and can it repair its dirtied reputation?
In this episode of The Big Question, Gianni Onorato, CEO of MSC Cruises, sat down with Hannah Brown to discuss how the cruise industry is responding to its biggest criticisms to ensure its survival.
How big is the cruise industry?
Gianni stressed that while their ships may be big, the cruise industry is not, with this segment making up less than 2% of the travel packages sold globally in 2025.
And while we’ve seen overtourism complaints in Barcelonablamed on cruises, their passengers only account for around 3% of the city’s daily visitors.
Despite this, cruise companies are working hard, like the rest of the travel industry, to take passengers to new destinations and spread tourist arrivals more evenly throughout the year.
Unlike airlines, which confirm their flight schedules less than 12 months in advance, cruise itineraries are set two years ahead to help destinations plan for the incoming visitors.
“The predictability of cruises allows small family businesses to decide if they want to add, for example, more tables and seats in their restaurants or in their bars because they know that it's for sure that they will have these people coming,” Gianni explained.
And the industry has become a vital part of the European economy, providing more than 445,000 permanent jobs across the continent.
Scaling up technology to clean up cruising
But overtourism isn’t the only worry. People are also critical of the cruise industry’s carbon emissions.
The most significant development to clean up the industry is the roll-out of dual-fuel engines, capable of seamlessly switching between traditional marine fuel and cleaner alternatives.
“In 2023, one of our ships, the MSC Euribia, had a four-day cruise from Le Havre to Copenhagen using biofuel and it was proved that together with other innovative measures for fuel consumption reduction, we were able to reach the target of zero,” Gianni explained.
Members of the Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA) operate 327 ships, accounting for about 90% of global cruise capacity. Only 30, or around one in 11, are equipped with dual-fuel engines, up from a single ship in 2018.
And although this is progress, it is slow. This is partly because affordable cleaner fuels are in short supply and partly because companies have to wait until the end of a ship’s 30-year lifespan to upgrade their fleet.
Gianni was confident, however, that most of the remaining ships in service will have been decommissioned and replaced in time to meet the EU’s target of a climate-neutral maritime industry by 2050.
In the meantime, he spoke passionately about the other technologies being retrofitted in the current fleet to dramatically reduce energy consumption on board.
“The air conditioning on the ship today is through an HVAC inverter that gives the opportunity to automatically regulate the level of air conditioning according to the number of people present in the room,” Gianni told The Big Question.
Cruise passengers are changing
While technologies, fuels and destinations have been changing, so too has the cruise industry’s clientele.
“In the past, cruises had this perception for being for old people. While now, there is a much younger demographic. The average age is 35-54 and this is very good because this can ensure the future of this industry,” Gianni explained.
He also added that solo travellers are a growing market for the company, with safety becoming an increasingly important consideration. Multi-generational holidays are also growing in popularity, allowing family members to enjoy separate activities as well as spending time together.
But the industry isn’t about to suddenly boom.
Almost all of the world’s cruise ships are built in Europe, with the four major shipbuilders based in the bloc: Italy, France, Germany and Finland. But the production is limited, so demand is likely to outpace supply.
While some might see this as negative, Gianni pointed out that it means the industry has controlled growth - a good thing for investors and its long-term future.
The Big Question is a series from Euronews Business where we sit down with industry leaders and experts to discuss some of the most important topics on today’s agenda.
Watch the video above to see the full discussion with MSC Cruises.

This mysterious hole on the Moon may open into a giant cave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:47:40 UTC
13:47:40 KST

This mysterious hole on the Moon may open into a giant cave
- Date:
- October 5, 2026
- Source:
- Planetary Science Institute
- Summary:
- NASA has selected the GIMLI project to investigate whether the Marius Hill Pit opens into a vast underground cave or lava tube. Using radar, seismic sensors, gravity measurements, and cameras, researchers will search beneath the lunar surface and estimate the size of any hidden void. Such caves could preserve clues to the Moon’s volcanic history and potentially provide protected shelters for future astronauts.
- Share:
NASA has chosen a proposal led by the Planetary Science Institute to determine whether a potentially large cave stretches underground from the opening of a pit on the Moon. If such a cavern exists, it could eventually offer astronauts natural protection from radiation and the dramatic temperature changes experienced on the lunar surface.
The project will receive funding through NASA's Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon (PRISM) program. PRISM sends scientific instruments to the lunar surface aboard spacecraft supplied by providers participating in the Commercial Lunar Payloads Services (CLPS) initiative.
GIMLI Will Probe Beneath the Moon
The selected project, known as the Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation, or GIMLI, is led by PSI Associate Director and Senior Scientist Than Putzig. PSI is working with Honeybee Robotics, which will construct much of the mission's equipment and instrumentation. The instruments will travel aboard a lander and rover supplied through the CLPS initiative. PSI's work will also be conducted in partnership with the Norwegian Space Agency.
"GIMLI represents the type of ambitious planetary science that PSI was built to pursue," said PSI Director and CEO Amanda Hendrix. "Than and his team are taking a scientific question we've been studying from orbit and have developed a way to investigate it directly on the Moon. We're excited to have PSI leading this effort and to be partnering with NASA and Honeybee Robotics to learn more about the Moon and its volcanic past."
Scientists studying the Moon from orbit have found compelling evidence that caves and lava tubes could be hidden beneath its surface. GIMLI will concentrate on the Marius Hill Pit (MHP), a large opening located within one of the Moon's most volcanically varied regions. Like other pits identified on the Moon, MHP could provide an entrance into underground structures created by ancient volcanic activity.
Rather than relying only on observations from above, GIMLI will give researchers an opportunity to examine MHP directly from the lunar surface.
Radar and Seismic Sensors Will Search for a Lava Tube
"It's long been a desire of mine to reintroduce intentional active-source seismic methods to planetary science, as it has essentially not been done since the Apollo astronauts conducted the first seismic surveys on the Moon," shared Putzig. "Combining that method with ground-penetrating radar and gravity measurements makes it all the more exciting, as these methods together will allow us to get a much better understanding of subsurface properties -- including the anticipated detection of a lava tube extending away from the Marius Hills pit."
To investigate what lies underground, GIMLI will combine ground penetrating radar, seismic sensors, and a gravimeter. Cameras will also photograph the lunar surface and the exposed walls of the pit. Used together, these instruments will search for a possible underground void extending from MHP and, if one is detected, help scientists estimate its dimensions.
Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, will be PSI's commercial partner on the project. The company will provide project management services and construct instrumentation for the active source seismic system, the gravimeter, and the cameras. Honeybee Robotics will also help integrate the scientific instruments onto the lander and rover. Along with PSI, it will lead instrument operations after the spacecraft reaches the lunar surface.
Even No Cave Would Reveal New Lunar Geology
The mission could still produce important discoveries even if researchers find no cave or lava tube. Its measurements could help address another major question: How did the Marius Hill Pit form?
By examining the material surrounding and beneath MHP, scientists could gain new clues about the pit's origin as well as the geology and volcanic history of the wider region.
The team also plans to study more than the possible underground structure. The surrounding area has experienced a long history of volcanic activity, and the walls of MHP expose layers of regolith and lava flows that normally remain buried. Examining these layers could show how lava once moved across and beneath the lunar landscape and whether individual eruptions were separated by long intervals.
Lunar pits are valuable not only because their walls expose otherwise hidden geology. Any underground spaces connected to them could also preserve evidence of the volcanic processes that helped shape the Moon.
A Window Into the Moon's Volcanic Past
"Confirming a substantial lava tube would give us an insight into how volcanism operated on the Moon," explained Gareth Morgan, PSI Senior Scientist and Deputy Principal Investigator on the GIMLI program. "Lava tubes are a common feature of basaltic volcanism on Earth, so identifying them on the Moon means we could use knowledge of such terrestrial caves to better understand lunar history."
In addition to PSI and Honeybee Robotics, the GIMLI team includes Co-Investigators from Boise State University, Johns Hopkins University, the Lunar and Planetary Institute, and the University of Oslo. The Norwegian Space Agency will provide the ground-penetrating radar.
Story Source:

Australia's World Cup squad is a sign of the changing times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:46:15 UTC
13:46:15 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
analysis
Australia's World Cup squad a sign of the changing face of international rugby league
The depths of Australia's star power means the Kangaroos will always name squads oozing with class and Kevin Walters's combination for this year's World Cup is no exception.
It's a side with major success stories, young and old and in-between.
James Tedesco's return three years after his last Test caps the 33-year old's resurrection and after he ran the ball to hell and back in the grand final to win the Clive Churchill Medal, there can be no doubt that, at an age where many players best days are only just a memory, he is once again the best fullback in the world.
The inclusion of Dolphins flyer Jack Bostock, who will almost certainly see a Test debut in the World Cup opener given the side's shortage of wingers, heralds the start of a new generation wearing green and gold.
At 26, David Fifita is no longer a youngster in rugby league terms but his looming Australian debut is both a long time coming and well-earned following his strong finish to the year with Souths.
The one-time prodigy has longed seemed a player of limitless possibilities but only now, eight years after his NRL debut and three years since he last played for Queensland, will he get the chance to be a Kangaroo.
But the Australian squad also reveals the new truths about representative football, that the disconnect between State and Origin and Test matches is wider than ever before and may never be stitched back together again.
It's a process that began with Origin's gradual but unmistakeable rise past Test football as rugby league's biggest stage then continued when a host of players chose to represent Pasifika nations over Australia while retaining their Origin eligibility.
The final change came earlier this year when the NRL allowed players to represent New Zealand or England and still being available for Origin selection.
Both of those eligibility changes reflect the changing face of rugby league and the people who play it and the game is better for them.
But it does require a reset of over a century's worth of thinking that interstate football is the pathway to national selection.
This has not been true for some years now, but there's a reason old habits have a hard time dying.
And while Australia will never be hard up for talent, some of the more eyebrow-raising picks prove this old adage is as antiquated as Kangaroo tours that travel to England by boat.
Not one of the Queensland outside backs is in the side at all. Kalyn Ponga, Robert Toia, Jojo Fifita, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow all would be, but they're playing for other nations while Selwyn Cobbo is injured.
That's how we end up with Brisbane's Kotoni Staggs, a fine centre who had a tough year, making the side despite being dropped by New South Wales for the Origin decider after a horror night in Game II at the MCG.
Latrell Mitchell missed the entire series through injury and has only started one match in the past five months but he's made it, while Tom Trbojevic is a likely starter on one wing despite not having played rep football for two years and not playing a match on the flank since 2018.
Likewise of the 12 men who played in the forwards for New South Wales, only Blayke Brailey, Isaah Yeo, Liam Martin and Cameron Murray have made the squad.
Hudson Young and Payne Haas are both out with injury, but Haumole Olakau'atu and Addin Fonua-Blake will both line up for Tonga while Victor Radley is with England.
So Reuben Cotter makes the squad despite an underwhelming season with the Cowboys and a lacklustre series for Queensland.
His selection over Dolphins hardman Max Plath, who does a similar job with similar attributes whilst offering the same versatility and is coming off a far superior season for club and state, is perhaps the hardest pick to understand.
Plath, along with Newcastle's Fletcher Sharpe and South Sydney's Tallis Duncan can count himself most aggrieved at missing out but it's hard to take up too much issue with Walters's squad, even if it's short of wingers.
This is the hand the Australian coach has been dealt for his final tournament before he departs to take over Super League side St Helens.
The eligibility changes and the fact that Test football misses out on players who pick up injuries during club seasons that are getting longer and longer all the time means sometimes his options are a bit more limited than he would have liked.
Australia are still the pick to win the World Cup and will be warm favourites in every game they play, beginning with their tournament opener against New Zealand next Thursday night in Sydney.
Walters is attempting to solve a puzzle no other Kangaroos coach has ever had to face and there is no one-size-fits-all philosophy in the battle between fitness, function and form when it comes to selecting a player.
But when numbers are scarce, and for the Kangaroos they're a lot shorter than they used to be, the first two are more important than the last.

Israel’s southern ‘drone hunters’ prepare for worst-case scenarios on peaceful borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:39:47 UTC
13:39:47 KST

The IDF’s Paran and Yoav brigades are responsible for vast stretches of Israel’s borders with Egypt and Jordan, where commanders have spent recent years confronting a growing threat from drones used to smuggle weapons and drugs into the country.
Military estimates indicate that thousands of drones crossed the borders over the past two years, while hundreds of smuggling attempts were recorded last year. During the recent holiday period, as Israelis traveled across the south, troops remained on alert.
The IDF’s 80th Division includes the mixed-gender Caracal and Bardelas battalions, whose male and female combat soldiers fought during the Oct. 7 Hamas attack. Travelers along Route 10, through the Arava and even near Eilat may encounter troops from the units deployed along the border.
Maj. S., 26, deputy commander of the Caracal Battalion, immigrated to Israel from Belgium a decade ago. She said her family made aliyah for two reasons: Zionism and antisemitism. Her father had served as a lone soldier in the Golani Brigade and became an inspiration for her own military service.
“When I became an officer, it fulfilled a dream of my great-grandmother, a Holocaust survivor, who saw it as a kind of victory over the Nazis,” she said. “Although she did not live to see me wearing the rank, I’m sure she would be proud of me.”
On Oct. 7, S. left her home in central Israel with her driver, joined her brigade command post and went to fight in Kibbutz Holit. She remained in the Gaza border area for about a month as the commander responsible for the community of Pri Gan before returning to her original sector.
She is expected to begin academic studies this summer as part of the IDF’s Ofek program, designed for senior combat officers and generally intended for officers being groomed for battalion command.
“I arrived in the Gaza border area with my soldiers and we fought in Holit,” she said. “We took part in the battle alongside Caracal’s female tank crews and Bardelas.”
The debate over women serving in combat roles, she said, is answered by what the units have already done in the field.
“I think the proof is right in front of us,” she said. “In the Border Defense Corps, and in Caracal in particular, we have some of the best female officers there are. Women are serving as combat soldiers in key positions and doing good work. We are proving to everyone that it can work.”
“In Caracal, we all carry out the same missions, live shoulder to shoulder, fight shoulder to shoulder and train shoulder to shoulder,” she added.
Lt. Col. D., 37, deputy commander of the Paran Brigade, said the desert terrain presents challenges of its own, while the threats along the sector continue to evolve. Drones, he said, have emerged as one of the most prominent.
“They were always there in one form or another, and the enemy used them in wars,” he said. “We understand that the threat developed further over the past two years. We began seeing and identifying them being used more frequently.”
According to Israeli prosecutors, thousands of smuggling attempts involving drones have been carried out since 2025, including with aircraft capable of carrying tens of kilograms. The cargo has consisted primarily of weapons and drugs.
D. said the number of smuggling attempts has now fallen dramatically. Officials in the Ramat Negev Regional Council, which previously experienced hundreds of such incidents, likewise say the numbers have dropped and are no longer disrupting everyday life.
“We are preparing for terrorist activity,” D. said.
Asked whether the Israel-Egypt border has become less violent, he said the situation remains fluid.
“It changes. I can’t reveal too much, but I can say that in the past there were quite a few incidents here. Today we are identifying fewer and fewer of them along the border,” he said.
“The drones were hit, and we are more proactive and aggressive wherever we can be. It has a direct effect, and you can clearly see it along the border.”
For troops watching the skies, he said, there is no way to assume that an unidentified drone is carrying contraband rather than posing a security threat.
“When something is spotted by surveillance, I don’t know whether it’s a drone smuggling drugs to Tel Aviv,” he said. “As far as I’m concerned, it is an enemy drone, and I have to do everything I can to prevent it from reaching its destination.”
“And even though this is a border of peace, we prepare for any incident or extreme scenario,” he added.
The Yoav Brigade, responsible for the border area near Eilat and along the Jordanian frontier in the Arava, is confronting the same aerial threat.
Its deputy commander, Lt. Col. A., 35, originally from Mitzpe Ramon and now living in Eilat, was serving with the IDF’s School for Infantry Corps Professions and Squad Commanders when the war broke out. He and other troops headed to the Gaza border area in Namer armored personnel carriers, deploying to Kibbutz Kissufim and Nahal Oz to reinforce the Golani Brigade’s 51st Battalion.
He moved to Eilat only two weeks ago for his new role, after previously serving as operations officer in the 80th Division, where he became closely familiar with its mixed-gender battalions.
“The integration of women and men creates something special,” he said. “It makes operations more effective. The synergy between male and female combat soldiers is ultimately a good one.”
“There is a difference between a combat battalion made up entirely of men and the mixed battalions,” he added. “Integrating women into combat brings professionalism and attention to detail. That is what I experienced.”
“We will be there to guard and protect Israel’s civilians in Eilat and the Arava,” he said.

Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the National Security Commission, made the remarks on the sidelines of the memorial ceremony for the sister of Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

Trump says "125 million Indians voted in presidential election today."
US President Donald Trump on Monday confused India with Brazil, claiming that 125 million people had voted in an Indian “presidential election”, while also questioning the integrity of the American voting system.In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, “125 Million People voted today in the first round of India’s Presidential Election. The results came out shortly after the vote closed, on the same day!”He then compared the alleged election results with the US electoral process, writing, “In Detroit, Philadelphia, California, and numerous other US Cities and States, the results, with much smaller numbers, will often take weeks to Rig, I mean, calculate. Voting in America is corrupt!!!”However, India did not hold a presidential election on Sunday. The President of India is elected indirectly by an electoral college and not through a direct nationwide popular vote.
Trump's remarks came after Brazil held the first round of its presidential election on Sunday, with incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro advancing to the October 25 runoff.With 99.99% of the votes counted, Bolsonaro secured 47.03% of the valid votes, while Lula received 45.16%, according to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.
The figure of around 125 million mentioned by Trump is close to Brazil's total valid votes, which stood at about 125.27 million, suggesting he may have confused the Brazilian election with India.Neither Bolsonaro nor Lula crossed the 50% threshold required to win in the first round, triggering the October 25 runoff, BBC reported.Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, outperformed expectations in the first round and finished ahead of Lula. His strong showing has raised the prospect of a shift to the right in Latin America's largest economy.Brazil has used electronic voting for decades, and electoral authorities said the first-round voting process proceeded smoothly.The Organization of American States' electoral observation mission said “the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions.”
The rapid announcement of results has also been cited as a strength of Brazil's electronic voting system.“When results take a lot of time, it creates an opening for people to cast doubt on the results, to say there’s been a problem,” Josemar Lauriano Pereira, a 46-year-old lawyer in Rio de Janeiro, told the Associated Press.Trump's post drew reactions on social media, with users pointing out that India does not elect its president through a direct popular vote.One user posted, “Trump living in a different world? Is a presidential election taking place in India? President Donald Trump made the incorrect claim that 125 million people voted in India's "presidential election" today.”Another said, “What is my blud Donald Trump smoking? Why is he mentioning India instead of Brazil when talking about the election?”
Kanchan Yadav is a writer at The Times of India, where she covers business, politics, international affairs and social issues. Putin began this year's winter strike campaign against Ukraine earlier, and ISW explained his calculation
Kyiv • UNN
Russia began its winter strike campaign back in September, attacking Ukraine's energy sector and critical infrastructure. ISW explained the Kremlin's calculation.
Ukraine's successes on the battlefield in 2026 are likely forcing Vladimir Putin to reconsider his initial strategy for achieving victory in the war. The Kremlin is increasingly betting on large-scale strikes against Ukraine's energy and critical infrastructure in winter, according to a report by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), UNN writes.
Details
Analysts believe that Russia has already begun its winter strike campaign for 2026–2027. It started in late September—before the beginning of the heating season.
According to ISW's assessment, the Russian leadership may be counting on systematic strikes against energy facilities and other critical infrastructure making civilian life so difficult that this will increase pressure on Ukraine and force it to agree to Moscow's demands. Inserted markdown text
Russia started the winter campaign earlier
ISW points out that Russia has attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure every winter since 2022–2023. However, this time the campaign began earlier than usual.
Analysts suggest that in this way Russia is trying to take advantage of its new strike capabilities before Ukraine can scale up effective means of countering Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
In just one week, from September 27 to October 4, Russian forces used more than 1,900 attack drones against Ukraine, including more than 800 jet-powered drones, around 1,700 aerial bombs, and 25 missiles.
ISW believes that the Kremlin is also trying to portray the intensification of the strikes as a "response" to Ukrainian attacks on Russian territory. At the same time, analysts note that the Russian Federation has been systematically striking Ukraine since the very beginning of the full-scale invasion.

Taiwan improves drone ship AI training
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:20:42 UTC
13:20:42 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ocean Affairs Council said Friday that drone vessels in Kaohsiung have completed maritime missions using its in-house AI, according to a press release.
The council said it combined AI patrols with federated learning for larger drone ships to validate in open seas. It added that the closed training method does not leak sensitive data such as images of key installations.
Federated learning involves a central server assigning a training model to individual units. The drones complete mission objectives and pool the data, like students turning in homework.
The council said its team conducted a stress test in high waves dotted with chaotic light sources, where the vessels completed point-to-point navigation, strafing maneuvers, and carpet searches. It also tested a three-second manual commandeering mechanism in the event of a signal cutoff.
The council said the boats accurately identified more than 90% of all targets within a reaction window of more than 15 frames per second for each marker. It noted that all units showed acceptable memory retention by remembering more than 90% of acquired objects.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:20:28 UTC
13:20:28 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — LGBTQ+ rights groups called Sunday for an independent investigation into a police raid on a gay bar in Taipei's Ximending district, alleging excessive force, procedural violations, and discriminatory treatment.
The Taiwan Tongzhi Hotline Association and several other gender-equality groups issued a joint statement on Saturday. They urged the Taipei City Government to investigate the operation, release legally disclosable records, and establish guidelines for police handling of LGBTQ+ venues.
Police said the operation was conducted after receiving multiple complaints and gathering evidence of alleged public indecency. Officers obtained a search warrant from the Taipei District Court after prosecutors directed the investigation, according to the Wanhua Precinct.
The 44-year-old manager was brought back for questioning on suspicion of public indecency, and 51 customers were cited under the Social Order Maintenance Act, police said. Officers reportedly found people without shirts as well as used condoms and lubricant at the venue, per CNA.
The groups said witnesses reported that officers ordered people to squat, prohibited them from talking or using their phones, and allegedly refused to show the search warrant to people at the scene. They also accused an officer of making a derogatory remark about a person with a disability.
The Wanhua Precinct later acknowledged that an officer had behaved inappropriately after reviewing video footage and said the officer had been disciplined. Police also said they would strengthen training on respecting social diversity and protecting citizens' rights.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) said Sunday that police had a search warrant but that any inappropriate conduct should be reviewed and clarified, per CNA.
The LGBTQ+ groups said the incident recalled a period when gay venues faced frequent police surveillance and raids. They called for an independent investigation and stronger protections, and an end to stigmatizing descriptions of LGBTQ+ venues and culture.

Taipower urges support for supplementary budget to ease financial pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:20:16 UTC
13:20:16 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipower on Sunday urged the legislature to support the Cabinet’s NT$71.1 billion (US$2.24 billion) cash infusion allocated in the 2026 supplementary budget, citing the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran on fossil fuel prices.
Following a utility rate meeting on Sept. 18, the Ministry of Economic Affairs announced that electricity rates for state-owned Taipower would remain unchanged, per NOWNews. Taipower said that, as energy prices remain volatile and a government cash infusion is still possible, the company has prioritized securing the funds.
Taipower said the war in the Middle East had caused it to spend NT$70 billion more on natural gas between March and August compared with the same period in 2025. The company said the cash infusion is necessary to ease the financial burden incurred by absorbing the impact of international energy prices for the broader public.
In addition to providing financial support for Taipower, the Cabinet plans to allocate NT$109.8 billion in cash and NT$233.8 billion in capital investment to CPC Corp., through the supplementary budget, per UP Media. The economic affairs ministry warned Sunday that CPC’s efforts to stabilize energy prices had resulted in a NT$127.6 billion deficit, potentially affecting the company’s borrowing capacity and its ability to negotiate prices.
Vice Economics Affairs Minister Lai Chien-hsin (賴建信) said CPC’s price stabilization efforts had kept the price of gas at NT$20.01 per kilogram, absorbing the NT$20.37 per kilogram cost caused by the price shock.
Lai warned that if CPC were unable to stabilize prices, monthly costs for an average household could increase by NT$712. Night market vendors could see their monthly costs rise by between NT$1,425 and NT$14,000, depending on the business in question.
Still, opposition lawmakers have voiced disagreement with the move.
KMT Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) argued that the DPP’s energy policy, which has significantly increased the role of natural gas in the country’s power generation, has contributed to financial difficulties at state-run enterprises, per UDN. She said the opposition would thoroughly review the government’s supplementary budget proposal.
TPP Legislator Hung Yu-hsiang (洪毓祥) urged the government to separate social welfare funding from cash infusions for Taipower and CPC. He said budget allocations for senior farmers and the public could be prioritized, while funding for state-owned enterprises should undergo a more methodical review.
Commenting on CPC’s financial situation, Southern Taiwan University of Science and Technology Professor Wei Hui-shan (魏慧珊) said the cash infusion would eliminate the deficit the company incurred through its price stabilization efforts in 2026, per Tai Sounds. She said the capital increase would also help prevent CPC’s debt-to-capital ratio, which stood at 93% in August, from worsening.
Wei warned that if CPC’s liabilities were to exceed its capital, the company could face bankruptcy and restructuring, potentially resulting in a credit-rating downgrade and reducing its ability to purchase energy on international markets.
Regarding CPC’s financial difficulties, Wei said the company has served as a price stabilizer since the COVID-19 pandemic began in 2020, accumulating massive deficits after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. She added that the government’s policy of replacing coal-fired power generation with natural gas had contributed to CPC’s rising debt-to-capital ratio, which increased from a relatively healthy 60% to 93%.

US importer recalls 37,000 squishy toys due to ‘deadly ingestion hazard’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:16:00 UTC
13:16:00 KST

US importer recalls 37,000 squishy toys due to ‘deadly ingestion hazard’
A US-based toy importer has recalled about 37,000 squishy toys from stores nationwide due to a “deadly ingestion hazard”.
A notice on the US Consumer Product Safety Commission’s website, which gave the recall date as Oct 1, said the two types of toys affected are Squishy Dumpling Toys and Crazy Squib Ball Toys.
These toys are manufactured in China and imported by ABC Trading, which is based in Vernon, California.
They were available at ABC Trading’s stores in Los Angeles and other stores nationwide from April to June for about US$0.41 to US$1.25.
The commission said the toys had violated the mandatory product safety standard in the US, as the water beads inside them can expand larger than permitted, posing risks if ingested.
“If a water bead is ingested, it can pose ingestion, choking, and intestinal obstruction hazards inside a child’s body, resulting in severe discomfort, vomiting, dehydration and a risk of death to a child,” the commission added.
Both types of toys come in multiple translucent colours, and contain glitter and water beads.
Model 3655 of the squishy dumplings feature a cartoon face and come in a tan plastic container shaped like a bamboo steamer. These also have the words “SQUISHY DUMPLING” printed on the front of the removable package labelling.
Meanwhile, model 3984 of the crazy squib balls are individually wrapped in a white netting, with the words “CRAZY SQUIB BALL” and “Squeeze it! Throw it!” printed on the front of the package labelling.
The commission has advised consumers to stop using the squishy toys immediately and contact ABC Trading for a full refund.
There have been no incidents or injuries related to the toys reported so far, it added.
According to CNBC, sales of squishy toys in the US quadrupled in 2026, reaching US$297 million (S$380.30 million) in June.
The toys’ relatively low prices and high social media appeal have been cited as the main reasons driving their popularity.
The recall comes amid heightened scrutiny across the world over the safety of squishy toys, especially for children and young people.
In August, nearly 20,000 illegal squishy toys were seized in Thailand due to substandard products that may expose children to chemicals linked to cancer and other health risks.
Some squishy toys are designed to resemble food and contain added fragrance, which increase the risk of young children putting these toys in their mouth, local media The Nation had reported.
The Thai authorities had begun closely monitoring squishy toys after they became highly popular on social media, with a particular focus on TikTok and shops with high follower numbers and strong viewing figures.
Singapore has also seen a resurgence of interest in squishy toys, with a number of independent stores popping up over the past year.
Videos selling these toys have garnered millions of views online, with some brands also opening physical stores in places such as Suntec City and Chinatown.
In Singapore, stocks of popular squishy toy brand NeeDoh have run out, with the next major shipment expected in mid-October, according to NeeDoh Singapore’s official website.
“We’ve been blown away by the demand for NeeDoh this year, and we’re grateful for your support through a long wait,” the brand wrote on its website.
Singapore’s Consumer Product Safety Office (CPSO) has advised customers to choose squishy toys from reputable brands and sellers, and to avoid toys with a strong or unusual smell.
CPSO has also urged customers to check their toys regularly and to stop using any toys that are damaged, leaking, smelly or deteriorated.
“Supervise young children and never microwave or intentionally heat squishy toys,” CPSO wrote on its website.

Don’t know? Blame Russia: Finnish president takes page from NATO chief’s playbook
Published 5 Oct, 2026 04:09 | Updated 5 Oct, 2026 09:27
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has blamed Russia for a wide range of security concerns facing the EU, including the influx of migrants over the summer into Ceuta, Spain’s enclave in Morocco. He later admitted that he did not know the situation in Ceuta “well enough to take a position.”
Stubb made the remarks in an interview with Spanish newspaper El Mundo over the weekend. Asked about potential hybrid threats posed by Russia, Stubb said the country would try to interfere with the upcoming Spanish election.
Madrid “should expect some form of sabotage or hybrid attack. It could be related to information warfare or a campaign that threatens their democracy,” he claimed.
The president went on to allege that Russian-backed cyberattacks are “happening as we speak against Spanish banks and other targets,” without citing specific evidence.
“They send asylum seekers to our border, as we have also seen in Ceuta,” he said, accusing Russia of committing acts of sabotage throughout the EU.
He also mentioned cases in which Russian-linked ships were accused of cutting undersea telecommunications cables in the Baltic Sea and the recent incident at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport, where explosives-laden drones were found near Ukrainian cargo planes. Germany blamed Moscow and ordered the closure of a Russian consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural center in Berlin. Russia dismissed the accusations as “nonsensical” and denied any involvement.
Pressed further about Russia’s alleged role in the Ceuta crisis in late July, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the enclave, Stubb admitted that he did not “know the matter well enough to take a position.”
Reuters reported at the time that migrants had been encouraged by viral videos and misleading claims about Spain’s asylum and migration rules. Spain later accused Russian- and Israeli-linked networks of spreading disinformation regarding the crisis, which both countries denied.
Stubb’s interview came after NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte encouraged members of the bloc to attribute incidents to Russia whenever they are sure or “almost sure” that Russia is responsible.
“When able, when you are sure it is the Russians, or almost sure it is the Russians, attribute it to the Russians,” Rutte said this week.
Direct conflict unlikely
Asked about the possibility of a direct conflict between NATO and Russia, however, Stubb dismissed it as negligible.
“Do we expect Russia to attack? The answer is no. We have no evidence of that,” he told El Mundo.
According to the Finnish president, EU leaders have a “communication problem,” as some have been “acting in an alarmist way and conflating [hypothetical] scenarios with the perception of the threat.”
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius urged officials this week not to “exaggerate” when making alarmist statements about Russia and said there is no evidence that the country is planning to attack NATO. Rutte has also said there is “no imminent threat to NATO territory.”
Nevertheless, EU officials have argued that the bloc, as well as NATO, should be prepared for a potential clash with Russia. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the country must be ready for a conflict by as early as 2028. The German government amended its constitutional debt brake to fund military spending and passed a 2026 budget allocating a record €108.2 billion ($121.5 billion) to defense and €11.5 billion in military assistance for Ukraine.
Russia has stated that it would not attack any NATO country unless attacked first – warning, however, that Western military aid to Ukraine makes a dangerous escalation more likely. President Vladimir Putin has argued that European politicians are stirring tensions with Russia to distract voters from problems at home.

Brazil heads to a runoff presidential vote after Bolsonaro and Lula fail to acquire outright majority needed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:08:45 UTC
13:08:45 KST

Flávio Bolsonaro, Brazilian senator, presidential hopeful and son to embattled former leader Jair, says he is “very happy” to have led in the first round and heading into the runoff, with incumbent Lula expressing disappointment over “unexpected” results.
Flávio Bolsonaro, a Brazilian Senator and ally of US President Donald Trump, and Brazil’s incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off in a runoff on the 25th of October 5 for the top job of Latin America’s powerhouse economy after neither won a majority in Sunday's presidential vote.
The country’s electoral court in the capital Brasilia said neither the 80-year-old incumbent, seeking his fourth non-consecutive term, nor the 45-year-old son to embattled former President Jair Bolsonaro garnered the majority vote needed for an outright win.
The court had Bolsonaro with just over 56 million votes while Brazilian political veteran Lula sat at around 53.7 million. The data was announced after local election officials reported 99.8% of the votes counted for the country’s next presidential term, set to begin 5 January.
The winner will be in charge of South America’s biggest economy and a population of 214 million. A win for Bolsonaro would increase US influence in the country, while a win for Lula would likely continue to distance Brasilia from Washington and instead deepen its ties with China.
Flávio Bolsonaro addressed the press and a small group of supporters, including some wearing green and yellow Brazil jerseys and one woman wrapped in the Israeli flag, outside his Brasilia house.
“Brazil wants change, that’s the reading of what happened today,” Bolsonaro said. “It’s the end of the Workers’ Party era,” he added, referencing Lula's party.
Lula, seeking to be encouraging ahead of an uphill battle to beat Bolsonaro in the upcoming runoff, said the result was “unexpected” as he had thought he could win in the first round.
“Tomorrow we start a new campaign,” said Lula. “I am very good in the knockout stage. We will see who has the best plan.”
Both Lula and Bolsonaro will have three weeks to reach moderate voters who did not support them in the first round.
Augusto Cury, a writer who finished in third place with 3.4 million votes, said he would not endorse either in the runoff. Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, two candidates who garnered about 5.3 million votes combined on Sunday, have previously said the same.
In the campaign ahead, Lula is expected to try to capitalise on the popularity of his social policies and his rival’s many legal woes.
While the once widely popular Lula saw his approval ratings plummet during his third term, standing up to the US gave him a boost. He still enjoys a strong base of supporters who credit his social policies for improving millions of Brazilians’ lives.
But the incumbent faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same Supreme Court justice who led the investigation into his rival Jair Bolsonaro, and subjected him to house arrest following his conviction of plotting a coup to subvert democracy after the last presidential election.
Justice Alexandre de Moraes is accused of having been in contact with disgraced banker and head of the Banco Master financial institution, Daniel Vorcaro, who had messaged him several times seeking legal advice.
Both candidates face image problems; Roughly half of Brazil’s population disapproves of the Bolsonaro family, and the other half disapprove of Lula’s Workers' Party, according to multiple polls.
Four years ago, Lula beat then incumbent Jair Bolsonaro by about 2.1 million votes.
While Sunday was a successful night for Bolsonaro, nothing is won yet. Both will need to tap into to the other candidates’ base to launch a successful presidential bid, which may force them to concede on certain policy goals to receive an endorsement.
The three other main candidates – Cury, Santos and Caiado – hold roughly 8.73 million or 7.5% of eligible votes between them.

Amid Blue-Wave Panic, Republicans Still Hopeful About New Hampshire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:07:00 UTC
13:07:00 KST

The DC Brief
Twice A Week
Essential context on the people, politics, and issues driving Washington.
From afar, Republicans’ Senate map looks pretty smudged at best. This was the year in which the GOP was favored to hold their majority, and Democrats’ aspirations for taking back control were viewed as pipe dreams. But here we are, in October of an election year, with polls showing Democrats potentially leading in competitive Senate races in Michigan, Ohio, North Carolina, Georgia, even Texas. The fact that reporters in Washington are now setting alerts for Senate contests in Alaska, Iowa, and South Dakota says as much about the fast-moving environment as President Donald Trump’s terrible standing in the polls.
But New Hampshire, whose independent streak sometimes borders on contrarian, may be Republicans’ best chance for an upset over a Democratic contender—in this case Rep. Chris Pappas. And the GOP is throwing more money into the Live Free or Die state in hopes of making it happen.
Why Republicans are hopeful about New Hampshire comes down to one word: Sununu.
The Republican candidate, John E. Sununu, is not only a former Senator, but part of a New Hampshire political dynasty. Both his father, John H. Sununu, and brother, Chris Sununu, are former governors of the Granite State. The Sununu name is about as bullet-proof in New Hampshire as the party could find. His one term in the Senate from 2003 to 2009 was well-regarded in the state for his willingness to cross party lines, particularly his opposition to the post-9/11 PATRIOT Act over provisions that were anathema to the libertarian-minded New Hampshire voters.
In Michigan and Georgia, two other states Republicans are targeting for Senate flips, Reps. Mike Rogers and Mike Collins have struggled to convince voters they will be more than Trumpist Yes Men. No one is really confusing any member of the Sununu clan for a MAGA cheerleader. His family has long been seen as aligned with the Bush wing of the party—his father was George H.W. Bush’s White House chief of staff—and his brother was a prominent Trump critic.
When Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced her plans to retire last March, Democrats quickly coalesced around Pappas as her successor. A former state legislator, and small-business owner, Pappas’ ethos matches the vibe of voters in the famously fickle state—no one would mistake him for a democratic socialist or a woke culture warrior.
The race is now in an odd limbo state, where the Democrat appears to have the advantage, but a closer look reveals why Republicans aren’t giving up. A New York Times poll released late last month week found Sununu trailing by five points. But it also found 42% of New Hampshire voters think the Republican nominee “has good character.” Among independent voters—who normally decide elections in New Hampshire—Sununu has a 10-point advantage over Pappas on the character question.
Yet the same poll has Trump at 60% disapproval among all New Hampshire voters, and that number hits 65% among independents. If the final five weeks of this campaign become nationalized—as many Democrats hope—then that number could be an anchor heavier than any political pedigree.
All of this uncertainty comes as the conservative Senate Leadership Fund announced $17 million in spending for Sununu, the Trump-backed No Going Back PAC is ready with $10 million in ads, and the Koch-minded Americans for Prosperity Action is already on the record with more than $2 million. In all, by most estimates, outside spending has already topped $50 million in a race with fewer than 1 million registered voters.
The pace of spending has left both campaigns frustrated. As New Hampshire Public Radio reports, Sununu acknowledged how the noise complicates things during a stop last week. “You’ve got to work really hard to keep your message focused to break through to make sure people can appreciate you for who you are, what you have to offer, what kind of leader you will be,” Sununu said.
That hasn’t meant an easy glide for Pappas, though. “It’s crazy. This is no way to run a democracy. The fact is we’ve got to get big money out of politics,” Pappas said last Monday during an interview with Boston 25 News. “It’s very clear we are being outspent.”
Senate Majority PAC, the super PAC aligned with Senate Democrats, announced an initial $10 million commitment to help the 46-year-old four-term House member perhaps become the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. It’s a big outlay, but still dwarfed by Republican dollars.
Democrats know they have to keep the New Hampshire seat to have any shot at becoming a majority in the new Senate, but Pappas may face an enthusiasm shortage. While 75% of Democrats say they’re satisfied with Pappas as their nominee, it’s certainly short of the 85% of Republicans who say the same about Sununu. In a state that small, the enthusiasm gap and party unity really matter.
Another polling dynamic keeps getting flagged by Republicans working in New Hampshire or those keeping an eye on the race from Washington: while Democrats have a 9-point edge in voters who would rather see a Democratic Senate than a Republican one, Pappas’ lead in the poll is just five points. Add in that 8% of voters who prefer a Democratic Senate but claim that they plan to cast a ballot for Sununu anyway, and it’s clear this race is far from decided.
Of course, if a blue wave does swamp Senate races across the country, anyone who’s followed New Hampshire politics for a spell would not be at all surprised to see it bucking the trend. Such a move would be very on-brand for New Hampshire.
