Japan’s Potential as a ‘Third Option’ for ASEAN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:06:00 UTC
13:06:00 KST

The countries of ASEAN have traditionally sought to maintain their autonomy under the banner of “centrality,” avoiding excessive dependence on any particular external power — the United States, China, or others — through what might be called an omnidirectional strategy. Expanding cooperation across as many extra-regional partners as possible in areas such as trade, investment, and infrastructure development has been a useful strategy for building the foundations that sustain that autonomy.
Among the challenges this entails, none is more important than determining how to engage with the United States and China, respectively, and how to keep a balance between them. The United States remains the world’s preeminent military power and occupies the central position in the global financial and monetary regime. It is also the largest source of investment in ASEAN and the largest export market for many ASEAN member states. As such, its influence in the region should not be underestimated. Yet the second Trump administration’s highly unpredictable foreign policy is eroding American soft power, while China is intensifying its outreach to the Global South, including ASEAN countries. China’s cooperative relationships with the ASEAN states are clearly deepening.
Beijing presents its relationship with ASEAN countries as an opportunity, one offering member states the potential for greater stability and development. Evidence for this can be found in China’s four major initiatives for engagement: the Global Development Initiative (GDI), the Global Security Initiative (GSI), the Global Civilization Initiative (GCI), and the Global Governance Initiative (GGI). The GDI, which calls for invigorating the global economy and advancing win-win cooperation toward stronger, greener, and more balanced development, and the GSI, which calls for a common, inclusive, cooperative, and sustainable approach to security, are the cornerstones of these initiatives.
In response to this Chinese outreach, ASEAN countries have uniformly endorsed the GDI. ASEAN’s principal documents welcome it, and all ASEAN countries have joined the Group of Friends of the GDI at the United Nations. For ASEAN countries, more active investment, financial support, and technical assistance from China channeled through the GDI aligns with their own development needs. The GSI is a different matter: while Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, and Timor-Leste have explicitly expressed support, ASEAN as a whole has not. Malaysia, however, has indicated a willingness to begin consultations on joining the GSI. In August 2026, Indonesia and China also agreed to strengthen joint military exercises, defense industrial cooperation, and technology cooperation.
ASEAN countries have not, however, abandoned their commitment to autonomy. In March 2025, for example, in response to the launch of the second Trump administration, ASEAN established the ASEAN Geoeconomic Task Force (AGTF); in response to the Middle East crisis, this was subsequently reorganized in March 2026 into the ASEAN Geoeconomic Group (AGG). The AGG is examining what measures ASEAN should adopt amid intensifying geoeconomic competition — measures of existential significance for the bloc. For ASEAN countries grappling with the “geoeconomic turn” as a new challenge, maintaining an omnidirectional strategy and expanding cooperative relationships with third partners beyond the United States and China is becoming ever more critical to securing their autonomy.
Japan should recognize these needs and play a role as that third partner, or option, for ASEAN countries. Potential areas for cooperation are wide-ranging: energy security, environment and green transformation (GX), digital infrastructure including AI and semiconductors, infrastructure development, and security cooperation through defense equipment transfers and capacity-building support. The Updated FOIP announced in May 2026 also signals Japan’s intention to reinforce a range of issues that ASEAN countries consider important. Japan should make full use of the key schemes it has available for deepening cooperation with ASEAN: the Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC), the Partnership on Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia (POWERR Asia), Official Security Assistance (OSA), and an ODA framework that now makes it easier to leverage private-sector financing.
RCEP, the broad mega-FTA encompassing Japan, ASEAN, and other regional partners, is due for review in 2027. Japan and ASEAN should work together in maintaining a freer and more open rules-based regional economic order. Beyond that, supporting ASEAN countries in their efforts to expand their role in broader global forums, and working together to uphold a rules-based international order, will become increasingly important.
The annual survey “The State of Southeast Asia” conducted by the Singapore-based think tank ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute has shown consistently that Japan commands the highest level of trust among extra-regional countries from ASEAN nations. The reasons behind this deserve attention. According to the latest edition, published in 2026, the top response to the question of why Japan is trusted was: “Japan is a responsible stakeholder that respects and champions international law” (41.4 percent). This was followed by “Japan has vast economic resources and the political will to provide global leadership” (22.7 percent). In working with ASEAN countries to sustain a desirable regional order, Japan’s reputation as a supporter of the rules-based international order may be its most valuable asset.

====================================================================================================

The foreign minister also referred to meetings with neighbouring countries, including Persian Gulf states, and stressed Iran's decision to continue building confidence among regional countries based on the principle of good neighbourliness, in order to strengthen cooperation and coordination to enhance regional peace and security.
Referring to meetings with European parties, he stressed that Iran has conveyed its positions on the need for European countries to adopt a responsible and independent approach to West Asian issues. He cited repeated admissions by NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte about extensive direct European participation in illegal and aggressive US and Israeli attacks on Iran, and demanded that European countries be held accountable for their role in designing and carrying out the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran.
Condemning US "inhumane and illegal" sanctions against Iran, Araghchi stressed that sanctions, pressure and threats cannot shake the Iranian nation's determination to defend its rights and dignity.
In his speech, Araghchi thanked the diplomats for arranging his and the president's meetings in New York. "I met with 42 foreign ministers in New York. The president met with almost 10 heads of state, and all of this was thanks to the efforts and coordination you made."
He said Iran's presence in New York this year was very strong and effective. In addition to the many meetings, there were many interviews, the president's speech at the General Assembly and other speeches Araghchi gave at side events, and meetings with thinkers, political elites and intellectuals in New York. Most important, he said, was the plan Iran presented this year to resolve existing disputes and the ongoing war between Iran and America, known as the seven-day plan, under which the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened within seven days if accepted.
Iran's presence at this year's General Assembly was very effective and active. The political atmosphere in New York this year was affected by Iran's plan and Iran's very broad presence, and it became clear to everyone that Iran remains serious about diplomacy and finding a peaceful solution.
"As we are serious in defending ourselves, we are firm and serious in both defending ourselves and advancing diplomacy. If our enemies again take the path of military confrontation, they will receive a firmer response than before, and we will defend ourselves more strongly than before. On the other hand, if they seek diplomatic paths, we remain ready to reach a just and honourable solution through diplomacy to end this war."
Araghchi said Iran explained its positions clearly. The level of interest from different countries in meeting Iran, learning its views and understanding its plan was very significant. "The perception some in America may have had that they could turn Iran into an isolated country was completely defeated, and Iran played its role in New York as a powerful and respected country in the international community, showing that it still has logical positions and has a solution both for war and for peace."
He said the US claim that it expelled the Iranian delegation, regardless of its truth, is noteworthy because Iran went to New York and returned according to its own pre-set schedule. "This claim by the American side is truly strange. On the one hand, they admit they acted contrary to their obligations as host of the United Nations and are not a worthy host for the organisation, and on the other, they showed how angry they are at the presence of the Iranian delegation in America, exactly as if the host of the Olympics, when its team loses, expels the athletes of another team. This behaviour is just as childish and contemptible."
Araghchi said Iran's diplomats had a brilliant presence at the General Assembly. "We were present in all arenas, conveyed the voice of the Iranian people to the world, and delivered the message of the Iranian people for peace and logical and peaceful solutions.
We explained our conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz clearly to everyone. All these conditions are consistent with the commitments the United States must accept."
He said meetings with neighbouring countries, especially Persian Gulf states, were very effective, respectful and friendly. "We have begun a new path to build trust between neighbouring countries and the Islamic Republic of Iran, and especially in the Persian Gulf, we are traversing this path well."
"Our brothers and sisters in the Persian Gulf are accompanying us on this path, and a shared will has formed to create peace, stability and security in the Persian Gulf region with the participation of the region's own countries, which is now being seriously pursued."
He said he also had many meetings with European countries. "You are all aware that our dialogue with European countries is very frank, and we hope European countries will reconsider their approach towards the Islamic Republic of Iran."
Araghchi said the NATO secretary-general's admission of European participation in the US war against Iran was a heavy admission. "He clearly said that more than 5,000 American warplanes flew from bases in Europe to attack Iran, and we are still waiting for European countries to answer why they effectively participated in this war against Iran. European countries must reconsider their approach towards Iran."
He said Iran hopes America will choose the path of wisdom and rationality, but if it again moves toward military solutions, "we are more prepared than before and will take whatever action is necessary to defend ourselves. If they choose the path of diplomacy, we remain ready."
"America has lost both in war and in diplomacy in the past. Testing the path of sanctions and new sanctions will bring them no benefit. There is no military solution and no solution based on more sanctions; only a solution based on negotiation, justice, fairness and diplomatic dignity can be effective and find a final solution to end this war and the illegal and unjust aggression that has been launched against the Islamic Republic of Iran."

IDF Chief Zamir marks three years since October 7: “The IDF failed in its supreme mission to protect the citizens of the State of Israel"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:04:18 UTC
13:04:18 KST

‘The IDF failed to protect the citizens of Israel:’ Zamir marks 3 years since Oct. 7th
Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir acknowledges the military’s failure to protect civilians, promises thorough inquiries and calls for renewed vigilance as flags are lowered to half-mast at the Knesset
Israel began memorial observances Monday marking three years since the October 7 terrorist attack and massacre, with ceremonies honoring the victims and a stark acknowledgment of responsibility from IDF Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir.
In a special order addressed to soldiers, commanders, reservists and civilian employees, Zamir placed the military’s failure at the forefront of his message.
“The IDF failed in its supreme mission to protect the citizens of the State of Israel,” he wrote, recalling the breach of Israel’s borders on Simchat Torah in 2023.
His message combined mourning for those murdered, abducted and killed in battle with a commitment to investigate the failures of that morning, implement lessons and prepare the military for future threats.
Communities transformed into battlefields
Zamir described the devastation inflicted on communities across the Western Negev, where familiar landscapes became scenes of violence.
“In the wheat fields, the orchards, the homes of the kibbutzim, and the towns of the Western Negev, places where the roots of life and settlement were planted, the enemy sowed fire, ruin, and destruction,” he wrote.
Roads connecting communities became battlefronts, fields turned into battlegrounds, and family homes became sites of massacre and abduction.
Three years later, he said, “an entire nation bows its head in mourning.”
The order honored civilians murdered in their homes, young people killed after going out to dance, hostages murdered in captivity, and soldiers and members of the security forces who fell in battle. It also remembered members of local rapid-response and rescue teams who rushed to confront the attackers and help those under fire.
Zamir expressed solidarity with the wounded, those affected by the war and bereaved families, saying the memory of the victims remained a constant reminder of the military’s responsibility.
Accountability and the public’s trust
Alongside remembrance, Zamir emphasized the obligation to examine what went wrong and turn the findings into meaningful change.
“It is our duty to conduct thorough inquiries and ensure that lessons are implemented, so that we may prove ourselves worthy of the trust the people have placed in us,” he wrote.
He pledged to preserve the stories of the fallen and use their courage, dedication and camaraderie to educate future generations of soldiers and commanders.
The chief of staff also paid tribute to the military and civilian response to the attack. He described soldiers rushing into the line of fire, reservists repeatedly leaving their families to serve, and civilian employees working beyond their usual hours to support the war effort.
“In the darkest moments, the cohesion and exemplary spirit of Israeli society shone through,” he wrote.
A pledge to confront emerging threats
Turning to the campaign that followed October 7, Zamir said the IDF had fought on multiple fronts, defended communities and borders, struck capabilities threatening Israeli citizens, and rescued and brought home hostages.
He said the military had also adapted its methods to confront evolving threats.
“We will not allow our enemies to build up their strength unchecked; we will identify threats as they emerge and strike them with determination and might,” he wrote.
Zamir called on troops to carry both the memory of the fallen and the lessons of October 7 into their service, while continuing to strengthen the armed forces and uphold their values.
“This is our duty to the fallen, our responsibility to the citizens of Israel, and our vow to future generations,” he said.
Flags lowered at the Knesset
At the Knesset in Jerusalem, national flags in the plaza were lowered to half-mast Monday morning as part of the memorial observances.
Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, Director-General Moshe “Chiko” Edri and Knesset Security Officer Chief Superintendent Yuval Hen attended the ceremony, accompanied by the Knesset Guard’s honor guard.
The ceremony brought the anniversary’s message of remembrance to Israel’s parliament as the country honored those lost and reflected on the responsibility to prevent another such catastrophe.

Across China: A Chinese county's violins go global
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:03:14 CST
13:03:14 KST

ZHENGZHOU, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- A knife turns gently against a scroll taking shape in a workshop. The craftsman blows softly, sending fine shavings dancing in a ray of sunlight, and the air is filled with the scent of spruce and maple.
The scene could easily belong in Cremona, Italy. Yet it is unfolding in Queshan, a county of about 374,500 people in central China's Henan Province that has quietly become one of the world's major sources of handmade violins.
The craft originated in 16th-century Italy and spread across the globe by the 18th century. In the 1980s, villagers from Queshan joined the tide of migrant workers heading to faraway cities. Many found jobs in violin factories in Beijing. Over the years, they built a reputation as master craftsmen. Some even ran their own workshops.
In 2015, Queshan began calling its natives home and laid plans for a violin industrial park. More than 60 luthiers returned to start businesses, assigning production roles to households where villagers can be trained and employed.
Unlike factory workers on city assembly lines, Queshan's craftsmen often specialize in a single stage, sawing timber, carving plates, fitting bodies, or cutting scrolls. They can also take components home and set their own hours.
He Ruixia is one of those returnees. "My hours are flexible, and I'm paid for each piece I finish," she said, bending over a violin while her husband assembled a cello nearby.
"Since I came back, I earn more and I'm happier," she said. "It's easier to look after my family and still get my work done."
The instruments she makes will be shipped from the northern port of Tianjin to the United States, the biggest overseas market for Queshan violins by both volume and value.
Queshan holds more than 80 percent of the domestic market for mid to high-end handmade violins, according to Jiang Baolin, secretary-general of the Queshan Handmade Violin Makers Association.
Taking advantage of the digital age, local workshops are now reaching buyers through social media. In a livestream at a factory in Zhugou Township, a host works with a musician testing instruments live as customers from Australia, Russia and France place orders online.
"Cross-border e-commerce presents our violins to customers across the globe," Jiang said. "Short videos and livestreaming enable overseas customers to see for themselves the quality of Chinese violin-making. People in the trade have long known that good handmade violins come from Queshan, but there was no channel to buy them before."
Today, violins made in Queshan are sold in more than 30 countries and regions, including the United States, Italy, France and Germany. The county has built a complete industrial chain spanning timber processing, accessory carving and spray-painting. Its 144 violin-making and supporting businesses employ more than 2,600 local people, who turn out about 400,000 violins a year, generating an annual industrial output of 600 million yuan (89.5 million U.S. dollars).
The industry has also been a path out of poverty. In February 2020, Queshan was among the last 14 impoverished counties in Henan Province to be removed from China's poverty list.
The violin continues to inspire the next generation. According to Jiang, several primary schools in the county offer violin classes, giving children a chance to learn the instrument their own families make. "Several young people are now studying at conservatories in Beijing, Tianjin, Xi'an and Shanghai," he said. ■

WELLINGTON, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Stronger-than-expected U.S. economic performance is putting upward pressure on New Zealand mortgage rates as higher U.S. bond yields have pushed up New Zealand wholesale swap rates, a key benchmark for fixed mortgage rates, Kiwibank said on Monday.
Strong U.S. economic performance could lead financial markets to price in higher interest rates, with expectations for rates to remain higher for longer, the New Zealand state-owned bank said in its weekly economic commentary.
As a small economy, New Zealand's wholesale funding costs are influenced by international developments, with higher U.S. bond yields pushing up New Zealand wholesale swap rates, which can mean higher fixed mortgage rates, Kiwibank said, adding that wholesale interest rates tend to move together globally, particularly at the long end of the curve.
Interest rates have risen sharply around the world, with U.S. rates at their highest level in 25 years, Kiwibank said, noting the difference between New Zealand's two-year and 10-year government bond rates has widened from 100 basis points in May to 120 basis points.
It said the weaker New Zealand dollar, which has fallen below 56 U.S. cents, could benefit the economy by supporting exports and making New Zealand cheaper for foreign investment and purchases. ■

Interview: UN official highlights GDI's role in advancing sustainable development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:02:54 CST
13:02:54 KST

by Ada Zhang
UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Five years after China proposed the Global Development Initiative (GDI), its focus is shifting increasingly towards practical cooperation that addresses the priorities of developing countries, a senior UN official has said.
"Five years on, the Global Development Initiative is showing how shared ambition can translate into practical support for development," Dima Al-Khatib, director of the United Nations Office for South-South Cooperation (UNOSSC), told Xinhua in a written interview.
The initiative, she said, has "provided a platform for mobilizing partnerships, knowledge and resources in support of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development."
According to a United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) China publication, more than 600 projects under the Global Development Project Pool had been implemented or were in progress by the end of 2024. The associated Global Development Capital Pool had mobilized 14 billion U.S. dollars in financing commitments as of March 2025.
"These mechanisms illustrate how cooperation under the GDI is supporting development financing and implementation," Al-Khatib said.
Al-Khatib pointed to China's longstanding cooperation with UNOSSC, which spans more than two decades.
"The strength of South-South cooperation lies in helping countries turn each other's experience into solutions that work for their own communities," she said.
One example is the Global South-South Development Center Project, which entered its second phase in 2025 under the China-United Nations Global South-South Development Facility.
Working with the China International Center for Economic and Technical Exchanges, the project aims to strengthen a network of more than 60 technical institutions to facilitate cooperation among developing countries.
In West Africa, a rice initiative involving the World Food Programme, the African Union and other partners combines technology and training to improve agricultural productivity, reduce post-harvest losses and support rural livelihoods.
She also highlighted cooperation on digital development, including e-commerce training that reached participants from more than 90 countries, followed by field studies in China for policymakers from 22 developing countries.
With just four years left to meet the 2030 deadline, Al-Khatib said the GDI can support accelerated Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) implementation by connecting nationally identified priorities with technologies, technical expertise, financing and capacity development.
In September 2025, China and the United Nations announced the China-UN Global South-South Development Facility, with 10 million dollars in budget support for the 2025-2030 period.
Established under the United Nations Fund for South-South Cooperation, the facility supports cooperation under the GDI in areas, including agriculture, technology and digital development, according to UNOSSC.
Al-Khatib said the facility's first call for proposals, which concluded in August, attracted 107 proposals from 16 UN agencies and entities, covering 115 countries across the Global South.
"The next phase may prioritize country ownership, measurable results and the adaptation and scaling of solutions suited to local circumstances," she said.
Looking ahead, Al-Khatib emphasized the importance of aligning cooperation with the SDGs, UN social and environmental standards, and UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks.
"The objective is to enable developing countries to adapt, co-create and sustain solutions, and share their experience across the Global South, guided by the commitment to leave no one behind," she said. ■

Feature: Building a personal bond along the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:02:20 CST
13:02:20 KST

BISHKEK, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Since a railway project launched in late 2024 connecting China, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, Chinese and local construction workers have worked side by side diligently.
The railway, a landmark Belt and Road cooperation project personally promoted by the leaders of the three countries, has brought together specialists and workers from China and Central Asia. Among them are Chinese engineer Yang Dong and Kyrgyz construction worker Zholboldu Korchubaev.
Yang has more than 40 years of experience in railway construction. As the technical director of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway project, he oversees training for Kyrgyz construction workers. Before long, Yang formed a friendship with 32-year-old Korchubaev from Kyrgyzstan's Jalal-Abad region.
For Korchubaev, working on the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway has been life-changing. "Our country has never had such a modern railway. Joining this project for me isn't just a job, but a way for me to grow and realize my dream," he said.
Before he became accustomed to the new equipment and technology, Korchubaev considered giving up. Yang stepped in and showed him the ropes.
Through repeated practice, he mastered the required skills. He became proficient in rebar welding and operating various types of equipment and well-versed in railway construction standards and regulations.
"Yang generously shares his experience, and we are working together on a great project. This friendship is especially valuable," he said.
Yang is particularly proud that Korchubaev can now perform various tasks independently. He, too, faced difficulties during his early days working in Kyrgyzstan.
"Among them were the harsh winter weather and the language barrier," Yang said, adding that Korchubaev helped him adapt to the climate and introduced him to local customs. "I'm so glad that through this major project, I learned to communicate with people from another country and with a different mentality," the Chinese engineer said.
Speaking about the prospects of the railway, Yang said it would facilitate travel between China and Kyrgyzstan, promote infrastructure development in the villages and towns along the route, and improve education and healthcare, thereby raising living standards among the local population.
Korchubaev believes the new railway would lead Kyrgyzstan to prosperity.
"Freight transportation will become more convenient, helping bring more factories to the region and create jobs. Young people will have more opportunities, and children will be able to see the world," he said.
For both Yang and Korchubaev, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway is not only a transport link but also a bridge of friendship and cooperation.
"Over more than a year of working together, builders from our countries have already become one big family," Yang said.
Korchubaev said that through their joint work, he had truly experienced the diligence and kindness of the Chinese people.
"This railway has brought the peoples of our countries closer together and will further strengthen cooperation between us, allowing the flower of friendship to bloom even more luxuriantly," Korchubaev said. ■

Ball in UK’s court: EU ambassador says Brussels will be ‘ready to engage‘ after country decides what it wants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:00:48 UTC
13:00:48 KST

Jukka Salovaara, the newly installed European Union ambassador to the UK, is likely to become a ubiquitous figure in national politics as the Andy Burnham government grapples with the question of its future relationship with the European Union.
Burnham has been clearer than his predecessor Keir Starmer in saying that what exists now is not working and that a full range of options, including rejoining, has to be on the table ahead of Labour’s next election manifesto.
Salovaara, aged 58, sees his role over the coming years as a “facilitator”, testing both sides like a good diplomat on what might fly and what will not work. He will not sit at the negotiating table, but he will be “very close to it”.
“Everyone tells me my job is explaining London to Brussels and Brussels to London”. The UK, he says, remains “the European Union’s first and foremost partner”. When the two have made agreements, it has always been to “our mutual benefit”.
A former permanent secretary in Finland’s foreign ministry, who also served as his country’s ambassador to the UN, this is his first job with the European Commission, but not his first posting in the UK. As a young diplomat in the summer of 1996, he handled European affairs in London for Finland at the onset of Cool Britannia, just as Tony Blair was on the cusp of gaining power.
“The 1990s was such an optimistic time,” he says of that era. “World trade was growing. Interdependence was expected to provide security, and global norms and rules were strengthening. There was a feeling that globalisation and a rising tide would lift all boats.” The Labour government, he recalls, came “very close” to joining the euro.
Since then, different ghosts have dominated UK politics. His office in Smith Square is just one floor up from that used by Margaret Thatcher in Conservative Central Office. The building was also a haunt for Nigel Farage when he was an MEP.
Burnham’s first EU summit is now pencilled in for November. Salovaara says issues such as how UK traders can avoid being caught up in the EU’s plans to prevent subsidised Chinese products flooding European markets will not be up for decision. The EU will not have completed its own legislative proposals by the time of the summit.
Salovaara says there are plenty of themes – food standards, linking the UK and EU carbon emissions trading scheme, youth mobility, and security – to keep the summit meaningful. On food, he points out: “When we have common standards we don’t need border checks. Nearly 60% of the UK’s food exports go to the EU market and 70% of the UK’s food imports come from the EU. Losing the red tape carries a lot of benefits.”
Negotiations between the two sides over the details of any “youth experience scheme”, including the number of 18-to-30-year-olds able to participate and the rights to work and study they would enjoy, are still under way. The UK has initially offered 50,000 places a year, according to EU officials, but Brussels is pushing for 150,000.
As to the parameters of a future relationship, Europe must wait to see what the UK wants rather than setting out a collective opinion of its own, he says. “The ball is very much with the UK in terms of having this debate then looking at the options … and then the EU [will be] ready to engage.
“The approach up until now had been step by step, but this prime minister wants to assess all the options.”
But he acknowledges the difficulties. Charles Grant, the head of the Centre for European Reform, has said he cannot envisage Europe wanting the UK back as a full member unless there is a political consensus to rejoin inside the UK. Salovaara admits: “When you do something that is very fundamental it usually makes sense to have a strong consensus, but it is for the UK to decide if consensus must be proven through a further referendum.”
He runs through the other options in the regulatory staircase – such as joining the EU single market or customs union – but points out other novel, if as yet undefined blueprints are evolving, including associate membership, which is the option being proposed for Canada.
Another scheme – associated with Alexandre Adam, chief adviser to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen – proposes that countries, including those locked in the Balkans EU accession waiting room, join the EU but without full rights of market access, which would be granted in time in return for commitments to democracy.
He points out that in the 1990s, European Economic Area countries such as Norway saw the relationship purely in economic terms, but have since come to see it as a more political relationship. “Look at how much Norway is integrated into what the EU does with Ukraine. Everyone is looking for a broader relationship with the EU.”

Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:00:48 UTC
13:00:48 KST

Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls.
The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC.
Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.
Writing in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, Dr Roselyn Campbell, author of the study from Purdue University in the US, notes: “While Aha, the first ruler of the First Dynasty, seems to have only had a few subsidiary burials, his successors included hundreds of subsidiary graves around their tombs and enclosures.”
The graves of the retainers were excavated in the 1920s by the English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who believed them to be an example of human sacrifice – a view some later experts agreed with.
But there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died.
Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge.
“This question of whether or not retainer sacrifice was practised in Egypt has been debated for over a century, but this is the first study to examine the human remains from the tombs themselves,” Campbell told the Guardian.
Campbell reports that 18 of the skulls showed signs of potentially lethal trauma such as fractures and – in one case – a chopping injury to the eye.
Campbell believs Petrie may have seen the skull fractures but did not realise they were injuries that occurred around the time of death, rather than arising as a result of later damage.
The fractures, she adds, are unlikely to have been caused by a mace – a weapon often depicted in ancient Egyptian art as being used by a victorious king to smite his enemies. Instead they are more likely to have been caused by flat, wide objects made of wood or antler.
“For the crania without trauma, we cannot be certain they were sacrificed. It’s quite possible that some of the retainers were sacrificed, while others were not,” she said. “With such a small sample size of the original burial population, we simply can’t see the full extent of these funerary rituals, nor can we be sure that this sample is truly representative of all the retainers.”
Campbell noted the number of subsidiary graves tapered off quickly and seems to have disappeared with the beginning of the Second Dynasty.
Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, said while the idea of retainer sacrifice was not totally new, “this paper is one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains”.
She added: “The practice was short-lived, with people being replaced by statuettes. Possibly some or all retainers felt that this was a boon and that they would enjoy an eternal life in the service of the god-king, though they might also have resented it, been terrified, and tried to escape this fate.”
Dr Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University, Alabama, said similar sacrifices had occurred across different cultures and times, adding that not everyone at the Egyptian site may have been compliant.
“If you really think about what those scenes would have looked like, it would have been very gruesome,” she said. While noting that the study only involved a small number of skulls from the burial site, “the idea that some of the people may have been violently killed, I think, is something that in reality we might expect”, she said.

To cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest shark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:00:47 UTC
13:00:47 KST

‘When I accidentally catch a shark, I bring it to my dogs,” Henrik Jensen, a 27-year-old from Greenland’s west coast, says casually. “I don’t let it back down because [the sharks] bully me and cut my lines.”
Jensen has fished for halibut in Ilulissat, Greenland’s third largest town, for a decade. He works an hour north of the town’s main iceberg-laden fishery, which sustains the livelihood of nearly 400 fishers. There, the halibut are bigger and more plentiful, but so are the Greenland sharks.
“This year I’ve lost around 6,000 hooks in total. Sometimes we lose 30,000 Danish krone [£3,440] a day,” says Jensen.
The Greenland shark is one of the least understood species on the planet. As well as being the world’s slowest shark, it is the second-largest carnivorous species, after the white shark, according to the Shark Trust. Reaching about six to seven metres in length, they can live for more than 400 years. For a long time they were thought to be completely blind, although scientists have recently discovered this may not be true.
The sharks inhabit a vast range across the deep and cold waters of the north and west Atlantic, but their attempts to feed on the northern fisheries’ main catch – Greenland halibut and Atlantic cod – often see them tangled in gear and brought in as bycatch.
This acrimonious coexistence has been documented ever since targeted fishing for the sharks’ liver oil ceased in the 1960s, but it came to a head earlier this year. The Avannaata municipality, of which Ilulissat is the administrative seat, approved a controversial plan to cull 1,000 sharks, offering 300 krone for every heart of a Greenland shark.
Lars Erik Gabrielsen, mayor of the municipality, says: “We need to safeguard the income of fishermen and the catch so that we can continue to eat the foods that we have relied on for generations.”
For many fishing inshore, working in small teams on dinghies, it brought a longstanding issue to a head. Timotheus Petersen, chair of the fishing association in Kullorsuaq, says: “Our longlines are expensive – one costs 1,599 krone. When the sharks cut our lines, we cannot finish fishing. We have to spend more money and buy new gear.”
The plan was eventually dropped after the government questioned its legality, but the prospect of a future cull remains.
In its decision to approve the cull, Avannaata council cited a similar scheme from the early 2000s in the former Aasiaat municipality, where a bounty of 200 krone was offered. According to a 2007 report from the Danish Technical University, another scheme between 1986 and 2001 in the former Uummannaq municipality brought in 19,697 hearts.
But the marine conservation group Oceans North Kalaallit Nunaat (ONKN) argues that culls do not resolve the issue, highlighting the migratory nature of the species, which can swim up to 1,200 miles (2,000km) a year. “Sharks removed in north-west Greenland would quickly be replaced by individuals arriving from other regions,” ONKN warned.
Many fishers also do not consider 300 krone worth the effort of hauling a shark onboard. “It’s difficult to catch them,” Jensen says. “You need bigger hooks and chains for the lines, so I don’t think anyone wants to try.”
But the debate around a possible cull is alarming conservationists. “If somebody says, ‘I’m going to cull a couple of thousand Greenland sharks’, that’s a disaster in my opinion,” says Prof Nick Dulvy, a marine conservationist at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia.
The Greenland shark is believed to become sexually mature at 150, which means the species replaces itself extremely slowly and will not rebound from a cull quickly. It is still recovering from targeted fishing throughout the 19th and mid-20th centuries, when, at its peak in 1948, 58,000 were landed.
“They are probably – biologically – the most sensitive species in the ocean to overfishing,” Dulvy says. Globally, it is estimated that 3,500 sharks are caught every year as bycatch and the population remains in decline.
Greenland’s fishing community highlight their longstanding problem with the sharks, but do not say why it has suddenly escalated. Jenseeraq Poulsen, the director of ONKN, suggests it is due to mounting pressures within a fishing industry that accounts for about 25% of Greenland’s GDP.
“If every Greenland shark in Baffin Bay vanished tomorrow, the inshore fishery in Avannaata would still face too many boats working a quota under pressure, rising costs and no alternative employment,” he says. “When margins are narrow, a longstanding nuisance becomes intolerable.”
Even though the price of halibut continues to rise, according to the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources, the average size of the fish is decreasing annually. While Jensen maintains he can still make a good living from fishing, he describes putting fewer hooks out and bringing in fewer fish, suggesting this is due to overfishing by offshore trawlers.
For some of those fishing these waters, however, the shark is not the leading cause of losing gear. “There are more and more ‘ghost lines’ and they are too heavy to pull up by the machine we use,” Jensen says. Ghost lines are discarded or lost gear that can get entangled with new lines, breaking equipment and trapping marine life.
Halibut Greenland, a cooperatively owned fish-processing company in Ilulissat, provides funds to clean up ghost gear in the area, which ONKN views as more effective than a shark cull. Poulsen also proposes a gear-loss compensation scheme, as well as funded trials of acoustic shark deterrents.
Rebekka Nygård Bak, an adviser to Greenland’s Ministry of Fisheries, Hunting, Agriculture and Self Sufficiency, suggests new bycatch-friendly equipment regulations could be a solution. She says a campaign for better bycatch reporting will also be key to any next steps.
For Poulsen, the sharks and those fishing these waters are two components of the same ecosystem, facing growing pressures in changing seas. “The shark is the visible, tangible version of a problem whose real drivers are structural,” he says.

Exiled separatist leader is likely to return to a very different Catalonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:00:47 UTC
13:00:47 KST

After years of legal wrangling, Spain’s constitutional court is expected to remove the last obstacle to the return of the former Catalan president Carles Puigdemont after nearly nine years in exile this week.
Puigdemont fled in 2017 to avoid being jailed for his part in the failed and illegal independence push for which nine of his colleagues were imprisoned on sentences of up to 13 years, although all were released within three years.
If on 6 October the court decides, as expected, that the charge of misuse of public funds is covered by the amnesty law passed by the Spanish parliament in 2024, Puigdemont should be free to return without fear of arrest.
But will he come back like Lenin, leaping from the train in St Petersburg to galvanise the faltering revolution, or as yesterday’s man, the last of the Romanovs, bound for the dustbin of history?
Whether he returns in triumph or, as he reportedly departed, in the boot of a car, Catalonia today is very different from the place he left nine years ago.
Firstly, the political climate has changed beyond recognition. The fervour of mass demonstrations and constant conflict and provocation between Barcelona and Madrid has given way to a climate of cooperation.
Since 2024, the region has been governed by the Socialists’ party of Catalonia (PSC), the first time since 1980 that a non-nationalist party has been in charge. Led by Salvador Illa, Spain’s health minister during the Covid epidemic, it has ushered in an era of entente with Madrid, where the Socialist Workers’ party, to which the PSC serves as a regional section, is also in the driving seat.
Another change is that those young people who got fired up about independence are not only older now but face issues that are more pressing than sovereignty, principally jobs and housing. Wages are low, rents high and mortgages mostly out of reach. As a result, 82% of Catalonia’s 18- to 30-year-olds still live with their parents. On Friday Puigdemont’s Junts per Catalunya (Together for Catalonia) voted down the government’s progressive housing proposals, a move that won’t endear them to young Catalans, nor to their parents.
The other big change since 2017 is demographic. When Puigdemont went into exile, 13.8% of the Catalan population was foreign-born; the figure today is 18.7%. This shift is most marked in the capital, Barcelona, where 32% of residents are immigrants representing 118 nationalities, a figure that rises to 50% in the 12-35 age group.
For nationalists, this raises the question: who is a Catalan? Jordi Pujol, the Catalan president from 1980 to 2003, insisted that a Catalan was anyone who lived and worked in Catalonia.
Things are a little different now. Out of the disillusion of the independence movement has risen Aliança Catalana, a far-right nationalist party whose leader says “there isn’t room for everyone” in Catalonia.
Specifically, there would be no room for Muslims, not even those born in Spain, which by implication would include, for example, the Barcelona and Spain football star Lamine Yamal.
This has dragged Junts, traditionally the party of the Catalan bourgeoisie, to the right as those on the ethno-nationalist margins gravitate towards the unselfconsciously racist Aliança, whose positions on sovereignty are otherwise barely distinguishable from Junts’.
Over the past 25 years, Catalonia, and above all Barcelona, has gone from being a bicultural, bilingual Catalan-Spanish society to one that is multicultural and multilingual.
Puigdemont’s pitch is based on identity and a historical sense of grievance at Spain’s perceived abuse of and disdain for Catalonia, a sentiment shared by many, perhaps most, Catalans.
This ingrained sense of difference and grievance isn’t going away, but his vision may prove a harder sell than it was 10 years ago.
As demography changes, so does identity. Immigrants now make up nearly a fifth of the population, have their own identity issues and have no particular beef with Spain. As for independence, support never did reach 50%, and now hovers in the low 40s.
Besides, as people migrate in search of a better or perhaps a more interesting life, it is becoming increasingly likely that the parents of those living in Catalonia will be from different countries, and their sense of national identity is multiple or simply not that important.
Puigdemont’s lifelong dream is for Catalonia to take its place among the world’s independent nation states. Yet perhaps he is a man out of time and the nation state he craves, with its monocultural, monolingual badge of identity, has passed its sell-by date.

Ceramiche Keope unveils trio of stone-effect surfaces for "varied and cohesive" interiors

Ceramiche Keope unveils trio of stone-effect surfaces for "varied and cohesive" interiors
Promotion: Italian brand Ceramiche Keope has launched a porcelain tile collection called Grace Atelier, featuring stone-like surface designs available as monolithic slabs and geometric mosaics.
Ceramiche Keope's Grace Atelier collection includes three surfaces that aim to recall geological sites in Europe: Grace, Grace Fossil, and Grace Lithos.
"The project is built on four pillars: the deep synergy within the collection, enabling the creation of multi-material projects; the progressive evolution of graphics and textures; a versatile colour palette; and signature mosaics, which introduce decoration as an integral part of the architectural language," said Ceramiche Keope.
"These elements allow the different facets of Grace Atelier to interact while each retains its own identity."
The Grace tile design, which was already an established product at Ceramiche Keope, forms the basis of the new Grace Atelier collection.
Grace has a simple and understated surface design, informed by limestone from the region of Saint Antoine d'Auberoche in France.
Grace Fossil features a more graphic surface design, drawing on the British Portland Stone used to build Buckingham Palace and the fossil-rich Bavarian Jura Stone.
It has a cloud-like appearance with details of primordial-inspired textures.
Ceramiche Keope referenced the layered, streaking surface seen in the Villeneuve quartzite of the Alps for Grace Lithos, which is available in two iterations – Essential and Wild.
Essential has a subtle appearance, while Wild has a bolder veined design with eye-catching colour contrasts.
The trio of tiles in the Grace Atelier collection share the same colour options, ranging from bright, luminous tones to neutral greys and warming shades.
"This outlines a true visual and tactile evolution: from the graphic purity of Grace to the greater depth of Grace Fossil, all the way to the bolder character of Grace Lithos," said Ceramiche Keope.
"This gradual progression allows you to choose different levels of intensity or combine them within the same project, creating spaces that are both varied and cohesive," it continued.
"Unifying the entire project is the colour palette, conceived as a true stylistic key to foster harmonious combinations among the different textures."
Ceramiche Keope also collaborated with designer and art director Margherita Rui to create Fragments of Grace, an exclusive mosaic series that expands the creative versatility of the Grace Atelier architectural system.
Conceived as a Déco Mosaic Laboratory, the range combines porcelain stoneware surfaces with glossy glazes and subtle metallic-effect accents across geometric compositions.
"The collection balances the rigour of Modernism with the visual richness and geometries of Art Déco, transforming decoration into an authentic structural design element," said Ceramiche Keope.
"Fragments of Grace is divided into four collections – Tressé, Domus, Avenue, and Pince – in which material, light, and rhythm blend through interlacing patterns, geometric shapes, metallic details, and exquisite glossy enamel backgrounds," it continued.
"The mosaic thus transcends its purely ornamental role to become a genuine element of architectural language, capable of further connecting the different facets of the system."
Grace Atelier was recently awarded the ADI Cersaie Award 2026, a prestigious recognition for design excellence, acknowledging its comprehensive and versatile range system and its "strong material, chromatic and compositional coherence".
To learn more about Ceramiche Keope, visit its website here.

Securing energy and trade flows in geo-economic conflicts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Decades ago, the world treated global trade as a neutral ground that helped energy markets in becoming more integrated, as we still see them today. The standard view in policy circles was that trade made countries more secure and stable. Governments therefore now use tariffs and export controls as a chokepoint of power. Today interdependence between countries became a double-edged sword. Europe, for instance, faced this back in 2022, when the Russian gas that it long treated as a reliable commodity became a prominent tool of pressure overnight.
Despite the shifts towards digital economies and the massive investments that countries have been pouring in it, a major share of world trade still goes through narrow water ways. The Strait of Hormuz, Suez Canal, bab el-Mandeb Strait and many more corridors could lead to world trade disruption if partly closed. In 2023 attacks on merchant ships in the Red Sea led to big containers switching their usual route through the Suez Canal and going around Africa instead. It resulted in higher insurances, increased fuel consumption and longer delivery times. At the same time, extreme drought forced the Panama Canal to cut daily Transits. Two of the worlds key sea shortcuts were constrained at once. Securing energy and trade flows in geo-economic conflicts is no longer only about protecting ships and pipelines; it is also about building systems flexible enough to absorb shocks that are now certain to come. The Hormuz crisis of 2026 made that lesson costly, and the states that act on it now will set the terms of the next era of global trade.
Despite the shifts towards digital economies and the massive investments that countries have been pouring in it, a major share of world trade still goes through narrow water ways.
Two years later, on the 28th of February 2026 as the US-Israel-Iran war started, The Iran Revolutionary Guard shut the Strait of Hormuz to control the oil that was being exported from the Gulf Cooperation Council. Within two weeks, the International Energy Agency ‘IEA’ reported that the exports through the Strait of Hormuz had fallen to a tenth of normal flows. Asian importers took the worst hit, as they highly depend on the Gulf’s crude. The damage, however, showed up in prices other than oil; for instance, urea fertilizers also flow through the strait, and its supply disruption led to higher food prices. Gulf countries demonstrated their resilience by finding alternatives to exporting away from the strait of Hormuz. The UAE, for example, Created the Habshan-Fujeirah line, which started construction in 2008 and was finished in 2012, to secure energy trade even if faced by geographical obstacles. Securing energy and trade flows is a significant topic to be discussed at the TRENDS Annual Forum on October 12, 2026, under the theme “Sustainable Security: The Post-War Future of the Middle East”.

The Future as Propaganda: Soviet Architecture in Kazakhstan and the Imagery of a New Era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Practically every history book records 1961 as the year man first reached space, an achievement that placed the Soviet Union at the center of the space race. What not everyone knows is that Yuri Gagarin's journey began in a seemingly unlikely place, more precisely in Kazakhstan. From the Baikonur Cosmodrome, Gagarin set off beyond Earth, inaugurating not only a new era of space exploration but also a history of technology and ambition that would transform this landscape.
At the time, Kazakhstan was one of the republics that made up the Soviet Union and occupied a strategic position at its southern edge, stretching across a vast area between Europe and Asia. Its territorial size and low population density made the region particularly important for large Soviet projects, which found there extensive areas available for military, industrial, and scientific facilities. The Baikonur Cosmodrome itself became virtually a planned city built in the desert.
The transformation of this territory, however, was part of a much broader project. It was about constructing — and selling to the world — a particular idea of the future, conceived by the Soviet regime around the ideals of a modern socialist society. This vision of the future found expression in different spheres, including architecture.
Buildings, monuments, and spacecraft, through their monumentality, each contributed in their own way to constructing this image; if the Soviet state was capable of sending a man into space and erecting grandiose structures, it was also capable of commanding the world around it.
Architecture and the Imaginary of the Future
But, within architecture, what exactly did this future that the Soviet Union sought to project mean? It was not simply about imagining what cities or technologies might look like in the decades to come, but about creating the sense that a new era was already beginning, and that it would belong to the USSR.
It is within this imaginary that architecture takes on a particular role. Futurism emerges in iconic volumes that break with tradition, large-scale structures, and avant-garde construction solutions. This language also finds an interesting parallel in space exploration. Domes, circular volumes, monumental structures, and unconventional geometries can, when viewed today, evoke machines, spacecraft, or other elements associated with the conquest of space. This does not necessarily mean that these buildings were intended to represent rockets or flying saucers, but rather that they participated in the same imaginary of the future, in which formal boldness and technical capability signaled a society that sought to remain ahead of its own time.
In Kazakhstan, this connection can be seen in buildings such as the Kazakh State Circus and Republic Square, both in Almaty, whose circular forms and domes may, to a contemporary eye, resemble objects that have landed on the city. At the same time, elements inspired by yurts, ornamental patterns, and references to Central Asian visual traditions coexisted with this radically modern-looking architecture. The result was a landscape in which different temporalities came together.
This combination was not exclusive to Kazakhstan. In different Soviet republics, space exploration became part of a broader visual repertoire, appearing in murals, monuments, and public buildings. A mosaic in the Tajik capital, Dushanbe, for example, depicts Avicenna, the great Persian philosopher, alongside Soviet cosmonauts, all contemplating the star-filled cosmos. This carefully constructed visual narrative was conceived to place national history within the context of a progressive socialist future.
Engineering and Futuristic Solutions
The futurism of Soviet architecture in Kazakhstan was not only expressed in its forms, but also in the technology behind them. Large-span structures, domes, reinforced concrete, and experimental construction systems made it possible to create buildings that, for their time, seemed to anticipate future architecture. Engineering itself became part of visual language; what had previously remained hidden within the structure was now revealed.
Seismic conditions, for example, led to important experimentation in Almaty. Rather than simply reproducing rigid urban models, architects and engineers had to develop structural systems capable of absorbing ground movements. Stepped towers, interconnected volumes, and more complex geometric configurations became part of the landscape.
An emblematic example is the Hotel Kazakhstan, completed in 1977. Built in one of the city's most seismically active areas, the building uses a monolithic reinforced-concrete core and structural systems designed to increase its resistance. The very possibility of constructing a tower of this scale in a territory subject to strong seismic activity represented, at the time, a testament to the capabilities of Soviet engineering.
A Future That Remained
The end of the Soviet Union did not necessarily mean the end of this imagination of the future. In independent Kazakhstan, the idea of creating a landscape capable of representing modernity and progress remained present, but now under a different political and economic project. If, during the Soviet period, this vision was shaped by the socialist state, its architects, and its engineers, in the new Kazakhstan it would also be projected through major international firms and megaprojects capable of rapidly transforming the urban landscape.
The relocation of the capital to Astana, beginning in 1997, became one of the clearest expressions of this vision. Within a few decades, the city had been transformed into a kind of architectural laboratory in the middle of the steppe, bringing together monumental buildings and deliberately extraordinary forms. Structures such as the Khan Shatyr, a gigantic translucent tent, and Nur Alem, the glass sphere built for Expo 2017, described as "reminiscent of space objects," revive characteristics that were already present in the Soviet architectural imagination, such as large scale and structural experimentation.
This shows that, even in a different political, economic, or technological context, the belief remains that an extraordinarily constructed landscape can function as a symbol of a country seeking to present itself as modern and technological, in a constant effort to anticipate the future.

A climate nightmare lurks in the Atlantic. Europe is starting to pay attention.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

From Reykjavík to The Hague, European governments are starting to prepare for a literal sea change that would end life as we know it on the continent.
In the depths of the North Atlantic, a vast system of swirling currents known as the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or AMOC, carries warm tropical waters north, preventing Europe from freezing. But as humans continue pumping planet-warming gases into the atmosphere, this oceanic heat pump will weaken. It might even fizzle out.
A colder-than-usual patch of water just south of Greenland, nicknamed the “cold blob,” has some scientists worried this slowdown is already well underway. Other researchers have examined climate models, surveyed sea temperature records and ran simulations to conclude that the ocean could turn on us sooner than previously thought.
While this process would unfold over many decades, a severe slowdown or collapse of the AMOC would disrupt Europe’s agriculture, infrastructure, welfare and economy on a scale that would make this past summer’s heat and fires look like mild memories of calmer times. The continent could face glacial winters and dry summers, surging sea levels and ferocious windstorms.
Until recently, this prospect was considered remote: A nightmare scenario trotted out to warn of the catastrophic dangers of unchecked climate change. But as research on the likelihood of a major slowdown or — less likely — a total collapse mounts, governments are beginning to take it seriously and trying to work out how to minimize the damage.
Iceland has declared an AMOC collapse a national security risk. The Netherlands is investigating what a slowdown might mean for its sea defenses. Finland is examining the potential consequences. The United Kingdom is spending millions on an early-warning system. And Nordic ministers have begun discussing the threat.
For policymakers, the AMOC’s instability poses an unusual challenge: How do you prepare for a far-off disaster that may never happen — but that, if it does, would disrupt life in Europe on an unthinkable scale? But governments are increasingly concluding uncertainty itself is no excuse for waiting.
“It is irresponsible to wait for absolute certainty before preparing,” Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson, Iceland’s climate minister, told POLITICO. “Because, by the time the consequences become undeniable, it may already be too late to prevent them from happening.”
“This is not about panic or alarmism,” he added. “It’s just responsible governance.”
The sense of alarm has also reached Brussels, where last year the European Union’s green transition chief Teresa Ribera suggested adding the AMOC “to the list of national security acronyms in Europe.”
That sinking feeling
The AMOC’s engine lies in the North Atlantic, where cold, salty water sinks deep into the ocean. That sinking helps pull more warm water north — driving a circulation that has shaped Europe’s climate for millennia.
It helps explain why Paris doesn’t have Ottawa’s cold winters, even though the French capital lies slightly to the north of the Canadian city. It’s also part of why Iceland and Europe’s northern countries don’t suffer a Siberian climate.
But climate change is now threatening to disrupt this long-stable motor. As Greenland’s ice sheet melts and heavier rainfall adds more freshwater to the North Atlantic, the sea becomes warmer and less salty — and therefore less dense. It sinks less readily, weakening the circulation.
This can set off a feedback loop: Weaker currents carry less salt north, further freshening the water and slowing the AMOC even more. The fear is that, with enough warming, the churn could slow significantly or even stop.
If that sounds familiar, chances are it’s because of the 2004 disaster movie “The Day After Tomorrow,” which imagines the shutdown of Atlantic ocean currents triggering a flash freeze that plunges the world into a new ice age overnight. There is no evidence that such an extreme and rapid scenario is possible.
And yet, the danger isn’t confined to some distant future. Even if a full AMOC collapse would unfold over many decades, likely beyond the end of this century, parts of the system could start failing much sooner — with consequences felt well before the currents grind to a halt.
“Bits of the AMOC could begin collapsing on the journey to the full collapse,” said Laurie Laybourn, a fellow at Chatham House and director of the Strategic Climate Risks Initiative. “It’s a process that would have disruption along the way.”
Scientists are particularly worried about the subpolar gyre, a circular current south of Greenland that helps power the AMOC. Some studies suggest its water-mixing function could begin shutting down as early as the 2040s, triggering major changes within as little as a decade.
A collapse of the gyre wouldn’t plunge all of Northern Europe into the deep freeze associated with a full AMOC shutdown. But it could bring significantly colder winters and increase the risk of drought.
“When exactly is hard to say, but I do think there’s a substantial risk that it can happen within the coming 20 years,” said Swinda Falkena, a researcher studying the subpolar gyre at Utrecht University. “It basically would mean you need to start planning now.”
For the AMOC as a whole, scientists still don’t know at what point the currents could cross their so-called tipping point, after which a collapse into a very weak state becomes inevitable. Nor do they know how close they are to crossing it. Estimates range from global warming of 1.4 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial temperatures — a level the world has just reached — to 8 C.
Just how much the currents will be disrupted remains a matter of debate; scientists are also still arguing over whether the slowing has already started. But they all agree that as the climate continues to warm, the AMOC will diminish.
In 2023, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change — which releases reports that represent the current scientific consensus — concluded that the AMOC “is very likely to weaken over the 21st century,” with its strength falling 24% to 39% below pre-industrial levels.
The IPCC also expressed “medium confidence” that “an abrupt collapse is not expected before 2100” — but research published since the report’s release has raised the possibility that the system could reach a tipping point much earlier.
Two recent studies placed that threshold around the middle of this century. A separate paper found that even if planet-warming emissions are reduced, a collapse is more likely than not to begin before the end of the century. Yet another suggested that even with mild warming, the risk of an AMOC shutdown is around 25 percent. And a study this year concluded the currents would lose half their strength until 2100. (In contrast, one recent paper found complete collapse unlikely this century.)
“The risks,” said Jóhannsson, the Icelandic climate minister, “are appearing more serious than previously understood.”
Freezing future
Scientists are starting to sketch out what Europe could look like after an AMOC collapse, drawing on climate models and research into the currents’ effect on temperatures, rainfall, sea levels and ecosystems. The picture they paint, in published studies and interviews with POLITICO, is dramatic.
In winter, storms could lash the continent, fueled by the stark temperature difference between a newly frigid north and the warm-as-ever south.
Arctic sea ice could push south toward Scotland and the Nordic fjords. Icebreakers might be needed in the Baltic Sea. Amsterdam’s canals could freeze solid, as cold snaps send temperatures plunging to minus 20 C in the Netherlands and minus 40 C in Scandinavia.
Drought in West Africa could drive migrants northward as the tropical rainbelt gets pushed south. Meanwhile, Iceland could face economic devastation as fish stocks collapse, according to a scenario researchers drew up for the Nordic Council of Ministers.
Along Europe’s North Atlantic coast, higher sea levels could worsen flooding and push saltwater into low-lying farmland. Summers would still bring extreme heat, but a decline in rainfall could compound water shortages. One paper found that in the U.K., land suitable for crop farming would fall from 32% today to 7% after an AMOC collapse.
Concern over these possible impacts are starting to shape government planning. Iceland, which has declared an AMOC collapse a national security risk, brought the threat to the Nordic Council of Ministers this spring. “We discussed preparing a joint risk assessment for the Nordics,” said Jóhannsson.
In Finland, Climate Minister Sari Multala launched an assessment this summer of what an AMOC slowdown could mean for the country, including its consequences for the climate, the Baltic Sea and key sectors such as agriculture, energy and transport.
“It would be quite obvious that if the temperature were to drop so drastically as the worst-case scenarios are, the living conditions in Finland would deteriorate very much,” she told POLITICO. “Because I think we are on the front line when it comes to this tipping point, we want to be the ones that are having the best knowledge around it.”
The Netherlands is conducting a similar assessment, with a particular focus on the threat to its sea defenses. The Dutch Delta programme commissioner — a government appointee charged with protecting the country from water-related threats — is working to include the weakening of the AMOC as a “what-if scenario” in the country’s preparedness plans. Studies suggest an AMOC shutdown could add roughly half a meter to sea-level rise along parts of the North Atlantic, on top of the increase already caused by global warming.
“The speed is uncertain, the moment is uncertain, and the impact is uncertain,” said Saskia van Vuren, who advises the Delta commissioner on the AMOC. But it is already affecting planning on the ground. “We should acknowledge that ice sheets may be present [on rivers] in the future,” she added, pointing to ongoing river-restoration projects.
Still, major uncertainties remain. There’s a chance global warming cancels out any AMOC-related winter cooling, for example.
Yet “uncertainty is not a reason for inaction,” said Walid Oueslati, head of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s climate division, who oversaw a report on how policymakers can approach such risks. “It’s a reason for better risk management.”
“Governments deal with uncertain risk every day,” he added, citing “the financial crisis, for example, or the pandemic, or earthquakes and other natural hazards.”
Ocean watch
One of the first lines of defense against an AMOC collapse is noticing when it starts. Governments and scientists are investing in early-warning systems to detect when critical parts of the circulation begin to approach a tipping point.
The British government has poured £81 million (€94 million) into a research program to create an early-warning mechanism for two key AMOC-linked systems that may themselves be approaching a point of no return: The Greenland ice sheet and the subpolar gyre.
“We’re trying to bring together teams to better observe, model and forecast tipping points, so that we might be able to respond better to them,” said Gemma Bale, one of the two scientists leading the program.
The program — and any effort to track the AMOC — depends on reliable, long-term observations of the ocean, she added.
Researchers have strung moorings across the Atlantic to measure the currents; one such array, known as RAPID, is the longest-running observational program with 20 years of consistent data.
“It’s the only thing that directly tells us how the AMOC is changing day to day, month to month, year to year,” said Penny Holliday, chief scientific officer at the U.K.’s National Oceanography Centre, which co-leads the project. So far, the array has recorded a slight decline in the AMOC, though scientists aren’t yet sure whether climate change is responsible.
But the monitoring network remains precarious. Many of the arrays are financed through short-term research grants, some of which run out by 2028, leaving decades-long observation programs vulnerable to shifting government priorities.
In the United States, for example, President Donald Trump’s administration decided to cut ocean observation funding and dismantle the buoys earlier this year, then backtracked after an outcry.
For scientists, the episode underscored the problem with treating long-term ocean monitoring as a string of short-term research projects. What they want instead is a permanent, internationally funded observing system — infrastructure on the scale governments already support for weather forecasting or space research.
“If we could get together collectively … then we would have an early-warning system,” said Holliday. “We’d be able to tell every nation whether that model-predicted AMOC decline has already started.”
The European Commission made a start this summer, announcing €92 million in funding for ocean observation; a pledging event in September raised the amount to €220 million. AMOC scientists welcomed the money but said a reliable Atlantic-wide system would require far more.
“You need about €500 million or €1 billion per year, and then you can measure the shit out of the oceans,” said Sjoerd Groeskamp, a researcher at the Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research. “Which sounds like a lot, but it’s not. The particle accelerator [at CERN] has a budget of €1 billion per year, right? The James Webb telescope was €10 billion.”
Groeskamp has teamed up with a handful of European Parliament lawmakers to lobby the Commission for an additional €25 million per year to monitor the AMOC.
Mohammed Chahim, a center-left Dutch MEP who led the campaign for extra funding, said Brussels should “create a structured financial program for ocean monitoring, like we’re doing for space.”
“AMOC is one of the biggest concerns I have,” he added. “If you look at the economic damages that we could see through AMOC, spending a couple of million or a couple of hundred million for a long-term observatory program plays an essential role.”
Win-win preparedness
Even if observational data only tells governments that an AMOC collapse has become inevitable — providing a late rather than early warning — that information would still matter, given the decades over which its impact would unfold.
“Once we know that the tipping point has been crossed, that the AMOC won’t suddenly recover but will continue to decline over the coming decades, that has a major impact on what adaptation measures are taken,” said Stefan Rahmstorf, an oceanographer at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.
In the meantime, experts say there’s a range of “no-regret measures” policymakers can take that will protect their citizens if the currents collapse, and benefit countries even if the AMOC remains stable.
“There are win-win situations, such as improving home insulation, that help both against global warming and in the event of a significant cooling,” said Rahmstorf.
Many of the impacts of an AMOC shutdown would compound problems Europe already faces as the planet warms, including drought, extreme weather and rising seas. That means much of the necessary preparations are familiar: strengthening infrastructure against weather extremes, investing in coastal flood protection and building less brittle supply chains.
“We can identify some things that are no regrets,” said Laybourn, the Chatham House fellow. He pointed to retrofitting buildings, restoring nature to make agriculture more resilient and supporting countries in Africa where monsoons could be disrupted. “There are some things that work no matter what’s going to happen.”
The most important no-regret measure is also the only one scientists say can reduce the risk of the AMOC collapsing in the first place: cutting planet-warming emissions.
“The main response must be to stop dithering and delaying when it comes to reducing emissions and phasing out fossil fuels,” said Rahmstorf.
That is true even for parts of the system that could destabilize sooner, such as the subpolar gyre. “To reduce the risk of this happening, the only real thing you can do is just slow down global warming,” said Falkena, the Utrecht University researcher. “Reduce emissions as fast as you can.”
That message is increasingly being echoed by governments most exposed to the threat.
“The most important thing we can do to limit temperature increase is to reduce emissions rapidly,” said Norwegian Climate Minister Andreas Bjelland Eriksen when asked how his country is approaching the risk of an AMOC shutdown.
Iceland’s Jóhannsson compared his country’s reaction to the AMOC threat to the way rising seas have pushed Pacific island states to demand stronger global climate action.
“For us, the possibility of AMOC collapse is not an abstract scientific question,” he said. “It’s basically an existential one, because we know the destabilization of AMOC would bring profound disruption to our infrastructure, our ecosystems and our way of life.”
