Singapore turns matchmaker amid rock-bottom birthrate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
03:48:17 UTC
12:48:17 KST

Singapore turns matchmaker amid rock-bottom birthrate
City-state launches dating platform for government workers, drawing curiosity, amusement and scorn.
Singapore – Nur Aisyah, a 30-year-old civil servant, has spent the past couple of years looking for a partner, with little to show for it.
Nur rarely meets men through work or her hobbies and finds dating apps such as Tinder and Bumble “terrible”, with potential suitors either putting scant effort into their profile or struggling to hold a conversation over text.
Nur is open to having children but also struggles to imagine raising them in a city where housing and childcare costs are high, and where the burden of childcare typically falls hardest on women.
“I feel slightly pessimistic about the future as a whole,” Nur, who asked to use a pseudonym, told Al Jazeera.
So when Singapore’s technology agency GovTech recently rolled out FirstDate, a dating platform for public servants that uses a Nobel-winning algorithm, Nur signed up out of curiosity
“It’s more of the mindset of ‘Why not?’” she said. “It makes quite a funny story if something did come out of this.”
Born out of GovTech’s annual hackathon, where staff develop and test new ideas, FirstDate is being piloted among single government employees aged 21 to 35.
Participants log in using their national digital ID and answer a survey about their interests, habits and values before being matched with one prospective partner at a time.
Sign-ups for the pilot closed on Monday.
GovTech has told local media that no decision has been made on whether to expand the service beyond employees at government agencies.
Singapore’s decision to get into the matchmaking game is its latest attempt to lift a birthrate that has sunk to historic lows.
Fewer than 30,000 babies were born in the Southeast Asian city-state in 2025, bringing the fertility rate to a record low of 0.87.
In August, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a series of new measures to support families, including almost 70,000 Singapore dollars ($55,000) worth of financial benefits for every child from birth until age 17.
For Singapore, whose six million people are practically the city-state’s only resource, the prospect of a shrinking, fast-ageing population is existential.
In February, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong warned that without intervention, the citizen population could begin to shrink by the early 2040s, leaving fewer workers to care for the elderly.
Singapore already leans heavily on immigration to meet its workforce needs, with the government expecting to take in 25,000 to 30,000 new citizens annually over the next five years, a politically sensitive influx in a country whose 6.2 million inhabitants fill an area less than half the size of London.
Yet even as Singapore’s bureaucrats urge people to have babies, many Singaporeans have enthusiastically embraced a child-free lifestyle, preferring to reap the benefits of living in a double-income household with fewer bills or to lavish their attention on pets.
Singapore has never been shy about meddling in matters of the heart.
In a 1983 speech that sparked what became known as the “Great Marriage Debate”, Lee Kuan Yew, Singapore’s founding father and longest-serving prime minister, warned that graduates, especially women, were marrying late and having fewer children than the less educated.
The following year, Lee’s government introduced the controversial Graduate Mothers’ Scheme, which prioritised the children of university-educated mothers in school admissions.
Around the same time, the government established the Social Development Unit (SDU) to organise events where graduate singles could mingle, prompting some Singaporeans to joke that the body’s initials should stand for “Single, Desperate and Ugly”.
Critics called the agency elitist, and a separate body for those with only secondary school qualifications followed in 1985.
“We have a highly interventionist government, even in a private sphere of love and marriage,” Tan Ern Ser, adjunct principal research fellow at the Institute of Policy Studies in Singapore, told Al Jazeera.
Tan said that although past governments’ attempts to play matchmaker were neither “significant nor cost effective”, Singapore’s current generation of bureaucrats is no less eager to involve themselves in the dating game, using the power of technology.
Still, Tan said, a government-backed platform does not mark a return to the era of arranged marriages, and “couples who are identified as compatible could still have a love match.”
FirstDate relies on the Gale-Shapley algorithm, devised by mathematicians David Gale and Lloyd Shapley in 1962, which pairs people according to the ranked preferences of each side.
Shapley shared the 2012 Nobel memorial prize in economics for discovering the algorithm, versions of which are used in school admissions and medical residency placements.
“This is a fundamentally different approach from most dating apps,” Jean Liu, an associate professor of psychology at the Singapore Institute of Technology, told Al Jazeera.
“It is more akin to offline matchmaking, with endless profile swiping replaced by a single match.”
That FirstDate grew out of a hackathon, Liu said, reflects “an appetite to innovate on the nation’s ‘hard problems'”.
Whether it will help people find love any better than mainstream dating apps is another matter.
Questionnaires have limited value in predicting whether two people will hit it off, and the matches are only as good as the pool of people who join, Liu said.
“The process may break down if too few people sign up.”
The app’s greatest value, Liu said, may be in giving the government an opportunity to evaluate and publish dating data, something app companies, which treat their algorithms as sensitive company information, rarely do.
Singapore is not alone in trying to pair up singles.
Tokyo’s metropolitan government launched Tokyo Enmusubi, an AI-powered dating app, in 2024, while the Seoul government’s “Seoulting” programme hosts curated blind dates at landmarks such as the Han River.
Online, Singaporeans’ reactions to their government’s latest bid to play cupid have ranged from scorn to amusement.
Some commentators have dismissed FirstDate as a waste of public money, while others have joked about “state-assigned spouses” and whether finding love will now be included among their work targets.
Jamie, a government employee who works in education, received the email inviting her to join the platform but has no plans to sign up.
“I think it’s quite cringe. It just sounds like someone is trying too hard,” Jamie, who declined to give her last name, told Al Jazeera.
“Our social skills have atrophied. I am so exhausted after work that I just want to go home and lie down,” Jamie said.
She said she does make an effort through community groups, but has yet to meet anyone who shares her values or is emotionally ready for a relationship, so “nothing happens”.
Jamie said she also wonders about privacy.
“What kind of data are they collecting in order for a match, and what are they doing with said data?” she said.
According to FirstDate’s website, profiles are visible only to a person’s match, contact details are shared only when both parties agree, and data will not be monetised or shared with third parties except where the law requires or permits.
For Teo Kai Xiang, a PhD student and former Straits Times journalist, dating reduced to a list of preferences reflects “a deeply transactional and instrumentalist view of love”, in which partners become “co-owners of a financial venture” and “breeders of sought-after children”.
That mindset, Teo said, is sharpened by Singapore’s public housing system, where the rational move for couples chasing subsidies is to apply for an apartment before marriage.
This algorithm “does not fix or challenge this HR interviewer mindset”, said Teo, who also questions why those aged 36 and above are excluded.
Though he welcomes the experiment, Teo would like to see the government do more to revive the city-state’s third spaces and nightlife instead of “ramming pro-fertility rhetoric down our throats”.
The bigger barrier to dating, he said, is cost – from pricey late-night transport to high rents that keep many singletons living with their parents into their 30s.
Singles cannot buy public housing, home to about 80 percent of residents in Singapore, on their own until they turn 35.
“The truth is that we don’t really know what exactly makes love work, such that we can articulate and implement it on a societal scale,” Teo said. “It’s too messy, too complex, too idiosyncratic, and too human.”

US: FBI arrests woman accused of spying for China
October 5, 2026
US officials announced on Sunday that a woman had been arrested by the FBI and accused of spying for China in the United States.
Wanying Z., 34, of Irvine, California, was detained at at Los Angeles International Airport ahead of a scheduled flight to China.
She faces charges of acting as an unregistered foreign agent.
The woman "traveled to Seattle in 2025 and, at the direction of (People's Republic of China) officials, surveilled a close relative of a Taiwanese government official, sending photos, videos and license plate information to those officials," First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said in an online post.
He added that Z. "coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection."
The woman is due to appear before a Los Angeles federal court on Monday, Essayli wrote.
Who was the alleged target of surveillance?
The FBI said Z. was spying on a son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te. While the US agency did not provide the target's name, they later shared a New York Post report identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, who is reportedly a US resident.
In an X post, FBI Director Kash Patel celebrated the arrest, warning foreign adversaries that "America is no longer a safe place to run your espionage operations."
"Allegedly surveil a foreign leader's family on US soil for the PRC — and try to catch a flight back to Shanghai? Not happening," Patel added.
Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party advocate for Taiwan's distinct identity from China. Their statements often irritate Beijing, which considers the island Chinese territory.
While Washington does not have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, the United States is the island's most important international supporter and supplier of weapons.

No US vessel present near Iran: IRGC chief adviser
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
03:39:59 UTC
12:39:59 KST

Brigadier General Ali Fadavi, head of the advisory group to the commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said in a special television interview on Sunday night that the Strait of Hormuz has been firmly under Iran's control throughout these long months.
Fadavi said America's military power is sea-based, meaning its navy incorporates both land and air forces, and that the manifestation of American military power is therefore in its navy.
"The Americans have been present in the Persian Gulf since 1853, but now for the first time, no American vessel is present not only in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Sea of Oman, but even in the northern Indian Ocean," he said.
"The Americans have fled and moved more than a thousand kilometres away from our borders. This did not happen at their own choosing, but is the result of the authority of the Islamic Republic of Iran and the IRGC Navy."
Fadavi said Americans claim they can move a maximum of three to four million barrels of oil through the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz and outside the area Iran has officially announced, a figure that is insignificant compared with the volume of oil transiting the strait.
Previously, he said, more than 20 million barrels of oil officially passed through the Strait of Hormuz each day, and a quantity of oil was also exported unofficially. Forty-six percent of the world's oil exports passed through the strait. The 20 percent figure often cited relates to global oil consumption, because many countries consume their own production and do not export, he said.
"Now oil exports through this route have faced fundamental disruption, and this has had a broad impact on the global economy, America and Europe."
Fadavi said Americans imagine that because they have great power, whatever they say must be implemented, while geographically and regionally they have no connection to the Strait of Hormuz and are more than 10,000 kilometres away from the area.
"Iran and Oman must formulate the rules governing the Strait of Hormuz, which has been done and we have agreed on it. We are now applying these same rules, and they have so far been implemented," he said.
Fadavi said that despite having vast financial and military power and a military budget equal to the combined military budgets of the world's countries, the Americans have not been able to impose their demands in the Strait of Hormuz.
"This has had a direct impact on the world economy and even America's own domestic economy, which is why the Strait of Hormuz issue remains the main axis of negotiations."
On escalation, Fadavi said Americans are forced to use their vessels to escalate tensions because air power alone cannot impose sovereignty. "Even if they bomb an area every day, as long as they do not have a physical presence, they cannot impose their demands."
He said American vessels are exposed to threats and vulnerability against the IRGC Navy. "They tried several times to bring their military vessels into the Strait of Hormuz, but they were attacked by the IRGC Navy and Aerospace Force. Taiwan ends Asian Games with five gold, 17 silver, 33 bronze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
03:32:51 UTC
12:32:51 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games officially concluded Sunday, ending two weeks of competition in which Taiwan won five gold, 17 silver, and 33 bronze medals for a total of 55.
Taiwan finished 15th in the overall medal standings. The five gold medals marked the country's lowest gold-medal tally at an Asian Games since the 1990 Beijing Games, when Taiwan won no gold medals, per ETToday.
The result was also a significant decline from the 2022 Hangzhou Asian Games, where Taiwan won 19 gold, 20 silver, and 28 bronze medals for 67 medals overall, ranking sixth. However, the elimination of roller/inline sports, where Taiwan won seven gold medals, was a major reason for the decline.
Taiwan's five gold medals came in soft tennis, swimming, athletics, boxing, and tennis. Yu Kai-wen (余凱文) and Huang Shih-yuan (黃詩媛) won the mixed doubles soft tennis title. Swimmer Wang Kuan-hung (王冠閎) won the men's 200-meter butterfly in 1 minute, 55.05 seconds, becoming the first Taiwanese male swimmer to win an Asian Games gold medal, per Taiwan Olympic Committee.
Fu Chao-hsuan (傅兆玄) won the men's high jump after clearing 2.25 meters, matching his season best. He became the first Taiwanese man in 60 years to win an Asian Games athletics gold medal, since Wu Ah-min (吳阿民) won the men's decathlon in 1966.
Boxer Lin Yu-ting (林郁婷) added Taiwan's fourth gold medal after moving up from the 57-kilogram class to 60 kg. She defeated China's Yang Chengyu 5-0 in the final to win her second consecutive Asian Games boxing gold medal.
Hsieh Su-wei (謝淑薇) and Liang En-shuo (梁恩碩) secured the fifth and final gold medal in the women's doubles tennis competition, defeating fellow Taiwanese players Chan Hao-ching (詹皓晴) and Wu Fang-hsien (吳芳嫻) in the final.
Another highlight in the boxing ring was Chen Nien-chin (陳念琴), who reached the women's 65-kg final before losing 3-2 by split decision to India's Parveen Hooda. Chen settled for silver after a closely contested bout.
The younger generation also made history
Fourteen-year-old Lin Yi-fan (林逸凡) won silver in the women's park skateboarding event, giving Taiwan its first Asian Games medal in skateboarding. Twelve-year-old Ku Yong-yan (辜泳諺) then won silver in the men's park event later the same day, breaking Lin's record as Taiwan's youngest Asian Games medalist.
Taiwan did not win a medal in breaking, but Sun Zhen (孫振), competing as B-Boy Quake, drew attention by wearing bubble-tea-themed earrings during the competition. He said the accessory was a way to promote bubble tea and Taiwanese culture internationally.
Traditional medal-producing sports also contributed to Taiwan's overall haul. Weightlifting, taekwondo, badminton, table tennis, and shooting all produced medals, but none won gold at Aichi-Nagoya.
The games concluded with the Olympic Council of Asia flag being handed over to Qatar, which will host the 2030 Asian Games in Doha. The closing ceremony was held Sunday evening at Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium, where the handover ceremony featured a horse and rider representing the next host city, per ETToday.

US Monitors Suspected Plague Case In Russia As Calls Grow For Travel Restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
03:32:35 UTC
12:32:35 KST

More than 60 staff at a Russian plague research facility have been isolated following the death of a laboratory worker, sources told RFE/RL's Siberia.Realities, and the United States said it was monitoring reports of a suspected case of pneumonic plague.
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was hospitalized on September 29 and died at a hospital early on October 2, according to news reports and sources.
Independent Siberian news outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal) reported that Shipilova accidentally broke a test tube containing pneumonic-plague bacteria on September 25 while working at the institute. Russian authorities have not publicly confirmed that account.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's consumer and public-health watchdog, said Shipilova had been diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology," meaning that its cause was unknown. The agency said additional testing was conducted because of her professional activities but did not detect microorganisms associated with her work.
Rospotrebnadzor also said no accidents involving pathogenic microorganisms had been recorded at the institute.
Asked about the matter before leaving on a trip to Europe on October 5, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "watching and monitoring it closely."
"I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on," Rubio said.
In a Telegram post on October 5, regional Governor Igor Kobzev said the "sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk" and the nearby district where Shipilova had been hospitalized "is currently stable." He added that no new cases of institute employees seeking medical care had been reported in recent days.
At the same time, authorities have imposed precautionary measures. About 200 people who may have had contact with Shipilova were placed under medical observation or isolation, many of them at hospitals in the area, according to media reports.
Staff at the anti-plague institute have been confined to the facility since October 2, sleeping on floors and chairs while awaiting test results, two independent sources among employees and their relatives told Siberia.Realities. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the situation and fears of repercussions.
"They locked everyone inside for isolation starting Friday (October 2), more than 60 people," a relative of an institute employee said, adding that "by Saturday (October 3), not a single positive test had been found. They're sleeping there on the floor and on chairs. There are, of course, no beds. Relatives were allowed to bring food through the checkpoint."
Former colleagues of Shipilova said the institute has strict biological-safety measures, including plague vaccinations for interns.
Quarantine has also been reported at two Irkutsk hospitals and a maternity hospital, with visitors barred and patients unable to leave for up to six days.
On October 3, the Irkutsk Aluminum Plant in the nearby town of Shelekhov introduced a mask mandate.
The measures have fueled speculation because Russian officials initially avoided publicly referring to plague, while local and independent reports described a possible laboratory accident involving Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague.
The pneumonic form of Yersinia pestis, a bacterium that normally circulates among wild rodents and fleas, affects the lungs and can spread from person to person through respiratory droplets during close contact. The disease can progress rapidly, but modern antibiotics can be highly effective if treatment is begun promptly.
There is currently no publicly confirmed evidence of transmission among residents of Irkutsk.
US Monitoring Situation
Hours before Rubio spoke, a State Department spokesperson told RFE/RL said the department was "aware of reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia," and was "monitoring the situation closely with the CDC (the US Centers For Disease Control And Prevention) and our other interagency partners."
The State Department urged Russian authorities to "share accurate information quickly and openly," while noting that plague is treatable with commonly available antibiotics, particularly when treatment begins early.
The reports have prompted concern among some US lawmakers and former officials, including over Russia's history of biological-weapons research. There is no public evidence that the Irkutsk laboratory was developing plague as a weapon or that the worker's death was connected to an offensive biological-weapons program.
Republican Representative Don Bacon, a senior member of the House Armed Services Committee, spoke of longstanding Russian allegations that US-supported laboratories in Ukraine were involved in biological-weapons research.
"I remember hearing from anti-Ukraine voices about their so-called bio labs. It was Russian disinformation ops at their best. But in reality it is Russia with the bio labs," Bacon wrote on social media.
Russia has long accused Washington and Kyiv of running biological-weapons facilities in Ukraine, allegations both governments reject and independent investigations have found no evidence to support.
The Soviet Union maintained a large offensive biological-weapons program during the Cold War, despite being a party to the 1972 Biological Weapons Convention. Defectors and subsequent investigations documented military research involving pathogens including plague, as well as efforts to develop antibiotic-resistant strains.
In an April 2025 report on compliance with arms control commitments, the State Department said the United States "assesses that Russia maintains an offensive biological warfare program and is in violation of its obligations" under the Biological Weapons Convention.
Russia denies that, saying such facilities are aimed at developing defenses against pathogens.

Brazil heads to run-off as Bolsonaro pulls off shock first-place finish over Lula
- Flavio Bolsonaro surprised by leading the first round with 47%, ahead of incumbent Lula's 45%, forcing a run-off election on October 25.
- Bolsonaro family's political comeback is marked by multiple family members winning seats, despite scandals and Jair Bolsonaro's 27-year prison sentence.
- Lula warns of a fight between democracy and "barbarism," while voters express frustration over inflation, crime, and political fatigue in Brazil.
AI generated
BRASILIA – Right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro pulled off a surprise first-place finish ahead of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s Oct 4 election, which heads to a run-off vote in three weeks as neither clinched a majority.
In a result that defied opinion poll projections showing Lula in the lead, Bolsonaro scored 47% of the vote to the incumbent’s 45%.
If Bolsonaro triumphs in the Oct 25 election, the Latin American powerhouse will join a steady rightward march in the region in recent elections, a trend championed by US President Donald Trump.
The election results included a series of landslide wins for the right in Parliament in a massive setback to Lula, who at almost 81 is seeking a fourth term in office to cement his legacy.
“I admit I was convinced I would win in the first round. The game is about to start. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people,” the 80-year-old said.
The veteran leftist has branded the election a battle between democracy and “barbarism”, warning voters that Brazil’s sovereignty was at stake in the face of US pressure.
Bolsonaro was a little-known senator a few months ago when his father anointed him his political heir, unable to run himself as he serves a 27-year sentence for an attempted coup after losing a 2022 election bid.
However, his father’s powerful name won over the country’s conservative base, and he slid past Lula despite a campaign marked by scandals and mudslinging.
“I am truly happy with the result,” Bolsonaro said after results came through, hailing the “very real possibility” of a run-off victory.
Voters in the deeply polarised nation were jaded by familiar choices, and few voted with conviction.
Oscarina de Oliveira, a 62-year-old caregiver, told AFP she had planned to vote for Lula, as she always has. But “when I got there, I switched to Bolsonaro. Just to see what happens, to see if anything changes”.
Carolina Botelho, a political scientist at Rio de Janeiro State University, told AFP that the leading candidate in the first round has won every election in Brazil since the end of the country’s military dictatorship in 1985.
Bolsonaro dynasty
With 56 million votes, Bolsonaro’s first-round performance outdid that of his father Jair Bolsonaro in 2018, when he was elected, and in 2022.
It emerged during the campaign that Flavio Bolsonaro was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic Dark Horse about his father.
For many voters, this did little to move the needle.
“Things are truly terrible. As far as I’m concerned, the left just doesn’t work any more,” said tech worker Joao Batista, 36, in the Rocinha favela, saying he was fed up with the “horrible” prices of basic goods.
Flavio Bolsonaro highlighted on Oct 4 that as president he will have the possibility of appointing four justices to the powerful Supreme Court – which convicted his father and has been at the centre of key political and criminal scandals.
The elections proved a triumphant comeback for the Bolsonaro family after Jair Bolsonaro lost a re-election bid in 2022, leading to violent riots in the capital and his conviction in 2025 for attempting a coup.
Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro and another one of Jair Bolsonaro’s sons, Carlos Bolsonaro, both secured seats in the Senate.
Jair Bolsonaro’s youngest son Jair Renan, 28, was elected as a federal lawmaker.
Flavio Bolsonaro has cast himself as more “moderate” than his firebrand father, but his critics are concerned.
“Flavio is a danger to Brazil, he represents a step backward. We can see everything his father did... He really destroyed Brazil,” said Anderson de Almeida, a 45-year-old doorman.
Trump watching
Trump had said he was watching the election “very closely”, but did not endorse Flavio Bolsonaro.
The US President has wielded tariffs and sanctions to pressure Brasilia over complaints ranging from the trial against his ally Jair Bolsonaro to alleged unfair trade practices.
Lula repeatedly warned him not to “meddle” in the elections.
Revered for social welfare programmes that lifted millions out of poverty, Lula made a dramatic comeback to office in the 2022 elections after being jailed on a corruption conviction for 18 months.
The charges, thrown out on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him.
In his third term, he oversaw a drop in inflation and unemployment, but voters complain about a high cost of living and as in many Latin American nations, citizens are fed up with high levels of crime and violence. AFP

US coastguard suspends search for six on board crashed medical jet
Debris found off Nantucket island after the air ambulance disappeared while flying from Bermuda to Boston.
The United States coastguard has suspended its search for six people on board a medical transport jet that crashed while flying from Bermuda to Boston.
“Suspending a search is not an easy decision,” Rear Admiral Matthew Lake, commander of the coastguard’s Northeast District, said in a statement on Sunday.
The search was called off after teams spent about 66 hours covering 4,445 miles (7,150km) by air and sea and confirmed that debris found off the shore of Massachusetts’s Nantucket Island came from the aircraft.
The Gulfstream G100 carried two pilots, two medical staff, a patient and a relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Canada-based Latitude Air Ambulance, told Canada’s public broadcaster CBC.
The four crew members were Canadian, and the two passengers were Bermudian, according to authorities.
In a statement on Sunday, Latitude Air Ambulance said, “Given the information shared by authorities and the conclusion of the search-and-rescue phase, we must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient’s family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died.”
Attention has turned to what happened in the jet’s final minutes, when flight-tracking data showed a steep descent and air traffic controllers struggled to re-establish contact.
Authorities have not determined what caused the aircraft to come down.
The aircraft had flown to Bermuda to collect the patient and was heading to Boston Logan International airport.
The US Federal Aviation Administration alerted the coastguard at about 2am on Saturday (06:00 GMT) after contact with the jet was lost.
Lake said at a Sunday news conference that the water around the debris was about 80 to 90 feet (24-27 metres) deep.
He offered condolences to the families of those on board and thanked the agencies involved in the operation.
Latitude Air Ambulance specialises in medical evacuation and repatriation flights, carrying patients home from other countries.
The company says its missions are normally staffed by two pilots and medical personnel.

Türkiye-led Antalya Declaration unites 21 countries on peaceful use of space

Delegates from 21 nations have endorsed the landmark Antalya Declaration during the International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in southern Türkiye, Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir announced.
The endorsement marks the first time a formal joint declaration has been adopted at the IAC's Ministers and Members of Parliament Meeting (MMoP).
A total of 32 participants, comprising government ministers, lawmakers, and heads of national space agencies, accepted the text, which reaffirms the International Astronautical Federation's (IAF) role in expanding international space partnerships.
The high-level session convened delegations representing 38 countries to debate the peaceful utilisation of outer space, emerging space missions, legal frameworks, and the integration of developing economies into the global space sector.
Türkiye's 2027 lunar mission
Türkiye is hosting the 75th edition of the congress from October 5 to 9, in Antalya, coordinated by the Ministry of Industry and Technology alongside co-hosts SAHA Istanbul and the Turkish Space Agency.
Kacir explained that the Antalya Declaration reflects President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's diplomatic vision of advancing peace through multilateral dialogue and constructive engagement.
"Progress in space is meaningful only when it produces tangible benefits for people on Earth," Kacir told delegates.
"The question before us is not only how far we can advance technologically, but how effectively we can turn these capabilities into greater security, resilience and prosperity for our societies".
Kacir highlighted the rapid commercialisation of the sector, noting that the global space economy reached a record $686 billion in 2025, with commercial ventures accounting for roughly 80 percent of total activity.
Reduced launch expenses and smaller satellites have significantly lowered barriers to entry for startups.
Domestically, more than 300 space-technology enterprises currently operate within Turkish technoparks, supported by the government's BiGG seed-funding mechanism and venture capital initiatives exceeding $750 million.
Kacir confirmed that Ankara has also initiated work on a dedicated space technopark and remains on track to launch its first domestically developed lunar spacecraft in early 2027, featuring an indigenous hybrid propulsion engine and an 80 percent domestic production rate.

NEW DELHI: Government is set to disallow diversion of sugarcane juice, syrup and B-heavy molasses for ethanol production in the 2026-27 ethanol supply year (ESY) starting November, amid an around 11% shortfall in sugar production from initial estimates for the 2025-26 sugar season and indications of a further decline in output due to drought in major sugarcane-growing states of Maharashtra and Karnataka.TOI has learnt that government will notify the decision soon, ahead of the start of the new ESY. While ethanol supply year runs from Nov 1 to Oct 31, sugar season in India runs from Oct 1 to Sep 30. Government specifies the quantity of sugarcane juice, syrup and B-heavy molasses that can be diverted for ethanol production to meet the mandatory blending target for the green fuel in petrol.The move comes at a time when domestic sugar supplies remain tight. Mills diverted about 30 lakh tonnes of sugar, or around 10% of total output, for ethanol production during the sugar season that ended on September 30. The new sugar season began on October 1 with opening stocks of around 37.5 lakh tonnes, compared with nearly 50 lakh tonnes a year ago.Industry sources said there was no scope for allowing further diversion of sugarcane juice, syrup and B-heavy molasses for ethanol, as ensuring adequate domestic sugar supplies remains a priority for both govt and mills.
With the possibility of a fall in output in the current season, particularly in Maharashtra and Karnataka, government would prioritise sugar availability over additional diversion for ethanol.Disallowing the use of sugarcane juice, syrup and B-heavy molasses for ethanol in 2026-27 would enable mills to produce more sugar from the available cane, helping augment domestic supplies and meeting consumption requirements.Government has said that the share of sugar diverted for ethanol has declined from around 12% in 2022-23 to around 9% in 2025-26. Besides, nearly three-fourths of ethanol produced in the country now comes from grains, particularly maize, reducing the dependence on sugar-based feedstock.
“Meeting the demand for 20% ethanol blending in petrol won’t be an issue. With indications of millers getting a better price, it won’t be a problem for them either. Government would have to continue with the ban on exports and may have to allow more imports as well,” an industry analyst said.Sugar production in the 2025-26 season was hit by crop diseases, waterlogging and adverse weather in key producing states. Against the initial production estimate of around 343 lakh tonnes, output was estimated at around 306 lakh tonnes in August, including the quantity diverted for ethanol production.After accounting for the diversion to ethanol, net sugar production in 2025-26 was around 279 lakh tonnes, barely enough to meet the normative domestic consumption requirement of 280-285 lakh tonnes.

US Coast Guard halts search for six people missing after medical transport aircraft crashes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
03:15:44 UTC
12:15:44 KST

The US Coast Guard has halted its search for six people who were on a medical transport aircraft that crashed off the coast of Massachusetts' Nantucket Island.
"Suspending a search is not an easy decision," said Rear Admiral Matthew Lake, commander of the Coast Guard's Northeast District, in a statement on Sunday.
"We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude for our partner agencies who helped support search efforts."
The Coast Guard said that after it found debris late on Saturday from a Gulfstream jet traveling to Boston from Bermuda, it searched for the passengers and crew on Sunday with aircraft and vessels on the water.
Four Canadians, two Bermuda citizens, on crashed aircraft
The aircraft, registered to Latitude Air Ambulance, left Bermuda at 12:41 a.m. on Saturday, according to data from flight tracking website FlightAware. Officials said four Canadians and two citizens of Bermuda were on the plane, which was headed for Boston's Logan International Airport.
Local TV station Boston 25 posted an audio clip of Logan's air traffic controller asking the Gulfstream pilot whether he was declaring an emergency. There was no response from the pilot.
"Given the information shared by authorities and the conclusion of the search-and-rescue phase, we must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude said in a statement on Sunday.
Latitude said it would work with the US National Transportation Safety Board, the Transportation Safety Board of Canada, and other authorities on recovery efforts and the investigation into why the plane crashed.

We are all grateful to the flydubai plane heroes but who is taking accountability? - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
03:15:22 UTC
12:15:22 KST

As is customary in Israel, the elation and pride felt last week over the miraculous rescue of the hijacked flydubai plane and the courage displayed by a group of ordinary, but extraordinary, Israelis who saved the 174 mostly Israeli passengers has morphed into a blame game of accusations and evasions.
However much we should be grateful for the heroic actions of the Indian pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, and the Israeli passengers – Tzvika Manes, Yaniv Hayun, Dr. Shota Musayev, Asaf Rajuan, and Tzvika’s wife, Tali Manes, who was the first to raise the alarm on board after hearing a suspicious commotion coming from the flight deck – it’s now incumbent on the relevant authorities to examine how the events were allowed to materialize in the first place and draw conclusions and develop a system that will prevent such potential tragedies from occurring in the future.
It was no secret that flights to and from Israel from the UAE present security risks. In fact, since the onset of Iranian attacks against Israel earlier this year, the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and Israeli security forces had barred El Al, Arkia, and Israir from flying to the UAE, pending an agreement between the nations to resolve security-related issues.
The ban had stemmed from concerns about baggage screening, not the risk posed by pilots employed by foreign airlines, N12 news site reported.
Who was in charge of vetting the pilots?
That appears to be the crux of the matter. Was any official Israeli body in charge of vetting the pilots who were flying into Israel?
Israeli regulations reportedly say pilots from states without diplomatic relations with Israel are prohibited from landing in the country. But there didn’t seem to be any mechanism in place – not by the Transportation Ministry, not by the Shin Bet, and not by the Mossad – to screen those pilots.
According to reports, pilots from unfriendly or hostile states – including Iran, Syria, and Iraq – have repeatedly landed planes in Israel in recent years. Those pilots have dual citizenship, with a second passport presumably issued by a nonbelligerent state, N12 reported.
A law stating that lists of flight crews would be sent to Israeli security agencies passed in 2023. On Saturday night, the Israel Tax Authority, tasked with reviewing incoming flights’ manifests, confirmed it had received the list of passengers and crew for flydubai flight 1073 before takeoff – a standard procedure for all flights under that legislation. The Mossad also had access to that list.
Transportation Minister Miri Regev said her ministry is not responsible for implementing security checks on incoming foreign pilots. The Shin Bet is responsible for security on Israeli carriers, and the Mossad is responsible for security on foreign carriers, she told KAN News on Saturday night.
“Those who are supposed to identify the crew are security officials,” she said. “We are not security officials. Those who are supposed to say what the threat level is, and whether you can travel to a given destination, are security officials.”
Tamir Uri, a senior official in the Transportation Ministry’s Security and Cyber Division, told Walla: “We have 120 airlines flying here. We are not the Shin Bet, and we don’t have people abroad.”
Netanyahu's government vows to fix security cracks
With nobody accepting responsibility, the body ultimately in charge, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, has vowed to fix the cracks in the process.
“Every pilot that is going to be flying into Israel, we are going to know the pilots’ identities, know who they are, and do some type of security check,” Prime Minister’s Office spokesperson Doron Spielman told Reuters last week.
Those might be welcome words, but how is it that such a system has not been in place and functioning already?
We’ve written on these pages that just as Israeli citizens had to take action due to government agency failure on October 7, 2023, Israeli citizens had to spring into action in the sky above Saudi Arabia to prevent a preventable tragedy from occurring. That’s not the way things should work.
As the euphoria over the midair rescue and achievements dissipates, it’s vital not only to conduct a proper investigation into the security gaps that enabled the hijacking, but also for all of the relevant authorities to stop shirking responsibility and work together to quash the likelihood that such a horrific event is ever able to get off the ground again.

FBI arrests California woman under suspicion of spying on Taiwan's president's son for China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
03:15:17 UTC
12:15:17 KST

US authorities arrested a California woman on Sunday and accused her of spying on a son of Taiwan's president at the behest of Chinese officials, the FBI said.
The FBI arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday before her planned departure to China, the agency said in a statement. Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.
Zhang surveilled a son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, the FBI said. The agency did not directly name Zhang's alleged target, but later shared a New York Post report identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, a US resident.
Taiwan's presidential office described Zhang's actions as a "typical case of transnational repression" and thanked the US government for protecting Taiwanese citizens.
"Our country expresses the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of nations," spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
China's foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The Justice Department said Zhang traveled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and subsequently sent them photos, video, and license plate information of the Taiwanese leader's son and his family.
Zhang used tradecraft to avoid detection and never notified Washington that she was acting for a foreign government, Bill Essayli, the first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.
It was not immediately clear whether Zhang has a defense attorney. She will appear on Monday in a Los Angeles federal court, Essayli said.
Taiwanese president pushes separate identity from China
Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan's separate identity from China, a position that frequently angers Beijing, which views the island as Chinese territory.
Washington does not have formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the United States is the island's most important international backer and weapons supplier.

Democrats projected to keep House majority as GOP turnout lags, CBS poll finds

Democrats are projected to maintain their majority in the House of Representatives in the 2026 midterm elections - a phenomenon driven by opposition to the Trump administration's policies and a Republican base that is less likely to vote on election day, according to a recent CBS News House estimate published on Sunday.
The GOP vote may be affected by the cost of living, the CBS report claimed, noting that Republicans were less likely than Democrats to say they would definitely turn out. What is more, Republicans who said their candidates are not talking about the cost of living were found to be less likely to vote.
The report also noted that, broadly speaking, voters see the Trump administration (not the previous Biden administration) as being responsible for the current state of the US economy.
Furthermore, while more voters oppose US President Donald Trump than support him, the CBS report noted that most Republican voters want a candidate who mostly, but not always, agrees with Trump. Similarly, Democrats do not want a candidate who agrees unilaterally with the national Democratic Party, per CBS.
Regarding international policy, CBS found that most voters - including one-third of Republicans - want an end to the war in Iran. Most feel the conflict has been a major factor in the high gas prices, the report noted.
US, Iran may return to fighting after midterm elections, reached 'diplomatic stalemate'
Against that backdrop, the US and Iran could return to fighting after the US midterms, having made little progress toward a diplomatic end to the conflict, Axios reported on Wednesday.
A diplomatic stalemate increases the likelihood of a return to fighting, with some US officials telling Axios that Trump may order a return to combat operations after the US midterm elections in November.
This follows separate talks in New York between Qatari mediators and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, along with a US delegation that included Jared Kushner.
The CBS survey was conducted with a nationally representative sample of 2,166 US adults interviewed between September 30 and October 2, 2026. The sample was weighted to be representative of adults nationwide according to gender, age, race, and education, based on the US Census American Community Survey and Current Population Survey, as well as the 2024 presidential vote. The margin of error for the total sample is ±2.5 points.
Esther Davis contributed to this report.

The “glue” holding your cells together has a surprising second job
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
03:12:55 UTC
12:12:55 KST

The “glue” holding your cells together has a surprising second job
- Date:
- October 4, 2026
- Source:
- University of Liverpool
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that E-cadherin, a protein best known as the “glue” holding cells and tissues together, has a surprising second job: helping epithelial cells swallow nearby dead cells. Using live zebrafish and mouse embryos, researchers found that cells can dramatically reshape their lower surfaces to engulf cellular debris while keeping their upper surfaces stable, allowing protective barriers to remain sealed.
- Share:
A protein best known for helping cells and tissues stay connected has another unexpected role. Researchers have found that it also helps epithelial cells, which form continuous sealed layers throughout the body, engulf nearby dead cells.
The discovery could have implications for chronic inflammation. Debris from dying cells is a major contributor to inflammatory responses, so understanding how tissues remove that material may reveal new clues about what happens when the cleanup process fails.
The study, published in Nature Communications, focuses on the E-cadherin complex. This molecular system includes E-cadherin along with three additional proteins. Together, they connect epithelial cells lining areas such as the skin, gut and airways, giving tissues the structural strength they need to remain intact. In these tissues, each cell connects to E-cadherin molecules on neighboring cells.
Cellular Glue Takes on a Cleanup Role
A team led by Verena Ruprecht examined epithelial tissues in living zebrafish and mouse embryos. They found that the same molecular machinery also gathers at the exact location where a dying cell comes into contact with the tissue.
The researchers wanted to know whether E-cadherin and its partners were attaching to the dying cell in the same way they normally attach neighboring epithelial cells. To test that possibility, they carried out two experiments.
First, they presented the tissue with dying cells that had been stripped of E-cadherin. The epithelial tissue removed those cells just as effectively as it removed normal dying cells. Next, the team introduced fat droplets that contained no protein at all but carried a signal normally displayed on the surface of dying cells. The epithelial cells engulfed those droplets as well.
"We were intrigued to find out that epithelial cells repurpose their molecular adhesion machinery -- the 'glue' that normally holds them together -- to engulf dying cells," says ICREA Research Professor Verena Ruprecht, senior author of the study.
How Cells Eat Without Breaking the Barrier
Engulfing something roughly the size of another cell presents a difficult mechanical problem. Epithelial cells are tightly packed into barriers that often need to remain sealed, even while individual cells reshape themselves to remove debris.
Live imaging revealed how they accomplish this. The upper and lower surfaces of the same epithelial cell can behave differently from one another. The lower surface stretches and bends around the dead cell, while the opposite side remains relatively unchanged.
That upper surface, which may face the outside environment or an open space such as the inside of a lumen, continues maintaining the tissue barrier. Measurements taken before, during and after engulfment showed that the area of the upper surface changed very little. By contrast, the lower surface underwent substantial deformation during the 'eating' process.
Ruprecht compares the behavior to a row of dancers standing with their arms linked. Their upper bodies remain steady while their feet perform increasingly complicated movements when a dying cell appears. "It's the same dancer with a different choreography," she says.
A Molecular Rope and Brake
The researchers also examined the mechanics that allow the cells to perform this cleanup.
One protein in the E-cadherin complex acted much like a rope. It connected the molecular assembly to the cell's internal skeleton, allowing force to be transmitted across the surface of the material being engulfed. When cells lacked this tethering protein, or lacked the specific region that attaches it to the skeleton, they could no longer swallow dead cells.
Another component behaved more like a brake on the cell's contractile machinery. Surprisingly, removing this brake did not make the cleanup process more effective. Instead, the cell became too stiff and lost its ability to properly remove dying cells.
The Same Mechanism Appears in Mammals
The team next investigated whether the process extends beyond zebrafish.
In early mouse embryos, blocking E-cadherin caused dying cells to remain uncleared. This matched the results seen in zebrafish and suggests that the mechanism is shared among vertebrates.
The new work builds on earlier research from Ruprecht showing that embryos can use epithelial tissues to cooperatively remove dying cells. That behavior represents a form of early innate immune defense.
Embryos are particularly useful for studying these events because they are transparent. Researchers can observe living cells and tissues directly at a level of detail that cannot currently be achieved inside the human body.
Could the Same Process Work in Adult Tissues?
An important question remains unanswered. Researchers do not yet know whether this same E-cadherin dependent mechanism operates in adult zebrafish or mice, or in any type of human tissue.
There are reasons to think it could. Epithelial tissues in adults are already known to remove dying cells in places including the retina, colon, airways and mammary gland. E-cadherin is also found throughout epithelial tissues in the body, and its structure has remained remarkably similar across species. Those characteristics make it a strong candidate for a more broadly used cleanup mechanism.
The potential medical importance comes from what can happen when dead cells are not removed efficiently. Dying cells that remain in tissues can eventually rupture and release their contents, contributing to chronic inflammation.
The findings suggest that successful cleanup depends on more than receiving the correct chemical signal to engulf apoptotic debris. Cells must also be physically capable of changing shape, applying force and wrapping around dead material without compromising themselves or the surrounding tissue.
"Studying the mechanisms of how dying cells can be removed efficiently from tissues is of very high relevance to human health," concludes Ruprecht.
The work was led by joint first authors Hanna-Maria Häkkinen, Marta Batet Palau and Laura F. Bianchi and supervised by Verena Ruprecht. It was funded by the Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation, the Human Frontier Science Program, the European Union's Horizon Europe program, and the "la Caixa" Foundation, with additional support from the European Social Fund. It made use of the CRG Core Facilities for Advanced Light Microscopy, Tissue Engineering and Protein Technologies.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Liverpool. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Hanna-Maria Häkkinen, Marta Batet, Laura F. Bianchi, Senda Jiménez-Delgado, Fabio Pezzano, Stefan Wieser, Luca Ciampa, Esteban Hoijman, Carina Vibe, Sofie Wijma, Verena Ruprecht. De novo E-cadherin/catenin complex formation controls basal epithelial mechanics and force transmission for apoptotic cell clearance. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76710-1

China Focus: Ancient temple draws visitors as cultural tourism booms in Shanxi
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:10:45 CST
12:10:45 KST

TAIYUAN, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- For years, Yang Liangen saw strangers as a threat.
After a series of break-in attempts at a 900-year-old temple in north China's Shanxi Province, Yang moved into the compound in 1997, sleeping behind its gates and guarding its rare sculptures and wooden structures.
Nearly three decades later, he eagerly waits for strangers to arrive. "We used to be afraid when people came," Yang said. "Now we hope they will come."
Located in Xiaonan Village in Jincheng City, Erxian Temple fully opened to the public in 2024 as interest in Shanxi's ancient architecture surged following the release of "Black Myth: Wukong," a blockbuster Chinese video game.
During China's National Day holiday that year, Yang counted 1,280 visitors in a single day -- a record for a site whose gates had long been kept mostly shut. The crowds have continued to grow, with more than 4,300 people visiting the temple from Oct. 1 to 3 this year.
The change at Erxian Temple reflects a broader shift across China, as growing interest in cultural tourism brings new attention to historic buildings that for decades were little known beyond their local communities.
Built in 1097, Erxian Temple is a major national cultural heritage site. Its main hall is known for rare Song Dynasty (960-1279) painted sculptures and an exceptionally well-preserved miniature wooden architectural structure known locally as the "sky bridge."
Dubbed China's "above-ground cultural relics museum," Shanxi is home to over 28,000 ancient structures. The province also preserves more than 12,000 painted sculptures and 24,000 square meters of murals from the Tang Dynasty (618-907) onward.
PRESERVED BEHIND THE GATES
For Yang, the new attention marks a dramatic change from the late 1990s.
Facing growing risks to the temple in 1997, Yang, then the village Party secretary, took responsibility for Erxian Temple and moved in with his wife.
The couple kept watch day and night. On one occasion, Yang's wife rushed outside with a flashlight after two people were spotted apparently chiseling through a wall, sending them fleeing.
No theft has occurred since Yang became its caretaker.
A major restoration completed in 2014 repaired the compound and revived its two-courtyard layout. Surveillance cameras were installed, giving the couple what Yang described as their first truly restful sleep in years. But the gates largely remained closed.
Visits by preservation experts became important opportunities for Yang. He followed them around, learning about Song Dynasty construction and the temple's rare architectural features.
As architecture enthusiasts began making their way to the village, Yang sometimes made exceptions to let them inside and shared what he had learned.
"They had come such a long way," Yang said. "Maybe they would only come once in their lives. How could I not let them see it?"
Over time, Yang turned himself from a guard into an unofficial guide.
FINDING NEW AUDIENCES
Years of restoration and improved security eventually made it possible for more people to see what Yang had spent decades protecting.
In late 2022, an upgrade of Erxian Temple's security system was launched. Around the same time, local heritage enthusiasts formed a volunteer association in Jincheng City to support heritage site caretakers, organize educational visits and train volunteer guides.
In August 2024, Jincheng began opening 18 nationally and provincially protected heritage sites to the public on Sundays on a trial basis before fully opening them in October. Erxian Temple was included.
"The temple didn't become popular overnight," said Zhang Jianjun, one of the association's founders. "Without all those years of preparation, we wouldn't have been ready when the crowds came."
The association now has more than 400 members, including Zhang Jie, a local charter driver who first visited Erxian Temple while taking customers around Shanxi in 2024. Standing among centuries-old sculptures and elaborate woodwork, he realized how little he knew about the heritage of his own home province.
"I felt ashamed, but also curious," he said. He began studying traditional architecture, joined the volunteer association and now shares what he has learned with tourists.
At the Hanging Temple in Datong City, Chen Ruiyan recalled a recent road trip she and her husband had taken from Guangdong Province to Shanxi, visiting more than a dozen historic sites across the province. Inspired by films and animations featuring Shanxi's ancient architecture, they had studied traditional architectural features before setting out.
"Beyond their aesthetic impact, ancient wooden buildings have a sense of quietness and vitality," Chen said.
Beyond Shanxi, efforts to preserve historic architecture are also bringing old buildings closer to contemporary life. In Fujian Province, traditional Tulou, or earthen buildings, are being preserved and given new uses, while in Guizhou Province, more than 12,000 endangered traditional buildings have undergone emergency restoration.
China's latest five-year plan for cultural heritage calls for stronger systematic protection while making preservation efforts more accessible and beneficial to the public.
Wang Chunbo, a researcher specializing in ancient architecture, sculptures and murals in Shanxi, said the growing interest in historic architecture reflects a deeper engagement with traditional culture among younger Chinese.
"Young people are no longer satisfied with simply checking a destination off their list," Wang said. "Historic buildings are becoming cultural spaces they can experience, engage with and share."
Li Junda, a university student studying anthropology in London, traveled to Shanxi after encountering Yang's story online. What struck him was how the temple's history was still carried by the people around it.
"At the British Museum, I saw many Chinese artifacts on display, identified simply by their dynasties," Li said. "Here in Shanxi, the heritage is still 'alive,' because villagers like Yang are here to tell the stories behind it." ■

Joseph Dauey, a Taijiquan enthusiast from Britain, practices Taijiquan in Chenjiagou Village of Wenxian County, central China's Henan Province, Aug. 26, 2026. Social media users in the West have recently embraced "Chinamaxxing," in which young people show interest in aspects of Chinese daily life.
Taijiquan, a kind of traditional martial arts, was born in the mid-17th century in Chenjiagou Village. Rooted in Chinese philosophy, traditional medicine and martial arts, Taijiquan has evolved into a wide range of styles and is now practiced in more than 180 countries and regions. For foreign visitors, Chenjiagou is naturally one of the best spots to experience the "Chinamaxxing" trend. The small village offers a tranquil and comfortable living environment which lets visitors get away from the busy pace of city life and immerse themselves in traditional Chinese culture. Flavio Bolsonaro (C), presidential candidate of Brazil's Liberal Party, is seen after the announcement of the first-round results of the presidential election in Brasilia, Brazil, Oct. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Lucio Tavora)
BRASILIA, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Brazil will hold a presidential runoff on Oct. 25 as official results showed Sunday that no candidate secured a majority of valid votes in the first round.
According to results released by the Superior Electoral Court, with over 99 percent of the ballots counted, Flavio Bolsonaro, presidential candidate of Brazil's Liberal Party, garnered about 47 percent of valid votes while incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party came in second with about 45 percent.
Under Brazil's electoral rules, a presidential candidate must secure more than half of the valid votes to win outright in the first round. Otherwise, the two candidates with the most votes advance to a runoff.
Following the announcement of the first-round results, both candidates made remarks on Sunday night.
Bolsonaro said at a press conference in Brasilia that he was satisfied with the election result and hoped to have the opportunity to serve Brazil and its people.
"Brazil wants change. I just need a mandate to put Brazilians at the center of my government, to tackle and solve Brazil's real problems," he said.
Speaking in Sao Paulo, Lula acknowledged that he had expected to win in the first round but described the result as a lesson from voters.
He pledged to campaign on economic development and social inclusion, and urged those who abstained in the first round to vote in the runoff.
"We have a second round, and it's time for the test, time to show the true picture of Brazil," Lula said. ■

21 countries adopt Antalya Declaration for peaceful use of space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
03:01:26 UTC
12:01:26 KST

Türkiye's Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir said Sunday that 32 participants from 21 countries had adopted and endorsed the Antalya Declaration, marking the first time a declaration had been endorsed at the International Astronautical Congress’ (IAC) Ministers and Members of Parliament Meeting (MMoP).
“We are particularly pleased that 32 distinguished MMoP participants from 21 countries, consisting of ministers, parliamentarians and space agency heads, have accepted and endorsed this declaration,” Kacir said.
He said the declaration reaffirmed the International Astronautical Federation’s (IAF) vital role in advancing global cooperation and called on other countries and international organizations that have not yet joined to adopt and sign it.
The meeting brought together ministers, lawmakers, parliamentary delegations, heads of space agencies and senior officials from international organizations representing 38 countries.
Participants discussed strategic issues including the peaceful exploration and use of outer space, space missions, space law, the integration of developing countries into the global space ecosystem and the development of a sustainable space economy.
Türkiye is hosting the 75th International Astronautical Congress from Oct. 5-9 in Antalya. The annual congress is organized by the IAF under the coordination of Türkiye’s Ministry of Industry and Technology, with the Turkish Space Agency and SAHA Istanbul as co-hosts. Anadolu is the event’s global communications partner.
‘Progress in space is valuable when it serves people on Earth’
Speaking at the meeting, Kacir said participants took pride in adopting a declaration that for the first time in the history of the IAC MMoP brought ministers, lawmakers and space agency representatives together around a common commitment to peace, responsibility and cooperation in space.
The Antalya Declaration for Space for Peace was initiated by Türkiye, the host country of IAC 2026, in line with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s vision of advancing peace through dialogue and international cooperation, he said.
“The text was developed through close consultations with the IAF and our international partners. Our goal is to build a common international framework for a peaceful, sustainable and responsible approach to space,” he said.
Kacir said the declaration reflected the “Spirit of Antalya,” characterized by openness, mutual respect and constructive engagement.
He also emphasized the growing importance of space-based capabilities to everyday life, economic activity and disaster management.
“Progress in space is meaningful only when it produces tangible benefits for people on Earth,” he said. “The question before us is not only how far we can advance technologically, but how effectively we can turn these capabilities into greater security, resilience and prosperity for our societies.”
‘The space ecosystem cannot advance without entrepreneurship’
Kacir said the global space sector was no longer driven solely by public funding, with private companies and startups increasingly becoming key drivers of growth.
“The global space economy reached a record $686 billion in 2025,” he said, adding that about four-fifths of that value came from commercial activities.
He said lower launch costs, smaller satellites and increased private-sector investment had lowered barriers to entry, allowing new players to enter a sector that had previously been dominated by a limited number of actors.
“However, innovation does not flourish on its own,” Kacir said, stressing the need for an ecosystem supported by public institutions, long-term financing and predictable regulations.
He said Türkiye had made entrepreneurship and innovation a central part of its technology policies.
“Our BİGG program is Türkiye’s largest public support mechanism for technology startups at the seed and pre-seed stages,” he said. “We have taken steps that will bring more than $750 million in additional resources to our venture capital ecosystem.”
More than 300 companies now operate in space technologies in Türkiye’s technoparks alone, he said, adding the government had also begun work to establish a dedicated space technopark in the capital Ankara.
Türkiye’s lunar mission
Kacir also briefed the delegations on Türkiye’s satellite development capabilities and planned deep-space projects.
“Our first lunar spacecraft, which we plan to launch at the beginning of 2027, will carry out its mission with a domestic production rate of more than 80% and a hybrid propulsion system developed by us,” he said.
The mission will serve as an international test of Türkiye’s engineering capabilities and its ability to turn its space ambitions into concrete results, he added.

Kai Tak Hospital opens this week: what you need to know before visiting
Hong Kong’s largest public hospital begins phased operations on Monday, starting with family medicine and specialist outpatient services
Hong Kong’s largest public hospital, built on the former airport site in Kai Tak, began its first phase of operations on Monday after more than a decade of planning and preparation.
The South China Morning Post looks at the hospital’s key features and what its opening means for the city’s healthcare development.
1. What makes Kai Tak Hospital special?
With a gross floor area of roughly 500,000 square metres (5.38 million square feet) and 2,400 beds, Kai Tak Hospital will be Hong Kong’s largest public hospital. It will gradually take over services from Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Jordan.
The hospital, which cost more than HK$36 billion, comprises five buildings on the site of the former airport’s south apron. Major facilities include 37 operating theatres and a 24-hour accident and emergency department.
It will also house Hong Kong’s largest pharmacy, the first in a public hospital to use an automated dispensing system capable of handling up to 3,200 prescriptions a day.

Three years after Oct. 7, Hamas still rules Gaza despite IDF control of 64%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
02:47:31 UTC
11:47:31 KST

Nearly three years after the October 7 massacre, Israel’s security establishment acknowledges that the Gaza campaign remains far from a decisive outcome. Despite major military gains and a large permanent IDF presence, the basic reality remains unchanged: Hamas still governs the territory.
The IDF currently controls about 64% of the Gaza Strip, deploying two divisions across roughly 30 outposts. Security officials say Israel’s defensive posture has been completely transformed since October 7. "If Hamas tries anything, it will encounter IDF forces at the front," a senior security official told Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth. "Our defense no longer begins at the border fence, but inside Gaza. We have stable and very strong control here."
Israeli forces are completing an anti-vehicle barrier consisting of a wide trench and an earthen embankment, while drilling into the ground at regular intervals to ensure no cross-border tunnels into Israel have been missed. The work is taking place east of the Yellow Line, which divides areas under IDF control from those controlled by Hamas.
Alongside its territorial presence, the IDF continues targeted strikes against Hamas personnel. Security officials said about 70 terrorists, including three brigade commanders, were killed over the past month.
"We will act against operatives and kill them one by one," officials said. "We wait patiently for the right moment to strike with very low collateral damage. There were opportunities when we did not strike immediately because of those considerations."
No political plan
The central unresolved problem is Hamas’ continued grip over Gaza’s population. Security officials say the absence of a clear political plan for who will govern the territory after the war has allowed the terrorist organization to remain in place despite the severe damage to its military capabilities.
"Everything entering Gaza today passes through Kerem Shalom, where we have some of the best scanners in the world for detecting prohibited items," one security official said. "Food, fuel and gas enter, but then Hamas takes control of it."
About 600 trucks enter Gaza each day with Israeli approval. Officials acknowledge that there is currently no effective way to prevent Hamas from profiting from the goods after they cross into the territory.
"The trucks enter, Hamas takes control of them and transfers the goods to merchants," officials familiar with the issue said. "It collects taxes and receives money. That is how it keeps its people going, and that is how it has weapons."
Military officials stress, however, that the money Hamas extracts from aid does not translate into significant military rebuilding and primarily helps it maintain governing control.
A senior security official said Hamas faces severe ammunition shortages and can no longer import raw materials as it did before the war. The group still commands tens of thousands of operatives, but many are young recruits who replaced experienced fighters killed or wounded during the fighting.
"It cannot recruit everyone it wants simply because it does not have weapons to give them," the official said. Hamas also has far less ability to train its forces, he added, because any identifiable training activity or visible weapons can trigger an Israeli strike.
"They do a lot of theoretical lessons, but there is no real training, so their operational capability has been damaged," the official said. "Hamas is mainly on the defensive."
The goal: demilitarization
The IDF says it is implementing government policy rather than determining Gaza’s political future. But three years after the war began, security officials say the lack of a long-term political framework remains a central factor behind Hamas’ continued rule.
Officials are deeply skeptical that negotiations under the Board of Peace plan could persuade Hamas to voluntarily disarm. "Everything depends on Hamas being demilitarized," a senior security official said. "I am skeptical that the organization will truly give up its weapons. It will put on shows, but we are not going to give up."
"We have a rough idea of how many weapons it has, and in Gaza you have no chance without weapons," he added. "For Hamas, giving up its weapons means ceasing to exist."
The continuing Gaza deployment also comes amid mounting pressure on Israel’s reserve forces, which have carried much of the burden across Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and the West Bank for three years. "There is no doubt we could not have done this without the reservists," the security official said. "Today you are simultaneously maintaining forces on the Syrian, Lebanese and Gaza borders and in the West Bank."
According to the official, most combat reservists have now served more than 500 days since October 7, equivalent to roughly half of the period since the war began. "Next year we will have to reduce reserve duty somewhat and thin out forces because there will be no choice," he said. "Wherever we can reduce the deployment, we need to. These are civilians with families."
