Can Australia Create Lasting Climate Impacts For the Asia-Pacific?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
02:37:00 UTC
11:37:00 KST

COP31 comes at a time when the world is facing the reality that it will soon exceed the 1.5°C global warming threshold enshrined in the Paris Agreement. Across the Asia-Pacific, extreme weather impacts are being felt more visibly and intensely, from the streets of Bangkok to towns across China and Nepal and the waters of the Pacific Ocean.
While these impacts are becoming more severe, global climate cooperation is facing tighter fiscal constraints and a more fragmented geopolitical environment. Elsewhere the need for strengthened cooperation is also being overshadowed by the discussion around energy security and the race for power availability for the technologies and infrastructure that will shape the future of industrial competitiveness.
In the coming days, with support from Australia and Pacific partners, up to 3,000 participants are expected to gather in Fiji alongside a leaders’ summit in Tuvalu for a Pre-COP31 preparatory meeting. This meeting will amplify voices from small state islands and explore what global solutions are needed and the speed required to protect countries whose exposure to climate impacts is rising despite their limited contribution to global emissions.
In November, Australia will then preside over the negotiations at COP31 hosted by Türkiye in Antalya. The global climate movement expects both countries to advance key outstanding agenda items, including mobilizing climate finance set out in the COP29 New Collective Quantified Goal on Climate Finance and advancing the phase-out of fossil fuels in the negotiation texts.
This will be a tough job. Last month, leaders of BRICS – a grouping of major emerging economies founded by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – met in New Delhi. The group has since expanded to 11 countries, accounting for 50 percent of the global population. The final endorsed text of the New Delhi Declaration has 34 mentions of climate, highlighting the importance of energy security but stating that “fossil fuels will still play an important role in the world’s energy mix, particularly for emerging markets and developing economies.”
Achieving an absolute consensus from 198 countries for phasing out fossil fuels, especially in the context of the U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement, is not easy. But there are practical areas where Australia’s leadership can create lasting impacts for Asia Pacific: electrification and energy security; the rules and infrastructure for clean trade; and climate finance and resilience for the Pacific.
Across major Asian economies, including China, Japan, Korea and Southeast Asia, electrification is growing at a fast pace. Pairing this with renewable electricity will provide significant opportunities for lower import bills and better environmental outcomes.
The opportunity is particularly immediate in remote and island communities. For fishing communities in archipelagic states like the Philippines and Indonesia, solar-powered cold storage could reduce post-harvest agricultural losses for farmers and fishermen and avoid high electricity costs while improving food security and incomes. Across the Pacific, countries spend up to 13 per cent of their GDP on imported fuels. Replacing diesel generation with solar, batteries and other renewable systems has strong implications for energy security, but will require upfront investment.
With its strong electrification focus, COP31 can make this opportunity more visible and therefore connect investment, technology and development finance with policy support. For businesses, this means creating opportunities to invest in renewable-powered electrification in industrial export-led economies. For communities, it means combining solar and storage with concessional finance and development assistance to replace ageing, expensive equipment and enable long-term resilience for farmers and fishermen.
The Asia-Pacific is a center of industrial activities. Some clean commodity corridors and supply chains are emerging in the region, such as the Australia to Singapore’s green and digital shipping corridor, or the potential Australia to East Asia iron ore green corridors.
These go beyond high-level political endorsement. Lots of work has been done and will need to be done to develop a shared view of how emissions are measured, which standards are recognized, how products are certified and whether infrastructure exists to move them from producers to customers.
COP31 can strengthen a clean commodities economy through global coordination efforts on measuring, reporting, and verifying carbon reduction standards and action agendas related to green trade and certification. But beyond the negotiation room and climate action agenda, there are various collaborations taking place. An example is reaching consensus on a Net-Zero Framework for marine fuels under the International Maritime Organization. The framework, if advanced further in December, will be fundamental to drive global progress beyond the shipping sector.
Australia’s clear goal for COP31 is to support the best possible outcomes for the Pacific, including mobilizing finance through initiatives such as the Pacific Resilience Facility. This is very important, but Pacific countries should not be presented only as vulnerable countries in need of assistance.
Their economies, food systems, cultures, and identities are closely connected to global natural capital and security. Fisheries, tourism, coastal protection, and other ocean-based activities can form the foundation of future economic development if this natural capital is protected, including vast ocean territories, forests, coral reefs, mangroves and freshwater.
Earlier this year, Australia and Fiji signed the landmark Vuvale Union Treaty, recognizing the deep interconnectedness between climate, people, prosperity, and peace across the Pacific. The treaty has made its message clear: rising sea levels are not only an existential threat to Pacific nations; they also have profound implications for Oceania’s security and future prosperity.
At the end of the day, countries and communities are deeply connected by climate. One country’s security and prosperity depends on the livelihood and resilience of others.

Israel bans UK Green Party leader Zack Polanski after ‘Zionism is racism’ vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
02:33:05 UTC
11:33:05 KST

Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar on Sunday barred Zack Polanski, leader of Britain’s Green Party, from entering Israel after the party conference adopted a resolution defining Zionism as a form of racism and supporting the establishment of a single Palestinian state throughout what it calls “historic Palestine.”
Polanski, who is Jewish and identifies as anti-Zionist, did not take part in the vote, which passed by 1,022 votes to 813. Before the vote, he had expressed reservations about parts of the motion. Asked whether Israel had a right to exist, however, he declined to answer affirmatively, saying instead that “human beings have a right to exist.”
Israel’s Foreign Ministry said the resolution “equates Zionism with racism, grants legitimacy to armed struggle against Israel and calls for the establishment of a Palestinian state ‘from the river to the sea,’ which means the destruction of the State of Israel.”
According to the ministry, “the resolution constitutes a clearly antisemitic text under the IHRA definition, since it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination.”
“Accordingly, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar has decided, as a first step, to declare Green Party leader Zack Polanski barred from entering Israel,” the ministry said, adding that the move had been coordinated with the relevant Israeli authorities.
Earlier, the Foreign Ministry issued an unusually sharp response to the resolution adopted at the Green Party conference in Brighton, saying the party “today ceased functioning as a political party and became an organization that supports terrorism.”
“The Greens have officially adopted the green color of Hamas and its ideological doctrine, which calls for the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” the ministry said.
It added that the resolution “grants legitimacy to armed struggle, calls for the establishment of a Palestinian state from the river to the sea, in practice the destruction of the State of Israel, and equates Zionism with racism.”
“This is no longer a political text,” the ministry said. “It crosses the boundaries of political discourse and, as long as it remains in place, constitutes a stain on the history of the United Kingdom.”
The ministry called on all British political parties, “first and foremost the governing Labour Party,” to reject the resolution immediately and unequivocally. Israel’s condemnation was also widely reported in the British media.
The resolution adopted at the Green conference defines Zionism as an “ethnonationalist political project” and calls for “one democratic state throughout historic Palestine.” It also reiterates the party’s demand for Britain to end arms trade with Israel.
The proposal triggered fierce disagreement within the party, with several senior and former Green figures opposing it, including Caroline Lucas, Adrian Ramsay and Carla Denyer.
Lucas warned before the vote that the resolution could create the impression that Jewish people were not welcome in the party, while Denyer cautioned that it could alienate Jews who strongly oppose the Israeli government and support Palestinian rights.
Polanski himself had sought changes to parts of the proposal before the vote and did not participate in the ballot.
Alongside Israel’s diplomatic response, Matan Bar Noy, head of the World Zionist Organization’s delegation to Britain and Europe, released a video filmed outside the Houses of Parliament and Big Ben in which he tore up a copy of the resolution.
The gesture echoed a famous 1975 speech by Chaim Herzog, then Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations and later president, after the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 3379 declaring that “Zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination.” That resolution was revoked in 1991.
“Zionism is the national liberation movement of the Jewish people and the expression of their right to self-determination in their historic homeland,” Bar Noy said.
“Fifty-one years after the UN adopted the shameful resolution equating Zionism with racism, and years after the world withdrew it, there are those trying to bring the same libel back through the rear door,” he said.
“Here, in the heart of British democracy, our message is clear: We will not accept an attempt to turn the Jewish people’s very right to self-determination into racism. I am tearing up this resolution and throwing it where it belongs, into the dustbin of history.”
Bar Noy said the decision was especially serious given rising antisemitism in Britain and what he described as an increasingly hostile climate toward Israel and the Jewish community.
“At precisely such a time, political parties are expected to show responsibility and fight hatred, not grant it legitimacy through the delegitimization of Zionism,” he said. “Criticism of the Israeli government is legitimate, and we can debate it. Denying the Jewish people’s right to self-determination is something entirely different.”
Israel’s ambassador to the European Union, Avi Nir, also attacked the decision.
“If Zionism is racism, then I am a proud racist,” he said. “In reality, I am a proud Zionist, while the real racists are the members of the British Green Party who supported this motion and opposed an amendment seeking to protect Jewish party members who pray in ‘Zionist’ synagogues from being targeted.”
Nir also invoked Herzog’s 1975 UN speech, quoting his declaration: “I do not come to this rostrum to plead the case of the Jewish people, or to defend the Zionist movement. I come to express our total contempt for this resolution and our refusal to accept it.”
“The Jewish people have been the victims of racism and discrimination for thousands of years,” Nir added. “We know the price of hatred and prejudice better than any other nation on earth.”
“It is a cruel irony that those who now accuse us of racism are themselves the perpetrators of discrimination and oppression,” he said. “This resolution is based on hatred, falsehood and arrogance. It will not change the reality of Israel’s existence, nor will it undermine the determination of the Jewish people to defend their country and their rights.”

It’s Time For Thailand to Amend Its Controversial Lese-Majeste Law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
02:20:00 UTC
11:20:00 KST

On September 26, 2023, my fellow human rights lawyer Arnon Nampa was imprisoned in Thailand for calling for the reform of the Thai monarchy. He has been behind bars ever since.
I had the opportunity to talk to him early last month at the Bangkok Criminal Court, where he appeared for a hearing in one of the remaining three lese-majeste cases he is facing under Article 112 of Thailand’s Criminal Code. This draconian provision punishes with prison terms of three to 15 years whoever defames, insults, or threatens the Thai king, queen, heir apparent, or regent. Eleven additional lese-majeste cases filed against Arnon have already resulted in 11 convictions and a cumulative prison term of more than 31 years.
When I met Arnon in court, he was barefoot, wearing his prison uniform. I was shocked to see he was being kept ankle-shackled the entire time, a clear form of ill-treatment and a violation of his right to be treated humanely and with respect for his dignity. I briefly spoke with him about his trial and expressed my full solidarity. When he was eventually escorted out of the courtroom to return to prison, he turned to me, and knowing I am from beer-loving Belgium, he smiled and promised me the next time he would meet me in Brussels for a beer. This rendezvous will likely have to wait many years.
A day earlier, I was in the same court for another lese-majeste case. This time, the defendant was a young woman pro-democracy activist, Tantawan Tuatulanon, known as “Tawan.” Visibly stressed but putting on a brave face, she reminded me of my own daughter – same age, same studies, same demeanor. This was the day of the verdict, which, as it happens in most lese-majeste cases, turned out to be a conviction. Her crime? She livestreamed on Facebook the relocation of a farmer sit-in protest in Bangkok to make way for the passage of a royal motorcade. She was violently arrested on the spot and charged with violating Article 112. The Criminal Court sentenced her to two years in prison without suspension. Tawan spent the rest of the day in the holding cell in the court’s basement, while awaiting the outcome of her bail application, which was successful and resulted in her temporary release pending appeal. I managed to talk to her through a phone line across a series of partitions to convey my support and encouragement.
In a striking and surreal contrast, just before Tawan’s verdict, the same judge had delivered another verdict, in which a convicted child sex offender was sentenced to six years in prison. His sentence was suspended for two years so that he could be free and have a chance to demonstrate he is “a good person.”
Like Arnon and Tawan, in recent years, hundreds of Thais have faced criminal prosecution under Article 112. About 30 of them are currently behind bars, with 19 serving prison terms of up to 50 years. Those who are on trial have little or no hope of avoiding prison. In a discriminatory move, Article 112 has been excluded from offenses covered by recently adopted legislation designed to promote a “peaceful society” to clear records, dismiss pending cases, and release individuals detained in connection with the political turmoil that Thailand experienced for two decades (2005-2025). In addition, authorities have made no progress in the adoption of alternatives to detention (such as home detention) for prisoners convicted of certain crimes – which should include non-violent offenses such as lese-majeste.
Like Thailand, my own country, Belgium, is a constitutional monarchy with the King as the head of state. In October 2021, the Constitutional Court ruled that Belgium’s lese-majeste law – introduced in 1847 and rarely used – violated freedom of expression and that monarchs were not entitled to greater protection than ordinary people for defamation. As a result, in Belgium’s current Criminal Code, lese-majeste can only be punished by a fine, and no deprivation of liberty is possible for those who insult the monarch.
This sensible reform could provide a blueprint for Thailand and would bring Article 112 closer to compliance with international human rights law. Indeed, under international human rights law, imprisonment is never an appropriate penalty for insult or defamation, including when insults are directed towards public figures, such as heads of state.
The task of reforming Article 112 falls exclusively on the Thai people. Nonetheless, like-minded states, including Belgium, must play a positive role by supporting such domestic efforts and backing them with calls for the amendment of Article 112 and respect for international human rights law.
Freedom of expression is a fundamental and universal right that protects all opinions, including those that shock, offend, or hurt – let alone those that call for the reform of the monarchy or question the appropriateness of royal motorcades. As Thailand has learned in recent years, without freedom of expression there is no “peaceful society.” It is as simple as that.

Rubio Heads To NATO Allies As Russian Threat, Middle East War Shape Agenda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
02:18:14 UTC
11:18:14 KST

WASHINGTON -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is visiting Iceland, Greece, and Portugal on October 5-8 for talks on security, defense, energy, economic cooperation, and technology as NATO allies face growing security concerns over Russia’s military activity and continued Middle East instability.
Rubio began in Reykjavik, where he is expected to discuss Arctic security and economic cooperation with Icelandic officials.
He will then travel to Athens for the sixth US-Greece Strategic Dialogue, with defense cooperation, energy, regional security, Ukraine, and the Middle East on the agenda.
In Lisbon, his talks will focus on defense, economic development, and technology cooperation, according to the State Department.
The three stops include different areas of US cooperation with NATO allies, from Iceland’s role in North Atlantic and Arctic security to Greece’s position in the Eastern Mediterranean and Portugal’s long-standing importance to US military operations in the Atlantic.
Iceland: Security And The Arctic
Iceland has no standing army but has long cooperated with the US and NATO on security because of its location in the North Atlantic.
Two former US ambassadors to Iceland -- who spoke on the condition of anonymity -- told RFE/RL that Rubio should expect Reykjavik to be receptive to further security cooperation, while also listening to the concerns of a country that places a high value on its independence.
“Icelanders are a fiercely independent people,” one ambassador said, adding that there has been continued US-Icelandic security cooperation since Russia’s invasion of Crimea in 2014.
Separately, Robert Gerber, a former US diplomat who served at the US Embassy in Iceland, said Rubio's visit could follow up on commitments discussed at a September meeting of Arctic countries on the margins of the UN General Assembly.
Those discussions included commitments by Arctic partners to take greater responsibility for their own security and the protection of critical infrastructure.
Gerber also pointed to his own experience in Iceland to illustrate the security concerns facing the country.
“When I was in Iceland on a regular basis, Russian aircraft or bombers or whatever would fly toward Iceland, do a loop of the island, and then fly back just to see how fast NATO planes would scramble,” Gerber told RFE/RL.
“The threat is real there, and it's been there for a long time,” Gerber said, adding that submarine warfare in the region is also a continuing concern.
Iceland's contribution to NATO differs from that of larger allies, Gerber said. The country hosts Keflavik Air Base, has contributed to Ukraine, and provides maritime and search-and-rescue capabilities through its Coast Guard.
Gerber said the protection of undersea telecommunications cables linking North America and Europe could also be an area for greater cooperation.
Russians In The Arctic
“Those obviously need to be hardened and protected because the Russians are up to all kinds of things in the Arctic,” he said. Iceland's Coast Guard, including its ships and helicopters, could also be important in an Arctic crisis, he added.
Gerber said he did not expect Rubio to persuade Iceland to make a major change in its defense spending. “Iceland's economy is relatively small,” Gerber said, adding that the country's approach to security is also shaped by its independent political outlook.
Eric Green, a former White House National Security Council official who also served as deputy chief of mission in Iceland, said Icelandic officials would also be looking for reassurance from Washington.
“It’s positive that Secretary Rubio is visiting NATO countries,” Green told RFE/RL, adding that Icelandic officials would want reassurance that Washington was no longer interested in making claims on Greenland based on what he called “spurious accusations.”
Green also said Iceland, a strong supporter of Ukraine, would welcome indications that Washington intends to do more to help Ukraine and Europe as Russia continues its war.
The Arctic has also become a focus of competition as melting ice opens new maritime routes and increases interest in the region's resources.
The former ambassador said Russia has strengthened its military presence along its Arctic coast, while China has sought to expand its presence through port, research and other initiatives in Iceland.
Greece: Defense, Energy, Regional Security
In Athens, Rubio will lead the US delegation at the sixth US-Greece Strategic Dialogue on October 6-7.
The dialogue, launched in 2018, provides a framework for cooperation on defense, energy, and other issues. The talks are expected to include the facilities and support Greece provides under the Mutual Defense Cooperation Agreement, as well as developments in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Geoffrey Pyatt, a former assistant secretary of state for energy resources and former US ambassador to Greece and Ukraine, said the dialogue was established as a way to advance bilateral cooperation independently of other regional relationships.
“When we created the Strategic Dialogue during my tenure as ambassador, the whole idea was to create a forum to advance the strong agenda of bilateral cooperation topics independent of any other regional relationships,” Pyatt told RFE/RL.
He said military cooperation, energy opportunities, and people-to-people ties, including education and investment, have remained consistent across Republican and Democratic administrations.
Pyatt also pointed to Greece's commitment to its European and transatlantic relationships. “Greece remains strongly committed to its European identity including the firm commitment to the transatlantic relationship,” he said.
Rubio's final stop will be Lisbon, where the State Department says he will discuss defense, economic development and technology cooperation with the country’s leadership.
Portugal's role in US security cooperation includes the Azores, where Lajes Air Base has long provided an important logistical and refueling location for US military operations in the Atlantic.

Pro-Russian party leads in elections in Republika Srpska
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
05:15:00 EEST
11:15:00 KST

Pro-Russian party leads in elections in Republika Srpska
According to early vote counts, the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, led by pro-Russian politician Milorad Dodik, has come out ahead in the elections in Republika Srpska, Bosnia and Herzegovina's predominantly Serb entity. Meanwhile, in the country's other entity, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, three of the four leading parties that have received the most votes so far hold a clear pro-Ukrainian stance.
Source: Bosnia and Herzegovinian web portal Klix.ba
Details: According to preliminary results reported by Klix.ba, with results processed from 89.45% of polling stations, the Party of Democratic Action (SDA) is leading in the parliamentary elections to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina's House of Representatives, having secured 30.63%, which amounts to more than 212,000 votes. The Federation is the country's predominantly Bosniak and Croat entity.
The Social Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina (SDP) is in second place with 15.27% (over 105,000 votes), while the coalition formed around the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina (HDZ BiH) is in third place with 13.89% (over 96,000 votes). In fourth place with 8.97% (over 62,000 votes) is the Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina (SBiH).
Meanwhile, according to Klix.ba, the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) is leading in the elections to the parliament of Republika Srpska, Bosnia and Herzegovina's predominantly Serb entity. The party is currently projected to win 34 seats based on the votes counted so far.
In second place is the Pokret Sigurna Srpska (PSS) party with a projected 12 seats, followed by the Serb Democratic Party (SDS) with 11. The Coalition for the State, consisting of pro-Bosnian parties from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is projected to receive two seats in Republika Srpska's parliament.
Overall, as reported by The Associated Press, Bosnia suffers from tensions between nationalist parties representing predominantly Muslim Bosniaks (who make up about half of the population), Orthodox Serbs (who account for about a third of the population) and a minority of Catholic Croats (who make up around 15% of the population).
Furthermore, the country has a complex system of state institutions created under the 1995 peace agreement brokered by the US to resolve inter-ethnic conflicts.
Therefore, Bosnia is currently divided into two political entities with a weak central government whose work is overseen by an international envoy: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with a population that is in the majority Muslim, and Republika Srpska, predominantly ethnic Serbs.
Even ahead of the elections, victory in Republika Srpska was projected for the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, the party led by the former president of the Republic and staunchly pro-Russian politician Milorad Dodik.
The politician was at the centre of the election campaign's focus, despite the absence of his name from the ballot paper due to being stripped of the right to hold public office. During the election campaign, Dodik stoked controversies that raised fears of renewed instability in the country.
Specifically, at his party's final rally before the elections, which was also attended by Igor Kalabukhov, the Russian Ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Dodik told supporters that Bosnia is "dead" and that "it is an impossible country that makes no sense whatsoever."
The parties that preliminarily took second and third place in the elections to the parliament of Republika Srpska do not position themselves as explicitly pro-Russian, but they do support Bosnia's neutrality regarding the Russia-Ukraine war.
In contrast, the centre-right SDA, the centre-left SDP and the centrist SBiH – which, according to preliminary results, are set to win in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina – hold a clear pro-Ukrainian and pro-Western stance. They have openly condemned Russian aggression against Ukraine.
The HDZ BiH, which will most likely take third place in the Federation elections, officially holds a stance similar to the two aforementioned parties but in practice sometimes adopts compromise positions, such as abstaining during votes on anti-Russian sanctions or entering into alliances with Dodik's political force.
Background:
- On 4 October, general elections took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina, during which a massive drop in voter turnout was recorded.
- Approximately 3.4 million people voted to elect three members of the country's multiethnic presidential council, members of the national parliament and leaders of the institutions of the country's two political entities.

Research into weight-loss drugs tipped for Nobel as award week opens

Research into weight-loss drugs tipped for Nobel as award week opens
- Research on hormones regulating appetite, especially GLP-1 linked to weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, is a strong contender for the 2026 Nobel Medicine Prize.
- Other Nobel possibilities include skin regeneration, immune system adhesion receptors, and advances in imaging or breast cancer research.
- The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize may go to broadly supported laureates like Save the Children or Ukrainian activist Mykola Kuleba amid anticipated lobbying and controversy.
AI generated
STOCKHOLM – Research into hormones that regulate appetite is on everybody’s lips for the Nobel medicine prize, to be announced on Oct 5 when the 2026 Nobel season kicks off.
The winners of the six Nobel prizes for medicine, physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics will be revealed daily from Oct 5-12.
The medicine prize, to be announced at 11.30am on Oct 5, could go to research that paved the way for weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro, Nobel watchers told AFP.
That could include microbiome research, the discovery of the leptin and ghrelin hormones regulating satiety and hunger, and research into a hormone released by the intestine after we eat which signals satiety, called “glucagon-like peptide 1” (GLP-1), which drugs like Ozempic mimic.
“A Nobel Prize recognising any of that work is a likelihood,” said David Pendlebury, who heads research analysis at data analytics firm Clarivate, which predicts potential Nobel winners based on the number of citations of their work.
“I would put GLP-1 at the top of the list, just because of its enormous worldwide clinical impact,” he said.
Many scientists have made significant contributions in the field, although three who have been regularly mentioned for the Nobel are Canadian endocrinologist Daniel Drucker, Danish physician Jens Juul Holst and Yugoslav-born American chemist Svetlana Mojsov.
Skin science or immunology?
If the Nobel Committee were to go in another direction, stem cell research into how skin regenerates and heals wounds could get the nod, with American cell biologist Elaine Fuchs and her British colleague, Fiona Watt, being recognised as leaders in the field, according to Annika Ostman, a science reporter at the Swedish public broadcaster SR.
The honour could also go to a new imaging technique, called optical coherence tomography.
The non-invasive technique uses reflected light to create high-resolution, cross-sectional images of biological tissues, particularly the retina and optic nerve, allowing doctors to detect and monitor disease.
Yet another field that may have caught the medicine committee’s eye is that of adhesion receptors in the immune system, identified by US immunologist Timothy Springer.
These receptors are molecular grips on immune cells that help them stick to blood vessels, enter tissues, and reach infections.
They are crucial for directing the body’s immune defences and are targets for research into treatments of several inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.
Research into breast cancer or DNA sequencing that helped combat coronavirus could also be honoured.
The medicine prize will be followed by the prizes for physics on Oct 6 and chemistry on Oct 7.
The literature laureate will be revealed on Oct 8, with some pundits suggesting that the Swedish Academy could follow up the 2025 award to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a woman writer, possibly from Latin America.
Argentinian author Samanta Schweblin, 48, could be one such pick, literary critic Lina Kalmteg told AFP.
Others often mentioned in Nobel speculation include Antiguan-American author Jamaica Kincaid, Chinese writer Can Xue, Australia’s Gerald Murnane and Alexis Wright, Thomas Pynchon of the US and Mexican writer Cristina Rivera Garza.
All eyes on peace
Perhaps the most keenly anticipated award is that due on Oct 9, the peace prize – the only Nobel to be awarded in Oslo.
For 2026, some experts have suggested the jury could choose a laureate who enjoys broad consensus, after the 2025 winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, stirred controversy.
US President Donald Trump lobbied intensively in 2025 to get the prize – Machado ended up giving him her Nobel medal – and the committee is aware he will be watching closely again.
“There’s always a lot of lobbying, and ultimately perhaps also attempts to exert pressure on the committee,” the secretary of the Nobel Committee, Kristian Berg Harpviken, told AFP in an interview.
“We’re very used to that.”
Among possible laureates in 2026 are a joint prize to Save the Children and Mykola Kuleba, a Ukrainian children’s rights activist campaigning for the return of Ukrainian children illegally taken to Russia from occupied territories.
Others include Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms, which is a vast network of volunteers who risk their lives to help people facing the double threat of war and hunger, and the Committee to Protect Journalists, after the deadliest year on record for the profession in 2025.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on Oct 12. AFP

Quebec separatists favoured to win Canada vote in test for Carney
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Quebec separatists favoured to win Canada vote in test for Carney
MONTREAL – Quebec separatists are favoured to win the election on Oct 5 in Canada’s majority French-speaking province, testing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s message of national unity to confront the United States.
Carney is popular in Quebec, and the expected success of the separatist Parti Quebecois (PQ) is not seen as a repudiation of his defiance towards US President Donald Trump, whose trade war and annexation threats have infuriated Canadians.
The PQ’s possible return to power after 12 years in opposition is tied to frustration over affordability and declining public services, rather than a growing desire among Quebecers to leave Canada, experts and polls say.
Recent surveys put support for an independent Quebec at roughly 30%.
Polls also give the PQ about 30% support, but in the province’s first-past-the-post electoral system, that could be enough to secure a majority in the 127-member National Assembly, with the federalist vote expected to split among several parties.
PQ leader Paul Saint-Pierre Plamondon, a 49-year-old lawyer known widely by his initials PSPP, insists he will call a referendum on leaving Canada if elected, just not while Trump is in office.
In August, he said a decision on Quebec’s independence “requires conditions that allow for an informed and calm debate”.
That debate should not be “hijacked by the theatrics of an unpredictable president”, he added, ruling out a referendum until at least 2029.
Quebec has held two previous votes on leaving Canada. Federalists won comfortably in 1980, but the 1995 result was excruciatingly close, with just 50.58% voting to stay in Canada.
‘Balance of power’
Polls in the province of roughly nine million people open at 9.30am local time, and the results should be known a few hours after voting ends at 8pm.
PSPP has attacked Carney’s federal government and said that, if he is elected premier, the relationship will be defined by a “balance of power”.
“There will be dialogue, but the condition for cooperation is that Quebec be respected,” he told public broadcaster Radio-Canada.
If Quebec is not respected, “I won’t sweep under the rug the fact that it’s unacceptable”, he added.
Carney is facing a complex set of conflicting forces.
His Liberal government enjoys broad support, and many Canadians credit him with leading national – and at times international – opposition to Trump.
But in addition to the possible return of separatist governance in Quebec, voters in the oil-rich province of Alberta will hold a non-binding vote in October on whether they want independence.
Asked on Oct 1 about the upcoming Quebec vote, Carney assured his government would work “with the next Quebec premier in a spirit of cooperative federalism”.
‘Abolish the monarchy?’
PSPP may not have majority backing for an independent Quebec, but his plans to target the British monarchy appear far more popular.
Canada is part of the British Commonwealth. King Charles III, Canada’s head of state, is represented in Ottawa by the governor-general. Lieutenant-governors represent the monarchy in the provinces, including Quebec.
In a 2025 Leger poll, 87% of Quebecers said they felt no attachment to the British monarchy, and only 31% expressed a favourable view of King Charles.
“There is nothing preventing (Quebec’s) National Assembly from acting as a sovereign parliament and passing a law that abolishes the activities of the lieutenant-governor and no longer allocates a budget to this masquerade that wastes money,” said PSPP.
He has proposed reallocating the lieutenant-governor’s budget to combat homelessness. AFP

Badenoch ally attacks Burnham’s ‘hope hard enough’ economic message as ‘absolutely mad’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Badenoch ally attacks Burnham’s ‘hope hard enough’ economic message as ‘absolutely mad’
Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary Helen Whately says Conservatives will present “very different view of the country” — and defends policy on pensions triple lock.
BIRMINGHAM, England — One of Kemi Badenoch’s most senior frontbench colleagues has branded Andy Burnham’s conference speech last week as “absolutely mad.”
Speaking to POLITICO, Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, argued that a “very different view of the country” will become clear at the Conservative Party conference this week.
“I see Andy Burnham saying, look, if we just hope hard enough, everything will be fine, and let’s achieve growth by taxing more and spending more, and more public ownership and more regulation,” she said. “To me, as a Conservative, that is absolutely mad. That is how you make our economy worse, and that is how you make people poorer.”
Advertisement
Her fierce attack on Burnham’s speech reveals a more combative approach from Badenoch and her shadow cabinet as the conference in Birmingham gets underway. Whately accused the prime minister of having the “wrong political philosophy and understanding of the economy.”
She left little wriggle room when she defended the party’s approach to the triple lock, a state pension increase guarantee introduced by the Tories — and now being tweaked by Burnham to fund a social care overhaul.
Over the weekend, Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Conservatives would commit to the triple lock “for this parliament” — without making an express pledge to keep it in the party’s next manifesto.
But the shadow work and pensions struck a more defiant tone. “Kemi is absolutely dead clear about it,” Whately insisted in her POLITICO interview. “The triple lock is Conservative policy. The answer to the problems that our country faces isn’t to go after pensioners. The answer is to get people working, and the core to my brief is to make savings from the welfare bill where we’ve got seven million people of working age on out-of-work benefits. Let’s get some of those seven million people into work.”
Childcare drive
Whately also defended the Conservative Party’s pledge to offer free childcare to parents earning over £100,000. The current “cliff edge” means parents in England lose out on tens of thousands of pounds of childcare support when they reach this income.
The former Conservative MP Miriam Cates has questioned whether the policy might harm support for parents who want to stay at home rather than get back into the workplace as soon as possible, and risks treating them as “economic units.”
Advertisement
But Whately said: “I’ve had those arguments sometimes with colleagues, Miriam included, about whether we should be doing the kind of policies that some other countries do. I think Hungary was the obvious example of more paying people to essentially have children. Those are things are incredibly expensive. We’re not going down that route.”
“What we have to do is we have to make sure that our tax system supports growth, supports the economy,” she added.
Whately vowed that the Conservatives would meanwhile clamp down on access to working-age benefits. “The way that we are assessing people for access to sickness benefits is very flawed,” she said. “A huge amount of assessments are done over the phone, just with forms, people not being seen in person… it means that those who really are sick are now having to sort of compete with all the benefits of those who have seen on the internet how they can most effectively make sure they maximize their claim.”
Pressed on whether the party’s opponents could seize on policies curbing access to social security — as has happened to the Trump administration in the U.S. as it clamped down on programs like food assistance — Whately said: “This is specifically about people who could and should be working. It isn’t a policy about people who have disabilities and who are on the Universal Credit health component.”
Whately was also pressed on her former friendship with Robert Jenrick, a one-time Conservative leadership contender who has defected to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.
The Tory conference center this year boasts a spoof Bayeux Tapestry on prominent display — which includes several images of Jenrick, the former shadow justice secretary. Whately and Jenrick were close colleagues until his switch to Reform earlier this year.
“I’m not feeling like we’re missing him right now,” Whately said. “I considered Rob a friend, and now he’s not a friend in my life … because of the way he behaved, and because he lied to people and deceived people.”

====================================================================================================

4 reasons for Kemi Badenoch to be cheerful — and 3 looming headaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Kemi Badenoch speaks to the media after visiting the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum in London on Sept. 11, 2026. | Alishia Abodunde/Getty Images
BIRMINGHAM, England — Britain’s Conservatives don’t get many opportunities to feel upbeat these days — but Kemi Badenoch is heading into party conference with a modest spring in her step.
The Tory leader — who in 2024 took over an outfit near-obliterated by its worst general election result in history — can point to disarray in her chief rival’s ranks, decent personal ratings and some clear dividing lines with Labour as just a few reasons to be cheerful.
Yet it’s still a massive road back for the once-dominant center-right party. Let POLITICO give you the view from Tory land as the West Midlands gathering gets going in earnest.
Advertisement
On the upside
1) Badenoch’s personal ratings are on the up
The British public’s view of the Tory leader has improved sharply since she took over.
YouGov polling last month found 32% of voters now have a favorable view of Badenoch, compared to 47% who view her unfavorably.
It’s hardly stirring stuff, but that net rating — of minus 15 — is 20 points higher than a year ago. And that is beginning to vindicate some party strategists’ belief that the more the public sees of Badenoch, the more it likes her.
Robert Jenrick delivers his keynote speech during the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham, England on Sept. 5, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
Badenoch also has no serious internal competitor trying to remove her, following Robert Jenrick’s defection to right-wing populist Reform UK earlier this year. Jenrick narrowly lost the Tory leadership race to Badenoch in 2024, and was widely seen as hankering for her job before his abrupt departure to Nigel Farage’s army.
“Compared to last year when lots of people were sharpening their knives to bring Kemi down, going into this conference the mood is actually very good,” said one Tory adviser, granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Kemi has found her voice and is doing well in taking the fight to Labour.”
2) Farage has had a messy summer
The party’s year has also been helped by the trials and tribulations of their chief opponents.
Advertisement
The Conservatives’ main competitors on the right, Reform UK, enjoyed stellar results at May’s local elections, and there was serious talk of them eclipsing the Tories as the U.K.’s real opposition.
Since then, however, Farage has faced months of scrutiny about his party’s finances, and spent the summer campaigning in a self-imposed by-election entirely focused on his own position.
“A year ago, it felt like Reform UK had cannibalized the British right behind them, whereas now that seems much more up for grabs,” says Keiran Pedley, the U.K. director of politics at polling company Ipsos. “It doesn’t mean that the Tories have won that argument, but at least there is an argument to be had.”
Nigel Farage speaks during a Reform UK rally in Doncaster, England on Oct. 1, 2026. | Christopher Furlong/Getty Images
Reform UK still leads the Tories in national voting intention, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls, and it has gained a real toehold in local government that will help it build out an election-fighting machine.
But, says Pedley: “If you’re a voter on the right of politics in Britain, maybe as you become less impressed by Nigel Farage, you’re also looking to Kemi Badenoch, hoping that she can be the answer.”
Farage was widely criticized for failing to declare a £5 million gift he received from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne in the 12 months before he became an MP, while there’s been a fresh flood of cash to Reform UK in recent months.
Advertisement
In an eve-of-conference interview with the Tory-supporting Spectator magazine, Badenoch claimed the megabucks donations have “encouraged quite a few people to give us a bit more” to stay on the field.
3) She’s stamped her authority on the Tory top team
Badenoch revamped her Shadow Cabinet at the tail-end of the summer recess in a bid to take the fight to Labour under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Mel Stride, who fought the 2024 leadership contest and was a staunch loyalist to ex-PM Rishi Sunak, was replaced as shadow chancellor by Andrew Griffith. Griffith spent decades in business before working for Boris Johnson, and though Labour has leapt on his time as Treasury minister during former Prime Minister Liz Truss’ budget meltdown, the Tories believe his private sector experience adds real heft.
Tom Tugendhat speaks during an event in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. | Paul Morigi/Getty Images for Concordia Summit
Priti Patel — a Boris Johnson-era Cabinet big-hitter — was moved out of her role as shadow foreign secretary, in favor of the well-respected Tom Tugendhat, an ex-security minister who also chaired the Commons’ Foreign Affairs Committee.
Though a more centrist, one-nation Conservative, he has accepted Badenoch’s more hardline policies, like pushing to leave the European Convention on Human Rights.
“At our conference, we will show the country that the Conservative Party is different from the one that lost the last election,” a Tory spokesperson said. “We will set out our plan to reverse Labour’s economic decline, build a stronger economy and a stronger country, and get Britain working again.”
Advertisement
4) Andy Burnham has opened up space for a grey vote challenge
The biggest announcement from Burnham’s first conference speech as Labour leader has the potential to be a gift to the Tories, who have long felt able to rely on support from Britain’s older voters.
Burnham has vowed to reform the “triple lock” — introduced by the Tories when they were last in office and all but guaranteeing generous annual state pension rises — a move that opens up space for the Conservatives to go on the attack.
Privately, plenty of Tories would love to make the same move, because of the strain the triple lock places on the country’s public finances. “Literally no MP or party official think keeping the triple lock is a good thing,” the same adviser quoted above said. “It just boxes the party and the leadership in.”
Andy Burnham is seen during the Labour Conference in Liverpool, England on Sept. 30, 2026. | Christopher Furlong/Getty Images
But that hasn’t stopped Badenoch and her team from going straight on the attack. “His proposal to change the triple lock is already falling apart under scrutiny, and it won’t generate enough savings to fund a nationalized care system for another two decades, which means more tax rises are inevitable,” she said of Burnham last week.
On the downside
1) The Tories haven’t broken through in national polls
Despite Badenoch’s improved personal position, the Conservatives still lag in national polls and don’t appear anywhere close to forming a House of Commons majority after the next election.
POLITICO’s Poll of Polls has seen the party slip into third place behind Labour and Reform UK ever since Keir Starmer’s resignation as PM. Hovering around the 18% to 19% mark, they’re still polling lower than the national 23.7% vote share Rishi Sunak sank to in 2024.
Advertisement
Pedley warns there’s a difference between voters liking Badenoch as leader and believing the Tories have “the right plans, the right team of leaders [and are] ready to govern the country credibly in the future.”
2) A divided right could give Labour a hand
Even with Reform UK’s bumpy summer, Farage’s party is a national contender — and splitting the right-wing vote in some constituencies could let Labour or the Lib Dems cruise through the middle.
So far, the Conservatives and Reform UK have both insisted there will be no electoral alliance between the pair.
The Tories argue it’s impossible to work with Reform UK thanks to Farage’s history of falling out with once-close allies, while Reform UK sees the Tories as damaged goods who’ve wrecked the country. (That hasn’t stopped them grabbing a fair few defectors, of course.)
3) The specter of Brexit returns
Burnham also made closer relations with the European Union a key part of his conference pitch — thrusting a largely dormant part of British political discourse back to the centre.
Demonstrators attend a Rejoin rally in London on June 20, 2026. | Brook Mitchell/Getty Images
And it’s a divisive one for the Tories, who have spent decades riven by splits about the EU. While many former supporters of staying in the bloc have now left the Conservatives, the increased salience of Europe could reopen old wounds.
Polling shows many voters believe Brexit — which the Tories presided over — hasn’t gone well. That’s not the same as wanting to rejoin altogether, but the Conservatives may now be forced to defend a project they’d just about moved on from.

Meet the 4 lawmakers vying to lead the Green charge in the EU Parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

BRUSSELS — The Greens in the European Parliament will on Tuesday pick new leaders, as the group seeks to reverse its waning influence amid Europe’s rightward shift and launch a comeback in the 2029 EU election.
The vote is part of the Parliament’s midterm reshuffle, with a host of top posts up for grabs. The Greens are voting now because Bas Eickhout resigned in May as leader of the group and as an MEP amid revelations of undisclosed relationships with staffers. Eickhout was not only the face of the Greens in the Parliament, but also one of the best-known MEPs in Brussels and in his native Netherlands.
With other group leaders expected to stay in post — or with succession deals already struck — the Green vote is likely to be the reshuffle’s only open leadership race, and as has long been the case, they’ll pick two co-chairs. The candidates are working the phones and going office-to-office to secure the backing of the group’s 53 lawmakers (the Greens are the sixth-largest group in the Parliament).
Advertisement
All four broadly back a shift from pragmatic dealmaking inside the Parliament toward more offensive mobilization, gearing up for a 2029 EU election in which they hope to reverse heavy losses in 2024, and getting lawmakers out of Parliament and onto the streets.
POLITICO spoke to all the candidates. The vote takes place on Tuesday, with a press conference scheduled for 6.15 p.m. to announce the winners.
Terry Reintke — the continuity candidate
Germany’s Reintke has helped lead the group since 2022 and is widely expected to win one of the two co-chair posts. “I’m quite optimistic, quite confident,” she said in an interview.
Reintke says she believes the Greens can exert influence through pragmatic dealmaking, but also wants to take a more assertive approach.
Terry Reintke takes part in a vote during a plennary session at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on May 20, 2026. | Sebastien Bozon/AFP via Getty Images
The group “is really longing to focus more on external communication … to be more outspoken, to be more with the people, to go more outside of the European Parliament, to be more on the ground,” she said, adding that “this is … a sort of politics that I come from, that I was raised with.”
Such a change does not mean removing the Greens from the majority that supports the Commission, Reintke argued. Despite its rightward shift and rollback of green policies, the group can still secure wins by negotiating, she said, citing as an example the EU’s 2040 climate target, which falls short of Green ambitions but remains in place.
Advertisement
“I think this is going to stay,” she said of the pragmatic dealmaking. On some occasions, however, when the group considers it can’t win anything from a deal, “we are ready to also go into oppositional mode.”
That captures the tension shaping the race. Some national delegations within the Greens favor compromise and continued support for Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, while others want a tougher stance against her executive, which is dominated by the conservative European People’s Party.
Nicolae Ștefănuță — the grassroots newcomer
Ștefănuță joined the Greens in 2023 after defecting from the liberals. He ran as an independent in the 2024 EU election, gathering more than 100,000 signatures urging him to stand and 300,000 votes, according to his pitch for the leadership. He has put that grassroots success at the heart of his bid.
Nicolae Ștefănuță is pictured at an exhibition at the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Nov. 25, 2025. | Magali Cohen/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
“I have this special expertise in winning, in doing modern campaigns that we need to do in Europe to fight off the far-right,” he said.
He is also playing the geographic-balance card as the group’s eastern and southern wings seek a more diverse leadership. “I’m from the East and I’ve been … working with everybody, no matter what the region,” he said.
“I have a confidence to really build bridges between all the members of the group and be really a uniter.”
Advertisement
Like Reintke, Ștefănuță says the Greens should strike deals where possible. “I don’t believe in automatic opposition,” he told POLITICO.
He is courting smaller delegations by promising to give them a greater voice and prevent the priorities of larger national groups from dominating.
“I am also running against the idea of maintaining the status quo. We have not always done things right. We should not be complacent,” he wrote in his email pitch to fellow MEPs, in an apparent dig at previous leadership.
“We have not always treated everyone with understanding. The 13 one-person delegations of this group sometimes feel lonely. Instead of asking what they deliver, why don’t we ask what they need? How can we help you?” he wrote.
Isabella Lövin — the former minister
Lövin is selling experience, reliability and a network she says can help shape EU policy.
She served as Sweden’s international development minister, environment minister and deputy prime minister between 2016 and 2021, after a stint as an MEP from 2009 to 2014.
Advertisement
Her goal for the next two-and-a-half years “is to make the Greens as relevant as possible” to fight the far right and put Europe back on “a course” toward sustainability, reduced inequality and less dependence on fossil fuels.
“We should never give up on trying to influence the legislative work,” she said, while also becoming “more vocal on issues which really are understandable to our voters.”
Her experience among EU ministers “could also open a few doors to have us [be] more relevant in discussions,” she said. “I have a very extensive network throughout Europe, all colleagues, both green and not green, to try to kind of … navigate these very, very stormy waters and make us relevant through that.”
Isabella Lövin is selling experience, reliability and a network she says can help shape EU policy. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Lövin said her profile complements Reintke’s activist and grassroots links, and she expects Reintke to be reelected. Together, they “can cover many areas and speak to different audiences,” she said.
She acknowledged divisions over how pragmatic versus oppositional the Greens should be, and said the group should allow each delegation to do what’s best in a national context. “My leadership style is always to listen to everyone and try to find a good joint idea about how to go forward,” she said.
“We should focus more on how to communicate and to help smaller delegations to communicate back home.”

Sara Matthieu — the policy hand
Flemish MEP Matthieu casts herself as both a grassroots campaigner and pragmatic dealmaker with extensive policy expertise — pitched somewhere between Ștefănuță and Lövin.
Inside Parliament, Matthieu says the Greens must stand their ground and be “super clear” on issues such as further environmental rollbacks.
“I do think we need to be clearer in some of those battles, where we really have to say, ‘guys, now as a Commission, but also as a Parliament, you are taking it too far. This is really not acceptable anymore.’”
Sara Matthieu participates in a plenary session of the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Sept. 15, 2026. | Philippe Buissin/European Parliament
At the same time, the Greens must keep pressing the Commission for results, she said, citing von der Leyen’s recent heat action plan as a product of the group’s “pressure.”
“It’s not just the battle inside of the Parliament that we need to win, it’s also outside. It’s out on the streets and it’s conquering people’s hearts with the message.”
“For the last two-and-a-half years, we have been the adults in the room, holding the center together while the EPP had no problem relying on far-right majorities to get its way. We did a lot of damage control against this Commission’s reckless deregulation agenda. With me as co-president, we will shift our priorities,” she wrote in her program sent to fellow lawmakers.

She says her policy expertise and track record set her apart. She helped shape the group’s green industrial strategy and has taken a leading role in the Parliament’s environment committee (she was previously on the employment committee).
Matthieu pointed to “a lot of knowledge on green policies, on climate policies, on protecting people’s health … that is something that sets me apart.”

WASHINGTON – US authorities arrested a California woman on Oct 4 and accused her of spying on a son of Taiwan’s President at the behest of Chinese officials, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said.

Brazil’s presidential race: Three key takeaways from the first round
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
01:55:50 UTC
10:55:50 KST

Brazil’s presidential race: Three key takeaways from the first round
Flavio Bolsonaro beat polling expectations as Brazil’s right gained ground, setting up October 25 run-off with Lula.
Brazil’s closely watched presidential election is heading to a second round between leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, prolonging a deeply polarised race with major implications for the country and the wider region.
Brazil’s electoral court confirmed on Sunday that the two candidates will advance to a run-off on October 25 after neither won the majority needed to secure the presidency outright, with Bolsonaro leading at 56 million votes to Lula’s almost 53 million.
Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term after a political career spanning nearly five decades.
Bolsonaro, 45, is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro and is trying to return his father’s right-wing movement to power, even as the former president serves a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.
The election comes at a pivotal time for Latin America’s largest economy. Brazilians are grappling with concerns over crime and the cost of living, while the country faces an increasingly tense relationship with the United States. The vote is also being closely watched across a region that has shifted sharply to the right in a series of recent elections.
While a second round was widely expected, the first-round result did not play out quite as pollsters had predicted.
Here are some of the key takeaways from the election so far.
Brazil is heading for another Lula-Bolsonaro run-off
With nearly 99 percent of votes reported, Bolsonaro had about 47 percent of valid votes, compared with 44.9 percent for Lula. Neither reached the 50 percent threshold needed to win in the first round.
That sets up another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown, four years after Lula narrowly defeated former President Jair Bolsonaro. This time, he will face the former president’s eldest son.
The race could be extremely close, as polling ahead of Sunday’s vote suggested Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro were roughly tied in a potential run-off.
That puts voters who backed one of the other 10 candidates in the first round at the centre of the fight for the presidency over the next three weeks.
Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, who together received about 5.3 million votes, have previously said they will not endorse either candidate in the run-off.
Flavio Bolsonaro did better than polls suggested
Most polls leading up to election day predicted the race would be pushed into the second round, but had Lula finishing the first round ahead of Bolsonaro.
Instead, Bolsonaro emerged with a lead of two percentage points, raising questions about why the final polls underestimated his support.
On Sunday, Bolsonaro said the results showed that Brazilians want change.
Analysts told the Reuters news agency that Bolsonaro may have benefitted from “protest votes” from people who may have preferred another candidate but saw defeating Lula as the priority. Many had been expected to shift their support to Bolsonaro only in a second round, meaning this could have consequences for his support in three weeks.
“The protest vote foreshadows what is to come in the run-off,” political analyst Rafael Favetti told Reuters. “While this should benefit Flavio Bolsonaro now, his growth potential in the second round drops precisely because that support has already been front-loaded.”
After the results came in, Lula said the votes were “unexpected” but that he would come back stronger in the run-off.
“I admit, I was convinced I would win in the first round. The game is about to start. We are in extra time. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people,” the 80-year-old said.
The right had a strong night in Congress, too
Bolsonaro’s surprising performance in the first round was part of a broader show of strength for Brazil’s right.
Right-wing parties, led by Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL), were performing strongly in both houses of Congress, with the PL on track to emerge as the largest force in the Chamber of Deputies and making gains in the Senate.
This included victories for other members of the Bolsonaro family, including former First Lady Michelle Bolsonaro, Flavio’s stepmother, who won a Senate seat in the Federal District, her first elected office.
His brother, Carlos Bolsonaro, was elected to the Senate in Santa Catarina.
The results show that the political movement built around former President Jair Bolsonaro – known as “bolsonarista” – remains a powerful electoral force, even with the former president barred from running himself.
“The fact that far-right candidates for the legislature have exceeded all expectations suggests a deeper popular grounding for the bolsonarista project than many expected,” Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and author of a book on Lula, told Al Jazeera.
“Millions of Brazilians right now evidently feel the right best reflects their values and vision for the future,” he added.
The congressional results matter beyond election night, too. Both houses were already dominated by conservative lawmakers, and a stronger right-wing presence could make it even harder for Lula to push through his agenda if he wins another term.
A Bolsonaro victory, meanwhile, could give him more room to pursue his own priorities, including his pledge to seek an amnesty for his father.

ISW analyses why Russia is rushing to strike Ukraine's energy infrastructure
Analysts from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) have said that Russia is beginning its campaign of strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure earlier than usual, before Ukraine can develop effective measures to counter Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
Source: ISW report on 4 October
Details: The report said that the Russian Defence Ministry had set out its main rhetorical justification for the upcoming brutal Russian campaign of strikes against Ukraine's critical infrastructure in the autumn and winter of 2026-2027.
The Russian ministry presented the escalation as a response to "alleged Ukrainian strikes against Russian civilian targets in multiple instances since June 2026".
ISW analysts suggested that Ukraine's battlefield successes in 2026 appear to be "forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to reevaluate his original theory of victory in Ukraine and shift focus to compelling Ukraine to surrender through the winter 2026-2027 long-range strike campaign, as opposed to advances on the battlefield". [N.B. Ukrainska Pravda does not recognise Putin as president – ed.]
The report added that this "strike campaign aims to make civilian life in Ukraine unbearable such that Ukraine will capitulate to Russia's demands".
Russia has conducted similar campaigns of strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure every winter since the winter of 2022-2023 and is likely to begin its strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure earlier than usual this year, before Ukraine can develop effective measures to counter Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, which have already caused significant damage.
Quote from the report: "The Russian MoD's rhetorical framing is attempting to justify the intensification of its strike campaign, which will target Ukraine's already-degraded energy infrastructure and other critical infrastructure, to Russians and the international community."

He was the best forward in the grand final, but Whyte's best is yet to come
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
01:50:46 UTC
10:50:46 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Best is yet to come for Naufahu Whyte following NRL grand final victory
The 2026 NRL grand final was the kind of game they'll talk about for years to come.
As it goes further into history and the old stories come out at reunions and in front bars and on podcasts, they'll talk about Kalyn Ponga's try, Newcastle's heroic defence, Mark Nawaqanitawase's whole deal and the big finish.
They'll talk about James Tedesco winning the Clive Churchill Medal and maybe someone will remember his exact number of running metres — an obscene 388.
But what's certain is that at least one person will argue, passionately and adamantly, that Naufahu Whyte was the best player on the field.
There's no wrong answer between Tedesco and Whyte, who were the Roosters' best in the 19-18 victory.
Together, they combined for 55 runs and add Whyte's metres gained (187) to Tedesco's total and they carried the ball for more than half a kilometre.
Where Tedesco had 12 tackle busts, two forced dropouts and a try assist, Whyte forced several errors with his brutal defence, affirmed his status as one of the best forwards in the game and created the ruck speed that helped lead to Nawaqanitawase's crucial second-half try.
Winning the award as a middle isn't easy either, because even though you never win a comp without a few good ones, they always seem to miss out.
Sam Burgess was the last middle forward to win the Churchill medal when he led South Sydney from the front in 2014. Before then, you have to go back to Brent Kite in 2008 to find the last front-rower to do it.
For his part, the 24-year-old was happy to defer to his skipper.
"He deserves it; he's been doing it all year," Whyte said.
"I have big love for my captain and what he's done for the game. I'll say he's the best fullback in the game ever. That's my brother."
While Tedesco took home the medal, Whyte's own trophy cabinet has become cluttered in a short space of time.
His premiership ring will vie with the Dally M Prop Of The Year award he won last week for pride of place, but if Whyte keeps up this form, there's sure to be more to come.
Especially if Whyte is telling the truth when he says there's still major improvement in him despite dominating on the game's biggest stage on Sunday night.
"I know this isn't my best. It's far from it. I'm still just at the start of my career. There's a lot of work to put in," Whyte said.
"In the grand final, I had to take it next level. It's not easy winning a grand final, and the Knights were always going to show up, so I had to push myself.
"Taking carry after carry, that's what I'll do for my brothers. It's paid off for me so far.
"We came in confident we would get the job done, even down six, because that's the belief we have in each other, that's the belief we have in this team."
That belief proved crucial for the Tricolours as they claimed their first premiership since 2018-19, especially in coming back from 12-0 down with a Knights ambush eminently possible.
Whyte, who watches highlights of those games all the time, now has a version of it that he can not just replay but relive.
"Everything is going through my head and my heart now. I just want to embrace this moment and enjoy every part of it, because it's the best feeling ever," Whyte said.
"I screamed, had tears of joy; I was all over the place. All the hard work it took to get here — I'm speechless, brother, I really am."

Can the KKK find a new foothold in the US?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
01:47:13 UTC
10:47:13 KST

Can the KKK find a new foothold in the US?
The infamous hate group is trying to rebrand itself as the ‘Knights Party’ in an attempt to grow its base.
Experts have warned over the past decade of a resurgence in white supremacy in the United States, fuelled in part by the mainstream influence of political figures like President Donald Trump.
Just this year, the Public Religion Research Institute released the results of a 2025 survey that asked more than 20,000 US adults to evaluate the statement, “Immigrants are invading our country and replacing our cultural and ethnic background.”
That belief is the cornerstone of the great replacement theory, a conspiracy that falsely claims that immigrants, Jews and nonwhite groups seek to supplant white people in Western countries.
The research institute found that 32 percent of respondents – nearly one in three – nevertheless agreed with the idea.
Critics have accused right-wing leaders like Trump of normalising such views, through rhetoric that paints immigration as an “invasion” and “an assault on Western countries”.
Trump has also been accused of cosying up to white nationalists, even dining in 2022 with Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes, a key figure in the movement. When white nationalists engaged in a deadly clash with protesters in Charlottesville, Virginia, in 2017, Trump said there were “fine people on both sides”.
Al Jazeera correspondent Phil Lavelle travelled to Boone County, Arkansas, to see whether one of the most infamous white supremacist organisations in US history had seen a bump in its influence midway through Trump’s second term.
He spoke to Thomas Robb, the head of what was formerly known as the Knights of the Ku Klux Klan, a white supremacist group founded in the 1970s by David Duke.
What Lavelle found was a group seemingly eager to rebrand. The group had shortened its title to The Knights Party, and members told Lavelle they were trying to re-centre their message around family and faith.
But when Lavelle asked if a Black person would be welcome at the group’s church, Robb’s answer was simple.
“No,” Robb responded. “Because this is a white nationalist church.”
The Ku Klux Klan (KKK) has a long history of racism and violence in the US. The movement began at the end of the civil war in 1865, as a response to government efforts to expand civil rights to Black people and other minority groups.
Through lynchings and other targeted acts of violence, the KKK attempted to block non-white participation in government and maintain racial divides.
Robb, a Christian pastor, took over as the head of the Knights of the Ku Klux Klan – a faction of the KKK – in 1989. He has since attempted to broaden the group’s appeal.
He changed his title from “grand wizard” to “national director”, allowed new members to participate confidentially by mail, and distanced himself from KKK violence in public outreach campaigns.
Still, he has adhered to the racist philosophy his organisation is known for.
“What do you make of politicians like Zohran Mamdani or Abdul El-Sayed?” Lavelle asked Robb in his interview, referencing two high-profile US politicians who identify as Muslim.
“Well, first off, they’re not Americans,” Robb said. When Lavelle pointed out that El-Sayed was born in Michigan, Robb brushed off the contradiction. “I don’t care where he’s born. He’s not American.”
He proceeded to draw a distinction between the children of white and non-white immigrants. Only the children of white foreigners can be American, Robb said, “because they’re white”.
The Knights of the Ku Klux Klan is one of dozens of white supremacy organisations operating in the US.
The Southern Poverty Law Center, an advocacy group, estimates that there are at least 152 such groups active in the US today, part of what it calls a rising trend over the last decade.
Just this year, another white supremacist organisation, the Patriot Front, marched through Washington, DC, during the Independence Day holiday.
Critics say Trump, at times, has echoed their rhetoric. Trump told The New York Times earlier this year that “white people were very badly treated” in fields like academics.
He also instructed his second administration to dismantle diversity initiatives, and under his leadership, the government has launched probes into whether universities and companies like Nike discriminate against white people.
In addition, Trump has given priority to white South Africans in refugee admissions, falsely claiming they are the subject of a “genocide”.
Robb claimed the current rise in white nationalist sentiment began well before Trump, in 2008, during the election of Barack Obama, the country’s first Black president.
“People are beginning to stir and being angered by what they see happening to the country,” said Robb. “So we’re kind of a voice for that.”
Still, Robb acknowledged public wariness of joining a white supremacist group like his. “As for people actually to become members, that’s kind of a line they [are] a little hesitant to cross sometimes,” he said.
He also declined when asked to provide membership numbers or provide evidence for his assertion that support for his movement “is growing”.
“Maybe we’re wrong. Maybe everybody hates us. I don’t know,” Robb said.

Dating app from ex-Tinder executive lets strangers play matchmaker
