Dating app from ex-Tinder executive lets strangers play matchmaker
- A new dating app, Rivet, launched by former Tinder executive Taru Kapoor, lets volunteer "matchers" vote on strangers' compatibility to reduce swiping burnout and improve match quality.
- Rivet uses AI and community votes to create compatibility scores, offering users curated matches and features like visual blending of photos and social matchmaking events.
- The app gamifies matchmaking with rewards, leaderboards and live events to engage users, aiming to provide affordable, human-curated dating experiences beyond traditional algorithms.
AI generated
NEW YORK – A former Tinder executive launched a new dating app that invites the community to vote on strangers’ compatibility, putting a twist on courtship at a time when singles have grown exhausted with swiping.
Rivet, which opens to US users on Oct 8, relies on a pool of volunteer “matchers” who rate whether two given people might be compatible.
The idea is to prioritise quality connections over quantity, giving daters just a few pre-vetted options at a time, founder and chief executive Taru Kapoor said in an interview. That may include some prospects who fall outside the user’s typical preferences.
“It surfaces a lot of people that you may otherwise swipe past, especially because when you’re swiping through like 200 people on Bumble or Hinge, and people get faster and faster, more and more transactional and judgmental,” said Kapoor, who spent eight years at Tinder and was a general manager for several Asian markets.
Dating-app companies have been making major changes to their products in a bid to lure back singles who have reported burnout.
Bumble and Match Group’s Tinder host in-person meet-ups to get people off the app and keep users engaged. Bumble has also added an artificial intelligence-powered matchmaking tool as an alternative to swiping, and it gives men a chance to make the first move, not just women.
New York-based Rivet, which raised US$10.5 million (S$13.4 million) in seed funding and has been testing in select markets, is available on iOS and Android. It is free to join, but some features are paywalled, including the ability to message someone without having been matched by the community first.
The platform is built on the premise that aggregating wisdom from a crowd can help cancel out individual biases for better results.
Users fill out their profiles with information about what they are looking for, and the algorithm suggests potential pairings. Matchers then review the profiles and cast their vote, resulting in a composite compatibility score. High-scoring pairs are matched and can choose to start chatting.
“It’s very easy for most of us to look at a friend who may be dating the wrong person and ask, ‘Why?’” Kapoor said. “Most humans are actually pretty good at reading other people.”
People also tend to be “more objective and rational”, she added, when they are outsiders looking in on someone else’s life.
Rivet is not the first dating platform to outsource matchmaking to a community of volunteers.
In 2025, American reality star Bethenny Frankel launched the Core, where daters receive curated matches from their peers.
It is unclear if either of these alternative dating platforms has a chance of pulling in large numbers of users.
Kapoor’s app is attempting to stand out with an AI-powered visualisation feature that blends photo pairs together, helping users gauge vibe and height compatibility side by side.
“Humans introducing humans is the oldest technology,” Kapoor said. “A lot of people are turning to matchmaking – human curation – more than before, but it’s very expensive. If you can afford a US$20,000 matchmaker, great. But if you can’t, how about I give you several different matches for free?”
Rivet tries in different ways to gamify the experience to persuade people to return. Matchers can earn “karma currency” when successful matches are made, which can be redeemed for profile perks, direct introductions, cash rewards or gift cards. (The ability to reach out to someone without having matched costs 1,000 in karma points for one message. A pack of 3,000 karma costs US$9.99.)
The app also includes features such as weekly top-matcher leaderboards, live events and promotions that cover half the cost of a first date.
“People can log onto the app and there are social match events happening live, with a host and a pair on the screen,” she said.
“A lot of people join in and then the audience asks questions. We are bringing this energy of sort of making the crowd your wingmen.” BLOOMBERG

Bank of America met with Australian super funds and delivered a warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
01:44:38 UTC
10:44:38 KST

analysis
Rising rates could 'bite' into Australia's $4.5 trillion superannuation sector, Bank of America warns
What would it take to put the global economy into a tailspin?
The Bank of America, which is worth roughly $US275 billion ($395 billion), and dependent to a degree on functioning financial markets, is asking itself that question.
The answer lies in the cost of debt.
Low productivity, excess demand, the boom in artificial intelligence and the Iran war are all pushing up the cost of borrowing.
Despite this, interest rate increases have not yet done too much damage to share markets, property prices, or indeed many advanced economies.
But the Bank of America's head of interest rates strategy Mark Cabana has estimated the cost of borrowing, or level of interest rates, that would cause financial damage.
He says we are not far from that point.
Interest rates are still benign
The Federal Reserve is the US equivalent of Australia's Reserve Bank.
It recently raised America's benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to between 3.75 and 4 per cent.
The trillion-dollar question many central banks are asking themselves is what interest rate level will work to lower overall demand in the economy?
And crucially, when does the cost of borrowing become financially dangerous?
Mr Cabana, who was previously an analyst at the New York Federal Reserve, said the recent US bond market sell-off had led to yields rising to multi-decade highs.
He also said the sell-off was not severe enough to cause steep falls in asset prices.
Bond yields rise when their prices fall.
Yields also rise ahead of increases to central bank interest rates.
"We expect that rates will continue to rise and that the curve will continue to flatten in the US, but also likely globally, simply because the level of interest rates today is not restrictive," Mr Cabana said.
Put simply, Mark Cabana does not believe US interest rates are currently high enough to significantly slow economic growth.
"What that means is that interest rates have not risen high enough to actually see [in macroeconomic data] any type of slowing," he said.
"So it seems like the market is generally comfortable with the extent of the rate move thus far."
US interest rates heading higher
Goldman Sachs has pushed its forecast for the next US interest rate hike to December.
It did this after a softer than anticipated inflation reading last week cooled expectations the Federal Reserve would hike rates again in October.
A December rate hike would push the fed funds target to between 4 and 4.25 per cent.
This interest rate level, Mark Cabana believes, is approaching the economic and financial danger zone, with greater concerns if expectations push into the high 4s and mid-5 per cents.
"That might be more consistent with some signs that we start to see a tightening of financial conditions and slowing in macroeconomic growth," he said.
Interest rate tipping point
Australia is already seeing a cooling of the housing market and the share market is also well off its August highs.
The Australian government's 10-year bond yield, the interest rate it needs to pay to borrow money for a decade, has risen to its highest level since 2011.
All working Australians would be mindful of this because it has direct implications for their superannuation balances.
Mr Cabana recently visited Sydney to, among other things, address the nation's superannuation heavyweights.
"I know that they are extremely focused on this question as well [of when interest rates will be restrictive to growth]," he told The Business.
Loading
Australian superannuation funds have tens of billions of dollars' worth of Australian workers' cash tied up on Wall Street, including the big tech companies.
"Our guidance to them would be that they should become much more concerned if you do see that macro data continue to be strong, and that financial conditions are not showing signs of caring,"
Mr Cabana said.
Put simply, he is saying that if the US economy continues to grow, and inflation pressures persist, US interest rates will need to push higher.
Inflation worry is front and centre
Others see more leg room for asset prices to stretch out.
Floodlines Research founder Anna Wu believes the investment boom underway, particularly in artificial intelligence (AI), will overwhelm any short-term financial market gyrations.
"Past rate hiking cycles have taught investors tough lessons, especially 2022 when the Fed lifted rates from near zero to above 4 per cent in nine months, and to above 5 per cent by mid-2023," she said.
"Equities fell because rising rates hit valuations before company profits could catch up."
Ms Wu believes this time is different.
"We are in a slightly different regime now," she said.
"Bond markets expect inflation to stay around its five-year average.
"That means US yields are rising largely because investors expect stronger growth, not runaway prices."
Anna Wu draws the distinction between inflation worries and interest rates responding in a healthy way to the growing US economy.
"Investors should be risk aware,"
she said.
As Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock put it last week when asked if the RBA would need to push the economy into recession to achieve its inflation target, "I guess, possibly."
She added that, "The scenario that I'm thinking of there is if inflation expectations get away from us."
"If that gets away, then that is a circumstance in which I think you might need to have quite a dramatic slowdown in the economy. That's our worry," Ms Bullock said.
It is clearly something Mr Cabana and the Bank of America are worried about too.

What's next?
The Kangaroos will begin their World Cup against New Zealand on October 15.

Denis Becirovic has secured another term as the Bosniak member of Bosnia and Herzegovina's tripartite Presidency, while Darijana Filipovic of the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) has won the Croat seat, according to preliminary election results.
Figures from the Central Election Commission covering 100 percent of regular polling stations showed Becirovic winning 207,281 votes, defeating Bakir Izetbegovic of the Party of Democratic Action (SDA), who took 184,602.
In the Croat contest, Filipovic secured 106,984 votes, unseating the incumbent alignment held by Zeljko Komsic, ahead of Slaven Kovacevic on 70,167.
Incumbent Zeljka Cvijanovic of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) led the Serb member race.
"Our path toward the European Union and membership in NATO must be resolutely continued," Becirovic said after declaring victory, urging Brussels to offer stronger backing and insisting that peace in southeastern Europe underpins wider European stability.
Izetbegovic conceded defeat, though he noted the SDA improved its parliamentary share by roughly 25 percent.
Republika Srpska outcomes
In the Republika Srpska entity, SNSD candidate Savo Minic led the presidential race with 202,245 votes over Serb Democratic Party rival Branko Blanusa on 160,936.
SNSD leader Milorad Dodik declared a sweep across entity and state levels, linking his party's position to US President Donald Trump's victory.
Dodik reiterated demands for a return to the "original Dayton" framework, calling for powers over the armed forces, border police, intelligence services, and indirect taxation to revert from state institutions to Republika Srpska.
Sunday's election marked the first nationwide deployment of biometric identification, electronic ballot scanners, and surveillance across polling stations.
Election Commission President Jovan Kalaba confirmed the scanners operated without disruption, allowing preliminary returns to emerge within an hour of polling stations closing.
Overall voter turnout dropped sharply to 41.48 percent among the 3.4 million registered electorate, a decrease of 9.97 percentage points compared to the 51.45 percent recorded in the 2022 general elections, representing approximately 319,000 fewer ballots cast.

Someone has asked you to help meet one of their needs, and you feel like you should do it. Perhaps…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
01:33:12 UTC
10:33:12 KST

Someone has asked you to help meet one of their needs, and you feel like you should do it. Perhaps you feel this way because you have a desire to make them happy, or you want to avoid their anger at failing to help, or simply because you believe you should help when you can. If you are attached to any of these intentions, you will feel motivated to do what has been asked of you.
Your helpful actions will be compassionate ones, since they help to meet someone’s need. This is true even though you are not motivated by an awareness of need. In this way, many of the things you do throughout life are compassionate, even if you do not recognize them as such.
At the same time, since you are taking action because of attachment to an intention, you might feel annoyed, frustrated, or even resentful at having to help. Perhaps you wanted to do something else, and now you feel forced to undertake this demanding task out of obligation. This can happen even when the person you are helping is someone you care about deeply. You might then feel guilty over having these feelings, which are actually forms of suffering produced by attachment.

Israel bars British Green Party leader over ‘Zionism is racism’ policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
01:32:48 UTC
10:32:48 KST

Tarek Chouiref
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Israel decided Sunday to bar the leader of the Green Party of England and Wales from entering the country after his party adopted a policy declaring Zionism a form of racism.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar ordered the ban on Zack Polanski in coordination with relevant Israeli authorities, the Foreign Ministry said.
Earlier Sunday, Green Party members approved the motion at their conference in Brighton, making opposition to Zionism part of the party’s official policy.
The motion describes Zionism as a racist ideology and backs a single democratic Palestinian state across historic Palestine with equal rights for all.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry accused the party of legitimizing armed resistance against Israel and denying Jewish self-determination, saying the policy amounted to antisemitism under the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition.
Earlier, the ministry accused the Greens of having become “supporters of terrorism” and called on British political parties, including the governing Labour Party, to reject the motion.
The Green Party rejected any equation of anti-Zionism with antisemitism, describing Zionism as an ethnonationalist political project.
The party has also reaffirmed its support for Palestinian self-determination, the right of return and a full arms embargo on Israel.

Verstappen wins F1 Bahrain GP in Malaysia, Antonelli extends title lead
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:32:01 CST
10:32:01 KST

by F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
SEPANG, Malaysia, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Max Verstappen claimed his first victory of the 2026 Formula 1 season in a rain-hit Bahrain Grand Prix at Malaysia's Sepang International Circuit on Sunday, while championship leader Kimi Antonelli took a major step toward his maiden world title after Mercedes teammate George Russell retired late in the race.
Verstappen, who started from pole position, recovered from a poor start to finish 2.3 seconds ahead of Antonelli, securing Red Bull's first victory with its own power unit. Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton completed the podium after a remarkable recovery from a disastrous early tyre gamble.
The race, relocated from Bahrain to Malaysia because of unrest in the Middle East, was delayed by more than 90 minutes following torrential rain and a series of technical problems during the formation laps.
The conditions also represented unfamiliar territory for the entire field, with the race marking the first time the new generation of F1 cars had been driven in significantly wet conditions. Introduced at the start of 2026 under sweeping new technical regulations, the cars had previously encountered little opportunity for teams and drivers to assess their behavior in sustained heavy rain.
Several cars, including Verstappen and Hamilton, slowed dramatically during the formation procedure, apparently because of a software issue caused by low-speed running in wet conditions. The resulting confusion over the starting order raised questions about race control's handling of an unprecedented situation.
When racing finally began, both front-row starters lost ground. Mercedes pair Antonelli and Russell swept into first and second, while Verstappen initially struggled to capitalize on his pole position.
Hamilton's afternoon appeared ruined almost immediately. The seven-time world champion, along with teammate Charles Leclerc and the two McLarens, gambled on starting on soft slick tyres despite the circuit remaining wet, while the Mercedes and Red Bull pair started on intermediates.
The decision proved costly, with Hamilton and the other slick-shod drivers tumbling down the order and losing almost a minute to the leaders in the opening laps.
Verstappen, meanwhile, recovered to challenge the Mercedes drivers and eventually overtook Antonelli following a safety car period, establishing control of the race as conditions improved.
The Dutchman's victory came after he had won the previous F1 race at Sepang in 2017, before the Malaysian Grand Prix disappeared from the calendar.
"It's a really nice one after the year that we've had and the progression that we've made," Verstappen said. "I'm incredibly proud of everyone."
Hamilton's fortunes improved as the circuit dried. Having remained on slick tyres, he steadily recovered through the field before a late safety car allowed him to switch back to soft tyres.
He subsequently overtook Red Bull's Isack Hadjar for third with three laps remaining, completing an unlikely podium finish.
The decisive championship development came when Russell, running third, suffered a suspected power unit failure five laps from the finish. His retirement allowed Antonelli to extend his championship lead from 66 to 84 points, dealing a potentially decisive blow to his teammate's title ambitions.
Ferrari's Charles Leclerc finished fourth ahead of Hadjar, with McLaren's Oscar Piastri sixth and Liam Lawson seventh for Racing Bulls.
Fernando Alonso scored his and Aston Martin's best result of the season with eighth, ahead of McLaren's Lando Norris and Lawson's teammate Arvid Lindblad.
Verstappen's victory underlined Red Bull's recent resurgence following a difficult start to the season, with the team's latest aerodynamic upgrades having delivered a significant improvement in performance.
The Dutchman is the sixth different Grand Prix winner so far in 2026, with Red Bull the fourth different team to have tasted victory this year.
The next round of the 2026 Formula 1 season is the Singapore Grand Prix at the Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 12. ■

Svetlana Kobiakova (R), a Russian Taijiquan coach, teaches Taijiquan in Chenjiagou Village of Wenxian County, central China's Henan Province, Aug. 26, 2026. Social media users in the West have recently embraced "Chinamaxxing," in which young people show interest in aspects of Chinese daily life.
Taijiquan, a kind of traditional martial arts, was born in the mid-17th century in Chenjiagou Village. Rooted in Chinese philosophy, traditional medicine and martial arts, Taijiquan has evolved into a wide range of styles and is now practiced in more than 180 countries and regions. For foreign visitors, Chenjiagou is naturally one of the best spots to experience the "Chinamaxxing" trend. The small village offers a tranquil and comfortable living environment which lets visitors get away from the busy pace of city life and immerse themselves in traditional Chinese culture. Halis Sunnetci
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Portugal maintained their perfect start to the UEFA Nations League with a 2-1 comeback victory over Norway on Sunday, making it four wins from four in League A Group 4.
Norway took the lead in the 36th minute through Kristoffer Ajer, who controlled Martin Odegaard's forward free kick before firing a right-footed strike from outside the box into the top-left corner.
Portugal responded just two minutes later as Joao Cancelo collected a loose ball on the edge of the area and struck a powerful effort into the top-right corner to make it 1-1.
The hosts completed the comeback in the 79th minute. Vitinha picked out Joao Felix at the back post, and the forward squared the ball for Goncalo Ramos to finish from close range.
Norway striker Erling Haaland was kept quiet by Portugal, failing to hit the target with either of his two shots before being replaced by Jorgen Strand Larsen in the 67th minute
Portugal ended the match with 10 men after Francisco Conceicao received two yellow cards in quick succession in the 86th minute.
The victory moved Portugal to 12 points from four matches, extending their perfect start despite the absence of Cristiano Ronaldo, who left the national team camp earlier in the week.
Denmark moved into second place in Group 4 with six points after beating Wales 1-0 away.
Rasmus Hojlund scored the only goal from the penalty spot in the 75th minute after Wales goalkeeper Danny Ward fouled Gustav Isaksen inside the area.
Norway and Wales remain on three points.
Netherlands beat Serbia as Greece hold Germany
The Netherlands earned a 2-1 home victory over Serbia in League A Group 2, with substitute Joshua Zirkzee scoring the winner.
Teun Koopmeiners put the Dutch ahead in the 31st minute when his free kick from the right went through the penalty area and found the bottom corner.
Serbia responded four minutes later through Mihajlo Cvetkovic, who headed Aleksa Terzic's cross into the far corner to send the teams into halftime level at 1-1.
Zirkzee, introduced at the break, restored the Netherlands' lead in the 71st minute, tapping into an empty net after Tijjani Reijnders sent Denzel Dumfries' low cross back across the six-yard box.
In the group's other match, leaders Greece and Germany played out a goalless draw.
Germany thought they had taken the lead through Jonathan Burkardt in the 32nd minute, but the goal was disallowed following a VAR review for a handball in the build-up.
The result left Greece and the Netherlands level on eight points. Germany have five points, while Serbia remain without a point.

01:24:47 UTC
10:24:47 KST

US Marine arrested over killing of woman in Okinawa
A US Marine has been arrested on suspicion of killing and robbing a woman in Okinawa, the Japanese authorities have said.
The victim, identified as Anna Yagi, 39, was found dead in a hotel room in Naha, the prefectural capital, on Saturday. Okinawa is home to several major US military installations and tens of thousands of US service members.
Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan, is accused of strangling Yagi and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations.
Surveillance footage reportedly shows a man believed to be Ballard entering the hotel with Yagi and later leaving alone with what appeared to be her belongings. Police located him in an entertainment district late Saturday.
The Marine Corps confirmed that Ballard is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force and said it is cooperating with the authorities.
“The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to US bases,” newly elected Okinawa Governor Genta Koja told reporters. “It is absolutely unforgivable, and we are outraged.”
“I must say, discipline and troop education are not working at all,” he added, referring to measures introduced by the US military following a series of sexual assault cases involving American personnel on the island.
The Japanese government lodged a formal protest with Washington on Sunday. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi demanded full cooperation with the investigation, stricter discipline among US personnel, and “thorough measures” to prevent similar incidents.
“The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and heinous incident is a matter of profound regret,” she wrote on X, extending sympathy to the victim’s family.
Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned US Ambassador George Glass, who pledged full cooperation with the investigation.
Okinawa accounts for just 0.6% of Japan’s territory but hosts 70.3% of the land area of US military facilities in Japan that are exclusively used by US forces, according to the Okinawa prefectural government.
Concerns over crime, aircraft noise, and pollution have fueled longstanding opposition to the bases. The 1995 abduction and rape of a 12-year-old girl by three US servicemen sparked mass protests. Demonstrations against the US military presence have continued, with a 2018 rally drawing an estimated 70,000 people.
In June 2024, Tokyo formally protested two alleged sexual assaults involving US personnel and delays in disclosing the cases. The Marine Corps subsequently stepped up sobriety checks and off-base patrols, while US Forces Japan later barred service members from off-base drinking establishments from 1:00-6:00 AM.
Despite the measures, further sexual assault allegations involving American personnel followed. In January 2025, then-Chief Cabinet Secretary Yoshimasa Hayashi urged US Forces Japan to tighten discipline and take stronger measures to prevent further incidents.

Pro-Israel Flávio Bolsonaro leads Lula as Brazil election heads to runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
01:22:31 UTC
10:22:31 KST

Brazil’s presidential election will be decided in an October 25 runoff after conservative Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro unexpectedly finished the first round ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, though neither secured the majority needed for an outright victory.
With about 97% of the vote counted, the 45-year-old Bolsonaro had 47.45%, compared with 44.66% for Lula, 80. Polls had generally predicted a much closer contest with Lula slightly ahead, though neither candidate had been expected to cross the 50% threshold.
Bolsonaro had said before the vote that he was counting on "protest votes" from Brazilians motivated more by opposition to Lula than support for him. "I am very happy with the results. Brazil wants change," he said after the scale of his first-round showing became clear.
Lula acknowledged the surprise. "These were unexpected results," he said. "I was sure I was going to win the election in the first round." He added that "a new campaign begins tomorrow," describing Bolsonaro as representing "uncertainty for the country."
Flávio Bolsonaro has served in the Senate since 2019 and is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, a close supporter of Israel who governed Brazil from 2019 to 2022. The elder Bolsonaro was later convicted over a plot to overturn his election defeat to Lula and sentenced to 27 years in prison. Because of health issues, he is currently serving his sentence under house arrest. His son has promised to pardon him if elected.
Lula previously served as president from 2003 to 2011. He was later convicted on corruption charges and imprisoned, but the convictions were annulled, allowing him to return to politics and narrowly defeat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022 by just 1.8 percentage points. Although Lula initially said that term would be his last, he is now seeking a fourth term as president.
The campaign has focused heavily on Brazil’s struggling economy, the cost of living, organized crime and relations with US President Donald Trump. Flávio Bolsonaro has promised a tougher campaign against powerful criminal groups and has proposed designating some of them as terrorist organizations, a move Lula opposes. He has also pledged to repair relations with Washington after repeated clashes between Lula and Trump.
Relations with Israel have also emerged as a clear dividing line. Like his father, Flávio Bolsonaro is an outspoken supporter of Israel and has repeatedly appeared at rallies alongside Israeli flags. During a visit to Israel earlier this year, his fourth, he pledged to move Brazil’s embassy to Jerusalem if elected.
"Brazil must stand with Israel, with the Jewish people and with democracies fighting terrorism," Bolsonaro said during the visit, accusing Lula of antisemitism. He also promised that Brazil’s next president "will not be persona non grata in Israel."
Lula, by contrast, has become one of Israel’s most outspoken international critics since the Gaza war began. Although he condemned Hamas after the October 7 massacre, he later accused Israel of genocide and compared its actions in Gaza to those of Hitler. Brazil recalled its ambassador from Israel in 2024, and Lula’s government declined to approve a new Israeli ambassador in Brasília the following year.
The result sets up three more weeks of campaigning in an intensely polarized race. Bolsonaro will seek to consolidate voters who backed other candidates in the first round, while Lula will try to reverse an outcome he acknowledged he did not expect and hold on to the coalition that returned him to power four years ago.

====================================================================================================

Are we living in a simulation? A question 2,500 years in the making
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
01:09:20 UTC
10:09:20 KST

The possibility that the world around us might be an illusion has long occupied the realms of philosophy and religion. Across cultures and centuries, people have envisioned hidden realities lying beyond the world we can see and experience. In the modern world, that ancient skepticism has been repackaged into a technologically advanced hypothesis: Some modern thinkers wonder whether the universe itself could be a computer simulation.
Although the idea sounds like a premise straight out of a movie, that hasn't stopped philosophers, scientists, and technology moguls from debating whether the hypothesis can actually be tested. One of its most famous proponents is Elon Musk, a man as controversial as he is influential, who famously said, "there's a one in billions chance we're in base reality."
Musk's provocative statement rests on a philosophical argument first formulated by Nick Bostrom, a Swedish philosopher at the University of Oxford.
Bostrom's argument is more subtle than the simple claim that we live in a simulation. He asks: If a technologically advanced civilization survives long enough, will it eventually develop the capacity to create hyper-realistic simulations of worlds populated by conscious beings? Such a civilization might run countless virtual realities to study, for instance, its own history – what Bostrom calls "ancestor simulations".
Fantastic worlds
If so, he argues that we are confronted with a trilemma, meaning at least one of the following three scenarios must be true: First, civilizations may go extinct before reaching the technological maturity required to create simulations. Second, even if civilizations develop the necessary technology, they may choose not to use it, perhaps for ethical or other reasons.
The third possibility follows if neither of these constraints applies: advanced civilizations survive, develop the technology, and choose to use it. In that case, they could potentially run countless numbers of ancestor simulations. The upshot could be that the number of simulated beings would vastly outnumber those living in the original, base reality, raising an uncomfortable statistical question: why should we assume we potentially belong to the privileged minority living in the original world rather than to the larger population inhabiting simulations?
Moreover, an advanced civilization could, in principle, simulate conscious beings with no evolutionary or physical connection to its own history, Bostrom adds: "They could also run simulations in which they don't think are like anybody's ancestors - completely fantasy worlds. In theory, we could be in one of those," he says.
According to that third possibility, what we perceive as the physical universe, including Earth, and even our own bodies, would be nothing more than just part of an extraordinarily advanced computational simulation.
Meanwhile, a paper published in 2025 by physicists pushes back against the hypothesis, arguing that the sheer computational math required to run such a simulation makes it mathematically impossible, meaning base reality is the only possibility left, ergo we are real.
Yet, the conclusion may be premature. The math may rule out the kind of simulation we can currently imagine, but that doesn't necessarily answer the bigger question. Maybe the problem isn't that the universe can't be simulated, but that we still don't understand what a simulation would really look like?
In fact, the argument isn't just about some modern matrix. These people are addressing a question that goes back thousands of years. Classical thinkers recognized that human perception is a notoriously fallible instrument, and faced the same core dilemma: if our perceptions can be fooled, or if our senses are inherently flawed, why assume the world they present is the ultimate truth?
What is real?
One of the earliest skeptics was Plato. Writing in the fourth century B.C.E., in his work "The Republic", a dialogue exploring politics, education, knowledge, and reality, Plato presented his famous "Allegory of the Cave" to challenge how humans perceive the world around them.
Plato asks his readers to picture prisoners bound inside a dark cave since birth, securely restrained so their heads face a blank stone wall. A fire burns behind the prisoners and a raised walkway sits between them and the fire. People walk along this path carrying statues and objects, casting flickering shadows onto the blank wall. Having spent their entire lives seeing only these projections, the captives take them as actual reality. They give them names, track their patterns, and build their entire worldview around them, completely unaware of the real objects, the people carrying them, or the external world outside the cave.
Plato's core message extends far beyond a simple optical illusion. The prisoners do not just mistake what they see; they fundamentally misjudge surface appearances for true reality.
Earlier philosophers such as Parmenides argued that "What-Is" (reality) is unchanging and unified, while change and motion belong to the realm of subjective appearance. Later thinkers like Plotinus went further, regarding the material world as the lowest level of a reality that ultimately proceeds from higher, immaterial sources.
Collectively, Plato and his successors suggested that human beings typically perceive only a small fraction of existence, while remaining unaware of the deeper principles underlying it.
Meanwhile, skeptics like the philosopher Sextus Empiricus pushed the epistemological problem further. Rather than claiming the senses can deceive, Sextus argued that they are so easily deceived that we can never truly know whether things exist as they appear.
The tension between perception and reality also echoed through the Roman period. The Stoics argued that impressions and judgments trap humans in false perceptions, leading them to mistake surface events for the actual truth.
But is that really a particle?
Moving onto today, science is effective at describing and explaining how the observable universe works, but a model's ability to predict observations does not innately establish what lies beneath them.
Equations may describe the fundamental structure of reality, or may simply govern the specific version of reality available to us. That possibility leads to one of the simulation hypothesis's most difficult problems: testability.
The particles we detect, the physical constants we measure, and the laws we use to interpret our experiments could all be features of the simulated environment. A sophisticated simulation could be designed to behave exactly like a non-simulated universe.
But if such a simulation is indistinguishable from reality, what evidence could ever prove it?
This is where Plato's cave dwellers and the inhabitants of a simulated universe find common ground.
The true dilemma goes beyond the idea that appearances can be deceptive. The real problem lies in the instruments we use to experience reality: our senses, our scientific tools, and even the physical laws themselves are all embedded within the system we are trying to analyze. As the cave allegory shows, an observer may be trapped within a framework that defines the very limits of what can be observed. The simulation hypothesis turns the ancient philosophical dilemma into a technological one.
Ultimately, the question is not whether our senses deceive us, but whether the universe is a self-contained digital cage, engineered by its creators so that it would always remain invisible to its dwellers. Maybe the authors behind the 2025 paper in the Journal of Holography Applications in Physics suffer from the same blindness.
Deleting every T. rex
This leads to one of the most delightfully alien questions related to the simulation hypothesis: What does it say about the dinosaurs who inhabited the planet long before us?
Viewed through the lens of computational optimization, the dinosaur era spanning over 150 million years represents a plateau in evolutionary progress relative to its potential "computational cost". Millions of years ticked by, and none of them built cities, invented anything, or actually did anything really surprising. Technologically, the dinosaur era was a snooze-fest. So, what does one do when a game gets boring? One clears the board.
Rather than deleting every T. rex one by one, the hypothetical operators could have triggered a massive "wipe", an asteroid strike being a way to clear the old save file in one apocalyptic sweep.
From this perspective, the dinosaur fossils would not be evidence of an old simulation gone wrong, but traces of a deliberate reset, clearing the board to make room for something more interesting – us.
However, Bostrom argues that the extinction of the dinosaurs could simply reflect an extinction that occurred in the underlying reality being modeled.
What about the roughly 65.7 million years between the extinction of the dinosaurs and the emergence of Homo sapiens? It is an awfully long time to wait for the next interesting result.
Even this apparent delay fits into the analogy, as a simulator does not need to render every moment at real-time speed. Just as we skip to the good parts of a film, millions of years could easily have been fast-forwarded into mere computational seconds.
Dinosaur extinction need not have been a deliberate intervention. As he puts it, "if we are in a simulation, their extinction within our simulation would plausibly simply accurately reflect that fact in the underlying reality which it is attempting to model."
In short, according to Bostrom, they were the real deal, we're not. A "reset" would not necessarily leave traces in a later simulation unless the simulators deliberately carried information from one simulation into another. The fossils therefore cannot, on their own, be interpreted as evidence that an earlier simulation was erased.
This brings the simulation hypothesis back to its most profound question. The challenge is not whether the universe could be a simulation, but if there could ever be evidence capable of telling an observer inside that universe that it is one.
The ultimate deception
More than 2,000 years after Plato, the 17th-century French philosopher René Descartes proposed a famous thought experiment: What if a powerful "evil deceiver" dedicated all its energy to manipulating our perceptions? Perhaps the external world doesn't exist as we see it. What if everything one sees, touches is being systematically manipulated or completely fabricated?
Descartes was not trying to expose a grand illusion about the physical world. His goal was more elemental: to dismantle every shaky assumption until he hit bedrock certainty.
That method of radical skepticism is what led to his famous conclusion: "I think, therefore I am". Even if someone was manipulating the universe around him, the very act of being deceived proved that a conscious mind existed to experience it. That same foundation is at the core of the modern simulation debate.
But this raises an even more uncomfortable question that the simulation hypothesis cannot answer through technology alone: if we discovered that our reality was artificial, would that make human life less valuable?
Bostrom doesn't think much would change even if people decided they were only simulated. "We quickly get used to many things, and in any case most of what we do doesn't seem to be strongly influenced by any theoretical beliefs about the nature of reality that we might happen to hold, which, incidentally, is probably a good thing, given the unreliability of many such beliefs that people have," he says.
By his thinking, discovering that we are a figment of somebody's imagination could transform our picture of the universe without necessarily transforming the everyday experiences that make up our lives.
That distinction is important. The simulation hypothesis might tell us something radically different about what reality is made of, but it does not automatically tell us that experiences inside that reality are worthless.
It could, however, change the stories people tell about unexplained events. "In the past, people might have tried to explain mental illness with reference to demon possession, later with reference to Freudian constructs, and if they believe the simulation hypothesis, they might infer that there is a glitch in the matrix," he says.
In that sense, simulation theory could become another framework for explaining mysteries. "New 'religious' ideas might arise with technical vocabulary rather than supernatural.
But the impulse would be familiar: if there is a hidden reality behind our world, there is an explanation for why we are here.
The question of death becomes even stranger. If our reality is simulated, then what exactly is death? Is it the end of a particular simulation instance, or a transition into some other state of existence? We have no answer. We struggle to understand death in the world we can touch, let alone in a reality running on a server beyond our comprehension.
Whether our reality is crafted from shadows, Cartesian trickery, or lines of quantum code, the ultimate realization is the same: the boundary between the artificial and the real may be invisible to us. If a simulation is complex enough to generate a conscious mind capable of questioning its own existence, does the underlying medium - code or stardust – truly matter? Perhaps the question itself is a trap. The programmer and the cosmos blur together when the observer becomes sophisticated enough to wonder about the nature of reality.
Perhaps the most frustrating implication of a putative discovery that the universe is an artificial creation is that it would not solve the mystery of its existence. After all, if our universe has programmers, who programmed the programmers? And who programmed their reality? At some point, "Who created us?" simply becomes "Who created them?" The only comforting part of the question, whether we are flesh-and-blood mortals or equations running on a machine, is that the doubt itself is a proof of our existence.

Nearly 1,500 migrants arrive in Myanmar from Malaysia despite UN warnings

Nearly 1,500 migrants arrive in Myanmar from Malaysia despite UN warnings
Malaysia continues mass refugee deportations despite warnings from the UN about unsafe conditions in an active war zone.
Nearly 1,500 Myanmar refugees and migrants deported from Malaysia have arrived in their war-ravaged country under an opaque repatriation scheme heavily criticised by human rights groups and the United Nations refugee agency.
The 1,479 returnees, transported from Malaysia on board two navy warships and a hospital ship on Tuesday, arrived in southern Yangon early Sunday, Nay Lin Tun, a regional government minister, said.
They are among 5,000 Myanmar nationals who will be repatriated in stages from Malaysia, where more than 10,300 others are being held in immigration detention centres, according to the country’s Home Ministry.
Malaysia insists all returnees agreed to voluntary repatriation, but rights monitors have raised concerns that Myanmar refugees had little choice and warned that conditions for return remain unsafe.
The UN refugee agency said this past week that its staff were not allowed to meet the Myanmar nationals to confirm whether their decisions to return “were genuinely free and informed”.
Rohingya make up the majority of Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, but it remains unclear how many members of the persecuted Rohingya are among the returned group.
The deportation was carried out during escalating raids on refugee communities in Malaysia by immigration officials, which led to the detention of more than 50,000 refugees in 2026.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced the repatriations in July against a backdrop of rising xenophobia towards refugees, particularly the Rohingya.
Kuala Lumpur is moving ahead with plans to return a second group of more than 3,500 refugees and migrants, saying they have caused financial, social and security burdens.
While Malaysia is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants, it is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
This includes more than 126,000 mainly Muslim Rohingya refugees.
Myanmar pledged last month that returns will be “safe and dignified”.
But Yap Lay Sheng, a senior human rights specialist with Fortify Rights, told the AFP news agency: “There’s no telling how the regime would treat returnees.”
Myanmar has been accused of committing genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority. Earlier this year, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) opened its first genocide case it has heard in full in more than a decade.
The UNHCR and rights groups said returnees could face persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone. Myanmar has been embroiled in a civil war since the military seized power from the elected government in 2021.
The war has killed more than 100,000 people since the coup, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) project.
Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing, the military coup leader who was installed as civilian president in April, is expected to visit Malaysia soon to discuss the repatriation scheme.

Ethiopia’s forces retake Mekelle amid renewed Tigray fighting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
01:03:54 UTC
10:03:54 KST

Ethiopia’s forces retake Mekelle amid renewed Tigray fighting
The capture of Tigray’s regional capital revives fears of another prolonged conflict, displacement and crisis.
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – The capture of Tigray’s regional capital Mekelle by Ethiopian federal forces and allied Tigray Peace Force fighters has revived painful memories of the 2020–22 Tigray war, with residents fearing a return to prolonged violence, displacement and economic hardship.
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) confirmed on Saturday that it had withdrawn from Mekelle, saying its regional administration would temporarily operate from another location. Government forces and allied fighters entered the city on Saturday, with a pro-government militia source, a humanitarian worker and a Mekelle resident confirming to the Reuters news agency on Sunday that they were in control of the city.
The development comes less than four years after the Ethiopian government and the TPLF signed the Pretoria agreement that ended two years of devastating fighting.
Berihu, a 32-year-old bajaj driver in Shire, northwestern Tigray, said the latest fighting had been particularly difficult to watch.
“I feel very heartbroken knowing that Tigray has gone back to full-scale war,” he said in a phone interview with Al Jazeera. “We have already seen what the last war did to our people, and now it feels like we are going through it all over again.”
The 2020–22 war killed hundreds of thousands of people, according to estimates, displaced millions and caused extensive damage to infrastructure and livelihoods.
The African Union-facilitated agreement, signed in Pretoria in November 2022, ended the large-scale fighting, but key issues, including the status of disputed territories, the return of displaced people and the disarmament of Tigrayan forces, remained unresolved.
In July, the TPLF said the Pretoria agreement had effectively collapsed, accusing the federal government of failing to implement key provisions. The federal government rejected that characterisation, saying it remained committed to the peace process while accusing the TPLF of undermining the agreement.
The political dispute was accompanied by growing military tensions, including reports of sporadic clashes and drone strikes in parts of Tigray. The two sides also traded accusations over troop movements and preparations for renewed fighting.
The capture of Mekelle marks a major development in the renewed conflict, putting the city once again at the centre of the fighting.
Fear spreads beyond Tigray
In Addis Ababa, the developments have also alarmed residents who remember the consequences of the previous war.
Abel, a 30-year-old shopkeeper, said the fighting had felt distant until explosions were heard in the capital.
“I woke up and heard that my city had been hit,” he said. “You hear about fighting in Tigray, and it feels far away. But when you hear about explosions in Addis Ababa, you start asking yourself what will happen next.”
Diplomatic sources said explosions were heard in several parts of the capital, including near the headquarters of Ethiopia’s military. Reuters separately reported that a source linked to an opposition alliance claimed the group had carried out drone strikes in Addis Ababa, including against military facilities. The claim could not be independently verified.
For Abel, the economic consequences are as concerning as the fighting itself.
“If the war becomes bigger, ordinary people will suffer,” he said.
Bisrat, a college student in Addis Ababa, said the overnight explosions had reinforced his fear that Ethiopia could be entering a much wider conflict.
“If Ethiopia goes into a full-scale war, ordinary people will suffer,” he said. “I fear seeing another Sudan.”
Sudan has been engulfed in war since April 2023, when fighting broke out between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, displacing millions and creating a major humanitarian crisis.
The current fighting also involves a wider set of actors than the Tigray war that ended in 2022. The TPLF is part of a broader opposition alliance that includes armed groups from several parts of the country.
Fighting has also spread into Afar, while relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have sharply deteriorated.
Ethiopian officials have accused Eritrea of interfering in Ethiopia’s internal affairs and supporting forces opposed to the federal government. Eritrea has rejected the accusations.
On Thursday, Ethiopia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced the closure of its embassy in Asmara and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats persona non grata, saying they had been involved in activities that posed a threat to Ethiopia’s national security.
Eritrea subsequently announced that it was severing diplomatic relations with Ethiopia.
The diplomatic rupture has added to concerns that the renewed fighting could acquire a wider regional dimension.
Mekelle changes hands again
In Mekelle, residents were left trying to understand what comes next after the TPLF withdrawal.
Goitom, 37, said there was a period of uncertainty after TPLF forces left the city, with what he described as a security vacuum allowing theft in some areas, including government offices.
“On Friday night, we were hearing gunfire but did not know what was happening,” he said.
By Saturday, Ethiopian federal forces and allied fighters had taken control of key locations, including the airport, according to Goitom. Reuters and The Associated Press news agency also reported that government-aligned forces had entered Mekelle following the TPLF withdrawal.
“It feels like we are back to square one,” he said. “We have already seen what war can do to this city and to our families. People are worried about what will happen next.”
The TPLF, however, portrayed the withdrawal as a tactical decision rather than an end to the fighting.
In a statement issued on Saturday, the group said it had “temporarily moved out of Mekelle” and that the regional government would “operate from somewhere else”. It said the decision was intended to prevent further destruction in the city and indicated that its forces would continue the conflict from other positions.
For the federal government, the capture of Mekelle represents a significant step towards restoring federal control over the region.
Abraham Belay, former president of the Tigray Interim Administration, said on Sunday that preparations were under way to establish a new interim administration in Tigray, with the aim of holding regional elections within months.
“We are working to establish a new administrative structure that will enable the people of Tigray to govern themselves,” Abraham said in an interview with Fana Broadcasting Corporate.
He said new administrative structures would be organised from the kebele level upwards, with community participation, before regional elections were held.
The competing accounts leave the next phase of the conflict uncertain. The federal government says it is seeking to restore its authority and establish a new regional administration, while the TPLF says its forces will continue fighting from elsewhere.
Civilian fears return to the fore
For people who lived through the previous war, the return of fighting has brought back fears of displacement, destruction and another prolonged humanitarian crisis.
Berihu, the bajaj driver, said he had seen villages bombed and civilians caught up in the fighting during the previous conflict, experiences that have shaped his fears about what could follow.
“It is painful to even think that civilians could once again bear the cost,” he said.
After years of displacement, loss and disruption, he said, many people in Tigray simply want the fighting to stop.
“We have already suffered enough,” Berihu said. “We just want peace. We don’t want to go through the same thing again.”

Auction clearance rate sinks to three-month low as property market slows

Auction clearance rate sinks to three-month low, Sydney and Melbourne property a 'drag' on results
In short:
Property sales for the spring season are off to a weak start.
It comes off the back of two long weekends in major capital cities and the RBA lifting the cash rate again last week.
What's next?
Some economists predict capital city property prices could fall 10-15 per cent from peak to trough.
Australia's auction clearance rate has slumped to a three-month low, while new data shows the number of unsold homes has surged by more than 20 per cent in the past year.
Less than half the auctions that occurred across the country last week resulted in a successful sale.
The preliminary clearance rate in the past week fell to 48.2 per cent, its lowest since late June (47.4 per cent) and the second-lowest preliminary reading for the year so far.
It has also been hovering at or below the 50 per cent mark for several months, coinciding with a steep decline in property prices and weak sentiment in the housing market.
In the past week, 1,223 auctions were held in the nation's capital cities.
So there were 12.8 per cent fewer auctions than the previous week. It was also a significant 47.5 per cent drop from a year ago, according to new data from property research firm Cotality.
Sharp fall in number of auctions held
Cotality's research director Tim Lawless said the weak result came off the back of long weekends in some states and the Reserve Bank's decision to lift interest rates for a fourth time this year.
It also comes after changes in this year's federal budget that sent shock waves through the property sector, including heavily restricted negative gearing, and in many cases higher capital gains tax for sellers.
Sydney and Melbourne "have been a drag on the national result", Mr Lawless said.
In Sydney, 304 auctions were held in the past week, down 61 per cent to the week before. It was also a 38.5 per cent drop compared to a year ago.
There were 670 auctions held in Melbourne. That was a 136 per cent jump compared to the previous week when the city was having the AFL grand final long weekend.
But in the past 12 months, the number of auctions held in Melbourne has dropped 45.6 per cent, the largest decline of any capital city.
Property taking up to six months to sell
Another real estate analysis firm, SQM Research, also released new data, showing some homes were sitting unsold on the market for as long as six months.
Homes that sat unsold for more than 180 days were clogging the market, with 10.5 per cent more older listings compared to a year ago.
Spring's traditional selling boom has ground to a halt so far this season, with the number of unsold homes across the country totalling 276,000, a 21.6 per cent annual increase.
"The bulk of the increase is property that has been on the market for one to six months and hasn't sold," SQM Research director Louis Christopher said.
"In Sydney, fewer vendors are listing than a year ago, yet total stock is up almost a fifth. That's a demand problem, not a supply surge."
Forced sales on the rise
Brisbane and Adelaide have had the largest increase in the number of properties available for sale, up 43.5 and 39.5 per cent respectively, according to SQM's data.
Melbourne, meanwhile, had 30.3 per cent more homes up for sale than it did a year ago.
Perth's figure was up 21.3 per cent, while Canberra's was up 17.8 per cent.
SQM's figures also showed there were 4,872 distressed sales across Australia in September, which was a 29 per cent jump compared to the same period last year.
It follows the ABC reporting last week that Australian housing values had dropped for a sixth straight month, with many economists warning there will be further price falls ahead.
Mr Lawless said Australian households were "deeply pessimistic" about the cost-of-living crisis, interest recent hikes and the budget's changes to property taxes creating "less favourable conditions".
"Homes are taking longer to sell, auction clearance rates have held below average and advertised stock levels have risen across many markets," he said.
